en: Preface to the *Zhengmasu* (Orthodox Pulse Commentary) on the *Mahāśrī-śūraṅgama-sūtra*, composed by the śramaṇa Jiaoguang Zhenjian of West Lake, Capital City.

The fundamental source of awakening, the ocean of the mind, exists within the bonds of saṃsāra; it is named the Tathāgatagarbha-citta. Its nature is a profound stillness, the very substance of the celestial realm of reality, and is designated as Śūraṅgama.
It is solemnly fixed. Not only are the mundane and supramundane realms fundamentally unmoving from the outset, but moreover, both the sentient and the insentient are, by their very nature, unborn.
Alas, how is it that the blossoming of flowers obscures the eyes and dreams sink into the long night? Within the unmoving, one perceives shifting and transformation;
within the unborn, one undergoes the cycle of birth and death. If this is so, then how could this be merely the delusion of those outside the Buddhist fold?
One runs, yet cannot escape the torrential flood. Although such provisional practitioners of the Lesser Vehicle exert themselves with toil, they likewise fail to avoid the subtle currents.
This is because they have not yet perceived the fundamental samādhi of the true nature (*t’ien-chên*); they merely attack the bound consciousness through the withered dhyāna of dry meditation.

What is called taking birth-and-death as the cause will ultimately yield no real fruit. Therefore, our Śākyamuni Buddha realized this during the causal stage as the secret cause, and realized it upon attaining the fruit.

This is the ultimate fruit. It is the Sea-Seal Samādhi at the site of tranquility. It is not that [the Buddha] does not wish to universally bestow the essence of the finest cream (amṛta), yet because one is deluded by the darkness of dreams and sleep, it is necessary to undergo refinement through various means.
When the capacity [of the practitioner] has matured, he reveals the primordial mind; the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka* first opens the way, while this sutra speaks of the final conclusion.
He shows that much learning may lead to downfall, and warns against the madness of mere intellectual wisdom, urging the power of diligent effort toward profound dhyāna. Thus he answers.

The "Determination of the Mind" (Dingzhengxin) section refutes the total delusion regarding false meditative concentration found among ordinary people and followers of the Lesser Vehicle; such must indeed be false concentration. Only after completely abandoning it can one hear of the Great Concentration.
Consequently, this section points toward the six sense faculties to reveal the nature of seeing, enabling one to personally verify the unmoving, fundamental reality.
It integrates the four aggregates to demonstrate the hidden mind, enabling one to fully understand the eternally abiding self-substance. Furthermore, it extends to the seven...
"Great! It is most manifest and all-pervasive. Ānanda then praised the Immovable Honored One for his rare samādhi.

This was still before he had requested instruction on cultivation; yet, as for the *Śūraṅgama-rāja* (King of Heroic Prowess) for which he offered thanks, how could it be anything other than the fundamental samādhi of one's own nature?
This section first answers Ānanda, returning delusion to the truth to reveal the unchanging essence of the *śūnyatā-garbha*.
Below, it responds to Pūrṇa, showing how delusion arises from the truth to reveal the functional utility of the non-empty that accords with conditions.

Furthermore, it simultaneously clarifies both nature and appearance, demonstrating that seeing emptiness and non-emptiness are both without obstruction, thereby perfectly manifesting the entire essence and great function of the Threefold Treasury (*tripiṭaka*). Only then can one know.
The essential substance of the samādhi that is ultimately firm and solid regarding all phenomena is, from the beginning, spontaneously perfected and penetrates the very source of reality.

This *Lengyan* (Śūraṅgama) samādhi—immovable and indestructible—is not produced through artificial effort. It is what is called the subtle and secret contemplation of *śamatha*, wherein all [delusions] are exhausted without remainder.

Compared to this, the samādhis of forced mental cultivation that involve the conceptualizing mind and its shadow-like images are as different as heaven and earth; they cannot even serve as a metaphor for it.
However, although concentration is inherently present, as long as the faculties and fetters have not been opened, its essence remains intact yet its function never manifests.

Therefore, those whose minds are ready seek entry by contemplating how to find the door within the house; the Tathāgata reveals the certainty of the method and points to the faculties to clarify the knots.
Within this, the enumeration of numbers was intended to lead them toward choosing the perfect; the examination of objects was meant to clarify that they are exhaustible.

When doubt arose regarding annihilation, he struck a bell to verify its non-extinction; when doubt arose regarding the existence of something separate, he manifested as a Buddha to testify that there is nothing else.

Thus it continued until he tied a cloth into six knots to demonstrate their sequential order, secretly bestowed his instructions so that all the elders were enlightened, and finally issued his command.

In Mañjuśrī’s selection, he singled out the "ear-door" of Avalokiteśvara. This is because the true reality of quiescent extinction must first manifest before the wondrous functions of perfect response can fully emerge.
This is truly what is meant by the "illusory-like samādhi," wherein one transcends the stage of no-more-learning with a mere snap of the fingers.
As for the three trainings of the practice site and the secret mantras of the four types of giving, these are merely for the purpose of cultivating perfect penetration.
Those with heavy hindrances merely apply the preparatory practice; it is not that there are separate alternative methods. This is like entering through the gate of a magnificent mansion:

while one has entered, there are still successive stages to be traversed before ascending to the hall and entering the inner chamber. Therefore, the practitioner, according to their capacity, follows this by requesting the [appropriate] stage.

The Buddha then added the preparatory practices (*prayoga*) and established the three gradual stages as the "Perfect Penetration" (*yuan-tong*). These three gradual stages were further condensed into the "Dry Wisdom" (*śuklavidarśanā-bhūmi*).

From this point, one enters the central flow within the mind; by doing so, one is born into the Buddha-family and termed the "Ten Abodes" (*daśa-vihāra*). Performing the Buddha-work is termed the "Ten Practices" (*daśa-caryā*).

Gathering these back into the three stations is termed the "Ten Dedications" (*daśa-pariṇāmanā*). Realizing the single truth is termed the "Ten Grounds" (*daśa-bhūmi*). This continues up to the stage of Equal Enlightenment (*samāpatti-bodhi*).
The ocean of nirvāṇa is the ocean of great quiescent extinction; therein, birth and death are eternally stilled.
The ocean of wondrous enlightenment is the ocean of the fruition of myriad virtues; therein, bodhi is eternally perfected.

Looking back and saying that returning to that which is unobtainable clarifies that one merely returns to the original unmoving essence and manifests the treasures of one's own original home—these are not obtained from without. How could it be?
"Are they not likewise neither cause nor effect, empty and yielding nothing? This is precisely by relying on *dhyāna* that one cultivates and advances toward the stages of sainthood;
thus, the Great Samādhi of Śūraṅgama brings both beginning and end to completion. Therefore, these five names are concluded and entrusted for your upholding."

As for the exhortation to depart from the five māras and the instruction on consciousness regarding the seven realms of existence, these are likewise essential points from the preceding text, merely restated here with particular emphasis and detail.
How could such profound compassion ever come to an end? Thus, this sutra is the ultimate reality and final destination of the One Vehicle, the perfect and sudden teaching.
Regarding awakening through understanding, the secret cause is inherently present and does not require seeking from without; regarding cultivation and realization, [it is as follows...]

This is the wondrous gateway of definitive meaning (*nītārtha*), requiring no strenuous effort. It is the essential path by which the Tathāgatas of the ten directions attained Bodhi; there is none who can transcend this gateway.

Yet, while the scriptural text itself is clear, its commentaries are often crude and superficial. Since the correct pulse [of the teaching] has been lost, the original intent has frequently been distorted.
Subsequent scholars have pointed out these errors, even to the extent of filling entire volumes. However, those who merely study the primary text...

Many have lamented in despair over the texts without being able to resolve their doubts regarding what to follow or reject. I, Jian, am a follower of the Buddhist tradition who has wandered in delusion through the long night;

as a latecomer to the school, I rely on the grace of the sages and saints to have awakened a meager root of goodness. Having by chance caught a glimpse through the gate of the magnificent palace, I feel pity for those looking out from within its walls.
I venture to set forth my limited views, requesting correction from the Great Masters. This is truly not a reckless presentation of personal opinions intended to disparage the ancients.
Worthy one, I have reflected that you intend to comply with the Buddha’s words to assist future students. Whether you judge me as right or wrong, I feel neither concern nor desire to escape it.
My hope is merely that we may briefly form a bond of joyful affinity, so that the Avīci Hell may be universally shattered and a Land of Bliss established;

that through the opening of wondrous awakening, all may return to Great Samādhi and realize Bodhi. In days to come, beneath the assemblies of the various Buddhas, would we not surely be companions and kin? Sincerely...
A brief summary is provided here to serve as the preface to the work; the full details are contained in the "Hanging Instructions" (Xuànshì).
*The Correct Pulse Commentary on the Great Buddha-Crown Śūraṅgama Sūtra*, Fascicle One.
Composed by the Śramaṇa Jiāoguāng Zhēnjiàn of West Lake, Capital City.
Regarding the title of the sutra, the term "shu" (commentary) follows; it refers to that which resolves and explains thoroughly so as to prevent any obstruction.
This is the general name for such annotated exegesis. As for the specific designation "Zhengmai" (The True Pulse), this is a particular title for the commentary.

This is because, although this sutra consists of tens of thousands of words and its text is extensive, the Sage’s words are sublime in both expression and meaning, with the beginning and end illuminating one another like a pulse.
It is interwoven and penetrating; there is no place where it does not correspond or where it does not interpenetrate.

Most traditional commentaries merely explain according to the literal text, failing to look back and forth across the beginning and end, or else presuming to trace the original intent without having grasped its fundamental meaning.

Consequently, earlier and later sections fail to correspond, and the flow of the discourse becomes mutually contradictory. This present commentary does not dare to offer arbitrary interpretations beyond the text;

rather, it seeks only to follow the original flow of the scriptural discourse as closely as possible, providing a detailed exposition so that the preceding and succeeding parts correspond and the flow of the discourse remains coherent.
For this reason, it is titled *Zhengmai* (The Correct Pulse). Part One begins:
Three. △ First, the Title:
*The Great Buddha-Uṣṇīṣa Tathāgata’s Secret Cause, the Cultivation and Realization of the Definitive Meaning of the Myriad Practices of All Bodhisattvas, the Śūraṅgama Sūtra*.

(This single title encompasses the entire sūtra; its meaning is indeed vast and inclusive. It consists of twenty characters and more phrases than other titles, yet the text is not brief. How could a rough explanation suffice to exhaust its underlying principles? Now, this commentary shall provide a somewhat more detailed and thorough exposition.)

I urge you to strive to bring forth its illuminating insights; I hope you will not weary of the detail. For what is there that is excessive in condensing a scripture of tens of thousands of words into a text of only a few leaves? This is the full title.

That is to say, from among the five types of titles spoken by the Buddha himself within the sūtras, nineteen characters are taken in brief (the first three characters are taken from the beginning of the first title;

the next eight characters are taken entirely from the name of the third title; and the final eight characters are taken from the end of the fifth title. All others are not taken, hence it is said "taken in brief").

A single character, "sūtra" (經), is added. Essential points are selected (choosing what is urgent and immediate while omitting what is slow and superficial), thereby encompassing the broad (though at first glance there may seem to be omissions, in reality the essentials encompass the vast, and thus nothing is truly left out).

Briefly stated: although the five titles appear extensive in their phrasing, when summarized by their essential meaning, they concern nothing other than the object and wisdom, the capacity and benefit, and the nature and cultivation—the subtle and wondrous cause and fruit. This will become clear from the detailed analysis of the five titles in their respective sections below.

Now, the "Secret Cause" (*miyin*) constitutes the object; the "Definitive Meaning" (*liaoyi*) constitutes the wisdom; the "Bodhisattvas" constitute the capacity; and "Cultivation and Realization" constitute the benefit. As for "nature and cultivation," these are fully covered by the third title and need not be further elaborated here. The Secret Cause and Definitive Meaning represent the "subtle and wondrous"; the myriad practices of the *Śūraṅgama* represent the "essential"; and the cultivation of the definitive meaning represents the "cause."

The realization of the definitive meaning (*nītārtha*) constitutes the fruit. This is accomplished by means of these nineteen characters, which encompass the entirety of the five topics; how could there ever be any omission? This was achieved through the skillful artistry of the compilers.

It is divided into seven sections for the sake of easy explanation: first, the Great [Perfection]; second, the Buddha-Crown; third, the Secret Cause of the Tathāgata; fourth, the Definitive Meaning of Cultivation and Realization;
fifth, the Myriad Practices of the Bodhisattvas; sixth, the Śūraṅgama; and seventh, the Sūtra itself.

Furthermore, according to the five titles, both the Exoteric and Esoteric aspects are revealed (though the second title refers to the esoteric intent; while it does not explicitly reveal the first half, it actually concerns the power of the secret mantra).

Now, among these seven sections, the second and third should also concurrently represent the secret mantra (since the mantra originally emanated from the light of the Buddha’s crown, and furthermore, this mantra gives birth to all Buddhas).

Nevertheless, from the perspective of the Esoteric, there is no room for explanation (it cannot be translated [into Chinese]; how could one permit an explanation that would clarify what follows the mantra?). Moreover, the Exoteric and Esoteric are definitively distinct.

The second [point] (the sūtra itself reveals the mantra; the mantra is the esoteric sūtra—this is known by inferring the meaning of the sūtra to understand the mantra). Therefore, both are here explained according to their manifest meanings, yet the esoteric significance is implicitly contained therein.
Although the seven sections together form a single title, among them there are the empty and the substantial, the universal and the particular;
these should first be distinguished so that they do not become confused. Sections one, two, and seven are all empty and universal.

The middle four sections constitute the actual dharmas. If one discusses the particular and the universal within these four sections, then the first three sections each have their own specific limitations, while the fourth section is universal (being the general essence of the *Śūraṅgama-samādhi* that determines the distinct characteristics of the preceding three).
The first [section] consists of words of praise, possessing vastness, inclusiveness, pervasiveness, multiplicity, profundity, primordially, and eternally.
It eternally transcends eight meanings; it possesses the two meanings of "venerable and noble" and "profound and mysterious," which are symbolized by the Buddha’s Uṣṇīṣa.

Because of these various meanings, it is called "Great. By applying this term to the dharmas below, one knows that the Secret Cause is the Great Cause, the Definitive Meaning is the Great Meaning, the myriad practices are the Great Practices, and the Śūraṅgama is the Great Samādhi. Possessing all these...

Great! This is what constitutes a Great Sūtra. (The reason it does not mention the title "Buddha-uṣṇīṣa" is that even if it were mentioned, it would only refer to the actual reality symbolized by it, rather than its physical marks and signs; therefore, it is not mentioned.)

How much more so for those who are honored and sublime, who likewise share this great intent; why labor further to praise them? Furthermore, the secret cause is principle (*li*), the definitive meaning is teaching (*jiao*), and the myriad practices are conduct (*xing*).
The *Śūraṅgama* is the fruit. It is so called because the Great Samādhi contains within it the ocean of the two ultimate fruits of original enlightenment.
Its initial designation as "Great" is intended for those who would uphold this sutra:

that they may rely on the Great Teaching to understand the Great Principle, invoke Great Practice by conforming to the Great Principle, and realize the Great Fruit through the fulfillment of Great Practice. Since it is not a substantial dharma, it is empty (the single character "xu" is used).

Regarding the mention of "Great" (*mahā*): it has not yet been determined what kind of phenomenon is "great," and thus it remains abstract and unreal. The traditional claim that this refers directly to the "greatness of essence" (*svabhāva-mahat*) is incorrect; for if it were so, why would it not be listed alongside the "Extensive Teachings" (*vaipulya*)?

Furthermore, how could it be definitively called the "greatness of essence" when it pervades all phenomena? Thus, it is "universal" (*vyāpin*). Second, regarding the "Buddha-uṣṇīṣa": among the thirty-two marks of a Buddha’s body, this is the first, known as the "mark of the invisible crown.
It is situated at the center of the blue-black curls of hair, surrounded by a crimson hue, like [the color of] spring...
When a mountain emits the sun, its summit cannot be seen; yet when he first descended into birth, one should have taken the ninth stage (*navamī-bhūmi*) as his wet-nurse.

Even if one were to traverse worlds as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, one would ultimately still be unable to see it. That this is now pointed out serves as a symbolic representation of the Dharma.

While the metaphor is also applicable in this way, it merely differs in the degree of intimacy of the meaning conveyed (using similar objects to illustrate a point is called a "metaphor," yet one never uses the actual name of the object within the metaphor).

Because it refers directly to the Dharma, it is distant rather than intimate. If one were to take the most excellent name and appearance and refer directly to the Dharma, this would manifest its excellence as a sign; it is not merely because of similarity that it is intimate.

Now, taking the Supreme, Unsurpassed, Most Sublime, and Invisible Buddha-Uṣṇīṣa, we refer directly to the underlying real Dharma to signify that it is identical to the formless Buddha-Uṣṇīṣa—both supreme and sublime.
[Question: Practice is a meritorious achievement; why is it called "honorable and noble"? Why is ardent cultivation called "invisible"? [Answer: It is because of the nature (*dhātu*).

The cultivation that arises encompasses the ocean of fruition; thus, it remains noble. Furthermore, rooted in the definitive meaning (*nītārtha*), cultivation is itself non-cultivation. It is subsumed within the *Śūraṃgama-samādhi*: "The source of movement is unmoving.

Therefore, even the five eyes cannot perceive it. Because it is not a substantial dharma, it is empty. (It has not yet been determined what specific dharma is indicated. Because it universally indicates all dharmas, it is pervasive. The *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka* is the complete body of the Buddha.

This sutra is the crown of the Tathāgata. It reveals that this scripture contains the essential meaning within the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka* (such as the knowledge and vision of the true reality, the Buddha-wisdom, etc.), while further penetrating the most sudden, perfect, and ultimate principles (such as "resting is itself bodhi" or "the manifestation of lands on the tip of a hair"). It is because it ultimately and truly embodies the entire Buddha-body;
its sudden and perfect meaning is so supremely honored and wondrous that it is identical to the *uṣṇīṣa* (crown protuberance) of a Buddha. This causes those who see its title to understand [this].
This is not a teaching of expedient gradualism. The middle four sections are what the Great One (the Buddha) extols, what the Buddha-Usnīṣa symbolizes, and what this sutra elucidates;

therefore, they constitute the True Dharma. Now, as for the third section, "The Secret Cause of the Tathāgata," it is one of the ten titles of a Tathāgata, modeled after the titles used by previous masters.
If explained according to its literal characteristics, it refers to the single body of all Buddhas.

The same applies to the application of wisdom. Therefore, the later Buddha is like the former Buddha’s second coming. If one were to provide an explanation according to the principle, there would be many varieties that could not be fully exhausted depending on the depth of the teachings.
Now, based on the ultimate reality: as for "coming," it refers to original enlightenment (mūla-bodhi); as for "coming back," it refers to initial enlightenment (ādi-bodhi).
That which is the beginning, the source, and the ultimate is called the Tathāgata; this refers to the person who has attained the fruit.

It is also the title bestowed after the paths of the various Bodhisattvas mentioned below. Regarding the "esoteric cause": this distinguishes it from the manifest causes that can be seen through the practice of phenomenal characteristics.
Here, we take the Tathāgata during his time as an ordinary being, who suddenly awakened to the perfect, profound, and unarising-and-unperishing wondrousness at the gateway of the six sense faculties.
This clarifies the true mind. This mind is the fundamental basis for the four categories and the seven elements. Its actual nature fully possesses the three *tathāgatagarbhas*.
It is the totality of great essence and great function; it has been the Buddha from the very beginning. How could it be merely the causal nature?
It is also the resultant nature itself, for there is no separate realization for the Tathāgatas, and even at the time of realization, not the slightest hair’s breadth is added.
Supplement: This refers to attaining perfect enlightenment from the very first moment of generating the bodhicitta. As the Buddha himself stated in the sutras:
"I unite the non-extinguishing and non-arising with the Tathāgatagarbha; and this Tathāgatagarbha is solely wondrous, enlightened clarity, perfectly illuminating the Dharma-realm.
The meaning of this can be seen therein. However, the reason it is considered the most esoteric is that it constitutes the two faculties.
The fundamental essence within the fundamental: that which is called the luminous source of consciousness, the primordial, pure substance of bodhi and nirvana. The Buddha said:

"That all sentient beings fail to achieve supreme bodhi, and instead become śrāvakas, pratyekabuddhas, various devas, non-Buddhists, or māras, is entirely due to their failure to comprehend this fundamental essence and their consequent confused practice. This leads to the subsequent verse.

Furthermore, it says: "It is never revealed. This sufficiently demonstrates that the *tathāgatagarbha* nature inherent within the faculties is a most profound and esoteric dharma, difficult to fathom and difficult to know.

[Question: Since this is already the nature of the fruition (*phala*), why is it further called the cause (*hetu*)? [Answer: Only after one perceives this nature does it become the ultimate fruition; yet the cause must still be cultivated and perfected before the ultimate fruition is attained.

Moreover, the two characters for "esoteric cause" (*mimi yin*) eliminate the faults of two types of people: first, the character "esoteric" (*mi*) eliminates the fault of those attached to signs (*nimitta*) in the provisional teachings, because they do not realize that the fruition is inherently and secretly present.

Nature. Even if one practices for kalpas as numerous as dust motes, there will ultimately be no real fruit. Second, by means of the character "cause" (yin), the text eliminates the fault of those with wild wisdom in the Perfect Teaching (Yuanjiao). This is because they do not realize that this nature is itself the true cause; relying on their own innate spontaneity, they abruptly abandon cultivation and realization.

Even if they attain liberation from fetters, their adornments remain incomplete, and they will never reach the ultimate. This meaning is most subtle and profound. From the beginning of the sutra’s request for certainty up to the first half of the fourth fascicle, the sense of light ease is such that one attains what has never been attained before;
this is precisely the secret cause. Now, this section is the [Avataṃsaka]... (Note: The provided text fragment ends abruptly. The translation reflects the available portion.)
Among the three names requested for this difficult task, "Exquisite Śamatha" refers to the fact that the nature of the Tathāgatagarbha is the fundamental, inherent concentration;
thus, one who suddenly awakens to and thoroughly penetrates this state does so precisely through subtle and profound contemplative observation.

Fourth, regarding the cultivation and realization of the definitive meaning (*nītārtha*): although the preceding section has fully revealed that the self-nature is inherently endowed, spontaneously present, and primordially accomplished, since it is called the "esoteric cause" (*guhyahetu*), how could it obstruct cultivation and realization?
Therefore, even while one may savor the fact that the *tathāgatagarbha* is already known, [one must still practice].

This is further illustrated by the metaphor of not yet entering a magnificent mansion. From this, the gateway to the definitive meaning (*nītārtha*) is opened, demonstrating the sequence for untying the knots.

One must necessarily untie the six knots—[the objects of] movement and stillness, the faculties, perception, emptiness, and cessation—and transcend the three emptinesses—[the emptiness of] persons, phenomena, and both—before it constitutes the cultivation of the definitive meaning.

Only after attaining the two excellences—[the upper] sameness and [the lower] integration—and manifesting the three functions—the thirty-two responses, the fourteen fearlessnesses, and the four inconceivables—does one truly [attain realization].

This is the proof of the definitive meaning (*nītārtha*). However, there are two senses in which something is called "definitive. First, it is because it employs the sense-faculties (*indriya*) rather than consciousness (*vijñāna*).

For if one employs consciousness, one takes arising and ceasing as the fundamental cause for cultivation; this is like steaming sand to make rice—the sand is not the basis of rice, and thus it will ultimately fail to produce the eternally abiding Bodhi.
Therefore, such an approach is not definitive. If, however, one employs the sense-faculties...

The nature of non-arising and non-ceasing serves as the mind for the causal ground. Just as when vessels are fashioned from gold, every vessel is entirely gold, one will certainly be able to achieve unsurpassed bodhi;

therefore, this is the definitive meaning (*nītārtha*). Furthermore, while the use of any sense organ already constitutes the definitive meaning, the specific selection of the ear-faculty is the "definitive meaning within the definitive meaning," because it transcends the twenty-four holy ones.
It is uniquely sublime. It is the essential gateway to the single path of nirvana for all Buddhas of the ten directions and the three periods of time.
How could there be any definitive teaching on cultivation and realization that surpasses this? Second, cultivation arises from nature; thus, the cause encompasses the ocean of fruition.

Therefore, while relying upon the secret cause where there is no cultivation or realization within the ocean of fruition, it does not preclude illusory cultivation and illusory realization. Thus, one cultivates...
There is no cultivation. It is not a defiled cultivation of phenomenal characteristics; it is realization without anything realized, for it is not a newly achieved actualization.
Thus, it is definitive (nītārtha) and not provisional (neyārtha). [Question: Is the cultivation of the preparatory practices for the site of practice definitive? Answer:

Within the site of practice, concentration and wisdom remain as before—the perfect penetration of the ear organ—only supplemented by the precepts, the site of practice itself, and the recitation of mantras. Since they are equally definitive, they are not described separately. Please refer to the sutra text from the latter half of the fourth scroll onwards.
The "Gate of the Flowered Mansion" extends through the first half of the seventh fascicle to the "Mantra Protected by a Hundred Spirits"; this is precisely the definitive meaning (*nītārtha*).

Now, this section corresponds to the "Wondrous Samādhi" among the three names requested by Ānanda, for it takes this "Perfect Penetration of the Ear-faculty" as the foremost "Illusion-like Samādhi. Fifth, the various Bodhisattvas...
"Ten-thousand practitioners" (*wanxingzhe*) is a brief rendering of the Sanskrit term *bodhisattva*. In full, it is *bodhisattva*, which translates as "enlightened sentient being.

This is because they have awakened to their own portion [of reality] yet have not fully exhausted their emotional afflictions (*kleśa*). Furthermore, they seek great enlightenment above while transforming sentient beings below;
thus, they are those on the causal stage of practice and are also designated by the title preceding the path of the Tathāgata. It is in this sense that one speaks of "all bodhisattvas."
"Those" refers to the fifty-five stages of the various sages as categorized in the original sutra. "Ten thousand practices" refers to the practices cultivated sequentially throughout these stages:
for example, in the stage of the Ten Faiths, one fully develops the faculties and powers to plant the seeds of Buddhahood;
in the Ten Abidings, one is born into the Buddha-family and becomes a son of the Buddha; and in the Ten Practices, one extensively cultivates the six perfections to perform the deeds of a Buddha.

Within the ten dedications (*pariṇāmanā*), one turns back the Buddha-activities toward the Buddha-mind. In the four preparatory stages (*prayoga*), mind and Buddha are merged and numerical distinctions are extinguished.

In the ten stages (*bhūmi*), one accords with *tathatā* and covers over *nirvāṇa*. At the stage of Equal Enlightenment (*samyak-saṃbodhi*), one reaches the limit of Buddhahood and destroys the mark of birth.
These practices should be immeasurable; that they are now said to be "ten thousand" clarifies that they are numerous rather than being restricted to a fixed number. One should know this.
These myriad practices build upon the previously explained definitive meaning (*nītārtha*) and advance further into the profound and mysterious.
Not only do they involve a cultivation identical to non-cultivation and a realization identical to non-realization, but they also reach the ultimate refinement, the divine, and the wondrous.
In brief, their foundation lies in the three *tathāgatagarbhas*, and their final consummation resides in the unobstructed *dharmadhātu*. Please examine the latter five of the ten practices in detail.
It is clear that all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*) are the great practice of the unobstructed Dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu*).
From the latter half of the seventh fascicle, where Ānanda requests his position, until before the name of the sutra is concluded, this constitutes these myriad practices.
This section corresponds precisely to "wondrous *dhyāna*" among the three names requested by Ānanda; it serves to describe Ānanda’s realization.

As for the passage: "Having already spoken of the sudden awakening to *dhyāna* (meditative concentration) and the cultivation of advancement through the stages of sainthood, the Buddha further states that within *śamatha* one employs various forms of *vipaśyanā*.
This reveals the abiding and maintaining of the self-nature which is fundamentally settled (*prakṛti-pratiṣṭhita*).

This is because it simultaneously encompasses the two preceding [stages], wherein concentration and wisdom are perfectly integrated, flowing into the Middle Way. [Question: Why does this proof of the definitive meaning not include the subsequent stages? [Answer: Because there are no lower [stages] among the myriad practices.

One should immediately include it therein. If these were fully included [within the stages], where would the myriad practices go? Moreover, how could the supreme, perfect penetration be allowed to remain without realization? As for the two categories of "excellence" and so forth, what are they if not realization?

You ask whether the stages should be considered realized practice, lest they be confused with cultivation; yet if you now take the stages as practice, does this not subordinate realization to cultivation? Answer: The various stages are precisely the positions of practice, and furthermore, one enters deeply into true cultivation; thus the sequence of stages is established. Just as when cultivation reaches its conclusion, it should be the Buddha-stage, one should know that such is the meaning of the name "Bodhisattva."

This is a designation for one whose causal practices are not yet fulfilled. If the causes were already fulfilled, one would immediately lose the title of "Bodhisattva. Furthermore, the Sūtra reiterates the myriad practices following the section on cultivation and realization; this is also a silent indication that these [practices] belong to this specific stage. Yet, those who understand this are few. Question:

If this is so, then perfect penetration would lack the myriad practices, and the various stages would fail to be established as definitive meanings. Would this not constitute two major errors? Answer: All of this is skillful means and does not constitute a fault. For it is the priority of the beginner to focus with single-minded dedication.

Furthermore, regarding the section on "Discernment" (jiǎnbié): how could one disdain the myriad practices? Even if one possesses a perfect, integrated understanding (*yúnróng shèngjiě*) that is fully endowed with all the *pāramitās* in every thought-moment, this remains merely "endowed in principle" (*lǐjù*) rather than "constructed through practice" (*shìzào*). Therefore, it is designated as "definitive meaning" (*liǎoyì*) without requiring the performance of the myriad practices;

this is intended to ensure that the practitioner remains focused and undistracted. If one contemplates Mañjuśrī’s verse on discerning the various gates, one will believe that this intention is not empty. As for the definitive meanings of the subsequent stages, they are even more evident;

indeed, if the initial stage of "turning the hearing back" (*fǎnwén*) is already considered definitive, it goes without saying that the definitive nature of those who have entered the sage-stages and cultivate deeply is self-evident. However, because those in the various stages are generally able to manifest infinite bodies and extensively promote the two benefits (*èrlì*), the myriad practices are specifically highlighted here.

He also silently exhorted him to bring all the perfections (*pāramitās*) to completion, for one must not consider a small measure as sufficient. If one understands the purport of the seven exhortations within the eighth stage (*bhūmi*), one will believe that this intention must certainly exist; how much more so when it accords with this classification in both the sūtras and the meditative concentrations (*samādhis*).

"Equitable, hidden, and compliant; it generates the sequence most profoundly. The wise should examine this. This summarizes the three preceding sections, which consist entirely of the three names requested by Ānanda;
they encompass the entire body of the formal exposition and collectively gather the specific titles of the Great Samādhi.
Regarding the sixth section, "Śūraṅgama" is the general name for the Great Samādhi. It perfectly contains the three aforementioned specific titles and constitutes the entirety of this single samādhi.
One should know that this samādhi is fundamentally different from the conventional *śamatha* and *vipaśyanā*.

For while conventional *śamatha* and *vipaśyanā* belong entirely to the realm of cultivation, here the self-nature is established as the object of truth (*satya-viṣaya*) in relation to *śamatha* and *vipaśyanā*; thus, their essential natures are distinct.

It does not take self-nature as its substance; rather, it takes that very [non-appropriation] as the essence of concentration (*samādhi*). Therefore, in its state as concentration, the initial mind and its object are two;
only when one reaches full maturity do they become one. Thus, *śamatha* and *vipaśyanā* belong entirely to the realm of cultivation;
they are not the actualization of self-nature, but merely serve to induce concentration. This, however, is not so.
In the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra*, the Buddha himself explains the *Śūraṅgama* as "the ultimate solidity of all phenomena.
Ancient masters have clarified that this refers to penetrating to the very source of reality—unmoving and indestructible. Upon careful examination of this meaning, it is entirely clear:
the *Śūraṅgama* is taken to be the perfect concentration inherently possessed by one's own mind; how could it ever be taken as the arising of the mind in response to external objects?
Regarding the fact that *śamatha* and *vipaśyanā* constitute the essence of meditative concentration (*samādhi*), one must further understand this:

the essence of concentration consists entirely of the self-nature of the direct cause (*hetu*), while it briefly incorporates both the understanding-cause (*jñāna-hetu*) and the conditions-cause (*pratyaya-hetu*). Furthermore, these incorporated understanding- and conditions-causes are also intrinsically possessed within the nature itself, being neither sequential nor horizontal;
they differ from what is taught in the provisional vehicles as being "subsequently attained. Within the Tiantai school, there is also this [teaching].
However, that [previous] system of *śamatha* and *vipaśyanā* does not take the fundamentally unmoving essence of the direct cause (*hetu*) as its definitive basis;

rather, it attributes the merit of realization primarily to the "revealing cause" (*vidyā-hetu*). Although it speaks of the inherent nature (*prakṛti-prakṛta*), its intent is largely toward cultivation and accomplishment.
Therefore, it is certainly different from this [present teaching]. In the present sutra, *śamatha* takes the entire, inherently endowed, and fundamentally unmoving nature as its basis.

It is neither extinguished nor lost, nor does it return; the four categories (the five aggregates, six sense bases, twelve entrances, and eighteen elements) are eternally abiding, and the seven great elements (earth, water, fire, wind, space, seeing, and consciousness) are all-pervasive.
This extends even to the delusions of the ten afflictions (ignorance along with the three subtleties and six coarsenesses) and the three continuities (the world, sentient beings, and karmic fruits).

The reality of the four meanings of "fundamentally and eternally illusory" (namely: one being infinite and the infinite being one; the large appearing within the small and the small appearing within the large), as well as the three aspects of the Tripitaka (namely:

emptiness, non-emptiness, and both emptiness and non-emptiness), are primordially and spontaneously perfected. Such meanings are entirely identical to the ultimate firmness of all phenomena, penetrating the very source of reality—immovable and indestructible—as if two halves of a tally were joined.
All of these are taken entirely from [the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra*].
The mind is fundamentally endowed with perfect concentration, which constitutes *śamatha*.

If, upon receiving the teaching, one’s understanding is opened and clarified such that the illuminating essence manifests before one, then taking this very essence of illumination is termed "subtle and secret contemplative observation" (*sūkṣma-guhyāvalokana*).

One does not take conceptual thought or cultivation as "contemplation" (*vipaśyanā*); therefore, it is further qualified by the term "subtle and secret. This was personally named by the Buddha himself; how could there be any doubt? It should be understood thus.

"Knowing" is the complete taking of the nature of the direct cause (*hetu-hetu*), briefly supplemented by the revealing cause (*jñāna-hetu*)—that is, intellectual understanding (for at the beginning, wisdom is predominant;
yet it arises from the stability of the nature, and is thus the wisdom within concentration)—as the essence of *śamatha*.

Furthermore, the complete taking of the nature of the direct cause, briefly supplemented by the contributing cause (*ālambana-hetu*)—that is, the practice of "listening inwardly" (for at the beginning, the cultivation of concentration is predominant; yet it proceeds by following after understanding, and is thus the concentration within wisdom)—is the essence of *samādhi*. Moreover...

It fully adopts the nature of the primary cause (*hetu*) and simultaneously encompasses both the conditional and the primary causes (that is, the equalizing flow of samādhi and prajñā within the central mean).

However, because it penetrates deeply into the fundamental samādhi of the *tathāgatagarbha* nature, it never deviates from the nature-samādhi from beginning to end; this constitutes the essence of *dhyāna*. [Question: Since you state that understanding is opened through receiving the teachings, this clearly refers to "subsequently attained" [knowledge].

Why then do you say it is "naturally endowed"? If that were so, why would one not understand prior to being taught? [Answer: This is precisely where the provisional schools are deluded. They take only correct analytical discernment as the primary cause for enlightenment, failing to realize that inverted discernment is fundamentally of the same substance as correct understanding. If it were not originally endowed [within the nature], how could it arise?

By what means can this essence be transformed into right understanding? It is because the teachings of definitive meaning (nītārtha) state that ignorance is itself clarity. Please clarify this through an analogy: right understanding and discernment are like water flowing eastward; inverted discernment is like water flowing westward.

Now, taking what was inverted and turning it into correct understanding is like changing a westward-flowing stream into one that flows eastward; previously, such a flow did not exist—on what basis, then, could there have been a transformation? By this analogy, one should understand that all delusory activities within the state of delusion are inherently endowed as the *pratyaya-hetu* (conditioned cause).

This is what Tiantai refers to when he speaks of "cultivating in reverse. Other schools, failing to grasp this principle, attempt to force a classification using the three types of *śamatha-vipaśyanā*, resulting in a total lack of coherence and leaving no place for their positions to be situated.
They either supplement [the meaning] beyond the literal words or merely seize upon one or two superficial similarities.
[The opponent] speaks thus, attempting to explain it by force, yet it utterly lacks any rational meaning. Now there are three points to clearly distinguish this samādhi.

First, this is a wondrous samādhi (*miaoding*). It is precisely because its nature is inherently and spontaneously possessed, naturally unmoving, and not something to be accomplished through cultivation.
Even while remaining in the state of delusion amidst movement, its essence remains as it is; therefore, it is called "wondrous. Otherwise, how could it be said to be "thorough" (*che*)?
This is the samādhi of the source of the Dharma, which is unmoving and indestructible.

Based on this, any practice of *śamatha* and *vipaśyanā* that does not accord with the nature itself but seeks effort elsewhere is not a sublime samādhi. Second, it is said: "This is the perfect samādhi.
For this samādhi does not merely take the immovability of one's own mind as its sole object; rather, it encompasses all dharmas and all phenomena.

All are fundamentally unmoving, constituting a single, unified essence. As the Sūtra says: "The Bodhisattva, abiding within samādhi, perceives that the seer, the objects of seeing, and all perceived forms are like flowers in the sky—originally non-existent.

This seeing and its objects are originally the wondrous, pure, and luminous essence of bodhi. This refers to the fact that the ocean of the mind is fundamentally tranquil; therein, the myriad phenomena are stilled and coalesce, collectively forming a single state of concentration.

Otherwise, how could it be called the samādhi in which all things are unmoving and indestructible? Based on this, anything that does not encompass the myriad phenomena [cannot be considered true samādhi].
As for those who alone restrain their single mind and remain unmoving, these are all concentrations that are not yet perfected. Third, it is said: "This is the Great Concentration (Mahāsamādhi).
Precisely because of this concentration, even while remaining in the state of delusion, one has never wavered from the fundamental; after awakening and understanding, [one remains so]."

How could there be emerging from or retreating from it? You should know that once this samādhi has spontaneously given rise to understanding and the practice of the path, until one reaches Buddhahood through the successive stages, there is ultimately no emerging or retreating;
how much less could there be its destruction? Otherwise, how could it be called the ultimate, steadfast samādhi?
Based on this, any state involving entering, abiding, or emerging—even if it lasts for a long time—is not considered "Great."
This is indeed *samādhi*. One may know this clearly by examining it in detail. The conventional practice of *śamatha* and *vipaśyanā* is entirely dissimilar to this.

In the sutra text, the request for *samādhi* occurs first, and the request for the title occurs later; this [title] thus encompasses the entire content indicated throughout the preceding three sections.
To take the Great Samādhi as the name of the entire sutra, both in its general and specific aspects, is unsurpassed in its subtlety. This is the seventh sutra.
This [term "emptiness"] is "false" because it is a text that explains the four aforementioned real dharmas; it is "universal" because it universally explains all dharmas.

Furthermore, as a general title for various sutras, it merely adopts the sense of the expressive designation and does not adopt meanings such as "nature-detached" or "immediately true," since the distinction between the false and the real has already been made.

According to the Tiantai school, this [term] also pertains to that which is expressed. As for its essence, it consists of phonemes (*śabda*), phrases (*pada*), names (*nāman*), and syllables (*vyañjana*), encompassing both the provisional and the real.
Among the four realities of the single term *sūtra*, it primarily refers to the sacred teachings of the sages; it partially corresponds to the *xi jing* (席經).

Furthermore, while the sacred teachings of this land are called "jing" (經), translating it here as "jing" reveals that it is the sacred teaching of the Western Land. Moreover, this term is glossed as "constant" (*nitya*).
It is said that this has remained unchanged throughout the ages, from antiquity to the present.

The intent of the Śākya Sage’s teaching in that region—to manifest the principles for the ten directions and the three periods of time—is identical [to our own], though its scope is vast. Other aspects, such as its comprehensive integration and so forth, are omitted here to avoid prolixity;

they cannot be fully detailed. If one wishes to know its extraordinary excellence, it entirely follows from what it explains. As for the subtlety of its literary expression, it is rooted in the Tathāgata.
This work is refined in its principles and skillful in its rhetoric, further enhanced by the artistry of Feng and Xiang in its polishing;

it is exceedingly ornate and elegant, such that no reader fails to offer three sighs of admiration. Since the author of the sutra has already provided a title for it, this commentary relies solely upon the sutra to extract its meaning.
Its subtle implications are inexhaustible, and the text has been slightly expanded for greater detail. May those who observe it take the opportunity to study and savor it.

(There are two traditional methods of interpretation. First is the *pratipakṣa* (correlative) interpretation, which briefly comprises six pairs: 1. the pair of the praiser and the praised; 2. the pair of the indicator and the indicated; 3. the pair of the signifier and the signified, which is self-evident; 4.

the pair of nature (*prakṛti*) and cultivation (*bhāvanā*), which corresponds to sections three and four; 5. the pair of movement and stillness, corresponding to sections five and six; 6. the pair of the general and the particular, where sections three, four, and five are the particulars and section six is the general. Second is the *viyoga-samāsa* (separative-combinative) interpretation, which briefly provides four explanations. First: "Great Buddha-Usnīṣa" is the indicator and praiser; as it is merely a verbal designation, it is inferior.

"The Secret Cause of the Tathāgata," etc., are the indicated and the praised; as they are the true principle of nature and cultivation, they are superior. The particle "of" (*zhi*) added below "Buddha-Usnīṣa" is interpreted according to the *taddhita* (dependent) compound.)

The *sūtra* is the signifier (*vācaka*), consisting merely of sounds, names, phrases, and syllables; thus it is inferior. That which is above [the *sūtra*] is the signified (*vācya*), consisting of the sublime meanings of the fundamental nature (*prakṛti*), cultivation (*bhāvanā*), and so forth; thus it is superior. The word "above" added before *sūtra* is a *tatpuruṣa* compound (dependent determinative). Thirdly, the *sūtra* is the very essence of the teaching.

The above [explanations] all concern the application of cause, effect, cultivation, and realization. By adding the character "is" (即) before "sūtra" (經), it is a *karmadhāraya* (持業釋) compound. Fourth, the four [aspects] encompass the six sections; these are what the sūtra possesses. By adding the character "not" (非) before "sūtra," it is a *bahuvrīhi* (有財釋) compound.

The rest is as in the case of the title "Mahābuddhoṣṇīṣa Sūtra" or "Śūraṅgama Sūtra," where one may apply similar reasoning to the preceding explanations. Furthermore, according to ancient conventions, there are three types of titles: those based on person, dharma, or metaphor; these may be single, compound, or complete. This title contains all three.

Thus, it does not abandon the ancient conventions and is provided here for reference. There is yet another point: I shall expand upon this in the commentary (*śāstra*) to resolve the points of contention regarding previous interpretations that were not entirely satisfactory. For the most part, I have simply not adopted them, rather than refuting them further. However...

This appears to be correct but is actually erroneous. Fearing that people might harbor doubts and fail to reach a decision, thereby being hindered in their discernment of what to adopt and what to reject, I shall now briefly present one instance from the outset as an illustration for the rest.

This follows the traditional interpretation; however, while this current title seems concise and its exposition appears thorough, it is not realized that there are two inconveniences that obstruct the profound intent of the Buddha. First, it is too perfunctory and does not capture the essence. Generally, one who explains a sutra must first honor the original text and explain it point by point.

For example, regarding the "Secret Cause" (mimi yin), one must state exactly what kind of dharma it is and identify which specific passage in the root sutra corresponds to it. Only after each point has been explained, and any remaining implications have been further elaborated upon, can it be considered a well-composed commentary. Now, however, the "Secret" [Cause] is not explained at all.

To merely take up such terms as "causes" (*hetu*) and so forth, and continue to handle and turn them over in one's hands, is to be debating the literary form; it is not an interpretation of the literary form. How could this possibly allow both the text and its meaning to be fully elucidated? This error is still relatively minor. The second [error] is to obscure the essential intent and to misrepresent the scripture.

This refers to those who, in their commentary on the passage "below the Tathāgata," employ the teachings of the Chan school to hold everything firmly in check, sweeping away the "mysterious causes" (*guhyahetu*) and so forth all at once, claiming that only then does one reach the ultimate principle of "neither cultivation nor realization. If this were the case, then the First Noble Truth would reside entirely outside the scope of the scriptures.

In reality, it is precisely by employing the Chan school’s "returning path and letting go" below [the section on the Tathāgata] that [the scripture] accommodates sentient beings by conforming to the "mysterious causes" and so forth. It continues to permit both cultivation and realization, establishing all these as provisional expedients in accordance with worldly conditions. If this is so, then...

The essential purport of the sutras is entirely established within the second gate. Yet, taking the Buddha’s perfect and ultimate intent, you have instead relegated it to the depths of the *Vajracchedikā* and the *Laṅkāvatāra*. This is because you have not at all understood what the "esoteric cause" (*mi-yin*) and the "definitive meaning" (*liao-yi*) truly are. To hastily and recklessly argue in such a way is a profound distortion of the sutras;

this error is no small matter. I shall now attempt to clarify it. Regarding that which is called the Tathāgata’s resultant essence: its essence is primordial. Why would it require an esoteric cause? Yet you fail to realize that this very esoteric cause is precisely the primordially present resultant essence, which is without cultivation and without realization.

Regarding that which is called the Bodhisattva’s path and function: its function is non-action. What, then, constitutes the myriad practices? Yet you fail to realize that these myriad practices are rooted in the definitive meaning; that cultivation is itself non-cultivation, and that they are subsumed within the "moving source" (*dong-yuan*) of the *Śūraṃgama Sūtra*.

"Immovable" is precisely the functioning of the path of non-action (*anabhisaṃskāra*). Speaking thus, why should one rely on what is borrowed or what is different? How could one fail to recognize a person and yet still address them by name with slander? One should know that this sutra is not only the primary meaning (*paramārtha*) in terms of rational principle;

all things and all phenomena (*dharmas*) are the primary meaning, because all phenomena are ultimately firm and solid, as they all transcend the names and characteristics (*nāma-lakṣaṇa*) of both the Great and the Small Vehicles.

How could there be a primary meaning outside of this sutra? There are many such examples among the various commentaries; for those who do not accept this hereafter, I have no leisure to debate at length. The title is hereby concluded.
△ Second, the section on the translators, which is divided into three parts. First, the primary translator:
"The Indian Śramaṇa Paramiti translated.
"Indian" refers to the birthplace of the primary translator; it is the general name for the countries of the Western Regions, which here is called the "Moon Country. It contains...
The succession of sages and worthies in their transformative influence is like the moon shining upon the world. This land lies at the center of Jambudvīpa, spanning over ninety thousand *li*.
It is divided into five regions and comprises more than seventy kingdoms; those in the east, west, south, north, and the center are all named Tianshu (India). This master—
A native of Central India—a land where Buddhas are born. This refers only to a general designation, and it is not yet known which specific country it denotes.
"Śramaṇa" is a general term for a disciple of the Śākya; here it is translated as "diligent and quiescent," meaning to diligently practice wholesome dharmas and to extinguish unwholesome deeds.
It is also said that because one quiets the mind and reaches the fundamental source, one is called a śramaṇa. "Prajñāmitra" is translated here as...
Ji-liang (Extreme Measure): A specific name for the chief translator; an Indian monk of talent and wisdom. "Translator" (yi-zhe):

Refers to both the Chinese characters and the phonetic transcription used to transform Indic language into the language of China (Huayan). (For the Indic script of the West differs entirely from this [Chinese]; if one were to examine the Indic original, not only would one not understand the language, but one would also fail to recognize the characters themselves.

It is necessary first to follow the Indic pronunciation and substitute it with characters from this land [China], which are termed "transliterated characters" (fan-zi). Only after these transliterated characters can the text be read. However, even when the phonetics match those of a mantra, one still does not know what kind of language it is; thus, one must also be proficient in both.)

Regarding the spoken sounds of the two countries, each was translated from Sanskrit into Chinese, which is called "Fan-yin" (foreign sound). The person specially appointed as the chief translator was [Guṇabhadra].
Because this sutra had not yet arrived, its great fame reached him first; for eighteen years, Tiantai faced westward, bowing and seeking it, yet in the end he did not succeed in seeing it.

In that country, it was prohibited as a state treasure. The Master secretly concealed it and brought it across the sea. In the early years of Emperor Zhongzong of the Tang dynasty, he arrived at Guangzhou.
It happened that Prime Minister Fang invited him to translate it at Zhi-zhi Temple.

He returned quickly to avoid the difficulty of being held accountable for violating the border regulations (the King had therefore punished the frontier officials for the Master’s secret passage). Indeed, despite the hardships of violating prohibitions, his resolve was ever more intent on benefiting this land.
His merit is unsurpassed. Furthermore, he possessed comprehensive wisdom and eloquence, presiding over the translation bureau until his work was completed and he withdrew from public office;
it is truly fitting that he be ranked first to honor his great foundational service. △ Second, the translators of the language.
The Śramaṇa Mīghaśikya from the country of Udyāna translated the terminology. Regarding the country of Udyāna:

according to the *Mingyi zhong* (Compendium of Names and Meanings), it is the country of Uddiyāna, which has been erroneously transcribed as Wuchang; its pronunciation is identical to that of Chang. It is suspected that this is indeed that country.
"U" here means "garden" (*vana*), referring to the gardens and parks of ancient great kingdoms. It is a country of Northern India.
This is an alternative name for [the term] *Migya Śākya*, which means "Capable of Subduing. Regarding the term "translator" (*yi-shuo-zhe*):

since the title of "Master of Esoteric Truths" (*mi-di*) encompasses all such matters and lacks a specific office, it is simply called "translation. This [term "translator"] designates a specific official who specializes in those duties.

It is also called "one who conveys the language" (*du-yu*), meaning one who is fully proficient in both Chinese and Sanskrit, transforming Sanskrit into Chinese; this refers to the transcription of foreign sounds.
[This is] all. △ Third, the person who provided the literary polish:
Transcribed by the Bodhisattva Precept Disciple Fang Rong, formerly Grand Master for Rectifying Counsel, concurrently Minister of the Department of State Affairs and Director of the Secretariat.
The Chapter on the Bodhisattva Precepts is so extensive that it cannot be fully recorded here; those who may practice as laypeople should receive them.

The sutras state that when kings and ministers assume their positions, they ought first to receive these precepts. Thus, not only will the deities of the precepts provide protection, but by guarding virtue and preventing wrongdoing, one will ultimately cultivate the seeds of sainthood.
As for disciples, they take refuge in the Triple Gem as their Great Master. The former...
"Old" refers to his former official title, which was his previous office; he has currently been demoted to Guangzhou. Because only his surname, Nánquán, is known, it is stated thus.
"Zhèngyì" (Correct Counselor) is a title for an official of the Censorate as recorded in the histories. "Dàfū" (Grand Master) refers to...

It is appropriate to greatly support those who are eminent in talent and hold high office. As for "together," it means that since his subordinates and assistants were not few, he collaborated with them in governance.
The Secretariat (Zhongshu) and the Chancellery (Menxia) were both names for the inner ministries and the palaces of the Left and Right Ministers.

However, the Secretariat primarily managed imperial edicts, while the Chancellery primarily issued administrative policies. Thus, Rong concurrently exercised authority over both ministries. Therefore—
Both are recorded here. Regarding the term "pingzhang" (平章): the text states, "to pingzhang the hundred surnames. "Ping" (平) means to level or equalize; "zhang" (章) means to manifest or clarify.

This refers to impartially managing administrative affairs and clearly manifesting the laws and regulations. "Shi" (事) refers precisely to these administrative affairs, laws, and regulations, and so forth. [End of note by] Fang Rong.
This was the father of Fang Guan. Both father and son served as Prime Ministers.

However, the details of Rong’s service appear briefly in the biography of Fang Guan, stating that he served during the final years of Empress Wu and was demoted in the first year of the Shenlong era of Emperor Zhongzong (*The Old Annals* notes that at the time of this translation, the year was given as the twenty-third day of the fifth month of the first year of Shenlong;
perhaps this records the date the work began, rather than when it was completed). The scribe (*bishou*) was also from the translation hall.
Within this [process], there is the designation of "specialized officials for specific duties," who are those that take up the pen to finalize the written text.

(Regarding the initial transcription of foreign characters, one must understand how to substitute them with corresponding Chinese characters—such as *dvandva*, *tritaya*, *mūrdhanya*, or *pluta*—and as for the foreign sounds themselves, one must consult experts on both Chinese and Sanskrit to ensure they correspond accurately before setting pen to paper; all of this is a difficult task.

Even emperors have personally held these offices. As for the refinement of the prose (*runden wen*), officials were traditionally established separately for this purpose; if the scribe (*bishou*) were otherwise, the result might be clumsy.
Regarding the phrase "polishing the text" (*runwen*): it refers specifically to the act of refining the literary style. Minister Fang (Fang Xuanling) also concurrently held this office;

therefore, his name and that of the sūtra alternate in manifesting his contribution. Now, although the request for translation, the transcription of the text, and the polishing of the style were submitted to the inner court and thus not immediately distributed, they were later recovered from the private collection after Shenxiu entered the palace and transcribed them.
Originally, it was ultimately brought into circulation. Thus, did not Rongzhen (Jizang) indeed perform a great service to this sutra?
The section on the translators concludes.
△ Third, the division of the sutra text into three parts: First, the Introduction. Now, as for the three divisions of the Introduction, the Main Body, and the Circulation, they begin with the Way.

Peaceful. And [it] was verified by Bandhuprabha (Dao’an was a monk of the Qin dynasty; he had not yet seen the Western versions, so he first divided them into three parts. Everyone criticized him, but later when the treatise of Bodhisattva Bandhuprabha arrived, it was indeed so).

This method of interpreting the sūtras is universally applicable. Now, regarding the initial preface: it is intended to introduce the subject matter. It is further divided into two parts: first, the sixfold sequence of authentication (*ṣaḍ-vidha-pratyaya-nidāna*).
This preface is common to all sūtras and is also called the "General Preface. Ānanda [recited it] for the Buddha...

At the time of his parinirvāṇa, the Buddha requested that these [introductory formulas] be placed at the beginning of all sūtras, so that those who witness their presence may recognize them as authentic Buddhist scriptures and develop faith and acceptance;
otherwise, many would be spurious and unworthy of belief. As for the "six kinds," they refer to the six accomplishments:
first, faith; second, hearing; third, time; fourth, the teacher; fifth, the location; and sixth, the assembly. It is not permissible for even one of these to be missing.
Therefore, it is called "accomplishment. Now, for the sake of convenience in the text, and to balance the detailed and abbreviated versions, we shall simply divide it into three parts.
First, the indication of faith and hearing: "Thus have I heard."
