At that time, King Prasenajit prepared a vegetarian feast for the anniversary of his deceased father’s death and invited the Buddha to the inner palace, personally escorting him there.
"Come! Prepare an extensive array of rare delicacies and unsurpassed, exquisite flavors, and further personally invite the great Bodhisattvas.
Gu-shan says: "Bimbasāra; this is translated as 'Victorious Army' (Shèng-jūn). Wén-líng says: "He is the King of Śrāvastī."

In the past, during the era of Buddha Dragon-Light (Nāgaprabha), he had already attained the fourth bhūmi; he was likewise one of great spiritual authority (*mahopāya*). As for the "day of his name" (*mingri*), it is a day of taboo.
When a filial son speaks of the day his parent passed away, he is immediately overcome with grief; therefore, he conceals the name and does not dare to speak of it.
According to worldly custom, on this anniversary each year, one alters one’s clothing and diet to manifest grief as if it were the first day. [End of Inner Section]

I instructed him to perform meritorious deeds for the afterlife to provide for his father. Now, as the anniversary of his father the King’s passing coincides with the *pravāraṇā* ceremony, he has observed a fast to provide for his parent.
"The palace quarters" refers to the attendants on the left and right of the inner court, like the armpits (*bāhu-kakṣa*) of a person.

“Rare delicacies” (*zhēnxiū*) refers to precious and valued foods. “Invite” (*yán*) also means to welcome and summon. There are six levels of invitation for the Buddha, which demonstrate the height of reverence:

first, as for the location, it is internal; second, as for the welcoming, it is personal; third, as for the arrangement, it is extensive; fourth, as for the delicacies, they are rare; fifth, as for the flavor, it is exquisite;
sixth, as for the companions, they are identical. “Companions are identical” means that the respectful attendants are the same as the host.
It was not that he was urgent with the host and lax with the attendants. △ Second, the ministers and citizens provide offerings.
Within the city, there were further elders and lay devotees who simultaneously fed the Sangha, awaiting the Buddha’s arrival to respond to them. The Buddha commanded Mañjuśrī.
The assembly consisted of bodhisattvas and arhats who attended to the various hosts of the ritual feasts.

Among them were elders whose virtue, age, rank, and emoluments were all preeminent; these belonged to the class of ministers. As for the lay practitioners (gṛhapati), they delighted in discussing profound and renowned names.

He dwelt in purity as if he were not in office, appearing merely like a recluse. Those who simultaneously provided meals for the monastic community were moved by the Buddha’s transformative ritual and practiced giving in accordance with the teachings.
However, those among the ministers and subjects who waited solely upon the Buddha did so out of reverence for their former sovereign.

When the host is present, the guests will surely arrive. When the Buddha commands that offerings be distributed according to need, it causes those who are without discrimination to obtain equal merit.
If one can practice giving with an impartial mind, then even after the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa, the merit will likewise be without inequality.

The sixfold introduction for establishing faith is now complete. △ Second, showing the introductory section on the occasion of the descent [of the Bodhisattva]. This introduction varies from sutra to sutra.
It is also called the "Separate Introduction" (*pṛthag-nirdeśa*). Because each sutra is introduced by its own specific circumstances and conditions, they differ from one another;

for example, the *Mahā-amitābha-sūtra* introduces itself through color, while the *Saddharma-puṇḍarīka-sūtra* introduces itself through light, and so forth. In the present sutra, the falling into a brothel serves as the occasion for the introduction.
Regarding the term "showing the fall," it refers to Ānanda, whose secret virtues are equal to those of the aforementioned leaders.
He was not an actual śrāvaka; his falling into a brothel was merely a manifestation intended to inspire the Great Teaching.
Furthermore, this sutra seeks to clarify that those who rely on extensive learning (*bahuśruta*) without practicing meditative concentration (*samādhi*) lack the power to resist the demon of desire;
how then could they transcend birth and death? Thus, by showing a person of great learning falling [into temptation], it serves as an exhortation.
"One who is widely learned" refers merely to the power of exertion within great concentration. Yet, the reason Ānanda must necessarily be employed is twofold:

first, because he is foremost among those of wide learning, it is made evident that what one has heard is not to be relied upon; second, because he is the Buddha’s cousin, it is likewise made evident that other [aspects] are not to be relied upon.

(At this point, since it is revealed that Ānanda is a Great Power Bodhisattva, that is sufficient for understanding. As for the subsequent text, it simply proceeds based on the perspective of the manifested Śrāvaka.)

[The Master] waved his hand and said: "Only by doing so can one truly inspire and draw forth those of the ordinary and Hinayana vehicles. This is because the profound stages are provisionally manifested through the shallow stages; thus, one must be able to fully exhaust the emotional states of the shallow stages.

For instance, when those who cling to delusions and perverse arguments are moved to tears of realization, it is precisely for the sake of exhausting their emotional states and thereby eliciting the hearts of those who are truly authentic, skillfully causing them to give rise to joy and realization. It is not necessary to further clarify point by point that [the provisional] is not the ultimate truth, which would only lead to excessive hesitation.

This is divided into three parts. First, the causes and conditions of falling into error. There are four such causes and conditions; if even one is missing, one does not fall. This is further divided into four sections. First, the separate invitation from afar.
[The Buddha] was traveling. Only Ānanda remained; having previously accepted a separate invitation, he had traveled far and had not yet returned, so he could not take his place in the assembly.
"Ānanda" is translated here as "Joyful Celebration. On the day the Buddha attained enlightenment, King Śuddhodana’s younger brother, King Droṇodana, further reported [the news].
A son was born, and Śuddhodana bestowed upon him the name "Ānanda" (Joy). He was the Buddha’s younger cousin. Regarding those who had previously received separate invitations:
this refers to those who had already accepted invitations for various specific matters prior to the *pravāraṇā* ceremony; they were thus occupied and could not attend. They are listed next.
Since he has traveled far away and has not yet returned, he has had no leisure to attend this assembly for the *prātimokṣa* (self-indulgence) ceremony.
Were it not for this long journey, how could he have fallen [into such a state]? Therefore, this constitutes the first condition. △ Second, returning alone without a companion.
Since there was neither an *upādhyāya* nor an *ācārya*, he returned alone on the road.

Regarding the *upādhyāya*, the Buddha stated that there is no person above him who may be called "Upādhyāya" (*upari-adhyāya*). Furthermore, seniority among the seats is divided into upper, middle, and lower based on the depth of one’s summer retreats (*varṣa*);
those who have completed forty summers are designated as the *upādhyāya*. As for the *ācārya*, this is translated as "Preceptor of Conduct" (*gui*).
Fan [Zhu] stated: "The Vinaya regulations stipulate that when a single monk travels afar, he must be accompanied by two masters to assist him;
this is to strictly regulate one's movements. Now, to travel without these two masters as companions constitutes the second condition for falling into error.
△ Third, begging for alms without provisions.
On that day there was no alms-food. At that moment, Ānanda took up his *pātra* (alms-bowl) and went through the city where he was traveling, begging in regular succession.
Regarding the fact that there was no alms-food on that day: at the place where he stayed for the night, no one offered him a meal.

This was so that there might be a path for him to obtain food, allowing him to proceed without falling into negligence; this is why it is called the third condition. The *pātra* is the bowl. It should...
The size [of the alms bowl] depends merely on one's own capacity for food. △ Fourth, practicing universal compassion:

with an impartial resolve, one should beg without discriminating between the pure and the impure. Even if one were to follow the constant rule of the Śrāvakas by begging only from pure households, there would still be no falling into error;
therefore, this fourth condition is a crucial point for avoiding such errors. This further divides into two parts. First:
One practices impartial compassion within the mind.
From the very beginning of seeking a donor until the very end, one takes them as the host of the feast, regardless of whether they are pure or impure, of noble lineage or a *caṇḍāla*.
Only then does one practice impartial compassion, making no distinction between the lowly and the humble, resolving to bring all sentient beings to perfect fulfillment.
"Immeasurable merit. Regarding "one who first seeks":
Ānanda had not previously given rise to this mind; he only now begins to seek it. "Dānapati" (檀越) is translated here as "donor.
Regarding "one who comes last": this refers to one who has never previously possessed a virtuous mind or practiced giving. [The original term] is in Sanskrit...

*Kṣatriya* is the literal Chinese translation for "noble clan," referring to the royal lineage. From the *kṣatriyas* at the highest level, there is no one among those who are noble and pure who is excluded.
*Caṇḍāla* means "butcher" in this [Chinese] context; they are families that slaughter living beings.

In the Western Regions, they are considered the most base and lowly, not permitted to live together with respectable families. They carry distinctive insignia while traveling, and people likewise avoid them. At the lowest level...
"Cāṇḍāla" refers to those who are lowly and defiled, leaving none out.

Furthermore, the statement "without selecting the lowly and base" means that while both the noble and the base are included, the intent is to universally embrace the lowly and defiled; this is the new sense of equality in the present context.
The final three phrases further clarify the universality and greatness of his vow, intending that even those without merit may achieve accomplishment.
This is of immeasurable merit. △ Second, [the section on] manifesting impartial compassion:
Ānanda already knew that the Tathāgata, the World-Honored One, had rebuked Subhūti and Mahākāśyapa for having minds that were not impartial as Arhats.
He now reverently looked up to the Tathāgata to expound the unobstructed [teaching] and resolve all doubts and slanders.

"Already known" means that [the truth] was already known long ago at the assembly of Vimalakīrti. "World-Honored One" (Bhagavat) refers to one who fully possesses the virtues of the ten titles and is revered by those in heaven and among humans.
Therefore, although the ten titles were previously set forth, the term "World-Honored One" is used here as a comprehensive designation;
this is the intended meaning. "Reproach" means to censure. That is to say, the Tathāgata did not—[regarding Vimalakīrti’s...]
If one rebukes something as being wrong, one immediately knows that the Tathāgata has already rebuked it and need not do so again.
How much more so when Vimalakīrti reveals that he is the Golden Grain Tathāgata—how would he differ from Śākyamuni? Subhūti, one abandons the poor to beg from the wealthy.
His intention was to restore their roots of goodness, fearing they might fall into ruin; furthermore, there was no difficulty in diminishing his own merit.

Mahākāśyapa abandoned the wealthy to beg from the poor, intending to pity those who had long suffered and to plant the causes for their future happiness, while also avoiding the criticism of seeking out the rich.
Thus, despite his status as an Arhat, he performed this act of apparent inequality; therefore, the Buddha rebuked him.

It is not so. "To open and elucidate the unobstructed" means to rectify the aforementioned two types of people who each have limitations, and now to develop and clarify the universal mind that is free from such restrictions.
"To deliver those who harbor doubts and slanders" means to deliver those sentient beings who are suspicious and slanderous.
This is to ensure one is exempt from suspicion and slander; for it is generally the case that those who are excessively poor invite suspicion, while those who are excessively wealthy invite slander.

This concludes the section on the causal conditions for falling into error. △ Second, the actual descent into the chamber of lust, which is further divided into three parts: first, the deliberate application of strict precepts.
He proceeded toward that city moat, walking slowly through the outer gate. He maintained a solemn and dignified demeanor, reverently observing the rules of the fast.

The "moat" refers to a waterless ditch surrounding the city; the "outer gate" is the city gate. As for the "rules of the fast," these are the regulations observed when approaching the ritual of fasting.
The reason for such meticulous attention to solemnity and restraint is that, once the resolve has been made, one does not discriminate between purity and impurity.
One must redouble one's self-restraint before one can hope for freedom from obstacles. II. Power Insufficient to Overcome Evil.
At that time, Ānanda, while on his alms-round, passed by a brothel and encountered the girl Mātangī, who possessed great illusory powers.
By means of the *sāṃvāraka* mantra of the former Brahmā, she drew him into the seat of lust;
"next" refers to the place where he subsequently passed through. Generally, illusionist arts take the transformation of false and deceptive objects as their technique;
these, however, merely delude people and cause them to lose their original mind. They do not—
Awakening follows along with them. "Mātanga" means "original nature" in this language. This woman had the karmic connection of lustful desire with Ānanda over many kalpas;
there is a separate *Daṅga Sūtra* that records this in great detail. Now, she has encountered this delusion again because of her habitual karma.
"Sāvikāra" means "Golden Head" in this language. She bound her fingers and ate half a grain of rice. For...
He was an ascetic. The incantations he transmitted were falsely claimed to be those of Brahmā.
To draw Ānanda into the seat of lust, he relied on the fact that Ānanda possessed the twenty marks of a Buddha and his complexion was as beautiful as silver; thus, Tiṅga conceived a desire for him.
Using a spell, she covered food with a cloth and gave it to him; by the power of the spell, Ānanda was unaware and followed her into the seat of lust.

This matter can only be practiced without obstruction by Bodhisattvas; Ānanda, however, manifested himself as being at the stage of the first fruit of the Śrāvaka, thereby demonstrating that his power was weak and thus unable to overcome the evil one. △ Third, the essence of the precepts is in peril.
He lewdly stroked [her body], on the verge of destroying the essence of his precepts (*śīla*).

The essence of the precepts is precisely the mind that guards them; because of the power of the "precepts co-arising with the Path" (*mārga-sahaja-śīla*) of the first fruit (*srotāpanna*), although his body was close, his mind had not yet moved.

Nevertheless, to say he was "on the verge of destroying" them is already perilous; therefore, it is categorized as being in a state of imminent danger. (Some attribute this "being on the verge of destruction" to Yaśodharā, while others...)

"Ānanda, I do not know what it is that you find so unacceptable about this manifestation; why do you seek to shield him? Furthermore, if he were not on the verge of death, what need would there have been to rescue him?
Thus ends the section on falling into the chamber of lust. △ Third, the Tathāgata’s rescue and liberation. This also has three parts. First, the swift return to the assembly.

The Tathāgata knew that she had employed sorcery; having finished his meal, he returned. The king, along with the ministers, elders, and householders, all followed the Buddha, wishing to hear the essential points of the Dharma.
As for knowing that the practitioner’s arts were being employed, the Buddha perceived it clearly with his Buddha-eye; there was nothing far away that was not before him. Zizhong said:
"It is the Tathāgata’s constant custom to preach the Dharma after the conclusion of a fast. Since he has now returned so quickly, he must have a specific purpose;
therefore, the assembly followed him. II. Preaching the Mantra to Dispatch the Rescue.
At that time, the World-Honored One emitted from the crown of his head a hundred-jeweled light of fearlessness.

From within this light, a thousand-petaled jeweled lotus emerged, upon which a manifested body of the Buddha sat in the full lotus posture. He proclaimed a divine mantra and commanded Mañjuśrī to take the mantra and go forth to provide protection.
"At that time" means at the moment when [the world] was about to be destroyed but had not yet been destroyed; it is neither before nor after.
"The crown" refers to the usnīṣa made of a hundred jewels, signifying that the myriad things are fully contained within it, such that nothing is sought that is not already present.

Seeing the compassion of his gathering-in, one sees the majesty of his subduing, wherein all heterodoxies are simultaneously subdued and no evil remains unsubdued. Thus, light is emitted from the crown. And...
Furthermore, it is expounded through the transformation Buddha (*nirmāṇakāya*). This is precisely what Master Huan refers to as the "unconditioned mind-Buddha" and the "unsurpassed mind-dharma.
Moreover, it is manifested from the crown of the head, signifying the most honored among the honored and the most secret among the secret.

The transformation Buddha upon the lotus seat also clarifies its essential role as both cause and fruit. As for *paryaṅka* (cross-legged posture), it means sitting with the feet folded; the details are fully explained [elsewhere].

Regarding *śamatha* and *vipaśyanā*, this divine mantra possesses the four *siddhāntas* (purposes) and contains the subtle and profound principles of the essence; it wields unfathomable majestic power.
That one must command Mañjuśrī is because, without the fundamental great wisdom, there would be no means to provide the practical utility for those of extensive learning.
△ Third, refuting the heterodox and returning to the orthodox.
The evil spell was extinguished. He led Ānanda and Mātaṅgī back to the Buddha’s presence.
By the power of this divine spell, the malevolent incantation was dissolved; Ānanda was as if awakened from a dream, and Mātaṅgī’s lustful mind suddenly ceased.
Her latent roots of goodness were awakened, she realized the first three fruits of the path, and resolved to leave the household life; thus, she also came along with them. Mātaṅgī.

Since the provisional and the ultimate have not yet been definitively established, there is nothing that cannot be done according to the circumstances. The introductory section (nidāna) is now concluded.
△ Second, the main body of the teaching (śarīra). Regarding the main body: the introduction is the beginning and the dissemination (pariṇāmanā) is the end;
this section lies between the two pillars, wherein questions and answers unfold the full intent of what is most highly revered within the sutra. Furthermore,
This is divided into two parts. First, the sutra fully demonstrates the beginning and end of the sublime samādhi.

Although both this section and the subsequent one constitute the primary teaching (*samyak-artha*), they are still distinguished as the primary and the auxiliary; this section is the primary, while the subsequent section is the auxiliary.

Within the primary section, the Buddha answers only the question posed by the immediate disciple regarding samādhi; therefore, throughout the entire sutra, there is no other intent than the beginning and end of this single samādhi.
It is further divided into three parts. First, Ānanda’s earnest plea, which is itself divided into two sections. First, the plea for the wondrous samādhi:

Ānanda beheld the Buddha, prostrated himself, and wept with grief, lamenting that from time immemorial he had been devoted solely to extensive learning (*bahuśruta*) without fully perfecting his power of the Way (*mārgabala*).
With earnest and respectful entreaty, [he requested] the initial expedient means for attaining Bodhi— the wondrous śamatha, samādhi, and dhyāna— of the Tathāgatas of the ten directions.
I prostrate with weeping compassion and thank you for the grace of your rescue. To recount our many lives from beginningless time, I have consistently been biased in my habitual practice.
"The power of the Way" refers specifically to the power of concentration (*samādhi*). I particularly regret these two faults:

first, that because I did not realize I had fallen [into error], lustful desire arose; this was merely a case of one's strength being unable to overcome the perverse. Second, that I gave rise to inferior [states of mind].
"I request meditative concentration. This request is twofold: first, a sincere regret that one has heard only partial teachings and lacks great power of meditative concentration;

second, a simultaneous remorse for the weak power of the Small Vehicle (Hīnayāna) which fails to subdue the forces of Māra. Therefore, he requests concentration below, precisely in order to alter the path of partial hearing.
To necessarily seek the Buddha-concentration is precisely for the purpose of turning back the mind of the Hīnayāna. The earnest entreaty below is the formal request for concentration.
To speak of the "Tathāgatas of the ten directions" is to seek the method of universal cultivation common to all Buddhas; this already serves as a check against the Lesser Vehicle.
Furthermore, to say "attaining the realization of Bodhi" is to further seek the cause for the ultimate fruit of complete verification; this again serves as a check.

Regarding the "expedient vehicle" (wherein, although one practices the Mahāyāna through expedient teachings, one ultimately cannot achieve unsurpassed bodhi)—*bodhi* here is translated as the "path of awakening.
This is the fruit of the perfection of the Buddha’s three wisdoms, the supreme and ultimate goal. These terms are merely used provisionally for the sake of distinction;

the specific name will be revealed below. The single character "wondrous" (*miao*) further distinguishes it from that which is not wondrous, yet the intent of this distinction is even deeper—this refers to the title itself.
Within the *Śūraṅgama-samādhi*, the meanings of "nature" (*xing*), "intent" (*yi*), "perfection" (*yuan*), and "greatness" (*dai*) must all be present;
if even one is missing, it cannot be considered wondrous. This is because the three—*śamatha* and so forth—are common names for meditative concentration (*samādhi*) shared by all vehicles.

If they were not distinguished, there would be confusion with those other concentrations. (However, this was because Ānanda did not understand that the concentration he should practice is a name unique [to this vehicle]; therefore, the common name was cited and then qualified.)

Seeking the Buddha’s definitive revelation, the Buddha subsequently relied upon that which had been selected [by the assembly] to extract and reveal the *Śūraṃgama-samādhi-rāja*. Thereupon, the great assembly naturally came to know that this *Śūraṃgama-samādhi* is the very samādhi by which the Tathāgatas of the ten directions attain Bodhi.

Thus, is the *Śūraṃgama-rāja* not indeed the name of a wondrous samādhi that is unique? Generally, common names are largely identical; if they are not distinguished, they lead to confusion. Unique names are fundamentally different; if they were not used, there would be no need for further distinction.

Previously, the *Śūraṃgama* was taken as the general title while *śamatha* and so forth were treated as specific names. While it is certainly not an error to take "unification" as the general principle and "the three" as the specific branches, one fails to realize that this distinction between the common and the unique is even more significant.
The profound significance [of these terms] must still be understood. As for the three names beginning with *śamatha*, the translators did not provide translations;

they were certainly treated according to the principle of "respecting the original" (one of the five reasons for not translating). Nevertheless, their profound significance remains that these constitute a particularly sublime form of meditative concentration (*samādhi*), which cannot be equated with the conventional meaning [of the term].
[In common usage,] *śamatha* is translated as "cessation" (*zhi*), which is a specific name for concentration, taken in the sense of "tranquility. *Samādhi*...

To mention it briefly, this term may be written as *ti*, or as *di*, or further with the addition of the character *po* (波), or as *boti* (波底), or simply as *samādhi* (三昧); these are merely variations in the pronunciation of the Sanskrit sound. However, all three characters are read in the departing tone (*qùshēng*). In Chinese, this is translated as "Right Concentration" (*zhèngdìng*).

Some refer to it as *samāpatti* (correct reception). In the *Commentary on the Perfect Enlightenment Sūtra*, it is translated as "equal attainment" (*ting-zhi*). "Equal" (*ping-deng*) means dwelling in equilibrium, being free from both dullness and agitation. "Attainment" (*zhi*) means reaching a superior concentration and a superior state. Its meaning is the dissolution of illusions.

*Dhyāna* (meditative absorption) is here called "calm contemplation" (*jing-lü*), which is the dual fusion of concentration and wisdom; however, in the *Perfect Enlightenment Sūtra*, it takes "quiescent extinction" (*ji-mie*) as its meaning. While these various meanings mostly pertain to the effort of practicing meditative concentration and thus have little to do with the nature of concentration itself—making them still applicable across the various vehicles—this present Great Samādhi...

Since the meaning is extraordinary, one should not necessarily adhere rigidly to these conventional interpretations. If those who study the meaning wish to examine the Buddha’s responses in detail to determine their significance, they will be without error in ten thousand cases.

This is because the Buddha’s wisdom discerns the capacities of beings; his responses must correspond to the questions asked. If they did not correspond, how could they constitute a teaching that accords with both principle and capacity?

Therefore, in my "Provisional Exposition," I clearly demonstrated that the question and answer do not correspond. Examining the Buddha’s responses, there is still a general heading followed by specific answers.
Second: The general title refers to the Śūraṅgama King (the text states: "There is a samādhi named the Śūraṅgama King... even unto the Path of Sublime Adornment";
thus we know that the Śūraṅgama King is the collective heading for these three names). It should certainly be explained by taking the meaning of "nature-concentration" from the title itself.
There is certainly no error. If one were to provide a separate response, further discussion would be required; a detailed exposition has already been presented as a preliminary indication.

Here, only a brief summary is provided, consisting of three points. First, the *Tiantai Zhiguan* (Stilling and Contemplation) is not adopted for harmonious interpretation, because although that work relies on the truth of nature (*xingdi*), it takes the cultivation of practice (*xiucheng*) entirely as definitive.
This [present work], however, takes the nature-determinacy (*xingding*) entirely, while briefly incorporating [the other].

Because the meaning is that of cultivation and realization, the second [point] does not take up the three names individually, but rather treats them as a complete set to constitute "perfection" (*yuan*).
This answers with the meaning of perfection by following the sequence of the three names in the Buddha’s sutras, because it specifically takes up the three *tathāgatagarbhas*.
The third [point] does not restrict itself to conventional translations and commentaries; for one must conform to the subsequent answer-text of the Buddha, as restriction would fail to be exhaustive.

Because they correspond [to one another], if one understands these three meanings, then one will know that although the explanations below differ from what was previously heard, this does not constitute a fault.

Now, regarding *śamatha*: according to the Buddha’s answer below, it takes as its meaning the opening of understanding and illuminating realization of the inherently endowed, immovable, non-arising, and non-ceasing, all-pervading mind;
that is, the *dharmatā-nimitta* (the true cause) of *buddhadhātu* (Buddha-nature), briefly including [the other two natures].
The *liǎoyīn* (cause of realization) constitutes the essence of *śamatha*; it is the wisdom that is inherently complete and identical to meditative concentration (*samādhi*).

[Question: Since one has already taken up the mind itself, one then applies effort; why, then, is it called both "concentration" and "wisdom"? [Answer: Because the perfect and ultimate meaning possesses all virtues, these are not attained through cultivation within the ocean of self-nature.

Therefore, the Buddha also referred to *śamatha* as "subtle and secret contemplation. Thus, although the term "contemplation" is the same, the distinction of "subtle and secret" is unique to this context. This is because "contemplation" here takes understanding and insight as its basis, rather than taking cultivation and practice as its basis. Concentration and wisdom should be understood in this same manner. *Samādhi*.

Regarding the term "ti" (to enter): according to the Buddha’s subsequent answer, it refers to entering by stepping upon the previously explained "liberated understanding-nature concentration" (*jiejingding*).
It signifies the cessation of conceptual understanding as practice arises, taking "quiescent concentration" as its meaning.

Furthermore, it constitutes the essence of *samādhi* by briefly incorporating both the "causal nature of Buddhahood" (*zhengyin foxing*) and the "conditional causes" (*yuan-yin*), which is precisely the concentration that is inherently endowed with wisdom (*xingju ji hui zhi ding*). (In this context, the "nature of hearing" is identical to the "seeing of nature" through liberated understanding mentioned in the preceding text.)
The first three [aspects] refer to the substantial nature of the Tathāgatagarbha; by relying upon this, one accomplishes the Vajrasamādhi.

As for *dhyāna* (meditative concentration), according to the Buddha’s subsequent answer, it refers to the meaning of entering deeply into the profound stages immediately after initial realization, wherein one simultaneously relies upon the preceding samādhi and prajñā, flowing into the center of the center, gradually realizing the successive stages until reaching the ultimate.

This also refers to the *dharmatā-nimitta-buddhadhātu* (the Buddha-nature as the true cause), which briefly incorporates the *pratyaya-nimitta-buddhadhātu* (the Buddha-nature as the contributing condition).

The realization of these two causes constitutes the essence of *dhyāna*; it is the meditative concentration and wisdom that are inherently complete and mutually integrated. (This must begin from the stage of "Dry Wisdom" (*śuṣka-prajñā*) onward to truly belong to *dhyāna*.

This is because the third gradual stage is where the text first concludes by stating: "From this point on, one gradually cultivates according to the practices undertaken, establishing the stages of the sages," and only at the end does it describe Ānanda’s sudden awakening to *dhyāna* and his progress through the sage-stages.

Regarding the initial expedient means, the traditional texts rely solely on those among the various methods of universal liberation (*sarva-vimokṣa*) that serve as the initial expedient means for entering the Path.
[The text] speaks of this, designating the ear-faculty (*śrotra-dvāra*) as the primary expedient for initial entry.
Although those of both ancient and modern times have all followed and believed this without doubt, there is now another explanation; let the wise judge it.

Only terms such as "Great Buddha-Usnīṣa" (大佛頂) and so forth refer specifically to this particular concentration.

That the Tathāgatas of the ten directions "transcend through a single gate" means they perceive this as the essential path traversed by all sages for liberation from birth and death.
The "Path of Sublime Adornment" signifies the direct way leading to the ultimate fruit.
For the Buddha’s ultimate fruit is called the "Ocean of Sublime Adornment," which refers to the adornment of the myriad virtues inherently present within the nature.

It arises in accordance with whatever it encounters; that is to say, at the very moment one grasps at a particular object, the mind is immediately present there.
Nowadays, people falsely claim that by thinking of a thousand *li*, they can reach a thousand *li*, and by thinking of ten thousand *li*, they can reach ten thousand *li*.
