"Confused" means that the mind is mixed up with them and cannot achieve the state of the Middle. The final three lines provide the explanation. "The thing is not" means the sense-object is not...
There is cognition. That which constitutes the essence of cognition is the sense-faculty; it is the sense-faculty that possesses cognition. Regarding the phrase "standing as opposing adversaries":

this means that if your mind were to take the connection between the sense-faculties and their objects as its essence, then half would possess cognition and half would lack it, standing in opposition to one another.
Falling into these two extremes, how could it be the Middle? Second, it is neither inclusive nor alternative. Being inclusive of both is not established;
being neither knowing nor not-knowing means it lacks any essential nature. What, then, would be the characteristic of the Middle?
"Simultaneously not being either" means that the substance of the mind is entirely unconnected with these two dharmas, the sense organ and the object.
"Neither knowing nor not-knowing" means that this substance of the mind is neither the knowing of the organ nor the non-knowing of the object.
The final two phrases state that since its essential nature does not even exist, upon what could a middle position be established? The formal refutation is now complete. △
Second, refuting [the notion of] conjunction.
Therefore, one should know that it is impossible for [a thing] to exist in between;
thus the refutation of "in-between" is concluded. △ Seventh, refuting non-attachment. This is divided into two parts. First, Ānanda [argues] that because one is not attached to various...
Objects serve as the mind. Furthermore, there are two [points]. First, citing the Buddha’s former teaching:

Ānanda addressed the Buddha, saying, "World-Honored One, I have previously seen the Buddha together with his four great disciples—Mahāmaudgalyāyana, Subhūti, Pūrṇamaitrāyaṇīputra, and Śāriputra—jointly turning the wheel of Dharma, constantly speaking of the awakening, knowing, and discerning of the nature of the mind."
Since it is neither within, nor without, nor in between, it has no location at all.

This refers precisely to the deluded mind that perceives and so forth; for it was already refuted in the preceding section on "in between. Thus, when one searches for it in these three locations, it is simply not found.
△ Second, explaining and requesting a definitive resolution.
"Non-attachment to all things is called the mind. Does this mean that my non-attachment is called the mind?
These first two lines are Ānanda’s own interpretation intended to establish his point; they are not the Buddha’s original intent.

When the Buddha said that [the three] do not exist, he was precisely referring to the meaning of "lack of substance" within the preceding two points. Yet, Ānanda uses this to corroborate that non-attachment constitutes the mind.
This is what is meant by saying that the mind has a substance, yet it is merely non-attached.

However, upon examining these words carefully, although the intention was not to realize that the deluded mind lacks substance, they have nonetheless forced the conclusion that it has no location. For if it is said to be non-attached, how could there be a location?

The false conceptualization, its arguments exhausted, arrives at this point of its own accord. Herein lies a hidden objection: the objection states that the Buddha’s inquiry into the location was originally intended to reveal...
"Non-abiding is now already non-abiding. How can it be further refuted? The answer says: "The Buddha’s point of reference (pramāṇa) clearly demonstrates non-abiding.
The Buddha’s demonstration of non-abiding is intended to lead one to realize the absence of intrinsic nature (niḥsvabhāva). Now, realizing this non-attachment is itself the essence of the mind.
Although this is non-abiding, one clings to the existence of an intrinsic nature; therefore, it is refuted. The final two phrases express the intention of not daring to decide for oneself."
△ Second, the Tathāgata refutes [the mind] by means of the existence and non-existence of all things. This turns to refute the essence of the mind by means of the essence of things.
It is divided into two sections. First, the direct refutation, which is further divided into two. First, the simultaneous inquiry into existence and non-existence.

The Buddha told Ānanda: "As for your statement that the nature of the mind which perceives, knows, and discriminates has no location whatsoever—if all things in the world, including empty space, water, land, flying creatures, and all other objects and phenomena, are called 'everything,' and you do not cling to them, then does this [nature] exist or does it not exist?"
This merely examines whether the substance of things exists or not. "The void of the world" refers to the place where things reside.

"Water, land, and flight" distinguishes the categories of things. The two lines beginning with "All that... serve as a summary to provide the final explanation. The final two lines restate your claim:
"If you say you do not cling to any things, then is the substance of those things existent or non-existent? △
The two pairs demonstrate that [the thesis] is not established. Furthermore, there are two [points]: first, non-existence itself is not established;
second, if it were non-existent, it would be identical to the hair of a tortoise or the horns of a rabbit—how then could it be non-attached?
The "hair of a tortoise" and "horns of a rabbit" are used as metaphors to clarify that they have no substance. This means that if all things were fundamentally and ultimately without substance...
If you claim that the mind has nothing to which it is attached, to what would it not be attached? This is merely the absence of substance in all things;
it does not establish the meaning of non-attachment. △ Second, "How could existence possibly be established? This also has two parts. First, the formal definition.
There is that which is not clung to; it cannot be called non-existent.
To the preceding statement, "If one says that all things have an essence, I simply do not cling to them," the next sentence provides a definitive conclusion:

If this cannot be called "non-attachment," then [it follows that] where there are no marks, there is nothing; and what is not non-existent is precisely a mark. Since a mark exists, it is present; how then can there be non-attachment? △ Second, the explanation for establishing [the point].
Where there are no marks, there is nothing. What is not non-existent is precisely a mark. If a mark exists, then it is present. How can there be non-attachment?

This explanation follows from what precedes it. One might ask: "By what means should this be understood? The subsequent passage provides the answer. The first two lines concern the mutual opposition between non-existence (*abhāva*) and existence (*bhāva*).

For instance, if one speaks of "non-characteristic" (*animitta*), it implies an absolute absence of any entity; yet, that which is not non-existent must necessarily constitute a characteristic of existence.
The third line states that the characteristic of existence and the attachment to existence are causally related. As it is said: "As soon as one says 'existence'..."
The characteristic has already been attached; how then could there be non-attachment? The character "in" (在) should be read as the character "attached" (著).

This means that because these various things possess a substantial body, the principle of non-attachment cannot be established. The refutation is thus concluded. △ Second, the conclusion of the refutation.
Therefore, one should know that it is impossible for anything to be called the "awakened knowing mind" while remaining unattached to all things.
Indeed, when the seven locations are all found not to be [the mind], deluded attachment is exhausted; yet worldly people still calculate a dwelling place for the mind.
It does not go beyond this. Upon reaching this point, that which one has habitually relied upon as the mind is found to have no abiding place whatsoever that can be traced.
If this is the case, do those who hear of these methods of investigation for the first time know how to cherish them?

However, upon examining these seven instances where the location is definitively established, there are only four such locations: namely, first, the internal; second, the external; third, within the sense organs;
and fourth, between the sixth sense organ and its object. The fourth remains within the internal;
the fifth has no fixed location; and the seventh lacks even a location. Furthermore, one set of four [instances] cites the consensus of the various schools.

The first two [sections] involve conjecture based on one's own views, while the latter three cite scriptural teachings with erroneous interpretations; such is the distinction, which the wise should discern.

Having concluded the implicit demonstration that false consciousness has no locus, [the text proceeds to] the second section: exposing the refutation of false consciousness as being the mind. Regarding the preceding section:
Regarding the first three types of non-ultimate meanings, [the text] had merely addressed the attachment to the third—the existence of a location.
Now, in this section, by denouncing it as "not mind," it finally refutes the attachment to the first—that it is mind. This is divided into three parts.
First, Ānanda reproaches himself and requests instruction, which is further divided into three. First, the propriety of the reproach and request.

At that time, Ānanda rose from his seat amidst the great assembly; he bared his right shoulder, knelt with his right knee on the ground, and with palms joined in reverence, addressed the Buddha, saying:

△ Second, the words of self-reproach for requesting instruction. This is further divided into two parts. First, self-reproach for not knowing the location of the mind. This is further divided into two.
First, reproaching oneself for not having realized [the truth] due to relying on pride and affection.
I am the youngest brother of the Tathāgata. Having received the Buddha’s compassionate love, although I have now left the household life, I still rely on his indulgent affection;
for this reason, despite my extensive learning, I have not yet attained the state of outflow-free liberation.

*Kauṇḍinya* also means "loving-kindness. Just as children at home often rely on the affection of their fathers and elder brothers and do not diligently apply themselves to their tasks, their habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*) remain unextinguished;
thus, even after leaving the household life, they still rely [on such attachments]. The final two lines clarify that he has not yet diligently cultivated realization;
this is included within the praise of his virtues regarding the manifestation of untainted liberation (*anāsravavimukti*). △ Second, rebuking his fall into lust due to ignorance of the proper place.
They are unable to subdue the Śābarī spell and are turned by it; they sink into brothels because they do not know where the true limit (bhūtakoṭi) leads.
As for this "true limit," since they have not realized that the mind they cling to is illusory, they continue to call it the "true mind" and the "actual limit."

The character "詣" (yì) is conventionally glossed as "to go. However, upon carefully examining the intent of the scripture here, it seems to carry the meaning of the character "在" (zài), "to be at" or "to abide in.

Thus, the phrasing chosen by the translator is somewhat unstable. This is because, although the Buddha had previously refuted the location [of the mind], he had not yet explicitly stated that there is no mind and no location;
therefore, Ānanda’s search for a location for the mind remained unresolved. Furthermore—
This rebukes him for not knowing the true mind and its actual locus. △ Second, seeking the Buddha’s separate explanation of the true locus.

This follows upon the preceding words of self-reproach; since he regards his ignorance of the mind’s location as a regret, it is evident that his intent in questioning must still be to seek that location.
Furthermore, this approach is a fixed sequence for engaging in debate with others. Since the Buddha has already [spoken] seven times...
He refutes all the points he has stated as being incorrect. Ānanda, do you not hope that the Buddha will separately explain the true point?
Furthermore, there are two parts: first, the formal request for instruction.
I only pray that the World-Honored One, out of great compassion and pity, will reveal to us the path of *śamatha*.
As for this path of *śamatha*, it is because we do not know the location of the mind that there is no way to cultivate correct contemplation.
I pray that the Buddha will clearly point out where this mind precisely resides, so that it may serve as the path for true contemplation. This...
This is precisely the true meaning of Ānanda’s words. △ Second, [the passage] also serves to eliminate evil views, causing all icchantikas to destroy their *mleccha* [ways].
"Icchantika" translates as "one who has severed the roots of goodness";
the intent here encompasses all non-Buddhists (*tīrthika*). "Destroying" (*huī*) means to demolish. "Mleccha" (literally *mili-li-che*)...
“*Śakaṭa*. This is translated as ‘evil view. The intent is that if the Buddha were to reveal the place where truth resides, then my sevenfold exposition would all become false views;
how much more so the evil views expounded by all the non-Buddhists? Would they not all be utterly destroyed?
△ Third, earnestly requesting to join the assembly.
Having spoken these words, he prostrated himself with his five limbs touching the ground. The great assembly likewise waited expectantly with longing, yearning to hear his instructions.
"Yearning with longing" means being like one who thirsts for a drink. "Waiting expectantly" means being like a bird looking out intently. "Yuan" (欽) means reverence.
The section on "Taking Responsibility for One's Own Person and Requesting Instruction" concludes. △ Second, "The Tathāgata Manifests That It Is Not Mind," divided into three parts.
First, "Manifesting the Refutation to Reveal All Phenomena," further divided into five. First, "Manifesting that All Wisdoms are About to Appear."
At that time, the World-Honored One emitted various kinds of light from his face. The radiance was so brilliant as to be like hundreds of thousands of suns.
"Face" refers here to the eyes, ears, nose, and tongue; because these grasp this consciousness, they allow delusion and inversion to run wild, thereby blocking all gates of wisdom.
All [the previous states] no longer appear before him. Now, as consciousness is about to be shattered and various wisdoms are about to manifest, he uses manifold rays of light to symbolize this.
Second, to symbolize that the various consciousnesses are about to be shattered:
throughout all Buddha-worlds, the earth quakes in six ways.

Regarding the "six quakes": these refer to shaking, leaping, trembling, rising, roaring, and striking. This precisely symbolizes that the deluded consciousnesses of the six sense bases (*ṣaḍāyatana*) are about to be destroyed.
Question: According to what the Buddha has refuted, it seems to concern only the sixth [consciousness]. Why do you now say that all six sense bases are simultaneously destroyed? Answer:
Since it is said that they involve "discrimination based on objects," the first five are not without discrimination. Furthermore, Ānanda clearly stated: "The eye... [and so forth].
With form as a condition, eye-consciousness arises; yet the Buddha refutes this with a twofold intention.
Since eye-consciousness is thus refuted, the remaining four may be understood to be refuted as well. △ Third, the obscuration is about to be cleared away.
In this way, the lands of the ten directions, as numerous as motes of dust, are all opened and seen at once.

This is because this consciousness, conditioned by sensory objects, obscures itself; following every thought, it becomes partial and restricted, constantly dwelling in darkness and unable to see the immeasurable realm of wisdom.
Now, in order to shatter and reveal it, this manifestation appears to symbolize it. △ Section Four: Manifestation.
The barriers were about to close.
Through the Buddha’s majestic spiritual power, he caused all worlds to merge into a single realm.
Because these consciousnesses grasp at phenomena and grasp at a self, discriminating between self and other, they have all become separated by barriers; now, consciousness has shattered them.
They naturally merge into one; therefore, this is symbolized. △ Fifth, the symbolization of the cessation of the cycle of transmigration:
within that world, all the great Bodhisattvas dwell in their respective native lands, joining their palms in reverence and listening attentively.
Because one takes this consciousness to be the mind, one wanders through vast eons.
Even if one attains the *nirvāṇa* of the Lesser Vehicle, it is like a traveler in a foreign land who cannot maintain the total illumination and function of their original ground.

Now, by destroying this consciousness, one returns to the original ground and perfects its illuminating essence; therefore, this sign is used to represent it. II. Universally Demonstrating the Two: Reality and Delusion.

The Root. To mistakenly perceive that which is fundamentally non-existent as being grasped at is the root of delusion; this is what is called "grasping at the semblance. To fail to recognize that which is fundamentally existent as such is the root of confusion;
this is what is called "confusion regarding the real. This is divided into two parts: first, citing the faults and their origins, wherein both are indeed faults.
This further divides into two: first, the explanation by way of phenomena (*dharma*). This further divides into two: first, enumerating the various faults. This further divides into three.
First, one arbitrarily incurs the fault of being submerged in human suffering.
The Buddha told Ānanda: "All sentient beings, from time immemorial, have experienced various inversions; the seeds of karma arise spontaneously."
It is like the *akṣa* cluster.
Ordinary worldlings who do not know how to practice are like this. *Akṣa* is the name of a fruit from the Western Regions; it does not exist here in this land.

A "cluster" refers to three fruits always forming a single cluster; this serves as a metaphor for how the three—delusion, karma, and suffering—are necessarily gathered together throughout the three lives.
△ Second, the fault of those who practice with provisional [intentions] for the Lesser Vehicle.
Various practitioners are unable to achieve unexcelled bodhi; instead, they end up becoming śrāvakas or pratyekabuddhas.

"Those who do not achieve unsurpassed bodhi" refers specifically to those Bodhisattvas of the provisional teachings who attain Buddhahood within the four dhyānas, for they have not yet reached the two practices of the Perfect [Teaching].
"Śrāvakas" are those who hear the vocal teachings of the Four Truths.
"Pratyekabuddhas" are those who understand the manifest [truth] and all who uphold the Small Vehicle teachings. △ Third, the faults of ordinary persons and those in training.
Furthermore, there are those who have become non-Buddhist deities, Māras, and their retinues—those who have rebelled against the Buddha’s orthodox teaching and whose minds wander outside the Way.

There are also the various devas who uphold the Buddha’s precepts and meditative concentration, joyfully seeking pleasant fruits rather than seeking liberation. *Māra* means "the slayer" (or "killer"); they are addicted to and protect the realms of desire.
They afflict and harm those who practice correctly. All of them obtain the superior fruit of their equipment;
they are born in exalted places and possess transformations and supernormal powers, merely claiming for themselves that the Path has been realized. △ Second, the general explanation of the causes.
This is entirely due to not knowing the two kinds of fundamental natures and practicing in a state of confusion.
These are the two fundamentals of the Real and the False. "In a state of confusion" means mistakenly taking the false to be the real and practicing the false alone;
it does not mean practicing the real and the false together. △ Second, the explanation by analogy.
It is like boiling sand in the hope of producing a fine meal; even if one were to pass through kalpas as numerous as motes of dust, one would ultimately never succeed.
"Kalpa" (劫麼) here means a long period of time. "Motes of dust kalpas" (塵劫) refers to a number of kalpas measured by the count of motes of dust, representing an extremely long duration.

The false does not become the true; therefore, it can ultimately never be attained. This concludes the section on citing errors and revealing their causes. △ Second, the inquiry and explanation of the names and essence.
This also has two parts: first, the inquiry.
What are the two kinds?
△ Second, the formal explanation, which is further divided into two parts. First, the name and essence of the delusive root as it is grasped.
Ānanda, the first is the root of birth and death from time without beginning; this is that which you and all sentient beings now employ through clinging.
"That which takes the mind as its self-nature" refers to the name given to the root of beginningless birth and death. "Then you" below points to its substance;
this substance is merely a false substance that has no substance. It is precisely what was not found in the seven rounds of reflection upon deluded thought in the preceding passage.
This refers to the section [of the text] and what follows below, which will subsequently be refuted and dismantled. △ Second, the true source that is deluded regarding:

"The second is the fundamentally pure essence of bodhi and nirvana from time immemorial; it is this very consciousness-essence (vijñāna-garbha) of original luminosity within you now, which is capable of giving rise to all conditions, yet is itself that which is left behind by those conditions."
This refers back to the "eternally abiding true mind, the essence of pure luminosity" determined in the preceding text, providing a further detailed clarification.
The phrase "The second" below introduces its name; the phrase "Then you" below points to its essence. This essence is precisely the truly existent, ultimate essence.
Regarding the claim that both the false and the true are called "beginningless," it is like gold and sand: both are without beginning.
As for "beginning," it cannot be questioned in terms of priority or sequence; this is the correct teaching within Buddhism, differing from the "having a beginning" held by non-Buddhists.

"Bodhi" refers, among the three types [of bodhi], specifically to *tathatā-bodhi* (true-nature bodhi). "Nirvāṇa" is translated as "perfect quiescence" (*yuánjì*): the true is fundamentally perfect and the delusive is fundamentally quiescent.
This refers specifically to *prakṛti-viśuddha-nirvāṇa* (nirvāṇa of intrinsic purity) among the three types. These are taken in order according to their basis.
Speaking from the principle of the wisdom that realizes suchness (tathatā), it is said to be "originally pure" (*ādi-viśuddha*).

"Origin" (*yuan*) means the fundamental source. It is not something produced by the cultivation of abandonment or the removal of obstructions and defilements; rather, it is now manifest as being inherently complete without depending on subsequent cultivation. Regarding "the essence of consciousness, originally luminous":

this refers to the nature of perfect stillness and non-arising/non-ceasing inherent in the six sense faculties. "Essence of consciousness" (*vijñāna-dhātu*) is its general name; fundamentally, it is simply...
It is a single entity. If one were to list its distinct names according to the six sense faculties, they would be the six essences of seeing, hearing, smelling, tasting, touching, and cognizing.
As the *Sūtra of the Five Scrolls* states regarding the testimony of all Buddhas:

"If you further wish to know unsurpassed Bodhi—which enables you to swiftly realize blissful liberation, quiescence, and wondrous permanence—it is none other than your own six faculties; it is not some other thing. This is verified by such evidence.
The fundamentally pure essence of Bodhi and Nirvana specifically points to the refined faculties of seeing, hearing, and so forth among the six sense organs.
This is why, after the destruction of consciousness, the text first reveals the nature of seeing as the wondrously luminous original mind. The old commentaries fail to comprehend this entirely;
thus, they mistakenly interpret it as the destruction of seeing itself. Furthermore, one should know that when the Buddha explains the verse, he refers to *ādāna-vijñāna*.

"Subtle consciousness. This refers precisely to the essence of this consciousness. Although it is also designated by the name "consciousness," it is actually the ocean of the eighth consciousness, and is not like the preceding six consciousnesses which are illusory and without substance.

Because it is the foundation for true cultivation, within the practice of perfect penetration, one directly selects the auditory faculty—the nature of hearing—which is likewise the essence of this consciousness. Furthermore, this is what is utilized from beginning to end throughout this sutra.
The reason this work is so distinct from other sūtras is that it takes these capacities and natures as its foundation.

One should understand that what is contained within these two foundations is such that the subsequent sections are longer than the preceding ones; the former extends to the middle of this fascicle, reaching the point where consciousness is thoroughly refuted.
Later, at the end of the second fascicle, [the text] refutes the combination [of consciousnesses] until it is exhausted. However, the true original text is merely indicated here.

"Originally luminous" means that it is inherently luminous from the beginning, not resulting from cultivation or cessation. "The various conditions" refers to the six evolving consciousnesses (*pravṛtti-vijñāna*).

As the *Laṅkāvatāra-sūtra* says: "The ocean of the storehouse-consciousness (*ālaya-vijñāna*) abides eternally; moved by the winds of objective realms, the various waves of consciousness surge forth."
And thus they arise. This shows that the preceding six [consciousnesses] are all waves produced from this ocean of consciousness; therefore, they are false and illusory. Regarding what was omitted:
it states that while the preceding six are able to universally perceive all objects, they alone [fail to perceive] the fundamental ocean of consciousness from which they arise.
The self cannot perceive itself. It is like the vision arising from the eye, which can see all things yet cannot see the eye itself.

Even when awakening occurs, one must remain in a state where not a single thought arises to be able to realize it through silent resonance. If the six consciousnesses stir, the essence is immediately obscured.
Therefore, if a student does not relinquish the mind that pursues conditions, they will ultimately be like one born blind, failing to see their nature.
Because one clings to and recognizes the conditioned mind, the original luminosity is inevitably lost; hence it is said that "it is lost by the conditioned. (Question:

Regarding Consciousness-Only, why is it said that the seventh consciousness takes the seeing-part of the eighth consciousness as its self? Answer: The verse says: "Following conditions, it clings to a self; its measure is non-valid cognition (*apramāṇa*). Since it is non-valid cognition, how could it truly be a perceiving subject? However, this is called the "true source."
This is the true cultivation of the root, for it is certain that one can thereby achieve *bodhi* and *nirvāṇa*. The formal explanation is concluded.
III. Conclusion and Return to the Source:

Because sentient beings have neglected this fundamental luminosity, although they act throughout their entire lives, they do not realize it themselves, and thus they enter the various realms of existence in vain.
This knot, while appearing to be a single knot of delusion regarding the Truth, is in fact also a simultaneous knot of attachment to the false;

for delusion regarding the Truth arises precisely from attachment to the false. It is because the causal conditions do not reach it that one ultimately fails to see it, thereby becoming eternally deluded.
To "act all day long without being self-aware" refers to the lack of knowledge regarding daily activities, such as seeing and hearing, which are like various refined essences.
They do not depart from it for even a moment, yet they ultimately do not know that it can be used as the fundamental capacity for true cultivation to reach the stage of Buddhahood;
therefore, they never perceive its entire substance nor attain its great function. "Wang" (枉) means to be bent or constrained.

It is said that originally one ought not to receive [rebirth], yet one yields and accepts it through distortion. "The various realms" refers to the seven realms. Indeed, this essence of consciousness is inherently possessed by sentient beings;
its substance pervades the ten directions and its function extends throughout the *asaṃkhyeya* worlds. It cannot be confined by any of the realms.
Yet, due to a lack of awakening, one willingly undergoes the cycle of saṃsāra—is this not a profound distortion? This is the ultimate admonition. Universal.

The demonstration regarding the two fundamental attachments is concluded. △ Second, the direct refutation that deluded consciousness is not the Mind. This refers to the "deluded mind of craving and attachment" previously investigated;

the reason for raising and investigating it again now is that, since the text used to demonstrate the fundamental source through the process of refutation is extensive, the characteristics of the Mind mentioned previously have become submerged and obscure.
If it were not raised and investigated again to bring it before us, against what would we then confront [the truth]?
This is the language used to refute and dismantle [the opponent's position]. The purport of the repeated inquiry lies solely herein. It is divided into three parts.
First, the Tathāgata’s repeated inquiry and direct rebuke, which is further divided into three. First, the descent of the inquiry to be addressed.
Ānanda, if you now wish to know the path of *śamatha* and desire to emerge from birth and death, I shall ask you again.
The intent of this question and answer differs from before. Previously, Ānanda sought the location of the mind as the path;
the Tathāgata, however, takes the realization that this deluded consciousness has no substance and no location, and seeks the true mind elsewhere, as the path of *śamatha*.

This is the path. △ Second, the inquiry that causes [the truth] to manifest before one’s eyes. This also has three parts. First, a detailed inquiry regarding seeing. This also has three parts. First, a general inquiry regarding seeing:
At that moment, the Tathāgata raised his golden arm, bent his five fingers, and said to Ānanda, "Do you see this now?"
Ānanda replied, “I see it.
As for the “five wheel-fingers,” the tips of the Buddha’s fingers all possess the markings of thousand-spoked wheels;
when they are bent, they form the appearance of a clenched fist. △ Second, a specific inquiry into what was seen.
The Buddha asked, "What do you see? Ānanda replied, "I see the Tathāgata raise his arm and bend his fingers into a radiant fist, illuminating my heart and eyes."
△ Third, specifically interrogating the capacity to see.
The Buddha said: "With what do you see? Ānanda replied: "I and the great assembly all see with our eyes.

These three preceding sections have, for the first time, used interrogation to determine the capacity to see and the object seen; however, they have not yet interrogated the mind. Therefore, [the text continues]: Great...

The topical outline (*ke*) provides a detailed examination of "seeing. (Within this section, the author first examines "eye-seeing," which implicitly contains profound meaning; this was already indicated in the small note beneath the "Examination" heading in the preceding text.

Now, because it is being re-examined, it shall likewise be further clarified. In the preceding text, the Tathāgata asked: "What do you see? Who is it that loves and delights? The intent was already deeply contained therein, yet the phrasing remained somewhat obscure and brief.

Here, however, there are three points of rigorous and repeated inquiry; students must not fail to take note. First, [the Buddha] raised his fist and said to Ānanda: "Do you see now? Ānanda replied: "I see. Second, he said: "What do you see? Ānanda answered: "I see the radiance and the fist. Third, he said: ... )

"By means of what do you see? Ānanda again replied only that he sees with his eyes. Thus, while the Tathāgata may be said to have revealed the truth layer upon layer, Ānanda may be said to have missed it point after point.

Seeing that from beginning to end Ānanda was unable to grasp it or directly recognize the nature of seeing as the mind, the Tathāgata had no choice but to descend to the common level and linger further, asking: "What is your mind when my fist shines forth? This meaning is extremely profound and difficult to know; therefore, I have specifically disclosed it for those who have attained the essence of the school.

Question: Master Huan also said at this point, "When the golden fist is raised, one must directly recognize the fundamental luminosity within the dust-like appearances. If the delusory marks have not yet been removed, one still mistakes the thief for the son. Have you not thoroughly understood this meaning? Answer: This is precisely what is called "resembling it. It resembles it, but it is not yet it.

Therefore, Master Huan had not yet fully penetrated the seeing-nature; that which he saw was merely the fundamental luminosity. Zheng said: When the Tathāgata raised his fist to test the seeing, Master Huan spoke right then and there about needing to recognize the fundamental luminosity. How can this not be a penetration of the seeing-nature? Answer:

If one had truly penetrated and realized the seeing-nature as being the fundamental luminosity at this point, then upon reaching the chapter on "The Blind Man Staring into Darkness," he would not have followed the crowd in saying that the seeing was destroyed. Question: What, then, did he take to be the fundamental luminosity?

Yes. [The Master] replied: "That person has merely received in a general way the names 'the Eye of the True Dharma' and 'the Wondrous Mind of Nirvana' as spoken by the masters of our school; he takes these as his fundamental clarity. However, in reality, he has not yet personally realized that seeing one's nature before one's eyes is itself the Wondrous Mind of Nirvana.

This is what is called a semblance of direct perception (*pratyakṣa*), rather than true direct perception. One who understands words certainly cannot grant full approval based on a mere accidental coincidence of a single phrase.

There are still many instances elsewhere where Master Huan appears to be correct but is actually mistaken; is this not the very source of his failure to penetrate through? △ Second, responding to the inquiry regarding the mind.
The Buddha said to Ānanda, "Answer me now: when the Tathāgata bends his fingers into a fist of light to illuminate your eyes and mind, your eyes can see it;
but what constitutes your 'mind' that is illuminated by my fist?"
The preceding text asks: "What is it that is seen? Who is it that loves and delights? This section should be understood as merely two successive inquiries into the mind.
△ Third, answering by citing the mind.

Ānanda said, “The Tathāgata has now questioned me regarding the location of the mind. As I have used my mind to investigate and pursue it, that which performs this investigation—I shall take that to be the mind.”

The mind that "pushes to the limit" and "seeks out" is precisely what Ānanda previously described as his own contemplation of love and delight, as well as what the Tathāgata identified as the mind of deluded conceptualization and攀緣 (pān-yuán, clinging to objects).
The preceding passage states: "Because I beheld the Tathāgata’s sublime marks with my eyes, a mind of love and delight arose.
Taken together with this section, these should both be instances where he presents his own deluded mind. However, in the preceding [passage]...

Furthermore, consider this point of refutation. Herein, [the Buddha] directly refutes that it is the mind. Having completed the investigation that caused it to manifest before him, △ Third, the direct rebuke that it is not the mind:
The Buddha said, "Tsk! Ānanda, this is not your mind."

"Ha! [Ānanda] raised his voice in a shout of alarm, causing him to awaken in great terror. Of the three types of "not being the true mind" mentioned previously, this passage specifically refutes the first:
that [the mind] is not the heart. Having completed the repeated interrogation and direct rebuke, the second section follows:
Ānanda’s startled inquiry for its name.
Ānanda was startled; he withdrew from his seat, joined his palms, stood up, and addressed the Buddha: "This is not my mind. What should it be called?

"Startled" (*jué rán*) describes an expression of alarm and astonishment. Having long relied upon this [mind] as his own, knowing nothing else, when it is suddenly snatched away, there is no one who would not be startled.
△ Third, the Tathāgata names it and reveals its transgression.
The Buddha told Ānanda: "These are the false appearances and perceptions of external objects that delude your true nature.
From your beginningless past until this present life, you have mistaken a thief for your own son; thus you have lost your original constancy and consequently undergo the cycle of rebirth."
"Phenomena of the external objects are false appearances and perceptions"—these six characters constitute its original name.

Since Ānanda, having heard that it was not the mind, requested its original name, the Buddha directly pointed out the original name in response. "Phenomena of the external objects" refers to the six sense-objects currently confronted before one.
"False appearances and perceptions" means that these thoughts and perceptions necessarily carry the marks of those objects; they are false and illusory.

It appears only momentarily; how could it possess any substantial reality? Therefore, in the subsequent section on "Revealing and Manifesting," there is nothing more than a detailed explanation of the meaning of this name.
From the words "Because of you" (*yūr*) onwards, the faults of erroneous recognition are set forth.
"Recognizing a thief as one's son" means mistaking that which is not the mind for the mind. "Losing the original permanence" refers to being deluded regarding the true mind.
One does not recognize it [as the mind]. It is like a person who, having already recognized a thief as their son, no longer seeks out their true son.

Those who undergo cyclic existence do so because they have recognized what is not the truly permanent mind; thus they flow long through birth and death, just as one constantly suffers at the hands of a thief-son who plunders them.
The explicit refutation that the deluded consciousness is not the mind is hereby concluded. △ Third, the analytical refutation of the deluded consciousness.
"Without substance. This section explains that the consciousness-mind is ultimately empty and non-existent, being utterly annihilated and not the mind at all.
It is divided into two parts. First, Ānanda describes his fear and requests instruction. This is divided into four sections. First, he describes how he has used only this mind.
Furthermore, there are three [reasons]. First, one leaves home using this mind.
Ānanda addressed the Buddha, saying: "World-Honored One, I am the Buddha’s beloved younger brother; because my heart loves the Buddha, he caused me to leave home."
△ Second, utilizing this mind for wholesome purposes:

"Why should my mind offer sustenance to the Tathāgata alone? It shall instead travel throughout lands as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, serving all Buddhas and spiritual friends (*kalyāṇamitra*).
With great courage and vigor, it shall perform all difficult practices and dharmic deeds—all of these are accomplished by means of this very mind."
These preceding and following sections are all provisional hypotheses and estimations; it is certainly impossible to function apart from this mind and act otherwise.
△ Third, employing this mind to commit evil.
Even if one were to slander the Dharma and forever lose their roots of goodness, it is still because of this mind.
2. Describing that apart from this there is nothing else:
If this illumination were not the mind, I would then be without a mind, identical to earth or wood; for apart from this awareness, there is nothing.
There is nothing further that exists.
The final two lines mean that once one relies on the Buddha’s relinquishing of this [mind], and further examines it through contemplation, then there is utterly no separate mind to be found.
△ Third, describing the astonishment and doubt of oneself and others.
"How is it that the Tathāgata says this is not the mind? I am truly alarmed, as are all those in this great assembly; there is none who does not harbor doubt.
From the heavens to the human realm, among the ordinary, the externalists, the provisional, and the followers of the Small Vehicle, there is none who does not declare this to be the mind.

Thus, Ānanda’s alarm and doubt are the same as mine. Even if one attains realization through meditative concentration (*dhyāna-samādhi*), it is likewise because one has mastered and stilled this very mind."
△ Fourth, seeking the Tathāgata’s instruction:
"I pray that you will deign to show great compassion and reveal what I have not yet understood.
Furthermore, I beg for instruction: how is it that this is not my own mind? How is it that these are called the false appearances of external objects?"
[Ānanda] reflects: "This has not yet reached the point of seeking an explanation of the true mind. Ānanda has finished recounting his terror and requesting instruction.
II. The Tathāgata’s Consolation and Revelation. This section also has two parts: 1. Consolation and the Granting of Assurance.
One should know that this section is not the formal exposition of the true mind; rather, because Ānanda was terrified and had no other recourse, [the Buddha] provisionally granted him assurance.
This was done to comfort them from their alarm and fear. Furthermore, it is divided into three parts. First, the profound intent behind the bestowed teaching is set forth:
At that time, the World-Honored One revealed this to Ānanda and the great assembly, desiring to cause their minds to enter the patience of the non-arising of dharmas (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*).
As for the patience of non-arising (*anutpattika-dharmakṣānti*), it is first realized from the first stage (*bhūmi*) onward in the Separate Teaching (*pratyekavyavasthāna-śāsana*).

In the Perfect Teaching (*yuanjiao*), it is that which is realized at the stage of abiding (*zhù*). Abiding in this patience, one perceives not even the slightest dharma arising within or without the three realms, nor does one perceive the slightest dharma ceasing.
Transcending emotion and departing from views, each and every thing, in its very essence, is identical to True Suchness (*tathatā*) and the Real Mark (*bhūtalakṣaṇa*). Furthermore...
This is precisely the ultimate firmness of all phenomena.

That sentient beings are unable to realize and enter this state is precisely because they mistakenly take deluded thoughts of arising and ceasing to be the mind; therefore, they remain forever separated from this patience and are unable to enter it.

Now, in order to shatter that [notion of] arising and ceasing and to reveal non-arising, the Sūtra provides this preliminary indication to demonstrate the profound benefit of the Tathāgata’s bestowed teachings.
Later, when describing the attainment of awakening, it says: "All that exists in the world is precisely the wondrous clarity;
one attains the fundamental wondrous mind, which is eternally abiding and imperishable. Is this not the meaning and characteristic of this very patience? △ Second.

Manifesting that he has always taught "Mind-Only," [the Buddha] stroked Ānanda’s head upon the lion throne and addressed him, saying: "The Tathāgata has always taught that all phenomena arise [from the mind]."
All is manifested by the mind alone. All causes and effects, the worlds, and even the finest atoms, derive their substance from the mind.

Regarding the arising of all phenomena, sentient beings are deluded about their true source and falsely claim that each of the myriad things has its own specific origin, such as the notion that water is produced from gold or fire from wood; this is precisely what is meant by "manifested by the mind alone."
The Holy Teaching directly points to the fact that the single fundamental substance of the true mind manifests in accordance with conditions. These two phrases present a direct contrast;
the first briefly provides a general indication, while "All things below" details them through specific enumeration.

This encompasses everything from cause and effect, ordinary beings and sages, provisional and real, extending from the vastness of the world down to the smallest atom, including all that is defiled and pure, coarse and subtle; all are formed by the causal mind.
As for its substance: it is that which manifests solely from the mind. That is to say, the myriad dharmas are devoid of the true mind;
not even so much as a mustard seed can be found. △ Third, citing an analogy to show that the true mind possesses substance.
Ānanda, if one were to examine the root source of everything that exists within all worlds—even down to blades of grass, leaves, and strands of thread—they would all possess a substantial nature.
Even empty space has its name and appearance; how much more so the pure, wondrously pure, and luminous mind, which is the essence of all minds, could it be without a substance of its own?
"Knots of thread" refers to things such as silk and hemp; by citing the most minute and subtle, it serves as a metaphor for the coarse and large. "To interrogate" means to pursue and question.
"Root, source, essence, and nature" likewise refer to what are described in the world as causes and conditions, as well as specific characteristics (*svalakṣaṇa*).

The two characters for "space" (*ākāśa*) are named for its vast emptiness and lack of obstruction, serving as a description of its appearance. This cites that which has no substance to serve as a metaphor for that which has substance.
Furthermore, its own essence being free from defilement is called "purity" (*viśuddhi*). Being unstained while dwelling amidst defilement is called "wondrous purity.
Its profound stillness and vacuous spirituality is called the "luminous mind. Regarding "the nature of all minds": it means that this [mind] serves as the mind-nature for all phenomena (*dharma*).
This ocean of mind is vast and pervasive throughout the *dharmadhātu*; all phenomena are merely images manifested within this ocean of the true mind.
It lacks intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*), because it takes this mind as its true nature. The phrase "lacking intrinsic nature" itself is a term used for emphasis;
it means that since the objects manifested still possess intrinsic nature, how could the manifesting mind itself lack intrinsic nature?
It is certain that the true mind must possess intrinsic nature; you merely cling to [this notion] due to your own attachments.
Because of this deluded mind, one is confused regarding that true substance. How could it be that there is nothing else apart from this?

Having concluded the consolation that [the substance] exists, [the text now proceeds]. 2. Revealing the Falsity. Although the faults were previously identified by name, it was not yet clarified what constitutes their falsity;
therefore, this section begins to reveal it. However, the three types mentioned in the preceding text are not truly real.
Within this section on the meaning, this division specifically explains the refutation of the second point: the lack of intrinsic nature (*anātman*). Furthermore, it is subdivided into two parts:
first, the appearance of existence based upon objects; and second, a counter-objection that [the object] must exist independently of the sensory field.
If you maintain that the nature apprehended by the discernment of vitarka and vicāra must necessarily be the mind, then this mind should exist as a distinct,
complete entity, separate from all objects of the senses— namely, the spheres of form, odor, taste, and touch— and their activities.
"Attachment" means firmly clinging to former views and refusing to let them go. "Discrimination" refers to the spontaneous functioning of the scattered mind.

"Applied and sustained thought" (vitarka-vicāra) refer to the functions of investigating principles and making deductions; the former is coarse while the latter is subtle, yet both possess a distinct and non-obscured character.
Therefore, they are called the "nature of that which is cognized. This is precisely the deluded consciousness (*vikalpa-vijñāna*). It must be the mind.
One must certainly recognize this as one's own mind. This first establishes the direction and then raises an objection from below:

regarding form, odor, taste, and touch—briefly citing these four sense-objects (*viṣaya*)—and including all sense-objects by further encompassing sound and mental phenomena (*dharma*), as well as all activities.
All are composed of dust. As it is said, "dustly affairs" and "dustly karma. Now, at the inception of engaging in affairs, they are called "affairs";
once the affairs are completed, they are called "karma. There is another category, the "complete nature," which allows one to let go so that one may exist independently of dust.
△ Second, the correct statement that one cannot be separated from objects. This is further divided into two sections. First, external conditions are not abandoned:
as you are now, receiving and listening to my Dharma; this constitutes discrimination arising because of sound.
To single out the sense-object of sound (*śabda-viṣaya*) is certainly to take a presently perceived object as an example for the rest;

it is also to encompass the inferior by means of the superior. This refutes the second [view]: the mind that takes the Buddha’s vocal teachings as its condition. △ Second, maintaining internal focus without departing.

Even if one were to extinguish all seeing, hearing, sensing, and knowing, and internally maintain a state of profound stillness, it would still be a matter of the conceptual shadows of mental objects (*dharmaviṣaya*).
This "seeing, hearing, sensing, and knowing" refers to the first five consciousnesses (*pañca-vijñāna*) along with the concomitant mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*);

the four [consciousnesses] subsume the six, as smelling and tasting are combined into a single "sensing. "Extinguishing" means to cease the external objects and the discursive observation of these various consciousnesses.
It is immovable. "Profound stillness" refers to the tranquil state within the inner mind. This section specifically encompasses all those who practice and study;

thus, this state is the object maintained by ordinary beings, non-Buddhists, and those of the provisional and limited vehicles while in meditative concentration, and it is that which they take as their realization to be the *dharmatā* (the nature of phenomena).
"Dharma-object" (*dharmaviṣaya*) refers to the original name of this state, as it is said: "Fundamentally not..."
The nature of phenomena (dharmatā) is fundamentally the object-field of phenomena (dharmālambana). Discrimination is the mind that clings to this object.

As for "shadow-phenomena," it means that both this object and this mind are merely light and shadow, entirely lacking substantial reality. This applies generally to all non-Buddhists, those of provisional or limited capacities, and the followers of the Lesser Vehicle.

One clings to this profound stillness, taking it to be the deep locus of the dharma-nature (*dharmatā*), yet does not realize that it is still merely a mental object (*dharmālambana*) perceived by deluded consciousness.
Furthermore, one clings to the thought that because the mind apprehending the object has already detached from external dust, it is no longer discursive;
yet one fails to realize that as long as one has not departed from mental objects, it remains nothing but discrimination. Such is the reason why this state constitutes a mental object.
There are two [types of practitioners]. First, those of the common worldlings, non-Buddhists, and the Hīnayāna do not realize that all phenomena are fundamentally empty.

They merely abandon external objects while focusing on the internal; it is like not removing objects outside a mirror—the reflection within the mirror remains constantly present, being only similar [to its source] and motionless.
In reality, they never cease to keep external dharmas in mind; how could they possibly eliminate their reflections? The reflection is itself the dharma.

It is also a mental object (*dharmāyatana*). Second, there are bodhisattvas of the provisional teachings who, although they have realized the emptiness of phenomena (*dharma-śūnyatā*), have not yet heard this sutra.

They maintain that there are twelve types of mental objects. Now, in moments of profound stillness, although they are free from the six [objects] of light, motion, penetration, sweetness, cohesion, and birth, they have not yet been freed from the six [objects] of darkness, stillness, obstruction, blandness, separation, and cessation; therefore, these too are mental objects. As for...
There are two reasons why the mind that guards its objects serves as the basis for discrimination. First, since the objects are dharmas (mental objects), their substance does not exist inherently;
they become distinct only by relying entirely upon discrimination. If one does not discriminate, the objects immediately sink into oblivion;
therefore, one must constantly discriminate. It is like a flowing stream without waves: it appears tranquil from afar, yet in reality it is not.

Second, ordinary beings, non-Buddhists, and those of provisional or limited capacity all take the contemplation of the six consciousnesses as their *vipaśyanā* (insight) and the retention of the six consciousnesses as their *śamatha* (calm abiding).
Since there is no separate essence of concentration or wisdom apart from the six consciousnesses, their fundamental nature is inherently one of conceptual discrimination.
How could one possibly escape this? For objects are the dust of phenomena (dharmas), and the mind is discrimination.

Objects cannot indeed be separated from the mind, nor can the mind be separated from objects. To claim to be pure while being entirely defiled, and to claim to be tranquil and settled—how can this be?

In truth, it flows entirely as a continuous stream. Generally speaking, when the profound teachings of the higher dhyānas are not clearly understood, those who merely delight in stillness and concentration have never been able to transcend this state.
Yet they remain constantly within the realm of arising and ceasing, ultimately failing to realize their own error.

I exhort those who cherish meditative concentration (*dhyāna*): they should still investigate this scripture with their whole hearts before they may proceed. Furthermore, by means of this, one comes to know that all provisional vehicles (*upāya-yāna*) possess concentrations characterized by entering and emerging;

these are all subtle forms of discrimination. This is because they rely entirely upon a subtle discriminating mind to maintain that state of quiescence. If one does not discriminate at all, the state of quiescence is immediately lost, which is called "emerging from concentration. How could the Great Samādhi of the *Śūraṅgama Sūtra* be like this?

I request you to examine the explanations provided in the title [of this work] to realize for yourself that it differs from this. This is precisely the refutation of the fourth [view]: the mind that enters quiescence by suppressing distraction. Relying on objects (*ālambana*).
The section on "that which appears to exist" is concluded. △ Second, "the absence of reality apart from objects. This is further divided into two subsections.
First, temporarily conceding that what is apart from existence may be granted as mind:
I am not commanding you to insist that it is not mind; rather, you must examine the mind with subtle discernment. If it is apart from the preceding objects...
The nature of conceptual differentiation is precisely your own true mind.
This is not a command for you to grasp it; it does not force you to rely upon it as something fixed. Rather, I am merely instructing you from below to bring about your own liberation.
"If it were apart from the lower realm" is a concessive statement. "That which possesses a discriminated nature" refers to having a self-substance that is separate from objects.
"This is precisely your own mind" is a temporary concession. △ Second, following the refutation: the various non-existent things cannot be taken as the mind.
Furthermore, it is divided into three sections. First, "being devoid of objects" refers to the shadows of sensory objects.

If it is the nature of discrimination (*parikalpita-svabhāva*), then being devoid of objects means having no essence; this is precisely the matter of the shadows of the discrimination of external objects.
△ Second, the shadows of objects are identical to annihilation.
Objects are not permanent; when they undergo transformation and perish, this mind becomes like the hair of a tortoise or the horns of a rabbit.
Since the shadows of discrimination manifest entirely by relying upon various objects, if the objects undergo transformation and perish, how could the mind possibly remain? It is as follows:
When the form perishes, the shadow naturally vanishes; thus, it is like the hair of a tortoise or the horns of a rabbit—both are names for things that lack substantial reality.
This is why they are used as metaphors. △ Third: Who could achieve the Ultimate Way through annihilation?
In that case, your Dharma-body would be identical to annihilation; who then could cultivate and realize the patience of the non-arising of dharmas?
To say the Dharma-body is annihilated is to follow Ānanda’s inclination and grasp the mind that conditions sensory objects as being the Dharma-body.
This is why provisional small dharmakāyas are not yet truly permanent and ultimately lack a real fruit;
for they do not depart from the shadows of sensory dust—what is called "steaming sand to make rice. Non-arising patience is as explained before.
Thus, the Tathāgata has completed his exhaustive refutation of the three delusions. II. The assembly realizes their error and is unable to respond.
At that moment, Ānanda and the great assembly were silent and lost in self-reflection.
"Silent" means they remained still while relying on the Buddha’s subtle examination; "lost in self-reflection" means they realized that, apart from sensory objects, there was no substantial entity.

Furthermore, having previously reproached themselves for not knowing the location of the mind, they had still hoped for the Buddha’s words; now, hearing the Buddha directly rebuke it as "not the mind," they were struck with alarm and doubt.

Regarding their contentious debates, once they received the Buddha’s teaching on the absence of intrinsic nature (*anātman*), they finally realized that even "nature" is fundamentally non-existent; how, then, could there be a place of abiding?
Thus, the three delusions were completely shattered and the three attachments entirely dissolved; consequently, they remained silent and ceased their disputations.
Therefore, that which they had habitually relied upon as their core self suddenly vanished into the profound stillness, leaving no trace to be sought, yet they remained uncertain as to what this was.
This refers to the mind. It is like a person who has lost a precious object; therefore, it is called "losing oneself.
This concludes the refutation. △ Third, the summary and judgment.

The Buddha told Ānanda: "All those practitioners in the world who have attained the nine successive meditative absorptions (*navānupūrvavihārasamāpatti*) in this present life yet fail to achieve the exhaustion of outflows (*āsravakṣaya*) and become Arhats, do so because they cling to these deluded thoughts of birth and death, mistaking them for reality."
Therefore, although you have now attained much learning, you have not achieved the fruit of sainthood.
The preceding passage provides a general judgment on sentient beings’ mistaken recognition, stating:

"All sentient beings continue in the cycle of birth and death because they employ various false conceptions; since these conceptions are not true, there is transmigration. Following this self-judgment, he then proceeds to provide a detailed explanation.
This refutes the three delusions. Having completed the refutation of delusion, this section therefore concludes by returning to the previous judgment, as that was the original intent of the text.
"The various practitioners in the world" refers to all sentient beings mentioned previously; it does not merely indicate those within the [three] realms.

According to this sutra, those at the stages of the three levels of worthiness (*tri-śaikṣa*) and the four stages of application (*catur-prayoga*) are termed "worldly. A detailed examination of the subsequent text indicates that this specifically refers to ordinary worldlings, non-Buddhists, and followers of the Hīnayāna;

however, the underlying intent encompasses the provisional teaching (*upāya-deśanā*) bodhisattvas as well. Regarding the nine successive attainments (*navānupūrvavihārasamāpatti*), namely the four dhyānas, the four formless attainments (*ārūpyasamāpatti*), and the attainment of the cessation of sensation and perception (*saṃjñāvedayitanirodha*):
in the Hīnayāna system, the first eight are accomplished while still in the stage of an ordinary person (*pṛthagjana*), whereas the ninth is attained by an undefiled noble one (*anāsrava-ārya*).

It is established by way of stages. As for the current statement that one cannot attain the exhaustion of outflows and become an Arhat, you should know that what is called the "outflow-free stage of the noble ones" is merely a provisional concession granted to encourage progress. The *Lotus Sūtra* refutes this, saying:
"You should observe and deliberate; the nirvāṇa you have attained is not the true reality. Since it is not true nirvāṇa, how could it be called true?
"Are the outflows exhausted? Therefore, Changshui’s assertion that the ten stages constitute the Arhatship of exhausted outflows is beyond doubt.
Speaking from the ultimate perspective, even the Buddha of the provisional teaching is not merely one who still abides in the two practices of the Perfect Teaching;

this is entirely due to the latter two phrases, which correctly serve as the words of judgment. That is to say, it refers back to the previous statement: "By means of deluded thoughts, one undergoes cyclic existence. This is because...

From this we know that the aforementioned birth and death must necessarily include the transformation-death (*pariṇāmi-maraṇa*), and that the cycle of rebirth (*saṃsāra*) likewise encompasses *nirvāṇa*.

That Ānanda ultimately returned [to the world] can still be seen from his underlying intention; for in the Hīnayāna teachings, it is permitted that all four fruits of the path are attained by noble ones (*ārya*), and Ānanda had already reached the first fruit.
Yet you claim they are not noble (*ārya*). How could one destroy the first [stage] and yet remain within the four?

It is certain that the ten stages (*daśabhūmi*) alone constitute the noble fruit of partial realization (*pradeśa-prativedha*). This is precisely the refutation of the mind that seeks realization outside the fifth stage.
The refutation of the grasping at a deluded mind to open the path of *śamatha* is hereby concluded. II. Revealing What Was Omitted.
The true nature causes one to see the essence of the *tathāgatagarbha*. The preceding section concerns the false foundation, which has already been refuted and is no longer employed;
this present section concerns the true foundation, which is the essential practice that must necessarily be utilized. The Buddha said: "Sentient beings have cast aside this original luminosity."
They enter erroneously into the various realms of existence; therefore, the titles of these sections employ the characters left behind [by the Buddha].

Nevertheless, because the six sense organs currently possessed by us universally constitute the substance of all phenomena, this section begins with the eye organ and unfolds until it reaches the four sections on the seven elements (*mahābhūta*).
This is divided into two parts. First: Ānanda abandons the false and seeks the True. For a long time, he has clung to deluded consciousness as his mind. Most...
That which was previously difficult to relinquish, I now realize to be illusory and have only begun to abandon it, seeking instead the true mind. (Third section:
First, an expression of sorrowful emotion.
Having heard this, Ānanda again shed tears of grief; prostrating himself with his five limbs touching the ground, he knelt for a long time with palms joined and addressed the Buddha, saying:

Generally, it is only after one has attained deep awakening that compassion arises. One may awaken to the falsity [of existence] and grieve for long-term suffering; or one may awaken to the Reality and grieve for its long-term loss.
What we have here is the compassion arising from the awakening to falsity. II. A Retrospective Account of Painful Remorse.

This section on the two children contains two points of profound significance regarding their falling into the chamber of lust; the text reveals this here. It is divided into two parts: 1. The manifestation of the two children’s fall into the chamber of lust. 2. The two kinds of profound intent. The text is presented as follows. (Divided into two)
Section One: Repenting of Relying on the Tathāgata and Failing to Cultivate Great Samādhi.

Since I followed the Buddha to resolve upon the mind of enlightenment and leave the household life, I have relied upon the Buddha’s majestic spiritual power, constantly thinking to myself that there was no need for me to practice.
I thought that the Tathāgata had bestowed this samādhi upon me, not realizing that body and mind are fundamentally not interchangeable.
Having lost my original mind, although my body has left the household life, my mind does not enter the Way; it is like a destitute son who abandons his father and flees.
This section shows that others cannot be relied upon. "Grace" (hui) refers to a bestowed favor. "Samādhi" is translated here as "right concentration" (zhèngdìng);
it is also called "right reception" (zhèngshòu). Entering this right reception means not receiving any other objects. "To act on behalf" (dài) means to substitute.
Just as a fool, driven by haste, may cause another to eat on his behalf yet remains unsatisfied himself; so too is one who has lost their original mind.
By awakening to the deluded mind, one finally realizes that failing to see one's own mind is not entering the Way. This is like the metaphor of abandoning one’s father:

the Buddha and sentient beings are from the beginning one and the same Dharmakāya. As for the Dharmakāya, it appears separate while in reality it is united; it appears distant while in reality it is...
This is truly intimacy. Now Ānanda recognizes the false while neglecting the true; he appears to be close but is actually distant, and seems intimate but is actually estranged.

This is what is meant by "facing each other across a thousand li. Thus it is said. Contemplating this, those who do not practice themselves but merely seek for empowerment [from others] can also be warned by it.
2. Repenting of Relying on Much Learning While Ultimately Attaining Nothing Real.

Today I have come to know that although one may possess much learning, if one does not practice it, it is equivalent to having heard nothing at all; it is like a person who speaks of food but can never satisfy their hunger with words alone.
This section demonstrates that learning alone cannot be relied upon. Contemplating this, one sees that to rely merely on scholarship without genuine cultivation is in vain.
This should serve as a warning. △ Third, expressing delusion and seeking instruction:

The two obstacles are the afflictive obstacle (*kleśāvaraṇa*) and the cognitive obstacle (*jñeyāvaraṇa*). The afflictive obstacle consists of the two delusions of views (*dṛṣṭi*) and thought (*vitarka*).

"Views" refers to the delusions of intentional discrimination, namely the ten fetters (*saṃyojana*). "Thought" refers to spontaneous craving and attachment, namely the four fetters of greed, hatred, ignorance, and pride.
The former is coarse and the latter is subtle; both collectively arise from the grasping at a self (*ātma-grāha*) and are able to obstruct persons.

The "obstacle of phenomena" (*vastu-āvaraṇa*) is so named because it consists of excellent and sublime worldly matters; thus, it is an *adhikaraṇasamāsa* (locative determinative compound), meaning that the afflictions themselves are the obstacle.

As for the "obstacle to the knowable" (*jñeya-āvaraṇa*), it is also twofold: first, the grasping of objects, which refers to failing to realize that external objects are mind-only, and instead asserting that they truly exist outside the mind, thereby having something to be sought and grasped;
second, attachment to phenomena (*dharmatṛṣṇā*), which refers to failing to realize the emptiness of intrinsic nature regarding what has been cultivated and realized. And...

The arising of attachment is likewise coarse at first and subtle later; all of this constitutes the clinging to phenomena (*dharmagrāha*), which can obstruct the principle of the emptiness of phenomena (*dharmanairātmya*).

Therefore, it is called the "obstruction regarding principles" (*tattvāvaraṇa*). However, the two characters for "the knowable" (*jñeya*) are not themselves the obstruction; they are in fact the very principle of the emptiness of phenomena.
It is named according to the principle of that which it obstructs; therefore, it is called "the knowable" (*jñeya*). This does not mean that the obstruction itself is the "obstructed knowable";

rather, it refers to the obstruction that is capable of obstructing the knowable, following the *tatpuruṣa* (dependent) compound analysis. It is also termed the "obstruction to knowledge" (*jñeyāvaraṇa*), which refers to the wisdom regarding the emptiness of phenomena (*dharmaśūnyatā-jñāna*), as explained by the same principle as before.

Saṃsāra refers to the two kinds of birth and death. "Within this" means within the body and its objects. It speaks of wandering through kalpas as dust.

[They] all turn back because they do not depart from the realm of the body. Ordinary beings are driven in cycles by birth-and-death through segmentation (*pariccheda-maraṇa*) within the coarse realm of the body;
those of the provisional and small vehicles are driven in cycles by birth-and-death through transformation (*pariṇāma-maraṇa*) within the subtle realm of the body.

The final phrase, which reproaches them for taking [this state] upon themselves, means that it is not due to the driving of demons or the coercion of ghosts, but rather arises solely from their own abandonment of the immovable [nature].
The fundamental nature merely takes for itself the body and its objects within the cycle of transmigration.

It has often been said that those who have only recently begun to study the Way immediately know to seek the "master of the house," yet they instead recognize many transient guests who cling to objects of perception and cannot remain still, while failing to realize that the seeing-nature, which is brightly manifest and eternally abiding right before one's eyes, is the true master of the house. As soon as they hear of Prajñā, they...

To speak of "true emptiness" while closing one's eyes to engage in suspended contemplation of the shifting dust of sensory objects, yet remaining ignorant of the seeing-nature (dṛṣṭi-svabhāva) that is vast and unmoving right before one’s eyes—this is precisely true emptiness.
How wonderful is this sublime instruction of the Dharma King! Practitioners should repeatedly examine and realize this;
there will surely come a moment of sudden enlightenment, at which point you will finally believe [the truth] and no longer feel regret.
The Primordial Existence has long been so.

△ Third, revealing that seeing is not extinguished; this demonstrates the meaning of permanence. It is divided into three parts. First, the assembly attains realization and requests further instruction.
Furthermore, there are two parts. First, the narration of the assembly’s realization. This is further divided into three sections. First, attaining the peace of realization:
At that time, Ānanda and the great assembly, having heard the Buddha’s instructions, felt their bodies and minds become tranquil and composed.
The one who was composed became startled and suspicious when the Buddha rebuked him for having "no mind.
Upon hearing that he must distance himself from sensory objects and sever all attachments, he became even more unsettled.

The reason for this was that, because he had previously seen no mind apart from consciousness itself, he now felt that what the Master pointed out among his faculties was something entirely distinct—a state of tranquil immobility. Consequently, his alarm and suspicion were instantly stilled. This is why...
Peace and Bliss. △ Second, repenting of former deluded attachments:
I reflect that since beginningless time, I have lost my original mind and falsely identified with the shadowy phenomena of discriminating sensory objects.
Only upon seeing the unmoving mind do I realize that consciousness was but a shadow of external dust. Therefore, I repent for my delusion of the truth and pursuit of the false. △ Third, by...
This metaphor illustrates joy.
Today I have attained awakening, like a child who has lost its mother suddenly encountering a compassionate mother.
To turn one's back on the truth and cling to delusion is like a child turning its back on its mother; the life of wisdom is in peril, like a child about to die from lack of milk. Now I see...
The fundamental mind is like suddenly encountering a compassionate mother; the life of wisdom is restored as if one were being nourished by milk at birth.
△ Second, the general and specific requests, which also has two parts. First, the general request of the assembled multitude.
With palms joined, he paid homage to the Buddha, wishing to hear the Tathāgata reveal the true and the false within body and mind, the reality and the illusory,
and the nature of the two kinds of illumination— arising and ceasing before one's eyes, and non-arising and non-ceasing.
The first sentence expresses gratitude for what preceded and a request for what follows. "Mind" refers here to the previously mentioned seeing-nature.

Although those of the Lesser Vehicle know that the body is impermanent, they remain consistently deluded in taking seeing to be the eye, which perishes along with the body. Although you have now briefly realized it, this is precisely the unmoving mind;
yet, because you have been mired in delusion for so long, you truly lack the wisdom and discernment to illuminate it yourself. This seeing is like...
"Why does it not perish along with the physical body? Thus he sought the Buddha to clarify this point. II. King Bimbisāra’s Separate Request.

This was intended specifically to eliminate the view of nihilism (*uccheda-dṛṣṭi*), though it incidentally addresses other matters; hence it is categorized as a "separate request. However, there are two reasons why the King initiated this inquiry:
first, because the King’s aged appearance made it easy to demonstrate the nature of transformation and transience; second, to reveal the [nature of the] body.

Regarding impermanence, even the most noble cannot escape it. (The questioner asks the Buddha about the fundamental nature; the primary intent is fundamentally to reform the provisional school’s view of the causes of birth and death, thereby establishing the true causal mind for attaining Buddhahood.)

"What leisure have we to first refute the most shallow view of annihilation held by ordinary people? [The author] replies: "Those of provisional, Lesser Vehicle (Hīnayāna) capacity who are dull and obstructed are truly pitiable; even those among the worldly non-Buddhists who are lost in delusion ought to be rescued with compassion. How much more so for those who have lost their fundamental nature and undergo the cycle of rebirth—for none is more calamitous than the view of annihilation.

Since the Buddha’s compassion is impartial, he uses this point to provide a warning and awakening; thus, while it is addressed concurrently with other views, it is not the primary focus. In the teachings of this land, it is often said that when a person dies, the spirit follows the dispersal of the vital breath and no longer remains.
This is a great delusion; I ask that you ponder this deeply. This is divided into four sections. The first is: Erroneous Delusions Prior to the Teaching.

At that time, King Prasenajit rose and addressed the Buddha: "In the past, before I had received the instructions of the Buddhas, I encountered Kātyāyana and Ajita Keśakambalin, both of whom said that after this body dies, it is annihilated and ceases to exist; they called this 'nirvāṇa'."
Kātyāyana means "shearer of hair" in this language. Pūraṇa Kāśyapa means "non-doing. These two were among the six heterodox teachers;

though their doctrines differed, both primarily adhered to the view of annihilationism (*ucchedadṛṣṭi*). While *nirvāṇa* has many meanings, its essential significance remains the absence of arising and ceasing.
One who attains *nirvāṇa* possesses a single, eternal nature, far removed from birth and death. Now, [this] is contrary to...
To hold that the nature of the self is annihilated upon death and to regard this as *nirvāṇa* is truly a heterodox teaching.
It appears that King Ajātaśatru had already fallen under this delusion before he ever heard the Buddha’s teachings. △ Second, his continued doubts after receiving the instruction.
Although I have encountered the Buddha, I still harbor solitary doubts.
The fox is a beast of doubt; when crossing water, it listens for the sound of the ice, inevitably wavering back and forth many times. A person with doubts is like this;
