this [story] is also shown as an analogy, hence it is said so. △ Third, the wish to hear that [the Dharma] does not perish.
How is this manifested? It is by realizing that this mind is the ground of neither arising nor ceasing.

This "mind" refers to the nature of seeing (*darśana-svabhāva*). One seeks the Buddha’s revelation that this nature is indeed neither arising nor ceasing; once this is so, there will be no long-standing doubts that are not resolved.
△ Fourth, clarifying that the minds of the assembly are the same.
Now, as for this great assembly, all those who possess outflows (āsrava) wish to hear [this teaching].

If we base ourselves on the elimination of the coarse delusions of the view of existence (bhavadr̥ṣṭi), then these "those with outflows" seem to refer only to ordinary worldlings within the realms and to the Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas who are still in training (śaikṣa).
However, if one distinguishes the true and eternal nature of the view, then even the four fruits of the Lesser Vehicle and the three stages of the Separate Teaching (pr̥thagvidyā) are included.
One must also point this out universally, because they have not yet clearly perceived that the nature of mind is the true, eternal mind.

△ Second, the Tathāgata’s interrogation and revelation of non-extinction, divided into three parts. First, revealing that the body undergoes change, which is further divided into two. First, briefly demonstrating its transformation and extinction, which is subdivided into three.
First, interrogating to establish that it must necessarily perish.
The Buddha said to the Great King: "Your body is present now. I ask you again: is this physical body of yours permanent and indestructible like a diamond, or is it subject to decay and destruction?
"World-Honored One," [the king replied], "this body of mine will ultimately undergo transformation and perish."
The meaning of this can be understood. △ Second, the inquiry into the cause of cessation is divided into three parts. First, the strange question regarding prior knowledge:
The Buddha said, "Great King, you have never before brought about cessation; how then do you know of its cessation?"
△ Second, a brief presentation of the signs of transformation:
"World-Honored One, although this body of mine, subject to impermanence and decay, has not yet perished, as I observe it before me, it shifts and passes away from moment to moment;
it is ever-new and never abides, gradually wasting away like fire turning to ash."
△ One clearly knows that extinction is inevitable;
death and passing ceaselessly continue. One decisively knows that this body must undergo total extinction;
because it now migrates and passes away without abiding, one knows that it will ultimately end in extinction and nothing more. Why wait for actual death before [realizing this]?
"To know extinction! These few words alone are sufficient to awaken one to impermanence;
how could those who are intensely greedy for worldly affairs not be struck with trepidation? △ Third, he granted approval to these words.
The Buddha said, "So it is.

He thus certified that what was spoken was not erroneous. This concludes the brief demonstration of the simultaneous cessation of both [afflictions and karma]. II. A detailed account of transformation and cessation, divided into three parts.
1. Causing the comparison of old and young, which is further divided into two. A. Asking the question intentionally to prompt the narration.
"Great King, your current age has already reached the state of senescence; how does your countenance compare to that of your youth?

My previous remarks were brief and general, not yet exhaustive in their detail. I now therefore cite the vast disparity between old age and youth to allow them to be compared, drawing out the contrast so that you may describe it in full detail.
2. An Exaggerated Description of Their Differences.
“World-Honored One, in my former childhood, my skin and flesh were moist and lustrous; as I grew into adulthood, my blood and vital energy were full and robust.
Now, in my declining years, pressed by old age and senility, my physical appearance is withered and haggard, my spirit is clouded and dim, my hair is white and my face is wrinkled;
before long, I shall pass away. How can this be compared to the time of my full vigor?”
The Buddha questioned those old and young; the King was among those who had reached full maturity. He elucidated three stages to demonstrate their differences.
"Mao" (耄) merely signifies being old and forgetful; it need not be restricted to a specific age. "Xia" (下) refers to withered decline, while "hunmei" (昏昧) explains "mao.
Having white hair and wrinkled faces are further manifest proofs that one will not remain so for long. As for the elderly, they are at peace.
One might remain complacent and unaware of fear. △ Second, instructing him to describe the state of transformation in detail. This section has two parts. First, the Tathāgata’s introductory question:
The Buddha said, "Great King, your physical appearance should not have suddenly decayed."
△ Second, King Prasenajit provides a detailed response. This is divided into two parts. First, he states that he did not perceive his gradual arrival.

The King said, "World-Honored One, the transformations of the subtle shifts [of time] are truly beyond my perception. Yet, as cold and heat have passed and flowed on, I have gradually arrived at this state."

It shifts secretly without being noticed; even Zhuangzi used the metaphor of a boat being carried away by a night torrent. He spoke of the secret shifting of *zhaohua* (the transformative power of nature), yet how could he have known it was the transition brought about by the *xingyin* (formative aggregate)?
II. Investigation and Explanation through Inference. This has two parts: 1. A coarse inference, limited for now to a period of ten years.
Why is this? At the age of twenty, although I was called young, my appearance was already aged compared to when I was ten.
At thirty, I was further declined than at twenty; now at sixty, I have passed that by two decades. When I observe myself at fifty, I see I was truly robust and strong.
Spontaneous unawareness persists until one begins to discern it through intentional reflection and deliberation.
Although this stage allows for awareness over a long duration, how could one truly know that twenty or thirty years have already passed since childhood, resulting in such senescence?
Thus, even the young should be alerted to impermanence. △ Second, detailed analysis down to the moment (kṣaṇa).

World-Honored One, I observe their secret shifting; although this decay and falling occurs within the span of ten years, if I were to contemplate it with subtle discernment, would the change be limited to a single decade or two?
In truth, it is the change of years. But does it stop at the change of years? It is also accompanied by the transformation of months.
Not only is there transformation by the month, but there is also migration by the day. Upon deep reflection and careful observation, [it changes] in every kṣaṇa.
In the interval of a single kṣaṇa or thought-moment, there is no staying still.
This section traces [the limit] to the most fleeting of times; even so, it is that which the coarse minds of ordinary beings fail to perceive.

In the *Shangshu*, "passing away" (*cu*) refers to the soul (*hun*) ascending to heaven, and "falling" (*luo*) refers to the spirit (*po*) returning to earth; these are alternative names for death. Now...
The sutras simply state that the daily departure of one’s youthful appearance constitutes "passing away" (tsu), and the daily transition of the signs of aging constitutes "falling away" (lo).

The term "ji" refers to twelve years; this merely changes the phrasing of the previously broad enumeration. From a year down to a kṣaṇa, these are precisely what is meant by "subtle shifting that goes unnoticed.
A kṣaṇa is so brief that it is contained within a single thought-moment (citta-ekakṣaṇa); in the teachings, this is called "one thought."
It comprises ninety kṣaṇas; taking the piercing of ninety sheets of paper with a sharp blade as one nimeṣa (nien), one may calculate the divisions of kṣaṇas accordingly.
△ Third, the conclusion that [the mind] must necessarily cease.
Thus, one knows that my body will ultimately undergo transformation and extinction.

Although this was spoken by the Tathāgata to detail the characteristics of the physical body’s moment-to-moment transition and decay, it is intended to reveal that the subsequently perceived nature is entirely devoid of transition or decay.
Nevertheless, it can also serve as a basis for cultivating the disenchantment of observing the impermanence of the body. However...

Wǔquán was briefly weary of this; he took ash to sever the fruits [of rebirth] and sought a transformed body—this was merely his former view. Now, we cause him to rely on the understanding of the Perfect Person (*yuanren*):
it is simply a matter of suddenly realizing the permanent nature (*changxing*) without departing from within the sense organs. The demonstration that the body undergoes transformation is complete.
△ Second, pointing out that the seeing-nature (*jianxing*) is without change. This is divided into four sections. First, questioning and determining the lack of knowledge.
The Buddha said to the Great King: "You see that transformations and changes ceaselessly shift; you have realized this extinction.
At the very moment of extinction, do you know that within your body there is something that does not perish? King Prasenajit joined his palms and addressed the Buddha: "I truly do not know."
It does not perish within perishing; this is what the true King has failed to perceive. Let him know it early; how could he then be deluded by the view of annihilation?
2. Granting the Instruction:
The Buddha said, "I shall now show you the nature that is neither born nor extinguished."
△ Third, citing the observation of the river:
"Great King, at what age did you see the waters of the Ganges? The King replied, "When I was three years old, my compassionate mother took me [there]."
He paid his respects to the deity Jīvaka. As he passed through this stream, he immediately recognized it as the waters of the Gaṅgā River.
"Jīvaka" translates here as "Long Life. He visited this celestial deity to pray for longevity. △ Fourth, a detailed exposition on the unchanging nature, which has two parts.
First, demonstrating that what was seen remains unchanged; that which was seen was the water within the Gaṅgā River. [The following is] the cause for this.
The water seen does not differ; it merely serves to reveal that the nature of the seer is unchanging. Furthermore, this is divided into three parts.
First, following upon the preceding discussion of transformation and cessation, the Buddha said:
"Great King, it is as you have said. At twenty years of age, one declines from the state of ten years, and so on until sixty."
The sun, moon, years, and seasons shift and change from moment to moment.
△ Second, have them compare what they see:
"When you first saw this river at the age of three, and then reached the age of thirteen, how was its water?"
△ He answered directly and without wavering.
The King said, "It is exactly as it was when you were three years old; there is not the slightest difference, even up until this year at sixty-two."
The first section, demonstrating that the seen is unchanging, is concluded. △ Second, demonstrating that the seer is unchanging.

The "seer" refers to the nature of seeing within the sense organs; it is presented as the capacity revealed by the object of seeing, which makes it easier to awaken to. This is divided into three parts. First, following up on the previous discussion of the changing body.
The Buddha said: "Now you yourself lament that your hair has turned white and your face is wrinkled; yet your face must certainly have been more wrinkled than it was in your childhood.
2. To cause him to compare the capacity for vision:

"At this present time, as you look at this Ganges River, does your vision differ from the vision you had when looking at the river in your childhood? Is there any difference between your being a child and your being an old man?"
△ Third, he answered directly and without wavering.
The King said, "No, World-Honored One.
[The Buddha] asked regarding one who is intelligent despite old age and does not decline: such a person may be said to be unchanging. However, there are many whose eyes grow dim with old age.
Question: Regarding "darkness," what does this refer to? Answer: This refers simply to the dimness of the eye; it has no bearing on the nature of seeing (*darśana-svabhāva*).

If we were to discuss only the eye, there are indeed those who are naturally deficient, dull, or blind from birth—why wait until old age? Furthermore, in the previous section on "seeing," there was already the analogy of a blind person gazing into darkness.
That example acknowledges that one perceives the entirety of the darkness, yet this does not impair the essence of seeing itself.

How could this merely refer to the obscuration of the visual organ? One should know that herein we are simply using the King Ajātaśatru’s unimpaired eye as a means to verify that the nature of seeing is immutable;
it does not claim that the physical eye itself is immutable.
How, then, could one intentionally take his diseased eye as a point of contention? This concludes the section on the immutability of seeing. △ Third, the formal presentation of the two natures.
Previously, during the general inquiry, you wished to hear about the two natures of arising-and-ceasing and non-arising-non-ceasing that clarify the nature of the mind.

The Tathāgata has already led you through the observation of the river to verify and establish this point; now he shall set forth these two natures to conclude by returning to what was previously requested.

This section is further divided into two parts: first, a detailed explanation and their differentiation; and within that, first, distinguishing between change and non-change based on the wrinkling [of the face].
[The King] said, "It changes. The Buddha said, "Great King, although your face has grown wrinkled, this essence of seeing has never been wrinkled. That which wrinkles is subject to change;
that which does not wrinkle is not subject to change."
△ Second, distinguishing between extinction and non-extinction through the transformation of causes.
That which undergoes transformation is subject to extinction; that which does not transform is fundamentally without birth or death. How could birth and death be experienced within that?

Since King Ajātaśatru already anticipates the inevitable destruction of the body due to its decay and transformation, why does he not likewise anticipate that this vision will certainly not perish after death because it is unchanging?
This can serve as a profound catalyst for awakening.
"Within" refers to within the body itself. Those who undergo birth and death do so together with the body.
It perishes. Since it does not undergo transformation together with the body, it certainly does not perish together with the body.
Often, the masters of our school say that the indestructible nature-body exists without departing from within the body;

this refers precisely to the natures of seeing, hearing, and so forth within the sense organs, and does not mean that there is a separate life-force or destiny within the heart-mind or inside the viscera—just as Ānanda [initially thought].
First, they cling to the consciousness within the body as the mind.

Second, they are rebuked for maintaining the view of annihilationism (*ucchedadṛṣṭi*), yet they still cite Makkhali Gosāla and others, asserting that after this body dies, everything is utterly extinguished.

Makkhali—here translated as "One Who Does Not See the Path"—and the others mentioned in the preceding invitation refer to two individuals who were likewise of the same class of nihilistic heretics (*ucchedavāda*).
Thus, the Buddha’s reprimand was presented in contrast to the King’s invitation. This concludes the section on the Tathāgata’s inquiry into and clarification of the doctrine of non-extinction.
△ Third, the King and the others were filled with the utmost joy and celebration.

When the king heard these words, he came to believe with certainty that after death one leaves this life to pass into another. Together with the great assembly, he leaped for joy and experienced a wonder never before known.

Although the king’s original purpose was to eliminate the delusion of the ordinary person’s view of nihilism (uccheda-dṛṣṭi), he acted as if joining the inquiry; therefore, he now proceeds solely on this basis.
O King, [the Buddha] merely bound those of one class who harbor nihilistic views, rejoicing only in their nature of proceeding toward rebirth;

it was not that he universally bound the entire assembly to share in this joy. Because abandoning birth and proceeding toward rebirth is precisely the "human characteristic" (*pudgala-lakṣaṇa*) among the four characteristics, the provisional and small vehicles rejoice in this;
however, this is a detriment rather than a benefit. Question: Do the provisional and small vehicles not have any joy at all? Answer: [They do.]
He will surely rejoice. Apart from consciousness and mind, there exists this fundamental, eternal nature;
from this point, by cultivating the Great Samādhi, the attainment of Bodhi is truly within reach. [The interlocutor] asks: Why does the author of the sutra conclude solely with reference to the King?
[The answer is: The King’s question was merely incidental; the intention was simply to resolve and sever misconceptions on this particular occasion. To sever misconceptions...
Since it has already been removed, its purpose is exhausted; why not conclude it? [Question: Why is the joy of the assembly not formally concluded? [Answer: There are two reasons for this.
First, regarding the joy of minor realization, there is no necessity to conclude it again. This refers to the joy of awakening that occurs at each successive stage.
At the beginning of this section, it was already stated that body and mind were at ease, and so forth. If one were to conclude it once more, it would merely be redundant.

The same words as before. Why use such redundancy? Second, the joy of great awakening must await the final conclusion, for the mind has not yet fully opened and remaining doubts have not been exhausted.
While Ānanda and the others were about to raise various questions, what leisure was there to conclude with joy?
It was only at the end of the third fascicle that the conclusion was made, saying: "Each knows for themselves that the mind pervades the ten directions," and so forth.
Having attained the fundamental wondrous mind, which abides eternally and is indestructible, they prostrate to the Buddha with palms joined, experiencing what they have never known before;
this is the joy of the entire assembly. The demonstration that seeing is indestructible is complete. △ Fourth, the demonstration that seeing is not lost.

If one relies on the title of this section, it is sufficient to fulfill the meaning of the character "constant" (*chang*) from the previous section. This is because the preceding section was explained in terms of the future, as it were:

"It shall remain ultimately indestructible until the end of the future. This section is explained in terms of the past; as it says, "From beginningless time, it has been inherently present without omission.
Since this refers exclusively to its vertical pervasiveness, there is no doubt that it pertains to the character of "permanence" (*nitya*).

Furthermore, according to the text’s revelation that its essence encompasses all phenomena and its magnitude reaches the limits of empty space, it may also be regarded as corresponding to the "Tathāgata" of the subsequent section.
This demonstrates the meaning of pervasive perfection. Furthermore, in the preceding text, he requested an explanation of the nature of the mind as quiescent and eternal.

The first two sections have already answered the two characters "quiescent" (*jì*) and "eternal" (*cháng*). This current section, concerning its vastness and pervasive perfection, truly constitutes the nature of the mind;

it answers the two characters "mind-nature" (*xìng-xīn*) in their entirety. All three interpretations are valid; one should examine them carefully. This is divided into two parts. First: Ānanda, having attained realization, turns back...
Doubting his previous words, Ānanda rose from his seat, prostrated before the Buddha with palms joined, and knelt on one knee to address the Buddha: "World-Honored One,
if this seeing and hearing are indeed neither produced nor extinguished, why does the World-Honored One say that we have lost our true nature and act in a state of inversion?"
I pray that you will arouse compassion and wash away my defilements.
Above, you have cited what was seen; here, I further add what was heard. This sufficiently demonstrates that the Buddha’s words were given according to the occasion.

In reality, the four natures and six consciousnesses are all subsumed within the nature of seeing. That it must be neither arising nor ceasing is precisely the source of one's doubt. As for the passage above:

In the section [on "Immovability"], the text says: "That which is unchanging fundamentally lacks birth and extinction. This is correct. That one has lost the true nature and acts in a state of inversion is precisely what is being questioned;

yet this point is found within the section on "Immovability," which is the full text of that passage. Because the subsequent doubt arises from the preceding [text], it is not a doubt directed at the Buddha.
It is merely a contradiction of one's own words. However, since the Buddha has already stated that there is no extinction, by what...
Regarding the causes and conditions: since it was previously stated that there is "loss," the Buddha subsequently demonstrates this.

However, he speaks of "loss" because of inversion, not because of annihilation; thus, one can see that it is not a true loss. Therefore, the entire chapter fully demonstrates the characteristics of how inversion does not constitute loss.
While various commentaries merely clarify inversion, they completely forget to mention non-loss; it is unclear why this is so.
This is to dispel Ānanda’s doubts; please examine the present explanation carefully, for you shall naturally discern its merits and defects.

△ Second, the Tathāgata’s elucidation: the fault of explaining based on inversion. Regarding this, the old commentaries contain errors; if these are not clarified in advance, [the confusion will persist].
Not only would the fundamental purport of the sutra ultimately fail to be revealed, but even the current correct interpretation would, on the contrary, appear erroneous.

The commentary states: "To hang [the head] downward is 'correct' (zhèng); to stand [it] upside down is 'inverted' (dào). This statement is incorrect; moreover, it contradicts the phrasing at the point where it joins with what follows.
This is because the author mistakenly understood the four characters "shǒuwěi xiānghuàn" (head and tail exchanged), thereby resulting in this error.
Having reached this point, it is not that the beginning and end have been confused; rather, it precisely clarifies that there is no loss. It is not intended to describe a state of inversion.
This is because whether an arm is held upright or inverted has no fixed standard. Both Ānanda and the Buddha merely followed worldly convention.

However, while it is easy for people to understand that an arm, though inverted, does not lose its identity as an arm, it is difficult for them to understand that the mind, though inverted, does not lose its identity as the mind.

Xiao [responds]: "This is merely using the principles of the *Yi* to challenge the difficulty. Please examine the present explanation, which is divided into two parts. First, the analogy that turning the arm over involves no error.
This is further divided into three sections. The first is to determine the characteristics of the arm being turned over."
Thereupon, the Tathāgata extended his golden arm; with his wheel-marked hand pointing downward, he showed it to Ānanda, saying:
"Do you now see my *mudrā* hand as upright or inverted? Ānanda replied: "The sentient beings of the world consider this to be inverted;
yet I do not know who is upright and who is inverted."

*Mudrā-hasta* (Mother-dhara-hasta) is here translated as "Seal-Hand," referring to one of the marks of physical excellence (*lakṣaṇa*). It is unclear who is correct and who is mistaken regarding this;
for there is no fixed standard for what constitutes an upright or inverted position of the arm. Rather, it follows worldly convention to describe this downward-hanging position as "inverted."
△ Second, the correct characteristics of the two crossed arms.
The Buddha told Ānanda: "If people of the world consider this to be inverted, then by what standard do people of the world determine what is upright?"
Ānanda said, "If the Tathāgata extends his arm with cotton-wool on his hand and points it toward the sky, that is called 'upright.

The Buddha’s intention was this: since the arm itself has no fixed state of being upright or inverted, and because the world regards it as inverted, he followed that convention and called it inverted.
He then asked the world what it considered to be upright, intending to follow that as well and designate it as upright."
This is merely intended to provide an analogy without error; it is not meant to adjudicate the right or wrong of what constitutes correct or inverted [perception].
△ Third, clarifying that inversion is not a loss:
The Buddha then raised his arm and said to Ānanda, "If this were an inversion where head and tail were exchanged, then all people in the world..."
"First, looking up" refers to raising the arm;
this takes the upward-pointing gesture as the primary one. As for these two lines regarding the inversion of head and tail, they precisely clarify that there is no fault in such inversion.
This is because when the Buddha raised his hand upward, he was already conforming to worldly convention.
This completes the formation. It then says: "If one were to take this arm and hang it upside down, it would merely be a case of exchanging the upright head for the downward-pointing tail;
how could this truly cause the loss of the arm? These are the final two lines.

The first point is "sameness" (*sama*). "Twofold" (*dviguṇa*) means "many. For instance, if one says that the inversion of the mind is not lost, this is something that people of the world find difficult to understand.
However, the inversion of an arm being not lost is something seen by everyone alike without difference; it is witnessed by many rather than just one person.
This is intended to show that it is clear and easy to see, and thus one should attain awakening through this analogy. Furthermore:
This accords with the following analogy; there is no contradiction whatsoever. △ Second, the analogy based on the absence of error regarding the inversion of the mind, divided into four parts.
First, a brief application of the analogy according to the names to establish the certainty.

Thus you should know: when your body is compared with the pure Dharma-body of all Tathāgatas, the body of a Tathāgata is called "Right Universal Knowledge," whereas your bodies are designated as "inverted by nature."
The pure Dharmakāya is both form and essence, both existence and emptiness. The manifestation of the thirty-two marks is itself the Dharmakāya;

it is not like the conditioned, untainted final body of the Buddha according to the Characteristics School (Lakṣaṇavāda), nor like the view of the Emptiness School (Śūnyatāvāda) which deprecates forms as false and considers the reward and transformation bodies to be unreal.
In this School of Essence (Svabhāvavāda), mountains and rivers are fully revealed, and the myriad phenomena...
All is as stated. Those who claim that the *nirmāṇakāya* (emanation body), the *saṃbhogakāya* (enjoyment body), and the *dharmakāya* (dharma body) are distinct entities shall fall into hell.

As for those who use analogies to bring forth the truth, they are instructed to realize the nature of the body and mind by means of the arm. To realize that the mind encompasses all phenomena is correct knowledge (*samyag-jñāna*);

to realize that all phenomena are the mind is pervasive knowledge (*sarvajña*). The Tathāgata’s realization of this is called "Correct and Pervasive Knowledge" (*samyak-sarvajña*). The body is like the fingers upon the arm.

This is not something newly acquired. To grasp at the physical body as encompassing the mind is inverted cognition (*viparyaya-jñāna*); to grasp that there are phenomena external to the mind is inverted view (*viparyaya-dṛṣṭi*).

Ordinary beings and those of the two vehicles cling to this, which is termed "inverted nature" (*prakṛti-viparyāsa*). That the body hangs down like an arm is not a true loss; this is merely a brief synthesis.
A detailed synthesis follows in the subsequent text. II. Investigation and Manifestation of the Body’s Lack of Correctness or Inversion.
"Examine this thoroughly as you wish: between your body and the Buddha’s body, where is the designation 'inversion' located? By what name is it called 'inversion'?
At that time, Ānanda and the great assembly stared fixedly at the Buddha; their eyes did not blink, and they could not discern the location of the inversion of body and mind.
Although this demonstrates the non-erroneous characteristic of the body, it also reveals that Ānanda and others do not clearly understand the true meaning of inversion.
The intention is that for all things, names and characteristics are generally inseparable; therefore, one is led to seek the characteristic by following the name.
For example, if "black" is the name, then when contrasted with a white object, the characteristic of black must necessarily be clearly visible, standing in stark contrast to the white.
"Distinct. Now, since your body is already named 'inversion,' it ought to possess the distinct characteristics of inversion when contrasted with my body of perfect universality;
only then could it be said to be utterly separate from my perfect universality. Yet, as you observe now, where exactly does this inversion reside?
For this reason, none of you have ultimately been able to find the distinction between inversion and correctness."
Regarding the characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*): the reason they cannot be apprehended is that these names possess three meanings that are profoundly deep and differ from other names.
First, the meaning does not reside in the substance itself. This is because although the name resides in the body, the meaning follows the mind.
Second, it is not something that can be perceived through mutual observation; it can only be sought through its meaning, unlike material objects which can be observed through their mutual forms.
This is indeed so. Thirdly, it is not that these [three] exist elsewhere within the mind; rather, they are merely the deluded views of sentient beings who are inverted.
The mind, in reality, does not rely upon them, for it is by virtue of their being truly inverted that one recognizes this inversion.

Since even within the mind this inversion cannot be apprehended, how could it possibly be seen as residing in the body? The following text will fully demonstrate this, so that you may understand it through its meaning.
Seek it! △ Third, a detailed exposition on how correctness and inversion arise from the mind, divided into three parts. First, the Tathāgata’s compassionate address to the assembly.
The Buddha gave rise to great compassion, feeling pity for Ānanda and the great multitude; he uttered a voice like the ebb and flow of the ocean, addressing the entire assembly.
Compassionately pitying their delusions, they do not even know where [the truth] resides; how, then, could there be an opportunity for awakening?

One must not miss the opportune moment; this is called the "Sound of the Ocean Tide," for it is when their dazed gaze is fixed upon the world that they are precisely at the time when they may be taught.
II. Quoting past teachings to clarify the correct characteristics. This section corresponds exactly to the metaphor of the arm being raised upward.
This is divided into three parts. First, showing that this is the teaching for ordinary beings:

"O sons of good family, I have always said that all the teachings spoken by the Buddha reach the stage of omniscience; yet sentient beings each understand them according to their own kind, as in the following example."

All things are created solely by the mind. Those of the ordinary and small vehicles understand them as being created by karma; those of the provisional teachings understand them as being created by consciousness.

The Perfect and Sudden teaching directly realizes that they are the manifestations of the true mind. Now, based on this profound meaning, I shall re-explain the former teachings. △ Second, all phenomena are manifested solely by the mind.
The various conditions of form and mind, as well as all the objects of cognition associated with mental factors, are manifested solely by the mind.
"Form" refers to the eleven types of material phenomena (*rūpa-dharma*). "Mind" refers to the eight consciousnesses, the mental phenomena (*citta-dharma*).

"Various conditions" refers to the four conditions that give rise to the mind and the two conditions that give rise to form. "Mental factors" refers to the fifty-one mental concomitants (*caitta-dharma*). "All objects of cognition" refers to...
"Phenomena" (*dharma*) refers extensively to all activities—whether good or evil, deviant or correct, mundane or supramundane—including the gates of dharma concerning cause and effect.
"Mind-only" (*cittamātra*) refers to the mind of the single true *dharmadhātu* inherently possessed by sentient beings;
it is also the *tathāgatagarbha*-mind, the substantial reality that manifests all phenomena. Therefore, it is said that "all is manifested by mind alone. This section emphasizes this point.

First, the manifestation of characters: seeing that the myriad dharmas are precisely the mind. (Question: Previously it was stated that seeing the nature is the essence of the ālayavijñāna, which is the Tathāgatagarbha-mind, and is also the substantial reality of the myriad dharmas.)

It appears to function as that which manifests. Now, since the "mind" within the phrase "matter-and-mind" encompasses all eight consciousnesses, the *ālayavijñāna* has already become that which is manifested. Yet, the "mind" of "mind-only" (*cittamātra*) must refer to a distinct, purely true mind. How can one still take the *tathāgatagarbha*-mind to explain it? Answer: The first seven [consciousnesses] and so forth are merely that which is manifested;

the True Mind is merely that which manifests. However, this *ālayavijñāna* functions as both subject and object: in relation to the True Mind, it is demoted to the status of the manifested; in relation to the myriad phenomena, it is elevated to the status of the manifestor.

This is because it is fundamentally non-dual in essence with the True Mind, differing only in that it carries delusion. Therefore, in this present text, even when speaking of the True Mind, it remains strictly within the realm of what is shown and seen, for sentient beings’ direct perception (*pratyakṣa*) is nothing other than this.
This may be indicated. In the sutras, this meaning predominates. We shall wait until the next section to explain it most thoroughly). △ Third, the myriad dharmas are ever-present within the mind.
Your body and your mind are both objects manifested within the wondrously luminous, true essence—the wondrous mind.

The body consists of the five sense organs; the mind consists of the eight consciousnesses and their associated mental factors (*caitta*). All other elements are subsumed within the word "all. It is called "wondrous" because it belongs neither to emptiness nor to existence.
It is called "luminous" because it is far removed from the darkness of ignorance. It is called "true" because it is the substantial reality of all phenomena.

"Essential. To possess these various meanings is called "wondrous. Regarding that which appears within the mind: it is said that the wondrous mind is like the ocean, while the myriad dharmas are like reflections within the ocean.
The mind encompasses all without exterior; thus, the myriad dharmas are entirely within the mind.

This section emphasizes the character "one" (一), showing that the mind encompasses the myriad dharmas. This accords with the previous section’s statement that the myriad dharmas are identical to the mind. This...
The mind-encompassing category subsumes all phenomena; this is the true characteristic of the mind, which is ever-unobscured.
This is the body of Right Universal Knowledge (*samyak-saṃbuddha*). It should further be stated: "It is no different from my raising a hand; how could there be anything else to be attained?"
This *manas* must certainly exist; it is simply that the text is concise. Having concluded the explanation of the correct characteristics by citing the ancient teachings, [the text now] proceeds to:
△ Third, rebuking the neglect and recognition to clarify the characteristic of perversion. "Neglect" (*wei*) refers to neglecting the True; "recognition" (*ren*) refers to recognizing the delusory.
It rebukes them for becoming inverted solely because they neglect the True and recognize the delusory. This makes it clear that this is a perversion of delusion, not a perversion of the Mind itself.
It is further divided into three parts. First, the reproach for abandoning the true and recognizing the false:

"How is it that you all have lost the fundamentally wondrous, perfectly marvelous, and luminous mind, and the jewel-like, brilliant, and wondrous nature, thereby recognizing delusion within awakening?"
The meaning of the previous question was: "By what causes and conditions is it said to be 'lost'? This section provides those very causes and conditions.
It refers to abandoning the Truth and identifying with the delusory; though one has not actually lost it, in meaning it is equivalent to having lost it.

The two characters "Original Wonder" (Benmiao) are spoken of separately to indicate that it is not produced through cultivation; it is fundamentally free from the constraints of existence and non-existence, and is sovereign.
The meaning of liberation. The two phrases, "the mind that is perfect, wondrous, and luminous" and "the nature that is jewel-like, bright, and wondrous," correspond to one another.

"Perfect" (yuan) refers to its pervasive integration and dynamic flow; this is the characteristic of its function (yong). "Jewel-like" (bao) refers to its purity and solid reality; this is the characteristic of its essence (ti).

Thus, following Master Huan’s interpretation, "mind" (xin) and "nature" (xing) are used interchangeably as essence and function. As for the mind, it arises from the wondrous toward the luminous; it is perfect...
Fusion and illumination are as the light of a mirror; its nature is thus luminous and wondrous,凝然湛寂 (stabilized and profoundly tranquil), like the substance of the mirror.

This interpretation is excellent. When "mind-nature" (xinxing) is mentioned alone, each term encompasses both substance and function. When "mind" and "nature" are raised together, substance and function are temporarily distinguished.
This is merely establishing meaning based on the phrasing; it is not fixed. This [critique] precisely accuses [the opponent] of neglecting the True.
The final phrase rebukes the recognition of the delusory. "Awakening" refers to the two preceding sections: that the myriad dharmas are the mind, and the mind encompasses all beyond the dharmas.
"Delusion," conversely, is their diametric opposition: it means regarding all dharmas as being outside the mind, while the mind falls within the dharmas.
Regarding "recognizing delusion within awakening" means that although one’s views are deluded and inverted attachments, the true mind and the myriad dharmas have never actually depended upon them.

The result is the formation of perversion. It is like a person who mistakes east for west; while the directions themselves do not actually shift, one falsely conceives of perversion within that which is non-perverted.
Therefore, it is said: "To mistake awakening for delusion. II. Detailed Elucidation of the Characteristics of Mistaking and Forgetting.
The preceding section merely provided a heading; this current section fully explains and establishes it. This is divided into two parts. First, the explanation by way of principle (*dharma*).
Furthermore, there are two [points]. First, to manifest the characteristics of misrecognizing the delusory. This is further divided into four parts. First, erroneously recognizing the physical world:
mistaking the state of obscured darkness for emptiness; within this emptiness and obscured darkness, the accumulation of darkness forms matter.

This section [addresses] the erroneous recognition that mountains, rivers, and all phenomena exist as real entities external to the mind; it correctly shows that the myriad dharmas are, in fact, the mind itself.
However, both this section and the following one are excellently annotated by Master Yuan; I have now adopted them in their entirety. Regarding "the darkening becomes emptiness":
because one is deluded regarding the luminosity of the nature, ignorance (*avidyā*) is produced. Due to this ignorance, it transforms into stubborn emptiness (*jaḍa-śūnyatā*). That is to say:
The subsequent scripture states: "From delusion and ignorance, empty space arises. Regarding the phrase "within the darkness of the void, the darkness coalesces to form matter":

this refers to the union of the transformed inert emptiness and the transforming ignorance; these two dharmas combine to give rise to the four great elements, which constitute the external matter of the mountains, rivers, and environment as the *parigraha* (retributive support).
This is what is meant by "the clarity of thought forming the land. △ Second, erroneously identifying the root-body.
"Material form is mixed with deluded conceptualization; the characteristics of conceptualization constitute the body.
This section refers to the false identification of the five aggregates and the four great elements as the characteristics of one's own body. Master Yuan says:

"By means of the material form of the four great elements mixed with the mind of deluded conceptualization, the internal material form of the primary retribution of sentient beings arises. 'Conceptualization' refers to the deluded mind; 'characteristics' [refers to the resulting forms]."
This refers to false form. When form and mind conjoin, the five aggregates are complete; thus, that which possesses cognition and awareness is the sentient being.
△ Third, erroneously identifying the nature of the mind:
gathering conditions within, it stirs; rushing outward, it gallops away. Taking this state of confused turmoil as the nature of the mind.
Regarding this section: it refers to falsely identifying the discrimination of conditioned objects as the characteristics of one’s own mind.

As for "accumulating conditions," Master Huan explains it by saying that in the *Awakening of Faith*, there is a delusory "conditioned vapor" (*yuanqi*) that accumulates therein; this is most excellent.
However, my humble opinion differs from that of Guifeng. Now, as for this "conditioned vapor," it refers to the spirit, consciousness, soul, and will, which reside latently within the five viscera.
This [self] is falsely established by the habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*) of ego-clinging (*ātma-grāha*). "Within it" means within the body.

"Accumulated" refers to being bound together as the life-faculty (*jīvitendriya*), tethered to birth and death. Indeed, although the self is fundamentally void and non-existent, through long eons of firm clinging, it has accorded with false principles;
thus, to preserve it is to live, and to sever it is to die. This is what is meant by... from... [the source].
That which is ultimately unformed is ultimately existent. As for "inner agitation," it is as the saying goes: "If there is movement within, one's essence will inevitably be disturbed.
We see clearly that when mental anxieties and labors are excessive, the five viscera fall into illness accordingly.

This is why sentient beings for the most part do not believe that life and nature are fundamentally non-existent within the body. As for "rushing outward and running wild," this refers to pursuing sensory objects and being preoccupied with discursive thoughts.

These two phrases, although speaking generally of deluded consciousness (*vikalpa-vijñāna*), suggest that the two characters "gathering" (*ju*) and "conditioning" (*yuan*) sustain the life-root (*jīvitendriya*), appearing as the functional power of the eighth [consciousness].
"Inner agitation and outer rushing," and the "leaping-up of delusive thoughts" (*parikalpa*), appear to be the karmic activities of the first six [consciousnesses].

As for the phrase "the state of murky confusion": it is "murky" because of gathering conditions and deluded attachment; it is "confused" because of inner agitation and outer rushing. To mistakenly recognize this...

Those who are deluded and confused take this as the functioning of the numinous spirit and falsely claim it to be the nature of the mind. You previously asked whether seeing the nature is the substantial reality of the eight consciousnesses;
now you further claim that "gathering conditions" is the functional capacity of the eight consciousnesses. How can you distinguish between gain and loss? Answer:
This consciousness is a synthesis of the true and the false. Therefore, "seeing the nature" takes one portion of the True Principle (*tattva*), while "gathering conditions" takes its...
This is one part of deluded sentiment. Generally speaking, when it is said that the eight consciousnesses "leave later and arrive first," these are all spoken of according to deluded sentiment;
hereafter, follow this pattern. △ Fourth, resulting in perversion.
A single delusion becomes the mind, which is decisively mistaken for being within the physical body.
The preceding two sections were still merely the causes of inversion; it is in this section that the great inversion is fully established.

For the mind has turned back and entered into the body, such that the myriad dharmas are all encompassed outside the mind, whereas in reality, it is the mind that encompasses the myriad dharmas. Therefore...

This is indeed a perversion. Alas! Were it not for the Buddha’s teaching of definitive meaning (*nītārtha*), who would not reckon that one's life-force (*jīva*) resides within the body and that all phenomena (*dharmas*) exist solely outside the mind?

Yet, while the Daoist teachings are particularly extreme in reckoning that life-force resides within the body, even the Lesser Vehicle (*Hīnayāna*) remains thus in its doctrine regarding phenomena as being external to the mind. This is likewise true of the Perfectly Complete Enlightenment (*Samyaksaṃbodhi*).
How profound it is! II. Revealing the signs of those who have abandoned the truth:
they do not know that from the physical body outward to the mountains, rivers, empty space, and the great earth—all are things within the wondrously luminous true mind.
The mind is within the body; it is merely a matter of deluded views and false attachments.
How could the infinite Great Mind ever truly enter the body based upon such deluded views? It is exactly like mistaking east for west, while the east remains truly not west.
Therefore, the body and empty space remain as they were within the mind, and the Great Mind relies [upon them].
The "old" [nature] is encompassed within the Dharma, yet it is simply not perceived when one is deluded. Thus, these two characters, "not knowing," constitute the very essence of inversion;
how could there be any substantial entity to be found? The explanation by way of the Dharma is complete. △ Second, the explanation by way of analogy, divided into two parts:
1. An analogy for abandoning the True and recognizing the False.
It is like discarding hundreds of thousands of vast, clear oceans and recognizing only the substance of a single floating bubble;
one loses the mind that encompasses empty space and the great earth, failing to acknowledge it.

This is like discarding hundreds of thousands of oceans while merely recognizing the "self" within this tiny body—just as if recognizing only a single bubble. △ Second, the analogy for taking the delusive as real.
Truly, you have taken the eye for the entire tide and exhausted the vastness of the ocean;
yet through successive perversions and attachments, you claim that the heart within the square-inch of the body can encompass empty space and the great earth. It is like...
It is said that a single bubble encompasses the entire great ocean. Question: How does this differ from [the statement] that a single pore contains the entirety of the oceans of lands?
Answer: Because he has realized that the nature of all phenomena is the totality of the Dharma-realm, a single hair, being in accord with that nature, encompasses everything without exception.
As it is said, "A true mani-jewel is worth an entire kingdom"—this is indeed not false.

Yet, those who do not penetrate the true nature (*dharmatā*) of all phenomena merely take their deluded and agitated conceptualizations and falsely calculate them within the body; they further perversely cling to [the self] as being able to encompass empty space and the great earth.
Since even this has no essence that can be found, by what means could it extensively encompass anything? It is like saying a bubble on the water is of great value.

"One country" refers to the true state of great delusion; how could it be the same as [the former]? Having thoroughly elucidated the characteristics of failing to recognize what has been left behind, [the text proceeds to] three:
a profound censure of the extreme depth of this deluded inversion.
"You all are people who are doubly deluded within delusion.
You have abandoned the Great Mind to identify with fleeting thoughts; it is like discarding the ocean to identify with a bubble.
You are already deluded, yet you further cling to these fleeting thoughts as the Great Mind—like claiming a bubble is the ocean. This is a doubling of your delusion. Therefore it is said:"

Those lost in delusion are twice as many. The detailed demonstration that the correct and the inverted both arise from the mind is hereby concluded. △ Fourth, combining this with the previous analogy shows there is no error:
it is like my hanging down my hand; they are without distinction. The Tathāgata calls such people those who are to be pitied.
This section summarizes the aforementioned erroneous attachment that recognizes the delusive while neglecting the real, concluding with the previous analogy:
it is merely like an arm hanging downward; how could there truly be anything lost? Thus, the teaching and the analogy do not contradict one another.
Had the upward-pointing position been considered inverted, one would have said, "It is like my hand pointing upward"; how then could one have said, "the hand hanging down"? Consider this carefully.
The Tathāgata calls them objects of compassion. As it is said: "If one were to actually lose what is truly one's own, that might not seem a cause for deep pity;
but now, though there is originally nothing lost, they are as if constantly losing it—like one who possesses a jewel yet remains in poverty.

Therefore, their kinsmen and friends sigh with sympathy and reprimand them earnestly. Herein, both aspects are clarified: although they are inverted, they do not lose [the nature]; and although they do not...
This would result in error and inversion. To understand the former meaning is not to isolate the inherently existent;

to understand the latter meaning is not to abandon cultivation. This is also the principle that nature and cultivation do not obstruct one another. (Previously, when Ānanda heard the rebuke that it was not the mind, he was startled and thought that if he abandoned this, there would be nothing else—reducing him to being like earth or wood.

The Tathāgata comforted him, merely granting that the true mind has a substance, but this was not yet the formal revelation of the true mind. It was like promising someone an object and only giving it to them on a later day. Changshui [Zhuan] stated at that point: "The true mind was revealed," because of that promise.)

What true benefit could there be in this? Therefore, within this section on "Non-Loss," the two aspects of the correct and the inverted are precisely the main text that reveals the True Mind. At this point, Ānanda finally realizes that beyond the objects of the sensory conditions, there exists such a vast and great essence of mind, and that what the Tathāgata promised is indeed not false.

To compare this with his previous words of promise, it is truly profound and flavorful to contemplate them together. It can be seen that in interpreting Buddhist scriptures, it is essential to be able to detail the flow of the discourse; one must not be careless or misinterpret the meaning.
However, while this section seems to complete the first cycle of investigating the mind, the subsequent six rounds of inquiry serve to search out and resolve remaining doubts.
Thus ends the section on demonstrating that seeing is not lost. △ Five: Demonstrating that seeing has no source of return.

Looking back at the preceding sections, one can say that the Buddha’s instruction was given with his whole heart and full disclosure. Yet Ānanda was unable to fully comprehend it and harbored various doubts;
therefore, there are the subsequent sections below. Had the Buddha intended even slightly to refute the nature of seeing, this would have been superfluous.
One might doubt this; would you truly be willing to accept it? The words that shatter deluded views are sufficient to know that [the former interpretation] is incorrect.
In this section, "returning" implies "departing. While the heading specifically indicates the sense of departure, the text itself contains the sense of arrival.

This merely clarifies that there is no coming or going. Examining Ānanda’s prior request for the simultaneous fulfillment of both the meanings of "quiescence" (*śānta*) and "permanence" (*nitya*), it is divided into four parts.

First, Ānanda seeks a definitive resolution regarding what to adopt and what to reject; this is further divided into four sections. The first describes how, although he has heard the Dharma and awakened to his original mind...
"Ānanda, having received the Buddha’s compassionate salvation and profound instruction, I wept and joined my palms, addressing the Buddha:
'Although I have received such wondrous sounds from the Buddha and awakened to the wondrous, luminous mind—the fundamentally perfect and eternally abiding ground of the heart—'"
"The Compassionate Savior" refers to saving [beings] from their inverted states and their sinking into suffering.

"The Profound Instructor" refers to instructing them so that they may fully comprehend Perfect Universal Knowledge (*samyak-saṃbuddha*). Because he was moved by the Buddha’s profound compassion, he came to shed tears.

Even the single character "though" (*guān*) implies that there is still something he suspects he has not yet fully comprehended. The final two lines summarize the three preceding sections. They encompass...
Encompassing empty space is called "round" (*yuan*); pervading all phenomena is called "full" (*man*). This restates the meaning of the preceding section on "not losing.

"Constant" means not ceasing; "abiding" means not moving. These merely restate the two preceding sections. △ Second, clarifying the mind that does not abandon the conditions for awakening to the Dharma.
Yet I have awakened to the Buddha’s manifested voice of Dharma and my present mind perceiving that mind; this is truly what one should look up to and revere.
This passage describes how, upon receiving the teaching and awakening to the Way, he attributes the entire merit to the mind of listening and mental engagement with the Dharma.
For Ānanda, a man of vast learning who values the Dharma above all else, regarding this kind of mind that perceives and awakens through the conditions of the Dharma, it was even more so...
"It is difficult to relinquish. This means: one might perhaps be able to cast aside a mind that conditions objects through separate seeds;

however, when I now realize the Dharma taught by the Buddha, I am currently employing this conditioning mind to receive and comprehend it, relying upon its very function. How could I suddenly abandon it?
△ Third, explaining why he does not yet dare to claim the original mind as his own.
I have merely attained this mind, yet I do not yet dare to recognize it as my original, fundamental mind-ground.

This "mind" refers to the wondrously luminous essence of the mind described above. Because one does not abandon the mind that takes the conditions for awakening as its object, it is said that one has "merely attained" it;
conversely, regarding the perfect, eternally abiding true mind, one still dares not recognize it as the original, fundamental mind.

As for the stage of "ground" (bhūmi): one ought to recognize this [truth] by relinquishing that [delusion]. Now, since you cannot bear to relinquish that mind which conditions [objects], you likewise do not dare to recognize and take hold of this [truth].
Furthermore, if you were to relinquish this mind that conditions phenomena, what would there be to receive and uphold the Buddha-dharma hereafter?
Even if you did not begrudge this conditioning mind, would you not nonetheless value the Buddha-dharma alone? This is the same as what follows below.
The text asks: "How can one know that this is my true nature? A certain class of people conversely doubts the meaning of the True Mind.

Traditionally, they have pointed to the conditioned mind (*yuanxin*) as being this mind; this is utterly devoid of meaning. Truly, since they still stubbornly cling to it and refuse to let go, how could they dare to recognize it [as the True Mind]?
4. A Prayer for the Tathāgata to Resolve What to Accept and What to Reject.
I pray that the Buddha, out of compassion, will proclaim his perfect voice to uproot my doubts and lead me to the unsurpassed path.
This perfect voice possesses three inconceivable qualities: first, those from different regions and diverse species all hear it as their own fundamental language;

second, whether their capacity be great or small, shallow or deep, all benefit according to their understanding; third, even those separated by distance who possess the karmic affinity perceive it as being right before their eyes.

As for the root of doubt: it takes both the conditioned mind and the true mind as its object, holding to both without resolution. Because this root is deep within the mind and difficult to uproot, one seeks the Buddha to extract it.
The "Unsurpassed Way" refers to *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*. It is like a person who is confused at a forked road; a guide points out the way.
Only then may you resolve this single point and depart. △ Second, the Tathāgata refutes and reveals the two minds. "Refute" means to refute the mind that relies on conditions;
"reveal" means to reveal the nature of seeing. This is divided into two parts. First, refuting the conditioned mind as having a point of return, which is further divided into three.

First, first refuting the dharmas that serve as objects—namely, the sounds of the Dharma being preached now. Because the depth of the mind that relies on conditions has not yet been abandoned, it is entirely... [text continues]

Because one holds the Dharma in high esteem, one must break through the notion that phenomena are not real; thus, the mind that takes them as objects naturally relinquishes them. This is divided into three parts.
First, the teaching on the Dharma:
The Buddha told Ānanda, "If you still listen to the Dharma with a mind that takes objects as its basis, this Dharma is also merely an object; it is not the attainment of the nature of reality."
The "condition" of the mind-condition refers to the object of perception (*ālambana*). The "condition" of the dharma-condition refers to the sensory objects (*viṣaya*).
Since the sound of the Dharma is subsumed under the sensory object of sound, it is likewise not ultimate reality. If it falls upon paper and ink, it is even more clearly a sensory object of form.

The final phrase precisely reveals the reason why these are not ultimate reality. "Dharmatā" (the nature of phenomena) is the true principle. Master Yuan said: "The teachings expound the true principle; the principle is the multitude..."

The mind that gives rise [to phenomena]. Therefore, one knows that the wondrously luminous ground of the mind is precisely the true principle (*tattva*). How could one possibly cling to the verbal teachings as being the true principle?
△ Second, the explanation by way of analogy, which is further divided into two parts. First, the analogy of observing the mind based on the Dharma.
It is like a person pointing out the moon to another with their finger; that person, by means of the finger, should look at the moon.

The "upper person" (the one pointing) is a metaphor for the speaker of the Dharma; the "two lower persons" (the one being pointed at) are metaphors for the listeners of the Dharma; and the "finger" is a metaphor for the Dharma itself.
The moon serves as a metaphor for the listener’s own mind; pointing at the moon serves as a metaphor for the speaker revealing the mind.

Just as one should look at the moon because of the finger, so too, upon hearing the teaching, one should naturally turn to contemplate the mind. △ Second, the metaphor of grasping the finger while forgetting the moon.
Furthermore, there are two [points]. First, the direct illustration of grasping at what has been forgotten:

if one again observes the finger and takes it to be the body of the moon, this is a metaphor for those who merely cling to the Buddha’s verbal teachings without understanding how to turn back and observe their own minds. Second, the dual presentation.
There are two faults. This is divided into two parts. First, the fault of losing both the object and the means.
How could this person merely lose the lunar disc? They would also lose their finger. Why is this? Because the finger pointed out was for the sake of the bright moon.
It should rightly be said: This person not only fails to comprehend his own mind, but he also does not understand the intent of the teaching. Why is this?
Because he takes the teachings of others to be his own mind; since he cannot distinguish between self and other, how can he know the intent of the teaching?
△ Second, the fault of being simultaneously deluded regarding the characteristics of phenomena (*dharmalakṣaṇa*).
It is not merely that they have lost the finger; they also fail to recognize light and darkness. Why is this?
Because they take the very substance of the finger to be the nature of the moon’s light, and thus they lack any discernment of the two natures of light and darkness.
One should rightly say: This person not only fails to understand the meaning of the teaching, but also fails to comprehend the essence and characteristics of the mind of the teaching.
Why is this? The teaching takes the sensory object of sound as its essence and takes the absence of self-reflective awareness as its characteristic.
The mind takes spiritual cognition as its essence and takes inherent, original awareness as its characteristic. This person [takes] the sensory object that lacks reflection...
This is because there is a mind that illumines; since "illumination" and "non-illumination" are not two distinct things, this can be clearly seen by examining the Dharma and its analogies in detail.
△ Third, the conclusion and determination.
You are also like this.

To say that your deluded mind is deluded regarding the teaching, and that the essence and characteristics of the mind deluded regarding the teaching are no different from the lost moon, the lost finger, and the lost light and darkness—is precisely the same.
The refutation of the dharmas that serve as objects of perception is now complete. Part Two.
One must first refute the mind that takes [the teaching] as its object before one can uproot the very foundation of the mind that clings to and does not relinquish that object;

this is because the primary task is to refute the mind that takes the object as its focus. This section is divided into three parts: first, the direct refutation of the mind that takes the sound of the teaching as its object, which serves to distinguish it from subsequent objects such as forms and so forth, as these are treated incidentally.
This is because [the objection] arises solely due to the failure to relinquish the mind that takes the Buddha’s vocal teachings as its object.
This is refuted. Furthermore, even granting for a moment that apart from sound there must exist [consciousness],

if you take this discriminating mental state regarding my spoken words as being your mind, then this mind itself ought to possess the nature of discrimination independently of the discriminating sounds.
One discriminates the sounds of dharmas and then takes that which is capable of discriminating as one’s own true mind; this is precisely not abandoning the conditioned mind.
One lets this mind go downward, causing it to leave behind the sensory object of sound and seek the self-nature of discrimination itself.

△ Second, the illustration clarifying that there is no nature apart from sound. This is further divided into two parts. First, presenting the analogy. This is further divided into two. First, the actual application of the guest... [text fragment]
Metaphor:
It is like a traveler who stays at an inn; having halted for a short while, he departs and never remains permanently.

The previous Buddha used the metaphor of a guest solely to represent the body and its objects. I, however, say it also represents the mind that conditions the body and its objects. This [is the teaching of] this Buddha.
Using the guest as a correct analogy for the conditioned mind. Second, it is shown by contrast through the host:

although the attendant at the pavilion goes nowhere and is thus called the "host of the pavilion," this passage uses the contrast merely to show that the conditioned mind is not the host; in reality, it is the nature of seeing itself that constitutes the host.
...so it is. △ Second, the application of the principle (*dharmasama*). This also has two parts. First, the application of the primary subject to the analogy:
"This too is likewise. If it were truly your mind, then it would have nowhere to go."
It is said that one should be like the innkeeper. △ Second, the subsequent application of the guest analogy.
How is it that by departing from sound, there is no nature of discrimination?

Regarding "departing from sound, there is no nature," does this mean that one merely stays for a short while like a guest and then departs? This is precisely the refutation of [the notion of] conditions.
The examination of the mind regarding sound is concluded. △ Second, the simultaneous refutation of the mind that perceives form:

This is not merely the case with the discriminative mind regarding sound; even when one discriminates one's own appearance, it is devoid of all phenomenal characteristics and lacks any nature of discrimination.

The "discriminating mind regarding sound" refers to the discriminating mind directed toward sound. That sound has no intrinsic nature apart from form can be understood by applying the same principle as that which holds for sound having no intrinsic nature apart from itself.
△ Third, the mind that extensively reaches and conditions phenomena.
In this way, up to the point where all conceptual discrimination is entirely absent—neither form nor emptiness—the Kauśikas and others mistakenly regard this as the "Primal Truth" (Tattva).
It is free from the conditions of all dharmas and possesses a nature devoid of discrimination.
The phrase "and so on, up to" follows the same pattern as the preceding two sense-objects, sound and form.

It refers to the intermediate categories—excluding smell, taste, and touch, as well as half of the objects included in the sphere of mental phenomena (*dharmāyatana*)—which constitute the objects of arising. By setting aside the other half, which constitutes the objects of cessation, they are combined and designated as the "Primal Essence" (*mūlatattva*).

"Completely devoid of conceptual discrimination" means that regarding the five sensory objects mentioned previously, as well as the objects arising from the sphere of mental phenomena (dharmāyatana), one does not engage in conceptualization;

this is what is meant by "internally maintaining a state of profound stillness. "Neither form nor emptiness" refers to the objects of focus of the last three of the eight meditative absorptions (dhyāna).
Because it is detached from all forms and so forth that constitute the objects of the previous four [dhyānas], it is not form (*rūpa*).

Furthermore, because it is detached from the infinite space that constitutes the object of the Sphere of Infinite Space (*ākāśānantyāyatana*), it is not space. Indeed, from the Sphere of Infinite Consciousness (*vijñānānantyāyatana*) up to the Sphere of Neither-Perception-Nor-Non-Perception (*naivasaṃjñānāsaṃjñāyatana*), all objects of focus are this very realm;
it is simply the cessation of sensory objects within the sphere of mental phenomena (*dharmāyatana*). Kauśali—this is the Chinese translation.
This is not clearly explained. It refers to Makkhali; only when these three characters are joined together do they form a single name, which is actually his mother’s name.
This follows the precedent of naming someone after their mother. Those who are ignorant fail to understand this and establish [the name] erroneously.
"Ming" (冥) means obscure and indistinguishable; "di" (諦) is merely a false claim of reality. For the non-Buddhists establish twenty-five *tattvas* (truths), the first of which is titled...

Regarding the "Ultimate Truth of Obscurity" (*tattvārtha*): they claim that the primordial obscurity gives rise to cognition (*buddhi*), which is the original source of all phenomena and is honored as the supreme principle.
This is precisely equivalent to the view that it is neither form nor emptiness. The word "zhū" (諸) in the final two phrases is an auxiliary particle;
it functions identically to the "li zhū sè xiàng" (離諸色相) in the preceding section. The meaning is that even if the mind’s conceptual discriminations were entirely absent, it would still be merely...
This merely involves being free from coarse discrimination; as for the subtle, continuous flow, it is certainly not yet perceived.

Even if the objective realm of form and emptiness were entirely exhausted, one would only have become free from coarse objects. As for the matter of extinguishing the shadows of sensory dust, one certainly cannot be free from them.
If one were free from the conditions of the sensory dust of all phenomena, that would be the nature of non-discrimination, which is the same as the aforementioned freedom from sound and form.
"Non-existence" means that there is no distinct category [of self-nature]. Having completed the refutation of the mind that acts as the perceiver, [the text continues: Third, the conclusion:
if this mind has a place of return, then your own mind-nature must each have its own place of return; how then can it be the master?
In summary, these six sense bases condition the mind; each arises according to its respective object and likewise ceases according to its respective object.
It is like a shadow following a person: from whom it originally came, to that very person it returns and vanishes.
Therefore, it is said that there is a "return. As for what constitutes the "host," this refers merely to a guest who stops temporarily and then departs;
how could such a one be the host who remains eternally, neither going nor coming? The first section, "Refuting the Conditioned Mind as Having a Return," is hereby concluded.
II. Revealing that the Fundamental Mind Has No Return. In this section, the focus is specifically on revealing that the True Mind neither goes nor comes.
The permanently abiding [nature] is the host; it is vastly different from the adventitious, object-contemplating guest-mind, which stops for a moment and then departs.
This is why Ānanda was led to decisively abandon the guest and take the host as his master. This is divided into two parts. First: Ānanda requests instruction on that which does not return.
Ānanda said, "If my mind-nature has various points of return, then why does the Tathāgata say that the wondrous, luminous, original mind has no point of return?
I only pray that you will deign to show compassion and explain this for me."

△ Second, the Tathāgata provides a detailed explanation and demonstration, which is further divided into four parts. First, using the analogy of the finger to point out that the seeing-essence is precisely the True [Nature].
The Buddha told Ānanda: "Furthermore, as for your seeing me—this seeing-essence is the fundamental source of clarity. Although this seeing is not the wondrous, supremely clear mind,"
Just as a second moon is not the reflection of the moon,
so too, when you say you see me— that which is the luminous essence of your seeing— it is this very substance of the capacity to see,
the function of spiritual clarity, that emerges from the original source. This is merely citing its name for the time being.
This metaphor is indeed precise. Although it says "not yet wondrously brilliant," it subtly reveals the sense of being accompanied by delusion.
Since this mind is already one of the six types of clarity and is manifest and lucid in every location without obstruction, it inherently possesses the essence of brilliance.
It is only because the two kinds of inverted views and delusions have not yet been eliminated that it is said, "although not yet..."
"Subtle and brilliant" (*miao jingming*): this indicates that while he already possesses brilliance and clarity, he merely lacks subtlety. However, observe the single character "though" (*sui*);
it is used temporarily to suppress [the notion], yet within the analogy, it immediately elevates the essential truth. As for the phrase "like a second moon, which is not a reflection of the moon":
there are three aspects to the moon. The first is the pure [moon] in the heavens.
Regarding the moon: the second is when a person presses on their eyes with their hands while looking at the moon, whereby two moons appear;
that which is produced by the pressing is taken as the "second moon. The third is the reflection of the moon in water. The intention is to use the first moon as a metaphor for the pure, true mind;
the second moon as a metaphor for the luminous essence of seeing; and the third moon as a metaphor for the discrimination of sensory objects.
Now, when it is said that the essence of seeing is like a second moon, it clarifies that although it is not itself the true reality, it is in fact not a different substance from the true mind.

It merely carries ignorance; once this is removed, it is the truth. This is also like the second moon, which does not differ from the true moon in terms of being illusory versus real, nor is there any vast separation between them;
it is simply due to an extra pressure on the eye, and once that is released, it becomes pure.

That which is not the reflection of the moon clarifies that it is not the mind that takes external objects as its conditions; rather, it is merely a shadow of the preceding sensory objects, like the moon in water.
This differs from the true moon by being separated from it by a vast distance above and below; their natures as void and real are fundamentally dissimilar.
If one intends to cause people to definitively abandon the third month and definitively recognize the second month, then the first month is not far off and is already present.
(Question: Why not point directly to the pure and true mind, but instead employ this indirect indication and take such trouble to explain it?)

The answer to the previous statement—that it is made perfectly clear by awaiting the subsequent section—is precisely this point. For the ultimate mind that is free from delusion and purely true is possessed only by the Buddha. Even those at the stage of Equal Enlightenment still carry the ignorance of the "mark of birth" (*jāti-lakṣaṇa-avidyā*);

how much more so for those in the stages prior to the [Bodhisattva] grounds, including ordinary beings up to the fifth dwelling? What purely true mind could possibly exist before them? Nevertheless, although the truth is not yet pure, its essence never changes.

It is like gold within ore: apart from the ore, there is no gold; it is simply that the ore may be genuine or counterfeit, and unless one is a skilled smith, one cannot discern the difference. Therefore, the Buddha points directly to the fundamental nature as the mind, just as one points to the ore while speaking of gold. The gold is already present within the ore; it does not exist separately outside of the ore. In this context, it is simply because their ignorance has not yet...

[The text] is dissected. Yet, there remains a lingering delight in the single word "wondrous" (miao). Therefore, the Buddha briefly suppressed and elevated [the discussion], intending only to manifest its essential truth. This is not like the critique of conditioned objects (*ālambana*) for being without substance in the absence of mind. Various commentaries have erred here;

they are excessive in their treatment and too light in adding the name "conditioned objects," thereby conflating it with the three months [of the *Śrīmālā-sūtra*]. By insistently seeking a place of return, they seem to openly oppose the Buddha’s words. Even if there were logical grounds, this would greatly hinder realization and merely incite hesitation in others.

To dare not directly acknowledge the seeing-nature as the mind is a failing that is no small matter. It is because one does not realize that the *pratyakṣa* (direct perception) of sentient beings is inseparable from this nature within the sense-faculties and that there is nothing else to point toward.

Therefore, when the Patriarchs gave instructions, they mostly took it from the gates of the six faculties; this was to honor the Buddha’s secret mandate. During practice, one need only request to recognize this nature, and there will never be even a single failure. It is like someone buying gold ore: although it is not pure gold at the moment, true gold can ultimately never be obtained apart from the ore.
