If one were to discard the ore in search of the gold, not only would the gold be discarded along with it, but one would surely become confused by brass, and true gold would remain forever unseen. Is this not deeply regrettable? △ Second.
I grant that you may be shown the principle of non-return;
you should listen attentively. Now I shall show you the ground of non-return:

it is the essence of the clarity and brightness of seeing, which is without anything to return. △ Third, fully demonstrating that the eight characteristics all return. The old [commentary] takes the eight...

Furthermore, regarding the "discrimination of seeing" (*jien*), in response to the previous seven inquiries seeking the mind, I have already provided my analysis. Those seven inquiries were indeed superficial remarks;
yet you now single out these eight "returns" (*huan*) as the means for discriminating seeing, while still contrasting them with the previous seven inquiries—this is even more reckless speech.
Throughout the ten preceding sections, all were intended to demonstrate the nature of seeing (*jianxing*); yet you point exclusively to the eight returns, neglecting the rest.
In what dharma do they all discern? Furthermore, the preceding seven locations constitute seven major sections;
how could they be set in opposition to this single section? Now, I shall revise them collectively by stating: "The Seven Locations refute the mind, while the Ten Chapters reveal the seeing.

Thus, not only will the number of items correspond, but the essential principles of the mind’s delusion and the seeing’s truth will also be clearly distinguished. Furthermore, these shall be divided as follows:
The three categories collectively enumerate the eight characteristics.
Ānanda, this great lecture hall is wide open to the east. When the sun rises in the sky, there is brilliant illumination;

at midnight during a dark month when clouds and mist shroud the heavens, it is again dark and murky. Through the openings of doors and windows, one perceives transparency; yet through walls and buildings...
In the interval between these, one again contemplates the blockage; in the place of discernment, one again perceives conditions. Within the stubborn void, there is everywhere the nature of emptiness;
when the image of dense turbidity arises, it entangles the dark dust; yet when the sky clears and the mists subside, one again contemplates purity.
These eight types are all objects of form (*rūpa-viṣaya*). They are all the objective spheres confronted by the eye. Each possesses both an essence (*svabhāva*) and a characteristic (*lakṣaṇa*).
For example, the solar disk is the essence and its brilliance is the characteristic; the night’s darkness is the essence and its gloom is the characteristic.
Even down to doors, windows, walls, and buildings, their differentiation as emptiness, turbidity, clarity, and serenity are all its substance (*tī*).

Whether they are pervious or obstructed, empty or dense, pure or turbid, these are all its appearances (*xiàng*). These eight types of dust form four pairs; the intention is that each pair takes the opposites of their respective appearances as a contrast.
That is to say, light and darkness, up to density and purity, are opposites. Only the dust of empty space is turbid.
The inversion of essence and characteristics will be seen again in its proper place below.
"Discrimination" (*fenbie*) refers to the discrimination of external objects (*qianchen*), pointing to various things as being like a place where pines, thorns, cranes, and crows are mixed together.
"Conditions" (*yuan*) refer to various distinct appearances, pointing to such differences as straight versus curved, white versus black. What follows, "the stubborn void" (*wanxu*), is as follows:
"In a place where all things are entirely absent, that which is pervasively emptiness" refers to seeing nothing but a single characteristic of space in utter stillness.
This is because "form" (rūpa) is the distinct [different] color, while "emptiness" (ākāśa) is the identical [same] color; identity and difference are opposites, forming a pair.
Furthermore, this is evidenced by the later passage of the sutra, which states that empty space is the same and the world is different. As for the old commentary, it... [text truncated]
If one discriminates by means of a discriminating mind, then what difference is there between the characters below that serve as objects and those above?

Furthermore, how can they be perceived? Moreover, with what would the empty space below be contrasted? This is because all eight types [of elements] take on the characteristics of sensory objects and thus possess a "return" (reversion).
This demonstrates that the nature of seeing does not return along with the objects; rather, it exists as a complete nature distinct from the objects.
This differs from the previous major section, which held that the perceiving mind returns with the objects and lacks a nature apart from them.

Why, then, must there be further conceptual differentiation introduced here? The characters are the same, but their meanings differ; one must skillfully discern this. △ Second, each returns separately.
Regarding the original causes, there are two further points. First, returning to the original causes:
"Ānanda, you have all observed these various changing phenomena; I shall now cause each of them to return to its respective original source."
The various marks of transformation are the aforementioned eight kinds of marks; their original causal basis is the aforementioned eight kinds of substance.
Part Two: Investigation and Detailed Explanation. This is further divided into two sections. First: Explaining the Formation of the Single Mark.
"What is the fundamental cause? Ānanda, these various manifestations of light return to the sun. Why is this? Without the sun there would be no light;
since light is dependent upon the sun, it therefore returns to the sun."
Therefore, regarding the day of return: just as it is said that those who come together with the solar disc also depart together with the solar disc.
△ Second, establishing [the point] through analogy.
Darkness returns to the black moon; penetration returns to doors and windows; obstruction returns to walls and eaves; dependence returns to discrimination;
stubborn vacuity returns to emptiness; stifling turbidity returns to dust; and clarity returns to a cloudless sky.

In this context, when one contemplates emptiness, it returns to emptiness; when one contemplates turbidity, it returns to dust. This sufficiently verifies that the substance and characteristics previously [discussed] were inverted.
Other cases may be understood by analogy. The section on returning each to its original cause is concluded. △ Third, further clarifying the comprehensive exhaustion [of all phenomena].
Thus, all that exists within the world does not transcend these categories;
it is merely the grasping of the visual forms (rūpa) that correspond to the eye. Having fully demonstrated this, the exposition of the eight characteristics is now complete.
△ Fourth, the exclusive manifestation of the nature of seeing as having nothing to return to.
You perceive these eight kinds of objects through the luminous nature of seeing; toward which of them would you wish to return? Why is this?
If you were to return to light, then when it is not light, you would no longer see darkness. Although there are various distinctions such as light and darkness, the seeing itself has no distinction.

Regarding the statement that "seeing" is also of eight kinds: when the aforementioned eight characteristics are enumerated, each individual characteristic must be confronted with the nature of seeing.
If the nature of seeing were absent, by what means could one apprehend these characteristics? Therefore, seeing is also said to be of eight kinds in accordance with the characteristics.
As for the phrase "to whom should it be returned": this refers to the fact that the nature of seeing, within these eight characteristics, ultimately...
"With what characteristic does it return? This question below seeks to clarify that, in reality, there is no returning.

For if it were to return together with a single characteristic, by what would the various characteristics be perceived? Now, as each of the various characteristics undergoes transition, they are all individually perceived.
Thus, one can know that within the nature of seeing, the eight objects of perception come and go of their own accord.
They compete with and usurp one another; yet the substance of this seeing is luminously constant, unmoving, and unchanging.
How could it be the same as the mind previously described that pursues objects and returns along with them? The Tathāgata has finished refuting and revealing these two minds.
△ Third, concluding the previous discussion to determine what to adopt and what to discard.
"Those things that can be returned do not naturally belong to you; as for that which cannot be returned by you, if it is not you, then who is it?
'Those things that can be returned' is a general summary of the aforementioned six types of objects—sound, form, and so forth—which accompany the mind and return along with their sensory objects.
'They do not naturally belong to you' means that since they all pertain to external objects, they do not inherently belong to you. [This is a definitive conclusion.]
"You must certainly relinquish it; you need not cling to it with stinginess.
'If it does not return to you' refers to the fact that the essence of the eight kinds of seeing subsequently does not return along with the sensory objects. 'If it is not you, then who?
means that since it does not belong to the objects, it naturally belongs to your own fundamental mind. You must definitely recognize it and must not hesitate."
Thus it is. △ Fourth, the conclusion lamenting one's own delusion and drowning:

"Know that your mind is fundamentally wondrous, luminous, and pure; yet you have become confused and bewildered by yourself, losing your original nature and undergoing the cycle of rebirth within birth and death."
They are constantly drifting and drowning; for this reason, the Tathāgata is called "one who should be pitied.

The mind is the seeing of nature (*citta-darśana-svabhāva*). The original characters fundamentally encompass the three characters "wondrous," "pure," and "luminous. This is that which is inherently possessed and presently manifest.
The meaning of not being attained through cultivation is that while one is not displaced by the various sense-objects (*viṣaya*), the mind of discernment (*ālambana-citta*) cannot surpass them;

this is called "primordial wondrousness" (*mūla-mādhurya*). That while one is not obscured by the various sense-objects, the mind of discernment cannot be obstructed is called "primordial luminosity" (*mūla-prakāśa*).
It is not defiled by any sensory objects (*viṣaya*), yet the mind that takes them as conditions cannot doubt or confuse it; this is called "fundamental purity.

Those who are bewildered and distressed cling to and treasure the mind that takes conditions as its object. Those who lose their fundamental nature, conversely, harbor doubts and abandon the fundamentally wondrous, luminous, and pure [nature].

That they undergo the drifting and drowning of saṃsāra is entirely what they have chosen for themselves; thus, they are to be pitied. The demonstration that the seeing has no place to return is hereby concluded. △ Six.

This major section demonstrates that [the faculties] are distinct and not intermingled. It appears that the ancient commentary was entirely unaware of this; its questions raise doubts where there should be none, and its answers offer no explanation at all.
Thus, it constitutes a general misunderstanding and cannot withstand critical correction. I merely request that you carefully examine my present interpretation.
When one realizes this for oneself, right and wrong will become manifest and not difficult to distinguish. Furthermore, it is divided into two sections. First:
Ānanda, confused by the intermingling of objects and perceptions, doubts the self-nature.
Ānanda said, "Although I recognize that this nature of seeing has no place to return, how can I know that it is my true nature?

This doubt arises because, while he has received the Buddha’s previous instruction that this seeing does not return along with various phenomena, it remains in fact constantly intermingled and indistinguishable from objects such as those moving in water, on land, or through the air. Now, in the midst of these various objects...
We shall now distinguish what constitutes the nature of the view of self (*ātma-dṛṣṭi*) and what constitutes the characteristics of phenomena (*dharma-nimitta*).

To say that these are "inseparable" is because the intent of this question naturally accords with and clarifies the intent of the following answer. The emphasis lies solely on the character *wo* (self);
it does not emphasize the character *zhen* (true). Therefore, the interpretation of Wuxing is incorrect. △ Second, the Tathāgata [explains] the view of phenomena.
To clearly distinguish the self-nature, one first sets forth the subject and object.
When wishing to investigate and analyze, one must first list the nature of the perceiving subject and the objects perceived;
only then can one select and differentiate among them. This is divided into two parts. First, listing the nature of the perceiving subject, which is further divided into two. First:
The noble assembly beholds it. Furthermore, this is divided into three parts: first, the vision of the śrāvakas.
The Buddha addressed Ānanda: "I now ask you: at present, you have not yet attained the untainted purity; yet, by relying on the Buddha’s spiritual power..."
He sees as far as the first dhyāna and attains unobstructed vision; yet Ānanda, while seeing Jambudvīpa as clearly as looking at an *āmra* fruit in the palm of his hand,
had only just realized the first fruit [of the path] and thus had not yet attained the outflow-free (*anāsrava*) state, nor was his divine eye yet capable of seeing at a great distance.
Relying on the Buddha’s supernatural power, one can then see the First Dhyāna. However, by the power of the First Dhyāna alone, one can see only a single four-continent world system (*cāturdvīpaka*).
Anuruddha—meaning "the Undying" in this language—once received inexhaustible merit due to his past offerings. He was the Buddha’s younger cousin;

having been rebuked for sleeping during the day and subsequently losing his eyesight through excessive asceticism, he attained the fruit of Arhatship and acquired the divine eye (*divyacakṣus*), whereby he sees the great trichiliocosm.
It is like observing fruit in the palm of one's hand. Now, you mention Jambudvīpa; how could it possibly be inferior to the first fruit (srotāpanna)?
I suspect that "Sahā World" (娑婆界) is a scribal error by the amanuensis. Furthermore, the four views proceed from the narrow toward the broad, and their sequence can be clearly understood.
*Āmalaka*—this is translated as "difficult to distinguish. One might mistake a peach for a plum, as it is difficult to tell whether it is raw or ripe. In this land...
This is what is absent [in the previous stage]. △ Second, the vision of the Bodhisattvas:
The various Bodhisattvas see hundreds of thousands of worlds.
A single trichiliocosm constitutes one world; that which the Bodhisattvas see accumulates up to hundreds of thousands. In reality, those on the stages (bhūmi) see even more.
Although these are also extremely vast, they are all collectively limited. △ Third, the vision of the Tathāgatas:
The Tathāgatas of the ten directions exhaustively reach all pure lands as numerous as motes of dust; there is nowhere they do not gaze.
When exhausted, there is no limit; their number is like that of motes of dust, such that they cannot be counted. To the vision of the Buddha-eye, the pure and the defiled are all identical.
Thus ends the vision of the pure assembly of sages. △ Second, the vision of the ordinary class.
Sentient beings perceive with a clear vision that does not exceed a mere inch or two.
This "not exceeding a mere inch or two" has two meanings. First, it expresses the inferiority of [ordinary] beings in contrast to the superior.

From the various sages up to the Tathāgata, when compared to sentient beings—even if one exhaustively measures their capacity—it does not exceed a mere inch or two. Second, it [serves to] encompass...
All contain the impulse of life. Above, they are equal to the Tathāgata; below, they must be equal to even the most minute insects.
Thus, they extend broadly to the furthest reaches of the world and contract narrowly to no more than a fraction of an inch.

This is to say that although their perceived capacities differ, they are all equally the nature of seeing itself. The enumeration of the nature of seeing is hereby concluded. II. Enumeration of the Objects Seen.

"Ānanda, let us observe the palaces where the Four Heavenly Kings reside. Surveying all that lies between—beings moving on water, land, and through the air—we see various forms, both obscured and luminous;
yet none of them are anything other than the obstructions left behind by the mind’s discrimination of external objects."
This passage refers specifically to what Ānanda personally witnessed, intended for him to examine and discern for himself.

The Four Heavenly Kings reside on the four sides of Mount Sumeru (Dhṛtarāṣṭra in the east, Virūḍhaka in the south, Virūpākṣa in the west, and Vaiśravaṇa in the north), dwelling at the mountain’s midpoint at a height of forty-two thousand yojanas level with the sun and moon.
It mentions three locations: water, land, and the air; these three are cited here.
From the four continents above down to all things upon the great earth, wherever their various characteristics reside—regarding these "objective phenomena" (*viṣaya*) before one:
those encountered and remaining before the eyes are called "retention" (*sthiti*); those that obstruct and block passage are called "impediment" (*āvaraṇa*).
This refers to the retention and impediment of vision and hearing. Having first enumerated the subject and object, this section is complete. II. Selection from among them. This has two parts. First:
First, let him choose for himself.
You should distinguish between self and other within this.
"Within this" refers to the seer and the seen. "Self" is the nature of seeing; "other" refers to all [objects].
Regarding the objects: first, I have had you choose for yourself because I wish for you to examine them in accordance with my instructions, so that you may attain true knowledge.
Second, I shall now choose for you by proxy:
I will now lead you to discern among these appearances who is my own substance and what constitutes the characteristics of external objects.
The "one who chooses on your behalf" knows that you cannot discern [the truth] yourself, and thus causes you to borrow the Buddha’s wisdom and eloquence so that [the distinction] may become clear.
"To lead you" means to lead Ānanda’s vision; "to choose within the vision" means to choose within the Buddha’s vision.
The essence is precisely the essence of the vision. Having finished the selection therein: △ Third, the objects and vision are clearly distinguished.
Furthermore, there are four points. First, to correctly state that objects are not the seeing:
Ānanda, exhaust the source of your seeing. From the palaces of the sun and moon—which are objects and not you—down to the seven golden mountains, observe them thoroughly and completely.
Although they possess various kinds of light, these too are objects and not you. Continue observing further: the rising clouds, the flying birds, and the blowing wind.
Dust arises. Trees, mountains, rivers, grasses, weeds, humans, and livestock—all these things are not you.
To exhaustively reach the source is the very faculty of the eye (*cakṣur-indriya*). It is as the saying goes: "exhaust the power of your eyes.

The palaces of the sun and moon are the most superior of objective phenomena; the seven golden mountains and so forth are the intermediate objective phenomena; and the sevenfold [rings] outside Mount Sumeru are...
The surrounding [walls]—namely, (1) Dvāravatī, (2) Yāmakuṇḍalā, (3) Dāruka, (4) Sudarśanā, (5) Aśvakarṇā, (6) Hastikāśyapā, and (7) Mīnadvīpā—are all composed of pure gold.
Among these, light is the most abundant; therefore, it is called "various. "Gradually descending" refers to the characteristics of the lowest objects.
Even the rising clouds and soaring birds, when viewed from the Golden Mountain, occupy the very bottom. Your name corresponds to objects; this is precisely the seeing-nature.
Because the three preceding sections stated that objects are not you, this section is the definitive statement that objects are not the seeing.
△ Second, the correct statement that seeing is not an object:
"Ānanda, although these various natures of objects, whether near or far, differ from one another, they are all equally what is beheld by your own pure essence of seeing.
Thus, while the categories of objects have their own distinctions, the nature of seeing has no difference. This subtle, wondrous, and luminous essence is truly yours."
Regarding the "seeing-nature" (jìngxìng):
in the preceding section, it was stated that all things universally are not seeing. In this present section, from among all things, the seeing-nature is singled out;
it is manifest that it is not a thing. Thus, this section is the definitive statement that seeing is not a thing. Nevertheless, there is a distinction in the selection.
This Dharma is likewise merely a matter of discerning and distinguishing based on the differences between existence and non-existence.

For while the myriad objects arrayed within the nature of seeing manifest in a thousand forms and ten thousand appearances—this is "existence with difference"—the nature of seeing shines universally upon all these objects, illuminating them as a single, radiant clarity—this is "non-existence without difference. Yet, regarding this non-differentiation...
How could its essence ever be confused with the differentiated characteristics of material objects? Therefore, he concludes by saying: "Truly, your seeing-nature is not a thing.
△ Third, the refutation that seeing is not a thing. In the preceding two sections, the analysis of material phenomena and the seeing-nature has already been made clear.
From this section and the one following it, he reverses the terminology.

This section analyzes [the preceding argument] by using parallelism to clarify the two previous points, thereby making them more distinct. This specific section uses parallelism to clarify the previous point that "seeing is not an object.
Continuing from the preceding meaning, it states: "Objects are diverse, yet seeing is not diverse; this is sufficient to know that seeing is not an object.
From this, it proceeds to turn the argument around, saying: "If seeing were an object, then you... (and so forth).

The meaning of these words is self-evident. Because this point was not clarified in previous [commentaries], it led to a narrow-minded view that suspects there is no connection between them and that there are missing passages elsewhere;
this is truly a case of error being transmitted as error. Furthermore, there are two [sections]. First, the determination that [the object] is not a material thing.
This is divided into two. First, using a reductio ad absurdum to refute its visibility. This is further divided into three. First, if it were a material thing, it would necessarily be visible.
If you see these objects, then you can also see my seeing.
This section reverses the previous section, stating: "If my extraordinary nature of seeing were not present when seeing differentiated objects..."
If this seeing were identical to that object, then the nature of seeing would itself become something visible.
Consequently, you should also be able to see my seeing. Why? Because if seeing is an object, it must possess distinct characteristics;
would it not then be clearly visible? In truth, this is not so; I have merely provisionally conceded this point to expose its fallacy. 2. The Visible.
One must necessarily rely on those of like view.
Those of like view are said to "see me.
Because the phrasing of the preceding passage was difficult to comprehend, these two sentences are treated as a separate section. The meaning is that the vision of seeing me is, in reality...

There is no trace upon which to rely. If one takes from that [the claim that] when perceiving an object shared by both self and other, one then says that one perceives my perception—△ Third, the difficulty regarding whether it is seen or not seen.
"When I do not see, why do you not see the place where I do not see?
This means that my observation of things is truly not fixed: at times, when I cast my gaze and grasp at appearances, I see things;
at other times, when I withdraw my vision and detach from appearances, I do not see. If you were in the position of seeing what I see, you would see it as I do."
These are merely mistaken words claiming to perceive my perception.
If, when I withdraw my gaze and detach from forms, I do not see objects, why then do you not also see the very substance of my non-seeing and point out its location?
This is intended to clarify that if one cannot see at the time of non-seeing, how could one truly see at the time of seeing? It is not so.
It is merely the refutation of erroneous attachments. Having first used the "turning back" of the objection to refute the notion that [the seeing] is a visible object, this section is now complete.

II. Following up by opening two paths to jointly prove that the nature of seeing is not a material thing. Taking up the aforementioned point regarding the place where nothing is seen, he opens two paths—either seeing or not seeing—and uses both as counter-evidence to prove that the nature of seeing is not a material thing.

This is the fundamental intent of this section; it is extremely... (Note: The final character "極" appears to be an abbreviation or fragment, likely intended to mean "extremely clear," "fundamental," or "ultimate.")

The text is concise and subtle, yet its phrasing is somewhat obscure and abbreviated. Consequently, ancient commentators have interpreted it through successive layers of fragmentation, causing the original intent to become increasingly darkened.
For instance, their laborious and artificial attempts—such as reducing the fivefold structure of the *Guanjing* to three while obscuring two—are entirely incorrect.
Please examine this explanation in detail; you may perhaps laugh at it. This shall be divided into two sections. First, the proof through what is visible:
whether seen or unseen, it naturally is not that which possesses the characteristic of being unseen.

Regarding "if one sees that which is not seen": it means that if you maintain the claim, "I have already seen the place where you do not see," then [that which is] "spontaneous" (svabhāva) does not depend upon the expenditure of effort.
That characteristic of non-seeing is precisely the differentiation of various phenomena.
It is precisely at the time when [the self] is not seen that this nature is the substance of my non-perception, and all phenomena are the characteristics of that non-perception.

As for the statement that "naturally it is not those characteristics of non-perception," this means that since my perception has already departed from phenomena, you further perceive my own substance;
this, then, does not require the expenditure of effort to argue—it is naturally so. My perception is natural.

It is not that the nature of seeing does not perceive the characteristics of objects. Why is this? Having already transcended objects, it perceives them anew; how could it still be confused with the objects themselves?
(The point where commentators have fallen into error regarding this passage lies precisely in the phrase "it is not that the nature of seeing does not perceive the characteristics of objects.

Now, I shall restate this by examining both the time when objects are seen and the time when they are not. For at the very moment one sees an object, the nature of seeing is the essence of the "I" who sees, while all objects are the characteristics perceived by it. When it comes to the time when objects are not seen...)

Thus, seeing-nature is my own self, the substance that does not see; all phenomena are the appearances that it does not see. Therefore, when it is now said that [seeing-nature] is "not those appearances which it does not see," this means it is not those appearances that are unseen by it.

This refers specifically to all phenomena, namely the two characters "non-phenomena" (fēiwù). When these are joined with the preceding two characters "spontaneously" (zìrán), they form the same phrase as the later sentence, "spontaneously non-phenomenal" (zìrán fēiwù).
Thus, my categorization shows that both paths—what is visible and what is invisible—are equally established as being non-phenomenal. △ Second, proving through the unseen.
If you do not perceive the ground of my non-perception, it is naturally not a thing.

This is even easier to explain than the preceding section. When I am in the state of non-seeing, if you cannot perceive the essence of my seeing, then there is no need to expend further effort in debate; it follows naturally that my seeing is not a thing.
Why is this? If even that which is visible is not a substantial entity, how much more so that which cannot be seen—how could it possibly share the characteristics of material things?

Thus we know that these two categories are fundamentally as concise and direct as this. Let the wise examine this in detail. Having completed the definitive analysis that they are not substantial entities, [the text] proceeds to:
Two, concluding the establishment of their own nature.

"How can it not be you? Continuing from above: since it cannot be seen, and furthermore, as each successive stage is shown not to be a material thing (*vastu*), how can it not be your own self-nature (*svabhāva*)?
The refutation by way of inversion—that seeing is not a material thing—is hereby concluded. △ Fourth, the refutation by way of inversion that material things are not [seeing].

[The Master] said: "To see. This follows the previous section on the principle that when an object is not seen, it is not seen; this constitutes the category of "seeing. It is divided into two parts. First, the analogy of the confusion of objects leads to the confusion of persons.
Furthermore, at the present time when you see an object, since you see the object, the object must also see you; thus, their essential natures would become entangled and confused.
Then you, I, and all the world would fail to be established.

This point is somewhat obscure and abstruse; even the ancient commentaries offer no definitive attribution. When encountering the passage regarding "the object," one should supplement it with the following sentence:
"If the object were seeing, then it would be clearly manifest. As for the section stating that "the object is confused," there is...
Sentience and insentience cannot be divided. As for those who are confused regarding persons, your seeing and my seeing cannot be distinguished.
Although things may be generally categorized together, they are now treated by analogy with persons; thus, they are classified as insentient. The meaning is this:
when you now perceive various distinct objects, if those objects were themselves the very act of seeing, then at the moment you see an object, that object would also [be the seer].

"You shall immediately perceive that the essential natures of sentient and insentient beings are in a state of chaotic intermingling, such that there is no longer any distinction between the animate and the inanimate.
This is what is meant by 'the confusion of things. The final three phrases then provide an analogy:
if even sentient and insentient beings cannot be distinguished, it is all the more impossible to differentiate one sentient being from another. Therefore, when you see me, you instead become me."
It is seen in you; there is no one among the people of the world who is not like this. They destroy the worldly distinctions of "self" and "other," yet they are unable to establish [a true self].
This is merely a temporary indulgence; logically, it is impossible. The correct principle is fully revealed in the following section.
△ Second: The division of persons establishes the division of things.
"Ānanda, when you see, it is you and not me. Since the nature of seeing is all-pervasive, if it is not you, then who is it?
This section serves to turn [the discussion] to reveal the correct principle. It means that when you see me, if it is fixed as such, it is simply your seeing and not my seeing;
the distinction between 'you' and 'me' is clear and has never been confused or disturbed. This is the portion concerning the person. The final two lines [refer to this]."

He then proceeded with an analogy: "If sentient beings do not even become confused or intermingled with one another, then although your seeing-nature pervades all things—both sentient and insentient—they remain clearly and utterly distinct.
How could it ever come to the point that it becomes mixed into all these objects and is no longer your own self-nature? 4. Rebutting the Doubt Regarding Self-Nature.
Why do you doubt your own true nature? You consider your own nature to be unreal and seek the truth by taking refuge in me.
To doubt one's own true nature is to mistake that which is fundamentally one's own nature for something mixed with external objects. You consider your own nature to be unreal.
"You who take my words while seeking the truth," he said, "claim that the true nature resides within you.
Yet, you do not believe it to be true yourself, but instead take my words to seek the truth [within]. Your delusion is extreme. This concludes the section on "Manifesting Vision as Unmixed.

[The following] consists of two sections: "Manifesting Vision as Unobstructed" and "No Return. These have already demonstrated that [vision] must be the self-nature; this concludes the section on "Unmixed."
In this section, the pervasiveness of the essence is further clarified, which subsequently gives rise to doubt. [Ananda] thinks that the true nature must have a fixed essence;
why then is there no single, pervasive, true self that ought to attain mastery? Why, instead, is it constantly obstructed by external objects?
To resolve this doubt, the Buddha provides this section on the demonstration of non-obstruction. It is divided into two parts: first, Ananda’s doubt regarding the seeing.
It is indeterminate yet obstructive. Furthermore, there are three points. First, taking up the preceding thread of doubt, Ānanda addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One, if this nature of seeing must be mine and not that of another..."
The text here is also incomplete. If this were the case, one should supplement the line following "the nature of seeing" by adding: "is fundamentally all-pervasive.
Only then would the two concepts of true nature and true self fully resolve their points of doubt, and moreover, they would correspond with the subsequent passage.
△ Second, the simultaneous presentation of two views:
"I and the Tathāgata observed the Treasure Palace of the Supreme Treasury of the Four Heavenly Kings, residing in the palaces of the sun and moon; this vision was all-encompassing."
Throughout the Sahā world-system, he returned to his monastery; there he saw only the monastic grounds and the hall of the pure mind, beholding only the eaves and corridors.

As for the Hall of Supreme Treasures (*Vijaya-kośa*), it is within the Hall of the Heavenly Kings where all manner of jewels are present; hence it is called the "Supreme Treasury. The palaces of the sun and moon are both composed of *maṇi* jewels;
their halls, terraces, and ponds are filled with devas and humans. Although the sun palace consists of fire-*maṇi*, [it remains cool].
The *nirvāṇa* is accomplished, yet it is likewise cool and identical to the moon; it is only that its light is superior and, when cast downward, produces heat (one may test this with a fire-mirror:
when the light is cast down to produce burning, one can know that the substance itself is not actually hot). Ānanda sometimes resided with the Buddha on this mountain. Gu Shan says:
"In the beginning, the heavens saw only a single four-continent world (*cāturdvīpaka*). To say 'pervading the Sahā world' refers to a single minor *kṣetra*, not the Great [Thousandfold World]."
"Thousand. "Gārala. This is translated as "garden. This merely cites two types of perceptual measurement: the pervasive and the non-pervasive.
Below, he poses a strange question to gauge [the Master's understanding]. △ Third, expressing doubt to request instruction, divided into three parts. First, a strange question regarding uncertainty.
World-Honored One, this vision is thus: its substance is originally pervasive throughout a single realm, yet now within this room, it fills only the room.

Since my mind suspects that if it is said to be pervasive, it must be constantly pervasive, then while it was originally pervasive throughout a single realm in the sky, it is now [pervasive] in the room.
Why is it that within a single room, there is such uncertainty regarding its size? Second, [considering] the obstruction as the cause for measurement:
does this vision contract the large into the small, or is it that the walls and buildings have squeezed it and severed it?
Following the aforementioned uncertainty, one follows emotional delusions and remains undecided between two possibilities.

One suddenly perceives that the vision of a single world has shifted, yet it now fills only a single room. Is this because the vision was originally confined within the inner chamber, such that the large was reduced to the small?
Or is it because it was partitioned and severed by the walls? It must be due to the walls of the room...
It is simply because of obstruction that this occurs. Although one may see the body itself contract, it must also be due to spatial restriction for this to happen.

For example, when passing through a low doorway, one bends the torso and arches the back; this too is caused by obstruction. This is indeed the calculation of ordinary people, who certainly do not go beyond these two pillars;
yet they remain settled in this state without realizing their doubt. Ānanda has stepped forward to pose questions and provide clarification on all such matters.
I, a seeker who investigates the mind, shall surely attain great enlightenment by examining the Buddha’s responses through this very question.
You must take this most seriously. △ Third, the summary conclusion and request for instruction.
I do not now know where this meaning resides. I pray that you will bestow your great compassion and expound it for me.
This "meaning" refers to the location of the expansion and contraction of the Great and Small [vehicles], which is to say, its definitive location.
He asks by which of the four meanings the Buddha is definitively located, seeking a resolution from the Buddha. II. The Tathāgata explains the reasons for each case and instructs him.
This is divided into two parts. First, a general overview:
The Buddha told Ānanda, "All worldly activities, whether great or small, internal or external, each belong to their respective objective conditions."

One should not say that there is expansion and contraction to be seen in all activities, including other categories such as square, round, above, and below—these being the objects of the external environment, namely things such as celestial palaces, monasteries, and various articles.
This clarity is not fixed; it depends solely upon the object. "Expansion and contraction" here refers generally to continuity and discontinuity.
If one says that [the mind] contracts and is severed, then the nature of the mind remains intact.

When the mind clearly perceives that its fundamental source does not undergo contraction or severance due to obstructions, it becomes evident that the essence of seeing is ultimately incapable of being obstructed by material things.
That sentient beings falsely perceive the shifting of size has a distinct underlying cause, yet they do not truly know it themselves. This underlying cause is found in the following sections.
Section. △ Second, the detailed explanation of "giving" and "teaching. "Giving" (釋) refers to revealing the fundamental cause; "teaching" (教) refers to bestowing the methods for liberation.
This is divided into two parts. First, the analogy of forgetting objects through teaching. This section uses an analogy to clarify "objects" (*dust*);

that is, it reveals that the reason [the mind] is not fixed is due to objects, and teaches the forgetting of those objects, which is itself liberation. Furthermore, this has two parts. First, clarifying the non-...

It is determined by the object. Furthermore, there are two [points]: first, showing that both are indeterminate; second, referring to the settled and the unsettled. Furthermore, there are three [points]:
first, briefly citing a single analogy.
For example, seeing a square void within a square vessel is a metaphor for perceiving the Great [Dharmadhātu] within a single realm (*dhātu*).
Square and round are fundamentally used to illustrate one another; by citing one, the others can be understood by analogy.
△ Second, opening the path with two questions.
I ask you again: Is the square space seen within this square vessel definitely square, or is it not definitely square?
This is analogous to the view of a single realm within the Dharma; is that which is perceived definitely great, or is it not definitely great? △ Third:
Both meanings are neither.
If space were restricted by shape, then when placed in a circular vessel, empty space should not be circular; if it were unrestricted, then within a square vessel, there should be no square space.

Within the Dharma, if concentration were substantial, then entering a room, one’s vision should not be limited to that small space. If it were not substantial, then being within a boundary, its pervasiveness should not be universal.
This clarifies that if the objects of the boundaries, rooms, and so forth exist as discrete entities, then both meanings—substantiality and non-substantiality—are indeterminate;
to claim that there is both substantiality and non-substantiality is entirely incorrect. △ Second, showing the nature of meaning.
It has no location.
You say that you do not know where this principle resides; yet such is the nature of the principle—how could it have a location?

You speak of not removing the various sense-objects (*dharmas*); thus, the nature of the principle is fundamentally neither fixed nor unfixed. How can you insist on seeking it [as something specific]?
Its certainty lies therein. The demonstration that uncertainty arises from external objects is complete. II. Teaching that by forgetting objects, [the mind] is naturally pervasive.
Ānanda, if you wish again to enter a state that is neither square nor round, you need only remove the squareness of the vessel; the substance of space itself has no fixed direction.
You should not say that one must further remove the directional characteristics and locations of empty space itself.

Both the square and the round are indicated by the title, yet here only the square is discussed; this is a brevity of expression, but the meaning must necessarily encompass both. The *Dharmapada* says:

"If one wishes to enter [the state where there is] neither large nor small, one need only forget the boundaries of the chamber; one should not say that one further removes the characteristics of largeness and smallness within the nature of seeing.
Why is this? The nature of seeing is fundamentally without largeness or smallness; largeness and smallness arise only due to external objects."
When dust is forgotten, the great and the small vanish. Once the nature of seeing is realized, what further need is there to eliminate anything?

It is just as empty space is fundamentally without squareness or roundness; these qualities arise only from the vessel. When the vessel is removed, squareness and roundness vanish. What further need is there to eliminate anything from empty space?
Nevertheless, the effort of forgetting dust lies within the causal stage of initiating practice; it consists simply of contemplative visualization.
One merely realizes that the chamber of the elements is fundamentally empty, and thus immediately ceases all grasping; it is not a matter of further conceptualizing emptiness.

When contemplation becomes thoroughly matured, the mind-ground suddenly opens up, and the body vanishes into vast emptiness such that the chamber of the elements is no longer perceived. This is merely a semblance of non-obstruction, not the true state.
However, this location is most difficult to penetrate. If one becomes attached to it and considers it the ultimate, one falls into the extreme of "one color" (ekavarṇa) and will no longer open up.
Only when the power of contemplative practice reaches its peak and the aggregate of form (rūpaskandha) is completely exhausted will the ten directions open wide.
There is no longer any darkness; within and without the realm of the body, the reflected image becomes clearly manifest, like seeing fruit in the palm of one's hand.

This is the true state of non-obstruction. This is precisely the point of reaching the fruition within the stages of entry (*praveśa-bhūmi*); at this stage, all afflictions, whether great or small, shall never arise again.

However, this is merely non-obstruction in terms of essence (*svabhāva*), not non-obstruction in terms of function (*vṛtti*). As for the non-obstruction of the Great Function (*mahā-vṛtti*), it lies further below.

Section. Furthermore, one should know that this "forgetting of objects" (*wangchen*) is identical in its function to the "forgetting of the object of entry" (*rushi wang suo*) within the subsequent "Perfect Penetration of the Ear-faculty.
This concludes the analogy for forgetting objects through teaching. II. Refuting Erroneous Teachings Regarding the Transformation [of Consciousness].
This section is divided into two parts. First, revealing the origin of the error. This is further divided into two. First, revealing the error through a counter-argument.

If it were as you ask—that when entering a room, the seeing faculty contracts and becomes small—then when you look up at the sun, would you pull that seeing faculty out until it is level with the face of the sun?
Furthermore, if walls and houses can obstruct and sever the seeing faculty, yet a small aperture is pierced through them, how could there not be a trace of continuity?
This interpretation is not correct.
When one perceives that the sun has expanded, how could it be that one is exerting force to pull it so that it appears expanded at the edge of the sun?

If perceiving the sun does not involve expansion, one should know for oneself that entering a room does not involve contraction. Furthermore, when one observes a hole being pierced, how could it be that [the process] continues...?

If you see that there are traces of continuity, it means the piercing was conscious; if there are no traces of continuity, you will know for yourself that there were no marks of interruption between the two.
II. Explaining the Cause of Obstruction:
All sentient beings, from time immemorial, have been deluded by taking themselves to be external objects. Having lost their original mind, they are turned around by these objects.
Therefore, within this, one contemplates the great and the small.
This constitutes a delusion regarding four aspects: first, delusion regarding objects; second, the loss of the mind; third, being subject to transformation; and fourth, the formation of obstructions.

The intent is to clarify that while the fundamental nature of seeing cannot be obstructed, and objects fundamentally cannot obstruct, sentient beings ultimately come to form obstructions. This is not [due to the nature of things].

It is because of the obstruction of external objects that there is contraction and fragmentation. This arises solely from the failure, since beginningless time, to realize that all things are already [within oneself], leading to the delusion of taking the self to be an object.
Consequently, one loses the fundamental mind in which all things are of one body.

Since objects no longer belong to one's own mind, they not only fail to follow the movements of the mind, but instead cause the mind to revolve around them. Therefore, one is constantly obstructed by objects.
Whether observing the great or the small, none possess the capacity for autonomy. These four categories may be distinguished; thus we know that the substance of things is fundamentally the mind.
To be deluded by it and take it as "things" is to allow them to obstruct the mind. It is just as ice is fundamentally water, yet when it freezes into ice, it obstructs the water.
One can see that the cause of this obstruction lies precisely in one's own delusion, whereby one is turned around by objects. How could it be otherwise?
Is it because of contraction that this occurs? Question: If observing the small is considered a transformation of the object, is it the same when observing the large?

Answer: Just as seeing a single realm restricts one to that single realm—it is precisely a transformation of the realm—how could it possibly extend beyond the realm or transform the realm within a room?
It is undoubtedly the same case of a transformation of the object. This concludes the section on exposing errors regarding the source [of these views].
△ Second, teaching by means of the transformation of objects. This also has two parts. First, the designation that transforming objects is identical to the Buddha:
"If one can transform objects, then one is equal to the Tathāgata.
This briefly reverses the fourth [point], "becoming an obstacle," to serve as the general heading for the following section. As for "transforming objects":

This refers to such wondrous functions of the various profound gates as "the small encompassing the large," "the large entering the small," "the large manifesting within the small," and "the small manifesting within the large.
Since these ten profound gates are realized only by the Buddha, one who can thus [penetrate them] is identical to the Tathāgata.
These exclusively directly manifest the great function of non-obstruction; it is only in the following two sections that the fourfold [classification] is established.
Detailed Explanation of the Barbarians. △ Second, the clarification of sovereign non-obstruction, which is further divided into two parts. First, the sovereignty of the body:
body and mind are perfectly luminous, remaining unmoved from the site of enlightenment (*bodhimaṇḍa*).
In delusion, the body is but a tiny fragment, confined and stagnant within its shell; the mind is obscure, following objects with partiality and limitation.
Thus, it is turned around and becomes an obstacle. Now, however, all things are one body—perfect and without partiality; one realizes that all things are oneself.
It is luminous and not obscure. The body is like empty space; the mind is as tranquil as the ocean. All things exist within the body and mind.
What thing can shift or move the body and mind? Therefore, it is called the Immovable Site of Enlightenment (*acalā-maṇḍala*).

Third: The intent of the inquiry throughout the one lifetime.
At that time, Mañjuśrī, the Dharma Prince, took pity upon the fourfold assembly.
Fourth: The ritual of the inquiry.
In the midst of the great assembly, he immediately rose from his seat, prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, joined his palms in reverence, and addressed the Buddha as follows.
△ Second, the words of the second inquiry, which are further divided into four parts; first, indicating the doubts of the assembly.

World-Honored One, this great assembly has not yet awakened to the meaning of the Tathāgata’s clarification regarding the two kinds of refined vision—the seeing of form and the seeing of emptiness, and what is and what is not.
These "two kinds" refer to the meanings of "is" and "is not. Form and emptiness collectively encompass all things; [this concludes] the final phrase.
In essence, the single character "yi" (meaning/point) doubly penetrates both "is" and "is not," thereby forming two meanings.
"Is" refers to the meaning of having no view of "is"; "is not" refers to the meaning of having no view of "is not.
Reading it superficially, it appears to lack two instances of the character "wu" (no), which is merely an abbreviation of the phrasing. △ Second, recounting the opinions of the assembly.
World-Honored One, if these preceding conditions—the forms, emptiness, and so forth—are that which sees, there should be something pointed out;
if they are not that which sees, there should be nothing beheld. Yet now, we do not know where this principle leads, and for this reason we are struck with fear.

Regarding that which "should have something to point to," one wonders why it cannot be pointed out. Regarding that which "should have nothing to gaze upon," one wonders why it cannot remain without gazing.
The meaning consists precisely of these two aspects: neither being nor non-being. That to which they return is the causal basis for those two meanings.
△ Third, examining the faults of the assembly.
This is not because his past roots of goodness were meager;
it is said that he was not like those with shallow roots of goodness who cling to existence and lack certainty.
He was not one of those who, out of frivolous doubt, would perversely distort and confuse the Buddha’s words. △ Fourth, seeking the Buddha’s instruction.
I only pray that the Tathāgata, through his great compassion, will clarify and reveal: what are these various objects and this essence of seeing fundamentally?
Within them, there is neither "is" nor "is not."
If one seeks to ask the Buddha what this "original state" is, then the causes and conditions of "is" and "is not" will naturally manifest themselves.
The final phrase, with its single word "none" (wu), doubly penetrates both "is" and "is not. It is as if one were to say:
"What is this seeing and these objects originally? Are they then neither 'is' nor 'is not'? This accords with the preceding discussion of "is," "is not," and "neither is nor is not."
The meaning is that this is the upper penetration; this is the lower penetration. Sentences of these two types are most numerous; all subsequent ones follow this pattern.
Thus, having raised their doubts by means of the absence of right and wrong, [the text proceeds]. △ Second, enlightening them as to why there is no right or wrong.

In the preceding section, Mañjuśrī described the assembly’s doubts as to why there is neither "is" nor "is not. Therefore, in this section, the Buddha clarifies the reason for this. It is divided into three parts.
The first part concerns the ultimate truth where there is neither "is" nor "is not. One should know that this section is entirely the perfect contemplation (*parivarta-darśana*) of all the sages;
practitioners of the Great Samādhi should earnestly investigate its meaning. If one can abide permanently within this state, [one will attain liberation].

If one is not deluded in every thought-moment, what doubt can there be regarding the attainment of Buddhahood? This is divided into four parts. First, citing the right concentration of the various sages:
The Buddha addressed Mañjuśrī and the great assembly, saying, "The Tathāgatas of the ten directions, as well as the great Bodhisattvas, abide within their own self-established samādhi."
Great Bodhisattva. There are two meanings to the phrase "solely taking those with the profound mind" from within the Perfect and Sudden Teaching (*yuan-dun jiao*).
First, it means "exclusively," signifying that this does not share the intent of ordinary people, non-Buddhists, or those of provisional and limited capacities.

Second, it means "from [the beginning]," referring to the state of remaining constantly present from the stage of generating the bodhicitta until the stage of attaining Buddhahood—what is called "the *nāga* is always in meditative concentration. There is no...
There is no fixed time; it pervades all four modes of deportment and does not consist solely of sitting. Nor is there any coming or going.
Samādhi is simply another name for the three samāpattis and is the general designation for the *śūraṅgama-samādhi*. However, this concentration is not produced by forcibly restraining the mind;
rather, its nature is inherently thus. Since beginningless time, one has been deluded regarding it; now, one merely does not remain in ignorance. △
Second, one realizes that delusions have no substantial reality.
Both the seeing and the conditions for seeing, as well as the perceived characteristics, are like flowers in the sky; they fundamentally do not exist.
In the preceding section, Mañjuśrī raised both the various objects and the seeing-essence (*darśana-viśuddhi*) as questions; now, the response likewise raises both in turn.

Thus we know that in this section, the single character "seeing" (jiàn) refers to the essence of seeing (jiàn-jīng), while the four characters "conditions for seeing," "conceptions," and "phenomena" (jiàn-yuán xiǎng-xiàng) refer to all objects.
Furthermore, "conditions for seeing" refers to the six sense-objects, such as form and space, and "conceptions" refers to the consciousness-mind of the six sense-bases.

"Phenomenal marks" (*xiāng*) refer to the physical forms of the six sense organs. The preceding text states, "The marks of perception constitute the body," which implies that the sense organs and consciousness are combined to form the bodily form.
Here, however, "the marks of perception" specifically refers to the mind-body complex.

This is because, within this context, the nature of seeing is integrated with the myriad external objects as well as the internal body and mind, forming a unified whole. To clarify their manifold differences is delusion;...
The single essence is originally true. This fundamental text clarifies that delusions are all like the seeing of flowers in the sky by one with an eye disease;
they do not exist because they are not created, for their original nature is non-existent. △ Third, realizing that delusion is identical to the one true reality.
This seeing and its objects are fundamentally the wondrous, pure, and luminous essence of bodhi.

Because the characteristics of perception enter into and are subsumed within conditions, one should know that the single word "conditions" (ālambana) subsumes the triad of faculties, objects, and consciousness;
it is merely set in opposition to the essence of seeing. The two words "fundamentally are" (yuan shi) directly answer Mañjuśrī’s question regarding seeing. His question was: [seeing]...
"What is the fundamental nature of this seminal essence? Now, the answer is given: "Its fundamental nature is the wondrously pure and luminous substance of Bodhi.
Among the three types of Bodhi, this refers specifically to the True Nature Bodhi (*tathatā-bodhi*).

It points to the fundamentally awakened true mind, which from the very beginning has been incapable of being bound, incapable of being defiled, and incapable of being obscured. This is the process of subsuming the delusive within the True.
This, too, is a case of subsuming function back into the essence. △ Fourth, concluding that there is neither "is" nor "is not":
"How could there be 'is' or 'is not' within this?

This intends to clarify that if all phenomena and the essence of seeing possessed two distinct natures, then one could speak of "seeing" and "not seeing. However, since they do not, such distinctions cannot be made.
This is the view. Now, regarding this single, wondrously pure, and luminous essence of Bodhi—by what means could one say it "is" this, or that it "is not" this?
This is why there is neither the view of "it is" nor the view of "it is not. [The interlocutor] asks: At the beginning, the Buddha took "seeing" alone as the nature;
yet he went so far as to clarify that it does not associate with the body, mind, or the myriad things. This seems to imply that seeing alone is truly real.
Yet all else is false, leading one to rely solely upon the nature of seeing (*darśana-svabhāva*). Now, when discussing the false, the nature of seeing is demoted to being equally a flower in the sky;
yet when discussing the true, all phenomena are elevated to being equally the true essence. This is indeed a discourse that reaches the ultimate limit of principle.
However, as for the human application of the mind, how is one to know where to turn? The answer is found in the following passage, which contains the fundamental basis.
The previous analogy did not resolve this difficulty; therefore, I shall now provide another analogy to further clarify the point.
True Suchness is like the water of a great ocean; the seeing-essence is like the light of that water; all objective phenomena are like reflections within the water.
It is only because the ignorant mistake the reflection for reality that they, conversely, forget the water itself. Now, I wish to cause them to abandon the reflection and recognize the water.
The substance of that water was so crystal clear that its form could not be seen; therefore, he first had him recognize the light upon the surface of the water.
Thus, he successively rejected the reflections as false and praised the light as real, desiring that he should come to know the water through the light itself.
Yet that fool further claimed that the light and the shadow each have their own distinct substance, groundlessly giving rise to disputes over right and wrong; therefore, [the master] spoke again.
It clarifies that both the light and the shadow lack any inherent substance (*svabhāva*), and that they are entirely nothing but water, which is their true essence.
Thus, one knows that although both light and shadow are said to be empty, when comparing light to shadow, the shadow undergoes arising and ceasing while the light has no coming or going;
the shadow is partial and localized, whereas the light is pervasive and all-encompassing. Furthermore, although both light and shadow are identical to the water, yet when [one] takes...
A shadow carries the peril of drowning, whereas consciousness possesses the benefit of attaining water.

Furthermore, a shadow is merely that which is reflected by external objects, while light is actually the self-substance itself, with nothing remaining beyond it. Thus, through this analogy, one may examine the relationship between the essence of seeing and the myriad dharmas:
although they are equally false and equally true, their distinctions in terms of gain and loss must still be discerned.
It is so. The ultimate truth of oneness is ultimately free from right and wrong. △ Second, the general metaphor for this oneness of truth, which has two parts.
First, the Buddha’s metaphor for the oneness of truth seeking out right and wrong.
Mañjuśrī, I now ask you: apart from you, Mañjuśrī, is there another Mañjuśrī who is Mañjuśrī, or is there no such Mañjuśrī?
The phrase "apart from you, Mañjuśrī" takes the single person of Mañjuśrī as a metaphor for the essence of the one true reality. Regarding the words "is there another," etc.:
The second line uses "is" (*suo*) as a metaphor for the perception of all phenomena. The final line uses "is not" (*fei*) as a metaphor for the non-perception of all phenomena.
The character "non" (*wu*) is identical to the character "not" (*fei*). At that time, it would have been more excellent to use only the character "not.
The translator was perhaps slightly over-refined in his choice. The meaning is this: although you, Mañjuśrī, possess but a single body, now, with respect to this very body—
Within this, is there yet another place that is Mañjuśrī? Or is there a place that is not Mañjuśrī?
△ Second, Mañjuśrī directly answers that there are no two aspects. Regarding this section, both of Wu-xing’s three correlations are correct;
however, because it is obscure and abbreviated, it is difficult to clarify. It is divided into three parts: First, accepting the single aspect.
"So it is, World-Honored One. I am truly Mañjuśrī.
Thus, the World-Honored One, having acknowledged the Buddha’s intent, gave a direct reply. "I am truly Mañjuśrī" means that there is only this single person;
this answers the previous analogy of "one true [reality]. 2. Answering regarding the absence of dual characteristics.
Furthermore, there are two [points]. First, there is no such thing as "being.
There is no such thing as Mañjuśrī. Why? If there were such a thing as "being," then there would be two Mañjuśrīs.
This answers the previous analogy regarding the emptiness of form and the absence of the view of "being. As for "there is no such thing as Mañjuśrī," it means that since I am merely...

"A single body. It cannot be further explained in this regard; this one phrase is definitive. Why is this? It is because [the text] raises a question and then provides an explanation to establish the point.
To say that it is "only" spoken of in this way implies that two Mañjuśrīs would be required—one right and one wrong—before one could contrast the wrong with the right to speak of what is correct.
Now, since there is only one, there is no "right" [to contrast]. This is expressed through a rhetorical inversion to reveal the truth. △
The second [point] is that there is nothing that is not the characteristic. However, today I am not without Mañjuśrī;
this answers the previous analogy of form being empty and non-existent yet not being without seeing. Following from the above, it is said that even this cannot be spoken of.
How much more so can it be said regarding "non-existence"? Since the two characters for "non" (fei) and "nothingness" (wu) share the same underlying meaning, they may be interchanged;
thus, it is clear that "non-non-Manjushri" is simply "Manjushri. Furthermore, following the character for "nothingness" (wu), another interpretation may be made.
Regarding the Buddha’s question: one may say "it exists" only if it exists as a replica of its original essence;
one may say "it does not exist" only if it is entirely non-existent along with that original essence. Now, Mañjuśrī, as for you:
do you exist as a replica of your original essence, or are you entirely non-existent along with your original essence? As for your response, it likewise follows this principle.

This constitutes a response. It is not necessary to change "non" (非) to "is" (是) in order to respond; this merely shifts the level of the discussion from the realm of existence and non-existence to that of "is" and "is-not.
While this is quite smooth in terms of the phrasing, the underlying meaning is somewhat difficult to discern. I have provisionally retained it for reference.
△ Third, concluding on the mark of non-duality.
Within this, there is in reality neither the mark of "is" nor "is not.
Because it is one, it is without duality. △ Third, the general application of the Dharma to the analogy:
The Buddha said, "This wondrous clarity of vision and these various empty objects are likewise thus."
This passage cites both the "view" and the various objects to show that they are identical to Mañjuśrī; they are merely a single essence.
Therefore, there is neither this "view" nor the absence of such a "view. This single essence is none other than the wondrous, pure, and luminous essence of Bodhi.

Having completed the definitive analysis that fundamentally there is neither right nor wrong, [the text proceeds to] △ Third, teaching the method for transcending right and wrong. Previously, one desired...
He explains that because there is no such thing as right or wrong, the two delusions combine to form one truth; thus, within this single truth, he provides a general analogy and a general synthesis.
Now, wishing to teach the method for transcending right and wrong, he causes the one truth to arise as the two delusions;
thus, regarding truth and delusion, he provides distinct analogies and distinct syntheses. Above, there are these three parts: the teaching (dharma), the analogy (upamā), and the synthesis (upanaya).
Section. Now, following the subsequent sections, this is further divided into three parts:

First, it reveals that the two aspects of truth and delusion are originally the wondrously luminous, unsurpassed Bodhi—the pure, perfect, true mind—which has falsely manifested as form, emptiness, hearing, and seeing.
"Fundamentally this" refers to first revealing its true nature in contrast to the delusions that follow below. "Wondrously luminous" signifies the non-duality of quiescence and illumination.
"Unsurpassed Bodhi" refers exclusively to the resultant essence of original enlightenment (*mūla-āśraya-parāvṛtti*); it does not refer to that which was realized beneath the tree.
This resultant essence is inherently possessed by every person; even though a Buddha realizes it in accordance with phenomenal conditions, there is not even a thread [of difference].
It is merely added to manifest that which is inherently present; hence it is called "unsurpassed. Being inherently free from defilement is called "purity";

being inherently free from deficiency is called "perfection. Taken together, these various meanings constitute the single true mind. The preceding section clarifies only the essence of this single true mind as the fundamental reality.
As for "that which is falsely constructed," this refers back to the aforementioned fundamental reality and serves to reveal its false appearances.
It is said that its basis arises from the single reality, which falsely manifests as two divisions: form and emptiness. These are subsumed under the objective division (*nimittabhāga*).

Hearing and seeing are subsumed under the subjective division (*darśanabhāga*). However, since it is said to be "delusory," it is not substantially existent. Yet, although it is not substantially existent, [it functions].
They appear distinctly different; hence, many are deluded. △ Second, separately citing two metaphors for the True and the False, which is further divided into two sections:
First, the moon and its reflection ultimately lead to the fallacy of "is" and "is not."
It is like a second moon. Who is this moon, and who is not the moon?
Just as the written characters rely on delusion to speak of two parts, these two parts are like the two circles seen when pressing on the eyes;
yet they differ from what preceded. The former was a single metaphor for seeing, whereas this one serves as a combined metaphor for both form and emptiness. Furthermore, it is due to...
This, then, reveals that the essence of seeing is like the fundamental substance of a twisted ribbon, while form and emptiness are like the secondary circles produced by the twisting.
Once these two circles are seen, both fall into delusion; who then is right and who is wrong?

The old commentary directly asserts that there is neither right nor wrong in this clarity, which seems to accord with the analogy of Mañjuśrī, yet it somewhat loses the sense of their disparity. Now, I shall harmonize the phrasing.
This appears in the subsequent text; it has no connection with what precedes it. It is merely the conjecture of a deluded person, intending to fabricate two wheels.

Although these do not truly exist, they appear distinctly different. If the ignorant were to cling solely to this, they would inevitably engage in vain speculation as to which is the true moon and which is not.
This cycle of dispute over right and wrong could never reach a conclusion.
To forget this is to fall forever into the duality of right and wrong; one will certainly be unable to emerge from it. △ Second, the single moon finally transcends right and wrong.
Mañjuśrī, there is only the true single moon; within it, there is naturally neither a "right" moon nor a "wrong" moon.

If one knows that the original month is but a single entity and fundamentally lacks two cycles, then there is inherently nothing of right or wrong to be spoken of, and one forever transcends the conceptual proliferation of deluded conjectures.
Since the "two months" in the old commentary already lack right and wrong, what need is there for the "one month"?
Furthermore, how would this relate to the subsequent text? △ Third, the application of the Dharma to each of the two metaphors, divided into two parts. First, the application of the two.
In the end, one falls into the trap of right and wrong.

Therefore, when you now observe this and those sensory objects, variously manifesting them, this is called delusive thought (*vikalpa*). You are unable to transcend the notions of "is" and "is not" within them.
These two characters [“dust” (chén) and “various” (zhòngzhǒng)] directly follow from the two preceding metaphors. The meaning contained within these terms—“dust” and “various”—is not shallow;
rather, they represent the Buddha’s compassionate instruction that the points of inquiry must be fully resolved. “Seeing” refers to the seeing-essence (*darśana-vijñāna*).
“Dust,” however, encompasses both the internal—body and mind—and the external—the myriad phenomena. Nothing is excluded. Mind, too...
"Belonging to the objects" means that it takes the objects as its shadows. "Various manifestations" refers to the body and mind;

when viewed from the perspective of the nature of seeing, it is prior [to the objects], yet when viewed from the perspective of the myriad things, both "seeing" and "not seeing" are equally false and deluded thoughts, failing to attain the reality, and ultimately unable to transcend this state of "seeing" and "not seeing. It is just like...
One may observe a second moon and indulge in arbitrary conjectures, yet in the end, one does not transcend the false discourse of whether it is that moon or not a moon.
△ Second, only when the single moon is unified do right and wrong emerge.
It is because of this nature of true, refined, wondrously enlightened clarity that it enables you to distinguish "the finger" from "not the finger.
Speaking of its essential substance, it is called "true refinement"; speaking of its illuminating function, it is called "wondrous enlightenment.

"Clarity" (ming) unites this substance and function, and is thus collectively designated as "nature" (xing); this is a *dharmadhāraya* compound. For the preceding [section] brought delusion back to the True, subsuming function into...
It is called "essence" (*tǐ*) because it is the fundamental substance. When it arises from the True as delusion, it belongs to the function of following conditions; thus it is called "mind" (*xīn*).
This is the harmonious integration of essence and function, hence it is called "nature" (*xìng*); in total, it is nothing other than the One Reality. As it is said:

"If you can thoroughly understand that the essence of seeing and the myriad things of body and mind are fundamentally the One True Nature, originally constituting a single entity, only then will you attain sudden enlightenment."
The myriad dharmas are entirely devoid of any distinction between self and other.

Why then would you be willing to propose that the nature of seeing is located before the body and mind and claim it can be pointed out, while claiming it cannot be pointed out when it is within all things?
It is just like observing the first moon: once one has falsely attempted to grasp it, such efforts become futile and both right and wrong naturally exhaust themselves.
This reference to "the finger" precisely corresponds to the previous point that, since there is a location, it is not the case that there is no pointing finger.

Furthermore, at first one stubbornly clings to what is before one, as if falsely claiming it can be pointed out; yet when examining it in detail against the object, it seems again as if it cannot be pointed out.

All of these are delusions caused by false conceptualization; they involve futile and chaotic attempts at measurement and estimation. Now that you have awakened to the single truth, these doubts are suddenly severed.
Therefore it is said: "Pointing out what is beyond pointing. The demonstration that seeing is undifferentiated is complete. △ Ninth: The demonstration that seeing transcends emotion.
All natural causes and conditions are merely the calculations and attachments of false emotions. This present nature of seeing is entirely not...

This belongs to this category; therefore, it is said to "transcend the realm of emotion. This is divided into two parts. First, the direct refutation of emotional conceptualization, which is further divided into two. First, the specific refutation according to the questions asked, which is further divided into two.

First, that [the self] is not spontaneous (*svayambhū*), which is further divided into two. First, Ānanda raises a doubt regarding spontaneity based on the meaning of pervasiveness and permanence, which is further divided into three.
First, acknowledging that the nature is pervasive and permanent.

Ānanda addressed the Buddha, saying, “World-Honored One, it is truly as the Dharma King has said: the awareness that conditions the objects of perception pervades the ten directions, remaining profoundly still and eternally abiding;
its nature is neither arising nor ceasing.”

This is because one uses the true seeing that is capable of seeing to see the deluded seeing that is seen; yet, this true seeing is itself not deluded seeing.
This meaning is difficult to distinguish, therefore it is illustrated by analogy using four points that are easier to discern.

However, as for why the seeing one perceives is considered delusive, while the true seeing is not considered delusive, I shall clarify this point of confusion after the Buddha’s subsequent explanation, revealing it from within myself.

Having reached the ultimate point in the preceding ten demonstrations of seeing—which revealed the True by means of the Delusive—I shall now dissect the delusion to bring forth the True; thus, this section serves to initiate that process. △ Third, Reprimanding and...
Exhort yourself further. Once more, there are two points. First, the reprimand:
"Even seeing is already detached from seeing; seeing cannot reach it. Why, then, do you again speak of causes and conditions, spontaneity, and the characteristics of their conjunction?"
"Even seeing is still apart from seeing" means that this true seeing is still apart from the self-characteristic of the essence of seeing.
"Seeing cannot reach it" means that even the essence of seeing cannot reach it. This is truly because when there is deluded seeing, [the essence remains beyond it].
True vision is entirely hidden. When true vision manifests before one, false vision has already become empty; therefore, it can ultimately never be reached.
As for the passage beginning with "How could," this further rebukes their stubborn attachment to their former tenets, making them even more inaccessible.
