Regarding the statement that the "conjunction" has not yet been explained, yet they speak of reaching the "characteristics of conjunction"—this is merely a type of conceptual proliferation similar to [theories of] causes and conditions, and is not [in accord with the truth].
They are those who have abandoned [all attachments]. △ Second, the exhortation:
"You śrāvakas are narrow-minded and lacking in discernment; you are unable to penetrate the pure true reality (*dharmatā*). I shall now instruct you."
One should contemplate this well. To become weary or indolent on the sublime path to Bodhi is called "narrow.
To be content with meager attainment is called "inferior. To lack the wisdom of discernment is called "ignorance.

To regard the parikalpita (imagined) and paratantra (dependent) natures as having no relation whatsoever [to reality] is called "pure. As for the true nature (*dharmatā*), it refers to both the Śūnyavāda and the Svabhāvavāda schools.
The distinction between the crooked and the straight is slight. The school of Emptiness (Śūnyatā) maintains that all phenomena possessing marks are entirely illusory.

Although this implies that emptiness and form are non-dual, one must perceive that all marks are not marks before they can be considered the true mark (dharmatā). According to this principle, one must dismantle illusory marks.

Thereafter, the true mark (*dharmatā*) is revealed. In the School of Nature (*xingzong*), mountains and rivers are entirely the manifestation of the *dharmakāya*, and the myriad phenomena are, in their very substance, reality.
Based on this, one directly reveals the true mark through the very phenomena themselves.

The two meanings [of the preceding discussion] are fully contained in the following text, from "from here until" onwards, where the aggregates (*skandha*), bases (*āyatana*), and elements (*dhātu*) are all treated as half-identical to the School of Emptiness (*kongzong*), because both schools alike destroy the false to reveal the true.

Nevertheless, because it follows both negation (*pratiṣedha*) and affirmation (*vidhi*), it differs from the "unmanifest" (*avijñapti*) of the school that maintains emptiness; thus, it is said to be "half-identical. The seven great principles are identical to the latter meaning;
therefore, the Buddha reiterates them, and the text clarifies them once more. Only by attaining this can one reach the ocean of fruition; hence, it is called the "Sublime Path to Bodhi.
One must exert oneself to the utmost, lest one become lax and retreat midway. This concludes the discussion on the ten sections above.
The first section reveals that it is detached from both faculties and objects, standing aloof as a solitary, radiant spiritual light.
The second section reveals that it is free from both body and environment, remaining concentrated and fundamentally unshakable.
The third section reveals that it shall never perish throughout the limits of the future. The fourth section reveals that it has been inherently present since beginningless time.
The fifth section reveals that it neither departs nor returns, standing aloof from all things and eternally abiding.
The sixth section reveals that it is neither mixed nor confused, transcending all forms and standing solitary as a unique banner.

The seventh section reveals that its nature is fundamentally autonomous, revolving all phenomena while remaining unrestricted by size. The eighth section reveals that its essence is inherently integrated.

Rong likens this to the single moon, wherein right and wrong cannot be distinguished. The nine sections reveal that his various mental states do not fall into the distant or transcend the external calculations of provisional schools.
The ten sections reveal that even his own characteristics are detached from transformation, entering into pure truth and non-delusion.
When the manifestation reaches this point, it may be called the ultimate of manifestation. The old commentaries generally treat it in this manner.
This reveals the underlying intent, which is entirely for the purpose of shattering [false] views. This is one reason why I could not help but provide this detailed commentary once again.
Specifically, it is because even within the deluded state of sentient beings, there still remain two kinds of delusive views that have not been eliminated;

therefore, it is said that "the true is revealed while carrying along the delusive. The section on "revealing the true while carrying along the delusive" is complete. △ Second, "Distinguishing the Delusive to Reveal the True. (2)
The various deluded views of perversion are like jade hidden within its ore; yet the true essence perceived therein is like the jade existing within the ore.

Therefore, the truth is revealed while still accompanied by delusion, just as one points to the ore to describe the jade. Although it is precious and not false, the coarse stone has not yet been split open.
A beautiful jade has not yet been polished; this [process] involves dissecting the false to reveal the true, like cutting through a raw stone to produce jade, whereby its brilliance shines forth.

Therefore, the previous deconstruction of consciousness—which deconstructed it until it was found to have no substance—constituted a "true deconstruction. This present dissection of the false reveals the actual substance;
what is called "not ultimately deconstructing" is that which appears to deconstruct but actually manifests [the truth]. This may be summarized as follows:
To refute this, it is divided into two parts. First, the request for permission to provide a provisional response. The intent of the request is far-reaching;

the actual response is found in the subsequent text, as it is not restricted to the original subject matter. Therefore, the Buddha granted the request accordingly. Nor is it restricted to the immediate context; hence, it is termed a "provisional response" (*kṣaṇika-prativacana*).

This section is divided into two parts. First, Ānanda’s request for instruction, which is further divided into two. First, the statement of his intention, which is further divided into two. First, the statement that he has not yet attained realization.

Ānanda addressed the Buddha, saying: "World-Honored One, although the Buddha, the World-Honored One, has expounded for our sakes the nature of causes and conditions as well as spontaneity, and the characteristics of both harmony and disharmony, my mind remains unenlightened."
The four meanings, such as causes and conditions (*hetu-pratyaya*), are those necessarily possessed within worldly conceptual proliferation (*prapañca*).

Therefore, although the latter two were not previously questioned, they are now presented together. However, there are two reasons for the general statement that "they have not yet been opened": first, while the words are general, the meaning is specific;
specifically, it refers to the latter two, indicating that the four meanings have not yet been fully disclosed. Second, regarding the meaning...
"Related" means that conjunction is related to causes and conditions (*hetu-pratyaya*), while non-conjunction is related to spontaneity (*svabhāva*).
If it pertains to the latter two, then the former two are likewise not entirely abandoned; therefore, it is said in general that they have not yet opened.

However, the intention is solely to hope for a further explanation of the latter two; there is absolutely no hope that the Buddha would once again sweep away the former two. Thus, the old interpretation is incorrect.
...so it is. △ Second, describing his bewilderment:
Now, hearing further that "the seeing of seeing is not seeing," his confusion increases all the more.

Originally he had hoped only for the Buddha to explain the meaning of "harmonious integration" and so forth in sequence; now, because he does not understand that "the seeing of seeing is not [seeing]," [he is further perplexed].
[The Buddha] saw that their confusion and distress were urgent; therefore, he first sought to resolve this. Having finished stating his intention, [the assembly] made this plea:
"We humbly pray that your vast compassion will bestow the eye of great wisdom upon us, revealing and clarifying the luminous purity of our awakened mind. Having spoken these words, they fell silent.
Prostrating with tears of compassion, he received the holy command.
He who observes emptiness with the eye of wisdom—the Buddha revealed the pure reality (*dharmatā*), and Ānanda further requested the eye of wisdom.
Then it is certain that this [text] below will fully reveal the empty *tathāgatagarbha*. If even a subtle doubt remains in the mind, then awakening will not be clear and pure;
thus, one must resolve this confusion and open what has not yet been opened. Only then will the awakened mind be entirely clear and pure.
△ Second, the Buddha’s compassionate permission to speak, divided into two parts. First, about to demonstrate the sublime practice.
At that time, the World-Honored One, out of compassion for Ānanda and the great assembly,
was about to expound the sublime path of practice consisting of the various *samādhis* of the Great *Dhāraṇī*.
This is the sūtra-recorder’s narration of the Buddha’s intention. If one examines the two characters "about to" (*jiangyu*), the meaning therein is profound and far-reaching.

It pertains to volumes five and six; for generally, when one wishes to engage in wondrous cultivation, one first seeks true wisdom, and the extensive opening of true wisdom serves as the ground for that wondrous cultivation.
Therefore, while the Buddha is currently discussing the subtle and secret contemplation in close terms, the sūtra-recorder first [introduces it] from afar.
To introduce this: its purport is profound. *Dhāraṇī*—here translated as "total retention" (*saṃgraha-dhāraṇa*)—refers to the totalizing of all phenomena and the upholding of immeasurable meanings.
This is precisely for the sake of strengthening understanding and ensuring its universal perfection; yet, in practice, one should grasp its essential points.

Among the practices of definitive meaning (*nītārtha*), the cultivation of this sutra is the most essential and concise. Although *dhāraṇīs* pertain to both the Exoteric and Esoteric teachings, we shall here address them according to the Exoteric.
Thus, Guifeng’s commentary explains that he does not select the characters "many" (*duō*) or "one" (*yī*), but selects exclusively the character "non-existence" (*wú*).
This refers to the pure and perfect *bodhi*-mind. Now, one should likewise select the character "non-existence," which refers to the perfectly clear, non-arising, and non-ceasing faculty-nature.

The phrase "all *samādhis*" is a general title for the twenty-five perfect paths of penetration—the sublime paths of practice—while "the secret door of the ear" specifically points to the gateway of the auditory faculty. Such is the intended meaning.
Among all the gates of perfect penetration (*pariśuddha-mukha*), this is the wondrous gate of the ear.

With these two phrases, he explains the aforementioned *dhāraṇī*, revealing that within the gates of cultivation, the perfect penetration of the ear-faculty (*śrotra-indriya*) is itself the Great Total Retention (*mahā-dhāraṇī*). This does not follow the old commentaries which levelly divide it into concentration and wisdom, or shamatha and vipaśyanā;
rather, it accords with what follows: when Ānanda requested entry into the "flowered chamber," he immediately attained the *dhāraṇī* and entered the Buddha’s [wisdom].

The phrase "knowledge and vision" (*jñānadarśana*), as well as the Buddha’s permission stating, "I shall open the path for the sublime practice of the Unsurpassed Vehicle," and further saying, "One shall not give rise to weariness regarding the sublime *samādhi* of the Buddha-Tathāgata"—the meaning of these words is entirely consistent.
This sufficiently serves as evidence that this passage is a pre-indication of the subsequent gate of cultivation. II. First, opening the true wisdom. This has three parts. First, clarifying its...
He was not yet enlightened.

[The Buddha] said to Ānanda: "Although you possess a powerful memory, it merely increases your erudition; regarding the subtle and secret contemplation of śamatha, your mind is still not yet enlightened."
This is addressed to those who rely on extensive learning yet indulge only their mouths and ears, failing to realize the true meaning.
*Śamatha* is the fundamental, innate meditative concentration; "subtle and secret contemplation" (*vipaśyanā*) is the inherently endowed essence of illumination manifesting clearly before one.

Examining distinctions and giving rise to the mind to contemplate objects is called "coarse observation. Examining distinctions to regulate the body and sit in stillness, observing the signs of entering and emerging from samādhi, is called "subtle."
It is called "mysterious" (*mi*). Furthermore, to be free from delusion and cut off from marks is called "subtle" (*wei*). To realize that within marks there are no marks is called "mysterious.

Therefore, what is now taught—the seeing of seeing as non-seeing, up to the pervasive presence of the seven elements—is precisely the subtle and wondrous contemplation that is free from delusion and cut off from marks.
The two answers given by Pūrṇa Maitrāyaṇīputra in the following text are precisely the contemplation of marks and marklessness, which is the secret observation.
One should know that this intention illuminates the three Tathāgatagarbhas to their full extent; this is called true wisdom (*bhūta-jñāna*).
Only through this true wisdom can one subsequently engage in the wondrous cultivation. II. Properly Granting the Permission to Reveal.
Listen attentively now; I shall analyze and explain this for you.
△ Third, it also benefits those of the future, enabling all those with outflows in the coming ages to attain the fruit of Bodhi.
If even those with outflows (*sāsrava*) can still attain Buddhahood, it goes without saying for those without outflows (*anāsrava*).
△ Second, the detailed analysis and exposition, which is divided into two parts. First, the explanation of his confusion and distress.

Because Ānanda had not yet had his confusion and distress resolved, and because his confusion and distress became even more urgent as both [the former and latter] were presented together, the Buddha now first explains away his confusion and distress. This has already been clarified previously; herein—
Furthermore, there is no intention of repeatedly brushing away [delusions], as they resolve naturally; do not seek them by force. This is divided into three parts:
first, the dual presentation of the two views; within the single false view, it is divided into two, yet these are not two distinct views of truth and falsity. This is further divided into two:
first, generally exposing their faults.

Ānanda, all sentient beings transmigrate through the world due to two kinds of inversion; through the delusion of discriminative views, they arise in their respective places and revolve according to their respective karma.
This clarifies that if false views persist, such faults will arise; therefore, one must analyze and distance oneself from them.

This applies not only to ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*) but also includes those of the Lesser Vehicle (*hīnayāna*). It encompasses not only the segmented existence (*prātibhāsika-vaipākika*) of the seven realms of rebirth within the cycle of birth and death (*saṃsāra*), but also the transformational existence (*nairmāṇika-vaipākika*) of the two vehicles.
Since this is an object of delusion for both the ordinary and the Lesser Vehicle, it concludes [the section].
This is because the goal lies in the perfection of the nature of bodhi, which is neither arising nor ceasing. However, these two phrases first provide a general indication of the great affliction;
what follows below traces its origin, showing that it all results from the deluded perception being able to manifest objects, thereby giving rise to karma.
As for the mention of "two," this refers to the subsequent categories of "common" and "distinct. To speak of "inverted discrimination" is precisely to see [the truth].

This is the essential nature and characteristic of delusion (*mṛṣā*). It refers to: mistaking the particular for the universal (mistaking a realm that is originally one’s own mind manifesting through individual karma as a realm existing externally to the mind, shared in common with others);

mistaking the universal for the particular (mistaking a realm that is originally manifested by one’s own confusion and shared by all beings as a realm existing externally to the mind, having no connection to oneself);

and mistaking the empty for the real (mistaking what is originally a hollow shadow of afflictions and karma as a truly existent object with fixed characteristics existing externally to the mind). Regarding these three types of delusion, traditional commentaries have understood only the last one, while remaining ignorant of the first two. Up to...
This shall be elucidated below. One constantly maintains such views and interpretations; therefore, it is called "perverted discrimination.

However, this discrimination is simply a spontaneous, vivid, and unobscured state—what is known as "subtle continuous-flow discrimination," rather than the coarse discrimination of intentional calculation.
Generally termed "delusive views," its essence is precisely the subtle *ālayavijñāna*.

Within the seeing-part (*darśana-bhāga*), one portion is deeply deluded; this is what is referred to in the subsequent text as the "innate ignorance (*sahaja-avidyā*) that is the root of birth-and-death" as proclaimed by all Buddhas.
This passage reveals the essential nature and characteristics of the false seeing.

The final two phrases clarify that the manifestation of objects and the arising of karma constitute the fundamental cause for triggering the cycle of saṃsāra. The character *dāng* (當) is pronounced in the departing tone (*qùshēng*). As for "in its own place" (*dāngchù*):
The mind of the entire dharma-realm universally constitutes the locus of delusion; though fundamentally no such locus exists, it is merely called a "locus.

As for "arising," this refers to the manifestation throughout the entire dharma-realm of all worlds, both sentient and insentient—a point made in the subsequent text when it says, "within that which is devoid of sameness or difference, there blazes forth the formation of difference.
This is simply due to the manifestation of delusion and the subsequent invitation of karma.

This refers merely to the manifestation of the objective field of the homogeneous class (*sabhāga*). Regarding "when one acts," it means that within the very sphere of delusion at that particular place, one grasps and creates karma.
Regarding "transmigration," it means that one undergoes retribution according to karma, flowing on in succession to form boundless saṃsāra.
This indicates that it is not only delusion that manifests, but is further summoned by karma; thus, it is established as the objective field of individual karma.

Regarding the statement that both "location" and "karma" are "destined" (*bhavya*), this reveals two meanings: First, "destined location" reveals the meaning of immobility. It is like what is seen in a dream:
though there are immeasurable objects and immeasurable movements, one does not leave the bed or pillow; not even an inch is moved.

Second, "destined karma" reveals the meaning of the absence of external things. It means that these are merely produced by the illusion of one's own karma, which is falsely grasped and falsely experienced.
There is nothing else whatsoever. Thus, one sees that delusion can summon such great calamities;
therefore, it must not be left unawakened to, nor unshunned. △ Second, listing their names individually.
What are the two kinds of views? First is the deluded vision arising from the individual karma of sentient beings; second is the deluded vision arising from the common lot of sentient beings.
Now, the realm of the Mind-Only extends to the furthest reaches of the ten directions; it is my single mind alone, fundamentally devoid of any distinction between kin and stranger, or near and far.
Yet, now, being deluded by the false vision of seeing, one is unable to dwell in the Buddha’s entire body or receive [the Dharma] with the Buddha’s entire body.
Thus, there are those who perceive what they themselves maintain and currently enjoy as objects of intimacy;
and there are those who perceive what others maintain and do not personally enjoy as objects of distance.

However, these objects of intimacy are not merely the manifestations of delusion, but are further compounded by karmic bonds. For it is one's own karma that brings them forth, which then returns upon oneself.
Grasping and attachment. It is not that there exists outside the mind a real place where one dwells together with others;

therefore it is called "delusive vision through individual karma" (arising specifically from inverted discrimination, whereby one delusively sees what exists outside the mind as real and shared with others—how could this be true?). As for those who are distant, although they are not bound by karma, [they appear due to such delusion].
Yet it manifests solely through delusion; for one shares the same delusions as the multitude and consequently shares the same views as the multitude.

It is not an external reality existing apart from the mind that has no connection with oneself. Therefore, it is called "common delusory vision" (also because of inverted discrimination, one delusorily perceives an external reality existing apart from the mind that has no connection with oneself—how could this be real?).
One should know that this differs from the old interpretation. The old view held that "distinct karma" referred to a single individual.
If one were to define "commonality" (*sabhāgatā*) in terms of many people, it would contradict the principle that all phenomena are but manifestations of mind.

Now, we consider only Ānanda’s single mind as simultaneously possessing these two kinds of deluded vision; we merely distinguish them by classifying their karmic differences as distinct visions and their shared delusions as common perceptions.
Taking Ānanda as the model, one can apply this to all sentient beings: every person possesses both of these.

Only by planting these false views can one fully exhaust the principle. △ Second, each provides an easy example. The old interpretation claims that both "eye-disease" (*cakṣur-roga*) and "calamitous signs" (*upadrava*) serve as metaphors;
using them to illustrate the subsequent "one place" and "many places" contradicts the later text, leading to endless errors.

I have no time for a detailed refutation. Now, both are the term *dharma* (translated here as "phenomenon" or "principle") according to the literal character; it is merely a word used to introduce a phenomenon. However—
There is a distinction between that which is difficult to perceive yet easy to know; there is evidence for this in the subsequent text.

This is because, although the objects of immediate proximity are individual karmic products (*pratyeka-karma*), they are in fact shared and perceived by the multitude. Thus, it is truly difficult to discern whether they are distinct or illusory.
As for the vision of a circle of light (lamp-wheel) during an optical aberration, this is yet another instance within the distinct [categories], the most vacuous among the vacuous;

it is that which is most easily known to be distinct and illusory. Although distant objects belong to the same class of shared experience (*sabhāga*), because they appear suspended far apart from oneself and each is experienced differently, it is truly difficult to realize that they are the same.
It is delusion. As for the phenomena of pestilence, evil omens, and calamities, these are the "same within the same" and the "delusion within delusion";
thus, it is still relatively easy to know that they are the same [in nature] and empty.

Therefore, the Buddha cited the easily understood examples of optical distortions and calamitous signs in order to illustrate the subsequently mentioned cases—those occurring in a single location or multiple locations—which are difficult to understand. Question: The Buddha should clarify this next.
"Why are there no commonalities or differences? [The answer is: The Tathāgata’s words are never uttered in vain; his speech invariably dispels delusion.

Since he has already indicated "perversion" (*viparyāsa*) and further enumerated "distinctions," the "commonality of distinct karma" (*bhinna-karma-sabhāgatā*) must necessarily be an object of confusion for sentient beings.

If it were not present in the initial indication, why would he not clarify it accordingly? If it were absent from the final conclusion, what need would there be for such a forced addition? It is merely to follow the Buddha’s golden words with complete precision.
However, the reason this section on the "Conjoined Illumination" is abbreviated is that its primary intent is to emphasize the falsity of seeing, thereby resolving one's confusion and bewilderment.
It is divided into two parts. The first concerns the false vision of individual karma, which is further divided into four sections. First, it begins with an inquiry.
What is meant by "delusive vision resulting from individual karma"?
Second, [the Buddha] describes what is seen:
"Ānanda, it is like a person in the world who has a red film over their eye; at night, when they look at a lamp-light, they see a separate circular halo of five colors."
It is layered and overlapping.
Although the eyes are but floating organs, when sentient beings gather their vision within them, this is precisely where the essence of seeing resides.

Although the cataract is a disease of the floating organ, it actually arises because of the nature of seeing; only through the presence of this nature does such a disease exist. Thus, it is also the nature of seeing itself.
The disease of the eyes causes the lamp-circle to appear as a reflection of that disease.

Specifically, the clear eye constitutes the fundamental disease of vision rooted in ignorance (*avidyā*), whereas the red cataract is a peripheral disease of vision belonging to the secondary branches of the physical sense-organ.

The body and its objects are reflections of the fundamental disease of vision, while the lamp-circle is a reflection of the peripheral disease of vision. Using this reflection of the cataract as an analogy, there is...

These two aspects are easy to understand. First, it is easy to know that this is a separate karmic activity (*bipākakarma*), because one clearly knows that the lamp-circle is an object seen exclusively by oneself.
Second, it is easy to know that this is a false perception, because one also clearly knows that the lamp-circle does not exist as a reality.
Therefore, this is presented first to serve as the primary analogy, with the intention of using it to illustrate the latter two cases.

It is difficult to understand deeply. Furthermore, from the section on the Buddha’s downward descent—specifically the chapter on "Departing from the Causes of Delusion" and so forth—all explanations are provided with detailed clarity by relying on these easily understood and applicable methods; what follows below is summarized in a single word.
Therefore, one must clearly correlate each point with its corresponding example; only then will the subsequent text be self-evident without requiring further elaboration.
Now, consider that the seeing-nature possessed by the eye is of the same substance as the seeing of the body and objects later on; there is no difference between them.

However, while this [initial state] carries both the primary and secondary ailments, the latter state has only the primary and lacks the secondary; therefore, they are used as analogies for one another.

The cataract serves as an analogy for ignorance (*avidyā*); the lamp serves as an analogy for the realm within; and the wheel serves as an analogy for the body and its objects. This should be understood in conjunction with the subsequent text.
This serves to illuminate [the truth] without error. △ Third, the realization that there is no reality to it. This is further divided into two parts.
First, examining the two locations:
"What do you think? Is this circular light manifested by the lamp-light at night the color of the lamp, or is it the color of what is seen?"
For example, it is asked: "Are these bodies and objects manifested within this triple world truly existent within that realm?
Or is the nature of your seeing truly existent? △ Second, refuting their identity or difference. This also has two parts. First, refuting that the lamp is identical to the seeing.
Ānanda, if this were the color of the lamp, it would not belong to the person with the cataract; why then do they not both see it?

Yet this circular image is seen only by the one with the cataract. If it were the seeing of the color, then once the seeing has become the color, what would you call that person with the cataract who sees the circular image?
First, by means of the absence of cataracts, one sees that it is not the lamp that is broken. Those who lack cataracts may be used as an analogy for all Buddhas;
they have utterly severed ignorance and are thus identical to those without the ailment of cataracts. The analogy states:

if the body and its objects were truly existent within the realm, how could those who have utterly severed ignorance fail to see them? Why must it necessarily be only those with ignorance who then perceive them?
Next, using the fact that color cannot see itself to refute the notion that seeing is inherent in the object, the analogy is stated:
"If the body and its objects were identical to the nature of seeing as a real entity, then the nature of seeing would have already become the body and its objects, and thus it could not see itself.
Now, as for that which sees the body and its objects—what else is it that performs this seeing? △ Second, the refutation of the separation between the lamp and seeing.
Furthermore, Ānanda, if this circular shadow existed separately from the lamp, it should appear when one looks at a screen, a curtain, or a table from the side.
If it existed separately from the act of seeing, it should not be within the range of visual perception. How then is it that a person with cataracts sees this circular shadow with their own eyes?
First, by observing laterally that there is no substance, one refutes the separation from the lamp. The analogy is as follows:
if you further calculate that the body and its objects exist with a separate substance outside those realms, then one ought to perceive the body and its objects even beyond the realms in nirvana.
It may be asked: "When the followers of the Two Vehicles transcend the triple world (*traidhātuka*), they perceive emptiness;

how does this differ from the Buddha? Answer: The Buddha is the triple world itself, yet he does not perceive it as a body or an object. This is like a person without cataracts who does not see the floating hairs before a lamp. The followers of the Two Vehicles are like those with cataracts;
they must move away from the lamp toward a screen or similar object before they no longer see them. Yet, this is not true non-perception. Furthermore...

[The opponent] returns to the old position that [the object] exists as before. Next, [the Master] refutes the separation from seeing by means of the argument that "nothing can be beheld except by the eye. He provides an analogy, saying:

"If you further argue that the body and its objects exist apart from the nature of seeing and possess their own independent substance, then by what means could one know that the body and its objects exist?
Why, then, do ignorant people insist on using the nature of seeing to perceive them? Having thus concluded that they are utterly devoid of reality. △
4. A Detailed Exposition of the Cause of Delusion. The preceding section merely pointed out that neither identity nor separation applies; this was sufficient to demonstrate their falsity.

However, it did not yet reveal the underlying cause of this delusion nor the essence of the "sickness-free" vision. This present section provides a complete exposition of these matters, divided into five parts.
The first point specifically indicates the cause of delusion.
Therefore, one should know that while form actually resides in the lamp, the visual disorder perceives it as a shadow.
Regarding the phrase "form actually resides in the lamp," this means that those five colors must actually exist upon the lamp before they can manifest. This is because...

It is not the case that curtains and the like do not appear without the principle of being separate from a lamp. Regarding the statement that "seeing the disease constitutes the shadow": although it appears without being separate from the lamp, it is in reality not the shadow of the lamp itself;
rather, it is the shadow of the visual disorder (the *timira* disease) upon the eye. This refers to the two characters for "seeing the disease."
This is precisely the false cause of reality. However, according to the preceding analogy, mountains and rivers must actually exist within the boundary to be seen;
yet they do not truly exist within that boundary either, being merely shadows of the fundamental sickness of vision.
△ Second, the essence of vision has no involvement [with objects].
The shadow and the seeing are both cataracts; the seeing of the cataract is not itself a disease.

The first phrase restates the previous "disease-shadow. The character "seeing" (jiàn) above refers to the "sickness of seeing" (jiàn-bìng); it is an abbreviation for the word "and" (yán). It should properly read:

"The shadow and the sickness of seeing are both merely a single cataract. The intent clarifies that the shadow and the disease are of one substance (*ekātmya*); they have never existed as separate entities.

The shadow is not itself the eye disease, nor is there such a thing as an eye disease without a shadow; therefore, it is only when the shadow and the disease coincide that they are termed a "defect" (*śaṅ*).
Thus, it is said that both the shadow and the seeing are defects. The second phrase specifically points to the subject that sees—the very essence of the defect's vision.
The constant absence of illness is fundamentally unrelated to the cataract. If what you perceive were the cataract itself, it should not be able to see itself.
Now, since you clearly see the cataract, how could the seeing-substance that perceives it be identical to the cataract-illness that is seen?
This point is of the utmost importance; it is precisely because there exists this substance of seeing that is free from illness that one is able to see the seeing.

This is not what is meant by "seeing. It does not refer to a person with the visual affliction of cataracts; there will be an illumination on this later in the text, where it shall be pointed out in due course.
△ Third, admonishing people against their deluded sentiments.
One should ultimately not say, "This lamp is the seeing," nor that "within this there is that which is neither lamp nor seeing.
Observe the two characters "should not" (bù yīng); they are words of admonition and prohibition.

This implies that since [the object] is merely a pathological reflection and lacks any substantial reality, to speak of it as being either identical to or separate from the subject is in both cases contrary to reason; therefore, one is cautioned against such assertions. △ Fourth, the illustration for clarification.
For this reason, it is like a second moon: it is neither a substantial entity nor a reflection. Why is this? Because the perception of a second moon is produced by pressing [the eye].
Any person of wisdom should not say that the source of this pressed organ is a form or not a form, or that it is apart from seeing or not seeing.

Regarding the statement, "This analogy is neither the substance nor the reflection," according to the subsequent text: since the substance is perceived by way of the moon's form, it is used here to distinguish between what is correct and what is incorrect.
Thus, this should be understood as a dual designation based on perceiving both the substance and the moon's reflection.

Therefore, "not the substance" means it does not belong to the substance that is perceived; "not the reflection" means it is not manifested by the moon's reflection. This leads to the following inquiry.
Commentary: This correctly elucidates the second month. The true cause of delusion lies solely in the single character "niē" (捏).

For when one "niē-s" [grasps at] it, it exists; when one does not "niē-s" it, it is non-existent. This is identical to the previous case of the lamp-circle: the true cause of delusion lies solely in the single character "bìng" (病).
Therefore it is said that seeing the disease constitutes the shadow; for it manifests through the disease, and does not manifest in the absence of disease.
Because it is manifest. Regarding the final two lines, Wu’s commentary states: "It merely takes up both 'is' and both 'leaves behind,' thereby forming the shape of the moon.
"Both 'is' and 'non-shape'" is equivalent to saying "it is the moon and it is not the moon.

"Both 'leaves behind seeing' and 'leaves behind non-seeing'" is equivalent to saying "it is not seeing and it is seeing. For leaving behind seeing is itself non-seeing; leaving behind non-seeing is...

This is precisely "seeing"; it is merely a matter of literary technique. In the main point, the moon is contrasted with seeing to simultaneously negate the reality or unreality of the cataract and the wheel;
the intent is to clarify this through metaphor. The lamp is contrasted with seeing to simultaneously negate the identity or difference between the cataract and the wheel.
Thus, reality and unreality are likewise identical and separate. △ Fifth, the analogy is applied to the Dharma to reveal the truth.

This is also like that; it is produced by a cataract in the eye. Now, whom can one name as being the lamp or the seeing? How much more so regarding the distinction between what is not the lamp and what is not the seeing?
As seen above, the two moons are not real; the pressing [of the eye] is their sole root cause. The wheel of lamps is fundamentally non-existent; it is only...
The cataract is the very root of the disease. Since it is fundamentally and utterly illusory, on what basis can one speak of its identity with or separation from [the lamp]?
Furthermore, since both identity and separation are absent, this further demonstrates its utter illusoriness. Indeed, the cataract and ignorance are both like the pressure upon the eye;
the lamp-halo, the body, and the environment are all like the two moons. This analogy makes it easy to see. Thus ends the discussion on the illusory vision of individual karma.
[End of section]. △ Second, the deluded vision shared by those of the same class (*sabhāga-viparyāsa-darśana*). This is further divided into three parts. First, the initial inquiry:
"What is meant by the 'deluded vision shared by those of the same class'?

This corresponds to the previous inquiry. △ Second, the description of what is seen. This is further divided into two parts. First, a general enumeration of the continent and the country. This is further divided into two parts.
First, regarding the number of islands within the ocean:
Ānanda, in this Jambudvīpa, excluding the waters of the great oceans, there are three thousand islands upon the intermediate plains.
The "great oceans" refer to the salt-water seas outside the seven golden mountains. The "plains" refer to land devoid of water, which is encircled by water.

Landmasses are called continents (*dvīpa*). Because there is one large one and the rest are small, their number totals three thousand. This refers specifically to the continent on the southern side of Mount Sumeru.
II. The Number of Countries within the Continents. This is further divided into two parts: 1. The Number of Countries in a Single Continent.
The central great continent, measured from east to west, contains a total of two thousand three hundred large kingdoms.
"Great continent" here specifically refers to Jambudvīpa; by citing the large kingdoms, the small ones are implied. △ Second, the number of countries on the small continents.
As for the other minor continents within the various oceans, there may be two or three hundred kingdoms among them, or perhaps only one or two,
up to thirty, forty, fifty, or sixty.
These are all situated outside the great continents. This concludes the general enumeration of the continents and their kingdoms.
△ Second, the specific enumeration of what is seen. This also has two parts. First, two kingdoms on the same continent.
Ānanda, suppose further that within this [continent] there were a small island with only two countries.
Taking the smallest island and the least of the two countries as a comparison, one may thereby illustrate the vast majority. △ Second, what is seen by one country.
If the people of a single nation collectively experience adverse conditions, then the sentient beings of that small continent will behold all manner of inauspicious phenomena;
they may see two suns, or two moons, or even such portents as halos, solar spots, and jade rings.
Comets, meteors, flying stars, and shooting stars; the "burdened ear" (*fǔ'ěr*) and rainbows;

various evil portents such as halos (*yùn*), eclipses (*shì*), girdles (*pèi*), and rings (*jué*)—all of which accompany the sun and moon: a halo is that which encircles them; an eclipse is their partial or total obscuration;

girdles and rings are the manifestations of calamitous vapors near the sun and moon. Comets, meteors, flying stars, and shooting stars are the disaster-omens of the stars; they are characterized by starlight pointing in a biased direction.

It is said that when [the vapor] radiates in four directions, it is called a *pō* (comet); when it moves horizontally, it is called a *fēi* (flying meteor); when it descends and pours down, it is called a *liú* (flowing meteor).
The "fù'ěr" (ear-shaped halo) and the "hóngní" (rainbow and halos) are exclusively omens of disaster for the day. The "fù'ěr" forms by flanking the sun; the "hóngní" forms by reflecting the sun.
The final phrase encompasses all other such phenomena. Having finished setting forth what was observed: △ Third, concluding that they have no actual substance.
It is merely seen in this country, while the sentient beings of that country have never seen it, nor even heard of it;
though they share the same celestial phenomena, its presence here and absence there is sufficient proof that it is not real. This teaching is a point of falsehood.

Compared with other cases of individual karma, it is both abbreviated and detached, and furthermore lacks the cause of falsehood. "Abbreviated" means the intention is to conform to what precedes; "lacking" means leaving it for later.
This is an example cited within the section on "descending and ascending. Furthermore, this [case] is easily understood in two respects.
First, it is easy to know that it is a common perception (*sabhāga*), because it is clearly known to be shared by everyone in the country.

Second, it is easy to know that it is a false perception (*vitatha-darśana*), because it is also clearly known that it is not seen by those in other countries. Therefore, this is first presented and taken as [an illustration].
This serves as an analogy; it is also intended to provide an analogy for the two subsequent layers that are difficult to understand.

Having completed the presentation of each easy-to-understand analogy, △ Third, the combined clarification through progression and regression, divided into two parts: First, the general indication of the analogical method.
Ānanda, I shall now for your sake clarify these two matters by advancing and retreating through the text.
Regarding this section, although the old commentaries mark it as being here, they instead skip over many subsequent passages and select only a few lines to establish its meaning.
Consequently, based on their limited perspective, they claim it is a misplaced passage (*kōkan*) and wish to rearrange the text. Now, in this [work],...
Although I did not dare to alter the printed edition, those who lectured on it all copied and taught it as an authoritative treatise.

Now, having examined it repeatedly and in detail, I find that they failed to understand the original intent and instead claimed the scripture was erroneous. If this were indeed altered, [it would be a grave error].

This greatly confuses the Buddha’s intent; it is deeply necessary to be cautioned against this. One should know that from this point onward, up until the end of the "Section on Confusion," three successive sections follow the same pattern;
all are the main text where advance and retreat are explained together. Furthermore, this method of advance and retreat differs from previous explanations.

For when the Buddha expounds a sūtra, it is like a person entering a house: proceeding from the front toward the back constitutes "advance," while returning from the back toward the front constitutes "retreat."
This concerns "regression. However, there are two interpretations, both of which are logically consistent; let the wise examine them.
First, if one follows the examples found in the extant text, then the three sections are divided such that advancement and regression are explained in conjunction. That is to say:

the first example ("For instance, you today perceive mountains and rivers") explains advancement in conjunction with the following. The second example ("For instance, the false perception of a single person in a separate karma") explains regression in conjunction with the following. The final example...

(For example, within the three thousand continents of Jambudvīpa) this is further explained through progressive synthesis. Second, if one considers the profound intent regarding the points of conjunction, then each of the three sections has its own progressive and regressive synthesis.
That is to say: the first conjunction (*sarvam etad yāvat sādhyam*) explains the progressive and regressive synthesis in terms of the lamp-circle’s reliance on and its primary manifestation;
the second conjunction (*sarvam etad yāvad utpannam*) explains the progressive and regressive synthesis in terms of the calamitous signs and the lamp-circle; the latter...
The section on "Knots" (from "the same is true for... up to "false death") explains the advancement and retreat of various nations by means of the signs of calamities;

this will become clear as each point is indicated in the text itself. II. Taking examples based on the Dharma. This also has two parts. First, explaining individual karma through an analogy. This also has three parts.

First, presenting the analogical principle and defining the delusion of the eye-ailment (*taimira*). Although this generally reiterates the previous discussion on individual karma, its intent primarily draws upon the detailed explanation [of the *Śrīmālādevī-siṃhanāda-sūtra*].

This demonstrates the meaning within the context of false causes, using the present capacity as an illustrative analogy. Furthermore, there are four parts. First, briefly citing the aforementioned dharma:
"Ānanda, it is like that sentient beings' individual karma of deluded vision."
This section provides a general summary, which the following three sections will detail.

To regard the "defective eye" (*taimira*) mentioned previously as a deluded perception resulting from individual karma (*bipākaja-viparyāsa*) and then insist upon it as a mere metaphor—this is the first proof. △ Second, the illusory object appears to exist.
Gaze at the circular reflection appearing within the light; although it appears as if it were an external object, its delusive substance is fundamentally non-existent.
Ultimately, for the observer, it is produced by a cataract in the eye. This cataract is simply the exhaustion of the faculty of sight and is not created by material form.
"To see exhaustion" means to perceive the illusory manifestation of the signs of exhaustion arising from illness. "Not produced by form" means it is not truly produced by material form.
This simply states that it is manifested solely by a single optical aberration and there is nothing else;
this is precisely the previous phrase regarding the shadow and the vision both being aberrations. △ Fourth: The True Essence is Not Illness.
However, one who perceives the visual aberration ultimately incurs no fault.
This is because the one who perceives the aberration is precisely able to perceive the very essence of that aberration.

For it is because the aberration does not perceive itself, whereas the perceiver of the aberration is the true essence of seeing; since that [essence] is inherently unimpaired, it is said there is "no fault. This is what was previously...
"Seeing the optical illusion is not the disease" is merely a phrase. △ Second, clarifying the application through the analogy by advancing and retreating.

This is divided into two parts. First, establishing the general meaning of the analogy. Regarding the previous classification, the words are general while the intent is specific; subsequently, the meanings are correctly aligned. This is further divided into two: first, establishing the general meaning of the analogy.
For example, when you today observe with your eyes the mountains, rivers, lands, and all sentient beings, these are all produced by the disease of vision that has existed since beginningless time.
"Example" (*dṛṣṭānta*) means they are of one and the same category; it signifies there is no difference. "Observing with the eyes today" clarifies what is manifest before one’s own presence.

"Abiding" refers to the state where one perceives nearby objects directly, as opposed to distant ones. The following two phrases—referring to the "relying" and the "supported"—should be understood accordingly.

The "sickness of perception from beginningless time" is none other than fundamental ignorance (*mūla-avidyā*). At its inception, it forms the *karma-vijñāna* (karmic consciousness), which then evolves into the two divisions of "perception" (*darśana*) and "phenomena" (*nimitta*).

Thus, perception is like a cataract or visual impairment, and phenomena are like the illusory wheel of a lamp-flame. From this point on, throughout vast eons, there has been no further purification. Therefore...
It is said: "The beginningless perception of illness. This section is the first instance where progression and retreat are combined for clarification.
If one follows the previous principle of dividing the text into three sections, this belongs to the category of progression for the purpose of combined clarification.

That is to say, it progresses from the preceding passage on the lamp-wheel, which clarifies the distinct karma that is easy to understand, to the subsequent passage on the environment and its inhabitants (*niśraya-vastu*), which clarifies the distinct karma that is difficult to understand; thus, the concluding phrases all consist of two characters.
It merely enumerates all sentient beings throughout the lands;

it states that these sentient beings of this land are all shadows of the fundamental sickness of views from beginningless time, identical in kind and no different from the shadows of the derivative sicknesses of views regarding the lamp-wheel.
This explanation is consistent and easy to comprehend. If one follows the latter meaning, each of the three sections has its own...
The principles for advancing and retreating are the same as before without difference; the distinction lies only in the points of conjunction, all of which consist of two characters.
These refer to the simultaneous mention of the lamp-wheel (the adornment) and its support (the dharma-realm), both of which are shadows of the eye-disease of beginningless time.
Therefore, they fully embody the meaning of advancing and retreating. That is to say, by advancing toward the lamp-wheel to merge with the light behind—the support and the adorned—one then...
The environment and its inhabitants are certainly shadows of the fundamental disease of vision carried by the nature of seeing since beginningless time;
they are analogous to the wheel of lamps. To take the subsequent environment and inhabitants as an illustration to clarify the preceding wheel of lamps, this wheel of lamps—
Furthermore, there are no shadows of the fundamental and derivative illnesses of seeing that have been carried by the nature of seeing since beginningless time;

this is the same principle as [the distinction between] the primary and secondary [realms]. Although they differ in being long-term or temporary, there is nothing that is not an illness of seeing produced through successive illusory manifestations.

This explanation is somewhat difficult to comprehend, yet its meaning is complete; reflect upon it. (Question: A cataract is merely a temporary ailment, whereas now you speak of an "illness of seeing" from beginningless time. I fear this is not so.)

The Buddha’s intention: This answer is based precisely on the Buddha’s intention. The subsequent passages apply this by analogy to the delusory, pathological, and evil signs of eye-disease (*taimira*). Later, it is also concluded that both are produced by the beginningless delusion of seeing; thus, one knows it is so. However, compared to the body and its objects, there is one additional turn, namely, that it "doubly carries" both the fundamental and derivative illnesses.

By tracing the derivative back to the fundamental, the fundamental and derivative are therefore concluded together. Question: Since the lamp-circle and the union of light illustrate the relationship between the environment and the sentient being (*āśraya-ālambana*), it is certainly easy to understand the illustration of the difficult-to-know.

But what is the intent behind using the lamp-circle to illustrate the union of the environment and sentient beings with light? Answer: While the falsity of the environment and sentient beings is indeed comparable to the lamp-circle and is difficult to know, the remote cause of the eye-disease is likewise the transformation of ignorance (*avidyā*), which remains not easily understood. Therefore, the Buddha mutually clarifies these points; therein lies a profound [meaning].

This is the underlying intent. The essential point is to reveal that both the fundamental and the derivative aspects of perceived illness are entirely the fault of beginningless ignorance (avidyā). Hereafter, all [sections] shall follow this pattern. △ Second, a detailed explanation corresponding to the preceding text, further divided into three parts.
First, a combined clarification that the delusory objects appear to exist.
The seeing and the objects of seeing appear as if they were present before one;
"seeing" refers to the act of seeing, while "objects" refers to the lands and sentient beings. △ Second, a combined explanation that the essence of delusion is fundamentally non-existent.
Originally, my enlightened clarity perceived the cataract of the object-conditioned; thus, the perception itself was the cataract.

This "enlightened clarity" refers to the fundamental enlightenment that has fallen into ignorance. To say it "perceived the cataract of the object-conditioned" means it saw the shadow of its own inherent ignorance.
To say "the perception itself was the cataract" means that what was seen by this enlightened clarity was [unreal].
"The shadow of the light" refers precisely to the eye disease. This phrase clearly conveys the meaning that both the shadow and the seeing are the disease.
△ Third, combining this with the true essence to show it is not the disease.
The luminous mind of original enlightenment perceives conditions; this perception is not an optical defect.

The term "conditions" (yuan) here refers doubly to both the seeing and the objects seen. Since the false seeing confronts the enlightened mind, it is also that which is perceived by the enlightened mind.
Thus, while the false seeing belongs among the various conditions, the enlightened mind is that which can perceive those conditions. And...
This is called "not an ailment. It is precisely because the preceding discussion on the essence of seeing being able to see the ailment is clearly and evidently consistent with this that we know:
whenever it is said that one "sees the ailment," it refers to the fundamental essence of seeing itself, not to a person who possesses the ailment of wisdom.
One should verify the holy words at this point; for it is precisely because this essence is fundamentally free from delusion.
Therefore, as the text proceeds, one realizes that upon awakening, one is immediately free from [delusion], with no further obstacles.

Thus we know that although the section on "Detailed Correspondence" (*xiangying*) sufficiently illustrates the underlying principle, it primarily serves as a foundation for the subsequent explanation of the "confusion" (*men*). (Regarding this body and environment perceived by Ānanda, there are two layers of difficulty in knowing them:

first, it is difficult to know them as being a distinct karmic enterprise (*bieye*), because his own perception does not differ from those of the multitude; second, it is difficult to know them as false perceptions, because he relies on the commonality of their vision to believe they must necessarily exist. Therefore, based on the former...)

That which is easily understood as having two layers within a visual aberration can be used as an analogy to understand this. Question: Since the body and the object are seen together, why is this compared to the separate perceptions of a visual aberration? Answer: Sentient beings rely upon the *dharmadhātu* of their own minds, yet through delusion they give rise to the dream-like *dharmadhātu*. Because these dream-like objects are nothing but mind and do not truly exist, they appear distinct and illusory.

Although the perception is shared by many people, it is merely that their karmic conditions are identical and thus they see the same thing. How could this be like the common teaching of other schools, which asserts a single, real, external entity? It is like a thousand lamps in one room, each with its own light filling the space;

or like a group of people with cataracts viewing a lamp, where the appearance of a wheel is the same for all, yet each person’s ailment is individual. When one person recovers, only that one person’s wheel disappears. Only then does one know that it was not a single shared entity, nor was it truly existent.

The detailed analysis of the dharma through analogy, advancing and retreating to clarify the point, is hereby concluded. △ Third, the conclusion: "Seeing seeing is itself detachment" explains the confusion and distress.
The *Complete Enlightenment Sūtra* states: "Knowing it is an illusion is itself detachment. This is precisely identical to "seeing seeing is not seeing"; therefore, this heading is named after it.
This is divided into two parts. First, the reinterpretation by taking up the superior meaning:

taking up the meaning of the single phrase "the object of superior cognition is not an eye-disease," one reinterprets the previous confusion regarding the seeing of seeing as non-seeing. This is further divided into two. First, using this to manifest transcendence.
To perceive that which is perceived is a cataract; awakening itself is not within the cataract.

"Perceiving that which is perceived is a cataract" refers to the two characters "awakening" (jue) and "condition" (yuan) mentioned above. "Awakening is not within the cataract" refers to the two characters "not a cataract" (fei sheng) mentioned above.
The meaning is that awakening is fundamentally real, while the cataract is fundamentally delusory. When one has not yet awakened to the cataract, awakening constantly falls into...

Within the cataract: as soon as one realizes it is a cataract, that realization emerges early from outside the cataract; thus, within the "separate karma," many manifestations are displayed solely to fulfill these two phrases.
The intent lies in revealing that the true source is transcendent and liberated, thereby explaining away the previous state of confusion and distress.
△ Second, turning back to explain the preceding words.
This is the seeing of seeing. Why, then, is it further called "awakening," "hearing," "knowing," and "seeing"?
The character *shí* (real) also carries the meaning of the character *zì* (itself). "Seeing of seeing" (*jiàn-jian*) refers to the preceding term and its prior category.

The character *jué* (awakening) corresponds to the upper *jian* (seeing), and the character *shěng* (eye-disease/hallucination) corresponds to the lower *jian* (seeing). Therefore, "awakening to the eye-disease" (*jué-shěng*) explains "seeing of seeing. "Not [the result of] eye-disease" (*fei-shěng*) explains... [the latter].

"It is not seeing. The meaning is this: when one awakens to the cataract, one is immediately liberated from the cataract; this is "seeing the seeing," which is to be immediately liberated from seeing.
How, then, could it again be called "seeing"? This is why I say it is "not seeing. As for "hearing, knowing, and perceiving," these are all equally possessed within the single substance.
Because it is difficult to examine the "seeing of seeing," the character was changed to clarify that these are not two separate things. △
Second, there is the interpretation by confronting what is before one's eyes. This points toward the present moment and is analogous to the "Penetration of the Principle" (zongtong);

it further provides an expository refutation while still returning to the intent of the teaching. Furthermore, there are two parts: first, a general indication that this is a cataract, which explains false seeing.
Therefore, when you now see me, yourself, and the ten classes of sentient beings in the world, you are seeing nothing but a cataract;
it is not that you are seeing the one who perceives the cataract.

To "see me" is to contemplate the Buddha’s marks and signs. Thus, know that as long as your own delusions have not been eliminated, even though you contemplate the excellence of the Buddha, [it remains a projection].
"Phenomena" (xiàng) are likewise shadows of cataracts. "And you" refers to Ānanda himself.

"The world" refers to the aforementioned mountains, rivers, lands, and the ten classes of sentient beings—all of whom are identical to the previously mentioned ten types of ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*).
"All are those who see the cataract" means they all see the aforementioned disease of the cataract. "Not one who sees the cataract" refers to the true essence that is capable of seeing the cataract.
These two phrases definitively determine that this is delusion and not reality. △ Second, specifically identifying what is not the cataract explains what is not "seeing.
That seeing is the true essence; its nature is not a cataract, and therefore it is not called "seeing."
"That" is a term referring to the dharmas. "One who sees the true essence" refers to one who is able to see the true essence of the optical aberration (*taimira*).

Furthermore, another interpretation holds that "that seeing" still points to deluded seeing, whereas "true essence" refers to the true seeing. This true essence is the actual substance of that deluded seeing;
therefore, it is called "seeing the true essence of that [delusion]. As for "its nature is not the aberration," this means that it is indeed the nature.
The substance is not delusion; these two phrases definitively establish that it is true and not false.
The final phrase concludes by resolving doubts: for delusion is not truth, and truth is not delusion. Thus, one knows that the true seeing-nature is fundamentally constant and detached from delusion.
This is why it is said that when true seeing perceives deluded seeing, it is immediately liberated from seeing. And...
It can no longer be designated by the term "seeing. Why are you so bewildered and distressed by this?

Since the world and its sentient beings are merely the delusory shadows of individual karma arising from one's own mind, ordinary people need not feel joy for the higher realms or aversion toward the lower ones through various forms of grasping;
nor do those of the Two Vehicles need to fear existence or sink into emptiness through various forms of weary detachment. They should instead quickly and diligently seek [the truth].
To see seeing and thereby eliminate one's own deep delusions means that one does not fall into the realm of the false body.

Among the three paths, this constitutes the initial awakening to the path of delusion; realizing that the three are fundamentally empty is still a state of proximate detachment rather than ultimate detachment.

The meaning of "distancing" (遠離) appears later in the section on the "homogeneous class" (*sabhāga*). Having finished illustrating individual karma (*pratyeka-karman*), [the text] next illustrates the homogeneous class (*sabhāga*).
This is divided into three parts: first, citing the illustrative phenomena to clarify the progression and regression together.

The traditional explanation holds that the clarification of progression and regression belongs exclusively to this section. The first six lines are established because the text exhibits the character of a dialectical exchange.

This is an error. Consequently, based on my limited perspective, I have intended to take the previously cited passage and place it above this section, while simultaneously moving the entire preceding section to follow "Original Awakening is Ever-Present.
Furthermore, I have taken the scriptural passage from the earlier section beginning with "What is meant by 'having a common lot' (*sabhāgatā*)?
and inserted it here. Thus, there are three instances of shifting back and forth, as well as the beginning...

The essential meaning of the concluding section on the "tail" has been lost by both [parties]. If one further examines this by comparing it with their respective doctrines and metaphors, the confusion becomes even more extreme.
Those who transmit and lecture [on these texts] fear contradicting the commentaries yet dare to violate the sūtras; this must be strictly cautioned against and brought to an end.

Moreover, upon now carefully investigating the sūtra text, not a single hair’s breadth of error is found. Therefore, I have interpreted it by following its original intent in every detail. Furthermore, at...
Each passage explains its respective reason in detail. I request that the wise apply themselves to its study and savoring, so that there may be further illumination.

One should know that this section constitutes the second instance where "advancing" and "retreating" are combined for clarification. According to the previous principle, these were categorized separately as advancing and retreating;
here, they are combined under the heading of "retreating" for the sake of clarification. This is because the subsequent shared karma is used to clarify the preceding individual karma. This...
This can also be easily summarized in three parts. First, to briefly cite the preceding method:

Ānanda, regarding the deluded perceptions of the common lot of those sentient beings—prior to the separate examples of individual karma mentioned above—it was first briefly cited, saying: "As with those sentient beings, [there are] deluded perceptions of individual karma."
[The text] says: "I see it. Now, even before this analogy regarding the *sabhāgatā* (homogeneity) is fully established, [the author] briefly cites it, saying:

"Just as that sentient beings' delusory vision of *sabhāgatā* is manifest and confrontational, who would dare to arbitrarily alter it? This is intended generally to cite the various calamitous signs observed by the people of the aforementioned country.
However, this section contains both the subjective (*kartṛ*) and objective (*karman*) analogies; if one were to correlate it distantly with the subsequent section, it serves as an analogy.
Regarding Jambudvīpa and so forth, this serves as the exemplifier (*dṛṣṭānta*) and that serves as the exemplified (*dārṣṭāntika*).

If one considers them in close relation to the primary text’s discussion of individual karma and deluded vision, then this serves as the exemplified and individual karma serves as the exemplifier. The reason why this is difficult to comprehend will become clear later;
please keep this in mind for now. II. Taking Individual Karma as an Exemplar. Question: Since the calamitous phenomena are already common [to all],...
Regarding the examples that are easy to understand: one should simply take the subsequent sections on Jambudvīpa and so forth as the examples.

Why must one further seek examples from other karmic activities? Answer: Following the brief presentation in the preceding text, the section that immediately cites and establishes the "eye-disease delusion" (*taimirika-vibhrama*) is entirely the section that cites the previous detailed exposition of the causes of delusion.
This is because it is only once the causes of delusion have been established that one may proceed to apply the analogy to what follows.
The identity of the body and its objects is false. Now, beneath this brief summary, we must likewise establish the cause of this falsity.
However, in the preceding section on the portents of calamity, the text originally lacked a detailed exposition of the cause of falsity.

This was because the Buddha’s intention was not to provide a separate explanation of the cause of falsity there, but rather to reserve it for this point so that it might serve as an illustration of the cause of falsity in the case of individual karma. For this reason:
This is merely taking an example to supplement what was not explicitly stated in the text. Question: Why is it so? Answer:

Although the phenomena of optical illusions (*taimira*) and portents (*upadrava*) are both easily understood through analogy, portents are somewhat more difficult to comprehend than optical illusions.

Therefore, this also uses the easy to illustrate the difficult, so that one may know they are of the same single category of falsity as those optical illusions. Only then does the cause of delusion become established.

This can be analogized to the case of Jambudvīpa and others below. The subsequent question is roughly the same as that of Wuxing. Furthermore, there are two parts: first, taking an analogy by way of inversion;
this refers to the false vision of a single individual through distinct karma.

Generally, one first presents the exemplifier (*dṛṣṭānta*) and subsequently applies it to the exemplified (*dārṣṭāntika*); this constitutes the proper order of analogy. Now, however, the exemplified is inverted and applied to the exemplifier;

therefore, it is said that "the analogy is taken by inversion. Inversion here means "reversal" (*pratyudāvarta*). Thus, according to the preceding meaning, this belongs to the category of reversal and should be explained as such. [Question: Why is it thus? [Answer:

To briefly present that which is of the same class (*sabhāga*) so that it may be easily understood, and then to use it as an analogy for that which follows, which is of the same class but difficult to understand. Therefore, one cannot help but first present the "same-class" [category] to correspond with the preceding "distinct" [category].

This is the section concerning the "abridgment and elevation" (*cu-jǔ*) within the [classification of] karma. However, because one specifically lacks the false cause for this, one must take an example from a separate category of karma; furthermore, there is no choice but to regress to that separate category and adopt it [as the model]. △ Second, the explanation by way of conformity (*shùn*).
Since the preceding text was forced and resulted in the inversion of subject and object, which ultimately remains inconsistent, the principle requires that the phrasing be reversed to explain it;

hence, it is called an "explanation by conformity. (Question: Is this not merely following the previous progression? Answer: It is simply viewed in light of the section on abridgment and elevation; the inversion of subject and object is, in the end, a regression.)
Furthermore, this section is divided into two parts. First, the headings are identical.
Regarding the person with diseased eyes, they are like those in a single country;

following the established precedent, the analogy for individual karma (*bipākakarma*) is placed first, while the analogy for shared karma (*sādhāraṇakarma*) follows later. Thus, it is briefly indicated.
This has been explained in detail according to the preceding section. △ Second, the illustration of the causes of delusion:
That vision of a circular shadow arises from the delusion of a cataract; this commonality of perception among beings is not clearly understood. It occurs within the karma of shared perception.
The arising of these malignant miasms is cited here as an example of individual karma; they are merely optical illusions caused by a delusive condition.

By analogy with this, the commonality [of the world] is likewise merely a malignant miasma caused by a delusive condition—how could there be any substantial reality to celestial phenomena? △ Third, a combined clarification of their shared origin.
Both are produced by the deluded views of beginningless time.
Regarding these two characters "both" (俱), there are no two interpretations; they simply rely on the latter meaning to mention both the wheel of lamps and the image of the calamity together.
This "both" and so forth is precisely because one infers from this point that what preceded was entirely the same as what followed.
Their commonality lies in the principle of advancing and retreating to achieve illumination. "Arising" refers to successive arising and spontaneous arising.

Although, according to what is manifest before us, these are all simultaneous events, when one traces them back through their successive transformations to the root, they are both beginningless false perceptions;
they arise from the fundamental source and extend outward to the branches. "Advancing and retreating to achieve illumination" means advancing the lamp-wheel to merge with the light.
As for the signs of calamity, these are indeed the misfortunes of an entire nation.
As for the lamp-wheel used to dispel those signs of calamity, it too is but the miasma and evil of a single person. Therefore it is said:

"Both are the delusive views of beginningless time, arising and proliferating through mutual influence. △ Second, advancing and retreating in accordance with the analogy to clarify the point. Regarding the aforementioned "nation":

As for the signs of calamity: since they are analogous to the shadow of a fault, the false cause has already been revealed. This [revelation] serves as the method by which this capacity can be analogized;
meanwhile, this Jambudvīpa and so forth serve as the object of the analogy. Proceeding from this, the matter is clarified through both progressive and regressive analysis.

This constitutes the third round of clarification through progressive and regressive analysis. Furthermore, according to the principle of the prior classification, this also represents a general statement.

The meaning is distinct; however, it is subsumed under "progression" (*pratipatti*) for the sake of combined clarification. That is to say, by progressing to the calamitous signs of one land, one combines and clarifies those of all subsequent lands.
If one follows the latter sense, they are properly aligned and divided into two parts. First, the general application to the world (*loka*), which is further divided into two.
First, the receptacle world (*bhājana-loka*), which is again divided into two. First, from the narrow to the broad.

For example, Jambudvīpa among the three thousand continents, together with the four great oceans; the Sahā world, extending throughout the ten directions—all are subsumed under the character "Example" (lì).
This is because it correctly inherits the preceding discussion on the delusive causes of the same category (*sabhāga-hetu*) as the governing principle for this section.
The ocean is fundamentally one cause, yet because there are four great continents on the four sides of Mount Sumeru, the ocean likewise conforms to those continents.
This refers to the four great elements. Within the Sahā world, there are ten billion sets of four continents; this is merely the land of a single Buddha-field of our Original Teacher.
As for the ten directions, the number of all Buddha-fields is immeasurable and boundless, such that even the dust motes of the sands cannot exhaustively represent their count.
△ Second, a general indication of the outflowing (sāsrava) realms.
"All contaminated lands" (*sarva-sāsrava-kṣetra*).

The term "all characters" (*sarva-akṣara*) collectively refers to the meaning of contamination within all lands, whether broad or narrow; this is contrasted with the "non-contaminated" (*anāsrava*) mentioned previously.
Here, in response to the capacities of the audience, it specifically indicates the Land of Common Residence (*saha-loka-dhātu*). △ Second, the world of sentient beings (*sattva-loka*).

"And all sentient beings" refers to the sentient beings of the aforementioned lands. Both the world of sentient beings (*sattva-loka*) and the world of the vessel (*bhājana-loka*) are objects perceived by one's own mind and the commonality of the group (*nikāya-sabhāga*).
It is not that a multitude of people collectively constitute the perceiver; this principle applies universally to the world.
The section concludes. △ Second, a combined explanation of their common delusiveness, further divided into two parts. First, a combined explanation of the preceding six characters:
they are all equally the enlightened clarity, the untainted, wondrous mind; yet seeing, hearing, sensing, and knowing are the conditions for the illusory disease.

If one follows the previous meaning, then "the same" (*tóngshì*) refers to both characters; it is likewise spoken of by universally citing all nations as being "the same" in their state of outflowlessness (*anāsrava*).
This, in turn, combines with the six characters "all are beginningless false views" (*wúshǐ jiàn wàng*) from the preceding illustrative capacity.
However, that [text] merely speaks of beginningless false seeing, without mentioning the reality upon which it depends.
This is the awakened, luminous, untainted, wondrous mind; this is the reality upon which it depends. Seeing, hearing, sensing, and knowing are the illusory conditions of disease;
these are the delusions that arise from it. Following the precedent above to illustrate what follows, it says: "These worlds seen by each of the ten directions..."
Although sentient beings differ in their various ways, the inauspicious sights they perceive in that single land are all of one kind;
