Now you say that light and darkness are both transcended and that there is ultimately no substance. How does this differ from the lack of substance in the mind that conditions [the senses]? Answer:

To explain briefly: previously, because sentient beings could not perceive the true mind by means of the mind that conditions [the senses], I pointed to the nature within the sense-faculties (the eyes) to enable them to recognize the true mind.
However, after it was established that "this is the mind, not the eye," I have merely manifested the nature and will no longer [rely on the faculties].
This treatise examines the sense faculties (*indriya*) in order to most thoroughly demonstrate that their true nature exists apart from sensory objects.

Now, because you have already realized this true nature yet still cling to the idea that the six faculties possess distinct substantial characteristics and have not yet integrated them into a single essence, it is necessary to further cause you to know that the six sense bases (*āyatana*) lack any inherent substance or characteristic.
Thus, it most rigorously refutes the delusion that they exist apart from objects while lacking any substance. Although it speaks of "seeing-nature," it is...
The self-nature of localized attachment within the sense organs is not the same as the previously mentioned seeing-nature that pervades the space beyond the eyes.
The former reveals the nature, whereas this [latter] refutes its characteristics; thus they differ. To investigate this further: this refutation of characteristics...
It is also intended that they be free from marks, which is precisely the wondrous nature of True Suchness (tathatā). Thus, the principle of revealing the nature remains fundamentally the same.
How could it be otherwise than the true shattering of the conditioned mind, such that it certainly has no substance? At the end of the fourth fascicle, Ānanda also poses this question;
one should again examine these passages in comparison. △ Second, "from whence it does not come. The preceding section inferred the falsity [of the mind].
This can be verified through analysis. This will be released later. Furthermore, there are two parts: first, a general enumeration.
Thus, Ānanda, you should know that this seeing does not come from light or darkness; it does not emerge from the sense organ; nor is it produced from space.
To assert that [consciousness] arises from the sense organs in accordance with worldly conditions is the correct view; the other two [positions] are merely defensive counter-arguments.
△ Second, the interrogation and refutation, which is further divided into three parts. First, it does not come from the objects.
Why is this? If [the eye] comes from light, then darkness would immediately cease upon its arrival; thus it should not perceive darkness.
If it comes from darkness, then light would immediately cease upon its arrival; thus it should not perceive light.
The first three characters constitute a general inquiry concerning the section on "Dwelling. Since light and darkness are mutually opposed, arising and ceasing naturally alternate with one another;
this can be understood as being identical to the previous refutation of causes and conditions. △ Second, [the analysis of] not arising from the sense organs.
If [the seeing] were produced from the sense organ, there would necessarily be neither light nor darkness. Thus, this essence of vision fundamentally lacks intrinsic nature;
consequently, the latter three phrases would necessarily not apply. Read them as a single breath, as if it said: "If one claims that the sense organ alone can produce the nature of seeing..."
Thus, one is doubly free from both light and darkness, revealing that the essence of vision fundamentally has no self-substance. △ Third, it does not come from space.

If it emerged from space, then when it looks forward at external objects, it should return to see its own root. Furthermore, if space were observing itself, why would your faculty of entry be missing?
The sense organs and their objects are empty and without substance. If one can emerge from [this state of] seeing, then both the organs and the objects will become visible;
furthermore, one would fall into the view of an external object and a self. △ Third, concluding the false and returning to the true.
Therefore, you should know that the eye-base (*cakṣur-āyatana*) is illusory; it is fundamentally neither produced by causes and conditions nor of a spontaneous nature.
It is empty because it lacks a substantial reality, and it is illusory because it comes from nowhere.

Furthermore, the reason it has no real self-nature is that its essence is precisely True Suchness (*tathatā*); and the reason it does not arise from the three locations is that it emerges from the storehouse consciousness (*ālayavijñāna*).
The nature [of the eye] is fundamentally the wondrous nature that is neither caused by conditions nor produced spontaneously; it merely manifests falsely as the eye-sphere (*cakṣur-āyatana*).

The following sections shall all be explained according to this principle. The section on the eye-sphere is concluded. II. The Ear-Sphere, divided into three parts: 1. Falsehood arises based upon the True.
Ānanda, it is like a person who, with two fingers, tightly plugs their ears. Because the faculty of hearing is strained, sounds arise within the head.
Both the ear and the strain are equally the signs of fatigue produced by the fixed gaze of Bodhi.
One stares with fixed eyes to see "flowers in the sky," which then transforms into stopping the ears to hear the ringing within the head.

Following the above, the first instance of the character *láo* (weariness/distress) refers to the hollow sound within the head, while the latter two instances of *láo* refer to all sounds perceived by the ears.

From this point onward, you should consult the preceding text to apply these principles; then nothing will remain unclear. This is because when the eyes are strained by staring, one sees only empty flowers;
when Bodhi is strained, then seeing, hearing, smelling, tasting, touching, and cognizing all arise simultaneously.

Therefore, it is said in each case that they are "the signs of strain from staring. II. Distinguishing Delusion as Having No Reality. This is further divided into two parts. First, [the absence of] substance...
It possesses a substantial entity. Furthermore, it is divided into two parts. First, its false manifestation based on objects:
due to the two kinds of false objects—movement and stillness—the faculty of hearing arises within the center; it draws in these objective phenomena, and this is called the nature of hearing.
When there is movement, there is sound; when there is stillness, there is no sound. △ Second, the absence of substance apart from sensory objects:
This hearing, separated from those two objects—movement and stillness—is ultimately without substance.
△ Second, [the section on] having no place from which it comes. This is further divided into two parts. First, a general heading and enumeration:
"Thus, Ānanda, you should know that this hearing does not come from movement or stillness; it does not emerge from the sense organ, nor is it produced from space."
△ Second, the interrogation and refutation. This is further divided into three parts. First, [the sound] does not come from the object. Why?

If it came from stillness, then as movement arises, stillness would immediately cease; thus one should not hear the movement. If it came from movement, then as stillness arises, movement would immediately cease;
thus there should be no perception of stillness.
△ Second, it does not arise from the sense organs.
If it were produced from the organs, there would necessarily be no movement or stillness. Thus, the essence of hearing is fundamentally without self-nature.
△ Third, it does not arise from space.
If hearing were to arise from space and possess the nature of existence, it would not be empty space. Furthermore, if space itself hears, what concern is that for your faculty of hearing?
This passage merely differs slightly from the text concerning the "returning to the root" regarding the nature of existence being non-empty;
all other points may be understood by analogy with the above. △ Third, concluding the false and returning to the true.
Therefore, one should know that the ear-base is false and illusory; fundamentally, it is neither produced by causes and conditions nor is it of a spontaneous nature.
Having concluded the discussion on the ear-base as above, [we now turn to] three: the nose-base. This is further divided into three parts. First, the false arises depending upon the true.
Ānanda, it is like a person who forcefully pinches their nose; after pinching it for a long time, they become fatigued, and within the nose they perceive a sensation of cold.
Based on that sensation, they distinguish between what is open and obstructed, or empty and solid, and so on even to various fragrant and foul odors.
Together with the nose and the fatigue, these are all but the appearance of exhaustion produced by the staring of Bodhi.
The sensation of cold is originally an object perceived by the faculty of the body. This [sensation] arises due to the strain of using the nose;
there is no separate fragrance or stench, but only the sensation of cold. Let us temporarily borrow this as an analogy: all fragrant and foul odors are likewise equally illusory.
Furthermore, this further confirms that the latter two instances of the word "strain" (*láo*) in the preceding passage refer to various forms and sounds. △ Second, the analysis.
Delusion is without reality. Furthermore, there are two aspects: first, it lacks a substantial essence; second, it manifests falsely by relying on sensory objects.

Due to the two kinds of false sensory objects—namely, "openness" and "obstruction"—the faculty of hearing arises within them. It draws in these objective phenomena, which is called the olfactory nature of hearing.
"Obstructed" merely refers to the absence of fragrance; it does not necessarily mean that the air is blocked. △ Second, the lack of substance apart from sensory objects:
once this hearing is separated from those two objects—obstruction and openness—it ultimately has no substance.
△ Second, "having nowhere from which it comes," which is further divided into two parts. First, a general indication and enumeration:
One should know that this hearing does not come from openness or obstruction; it does not emerge from the sense faculties, nor is it produced from space.
△ Second, the interrogation and refutation, which is further divided into three parts. First, [the sound] does not come from the object. Why?

If it came from the open space, then when it is obstructed, hearing would cease. How then do we know there is obstruction? If it exists because of the obstruction, then when there is openness, there would be no hearing.
How then could it manifest the sensations of fragrance, stench, and so forth?
△ Second, it does not arise from the sense organ.
If it were produced from the organ, there would necessarily be no alternation between penetration and obstruction. Thus, the faculty of hearing is fundamentally without self-nature.
The term "faculty" (*jī*) is merely a stylistic variation; it need not be said that it initiates hearing, because [hearing] arises precisely by negating the production from the organ. △
Third, it does not come from space.
If it were to emerge from space, then that hearing would naturally turn back to smell your own nose; for space itself possesses hearing—what connection would that have with your faculty of hearing?
Turning back, it smells your nose. As above, when returning, one should see the root. △ Third, concluding that the false returns to the true:
Therefore, you should know that the nose-faculty is empty and false; fundamentally, it is neither produced by causes and conditions nor is it of a spontaneous nature.

The preceding section on the Nose Faculty (*ghrāṇa-āyatana*) is concluded. △ Four: The Tongue Faculty (*jihvā-āyatana*). This is further divided into three parts. First: Falsehood arises based upon the True.

Ānanda, it is like a person who licks their lips with their tongue; by licking repeatedly until they become fatigued, if that person is ill, they perceive a bitter taste, whereas a healthy person perceives a slight sweet sensation.
Through this contrast between sweetness and bitterness, the immobility of this tongue-faculty is revealed.
At that time, the nature of stillness is ever-present. Both the tongue and weariness are equally the signs of weariness manifested through the staring of Bodhi.

This is the definitive meaning (*nītārtha*) of this sutra. Although there are two for each of the six sense objects, within the section clarifying how the first three delusions arise dependent upon the True, it only explains the movement and pervasion.
The following three entries all employ both [aspects], namely: added, stillness, detachment, and cessation. △ Two.

Discriminating that the false has no reality, it is further divided into two parts. First, there is the absence of a substantial entity; this is further divided into two. First, it manifests falsely by relying on sensory objects.
Due to the two kinds of false objects—sweet, bitter, and bland—the faculty of cognition arises within them. It absorbs these objective images, which is called the nature of the cognition of taste.
△ Second, the absence of intrinsic nature apart from objects.
This nature of taste, when separated from the two objects of sweet/bitter and bland, ultimately lacks any intrinsic nature.
△ Second, the fact that it comes from nowhere. This is further divided into two parts: first, a general heading and enumeration.
Thus it is, Ānanda. You should know that this perception of bitter and bland taste does not come from the sweet or the bitter, nor does it exist because of the bland;
furthermore, it does not emerge from the sense organ, nor is it produced from space.
△ Second, the interrogation and refutation, which has three parts. First, [the sensation] does not come from the object. Why?

If sweetness or bitterness were coming [from the object], then when the blandness is perceived, that [sweetness or bitterness] would have ceased. How then could one perceive the blandness? If it were emerging from the blandness, then as soon as the sweetness appeared, [the blandness] would have perished;
how then could one perceive the two characteristics of sweetness and bitterness?
△ Second, it does not arise from the sense organ.
If it were produced from the tongue, there would necessarily be no sweet, bland, or bitter objects; thus one knows that the gustatory faculty has no inherent nature of its own.
△ Third, it does not come from emptiness.

If it were to emerge from emptiness, then emptiness would possess its own flavor, which your mouth could not know; furthermore, if emptiness knew it itself, what concern would that have for your faculty of taste?
The "taste itself" is not the mouth; it appears different from the preceding [section] but emphasizes the following. As it says: "One should simply know the taste by means of empty space itself;
it is not necessary to use the mouth before one knows it. This is intended so as not to repeat what is stated in the subsequent text. △ Third, concluding the delusion and returning to the truth.
Therefore, you should know that the tongue-sphere is empty and false; it is fundamentally neither produced by causes and conditions nor is it of a spontaneous nature.
Having concluded the discussion on the tongue-sphere above, [we now turn to] △ Five: the Body-sphere. This is further divided into three parts. First: the false arises in dependence upon the true.
Ānanda, it is like a person who touches one warm hand with another cold hand. If the power of the cold is greater, the warm becomes cold;
if the efficacy of the heat prevails, the cold becomes warm. In this way, through the touch of their union, the awareness of separation is revealed.

When these forces interact and reach completion, they arise from the touch of exertion; thus, both the body and the exertion are equally the *bodhi* (enlightenment) manifested by staring into emptiness.

The characteristic of weariness (*āyāsa-lakṣaṇa*). This is because both hands are equally the body-faculty (*kāya-indriya*) and there is no distinct object of touch (*spraṣṭavya-viṣaya*); it is merely through the mutual overcoming of cold and heat that one falsely forms perceptions of contact and separation.
These are called false and weary characteristics. Furthermore, all such deluded perceptions within the sense-field of the body (*kāya-āyatana*) are likewise [false].
It is analogous to this. That which is "contact perceived through conjunction" refers specifically to contact involving the intermingling of cold and heat.

As for its being "manifested through disjunction," this is because the body is separated from sensory objects; since those of the Provisional and Lesser Vehicles do not comprehend this, it is manifested by way of the perception of conjunction.
As it is said: "When in conjunction, one knows conjunction; by this, it is naturally revealed that when in disjunction, one must also know disjunction. From the beginning...

This concludes the section. These two lines, "raising both the combined and the separated perceptions" and "engaging with the momentum," serve as a general conclusion, asserting that [the preceding analysis] was merely a futile exertion.
II. Distinguishing that Delusion Lacks Reality. This is further divided into two parts. First: There Is No Substantial Entity.
This is further divided into two parts. First: Manifesting Falsely by Relying on Objects.

Based on the two kinds of false objects—separation and union—the faculty of awakening arises in the midst of them; it draws in these objective phenomena and is termed the nature of cognitive awareness.
△ Second, its lack of substance when separated from objects.
This essence of cognition, apart from those two objects—separation and union, as well as opposition and compliance—is ultimately without substance.
Opposition and compliance are themselves the opposition and compliance within the context of separation and union; thus, there are only these two objects.

That is to say, whether it be separation or union, the perception of suffering is itself opposition, while the perception of pleasure is itself compliance. △ Second, "having nowhere from which it comes," which is further divided into:
2. First, a general enumeration:
"In this way, Ānanda, you should know that this awareness does not come from separation or union; it does not exist through opposition or conformity; it does not emerge from the sense faculties."
Furthermore, it does not arise from emptiness.
△ Second, the interrogation and refutation, which is further divided into three parts. First, it does not come from external objects. Why is this?

If it were to come when [the object] is present, it would have already ceased when [the object] is absent; how then could one perceive its absence? This also applies to the two characteristics of the agreeable and the disagreeable.
It is likewise so.
Although four characteristics are distinguished, they ultimately consist of only two objects. Second, [consciousness] does not arise from the sense organs.

If it were to emerge from the organs, there would necessarily be no four characteristics of separation and union, or opposition and compliance; thus, the cognitive faculty of your body would fundamentally lack intrinsic nature.
△ Third, it does not come from emptiness;
it must emerge within emptiness. Emptiness itself is aware of this; what concern is it to your entry?
This "entry" (入) and the following "entry" (入) both belong to this section [of the text], where the first two phrases are missing and only the latter two phrases remain. △
The three fetters falsely return to the True.
Therefore, one should know that the body-faculty (kāyāyatana) is empty and false; it is fundamentally neither produced by causes and conditions nor is it of a spontaneous nature.
Having completed the discussion on the body-faculty above, the six mind-faculties (manāyatana) are further divided into three parts. △ First: The False Arises in Dependence upon the True.

Ānanda, it is like a person who sleeps when weary; having slept deeply, he awakens. When he encounters sensory objects, he recollects them; losing that recollection is forgetting. These constitute his inversions.
Birth, abiding, change, and extinction follow one another in succession, returning to the midst of habitual conditioning without ever overstepping their order.
What is called the faculty of mental cognition, together with the mind and its weariness, is all but a state of exhaustion produced by the fixed gazing of Bodhi.

Following the principle of the various sense bases (*āyatana*) mentioned above, the faculties (*indriya*) are each singular; for example, the eye is simply called "seeing," and the ear is simply called "hearing," and so forth.

The objects (*viṣaya*) are each divided into two; for example, visible form (*rūpa*) is distinguished as light and darkness, and sound (*śabda*) is distinguished as movement and stillness, and so forth.

Now, the mental faculty (*manas*) should likewise be designated simply as "cognition" (*jñāna*), while mental phenomena (*dharma*) should likewise be divided only into arising and ceasing. Thus, one knows that waking and sleeping, recollection and forgetfulness, and arising and abiding [are all subsumed within these categories].

The eight characters for "differentiation" and "extinction" merely form a textual arrangement through their mutual interaction; in reality, they are all objects of the mental consciousness (*dharmāyatana*).

In truth, they consist solely of the two meanings of arising and ceasing. Furthermore, based on the preceding discussion of sleep and awakening, this should also be understood as an illustrative analogy of provisional designation.
For example, when the eyes are strained by staring, one perceives floating flowers; when the mind is exhausted by fatigue, the states of sleep and awakening manifest. This is the case. As for...
"Recollection and forgetting merely manifest the states of sleep and awakening. Awakening is the perceiving of objects; sleep is the loss of recollection.

This section concludes the preceding hypothetical illustration, which serves as an example for what follows. All instances of recollection and forgetting are identical to the states of sleep and awakening;
by means of this, the characteristics of the mental faculty (*manas*) are explained and established. As for "inversion," it refers to [the confusion of] beginning and end.

The meaning of "successive circulation" (cun-huan) refers to arising, abiding, change, and cessation, which are also equivalent to recollection and forgetting, differing only in their respective sequence of before and after.
Initial recollection is "arising"; the state of active recollection is "abiding"; the beginning of forgetting is "change"; and the complete exhaustion of forgetting is "cessation.

Regarding the two phrases "inhaling" and "practicing," Wuxing says that within these characteristics, the mental faculty returns to the four characteristics, which do not exist as distinct moments of before and after.
This is correct. Regarding the term "faculty of knowing according to one's will" (*yathābhiprāya-jñānendriya*), this is merely an explanation of its name based on its function;

let us not elaborate further, lest it be confused with the "nature of awakened cognition" (*bodhana-jñāna-svabhāva*) mentioned in the subsequent text. △ Second, the analysis of delusion as lacking reality, divided into two parts.
First, the absence of a substantial entity, which is further divided into two. First, the false manifestation based upon sense objects.

Based upon the two kinds of delusive objects—arising and ceasing—the faculty of cognition gathers within and draws inward the internal dust; seeing and hearing flow against the current, reaching a ground where the flow no longer reaches.
This is called the nature of cognitive awareness.

Arising and ceasing encompass all eight [characteristics] mentioned previously; they do not stop at abiding and change alone. Regarding the two phrases "seeing and hearing," according to the interpretation of Master Gusuan:

"recollection" refers to the mind's retrogressive engagement with the five sensory objects that have already fallen away, while "forgetting" refers to the state of being obscured and dwelling in a realm that has not yet been reached.

If one pursues it upstream, dust arises; if one does not reach it, dust is extinguished. That which is called the "nature of awareness" refers merely to the recollection or forgetting of sensory objects;
it is only a provisional designation for the nature of cognition. II. The absence of intrinsic substance apart from sensory objects.
This nature of awareness, apart from the two objects of waking and sleeping, arising and ceasing, ultimately has no substance.
Waking and sleeping are not the same as the "sleeping" and "waking" mentioned above; those are merely conventional designations referring to the state of slumber.

This [present discussion] concerns mental objects (*dharmas*), which consist merely of the clarity or turbidity of the spiritual mind. It does not point to sleep itself as being arising and ceasing; therefore, there are only these two.
Dust. △ Second, that it comes from nowhere. This is divided into two parts. First, a general heading and enumeration:
"Thus, Ānanda, you should know that this faculty of awareness and cognition does not come from waking or sleeping, nor does it exist through birth or extinction."
It does not emerge from the sense organs, nor is it born from space.
△ Second, the interrogation and refutation, divided into three parts. First, it does not come from the objects. Why?
If it came from the waking state, it would cease immediately upon falling asleep; what then would constitute sleep? It must exist at the time of arising, yet it ceases [upon awakening].

This is equivalent to non-existence; who would there be to undergo cessation? If existence arises from cessation, then birth is simply the absence of cessation; who then could know that which is born?

Whether awake or asleep, this merely expands upon the refutation of the [concept of] "mind," yet it remains the same as arising and ceasing. Thus, the Master [Huiyuan] maintains that both characters "shou" (to receive) and "er" (two) are actually the character "zhi" (to know);
they are merely a variation of the phrasing to form a complete sentence. △ Second, [the mind] does not arise from the sense organs.
If [consciousness] were to emerge from the sense organs, it would possess the two characteristics of waking and sleeping, opening and closing according to the body;
yet apart from these two entities, this cognizer is like a flower in the sky—ultimately devoid of intrinsic nature.
These two characters, "awake" (wù) and "sleeping" (mèi), comprehensively encompass the eight characters beginning with "arising" (shēng) and "ceasing" (miè).
This section is somewhat difficult to elucidate; however, based on the preceding texts, it becomes clear. For instance, it says:

"If you insist that [the objects] arise solely from the sense organs themselves and have no relation to waking and sleeping, you fail to realize that these two types of objects constantly accompany the body, opening and closing with it, never for a moment departing."
If you consider the faculty of cognition to be devoid of substance when separated from these two objects, it would then accord with various scriptural passages.
As for the body, its opening and closing refers to the flesh within the body; the mind is shaped like a lotus flower: it is bright when open and dark when closed.
△ Third, [it does not come from space].
If it arises from emptiness, it is inherently the cognition of emptiness; what concern is it to your sense-base?
△ Third, concluding that the false returns to the true:
Therefore, you should know that the mind-base is illusory; fundamentally, it is neither caused by conditions nor of a spontaneous nature.

(At this point, the entry into the analysis of the categories of the aggregates, elements, and sense-bases should be clarified. There are three types of distinctions in the deconstruction of phenomena: first, deconstruction by way of conditions. This means that the discourse does not restrict itself to the primary phenomenon, but extensively deconstructs external conditions. It is like extinguishing a fire:

one does not strike the fire directly, but simply removes its fuel, and the fire extinguishes of its own accord, because fire has no self-nature. Second, mutual deconstruction. This means that two phenomena stand in dependence upon one another; thus, they must be mutually deconstructed, just as a water-snake and water depend on each other, yet both become a source of affliction.)

To eliminate them is to drive away the *kō* (water-dragons) and cut off the source of water, or to drain the water and destroy the dragons' dwelling. These three methods involve breaking down from the essential point; there are two types. First, breaking down from the essential point via two factors:

it is like two pieces of wood standing leaning against one another; if one simply pushes one side over, both will fall. Second, breaking down from the essential point via three factors: it is like a bow made of the combination of sinew, glue, and horn, where the glue is the essential element; if the glue is merely removed, the sinew and horn will no longer form a bow.

Therefore, these six sense bases (*ṣaḍāyatana*) entirely involve breaking down the objects by means of their conditions; this refers precisely to those conditions. The following twelve bases (*dvādaśāyatana*) further include mutual interaction and the breaking down from the essential point via two factors. The four bases of eye-form and ear-sound involve mutual breaking down. The remainder...

The eight bases (*āyatana*) and two factors are analyzed by means of their essential constituents. Furthermore, among these, only the bases of body and tangibles are analyzed solely with respect to the sense faculties (*indriya*); the remaining six bases are all analyzed solely with respect to the objects (*viṣaya*). The subsequent eighteen elements (*dhātu*) are entirely analyzed by means of the three factors [faculty, object, and consciousness].

Although the text analyzes them according to their essentials, the underlying intent actually analyzes them all together; this is not the same as the case of the six sense bases (*ṣaḍāyatana*), where the primary intent lies in the faculties. This can be clearly seen upon examining the concluding sections. The analysis of the six bases is now complete. △ The thirty-two bases:
This is likely an expansion of the category of form (*rūpa*) and a contraction of the category of mind (*citta*), taught for those who are deluded regarding form but not regarding the mind.

Form (*rūpa*) is originally one; when opened, it becomes the five sense organs (*indriya*). Together with the six objects (*viṣaya*), these constitute the eleven bases (*āyatana*). Therefore, it is said that "form is opened.
If contrasted with the aforementioned five aggregates (*skandha*), it combines the four—feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness.

If contrasted with the eighteen elements (*dhātu*) below, it combines the seven—the six consciousnesses and the mind-faculty (*manas*)—and collectively subsumes them into the single base of the mind. Therefore, it is said that "mind is closed."
This is divided into two parts. First, a general inquiry:
"Furthermore, Ānanda, how are the twelve *āyatanas* (bases) fundamentally the Tathāgata-garbha, the wondrous true nature of *tathatā*?

'Āyatana' refers to a location or a fixed place. Because there are the six sense organs (*indriya*) and the six sense objects (*viṣaya*), there are twelve. This is the provisional teaching regarding their characteristics."

Establishing the Argument: The sense organs (*indriya*) are definitively internal, while their objects (*viṣaya*) are definitively external. Furthermore, the eye corresponds only to form, and the ear corresponds only to sound; each has a fixed location.
Now, to unify them within the single nature is precisely to refute those fixed locations.
The intent of this inquiry follows the above. II. Specific Refutations, divided into six parts: 1. The Place of the Eye and Form. Subdivided.
4. First, the two locations are indicated.
"Ānanda, you should now observe this Jeta Grove and its various springs and ponds.
The word "observe" (觀) is the locus of the root; what follows is the locus of the objects (dusts). All subsequent instances follow this pattern. △ Second, the pair.
This is raised as an objection.
What do you think? Do these [phenomena] mean that form arises and the eye sees it, or that the eye arises and takes on the appearance of form?

For those of ordinary and limited minds who hold that dharmas exist externally and that the sense faculties and their objects do not interact, this objection does not apply; this is explained according to the provisional [teaching].

The school that takes the mind as its primary principle asserts that mental phenomena give rise to the sense of existence. This means that form must first appear before seeing can arise; apart from form, there would be nothing for seeing to manifest.
Therefore, it is said that "form gives rise to the eye's seeing. Furthermore, the eye must first observe before form becomes manifest; apart from seeing, form cannot be apprehended.
Therefore, it is said that "the eye gives rise to the appearance of form. This is indeed a provisional teaching, skillfully cited to lead those who cling to dharmas gradually toward [the truth].
The object of consciousness-only (*vijñapti-mātra*) is not, in fact, a definitive teaching on non-arising; therefore, this objection is raised to refute it.
△ Second, the refutation through analysis of the text, which is further divided into two parts. First, the refutation of the arising of form from seeing.
Ānanda, if it were the visual faculty that produced the appearance of form, then when seeing empty space—which is not form—the nature of form would have to dissolve.

If it were to dissolve, everything would be revealed as utterly non-existent. Since the appearance of form would no longer exist, who would perceive the substance of empty space? It is the same for empty space as well.
"Seeing emptiness as non-form, the nature of form should be extinguished" means that since the eye arises in relation to form, the eye possesses the nature of form;

yet when seeing emptiness as non-form, the nature of form should be lost. "Extinguishing it reveals that everything is utterly non-existent" means that nature and characteristics arise in mutual dependence;
once the nature of form is extinguished, the characteristics of form should likewise vanish. Since the characteristics of form no longer exist, who [is there to see]?

Regarding the clarification of the substance of emptiness: it is said that emptiness is manifested at the boundary of form and its characteristics. Since the characteristics of form are absent, emptiness should likewise not be manifested.
"Emptiness is also like this" means that the eye gives rise to the appearance of emptiness; by this analogy, it can be understood. △ Second, refuting that the arising of form produces seeing.

Furthermore, if it were the case that visual perception arises from the dust of form, then when one contemplates emptiness as being non-form, seeing would immediately vanish. Once vanished, it would be entirely absent;
who then could discern between emptiness and form?

This is easier to understand than the previous point. Regarding "the seeing of non-form vanishes," this means that since there is no form capable of producing [seeing], [seeing] itself has nothing upon which to depend.
The view of birth is a non-view that is entirely devoid of clarity; therefore it is said, "Who clarifies emptiness and form?
According to the preceding section, there should likewise be the phrase "emptiness is also thus. △ Fourth, concluding the false and returning to the true.

Therefore, you should know that seeing and form-emptiness both have no location; thus, form and seeing—these two locations—are illusory, fundamentally neither produced by causes and conditions nor possessing an inherent nature.
"Having no location" means there is no fixed dwelling place, whether internal or external; this further clarifies that there is no location.

"False and illusory" means that, in their essence, they are one and not two. This is because the notion of mutual production arises precisely from the false attachment to the eye and form as being two distinct entities, failing to realize they are of one essence.

This false conceptualization arises through opposition. Now, regarding the falsity of these appearances: [...]* *Note: The provided source text ends mid-sentence. The translation reflects the available portion.*
Since there is no substance and it is a false manifestation, there are not even two locations; of what could one say that characteristics arise?

From the perspective of the true nature, one sees that form is of a single essence; from the beginning, it is simply this wondrous nature, which is neither caused by conditions nor produced spontaneously.

With what could characteristics arise? This principle applies to all subsequent cases. Now, regarding the observation of the beginning, it is said that both have no location; next, it is said that the two—
To dwell in falsehood is clearly a flat contradiction; this differs from the "correct refutation" above, wherein the six sense bases (ṣaḍāyatana) and their objects are merely mentioned in passing.
This concludes the two bases of eye and form. II. The Bases of Ear and Sound. This is divided into four parts: first, the enumeration of the two bases.
Ānanda, listen further to this sound of the drum being struck when the meal is prepared in this Jeta Grove, and the bell being tolled when the assembly gathers;
the sounds of the bell and drum continue one after another in succession.
The faculties and their objects follow the same principle as above. △ Second, the inquiry is raised by means of a pair:
"What do you think? Do these sounds come to the ear, or does the ear go to the place where the sound is?"
Examine the intent of the refutation below. Here, one phrase is missing: "Is it because there is no coming and going?

For indeed, having coming and going is the deluded sentiment of ordinary people and the Lesser Vehicle; the absence of coming and going is the conceptual proliferation (*prapañca*) regarding the characteristics of dharmas—namely, the so-called "cognition apart from [the object].
Now, both are refuted. Thus, the "double interrogation" must refer to the double interrogation of both the existence of coming and going and the non-existence of coming and going.

This constitutes the second calculation. △ Third, the refutation of the difficulty regarding the division of the text, which is further divided into three parts. First, the refutation of the sound reaching the ear:
"Ānanda, if this sound were to come from outside to the side of your ear—just as I am now begging for food in the city of Śrāvastī while staying in the Jeta Grove—then 'I' would not be present here.
This sound must then come to the location of Ānanda’s ear; yet Maudgalyāyana and Kāśyapa [would not hear it]."
If even they all hear it, how much more so the one thousand two hundred and fifty śramaṇas therein? Upon hearing the sound of the bell once, they all come together to the place of the meal.
This is an illustration of using the "single hearing" of sound to refute the notion of multiplicity. In the analogy, even a single body cannot go to two places simultaneously.
Regarding the locus: how could a single sound within the dharma-realm possibly reach many ears? It is evident that the calculation that sound travels to the side of the ear is false.
One should not find difficulty in this analogy by appealing to supernatural powers (*ṛddhi*). △ Second, refuting the idea that the ear reaches the sound.
Furthermore, if your ear were to go to the location of the sound—just as I have returned to dwell in the Jeta Grove within the city of Śrāvastī—then I would no longer exist [for you].
When you hear the sound of a drum, your ear has already gone to the place where the drum is; yet when the sound of a bell arises simultaneously, [how can it reach both?]
One should not hear them all simultaneously; how much less so the various sounds of elephants, horses, oxen, and sheep within them?

This refutes the notion that the ear goes out to hear many sounds by means of hearing a single sound. The meaning of the analogy remains as before: how could a single ear within the [analogy of] the Dharma travel everywhere to reach many sounds?
Thus, it is evident that the calculation that the ear travels to the location of the sounds is also false. △ Third, the refutation of the absence [of the ear].
Coming and going.
If there were no coming and going, there would likewise be no hearing.
For one who neither comes nor goes, the faculty of the ear and the object of sound each abide in their own respective positions; the two do not reach one another. Based on this, then—
Even if one were to respond with a voice, the ears would be unable to hear it. This is like two people, one in a city and one in a garden, who cannot reach each other and will never know one another.
It is also like fire and wood, which, remaining in separate places, can never burn one another.

Thus, the so-called "cognition through separation" regarding the characteristics of phenomena (*dharmalakṣaṇa*) is merely frivolous conceptualization (*prapañca*); how could it be the definitive meaning? △ Fourth, concluding the false and returning to the true.

Therefore, you should know that hearing and sound both have no location; thus, both hearing and sound are illusory in their respective domains, fundamentally neither produced by causes and conditions nor existing as a spontaneous nature.
Regarding the two views mentioned above—of coming and going, and of no coming and going—neither is correct. Why is this so?
It is simply because their characteristics are false while their nature is true. To speak of the falsity of their characteristics:
one should know that hearing and sound each pervade everywhere; neither has a fixed location. Thus, as for the two locations of hearing and sound themselves—
The substance [of these] is likewise unattainable. Expedient and limited [teachings] of the Lesser Vehicle are entirely devoid of real meaning.

Thus, since even the two [realms] do not exist, who could be said to come and go, or not come and go? Regarding the self-nature mantra, one should know that hearing and sound are not ultimately non-existent dharmas;
they are simply the single, wondrous nature that is neither caused by conditions nor produced spontaneously. Truly.

If there is no dual nature, with whom could there be coming and going, or not coming and going? Question: Since it is only a single substance, what fault is there in its being separate from cognition?
Answer: A single substance is not dual; how can one say it is separate? If there were truly such separation, how could there be cognition?
This is because, due to the absence of dual characteristics and the presence of a single nature, both dualistic reckonings are simultaneously negated.

It is precisely through the simultaneous negation of these two reckonings that it is revealed as a single essence without two locations. One should know that while the single essence is non-dual, it is specifically these two locations that are emphasized for clarity;
thus they are explained in detail. All other cases should be understood according to this principle. This concludes the section on the two locations of the ear and sound.
△ Third, the sense base of the nose and odors. This is divided into four parts. First, the designation of the two bases:

"Ānanda, you should again smell this sandalwood in the incense burner. If this fragrance were burned from only one *zhu*, its scent would be smelled simultaneously throughout the forty *li* within the city of Śrāvastī."

At a distance of forty *li*, the scent is perceived simultaneously; this immediately demonstrates that the nose does not encounter the smoke. The old commentary suspects that this violates the principle of "knowing through the conjunction of dharmas" (*dharmalakṣaṇa*).
It fails to recognize that this is the definitive meaning (*nītārtha*) of the *dharmatā* (the nature of phenomena), which precisely refutes the *dharmalakṣaṇa*.
How can one, on the contrary, use that [principle] to challenge this? According to the *dharmatā*, the sense faculties and their objects are each all-pervasive and of a single essence.

There is no [actual] contact. To speak of "separation" or "contact" with cognition is entirely mere conceptual proliferation (*prapañca*). However, since the nose constantly encounters fragrance, it necessarily meets with smoke;

thus, speaking of "contact" is not of definitive meaning (*neyārtha*). It is precisely this distinct fragrance that does not depend on meeting with smoke, and it is through this that [the perception] is correctly established.

The Buddha adopted this because it clarifies the definitive meaning that the sense faculties (*indriya*) and their objects (*viṣaya*) each pervade everywhere and do not depend on contact for cognition;
thus, there is a profound intention behind his choice. Furthermore, all things possess unique characteristics; it is not limited to sandalwood alone.

For example, the medicinal tree heals disease upon being seen, while poison applied to a drum harms people when its sound is heard. The eyes of an owl are dark during the day but clear at night. Wheat [ripens] in autumn...
That it flourishes in spring and withers in summer—how could all such things be rigidly bound by convention, such that one would not believe in their extraordinary nature?
△ Second, a detailed inquiry to provoke reflection:
What do you think? Does this fragrance arise from the sandalwood tree, or does it arise from your nose, or does it arise from space?
This refers solely to the investigation of the olfactory object (*gandha-viṣaya*). It is entirely without a place of origination; thus, these two factors must be refuted from their essential basis.

△ Third, the refutation through textual analysis, divided into three parts. First, the refutation of [the scent] arising from the nose, further divided into two. First, establishing that if it arises from the nose, it must emerge [from it].
Ānanda, if this fragrance were produced within your nose, and was thus designated as being produced by the nose, it ought to emerge from the nose.
2. Refuting the error based on its emergence and transformation is further divided into two parts: first, the incompatibility between essence and function.
The nose is not sandalwood. How, then, can there be the fragrance of sandalwood within the nose?
Being a physical body of flesh rather than a body of fragrance, how could it possess the function of emitting fragrance? △ Second, the name and its meaning are inconsistent.
"You say you 'smell' the fragrance; this should occur through the entry of the nose. Since the fragrance issues from within the nose, to speak of 'smelling' is not correct.
The character for 'hearing' (or 'smelling') is a name that takes 'entry' as its meaning; 'issuing forth' is not its meaning. 2. Refuting [the view] that it arises from space.
If [the fragrance] were produced from space, then since the nature of space is eternal, the fragrance should be eternally present. Why then rely on burning this withered wood in a brazier?
△ Third, refuting [the view that it] arises from the wood.
If it were produced from wood, then this fragrant substance would become smoke upon being burned; if the nose were to perceive it, it ought to be enveloped by the scent of that smoke.
Yet, before the smoke has even ascended far into the air, how is it that the fragrance is already perceived within forty *li*?
Even this visible [smoke] is not permitted to be the extraordinary power of a distinct fragrance, for it is accepted only through the habitual attachments of ordinary people;
thus, one falls into the view that fragrance arises from the wood. How much more so, then, to insist that it must be identical to ordinary fragrance enveloped in smoke?
This definitive meaning of non-arising is extremely profound and difficult to understand; it should be contemplated with deep reflection. △ Fourth, concluding the false and returning to the true.

Therefore, you should know that the fragrance and the nose, along with the act of smelling, all lack a fixed location. Thus, both the smelling and the fragrance are illusory in their respective domains;
fundamentally, they are neither produced by causes and conditions nor do they possess an inherent nature.

The two characters for "nose" (bi) seem to encompass both the physical organ (*bu-chen*) and the subtle faculty (*sheng-yi*). When the faculty is paired with its object, they still constitute two locations;

Therefore, it is said that both lack a location; this refers to the essential substance of the arising of these two locations—namely, smelling and fragrance.
It is utterly unobtainable. Up to this point, the delusions have been tied up; as for returning to the truth, the meaning is the same as above.
The two locations of the nose and fragrance are now concluded. △ Fourth, the location of the tongue and flavor, divided into four parts: first, the enumeration of the two locations.
