This is divided into three parts. First, the refutation of the ear arising from causes, which is further divided into three. First, the refutation by means of the ultimate sense-faculty (*paramārtha-indriya*).
Ānanda, if [the faculty] were produced by reason of the ear, then when the two characteristics of motion and stillness are not present before it, the faculty would fail to constitute cognition;
there would necessarily be nothing known. Since the "preceptor" (the faculty) is unestablished, what form or appearance could consciousness have?
As for the *paramārtha-indriya* (ultimate sense organ), it is composed of the eight pure elements (*dharmas*) and is held to possess the capacity for hearing.

Furthermore, it is the object perceived by the noble ones (*ārya*), which is not seen by the physical eye (*māṃsa-cakṣus*). Changshui said: "If the external object does not exist, the sense organ itself lacks cognition.
If it truly lacks cognition, what consciousness could there possibly be? △ Second, refutation based on the *vikalpa-indriya* (conventional sense organ). As for the *vikalpa-indriya*, it is...

It is merely flesh and ears. Composed of the eight coarse and floating elements (*dharmas*), it originally lacks the capacity for hearing. The classification under the two sense organs follows Changshui.
Furthermore, it is divided into two types: first, the absence of hearing when separated from the object.
If one grasps at "hearing by means of the ear," there is no distinction between movement and stillness; thus, hearing cannot be established.

To "grasp at hearing by means of the ear" is simply to grasp at the physical ear as being capable of hearing. The final two lines refute this notion of the mind, following the same analytical method as above.
△ Second, the physical ear alone is not the auditory element (*dhātu*).
What is the form of the ear? The various colors and tactile objects are called the element of consciousness (*vijñānadhātu*).

What is meant by "various colors and tactile objects"? Among the four types of sensory objects of the physical sense-faculties (*bhautikendriya*), two are briefly cited: namely, color, which can be seen, and touch, which can be grasped.

These are material things that possess form. If one were to take only these... [there would be no... (Note: The source text appears to be a fragment from a Buddhist scholastic commentary, likely discussing the relationship between the sense faculties, their objects, and the resulting consciousness. The final sentence is incomplete.)

It is subsumed under the category of feeling (*vedanā*) and does not belong to the class of mind-consciousness (*citta-vijñāna*). How, then, can it be established as the element of consciousness (*vijñāna-dhātu*)? △ Third, refuting [the position] by means of two faculties:
Furthermore, from what would the element of ear-consciousness (*śrotra-vijñāna-dhātu*) be established?
Regarding consciousness, from which of the two bases (āyatana) is its "element" (dhātu) ultimately established? The refutation of [the view that it] arises dependent on the ear is complete.
△ Second, the refutation of [the view that it] arises dependent on sound. This has two parts: first, the refutation by showing the simultaneous failure of both the sense organ and the object.
If auditory consciousness arises because of sound, then it has no relation to hearing. Without hearing, the locus of the characteristic of sound would cease to exist.
Changshui said: "If sound can produce consciousness, why rely on hearing? If there were no hearing, sound itself would not exist."
△ Second, the refutation based on the simultaneous existence of both the faculty and the object. This is further divided into three parts.

First, establishing that auditory consciousness arises from sound: you concede that the characteristic of sound exists because of the faculty of hearing; therefore, the hearing [faculty] should hear the auditory consciousness.
The first phrase establishes the premise. The two phrases beginning with "admitting sound" state that it is also admitted that there is hearing.
This is intended to rescue what was previously refuted; however, the final phrase refutes it once again by stating that if consciousness arises because of sound, it must be identical to that sound.
Then, at the time of hearing a sound, how could one avoid the fault of the auditory consciousness? △ Second, both paths are untenable. "Not hearing" is not the [auditory] element (*dhātu*);
"hearing" is the same as the sound. Regarding "not the element":

it means that the sound is not the element from which consciousness arises. "The same as the sound" is easy to understand. Although this explicitly demonstrates the double negation, the intended meaning is—
This further clarifies that the consciousness of hearing must necessarily exist. △ Third, establishing the absence of a knowing subject:
Since consciousness has already been heard, who is it that knows this hearing-consciousness? If there were no knower, one would ultimately be like grass or wood.
If one follows the former [position], the auditory consciousness becomes subject to the fallacy of being insentient.
For it is said that consciousness must differ from sound in order to be able to distinguish sound; yet now, having already been heard, it is identical to the insentient object of sound.
Furthermore, who would come to know this auditory consciousness? The final two lines conclude the refutation, thereby resulting in the fallacy of being insentient. △
The three [realms] would then mutually destroy one another;

it would be illogical for the Śrāvakas to intermingle and form the intermediate realm (*madhyama-dhātu*). If there were no intermediate position within the realms, from what then could the characteristics of "internal" and "external" be established?
If one claims that the sense organs and their objects arise together, then it would be illogical for sounds to intermingle to form the intermediate realm.

For once they are said to intermingle, they cannot constitute an intermediate state. The subsequent statement that there must be an intermediate position before internal and external can be distinguished follows from this.
Now, since there is no intermediate realm, how can one distinguish between internal and external realms? △ Fourth, concluding the illusory and returning to the true:

Therefore, one should know that with the ear and sound as conditions, the auditory consciousness-realm arises. Since these three locations are all non-existent, then the ear, the sound, and the auditory realm—these three—are fundamentally neither produced by causes and conditions nor are they of a spontaneous nature.

Hereafter, follow the above pattern. The three realms of the ear, sound, and auditory consciousness are concluded. △ Third, the realm of the nose, odor, and olfactory consciousness, which is further divided into four parts.
First, the enumeration of the three realms.
Ānanda, furthermore, regarding what you have clarified: with the nose and fragrance as conditions, the nose-consciousness arises.
Second, [the Buddha] interrogates this by means of a pair:
does this consciousness arise because of the nose, taking the nose as its constituent element (dhātu), or does it arise because of fragrance, taking fragrance as its constituent element?

As above. △ Third: Refuting the difficulty by combining the three parts. This is divided into three sections. First, refuting that [the sense of smell] arises from the nose. First, interrogating both organs together:
"Ānanda, if it arises because of the nose, then within your mind, what do you take to be the nose? Is it the physical form of the flesh, or the two nostrils?"
...the characteristic [of the nose]. This is done to apprehend and know the nature of movement through smelling.
△ Second, the refutation based on the ephemeral sense organ (bu-chén-gēn) has two parts. First, the transformation of its substance:
if one takes the physical form [of the nose], the fleshly substance is the body; what the body knows is touch.

This means that the olfactory faculty (*ghrāṇendriya*) transforms into the tactile faculty (*kāyendriya*), and the function of smelling transforms into the object of touch (*spraṣṭavya*). Second, they lose their respective names:
what was called the "nose" is now called the "body," and what was called "smelling" is now termed the "object."

This pair serves to refute the designation "noseless. That is to say, "name-body" (nāmakāya) refers to the name of the body and not the name of the nose; "name-contact" (nāmaspraṣṭavya) refers to the name of the object-field and not the name of the nose.
△ Third, refuting [the opponent's position] by following up on their denial of the [nose] element.
The nose itself has no name; how then can it be established as a constituent element (*dhātu*)?
△ Third, refuting both [the sense organ and its object] by means of the ultimate reality (*paramārtha*). First, a general interrogation regarding the nature of cognition:
If you take "olfactory cognition" as the basis, then within your own mind, what constitutes that which cognizes?
△ Second, a detailed analysis and refutation of the objection. This also has three parts. First, [the nose] does not know by means of the flesh;
if one takes the flesh to be the knower, then that which is the knowledge of the flesh is fundamentally contact and not the nose.
That is, the body mentioned above knows touch. △ Second, the refutation of the claim that it is empty space that knows, which is further divided into two parts:

(1) Refuting the notion that knowledge belongs to empty space while discarding the flesh, and asserting that empty space is the knower. If empty space were the knower, then empty space would know itself; consequently, the flesh should not be conscious.
The empty finger points to the nostrils; the fleshly finger points to the tip of the nose. This section addresses the fault of failing to realize that the flesh of the nose is falling away.
△ Second, grasping at emptiness as self while neglecting the body.
If this were so, then empty space would be you; your body would not be the knower. In that case, Ānanda, today you would have no fixed location.
For if the emptiness within the nostrils already possesses the nature of cognition, then all empty space should likewise be you.
Furthermore, since the flesh upon the nose lacks the nature of cognition, then all the flesh throughout your body should likewise lack cognition.
Based on these two points, the fallacy of non-existence follows: if space were you, then as space has no location, you too would have no location;
if the body lacks cognition, then even if the body had a location, [you would still not exist].
One should not fail to perceive in what location it resides. △ Third, the section "Non-fragrance" refutes the possibility of confusion with the arising of inferior fragrances.
This follows from the refutation of the nose-born consciousness-element, which leads to a further investigation: what constitutes the nose?

Having already refuted the superficial sensory organ (*buddhadhātu*), one now investigates the ultimate knowledge (*paramārtha-jñāna*): upon what does its substance depend? Thereby, both flesh and space are refuted.

Thus, it eventually reaches the fragrance; this is merely a refutation of the nose-faculty’s cognition of fragrance, not the same as the refutation below regarding the production of consciousness from fragrance.
Furthermore, it is divided into two parts: first, turning [the opponent's position] back upon themselves to expose their own fallacy.
If you take fragrance as your cognition, then that cognition belongs to the fragrance itself; what concern is it to you?

"Concern" means interference. Since you have shifted [the locus] so that your own cognition becomes the cognition of another's fragrance, and that [fragrance] possesses its own cognition, how does it interfere with you?
2. The Error of Appropriating Another as Self: This refers to taking external fragrance-objects (*gandha-viṣaya*) as arising from one's own nose.
Furthermore, there are two points. First, [the argument that] external factors must establish the internal:
if fragrant and foul odors necessarily arise from your nose, then those two types of flowing air—fragrant and foul—would not arise from the eranda tree or the sandalwood tree.
For a moment, external objects are set aside so that the internal sense organs may arise. △ Second, the nose is refuted by means of its "air" (qi).

This consists of two parts: first, refuting the nose by means of the air; this is the refutation of the one (the nose) by means of the two (the air). This further has three parts: first, the nose smells apart from the air.
The two things do not come to you; you yourself smell your own nose. Is it fragrant or foul?
Second, they cannot be smelled simultaneously:
if it is foul, it is not fragrant; if it is fragrant, it is not foul.
If it were the case that your nose originally perceived only stench, it would certainly not simultaneously perceive fragrance; and if it were fragrance, the opposite would hold true.
Third, regarding the simultaneous perception of both, which leads to a dualism:
if you were able to perceive both fragrance and stench at once, then you, as a single person, would have to possess two noses. Thus I question you.
"There are two Ānandas; which one is your own body?
This refutation is made because [the opponent] erroneously clings to the notion that fragrance and stench arise simultaneously within the nose.

It states that if fragrance and stench were produced together, one would necessarily possess two noses. These two noses do not refer to the physical nose, but rather to the *indriya* (sensory faculty).
Because the spirit of meaning is aware, it steps down upon the two nostrils and immediately seeks the two bodies. Second, breaking the qi from the nose:
this refers to one nose breaking through the two types of qi. This is further divided into two parts: first, the sense organ uniting with its object.
If the nose were a single entity, there would be no distinction between fragrance and stench.
Since you say that the sense of smell arises from the nose, and the nose is but one, the fragrances and stenches it produces should be a single undifferentiated whole.
2. The Conjunction with Objects Renders the Elements Obsolete.
What was foul becomes fragrant, and what was fragrant again becomes foul. Since these two natures do not exist, from what could the realms (*dhātu*) be established?
The first two lines cite the cases of fragrance and foulness to mutually negate them; the final two lines offer two interpretations to conclude the refutation.

According to one interpretation, because they mutually negate each other, both become non-existent. If this is so, then even the sense organ’s cognition lacks its own substance, let alone consciousness (*vijñāna*).
From what is the "element" (dhātu) established? Furthermore, it is said that the two energies are mutually identical and lack any fixed distinction;

how then can the consciousness-element be established based on what is discriminated? [This applies] to both cases. △ Second, refuting [the claim] that [consciousness] arises from fragrance. This is divided into three parts. First, establishing that [the subject] does not know the fragrance. This further has two parts.
First, granting for the sake of argument that it arises from fragrance.
If consciousness arises because of fragrance, and consciousness exists because of fragrance, then:
△ Second, refuting the doctrine by means of an analogy.
Just as the eye has the capacity for seeing yet cannot see itself, because consciousness exists because of fragrance, it should likewise not know fragrance.
Seeing exists because of the eye; since one does not see the eye itself, consciousness exists because of fragrance, yet it should not perceive that fragrance.
Second, both paths are untenable:
if it perceives, it is not produced; if it does not perceive, it is not consciousness.
Wenling says: To say that if one knows it, then it is not the arising of fragrance, or to say that if one does not know it, then it cannot be called consciousness—both are untenable.
△ Third, both realms are simultaneously refuted.

If fragrance were not known to exist, the fragrance-element (*gandha-dhātu*) would not be established. If consciousness did not know fragrance, then the element [of fragrance] could not be established on account of that consciousness.

"On account of the element" here refers specifically to the consciousness-element (*vijñāna-dhātu*), because the term "element" (*dhātu*) carries the sense of being a cause or basis. Continuing from the above:
if one does not know fragrance, it is not merely that consciousness is non-existent; rather, both the fragrance-element and the consciousness-element will necessarily fail to be established.
Why is this? It is because fragrance is not [as you claim] (and so forth). Fragrance is not that which knows its own existence; fragrance does not manifest through consciousness.
Based on this, the realm of fragrance (*gandha-dhātu*) would fail to be established, for fragrance necessarily manifests by depending upon cognition.
How could it be self-established apart from cognition? As for "consciousness does not know fragrance," this means that consciousness does not arise by taking fragrance as its object. Based on this...
In that case, the element of consciousness (vijñāna-dhātu) could not be established. Since consciousness must rely upon fragrance to exist, how could it establish itself in the absence of fragrance?
To summarize: "The loss of consciousness destroys the elements; the fault is inexhaustible. How, then, can it be said that consciousness arises because of fragrance?
△ Third, refuting the arising from mutual causation.
Since there is no intermediate space, the internal and external cannot be established. Those various natures of hearing are ultimately false and illusory.
Based on the above refutation, since the intermediate element of consciousness (vijñānadhātu) cannot be found, the internal faculties and external objects likewise fail to be established.
Now, if the internal and external are not established, that which arises from their conjunction lacks reality; and since the intermediate element does not stand, [the sense-spheres are non-existent].
That which arises through co-production is not real. Is the consciousness that smells and perceives not ultimately false and illusory?
△ Fourth, concluding the return from the false to the true:

Therefore, one should know that the nose and fragrance act as conditions to give rise to the realm of olfactory consciousness; yet these three locations are entirely non-existent. Thus, the nose and the fragrance...
Furthermore, the three factors of the fragrance element are fundamentally neither produced by causes and conditions nor are they of a spontaneous nature.

This concludes the preceding analysis of the three elements of nose, fragrance, and olfactory consciousness. IV. The Elements of Tongue, Taste, and Gustatory Consciousness. This section is divided into four parts.
First, the presentation of the three elements.
Ānanda, furthermore, regarding what you have clarified: with the tongue and flavors as conditions, the tongue-consciousness arises.
Second, he interrogates by means of a pair:
does this consciousness arise because of the tongue, taking the tongue as its constituent element (*dhātu*), or does it arise because of flavors, taking flavors as its constituent element?

△ Third, the refutation of the difficulty regarding the arising [of consciousness] from the three parts. This is divided into four sections. First, the refutation of its arising from the tongue. This is divided into two. 1. The sense organ transforms while the object perishes.

Ānanda, if it arises because of the tongue, then for all people in the world—whether eating sugarcane, *ume* plums, yellow lotuses, rock salt, or *xi xin* (Asarum sieboldii)— *Note: The provided text fragment ends abruptly. The translation reflects the available portion.*
Ginger and cinnamon have no flavor at all.
The first four flavors can be understood; the latter three flavors are all of the same pungent taste. Regarding "having no flavor at all":

if one considers that consciousness arises from the tongue based on the aforementioned causes, then it does not depend on external flavor-objects (*rasa-viṣaya*), yet the substance of the tongue itself is capable [of perception].

This is because it is established through conceptual discrimination; thus it is said as such. △ Second, the refutation of the teaching regarding the tasting [of the tongue]. This has two parts: first, the teaching that one must taste one’s own tongue:
"Taste your own tongue yourself—is it sweet or bitter?"
If one places the tongue upon itself, it has no taste of its own; thus, a difficulty arises. △ Second, both paths are untenable. This is further divided into two parts.
First, "Whose tongue would experience bitterness?
If the nature of the tongue were bitter, who would come to experience that tongue? The tongue does not experience itself; what, then, could be the cognizer?
"If the nature of the tongue were suffering"—this raises the single flavor as an example. "Who comes to taste the tongue?"—this is the initial counter-question.

The following two lines set forth the correct principle: "Who is it that perceives? This means that since the tongue does not taste itself, by what means could the tongue perceive its own state as suffering?
△ Second, [the section on] "if not suffering, to which realm does it belong?"
The nature of the tongue is not suffering; flavors do not arise of themselves. How, then, can a realm be established?
If it is said that the nature of the tongue is fundamentally not suffering, then all flavors would not arise within the tongue of their own accord, and there would be nothing to be cognized.
How, then, can a consciousness-realm be established? The refutation of the arising of the tongue is complete. II. Refuting the Arising of Flavor. Furthermore:
Furthermore, it can be divided into two [cases]. First, there is the non-establishment of the cognition of taste.

If consciousness arises because of taste, then consciousness itself would constitute the taste; being identical to the tongue-faculty, it should not be able to taste itself. How, then, could consciousness know what is taste and what is not taste?
Regarding "consciousness taking itself as its flavor": consciousness is itself the flavor. Yet the flavor does not know itself, which is like the tongue not tasting itself;
thus, ignorance is formed. II. Furthermore, the mutual destruction of characteristics has three parts. First, the many destroying the one.
Furthermore, all tastes do not arise from a single entity. Since tastes arise from many [causes], consciousness should likewise possess multiple entities.
Because there are many tastes, the unity of consciousness is undermined;

that is, if the tastes that produce it are inherently multiple entities, then the consciousness produced by them should also not be one. It is like a mother having many children—the children must also be many. △ Second, by...
One [entity] destroys many.

If the substance of consciousness were one, its substance would necessarily arise as a single flavor; thus, the various changing characteristics produced by the combination of saltiness, sourness, sweetness, and pungency would all become one uniform flavor, and there should be no differentiation between them.

By means of the oneness of consciousness, the multiplicity of tastes is destroyed. This means that since the consciousness produced is fundamentally a single entity, the tastes capable of producing it should likewise not be many;
just as when the child is one, the mother should also be one. Wuxing said:
"Salty, bland, sweet, and pungent"—these four flavors are mentioned briefly. "Harmonized" refers to the collective formation of various flavors.
"Co-nascent" refers to that which is unchanging by its very nature. "Transformed" refers to that which differs from its original state through burning or boiling.

I say that "transformed" specifically refers to things such as fermented wine and vinegar, while burning and boiling are secondary to it. △ Third, following upon the [discussion of] faults, the names [are given].
Regarding the meaning:
since discrimination is absent, it cannot be called consciousness (*vijñāna*). How, then, can it further be called the "tongue-flavor-consciousness element"?

By following the absence of discrimination, one ultimately loses the name of "consciousness. This is because the essential nature of consciousness is precisely discrimination; such is its definition. △
Third, the refutation of production from space:
Space should not give rise to your mind-consciousness.

According to the previous dual interrogation, this category [of production from space] is untenable; furthermore, among all the elements (*dhātu*), there is no instance of production from a flavor that lacks a locus of belonging. Moreover...
This seems somewhat redundant; one might suspect it is an interpolation, yet I do not yet dare to be certain.
Nevertheless, as the Buddha’s words are sovereign, there is no harm in opening a separate section according to the intention of Gushan. △ Fourth, refuting co-arising.
The tongue and taste come together; yet within this very union, there is fundamentally no self-nature. How, then, can the elements arise?
"Fundamentally no self-nature" means that although they combine to become one, there is no duality such that each retains its own individual nature.
"How, then, can the elements arise? means that since the faculty and the object have already merged into one and still lack self-nature, how could there be anything intermediate between them?
Does the void exist to provide space for the arising of the consciousness-element?孤山 (Gushan) says: First, by refuting the tongue, he refutes self-arising;
second, by refuting flavor, he refutes other-arising; third, by refuting the void, he refutes causeless arising; fourth, by refuting their combination, he refutes co-arising.
This interpretation is also excellent. It is not the case that the distinct realms are incomplete. Furthermore, one should know that this is the *prajñā* of intentional meaning (*saṃdhāya-bhāṣita*);

it merely refutes the false conceptualizations of the four modes of birth to reveal that all phenomena are non-arising. This further directly points to the single nature to show that all such conceptualizations are false;
only then does it constitute the truly definitive meaning (*nītārtha*). △ Fourth, concluding the return from the false to the true.
Therefore, you should know this: with the tongue and flavors as conditions, the tongue-consciousness element arises.
Since these three locations are all non-existent, the triad of the tongue, flavors, and the tongue-element are fundamentally neither caused by conditions nor of a spontaneous nature.
The tongue-element (*jihvā-dhātu*) is the tongue-consciousness-element (*jihvā-vijñāna-dhātu*). These, along with the two sections below, all take the sense-faculties as their specific names.

The remainder is to be understood by analogy with what precedes. This concludes the three elements of tongue, taste, and tongue-consciousness. △ Five: The body, touch, and consciousness elements. Divided into four parts.
First, it indicates the three realms:
"Ānanda, furthermore, as you have clarified, with the body and touch as conditions, body-consciousness arises.
Second, it interrogates both together.
Does this consciousness arise because the body is its cause, taking the body as its realm? Or does it arise because contact is its cause, taking contact as its realm?
△ This refutation through the combination of the three parts is further divided into three sections. First, the refutation of its arising from the body as its cause.
"Ānanda, if [the consciousness] were produced because of the body, there would necessarily be no conditions for the two types of mental application—conjunction and separation.

What, then, would the body cognize? Wēnlíng says: "Mental application (vitarka) and investigation (vicāra) are themselves the body-consciousness, which takes the two objects of conjunction and separation as its conditions.
If these conditions do not exist, then there is no consciousness. 2. Refuting that it is produced because of contact.
If [the sensation] were produced because of contact, there would necessarily be no "you" as a body. Who, being bodiless, could know union or separation?
By treading upon the state of having no body, it is determined that one certainly cannot know union or separation. △ Third, the refutation of co-arising has three parts.
First, the summary, the determination, and the manifestation:
"Ānanda, an object does not know by being touched; it is the body that knows there is touch.

Regarding "an object does not know by being touched," this means that an object alone cannot touch itself and thereby know [the touch]. Regarding "it is the body that knows there is touch," [this means...]
One must necessarily depend upon the conjunction with the body to know that there is contact.

First, this establishes that the cognition of contact must depend on the conjunction with the body, thereby revealing the basis for the formal refutation to follow. II. The Formal Refutation of Simultaneous Arising (sahaja), which is further divided into three parts:
1. The produced [contact] lacks the dual characteristics.
To know the body is itself contact; to know contact is itself the body. That which is contact is not the body; that which is the body is not contact. The commentary states:

"That which is produced" refers to consciousness (*vijñāna*). "Lacking dual characteristics" means lacking the characteristic of being simultaneously both sense organ (*indriya*) and object (*viṣaya*).

The first two phrases employ the logic of mutual identity to refute the possibility of their arising through co-production (*sahotpāda*). The two instances of the word "know" (知) are... [text truncated].

This refers to the cognition that was previously established as being manifest. As it was said above: "At the point where the body and touch meet, the nature of this cognition is indeed clearly manifest.
If one were to calculate based on this that [body and touch] arise together, one must examine whether this cognitive nature knows the body or knows the touch.
If you say it knows the body, then this cognition is simply the cognition of touch.
Why is this? Contact (*spraṣṭavya*) is the object of the body. This nature of cognition must be one with contact before it can be known in relation to the body.
To know contact is precisely to know the body; conversely, if this were not the case, [the conclusion] should ultimately state:
"This would belong to only one side; how could it be 'co-arising' (*sahabhū*)? One should note that the two instances of the word "identical" (*ji*) signify "cognition."

This means "the cognition is identical to contact" and "the body is identical to contact. One must not erroneously interpret this as "the body is identical to contact" and "contact is identical to the body.

The next two phrases use double negation to refute the possibility that they could arise through co-production. For example, it says, "this is cognition. Since it belongs exclusively to contact, it cannot simultaneously belong to the body;
therefore, it is said that "cognition is not the body. Since [the body] belongs exclusively to the body, it [cannot belong to contact].
It can be understood as belonging to both "touch" and "body. Therefore, it is said that "the body itself is not touch. At the end, the conclusion should state:
"In the end, it cannot belong to both extremes; how then could they arise together? Furthermore, one should simply record the two characters "not" (非).

This means knowing that the body is not [the knower] and knowing that touch is not [the knower]. One must not mistakenly write "touch is not the body" or "the body is not touch. △ Second, the capacity to produce.
The characteristic of non-resistance and the two characteristics of body and touch originally have no location. When conjoined with the body, they constitute the very self-nature of the body;
when separated from the body, they are simply the characteristics of empty space and so forth.

The commentary states: "That which can produce" refers to the body-faculty (*kāyendriya*) and the object of touch (*spraṣṭavya*). Regarding "the characteristic of being non-obstructive" (*apratigha-lakṣaṇa*):
it means there is no opposition between the two characteristics of internal and external. The first two lines establish the definition; the following four lines provide the explanation.

As for the meaning established therein, both "contact with the body" and "separation from the body" are expressed by the term "touch. The first two lines refer to touch being in conjunction with the body, thereby forming a single entity. It is not... [text truncated]

They may further be divided. The latter two phrases refer to the separation of contact from the body; this means they share the same characteristic as empty space. "Equal" (等) here signifies "the same.
This likely implies that, alongside [contact], their single substance is likewise non-existent.

Since both the uncombined and the separated states lack these two characteristics, the intent is to reveal that even these two characteristics have no locus; how, then, could they function as the co-arising conditions for consciousness?
It is rooted in this. △ Third, neither the subject nor the object is established;
since neither the internal nor the external is established, how can the middle be established? Since the middle cannot be established, the nature of both the internal and external is empty.
The first two lines [demonstrate that] because the causes—the sense organs and their objects—are not established, the resulting consciousness is not established.

The latter two lines [demonstrate that] because the resulting consciousness is not established, the causes—the sense organs and their objects—are not established. This applies both to the internal and the external.
This is also explained as above; however, the meaning is inverted, which is why it is said that they do not mutually establish one another.

A homologous analogy is that which shares the same characteristics as the subject (*dharmin*), thereby positively clarifying the subject.
A heterologous analogy is that which is contrary to the subject, thereby negatively revealing the subject. In this present sutra, the heterologous analogy is placed first, while the [homologous]...
The analogy follows later; see it for yourself in the subsequent section on the "Lower Parts. Furthermore, there are three [points]: first, restating the preceding words:
"Ānanda, as you have said, the four great elements combine to manifest the various transformations of the world."
△ Second, the distinct explanation by means of a dissimilar example. This also has two parts. First, clarifying that it is not the case that they do not combine:
"Ānanda, if the essence of those great elements were not a combination, then they could not intermingle with one another, just as empty space does not combine with various forms."
Regarding harmony and disharmony: when the nature (*dhātu*) and characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*) are examined in relation to one another, the various great elements (*mahābhūta*) are the characteristics;
the nature of these great elements is the *tathāgatagarbha*-mind. The first two lines establish this premise.
"Cannot be blended" means that the nature should not be able to follow conditions to form characteristics. This is a statement made by way of contradiction, yet it serves as an analogy.

The implication of this reversal is that it correctly clarifies how the fundamental nature follows conditions to manifest as phenomena, which is eternally distinct from the insentient and nihilistic nature of empty space;

therefore, it is not the case that there is no mutual integration. Question: Ānanda clung solely to the notion of integration. Why did the Buddha simultaneously refute non-integration as well, rather than merely refuting integration?
Answer: These two views are mutually dependent. If one were not to refute both, then the refutation of integration would remain incomplete.
Later, Ānanda would surely again consider this not to be a true conjunction; therefore, the Buddha first refuted it to block such shifting calculations.
△ Second, clarifying that it is not a true conjunction.
If they were to combine, they would be identical to a magical transformation: beginning and end mutually forming one another, arising and ceasing in continuous succession;
birth and death, death and birth, birth and death, death and birth—like a whirling firebrand, never coming to rest.
The first phrase establishes the definition. "Identical to transformation" means that they undergo change in the same manner as the [other] characteristics.
"Beginning and end" differ slightly from "arising and ceasing. "Beginning and end" refers to subtle aspects; "arising and ceasing" refers to the broad divisions.

Therefore, arising and ceasing each have their own beginning and end: for instance, arising is the beginning of abiding, and abiding is the end of arising; difference is the beginning of cessation, and cessation... [is the end of difference].

Regarding "the end differs from the beginning" and "beginning and end mutually establish one another": this means that because there is a beginning, there is an end; and because there is an end, there is again a beginning.
Regarding "birth and extinction continuing one after another": this means that birth leads directly to extinction, and extinction is followed in turn by birth.

Furthermore, "birth and extinction" applies to both the insentient (*nirjīva*), whereas "birth and death" is restricted to those with consciousness (*sajñin*). "Death and birth, birth and death" refers to the sequential order.
This is what is meant by [the term]. "Life after life" and "death after death" are discussed in terms of intervals.
For example, it refers to this present life preceding the next birth, and the previous death preceding the subsequent death. Alternatively, it is like the transformation of a molting insect:

having lived, one is born again; hence it is called "life after life. It is also like the end of the intermediate state (*antarābhava*): having died, one dies again; hence it is called "death after death."

"Death. This refers to the two lines beginning with "Like a spinning wheel," which state that the nature has no essence that does not change, yet constantly follows along with the shifting of phenomena, ultimately unable to return to the state of being without beginning or end.
This is an instance where the dharma itself is expressed through inversion, and the metaphor likewise reveals its meaning through inversion.
The mind, therefore, clearly demonstrates that appearances cannot actually transform the nature; it is not like a fire-brand wheel that never ceases. Thus, they are not a harmonious union. Question:
If this is so, why does the cycle of rebirth manifest now? Answer: It is as when the moon and the shore do not move, yet the cloud and the boat appear to move.
If movement were truly real, how could one realize it and cause it to cease instantly? The distinct explanation through a dissimilar analogy is hereby concluded.
△ Third, the general explanation of the concordant example:
"Ānanda, it is like water becoming ice, and ice returning to become water again.

The previous statement—that nature and characteristics are different, like two distinct substances—served as a dissimilar example; this statement—that nature and characteristics are identical—is the concordant example.

Because these two aspects exist, they are called "analogous examples" (*sādharmya-dṛṣṭānta*). Since ice and water are not two separate things, the statement of these two aspects precisely clarifies that essence and appearance are fundamentally not two things;
there are merely the two meanings of "changing according to conditions" and "remaining unchanging.
This analogy is employed to reverse the previous "dissimilar example" (*vaidharmya-dṛṣṭānta*); therefore, he calls out Ānanda again to initiate this point, saying: "Although the essence is one..."
Taste is able to form characteristics according to conditions. Since it is not like empty space, which remains uniform and does not combine with others, how can it be compared [to that]?
It should be understood as being like water’s ability to become ice. Although water is of a single essence, it can naturally congeal to form ice;
thus, while there is no actual combination of elements, it can manifest the appearance of combination. How could this be said to belong exclusively to a fixed nature?
Regarding that which is not in harmony: although their characteristics may differ in ten thousand ways, they can be fused back into the fundamental nature.
Since this is not like a whirling firebrand that never ceases, how should it be compared? It should be like ice returning to water.
For though water may congeal into ice, if it is melted, it remains as water; yet while [the world] seems to be in harmony, there is ultimately no such transformation. How could it be otherwise?

It may be said that this refers to being definitively harmonious and unified. One should contemplate the word "returns" (huan). This clearly demonstrates that the unchanging true cause is itself unchanging;
thus, it returns to being water. Precisely at the point where it returns to being water, one perceives that it is not a truly harmonious union.
If they were truly in union, they would undergo transformation. For example, when blue and yellow are combined, they transform into the causal condition [of green];

how could they then revert to being blue and yellow? To state the formal syllogism (pramāṇa) in summary: "The intrinsic nature and characteristics of the great elements (mahābhūta) are the subject (dharmin).

It is not the case that they do not combine, nor is it the case that they combine; this is the thesis (pakṣa). Because they do not change according to conditions, this is the reason (hetu). The concordant example (sapakṣa) is like water and ice."
The counter-example is like space or a fire-wheel; this meaning is most subtle and profound, and it should be treasured and contemplated.

Furthermore, one should know that while Ānanda inquired only about the characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*) of the four great elements, the Buddha answered by addressing both their nature (*svabhāva*) and their characteristics.

This is because, although the provisional teachings explain characteristics based upon nature, that nature is taught with intentional ambiguity (*saṃdhāya-bhāṣita*); they do not explicitly state that [characteristics] are identical to nature. Ānanda—

Having long practiced its teachings, they were deluded regarding the nature and followed after appearances; thus, they could not forget their calculations concerning the harmonious and the non-harmonious as they revolved in succession.
Now, the Buddha bestows upon them this teaching to wash away their former views; therefore, he presents both nature and appearance together, yet uses nature to dissolve appearance.
It is only when they attain mutual resonance and their natures are harmonized that one can simultaneously eliminate both dualistic calculations.

Furthermore, when the four categories were explained, each was in fact already harmonized with the others and returned to the fundamental nature; yet Ānanda had not fully grasped this, so [the Buddha] reiterated it to manifest it most clearly.
This concludes the general analogy of nature and characteristics. II. Detailed Explanation of the Seven Elements, divided as follows:
Seven sections. First, the element of earth, which further has three parts. First, defining its nature through analytical reduction:
"Observe the nature of earth: that which is coarse is the great earth; that which is subtle is the minute particle, down to the *paramāṇu* (the infinitesimal atom).
When you analyze the boundary of that most subtle form until it is reduced to seven parts, and further analyze those *paramāṇus*, they are immediately the reality of emptiness."

The first phrase indicates the essential nature (*lakṣaṇa*), which is intended to lead one to investigate the fundamental source and the substance of that nature. "Adjacent to the infinitesimal" (*paramāṇu-saṃnikṛṣṭa*) means being adjacent to empty space.
"To reach" (*yāvat*) means proceeding through successive analysis from the sevenfold coarse characteristics until reaching the infinitesimal.
The subsequent three phrases state that this "adjacent to the infinitesimal" refers to analyzing the boundary-phase of that ultimate subtle matter (*paramāṇu-rūpa*) into seven parts.
This is how the name "paramāṇu" (ultimate atom) is established. Read "the ultimate limit of the characteristics of matter" as a single phrase.
This means that this ultimate atom is the boundary of material phenomena (*rūpadharma*); beyond this, there would be no further characteristics of matter that could be called an ultimate atom.
However, if one takes a single ultimate atom and divides it into seven parts, only then does it become a *paramāṇu*; thus, it is even more subtle.
The "subtle" (*wei*) is that which reaches the ultimate limit of the ultimate. The final two phrases state that through further analysis, one eventually arrives at emptiness (*śūnyatā*).
△ Second, a detailed examination and discussion based on analysis, which is further divided into two parts. First: entering through analysis and determining what emerges.
Ānanda, if these neighboring atoms were analyzed until they became empty space, you should know that it is space that gives rise to the appearance of form.
This false calculation is much like a fool who, seeing the flowers of the sky vanish into the void, concludes that the flowers emerged from within the void.
Generally speaking, as long as one does not understand that the true source of the myriad phenomena arises from the *ālayavijñāna* (the storehouse mind), no one can truly emerge [from delusion].

This is their calculation. Thus, the calculations of the ordinary and inferior beings in the Western Regions are no different from those here in this land regarding how the Great Void coagulates to form shapes;
they are all similar. △ Second, the general restatement followed by a detailed refutation. This section has two parts.
First, the initial citation:
You have now asked, "By means of combination, the various phenomenal appearances of the world are produced.

This restates and confirms your original question. I shall now cite the "neighboring atom" (*paramāṇu*) to press you into the fallacy of combining atoms with space, thereby leaving you with no way to evade it.
This concludes the summary. △ Second, the detailed refutation. This is further divided into three parts. First, the refutation based on the emptiness of number and quantity:

"Consider for a moment this single *paramāṇu* (subtle atom). By how much empty space must it be combined to come into existence? It cannot be that one *paramāṇu* is formed by the combination of other *paramāṇus*."

The refutation of this [position] relies entirely on the single phrase, "How many voids are employed? For a conjunction must possess a numerical quantity—whether two or three—since they are conjoined to form a single unit;
hence the challenge: "How many are employed? (and so forth). The final two lines serve to preclude further attempts at defense. Suppose one were to defend by saying:
"My statement that they are conjoined refers only to the conjunction of material forms (*rūpa-lakṣaṇa*), not to the conjunction with space (*ākāśa*) in order to constitute matter."

Therefore, this is refuted by stating that it "should not be said" (and so forth). This is because, in the case of other coarse forms (*sthūla-rūpa*), if one were to say they are composed of those subtle forms (*sūkṣma-rūpa*), it might perhaps be logically consistent.
However, in the present case of the atom (*paramāṇu*), there is nothing subtler below it;
there is only empty space (*ākāśa*). Thus, it must combine with space. If it did not combine with space, how could it be that atoms combine to form atoms?
Yes. Even if one grants that synthesis occurs, there would be three fallacies. First, the fallacy of self-synthesis: for synthesis only brings about the self by means of the other;

there has never been a case where the self is synthesized by the self. Second, the fallacy of the synthesis of one: [if the self were to synthesize itself,] it would result in the synthesis of a single entity.
For there has never been a case where the combination of one produces one; there is only the combination of many to produce one.

It is erroneous to claim that the combination of three subtle [atoms] produces something subtle; there is only the combination of subtle [atoms] to produce something gross, never the combination of subtle [atoms] to produce something subtle.
Thus, if you maintain that various characteristics combine, then these *paramāṇus* must also be combinations. If this...
Since the "adjacent infinitesimal" (*paramāṇu*) is a composite, it must necessarily be formed by combining with space; this is intended to leave him with no room for evasion.
**2. Refutation by showing that matter cannot constitute space.** This uses the principle of mutual correspondence to expose his error.
Since Ānanda maintains that the various characteristics of matter and space each occupy half [of the whole], they ought both to be composites. Therefore—
This is refuted. Emptiness is not a composite; this is used as an analogy to demonstrate that visible form is not a composite. Furthermore, there are two points:
first, the fallacy of the difficulty in establishing emptiness;
and second, regarding the subtle particle (*paramāṇu*): if one analyzes it into emptiness, by means of how many material characteristics (*rūpa-lakṣaṇa*) would empty space be composed?
To say that the limit of form (*rūpa*) borders on space (*ākāśa*), it must join with space to constitute the limit of form-space;
likewise, to border on form, it must also join with form to constitute space. This is a refutation formulated in accordance with their own tenets.
However, since there is a deficiency in the lower part of the term "space," it should be supplemented as follows: "One should know that the characteristics of form give rise to space, yet [space]..."
Read this by connecting it with the final two lines. Thereafter, there is a further objection, for which a defense must be set forth. The defense states:
"Since you have already spoken of analyzing [form] into emptiness, why do you again question its synthesis?

Ānanda did not dare to raise such an objection because analyzing form into emptiness is the established doctrine of the Śrāvakas (the Lesser Vehicle), whereas the harmonious combination of all characteristics is the position of the present Ānanda.

This is his own statement. Therefore, by now following his own statement while contradicting his own teaching, it precisely demonstrates that his own statement and his own teaching are mutually contradictory;
this constitutes two of the nine fallacies of a thesis (*pakṣābhāsa*).
For this reason, although the Buddha intentionally set aside and conceded the challenge, Ānanda was likewise unable to offer a rebuttal. Why? Because he followed the analytical entry...

If [the opponent claims] it is not a combination, this contradicts their own current statement. If they rely on the combination yet contradict the refutation, they turn their back on their own former tenet.
Thus, being defeated on both counts, they remain silent and dare not argue. This meaning is most profound. 2.
Illustrating by analogy the fallacy of establishing form.
If form is conjoined, that which is conjoined with form is not empty; if emptiness is conjoined, that which is conjoined with emptiness is not form.
This statement sets forth the correct principle and refutes [the opponent] by analogy. The four propositions are not equal, for the first two propositions serve as examples to clarify the latter two.
As it is said: "If one knows that what is conjoined with form cannot become empty, then one knows [that what is conjoined with emptiness likewise cannot become form]."
It cannot be treated as form (*rūpa*). What was visible in the preceding section is precisely what makes it difficult; the intention here is to clarify this by applying the same principle by analogy.
The refutation that form does not constitute emptiness is now complete. △ Third, the refutation based on the meaning of the non-conjunction of emptiness and form.
Form may still be analyzed; how could emptiness be joined?
The first phrase is concessive; the second phrase is refutative. "Form may still be analyzed" means that form may still be analyzed so as to return to emptiness.

However, this may still be considered a provisional concession. In reality, it is the analysis of form (*rūpa*). Yet, while form itself can be analyzed, space (*ākāśa*) is not actually established through the analysis of form.
How so? To say they "combine" would mean that space definitely lacks the meaning of combination.
Briefly stated, there are four reasons why space cannot be said to combine: first, it is without form or obstruction; second, it is without quantity; third, it is without... [text fragment].
Regarding the limits [of atoms] and the fourfold lack of movement: based on these four points, how can they be reconciled? Later, the correct meaning shall be set forth by means of a reversal:
"If one knows that emptiness cannot be joined, then one knows that the *paramāṇu* (subtle atom) is not formed through conjunction.
Since the *paramāṇu* is not formed through conjunction, the earth element (*pṛthivī-dhātu*) is fundamentally not possessed of conjunction. Regarding conjunction—
[Objection: Is this then the ultimate reality? [Response: This, Ānanda, is merely based on coarse appearances; the Tathāgata investigates down to the most subtle atoms.
This is because, since you maintain that all phenomena are a combination of various characteristics, you must take the most subtle atom as the primary origin.

However, since the subtle atom borders upon space, it would inevitably lead to the fallacy of merging with space. Therefore, one must clearly understand that there is only the single void (ekākāśa), which cannot be [further analyzed].
If they are combined, then the calculations of harmonious integration can naturally be overturned and completely exhausted. How wondrous, how most wondrous!

△ Third, the conclusion that clarifies and refutes attachment. This is divided into two parts. First, the conclusion and clarification, which is further divided into two sections. First, the total embodiment of perfect interfusion.
You originally did not know that within the Tathāgatagarbha, the nature of form is true emptiness, and the nature of emptiness is true form;
it is pure and fundamental, pervading the entire Dharma-realm.
This section and the [sections on] the aggregates (*skandha*) and so forth both refer to the *tathāgatagarbha*; in principle, there is no lack of harmony between them, yet their meanings differ.
The single character "middle" (*zhong*) carries a distinct significance that must be clarified through analogy. It is like a wealthy elder whose storehouse contains limitless treasures;
whenever he has a residence, he invariably brings out the treasures from the storehouse and displays them extensively throughout the halls and pavilions. However...
It is merely one part out of ten million; for that which is deeply hidden and has not yet manifested is truly immeasurable.
The preceding four sections are like pointing toward a hall or pavilion’s treasures and stating that they are all items contained within the storehouse.
Now, these seven elements (*mahābhūta*) are like saying that this is only a small portion within the storehouse, while the rest remains unmanifested.
Each and every one is fully pervaded. However, according to the time and place, as many [applications] as are required shall emerge.

This is merely a matter of comparing the depth and shallowness of what has already been manifested and what has not yet been manifested; you should realize this for yourself. As for your fundamental ignorance, its meaning extends to the following section.
This section of the text is divided into five parts: first, the source and its development; second, mutual integration; third, the departure from faults; fourth...
The original text is complete. "Five circumferences, full" refers to a single phrase of the Tathāgata, pointing to its source and its course.

This is because, failing to realize that the source and course of the earth-element are originally things within the *tathāgatagarbha*, one falsely claims that form arises from emptiness and erroneously conceives of a process of combination.
It is for this reason that this single phrase points [to the truth]. Regarding the two—nature and form—...

These two phrases clarify their mutual integration. While those outside the provisional teachings (prajñā-upāya) largely reckon that nature is the principle of emptiness, they do not realize that internally, emptiness and form are mutually integrated.
It is for this reason that these two phrases are used to clarify it. There are three meanings to the transformation of earth into form.
First, the indication of the root and the demonstration of its vastness: Earth is the root of all forms (*rūpa*), and that which it encompasses is exceedingly vast.
Insentient things include gold, wood, tiles, stones, and so forth; sentient things include hair, skin, flesh, bone, and so forth—all are earth.
Therefore, among the phenomena subsumed under form (*rūpa*), earth (*pṛthivī*) accounts for seven or eight tenths. Second, these definitions are established to distinguish them from one another.
Generally, form possesses three meanings: color, shape and substance, and resistance. Each of these has both a "complete" (*paripūrṇa*) and a "partial" (*alpabhāga*) aspect.
Color is considered complete when it can be distinguished as black or white; shape and substance are considered complete when they can be grasped by the body in their own essence; and resistance...
Because their essences do not interpenetrate, they are considered incomplete. Thus, water is incomplete in its capacity for resistance;
fire is incomplete in both its substantiality and its resistance; and wind is entirely deficient in material form, and thus also incomplete in its resistance.

Only the great element of earth possesses all three meanings in full, and for this reason it is easily designated as "form" (*rūpa*), distinguishing it from those other three which are deficient and incomplete. These three [points] demonstrate:

This is consistent with various sutras. Generally speaking, when the Prajñāpāramitā and other sutras present dharmas that are fused with emptiness, they invariably take form-dharmas (*rūpa*) as the primary subject, applying this principle across more than eighty categories.
Now, in order to clearly demonstrate that this [text] shares the same intent as those sutras, it employs the term "form" (*se*).
"Nature" (*xing*) refers to its lack of characteristics; it is the principle itself rather than a phenomenal event. "Reality" (*zhen*) refers to its...
It is not mundane; it is the essence itself, rather than its function. "The nature of form is true emptiness" means that the form inherent in the nature is the emptiness of the true essence.
"The nature of emptiness is true form" means that the emptiness inherent in the nature is the form of the true essence.
"The nature of form is true form" uses language that integrates the nature with the great [reality]. "True emptiness" and "nature-emptiness" directly designate...
The meaning of the essence of nature (*xingti*) is expressed through inverted phrasing, and furthermore, it is established as a total fusion and identity.

This is because the two terms "nature" (*xing*) and "truth" (*zhen*) are non-different; they are used interchangeably like reflections. If they were not used interchangeably, there would necessarily be four permutations, as it is said:
The nature of form is true emptiness; true emptiness is the nature of form. The nature of emptiness is true form; true form is the nature of emptiness. Only then are the words and phrases complete.
Because the sutra encompasses the meaning while its text is concise, these lines are presented as mutual reflections. Question:

Is this the same as the common discourse found in the *Prajñāpāramitā* and other texts, which states that "form is itself emptiness and emptiness is itself form"? Answer: In truth, they are vastly different. For, regarding the *Prajñāpāramitā*...
In cases such as those, the meaning of "form is itself emptiness" and so forth is stated solely with reference to the various phenomena already manifested before one's eyes.
Here, however, we do not refer to these manifest phenomena before us; rather, we speak deeply of the Tathāgatagarbha, which contains all within it in its unmanifest state.
Thus, form and emptiness are fused into one, just as the later scripture says: "Originally, they were neither water nor fire."
This is precisely what that intention signifies. Therefore, this "nature-color" (dharmatā-rūpa) is the true color;

it not only distinguishes itself from substantial colors and the like, but truly reveals its difference from phenomenal characteristics—it is the color that is emptiness within the conventional truth. This "nature-emptiness" (dharmatā-śūnyatā) is the true emptiness;
it not only distinguishes itself from nihilistic emptiness and the like, but truly reveals its difference from phenomenal characteristics—it is the emptiness that is color within the ultimate truth.
This is so. Those who have traditionally spoken of essence and function, truth and convention, principle and phenomena together, have merely failed to investigate [the matter] thoroughly.
They do not realize that this refers only to the total embodiment [of essence], while the "great function" remains for the subsequent section. Let those with discerning eyes examine this in detail.

The two characters "pure and clean" (qingjing) indicate freedom from transgressions. This is because even form is already constrained by Prajñā—that is, form as emptiness—so how could it fall into the mundane?

As for the dyeing of phenomena, even emptiness is still constrained by the emptiness of form (*rūpa-śūnyatā*) within Prajñā; how could it fall into the stagnation in emptiness characteristic of the Two Vehicles?
From the outset, it has been free from faults and severed from non-existence. Among the two kinds of purity, it belongs to self-nature purity (*prakṛti-viśuddhi*).
The two characters "original" (*benran*) signify primordial possession; because they have existed primordially within the Tathāgatagarbha, they are what is called "all."

It is fundamentally inherent in the original nature; it is not newly produced through dependent origination. This phrase distinguishes [this teaching] from the delusions that bodhisattvas in the provisional teachings cultivate and eliminate.
The phrase "pervasive" (*zhoubian*) indicates complete fulfillment. To reach the limit where nothing exists outside is called "pervasive" (*zhou*).
"Zhou" (周) means "to encircle. To penetrate the interior of the unconditioned is called "pervasive" (biàn). "Pervasive" means "complete.
Although what preceded used the treasury of jewels as a metaphor, it cannot be compared to the worldly treasury of jewels. This is because, regarding a worldly treasury of jewels:

if all varieties of jewels were fully present, one could certainly not encircle and fill it with each one individually; yet if it were filled with a single type of jewel, it certainly could not contain various kinds.
They are fully complete. This is because both meanings do not constitute any obstruction;

whenever one great [element] is raised, it immediately pervades and fills the entire dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu*) without mutual interference. As for the "dharma-realm": "dharma" possesses two meanings, namely "guidance" (*vidhi*) and "sustenance" (*dhṛti*).

The *dhātu* (element/realm) has two meanings regarding its nature (*svabhāva*) and its differentiation (*vibhāga*). "Guiding" (*kai*) refers to following conditions; "sustaining" (*chi*) refers to remaining unchanging.

"Nature" (*xing*) refers to the emptiness of essence; "differentiation" (*fen*) refers to the accomplishment of phenomena. In their totality, they are unified within the One True [Dharma-realm]; in their particularity, they open into many varieties. This present Dharma-realm is as follows:
When unified within the single truth, there is no room for further deliberation.

When viewed from the perspective of its manifold aspects, it is precisely pervasive throughout the principle-dharmadhātu (li-fajie) and mysteriously pervasive throughout all phenomena-dharmadhātus (shi-fajie). This is because nothing apart from the single truth can ever be found.
Because it exercises sovereign control within this profound stillness, it is able to manifest in accordance with conditions and respond to circumstances without deficiency.
△ Second, the great function is infinite.
It accords with the minds of sentient beings and responds according to the measure of what they know.
This refers to its inherently possessed wondrous function, which is able to accord and respond; it is not the same as the "following of karma" mentioned previously. Regarding this:

These two phrases continue to connect with the preceding "manifesting according to karma" as a single breath. Furthermore, by examining the various "greats" (mahābhūtas) below, one finds that they truly arise from the cause of responding to the mind and measuring its capacity;
thus, one grasps the fundamental intent regarding their respective classifications.

Please examine the subsequent explanation: sentient beings encompass all nine realms of existence. Regarding the "mind," when spoken of in terms of faculties and natures, there are superior and inferior capacities; as for "capacity" (mātra),...
One knows through the mind that there are those who are great and those who are small.

If one approaches with an inferior mind and a limited capacity, then that which is responded to with coarse and meager forms will certainly not fail to correspond to that mind, nor will it fail to satisfy that capacity.
If, however, one can approach with a superior mind and a vast capacity, then that which is responded to will be extensive.
As for wondrous forms, there is nothing that does not correspond to the mind, nor is there anything that fails to satisfy its measure.
This is likewise true for all conditioned and unconditioned phenomena of the mundane and supramundane realms.

When considered in conjunction with the preceding section, the former concerns nature, essence, reality, and principle; this section concerns characteristics, function, the conventional, and phenomena. Thus we know.
To explain that "the color of the upper [element] is emptiness" as being equivalent to the manifestation of its functional aspect (*xiàng-yòng*) is incorrect.
Furthermore, since the aspects arise from the nature (*xìng*), one knows that the entirety of the aspects is identical to the nature; the same applies to essence and function (*tǐ-yòng*).

This is why it is said that the earth element (*dì-dà*) is the very nature within the storehouse consciousness (*ālaya-vijñāna*). Moreover, one should know that regarding the four categories beginning with the aggregates (*skandha*), all first involve the dismantling of the delusory aspects. However...
The subsequent conclusion reveals that because the nature is truly real, its meaning of "shattering characteristics" (prabheda-lakṣaṇa) still partially accords with the Śūnyavāda school.
However, these seven great elements (mahābhūta) here exhaustively reach the ocean-deep abyss of self-nature, from which all phenomena flow forth;

thus, they exclusively designate the reality of nature (dharmatā-satya), being utterly devoid of any superficial or deceptive terminology. This is truly the unique discourse of the Dharmatā school, not only far surpassing the Prajñāpāramitā, but...
This is also not different from the preceding text. The conclusion of this section is hereby completed. II. Refuting Attachment. "Phenomena manifest according to karma;
the ignorant of the world are deluded, taking them to be either caused by conditions or arising spontaneously. These are all merely conceptualizations and calculations of the conscious mind;
they consist only of verbal expressions and possess no real meaning whatsoever."
This section concerns the stage of delusion and the causal stage of the person who has attained awakening. First, it asks:
"If the essence is fundamentally all-pervasive, and its function responds to the mind according to its measure, then every manifestation of that essence would be sovereign and unimpeded.

Why, then, must one follow karma? The answer is: "Precisely because, since beginningless time, one has not awakened and has long been deluded regarding what is inherently present; consequently, [one is entirely unaware of it]."
Mastery! How could it be that only those in deluded states must follow defiled karma before they can manifest [it]?
Even for those who have attained awakening, they must likewise follow pure karma before they can manifest it. Therefore, these four characters possess both types of lack of mastery:
first, if one does not follow all the pure and wondrous forms of the mundane and supramundane realms...
Various pure karmas, though one wishes for them to manifest, cannot be made to do so.

Second, regarding the various defiled karmas of the three miserable realms and the four evil destinies—all their painful and impure forms—if one does not refrain from them, they cannot be prevented from manifesting even if one wishes otherwise.

Indeed, failing to refrain is precisely what it means to follow [the path of transgression]. Therefore, these four characters do not merely signify "non-... [but rather imply the active engagement in such conduct].
If one follows karma, then [the manifestation] cannot occur; furthermore, it indicates that if one follows karma, it must not fail to manifest.
Yet, in both cases, there is no possibility of autonomy. However, these four characters are precisely the cause for giving rise to the two subsequent delusions;
therefore, they are categorized under the following text. This is truly because the arising of karma seems to have a basis upon which it relies; thus, those of shallow worldly wisdom—
Sentient beings grasp at these proximate conditions for the arising of this [reality] and consequently delude themselves into regarding them as its causal nature;
they never realize that the perfectly integrated and unchanging essence pervades the entire Dharma-realm—what need would there be for causes and conditions?
Since the formation of karma appears difficult to alter or shift, ignorant sentient beings in the world cling to this present reality which seems so resistant to change.

Consequently, they are deluded into regarding this as a "natural nature," failing to realize the infinite function of responding to conditions according to the mind and manifesting in accordance with the capacity [of beings].
How could one remain mired in the notion of "nature"? All of this is merely being deluded by following one's own karma.
Had it been the case that one simply responded to the mind and its capacity without necessarily following karma, then all sentient beings would have attained realization of Mind-Only.

The essential point is that one does not fall into various delusions. (Question: Since an enlightened person must follow karma, does the Buddha also follow karma? Answer: While the Buddha was at the stage of a cause, he followed it.

However, once his causal practice was fulfilled and the fruit had manifested, he simply acted according to his mind; since there was nothing even as vast as "karma" to respond to, how could there be any karma to follow? This is except for those instances where he manifests [karma] without actually having real karma. Thus, we know that the functioning of the essence is everywhere sovereign.)

"Only the Buddha can do this. Question: We see before our eyes that Bodhisattvas possess mastery over their activities; why then do you say that only the Buddha can do it? Answer: Because the Bodhisattva’s cultivation is not yet complete, [their activity] still arises strictly in accordance with karma.

It is not that I am now excluding them from possessing mastery over their activities; rather, I am merely excluding them from being those who do not follow karma. However, when a perfectly realized Bodhisattva follows the karma of great mastery, the ten mysterious and wondrous forms they manifest are identical in essence to those of a Buddha.

Question: What is meant by "the karma of great mastery"? Answer: It refers precisely to the Ten Mysterious Gates of the *Avataṃsaka*, as well as the Contemplation and the Ear-Gate Samādhi of this very Sūtra. Furthermore, that which is to be known is awakening and understanding; that which is followed as karma is cultivation.

If one strives solely for practice without seeking perfect understanding, then the three great eons and six perfections will ultimately yield no real fruit; this is precisely because one’s own knowledge is narrow and one’s own capacity is limited.

If one devotes oneself exclusively to extensive learning without encouraging perfect cultivation, then the wondrous principles as numerous as the sands of the Ganges will only increase frivolous proliferation; this is precisely because one’s karma does not follow [the path] and the fruit will never manifest. From this we know that perfect understanding and perfect cultivation must be mutually consistent.

"The mind of consciousness" refers to the six consciousnesses. To analyze without confusion is called "discrimination" (vibhāga); to examine in detail and weigh is called "calculation" (abhinirūpaṇā-vikalpa).
This refers to pervasive conceptualization (*parikalpita*). "But merely" means in vain; to have words alone is the existence of phenomena as perceived (*yathābhāsa*).

"Lacking any real meaning whatsoever" is the non-existence of things according to principle (*yathātattva*). This [latter] constitutes conjunction, which includes that which arises from causes and conditions (*hetu-pratyaya*);

non-conjunction includes that which is spontaneous (*svabhāva*). Furthermore, another interpretation holds that "merely" refers to the ordinary person. To have words alone is to be inferred by analogy.
This is a term used for broad indication; such things as the notions of conjunction, as well as various overlapping views of affirmation and negation, are all included therein.

Both interpretations are valid. Now, if one does not understand essence and function, nor the two types of deluded attachments, then Ānanda’s meaning and that of the worldly convention would merely be mutually implicit and abbreviated reflections of one another.
This is the general intent of this entire section; all subsequent parts should be understood accordingly. The element of earth has already been discussed.
[The preceding section] concludes. △ Second, the fire element. This is divided into three parts. First, defining its nature through inquiry:
"Ānanda, the nature of fire has no self; it relies upon various conditions. Observe the households in the city that have not yet eaten:
when they wish to cook, they hold a magnifying lens in their hands and seek fire from the sun."
Regarding "non-self": this is what is meant by Wēnlíng when he says that fire has no substance of its own and takes form by dwelling within things.
Thus, one who grasps fire must rely upon firewood and the like; apart from firewood and such, there is no substantial entity to be seized. Jùlǐ says:
as for the *yángsuì* (sunstone), Cú Bào’s *Gǔjīn Zhù* states that it is made of copper and shaped like a mirror; when it reflects objects...
The shadow is inverted; when facing the sun, fire emerges. The *Huainanzi* states: "The yang-sui is the fire-mirror, and the fang-zhu is the water-mirror. The *Lunheng* says:
"On the day of Bingwu in the fifth month, one melts stones from the five directions to form a circle like a mirror with a concave center.
I have also seen this myself: when reflecting the sun, the spot where the light is focused ignites. A crystal bead used for focusing likewise burns in exactly the same manner.
...also. △ Second, a detailed investigation based on seeking [the truth]. This is divided into four parts. First, citing an example:
"Ānanda, that which is called 'conjunction' is like myself and you, along with these one thousand two hundred and fifty bhikṣus, who now constitute a single assembly.
Although the assembly is one, when its fundamental basis is examined, each possesses an individual body, and all belong to specific clans from which they were born."
Names: such as Śāriputra of the Brahmin caste, Uruvilvākāśyapa of the Kāśyapa caste, and so on, up to Ānanda of the Gautama clan.
This presents an example of conjunction; it is also a dissimilar example (*vaidharmya-dṛṣṭānta*). Its intent is to show that the fire element (*tejas*) discussed below differs from this example.
This refutation of the phenomenon is conducted by means of the characteristic of separability (*vibhakta-lakṣaṇa*) in order to refute the conception of conjunction.
For there must necessarily be the characteristic of separability as the basis for conjunction, only then can there be true conjunction. Therefore, [the text] presents...
A single community was harmoniously united, yet they separated into distinct lineages as a fixed rule.

This is clearly demonstrated by the fact that, in the subsequent sections on "Opening" and "Closing," there is no place from which fire arises; thus, the theory of harmonious union is manifestly false.
*Brāhmaṇa* here means "Pure Lineage. Wēnlíng (Wēnlíng) says: *Uruvilvā* means "Wooden Claw Forest. *Kāśyapa*.
This is called Mahāgovinda; Gautama means "Solar Lineage," though his clan name was later changed to Śākya.
△ Second, the formal determination:
Ānanda, if this nature of fire exists because of a combination of causes, [it would not exist when those causes are absent].
△ Third, the heading and inquiry:
That person holds a mirror and seeks fire from the sun. Does this fire emerge from within the bell, or does it emerge from the tinder?
"Regarding 'arising from the sun': 'That' refers to the hand below;
'this' is the fire below, which serves as the challenge. △ Four: Refuting by Pursuit. Divided into two. One:
Opening the Refutation and Examining the Examples. Again divided into two. One: Opening the Refutation. Again divided into three. One: Refuting [the claim] that it arises from the sun."
