Ānanda, if the sun were to come here, it would naturally burn the moxa in your hand, and the trees and forests from which it originated should all likewise be consumed by fire.

The first two phrases, "it would naturally" and so forth, are merely words of restatement; it is only the second two phrases, "the trees and forests from which it originated," that constitute the actual refutation. This means:
What difference is there between burning a forest and burning mugwort? △ Second, refuting the claim that it arises from the mirror:
If it were produced within the mirror, it should be able to emerge from the mirror itself and burn the mugwort; why then does the mirror not melt? Moreover, you yourself are holding it in your hand.
Since there is not even the appearance of heat, how could it melt?
The two phrases beginning with "spontaneously" (*zì néng*) are also citations; the single phrase "the mirror" (*jìng hé*) is the refutation. "Twisted" (*yū qū*) means to be entangled.
The three phrases beginning with "twisted you" (*yū rǔ*) provide the proof. △ Third, the refutation of [fire] arising from tinder.
If fire were produced from the moxa, why would it depend on the meeting of the sun, the mirror, and light before the fire could arise?
△ Second, the examination by analogy:
You should again observe closely: the mirror is held by the hand; the sun comes from the sky; the moxa grows from the earth; but from what direction does the fire come?
To "roam through" this means to examine it by analogy according to its origin. The "mirror" takes the three phrases as the example;
the "fire" examines it according to the two phrases. This examination has two meanings. First, it serves to refute the notion of a composite whole. For...
The previous section has already demonstrated that the three locations are non-arising; they are not like Śāriputra and others, who each have a specific clan from which they were born.
This principle is indeed certain. Furthermore, it says: "Moreover, while those three substances each have an origin, from where does this fire come?
Since it has no origin, how can it serve as the basis for conjunction? This is sufficient to see [the truth].
This is because it lacks the nature of being a composite. Second, to further investigate the source and origin:

the intention is that while those three [elements] each have a place from which they come, why should this fire alone have no place from which it comes? This is intended to lead people to examine its provenance.

The first section, "Opening and Refuting by Examining Individually," is concluded. II. "Refuting by Combining and Directly Examining" has two parts: A. Refuting by Combining; B. Direct Examination. A. Refuting by Combining:
The sun and its reflection are far apart; they neither blend nor unite.

The previous statement that there is no place from which they arise merely revealed the absence of a basis for blending and uniting; this, however, correctly clarifies the reality of their lack of blending and uniting.
To speak of something as "blending and uniting" requires that they occupy the same location and intermingle. How could this be?
There is that which is separated by a vast distance, yet acts as a means of unification; this is merely a matter of elliptical phrasing.
"Ai" (艾) is likewise the same as the mirror and the sun being distant from one another. △ Second, the direct examination.
Human light should not exist spontaneously without a source.

This direct examination differs from the previous example of examination. That [previous] inquiry—"From what does it proceed?"—is a question intended to cause the person to examine and recognize [the matter].
This statement—"It should not be without a source"—is a definitive judgment that establishes its having a basis.
This is what is meant. One [aspect] is doubting, while the other is resolving; thus they are not the same.
Although the phrasing is situated within the sections on "synthesis" (*he*) and "refutation" (*po*), the underlying meaning still carries forward from the preceding text:
"Since there is no place from which it arises when opened, and no characteristic of conjunction when synthesized, how could this fire exist of itself without coming from somewhere? It leaps forth—

It has not yet been refuted; it will be refuted in detail in the subsequent passages. (Furthermore, the four sections divided by opening and closing follow a sequence that closely resembles [the arguments] "not produced from another," "not produced from self," "not produced from both," and "not produced without cause.

Although the phrasing is similar, the underlying intent differs in each case. In the former [case], because people cling to the view that all phenomena have production, he refutes the characteristic of production in detail merely to reveal their lack of production.

In this [case], because they are ignorant of the true source of dharmas and falsely claim they arise from combination, he refutes them point-by-point and examines them accordingly, so as to lead them to realize the true original source. The detailed analysis is now complete. △ Third, the conclusion and manifestation.
Refuting Attachment. This section has two parts. First, the summary and clarification. This further divides into two. First, the total interpenetration of all phenomena:
"You still do not know that within the Tathāgatagarbha, the nature of fire is true emptiness, and the nature of emptiness is true fire; it is pure and fundamental."
Pervading the entire dharma-realm, as explained above.
△ Second, the infinite great function. This also has two parts. First, the explicit explanation of the great function:
it accords with the minds of sentient beings and responds to the measure of their cognitive capacity.
As stated above. △ Second, verifying its boundlessness:

Ānanda, you should know that when people hold a mirror in one place, a fire arises in another; yet if they were to hold it throughout the entire Dharma-realm, fires would arise filling the whole world.
Since these arise pervading the entire world, how could there be any fixed location?
Thus, by investigating the matter of seeking fire from above to verify the principle, it can be seen that responding to the mind according to its measure is without limit or extremity.
If even the present objects perceived by ordinary beings are thus limitless, it can be known all the more so regarding the sphere of the sages.
The conclusion and clarification are hereby finished. △ Second, the refutation of attachments.
They manifest according to karma. The world is ignorant and deludedly regards them as having causes and conditions or as being of a spontaneous nature;
these are all merely conceptualizations and calculations of the conscious mind, consisting only of verbal expressions and devoid of any real meaning.
The section on the fire element (*tejo-dhātu*) is concluded above. △ Third, the water element (*ab-dhātu*). This is divided into three parts.
First, defining its nature through inquiry: "Ānanda, the nature of water is not fixed; its flowing and ceasing are without constancy.
For instance, the great illusionists such as the sages Kāpiṭha, Kāśyapa, and Padma-mahāsattva, sought the essence of the moon to use for their mixtures."
This is like illusory music. These various masters, on a day during the bright fortnight, hold a *fangzhu* (concave mirror) in their hands to catch the water from the moon;
its flow and cessation are like the presence or absence of dew and rain, or the overflowing and exhaustion of streams and sources. Such is the general nature of water.
*Kapila* is translated here as "azure-blue. *Cakravāka* is translated as "mandarin duck. *Padmahasada* is not clearly established.
Wénlǐng says: "All four were followers of external paths (tīrthika) skilled in magical arts (*māyā*).

Their claims regarding the seeking of the essence of the moon and receiving the water within the moon follow the calculations of various masters concerning the emergence [of light] from the moon on the fifteenth night."
The day of the full moon is called the "white fortnight" (śuklapakṣa), and the period after the full moon is called the "black fortnight" (kṛṣṇapakṣa).
When the moon is at its zenith, its light is as bright as daylight; therefore, it is referred to as "day. *Fangzhu* refers to the *yinsui* (concave mirror) or the crystal bead.
Gu Shan cites Gao You’s commentary on the *Huainanzi*, which states: "A large clam, when wiped with heat and held toward the moon, produces water. This is clearly explained in the sutra.
He said: "The pearl is indeed produced from a clam; one uses the pearl to draw water, yet it should also be wiped when hot.
△ Second, a detailed examination of the request, which is further divided into two parts. First, the formal inquiry.
Does this water emerge from within the jewel? Does it exist spontaneously in the air? Or does it come from the moon?

△ Second, the sequential refutation, which is further divided into two parts. First, the analytical refutation by opening up the examples, which is further divided into two. First, the analytical refutation, which is further divided into three.
First, the refutation of its arising from the moon.

Ānanda, if it were derived from the moon, it would still be able to cause water to emerge from the pearl even from afar; all the trees and forests it passes through should likewise discharge flowing streams.
If they flow, why wait for what is produced by the *fangzhu* (the concave mirror)? If they do not discharge clear water, then it has not descended from the moon.

"Passing through" (*jing*) means "shining upon. It refers to the act of illuminating. Regarding "distant regions": this means that even the trees and forests through which the jewel passes are still considered distant.
Furthermore, when the moon is directly to the south, all the trees and forests to the south of the jewel are places it passes over in close proximity.
Alternatively, if the jewel is on level ground, then all the trees and forests atop high elevations are likewise [distant].
This refers to the places through which [the light] passes and reaches. This is a case of using the distant to prove the necessity of the near flow.
The following four lines concern whether there is flow or no flow; in all cases, they do not accord with reason. △ Second, refuting that [the light] arises from the pearl.
If [the water] came from the pearl, then water should constantly flow from within this pearl; why wait for the middle of the night to receive the white moonlight by day?
△ Third, refuting that it arises from space.
If it were produced from space, then since the nature of space is boundless, water would likewise be limitless; from humans to devas, all would be submerged and drowned.
How, then, could there still be those who travel by water, land, or air?
△ Second, the examination by analogy:
You should further observe closely that while the person ascends from heaven, the pearl is held in the hand, and the water basin for receiving the pearl is originally laid out by the person.
From what direction does the water flow here?

As for the case of "removing the basin and adding [water] from the void," since the void has no point of origin and cannot serve as an analogy, there would be no doubt that the basin lacks the person who provides the water;
thus, these two categories mutually involve exclusion and inclusion. Having completed the detailed analysis and refutation of the analogies. Part Two.
The combined refutation and direct examination are further divided into two parts: first, the combined refutation; second, the direct examination.
First, the combined refutation: The moon and the jewel are far apart; they are neither conjoined nor combined.
Second, the direct examination.
It should not be that the crystal exists spontaneously without a source;

this can be understood by analogy with what was stated above. The detailed investigation and analysis are hereby concluded. △ Third, the conclusion which clarifies and refutes attachment, divided into two parts.
First, the conclusion, which further has two sections. First, the total interpenetration and perfect fusion.
You do not yet know that within the Tathāgatagarbha, the nature of water is true emptiness, and the nature of emptiness is true water;
it is pure and fundamental, pervading the entire Dharma-realm.
The meaning is consistent with what was stated above. △ Second, the infinite great function. This also has two parts. First, the explicit explanation of the great function:
"In accordance with the minds of sentient beings, responding to the measure of their cognitive capacity."
△ Second, verifying its infinity:

If one holds a single pearl at one location, water emerges from that one location; if one holds them throughout the entire Dharma-realm, they emerge to fill the entire Dharma-realm, filling the world.
How could they have a fixed location?
△ Second, the refutation of attachments:
They manifest according to karma; the ignorant of the world deludedly regard them as being caused by conditions or as having a nature of spontaneity. These are all merely the mind of consciousness.
These are merely conceptual constructions and verbal designations; they possess no real meaning whatsoever.
The analysis of the element of water (*āpas*) is hereby concluded. △ Fourth, the element of wind (*vāyu*). This is divided into three parts. First, defining its nature by means of a sweeping motion.
Ānanda, the nature of wind has no substantial body; its movement and stillness are not constant.

When you regularly adjust your robes to enter the great assembly, the corner of your saṃghāṭī robe moves and reaches those beside you, whereupon a subtle breeze arises that brushes against the faces of those people.

The movement and stillness of the wind are not constant; this is easily seen by people. It should not be limited merely to the trailing of robes or the brushing against of robes, but rather should be understood as a general discussion based on the movement of the robes.
*Saṃghāṭī* is translated here as "the Great Robe" (Dàyī). △ Second, a detailed analysis concerning the brushing [of the robe].
Furthermore, there are two [points]. First, the interrogation:
Does this wind emerge from the corner of the *kāṣāya* robe and manifest in the void to produce that human face?

*Kāṣāya* is translated here as "dyed color. If translated according to its meaning, it signifies "leaving behind the dust" (*viraja*), "transcending the world" (*lokottara*), and so forth in various ways.
There are many translations; they are not cited here at length. △ Second, the refutation point by point. This also has two parts. First, opening the refutation and examining the examples.
This also has two parts. First, the opening refutation. This further consists of three parts. First, the refutation of [the view] that [the self] arises from clothing.
Ānanda, if this wind were to emerge from the corner of my *kāṣāya*, you would be wearing the wind; as the robe fluttered and swayed, it should have separated from your body.
Now, as I preach the Dharma, I have let my robe hang down within the assembly. Look at my robe: where is the wind?
There can be no place within the robe where the wind is hidden.

Your argument consists of three propositions: you claim that the robe is identical to the wind; since the nature of wind does not abide, it must therefore be distinct from the substance [of the robe].
I shall now present six propositions to lead you to observe and examine this matter closely. △ Second, refuting the notion that [the robe] arises from space.
If wind were produced from space, your robe would not move; for what reason is there no stirring? Since the nature of space is eternally abiding, wind should be constantly produced.

If there were times when there was no wind, space itself would perish. If the cessation of wind could be perceived, what would the state of the cessation of space be like? If there were such arising and ceasing, [space would not be eternal].
It is not called "empty space," yet it is named "empty space. How then does wind emerge?
This involves three refutations, which still encompass many meanings. Regarding the two lines concerning your robe: it should not be destroyed by depending on conditions.

Since it is already said that "emptiness arises," it must arise spontaneously; why then rely on the movement of the robe as a condition? [This concludes] the six propositions regarding the nature of emptiness.

This refutes [the claim] that their essential natures (*dharmatā*) are identical. It is said that emptiness has permanence as its essential nature, whereas wind has arising and ceasing as its essential nature.

Thus, according to the first two lines, if wind were to follow emptiness, it should likewise be permanent; according to the next two lines, if emptiness were to follow wind, it should likewise be subject to cessation.
Now, since neither is the case, it can be seen that their essential natures are ultimately different. [End of] the last [section].
The two phrases refute the fallacy of the emptiness of extinction, establishing merely that emptiness is without extinction.

If there were four phrases, it would mean that the name deviates from and destroys the true reality (*dharmatā*). This is because the meaning must correspond to the name, and the name must accord with the essence (*tattva*).
Now, considering the insentient, birth and cessation possess the meaning of having physical substance, whereas empty space possesses the name of lacking physical substance.
Therefore it is said: "If there were birth and cessation, it would not be empty space; thus one sees that the name and its meaning do not correspond."
Furthermore, the essence of space is defined by the absence of matter. When wind arises, there is matter and it is no longer empty;

therefore, it is called "empty space. Why does the wind arise? It is because one perceives that the name and its substance do not correspond. △ Third, the refutation of [the view] that it arises from the face.
If the wind arises from itself, then it should blow against the face from which that face arose; since you yourself have adjusted your robe, why do you instead brush against it?

"As for [the Master's question], 'Since you have adjusted your robes, why do you wipe them upside down?'"—how could it be that he waited only for the moment you adjusted your robes to then wipe them upside down, yet did not wipe yours?
It is because the wiping originated from his face and was directed back toward his own face;
therefore, it is called "wiping upside down. 2. Examining by Analogy.
Examine this with careful attention: your adjusted robes belong to the Dharma; your face belongs to that person; and space is tranquil, not participating in movement.
From which direction does the wind itself stir and come here?

The two lines concerning space do not follow the previous precedent of "taking from [the past]"; rather, they convey the meaning of wind and space being separated by their own natures, which is a characteristic that can be distinguished in the present.
One should not be dogmatic about this. △ Second, the combined refutation and direct examination, which also has two parts.
The first [element] is broken by the second;
wind and the nature of space are separated. They are neither conjoined nor combined.
This refers specifically to how the substance of wind and the nature of space are mutually estranged; they are neither conjoined nor combined, as was the case with the previous two.
The two versions differ slightly. This is truly because wind arises from space—a point commonly grasped by people—and thus many [treatises] refute the idea that it arises from space.
Here, the local dialect states that emptiness can produce wind; the underlying view is the same. The Buddha’s words are adapted to circumstances and lack fixed definition.
△ Second, the direct examination.
It should not be of the nature of wind; it does not arise from itself.

Having completed the detailed analysis based on the preceding "sweeping away" [of misconceptions], △ three, the conclusion that clarifies and refutes attachment, which is further divided into two parts.
First, the conclusion and clarification, which is further divided into two. First, the total integration and perfect fusion.
"You simply do not realize that within the Tathāgatagarbha, the nature of wind is true emptiness, and the nature of emptiness is true wind;
it is pure and fundamental, pervading the entire Dharma-realm."

Second, the infinite great function. This is further divided into two sections: first, the explicit clarification of the great function, which accords with the minds of sentient beings and responds to the measure of their cognitive capacity;
second, the verification of its infinity.

Ānanda, suppose you, as a single person, slightly move your robe; a subtle breeze arises, sweeping across the entire dharma-realm, filling the lands, and pervading the world. Could it have any fixed location?
△ Second, the refutation of attachments:
Phenomena manifest according to karma. Those in the world, being ignorant, deludedly regard them as having causes and conditions or as being of spontaneous nature.
All of these are merely conceptualizations and calculations of the conscious mind; they consist only of verbal expressions and possess no real meaning whatsoever.
The section on the Great Element of Wind is concluded above. △ Five, the Great Element of Space. This is divided into four parts.
First, defining its nature by means of an analogy involving excavation: "Ānanda, the nature of space is formless; it is manifested through matter.

For example, in places far from the river in the city of Śrāvastī, where there are various dwellings, families, and among the Brahmins, Vaiśyas, Śūdras, as well as the Purohitas, Caṇḍālas, and others who have recently established themselves..."
During the summer retreat, one digs a well seeking water. When one foot of earth is removed, there is one foot of empty space within;
likewise, when ten feet of earth are removed, one obtains ten feet of empty space in the middle. The depth of the empty space corresponds exactly to the amount of earth that has been excavated.
The first two lines state that it has no form or appearance of its own, but is manifested only in contrast to manifest color (*rūpa*).
The *Vijñaptimātra* school calls this the "manifest color of solitary emptiness" (*ākāśa-ekavarṇa-rūpa*), which need not be restricted to being manifested only by excavating earth. Wēnlíng says:

In India, the noble and the lowly are divided into four castes (*varṇa*), similar to the four classes of people here [in China]. The *Kṣatriya* is the royal caste; the *Brāhmaṇa* is the pure-vowed caste.
They are also called "Pure Conduct" (*śuddha-vṛtta*), for they maintain the Way, abide in rectitude, and keep their conduct pure and white.
Vaiśyas are merchants; Śūdras are farmers; these constitute the four castes (*cāturvarṇya*). Pahlavas possess sharp faculties; Caṇḍālas are executioners.
These, moreover, are clans distinguished by wisdom and folly. The *Mingyi ji* (Collection of Names and Meanings) states: "Caṇḍāla is translated here as 'butcher' (*vadhaka*)."
These are those who slaughter humans and livestock. In India, those who commit adultery and murder are treated as equally base as those who kill; they are still designated as "evil persons.
By national law, they are required to shake bells and carry banners to warn others to take a different path, so that they may not travel together with virtuous citizens.
Therefore, it is also translated as "ornamented banner. △ Second, a detailed analysis regarding the excavation. This also has two parts. First, the interrogation:
Is this emptiness produced by the earth due to the cause of digging, or does it exist because of the digging, or does it arise spontaneously without a cause?

△ Second, the sequential refutation. This also has two parts: first, opening the refutation by setting forth the points for examination; second, the opening of the refutation itself. The latter is further divided into three sections:
first, the refutation based on the absence of a cause.
Ānanda, if this space were produced spontaneously without cause, why was it not unobstructed before the earth had been excavated?
Why did one see only the great earth, with no penetration or passage whatsoever?

"Extremely remote appearance" means looking as far as the eye can reach. It is said that there was no void before it was excavated; this clarifies that [the void] exists because of excavation. How could this be established as being without a cause?
△ Second, refuting based on the emergence from the earth, which is further divided into two parts. First, refuting the existence of entering and exiting.
If space emerges because of earth, then at the time earth emerges, one should see space entering.
If earth emerges first and there is no entry of space, how can space emerge because of earth?
Since emptiness was not originally perceived prior to the act of digging, one must conclude that emptiness is established only after the earth has been excavated;

this is an objection based on the fact of the earth being unearthed. The underlying intent is to suggest that, since it is said emptiness exists only after emerging from the earth, it is therefore dependent upon the earth for its existence.
The earth must first emerge and the space subsequently enter, just as when one opens a pond to draw in water.
Therefore, it is said that "when the earth emerges, space should be seen entering. However, while the emergence of the earth can be perceived, what is the characteristic of the entry of space?
Thus it is said: "If the earth... [and so forth]. Since there is no observable characteristic of space entering, the notion that space exists because of the earth's emergence is untenable.
It is merely a product of deluded sentiment. △ Second, refuting the absence of entering and exiting.

If there were no entering or exiting, then the empty land and [the mountain] would fundamentally have no different causes. If they were not different, they would be identical; thus, when the land emerges, [the mountain] should likewise emerge.
"Why does space not come forth?

This is a record intended to prevent [the opponent] from shifting their argument. It continues the previous challenge: if one must say that the earth itself comes forth and enters, then why would space come forth or enter?

Thus, the objection is raised by means of the fact that space has no coming forth or entering. The intent is that, since it has been stated that space has no coming forth or entering, then as for the earth...
If it had not yet emerged, there would have to be emptiness [prior to it]; yet emptiness and earth are of one substance and cannot be divided.

Therefore, it is said that "then emptiness and earth would fundamentally have no different cause. Consequently, they would become one substance, leading to the fallacy that they emerge simultaneously. Thus, the objection is raised: "There is no difference" (and so forth).
△ Third, refuting based on the act of digging. This is further divided into two parts. First, refuting the claim that [the earth] emerges by means of digging.
If it were the case that the empty space is produced by the act of digging, then the empty space would be produced by the digging and should not be produced by the removal of earth.

The point is this: since you say that the empty space arises solely because of the digging and not because of the removal of earth, it should follow that one only produces empty space through the digging;

why then dig the earth? Therefore, it is said: "If it were produced by the digging, then the empty space should not be produced by the removal of earth. △ Second, refuting that it is not produced by the digging.
It emerges. It does not emerge because of the digging; rather, the digging itself emerges from the earth. How then can one see emptiness?
The intention [of this objection] is: if one says that emptiness is not caused by the digging and has no connection with the digging, then the digging should only emerge from the earth. It should...
One does not see emptiness; why then, as one digs, does one see emptiness appearing at every turn? Once the excavation is finished, [the space remains]. △ Second, the detailed examination:

You must further examine with utmost clarity and observe with the most profound discernment: the digging proceeds from the hand, which moves according to direction, while the earth shifts because of the ground.
"Such as this empty space—by what cause does it arise?
This repetition of the words is intended to ensure careful and thorough examination. "Moving according to direction" refers to selecting the site and applying effort.
"The earth is moved because of the ground" means that the earth is extracted from within the ground. Because it lacks a cause, it is not a substantial reality; therefore, it does not [arise].
Taking examples from tradition. △ Second, the combined refutation and direct examination. This also has two parts: first, the combined refutation.
Empty space and physical substance do not function for one another; they are neither in harmony nor in union.
The commentary states: To excavate that which must be excavated is to realize that emptiness is actually void. The previous discussion of wind and space concerned their natures being contrary;
this discussion of excavating emptiness concerns its function. In both cases, they turn away from the principle of mutual production through harmonious conjunction. △ Second, the direct examination.
It should not be [conceived as] empty space, for it does not emerge from itself.
Following the above, the detailed analysis based on the "drilling" has been completed. △ Third, the synthesis and awakening. Wuxing said:
"The reason why 'space' is added after the four great elements and collectively termed the 'five great elements' is that, although various sutras commonly speak of only four."

Since this differs from that, it is specifically mentioned. The same principle applies to the subsequent faculties and consciousnesses. This interpretation fully captures the underlying intent of this section.
Furthermore, there are two parts: first, the integration of nature through harmonious union.

If this empty space is by nature perfectly pervasive and fundamentally unmoving, you should know that the earth, water, fire, and wind presently manifest before you are all equally termed the "five great elements.
Their natures are truly and perfectly interfused; they are all the Tathāgatagarbha, fundamentally without arising or ceasing.

"Fusing nature" (*rong-xing*) refers to the fusing of the nature of emptiness. "Conjoining" (*he-hui*) refers to the meeting of the four great elements. The first three phrases conclude the nature of empty space.
As for the two characters "if this" (*ruo-ci*), they承接 (receive) the preceding refutation and lead into the following three characters "perfectly pervasive" (*yuan-zhou-bian*).
The character "perfectly" (*yuan*) is emphasized because, while ordinary discourse on emptiness also speaks of its pervasiveness, there are nonetheless material phenomena that possess obstruction.

That would not be complete; such a term implies pervasiveness, yet it is not a perfect pervasiveness. Now, it is said that the nature of emptiness is perfectly pervasive because form does not constitute an obstruction;
therefore, it is called "perfectly pervasive. This phrase concludes that this is precisely the true nature (*dharmatā*).

It is "unwavering," which is the same as the subsequent state of being without arising or ceasing. Thus, "pervasiveness" indicates that it is not the case that it exists here while being absent there.
That this does not exist while that exists expresses the sense of perfect fulfillment.

That it is immovable expresses the sense of eternal abiding—that it was not previously non-existent and subsequently existent, nor is it presently existent and subsequently non-existent. This phrase concludes [the discussion] by showing its freedom from all delusive appearances.
The above concludes the stabilization of the space element (*ākāśa-mahābhūta*). The direction toward the lower part signifies the intention of combining four to form five.
Regarding the three middle phrases, they first establish the union; "its name manifests before one" refers to the phenomena already appearing and manifesting directly before one's eyes.
It is stated that these are all the nature of the hidden essence (*tathāgatagarbha*); thus they are fundamentally distinct from the locations of the fetters and manifestations.

They are equally termed the "five greats" (*pañcamahābhūta*), yet while the names of the five greats are the same, the reality is that space (*ākāśa*) is newly admitted here as a "great. The final three phrases subsequently unify their substance.
"The nature is truly perfect and interfused" refers to the aforementioned "nature is perfectly pervasive"; "originally without arising or ceasing" refers to the aforementioned "original [nature]."

It is unshakable. However, the former [passage] refers solely to the single realization of the Great Emptiness (*ākāśa-mahābhūta*), whereas this [passage] refers to the unification of the five great elements (*pañca-mahābhūta*).

Both are, in essence, the single phrase "Tathāgatagarbha. In terms of the text, it encompasses all five elements; in terms of its meaning, it extends throughout both the preceding and following sections. The former extends to the true nature’s perfect interfusion (*pariniṣpanna-yoga*);

the latter extends to the fundamental absence of arising and ceasing. Together, they clarify the origins and details of the matter. Nevertheless, the *Record* treats these merely as four examples of emptiness. Furthermore...
It should be understood that it is not only this one who has newly attained the title of "Great.

Although those other four were also formerly called "Great," these titles were merely applied based on their presence in various places; in reality, they are obstructed by one another and lack mutual completeness, and thus are not truly "Great."
From now on, it is only when the nature of the treasury (tathāgatagarbha) is realized as perfectly interfused and eternally abiding that it can truly be called "Great.
Thus, although this is not a new name for "Great," it is in fact utterly distinct from what was previously compared to it. This is like Kāśyapa and others:

though they were long known as Śrāvakas and Arhats, it was only after the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka Sūtra* revealed and clarified the truth that they became truly so. △ Second, the exhortation to awaken and set forth.
"Awaken!
Ānanda, your mind is clouded and deluded; you do not realize that the four great elements are fundamentally the Tathāgatagarbha.
You should contemplate whether space is emerging, entering, or neither emerging nor entering."

In the preceding section, the Great Element of Space was used to illustrate the four great elements; this was intended to use the four great elements as an analogy to clarify the Great Element of Space.

In this present section, the four great elements are raised so that one may turn back and contemplate them by means of space; this is actually intended to use the Great Element of Space to elucidate the four great elements.
Those who are "obscured" have their emotional consciousness constantly darkened; those who are "deluded" are moved and confused by what is false. It is because of this obscuration that...

This is due to deluded perceptions; it is for this reason that such a state has come to pass. The previous attachment to the various characteristics of the four great elements as being in a state of total integration is precisely what is meant by this.
Since one is thus obscured and confused by the heterodox, one will inevitably turn away from the orthodox.

Consequently, one fails to realize that the four great elements are fundamentally the Tathāgatagarbha—neither integrated nor separate, yet also not non-integrated and non-separate. Below, the text then instructs one to contemplate the Great Emptiness.
This is to examine whether there is exiting and entering, or whether there is no exiting and entering.

The underlying intention is to cause one to realize that empty space is all-pervasive and immovable—neither exiting nor entering, yet not non-exiting and non-entering—and thereby realize that the four great elements are perfectly interfused, eternally abiding, neither a composite nor a conjoined entity, yet neither non-composite nor non-conjoined.
The text of the sutra clearly rejects both extremes in each case.
The ancients' commentaries all fall into one-sided extremes; therefore, I did not dare to adopt them. △ Fourth, the conclusion which clarifies and refutes attachment, also in two parts.
First, the conclusion itself, also in two parts. First, the total interpenetration and perfect fusion.
"You know nothing at all. Within the Tathāgatagarbha, the nature of awareness is true emptiness, and the nature of emptiness is true awareness.
Pure and fundamental from the beginning, it pervades the entire Dharma-realm."
The two phrases "the nature is aware of true emptiness" (*xing jue zhen kong*) modify the phrasing from the preceding section and, moreover, invert its meaning.
Previously, both were used to express the fundamental greatness (*ben da*) as being fused with emptiness; here, however, the fundamental greatness itself is the character for "emptiness.
If one were to follow the previous mode of fusion, the two phrases should both read "the nature is empty, true emptiness," and the wording could not be differentiated. Now...

If one replaces the "emptiness" (*śūnyatā*) of the preceding passage with the term "awakening" (*bodhi*), thereby changing "quiescence" (*śānti*) to "illumination" (*prabhāsvara*), there is no contradiction in meaning.
Thus, this "emptiness" (*śūnya*) here refers to the emptiness of space (*ākāśa*). If one were to follow the previous sequence without inversion, it should read:

"the true awakening-nature of the emptiness of nature" (*prakṛti-śūnyatā-bodhi-svabhāva*) and "the true emptiness of awakening-nature" (*bodhi-svabhāva-śūnyatā*). In the present text, the order is reversed; nevertheless, this is also unimpeded.
This merely serves to awaken people to its literary expression. △ Second, the infinite great function. This is further divided into two parts. First, the explicit explanation of the great function:
"In accordance with the minds of sentient beings, it responds to the measure of what they know."
△ Second, verifying its boundlessness:
"Ānanda, suppose there is one well of emptiness; emptiness arises within that one well. The empty space of the ten directions is also like this:
it completely fills the ten directions. How could it have a specific location?"
△ Third, the refutation of attachments:
Phenomena manifest according to karma. Those in the world, being ignorant, deludedly regard them as having causes and conditions or as being of a spontaneous nature.
These are all merely conceptualizations and calculations of the discriminating consciousness; they consist only of verbal expressions and possess no real meaning whatsoever.

The meanings are all consistent with what precedes. This concludes the Great Element of Space. △ Sixth, the Great Element of Seeing. This is identical to the Great Element of the Sense Organs (*indriya-mahābhūta*).
It subsumes all six sense organs, yet only the eye organ is cited as an illustration. However, it takes only the essential nature within the organ, not the superficial, physical form (*bu chen*).
Therefore, it speaks only of "seeing" and so forth, rather than "the eye" and so forth; the underlying intent is thus evident. It is divided into four parts. First:
The characteristics of the objects are defined according to their sensory domains.
Ānanda, the faculty of seeing has no intrinsic cognition; it exists because of form and space. As you are now in the Jeta Grove, it is bright in the morning and dark at night;
even if it were midnight, it would be light during the bright fortnight and dark during the dark fortnight. Thus, brightness and darkness alike exist because of seeing.

Analysis: Herein, the analysis is conducted entirely by means of the identity or difference between the visual faculty (*darśana*) and its object (*viṣaya*), in order to refute the false attachment to their conjunction.

However, as for the specific names of the characteristics of the object (*viṣaya-lakṣaṇa*), which vary in being two or three and in their combination or separation, they shall first be explained in general; they do not exceed [the category of] form (*rūpa*).

The four—emptiness, brightness, darkness, and [the fourth]—are merely mutual manifestations and concealments of one another. For instance, when speaking of "form and emptiness" as a whole, this combines brightness and darkness to contrast them with emptiness.

When speaking only of "brightness and darkness," this opens up form to include emptiness within it. If one speaks of "brightness, darkness, and emptiness," this opens up form to contrast it with emptiness.
As in the expression "seeing emptiness," this is emptiness encompassing form to contrast it with seeing. This is as explained in the text.
I point this out once more so that you may not be confused. "The seeing-consciousness" (*jian-que*) is synonymous with "seeing one's nature" (*jian-xing*).

"Lacking cognition" (*wu-zhi*) means that apart from sensory objects (*chen*), there is no separate object of knowledge. The phrase "because of form and emptiness" (*yin se kong you*) serves to explain the preceding sentence.

Because both light and darkness are simultaneously abandoned, the intrinsic characteristic (*zi-xiang*) of seeing no longer exists; therefore, it is said "because of form and emptiness. This refers to the union of light and darkness as a counterpart to emptiness.

Now, by means of these markers, he proceeds downward to enumerate the sensory objects currently manifest before one: "bright in the morning and dark in the evening" refers to the light and darkness of the day;
"the white moon and the black moon" refers to the light and darkness of the night. These are all equal to empty space itself.
"Because seeing is analyzed": it is because of this object that seeing is found to be analyzable. This merely indicates that seeing is established by relying upon the object;
one cannot say that the object is analyzed because of seeing. This serves solely to refute the conjunction of seeing, not to refute the object itself.
Herein, matter is opened up to encompass emptiness. △ Second, a detailed analysis regarding the object, which has two parts. First:
Investigation:
Does this seeing coexist with light, darkness, and great empty space as a single entity, or is it not a single entity?
Is it both the same and not the same, or both different and not different?
Xueli said: "These four propositions are: first, identity; second, difference; third, either identical or different; and fourth, neither identical nor different.
However, the scriptural text divides them into two identities and two differences, each forming a single proposition. This interpretation accords with the subsequent refutations.
Herein, form is also analyzed in contrast to emptiness. △ Second, the sequential refutation, which is further divided into two parts. First:

The opening of the refutation of the example has two parts. First, the opening of the refutation; this further has four parts. First, the refutation of the identity [of subject and object] within the formal restatement (*pratijñā*);

within the refutation of the identity of form (*rūpa*) and emptiness (*śūnyatā*), the inclusion of emptiness within form is opened up. This further has three parts. First, the statement that introduces the interrogative term.
Ānanda, if this seeing were fundamentally one and the same with light, darkness, and empty space, [it would follow that it could not perceive them as distinct].
△ Second, revealing the error by means of the objects. This is further divided into two sections: first, establishing that the characteristics are lost.
Thus, light and darkness—the two entities—are mutually non-existent. When it is dark, there is no light; when it is light, there is no darkness.
This first establishes the characteristics of external objects as they compete with and supplant one another.
The first half provides a general explanation, while the second half provides a specific explanation. △ Second, the actual demonstration of error.
If it were identical with darkness, then when light appears, vision would cease to exist. If it were necessarily identical with light, then at the time of darkness, it ought to perish.
If it perishes, how can one see both light and darkness?
Since you claim it is of one essence with darkness, then when light appears, darkness must perish; if so, how could vision not also perish? At that point—
The same applies to light. Regarding the final two phrases, which state that [the eye] perishes following darkness, how can it again see when following light?
The same applies to light; its error shall become manifest of itself. △ Third, concluding that they are not the same.
If light and darkness are distinct, how can it be established that seeing is without arising or ceasing?
This concludes the argument by following the previous point: while light and darkness may differ at will, the essence of seeing remains constant;
this naturally demonstrates that they are not a single entity. Thus far, all [discussions] have opened with form to encompass emptiness. The refutation of identity is complete.
△ 2. Refuting the Distinct [from Emptiness]. This section first cites the statement that "matter includes emptiness," and then, in the refutation, analyzes matter in relation to emptiness.
It further consists of three parts: first, citing and raising the interrogative phrase.
If this essence of vision were not of one substance with darkness and light:
△ Second, demonstrating that it is not separate from objects; this has two parts. First, instructing the contemplation by means of separation from objects.
"Set aside light and darkness, as well as empty space; analyze the source of seeing—what form or appearance does it take?
2. It has no substance apart from objects.
Apart from light, apart from darkness, and apart from empty space, this source of seeing is like the fur of a tortoise or the horns of a rabbit.
This directly cuts through [the misconception]. This, too, is a provisional statement that, by setting them apart, reveals their lack of self-nature.
△ Third, concluding that they are not distinct:
Light, darkness, and empty space—these three things are all distinct; from what, then, could "seeing" be established?

The character "yi" (異) in "ju yi zhi yi" (俱異之異) is read as the character "li" (離). This means that when these three are all separated [from one another], this seeing fundamentally lacks its own intrinsic substance;
therefore, it is said, "From what could seeing be established? The refutation of difference is now complete. △ Third, the refutation of being either identical or different.
Light and darkness are mutually opposed; how could they be identical? Apart from these three, nothing else exists; how could they be different?
All of this is the ultimate meaning, merely summarized in one place. The first two lines open up form to encompass emptiness;
the latter two lines open up form to confront emptiness. △ Fourth, refuting neither identity nor difference.
The divisions of space and the divisions of vision originally have no boundaries; how could they not be the same? Seeing darkness and seeing light—their nature does not undergo change;
how could they not be different?

The two phrases concerning the division of emptiness take emptiness to encompass form, thereby contrasting it with seeing. The two phrases concerning "seeing darkness" state that while the objects (dust) are distinct, the seeing is one;
thus they are clearly different. Therefore, it asks: "How can they not be different? This, in turn, opens up form to encompass emptiness.
△ Second, the examination by analogy:
You should examine this even more minutely; investigate it with subtle discernment; scrutinize it with precision and observe it with clarity. Light follows the sun; darkness follows the dark moon.
That which penetrates belongs to empty space; that which is obstructed returns to the great earth. Knowing this to be the essence of seeing, from what does it emerge?
You shall further utter three phrases to instruct him on the meaning of fixing his gaze: first, "examine minutely";
second, "minutely" is not merely minute, but is further refined as "subtly minute"; "examine" is not merely examine, but is further refined as "thoroughly examine"; next, "attentively."
Having already observed, one further investigates; moreover, one examines with precision and observes with scrutiny.

This also opens up form to face emptiness, while adding the penetration of obstructions, exhausting every detail. △ Second, the combined refutation and direct examination. This also has two parts: first, the combined refutation.
Seeing and cognition are empty and inert; they neither harmonize nor combine.
This is because their essential natures are distinct, and thus it is said that they do not form a union. This, moreover, is a case where emptiness subsumes form.
And this concerns the act of seeing. △ Second, the direct examination:
the essence of seeing should not be able to emerge from nowhere on its own.
Based on the above, the detailed analysis regarding the objects has been completed. △ Third, the synthesis for awakening, which has two parts. First, the integration of nature.
In summary:

if one perceives, hears, or knows that the nature is perfectly pervasive and fundamentally unmoving, one should know that the boundless, unmoving space, together with the shifting earth, water, fire, and wind, are all collectively termed the six great elements. Their nature is truly perfect and harmonious; they are all the Tathāgatagarbha.
Fundamentally, there is no arising or ceasing.

The intent of this section follows the previous one. This [phrase] generally encompasses the six faculties; that the awareness of the nose, tongue, and body is not explicitly mentioned is due to brevity.
The two phrases regarding "nature" and "perfection" also follow the same section as above. As for the subsequent "immovability" and "shaking," these both refer to the phenomenal aspect (*lakṣaṇa*).
He said: "The characteristic of emptiness is immovable; although the four characteristics appear to move, when combined, they are by nature all immovable.
The rest follows the above principle. △ Second, warning them to awaken.
Ānanda, your nature is submerged and you do not realize that your seeing, hearing, sensing, and knowing are fundamentally the Tathāgatagarbha.

You should examine this seeing, hearing, sensing, and knowing: are they arising or ceasing? Are they identical or different? Are they neither arising nor ceasing? Are they neither identical nor different?
Those who are submerged are mired in biased views and lack the wisdom for transcendence. This failure to awaken is to be contemplated as a cry for help, as previously described.

However, the principle within this case differs: that which fails to awaken is the *mahābhūta* of the four elements (*catur-mahābhūta*), whereas that which should be contemplated is the *mahābhūta* of emptiness (*śūnyatā*).
Thus, that which fails to awaken is the view of the great, while that which should be contemplated is likewise the view of the great.
Furthermore, "arising and ceasing" refers to their own substance, while "sameness and difference" refers to external objects.

The intent is to lead one to realize that seeing and the other faculties are neither arising and ceasing nor sameness and difference, yet they are also not non-arising and non-ceasing or non-sameness and non-difference. Thus, one knows that the nature of the store-consciousness (ālaya) is perfectly eternal;
it is neither a combination nor a non-combination. This constitutes a deeper awakening. The exhortation to awaken is hereby concluded.
△ Fourth, the conclusion that summarizes and refutes attachments. This also has two parts. First, the summary and clarification. This also has two parts. First, the total mutual interpenetration:

"You have never known that within the Tathāgatagarbha, the nature of seeing and the clarity of awareness, and the clarity of awareness and the essence of seeing, are fundamentally pure and inherently so."
"Pervading the entire dharma-realm.
The seeing-nature within awareness and clarity" means that the seeing within the nature is precisely the clarity upon awareness.

"The essence of awareness and the clarity of seeing" means that the essence of true awareness is precisely the seeing of the clarity of the nature. "Seeing-nature" and "clarity-seeing" are spoken of as...

"Nature-color is true color. This uses the term "nature" to describe the fusion with the Great [Dharmadhātu]. "Awakened clarity" and "awakened essence" are like saying "true emptiness" or "essential emptiness";
they directly refer to the meaning of the essential body of nature. Taken together, they do not go beyond the identity of nature and appearance.
Within this Tathāgatagarbha, before the true essence has been manifested, one must not take awakened clarity to be ignorance;
yet even its purity differs slightly [from that of the ordinary]. It should be said: "It is entirely seeing, yet this awakening is not the seeing of the sense-faculties' knots of ordinary beings;
it is entirely awakening, yet this seeing is not the dark, silent awakening of the Two Vehicles. Therefore, it is called "pure. Its fundamental nature remains as previously described. △
Second, the infinite great function. This also has two parts: first, the explicit clarification of the great function;
[it] accords with the minds of sentient beings and responds to the measure of what they know.
Second, the general categorization of the six sense organs. This also has two parts: first, the categorization of the entire body.

Just as with the faculty of sight, where seeing pervades the Dharma-realm, so too do hearing, smelling, tasting, touching, and the cognition of touch—these wondrous virtues are brilliantly pure and universally pervasive throughout the Dharma-realm.
"Seeing pervades the Dharma-realm" reiterates that the aforementioned seeing is all-pervasive within the Dharma-realm. Wénlíng says: "Tasting and touching..."

The tongue faculty perceives only when combined with flavor; therefore, it is also called "contact" (*spraṣṭavya*). "Perceiving contact" refers to the two faculties of body and mind. Regarding "wondrous virtue":
this means that seeing, hearing, and so forth are the functional manifestations of the wondrous nature. "Luminous and clear" means:
"Numinous clarity is not obscure" means it is slightly more than the sense of "awakened clarity" and "awakened essence.
"Pervading the entire Dharma-realm" refers to the fact that the complete body of universal seeing is perfectly interfused. △ Second, the categories of great function.
Filling the ten voids—how could there be any fixed location?

It is said that its manifestation constitutes a great function; according to the mind and responding to capacity, it is perfectly fulfilled (and so forth). The ten voids constitute the ten dharma-realms.
Furthermore, it may be like seeing, hearing, and so forth, according to the magnitude of its capacity, reaching the ultimate limit of that capacity, thereby filling the ten voids.

If considered in terms of arising and forming the root-body (indriya-kāya), whether it forms a single root-body or even manifests universally as immeasurable root-bodies, all are the great functions of responding to the mind according to its measure. △ Second, the refutation of attachments.
They manifest according to karma. The world is ignorant of this and deludedly regards them as having causes and conditions or as being of a spontaneous nature.
These are all merely conceptualizations and calculations of the discriminating consciousness; they consist only of verbal expressions and possess no real meaning whatsoever.

The meaning is consistent with what was stated above. (Question: Since this [passage] takes only the nature within the six sense organs (*ṣaḍāyatana*), it has already been revealed previously that their entirety constitutes the substance of the nature (*dharmatā*). Why, then, is there the need to laboriously integrate them again into the "Great" (*mahat*)? (Answer:

According to the specific intent of this sutra, both awakening and realization depend upon the six sense organs; therefore, it specifically revealed them previously as the entire body of the nature. However, according to the general intent of various sutras, only the *tathāgatagarbha* constitutes the universal characteristic (*sāmānyalakṣaṇa*) of the nature. Thus, here the six sense organs are once again integrated into the *tathāgatagarbha*.

Furthermore, among the various teachings, there are those with fixed characteristics—both general and particular—and those that are perfectly interfused and indeterminate. According to the fixed characteristics, the *tathāgatagarbha* is eternally the universal characteristic, while all phenomena are...

Regarding their distinct characteristics: according to the principle of the Perfect [Teaching], all phenomena can truly function as both the general and the particular. Previously, based on the Perfect principle, we took the particular to be the general; thus, the essence of seeing became the general characteristic of the fulfilled nature, while the myriad phenomena were its particular characteristics.

Now, based on fixed characteristics, the Tathāgatagarbha remains the general, while seeing and the six great elements remain the particulars. Although the general and the particular are not fixed, one still knows that these two perspectives do not contradict one another. This is truly because the previous revelation and manifestation...

The present "integration" (*róngrù*) likewise possesses the two phases of beginning and end. As for the initial phase, it emerges spontaneously from within the sense faculties; as for its subsequent phase, it unifies the myriad dharmas into a single essence, wherein the body, the sensory organs, and the physical world are all but illusory reflections within it—this is precisely the *tathāgatagarbha* herein.

The initial phase of the present [integration] also arises through the discernment of light and darkness before one's eyes, no different from the spontaneous emergence from within the faculties mentioned previously. As for its subsequent phase, it involves the convergence and manifestation of the true nature’s perfect interfusion, pervading the entire *dharmadhātu*;

this too is no different from the subsequent phase of the "unveiling" (*kāixiǎn*) discussed previously. However, within this context, the seven elements (*mahābhūta*) are all admitted to be equally interfused; furthermore, these are the myriad dharmas that serve as the basis for the principle of "perfect interfusion."

They contain one another. Yet, among them, the nature of seeing (*darśana-svabhāva*) alone is permitted to crown all phenomena; this is also the specific purport and essential core of this sutra. Therefore, while previously it was desired that one be skillful in awakening and cultivation, here it is desired that one be perfected in insight and understanding.
Let those with the eye of wisdom discern this. The section on the Great Element of Sight is concluded. △ Seven: The Great Element of Consciousness. This is termed the "Fourfold Analysis.
First, the designation based on the sense organs and objects. This further has two parts. First, the enumeration of the three dharmas.
Ānanda, the nature of consciousness has no source; it arises due to the six kinds [of sense bases]. From the faculties and objects, delusion emerges. Now, survey this assembly of noble ones;
let your eyes pass over them one by one.
Although the heading fully indicates three dharmas, the intent is merely to distinguish consciousness (*vijñāna*) by means of the faculties (*indriya*) and objects (*viṣaya*).

In the section on the nature of consciousness (*vijñānatva*), it states that it arises solely based on the six kinds of faculties and objects; thus, it refers only to the first six [consciousnesses]. As for why the seventh and eighth are absent:

because the eighth is identical to the great element of the faculties mentioned previously, and the seventh is likewise identical to the mental faculty (*manas-indriya*). [The character] "nature" (*xing*).
This refers to the body and its characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*), not the true nature (*dharmatā*). "Having no source" means it is like a wild fire:
its arising and ceasing have no point of origin. "Dependent on the sense organs and objects" means it arises through provisional reliance. The above establishes the thesis.

From "You now," below, he cites the visual consciousness presently before us, which falsely arises dependent on the sense organs and objects, as an analogy for the other five [consciousnesses], all of which are likewise so.
Contemplation is the faculty (*indriya*); the assembly of sages is the object (*viṣaya*); and the sequential investigation is consciousness (*vijñāna*).
△ Second, the distinction between the faculties and consciousness. Although this distinction is made in relation to objects, the intent of the confusion does not actually concern the objects at all.

This is because the essential natures of consciousness and objects are inherently distinct, whereas the faculties and consciousness have traditionally been difficult to differentiate; therefore, they are specifically distinguished here. This further divides into two parts.
First, distinguishing and clarifying the characteristic of the sense organ (*indriya*).
Its gaze surveys all around; it is simply like a mirror, without further analysis.

When the myriad phenomena are reflected therein, not a single thought arises—this is precisely the characteristic of the sense organ. Second, distinguishing and clarifying the characteristic of consciousness (*vijñāna*).
Within this assembly, you should identify them one by one: "This is Mañjuśrī; this is Pūrṇa;
this is Maudgalyāyana; this is Subhūti; this is Śāriputra."
This is precisely visual consciousness (*cakṣurvijñāna*), which also includes the clear and distinct mental consciousness associated with the eye.

However, as for the name "visual consciousness," it refers to the first momentary thought that arises in relation to a direct object (*svabhāvaviṣaya*), being free from names and phrases; thus, it follows the designation of the mental consciousness associated with the eye.

Discriminative conceptualization (*abhinirūpaṇā-vikalpa*) also arises in relation to an objective realm (*svabhāva-viṣaya*), giving rise to a second moment of thought that conceptually grasps names and words, such as when one designates "Mañjuśrī" and so forth.
This applies to the visual faculty; by extension, it is the same for the other four [senses]. As for the mental faculty (*manas*), however:
Apart from the first five consciousnesses, those that function independently and take their own objects—namely, the objects of solitary images—are also included in this category.
△ Second, the analysis according to the faculties and objects is further divided into two parts. First, the interrogation.
This consciousness cognizes: does it arise from seeing, or from forms, or from space, or does it emerge suddenly without cause? [Objection:

Since space can still be categorized as an object (*viṣaya*), [the question of] being without cause seems not to be addressed in terms of the sense-faculties (*indriya*) and objects (*viṣaya*). [Response: It must be discussed in terms of...
Since it cannot be established as causeless by relying on the sense organs and so forth, this is likewise discussed in terms of the sense organs and their objects.

△ Second, the sequential refutation. This also has two parts: first, opening up the refutation to examine the analogy; this is further divided into two: first, the opening refutation; this is further subdivided into four:
first, refuting that [consciousness] arises from the causal sense organ.
Ānanda, if the nature of your consciousness were produced within seeing, then in the absence of darkness, light, form, and emptiness—these four conditions—it would necessarily not exist;
since your seeing itself would fundamentally be absent, from what could consciousness arise?
"Seeing" is precisely the faculty (*indriya*). This statement means that if the object (*viṣaya*) is removed and there is no faculty, then the faculty has already been non-existent beforehand;
upon what basis could its own essence arise to produce consciousness? △ Second, the refutation of [the view] that [consciousness] arises from the object.

If the nature of your consciousness were produced from within forms and did not arise from the faculty of seeing, then since you would neither see light nor see darkness, and light and darkness would not impinge upon it, there would be neither form nor emptiness;
if those forms do not even exist, from what could consciousness arise?

"Phenomena" (*xiàng*) refers to the objects (*chén*). This statement means that if the sense organs are removed, there are no objects; thus, since the objects themselves lack their own characteristics (*sva-lakṣaṇa*), how could they give rise to consciousness?
The first line does not merely remove the organs. Since it is not the second line either, it still restates the intent of removing the organs from above.
It is only with the two lines concerning "light and darkness" that the fault of reducing them to non-existent objects is revealed. Light, darkness, form, and space are mutually identical.
The two phrases concerning "mutually using those characteristics" conclude that [the view] is incorrect. △ Third, refuting that it arises from empty space. This also has two parts:
first, restating the objection to open up the meaning.
If it were born from empty space, it would be neither characteristic nor vision.
The first phrase restates the challenging argument; the second phrase opens it up to form two meanings. △ Second, the refutation by combining examples.
This is further divided into two parts: first, the twofold refutation.

Without seeing, there is no discernment; one cannot know for oneself the brightness, darkness, form, or emptiness. These are not the extinction of marks nor the conditions of perception; seeing, hearing, sensing, and knowing have no place where they can be established.

The three propositions regarding "not seeing" are identical to those above: the sense organs are absent while objects are present. The three propositions regarding "not being characteristics" are identical to those above: objects are absent while sense organs are present.
△ Second, the combined refutation of both.

Abiding in this state where neither [form] nor [vision] exists, if consciousness were empty, it would be the same as a tortoise’s hair. If it were existent, it would not be identical to any object. Even if you were to give rise to your consciousness, what would there be to differentiate?
Wēnlíng says: "Abiding between this non-characteristic and non-vision, if the substance of consciousness were empty, it would be the same as a tortoise's hair."
If the substance of consciousness were existent, it would not be the same as material objects; since it itself lacks substance, how could it possess function?
△ Fourth, refuting production without cause:
If there were no cause and it emerged suddenly, why does one not perceive the bright moon at midday with a distinct consciousness?
To say that there is no moon at midday means that the consciousness which discriminates the bright moon cannot arise. If so, how could consciousness arise without a cause?
However, this scriptural passage is a form of rhetorical interrogation; having already completed the refutation, [the text proceeds as follows]. △ Second, the examination by analogy.
Examine this further with meticulous detail and profound scrutiny: you see that which relies upon your pupils and projects itself toward external objects;
it can be characterized as existing, yet cannot be characterized as non-existent. Given such conditions for consciousness, from what does it arise?
The first two phrases refer to the sense organs and their objects; the latter two phrases refer to form and emptiness. These four are said to be mutually unmixed.
One should minutely examine from where this consciousness arises. Having completed the detailed analysis and refutation by opening up each case, [the second part follows].
2. Combined Refutation and Direct Examination. This also has two parts: 1. Combined Refutation.
Consciousness is active while seeing is still; they are neither conjoined nor separate. Hearing, listening, sensing, and knowing are likewise so. Wēnlíng says:
"Consciousness possesses discrimination and is thus called 'active'; seeing lacks discrimination and is thus called 'still. Consciousness is active while seeing is still."
The natures are separated and distinct; seeing is separated from consciousness, and hearing and knowing are likewise so; none of these are in union. II.
Direct Examination:
It should not be that consciousness arises from itself without a source.
The preceding analysis regarding the faculties and their objects is concluded. △ Third, the synthesis for awakening. This also has two parts. First, the synthesis through the fusion of nature:
If this conscious mind originally has no source from which it arises, one should know that the discernment of seeing, hearing, sensing, and knowing is perfect, tranquil, and profound.
The nature does not arise from conditions; together with space, earth, water, fire, and wind, these are all uniformly termed the "Seven Great Elements. Their nature is truly perfect and interfused;
they are all the Tathāgatagarbha, fundamentally devoid of arising and ceasing.
"Fundamentally having no source" means that it does not arise from the conditions of the sense organs (*indriya*) and their objects (*viṣaya*).

Regarding "discerning seeing, hearing, smelling, tasting, touching, and cognizing," the narrow view holds this to refer to the preceding [passage on] the great elements of the sense organs. Following the previous two [cases of] the great elements, one should know that in all subsequent instances there is likewise no fundamental great element;

yet the old interpretation specifically points to the six consciousnesses (*ṣaḍ-vijñāna*). Since this differs from the preceding text and furthermore lacks the great elements of the sense organs, it is incorrect.

"How can it constitute the number seven? This critique from a limited perspective is indeed correct. It means that nature does not follow from conditions, nor does it belong to various causal factors.
The rest is to be understood according to the above. △ Second, warning to provoke awakening.
Ānanda, your mind is coarse and restless; you have not yet awakened to the fact that seeing, hearing, clarity, and cognition are fundamentally the Tathāgatagarbha.
You should contemplate these six bases of consciousness: are they the same or different? Are they empty or existent? Are they neither the same nor different, and neither empty nor existent?
As for those who are coarse and superficial: they lack the profound wisdom that is precise and penetrating, and are instead deluded by shallow discourses that cling to signs (*nimitta*).

The character "not" (*bù*) should be understood as applying to both "awakening" (*wù*) and "manifesting" (*fāmíng*). To understand (*liǎozhī*) is precisely to be aware (*juézhī*); it is merely an error in translation.

Alternatively, if "understanding" (*liǎozhī*) is attributed solely to the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*), then the character "awareness" (*jué*) is missing; this is either an error or an omission. Let the wise examine this in detail.

Regarding this: according to the latter explanation, "awakening" (jue) encompasses all three consciousnesses; this is a simultaneous abbreviation. Following the precedent of the preceding section, it refers only to the fundamental Great [Mind] in relation to the six consciousnesses.
"Identity and difference" are spoken of in relation to the sense organs and their objects; "emptiness and existence" are spoken of with respect to its own essence.

The rest follows the above. △ Third, the conclusion which clarifies and refutes attachments. This also has two sections. First, the conclusion and clarification. This also has two parts. First, the totality of the perfect circle.

Rong, you fundamentally do not know that within the Tathāgatagarbha, the nature-consciousness is luminously aware; this awakened, luminous true consciousness is wondrously enlightened and profoundly still,
pervading and encompassing the entire Dharma-realm.
"Nature-consciousness as clear knowing" refers to the consciousness of true nature, which is precisely the clear knowing of the wondrous brightness.

"Awakened clarity as true consciousness" refers to the clarity of original awakening, which is precisely the consciousness of true nature. "Nature-consciousness" and "true consciousness" are terms that express the integration of nature with the Great [Dharma-realm].
"Clear knowing" and "awakened clarity" directly signify the essence of the nature. In sum, these are all expressions of the integration and identity of nature-consciousness.
The meaning [of this] is as follows: that which is "pure and fundamentally so" transforms into the "wondrously enlightened and profoundly still.

This is because, although the sense organs (*indriya*) and their objects (*viṣaya*) stand in mutual dependence, they remain clearly distinct like images. As for the characteristic of consciousness (*vijñāna*), it has always been like flowers in the sky from the very beginning.

Therefore, regarding the aforementioned great elements, all are said to be "pure and fundamentally so. This [phrase]承接 (inherits/continues) the preceding [notion] that the greatness of nature (*dharmatā-mahattva*) and the greatness of characteristics (*lakṣaṇa-mahattva*) are mutually fused. Both...

This means that they are all free from defects and are fundamentally inherent. As for the Great Consciousness (vijñāna-mahābhūta), since it originally lacks both substance and form, and because it has already been integrated into the nature of awakening, its pervasive manifestation and emission are all spoken of solely in terms of the nature of awakening.
Therefore, it is directly designated as "wondrous awakening" (*prajñā*) being identical to the essential body of nature, without the necessity of further describing it as "pure" or "tranquil."

The nature is luminous; it is unnecessary to further state that it is inherently endowed [with all qualities]. That which "pervades the entire dharma-realm" is because the awakened nature is like a mirror and consciousness is merely like a reflection.
If one knows that the reflection is the very substance of the mirror, then one speaks of the pervasiveness of the reflection solely by way of the pervasiveness of the mirror.
Alternatively, if one refers to the perfectly consummate realm, one may also speak directly of how a single thought encompasses the ten directions.

Throughout the three periods of time, this is a sudden teaching that asserts the existence of the fundamental substance (youzong) while negating causes. If one were to investigate its cause, one would still employ the previous explanation, as it is said:
"For what reason? Because consciousness has no self-characteristic (*sva-lakṣaṇa*), for it is the very nature of awakening (*bodhi-svabhāva*).
Here, the reflection in a mirror serves as the corroborative analogy (*dṛṣṭānta*). II. The Great Function is Limitless.
Encompassing and exhaling the ten voids, how could there be any fixed location?
Regarding the phrase "this absence of following the mind corresponds to the measure," there are two meanings.

First, sentient beings themselves know that the various great elements mentioned in the preceding text take the sense organs as their internal endowment and external objects as their environment; neither possesses a portion of independent sovereignty.

Therefore, the Buddha taught that [the environment] accords with the mind and responds to its measure (*yathācittapramāṇa*). This reveals that it, too, is a phenomenon of the sovereign power of Mind-only (*cittamātra*).
As for consciousness and the mind, sentient beings have always known them to be phenomena that accord with their own sovereignty;
thus, there is no need to further state that they "accord with the mind and respond to its measure. These two are the self-nature of phenomena, namely, the mind.
This is precisely the consciousness-mind; its measure is the measure of consciousness. It no longer follows itself or corresponds to itself, just as the eye cannot see itself.

Encompassing and expelling the ten voids is also based on the awakening-nature manifesting through transformation. Yet, there is encompassing and there is expelling, and their characteristics are likewise not the same.

It is like a cloud: when movement is conceived, it contains [the rain]; when no thought is conceived, it emits [it]. If one relies on the Perfect Ultimate (yuanji), as explained in the preceding section, the conclusion and its manifestation are now complete.
△ Second, the refutation of attachments.
They manifest according to karma. The world is ignorant and deludedly regards them as having causes and conditions or as being of a spontaneous nature;
these are all merely conceptualizations and calculations of the conscious mind. They consist only of words and have no real substance.
The various consciousnesses arise only by means of their respective seeds, and these seeds must in turn depend on past karma;

therefore, one must follow the predominance of karma, as in the case of the two upper realms where nothing arises without a seed. The first five [consciousnesses] are inferior, like jellyfish, and fail to arise when lacking their seeds.

This applies to the sense-faculty consciousnesses of the eye and the others, all of which are to be understood according to the above. Question: At the beginning of this sutra, you first directly refute the [notion of a] conscious mind, as in the "Seven Stations" [Sūtra].
Through thorough investigation, the three delusions are resolved: names and meanings are all false and ultimately lack substantiality.
Even within the passage concerning the manifestation of seeing, he further refutes them by means of mutual comparison, never granting even the slightest concession.

Why, then, in the section on the eighteen realms, has he already granted that they are the Tathāgatagarbha-citta, the wondrous nature of True Suchness? Upon reaching this point, his praise becomes even more emphatic.
