Pervading the entire Dharma-realm and encompassing the ten voids, this is the complete embodiment of the nature itself, identical to that ultimate measure of the manifestation of the seeing-nature (*darśana-svabhāva*).
How can it be that what precedes is the height of delusion, while what follows is the pinnacle of truth? Answer:

The former refers to the awakening and cultivation of the beginner's mind, which must proceed from skillful means (*upāya*) to discern the true from the false and abandon the root of birth-and-death (*saṃsāra*).

To grasp the wondrous mind of *nirvāṇa*, consciousness must be completely shattered and definitively discarded. Subsequently, through the universal integration of perfect understanding (*yuanjie*), there is no phenomenon that is not true and no phenomenon that is not as it should be;
even down to the atoms of lands and the thoughts of kalpas, nothing is other than the single True Dharma-realm (*ekadharmadhātu*).

How much more so, then, could the conscious mind fail to integrate with the Dharma-realm? This principle is indicated in the "Hanging Exposition" (*xuanshi*) where both gates are simultaneously present. This is the intended meaning.

This is exhaustive; you should study and savor it with care. Furthermore, one must understand that while the preceding four sections each individually fused phenomena back into principle (*li*), they did not yet state that they collectively pervade the entire Dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu*).
Therefore, they represented only the modality by which principle and phenomena are unimpeded.

Now, the seven great elements (*mahābhūta*) subsume all phenomena, including the five aggregates (*skandha*) and so forth, and it is stated that each of these individually pervades the entire Dharma-realm. This is why...

This is the cause for the unimpeded interpenetration of phenomena and principle. For indeed, that contemplation takes phenomena as they accord with principle and fuses them into ten gates as the general cause.
This is because if there were only phenomena, they would obstruct one another; if there were only principle, there would be nothing further to be fused.

Now, because each and every phenomenon is harmoniously integrated according to the principle (*yathā-artha*) and is entirely without limit, there exists this profound gateway of the non-obstruction of phenomena (*dharmadharmāpratigha*).
Although this is discussed by defining their essential nature, it appears that the spatial and phenomenal aspects accord with the gateway of the principle without duality.
In reality, through these general causes, there are no gateways of myriad wonders—such as mutual inclusion and mutual containment—that do not arise.
"It is opened wide. [The questioner] asks: "If that is so, then the three dharma-realms (dharmadhātu) are fully present in their causal conditions.

Why then do you say, 'let us speak only of the one true [reality]'? [The answer: "The three dharma-realms are identical in their causal condition of subsuming phenomena (dharma) and returning them to principle (li).

This is in response to Ānanda’s false attachments; each instance of delusion is reconciled so as to return to the true and correct. It is solely for the purpose of subsuming phenomena and returning them to principle."
This merely involves the fusion of characteristics into nature; it has not yet reached the stage of arising characteristics from nature or accomplishing phenomena from principle.
Thus, within the Tripitaka, this properly belongs only to the *śūnyatā-tathāgatagarbha*.

Those who insist on judging it by means of the three contemplations and the three truths have failed to investigate with sufficient rigor. Let the wise reflect upon this. The Tathāgata destroys the false to reveal...

The first major section on the True One (Zhēnyī) is completed. △ Second, Ānanda’s realization, gratitude, and resolve for enlightenment. This is divided into two sections. First, receiving the instruction and attaining awakening;
this is all recorded by the scribe of the sutra. Furthermore, it is divided into two parts. First, the narration of receiving the instruction.

At that time, Ānanda and the great assembly, having received the subtle and wondrous instruction of the Buddha-Tathāgata, spoke based on the various passages within the section "Piercing through Delusion to Reveal the True. Indeed, the effort required for this great realization is not immediate;
therefore, we shall now summarize the preceding points and extract their essential meaning, so that you may understand the reality of the subtle and wondrous and how to pierce through delusion.

There are three parts to the refutation of the deluded mind: first, the sevenfold refutation which secretly demonstrates its lack of location; second, the double interrogation which clearly rebukes it as not being the true mind;
and third, the concession and withdrawal which decides that it has no substantial essence. Thus, this refutation of the deluded mind may be said to be extremely subtle and utterly refined.
In the section revealing the true mind, there are likewise three parts: first, the demonstration of seeing and so forth, which defines...

Regarding the nature of the sense faculties (*indriya-svabhāva*): first, it points directly to their essential substance; second, it demonstrates the aggregates (*skandha*) and so forth, extensively dissolving all phenomenal marks to clarify their single essence;
third, it demonstrates the stages (*bhūmi*) and so forth, most perfectly manifesting their perfect interfusion to reveal their total embodiment.
Thus, that which reveals the true mind may be said to be extremely subtle and utterly exquisite. Now, let us point to the nature of the sense faculties.
When all marks (*lakṣaṇa*) are fused, this simultaneously reveals the falsity of the myriad marks of both the environment and its inhabitants (*āśraya-adhiṣṭhāna*).

Thus, the principle that marks are false while nature is true is rendered completely clear and transparent. Therefore, the compiler summarizes and concludes here in order to manifest the fundamental basis for the awakening to follow.
II. Narrating the Awakening. Now, as for the subtle and profound contemplation of *śamatha*:
Although one should universally illumine the three *tathāgatagarbhas*, this is because Ānanda first realized the essence of the single true mind;

it is through this that his illumination penetrating the empty *tathāgatagarbha* is revealed. Nevertheless, as principle and wisdom are perfectly interfused, there is no partiality in the objective realm;
this is precisely the wondrous, enlightened clarity that universally illumines the dharma-dhātu of principle. This is divided into two parts. First, the realization of pervasiveness.
Furthermore, there are two [points]. First is the general heading:
"Body and mind are vast and open, attaining freedom from all obstructions.

"Body" refers to the Dharma-body; "mind" refers to the True Mind. "Vast and open" describes their pervasive nature. The subsequent sections provide a detailed explanation according to their divisions.
"Being without obstruction" means that the deluded body and deluded mind no longer bind, entangle, or create barriers. For the Dharma-body and true mind are fundamentally and spontaneously perfected;
yet, from time immemorial, they have been bound, entangled, and obstructed by the deluded body and deluded mind, such that one was never aware of this and possessed no autonomy at all.
Now, through being enlightened beneath these words, one attains great mastery. One attains...
This is a great enjoyment. △ Second, the detailed narration. This also has two parts. First, the mind is vast and empty. This is further divided into two.
First, the indication of the meaning of pervasive capacity.
This great assembly each and every one knows for themselves that their minds pervade the ten directions.

As for "assembly," their positions encompass both the profound and the shallow; as for "knowing," their awakenings encompass both realization and understanding. It is like a group of people situated within a dark environment;
though the space is fundamentally empty, vast, and expansive, because of the darkness they see nothing and mistakenly cling to it as narrow and confined. This is the stage of position.

Regarding those who realize through deep realization: perhaps the aggregate of form (*rūpa-skandha*) has already been exhausted, such that the ten directions open up like a sudden emergence from darkness into light, personally beholding the vast emptiness.

Regarding those who understand through intellectual comprehension at a shallow stage: perhaps the aggregate of form has not yet been exhausted, yet they give rise to great resolute conviction (*adhimukti*) in accordance with the words;
it is like hearing someone describe a scene in the dark, where one suddenly awakens to the original measure [of reality], vast and boundless.
One no longer gives rise to thoughts of narrowness. "Pervading the ten directions" means reaching the full extent of the ten directions;

it may also be understood as encompassing the ten dharma-realms. △ Second, the thorough awakening to the environment (the *niśraya-vipāka*). This has two parts: first, transforming the great into the small.
One sees the emptiness of the ten directions as clearly as observing an object held in one's hand.

Space is the greatest among the environmental retributions (*niśraya-vipāka*), for it is that upon which the vessel-world (*bhājana-loka*) relies; thus, it is also categorized as an environmental retribution.
The "leafy object" in his hand refers to the *palm-leaf* (pattraka). This is because in that region, characters are written upon palm leaves;

therefore, he constantly holds one in his hand. As for "seeing emptiness as like a leaf," it is because while empty space has no limit and cannot contain anything, the true mind is hundreds of thousands of millions of times greater than it, beyond all comparison.
It is only because one contemplates emptiness through the mind that emptiness appears small, like a leaf.
This section primarily conveys the principle that the seven elements are identical to the mind, which pervades the entire dharma-realm, thereby accomplishing this awakening.
△ Second, transforming the other into the self:
All things existing within all worlds are none other than the wondrously luminous, original mind of bodhi.
The first two lines refer to the myriad phenomena of the physical world (*bhājanaloka*), all of which belong to the *paratantra* (retributive) realm.

"Bodhi" refers to the essence of the fruit of original enlightenment (*mūla-avabodha*). This is what was meant in the preceding text: "This seeing and its objects are originally the wondrous, pure, and luminous essence of bodhi.
This wondrous luminosity is precisely the *tathāgatagarbha-citta*. Generally, those of the Hīnayāna view things as being non-mind; the provisional teachings likewise regard things as [external].
Delusion! Now I realize that all things are entirely mind; they are pure and true, without delusion.
This section largely encompasses the previous four sections on the aggregates (*skandhas*) and so forth, all of which constitute this realization through the *ālaya*-nature.

Reaching this point, the principle of refuting the deluded mind is finally and fully realized. One no longer identifies the discrimination of conditioned objects as the mind, nor is one again deluded by it.
Within the physical body (*rūpakāya*), one no longer deludes oneself by taking the self to be an object;

thus, doubts regarding "seeing" and "non-seeing," as well as the combination of the four great elements (*mahābhūta*), are suddenly and completely dissolved like ice. The mind is now utterly serene. △ Second, the body is utterly serene.
This is further divided into two parts. First, indicating the meaning of its capacity to encompass.
The essence of mind is all-pervasive and perfect, encompassing the ten directions.
The body takes this encompassing as its characteristic; when the four great elements combine and encompass the five viscera, this constitutes the physical body (*rūpakāya*).

When the essence of mind is all-pervasive and perfect, encompassing the ten directions, this constitutes the Dharma-body (*dharmakāya*). Therefore, whenever Buddhas and patriarchs speak, they do not depart from the body.
The phrases "the center and the body are the *bodhimaṇḍa*" and so forth all refer to the *dharmakāya*, not the physical body.
When a practitioner realizes that this *dharmakāya* is primordially and inherently complete, then whether walking, standing, sitting, or lying down, the body is constantly boundless;

thus, the immeasurable oceans of lands (*kṣetrasamudra*) all enter into the body. Generally, worldly people commonly say that the world is enveloped within space. However, [in reality,] space is itself contained within the body.

The body envelops the self; the self envelops the mind. Layer upon layer of confinement, there has never been any transcendence. Now, suddenly, the mind envelops the ten directions and the body encompasses the space beyond.
Inside and outside have been reversed; large and small have been transformed. This is truly what is meant by "wondrously being able to transform things."

Only those who can abide permanently within this body are capable of assuming the responsibility. Even coughing, spitting, turning the back, or shaking the head are none other than the intent of the Patriarchs.
As the four-fascicle text says: "The body contains the inexhaustible void of the ten directions. Thus we know this refers to the *dharmakāya*.

Moreover, this is discussed in contrast to the *nirmāṇakāya* mentioned in the subsequent passage; furthermore, it does not emphasize the preceding text. △ Second, the thorough realization of the primary retribution (*vipākaphala*).
Furthermore, there are two [aspects]. First, transforming the coarse into the subtle:
one reflects back upon the body born of one's parents as being like a single mote of dust blown into the empty space of the ten directions—sometimes present, sometimes absent.
The physical body that is produced belongs to the primary retribution (*vipāka*).

Because this causes one to lead forth the Dharma-body, which is void, expansive, and vast, encompassing even beyond the limits of empty space, the physical body appears small, insignificant, and merely provisional.

This is because it is perceived through comparison with its form. The empty space of the ten directions is a metaphor for the Dharma-body as the "shaper," while a mote of dust is a metaphor for that which is "shaped."
As for this physical body, whether it exists or perishes, its state is so vast and remote that it will soon dissolve into nothingness.
Indeed, that which was coarse and heavy in ordinary life becomes, at this point, so light and subtle as to be incapable of being a burden. △ Second, transforming the real into the void.
It is like a vast, deep ocean where a single bubble arises and vanishes; its origin and destination are nowhere to be found.
It is profoundly clear and unmoving; "vast" signifies the boundless. Regarding "its origin and destination are nowhere to be found": it arises from nowhere, and it vanishes to nowhere.
That which is normally solid and substantial becomes, at this moment, so light and empty that one does not even perceive its existence.

Furthermore, these two sections largely take up from the previous section on "Non-loss": that the physical body, extending outward to the mountains and rivers, and even all things, are objects within the True Mind;
as well as the section on "Non-differentiation," which states that all perceived appearances are like flowers in the sky.

This awakening is achieved through the intention that fundamentally nothing exists. Upon reaching this state, the principle regarding the body, objects, and adventitious defilements is finally fully realized.
One no longer identifies the five aggregates and the four elements as the self, no longer deludes oneself by taking them to be "mine," and no longer clings to them as being substantially real.
The realization of pervasiveness is thus complete. II. Awakening to Permanence.
He clearly knows for himself that he has attained his original, wondrous mind, which is eternally abiding and indestructible.
The meaning of this section is identical to the preceding one, yet the text here is much shorter because pervasiveness is itself the cause of eternal abiding;
furthermore, *nirvāṇa* also takes pervasiveness as its sense of "eternal. This is truly because the entire dharma-realm is, in its totality, [identical to]...
The mind is, for ten thousand kalpas, this Dharma-realm; for ten thousand kalpas, it is this mind. How could there ever be its extinction?

Therefore, there is no need for many words; the matter is settled by a single phrase. For one who knows clearly for themselves, it is as distinct as pointing at one's own palm—it is not realized through another.
Although the teaching relies upon the Buddha, the awakening comes from oneself; it is to see reality directly and arrive at self-confidence and self-realization.
The meaning of "consenting" (ken) refers to the fundamentally wondrous mind, which is one's original face. It is eternally pervasive throughout all things;

it is simply that, due to delusion, one does not recognize it oneself—it is not something newly acquired now. It is forever without beginning or end, abiding without coming or going. Because it is without beginning or end and without coming or going, it is never extinguished.
This also summarizes the aforementioned points of being unextinguished, non-disappearing, non-returning, and not being caused.
This awakening was not achieved through the principle of the "inherently pure and fundamental nature" (*viśuddha-prakṛti*) and so forth.

That the author of the sutra specifically details this passage between the Buddha’s discourse and the subsequent verses of praise is precisely to demonstrate the secret and profound essence of *śamatha*, so as to cause practitioners to fix their attention upon it.
Indeed, the entire effort of the preceding three fascicles is for the purpose of revealing this.

This is the essence of the most sublime and most secret contemplation. It is truly because sentient beings constantly transmigrate and those of the provisional vehicles do not reach the ultimate, all due to their failure to perceive this essence—just as one who gives birth does not see the child within the womb.

If a practitioner can, regarding what has been described here, maintain the oneness of mind and object, without erring in contemplation, then every thing and every situation will be clearly manifest before their eyes.
This is entirely the self-substance of the wondrous mind; it does not require even a hair’s breadth of effort.

Body and mind are from the beginning vast and pervasive throughout the world-systems of the sands. Provided one does not allow them to scatter, there has never been a case where such accumulation over years and months fails to open the mind.
One should know that fundamentally there is but a single essence. If one speaks of the nature of the true cause, it is the empty *tathāgatagarbha*.
Because there is nothing other than the single flavor of *tathatā*, if one briefly includes the "revealing cause" (*vyañjanahetu*), it is the secret contemplative observation of *śamatha*.
This is because one directly perceives one's own mind rather than engaging in conceptual mental cultivation (*manasikāra*).

If one does not further avoid the transgressions that would fill the heavens, then the direct pointing of the Mind from the West—the Treasury of the True Dharma Eye—is precisely this. However, that...
One enters directly into non-conceptuality (*avikalpa*). This is because one reaches this state of non-conceptuality through the conceptualization of skillful means (*upāya*);

their ultimate convergence is one. (Question: This appears to be the exhaustion of mental activity without remainder; however, *śamatha* is not yet concluded, and the latter two collections (*piṭaka*) have not been discussed. What is the intention there? Answer: It is subtle and secret contemplation.

Only here does one understand the meaning of the word "secret" (*mi*), for its essence belongs to the hidden and profound. Later, when both [methods] are employed to exhaust the most refined [aspects], it first belongs to the word "subtle" (*wei*). One should weigh and distinguish them accordingly. Having received the instruction, the awakening is complete. △ Second.
Praising and expressing gratitude for the arousal of the bodhicitta is divided into two parts. First, the verse of salutation and expression of thanks:
bowing to the Buddha with palms joined, having attained what was never before experienced, he spoke a verse in praise of the Buddha before the Tathāgata.
They attained what they had never before experienced. They said that from the past they had never attained such wondrous realizations, but only now have they finally attained them.

With the exception of those Bodhisattvas of the Perfect Teaching who have inherently possessed perfect understanding, all others—whether ordinary beings, followers of the Lesser Vehicle, or those of the provisional teachings—all attained what they had never before experienced.
Furthermore, this was likewise true for those at the initial stage of the Perfect Teaching, whether their understanding deepened further or they attained new realizations.
Second, the formal presentation of the verses. This also has two parts: first, the expression of praise and gratitude:
"O Wondrous, Profound, and All-Encompassing Sovereign of Immovability, The King of Śūraṅgama, rare in this world!
You have eliminated my inverted thoughts of billions of kalpas, And enabled me to attain the Dharmakāya without passing through the aeons of saṃgha."
The following section consists of Ānanda’s words. The first two lines are a praise. In the introductory verse, only the Buddha is praised;

because the Dharma is identical to the Buddha’s virtues, they are not mentioned together. However, in the commentary, the Buddha and the Dharma are still distinguished. The opening line praises the Buddha.孤山 (Gushan) says:
"Miao-zhan (Sublime and Profound)" praises the virtue of *prajñā* (wisdom) of the ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*); "Zongchi (Total Retention)" praises the conventional [truth].
The virtue of truth and liberation. Within the "Praise of Immovability," this refers to the virtue of the true dharma-body (*dharmakāya*).

Furthermore, because it is three yet one, it is called "wondrously profound" (*miaozhan*); because it is one yet three, it is called "total retention" (*zongchi*); and because it is neither three nor one, it is called "immovable."
The Venerable One is one of those who possess the ten titles. Because he has realized these three [truths], he is titled "World-Honored One" (Lokaguru).
One should praise only the Buddha’s three virtues, with the addition of the three truths merely to clarify them. The Middle Truth is itself the Ultimate Truth (Paramārtha-satya);
thus, when this one is added, the three aspects are complete. Furthermore, because this praise is inspired by the preceding revelation, the intent of the praise should be as follows:
This relates to the opening instruction. This is because that which was previously shown consists of the equal endowment of the living being and the Buddha;

it is only through one's own awakening that the virtues of the Buddha are subsequently perceived. First, within the section on the definitive nature of the faculties, there are ten instances of the primary instruction regarding the two views.
Manifesting the realization that the ocean of awakening is clear and pure, and the sky of nature is brilliantly radiant, vast and boundless—this is precisely the *prajñā* virtue of the Buddha.
Because it is based on this, he praises it as "wondrously profound. Next, within the section on synthesizing the four categories, all myriad phenomena are harmoniously integrated;
through the unfolding of both the general and the particular, one realizes that all forms are the nature and all things are the One Mind, appearing in their full, manifold splendor.
This is fully complete; it is precisely the virtue of the Buddha’s liberation. It is based on this that he praises it as *dhāraṇī*.
Later, within the "Perfect Manifestation of the Seven Great Elements," the great nature of these elements is unified and revealed as equally pervasive and all-encompassing.

One awakens to the fact that every sense organ and every object is entirely filled with the Dharma-realm, such that none undergo birth or extinction, and none come or go; they are nonetheless interpenetrating in their very presence—this is the Buddha’s Dharmakāya.

This is virtue (*guṇa*). Because it is based on this, he praises it as "immovable" (*acala*). The three and the one interact with each other, and the word "Venerable" (*bhaṭṭāraka*) is as explained previously.

However, these three virtues are that which is realized, while the "Venerable" is the person who realizes them. Next, the four characters praise the Dharma-Buddha. This refers to what was stated previously:
"There is a samādhi named Great Buddha-Crown Śūraṅgama King. This is it. In reality, it is now...
"Ultimately firm and in accord" is the title by which the King presides over all dharmas.

The three characters "rare in the world" offer a double praise for the fact that both the Buddha and the Dharma are difficult to encounter. For this reason, it is inherently difficult for a Buddha to appear in this Sahā world.
Even if he were to appear in the world, it would be difficult to preach this Dharma; it is like the *udumbara* flower, appearing but for a brief moment.

The final two phrases express gratitude. The preceding phrase expresses gratitude for the destruction of delusion. "Perverted conceptions" refers to the discriminative attachments to self and phenomena (*ātman* and *dharma*).
For example, it is like grasping at the discrimination of sense-objects as the characteristic of the mind, or reckoning the five aggregates and the four great elements [as the self].
One takes this to be the characteristic of the body; the deluded mind considers itself to be within the physical form. One identifies external objects as oneself and mistakes oneself for an object.
Regarding the myriad phenomena of body and mind, one claims they each possess their own substantial essence and characteristics.

All doubts concerning the four great elements, their harmonious combination, causes, conditions, and so forth—matters that have confused one for billions of kalpas—are now truly and simultaneously dissolved. (The following verse:)

Xie Xianzhen. Regarding "asaṃkhyeya" (asāṃkhya), as Gushan cites in the *Abhidharma-mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra*, one practices the six pāramitās for three asaṃkhyeya kalpas and plants the causes for the marks and signs (*lakṣaṇa-vyañjana*) during one hundred kalpas;
only then does one attain the fivefold dharma-body (*pañca-dharma-kāya*). Furthermore, as the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi* states:
"Before the stages [of the bhūmis], one passes through one asaṃkhyeya; from the first bhūmi to the seventh bhūmi, one completes two asaṃkhyeyas."

"A *kalpa* [of practice] spans from the eighth stage up to Equal Enlightenment (*samyak-saṃbodhi*); these constitute the three *asaṃkhyeya-kalpas*. Only thereafter does one attain the ultimate *dharmakāya*.

Now, it is said that one does not pass through [these stages], because the purport of the teaching is fundamentally different. One need only clarify the purport of the teaching, and there will naturally be no cause for doubt.
The old commentaries failed to distinguish the purport of the teaching, giving rise to groundless suspicions and resulting in a state of confusion and lack of certainty. I shall now resolve this."

However, there are two causes and conditions for why those of the past fell into confusion: first, their adherence to the *Abhidharma-mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra*’s interpretation of the provisional teachings on consciousness-only as being incomplete;
second, their obstruction by the text concerning the vows to eliminate delusions below and the realization of the two fruits.
Now, let us clarify this through the principles of the Perfect and Sudden Teaching (*yuantun jiaozhi*). Then the two delusions will naturally resolve themselves. This is truly because of this sutra.

For the most part, one ultimately enters the Perfect and Sudden (yuantun). According to the purport of the Sudden Teaching, prior to awakening, the Dharmakāya is inherently and spontaneously perfected.

With a single thought of turning the light back upon itself, one immediately becomes identical to what was originally attained. As it is said: "Simply by being free from delusive conditions, one is a Buddha of Suchness (tathatā).

In this state, there is no longer any discussion of realization versus non-realization, or accomplishment versus non-accomplishment. How could this be compared to the provisional and gradual teachings?
...its teaching, one must necessarily pass through *asaṃkhyeya-kalpas* before attaining it.
If you cling to that [teaching] while disbelieving this, it is like clinging to the slowness of a runner and disbelieving the speed of a flyer. How deeply you are stuck to the old strings!
Furthermore, if we examine the purport of the Perfect Teaching (*yuanjiao*), then sequential practice (*xingbu*) does not obstruct perfect interfusion (*yuanrong*); thus, although one has not yet—
Furthermore, when the cessation of delusions is perfected, there is no hindrance to fully attaining the Dharmakāya and being entirely the Buddha.
As previously demonstrated, one who is deluded regarding the mind within the physical body is termed "inverted in nature.
When, later on, one awakens and perceives the mind beyond the great void, would this not be called "Perfectly All-Knowing" (Samyaksaṃbuddha)? This Perfectly All-Knowing One is...

One attains the Dharma-body upon achieving perfect enlightenment. Thus, to cling to the present fruit while refusing to grant that Ānanda has attained the Dharma-body is a profound failure to grasp the essential meaning.

Furthermore, because perfect interfusion does not obstruct sequential progression, although one has fully attained the Dharma-body, it does not preclude further eliminating subtle delusions, further traversing the various fruits, and further becoming the ultimate Jewel King.
The latter part of this sutra states: "In principle, there is sudden awakening; through awakening, all is simultaneously extinguished.
In phenomena, there is no sudden elimination; they are exhausted through gradual stages. This may serve as clear evidence.

Thus, even if one subsequently passes through further *asaṃkhyeya-kalpas* to achieve the ultimate fruit of Buddhahood, it will not at all obstruct the attainment of the Dharma-body prior to these [gradual stages]. The two are entirely without mutual hindrance.
How much more so for the cultivation following the realization of the Perfect and Sudden (yuantun) teaching, wherein every thought-moment is the Buddha.
Although one may advance to sever the pervasive delusions (tonghuo), this still exceeds those who cultivate through provisional and gradual means by a factor of many eons per day.

Upon reaching the stage of abiding (zhouhou) and severing the distinct delusions (biehuo), there are those who attain the fruit of the Perfect teaching after a single lifetime, whereas others require vast eons. Thus, even if one were to say that [the gradualist] will not [attain it] again hereafter—

Even throughout incalculable eons (*asaṃkhyeya-kalpa*), there is likewise no obstruction. If one further grasps the profound principle that extension and brevity are simultaneous, then all the more can one not be constrained by length or shortness.
Question: If this is so, are Ānanda, Sudhana, and the Dragon Girl identical?
Answer: They are not entirely identical. This is because, although for a person of perfect enlightenment (*yuanren*) cause and effect are not strictly sequential, they nevertheless...
There is a distinction between the initial mind and the ultimate realization. If one discusses the initial mind, there is no difference;

yet when viewed from the perspective of ultimate realization, delusions vary in depth and faculties differ in sharpness or dullness. Because the Dragon Girl’s delusions were exhausted, her merit was perfected in a mere snap of the fingers;
because Sudhana possessed sharp faculties, he accomplished his task in a single lifetime. Thus, the initial mind and the ultimate realization are suddenly equalized. Now, within this assembly:

It is likely that there were not just these two individuals; however, Ānanda’s instruction was directed toward a specific class of practitioners—those of middling faculties who still possessed afflictions.
Furthermore, they merely resolved their minds in the same manner as those two, yet their previous attainment of the first fruit (srotāpanna) remained entirely unchanged.
Only after they aspired to become a "Jewel King" (a Buddha) and sought to ascend to supreme enlightenment did they finally seek [further progress].

This refers merely to the ultimate realization of those two types of individuals. However, because the sages value the initial resolve above all else, the fact that one attains the Dharmakāya in this very life carries profound significance.
As the Sūtra says: "The initial resolve and the ultimate realization are not different; yet between these two states of mind, the former is more difficult.
From this, it can be seen that whether one speaks of realized awakening (*zhèngwù*) or intellectual understanding (*jiěwù*), both equally attain the inherently existing Dharmakāya.
This is by no means the basis for making such a distinction. △ Second, the arousal of the mind (*cittotpāda*). This also has two parts. First, the actual arousal of the great mind.
This also has two parts. First, the general vow to repay kindness.
May I now attain the fruit and become a Treasure King, returning to deliver as many beings as there are sands in the Ganges.
Taking this profound resolve to serve every dust mote of a buddha-field—this is what is called repaying the Buddha’s kindness.

This is because the very attainment of the Dharma-body previously was already the initial resolve; now, subsequent to that awakening, one formulates the great vow in order to reach ultimate fulfillment.

Regarding the first two lines: the former primarily concerns self-benefit through the upward-seeking of the Buddha-realm, while the latter concerns benefiting others through the downward-saving of sentient beings.
Wēnlíng identifies the first line as the mind of wisdom and the second line as the mind of compassion.
The four characters at the end [of each vow] combine two minds and consolidate them into the "profound mind" (shinjin); of this there is no room for dispute.
Yet Gushan [Zhiyuan] interprets the first phrase as the vow to accomplish the Buddha-way and the second phrase as the vow to deliver sentient beings, even though the literal meaning is quite evident.
To claim that this subsumes the other two vows would seem to be a misconception. Now, the first phrase shall be taken to subsume the vow to sever afflictions (*kleśa*);
for it is only by completely severing all afflictions that one reaches the ultimate path of Buddhahood. The second phrase shall be taken to subsume the vow to study the dharma-gates (*dharmamukha*);

for it is only by thoroughly mastering the dharma-gates that one can extensively deliver sentient beings. The two characters "vow" (*yuan*) and "now" (*jin*) shall penetrate both [phrases] simultaneously.

"Descending to achieve Buddhahood and deliver sentient beings": contemplating the character "now" (jin) already implies the aspiration that one will soon achieve it without waiting for [the end of] kalpas (*asaṃkhyeya-kalpa*).
"Attaining the fruit" means attaining ultimate *bodhi*. "Jewel King" (*ratnarāja*) is also like the terminology in Confucian texts, where rank is referred to as a "great treasure.
"Returning to deliver" means that one does not merely vow to achieve Buddhahood oneself, but further vows to return and deliver others.

"Sentient beings" does not mean that one waits until after their accomplishment before delivering them. To claim that "serving the Buddha and delivering sentient beings" encompasses both [the adornment of lands and the service of the Buddha] while "delivering sentient beings" belongs exclusively to the latter is likely incorrect.

It would be more appropriate to explain this by means of "adorned buddha-lands," as this accords well with the two meanings of "dust-motes" (lands) and "buddhas" (service), without losing either sense.
Regarding "repaying the Buddha's grace," it refers to the simultaneous application of the two kinds of profound resolve (*adhyāśaya*) to adorn all things.
To the Buddha-land. This is to repay the Buddha’s subtle and wondrous grace of instruction. △ Second, specifically seeking realization and elimination.
This is further divided into two parts. First, seeking realization in the salvation of sentient beings.
I prostrate and request that the World-Honored One bear witness: I vow to enter first into this world of the five turbidities;
until not a single sentient being has attained Buddhahood, I shall never take *nirvāṇa* here.
I request that you provide proof; I pray that you will grant your majestic spiritual power so that [this vow] shall never deviate from its original aspiration.

The five turbidities (*pañca-kaṣāya*)—namely, the turbidity of the eon, the turbidity of views, the turbidity of afflictions, the turbidity of sentient beings, and the turbidity of life—are not the same as those described later in this sutra.
Their meaning refers specifically to one category within the Sahā world. Within this defiled realm, [a lifespan of] one hundred years...
Henceforth, during the age of the turbid and evil world, when all manner of evils flourish and beings are stubborn and difficult to transform—there are two preliminary intentions.
First, regarding the lands: although it is intended that one shall enter all lands as numerous as motes of dust, one must first enter those of the five turbidities.
This is because compassionate rescue prioritizes those whose suffering and hardship are most profound, just as King Wen of Zhou prioritized the widows and orphans. This is the aspect of compassion.

This is the mind [of resolve]. Second, regarding others: because those in the five turbidities are timid about entering [the path], one vows to be courageous in entering first, leading the multitude by example;
this is the mind of valor. *Nirvāṇa*—here translated as "extinction" (*mièdù*)—is an alternative name for *nirvāṇa*.
As the Master [Hui]ze cited two types, both should be embraced: first, not taking the solitary *nirvāṇa* of the two vehicles.
Second, not taking up the parinirvāṇa of the Buddhas. This is as Kṣitigarbha said: "Only when all sentient beings have been delivered will I realize bodhi.
This is the vast mind. This desire to deliver all sentient beings implicitly requires the vow to study the Dharma-gates.
△ Second, seeking the removal [of obstacles] upon attaining Buddhahood.
O Great Hero, of Great Power and Great Compassion, I pray that you will further examine and eliminate my subtle delusions,
so that I may quickly ascend to unsurpassed enlightenment and sit at the site of awakening throughout the worlds of the ten directions.

One who can shatter the solid core of sentient beings' delusions is called Mahāvīra (the Great Hero). One who can uproot the deep-seated roots of sentient beings' delusions is called Mahābala (the Great Powerful One).
To ultimately bestow upon sentient beings the joy of the two kinds of adornment (*dvividha-saṃbhāra*) is called Mahāmaitrī (Great Loving-kindness).

To ultimately uproot from sentient beings the suffering of the two kinds of death (*dvimaraṇa*) is called Mahākaruṇā (Great Compassion). These terms denote aspiration and thorough investigation regarding subtle delusions.

This refers to the *citta-saṃkleśas* as numerous as the sands of the Ganges as well as fundamental ignorance (*mūla-avidyā*). As for the separate afflictions (*pṛthag-kleśa*), it is as answered below to Pūrṇamaitrāyaṇīputra.

If we consider the case of Ānanda and his kind, the *saṃyojana-kleśas* (afflictions to be abandoned through cultivation) that he seeks to eliminate should also be included therein. This concludes the eighth fascicle of the *Sutra on the Binding of Karmic Retribution*.
Ānanda attained realization, severing the six grades of subtle afflictions of the mind within the three realms. He offered his thanks, saying:
"The Tathāgata has skillfully opened for sentient beings the subtle, sunken delusions; this is clear proof.
Yet, those who seek to eliminate these rarefied [afflictions] must pray that the Buddha, with his Great Heroic Power, applies it to shatter their substance and uproot them.

The character "zǎo" (早) has the same meaning as "jīn" (今). Those who ascend to unsurpassed enlightenment seek the Buddha so that he may empower them with great compassion (*mahākaruṇā*) until the two deaths are exhausted and the ultimate *dharmakāya* is realized.

Those who sit at the site of enlightenment (*bodhimaṇḍa*) seek the Buddha so that he may empower them with great kindness (*mahāmaitrī*) until the two adornments are fulfilled and they manifest upon the seat to preach the Dharma;
this is precisely the saving of sentient beings subsequent to fruition. This contemplation seeks to eliminate the subtle [defilements].
The delusions are manifest; this includes the vow to sever all afflictions (*kleśa*). The formal arousal of the Great Mind is now complete. II.
Concluding with Profound Vows:
"Though the nature of Śūnyatā may perish, The heart of Śakraka shall never waver."
Wenling says: *Śūnyatā* (Śunyata) is translated here as "emptiness" (*kōng*). *Śakala* (Shageluo) is translated as "solid" (*jiāngù*).
This means that while emptiness has no substance and can thus be extinguished, my mind is solid and shall never waver or turn back. "To waver and turn back" is synonymous with "to retreat.
This generally summarizes the preceding [sections on] seeking above and transforming below, making a profound vow for the mind: even if empty space were to come to an end...

My vow is inexhaustible. From the entry into the True Teaching (Zhengzong) up to this present exposition of the Dharma, it constitutes one complete cycle, titled "The Cycle of Destroying Delusion to Reveal Reality.
This first major section, which eliminates inverted conceptions and explains the empty *tathāgatagarbha*, is now concluded.

△ Second, examining and eliminating subtle afflictions, the latter two Tathāgatagarbhas are explained.
This also takes the verse from the end of the third fascicle on Ānanda’s resolve as its basis, which says: "I hope to further examine and eliminate subtle afflictions.

This is because what is discussed below constitutes the deep source from which delusion arises and the obscure root that forms obstructions. The latter two garbhas refer to the *Amogha-garbha* (the Non-empty Treasury).
It is with the treasury of emptiness and non-emptiness. Regarding the explanation of the Three Treasuries (Tripiṭaka) by ancient masters, there are two senses.
First, the *Commentary on the Perfect Enlightenment Sūtra* (Yuánjué shū) takes concealment, containment, and production as the three.

Second, the *Commentary on the Avataṃsaka Sūtra* (Huáyán shū) explains the three treasuries of emptiness and so forth in accordance with the sequence of the three greatnesses: essence, characteristic, and function. The present [text] seems to follow the latter sense, yet it is also slightly different from it. Above.

The *Kongzang* (Treasury of Emptiness) is entirely identical [to this]. As for the True Reality revealed therein, it is precisely the Greatness of Essence (*tǐdà*). When combined with the following two treasuries, their intended meaning differs.
This is because [the present section] explains the three treasuries—Emptiness and so forth—by means of the essence and function (*tǐyòng*), whether taken individually or as a pair;

yet, when the characteristics (*xiàng*) are integrated within the function, there is likewise no deficiency. This will become even clearer in the subsequent topical analysis (*fēnkē*). It is divided into two parts: first, the question and answer.
The refutation and examination of the various delusions is further divided into two parts. First, Pūrṇamaitrāyaṇīputra follows up on the preceding discussion to raise two doubts.

This request by Pūrṇa serves to indicate that the delusions discussed below are subtle and their principles profound; thus, those in the deep stage of the Aśaikṣas should all investigate them with thorough attention.
This is not spoken solely for those in training (*śaikṣa*). Therefore, [the text] now manifests two layers of excellence that surpass the previous [teaching] suited to the occasion.

First, the exhaustion of the delusions of the four abodes (*catur-vāsa-kleśa*) surpasses the previous state where such delusions were not yet exhausted. Second, the ability to preach through the four analytical knowledges (*catasraḥ pratisaṃvidah*) surpasses the previous state of merely being able to memorize [the teachings].

Furthermore, there are two parts: first, a general account of those who have doubts; second, a praise of the wondrous instruction. Within the latter, there are again two parts: first, the praise of the marvelous demonstration.
At that time, Pūrṇamaitrāyaṇīputra, rising from his seat in the midst of the great assembly, bared his right shoulder, knelt with his right knee on the ground,
joined his palms in reverent salutation, and addressed the Buddha, saying: "O World-Honored One of Great Majestic Virtue,
you have skillfully expounded for the sake of sentient beings the Tathāgata’s ultimate truth."
The courage to subdue [afflictions] is called "majesty" (wei); the compassion that gathers [beings] is called "virtue" (de).

To accord with the ultimate principle above and accord with inferior capacities below is called "skillful means" (shàn wéi). In its exposition, it discusses the One Truth while the Three Truths are fully contained within it;
moreover, in every truth and every phrase, it transcends the views of the Lesser Vehicle. Therefore, it is titled the Tathāgata’s Ultimate Truth (paramārtha-satya). △ Second.
He then raised his doubt, which is twofold: first, his own personal doubt, which is further divided into two parts. First, he recounts that he had not heard this before:
"The World-Honored One has always ranked me as the foremost among those who preach the Dharma; yet now I hear the subtle and wondrous sound of the Tathāgata’s Dharma."
It is like a deaf person listening for the sound of a mosquito from more than a hundred paces away; since they cannot see it at all, how could they possibly hear it?

Because he has attained a portion of the Tathāgata’s most supreme fourfold eloquence, he is foremost in preaching the Dharma. Regarding the phrase "the sound of the Dharma," it should be supplemented below as follows:
reflecting back upon the past, one then clearly recounts former events. The metaphor states that even when a deaf person is close to a mosquito, they do not hear it.
How much more so at a distance of a hundred paces! Even a loud voice at a hundred paces may not necessarily be heard, let alone the sound of mosquitoes and gnats.

This is an extreme description of how, since time immemorial, even those who have realized the stage of *aśaikṣa* (no-more-learning) and are skilled in preaching the Dharma have never, until now, heard this wondrous Dharma.
It does not mean that those currently in the assembly are like deaf people; rather, it means they have failed to hear it from the past until now. △ Second, seeking to sever delusions in the present.
Although the Buddha has now proclaimed and clarified that "I have eliminated delusion," I still have not yet fully understood this meaning to the point of reaching a ground free from doubt.

This is because, in my ordinary state, I was deluded into thinking that mountains, rivers, and so forth exist as real entities external to the mind; yet now, through the Buddha’s preceding discourse, it is revealed that these are nothing but the mind itself.

Furthermore, I am confused by the fact that the natures of the five great elements were previously described as mutually incomplete and deficient, whereas the preceding text has clarified that each of them is [complete].

"Universal" means causing them to eliminate these two delusions. This meaning—that both "original emptiness" and "universality" ultimately result in freedom from delusion—is seen in the detailed exposition below.
△ Second, the doubts of the assembly, which is further divided into two parts.
First, the Śaikṣas clarify their residual outflows.
"World-Honored One, as for those such as Ānanda, although they have attained awakening, their habitual outflows (*āsrava*) have not yet been eliminated.
The term "those such as" (*peyāla*) fully encompasses all those still in training (*śaikṣa*), including the *anāgāmin*.

"Attained awakening" refers to having previously received the Buddha’s sublime instruction, whereby they suddenly forgot the conceptualization of clinging to dharmas (*dharmagrāha-vikalpa*), and thus a resolute understanding (*adhimukti*) of the emptiness of dharmas manifested before them. Their "habitual outflows," however—
As for "not yet eliminated," it means that within that very self-grasping, the innate, subtle afflictions remain unbroken.
This is because profound awakening and shallow realization do not obstruct one another; however, as long as habitual outflows persist, both types of grasping will continue to arise deeply.
They should also be completely uprooted and removed. △ Second, those beyond training express their doubts and regrets:

Yet one still lingers in doubt and regret regarding the various outflows (*āsrava*).

These outflows consist of the outflow of desire (*kāma-āsrava*), the outflow of existence (*bhava-āsrava*), and the outflow of ignorance (*avidyā-āsrava*) within the realms. When these outflows are exhausted, one is no longer born within the three realms.

This passage concludes the account of the former realization, wherein the emptiness of self (*pudgala-nairātmya*) has been attained; it now reveals that what is being doubted below is the subtle clinging to phenomena (*dharma-grāha*). This is contrasted with [the previous state].
Learning can give rise to present doubt and also serves to plant its seeds for others. "Now, hearing" below correctly clarifies what has not yet been understood; "yū" (紆) means entanglement.
Doubt (*vicikitsā*) and regret (*kaukṛtya*) are two mental factors (*caitta*). Doubt belongs to the root afflictions (*mūlakleśa*), while regret belongs to the indeterminate factors (*aniyata*).

Among the three types of doubt—concerning self, others, and phenomena—it belongs exclusively to doubt regarding phenomena. Among the two types of regret—concerning the wholesome and the unwholesome—it belongs exclusively to regret.

"Evil! [This] refers to his regret for previously practicing the Lesser Vehicle (Hīnayāna) in a confused manner. Having already repented for what he practiced in the past, he still harbors doubts regarding what he has newly heard;

By stating that these are all the *tathāgatagarbha*, it reveals that they are precisely the mind; by stating that they are "pure and originally thus," it reveals that they are fundamentally empty.

Furthermore, although the phrase "pure and originally thus" appears within the sections on the seven elements (*dhātus*), the intent applies only to the first four sections, because of that one [principle].
First, by resolving delusion, one reveals the fundamental purity; for each [delusive phenomenon] returns to the truth, revealing it as the very treasury-mind (ālayavijñāna).
△ Second, the actual raising of the doubt:
How is it that the mountains, rivers, the great earth, and all conditioned phenomena suddenly arise, flowing in succession, ending and beginning again?
This doubt is twofold: first, the sudden arising of doubt at its beginning; second, the continuity of doubt at its end.
What is it, and by what causes and conditions does it arise? If one reads "what" repeatedly over the preceding sequence, these two doubts will become manifest of themselves.
From the mountains, rivers, and the great earth—that is, the world—including all conditioned phenomena as well as the karmic fruits of sentient beings, up to this point, there is doubt.

Regarding the phrase "suddenly arising at the beginning," the intention is as follows: since the fundamental mind (*cittaprakṛti*) is originally empty, why did the world, sentient beings, and karmic fruits suddenly arise at the very outset?
As for the "successive flow," this includes the aforementioned three—namely, the world and so forth—ending and beginning again;
this is the sense of continuity. These two phrases represent the aspect of continuity at the conclusion of the doubt. This is the intended meaning.
That is to say: since the *ālayavijñāna* (the storehouse consciousness) is fundamentally empty, even if it were to suddenly arise, it should likewise suddenly perish.

For what reason, then, does it continue to flow and evolve through vast eons without interruption? This question seeks from the Buddha a detailed explanation of its initial arising and subsequent continuity;
it is not merely a strange inquiry as to why it should not have arisen. Therefore, the Buddha subsequently provides answers regarding both the beginning and the end.
The details thereof. △ Second, the doubt regarding the five great elements being perfectly interfused. This also has two parts. First, restating the Buddha’s words:

Excellent.
Today, the Tathāgata has universally proclaimed for this assembly the true ultimate nature within the ultimate.

The Buddha’s statement that he does so "universally" further demonstrates the vastness of his compassion. Regarding the "ultimate within the ultimate," there are four [categories] according to the Dharma-lakṣaṇa school.

The aggregates (*skandha*), bases (*āyatana*), and elements (*dhātu*) constitute the ultimate truth of the world (*loka-paramārtha*). The Four Noble Truths constitute the ultimate truth of principle (*yukti-paramārtha*).

The true suchness (*tathatā*) of the two kinds of emptiness constitutes the ultimate truth of realization (*adhigama-paramārtha*). The single true *dharmadhātu* constitutes the ultimate truth of the ultimate (*paramārtha-paramārtha*). These differ only in that they do not integrate the conventional and the ultimate;
however, there is no difference in the ultimate truth established by the nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*). This is based on the Buddha’s later response regarding the arising of all phenomena.

The continuity [of this teaching] arises from the two types of awakening inherent in the nature. The answer is that the perfect fusion of the five great elements returns to the One Mind and the Threefold Treasury (Tripitaka), appearing clearly as the single True Dharma-realm. △ Second, showing the capacities of those for whom it is intended.

This causes those within your assembly who are śrāvakas fixed in their nature, as well as all those arhats and others who have not yet attained the two kinds of emptiness but have turned toward the Mahāyāna—

these are singled out from among the general multitude as the primary audience, while the phrase "and others" includes the remaining groups; since they are all of the four fruits of arhatship, they are described as "fixed."

"Directing toward the Supreme Vehicle" means directing [the mind] toward the definitive Mahāyāna. If one had already directed [the mind] toward the Supreme Vehicle prior to the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*, what further provisional [teachings] would there be to be opened?
Such reasoning is untenable; "etc. refers to those still in training (*śaikṣa*) as well as the multitudes of humans and devas.
△ Third, showing the benefits obtained.
All have attained the ground of the single vehicle’s quiescent cessation, the true *āraṇya*, the locus of correct practice.

The "single vehicle" is the one Buddha-vehicle; it is the great white ox-cart of the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka*. The "ground of quiescent cessation" is the essence of the fruit of original enlightenment (*prakṛti-bodhi*);
therein, the myriad delusions are fundamentally empty and the one reality is pure—this is what is referred to below as "only the wondrous."
The luminous clarity of awakening perfectly illumines the Dharma-realm; to speak in the ultimate sense, this is precisely the state of the perfect fusion of the Three Baskets (Tripitaka).
The Sanskrit term *araṇya* is also called *āraṇya*, which translates as "free from clamor and confusion.

Any place in the world suitable for quiet cultivation may be designated by this name. However, such places merely possess a quiet environment, which is provisional and not the true site of cessation (*śamatha*).
This is the original mind, fundamentally still, which has no connection with external objects; this is true detachment from clamor and confusion.
What the ancients meant by "placing it in one spot and sitting quietly for a moment" refers precisely to this. To practice while abiding in this state is like fashioning vessels from gold:
every vessel is gold. When the fruit arises based on the cause, every cause is the fruit. This is the direct, correct cause for attaining Buddhahood—nothing else is more direct.
Therefore, this is called the locus of correct practice; to depart from this is erroneous cultivation. △ Fourth, the exhortation to listen and permission to speak:

Within the gate of arising and ceasing (*utpāda-nirodha-mukha*), two meanings are distinguished: first, the meaning of awakening (*bodhi*); second, the meaning of non-awakening (*abodhi*).

Awakening is the true reality (*tattva*) upon which [all things] depend; non-awakening is the ignorance (*avidyā*) that depends [upon it]. Therefore, it is said that non-awakening exists based on fundamental awakening (*mūla-bodhi*).

Now, the text of the response fully accords with the intent of the treatise; thus, we know that this section refers to that very fundamental awakening which serves as the basis. Furthermore, there are two [aspects]: first, the Buddha...
He raised a question based on what has been commonly taught:
"Have you not always heard the Tathāgata proclaim that the nature of awakening is wondrously luminous, and that fundamental awakening is luminously wondrous?
When the Tathāgata speaks thus, he mostly expounds this true meaning for the sake of bodhisattvas; yet those śrāvakas present in the assembly have also universally [heard it]."
"Awakening through hearing" (wen-zhi) refers to the nature-awakening (*xing-jue*) and the original awakening (*ben-jue*), which manifest the meaning of awakening as the basis (*yi*).

As for the distinct designations of "nature" (*xing*) and "original" (*ben*), each has its own specific referent: "nature" expresses the single true reality-body (*tattva-dharmakāya*) that has not yet entered into phenomenal activity (*shiyong*);

thus, those who previously explained this in terms of the three truths did not realize that it lacks the conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*). "Original" (*ben*) expresses what is naturally and inherently possessed, regardless of whether it is produced through cultivation.
Those who previously attempted to explain this through the three contemplations failed to realize that it is not a matter of deliberate effort.

"Wondrous stillness" is luminous illumination; when wondrous and luminous, it is illumination within stillness; when luminous and wondrous, it is stillness within illumination. These two awakenings mutually reflect one another, revealing a state of perfect fusion.

Although this luminosity appears to be a function, it is nonetheless the illuminating function inherent within the essence, rather than a function involving engagement with external phenomena. The Tathāgata brought this forth...

Ignorance (*avidyā*) precedes all phenomena; it belongs to the very period prior to the kalpa of emptiness. Within this single segment of ultimate truth, there is only the mutual fusion of stillness and illumination;
how could there be any functional activity? To cite this alone serves two purposes: first, to show that ignorance and the myriad phenomena have no basis apart from this;
second, to show that stillness and illumination are complete in themselves and do not depend on false illumination. △ Second, Pūrṇa answers by means of the "Constant."
Pūrṇa replied, "Indeed, World-Honored One. I have often heard the Buddha proclaim this meaning.

The Buddha said: "When you refer to 'awakened clarity' (*jue-ming*), does this mean that the nature itself is luminous and is thus called 'awakening,' or does it mean that awakening is not inherently luminous and is therefore termed 'luminous awakening'?
This intent of the inquiry follows from the two preceding phrases concerning 'nature' and 'awakening'; thus, the word 'awakening' (*jue*) in this opening sentence refers to—"

The "awakening" (*jue*) in "nature-awakening" (*xing-jue*) and "original awakening" (*ben-jue*) refers to awakening; the "clarity" (*ming*) in "wondrous clarity" (*miao-ming*) and "clear wondrousness" (*ming-miao*) refers to clarity.

However, the character "wondrous" (*miao*) is not taken, and only the character "clarity" (*ming*) is used because there are two types of clarity—true and false—and it is the false clarity alone that constitutes the substance of great delusion.
When you refer to "awakened clarity" (*jue-ming*), you are likely speaking of the fact that when you preach the Dharma, you must always proclaim it.
This is an exegesis. Furthermore, the following section uses a pair of terms to pose a critical inquiry. The intent of the question is as follows:
Is it that the nature is inherently luminous, such that it is simply termed "awakening" (*jue*) and this already encompasses the meaning of "luminosity"?

Or is it that awakening is originally not luminous, necessitating the addition of luminosity to awakening so that they are termed together as "luminous-awakening" (*mingjue*)? For if it were simply termed "awakening," it would not require the false [duality].
"Clarity" refers to true awakening (*samyag-bodhi*). To refer to both as "clarity-awakening" while striving for a false and deluded clarity is what constitutes deluded awakening.

By posing these paired questions, [the Buddha] intends to lead Pūrṇa Maitrāyaṇīputra to personally determine what to adopt and what to reject. This is entirely similar to questioning Ānanda about where his mind resides and what constitutes his mind;
in both cases, the intent is to force him to expose what he has long mistakenly identified and then to refute it.
This refutes it. △ Second, Pūrṇa alone grasps at delusion.

This answer is as follows: If one were to call something "awakening" (jue) even without the clarity of illumination, then it would be a hollow name for awakening;

This is because, while the words seem to exclude a true awakening that lacks illumination, the underlying intent actually takes up a false awakening that possesses illumination. These two characters, "not illuminating" (buming), [reveal this].
This differs from what was stated above. The former was a provisional statement asserting that the source of awakening is not inherently luminous;

"If this manifestation is not the mind, then I am without a mind, identical to wood and stone. In both cases, one is compelled by the Buddha's interrogation to confront the habitual delusions and attachments one previously held.

This is because they do not perceive their own error. However, the six sense bases grasped by Ānanda are coarse consciousness, whereas that which Maitreya is deluded about is fundamental ignorance (*mūla-avidyā*).
Thus, the coarse and the subtle, the shallow and the deep, are utterly distinct. △ Second, the refutation as being ignorance.
The Buddha said: "If there is nothing that is illuminated, then there is no awareness of ignorance. That which has an object is not true awareness; that which lacks an object is not ignorance.
Furthermore, this ignorance is not the nature of the profoundly clear and luminous awareness."
The first two lines entirely quote Pūrṇa’s words: "If there is nothing that is enlightened" means that this very state is not enlightened;

As for what is clarified: it is the lack of clarity regarding awakening; one fears almost exclusively that there is no clarity regarding awakening, and thus insists on adding clarity to awakening.
Yet one does not realize that once this "addition" is applied, both meanings—awakening and clarity—are simultaneously lost. This is truly because:
The added clarity exists outside the essence; it is not originally possessed by the essence. It arises at times and ceases at others, existing at certain moments and being absent at others.

Thus, with respect to the arising of the mind, when there is something clarified, that clarity is not awakening, because the added clarity is superimposed upon awakening and is not inherently present within the essence of awakening.
With respect to the forgetting of the mind, when there is nothing clarified, awakening is not clarity, because from the beginning... [it has never been so].

This is because you have failed to realize that the essence of awakening is fundamentally luminous. This is merely what is meant by the statement that both having thoughts and being without thoughts equally lead to delusion and confusion.
Since it is neither awakening nor luminosity, both meanings are lost, and you have fallen entirely into ignorance (*avidyā*).
How could you take this ignorance to be the nature of your own awakening’s profound clarity? Furthermore, ignorance is not the same as the profound clarity of awakening.
As for "nature": ignorance is precisely non-awakening; it is merely turbid and dark, so how could it possess the quality of profound clarity?
Thus, although at the outset you feared only losing your luminous awakening, in the end you have come to lose your true nature entirely.
It has fallen entirely into ignorance. △ Third, concluding the formation of the root of delusion:
