(Question: All other sutras state that delusion is beginningless; why does this sutra alone speak of a beginning and an end? Answer: Although it is fundamentally beginningless, there is no impediment to speaking of the manifestation of a beginning.

To speak emphatically of a beginning does not contradict the principle of beginninglessness. Indeed, the Buddha’s teachings are of two kinds: first, provisional establishment (*prajñapti*), and second, the description of reality (*tattva*). If one speaks without provisional establishment, then reality will not be revealed; if one speaks without describing reality, then the provisional will lack ultimate significance.

For example, although there is originally no cultivation or realization, one speaks of cultivation and realization without any obstruction. This is all the more so since the sutras and treatises all state that "at the very first moment, the mind moved through non-awakening," and so forth.)
This is stated according to the meaning of provisional designation; thus, there is no contradiction in this initial exposition. Furthermore, there are two [categories]: first, the "initially subtle.

This section corresponds to the "three subtleties" of the treatise (*śāstra*). However, the method of the chapters differs: here, they are divided into two categories simply by correlating afflictions (*kleśa*) with their objects.

This is because noble ones (*ārya*) comprehend objects through wisdom (*jñāna*), whereas ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*) perceive objects through afflictions; both arise in continuous succession. Now, regarding this...
Generally speaking, because delusion and its objects correspond to one another, they are divided into two. First is subtle delusion:
awakening is not what is illuminated; based on illumination, an object is established. Once that object has been falsely established, your false subjectivity arises.

This refers only to the first two of the three subtle states; the third is still lacking. According to the ancient interpretation, the three subtle states encompass the entirety of the inversion of the evolving consciousness and its manifestations.

According to the present interpretation, the sequence consists only of the two aspects of karma and evolution. The first two phrases refer to the aspect of karma (*karmalakṣaṇa*) and the self-witnessing division (*svasaṃvedanabhāga*).

This is because the two characters "clarity" (*míng*) and "awareness" (*jué*) mentioned in the preceding text—where "clarity" is the deluded clarity that acts as the agent of illumination, and "awareness" [is the awareness of that].

Regarding the deluded awareness that is the object of illumination: although both subject and object are false and equally belong to ignorance (*avidyā*), when distinguished according to their essential nature, it is specifically the deluded luminosity of the subject that constitutes ignorance.
As for the deluded awareness that is the object of illumination, this refers to the "characteristic of activity" (*karma-lakṣaṇa*) mentioned in the preceding section;
in that previous section, it was merely mentioned incidentally and did not occupy its primary position. Therefore, the Buddha now connects [the discussion] here.

As stated in the preceding passage, the nature of awakening is fundamentally not an object of illumination; it is only because of the false addition of a "subject that illuminates" that it subsequently becomes established as an "object of illumination.

From this, one should know that the character *míng* (illumination) in the term "illumination due to [the subject] illuminating" (*yīn míng*) is precisely the false illumination of the "subject that illuminates" mentioned above, which is also what the treatise calls "non-awakening"—namely, ignorance (*avidyā*). Furthermore, the character *suǒ* (object) in the term "established as the object" (*lì suǒ*)...

This is precisely the deluded awakening elucidated in the preceding passage, and it is also what the treatise refers to as "the movement of the single thought-moment," namely, the *karmalakṣaṇa* (the phase of karma).
It is only here that this [term] reaches its proper locus. Furthermore, within the treatise, the movement of the mind based on non-awakening is designated as "karma";
and because the objective realm is established based on deluded luminosity, it is likewise designated as "karma. The underlying intent is entirely the same, yet—
This passage is further elucidated by the following discussion. It is because the *Śāstra* states that "the mind moves," yet does not clarify for what reason the mind moves;
whereas the *Sūtra* text reveals the fundamental cause, namely that false illumination is added to original enlightenment (*prakṛti-prabhāsvara*), thereby inducing this movement of the mind.

The two phrases beginning with "that which is perceived" (*yad upalabdham*) refer to the transformation of the aspect of the object-seeing (*viṣaya-dṛśya-bhāga*). One should know that the *Śāstra* designates this as the "aspect of the perceiver" (*darśana-lakṣaṇa*).

In the treatise (*śāstra*), it is stated that based on the movement of the mind, it transforms into the faculty of seeing. This is established by means of a causal argument and thus transforms into a false faculty.
The underlying intent is entirely the same, yet this [text] provides a further clarification compared to the treatise.

This is because while the treatise says that the movement of the mind transforms into the faculty of seeing, it does not explicitly clarify why it immediately becomes the faculty of seeing; the Sūtra, however, explains it as follows:
It arises because, through delusion, one takes the essence of awakening to be the perceived object; it is by means of this deluded object that a deluded subject is induced.
Thus, the deluded subject clearly unites with that which is capable of seeing. △ Second, the subtle objects.
Within the absence of identity and difference, the blazing intensity establishes difference; that which differs from what is different establishes identity because of that difference.
When identity and difference are thus manifested, one further establishes the absence of both identity and difference based upon this.

This is precisely the *nimitta-bhāga* (objective aspect) of the manifesting [consciousness]. The treatise designates it as the "characteristic of the objective field" (*viṣaya-lakṣaṇa*), and further explains it itself as the "manifesting characteristic.

The opening phrase is the fundamental basis for its establishment. Regarding the phrase "in the absence of identity or difference," this refers to the midst of the "evolving characteristic" (*karma-lakṣaṇa*). As the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi* states:

"Both the objective aspect (*nimitta*) and the subjective aspect (*darśana*) arise based upon the self-corroborating consciousness (*svasaṃvitti*). Here, "identity" (*samatā*) means the non-differentiated object, while "difference" (*visama*)...

This refers to the realm of differentiated objects. Within the characteristic of karma (*karmalakṣaṇa*), when discussed in terms of ultimate reality, since it is a single essence and a single characteristic where subject and object are not divided, there is, in fact, no such duality of objects at all.

From the second phrase onward, all refer to the objects that are established. "Blazing" (*cittara*) describes the intense appearance of a flame; although it manifests with great clarity, yet the flame...
It is bright only at night, which also signifies that it is manifest within the darkness.

Although this realm is manifest, it still remains within the fundamental consciousness (*mūla-vijñāna*) and has not yet become fully evident; therefore, it is like the light of a fire in the midst of a dark night.

Furthermore, although it exists within the fundamental consciousness, it is already blazing intensely, like a fire breaking out at night. How could it be the same as the previous two characteristics? For one of them is non-existent.

Regarding the objective realm (*viṣaya*): it is indeed impossible to know [its limits]. When ancient commentators saw the term "blazingly manifest" (*cittara*), they dared not define it as a subtle realm and instead interpreted it as the six coarse objects.
They failed to examine how the treatise itself explains the causes and conditions of arising and ceasing;
yet when the explanation reaches the *ābhāsajñāna* (manifesting consciousness), it states: "That which is able to manifest all objective realms is like a bright mirror."

It manifests as physical forms and images. Furthermore, it is said that according to the five sense objects (*pañca-viṣaya*), they appear immediately upon encounter, without any sequence of before or after.
How could this contradict the teaching in the present sutra regarding "blazing forth"? Therefore, one should know that this section is undoubtedly concerning the objective realm (*viṣaya*).
As for the phrase "blazing forth to become differentiated," it means that from within this state where there is neither sameness nor difference, various distinct forms and vessels suddenly appear.
The phrase "immediately binding darkness as the initial phase of form" refers to the present realm of differentiation.
The two subsequent phrases, "different from those," refer to the present realm of non-differentiation—namely, emptiness giving rise to the initial phase of great awakening.
The first character "yi" (different) signifies the sense of being dissimilar; the two subsequent characters "yi" (different) likewise refer to the aforementioned realms of differentiation. Now,

Since they are both distinct and yet dependent upon that distinction, it can be seen that this is entirely intended as an incidental clarification. This means that it is not a case of being different first and then becoming the same;
rather, at the very moment one perceives difference, one incidentally reveals the point of non-differentiation, which is precisely the "identical object.

To establish the terminology and grasp the underlying meaning is itself a manifestation. According to the conventional sequence of arising, the "bubble" (the individual) follows the "void" (the universal); first, the characteristics of the realm (dhātu-lakṣaṇa) arise.
Subsequently, following this [text], in accordance with the aspect of transformation (*pariṇāma-lakṣaṇa*), one first perceives the characteristics of the elements (*dhātu*).

This is stated thus because it incidentally reveals empty space (*ākāśa*). Whatever is appropriate is acceptable. The final three phrases are somewhat reminiscent of the characteristic of sentient beings (*sattva-lakṣaṇa*).
However, the reason they must clarify both difference and identity is that by contrasting difference with identity, this [nature] is revealed.
The realm of sentient beings is different from the two realms mentioned above. This is because it possesses a semblance of form and appearance, distinguishing it from the "same" realm;

thus, it is not identical to empty space, which is why it is said to be "without sameness. Furthermore, it possesses a semblance of movement and spiritual awareness, distinguishing it from the "different" realm;
thus, it is not identical to the physical vessel-world (the inanimate environment), which is why it is said to be "without difference. Question: Since it is already the world...
What is the difference between the "sentient beings of empty space" and the coarse objects [of the lower realms]? Answer: They still reside within the fundamental consciousness (*mūlavijñāna*);
they are manifestations of darkness that suddenly appear as flickering and indeterminate signs, serving merely as the embryo for the three dharmas within those coarse objects.

Question: The Treatise mentions the realm only in its undifferentiated totality, whereas the Sutra presents it with the full description of the three characteristics; how can these two accounts differ so much in their detail?
I fear this may not be appropriate. In response: Although the preceding heading of the *Śāstra* is general, its subsequent self-explanation is particularly detailed.

As previously cited, it states that "it can manifest all objective realms. The *Vyākhyā* (Commentary) takes up the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra* to explain this, stating that it possesses the seeds of the sense organs (*indriya*), the body (*deha*), and the receptacle world (*bhājana-loka*).
Furthermore, regarding the manifestation of the five objects (*pañca-viṣaya*), the *Vyākhyā* explains that while the five objects are cited for the time being, in reality...
It universally manifests all objective realms. Viewed from this perspective, the commentaries and sub-commentaries all speak of "all objective realms"—what would they not encompass?

Why then do they emphasize the three characteristics as being so numerous? Furthermore, regarding the explanation of the physical world (*bhājanaloka*), why would it not include both the common and the individual realms?

As for the mention of the "root-body" (*indriya-ātmabhāva*), why would it not refer to sentient beings with consciousness? Moreover, how could seeds fail to include both the subjective realm (*sattvaloka*) and the objective realm (*bhājanaloka*)? And furthermore...
Even the five sense-objects are not considered too many; why then should one take exception to the three marks being too broad?

Thus we know that if this section is categorized as the manifestation of characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*), then the sūtras and śāstras are of one accord. Furthermore, some assign these to the three subtle states (*tri-sūkṣma*). This intention is indeed circuitous. (Question:

Regarding the preceding exegesis on the sequence of the three marks, it was stated that when explaining the establishment of the object based on the cause of illumination, one says: "Because of delusion, there is the subject of illumination, which gives rise to the object of illumination, thereby establishing the mark of karma.")

Although this [passage] lacks the word "able" (*neng*), it is also logically consistent to supplement it by inferring the intended meaning. Furthermore, the subsequent sutra clarifies that the "ability" (*neng*) produced from the cause is explained as the "transformation of karma" (*ye-sheng-zhuan*). This is also the natural order of things.

However, since you claim that "deluded illumination" (*wang-ming*) takes the "karmic aspect" (*ye-xiang*) as its object of illumination, and the "transformative aspect" (*zhuan-xiang*) likewise takes the karmic aspect as its object of perception—how do these two differ? Moreover, why does the transformative aspect not take the objective realm (*jing-jie*) as its object of perception?

Answer: Your statement that "deluded illumination takes the karmic aspect as its object of illumination" is incorrect. This is because deluded illumination initially arises based upon fundamental awakening (*ben-jue*). Delusion takes fundamental awakening as its object of illumination; it did not originally intend for the karmic aspect to be so. Yet, fundamental awakening is fundamentally not an object that can be illuminated. For this reason, fundamental awakening...

Ultimately, it cannot be made manifest; rather, it is merely brought forth as the "characteristic of karma" (*karmalakṣaṇa*) to serve as that which is manifested. Therefore, the Buddha said: "Awakening is not that which is manifested; because of manifestation, an object is established. The meaning of this is clear. You next stated that the "characteristic of transition" (*vartalakṣaṇa*) falsely takes the characteristic of karma as its perceived object. These words are not incorrect.

For the characteristic of transition arises based on the characteristic of karma, and it falsely takes the characteristic of karma as its perceived object; originally, it did not intend to constitute a realm (*viṣaya*). Yet, since the characteristic of karma fundamentally lacks any visible characteristic, the characteristic of karma ultimately cannot be seen, and it is merely brought forth as a realm to serve as the perceived object.

Therefore, the Buddha said: "Since the object has been falsely established, your false subjectivity arises. Within the state where there is neither sameness nor difference, a blazing diversity is formed," and so forth. The intent of this is even more evident. This is...

Therefore, regarding the word "object" (*suo*) in the scriptural text, it connects with two instances of "subject" (*neng*)—the former being implicit and the latter explicit. Furthermore, the former is the subject that gives rise [to the object], while the latter is the subject that is produced. They are like a grandfather and a grandson; how can one say there is no distinction?

Regarding the word "subject" (*neng*), it likewise connects with two instances of "object" (*suo*)—the former being explicit and the latter implicit. Furthermore, the former is the locus of the subject that gives rise [to the object], while the latter is the locus of the subject that is produced. These too are like a grandfather and a grandson; how could they be conflated?

As for the statement in the *She lun* (Mahāyānasaṃgraha) that "the objective support of the evolving aspect cannot be known," this refers precisely to the initial moment of the evolving activity-aspect (*karmalakṣaṇa*). Yet, the Master Ji (Jizang) incorrectly pointed to the objective realm itself [as the referent]. Both of these cases involve the mind apprehending the mind; the true is hidden while the semblance appears.

This refers to that which is called "the non-illusory becoming illusory. It is like a person staring fixedly at their own eyes, not intending to see flowers in the sky; yet, because the eyes themselves cannot be seen, they merely bring forth the appearance of flowers in the sky. This analogy explains the Dharma in detail.

It is indeed thus. Question: The treatises speak of neither subject nor object; why then does the Sūtra elaborate so extensively? Answer: It is merely because their literary methods differ. The treatises follow a sequential order, where the lower arises in dependence upon the upper; therefore, they do not manifest subject and object. The Sūtras function like a chain of links, where the upper draws forth the lower.

Therefore, the subject and object are frequently discussed. Since it has already been repeatedly clarified within the section on Ignorance (*avidyā*) in the *Śrīmālādevī-siṃhanāda Sūtra*, why doubt that the "karmic characteristic" (*karma-lakṣaṇa*) is not the object? By harmonizing the texts and extracting their meaning, there is no inconsistency between the sūtras and the śāstras.
This concludes the initial section on the subtle. II. Gradual Manifestation of the Coarse. This corresponds to the six coarse aspects (*ṣaḍ-audārika*) in the treatise.
Here, too, we divide them into two categories by correlating the afflictions with their objects: first, the coarse afflictions.
Such disturbances, in their mutual interaction, give rise to weariness; this weariness, prolonged, produces dust, which naturally becomes turbid.
From this, the afflictions of dust and weariness are incited;
these constitute the first five of the six coarse states. The phrase "in such a manner" (rúshì) is a term referring back to the preceding text, indicating the state of disturbance.

The meaning lies entirely in the preceding section. If one takes the general cause broadly, then the three subtle states arise within the truly pure mind, all of which are manifestations of agitation and disturbance.
If one examines the specific cause for the production of the coarse consciousnesses, then it is solely the single characteristic of the objective realm (*viṣaya*).
This refers to what is called "the objective realm acting as a condition to develop the six coarse states. This is because that objective realm arises from non-existence.
When existence exists, existence and non-existence mutually oppose one another; when difference is established based on identity, identity and difference manifest each other.
Subsequently, by means of the boundary-phenomena of both unity and difference, the sentient beings who are neither identical nor different are revealed.
Thus, within the ocean of the *ālayavijñāna*, the winds of objective conditions stir in disorder, like flowers in the sky drifting aimlessly—how profoundly turbulent this is!

The *Laṅkāvatāra Sūtra* says: "The ocean of the storehouse consciousness (ālayavijñāna) abides eternally, stirred by the winds of objective realms. This is it. "Waiting" (*dai*) refers to conditional opposition;

the sense of "waiting upon one another" is precisely that of being conditioned (*pratyaya*). "Arising" (*sheng*) means growth. "Fatigue" (*lao*) and so forth refer to the coarse consciousnesses (*pravṛttivijñāna*).
Is it not the case that various coarse consciousnesses arise and grow with objective realms as their conditions? This is what the *Laṅkāvatāra Sūtra* means when it says:

"The various waves of consciousness surge and turn in succession. However, the two characters "arising" (*shēng*) and "exertion" (*láo*) correspond to the "characteristic of the arising of wisdom" (*qǐ chéng zhì xiàng*) in the treatise, which is the first of the coarse [aspects].
The treatise states: "Depending on objective realms, there arises the discrimination of the pleasant and the unpleasant."

Therefore, the Commentary states: "Upon the appearances manifested by the preceding manifesting consciousness (*nirvikalpa-vijñāna*), one fails to realize that they are manifestations of one's own mind;

thus, for the first time, the mental factor of wisdom (*prajñā*) arises, discriminating between the defiled and the pure, and grasping at them as having a fixed nature. This initial arising of the mental factor of wisdom and its discrimination is what is called the 'arising of weary toil'. Question:
Regarding the two aspects of evolving wisdom (*pravṛtti-jñāna*) and transforming wisdom (*parāvṛtti-jñāna*), both take objects as their conditions (*ālambana*). What is the difference between them?

Answer: The transformation-consciousness (pravṛtti-vijñāna) takes objects as its conditions; it is like a mirror in that there is no separate analysis. The consciousness of characteristics (nimitta-vijñāna) takes objects as its conditions without realizing they are manifestations of the mind;

it clings to them as external objects and discriminates between the defiled and the pure—this is what is called the "consciousness of discriminating phenomena" (vastu-pravicaya-vijñāna). This corresponds to the innate grasping at dharmas (dharma-grāha).
The two characters "labor" (lao) and "long" (jiu) refer to the characteristic of continuity (*saṃtati-lakṣaṇa*), which constitutes the second level of coarseness. Thus, "long" refers to—

Regarding the characteristic of uninterrupted continuity, the *Śāstra* states: "Because it relies upon cognition (*jñāna*), suffering and pleasure arise; the mind awakens and thoughts are produced, which correspond and continue without interruption.

The Commentary (*Vyākhyā*) explains that the uninterrupted nature of the two types of awakening constitutes one's own continuity, while the ability to further draw forth and sustain cyclic existence (*saṃsāra*) constitutes the continuity of others.
This corresponds to the aspect of conceptualization within the clinging to phenomena (*dharma-grāha*).
It is distinct. It is merely divided briefly into the defiled and the pure. This, moreover, transforms into the sensations of suffering and pleasure.

As these sensations arise within the continuums of oneself and others, the grasping at dharmas (*dharmagrāha*) becomes increasingly coarse; therefore, it is called "discrimination" (*vikalpa*). The two characters for "arousing dust" (*fa chen*) refer to the characteristic of grasping (*upādānalakṣaṇa*), which is the third level of coarseness.
"Dust" refers to the characteristic of defiled attachment. The *Śāstra* says: "Because the mind gives rise to attachment. "Arising" (*qi*) is synonymous with "rousing" (*fa*). That [text] says:
"Arising and grasping" (qǐzhù) is here rendered as "arousing dust" (fāchén); they share the same essential meaning. The *Śāstra* states:

"Based on the various ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*), their grasping and attachment become increasingly deep, calculating 'self' and 'what belongs to self,' and so forth. The phrase "the individual characteristics become turbid" refers precisely to the calculation of the characteristic of names (*nāmalakṣaṇa*), which constitutes the fourth coarse [delusion].
This is because the *Treatise* relies upon false attachments to differentiate the conventional characteristics of names and speech. The *Commentary* states: "Based on the preceding..."
This refers to the establishment of further provisional designations upon the characteristics grasped through inversion.

Now, taking up those who grasp at names and characteristics through inversion to an especially extreme degree—precisely because it accords with the turbidity of their own-characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*)—although this is one and the same intent, the stirring of dust is still shallow;

therefore, it belongs to the innate (*sahaja*) aspect of self-grasping (*ātmagrāha*). However, when the turbidity has already deepened, it belongs to the conceptualized (*vikalpita*) aspect of self-grasping. [End of] Section.

The second phrase refers to the "characteristic of initiating karma" (*karma-samutthāna-lakṣaṇa*), which constitutes the fifth coarse [delusion]. That text speaks of "initiating karma," while this text speaks of "arousing dust and so forth";
the meaning of the words is largely the same. The *Śāstra* states: "Relying upon names, one follows after names and grasps at them, thereby creating various kinds of karma.
The *Commentary* (*Śū*) states: "This means clinging to characteristics and calculating names; based on these coarse afflictions, one mobilizes body and speech to create all [karmas]."
Karma is the cause of suffering. There are eighty-four thousand afflictions (*kleśa*), which take the ten fetters (*saṃyojana*) as their substance;

when categorized according to the seven branches of body and speech and the four minds of the three periods of time, they fill this number. To speak briefly of the afflictions, there are six roots and twenty secondary ones.
If these are correlated with the eighty-four thousand afflictions, the number remains the same. In total, these are comprised of the views and thoughts (*dṛṣṭi* and *vitarka*). Regarding...
That which has not yet arisen belongs to the category of delusion; it refers to the aforementioned grasping at the two marks of names and forms.

Now, the Sūtra explicitly states "inducing," which refers to that which has already arisen and constitutes the mark of karma. Furthermore, both the defilements (*kleśa*) and the afflictions (*paryavasthāna*) must arise in relation to the seven branches of body and speech.
The commentary also states that they "activate" body and speech; thus, their meaning does not conflict, as [karma] necessarily...
Initiation is precisely what constitutes the meaning of "arising. Question: Since coarse objects have not yet been formed, how can there suddenly be body and speech? Answer:
Although the discourse is spoken in terms of the sequence from the initial arising, in reality, it is without beginning.

How could it truly be that before coarse objects were formed, body and speech were utterly non-existent? Furthermore, this treatise also speaks in terms of the initial arising; it must also be understood [in this way].
In the sixth [section], it is established that body and speech exist within the center. The commentary explains the arising of karma by clarifying the employment of body and speech.

If one were to insist that body and speech exist only in the sixth [direction], then upon what would the preceding marks rely to give rise to karma? And upon what would grasping and so forth rely to conceive of "self" and "what belongs to self"?
Although the words follow a sequential order, the meaning must be flexible and comprehensive; one should not be dogmatic. Furthermore, below...
Regarding coarse objects (*sthūla-viṣaya*): it is also not the case that they only come into existence after the five consciousnesses have fully arisen;
rather, this is merely a skillful elaboration because the words cannot be expressed all at once. One should understand this through spiritual intuition (*śen-hui*). △ Second, coarse objects.

Arising constitutes the world; stillness constitutes empty space. Empty space is the same; the world is different. That which is neither same nor different is truly a conditioned phenomenon (*saṃskṛta-dharma*).

This is precisely the characteristic of suffering bound by karma, serving as the sixth coarse [object]. The treatise says: "Because one receives retribution based on karma, one does not [attain liberation] by oneself..."

Regarding this, the *Śāstra* (Commentary) states: "Since the causal karma has already been established, the resulting fruit is inevitable; one will circulate through the various realms, bound eternally by birth and death.
Although the names and positions of this section of the Sūtra and the Treatise are identical, their underlying meanings differ. The Treatise clarifies that all phenomena are mind-only (*cittamātra*);

therefore, it provides a comprehensive explanation of the various consciousnesses (*vijñāna*), detailing the characteristics of the mind while treating the characteristics of the objective realm (*viṣaya*) more briefly. This is because...
The previous descriptions of objective phenomena (*viṣaya-nimitta*) and these present retributive phenomena (*vipāka-nimitta*) were also all based on consciousness;

they were presented in a concise and abbreviated manner without full detail in order to manifest that these are objects grasped by delusion. Thus, the Sūtra answers the question, "How do mountains, rivers, and so forth suddenly arise?

by presenting both mind and object together, yet providing particularly detailed exposition regarding the characteristics of the objective realm. Therefore, the subtle objective realm mentioned previously and this coarse objective realm [are treated with varying degrees of detail]. Text.

This is all detailed therein. Within it, the characteristics of worlds, empty space, and sentient beings are fully elucidated; furthermore, the characteristics of suffering bound by karma are annotated and categorized as "receiving retribution" (*vipāka*).
Now, in this sutra, the worlds and empty space constitute the "dependent retribution" (*niśraya-vipāka*), while sentient beings constitute the "primary retribution" (*mukhya-vipāka*);

thus, the intent accords with the category of receiving retribution. However, within these [worlds], purity and defilement, or suffering and pleasure, are not obtained through one's own autonomy. How is this inconsistent?

The treatise [states this], yet the Sūtra provisionally relies on the initial formation [of the continuum] with the intention that there is no returning; subsequently, there are three other types of continuities.
This point alone slightly diverges from the commentary. Having thus completed the reconciliation of the Sūtras and the treatises, we shall now explain the text according to its phrasing.
It should be understood that all of the above has been a sequential narration of their causal origins; it is only these six phrases [that follow].

Only then does one fully establish the intent of the response to the questions. The first four lines provide a definitive answer to the question: "How did the mountains, rivers, and the great earth suddenly arise?

The final two lines provide a definitive answer regarding all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛta-lakṣaṇa*). Taken together, they summarize the preceding discourse: based upon the awakened nature (*prakṛti-bodhi*), ignorance (*avidyā*) moves;

because of ignorance, the mind and its objects (*citta-viṣaya*) are produced; and conditioned by the mind and its objects, worldly afflictions (*kleśa*) arise. Thus it is said: [...]* *Note: The ellipsis indicates the omission of the intervening text.*
"Driven by the power of karma, it arises," and so forth. When explaining "arising" and "quiescence," one should not refer to time; rather, one should speak in terms of location. As it is said:
when arising constitutes the state of having characteristics, then mountains, rivers, and the great earth manifest as firm and fixed forms;
when quiescent and devoid of characteristics, then there is a vast, expansive, and desolate appearance of solid emptiness. The following two lines clarify this.
It does not depart from the subtle objects previously mentioned; rather, it is only upon reaching this point that they become determined and perfected.

Therefore, the two characters "ni" (in) and "shō" (is) constitute the character "soku" (that-is). This means that this emptiness is precisely the aforementioned common characteristic (*sāmānya-lakṣaṇa*), which only now becomes determined;
and this world is precisely the aforementioned particular characteristic (*viśeṣa-lakṣaṇa*), which only now reaches perfection. However, at this juncture, one should conclude as follows:
As for your question regarding how the mountains, rivers, and the great earth suddenly arise: they truly arise in this manner.

The final two lines provide a definitive answer concerning all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛta-lakṣaṇa*), clarifying that they do not depart from the preceding realm; it is merely a shift in literary expression.
The former refers to the latter as being identical to the former, while the present takes the former to manifest the latter. It is said that within that subtle realm, there is neither sameness nor...

The characteristics of their differentiation become manifest and certain at this point, thereby establishing the truly conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛta-dharma*) that constitute the karmic fruits of sentient beings.
He concludes again: "As for your question, 'How do the various conditioned characteristics suddenly arise?', they indeed arise in such a manner.
Although, in light of what preceded, these are all equally characterized by sudden arising, there remains the expression regarding the long-standing toil of mutual dependence.
This is because [things] arise from non-existence and must proceed from the subtle to the manifest. It is merely explained that the myriad phenomena first complete one cycle and then suddenly arise.
Furthermore, by observing the process of sequential severance during cultivation, this order is revealed;
the sequence of initial formation is provisionally taught so that one may easily awaken to the sequence of successive arising and not fall into confusion or bewilderment.
By understanding the sequence for severing the inversions, one will find it easy to practice and realize [the truth], avoiding confusion and disorder.
Furthermore, one should know that from ignorance (*avidyā*) down to coarse objects, the scriptures frequently employ the relationship between subject and object to link them sequentially;

this is intended to make known that subject and object are the very origin from which the myriad phenomena arise. After the practitioner has clearly distinguished between the true and the false, in a single thought-moment they suddenly—
Severing subject and object, one can bring the mind to stillness; all phenomena then sit back within their inherently pure and fundamental nature. As it is said:
"If one merely leaves behind delusive conditions, one is immediately a Tathāgata. This concludes the first section: the Sudden Arising. △ Second: Subsequent Continuity.
This section specifically answers the question regarding how things successively flow on, ending and beginning again.
The intent of this question was raised previously in the section titled "Raising Doubts. It is divided into three parts. First, the continuity of the world-system.

Although the principles herein resemble the concept of the mutual generation of the five elements found in non-Buddhist treatises, they are in fact not entirely the same; thus, one should not equate them point by point.
This is inconsistent. There are two inconveniences: first, the Five Elements are explained in reverse, while the meaning of the scriptures is obscured;

second, it causes those outside our teachings to believe that [the Buddhist view] does not transcend their own ideas. This is because those outside our teachings correctly maintain only that the Five Elements can form the world, yet they truly do not understand its ultimate source.
Even if they loftily postulate the Great Ultimate (*taiji*) or primordial chaos (*hundun*), [they remain ignorant].
Thus, they ultimately fail to recognize that this is the deluded perception of their own mind—the universal ignorance of the whole.
Now, I shall provide a clear and explicit instruction, precisely because it differs from the intent of those other teachings.

Yet, the old commentators have instead explained "awakened clarity" (*jue-ming*) as water, conflating it with the Tiantai doctrine of "Heaven first produces water," and placing it even below the "Ultimateless" (*wuji*) and the "Supreme Ultimate" (*taiji*).
How can one cause them to eliminate their old views and give rise to new awakening? Generally, the teachings of external schools mostly revert to transformation through the mechanism of yin and yang;
whereas our school points directly to the source of transformation within the nature and mind.

Furthermore, it demonstrates that the origin of heaven and earth arises from the ignorance within our own minds. This is truly vastly different from external doctrines and serves as an ultimate warning against error.
This is a misconception. Those who propagate the teachings do not simply refrain from drawing upon external doctrines; rather, they cause them to clarify internal principles.

To instead take internal teachings and apply them indiscriminately to external doctrines is an extreme error. As for the terminology employed within the internal teachings, they frequently utilize the "four great elements" (*mahābhūta*) rather than naming the "five elements" (*pañca-dhātu*).
Subsequent transformations and subsequent arisings are merely analogous to the five elements.

They are similar. Therefore, I shall now explain: regarding the four dharmas mentioned previously, they are entirely modeled after the "four great elements" (mahābhūta) as correctly interpreted by Mount Gushan.
However, while the first three great elements clearly arise based on the mind, the latter four dharmas are established with distinct terminology.
I have briefly adopted the theory regarding the parental elements (*dhātu*) of Wénlǐng to assist in clarification. This is further divided into three parts.

First, the primary element (*mahābhūta*) is that which can produce the four great elements. Although the four great elements arise from one another in succession, they are in fact all fundamentally produced by this primary element.

This is because each possesses the functional power to accomplish its respective task. What are termed "grasping and maintaining," "preserving," "transforming," and "containing" are all expressions of this meaning.
As for the final four dharmas, they do not possess this meaning; one shall see this for oneself upon careful observation.
Furthermore, they are divided into four specific categories, the first of which is the wind element (*vāyu-mahābhūta*).
Awakened clarity and empty dullness interact to produce agitation; thus there is the wind-circle that supports the world.
"Awakened clarity" refers to the fact that upon the essence of awakening, false clarity has already arisen, and this false clarity inevitably gives rise to bubbles within emptiness.
"Empty dullness" refers to the substance of inert emptiness, which is entirely dark and obscure; thus, this obscuring dullness and the preceding clarity stand in opposition and mutual dependence.
Regarding "the arising of agitation": this refers to what Wēnlíng called the mutual inclination of clarity and obscurity, whereby one is unaware that the mind is moving.
One should know that all the winds in the world are entirely the result of the stirring and turbulence of the deluded mind.

As for the wind-circle that supports the world, various sutras state that the very bottom of the world rests entirely upon the wind-circle; this is clearly evident, as it directly depends upon the deluded mind.
And thus it arises. △ Second, the earth element:

arising from the movement produced by space, solidity and clarity establish obstruction. That which is gold and treasure is the establishment of solidity within luminous awareness; therefore, there is the golden wheel.
Regarding the maintenance of the land, Gushan states:
"The earth and gold both possess the nature of solidity and thus belong to the element of earth (pṛthivī-dhātu). This is correct.
Since the nature of earth is hard, and nothing is harder than gold, gold is the essential, substantial body of the earth-element, produced through space."
"Shaking" refers to the mind being stirred by the obscurity of emptiness; it is like a person who, when overcome by sleep, experiences confusion and distress.
"Firm clarity establishing obstruction" refers to the firm adherence of awakened clarity, whereby delusion results in the formation of obstructions;

it is like one who, while in that state of being overcome, firmly insists on seeking passage and thus falsely perceives something solid pressing down upon them. From this, there is immediately felt the presence of all that is solid.

Because it has the characteristic of obstruction, it is said that the gold and jewels of the world are all manifestations produced by a portion of firm attachment upon the substance of luminous awareness.
For example, there are ancient accounts of those who, by concentrating their minds and binding their thoughts, were transformed into stone; this is also a minor verification.
This is indeed the inconceivable power and function of the numinous mind, yet it is also the principle of the inevitability of karmic retribution. The Golden Wheel.
Regarding the "Upholder of the Nation" (Dhṛtarāṣṭra): at the very bottom of the earth element lies the adamantine limit (*vajratala*).
This great element, too, clearly and directly arises in dependence upon the deluded mind. △ Third, the fire element.

The solid perception is formed from the jewel; the shimmering clarity emerges from the wind. As the wind and the metal rub against each other, there is the light of fire, which constitutes the nature of transformation.

This great [element] is indeed produced through the transformation of the two great elements of wind and metal; yet the solid perception and the shimmering clarity fully carry the characteristics of the deluded mind.
"Solid perception" refers to the deluded awareness of stubborn attachment. Because it establishes obstruction, it evokes metal, and thus the jewel is formed. "Shimmering clarity" refers to...
The delusion of stirring thoughts is luminosity. Because movement forms the characteristic of wind, wind arises. This is the cause for the emergence of fire.
Because one is solid and one is mobile, they rub against each other and produce fire. As it is said: "One hard and one soft rub and wash against each other.
That which functions as the nature of transformation is that fire lacks the function of sustaining or containing, yet possesses the capacity for transformation.
The functions of these [elements] become manifest only upon reaching the latter four.

Although the aforementioned three great elements arise in mutual dependence, they all carry the characteristics of the mind’s deluded awareness and deluded illumination; it is therefore appropriate for our own school to specifically clarify this.
How could we allow the meaning of water, earth, and wood producing one another to obscure it? △ Four: The Water Element.
The brilliance of the jewel produces moisture, and the fire-light rises as steam; thus there is a water-circle that contains the worlds of the ten directions.
This Great Square [Vajra-peak] alone employs the two great elements of gold and fire, without being accompanied by the mental aspect (*citta-lakṣaṇa*).

Since the previous three sections were accompanied by brilliance, this should be understood without needing to be stated explicitly. As for "the brilliance of the jewel produces moisture," it is because the brilliance upon the jewel already contains [the moisture].

The characteristic of moisture is like the luster of a pearl emerging from water; this is its verification. As for "the fire-light rising as steam," fire possesses a vaporous and turbid energy that can produce water.
It is like how, during times of intense heat, myriad things are often steamed until they exude water.
Thus, because of the brilliance of the jewel and further reflected by the fire-light, this is how the great element of water arises. It contains...

This also carries the sense of supporting and moistening. Regarding the "ten directions of worlds": in all worlds, beneath each one there is a water wheel (*āpa-maṇḍala*), as stated in various treatises.
A separate sutra states that the establishment of the world rests upon a earth wheel (*pṛthivī-maṇḍala*) which, in turn, rests upon a gold wheel (*kāñcana-maṇḍala*).
Yet they are equally the earth-element (*pṛthivī-mahābhūta*). The gold wheel rests upon the water wheel; the water wheel rests upon the wind wheel;
the wind wheel rests upon space (*ākāśa*); and space has nothing upon which it rests. Now, according to the sequence of arising from the mind, this is not entirely the same.

Furthermore, to reveal the ultimate reality, it is said that space rests upon ignorance (*avidyā*), and ignorance rests upon fundamental awakening (*mūla-bodhi*), because one perceives the myriad phenomena.
The Dharma begins with the mind of the union of truth and falsehood, for apart from this mind, nothing possesses its own inherent substance.

Thus, within our own tradition, it is only by revealing the mind that one attains the essential meaning. The section on how the "arising" produces the four great elements is complete. II. The Four Abodes Produced by Arising.
These four dharmas are precisely what is produced by the aforementioned four dharmas; they are what are called the world-systems and lands.
Furthermore, "sustaining and containing" refers to transformation; that is, sustaining, containing, and transforming. These are the four abodes.
Since the vessel-world (the physical environment) is fundamentally the dwelling place of sentient beings, these four directions now manifest the specific locations where sentient beings reside.

Therefore, it is said that there are four abodes. This does not contradict the teaching of the Lesser Vehicle (Hīnayāna), which states that all phenomena arise through the combination and transformation of the four great elements (*mahābhūta*).
However, the Lesser Vehicle has not yet realized that these four great elements are ultimately manifestations of the awakened mind.
Since the preceding passage clarified that the four great elements which constitute [the world] all arise based on the mind, we now reach the point of what is constituted by them.
Regarding the two "abodes" (*sthāna*): they merely demonstrate the transformation of the four great elements (*mahābhūta*) and do not further clarify the arising of the mind.

This is intended to lead one from the "mind-only" nature of the four great elements to the realization of the "mind-only" nature of all phenomena. Furthermore, these are divided into two parts: first, the general establishment of the two abodes; second, the specific explanation of the two abodes.
The "sea" refers to the dwelling place of water-dwelling sentient beings, while the "continent" refers to the dwelling place of land-dwelling sentient beings. Because they are the same...
Relying on water and fire as the generative forces, it is said that they collectively form [the world]. Furthermore, this is divided into two parts. First, showing the process of its arising:
fire ascends and water descends; their interaction produces solidity. The moist becomes the great ocean, and the dry becomes the continents and sandbars.

Although the four great elements (*mahābhūta*) equally constitute the functional capacity for transformation, among these four, the three great elements of fire, water, and earth are prominent in their manifest traces.
As for the element of wind, although its function in sustaining and agitating is not insignificant, it remains above that which has already been formed;
thus, its traces are not evident, and for this reason it is not mentioned. The first two lines specifically clarify the nature of fire and water.
The two great elements serve as the cause for the arising of the ocean and the continents where beings dwell. "Fire surges upward" means that the nature of fire is fundamentally to blaze upward.
"Water descends" means that the nature of water is fundamentally to moisten downward. "Mutual emergence" refers to the harmonious interaction of water and fire.
"Establishing solidity" refers to the formation of the vessel-world (the physical environment). This is like a ceramic vessel, which relies entirely upon the functions of water and fire. Next...
Regarding the statement that "the two locations which are the primary objects of accomplishment are also formed by the establishment of solidity":
this is because the ocean is not merely a matter of water; since it is only a vast depression into which water flows that is called an ocean, it is entirely a substance of solidity.
The "islands and sandbanks" refer to the four great continents and the various minor islands. △ Second, examining its elemental constituents.
For this reason, within that great ocean, flames constantly arise; within those islands and sandbanks, rivers and streams constantly flow.
For this reason—because of the principle that water and fire coexist there—the place where that great ocean originally arose as moisture should seemingly not have fire;
yet, because it does not forget the constituent elements of its mother, flames constantly arise.

A sandbank (*zhoutan*) is originally a place that should be dry; it ought not to have water. Yet, because it does not forget the vital essence (*qifen*) of its father, rivers and streams constantly pour into it.
This is because, within the doctrine of the Five Elements (*wuxing*) of the non-Buddhist teachings, water regards fire as its "wife" whom it overcomes (*ke*);
thus, fire is the mother residing in the second position. Fire, in turn, regards water as its "husband" who overcomes it. Therefore...
Water is the progenitor of the two abodes; now the great ocean has inherited the likeness of its father, yet it does not forget the constituent essence of its mother.
Therefore, fire arises within the sea. The islands and sandbanks have inherited the likeness of their mother, yet they do not forget the constituent essence of their father.
Therefore, there are rivers on the continents. All other cases should be understood by analogy with this. △ Second, the specific formation of the two abodes.

This is called "specific formation" (*bi cheng*) to distinguish it from "general formation" (*zong cheng*), as it is established through the evidence of the births occurring in those two abodes. This further divides into two parts:
first, the formation of mountain abodes.

The power of the water is inferior to that of the fire, which congeals into high mountains; therefore, when the mountain rocks are struck, they burst into flame, and when melted, they turn back into water.
This is the dwelling place of the sentient beings who inhabit these mountains. The first two phrases demonstrate the cause of their arising.
Regarding "the water being inferior to the fire," as Wenling says: "It is only after [one element] is inferior that yin and yang harmonize to produce offspring. Furthermore...
Water is the husband of fire; if it becomes too dominant, its power will inevitably extinguish the fire—how could it then give rise to another dharma?
Now, because the husband-water is inferior to the wife-fire, a high mountain is formed. The final three phrases verify their respective elemental natures;
this may be understood by reflecting upon the previous analysis. As for "melting and becoming water," it is like smelting the ores of the five metals.
All are completely reduced to liquid; this is it. △ Second, the formation of forest dwellings:

where the power of the earth is inferior to that of water, it is drawn up as grasses and trees; therefore, forests and thickets, when encountered by fire, become soil, and when subjected to pressure, become water.
This is the dwelling place where the beings of this forest reside. The first two lines indicate their origin; the final three lines verify their karmic affinity (*dhātu*).
The meaning of these points may be understood by analogy with what preceded. The exposition of the four types of dwellings is hereby concluded.
△ Third, the conclusion on the continuity of the seeds.
Mutually arising from delusion, they serve as seeds for one another; by these causes and conditions, the world continues in succession.
"Mutually arising from delusion" means that they produce one another through mutual delusion. "Serving as seeds for one another" means that first, the great elements arise from the deluded mind;
next, the four great elements are fully produced through successive transformation; and finally, from these various elements...
Thus, the four abodes are accomplished, and the receptacle world (*bhājanaloka*) upon which sentient beings depend is complete.
By this causal condition—that is, by these reciprocal causes and conditions—the worlds continue in succession:
through formation, subsistence, destruction, and emptiness, they end and begin again in an uninterrupted continuity. Every single cycle of formation proceeds in this very manner.
It revolves and arises. Therefore, once it has suddenly arisen, there will never be a time of purification. The succession of the world has concluded.

Furthermore, Pūrṇa, that the delusion of clarity is not caused by another, but rather that the clarity of awareness itself constitutes the fault.
To say "the delusion of clarity is not caused by another" means that the clarity attained by sentient beings necessarily arises from delusion;

The world is the root of both the real and the false. Since enlightened clarity (*jue-ming*) already belongs to the realm of subject and object, what follows will be discussed solely from the perspective of delusion.
This section is similar to the "suddenly arising" (*hu-sheng*) section previously mentioned, concerning the root of delusion. **2. The Three Characteristics are Localized as False.**
Once that which is falsely imagined has been established, the luminous principle does not transcend it. For this reason, hearing does not go beyond sound, and seeing does not exceed form.
"Once that which is falsely imagined has been established" refers to the characteristic of karmic activity (*karma-lakṣaṇa*) within that which is already falsely established.
