thus, the beginning and end correspond, and the synthesis is appropriately managed. Third, latent doubts are provoked, which are then set aside until their purpose is fully revealed in the subsequent text.
In that context, all such meanings are entirely lost. May the wise take care to examine and determine this for themselves.
Having concluded the resolution of doubts by means of the latter of the three collections (piṭakas), [the author] now proceeds to encourage practice by fully manifesting the three collections.

Because the preceding sequential three collections are urgent in their task of destroying delusion and achieving awakening, they both manifest in accordance with the deluded objects of sentient beings; there has not yet been the opportunity to encompass them universally.

The two conditions of the holy and the ordinary, and the two aspects of defilement and purity, are of one suchness throughout the ten realms, without duality, thereby fully manifesting the entire substance and great function of the *tathāgatagarbha* mind.
Now that the two delusions—coarse and subtle—have been successively shattered until exhausted, the wondrous luminosity is revealed, and the eye of the Way is perfected.
It is therefore fitting to exhaustively empty the spiritual treasury of all Buddhas and reveal it to the very bottom; thus, this [text] is a comprehensive synthesis.

This concludes the exposition, intended to manifest the perfect fusion of the Threefold Canon (*tri-piṭaka*). Question: The preceding words have raised a latent doubt; may I hear its resolution? Answer:

It is because the previous discourse extensively discussed how sentient beings currently dwell within deluded realms, wherein both essence (*svabhāva*) and characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*) are mutually unimpeded in their very substance.
Consequently, a doubt arises: "If this is so, then there should be no distinction between the holy and the ordinary, and all should equally perceive this non-obstruction. Why is it that we [do not]?"
Movement results in obstruction; yet how is it that only the Tathāgata attains non-obstruction? Thereupon, the Tathāgata, in response to their thoughts, individually revealed the reasons for this.
This is why there is the subsequent passage of perfect exposition (the "round demonstration"). [Old commentary:

Since it neither corrects errors nor infers the intent of this section, the preceding part of the scripture lacks a conclusion and the following part lacks an introduction. Furthermore, what textual continuity can be established? Those who read this text should carefully investigate and savor it. This is further divided into three parts.

First, the ultimate manifestation of perfect interfusion. (Question: The seven elements have already been concluded as being entirely and perfectly interfused; yet, while this subtle and exquisite exposition below also speaks of "ultimate manifestation," how does it differ from that? Answer: They are vastly different.

First, in the former case, each element is individually interfused with the others, and even when the seven elements are fully exhausted, they remain merely worldly phenomena. Here, however, the ten realms are universally interfused—how can they be compared? Second, while the former case involves the interfusion of characteristics and their entry into the nature, it has not yet spoken of the manifestation of all things or the unimpeded, wondrous function;

thus, they are difficult to equate. Furthermore, because it only manifests the emptiness-treasury, the Buddha simply says "pure and inherently so"—the meaning of these words is evident. It is specifically because its pervasiveness is deeper than the four categories, and furthermore...)

The emptiness of the ultimate truth (*paramārtha-śūnyatā*) is not the same as annihilationism like ashes; therefore, it manifests perfect interfusion. Furthermore, it is divided into two parts. First, based on the mind of delusion and enlightenment, one discriminates dependent origination.
Herein, the deluded mind of sentient beings is transformed into the wisdom-realm of all Buddhas, fully revealing the meaning of cultivation and realization.

For although the nature of sentient beings is inherently present, if one does not rely on enlightenment and apply cultivation, but merely gives rise to worldly afflictions (*kleśa*), [the nature remains obscured].

Yet, the immeasurable, sovereign, and unimpeded wondrous functions cannot be manifested. Therefore, although the Original Existence is emphasized prior to awakening in the Perfect Vehicle (Yuan-sheng), after awakening, one must necessarily cultivate its realization.
Furthermore, there are two [aspects]: first, regarding the defiled dependent origination, it reveals the causes for the emergence of obstructions.
This, in turn, has two [sub-aspects]: first, attachment results in the formation of obstructions. This, furthermore, has three [sub-aspects]: first, using characteristics to obscure the nature.
Pūrṇa, you have used the emptiness of form to overturn and supplant the Tathāgatagarbha;
this subtly dissolves our latent doubts regarding how movement could result in obstruction. Thus, form and emptiness overturn and supplant one another.

There are two interpretations. The first is the interpretation based on the initial stage: "Form" (*rūpa*) refers to that which is produced by the binding darkness; "emptiness" (*ākāśa*) refers to that which is brought about by obscurity;

and "overturning and seizing" refers to the false arousal of grasping at views. This is because it begins with the movement of the mind and the false arousal [of consciousness], and concludes with the accomplishment of grasping at views.

The second is the interpretation based on a slightly more proximate stage: here, "syllables" (*akṣara*) refers to the attachment to syllables, and "dharmas" (*dharma*) refers to the attachment to dharmas.

"Furthermore, 'overturning and seizing' collectively conveys the sense of turning one's back and rushing away. Those such as the heterodox schools turn their backs on emptiness and rush toward existence; thus, they overturn and seize emptiness with form.
Those of provisional and limited capacity turn their backs on existence and rush toward emptiness; thus, they overturn and seize form with emptiness.
This is because the former connects to the three subtleties while the latter cuts off the six coarsenesses; therefore, they are distinguished as being near to the beginning."
Both meanings are equally applicable. △ Second, the entirety of nature is identical to phenomena.
Thus, the Tathāgatagarbha, in accordance with form and emptiness, pervades the Dharma-realm.
This is True Suchness responding to conditions and corresponding with the deluded mind, universally forming all realms of form and emptiness.
Thus it is. △ Third, the conclusion regarding the various obstructions.
Therefore, within this, the wind moves and the space is clear; the sun is bright and the clouds are dark.
"Within this" refers to the dharma-realm of form and emptiness. "Clear" means stillness. Thus, movement and stillness obstruct one another.

Light and darkness mutually exclude one another. Among all obstructive phenomena, these four are cited as representative examples. In this manner, it should be understood by analogy that even earth and space cannot accommodate water and fire;
their mutual suppression and extinction follow the same principle. The section on the formation of obstructions through grasping is hereby concluded.
II. Tracing the Origin and Examining the End.
Sentient beings are deluded and distressed; turning their backs on awakening and uniting with the dust of sensory objects, they give rise to worldly toil and manifest the signs of the mundane world.
This section summarizes the essential points for guiding those who have lost their way, serving as a concluding summary of the preceding text. It is explained here in abbreviated form.
"Delusion and bewilderment" (*mimèn*) refer to the afflictions that arise; they internally encompass the three subtle [delusions] as well as the four coarse [delusions] mentioned previously.

This is also explained in connection with the initial stage. If one speaks from a more superficial perspective regarding the severing of the stream of existence, then in the lower realms and the three miserable destinies, having thought is "delusion," while in the higher realms and for the two vehicles, being without thought is "bewilderment.
Thus, what are called having thought and being without thought both ultimately return to the same state.
This refers to being bewildered and distressed. Furthermore, to turn one's back on awakening and unite with the sensory objects is the karma that is created;
it is called "turning one's back on awakening" because it opposes the true nature. To be intimately compliant with delusive phenomena is termed "uniting with the sensory objects.

Internally, this contains various attachments to signs and inversions regarding the realms of existence and emptiness; the mundane world of afflictions is the suffering thereby invited. Internally, it contains form and emptiness, light and darkness.
"All obstacles" refers to the sixth coarse level of the objective realm. At the conclusion, it should be stated:
"The reason you all constantly encounter obstructions is solely due to this self-delusion and self-contradiction; how could it be the fault of the nature or characteristics [of reality]?"

The explanation of the causes for the emergence of hindrance based on the defiled dependent origination is complete. △ Second, based on the pure dependent origination, the explanation of the causes for the emergence of non-hindrance follows.
This secretly resolves the latent doubt regarding the Tathāgata’s uniquely attained non-obstruction. It is divided into two parts.
First, the integration into non-obstruction, which is further divided into three sections. First, integrating the nature with the characteristics.
I [use] the wondrous marks, which are neither extinguished nor born, to harmonize with the Tathāgatagarbha;
this reverses the previous [explanation] by showing how the marks conceal the nature.

Since those present at the assembly had doubted why only the Tathāgata attained unimpededness, the Buddha, because he was about to explain the reasons for his own unimpededness, first said, "I use... Here, "yǐ" (以) means "to use."
"Subtle luminosity that neither perishes nor arises" refers to the selection and exclusion of the functioning consciousness-mind that arises and perishes in dependence on sense-objects.
This refers to the essence of non-discriminatory, immovable seeing, hearing, sensing, and cognizing within the six sense-faculties— as previously indicated in the Sūtra—
which thoroughly penetrates the four categories and seven elements as the Tathāgata-garbha, the eternally abiding, all-pervading, and wondrous nature of True Suchness.

It is so. "Integration" means fusion. The *tathāgatagarbha* is precisely that which, previously following along with form and emptiness, universally manifested as the characteristics of arising-and-ceasing and obstructive limitation.
The intended meaning is this: by what other means could I have attained all-pervasive non-obstruction?
It is simply by employing that perfectly湛 (zhàn) and non-arising, non-ceasing nature within the six sense faculties to fuse with those pervasive [characteristics].
It merely establishes the Tathāgatagarbha as the nature of form, emptiness, arising, and ceasing.

However, regarding the term "integration" (he), it carries the meaning of shedding the sense objects, turning back the faculties, and preventing them from flowing outward; in this regard, nothing surpasses the "Perfect Penetration of the Ear Faculty.
△ Second, all phenomena are entirely the nature.
The Tathāgatagarbha, however, is solely wondrous, awakened, and luminous, perfectly illuminating the dharma-dhātu;
this section corresponds precisely to the principle dharma-dhātu. It is said that the Tathāgatagarbha, when in a state of delusion, may manifest as form and emptiness, or as arising and ceasing.

Yet delusion is fundamentally and eternally empty; its appearances are not truly existent. Now, by means of this wondrously luminous and ever-abiding nature, the delusive appearances of arising and ceasing are found to be utterly unobtainable.

There remains only the wondrous purity—the nature of original enlightenment, profound and luminous—which is perfectly integrated and illuminating, pervading and encompassing the entire dharma-realm. This is what is called the union of suchness-wisdom with suchness-principle.

Abiding in the Great Treasury of Radiance (*mahā-ābhāsvara-garbha*) is none other than Avalokiteśvara. When quiescent extinction (*śānti*) manifests before one, it is the stage of the patience of non-arising (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*);
not even the slightest dharma is seen to arise or perish. What that [text] calls "quiescence" is here called "illumination.

Only when one possesses this profound mind (*gambhīra-citta*)—having entered the stage of full confidence (*śraddhā-paripūri*) in the Perfect Teaching (*vaipulya-yāna*)—does one accord with the essence of the Dharma-body of Quiescent Light (*śānta-prabhā-svabhāva*). Below this level, the Great [Vehicle] is fully manifested.
"Function" refers precisely to the fundamental ground-mind of the Tathāgata. △ Third, the conclusion establishes non-obstruction.

This is the karmic function of True Suchness arising in accordance with pure conditions. Previously, sentient beings acted contrary to its nature, yet True Suchness still conformed to defiled conditions.

When in accord with the principle of delusion, it forms the characteristics of the mundane world; how much more so now, when in accordance with the wondrous cultivation of the nature—how could there not be the manifestation of wondrous functions?
Nevertheless, herein lie two kinds of dharma-realms: the non-obstruction between principle and phenomena (*li-shi wu-ai*) and the non-obstruction between phenomena and phenomena (*shi-shi wu-ai*).
Master Wuxing has categorized these to illustrate their meanings and characteristics; for now, I shall merely follow his structural divisions. And...
I shall not adopt his interpretation. Instead, I will divide it into two parts. First, the presentation of the four meanings. Within this, first:
the infinite is one, and the one is infinite; the large appears within the small, and the small appears within the large.
"Therefore" refers to the preceding principle of the *dharmadhātu*, which serves as the general cause for these two realms.

This is because sentient beings, due to their prior delusion regarding phenomena (*dharma*), completely obstruct the principle; now, because the Buddha has awakened to the principle, he is able to harmonize phenomena.
"Within this" means within the *dharmadhātu* of principle. It is the natural principle that function arises from the essence. Regarding each of the four meanings below:
These two meanings each constitute a type of unimpeded dependent origination (*anāvaraṇa-pratītyasamutpāda*), both of which pervade the two realms.
First, speaking in terms of the Dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu*) where principle and phenomena are unimpeded: because principle cannot be divided, principle is one;
because phenomena have no limit, phenomena are infinite. However, since the one and the infinite are mutually constitutive, these two meanings [are unified] within the Dharma-realm.

Within the contemplation of the ten gates, eight gates are subsumed together. When principle pervades phenomena, when phenomena establish principle, and when principle is identical to phenomena—all are the one becoming the infinite.
When phenomena pervade principle, when phenomena manifest principle, and when phenomena are identical to principle—all are the infinite becoming the one.
As for the point where principle supplants phenomena, it is the infinite becoming the one; when phenomena conceal principle, it is the one becoming the infinite.
It is a measure (*pramāṇa*). Furthermore, because principle has no spatial limitation, it is "great"; because phenomena have spatial limitations, they are "small.
Yet, since greatness and smallness manifest to one another, these two meanings are subsumed within only two of the ten gates in this contemplation;
namely, the gate of the mutual pervasion of principle and phenomena. The intent is that each and every instance of the boundless true principle...
It is entirely pervasive within every atom, yet its principle is not small; this is the manifestation of the great within the small.
Since each and every atom fully contains the boundless ultimate truth, yet the atom itself is not large, this is the manifestation of the small within the great.
(A single atom may also be treated alone in relation to the principle; here, by means of the difficult, the easy is encompassed. This also serves to simultaneously clarify the two preceding meanings.

This can be seen through reflection. However, because the "mutually inclusive" (xiāng) aspect does not possess the meaning of mutual interpenetration (*xiānhù*) as found in the two gates [of the "identical" (*tóng*) and "hidden" (*yǐn*)], it does not correspond [to them].
If one must include it, it is subsumed under both the "identical" and "hidden" gates.

Next, speaking in terms of the *dharmadhātu* of the non-obstruction of phenomena and phenomena (*shìshì wú'ài*), and taking the concise and clear [explanation] as the standard, then the former two meanings—within the ten mysteries (*shí xuán mén*) of the *Huayan shū*—are provisionally subsumed under the "one-and-many mutually inclusive" gate.

The mutual inclusion of the characteristics of all phenomena consists of two gates. For example, a single atom, a single hair, a single body, or a single world-realm is "one," while many atoms, many hairs, many bodies, or many world-realms are "immeasurable. Regarding the principle of their mutual interpenetration, let us first explain it according to the gate of mutual inclusion:
a single atom is identical to many atoms, such that one becomes immeasurable; many atoms are identical to a single atom.
The immeasurable is one. Hairs, lands, and bodies are equal; the identity of the one and the many can be inferred by analogy with this.

If one adopts the "door of inclusion" (*shōyōmon*), then the character "identity" (*soku*) is changed to "entry" (*nyū*); this can be understood through reflection. This "identity" and "entry" refer exclusively to phenomena of the same category.

If one speaks of the intermingling of different categories, then whether it be atoms facing body-hairs and lands, or body-hairs facing atoms and lands, their mutual identity and mutual inclusion can all be understood by analogy.

Of the latter two meanings, they provisionally encompass the two gates of the "sovereign Indra's net" regarding the freedom between the broad and the narrow: minute particles and the tips of body-hairs are both "small," while boundless lands and boundless bodies are both "large.
The principle of their mutual manifestation is explained here according to the gate of the broad and the narrow.
Boundless lands exist within a single mote of dust, yet the ocean of lands does not become small;

this is the manifestation of the great within the small. A mote of dust encompasses boundless lands, yet the mote of dust does not become large; this is the manifestation of the small within the great (in this phrase, "character" [字] should be understood as "place" [處];

Although this possesses both...

Furthermore, when examining the Commentary (*Shu*), it treats "neither identical nor different" as the general underlying reason for each respective meaning;

however, for the sake of clarity in this diagram, I have omitted that qualification. Moreover, one should know that these four meanings should also fully encompass the ten [meanings] within this context.

[This concludes] the section on the Gates. Fearing prolixity, it has not been fully prepared. Just as in the "Ten Generations Separated by Dharma" [section], where a single thought-moment and an eon are no different, and a speck of dust and a Buddha-land are identical, why could one not apply this with diligent intent and exhaustive search?
This applies to every gate; I have merely provided these explanations for those who are clear and concise, so that they may understand the general principle.
Reflect upon this: thus, the Buddha, by means of sixteen characters, fully encompasses the two Dharma-realms and twenty [principles].

This is precisely the convergence of form into emptiness and the fusion of emptiness into form; where emptiness and form are unimpeded, all distinctions are extinguished and there is no place for dependence. The Immovable Bodhimanda pervades the realms of the ten directions. His body contains the infinite space of the ten directions;
within the tip of a single hair, he manifests jeweled-king lands, sitting amidst motes of dust and turning the Great Dharma Wheel.
Since there must be characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*) wherever there is meaning (*artha*), this section constitutes the characteristics of the four aforementioned meanings.

However, one must understand that while the meanings can be comprehensively subsumed, the characteristics are difficult to exhaustively detail; thus, I have merely provided examples for the remainder.

Consequently, the text of this sutra is divided into phrases of eight characters, which may also be arranged as four lines; yet, these need not correspond to each of the four meanings in their entirety.

I shall simply follow the flow of the text to assign these [terms] accordingly. The first two lines present the first two meanings within the non-obstruction of principle and phenomena (*li-shi wu-ai*):
the characteristic of the non-obstruction of the one and the many. This is shown by way of their pervasive inclusion, thereby manifesting these two meanings.
"The site of enlightenment" (*dao-chang*) refers to the principle; it is the *Avataṃsaka*'s True Dharma-realm (*eka-dharmadhātu*). This scripture is the wondrous Tathāgatagarbha.
The nature of *tathatā* (suchness) is also the site of the quiescence of the One Vehicle, eternally free from all marks of conceptual proliferation (*prapañca*) such as arising and ceasing;
it is the ultimate, true, and constant tranquility, and is therefore called the Immovable Site of Enlightenment (*acala-bodhimaṇḍa*).
The "ten directions" refer to phenomenal appearances, encompassing horizontally all Buddha-lands and exhausting vertically the ten dharma-realms. This is the Immovable Site of Enlightenment.

The "ability to pervade" is the subject, and the "ten directions of the world" are the object of pervasion. When we evaluate these two meanings, the immovable site of enlightenment (*bodhimaṇḍa*) is the complete totality of the single principle;
that which pervades the ten directions of the world means that within each and every phenomenon, it pervades by means of its entire totality.

If, however, one possesses sudden faculties from the very beginning, then even while within the stage of contemplative practice (*vipaśyanā*), one may completely subdue the five abodes of ignorance and enter directly by a single leap. This too is the supreme, pure, and luminous mind of Bodhi;
there is never any difference in quality between them. Do not be discouraged. As the Patriarch said: "But if one merely leaves behind delusive conditions, one is immediately as such."
As the Buddha has said, this accords with the meaning of "sudden cessation" within this context. That which pervades the *dharmadhātu* is manifested solely through cessation;

it does not come into existence for the first time because of cessation. What was stated previously—that all things existing throughout the entire world are none other than the wondrously luminous, primordial mind of *bodhi*—is precisely the meaning of pervading the *dharmadhātu*. As for "not obtained from others," even if...
He had his attendants point it out to him, yet the true principle was fully present within his own body; it was not something bestowed by others, being merely like a lamp transmitting its light.
△ Third, rebuking the toil of cultivation and realization.
What does it mean to "rely" (*ji*) on diligent toil (*qúláo*) and "be intent upon" (*kěnqìng*) cultivation and realization?

"Rely" (*ji*) means "to depend upon" (*jiǎ*) or "to require" (*xū*). Wúxīng says: "The flesh between the bones is called *kěn*; the knotted places of muscle and sinew are called *qìng*. This is from the *Zhuāngzǐ*:
"The butcher never once struck the sinews or the knotted muscles (*jìjīng kěncìng*). According to my own limited view, this refers to the laboring of sinews and the suffering of toil.

The meaning of "skeletal austerity" (*asthi-kṛcchra*) refers to the intention of ascetic practice. What is the source of this? It means that one need not intentionally strive with hardship to seek realization.

This is because those of the Sudden Teaching possess a sublime and wondrous place of awakening; they thoroughly understand that delusion is fundamentally empty while the True is fundamentally present.
One need only cease inverted discrimination, and in a single thought-moment enter non-discrimination. Since that which is fundamentally empty has no basis, what could there possibly be [to attain]?
It remains. Since that which is inherently present is unobscured, what could possibly conceal it? Therefore, it does not depend upon arduous cultivation for realization.
If this were the intention of Pūrṇa Maitrāyaṇīputra, such that he had no thought of practicing through effort, then what would the Buddha have had occasion to reprimand him for?
Nevertheless, those who wish to aspire to sudden cultivation must first seek sudden awakening. If their awakening has not yet reached great penetration, and...
To recklessly dismiss the cultivation of phenomena is to bring about one’s own downfall; it is also the height of folly and delusion. Be cautious!

Having finished demonstrating how to bring [the mind] to an immediate rest, △ third, the conclusion of the analogy and the deduction of the error, which is further divided into three parts: first, the analogy of original existence and non-awakening.
For example, suppose there is a person who has tied a wish-fulfilling jewel within their own garment, yet remains unaware of it.

The garment is a metaphor for the three conditions, the inverted discriminations, the three causes, the subtle flow of thoughts, and the state of being shrouded in layers by the fundamental ignorance of madness.
The jewel is a metaphor for the supreme, pure, and luminous mind of bodhi. From this branch...
Because the derivative ignorance and the fundamental ignorance wrap and envelop one another, although it exists, it is not perceived.
△ Second, the analogy of being deluded yet not having lost [the jewel]:
Having traveled far to other lands and wandered about begging for food, although he was truly impoverished, the pearl had never been lost.
To be entangled in emptiness while lacking sublime function is called "exhaustion" (*qióng*); to be obstructed by existence while having nowhere to retreat and hide is called "exposed" (*lù*).

Since both emptiness and existence are peripheral lands, they are like other regions. Wuxing said: To seek the pleasures of humans and devas or to take the benefits of the partial and small vehicles is like rushing about to beg for food.
As for "the pearl has never been lost": though ten thousand delusions rush past, the one true reality remains perfectly intact.
It was still there; even though he was poor, the pearl remained. △ Third, the analogy for awakening to that which is not newly acquired:
Suddenly, a wise person points out the pearl to him. His wishes are fulfilled according to his heart, and he attains great abundance.
Only then does he realize that the divine pearl was not obtained from without.
Wuxing said: "The Buddha is like the wise person; the teaching is like showing the pearl. To realize the principle and give rise to its function is to achieve great abundance.
Wénlǐng said: "The final two lines are a metaphor for the cessation of delusion and the manifestation of truth, requiring no effortful cultivation or realization.
[The phrase] 'achieving great abundance' is a metaphor for the fundamental essence pervading the Dharma-realm; the final two lines are a metaphor for not obtaining it from another. This...
Regarding the intermediate section: it originally accords with the *Vajragarbha* chapter of the *Sūtra of Perfect Enlightenment*, which states:
"If all sentient beings have been Buddhas from the beginning, why is there subsequently the existence of all ignorance?

However, while "all" refers to both the fundamental and the derivative, this scripture proceeds from the derivative back to the fundamental, stating that all delusions are entirely without cause and are empty by nature at their root. (Question: This sudden cessation [of delusion] and the faculty of hearing...)

Are [the methods of] Yuan and Tong the same or different? Answer: In their ultimate intent they are the same, yet they differ according to their respective stages. If an ordinary person of the broad ground, while in the stage of names, hears this Dharma-door and realizes thoroughly that the true exists while the false is empty, entering through the gate of the ear and forgetting the object, this is precisely not following worldly discrimination;

it is the immediate severance of the three conditions. If one still follows discrimination and does not sever the three conditions, how can it be called "entering the stream and forgetting the object"?

From this point on, by means of forgetting, non-arising occurs; by non-arising, exhaustion occurs; by exhaustion, emptiness occurs; and by emptiness, cessation occurs. Following this single path of rest, from the shallow to the deep, until quiescent extinction manifests before one—that is the manifestation of the Bodhi-superior-pure-bright-mind. This is entirely the same.

Furthermore, if Pūrṇamaitrāyaṇīputra has already exhausted the fetters of the faculties following the seventh stage of faith, what need is there to reverse the previous process? Moreover, by entering through the gateway of the ear, one simply brings to an immediate halt the conceptualization of the grasper and the grasped within awakening;

when quiescent extinction manifests before one, the supremely pure and luminous mind likewise manifests. This is because in the preceding stages, both the dual attachments to persons and dharmas were simultaneously stilled, whereas in this stage, only the attachment to dharmas is stilled;

thus it is said that they differ according to their respective positions. The direct answer to Pūrṇamaitrāyaṇīputra is hereby concluded. II. Simultaneously instructing Ānanda. Ānanda was originally the primary interlocutor, and he is now engaged through these doubts.
This arises from the inquiry of Pūrṇa Maitrāyaṇīputra; hence it is said that [the teaching] is presented concurrently. This is divided into two parts.
First, Ānanda follows the Buddha’s words and clings to the doctrine of causes and conditions (*hetu-pratyaya*). This is Ānanda’s third instance of doubting causes and conditions.

Initially, in the first section titled "The Manifested Vision Transcends Sentiment," he doubted that the nature of vision does not arise from causes and conditions. Second, in the section on the "Perfect Manifestation... [the text continues].

Prior to the seven major sections, there was a doubt that the myriad dharmas do not arise from causes and conditions. Now, this third section raises the doubt as to why the realization of the fruit and the attainment of the Way likewise do not belong to causes and conditions.
That there is a fruit without a cause is truly a matter of great doubt. The underlying intention seems to be this:
one has long heard that the Buddha rejected causes and conditions, yet within his words he also mentions causes and conditions; having spoken of causes and conditions, he then asks, "Why?"

Because he had cultivated and realized [the truth], he raised this question. Thus, while previously he was in doubt regarding nature and characteristics, now he is in doubt regarding cause and effect. This is divided into three parts:
first, the raising of the question.
At that time, Ānanda, amidst the great assembly, prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, rose, and addressed the Buddha:
△ Second, the formal inquiry. This is further divided into four parts. First, restating the Buddha’s words:
"World-Honored One, you have recently taught that because the three conditions for the karmas of killing, stealing, and sexual misconduct are severed, the three causes do not arise.
When this is realized within the mind, the nature of madness naturally subsides. This subsiding is itself Bodhi; it is not obtained from others."

The current explanation regarding those who commit killing, stealing, and sexual misconduct follows the *Tianru* (Heavenly Like) commentary, which provides a brief summary of karmic fruits while intending to encompass all sentient beings in the world-system.
If this were the case, the character "ye" (karma) would likely be an error for the character "deng" (equal/identical).

Furthermore, the character "yuan" (condition) refers to discrimination (*vikalpa*) and does not specifically denote the acts of killing and so forth. This interpretation is excellent, as it accounts for the fact that Pūrṇa Maitrāyaṇīputra was entirely devoid of the three types of karma.
How could it be that the Buddha further taught [them] in order to cause their severance? △ Second, the proof establishing the strange question:
"If these causes and conditions are thus clear and manifest, why does the Tathāgata suddenly abandon causes and conditions?"

The first two lines provide the evidence for the statement that the Buddha’s teaching is currently being expounded based on causes and conditions. The latter two lines pose a rhetorical question of surprise:
"If it is said to be based on causes and conditions, why then do you suddenly discard this and claim that delusion is causeless? Why rely on cultivation and realization?
This serves to clarify that the present teaching does not belong to the realm of causes and conditions. △ Third, the former teachings possess benefit.
“World-Honored One, it is through causes and conditions that my mind has attained awakening.
Is this principle not true not only for us young, newly ordained śrāvakas, but also for those in this assembly such as Mahāmaudgalyāyana, Śāriputra, and Subhūti?
Having heard the Buddha’s teaching on causes and conditions from an elderly brahmin, they resolved their minds toward enlightenment and attained the state of being free from outflows.”
The first two lines concern benefiting oneself; "World-Honored One" and the following concern benefiting others.
As for the term *brahmacārin* (梵志), it is a general designation for those who have left the household life in India, signifying that they possess pure aspirations and conduct.
The Sūtra records that Maudgalyāyana and others first encountered Uruvilvā-Kāśyapa and his followers while traveling on the road, and heard them preach the Four Noble Truths of arising and ceasing.

Through causes and conditions, one attains awakening and gains faith; only then does one see the Buddha and realize the fruit of Arhatship. △ Fourth, the current confusion with spontaneity (*svabhāva*).
To say now that *bodhi* does not arise from causes and conditions is identical to the "spontaneity" taught by Kauṣṭhila and others in Rājagṛha.
This establishes the ultimate meaning.

Observe that the two characters "now" (jin) in this statement directly refer to the present teaching on the absence of causes, primordial emptiness, and the cessation [of conceptualization] as being *bodhi*;
it does not require recourse to the preceding text. This serves the purpose of the sudden abandonment of causal conditions. Externally...
The Way is spontaneous, like one who naturally attains the Way after eighty thousand kalpas; it is like a ball of thread that comes to rest when it reaches its limit.
This signifies that everything is spontaneous and does not depend on cultivation or realization. The formal question has concluded. △ Third, the conclusion of the question.
I pray that you will deign to show great compassion and dispel my confusion. My thought is this:
if one relies on the Buddha’s words, they still involve causes and conditions; yet if one investigates the Buddha’s intent, causes and conditions are suddenly cast aside.
I now request a definitive resolution: does it remain as causes and conditions, or is it certainly not causes and conditions? Resolve upon one [position] so that there may be no further doubt.

They are bewildered and distressed. △ Second, the Tathāgata sweeps away deep attachments and rebukes their rigid adherence. This also has two parts. First, sweeping away attachments by means of a metaphor.
This also has two parts. First, sweeping away attachment to extend the intended meaning. This also has three parts. First, evaluating attachments based on the metaphor itself.
The Buddha told Ānanda: "It is just as with the case of Yantradatta in the city;
when the causal conditions for his madness are extinguished, the state of non-madness naturally emerges. Causal conditions and spontaneity reach their ultimate limit in this principle."
"Regarding 'the metaphor itself,' this refers to taking up the preceding metaphor. Regarding 'gauging the underlying sentiments,' this means gauging Ānanda’s two types of emotional attachments.
As it says: 'As for what you call "causality" and "spontaneity," let us now examine them by means of the previous metaphor of madness.'"

"If you must say that the nature of madness (and so forth) is exhausted in this principle," means that you can do no more than cling to these two paths—either as causes and conditions or as spontaneous occurrence (*svabhāva*).
To go beyond these two tracks would mean that your sentiments are spent and your reasoning is exhausted.
This is intended to gauge Ānanda’s thoughts and first establish a firm basis before proceeding to refute them below. This merely explains the analogy; if one were to apply it [to the actual case]:
Within the Dharma, one must attain the extinction of the causal conditions of ignorance, whereby Bodhi emerges spontaneously.

If it were otherwise, both the meanings of "primordial emptiness" and "primordial duality" would be lost, resulting entirely in two kinds of clinging attachments. II. Simultaneously Dispelling the Two Calculations.
This is further divided into two parts: 1. Simultaneous Dispelling with Respect to the Head. Regarding "with respect to the head," within the Dharma, this refers to Bodhi.
This prevents one from falling into the two dualistic views. Furthermore, there are two points. First, to dispel the notion of spontaneity:
Ānanda, for example, take the case of Yan-luo-da-duo (Śaṇmukha). His head was originally spontaneous; it was inherently so of itself. There is no "spontaneity" that is not inherent to itself.
For what reason or cause did he become terrified of his own head and run about in a frenzy?

The first two lines establish that "head" (shou) is "spontaneity" (ziran). "Originally spontaneous" (*ben zi qi ran*) reiterates the meaning of the preceding line, which is to say that since it is spontaneous;
"there is nothing that is not spontaneous" (*wu ran fei zi*) means that there is nothing that is not spontaneity.
It is said that [the head] should always exist naturally; one must not be startled by its sudden absence and fall into madness.
The final two phrases are an interrogation as to why he was suddenly startled by the absence of his head and ran about in a frenzy.

The "cause and condition" (*hetu-pratyaya*) likewise refers only to the meaning of the character "hence" (*gu*), and does not imply looking into a mirror; it merely indicates that once one has gone mad, one no longer belongs to oneself.

But let it be so. Within the Dharma, if one’s original nature were to belong to spontaneity (*svabhāva*), sentient beings would constantly perceive their own nature by themselves and there would no longer be anyone who wanders in delusion.
Why, then, are there still those who wander in delusion and turn their backs [on the truth]?
It is evident that *bodhi* does not belong to spontaneity. The general principle here is to refute spontaneity; we are specifically refuting spontaneity.
One cannot say that dependent origination (pratītyasamutpāda) refutes spontaneity (svabhāva), for such mutual refutation constitutes sophistry (vibhrama), as previously argued.
△ Second, the clearing away of dependent origination. This also has two parts: first, a counter-interrogation of the opponent's statement.
If the head exists naturally, why does it not naturally perish due to causes and conditions?

Although the text mentions both together, in reality it places sole emphasis on causes and conditions; although the language refers to madness, it actually distinguishes the matter solely in terms of the head.
If the head exists naturally, the head must have existed from the very beginning. As for "madness due to causes and conditions," this refers to looking into a mirror.
Consequently, one becomes terrified that there is no head. If this were the case, it would not be a genuine cause and condition at all.
Why? If it were a real cause and condition, why was this head not originally present by itself, such that through the causal condition of looking into a mirror, it would truly be lost?
One must truly lose one's head before it can become a genuine cause and condition. As it is said in the Dharma:

"If the wondrous nature of Bodhi existed naturally from the beginning, yet was subsequently not seen because it ran counter to the conditions of ignorance, and one consequently claims that this nature belongs entirely to causes and conditions—then one has truly lost that nature, and only then will one believe that causes and conditions are not false."

Now, why would it not be a true loss if it were not due to causes and conditions? This interrogation is intended to cause him to examine himself. II. Second, the formal conclusion of its falsity: "The original head was not lost;
it was only through madness and fear that it falsely appeared. It has never undergone any change; how could it depend upon causes and conditions?"
The first two lines express the primary meaning, concluding that the head remains intact and undiminished;
it is only through baseless delusion and fear that one falsely claims the head is lost. The final two lines set forth the reasons why this is not the case, as it is said:
Precisely at the moment when one falsely fears that one has no head, the original head is in fact without change.

And once one awakens to having a head and the madness ceases, what need is there for this head to rely upon causes and conditions? Regarding this, it is said in the Dharma: "The nature is fundamentally never lost."

To become deluded and turn one's back on it without cause is merely like having lost it; yet, even at the very moment of such delusion and apparent loss, the fundamental nature remains truly without change.
Furthermore, once one has seen this nature and shattered delusion, why would this nature depend upon causes and conditions?
This also refutes dependent origination; it specifically refutes dependent origination, rather than refuting dependent origination by means of spontaneity.
To speak roughly: if this head were spontaneous, there would be no madness or fear; if this head were dependently originated, it ought to have truly perished.
Now, because there is fear, it is not spontaneous; and because there is no [actual] loss, it is not dependently originated.
This can be clearly seen through detailed analogies drawn from the Dharma. It is simply a case of "neither of the two," and there is absolutely no "both of the two.

If one were to employ mutual refutation, then the former fallacy would be "caused by conditions" (dependent origination), while the latter fallacy would be "spontaneous existence" (arising without cause); thus it is called "confused equivocation.

Considering the subsequent text, which still requires these positions to be successively and thoroughly eliminated, how could this section instead allow for "neither of the two" to be inverted into "both of the two"?
△ Second, the simultaneous clearing away by means of madness. Regarding "madness," within the Dharma this refers to ignorance not falling into dualistic calculations.
This is divided into two parts. First, the clearing away of spontaneity (*svabhāva*).
Madness is natural by nature; madness and fear exist inherently. At the time before one has gone mad, where does this madness lie hidden?

"Madness is natural by nature" means that if madness originally arises from nature itself. "Madness and fear exist inherently" means that there must have always been inherent madness and fear from the very beginning.
The meaning of the following two lines can be understood through critical inquiry. If one [attempts to] reconcile this...
The Dharma is speech that has not yet gone mad; thus, the Dharma and its metaphor are difficult to equate.

This is because within the metaphor there truly exists a state prior to madness, whereas within the Dharma there is in fact no time that is not delusory. If this were so, one would fall into the error of asserting that ignorance has a beginning.
It can only be said that it is taken in this sense: within the state of being fundamentally pure and quiescent, where could delusion possibly lurk?
As the various patriarchs have stated, even the period prior to the empty kalpa is merely established as a conventional designation. △ Second, the dispelling of causes and conditions.
Non-madness is natural. The head is fundamentally without delusion; why then do you run about in madness?
"Non-madness is natural" means that if one were not mad, it would be natural. Furthermore, the two characters for "head" (shǒu) are spoken.
Inversion should indeed be madness; it is not natural, and thus one speaks of causes and conditions (hetu-pratyaya) by way of reversal.
This first phrase establishes the cause and condition through inversion; the following two phrases then build upon the former to interrogate and thereby refute it.

"The head is fundamentally without delusion" is equivalent to saying "the head is fundamentally not lost. The final phrase is the actual interrogation. The principle of the dharma should be stated as follows:
If it is argued that delusion is not spontaneous but possesses causes and conditions, then since its nature is fundamentally never lost, by what causes and conditions could it turn away from itself?
This concludes the first section, which simultaneously refutes these two views. △ Third, following this, the author extends his own intention.
If one awakens to the original head and recognizes the deluded running about, then both causes and conditions and spontaneity are equally mere conceptual proliferation.
Therefore, I say that when these three conditions are severed, that is itself the bodhicitta.
This reiterates the preceding refutation to once again extend one's own teaching on the meaning of "cessation is itself bodhi.

The first phrase reiterates the preceding point regarding the head, simultaneously brushing away [the notions of] the head being either spontaneous or caused by conditions, thereby realizing that the head is neither spontaneous nor caused by conditions.

The second phrase reiterates the preceding point regarding madness, simultaneously brushing away [the notions of] madness being either spontaneous or caused by conditions, thereby knowing that madness is neither spontaneous nor caused by conditions.
The latter two lines continue by stating: "If one understands in this way, then both views are merely conceptual proliferations (*prapañca*) and are entirely devoid of true meaning.

The corresponding principle should be stated as follows: "If one awakens to the fact that the nature of enlightenment is inherently complete, and further realizes that ignorance is fundamentally void."
These two views are indeed mere conceptual proliferation (*prapañca*). Having concluded the preceding section above, the following passage extends the author’s own intention.

As it says: "Because both of these are conceptual proliferations, I have previously stated that simply severing the conditions for the three kinds of conceptual proliferation is itself the true *bodhicitta*. This is because..."

For those who have not yet eliminated attachment to phenomena (*dharmagrāha*), the failure to forget the conceptualization of the three kinds of continuity is precisely frivolous proliferation (*prapañca*).

What was previously stated regarding "not following after conceptualization" is for the purpose of bringing this frivolous proliferation to a halt. When frivolous proliferation ceases, ignorance has no basis;

when awakening (*bodhi*) is free from obstacles, what further need is there to speak of its non-falsity? The clearing away of emotional attachments and the extension of the true meaning are hereby concluded. Part Two.

Wiping away all deluded emotions. This is divided into three parts. First, the prior presentation of two levels of arising and ceasing. This further has two sections. First, defining arising and ceasing in relation to bodhi:
when the bodhi-mind arises, the mind of arising and ceasing ceases; this, however, is merely arising and ceasing.
Continuing from the above: because the three conditions have been severed, although it is indeed Bodhi, one must no longer form the thought that "Bodhicitta is arising.
Why is this? If a Bodhicitta were to arise, then an arising-and-ceasing mind would cease;
this would still be a mind of arising and ceasing, not the true Bodhicitta. △ Second, regarding the natural arising and ceasing.
When both cessation and arising are exhausted, there is the path of non-effort (*anābhoga*). If there were such a thing as spontaneity (*svabhāva*), it would be clearly evident:
the spontaneous mind would arise and the arising-and-ceasing mind would cease; yet this too would be arising and ceasing.

To continue from what was said above: not only is this a mind of arising and ceasing; even if both arising and ceasing were exhausted, one must not give rise to the notion of spontaneity regarding the path of non-effort (*anābhoga*). Why is this?
If a spontaneous mind were to arise, then the mind of arising and ceasing would cease; yet this too would be entirely a mind of arising and ceasing, and not the true path of non-effort.

Because this [latter] layer is even more difficult to discern, the following provides a partial analogy. Having first completed the presentation of the two layers of arising and ceasing, (2) the analogy now clarifies that what is spontaneous is not the True [Mind].

That which is without arising or ceasing is called "spontaneous" (*tathatā*). Just as when various phenomena in the world are blended and combined into a single entity, it is called "the nature of combination";
that which is not a combination is termed "the original nature" (*prakṛti*).
In response to the preceding question: "Why is that which is spontaneous (*svabhāva*) still subject to arising and ceasing?
It is because those who reckon non-arising and non-ceasing to be spontaneity do so by establishing it in contrast to the non-spontaneity of arising and ceasing; it is not truly inherent.

To clarify this by means of an analogy: just as in the world, that which is formed through a mixture and becomes a single entity is called "the nature of combination" (*saṃyoga-svabhāva*), and in contrast to such combination, that which is not combined is designated as "the nature of spontaneity" (*tathatā-svabhāva*), these two terms—“spontaneous” (*tathatā*) and “nature” (*svabhāva*)—are originally established as mutually dependent designations. How could they be inherently existent? Spontaneity is...
It is naturally so. △ Third, only when one has utterly exhausted all deluded sentiments is it as it truly is:

"The fundamental nature is not 'as it is'; harmony is not 'union. Being both united and as-it-is, they are both transcended; being both transcended and united, they are both negated. Only this phrase is called the Dharma free from conceptual proliferation (*niṣprapañca*).

"Original suchness" (*benran*) is "spontaneity" (*ziran*); it is used by way of analogy. "Harmonious conjunction" (*hehe*) is "causal conditions" (*yinyuan*); it is designated by taking a category as a model.

"Original suchness is not suchness" refers to original suchness and that which is not original suchness. "Harmonious conjunction is not conjunction" refers to harmonious conjunction and that which is not harmonious conjunction.
"Both conjunction and suchness are transcended" means that both harmonious conjunction and non-conjunction are indeed both transcended.
It is "separation" (*li*). Both "original nature" (*benran*) and "that which is not original nature" are likewise separated from.

If one were to dismiss them individually, it would be shallower than the preceding phrase. Regarding "neither separation nor union" (*lihe jubei*): this refers to being doubly separated from both "separation" and "non-separation.
This character "union" (*he*) in "neither separation nor union" does not interfere with the character "union" in "harmony and union" (*hehe*); it is used specifically in contrast to "separation."
They are united; thus, they are not separate. Only with the final two lines is it permitted that there is truly no conceptual proliferation (*prapañca*).
For by repeatedly negating until there is nothing left to negate, one finally accords with the true path of non-effort, which is the true *bodhicitta*.
It is through the consciousness that one perceives frantic wandering; thus, as for the cause, one does not fall into dualistic views.
When one awakens to the original head, then as for the fruit, one does not fall into dualistic views. Thus, true non-effort is the true cause, and the true Bodhicitta is the true fruit.
Therefore, know that Ānanda’s current argument entirely concerns cause and effect. [This concludes] the section on the metaphor of the whisking away.

The section on "Sentiments" is concluded. △ Second, the thorough reprimand of those who cling to pedantic formalism. This is divided into two parts. First, the suppression and rejection of frivolous proliferation (*prapañca*). This is further divided into two. First, a direct rebuke of attachment to frivolous proliferation: The old teaching states that when the World-Honored One instructed Ānanda, he told him that diligent cultivation throughout kalpas must not be left to rely merely upon extensive learning (*bahuśruta*). If this were so, how would it differ from the previous meaning of "What need is there for laborious cultivation and realization? [which implies that such effort is unnecessary]. Thus, the two meanings are in conflict. Why? Because if one relies solely on extensive learning, one will never attain the fruit of the Way; yet, if one does not rely on extensive learning, one will fail to understand the Way. Therefore, the former statement was made to suppress the attachment to frivolous proliferation, while the latter was spoken to encourage the practice of cultivation. How could these two statements be contradictory? Furthermore, the old teaching says: "If you do not rely on extensive learning, you will not know the Way; if you do not cultivate diligently, you will not attain the Way. This means that if one does not rely on extensive learning, one will not know the Way; and if one does not cultivate diligently, one will not attain the Way. Thus, the former statement was made to suppress the attachment to frivolous proliferation, while the latter was spoken to encourage the practice of cultivation. How could these two statements be contradictory? This means that if one does not rely on extensive learning, one will not know the Way; and if one does not cultivate diligently, one will not attain the Way. Thus, the former statement was made to suppress the attachment to frivolous proliferation, while the latter was spoken to encourage the practice of cultivation. How could these two statements be contradictory? This means that if one does not rely on extensive learning, one will not know the Way; and if one does not cultivate diligently, one will not attain the Way. This means that if one does not rely on extensive learning, one will not know the Way; and if one does not cultivate diligently, one will not attain the Way. Not following after conceptual discrimination and remaining far removed from hatred and love—this is the place of correct practice. Thus, the true mark is brilliantly manifest.

When the Tathāgata attains the wondrously perfect true mind of Bodhi, it does not depend on further cultivation; it is the fundamental samādhi of suchness.

Furthermore, this mind and this samādhi cannot be fathomed or known by any sentient beings, including those of provisional or limited capacities;
therefore, they practice in confusion and ultimately achieve no real fruit. Thus, among the four real dharmas in the title of the sutra, this specifically pertains to the Tathāgata’s secret cause.

Therefore, I have now first determined that it belongs here. Although the old commentary’s classification as "cultivation" (*xiū*) is not incorrect in its underlying principle, its meaning is somewhat overly broad.
According to Tiantai’s judgment, the *yuán* (perfect) stage of abiding (*zhù*) is equivalent to the *bié* (distinct) stages of the *dì* (grounds);

only then can it be called "true cultivation" (*zhēn xiū*). Prior to this, it was not yet fully permitted to be considered cultivation. Now, at the initial understanding of the "perfectly penetrating faculty," one first attains the emptiness of persons (*rénkōng*); this is precisely [the point].
The stage of faith is essentially a semblance cultivation, not yet having entered true cultivation. The ancient commentary judges this as "cultivation" and the subsequent stages as "realization.
How could it be that there is no cultivation after this stage which lacks a fixed position?

Furthermore, within this stage, the fundamental nature and the wondrous mind prior to it are clarified and illustrated by the metaphor of a magnificent mansion, while perfect penetration is likened to entering its door; this clearly demonstrates the ascent into the hall.
One should know that entering the chamber and further practicing the various stages occurs later. This section discusses cultivation, yet it still pertains to the initial gateway of cultivation;

regarding realization, it is not without its initial stage of realization. Because the merit of perfect penetration has been achieved, one also enters and dwells [in the fruit] once faith is fulfilled.
Thus, while it is certainly incorrect to say that this section encompasses the entire stage of cultivation, it is likewise incorrect to say that this section...

Even the stage of non-attainment is not permissible. Therefore, this section now establishes the practice as belonging to *samādhi*, following the scriptural indications to enter deeply through a single gate, so that one may perhaps avoid those two faults. I do not know what those with discerning eyes will think of this.
[This section] is divided into two parts. First, selecting the faculty and entering directly; this has already been clarified several times previously. Regarding what is presented in this sutra...
Because this differs from the provisional and limited approaches, it relies solely on the faculties (*indriya*) rather than the consciousnesses (*vijñāna*).

Therefore, while previously the true beginning was revealed in the nature of the faculties, the present discussion of cultivation and realization concerns selecting the fundamental faculty for entry into perfect penetration (*pariniṣpanna-samyaktva*). This section is further divided into three parts.
First, Ānanda speaks by means of analogies to seek the gate of entry into realization. This also has four parts. First, he recounts and accepts the Buddha’s intent. This further has two parts.
First, he accepts the intent of opening the mind:
"World-Honored One, although I have now received such Dharma-sounds, I know that the Tathāgata-garbha, the wondrously enlightened and luminous mind, pervades the ten [directions]."
The "Spatial Realm" refers to the Tathāgata’s land of Pure Jewel Adornments, the Wondrous Enlightenment King, which nurtures and sustains the pure lands of the ten directions.
The previous passage spoke of the excellent opening of my mind; this section describes the characteristics of that mental opening.

It also comprehensively subsumes the power of the two complete divisions of the preceding section, clarifying that the essence of the mind is perfectly interfused, all-encompassing, and pervasive. Now, regarding what is...
Commentary: "The mind pervading the ten directions" refers to the pervasive intent; "nurturing the jewel-adorned lands" refers to the encompassing intent.
This indicates that one has attained great awakening through this faith and understanding, free from doubt. △ Second, receiving the instruction on the purpose of cultivation.
The Tathāgata further rebuked him, saying that his extensive learning was fruitless because he had not reached the stage of cultivation—“reaching” meaning to attain.
By recounting this, it is shown that the request to cultivate [the practice] is indeed in accordance with the Buddha’s intent.
△ Second, the main analogy regarding the gate of necessity.
I am now like a traveler who has suddenly been granted a magnificent mansion by the Heavenly King. Although I have obtained this great residence, I must enter it through its gates.

"Lu" (旅) refers to lodging on land; "po" (泊) refers to lodging on water. The *Chunqiu* (Spring and Autumn Annals) designates the King as "Heavenly" (*tian*). The translator has employed these terms accordingly.
The person is the sovereign. A deluded mind is like a traveler constantly dwelling in temporary lodgings; an awakened mind is like suddenly being granted a magnificent mansion.
This is a metaphor for the aforementioned mind that pervades all realms and contains all lands. Just as a house must have a door to be inhabited, the mind likewise requires a gate to enter.
This section provides an illustration; the following section applies the analogy to seek the gateway. △ Third, seeking the Buddha’s instruction has two parts:
first, universally seeking the path for entering the Great Vehicle.
I only pray that the Tathāgata will not abandon his great compassion, but will reveal to me and all those in this assembly who are shrouded in darkness,
so that they may cast aside the Lesser Vehicle and ultimately attain the path of the original aspiration for the nirvāṇa without remainder of one who knows the future.
"Being obscured" refers to looking out from outside the palace walls; it signifies that one ultimately and resolutely desires to attain [the goal], vowing never to stop.
"Nirvana with remainder" means that the followers of the Lesser Vehicle have ceased and severed the four abodes of views and afflictions (*dṛṣṭi-kleśa*), yet five abodes still remain.
The Tathāgata provisionally permits this as "nirvana with remainder," which is like a conjured city. Now, one wishes to advance toward the five...
Dwelling at the treasure-place of ultimate exhaustion, one therefore seeks the ancient path of the guide.
This joins with the previous description of the flowered mansion, for one now truly desires to obtain the gate and enter it. △ Second, specifically seeking the dhāraṇī of those still in training.

To cause those in training (*śaikṣa*) to subdue their former objects of attachment, attain *dhāraṇī*, and enter the Buddha’s knowledge and vision—this was specifically requested for those in training so that they might seek the expedient means of the initial mind and ensure its full completion.

Even those with the ignorance of the five stages (*pañca-vihāra-avidyā*) can likewise enter the gate. Below this, regarding perfect penetration, one first attains the path of the emptiness of persons (*pudgala-śūnyatā*) at the site of practice.

It can be clearly seen that only one fruit is permitted. As for "past攀緣 (pān-yuan)" [objects of clinging], this refers to the dualistic grasping at self and phenomena (*ātma-dharma-dvaya-grāha*) that has existed since beginningless time.

Although one has already awakened to and understood the views and knowledge through previous instructions, the reason one cannot enter [the state] is that these two types of grasping act as obstacles;
therefore, they must be subdued. The explanation of *dhāraṇī* is found in the second fascicle. A single thought-moment encompasses the three.

This is the method for entering the Perfect [Teaching] of the Treasuries. In the subsequent text, it says that by reversing the hearing in a single thought-moment (*ekacitta-kṣaṇa*) without laboring over various contemplations, until "tranquility manifests before one," one enters immediately through knowledge and vision. △ Fourth: A Prostrate Petition for Instruction.
Having spoken these words, he prostrated himself with his five limbs touching the ground; remaining in the assembly with a single mind, he awaited the Buddha’s compassionate instruction.
△ Second, the Tathāgata’s teaching on entering deeply through a single gate, divided into four parts. First, distinguishing the gates to determine two meanings.
Furthermore, there are two [sections]. First, opening the path for practice. Furthermore, there are two. First, identifying the capacity of the intended audience. This is further divided into two.
First, causing those present in the assembly to find peace of mind.
At that time, the World-Honored One, out of compassion for those among the assembly—both pratyekabuddhas and śrāvakas—who were not yet sovereign in their bodhicitta, singled them out for mention.
Although the Buddha’s mercy is universally extended to all, these two vehicles (the *śrāvaka* and *pratyekabuddha*) remain the primary audience; thus, he specifically highlights them.

This intention includes those still in training (*śaikṣa*), not only those beyond training (*aśaikṣa*). To "turn the small toward the great" refers to those of the two vehicles who have generated the bodhicitta. Not yet...
As for "those with mastery," this refers to those who have not yet found the gate through which to enter. △ Second, causing those of the future to resolve their minds [on enlightenment],
and for the sake of sentient beings in the Dharma-ending age after the parinirvāṇa of a future Buddha, causing them to give rise to the bodhicitta.
These sentient beings are not limited to ordinary worldlings and non-Buddhists; they also include those of the Hīnayāna. This is a mutual abbreviation that reflects upon the preceding section.
△ Second, clarifying the Dharma taught:
it opens the path of sublime practice for the Unsurpassed Vehicle (Anuttarayāna).

The Unsurpassed Vehicle is precisely the Single Buddha Vehicle. However, in terms of ultimate principle, the One Vehicle as the Common Teaching (*sādhāraṇa-dharma*) is still considered "with superior" (*sottara*);

it is only the One Vehicle as the Distinct Teaching (*asādhāraṇa-dharma*) that is truly "unsurpassed" (*anuttara*). The "Sublime Path of Practice" refers to the Perfect Penetration of the Ear-organ mentioned below.

Having concluded the opening of this path of practice, [the text proceeds to] △ Second, the Establishment of Doctrinal Gates, which is divided into three parts. First, the General Indication, which is further divided into two.
He single-mindedly resolved to seek it with diligence and proclaimed to Ānanda and the great assembly: "You all must resolutely resolve to attain Bodhicitta;
do not give rise to weariness regarding the wondrous samādhi of the Buddha-Tathāgata."
The followers of the Hīnayāna originally became weary midway through the five hundred *yojanas* and were content to linger at the conjured city.
Now, as if the conjured city has already vanished, they resolutely advance toward the place of treasure; therefore, they no longer feel weariness.
The wondrous *samādhi* is precisely the path for advancing toward the place of treasure. △ Second, the section on the meaning of teaching them to exhaustively investigate the mind.
One should first clarify the two meanings of the initial resolve for awakening, which is the arising of initial awakening from fundamental awakening.
"Initial resolve" refers to the right mindfulness that first arises when one begins cultivation.
"Resolve" means having a settled view and a settled reliance, free from hesitation. △ Second, the inquiry.
How are the two meanings of the initial mind determined?

△ Section Three: Determination. This is further divided into two parts. First, the determination that the cause is identical to the fruit, such that one enters *nirvāṇa* suddenly by clearing away turbidity.
The four characters "the cause is identical to the fruit" constitute the primary thesis of this first determination. "Clearing away turbidity" [is the second].

...and so forth; this is precisely the purport of this school. It is said that one must necessarily ensure that cause and effect correspond because, if cause and effect were dissimilar, one could not clarify turbidity and attain *nirvāṇa*. This is clearly visible in the scriptural text.
However, this principle is concise in wording yet profound in meaning. Its profundity lies in the fact that it extends all the way to the severing [of afflictions] by the Tathāgata.

"Result" (*phala*) refers to the ultimate and final realization. Furthermore, although this passage mentions both cause and result, its intent is to briefly clarify the remoteness of the realization of the result;

it does not compare [this result] to the fruit of the Small Vehicle’s teaching on the city, which merely corresponds to the seventh stage of faith (*śraddhā*) in the Perfect Teaching, nor does it compare it to the fruit of the Initial Teaching’s "gill-fish" stage, which merely stops at the second practice (*caryā*) of the Perfect Teaching. This is because those [stages] all involve birth...

Taking the extinction of the consciousness-mind as the fundamental cause for cultivation, yet because the cause and effect are not identical, one cannot reach the eternal fruit of Buddhahood from afar.
Therefore, it is necessary first to explain this primary determination. This principle is most subtle; it is divided into three parts.

First, one should examine with thorough scrutiny. This is further divided into two parts: first, examining by penetrating the essence, which involves directly investigating the cause and effect through diligent inquiry.
This is further divided into three parts: first, designating the root and turning the mind.

Ānanda, as for the primary meaning: if you wish to cast aside the vehicle of the śrāvakas, cultivate the bodhisattva vehicle, and enter the Buddha’s knowledge and vision—this bodhisattva vehicle does not fall within the three vehicles;
rather, it is the perfect and sudden One Vehicle. The Buddha’s knowledge and vision are detailed [in this].
In the section on the Three Pitakas: △ Second, to cause one to examine similarities and differences.
One should carefully observe whether the mind generated at the stage of the cause and the awakening at the stage of the fruition are identical or different.
△ A third time he resolved that they must be identical:

"Ānanda, if, during the stage of the causal ground, one takes a mind subject to arising and ceasing as the fundamental cause for cultivation, yet seeks the Buddha-vehicle of non-arising and non-ceasing,
such a thing is impossible."
Neither arising nor ceasing is precisely the wondrous virtue of nirvāṇa. Among the four virtues, "permanence" is cited as the essential;
this clarifies that the causes of arising and ceasing cannot constitute the fruit of true permanence. △ Second, the analogy for observing the world. As for those who observe the world:
Observe all phenomena by means of analogy. This is divided into two parts. First, regarding the examination of the world:
for this reason, you should illuminate the various vessel-worlds (*bhājanaloka*).
This is because of the cause. This principle refers to the principle that cause and effect must correspond. This phrase connects the preceding section to the following one.
"Illuminating the world" means observing universally the categories of the permanent and the impermanent, and examining them therein.

This phrase briefly indicates the subsequent section, which will then provide a detailed exposition of the method of contemplation. △ Second, the instruction to apply this analogy to observation, which is further divided into:
Second: First, contemplate that whatever is conditioned must perish.
All phenomena that can be produced are subject to transformation and extinction. Ānanda, observe the conditioned phenomena of the world:
which among them does not decay?

The first sentence briefly introduces all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛta-dharma*). The second sentence states that the Buddha has previously definitively determined them all to belong to the category of impermanence, namely, being like a dream, an illusion, a bubble, or a shadow.
"Ānanda," and so forth, instructs him to examine them in detail to verify whether this is indeed the case.
△ Second, observing that the unconditioned is indestructible.

Yet, one never hears of empty space being decomposed or destroyed. Why is this? Because space is not something that can be produced; therefore, from beginning to end, it is subject neither to decay nor cessation.

The first two lines borrow the analogy of empty space to elucidate the category of the eternal; the subsequent two lines further provide an inquiry and explanation regarding its non-existence [of decay].
As for the cause, the final two lines definitively establish that it is ultimately indestructible. This merely borrows the example of space to clarify the intended meaning:
if one seeks the indestructible causal mind, one must take the nature of non-action (*anabhisaṃskāra*) as the standard; one should not again employ the mind of arising and ceasing.
"Arising and ceasing" refers specifically to the consciousness-mind (*vijñāna-citta*), whereas the wondrous nature of non-action is the perfect clarity within the sense-faculties (*indriya*).

It is the nature of non-arising and non-ceasing. Having completed the formal contemplation [of this], △ second, to clarify the title of the section intended for removal and to reveal the purpose of the coming scriptural text:
One must inquire as to why, in the preceding passage, the nature of non-arising and non-ceasing was necessarily taken as the causal mind;
for it is because the ocean of the sentient beings' minds currently manifests as the five turbidities.

Turbid and agitated, it is never clear and still. Now, if one wishes to clarify it in order to attain the wondrous virtue of *nirvāṇa*, it is impossible unless one takes the perfect, profound, and unchanging nature as the causal mind.

Therefore, this section first clarifies the turbidity to be eliminated, while the subsequent text demonstrates the nature that can eliminate it, teaching the method for what to discard and what to adopt. This is the intent of this sutra.

This is the structural outline of the text. It is divided into two parts. First, a general demonstration of the five turbidities (*pañca-kaṣāya*).孤山 (Gushan) says: "The five turbidities in the present text are fundamentally different from those in other sutras.

In other sutras, the view-turbidity is established with the five sharp afflictions (*pañca-tīkṣṇa-kleśa*) as its essence, and the affliction-turbidity is established with the five dull afflictions (*pañca-manda-kleśa*) as its essence;

together, these constitute the ten underlying tendencies (*daśānuśaya*). Sentient beings merely grasp at the retributive fruits of these views and conceits, and thus this provisional designation is established."

Life (*āyus*) takes as its essence the maintenance of the physical and mental aggregates (*rūpa-citta*) throughout a single period; because it crushes the years and shortens the lifespan, it is called the turbidity of life. An eon (*kalpa*) has no separate essence;
it is simply named the turbidity of the eon (*kalpa-kaṣāya*) because the four turbidities gather together during that time. The present text is not like this;

rather, it defines the five turbidities based on the delusive thoughts of the five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*). Therefore, the subsequent passage states that within the aggregate of form (*rūpa-skandha*) there is "delusive solidity."

The aggregates of perception and feeling include such things as "empty clarity" and "deluded thoughts. This explanation of the current turbidity still relies on an inference based on later passages and is not yet thorough.

Now, according to the original text, it is simply a matter of casting the "great earth" of space and so forth into the "water" of the perfectly clear and tranquil seeing-faculty and so forth, thereby causing the seeing-faculty and others to become fragmented and disordered. That which is neither perfect nor tranquil is the very substance of turbidity.
Furthermore, this is divided into two parts. First, identifying the essence of turbidity:
The ocean of the mind is profoundly still, yet that which muddies it from within is the five great elements (*mahābhūta*), which constitute its actual substance.

Now, although both the external five great elements and the internal four great elements are equally turbid in nature, it is specifically the internal four great elements that most acutely press upon birth and death and utterly obstruct *nirvāṇa*.

Indeed. Therefore, it is in this subsequent section that there is much discussion regarding the elements within the body. Furthermore, there are three parts. First, the explanation of the four great elements within the body:
that which has the characteristic of solidity is earth; moisture is water; warmth is fire; and movement is wind.

The characteristic of solidity refers to things such as bone and flesh; the characteristic of moisture and so forth can be understood accordingly. Within the ocean of the mind, these things originally do not exist.

It is only from the binding of darkness into form, down to the conceptualization of characteristics into a body, that one is consequently turbidified by these objects and can no longer remain limpid for long.
△ Second, showing the partitioning of perfect luminosity.
Due to these four entanglements (*paryavasthāna*), they divide your profoundly still and perfect, wondrously enlightened, luminous mind into seeing, hearing, sensing, and cognizing.
That which is fundamentally free from turbidity is called "profoundly still" (*zhan*); that which is fundamentally free from partition is called "perfect" (*yuan*).
