Here, "sensing" (*jue*) and "mind" (*xin*) are mentioned together as both name and essence. Sensing is the essence of the mind; because it is perfect and unpartitioned, there is fundamentally a mutual integration between them.
It is wondrous; therefore, it is called "wondrous awakening" (*miao-jue*). "Mind" (*xin*) is a name for awakening. Because it is profound and not turbid, it possesses an innate, penetrating clarity;
therefore, it is called "clarifying the mind" (*ming-xin*). Possessing this profound, luminous, perfect, and wondrous nature is the state of original oneness.
When it is divided by the four great elements, this original state is entirely lost; there remains only the seeing of the eyes and so forth, up to the discernment of the intellect.
Turbidity creates separation; the originally limpid and perfect essence no longer remains. "Awakening" encompasses the three faculties of nose, tongue, and body, totaling the six sense organs.
△ Third, concluding the turbidities and indicating their number.
From beginning to end, the five turbidities are conflated. Regarding "beginning and end":

according to the subsequent text, it begins with the turbidity of the eon (*kalpa-kaṣāya*) and ends with the turbidity of life (*āyuṣ-kaṣāya*). △ Second, the turbid characteristics are clarified through analogy.
"What is meant by turbidity? Ānanda, it is like clear water, which is pure and pristine by nature. Then there are things such as dust, soil, ash, and sand, whose very essence is obstructive.
These two entities are such by their inherent nature that their qualities do not accord with one another.

Suppose there is a person in the world who takes that dust and soil and throws it into the pure water. The soil loses its obstructive quality, and the water loses its purity; their appearance becomes turbid. This is what is called [turbidity]."
It constitutes turbidity. Your five layers of turbidity are likewise so.
"Kindred" refers to their common category. "Obstruction" means having a physical mass. "Dharma-nature" (dharmatā) refers to the originally fixed characteristic from the very beginning.
"Mutually not following" (*xiāng bù xún*) means mutually not interfering with one another. "Earth losing its obstructive retention" (*tǔ shī liú ài*) refers to the dispersal of material forms.
The character *gǔ* (汩) is composed of the radicals for "sun" and "water," meaning it is like the reflection of the sun in water—darkly turbulent and unstable.

This concludes the general demonstration of the five turbidities (*pañca-kaṣāya*). △ Second, the specific demonstration of the five turbidities. This specific [demonstration] is the particularization within the aforementioned general [demonstration]. As for what is...

The demonstration of the various turbidities (*kaṣāya*) differs slightly from the previous general exposition. In the general section, it concerned only the internal four great elements (*mahābhūta*).

Now, in this second specific section concerning the turbidity of views (*dṛṣṭi-kaṣāya*), the remaining four turbidities include both the external five great elements and further combine the objects of mental consciousness (*dharmadhātu*), birth and death, and the six sense faculties (*ṣaḍindriya*).
However, the objects of mental consciousness are but reflections of the four great elements; [birth and] death...
Death is the conjunction and separation of the four great elements (*mahābhūta*); the six sense faculties (*ṣaḍindriya*) are the divisions of these four great elements.

Thus, within the general discussion, the intent regarding the four great elements and the six sense faculties is already largely exhausted. Within the specific discussion as well, external factors are few while internal ones are many; this should be examined in detail.
It is divided into five parts. First is the turbidity of the eon (*kalpa-kaṣāya*).
Ānanda, you see that empty space pervades the worlds of the ten directions; yet space and seeing are not distinct. Space exists but has no substance; seeing exists but has no awareness.
These interweave to falsely form [this world]. This is the first layer, called the turbidity of the eon.
Gushan said: "This turbidity depends upon the aggregate of form.

One should know that, generally speaking, 'turbidity' refers to the fact that while the fundamental seeing, hearing, sensing, and knowing are like clear water, the four internal great elements and the five external great elements are all like ash and sand.
Among these, the five external great elements turbidify the four natures; thus, the great elements and the natures each have their own shadows."

In brief, the "nature" (xing) refers to seeing as a representative example to cast light upon hearing and the other senses; the "great" (da) refers to emptiness as a representative example to cast light upon earth and the other elements.

The reason for singling out seeing and emptiness specifically is that both seeing and emptiness are each all-pervasive yet lack intrinsic substance (*svabhāva*), and thus their falsely interwoven appearances are easily clarified.
The first two phrases refer to the aggregate of form (*rūpa-skandha*) as the basis [of consciousness], for emptiness is its counterpart.
First, it is because of the manifestation of color. Regarding "seeing emptiness below," this refers to seeing emptiness, which is precisely the essence of turbidity.
"Having emptiness but no substance" means that while empty space can be seen, it cannot be grasped, as it lacks any solid form or mass.
"Having seeing but no sensation" means that although the seeing pervades all of space, there is no perception of sensations such as cold or warmth, just as when one looks into the midst of space.
It is like having fire that is seen but whose heat is not perceived. "Interwoven" means it is like warp and woof woven so densely that they cannot be separated.
"Falsely formed" means that although there are originally no two distinct characteristics, this false interweaving is nevertheless produced.

The final two phrases conclude by establishing the name "turbidity. The reason it is called the *kalpa-turbidity* (*kalpa-kaṣāya*) is precisely because within this state, all four great elements are simultaneously involved.

Mountains, rivers, and so forth undergo the kalpas of formation, abiding, destruction, and emptiness. Furthermore, this represents how sentient beings, from beginningless time, have been obscured by their own ignorance;
at the moment they become "empty," they immediately enter the kalpa-turbidity (*kalpa-kaṣāya*), which is not like the conventional view that it occurs after one hundred years.

If the ancient explanations were unclear or merely abbreviated, then the nature and the great elements would each be deficient. How could an "emptiness" devoid of substance still be considered a primordial unity?
[Question: "But when earth, water, and so forth are ablaze, are they not likewise turbid?

Furthermore, after the clarification of turbidity, does the nature that clarifies clarify only the faculty of sight and not hearing and the others? And does the turbidity that settles settle only in emptiness and not in earth and the others?
[Response: Please savor these words carefully; you should believe them to be true. 2. The Turbidity of Views (Dṛṣṭi-kāṣāya).

Your body currently manifests as being composed of the four great elements. Sight, hearing, awareness, and cognition obstruct and confine one another; water, fire, wind, and earth revolve to produce these cognitions.
Interwoven together, they falsely constitute existence. This is the second layer, called the turbidity of views.

Gushan said: "This turbidity depends upon the aggregate of sensation (*vedanā-skandha*). Within the profound and perfect [state], there was originally no physical form composed of the four great elements;

now, by clenching these four great elements together, it is made manifest. Thus, it constitutes the second layer of turbidity. The first two phrases refer to the aggregate of sensation upon which it depends.
'Clenching' (*po*) is precisely sensation; it is the act of receiving and taking in as the objective field of the body. From 'seeing and hearing' onwards, the turbidity is explicitly demonstrated."
"Substance" (*tǐ*) refers to that which is obstructed and partitioned. "Obstruction" (*liú'ài*) refers to being stagnant within form.

This means that while the four *dhātus* (elements) are fundamentally free from stagnation and obstruction, they become obstructed by the four *bhūtas* (great elements); thus, that which was without stagnation and obstruction comes to possess them.

"Revolution" (*xuán*) refers to being gathered into a self-substance. While the four *bhūtas* are fundamentally devoid of cognition, they are revolved by the four *dhātus*. [That which was] without...
As for "the one who perceives," there is indeed perception. As for "interwoven by delusion," it is like a single warp and a single woof woven so densely that they cannot be separated;
likewise, consciousness and non-consciousness are blended together without distinction, becoming as if interwoven.
The final two phrases conclude with the name of "turbidity. Regarding the turbidity of views (*dṛṣṭi-kaṣāya*), it is because of the four great elements...
Originally, insentient objects do not possess [feeling]. It is through the weaving of delusion that even the point of a needle or the prick of a blade of grass is experienced as pain.
For this reason, sentient beings firmly give rise to the view of self (*ātman-dṛṣṭi*), which serves as the king of all views; the sixty-two views are all subsumed under it.
This is called the turbidity of views (*dṛṣṭi-kaṣāya*). △ Third, the turbidity of afflictions (*kleśa-kaṣāya*).

Furthermore, within your mind, the nature of recollection, cognition, chanting, and study gives rise to knowing and seeing, allowing the six sense objects to appear. Apart from the objects there are no forms;
apart from awareness there is no nature. These forms and awareness interweave to falsely constitute existence. This is the third layer, called the turbidity of afflictions (*kleśa-kaṣāya*).
Gushan says: "This turbidity relies upon the *saṃjñā-skandha* (the aggregate of perception). The first two lines refer to the *saṃjñā-skandha* as the basis of reliance. Changshui says:
"Recalling past objects, cognizing present sensory fields, and reciting future objects. The lines beginning with "Its nature arises" (*xing fa*) correctly demonstrate the essence of the turbidity;
for while the *saṃjñā-skandha* is merely the basis of reliance, the essence of the turbidity that relies upon it is further the *dharma-viṣaya* (mental objects).

Gushan said: "The nature gives rise to cognition and vision" refers to the subject that grasps the six perceptions; "allowing the six objects to appear" refers to the characteristics of the six objects as they are grasped.
The "six perceptions" are the deluded cognitions of the six consciousnesses. The "six objects" consist of the five present sensory objects and the mental object (dharmadhātu) of the past and future.
"Apart from the objects there are no characteristics" means that if one's awareness is separated from the six objects, then that awareness has no [objective] form.

Regarding "their own-characteristics (svalakṣaṇa) are devoid of intrinsic nature apart from cognition": this means that if objects were separated from deluded cognition, the objects would have no self-essence.
These two factors depend upon one another; if one is removed, both vanish. Indeed, there has never been a cognition apart from an object, nor an object apart from cognition.
"Interwoven to form delusion" means that since objects and cognition cannot be separated, they are like warp and woof.
They are densely interwoven and cannot be separated. The final two phrases establish the name of the *kaṣāya* (impurity). "Fán" means agitation; "rǎo" means weariness.

Because sensory objects fill the mind, there is never a time when one is not weary and agitated; thus, it is called the *kleśa-kaṣāya* (impurity of afflictions). △ Fourth, the *sattva-kaṣāya* (impurity of sentient beings).
Furthermore, you arise and perish morning and evening without ceasing; your perceptions and views constantly desire to remain in this world, while the movement of karma perpetually shifts the lands.
These factors interweave to form delusion; this is the fourth layer, called the turbidity of sentient beings.

Gushan said: "This turbidity arises within the *saṃskāra-skandha* (the aggregate of formations). The first two lines refer to the *saṃskāra-skandha* as the basis, indicating the constant flux from moment to moment.
The lines beginning with 'knowledge and vision' (*jñāna-darśana*) specifically demonstrate the essence of the turbidity.

However, while the *saṃskāra-skandha* serves merely as the basis, the essence of the turbidity is further the cycle of birth and death (*saṃsāra*). This is because, within the profound and perfect [nature], there is fundamentally no birth or death. (As stated above)
Because the three turbidities encompass both the vessel-world and the body-mind, within this shifting vessel-world and the continuity of body and mind, there thus arise boundless births and deaths.
Those who wish to remain as they know and see [the truth] are born according to their habitual tendencies; yet among ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*), there are none who do not crave life.
As the movement of karma constantly shifts, death follows the flow of transformation; yet among ordinary beings, there is no portion of freedom.
"Mutually interwoven and falsely formed" means that one remains while the other migrates; it is like a warp and a woof woven so closely together that they cannot be separated.
The final two phrases conclude by establishing the name "turbidity. Because of this, one transmigrates through the seven realms of existence.
They manifest and transform the appearances of all sentient beings; therefore, it is called the turbidity of sentient beings (*sattva-kaṣāya*).

△ Fifth, the turbidity of lifespan (*āyuḥ-kaṣāya*): You who see and hear [me] are originally of no different nature. Yet, separated by the various sensory dusts, you give rise to differences without cause. Within your true nature, you know one another.

Functioning amidst mutual opposition, the criteria for identity and difference are lost; they interweave to form delusion. This is the fifth layer, called the turbidity of life (*āyus-kāṣāya*). Guishan says:
"This turbidity relies upon the *vijñāna-skandha* (consciousness-aggregate). The first two phrases also point to this relied-upon consciousness-aggregate."

However, this refers specifically to the eighth consciousness and does not include the first six. This is because the non-discriminative seeing and hearing within the sense organs (*indriya*) are precisely the "seeing-division" (*darśana-bhāga*) of the eighth consciousness.
Here, the distinction between identity and difference within the turbid substance is fundamentally made in reference to the sense organs, not the consciousnesses.

[Question: Since the preceding "turbidity of views" (*dṛṣṭi-kāluṣya*) was defined in relation to the body, it would seem to already encompass the sense organs; is this not redundant? [Answer: That [preceding definition] took the internal four great elements as the general characteristic of the body to manifest the view of self (*ātma-dṛṣṭi*) as the turbidity of views. This [present definition], however, takes the specific characteristics of the six sense organs to manifest their state of discordance [with reality].

Regarding the turbidity of lifespan (*āyuṣka-kaṣāya*), both the general and specific expositions do not consider it a primary [defilement]. Question: The ancient commentaries point to the six consciousnesses; why do you now reject that? Is it that the six consciousnesses alone are not turbid within the profound and perfect [nature]? Answer:

Within the turbidity of afflictions (*kleśa-kaṣāya*), it is established entirely based on the conceptualizations of the six consciousnesses. How could objects (*viṣaya*) themselves be able to constitute afflictions? Nevertheless, if this turbidity must be attributed to the consciousnesses, it applies only to the first five, because the sixth lacks the quality of "intermediate transition" (*vyavakiraṇa*) and is thus categorized separately within the turbidity of afflictions.

This also seems to be a brief explanation. However, based on the later Buddha’s clarification regarding the delusion of "one and six," and his principle of revealing the essence through the six sense faculties while showing that their functions are turned away from it, this appears highly reliable. Furthermore, since the basis is already the *vijñāna-skandha* (aggregate of consciousness), and the dependent is likewise consciousness, it would be self-reliant yet self-contradictory if it were not so;

let the wise judge this. [The phrase] "underneath the various objects" correctly indicates the turbid essence. Regarding "producing differences through separation": *(Note: This translation assumes the context of the *Śrīmālādevī-siṃhanāda-sūtra* or related commentaries on the nature of the *ālaya-vijñāna* and the *vijñāna-skandha*, where the "turbid essence" refers to the underlying ignorance or defilement within the aggregates.)*

That is to say, the four great elements combine to form the six sense organs; they isolate seeing and hearing so that each does not communicate with the others. The next two phrases establish their identity and difference:
in terms of their essential nature (*svabhāva*), their substance, and their mutual cognition, they appear identical rather than different;

yet in terms of their active functions, they oppose one another, thus being different rather than identical. Whether identical or different, these two cannot be fixed; hence it is said, "the standard is lost. As for their mutual...
That which is woven from delusion is also characterized by identity and difference. Just as when one warp and one woof are woven together densely, they cannot be separated.

The final two phrases conclude the definition of the "impurity" (turbidity). As for why it is called the impurity of life (*āyuṣka-kaṣāya*): it is simply because the six sense faculties are bound and obstructed;
life is entrusted to their midst, and since both essence and function lack autonomy, this constitutes the impurity of life. Alternatively...

When the faculties and their objects coalesce, life is sustained; when the faculties and their objects disperse, life departs. This is also a general principle. Discussing this from a higher perspective:
the wondrously enlightened, luminous mind is solely a single, profound, and perfect stillness; since it possesses neither interior nor exterior, how could there be any turbidity?
Now, since the self-obscuration that constitutes emptiness, it is externally submerged by the five great elements of the vessel-world, becoming the turbidity of the kalpa (*kalpa-kaṣāya*).
Slightly more internally, it is submerged by the physical characteristics of the four great elements, becoming the turbidity of views (*dṛṣṭi-kaṣāya*).

Further internally, it is submerged by the shadow-like reflections of the six sense objects, becoming the turbidity of afflictions (*kleśa-kaṣāya*). Consequently, the body and mind are interrupted and flow on through the realms.
Furthermore, it is turbidified by birth and death, becoming the turbidity of sentient beings (*sattva-kaṣāya*).

In terms of these four phases, both the internal and external are uniformly turbid, and the meaning of "clarity" (*zhan*) is entirely lost. Moreover, because of this, the various defilements become entangled and obstructed, so that the six sense faculties no longer function with harmonious integration.
In terms of this single phase, the meaning of "perfection" (*yuan*) is entirely lost. Therefore, one desires to restore the original state of clarity and perfection.
One must seek the method for clarifying turbidity; therefore, the subsequent text teaches the clarification of turbidity.

Having completed the explanation of what is to be removed, [the third section follows]: "Removing through the method of selection. In the preceding section, the turbidity to be removed was first shown; in this section, the method capable of removing it is next shown.
The removal of defilements depends upon the discernment of what to exclude and what to adopt. If this discernment is not clear, and...
If one’s grasping and rejecting are inverted, then turbidity cannot be eliminated, and the profound stillness and perfection can never be restored. This is divided into four parts.
First, showing the desire for sudden realization:
"Ānanda, you now wish to cause your seeing, hearing, awareness, and cognition to reach far back in accord with the Tathāgata’s permanence, bliss, self, and purity."

Seeing, hearing, smelling, tasting, touching, and cognizing—these are presently possessed by sentient beings; the nature within their six sense faculties is precisely Original Enlightenment (*mūla-bodhi*).

Perpetuity, bliss, self, and purity—this is the *nirvāṇa* without remainder of the Tathāgata, which is Ultimate Enlightenment (*atyanta-bodhi*). This is explained in the section on the "Perfectly Endowed Treasury of Emptiness.

Thus, although the profound and perfect Original Enlightenment of ordinary beings is identical to that of the Buddhas, because they possess the turbidity of sentient beings (*sattva-kaṣāya*), [it remains obscured].

Because one transmigrates through birth and death, one loses true permanence. Because there is the turbidity of afflictions (*kleśa-kaṣāya*), the objects of the mind (*dharmaviṣaya*) are vexed and disturbed;
thus, one loses true bliss. Because there is the turbidity of the eon (*kalpa-kaṣāya*), the realm of space is insentient; thus, one loses true self.

Because there are the turbidities of views (*dṛṣṭi-kaṣāya*) and life-span (*āyuḥ-kaṣāya*), the sense organs and the physical body are impure; thus, one loses true purity. This is according to their specific meanings. If, however, one considers them collectively:
In the case of the *xiang* (characteristics), each of the five turbidities simultaneously loses four virtues; therefore, they are vastly different from the meritorious virtues of the Buddha-fruit.

Now, if one wishes to immediately use these four natures—which possess the five turbidities—to remotely accord with the Tathāgata’s four virtues and thereby suddenly realize the ultimate fruit, this is truly the most supreme dharma-gate. 2. Determining What to Reject and What to Adopt.
One should first select the root of birth and death, which is established upon the nature of non-arising and non-ceasing, perfect and profound stillness.
"Selecting" means to discern and discard what is not to be used. The root of birth and death is precisely the consciousness-mind of the six sense bases;

however, at the beginning of the sutra, these were refuted through seven rounds of analysis to reveal that they are entirely not it. All heterodox schools, worldly paths, provisional teachings, and those of the Lesser Vehicle take this [consciousness] as their basis, yet they err.
These confused practices all result in causes that do not correspond to their effects; they are now decisively selected out and discarded.
This is because when the two kinds of roots were previously distinguished before the Buddha, this very mind was identified as the root of birth-and-death; thus it is known to be so.
That which is the unarisen and undying, perfectly湛 (zhan) and profound nature, is precisely what is inherent within the faculties, as revealed in the first ten sections of the Sūtra.
It reveals the clarity of the analysis of the two views: that which is proximate possesses the six sense faculties, while that which is remote encompasses the myriad dharmas.
All heterodox schools, worldly paths, and those of provisional or limited capacity are ignorant of this, remaining unaware even as they employ it daily. Now, we decisively adopt and rely upon it;
this is because the Buddha himself judged this nature to be the fundamentally pure essence of bodhi and nirvana. Thus, one should know it to be so. If this is the case, then...
The text’s preceding and succeeding passages summon and respond to one another, with its internal logic thoroughly interconnected; it is a most sublime principle.
The old commentaries fail to reach the fundamental root of birth and death, yet they arbitrarily label it the "functional activity of the five turbidities.

They further establish the nature of perfect stillness as their own "three gates of śamatha and vipaśyanā," entirely disregarding that such things already exist within the sūtra itself. Not only are these mere conjectures lacking any basis, but they also contradict the original scripture.
If that were so, the previous instructions would all become useless. Yet, how could those previous instructions not be relevant to this practice?
Examine this carefully. △ Third, subduing and severing through grasping. This has two parts. First, the method (dharma). This is further divided into two.
First, one achieves the ground of subduing.

By using profound stillness to revolve against the false and extinguish birth, one subdues the flow of delusion and returns to original enlightenment, thereby attaining the fundamental, luminous awareness that is devoid of the nature of arising and ceasing.
Regarding "as the mind of the causal ground":

the character *chéng* (成就, accomplished) in the preceding section is used merely as a verbal suffix; it properly refers to accomplishing this causal ground as well as the subsequent fruit-ground. *Yǐ* (以) means "by means of.
*Zhàn* (湛) refers to the aforementioned nature of perfect stillness that is neither arising nor ceasing. In relation to what precedes, it is the Tathāgata.
The nature of seeing (*darśana-svabhāva*) thus demonstrated is, in its ultimate sense, identical to the nature of hearing (*śravaṇa-svabhāva*) employed by Avalokiteśvara.
Its essence is fundamentally tranquil and immovable. This is verified by the preceding passage on the fingers and the flying light, as well as the subsequent passage on the striking of the bell.
It is the fundamental nature that is unmoving, unwavering, unborn, and unceasing. The extinction and arising of the false and illusory constitute the aforementioned five turbidities;
these are, in total, the deluded phenomena of birth and cessation. To revolve [the mind] through profound stillness is as stated in the subsequent text:

"If one abandons birth and cessation and maintains true permanence, the light of constancy will manifest before you, and the faculties, objects, consciousnesses, and the mind will dissolve away in their proper time. This is it.
Furthermore, the five turbidities are nothing more than the sense organs, objects, and consciousnesses.

To subdue [the delusions] and restore the original luminous awareness as the mind of the causal stage precisely signifies that within the cause, one takes the fundamental, true, and eternal as the cause, rather than taking that which is subject to arising and ceasing. This is explained according to the following analogy.
This appears to be the fulfillment of the mind of the ten levels of faith; it shall be further clarified when we reach the section on the "Parable of the City.
II. Severing [delusions] and entering the stage of fruition, after which one fully perfects the cultivation and realization of the stage of fruition.

From this initial stage (*prathama-bhūmi*) up to the stage of Equal Enlightenment (*samayakabodhi*), these constitute the cultivation of the ground of fruition; Perfect Enlightenment (*samyaksambodhi*) constitutes the realization of the ground of fruition. Question:
It was previously stated that once one has arisen within the five turbidities (*pañca-kaṣāya*), the four virtues have already been lost.

How can there still be this nature of perfect clarity and stillness (*pariśuddha-vyapagata-sthiti*) capable of establishing both the cause and the fruition stages? Answer: Although the five turbidities pervasively disturb it, the perfect clarity and stillness remains like space.

The Middle Kingdom has always been fundamentally void and non-existent. Although its perfect clarity is disturbed by the pervasive turbidity of the five defilements, it remains as unmoving and sovereign as the great void of space.
People merely delude themselves into abandoning this perfect clarity, instead taking the arising-and-ceasing mind within the five defilements as their cause.
In the end, they are unable to clarify the various turbidities; thus, this teaching is said to be a failure. But how could it truly be a failure? △ Second, the analogies. This also has two parts.
First, the analogy for subduing [the mind] to establish the ground of practice (*yindi*).
It is like settling turbid water by storing it in a still vessel; when it is deep and motionless, the sand and soil naturally sink, and the clear water appears before one.
This is called the initial subduing of adventitious afflictions.
The five turbidities cloud the [faculty of] views and so forth;

within the perfectly tranquil and profound nature, they universally manifest as the illusory signs of extinction and birth, just as silt and soil turbidity universally manifest the form of murkiness within clear water. Therefore, one must revolve the profound stillness to subdue delusion.
It is like using a still vessel to clarify water. The "still vessel" refers to the fundamental nature within the sense faculties (*indriya*).

In reality, the subsequent passage on "turning the hearing back toward its own nature" refers to being still, profound, and unmoving. "Gradually attaining the two kinds of emptiness" refers to the sand and soil settling of their own accord.
The final two lines provide the names of the objects to correspond with the analogy. [Jué] Li said: "The adventitious afflictions (*āgantuka-kleśa*) are explained in all the sūtras and śāstras."
This constitutes the afflictive hindrance (*kleśāvaraṇa*). Tiantai designates this as the "view-delusions and thought-delusions" within the realm of transmigration.

According to the Hīnayāna teachings, the stage where one first subdues these view-delusions and thought-delusions corresponds to the level of the Seven Sages; if one were to equate this with the "contemplative practice" (*guanxing*) of the Perfect Teaching, it would seem far too inferior.

Now, examining the intent of the sutra, it is only when one advances to sever the fundamental ignorance (*mūlāvidyā*) that it is said one severs view-delusions and thought-delusions. Although the delusions of dust and sand (*rajomaśa*) may also be severed [at this point],...

It is likewise stated simply as "subduing" (*fu*). Thus we know that the initial subduing of adventitious defilements must refer to one who has fulfilled the stage of faith (*śraddhā-pūrṇa*), having already severed the two delusions and also subdued ignorance (*avidyā*).
The Buddha’s words are given according to what is appropriate; do not be dogmatically attached to them. Furthermore, the *Wénshǐ Pútián* (Guanyin) Sūtra says:

"When birth-and-death is extinguished, quiescent extinction manifests. This corresponds to what is here called "revolving the false, extinguishing birth, and subduing [the mind] back [to its source]."

The fundamental awakening possesses a nature that is without arising or ceasing. What is the distinction in meaning between these two expressions? △ Second, the metaphor for severing [delusion] and entering the stage of fruition:
removing the mud so that there is pure water is called the permanent severance of fundamental ignorance.
The sand that was previously settled has not yet been removed; this is used as a metaphor for ignorance (*avidyā*) being suppressed but not yet severed.
Thus, the removal of the mud is a metaphor for severing ignorance. The clear water that appeared before is used as a metaphor for original enlightenment (*mūla-bodhi*) being limpid but not yet pure.
Thus, the pure water is a metaphor for ultimate, purified awakening. The final two lines provide the names and apply them accordingly.

Commentary: Jueli says that fundamental ignorance (*mūlāvidyā*) is described in various sutras and śāstras as the obstruction to what is known (*jñeyāvaraṇa*), the obstruction to wisdom (*jñānāvaraṇa*), and so forth;
Tiantai designates it as the "viewing and thinking" (*dṛṣṭi-kāma*) of the realm beyond. This [designation] also does not distinguish between the two aspects of dust-like and fundamental ignorance.
Examining the scriptural text now, since it states both "permanently severed" and "fundamental," it is clear this refers to the first stage (*prathamabhūmi*).

When the various afflictions to be abandoned have been eliminated, and even the arising marks of the state of Equal Enlightenment are exhausted without remainder, this is precisely the Tathāgata’s nirvāṇa without remainder.
How could the attainment of the fruit not be far off? For the subduing and severance [of afflictions] has already been completed. △ Fourth, the conclusion and verification of the ultimate fruit.
The luminous marks are pure and refined; all transformations and manifestations do not constitute afflictions, for they all accord with the pure and wondrous virtues of *nirvāṇa*.
Regarding "the luminous marks are pure and refined," as Qīngliáng stated: "Possessing ten thousand virtues, it is vast and free from even the slightest speck of dust. Gūshān said:
"All transformations and manifestations" refers to the manifestation of forms within the ten realms according to the responses of sentient beings' capacities. As for the ultimate principle:
They continue to manifest as the physical world, the body, and the mind, even manifesting as dwelling within birth and death;
yet their six sense faculties are mutually interfused, none of which are turbid, all becoming the unimpeded nirvana of wondrous function.

This is truly because, in the past, delusion gave rise to attachment to the self and phenomena, causing them all to become turbid and obstructed; now, with delusion exhausted and attachment empty, they are seen as manifestations of the mind alone.
It is sovereign and unimpeded; therefore, there is nothing that is not sublime virtue (*guṇa*). It is like when the mud has been exhausted and the water becomes pure:

no matter how much it is stirred, it will never become turbid again. This section fully reveals cause and effect. If one attains the ultimate fruit together [with the cause], it is not like the provisional teaching where the cause and effect differ, such as halting at the city of the *śrāvaka* on the way.
The sublime virtue of *nirvāṇa* is precisely permanence, bliss, self, and purity; it encompasses everything without exception.

Regarding the phrase "all ten thousand virtues are unified": it signifies the principle of encountering the source from either the left or the right, whether proceeding in accordance with nature or against it.
This concludes the meaning of definitively equating cause with fruit and suddenly entering nirvana by clarifying turbidity. II.

The Meaning of Definitively Untying the Knots from the Roots to Shed Entanglements and Suddenly Enter Perfect Penetration. "Untying the knots from the roots" refers precisely to the second determination.

This is the core principle [of this school]. Liberation from entanglements and the like is precisely the ultimate aim of this school. This refers to the reason why one must necessarily untie the knots from the root:
for if one does not proceed from the root, one cannot liberate oneself from entanglements and enter perfect penetration (*yuan-tong*) instantaneously.
This is clearly evident in the scriptural text. However, regarding this point, the meaning is concise while the expression is prolix. It is "concise in meaning" because...

Regarding the explanation of the perfect penetration (*yuan-tong*): it appears to pertain only to the initial stage of entering and abiding. Compared to the preceding meaning of *nirvāṇa*, this section is shorter.

As for the length of the text: since the essential meaning of the entire sutra and the practical application of its practice are both fully contained within this chapter, not only is this specific chapter longer than the preceding one, but the subsequent sections—explaining the two doubts and demonstrating the categories, as well as selecting the fundamental organ (*mūla-indriya*)—all serve to complete it.
Regarding the meaning of this section: one might ask why the cause and effect of the [first] great stage are explained so extensively at the beginning and so concisely at the end.
The answer is that there are two intentions. First, because this concerns the skillful means for those with a newly awakened mind.

For a beginner, what is most essential to know in detail is the practice prior to abiding; thus, it cannot but be explained in detail. Even if one were to discuss the practice after abiding in detail, [it would serve no purpose].
This is by no means a practical application for beginners. Second, because this is the ritual of the Perfect and Sudden teaching:
in the Perfect and Sudden dharma-gate, the practice consists solely of the stages prior to abiding; once one has attained abiding, one transcends directly into the subsequent mind.

This meaning is also very evident in the later passages of the present sutra, which will be further elucidated later. Regarding this section in contrast to the preceding section: the former was an explicit exposition.

The fruit is remote yet ultimate; this demonstrates that the causes are skillful and the realization is swift. Since even among the six sense faculties the sūtra selects the "perfect faculty," as the text says:
"Between the perfect faculty and the imperfect faculty, a day and an eon differ by a factor of ten million.
How much more so when comparing those who enter through consciousness or through objects—would it not be far more than a difference of a day and an eon? Thus we know.

This dharma-gate is most skillful and swift. For while a result may be distant yet entered with sluggishness, or a cause may be swift yet its realization shallow and near, neither can be considered superior.
Now, since its realization is both distant and its entry swift, this is why it is the most excellent dharma-gate.
Let those with the eye of wisdom discern it. [End of] Section.

II. First, the exposition on the untying of the knots, which consists of three parts. First, identifying the location, pointing out the root, and clarifying the knots, which further consists of three parts.
First, tracing the origin of the predominant cultivation of the mind.

The second meaning is this: you must certainly resolve to generate the bodhicitta, give rise to great valor regarding the Bodhisattva Vehicle, and resolutely abandon all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛta-dharma*).
Although the Buddha’s compassion in benefiting sentient beings is urgent, the bestowing of the teachings must await the arousal of the resolve.

This is what is meant by the saying, "One is not enlightened until one is provoked to indignation. The bodhicitta consists of the three aspects of aspiration—direct, profound, and great compassion—and it is also the essence of the fruit.

The Bodhisattva Vehicle is none other than the Single Buddha Vehicle; there are no two or three. It carries one to the precious destination. The fulfillment of the six perfections constitutes the aspect of practice.
This alone is the true cause. Examining the positions: the first phrase intends for one to aspire to enter the First Abode from the First Faith;

the second phrase intends for one to aspire to reach the stage of Equal Enlightenment and non-retrogression after the Abodes. "All conditioned marks" refers to the old practices of the provisional and the Small Vehicle.
This is because both the provisional and the Small Vehicle take the mind of birth-and-death as their fundamental cause for cultivation. As for that which they...
Even the realization of the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*) is not yet truly authentic, let alone the various conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*). As the subsequent verse states:

"The true nature of the conditioned is empty, for it arises through conditions and is thus like an illusion; the unconditioned has no arising or ceasing, and is as unreal as flowers in the sky. This is it.

Now, turning from the provisional and the Small Vehicle toward the real and the Great Vehicle, one must resolutely abandon them all. △ Second, a general statement on what should be known as a conclusion.

Regarding "abode" (*āyatana*): to speak of it in general terms means not to specify clearly which dharma constitutes the abode. This is divided into two parts. First, the explanation in terms of dharmas, which is further divided into two.
First, the actual instruction to carefully examine the root of delusion.
One should carefully examine the root of afflictions (*kleśa*). Since beginningless time, these have initiated karma and moistened rebirth; who creates them and who experiences them?

Regarding afflictions, according to the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi*, they are restricted to mental factors (*caitta*), are biased toward unwholesome phenomena, and consist merely of twenty-six categories, including the primary afflictions and secondary afflictions (*anuvyañjana-kleśa*).
This, however, is not the case here. One should follow the *Śraddhotpāda-śāstra*, wherein they encompass all wholesome, unwholesome, and indeterminate states within the realms of existence.
Furthermore, provisional [teachings] and those of the Lesser Vehicle refer to all such delusions as "afflictions" (*kleśa*), because they are both the deep source of the two kinds of death.

This term "root" (*mūla*) implicitly refers to the six sense faculties (*ṣaḍ-indriya*). Question: How does this differ from the "root of birth-and-death"? Answer: Birth-and-death is the fruit of suffering;
its root is the six consciousnesses (*ṣaḍ-vijñāna*). Affliction is the cause of suffering; its root is the six sense faculties. Question: [What further distinction is there?]

Do the faculties (*indriya*) give rise to the cause and consciousness (*vijñāna*) give rise to the effect, such that they do not interfere with one another? Answer: Regarding the afflictions (*kleśa*) produced by the faculties, the mind (*manas*) intends them as being of a general nature;

these are precisely the six consciousnesses (*ṣadvijñāna*), as in the *Vijñaptimātratā* [system]. The faculties follow the mental factors (*caitta*), yet they do not exceed the sovereign mind (*cittarāja*);
rather, they are opened out from the sovereign mind and combined into a single entity, which is itself the sovereign mind. This may be understood by analogy. Thus:

Afflictions are precisely the six consciousnesses; one should know that the six consciousnesses are the root of birth and death, and the six sense organs are, in turn, the root of the six consciousnesses.
Originally, they form a single continuity—how could they not be interconnected? "Karma" refers to what is created within the present aggregate.

"Arising" (*samutthāna*) and "formation" (*abhisamṣkāra*) are different. "Formation" refers to the actual accomplishment of the afflictions; "arising" refers to the source from which the afflictions emerge.

"Birth" (*jāti*) refers to that which is moistened by the intermediate state (*antarābhava*), namely, the ignorance consisting of aversion and attachment at the time of seeking a father and mother. Who performs [the action] and who experiences [the result]?
This is precisely to encourage self-examination and deliberation. Wuxing said: "That which initiates karma and moistens rebirth" refers to the afflictions (*kleśa*).
"Who acts and who receives" traces this back to the root. The intent is to clarify that the six sense organs (*ṣaḍāyatana*) act themselves and receive the results themselves.

Furthermore, one should know that the sense organs are the eight consciousnesses (*vijñāna*). The eight consciousnesses give rise to the six consciousnesses, which are entirely composed of afflictions. And...
They serve as the causes of suffering. The six consciousnesses bind and lead one through birth and death, thereby constituting the fruits of suffering.

While a coarse analysis suggests that the six consciousnesses alone create them, a subtle investigation reveals that it is actually the eight consciousnesses that act as their own creators. Furthermore, while the present observation seems to indicate that the six consciousnesses experience them, [the reality is otherwise].
Since the six decaying [faculties] are experienced solely by the eight consciousnesses themselves, it is said that "one creates and experiences for oneself.
However, rather than speaking of the eight consciousnesses, the text speaks of the six faculties; this is intended to make the matter easily understood by sentient beings in the present moment.
△ Second, the reverse demonstration to determine the locus of knowledge.
Ānanda, if you cultivate bodhi without carefully examining the root of afflictions, you will not be able to know where the false roots and objects are inverted.
If you do not even know their location, how can you subdue them and attain the rank of Tathāgata?
The false roots and objects encompass a very broad range of phenomena. "Roots" refers collectively to the physical body composed of the four great elements and the six sense organs.
"Objects" refers collectively to the insentient material world—including space—and the one true, pure mind.
Based on these two dharmas, they collectively constitute bondage. Although the root-body and the vessel-world are extremely vast, the actual points of bondage are most concise and not redundant;
one must certainly understand them before one can be liberated. This will be clear upon examining the following analogies.
△ Second, the explanation by analogy, which is further divided into two parts: first, the primary explanation using a common analogy.
"Ānanda, observe those in the world who untie knots. If they do not see where the knot was tied, how can they know how to untie it?
This is like making a knot with a rope: although all the strands together constitute the substance of the knot, the actual point where it is tied lies in only one strand.
If one does not truly perceive and recognize this, one will ultimately be unable to untie it. (2)
The negative example (vaidharmya-dṛṣṭānta) clarifies this:
you have not heard of space being torn asunder by you. Why is this? Because space has no form or shape, and thus lacks both binding and unbinding.

This analogy clarifies that what is being explained are the six faculties (ṣaḍ-indriya), not the absence of form or essential nature within the faculties themselves; rather, it refers to the six consciousnesses (ṣaṭ-vijñāna).
This refers to the entanglement of the two faculties of excellence (*śubha*) and inferiority (*aśubha*).
Because these two faculties possess mutual forms, they cause the wondrous nature that is inherently free from obstruction to falsely manifest as obstructed. Space has no such mutual forms.

This is because it serves as a counter-example (vaidharmya-dṛṣṭānta). By taking this, it is revealed by contrast that when the faculties (indriya) exist, the forms (ākṛti) have their relative positions, and where there is bondage, there must be liberation.
Furthermore, the secret manifestation of bondage and liberation is such that wherever these two faculties of form and shape exist, that is precisely the locus of bondage. Question:

When the Noble Ones (ārya) liberate the knots, do they all cause the two faculties to be extinguished like ashes? Answer: Not so. Although the faculties remain fully intact, [the Noble One] perceives...
When one hears the ten directions, they interpenetrate and manifest through mutual transformation; one simply remains unbound and unhindered.

If this is so, then not only is the body and its faculties unbound, but even the physical world (*bhājanaloka*) is free from obstruction. The following text will clarify this. Generally speaking, the discussion on the locus of bondage is now concluded.

△ Third, the specific identification of the sense organs as the locus of bondage. Although the commentary in the preceding section provided a somewhat indirect interpretation of the meaning of "roots" (*indriya*), [the present section provides the definitive identification].
Yet the sutra had not explicitly stated the sense organs; it is only in this section that they are clearly pointed out. It is divided into three parts.
First, the direct indication of their locations and substances:
"Those which are present before you—the eyes, ears, nose, tongue, as well as the body and mind."
The mind is the faculty. This directly points to the six faculties; they are the very substance of the locus where true reality is bound.
△ Second, exposing their faults and afflictions:
"The six serve as intermediaries for thieves, who plunder the family treasure themselves."
"The thief's intermediary" refers to an insider who introduces an external thief.

Just as an external thief in the world must rely on a treacherous person within the household to provide guidance and an invitation before he can successfully carry out a robbery, the "intermediary" is a metaphor for the six sense faculties; there is no doubt regarding this in the ancient commentaries.
The "bandits" are a metaphor for the six sense objects (*ṣaḍviṣaya*). Although these objects exist externally, their essence is fundamentally insentient;

therefore, it is not appropriate to describe them as bandits, nor is there any basis for such a claim in the original sutra. Now, according to the beginning of the "Seven Investigations," the Buddha said: "It is like dispatching an army to punish bandits."
One must know the dwelling place of the thief. Below, the text then interrogates the locus of the mind; this is the Buddha’s clear teaching that the consciousness-mind (*vijñāna-citta*) is the thief.
Question: When the mind is spoken of as an external thief, what is the basis for this meaning? Answer: Consciousness is the thief of sentient beings; thus, its significance is superior.

The substance of the dust is itself the shadow of the dust; thus, the teaching that they are external is also consistent. Regarding "plundering the great treasures of one's own house": the sense organs induce the arising of consciousness, which then gives rise to inverted discrimination.

Consequently, all the great treasures within the *tathāgatagarbha* are plundered and treated as the six external sense-objects (*ṣaḍviṣaya*), even to the point that the physical body loses its sovereignty. As the Sūtra says: "Because you mistake a thief for your son, you are deluded."

Delusion and ignorance give rise to the cycle of transmigration. As the Patriarch said: "The depletion of the Dharma-treasure and the destruction of merit—none of these fail to arise from the mind, intellect, and consciousness of others.
This is precisely it. △ Third, the manifestation as the locus of bondage.
Because sentient beings have been bound by entanglements within the world since beginningless time, they are unable to transcend the vessel-world (*bhājana-loka*).
"World" (*loka*) is synonymous with "world-system" (*loka-dhātu*). Another sutra states: "There are two kinds of worlds:

first, the world of sentient beings (*sattva-loka*), which refers to the physical bodies of sentient beings; second, the vessel-world, which refers to the insentient environment. These two phenomena alone comprise the entirety [of existence]."
Regarding all phenomena (*sarvadharma*), sentient beings are universally bound by duality and lack all autonomy; they are collectively constituted as knots.
However, the actual locus of these knots does not reside in the objective world (*bhājana-loka*), but exists solely within the six sense faculties (*ṣaḍ-indriya*).

Therefore, while those who are deluded seek liberation from the three realms (*traidhātuka*), those who have attained awakening merely resolve the six faculties. As this sutra states: "Because one is bound by the faculties, one cannot transcend the world. On the contrary...

When the faculties and their corresponding understandings are manifested, one does not merely attain mastery over the body, but also transcends to attain great mastery over the physical environment (*bhājana-loka*).
This is exemplified by the thirty-two transformations of Avalokiteśvara mentioned later; such is the nature of transcendence.

The section on designating the locations and pointing out the faculties and their knots is hereby concluded. II. Fully Manifesting the Quantities of the Six Faculties. The preceding major section has only just provided a general indication.

The source-roots (*indriya*) are the locus of the fetters (*saṃyojana*). Although the practitioner already knows that the untying of the fetters must proceed from the roots, there are six such roots while the untying occurs through only one;
thus, one must not fail to exercise discernment. To discern, one must thoroughly understand the number and measure of the six roots.
Without knowing their number and measure, on what basis could one choose? This section is therefore intended to clarify that number and measure. It is divided as follows:

2. First, a general discussion on the quantity of the fundamental objects (*mūla-vastu*). Regarding the quantity of the fundamental objects, there is no superiority or inferiority; they cannot be selected [as being better or worse].
Nevertheless, there are two reasons why this section must first be presented: first, to clarify that the arising of these quantities depends upon the mutual interpenetration of worlds;
second, to reveal that while the original function is fundamentally without superiority or inferiority, it is from [the perspective of] these [worlds] that superiority and inferiority arise.
It is merely according to the karmic power of various directions. This is divided into five sections. First, following the preceding [discussion], he raises a question:
"Ānanda, what is meant by the world of sentient beings?"

Observing these evidential terms, one should know that the "world" (loka-dhātu) spoken of here refers only to the body of the sense-faculties (*indriya-kāya*) and does not concern the physical environment (*bhājana-loka*).
This will be clarified again below. II. The actual explanation of the world has three parts: 1. Explaining the name.
"World" (*loka*) refers to temporal flux;
"realm" (*dhātu*) refers to spatial orientation. Since the world pertains to time, its meaning is defined by impermanent flux;
since the realm pertains to location, its meaning is defined by fixed spatial position. △ Second, indicating the essence.
You should now know that east, west, south, north, southeast, southwest, northeast, northwest, above, and below constitute the directions;
the past, future, and present constitute the time periods.
This "world" (*loka*) and "realm" (*dhātu*) are both spoken of in reference to the body. Question: While the world is beyond dispute, the term "realm" seems inapplicable here.
The physical environment (*bhājanaloka*) is stationary, so one may speak of fixed directions such as east and west; however, the body is constantly shifting—how can there be fixed directions for it?

Answer: There are two explanations for this. First, it is metaphorical (*upacāra*); that is, one borrows the east, west, and so forth of the physical environment to clarify [the orientation] within the body.
East and west are equal. These [distinctions] exist within the body; only left and right, front and back, and so forth, are as explained by Wenling.
Second, regarding reality: this refers to that which can be seen to shift outside the body; how could there be any perception of shifting within the body?
Just as the world is not truly immovable, yet there must also be times of movement and shifting;

so it is with the *Avataṃsaka* Sūtra’s description of worlds traveling and coming and going across hundreds of thousands of myriads of worlds, while the people within those worlds perceive them only as unmoving and unshakable—how could they possibly realize this?
One should know that within the body there is likewise a fixed location, yet from outside the realm, one perceives its shifting and changing.
What need is there for emotional calculations? △ Third, the summary of the numbers:
there are ten directions and three categories of flow.
The formal explanation of the worlds is now complete. △ Third, clarifying their mutual interpenetration.
"All sentient beings weave their delusive appearances into existence; within their bodies they trade and shift, and worlds intersect one another.
These first two lines discuss all phenomena in general, implying that in principle there are originally no sentient beings, who exist only after becoming deluded.
All sentient beings are formed by the interweaving of various delusions. Only the latter two phrases specifically point to the world.

The two characters "shen zhong" (within the body) sufficiently demonstrate that [the preceding discussion] pertains solely to the sense-faculties and the physical body (*indriya-rūpa*). "Trade" (*mao*) refers to the exchange between existence and non-existence.
"Transmigration" (*qiān*) means that things reach one another; it is like the worldly practice of merchants trading and exchanging various goods.
"Mutual interpenetration" (*xiāngshè*) carries the meaning of being interwoven and inseparable. This will be clearly explained in the following text:

this world’s mutual interpenetration is but one phenomenon within the process of false weaving and mutual formation. Indeed, false weaving, commercial exchange, and mutual interpenetration all share the same underlying intent.

It is simply that [the former] extends upward while [the latter] is restricted below. To construe the delusions of weaving as being fundamentally rooted in the sense organs and their objects is incorrect.

△ Fourth, the summary of the numerical quantities, divided into two parts: First, regarding the exclusion and inclusion of the number of realms (*dhātu*) and the number of worlds (*loka*), there are only three; yet the number of realms is ten.
If one does not exclude the number of realms through inclusion and exclusion to form four, one cannot combine them with the number of worlds to form twelve. Furthermore, it is divided into...
Second: one goes and six remain, leaving four.
Although the nature of these directions may be clearly established throughout the ten quarters, the world refers to them simply as east, west, south, and north.
△ Second, clarifying the reason for this:
"There is no fixed position above or below; there is no determinate direction in the middle.
Regarding this, the Master said: "As for 'no fixed position above or below,' this refers to the fact that both 'above' and 'below' are themselves the four directions."

Furthermore, apart from this, there is no "above" or "below"; therefore, it is said to be "without position. Regarding "the center having no fixed direction," this refers to the midst of the four intermediate corners (*koṇa*).
A corner derives its name from the intersection of two directions; since a single corner belongs to two directions, [it has no fixed orientation].
Therefore it is said that there is no fixed direction. ○ One should conclude by saying: "For this reason, the number of realms is only four.
△ Second, the formal summary of the intersecting numbers, divided into two parts. First, the intersection resulting in the original number.
The four numbers must be clearly understood as they interact with the world: three times four and four times three, revolving to twelve.
This constitutes the foundation of the layered numbers; therefore, it is called the "fundamental number. △ Third, the layered formation of the complete number.
"Flowing and transforming through three layers: one, ten, hundred, thousand.
"Flowing" means flowing from the first layer to the third layer. "Transforming" means changing the small into the many. Wuxing said:
"One, ten, hundred, thousand" is merely a general enumeration of the method for increasing numbers; it refers to increasing by one to reach ten, and so forth.
Ten becomes a hundred, and so forth. Now, for the time being, we shall explain the "three layers" as they apply to worldly phenomena. Regarding the first layer:

taking each of the four directions, one discusses the three periods of time for each, resulting collectively in twelve. Regarding the second layer: within the three periods of time in the eastern direction, each period transforms the number one into ten, resulting in thirty;
the same applies to the southern, western, and northern directions. Thus, with thirty in each of the four directions, they form one [layer].
This is one hundred and twenty. Thirdly, in the eastern direction, by transforming thirty into ten, it becomes three hundred.

The same applies to the other three directions. With three hundred in each of the four directions, they total one thousand two hundred. This analogy can be understood through the worldly engagement with the directions.
△ Fifth, a general summary of the beginning and end.
To summarize from beginning to end: within each of the six sense faculties, there are one thousand two hundred merits.
Here, the character "de" (merit) should be understood flexibly; it carries the meaning of the characters "yong" (function) and "neng" (capacity).

This is because the three periods of time and the four directions within the six faculties are merely the provisional designations of the dharmas of form and mind within *vijñapti-mātra* (consciousness-only), termed "non-associated formations" (*viprayukta-saṃskāra*).
Since these are entirely established based on the matter and mind within the sense organs, the functions and capacities of the six sense organs are all inherent within their own respective bases.
Throughout the three periods of time and the four directions, they are nowhere incomplete; they merely manifest their perfection by increasing from a small beginning.

It is likely unnecessary to force a correspondence with specific doctrinal characteristics (dharmalakṣaṇa), which would only lead to strained and artificial interpretations. Furthermore, the ancient masters stated that in India...
The transmitted three-layered commentary merely increases the number [of sections], as explained by Master Shangyue.
Furthermore, this intention is simply to enable the selection of faculties; it is necessary to clarify the quantity [of sections], yet it is not the locus of actual practice.
The true intent of practice lies solely in the "Perfect Penetration of the Ear-faculty. Changshui focused his mind on providing a profound interpretation.

To present a diagram to others and claim that the intent of cultivation lies solely therein—though this may have its own separate logical basis—it fails to recognize that it obscures the original, correct intent of cultivation.
It should be understood that the wise ought not to be deluded by such views.

Furthermore, these figures of one thousand two hundred are merely a general enumeration of what ordinary beings possess; they are not restricted to this particular region. Therefore, it is said that each is "complete."

This is not yet the supreme function of the true nature itself. As stated below, the beings of this region currently possess twelve hundred faculties each—ears, tongues, and minds—which are merely slightly more complete than other faculties;
how could they be as all-pervasive throughout the Dharma-realm as that which the Buddha has realized?
Therefore, one knows that the merit of the six faculties of a sage who accords with the truth must be immeasurable. (Wenling)
That is to say: this is merely a provisional reliance on worldly discourse. When the six are resolved and the one is forgotten, how could any numerical measure reach it?

This indeed constitutes knowing the words. The general discussion of the original numerical measures is hereby concluded. △ Second, the specific selection of numerical measures according to various regions.
This section is distinguished solely with respect to the Sahā world. If one were to rely on the preceding section, such a distinction would be impossible.

Now, because various regions possess varying degrees of excellence and inferiority, and because within the Sahā world there are three excellences and three inferiorities, it is still possible to single out one faculty as the most excellent;
therefore, a distinction must be made. This is divided into two parts: first, generally establishing the definitive determination.
"Ānanda, you must further determine the superiority and inferiority among them.

Second, specifically showing what is complete and what is deficient: if complete, there are one thousand two; if deficient, there are eight hundred. This is divided into six parts: first, deficiency of the eye-faculty."
As seen with the eye: the area behind is dark while the area before is bright; the front is entirely bright while the back is entirely dark.

Looking to the left and right, two-thirds [of the field] are obscured. Generally considering its function, its merit is incomplete; if one speaks of its efficacy in three parts, one part lacks virtue.
One should know that the eye possesses only eight hundred merits.
As for the Master’s statement that if one side has three hundred, and adding the front with the left makes nine hundred, this interpretation is untenable.

One should know that each of the four cardinal directions has two hundred merits, while the four intermediate corners have four hundred. What is currently seen by the eye consists of the front and the left.
To the right, three sides have already formed six hundred; together with the previous two corners totaling two hundred, they form eight hundred in total.
Only the rear side of two hundred and the two rear corners of two hundred are not yet visible; therefore, it is said to be "two-thirds.
△ Second, the ear faculty is complete.
Just as the ear listens all around, leaving nothing unhearing in the ten directions; when active, it reaches both near and far, and when still, it is without boundary.
You should know that the faculty of hearing is endowed with one thousand two hundred merits.
Sound is movement. "If" (若) is a term indicating similarity rather than reality; "near" (邇) means proximity.
"Movement as if near or far" means that when people of the world hear a sound, they necessarily know its distance. To speak according to reality, it is as stated in the preceding sutra:
Observing that both hearing and sound have no location, then proximity and distance likewise belong to emotional attachments and are not real.
Therefore it is said: "If one is still and without boundaries. This is like when people hear the silence of the absence of sound; how could they measure its distance?
When the faculty of hearing is perfectly attuned to the ten directions and hears this boundless silence, this is why the auditory faculty is the most excellent. △
Third, the deficiency of the nose faculty.

Just as the nose smells and perceives, it is through it that inhalation and exhalation pass; there is out-breathing and in-breathing, yet the intermediate junction is missing. This is verified by examining the nose faculty.
One-third is missing. One should know that the nose possesses only eight hundred merits.
Regarding the absence of the "middle intersection": it is like the regulated breath, which, having fully exhaled, pauses briefly before entering again;
this brief pause is what is called the missing middle intersection. This can be verified during the winter months. Since the breath thus has a deficiency, [the count is incomplete].
"How could its function be complete? Wēnlíng says: "When it goes out, it can grasp fragrance; when it comes in, it can smell fragrance.

Since there is no capacity in the interval between going out and coming in, the middle intersection is missing. Chángshuǐ says: "Going out, coming in, and the middle intersection together constitute three parts.
One part consists of four hundred [units]; because the middle intersection is missing, there are only eight hundred. △ Fourth, the tongue faculty is complete.
As the tongue proclaims, exhausting all mundane and supramundane wisdom, its expressions are methodical and its principles inexhaustible;
one should know that the faculty of the tongue is perfected with twelve hundred merits.
Gushan said: "If one takes up the capacity for verbal expression, one does not discuss the tasting of flavors;

if one takes up the tasting of flavors, its efficacy is inferior because it is a cognition based on conjunction (*saṃyoga*). Question: To proclaim the two types of wisdom, the wise are capable while the foolish are not.
Since there is such capability and incapacity, how can all [beings] possess the twelve thousand [dharmas]? Answer: Although the words of the foolish lack supramundane wisdom, they..."
Worldly wisdom already exists; how much more so when the subsequent text states:
"That which has spatial divisions" refers to words that may be limited, while "that whose principle is inexhaustible" refers to meanings that are universally pervasive.
In this regard, even the most coarse and superficial worldly speech penetrates the ultimate truth, as when the Patriarch attained enlightenment upon hearing lewd words—this is supramundane wisdom.
When Confucius heard the song of the child, his mind was alerted. This is worldly wisdom (*laukika-jñāna*).
If this is so, then even the words of a fool possess the perfected merit of the two types of wisdom. What difference, then, exists [between them]? △ Five: Deficiency of the Body-faculty.

Just as the body perceives touch, consciousness perceives the agreeable and the disagreeable when they are in contact; it does not know them when separated. Separation pertains to the single, while conjunction pertains to the pair.
By examining the body-faculty (*kāyendriya*), one finds that three parts are missing from one. Thus, one should know that the body possesses only eight hundred merits.
Gushan said: "As for 'separating the one and uniting the two,' when separated, there is no cognition; this is a deficiency of one part. When united, it is able to perceive;
because there are both opposition and compliance, it possesses both parts. △ Sixth, the faculty of mind is complete.

The faculty of mind silently accommodates all mundane and supramundane phenomena of the ten directions and the three periods of time—whether saintly or ordinary—encompassing them all without exception to their very limits.
You should know that the faculty of mind is thus perfected with one thousand two hundred merits.

"Silent acceptance" (*tūṣṇīmbhāva*) is different from the aforementioned "proclamation. That [proclamation] is the capacity for deliberation; this [acceptance] is the capacity for reflection. Question:

Regarding one who has attained thorough penetration of all phenomena (*sarvadharma*), they are able to encompass the ultimate limit (*koṭi*). One who has not yet attained such penetration does not possess this capacity.
Why, then, are the two [capacities] equal? Answer: The meaning is that the fundamental [nature] possesses this capacity, yet the ignorant are unable to bring it forth.
It is not the fault of the faculty of mind. For example, a sharp blade is inherently capable of cutting;
yet if a clumsy craftsman fails to hone it, this is not the fault of the blade. Now, we speak of all things as being complete simply by taking into account what is originally possessed.
The detailed exposition of the number of the six faculties is concluded. △ Third, instructing them to awaken to the perfect entry into the One.
In the preceding two sections, the sense organs were first designated as the locus of the knot; these merely demonstrated their relative superiority and inferiority.

In this section, one is finally led to personally realize that the most perfect faculty is to be cultivated and realized through a single gate alone. Therefore, it should be known that this section further serves as the basis for what follows.
The "Hand" (*shou*) is the essential point. It is divided into two parts. First, the synthesis and verification of the six awakenments as the perfection. This is further divided into three sections.
First, the fundamental basis for the desire to realize non-arising:
"Ānanda, you now wish to go against the current of the flow of birth and death, to trace back the root of that flow until you reach the state of neither arising nor ceasing."
"Going against the current" means not following its flow. "Desire" refers to the five sensory objects; these are called the five desires (*pañca-kāma*).

Although that which is uniquely perceived by the mind is but a reflection of these five sensory objects, this constitutes the six sense faculties flowing outward and rushing toward external objects, thereby creating boundless birth and death.
This is what is meant by "following the current of birth and death. To turn the faculties back and detach from the objects is to go against it and not follow it.
Furthermore, "returning to exhaust the source of the faculties" means proceeding from the shallow to the deep, striving to cause the source of birth and death to be exhausted.
In reality, since the six sense-faculties are the root of afflictions, they are the profound source of birth and death.

"Reaching the state of no-birth-and-extinction" means that when delusion is exhausted, the True manifests; one realizes the ultimate principle of true quiescence. According to the subsequent [section on] Avalokiteśvara’s Perfect Penetration...

"Flowing so as to forget its source and so forth" refers to reversing the flow of birth and death. "Hearing that which is heard until it is exhausted and so forth" refers to returning to and exhausting the root of the flow.
"Quiescent extinction manifests before one" refers to reaching the state of non-arising and non-ceasing. △ Second, causing them to verify this through six detailed investigations.
One should examine these six faculties of experience: which are conjoined and which are disjoined; which are deep and which are shallow;
which constitute perfect penetration and which are not complete.
The reception of sensory objects constitutes sensation (*vedanā*); the exertion of functional capacity constitutes activity (*kāritra*).

All six faculties possess these two; therefore, they are called the "six faculties of experience. The various instances of the particle *shui* (who) are precisely intended to prompt detailed investigation.

"Conjoined" refers to cognition through contact; "separated" refers to cognition without contact. A proximate nature is profound; a remote nature is shallow. These function as a single, pervasive intent.
To possess [these qualities] is to be fully pervasive; to lack them is to be incomplete. Now, examining the six sense faculties:

the eyes and ears are cognitions through separation; the three of nose, tongue, and body are cognitions through contact. Although the mental faculty (*manas*) is mostly through separation, within the "mental consciousness co-arising with the five" (*pañcavijñānakāyasamprayuktamanovijñāna*), the aspects of nose, tongue, and body also belong to cognition through contact.
Thus, these are combined with contact rather than being purely through separation. As for the objects perceived by the ears and the mind...

Quiescent cessation constitutes the nature of proximity. This means that as soon as one turns back the faculty of the ear, one immediately abandons movement and enters stillness; because this stillness cuts off clamor and distraction, it is the nature of proximity.
As soon as one turns back the faculty of the mind, one departs from arising and enters cessation; because cessation is devoid of origination, it is likewise the nature of proximity.

That which is perceived by the faculties of the eye, nose, tongue, and body—namely, darkness, obstruction, dullness, and detachment—constitutes the nature of distance. This is because, through darkness, [the faculties] do not [function].

If it is bright, it is clear; if it is obstructed, it does not penetrate. If it is bland, it lacks flavor; if it is separated, one is unaware. These are all far removed from the nature of the spiritual mind (xingling) and do not resemble it.
The circularity and deficiency of the scriptural text are manifest. △ Third, revealing the supreme advancement of perfect penetration.
If one can, within this, awaken to the faculty of perfect penetration, one will reverse that beginningless flow of fabricated deluded karma and attain the path of following perfect penetration;
compared to those with imperfect faculties, this will differ by a factor as great as a day versus an eon.

Although this section’s conclusion clearly demonstrates superior progress, the initial text actually intends for one to personally awaken to and resolve upon a single faculty (*indriya*) and practice accordingly.
In the preceding section, the primary aim was to have one investigate and examine the six meanings (namely: separation and combination, shallow and deep, complete and incomplete);

that it now merely says "awaken to the complete" is a brevity of expression. This is because, in selecting the faculty, one chooses the separated, the deep, and the complete, while discarding the rest.
This is a brief summary. Now, by examining the matter through six criteria, it becomes evident that only the faculty of hearing (*śrotra-indriya*) fully meets the requirements.
This is because, although the eye is likewise characterized by detachment (*viveka*), it does not possess the same depth or perfection;
although the tongue is likewise perfect, it does not possess the same depth of detachment; and although the mind is likewise deep and perfect, it does not possess the same purity of detachment.
Furthermore, among the three meanings of being "detached," "profound," and "perfectly complete," only the faculty of the ear possesses them all.

Therefore, the meaning of this passage should be supplemented as follows: "If one awakens to the detached, profound, and perfectly complete faculty... (and so forth), up to: "...one attains a penetration that is detached, profound, and perfectly complete.
Compared to those whose faculties are neither detached, nor profound, nor perfectly complete, their respective days and kalpas differ by a factor of ten million. Such is its significance.
This is complete. However, the Buddha’s words are concise and allusive; though the text is abbreviated, the meaning is fully contained. One should know this most clearly.
The subsequent verse says, "Those with the initial resolve enter right concentration, yet their speed differs beyond compare. This refers to the sense that days and kalpas multiply by degrees.
"The flow of fabricated karma" refers to the entanglement of sensory desires, flowing through birth and death. △ Second, causing entry into the One.
