Explanation of the six [sections]. In the preceding section, the character "awakening" (wù) is emphasized; its meaning encompasses both faith and understanding (*śraddhā-adhimukti*). In this section, the character "entry" (rù) is emphasized;

the text includes both cultivation and realization (*bhāvanā-sākṣātkriyā*). First, one must have faith and understanding in the single, most perfect faculty. Thereafter, one cultivates and progresses through that single faculty until entry is realized.
This briefly covers the complete process of the correspondence between cause and effect—namely, faith, understanding, practice, and realization. It is divided into four parts. First:
I shall now fully reveal the aforementioned quantities.
The six profound, perfect, and luminous qualities are the original merits; their quantities are as follows.

"Profound, perfect, and luminous" refers to the nature of perfect stillness and non-arising/non-ceasing within the first determination (*niścaya*), which is sufficient to clarify what was previously indicated.
The nature within the faculties is beyond doubt. The two characters "original" (ben) and "inherent" (suo) clarify that all sentient beings currently possess this [nature], each being identical;
it is not so because of cultivation or contrived effort. This meaning actually encompasses both the general discussion and the specific analysis;
the intent of these two sections is precisely the quantity of what is original and inherent. △ Second, causing them to select and cultivate.
"Follow whatever you can discern as suitable for entry; I shall clarify it for you so that you may progress. Question:

"What is the distinction between awakening (*wu*) and discernment (*ze*)? Answer: "To be luminous and free from doubt is called awakening. To decisively adopt and apply [the truth] is called discernment.
However, do not explain the fundamental root to them. First, cause them to awaken and discern for themselves, so that they may bring it forth through their own realization."
This refers to the progressive stages of advancement in accordance with that teaching. "Advancement" refers to the gradual cultivation of practice.
Therefore, this section, together with the following section, belongs to the category of cultivation. △ Third, setting forth the single reason for selection, which is further divided into two parts.
Generally speaking across the ten directions, there is no distinction;
the Tathāgatas of the ten directions all practice within each of the eighteen realms and thereby attain the perfect and unsurpassed Bodhi.
Within this, there is neither superiority nor inferiority.
As a verse says: "The nature of the Sage is all-pervading; both the direct and the inverse are skillful means.

Although it is said that these are the original skillful means practiced at the very beginning when the Tathāgata was cultivating the causes for enlightenment, when discussed comprehensively across the ten directions, they follow accordingly.
The mechanisms for this are a thousandfold and myriad; thus, one may enter and realize the truth through any of the various gates, as there is no superiority or inferiority among them.

Nevertheless, although the text is limited in its scope, the seven elements (mahābhūta) are in fact encompassed within it. Question: The subsequent verse states, "The Bhagavans of the ten directions / Enter the single path of the gate to Nirvana.
This refers to the faculty of hearing (the ear-root). How does this accord with [your previous statement]? Answer: Although that [verse] also...

The phrase "the ten directions" refers specifically to those of a single class of capacity, such as those of Avalokiteśvara, because those with a capacity similar to Avalokiteśvara also pervade the ten directions and the three realms.
However, the "ten directions" mentioned here represent a comprehensive discussion that does not restrict itself to a single class of capacity.
Thus, there are many gates. Second, because this [teaching] is tailored to the capacities of sentient beings, it is necessary to select one.
Since you are of inferior capacity and have not yet attained sovereign wisdom that is perfect within these [gates], I proclaim this so that you may enter deeply through just a single gate.
The inferior refers to those who are fully possessed of afflictions; even the four abidings remain entangled for them.

One who possesses the perfect wisdom of mastery can thoroughly penetrate the Dharma gates, entering each one without any further distinction between slow or fast. This is truly possible only for those at the profound stages.
This is not something that can be achieved by one who has newly entered right concentration. Therefore, I shall now conclude by clarifying the reason for selecting [this specific practice].
Question: Is Avalokiteśvara also of an inferior class? Answer: From the perspective of his current status, he is indeed a Tathāgata;

yet, when tracing back to his initial resolve, he also began from the stage of an ordinary being (*pṛthagjana*). Furthermore, regarding his initial skillful means, although [they may appear as such] among all Buddhas...
Each of these likewise accords with the capacities of those in a particular direction; they enter into the One alone. How could this apply only to Avalokiteśvara?
Furthermore, after Ānanda has entered the One, then through the entry into the One, all things are entered, and the perfectly sovereign wisdom will likewise manifest before him.
How could he remain forever inferior? The selection of one [entry] from among the six is hereby concluded. △ Four: Entering the One and Understanding the Six.
Entering into one [gate] without delusion, those six faculties of cognition are simultaneously purified.
This section belongs to the category of realization (*sākṣātkriyā*). To cause one to enter through a single gate is to achieve liberation through a single faculty.

Fearing that Ānanda might doubt that by liberating only one faculty, the remaining faculties would still be bound, he concludes and demonstrates that the liberation of one entails the liberation of all.
This is the explanation. According to the subsequent section on "Perfect Penetration," one should take the exhaustion of that which is heard as the entry into the state of non-delusion.
However, when a single faculty returns to its source, all six faculties are liberated. From this, the exhaustion of that which is seen occurs, and so on until the exhaustion of that which is known;
thus, the six faculties are simultaneously purified. The six points discussed above are an inferential verification of this.

The faculties have now been revealed in secret. Since one practices through awakening and realizes through practice, the general outline of the effort required to untie the knots has been roughly completed.
This concludes the first section: "The Instruction on Untying the Knots. II. Reiterating the Details in Response to a Question.
This inquiry differs from the subsequent doubts; for doubt arises from a lack of sufficient faith, whereas this [inquiry] establishes the truth through discernment.
This is not so. The question arises because his understanding was not yet thorough, and he requested further instruction for clarification;
thus, the Buddha provided a response below that merely supplemented what had been shown previously, making it more detailed and clear to increase his understanding, rather than resolving his doubts.
This is divided into two parts: first, Ānanda follows up on the previous discussion to pose a question.

Ānanda addressed the Buddha, saying: "World-Honored One, how is it that by flowing against the current and entering deeply through a single gate, one can cause the six faculties to become pure simultaneously?
This question arises specifically from the section on "Awakening to Perfection and Entering the One. Furthermore, within that section on Awakening to Perfection, it is only...
The first half of the question asks: "What is 'flowing with' and what is 'going against'? Within the section on 'entering one,' why does it only ask about the latter half?
How can one simply cause them to enter one, and how is it that one is thereby able to understand the six? This precisely clarifies the intent of this inquiry.
This concludes the subsequent portion of the answer. △ Second, the Tathāgata restates the response in accordance with the question.

"Restatement" means that it does not depart from the previous meaning, but rather refers to providing further detail. This section is divided into four parts: first, restating that the delusions and attachments remain deep; this section serves two purposes:
first, to reveal the reason why [the disciples] cannot achieve sudden realization; second, to clarify that the flow of desire still persists.

One must certainly oppose it; only then can one reach the state of no-arising and no-ceasing. This is further divided into two parts. First, directly clarifying that the grasping at a self has not yet been exhausted.
The Buddha told Ānanda: "You have now attained the fruit of Srotāpanna; you have already extinguished the world of sentient beings within the three realms."

Regarding the afflictions to be abandoned through seeing (*darśana-heya*): however, one has not yet understood that within the faculties (*indriya*), there are accumulated, beginningless, empty habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*). Those tendencies must be eliminated through the path of cultivation (*bhāvanā-mārga*) in order to be removed.

A *srotāpanna*—which in this [Chinese] context is called "Stream-enterer" (*preliu*)—refers to one who, in the Lesser Vehicle (*Hīnayāna*), has entered the state of a sage (*ārya*) from the stage of the worthy (*śaikṣa*).
Only upon reaching the first fruit does one truly join the stream of the sages. In the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra*, the Buddha himself explains:
"Srotāpanna is called 'entering the stream,' yet in reality there is nothing entered; because one does not enter form, sound, smell, taste, touch, or dharmas, one is named Srotāpanna.
Since this has been set forth as the Buddha’s own word, it accords perfectly with the present sutra; one should reflect upon this accordingly.
Take this. It is truly because not entering the six sense-objects is precisely to go against the current of birth-and-death (saṃsāra).
As for "sentient beings of the world within the three realms," this refers to that which is severed within the realms by the four abodes [of ignorance] and the afflictions of views and thought;

it is not that which is severed by those who have already transcended the world. Guishan said: "The delusions severed by the realization of the truths are the eighty-eight proclivities (*anuśaya*). Cultivation...
The delusions severed by the Path consist of eighty-one *cetanās* (volitions). Regarding "view" (*dṛṣṭi*): this refers to the stage of the Path of Seeing (*darśana-mārga*).

Since the first fruit of the Hīnayāna belongs to the stage of the Path of Seeing, and it is precisely at the first fruit that one severs the conceptualization of self-grasping—wherein conceptualization is termed "view"—these are also called "delusions of view.
These are the ten *anuśayas* (latent tendencies), which total eight when categorized according to the four truths across the three realms.
The eighteen constituents (*dhātu*). These are those whose initial fruits have already been extinguished by Ānanda. Within the faculties (*indriya*), there is empty habituation;
this is precisely the affliction of thought (*vicikitsā-kleśa*), namely, the innate grasping at a self (*ātma-grāha*). The "faculty" refers to the eighth *ālayavijñāna*.

According to the *lakṣaṇa-vāda* school, this consciousness is called the fundamental support (*mūlāśraya*). If one interprets "accumulated births" as many births, it would seem to contradict [the doctrine of] beginninglessness.

The characteristics are layered. Now, "accumulation" (*cita*) is explained as the seed; "arising" (*janman*) as the active manifestation (*samudācāra*); and "empty habituation" (*śūnya-vāsanā*) as the habitual tendency (*vāsanā*), which refers to the four proclivities (*anuśaya*).

These correspond to the eighty-one categories formed by the multiplication of the four proclivities across the nine stages of the three realms. Furthermore, one should know that the "bases" (*indriya*) are likewise the six sense faculties;

however, because the *lakṣaṇa*-school (the Abhidharma school) refers exclusively to the eight dharmas [of the five aggregates, matter, mind, and formations] as its object, they belong to the category of insentient material phenomena (*rūpa-dharma*). This...
Because the Sūtra directly points to the essence of the six subtle minds within the sense organs, these are precisely the *ālayavijñāna*.

Therefore, when the subsequent text states that Avalokiteśvara’s perfect penetration of the sense organs reaches its culmination, it corresponds to the fourth fruit [of the Śrāvaka] at the seventh stage of faith (*śraddhā-bhūmi*).

As for "that which must be abandoned through cultivation," this refers to what is abandoned during the stage of the path of cultivation (*bhāvanā-mārga*) in the Hīnayāna; for in the Hīnayāna, the second and third fruits belong to the stage of the path of cultivation, where they are finally severed.

Regarding the afflictions of thought (*kleśa*): since Ānanda has not yet entered the stage of cultivation (*bhāvanā-mārga*), he does not yet know what remains to be abandoned. △ Second, this further demonstrates that the attachment to dharmas (*dharma-upādāna*) remains entirely intact.
How much more so, then, regarding the specific divisions and numerical categories of arising, abiding, changing, and ceasing (*utpāda-sthiti-anyathātva-vināśa*) within this?
In this context, it still refers to the sense-faculties (*indriya*), indicating that apart from the *ālayavijñāna*, there is no basis for the various delusions. Guishan said:

"Arising, abiding, change, and cessation are themselves the ignorance of the same substance (*tongti wuming*). "Quantitative divisions" refers to the forty-two grades from the first stage (*prathamabhūmi*) up to the stage of Wondrous Enlightenment (*samyaksambodhi*).
Regarding the ignorance of the same substance, it is subsumed within the grasping at phenomena (*dharmagrāha*). It is divided into...
Separately from the co-arising subtle afflictions—namely, the *sands-of-the-Ganges* of ignorance—they are combined into a single stage of abiding (*sthiti*).

Tiantai designates this as the "view-delusion and thought-delusion outside the realms" (*jie wai jian si*); this is correct. According to the *Awakening of Faith*, among the three subtleties, the "phase of karma" (*ye xiang*) is the "phase of arising" (*sheng xiang*).
Following the three subtleties and preceding the two sets of six coarse phases, these constitute the "phase of abiding. As for the third of the six coarse phases:

The fourth is the characteristic of change (*anyathātva-lakṣaṇa*), and the fifth is the characteristic of cessation (*nirodha-lakṣaṇa*); the sixth does not participate therein. The commentary explains the meaning of these four characteristics as follows:

the initial movement of the mind is taken as arising (*utpāda*); the firm persistence of attachment to phenomena is taken as abiding (*sthiti*); the internal and external self and mine are taken as change (*anyathātva*);
and the exhaustive exhaustion and finality is taken as cessation (*nirodha*). This is according to the characteristics of the forward flow (*anuloma*). If, however, one considers them in reverse...
When the person who speculates is eliminated, those in the ten stages of faith awaken to the mark of extinction (*nirodha-lakṣaṇa*).

Those of the Two Vehicles and the three stages of the *śaikṣas* awaken to the mark of difference (*anyathā-lakṣaṇa*) [according to Tiantai’s judgment, where the seventh stage of faith in the Perfect Teaching is equated with the ultimate fruit of the Śrāvaka vehicle; this is here correlated with the three stages of the *śaikṣas*. It is feared that these are not the three stages of the *śaikṣas* in the Perfect Teaching, and the aforementioned "ten stages of faith" also seem to refer to the ten stages of faith in the Separate Teaching].

From the first stage up to the ninth stage, they awaken to the mark of abiding (*sthiti-lakṣaṇa*). From the ten directions up to the Tathāgata, they awaken to the mark of birth (*utpāda-lakṣaṇa*). This is the principle.
In truth, it is only the Tathāgata who directly perceives the characteristic of arising through immediate cognition (*pratyakṣa*).
As for the Ground of the Cloud of Dharma (*dharmameghā bhūmi*), it is merely the initial awakening of the mind within this very characteristic.

Therefore, one should know that these four characteristics are established by encompassing the five stages of dwelling (*pañca-vihāra*), proceeding from the subtle to the manifest during the process of flowing with the current, and from the shallow to the deep during the process of reverse severance; they do not refer to a single moment.

Those which possess the four characteristics also have their numerical divisions and counts. This clarifies that their quantity is extremely vast, a realm beyond the comprehension of those of the Two Vehicles.
This is because, while they are roughly divided into forty-two categories, if subdivided, they would be immeasurable.
The general purport of this section is to answer your previous question: "What is the flow? It refers precisely to the thoughts you have not yet severed.

The delusions, as well as the dust-like *avidyā* (ignorance) and specific secondary delusions, constitute the flow of desire (*kāma-āsrava*). These are still among those that must be countered and severed.

[The Buddha] remained silent.

This refers precisely to the sense of "mutual non-communication. These two characters explain the reason why [the elements] are not one.
It states that because their functions do not mutually communicate, they are definitively not one. The two characters "non-six" (fei-liu) are likewise words of definitive determination.

"Ultimately one" means that they function in mutual accompaniment. These two characters explain why [the self] is not six, stating that because they function in mutual accompaniment, it is definitively not six.
The final two phrases conclude by establishing the "double negation" (neither-one-nor-six), thereby simultaneously dispelling the delusions of both "one" and "six.
One must by no means further add "both" to create a sophistical confusion.
This is an error. △ Fourth, tracing the origin to delusion:

"Ānanda, you should know that these faculties are neither one nor six. Since beginningless time, due to inverted views and the cycle of transmigration, the meanings of 'one' and 'six' have arisen within the perfect and lucid [nature]."
This faculty is neither six nor one. Why is it that sentient beings are deluded regarding it as being either six or one?
To investigate the matter: the fundamental essence of this faculty has never been either one or six from time immemorial (and so forth).
"Inversion" refers to delusion and karma—corresponding to the three subtleties and five coarsenesses discussed in the treatise—while "sinking and changing" refers to the fruit of suffering.
This refers to the sixth of the coarse [delusions] within the treatise. "Round" means that while the functions are complete, the essence is fundamentally not one;

"tranquil" means that while the substance is one, it is fundamentally not six. As for the arising of the meanings of "one" and "six," this refers to ordinary worldlings at the level of common ground who grasp them as being six.
Shallow scholars cling to this as being "one," yet they never realize the fundamental truth that the Perfect is not one and the Stillness is not six;
how then could "one" or "six" be attainable? △ Five: Judging and Indicating the Appropriate Capacity.
"You, O Srotāpanna, although you have attained the extinction of six [objects], have not yet lost one.

According to the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra* cited by Gu shan, 'not entering into form, sound, smell, taste, touch, or dharmas' refers merely to the cessation of the six sense-objects (*ṣaḍviṣaya*).
However, the function of the sense-faculties (*indriya*) is to cognize these objects; since the objects no longer enter, the six functions of the faculties likewise cease."
Once [the practice] has been undertaken, one does not engage in it [further]. Moreover, this merely describes the non-engagement of its function; it does not mean the exhaustion of its essence.

It is only upon attaining the four fruits that the essence can be fully exhausted. According to the subsequent account of Avalokiteśvara’s perfect penetration—where movement and stillness do not arise—this corresponds to the dissolution of the six sense-bases.

Only when "hearing and what is heard" are both exhausted is the essence truly exhausted. That one has not yet forgotten "the One" is explained by Master Gusuan as being due to clinging to the existence of nirvana.

It is not so; yet it does not stop at the first fruit. The same applies to the four fruits, because that path achieves the exhaustion [of defilements] by extinguishing the six faculties as ashes, which constitutes *nirvāṇa*.
This is precisely what is meant when those of shallow understanding cling to this as being "one.
However, the reason for explaining this is that while ordinary people all know the attachment to the six [faculties], the two vehicles [do not].
The clinging to the one. Some people may not yet have reached this understanding; therefore, this judgment is presented here to demonstrate it.
This is because seeing [the one] and the ordinary person’s clinging to the six are both the same delusion and not the truth. △ Sixth, further clarifying through analogies, in two parts.
First, presenting the analogies, in three sections. First, the analogy of producing six from one.
It is like the great void of space, which permeates and unites with all vessels. Because the shapes of the vessels differ, the space within them is given different names.
The void of space is a metaphor for the nature that is perfectly still and profound; the various vessels are metaphors for the characteristics of the six sense faculties.

The differences in the vessels—such as being square, round, long, or short—do not inherently affect the void of space at all; it is only because they are combined with the vessels that one subsequently speaks of [different spaces].
To claim that space possesses distinctions is truly false. △ Second, removing the six [distinctions] to illustrate the oneness of space:

when one removes the vessels to contemplate space, one speaks of space as being one because it did not exist prior to the joining of the vessels; yet how could one say that space itself is one? Now, it is only after the removal of the vessels that...
To speak of "one" is likewise a false designation established through relative contrast; it is not the fundamental reality. △ Third, the analogy that the true essence is beyond interference:
That great void—how could it be "you"? How could it be established as either identical or different? How much less can it be called "one" or "not one"?
The first two lines refute the correct [misguided] views. Because the vessel is present, one speaks of emptiness as being different;
"different" means distinct. Because the vessel is removed, one speaks of emptiness as being the same; "same" means one. This is merely empty talk;
how could space itself be made to be either the same or different by your words? This—
The preceding section has already eliminated both "one" and "different. The final two lines serve as a precaution against further conceptual shifts; they represent yet another layer of refinement.
This is because, in the previous passage, "one" was established again after refuting "difference," and thus both "one" and "different" have already been discarded together.
Now, fearing that "not one" might be established again after refuting "one," these lines further add: "how much more so for 'other'? Therefore...
Once again, he sent both the "one" and the "not-one" together. Having finished providing these analogies, [the second section] follows:
"The six faculties of sensory reception that you clearly perceive are likewise thus."
This must be applied by correlating each of the three categories within the analogy. First, to correlate the analogy of "one becoming six," it says:

That perfectly clear and tranquil nature becomes obstructed and stagnated within the six sense faculties; because of these six faculties, one consequently claims that the nature is sixfold, yet one fails to realize this.

The six faculties originally have no interference with the perfectly湛 (zhan) and profound state; it is only because of the obstruction caused by karmic entanglement that they are subsequently termed the "six natures.

This is certainly a false conceptualization. Next, regarding the merging and elimination of the six to speak of them as one, the analogy is given: to dissolve the six faculties and establish the nature as one.

Yet this fails to realize that before the faculties were obstructed by entanglement, they did not exist [as such]; how, then, could one speak of a "one nature"? Now, because the faculties have been dissolved...

To subsequently establish "one" is likewise a false establishment based on duality; it is not the original reality. This is like the analogy of the end meeting the true essence without interference, which is also divided into two sections.
First, combining [the arguments] to refute the correct calculation: Because the faculties are bound together, you speak of the nature as six;
because the faculties are dissolved, you speak of the nature as one. This too is merely empty talk; how could the perfect and profound stillness belong to you?
Such discourse truly establishes the distinction between the "one" and the "six. This has already simultaneously discarded both the "one" and the "six.

Furthermore, one ought to guard against the following counter-argument: "If the 'one' is established by means of negating the 'six,' then both the 'one' and the 'six' have already fallen into mutual falsehood.
How much more so when, having refuted the 'one,' one further names it 'not-one'? Thus, both 'one' and 'not-one' are metaphors for the false."

It is not that there is no end [to such views]. It is feared that after the nirvana of the two vehicles (śrāvaka and pratyekabuddha) has been refuted, some might still conceive of a state that is "not-nirvana";
therefore, it is again dismissed. However, these six types of faculties and natures are both equally false;

how do they differ from the space within a vessel and its shape? Thus it is said, "it is also like this. The general meaning of this section answers the previous question by stating: "Because of this..."
The fundamental nature of the faculties is originally neither one nor six; therefore, when the "one" is understood, the "six" immediately dissolves.
The explanation of how the "one and six" arise from delusion is hereby concluded. △ Third, explaining how the knots of the faculties arise from the objects.

as a "floating root," its four sensory objects flow forth and rush toward forms.

"Subtle and perfect" refers to the nature; "subtle" also implies "tranquil. "Adhering" (*li*) means clinging and attachment. Through adhering to the tranquil [nature], seeing is produced.
This merely states that the tranquil nature is adhered to, whereby the initial deluded seeing arises, though the sense-roots have not yet formed.
The middle four lines next establish the ultimate sense-faculties (*paramārtha-indriya*). The first two lines above represent the establishment of the ultimate seeing-essence (*darśana-viśuddha*).

These are the ultimate sense-faculties composed of the four internal great elements (*mahābhūta*). Once these faculties are established, they constitute inversion.

That which flows and rushes toward form is the gathering of views; it is a perversion within the eye, wherein vision arises from the sensory object.

The general meaning of the five lower faculties should be inferred by analogy according to this principle.
△ Second, the ear is formed by gathering sound.

Due to the mutual impact of the two aspects of movement and stillness, within the wondrous perfection, the clarity becomes adherent and gives rise to hearing. The essence of hearing reflects sound, and by coiling back the sound, it forms the faculty.
The root of this faculty is termed the "pure four great elements," and for this reason it is called the substance of the ear; it is like a newly curled leaf.
The four sensory objects float upon the root-faculties, and as they rush toward sounds, they strike one another;
this means they do not tolerate each other. "Enveloping" (*juàn*) means to wrap around and grasp, which is the same as the meaning of "binding" (*jié*).
"Rushing toward sounds" refers to the continuous flow following sound. The remaining [explanations] are all to be understood according to the above. △ Third, grasping fragrance to form the nose.
Arising from the two aspects of penetration and obstruction, within the wondrous perfection, it adheres to the stillness to produce smelling. The essence of smelling reflects fragrance;

by taking in fragrance, it forms the faculty. The root of this faculty is termed the "pure four great elements," and for this reason it is called the substance of the nose. It is like a pair of hanging claws.
The four sensory objects float upon the faculties; they flow and rush toward fragrance.
"Mutually inciting" means they provoke one another. "Ingesting and absorbing" means taking in. 4. Grasping flavors forms the tongue.

Due to the intermingling of the two aspects of tranquility and transformation, within the wondrous perfection, the clarity adheres to stillness and gives rise to tasting. The essence of tasting reflects flavor, and by churning flavor, the sense organ is formed.
The root of this organ is termed the "pure four great elements," and for this reason it is called the substance of the tongue; it resembles a crescent moon at its first appearance.
The floating faculties pursue the four sensory objects, flowing and scattering as they rush toward flavors.
"Tranquility" (tián) is the taste of the flavorless; it is the flavor of the flavorless. "Change" (biàn) is the aggregate of the five flavors; it is the flavor of the flavorful.

These two—flavorlessness and flavor—are established as two poles by being set in contrast to one another. "Intermingling" (cān zá) refers to their blending together. One should rotate and grasp [the essence].
It is called "entanglement. Fifth, the body is formed through contact.

Through the two types of mutual friction—separation and conjunction—within the wondrous perfection, the clarity of stillness becomes adhered to, giving rise to sensation. The essence of sensation reflects back upon contact.

The impact of contact forms the sense-faculties (*indriya*). The source of these faculties is termed the "pure four great elements" (*mahābhūta*); because of them, they are called the "body. They are like the drumhead of a waist-drum;
the "floating faculties" [perceive] the four sensory objects, and their flow and escape rush toward contact.
"Mo" (摩) means "to join at the edge. "Luan" (攬) means "to grasp and take up. The waist-drum (*yaogu*) is commonly called the staff-drum (*zhanggu*). Its "sang" (顙) refers to the body of the drum;

Through the two kinds of continuity—arising and ceasing—within the wondrous perfection, the stillness becomes adhered to and gives rise to cognition. The essence of cognition reflects the dharmas, and by grasping these dharmas, the sense-organ is formed.

The fundamental source of this organ is termed the "pure four great elements," and because it functions through mental intention, it is called the "mind-faculty" (*manas*). This is like seeing within a dark chamber.
The floating sense-faculty of the four objects flows and rushes toward mental phenomena (*dharma*).

It is not called the "substance of the mind" (*manas-tattva*), but rather "mental intention" (*manas-cetanā*). This is because the floating sense-faculty of the mind is the physical heart-lump (*māṃsa-guḍa-hṛdaya*).

In general, when free from sensory objects, there are no fetters.

they will no longer rush toward external objects. This is the method for the ears, body, tongue, nose, and mind.

by inference, one knows that the sound has ceased and the hearing has likewise followed in its cessation. When it is struck again, there is no hindrance to the arising of sound."
Hearing likewise arises accordingly; therefore, this section uses the final two lines of the verse to refute it by saying:
"If hearing were to perish as soon as the sound actually perishes, then when the sound is absent, one should not know that the sound is absent.
Thus, you must next examine carefully: who is it that knows the absence of sound? Having thus finished refuting the view of annihilation (*uccheda-dṛṣṭi*), △ [the section ends].
Second, I shall now set forth the true and eternal correct principle.
Therefore, Ānanda, within the act of hearing, sounds themselves undergo arising and ceasing; it is not that your hearing arises and ceases with the sounds.
This causes you to hear whether the nature [of hearing] exists or does not exist;
this is precisely where the distinction is made and determined between that which arises and ceases and that which neither arises nor ceases.

Although the phrasing seems to repeat what was stated previously, this actually carries a further sense of mutual interpenetration that differs from the preceding text. Regarding the first two lines: within the act of hearing, sound is truly...
There is arising and ceasing. The final four phrases mean that although one hears within the sound, in reality, one does not follow its arising and ceasing.
This is not to be read separately from "for you"; rather, the character "hears" (聞) should be read in conjunction with the following phrase.

It states that it is not the case that the arising and ceasing of your hearing of sound causes your hearing-nature itself to sometimes exist and sometimes not. The refutation and establishment of the correct principle are now complete.
△ Fourth, rebuking the error of delusion regarding the precepts:
You are still inverted, mistaking sound for hearing; why then do you marvel at being deluded by taking the permanent to be intermittent? Ultimately, you should not speak thus.
Detached from all movement and stillness, as well as obstruction and openness, it is taught that hearing has no inherent nature.

The first four lines of the verse reprimand delusion. The underlying meaning is this: although the extremes of annihilationism and eternalism may be difficult to definitively distinguish, the faculties and their objects should be easy to differentiate.
Now, you are confused about sound being "hearing," yet you fail to distinguish even that which should be easily distinguished; how much less can you be expected to distinguish the faculties?
To be deluded into thinking that this constant nature within is subject to annihilation is indeed a difficulty in establishing certainty; it makes it even more impossible to establish.

In truth, the reason ordinary beings and those of limited capacity cannot decisively believe that the nature of the faculties is eternally abiding lies in the confusion between the faculties and their objects.
Because their coarse minds have not yet been able to distinguish them, the Buddha struck the bell to examine the matter in detail.
After [the confusion] has become muddled and mixed, one then clarifies and proclaims it; this is the most wondrous instruction. The final four lines warn against ceasing the erroneous arguments.
Regarding "adding closure where there was openness," this seems to clarify that the ephemeral sense organs (*bu chen gen*) are likewise unrelated to the nature of hearing.
The verification of permanence through striking the bell is complete. II. Verification of Permanence through Dreaming. Previously, Ānanda received [the teaching].
The Buddha’s principle that he is free from both movement and stillness, and fundamentally lacks the substance of hearing, has given rise to doubts regarding the annihilation of the auditory faculty.
Now, the demonstration of striking the bell serves to verify the presence of sound during movement and the absence of sound during stillness;

yet, this does not actually reach the point of verifying it by departing from both movement and stillness simultaneously. Therefore, he again cites the state of deep sleep to demonstrate this simultaneous departure from both movement and stillness.
This is verified by experience. It is divided into two parts. First, verifying that dreams are not obscure. This is further divided into four sections. First, dreaming of external, real objects:
for example, when a person is in deep sleep on a bed and pillow, and while they are sleeping, someone in their household pounds silk-cloth or husks rice.
One who sleeps lightly awakens at the slightest sound; thus, this does not serve as a valid analogy. Therefore, only deep sleep is taken—meaning the time when one is fast asleep.
"Beating the laundry" refers to the sound of the washing block; "pounding rice" refers to the sound of the mortar and pestle.
It may also be that both activities are performed simultaneously. △ Second, mistaking things within a dream.
In a dream, such a person hears the sound of pounding and mortaring, yet perceives it as something else—either as the beating of a drum or the striking of a bell.
Within the state of sleep, consciousness is clouded and objects are frequently distorted; hearing an external sound, one erroneously produces a different impression.
This is a common occurrence. Whether it be a bell or a drum, it is acceptable to take both together, as they are mutually implied by the subsequent text. △
The threefold discrimination is not obscured;
thus, even during a dream, one naturally wonders at the bell, taking it to be the sound of wood or stone.
This merely takes up the hearing of the sound as the faculty of the sense-base being unobscured, regardless of whether that perception is mistaken or not.
In the dream, he clearly saw him striking the bell; yet the sound was actually that of the pestle.
Therefore, within the dream, he marveled at how the resonance of this bell’s sound was like that of wood or stone. △ Fourth, describing the error upon waking.
At that moment, he suddenly awoke and immediately recognized the sound of the pestle. He told his family members, "While I was dreaming, I mistook this sound of pounding rice for the beat of a drum."
In a dream one perceives a strange bell; upon waking, one speaks of a drum. These are merely shifting reflections. The verification that the dreaming consciousness is not deluded is complete.
△ Second, the determination of its permanence. Based on this determined root-nature, it is established as permanent. Part One: It is not deluded whether separated from or in contact with objects.

Ānanda, while this person is in a dream, how could they recall stillness, movement, opening, closing, penetration, or obstruction? Although their physical form is asleep, the nature of hearing is not obscured.
"Movement" refers to motion; "stillness and movement" refer to the two sensory objects of motion and stillness. Furthermore, one adds opening, closing, penetration, and obstruction.

This refers to the ears and the flesh. It means that within this dream, not only are motion and stillness both transcended, but the sense organs (*indriya*) and their objects (*viṣaya*) are simultaneously abandoned.
In reality, for a person who is asleep, the entire body is forgotten; how could they still remember the opening and closing, or the penetration and obstruction, of the fleshly ears?
Your doubt—that when motion and stillness are both transcended, the nature of the sense organ (*indriyatva*) would be annihilated—is precisely what applies to this sleeping person during movement.
When the faculties and their objects are both forgotten in stillness, one should be entirely without perception. Yet now, you are still able to distinguish the sound of the pestle;
this proves clearly that the nature of hearing is independent of objects and does not perish. How can there be any further doubt?
△ Second, knowing that the form dissolves but the awareness is not obscured.
"Even if your physical form dissolves and the radiance of your life-force passes away, how could this nature be extinguished by you?
This advances the argument one step further, intended to show that it is not only unclouded during sleep;

based on this, you should also believe that it remains unclouded after death as well. As for the phrase 'how could it be extinguished by you,' does it mean [it is extinguished] by your physical form?"
...is extinguished. Does the nature of hearing also perish along with it? At this point, Ānanda should further pose a question.

He asks: "Since this faculty of the root is unrelated to motion or stillness and unimpeded by birth or death, why does the Tathāgata say that apart from motion and stillness, there is fundamentally no substance of hearing? The Tathāgata should answer: "I said..."

As for the statement that "dust has no substance of hearing": this means there is no accumulation of hearing within the ear; rather, it is the obstruction caused by the attachment to the ear as a faculty that constitutes the substance of hearing.
If this substance is forgotten, then the nature of hearing, which pervades the entire Dharma-realm, will finally manifest in its fullness.

How could it be allowed to turn into something that is severed or annihilated? This passage clarifies that from the very beginning there was no such substance of hearing, thereby revealing that it is inherently the *ālaya*.
This is not a difficult or erroneous interpretation; it is not a case of the Buddha’s own words being contradictory.

Otherwise, if the Buddha first stated that [the sound] is devoid of dust and lacks substance, and later stated that it possesses a body while devoid of dust, there would ultimately be no way to resolve the difficulty of this contradiction in his own speech.
Therefore, this question and answer ought logically to exist; that the scriptural text is missing it is solely because Ānanda was distracted by the striking of the bell.

The skillful demonstration through the dream-citation shows that the nature of the faculty of awakening is eternally abiding. One realizes for oneself that previous difficulties were erroneous and need not be investigated further.
Consequently, many later scholars have failed to understand what the phrase "originally having no substance of hearing" refers to.
This point has never been realized by others; its clarification is of great significance. Let the wise examine this in detail.
Wuxing said: "Previously, Ānanda raised doubts regarding the six sense organs and their objects being devoid of substance when separated.
It was for this reason that the Tathāgata specifically revealed the nature of hearing to be permanent; he truly wished to awaken the potential for the perfect penetration of the ear-organ.
Therefore, the subsequent verse says: "When sound is absent, there is no cessation; when sound is present, there is no birth. This holds true even when one is in a dream."

"Not for the sake of non-thinking, nor for the sake of non-existence"—all of these are taken from this [text]. Having finished citing dreams as proof of permanence, △ Four: Clarifying the Misunderstanding of the Teachings and Adhering to Them.
The preceding section merely elucidated correct understanding; this section provides warnings and exhortations for dedicated practice. It is divided into two parts. First:
Universally Clarifying the Misunderstanding of Permanence, whereby One Falls into Impermanence. This is further divided into two. First: Explaining the Pursuit of Delusion and the Loss of the True.

Because all sentient beings, from time immemorial, have followed after forms and sounds, flowing and turning with every thought, they have never awakened to the pure, wondrous, and eternal nature of their own essence.

The phrase "following after the two lines" refers to pursuing delusion; it speaks generally of following sensory objects (*viṣaya*) in one's flow, citing "form and sound" as a brief illustration to encompass all such categories.
This subsumes all other sensory objects. The final two phrases concern delusion regarding the Truth:

one fails to realize that the nature within the sense-faculties is pure and unstained, wondrous and unbound, eternally abiding and devoid of arising or ceasing. △ Second, the conclusion on the flow of impermanence.
Not following that which is constant, one pursues all that arises and perishes; thereby, birth after birth, one flows and wanders through defilement.
In the previous section, it was stated that wandering with every thought without awakening belongs solely to delusion.

Here, "not following that which is constant" means not maintaining the constant nature inherent within the faculties. "Pursuing all that arises and perishes" means rushing headlong in outward dissipation.

"Dust" refers to the various karmic actions created by dust. "Flowing and transmigrating through birth after birth" points to the inexhaustible fruits of suffering as one wanders through the six realms of existence;
therein, the three—delusion, karma, and suffering—are fully present without deficiency. Because they are deluded regarding the permanent, they ultimately fall into the impermanent.

△ Second, the instruction to maintain the permanent so that one will surely achieve Perfect Enlightenment. The above has alerted [the practitioner] to the boundless cycle of birth and death, but it is merely the cause.

The deluded do not know what to follow regarding constancy; for this reason, they are exhorted to maintain constancy, which will surely lead to ultimate accomplishment. "Maintaining" is synonymous with "following.
This is divided into three parts. First, maintaining constancy according to the orthodox teaching.
If one abandons arising and ceasing to maintain the true and constant:

the first phrase means not pursuing delusions, which is to say, not rushing toward the various sensory objects; the second phrase means maintaining only the truth, which is to say, turning the faculties back to reflect inward.
This is what is meant by "detaching from clinging and withdrawing within. In principle, this is precisely the subsequent entry into the stream of perfect penetration where one forgets the self.

This is merely a matter of diligent effort. △ Second, the six faculties being liberated and the one [mind] forgotten. This is further divided into two parts. First, the constant light manifests and the six faculties are liberated.
When the constant light appears before one, the sense organs, objects, consciousness, and the mind dissolve away simultaneously.

The first line immediately subdues [the delusions] and returns to the original truth, manifesting the fundamental radiance. The final two lines correctly describe the characteristics of the sixfold liberation.
According to the text, the eighteen realms have all been simultaneously dissolved; yet in principle, when the faculties are exhausted, the remaining objects naturally exhaust themselves as well.

This is precisely what was previously called "the nature of radiance manifesting its brilliance," whereby the other five types of attachment should be uprooted and completely liberated. Thus it is said. *Note: IAST diacritics have been applied to Sanskrit terms (e.g., *āyatana*, *dhātu*, *mūla-prakāśa*) as requested.*

Subsequently, when perfect penetration is achieved, that which hears and that which is heard should both be exhausted. II. When the reflected images are exhausted and the one-pointedness is forgotten:
conceptualizations and appearances act as dust, and cognitive consciousness acts as grime; when both are left far behind, then your Dharma-eye will, at that moment, become clear and bright.
In this context, "dust and grime" does not refer to coarse defilements. This is because, in the preceding section, the faculties, objects, consciousness, and mind have all been completely eliminated.
What is now described as occurring after this dissolution—the pure, tranquil, and unified essence within the mind—is itself the appearance of that very tranquility and unity;
it is yet another kind of extremely subtle dust that is difficult to remove. Sentient cognition (*vijñāna*)...

This is not coarse consciousness; rather, it is this very state of profound stillness and unity that acts as the mind capable of conceptualization, and is also termed "attachment to dharmas" (*dharmatṛṣṇā*), because one does not relinquish the realm of profound stillness and unity.
This emotional attachment to dharmas is yet another kind of defilement that clings closely to the body and is difficult to scrape away.
If one can distance oneself from both of these, then the Dharma-eye will immediately become clear and bright.

This is because coarse and subtle dust and defilements have been purified until nothing remains. According to the subsequent section on Perfect Penetration (*yuan-tong*), this stage should correspond to the point where "hearing does not abide" (*wen bu zhu*) and continues until "quiescence manifests before one" (*ji-mie xian-qian*).
Upon reaching this state, even the "tranquil unity" (*zhan-yi*) is forgotten;
how then could the six sense-faculties (*liu-gen*) remain bound? II. Resolving to Attain Perfect Enlightenment.
How could it be that they do not achieve unsurpassed perfect enlightenment?
Their supreme Dharma-eye is clear and bright; they appear to have just reached the first stage (*prathama-bhūmi*), yet now you grant them the ultimate fruit of finality.
It is truly because when the ground is authentic, the fruit will not be circuitous; thus, from the initial generation of the mind of enlightenment, one will necessarily achieve perfect awakening.
Having verified the nature of the faculties and resolved doubts regarding annihilationism, this concludes the examination.
The Correct Pulse Commentary on the Great Buddha-Usnīsa Śūraṅgama Sūtra, Scroll Four;
The Correct Pulse Commentary on the Great Buddha-Usnīsa Śūraṅgama Sūtra, Scroll Five.
Composed by the Śramaṇa Jiaoguang Zhenjian of West Lake, Capital City.

△ Second, the proof and explanation that resolves the doubt regarding the distinct origin of the fetters. Regarding "proof and explanation": this refers to explaining by means of the testimony of all present Buddhas who have attained realization together.
The old commentary states: "This restates the previous point that 'the bound was not seen,' and asks again how one can know and understand it."

If this were so, it would be utterly tasteless. This is because the preceding text clearly stated that the six [senses] act as intermediaries for thieves who plunder the family’s own treasures, providing a detailed exposition on the causes of the roots’ entanglement and the method for resolving them. Furthermore, the fault was verified by the striking of the bell;
why then did Ānanda suddenly fail to realize that the six sense organs are themselves the knots, thereby necessitating the Buddha’s laborious repetition of the answer? This is truly meaningless.
Furthermore, you should know that Ānanda has already understood that the six sense organs are the knots; yet he now requests further clarification regarding the origin of these knots.
This origin is precisely what the Buddhas below have described as the root of birth and death—the innate ignorance (*sahaja-avidyā*).

Because [Ānanda] does not realize that the very substance of the six sense organs is itself this [ignorance], and that there is nothing else apart from it, the Buddha provides the following answer: "If you wish to recognize and know this innate ignorance..."
The root of the fetters of birth and death is none other than your six sense faculties; there is no other thing that constitutes it. This is divided into two parts.
First, Ānanda seeks the source of the fetters elsewhere, which is further divided into three sections. The first is seeking the source by means of an analogy.
Ānanda addressed the Buddha, saying, “World-Honored One, although the Tathāgata has explained the second gateway of meaning,
when I observe those in the world who attempt to untie knots, if they do not know the origin from which the knot was tied, I believe such persons will ultimately be unable to untie it.”
The "original source of the knots" refers to the notion that, apart from these six sense organs, there exists a deeper root above them that serves as the fundamental origin of the knots.
This is merely Ānanda’s deluded conjecture; he assumes there must be such an origin and concludes that because it is unknown, it cannot be untied.
II. Citing an analogy to illustrate [the point]. This is further divided into two parts. First, providing...
"Combined and settled.
World-Honored One, it is likewise for me and the śrāvakas in training within this assembly.
△ Second, the detailed exposition of the text on opening and combining, which is further divided into three parts. First, a remote narrative of the entanglements of delusion.

Since beginningless time, it has arisen and ceased simultaneously with various forms of ignorance; although one may attain such roots of goodness from extensive learning and be called a renunciant, it is still like a quotidian malarial fever.

These accounts are all for those who do not know the root-source of the knots; they will ultimately be unable to untie them. The various forms of ignorance are precisely the five stages of dwelling (pañca-vāsabhūmi).

"Together extinguishing birth" refers to being constantly submerged in birth and death. Ānanda, it is precisely this co-emergent ignorance that constitutes the root of the knots of birth and death—what is called the "root-source of the knots.
How could he have known that the six sense faculties (*ṣaḍ-āyatana*) are themselves that very source?
One who has attained the roots of goodness is called a renunciant; this refers to those who have attained the minor fruits of the stage of training (*śaikṣa*).

As for the "malaria that recurs every other day," it means that at the time of attaining the fruit, one temporarily appears to be liberated, yet upon re-entering the cycle of birth and death (*saṃsāra*), one is again bound as before.

In truth, this applies not only to those in training; even an Arhat of the stage beyond training (*aśaikṣa*) remains so only so long as they do not enter *saṃsāra*. Once they do enter, [they are likewise bound].

This constitutes bondage precisely because one fails to comprehend the locus of the fetters; it has nothing to do with the consciousness-mind. Even if one suppresses or severs [the afflictions], one will ultimately not attain liberation.
△ Second, the prayer for the Buddha’s compassionate instruction.
I only pray that you, in your great compassion, will take pity on those submerged in suffering. Regarding today’s body and mind: what constitutes bondage?
From what is it called liberation? What is meant by "bondage"? What is the fundamental source of bondage? What is meant by "liberation"?
This refers to practicing what dharma to effect such liberation. Because the wording of the sutra is concise, many people have not yet understood this. △ Three.
It also extends to the future,
enabling sentient beings suffering in the future to escape the cycle of rebirth and not fall into the three realms of existence.
△ Third, the earnest plea for instruction.

Having spoken these words, he addressed the entire assembly. Prostrating himself with his five limbs touching the ground, he shed tears and, with uplifted sincerity, awaited the unsurpassed revelation of the Buddha-Tathāgata.
"Uplifted" (qiao) means like a bird spreading its wings while looking for its food. Ānanda had finished his separate search for the origin of the knots. △

Second, the Tathāgatas testify that there is no other substance. This roughly clarifies that outside the six sense faculties (*ṣaḍindriya*), there is no further entity, thereby establishing the fundamental source of bondage.
This is divided into three parts: First, the testimony of all Buddhas. That which is not separate from the six sense faculties is precisely the wondrous nature (*prakṛti*).
This is a teaching difficult to believe and difficult to understand. From the beginning of the sutra until this point, Ānanda has repeatedly received these instructions, yet he still—
Entrusting them with profound understanding, yet abandoning the easy to seek the difficult, the Buddha feared that his own words alone could not cause them to attain firm conviction;
therefore, he manifested all the Buddhas to provide testimony for their faith. This is divided into four parts. First, compassionately touching their heads. This is further divided into three.
First, compassionate mindfulness of those in the present.
At that time, the World-Honored One felt compassion for Ānanda and all those in the assembly who were still in training (*śaikṣa*).

Since the preceding section had already demonstrated that those beyond training (*aśaikṣa*) had attained understanding, and these doubts pertained only to those still in training, he showed particular compassion for them.
△ Second, his compassionate concern for future generations.
It also serves as the cause for transcending the world and acts as the eye for all sentient beings of the future.
As the future recedes further from the Sages, faith and understanding become increasingly difficult; therefore, he universally pities them.

To serve as the cause for transcending the world means that there is reliance upon cultivation and realization. To act as the eye for the future means that faith and understanding will not be deluded. △ Third, Samādhi.
He placed his hand upon the crown of Ānanda’s head. With his hand of Jambūnada purple-gold light, he stroked Ānanda’s crown;
this stroking was solely intended to express compassion and to provide protection. Having finished stroking the heads of the assembly out of pity for them, [the second section follows]: II. Movement.
Throughout the worlds of the ten directions, at that very moment, the Buddha-worlds of the ten directions shook in six ways, signifying that the six sense organs were about to be liberated.
△ Third, the response of the auspicious omens of all Buddhas, divided into two parts. First, each [Buddha] emits...
The light from the crown:
each Tathāgata, as numerous as motes of dust, dwelling within this world, has a precious light issuing from his crown.
This represents the wondrous nature within these faculties, which is honored as supreme and is a secret, invisible dharma. △
Second, the light comes to sprinkle the Buddha’s crown.

Simultaneously, that light arrives from that world at the Jeta Grove to sprinkle the Tathāgata’s crown, demonstrating that they have equally realized this nature and that there is no distinct nature. △ Third, the great assembly rejoices.
This great assembly attained what they had never experienced before.
It was certainly a rare and auspicious omen; yet it also symbolized that all sentient beings equally possess the capacity for sympathetic resonance and shared joy.
△ Fourth, hearing the words of the Buddhas, divided into two parts. First, the standard description of hearing the same voice universally.
Thereupon Ānanda and the great assembly all heard the Tathāgatas, as numerous as motes of dust throughout the ten directions, speaking with one voice and in unison.
That they spoke with one voice and in unison was to demonstrate that all Buddhas proclaim this teaching together; it is not a statement spoken by a single Buddha alone.
This is sufficient to inspire deep faith. The *Amitābha Sūtra* states: "You should all believe and accept my words, as well as what has been spoken by all the Buddhas.
This is precisely that meaning. It is also the same principle as the Buddhas' paths being identical during the Dharma-exposition of the Lotus Sūtra;

since this sūtra causes one to personally see and hear [the Buddha] within its light, it should be especially believed and accepted. II. Describing the Words of All the Buddhas. This has two parts. First, the address.
There is no other thing that forms this bond.
Excellent, Ānanda! If you wish to recognize and know that co-arisen ignorance which causes you to revolve in birth and death—the root of bondage—it is none other than your six sense faculties;
there is truly nothing else.
Co-nascent ignorance (*sahaja-avidyā*) is itself a distinct affliction within the same substance; it is the deepest source of birth and death.

It is called the "root of bondage" (*bandhana-mūla*) because "bondage" signifies being firmly fixed and not opening, while "root" signifies continuity and non-interruption; there is nothing else besides this.
It is said that these faculties are the primary source of innate ignorance (*sahaja-avidyā*) and the deeply rooted foundation of birth and death (*saṃsāra*).
Apart from these six faculties, there is no further root of bondage. △ Second, the instruction that there is nothing else to be liberated.

Furthermore, if you wish to know of unsurpassed bodhi—which enables you to swiftly realize blissful liberation, quiescence, and wondrous permanence—it is none other than your own six faculties; it is not some other thing.

Furthermore, it is stated that this is not merely the fundamental source of delusion, but is also the fundamental source of truth; for it is the chief of transgressions and yet the foremost of merits.
Supreme Bodhi belongs to the fruit of wisdom (*jñāna-phala*), which is precisely the *tathatā-jñāna* (suchness-wisdom) that is capable of realizing [the truth].

Bliss and so forth belong to the fruit of severance (*prahāṇa-phala*) consisting of the four virtues, which is precisely the *tathatā-artha* (suchness-reality) that is realized. "Bliss" refers specifically to the virtue of bliss (*sukha-guṇa*).
Liberation is my attribute, for "I" has the meaning of sovereignty. Quiescence is the attribute of purity;
wondrous permanence is the attribute of eternity. The phrase "not another thing" means that apart from this fundamental nature, there is no separate true source.
This is because the fundamental nature of the faculties is originally identical to the essence of Bodhi and Nirvana, which is primordially pure.
At the beginning of the sutra, the Buddha already determined this to be the true source; yet, the people there for the most part do not recognize it.
I have previously cited this to explain it, and all Buddhas have likewise realized it. II. The Tathāgata’s Explanation. This is divided into two parts: 1. Ānanda’s inquiry before his realization.
Although Ānanda had heard such a sound of the Dharma, his mind was still not yet clear. He bowed his head to the Buddha and said:
"How can it be that my cycle of birth and death and the wondrous, eternal bliss are both these same six sense organs and nothing else?"
[The disciple] harbors a doubt: "The Tathāgata has always taught the characteristics of dharmas; among the most essential and concise formulations, there are even the eighteen *dhātus* and so forth.
Why now do you speak only of the six sense organs (*ṣaḍ-indriya*), while the six objects (*ṣaḍ-viṣaya*) and the six consciousnesses (*ṣaḍ-vijñāna*) are not included?

II. The Tathāgata provides a detailed explanation to remove this doubt, which is divided into two parts. First, the prose section, which is further divided into three. The first part uses the standard to examine [the question], which is further divided into...
This consists of two parts: first, identifying the locations and the single essence.
The Buddha told Ānanda: "The faculties and their objects share the same source; bondage and liberation are non-dual.

Regarding the term "locations" (*āyatana*) mentioned in the analysis, it refers to the "faculties and objects" in the sutra, which subsumes the twelve *āyatanas*. This was because Ānanda harbored a doubt in his mind.
It says: "If we speak only of the six faculties (*ṣaḍ-indriya*), would it not be a neglect of the six objects (*ṣaḍ-viṣaya*)? Therefore, this opening sentence announces:
'Regarding the faculties and the objects, if one observes them by grasping at their characteristics, the faculties are the internal body and belong to the sentient;
the objects are the external vessel-world and belong to the insentient. They seem forever distinct. Yet one does not know that they are fundamentally but the One Mind, falsely divided.'"

Regarding the sentient beings and their physical environments: if one traces back the flow to its source, they remain but a single essence. How could there truly be twelve distinct essences for the twelve bases (*āyatana*)? This is precisely the school of Consciousness-Only (*Vijñaptimātra*):
both the objective aspect (*nimitta-bhāga*) and the subjective aspect (*darśana-bhāga*) arise based upon self-cognition (*svasaṃvitti*). Following this, it continues:

because the sense organs (*indriya*) and objects (*viṣaya*) share the same source, by taking up the organ, the object is simultaneously subsumed. Therefore, when bound, one is an ordinary being (*pṛthagjana*).
Flowing into and sinking into [suffering], these six sense faculties (ṣaḍ-indriya) are firmly established as the root of bondage.

Conversely, when one becomes a companion of the sages and attains sovereignty, it is likewise these six sense faculties that serve as the source of liberation. How could there be two separate entities?
△ Second, examining the consciousness to reveal its falsity.
The nature of consciousness is illusory, like flowers in the sky.
Ānanda may further harbor doubts in his mind, thinking: "Since the faculties and objects share the same source, the mention of the faculty alone suffices to encompass the object."
Why, then, are the six consciousnesses not mentioned? To address this, he further examines the matter, stating:
"Consciousness consists of false perceptions and conceptualizations regarding external objects, like flowers in the sky; it possesses no substantial reality at all.

Since it is neither the root of bondage nor the essential means of liberation, binding and liberation pertain solely to the faculties (*indriya*), and are in no way dependent upon consciousness. This concludes the section.

It is said: Since the six sense objects have no separate substance and the six consciousnesses are utterly void, all Buddhas unanimously declare that both bondage and liberation reside solely within the six sense faculties.

In truth, this very section on "marking and examining" exhaustively explains the words of the Buddhas without remainder; the subsequent prose and verse explanations merely serve to further clarify this point.
△ Second, a double explanation for clarification. The principle is fundamentally profound and subtle, yet the indicated text is obscure and concise;

fearing that it may not be fully understood, it is therefore explained again for the sake of clarity. However, within this section, only the indicated points are explained while the examined points are not, because they have already been eliminated and discarded.
This is divided into two parts. First, a double explanation of the common source of the faculties and their objects.

Ānanda, cognition arises from objects, and characteristics exist because of the sense organs; yet both characteristics and cognition lack inherent nature, being like two bundles of reeds leaning against one another.
"Cognition arises from objects" means that it is only by virtue of the six sense-objects (*ṣaḍ-viṣaya*) that the cognitions of the six sense-faculties (*ṣaḍ-indriya*) subsequently arise.

This phrase shows that the six sense-faculties must rely upon the six sense-objects to be established. "Characteristics exist because of the sense organs" refers to the six... [the six sense-objects].
Only after the sense organs exist do the characteristics of the six objects arise. This phrase shows that the six objects must rely upon the six organs before they can exist.
Regarding "the mutual lack of self-nature in appearance and perception":

it means that objects lack an independent self-nature apart from the organs, and the organs likewise lack an independent self-nature apart from the objects. The "mutually supporting reeds" (*jiaolu*) is a distinct type of plant.
It is coarser and larger than ordinary reeds; it must grow in pairs, standing with the two stalks entwined around one another.
Their two roots are knotted and joined together; if single, they fall to the ground and cannot stand on their own. Furthermore, its substance is solid on the outside and hollow within.

When it is said here that it is "like a *jalābu* (interlaced reed)," this refers to the prose description, which seems to take only the quality of being interlaced and unable to stand independently as the point of comparison. It is also like this.
The faculties (*indriya*) and their objects (*viṣaya*) each lack intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*); they share a single source and are of one essence.

This is why the subsequent passage introduces the idea that bondage and liberation depend solely upon the faculties. According to the verse, it still adopts the metaphor of the external being real and the internal being empty, to illustrate that both the emptiness and existence of the faculties and objects are non-existent.
Therefore, although the meaning of emptiness and existence is not explicitly stated in the current prose section, it should nonetheless implicitly contain both.
The purport of this refutation is that, as will be seen in the following text, the establishment of cognition based on non-seeing has a profound historical and doctrinal basis. II.
A further explanation of the non-duality of bondage and liberation:
"Therefore, when you now establish cognition within seeing and knowing, this is the very root of ignorance; when seeing and knowing are devoid of seeing, this is itself Nirvana."
It is untainted and truly pure.

Therefore, although these two characters—“is” (shi)—explicitly indicate that they follow from the preceding statement that since both the faculty and the object lack dual substance, bondage and liberation reside solely within the faculty, they also implicitly carry the further significance of following from the principle that both emptiness and existence are neither. One should know this.

"Seeing" encompasses the nature of the six sense organs. "Establishing knowing" refers to establishing the two types of knowing: emptiness and existence. Ordinary beings delude the nature of the six sense organs as being existent;
those of the Two Vehicles obscure the nature of the six sense organs as being empty. Neither has reached the principle that both emptiness and existence are non-existent.
"That which is the root of ignorance" refers to ordinary beings, who are fully possessed of the five abodes [of affliction]. And...

Those who have long been submerged in the realm of segmented birth all take delusion regarding existence as their fundamental basis. Those of the Two Vehicles still retain a remnant of the fifth [stage] and have not yet emerged from the realm of transformation;
they all obscure emptiness as their fundamental basis. "To be without views" means to be without the dualistic views of existence and emptiness.

Ordinary beings eliminate the view of grasping at existence within their sensory faculties and natures; those of the Two Vehicles eliminate [the view of emptiness] within their sensory faculties and natures.
This is the view of partial emptiness. Nirvana is the opposite of the two aforementioned types of birth-and-death.
"Untainted true purity" refers to being free from the ignorance of the five abodes mentioned above. As for the phrase "this is what is called":

it means that ordinary beings, having eliminated the first four abodes, first attain *sopadhiśeṣa-nirvāṇa* (nirvana with remainder) and untainted true purity—what is known as "this faculty first being liberated, first attaining the emptiness of persons."
The Two Vehicles, excluding those in the fifth stage, attain the ultimate *nirupadhiśeṣa-nirvāṇa*, which is untainted (*anāsrava*), true, and pure.

This scripture was spoken for the sake of ordinary beings and followers of the Lesser Vehicle; therefore, it makes such statements. If one possesses the great faculties from the very beginning, there is no necessity to distinguish between these two types of persons.

(Old Commentary: Both interpretations are incorrect. The former interpretation negates existence to grasp at emptiness, failing to heed the verse’s statement that both emptiness and existence are neither. The latter interpretation establishes the real and excludes the false, failing to heed the verse’s teaching that both the false and the real are equally false.)

These words are significant. To disregard them so flagrantly while still claiming to be in accord with the Buddha’s intent—how could such commentary and sub-commentary ever be considered easy to produce? Students should treat this matter with great care. Question:

Is this "knowledge and vision" (jñāna-darśana) the same as, or different from, the knowledge and vision in the *Lotus Sūtra* (*Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*) and the knowledge and vision taught after the "Perfect Manifestation of the Three Baskets" (*Tripiṭaka*) in this present sūtra? Answer: There is no separate dharma; it is merely that the manner of explanation and demonstration differs. In the *Lotus Sūtra*, the name is established but the meaning has not yet been explained.

Commentators have followed their own subjective sentiments, which lack scriptural evidence and are therefore far too superficial. In this sūtra, the Buddha himself explains it through his golden mouth. The "Perfect Manifestation of the Three Baskets" refers precisely to the Buddha’s knowledge and vision, which is taken to be the fundamental endowment within the store-consciousness (*ālaya-vijñāna*) of sentient beings, rather than something produced through cultivation and realization. However, regarding sentient beings...

The previous discussion concerning their manifestation in birth did not specify where they are possessed; thus, it was not yet definitive. Now, by pointing out the Tathāgata’s knowledge and vision within the nature of the six faculties currently present in sentient beings, this [explanation] is truly definitive.

It is not a matter of generality. For "knowing" (*jñāna*) is the internal faculty of the mind-organ (*manas*), while "seeing" (*darśana*) refers to the external five sense-faculties. Since the nature of these faculties is all-pervasive and eternally abiding, it constitutes the fundamentally pure essence of *bodhi* and *nirvāṇa*, wherein the three baskets (*tripiṭaka*) are perfectly complete.

If this is not the Tathāgata’s knowledge and vision, what else could the "single transmission" and "direct pointing" possibly refer to? They are, in fact, a secret pointing to this very reality. Yet, they are called "beyond the teachings" (*kyōge*) because one must transcend words and letters to turn the light back and see for oneself. If one merely follows the words, [one will miss the point].

To treat this as something outside the teachings is like attempting to speak of dreams before a fool; one must be careful. Having thus completed the detailed explanation, △ third, the general conclusion and dedication.
"How can there be room for any other thing within this?
This concludes and returns to the fundamental words of all Buddhas. "Within this" refers both to the binding within and the liberation within.

The intended meaning is that within the binding, there is only the root-binding (*mūla-grantha*), and there is no other entity capable of acting as the source of binding. Within the liberation, there is only...
This is the faculty of understanding (*indriya-prativedha*). Furthermore, there is no other entity that can serve as the primary source of understanding.
This is why all Buddhas unanimously state that there is no other entity whatsoever. The prose section concludes. △ Second, the verse summary, divided into two parts. First, the introductory verse.
At that time, the World-Honored One, wishing to restate this meaning, spoke in verse:

**II. The Verse Text.** This is divided into two sections: **A. The *Geya* (Repetition) Verses, which echo the preceding prose.** This is divided into two parts: **1. Direct Versification, which sets forth the examination.** This is divided into two parts:
**a. A Transcendent Verse examining the falsity of consciousness.** [In the Faxiang school, the five stages of *vijñapti-mātra* consist of four conditioned (*saṃskṛta*) stages.]
The fifth [point] concerns the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*). Now, the text of this verse clearly refutes both [theories].

Thus, we know that it is a "transposed verse" (*chāosòng*) intended to show that the nature of consciousness is false and illusory, like flowers in the sky. Generally, when the Buddha versifies his prose discourses, he frequently employs variations in phrasing, inversions, and non-sequential arrangements.

This is precisely what Tiantai did when he commented on the *Lotus Sūtra*, categorizing them as "transposed verses" (*chāosòng*) and "retrospective verses" (*zuīsòng*). Previous scholars failed to understand this.

Zhiyi’s verses transcend the nature of consciousness (*vijñāna-svabhāva*). [Your interpretation] forcibly explains them through such concepts as "the sense organs and objects sharing the same source" (*genchen tongyuan*);

the phrasing is highly inconsistent, so how could the meaning possibly be coherent? This is because you cannot omit what is doubtful. Now, please provide a separate explanation; let the wise discern it.
Furthermore, this shall be divided into two parts: first, the exclusion of the conditioned (*saṃskṛta*).
"In ultimate reality, conditioned phenomena are empty; because they arise dependently, they are like illusions.

This verse from the *Tattvasiddhi-śāstra* (Pal-zhen-lun) is identical in meaning to the [Prajñāpāramitā] Sūtra (as it completely refutes Vijñaptimātratā, it is the same as the Sūtra), though the phrasing differs slightly.
The first two lines state: "In ultimate reality, conditioned phenomena are empty; because they arise dependently, they are like illusions. The first line is entirely identical to the Sūtra. Qing...
Liang says: "That statement is inverted; it should read: 'The true nature of the conditioned is empty.

This means that the consciousness of the conditioned (referring here specifically to the first six [consciousnesses]—whether contaminated or uncontaminated—distinguished from the context of the *Sūtra on the Conditioned and Unconditioned*) lacks a true intrinsic nature, and is therefore called 'empty. This interpretation is most correct.

As for the subsequent line, if we apply the logic of formal inference (*anumāna*), then the verse of the treatise remains inverted (meaning the reason and the example are reversed), whereas the verse of the sūtra is correct."
