thus it is said that he withdrew to conceal his subtle mechanism. However, in his mind he hoped that the Buddha would not trouble himself to speak, but would instead command the various sages to speak individually. Thus...
The practitioner may naturally attain silent resonance through these words; hence it is said, "I hope for the Buddha’s secret transmission.
This is because the preceding phrase does not explicitly state a request, while the subsequent phrase conveys the request through its underlying intent.

Thus, the appropriateness of this skillful deployment by the Great Authority and the pedagogical intent of the teacher and disciple are fully revealed herein. △ Second, the Buddha commands the various sages to each speak. This...
I certainly concur with your previous intention and request; however, the reason for insisting that each person speak is twofold:

first, to demonstrate that the twenty-five gates universally encompass all phenomena, such that one may enter through any of them, yet to select only one gate here is to suit the specific capacities of those in this land, not because the nature of the sages is restricted to a single gate;
second, to show that each of the sages personally practiced and attained direct realization, rather than engaging in empty talk devoid of verification.

This is the method [of the scripture]. It is divided into three sections. First, the Buddha questions the various sages, which is further divided into two parts. First, the designation of the assembly to whom he addresses himself:
"At that time, the World-Honored One addressed all the great Bodhisattvas and the great Arhats whose outflows were exhausted within the assembly."
Relying solely on the subsequent passage, the Buddha stated that there is no distinction of superiority or inferiority among their practices.
Thus, these various names, ranks, and sizes of the Dharma gates—whether partial or complete—are all of one single flavor, perfect and real; there is no need for further doubt.
Why labor over such extensive disputation? If there were still distinctions of large and small, or partial and complete, then the Buddha’s later statement would become a falsehood.
How could such a principle exist? One should know that this sutra must indeed follow the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*.
Therefore, within this sutra, it directly permits the cultivation of bodhi through two practices without ever expressing any sense of astonishment or strangeness.

If it were prior to the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka*, then this sutra would have already discussed the true mark (*bhūtalakṣaṇa*) and the Buddha’s knowledge and vision (*buddhajñānadarśana*), yet the audience would each have known for themselves that their own minds pervade the ten directions.

[This is] the method. Even until the mind attains permanent abiding, these two attachments will be completely eradicated; there is no doubt that one will attain Buddhahood. What more, then, could the *Lotus Sūtra* reveal?
Even if it were to be preached again, what cause for such great astonishment would there be? Furthermore, Mount Gu said that the teaching had already been revealed, yet he also stated:
"Since their origins have been disclosed, all [teachings] refer to what was revealed by the Buddha in the *Lotus Sūtra*. And...
Wuxing fallaciously argues that this is not so, as if to say that Gushan’s claim that the various sages each reveal their own [teachings] is a grievous error.
Alas for these words! How could Gushan’s injustice ever be vindicated? Furthermore, Wuxing is obstinate;

he forcibly cites scriptures of provisional meaning to arbitrarily divide the Mahāyāna and Hīnayāna, asserting their superiority and inferiority with such clarity that they remain unmixed. This is truly a public defiance of principle.
The Buddha’s intent. At the end, you again cite the Buddha’s words and verses, claiming they are the definitive text for "opening the provisional to reveal the real.
Little do you realize that you are distinguishing between superior and inferior; if it were truly the Buddha’s word, it would not be so, and if it were the Buddha’s word, it would not be as you say.
If that were so, then your distinction between superior and inferior would not hold; how could both possibly be established as such?
Thus, while beginning with a horizontal critique of others' errors, you ultimately lack any certainty yourself. Your words are mostly of this kind; the wise should examine them.
Guishan’s words originally followed the Buddha’s intent and were fundamentally free from error. II. Relating the Admonition.
These words are further divided into two parts. First, regarding the result already accomplished:
"You bodhisattvas and arhats, having been born into my Dharma, have attained the state of no-more-learning."

Bodhisattvas and Arhats are both designated as those beyond training (*aśaikṣa*). This is precisely because, since the title "Arhat" is already applied to those on the stages (*bhūmi*), how could Bodhisattvas avoid the designation "beyond training"?
Moreover, they have realized the truth and understood delusion; for them, cultivation is itself non-cultivation. Yongjia said:
"The man of the Way who has transcended study and is non-active does not eliminate delusive thoughts nor seek the Truth. Master Zhi said:

Without giving rise to even a hair’s breadth of a mind for cultivation or study, one is eternally sovereign within the light of formlessness. This is the clear evidence of the Bodhisattva’s stage of No-More-Learning (aśaikṣa).
△ Second, the subsequent question on the skillful means for entering perfection.
I now ask you: when you first gave rise to the aspiration for enlightenment and awakened to the eighteen realms, which served as your perfect penetration?
By what skillful means did you enter samādhi?
It is evident that this does not inquire about the profound fruits of the present; rather, it asks only about the initial expedient means.

It does not state that the seven great elements are subsumed within the eighteen realms (*dhātu*), nor that the six sense objects (*viṣaya*) subsume the first five great elements, while the faculties (*indriya*) and consciousness (*vijñāna*) subsume the latter two great elements.

II. The Various Explanations of the Original Cause, in two parts: 1. The Brief Explanation by the Assembly of Sages. Because these are all expedient means for entering the Perfect [Teaching], they are thus described briefly.
It should be explained in full, for it can expand one's understanding of universal interpenetration (*yuanrong*).

However, because it would not accord with the spiritual capacities (*indriya*) of those in this land, it is only briefly explained here, lest practitioners engage in confused cultivation. This section is divided into four parts. First: the universal penetration of the six sense objects (*ṣaḍviṣaya*).

The Abhidharma school (Xiangzong) maintains that sensory objects (*viṣaya*) are the *nimitta-bhāga* (objective aspect) of the *ālayavijñāna*. This sutra, however, maintains that they are the *tathāgatagarbha-citta*.

If a practitioner can attain awakening through even a single sensory object, the nature of the *garbha* manifests before them; thus, the six sense-objects become the perfect penetration (*yuan-tong*). Question:

Is this the same as, or different from, the approach of the Gate of the Patriarchs (*Zongmen*), which enters the Way through seeing forms and hearing sounds? Answer: It is not entirely the same, yet...
Nor are they entirely different. For those in the Chan school, the point of awakening realized in the present life is not necessarily the same as the dharma-gate they practiced;
for instance, how could Lingyun have taken the peach blossom as his gate of practice? It was simply a matter of investigating with a state of doubt.
When the intensity of one's practice reaches its peak, there may suddenly be a momentary, piercing disclosure at the very point where forms are seen.

However, the current methods of contemplating the Four Noble Truths, impurity, and the tasting of medicine are mostly dharmas that are cultivated as objects of practice; it is only after long-term effort that realization is entered.

If this were the case here, I would not dare say they are the same. Nevertheless, those in the Chan school also have their own distinct causes and conditions, which a master with true insight can discern.
He knows this in advance. For example, if the conditions lie within the sphere of sound, one will certainly not attain awakening through the sphere of form;
this applies even to persons, sūtras, shouts, blows, and spoken phrases—all of which are fixed and cannot be confused.
When we trace this back to the past, it is likely that it was caused by such habitual practice. Otherwise, how could the master have known it beforehand? If...
This is not yet different from that of the various sages; I do not dare say it is otherwise.

Only cases such as those of Xiangyan and Guṇabhadra, who attained awakening through the scent and touch respectively, seem to be matters of sudden occurrence at a single moment, and thus resemble the awakenings in this very life found in the Chan school.

Let the wise examine this. Dividing [the objects] into six categories, first, regarding Dignāga’s treatment of sound-objects (*śabda-viṣaya*), they are divided into three sections. First, the composition...
The formal address was made.
The five bhikṣus, including Kauṇḍinya, immediately rose from their seats, prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, and addressed the Buddha, saying:
[The five bhikṣus understood and manifested... Part One, Scroll One. △ Second, the words of the formal address, divided into three sections. First, the narration of awakening to the sound.
The Teaching:
While I was at the Deer Park and the Cock Garden, I observed that when the Tathāgata first attained enlightenment,
he realized and clarified the Four Noble Truths through the Buddha’s voice.
The Deer Park and the Cock Garden were both sites where ancient emperors raised livestock.

When the five companions abandoned the Buddha to practice for themselves here, the Buddha, on the day he attained enlightenment, first sought them out and delivered them. Therefore, it is said that this was where the Tathāgata was first seen attaining the Way.
For the sake of these five men, the Buddha turned the Wheel of the Four Noble Truths three times; among them, Cunda was the first to awaken and become an Arhat. Thus...
It is said: "He attained clear realization of the Four Noble Truths through the Buddha’s voice. △ Second, receiving the seal of approval and being given a name:
The Buddha asked the bhikṣu, "I was the first to declare you 'understood. Thus, the Tathāgata conferred upon you the name Ajñāta (A-ruo-duo)."

"First called 'Understanding' (Ajñāta)" means he was the very first to attain realization. "Ajñāta" translates as "understanding"; his name accorded with his reality, for he was the foremost in realization.
Furthermore, that he was the first to receive deliverance was also due to his prior causes. △ Third, the perfection of the three sounds and the attainment of realization.
The wondrous voice is subtle and perfect. Regarding sounds, I have attained arhatship.
As for "the wondrous voice is subtle and perfect," it is because when the Buddha expounds the Dharma with a single sound, sentient beings each attain understanding according to their own kind.
When the Four Noble Truths were being taught, the śrāvakas of true practice only grasped the principle of arising and ceasing; yet the wondrous voice...

The Esoteric Perfect [Teaching] penetrates the unconditioned Four Noble Truths and reaches the Tathāgatagarbha mind. Dignāga secretly developed a profound understanding and realized the perfect and true principle.
If one aligns the Great with the Small, borrowing the name of the Small Vehicle’s fruition, his stage corresponds to that of the seventh stage of faith and above.

In essence, those who possess a semblance of great realization never truly deserve the name "faithful" (śrāvaka). They borrow the designation of a minor fruit with which they are temporarily equal to name themselves;

this is the case in all sutras. If names were taken entirely according to their literal reality, then other sutras would refer to the ten stages (*bhūmi*) as being the stage of an Arhat, and the dwelling place of a person of the Perfect Teaching (*yuan*) would be entirely on par with the distinct stages of the Separate Teaching. Therefore, the stage of perfect penetration is also what is meant by the Mahāyāna Arhat.
Han: This explanation is particularly profound; all subsequent [explanations] shall follow this pattern. △ Third, the conclusion of the answer regarding perfect penetration:
When the Buddha asked about perfect penetration, according to what I have realized, sound is supreme.

Regarding "sound as the supreme": the essence of the true teaching in this realm lies in purity within sound and hearing. These two characters, "sound" and "hearing," both constitute the essence of the teaching.
The faculty of hearing is that which Avalokiteśvara realized; now, the sense-object of sound is that which Dignāga realized.
This is because he gained power and attained awakening through the teaching of sound. He grasped the perfect purport of the Buddha’s Four Noble Truths and sought [it] therein...

These names and phrases are for the purpose of awakening the *cittagarbha*. For after the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* revealed and manifested the truth, who among the great assembly of humans and devas did not know that the Buddha’s various great disciples were all Mahāsattvas who concealed their inner realization while manifesting outwardly?

Furthermore, at the assembly of the *Śūraṅgama-sūtra*, countless great beings deliberated upon the perfect penetration (*pariśuddha-āyatana*). How could there have been any śrāvakas of actual practice who would not have reflected upon themselves?
How could one who falsely considers their own partial, inferior, and shallow realization to be audacious enough to equate themselves with the perfect penetration (*yuan-tong*) of the Mahāyāna?
Even granting such arrogance, for what reason would the Tathāgata falsely grant that there is no distinction of superiority or inferiority between them?

Viewed from this perspective, they must all have attained the perfect enlightenment of the Mahāyāna without doubt; as for those sūtras that are not yet fully understood, one need not be dogmatically attached to them.
Thus ends the section on the auditory object (*śabda-viṣaya*) by Dignāga. △ Second, the olfactory object (*gandha-viṣaya*). This is divided into three parts.
First, the prostration and formal address: Upānanda rose from his seat, prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, and addressed the Buddha, saying:
△ Second, the statement of formal announcement (*jñapti*). This is further divided into three sections. First, the narration of awakening to the nature of form (*rūpa-dharmatā*):
"I, too, when observing the Buddha’s initial attainment of enlightenment, observed the signs of impurity, gave rise to great revulsion and detachment, and awakened to the nature of all forms."

Regarding the practice of contemplating impurity—from the white bones and subtle particles returning to emptiness, where both emptiness and form are non-existent—thereby accomplishing the path of no-more-learning (*aśaikṣa*):
for those with excessive desire, the Buddha prescribed the nine contemplations (*navasaṃjñā*) as an antidote;
this is one of the five "cessation-of-the-mind" (*pañca-vinodana-citta*) practices. Indeed, among the gates of contemplation established by the Buddha, there are...
Common and uncommon: these are dharmas shared by both the Mahāyāna and Hīnayāna.

Furthermore, regarding the sharpness or dullness of the faculties (*indriya*) and the lightness or heaviness of the afflictions (*kleśa*), there are four permutations. This refers to those whose faculties are sharp but whose afflictions are heavy;

because they possess sharp faculties yet are prone to much desire for form and lust, when they practice the contemplation of impurity as an antidote, they still give rise to perfect awakening, which then increases.

This is what is meant by "water": it refers to contemplating that the sensory object of form (*rūpa-dhātu*) is fundamentally the *tathāgatagarbha*. This is because one has transcended and bypassed the nine stages of contemplation on impurity (*aśubha-bhāvanā*).
As for the non-existence of both emptiness and form, once the illness is cured, the medicine is discarded; thus, even the absence of characteristics is not exhausted.
The stage of No-More-Learning (*aśaikṣa*) follows the same principle as before. △ Second, receiving the seal and being named.
The Tathāgata conferred upon me the seal of ordination, naming me Upaśānta.
Wēnlíng says: *Upaśānta* is translated as "near" or "slight," and is also called "the nature of dust.
This means that subtle atoms (*paramāṇu*) are the smallest portions of form. △ Third: Attaining the Fruit through the Perfection of Form.
When the coarse colors have been exhausted, the wondrous color is subtle and perfect. From these forms and appearances, I attained Arhatship.
My previous statement that "emptiness and form are both non-existent" referred only to the exhaustion of appearances;

this present statement that "the coarse colors having been exhausted, the wondrous color is subtle and perfect" refers to the manifestation of the nature when appearances are exhausted. Yet, because it is still called "wondrous color," form remains unimpaired and is universally pervasive.
Contemplate all forms as being none other than the Tathāgata-garbha mind, which pervades the entire Dharma-realm. The Arhats may be understood according to the preceding explanation.
△ Third, the conclusion and response regarding the perfect penetration.
The Buddha asked about the perfect penetration of the faculties.

"According to what I have realized," [Ānanda] said, "the faculty of form is supreme, for contemplating form is the cause for entering into perfection. This concludes the section on the objective field of form (*rūpa-viṣaya*).
△ Third, the fragrance-field of Ghrāṇasena. This is divided into three parts: first, prostrating and making a formal statement.
The youth Fragrance-Veneration immediately rose from his seat, prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, and addressed the Buddha as follows.

△ Second, the words of his petition, divided into three parts. First, the narration of his realization regarding the sensory object of fragrance, further divided into three. First, the observation of conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛta*).
I have heard that the Tathāgata instructed me to carefully contemplate the characteristics of all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛta-dharma*).

"Careful contemplation" means to observe them with thorough and authentic scrutiny. Regarding "the characteristics of all conditioned phenomena," this refers to the verse on the manifestation of understanding, namely the sense organs (*indriya*), objects (*viṣaya*), and consciousness (*vijñāna*), and so forth.
△ Second, smelling fragrances in a quiet place.
At that time, having taken leave of the Buddha, I was in quiet seclusion within a pure chamber (*qingzhai*). I saw various bhikṣus burning aloeswood incense;
its fragrance was serene as it came into my nostrils.
Xie Li said: "Yan" means peaceful rest; "hui" means dark stillness. A pure room is called a "pure chamber."
○ Incense is but one phenomenon among conditioned things; that which is tranquil is signless. △ Third, the manifestation through incense:
I observe this vapor—it is neither wood nor space, neither smoke nor fire. As it departs, there is no place to which it clings; as it comes, there is no source from which it arises.
"By this, the conceptual mind is dissolved and the untainted (anāsrava) is revealed.
Wuxing said: "Generally, when speaking of the emptiness of nature (prakṛti-śūnyatā), one must examine the four natures.

Now, let us take wood as 'self,' smoke and fire as 'other,' their combination as 'both,' and emptiness as 'causeless. This resembles the Mahāyāna method of contemplating that what is illusorily existent is itself empty."

Regarding these characteristics: by contemplating these four natures, one realizes that the essential substance from which the fragrance arises is ultimately unobtainable, and thus the characteristic of fragrance is exhausted.
This interpretation is quite consistent with the Buddha’s method of deconstructing phenomena. As it is said: "Since fire does not exist in mere wood, it is not wood;

since the fragrance is not identical to the nature of space, it is not space; and since it does not arise from burning other substances, it is not those substances. Thus, the characteristic of fragrance is exhausted.
Therefore it is said: "It is neither smoke nor fire. Since the substance of the fragrance cannot be apprehended, it departs without attachment and arrives from nowhere.
By this, those whose conceptual minds are dissolved enter into non-discrimination; those who realize this are the ones who manifest the outflow-free (*anāsrava*).
The essence of the blazing incense is precisely the *tathāgatagarbha* mind. △ Second, receiving the seal and being named:
The Tathāgata sealed me, and I obtained the name "Incense Purity" (*Gandhavimala*).
△ Third, attaining the fruit through the perfection of fragrance.
Mundane odors suddenly vanish; wondrous fragrance becomes subtle and pervasive.

"I have attained Arhatship through Fragrance-Adornment" means that Fragrance-Adornment uses wondrous fragrance to adorn the Dharma-body. The two phrases regarding "mundane odors" likewise signify that when characteristics are exhausted, nature manifests.
The same applies to the Arhats as mentioned above. △ Third, the conclusion of the answer regarding perfect penetration:
"When the Buddha asks about perfect penetration, according to what I have realized, the fragrance of incense is supreme.
Although this and that of Bhadrapāla closely resemble the points of awakening in the Chan school, they still rely extensively upon conceptual discrimination.
This serves as the point of entry. In the ancestral school, it is not necessarily that there are so many [stages];

rather, when one's practice reaches its ultimate limit, everything is simply seen through with clarity wherever one touches. Nevertheless, although those who have attained awakening are identical in their vision of the Truth (*satya*), the depth of their realization varies according to their past roots (*mūla*) and cannot be fixed.
Yet, these various sages are likewise no different in their penetrating vision of the hidden mind (*citta*). And...
The stage of realization for those of initial resolve is definitely at the level of the seventh faith or above, extending through the first dwelling (*āśraya*); this realization is likewise the same.

Otherwise, it would be impossible to speak of it as being identical to the stage of perfect penetration. Hereafter, all cases shall follow this pattern. The section on the fragrance of incense and its corresponding sense-object is concluded.
△ Fourth, the medicinal king and the sense-object of taste, divided into three parts: First, prostration and formal address.
The two Dharma-Prince sons, Bhaiṣajyarāja and Bhaiṣajyasamudgata, along with five hundred Brahmā deities present in the assembly, immediately rose from their seats,
prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, and addressed the Buddha, saying:
Five hundred Brahmā devas were his accompanying retinue. △ Second, the words of his petition, which are further divided into three parts.
First, the narration of awakening to the flavors of sensory objects, which is divided into three. First, the past cause of tasting the medicine.

Since beginningless kalpas, I have served as a skilled physician for the world; with my own mouth, I have tasted the plants, trees, minerals, and metals of this Sahā world, numbering a total of one hundred and eight thousand varieties.
△ Second, being thoroughly proficient in the nature of medicines:
Thus he fully knows the tastes of bitter, sour, salty, bland, sweet, and pungent, as well as their combinations, natural occurrences, and transformations;
whether they are cold or hot, and whether they are toxic or non-toxic—he is able to know them all completely.
Gushan said: "When various flavors combine to form a single entity, it is called 'harmonized' (hehé). When they are used directly as they are, it is called 'co-nascent' (jùshēng).
When they are refined, roasted, or steamed, it is called 'transformed' (biànyì). △ Third, awakening through the very flavor itself."
Serving the Tathāgata, he thoroughly understood the nature of taste: it is neither empty nor existent; it is neither identical to the body and mind, nor is it separate from the body and mind.
By discerning the causes of taste, he attained enlightenment.

When the tongue comes into contact with medicine, a burning flavor manifests; therefore, it is not empty. Although it manifests upon contact with the tongue, it actually lacks any form or characteristic;
therefore, it is not existent. Furthermore, flavor is an invisible, resistant form (*sapratigha-rūpa*); because it is resistant, it is not empty, and because it is not seen, it is not existent.
Here, "body" refers to the tongue, and "mind" refers to the tongue-consciousness (*jihvā-vijñāna*). None of these medicines come [into being].
Thus, the tongue and its consciousness do not manifest of themselves as suffering and so forth; therefore, they are not identical to the body and mind.
Yet, if the gustatory consciousness does not taste the various medicines, how could it manifest suffering and so forth of its own accord? Therefore, they are not separate from the body and mind.

By investigating the causes of flavor one by one, analyzing where these causes of flavor actually exist, those who achieve awakening through this will suddenly realize that all flavors are but a blazing manifestation.
Originally, they do not arise from various medicines, nor from body and mind; they are fundamentally the Tathāgatagarbha, the nature of True Suchness (Tathatā).
△ Second, receiving the seal and the naming:
[The Buddha] bestowed upon me, his younger brother, the names of the two Bodhisattvas Bhaiṣajyarāja and Bhaiṣajyasamudgata, sealing them within this assembly.
As a prince of the Dharma, one who receives no separate title from the Buddha refers specifically to Śākyamuni as his teacher throughout kalpas of dust-like eons.
Regarding the stage of Bodhisattva realized at the time of initial awakening, it should correspond to the seventh faith or above, encompassing the first abode (*prathama-vihāra*). [End of fragment]

Two phrases clarify that although he has now attained a high realization and a profound stage, he does not change his original name. △ Third, the attainment of the fruit through the flavor of awakening:
having awakened to clarity through the flavor of the cause, his rank ascends to that of a Bodhisattva.
"Awareness-illumination" refers to the awakening of the storehouse mind (*ālaya-citta*). This concludes the initial expedient means of attaining the fruit through the flavor [of the practice].
△ Third, the conclusion of the answer regarding perfect penetration.
The Buddha asked about the perfect penetration [of the sense bases]. According to what I have realized, the faculty of taste is supreme.
This concludes the section on the medicinal king regarding the object of taste. 5. Bhadra’s Section on the Object of Touch, in three parts: First, prostrating and presenting his testimony.
Bhadrapāla, together with his sixteen companions, Bodhisattvas Mahāsattvas, immediately rose from their seats, prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, and addressed the Buddha, saying: Gu Shan says:
"Bhadrapāla" is translated here as "Worthy Protector" (Xiánshǒu) or "Worthy Guardian" (Xiànhù); it means one who personally guards what is worthy.
Virtue. It also protects sentient beings. ○ "Bodhisattva" (Kāishì) is an alternative name;
it is a title for one who has attained self-awakening and is further able to awaken sentient beings. △ Second, the words of the formal address, which are again divided into three parts.
First, the narration of awakening through the sense-object of touch, which is again divided into three parts. First, entering the room due to past causes.
We previously heard the Dharma from the Buddha King of Majestic Sound and left the household life. At the time of the monks' bathing ceremony, we entered the hall according to custom;
thus, we were of the same class as those who possessed overweening pride at the same time as the monk Never-Disparaging. △ Second, the immediate triggering of awakening.
Suddenly he realized the cause of the water: it neither washes away the dust nor washes the body; in the interval between them, all is tranquil, and one attains a state of non-possession.
"The cause of the water" means that the water serves as the guiding cause for awakening. In this section, one must not be confused by the discussion of touch.

Generally speaking, contact constitutes a sense-object (*viṣaya*). When the body-faculty (*kāyendriya*) comes into conjunction with the object of form (*rūpa-viṣaya*), there is an intense activity in the interval;
that which perceives cold, warmth, roughness, or smoothness is its characteristic. Now, at the time of bathing, the body touches the water and the water joins with the body;
there is an intense activity in the interval, and the sensations of cold and warmth manifest. By investigating this contact, one asks: by what cause does it arise?
There is. If you say that it exists because of washing away the dust and defilements, then since dust is fundamentally insentient, how could it manifest contact?
Therefore, the Sūtra says, "If one does not wash away the dust," which means that contact does not manifest by virtue of washing away the dust.
If you say that it exists because of washing the cognitive essence of the *indriya* (the faculty of ultimate meaning), then the essence of cognition is not something that can be washed.
"It may be applied. Thus, the Sūtra says: "Nor does one wash the body," meaning that the tactile sensation does not manifest because of washing the body.
"In between" refers to the space between the pushing away of the dust and the pushing away of the body. "Tranquil and secure" is the mark of thorough awakening and mastery.
"Attaining non-possession" means realizing that this tactile object has no place of origin and that its characteristics are exhausted.
The nature manifests; it is the wondrous true suchness-nature of the original Tathāgatagarbha. △ Third, the habitual tendencies remain and are now realized:
because past habits have not been forgotten, up until the present time, he has followed the Buddha into the homeless life and attained the state of no-more-learning (aśaikṣa).
Bhīṣmagarjitasvararāja attained the vision of the Truths; this was his initial resolve. Now, following Śākyamuni, he has realized the profound stage.
Second, receiving a name through the seal of confirmation: That Buddha named me Bhadrapāla.
△ Third, touching brings clarity and one attains the fruit.
Wondrous touch proclaims clarity; one dwells as a child of the Buddha.

This means that by touching the sensory object of touch (*spraṣṭavya*), one awakens to and enters the nature of the treasury (*tathāgatagarbha*). This is what is meant by "wondrous touch proclaims clarity. "Dwelling as a child of the Buddha" refers to—
This is the realization of the first stage (*bhūmi*). △ Third, the conclusion answering the inquiry on perfect penetration:
"The Buddha asked about the perfect penetration; according to what I have realized, the faculty of touch is supreme.
The section on Bhadrapāla’s faculty of touch is complete. △ Sixth, Kāśyapa’s faculty of mental objects (*dharmadhātu*), which is further divided into three parts. First, prostration.
The assembly addressed the Buddha:
Mahākāśyapa, the Bhikṣuṇī Suvarṇaprabhāsā, and the others immediately rose from their seats, prostrated at the Buddha’s feet,
and said to the Buddha:
Mahākāśyapa—translated as "Great Drinker of Light"—is identified among the three Kāśyapas; the details regarding the bhikṣuṇīs and others are self-evident.

△ Second, the words of the formal announcement, divided into three parts. First, the narration of awakening to the sensory objects (*dharmadhātu*), which further divides into three. First, the retribution induced by past causes.
In a past kalpa, within this world-system, there was a Buddha who appeared in the world named Candrasūryapradīpa. I was able to draw near to him, hear the Dharma, and practice its study.
After the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa, I made offerings to his relics and lit lamps to maintain the light, using purple-gold.

Because he smeared [fragrant paste] upon the image of the Buddha, from that time forth, in birth after birth throughout successive lifetimes, his body has always been perfectly full and a mass of purple-gold light.
Due to these two superior causes—having offered lamps and having smeared [the image]—he experienced a body of purple-gold radiance throughout kalpas, baring his chest to swallow the sun.
2. Furthermore, this was shared with his retinue.
These bhikṣuṇīs, such as the Bhikṣuṇī of Purple Golden Light, were my own attendants who simultaneously resolved their minds for enlightenment;
these bhikṣuṇīs share both identity of person and identity of fruit, while the others share only identity of fruit. △ Third: Attaining the Fruit through Contemplation of the Dharma.

I observe that the six sense objects in this world are subject to transformation and decay; by cultivating extinction through emptiness and stillness alone, my body and mind can pass hundreds of thousands of kalpas as if it were the snapping of a finger.
By means of the dharma of emptiness, I have attained arhatship.

Regarding the contemplation of the six sense objects (*ṣaḍviṣaya*): the correct contemplation takes the mental object (*dharmaviṣaya*) as the general category and the preceding five as the specific categories.

This is because one contemplates the fading shadows of the preceding five sense objects, thereby designating them as "six" by combining the general and the specific. As for "transformation and decay":

since the mental object relies upon the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*), it appears momentarily and then passes away; arising and ceasing moment by moment and thought after thought, one cultivates further practice out of weariness with this transformation and decay.

The contemplation of emptiness (*śūnyatā-vipaśyanā*). One enters the meditative absorption of cessation (*nirodha-samāpatti*). This absorption is able to extinguish the mental faculty (*manas-indriya*) and the objects of consciousness (*dharma-viṣaya*).
Because the concentration is profound, it can span vast eons as if they were but a moment. Wēnlíng states that he is currently at Mount Kukkuṭapāda, awaiting Maitreya’s entry into this absorption.

"I take emptiness as my dharma" means that through contemplation one shatters the dust of dharmas; when appearances are exhausted, the true nature manifests, and one awakens to and enters the *garbha*.
It is the mind. The Arhats were as before. △ Second, receiving the Buddha’s seal of approval:
"The World-Honored One declared me the foremost among those who practice *dhūta*.
Wēnlíng says: *Dhūta*—newly transliterated as *duōduō*—is translated here as "shaking off" (*dǒusǒu*), for it is able to shake off the dust of dharmas.
This is the title. △ Third, the Dharma-illumination extinguishes outflows (*āsrava*).
The wondrous Dharma is opened and clarified, thereby extinguishing all outflows.

The Dharma merges with the *garbha-citta* (storehouse mind), and thus there is wondrous opening and clarification. Once the *garbha-citta* has entered, one never again falls into the realm of outflows; hence it is said "to extinguish."
This is the fruit of the cessation [of suffering]. △ Third, the conclusion of the answer regarding perfect penetration. The Buddha asked about perfect penetration;
according to what I have realized, the *dharmadhātu* (the cause of phenomena) is supreme.

The section on the perfect penetration of the six objects (*ṣaḍviṣaya*) is complete. △ Second, the perfect penetration of the five faculties (*pañcendriya*). Regarding those who lack one of the six faculties, [the Buddha] retained the faculty of hearing.

The faculties (*indriya*) serve as the foundation; it is for this reason that they correspond to the capacities of those in this region. Upon examining the five faculties, one finds the term "revolving" (*xuanfan*) present in four of them.
This is because the dharma-gate of the faculty-nature is fundamentally the principle of revolving the faculties to detach from sense-objects (*viṣaya*).

The objects and consciousnesses are not so; this can be seen through careful contemplation. These are divided into five sections. First, the eye-faculty of Nārada, which is further divided into three parts.
Having performed a prostration and presented his request, Aniruddha immediately rose from his seat, bowed his head at the Buddha’s feet, and addressed the Buddha, saying:
"Changshui says: 'Aniruddha' is *Anuruddha*, which means 'Free from Poverty' (*Apauṇarbhava*) and is also translated as 'As One Wishes' (*Yathābhiprāya*)."
This is the Prince Śvetabhojana. In a past life, he offered a single meal to a *pratyekabuddha* and, as a result, experienced wish-fulfilling bliss for ninety-one *kalpas*.
△ Second, the statement of his confession, divided into four parts. First, the cause of being rebuked for losing his eyesight.
When I first left the household life, I was constantly fond of sleep. The Tathāgata rebuked me, saying I was of the same class as beasts. Hearing the Buddha’s rebuke, I wept and reproached myself;
for seven days I did not sleep, and thereby lost both my eyes.
Gushan said: The *Ekottarika Āgama* states that when the Buddha was at Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park preaching the Dharma to the assembly, Rāhula fell asleep there.
The Buddha rebuked him with a verse, saying: "Alas! Alas! Why do you sleep? You are like the species of snails, conchs, and clams."
He slept for a thousand years without hearing the name of the Buddha. At that time, Aniruddha remained awake until dawn, whereupon he lost his faculty of sight.
△ Second, receiving instruction on samādhi.
"World-Honored One, show me the Vajra Samādhi of Delightful Vision and Illumination.
'Delightful Vision' means that as vision turns inward, one forgets external dust; 'Illumination' refers to the manifestation of the radiance of the fundamental clarity.
According to the Perfect Penetration of the Ear Organ, this is the practice of turning vision back to see one's own nature. It is called the Vajra Samādhi because—"
The eye of insight manifests before one; it is as firm and solid as a vajra, indestructible, unlike the physical eye which is easily destroyed.
△ Third, one subsequently attains the eye of insight.
I do not rely on the eyes to perceive the ten directions; their essential reality is transparently clear, as if looking at fruit in the palm of one's hand.
"Not relying on the eyes" means not relying on the physical eye. "Essential reality is transparently clear" refers to the Tathāgatagarbha mind.
The fundamental luminosity is manifested; the mind’s eye opens wide. According to the Ear-Gate, it should be said: "At first, within the act of seeing, one enters the stream and forgets the object.
Once that which is entered has become still, the two aspects of light and darkness clearly cease to arise. This corresponds to the stage of the first fruit (*srotāpanna*).
At this point, the light of the mind should gradually manifest. As it increases in this manner, both the seer and the seen are exhausted. This is the stage...
The seven stages of faith and the four fruits of the śrāvaka path should immediately give rise to the Great Original Enlightenment and penetrate the vision of the ten directions.

Since these are identical to the perfect realization (yuanzheng), they should likewise be equal in their exhaustive vision that does not abide, even up to the manifestation of quiescent extinction (nirvāṇa).
The old commentaries compare the Āgamas and debate whether they belong to the Mahāyāna or Hīnayāna; however, none of these views are necessarily correct.

Since the Buddha has already revealed the source, all are equally included within the inner secret teachings. Regarding all that is cultivated and realized, what dharma is not perfected? △ Fourth, receiving the Buddha’s seal of certification.
The Tathāgata certified me, and I attained the state of Arhat.
As before. △ Third, the conclusion of the answer regarding perfect penetration:
When the Buddha asked about perfect penetration, according to what I have realized, by turning back the faculty of sight and tracing it to its source, this is the foremost.
"Returning to see" means that by reversing one's vision, one sees the self-nature. "Following the source" means that one realizes and enters perfect penetration.
This concludes the section on Nanda’s faculty of the eye. II. Zhouli’s Faculty of the Nose. This is divided into three parts: 1. Prostration and Petition.
Cūḍapanthaka immediately rose from his seat, prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, and addressed the Buddha, saying:
*Wenling* says: "Pantha" means "successor of the Way. *Changshui* says: "Panthaka" also means "snake-slave," as he was born by the roadside.
**II. The Words of His Confession.** This section is divided into four parts. First: Because of the deficiency in recitation and retention.
I lacked the capacity for recitation and retention, and possessed no nature of great learning. Having first encountered a Buddha, I heard the Dharma and left the household life;

yet, though I could remember a single verse of the Tathāgata, for a hundred days I would forget what came before when I learned what came after, and forget what came after when I learned what came before.
Changshui said: "In the past, he was a great Dharma Master who was stingy with the Buddha-dharma and did not constantly teach others.
Consequently, he was reborn dull-witted. Due to his past roots of goodness, however, he encountered the Buddha and left the household life.

When five hundred bhikṣus taught him a single verse together, he could not master it after ninety days. According to another sutra, when he was taught to recite 'broom,' he would remember 'broom' but forget 'sweeping.'"
"Having obtained the broom, one forgets the twigs. △ Second, following the instruction to regulate the breath:
"The Buddha, pitying my ignorance, instructed me to observe the rains retreat and to regulate the inhalation and exhalation.
At that time, I contemplated the breath, exhausting its subtle details down to the moments (*kṣaṇa*) of the conditioned formations (*saṃskāra*)—namely, arising, abiding, changing, and ceasing."

Changshui said: "The Buddha instructed one to count the breaths to collect the mind, and thereby attain awakening. Although the sutra speaks of "regulating" (tiao), this implies the meaning of counting as well.
Regarding "regulation," according to the Tiantai *Zhi guan*, one should distance oneself from wind-like breaths, gasping, and so forth, remaining subtle, continuous, and self-possessed.
As for counting, one proceeds from one to ten, or even to a hundred, and thereafter counts backward down to one. This is excellent.
Because of distant causes such as dullness and obtuseness, although one was originally deluded, the immediate conditions were also due to distraction;

therefore, one employs counting the breaths to collect and stabilize the mind so that it is not mixed with other objects. However, one counts the exhalation but not the inhalation, for counting both leads to illness.

At that time, I looked downward and observed the cessation of the breath in detail. Once concentration is attained, the meditative absorption becomes subtle and profound, reaching the ultimate limit of the four characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*). [This refers to] the exhalation.

Inhalation possesses all [four phases]. The initial arising is called "birth" (*jāti*). Its non-interruption is called "abiding" (*sthiti*). Its gradual attenuation is called "change" (*anyathātva*). Its cessation is called "extinction" (*nirodha*).
Conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*) are the flux of these [phases] such as birth; the shortest moment (*kṣaṇa*) consists of ninety *kṣaṇas*, which describes its extreme subtlety.

Regulating the breath is similar to the sixfold marvelous gate of counting, following, and stopping; the remainder is similar to contemplation (*vipaśyanā*). Returning [to the source]— *Note: The final term "還" (huán) likely refers to the practice of returning the mind to the source or the completion of the cycle.*
The details regarding purification are in the subsequent section. △ Third, awakening and attaining the fruit:
their minds become suddenly enlightened, they attain great non-obstruction, and eventually, with the exhaustion of outflows, they become Arhats.
"To be suddenly and unimpededly enlightened" means to attain sudden awakening at the very limit where the breath ceases; the faculty of the nose then penetrates the *tathāgatagarbha* nature.

This is what is meant by "the sacred nature is all-pervasive. Since the *tathāgatagarbha* nature is pure and serene, the myriad dharmas are clearly reflected within it, free from any further obstruction or partition.
How could there be any recollection or forgetfulness? Therefore, it is said that one attains great non-obstruction. This applies equally to Arhats whose outflows are exhausted.
The same applies as before. △ Fourth, receiving the Buddha’s seal of approval:
dwelling beneath the Buddha’s seat, he was certified as having attained the stage of no-more-learning (*aśaikṣa*).
The same applies as before. △ Third, concluding the answer on perfect penetration.
The Buddha asked about the perfection of penetration (*pariśuddhi*). According to what I have realized, "reversing the breath to follow emptiness" is the foremost method.

"Reversing the breath to follow emptiness" means simply observing the breath as it returns to its state of empty extinction; thereby one awakens to and enters the *tathāgatagarbha* nature, thus achieving the fruit of perfect penetration.
[Objection: The nose has smelling as its function; why, in this "revolving of the faculties," do you not take up the reversal of that function?

"Smell. This refers to taking up the reverse breath. Why? The answer is that the nature of smelling is precisely dependent upon the breath; what is called exhaling to take up fragrance and inhaling to perceive fragrance.
However, for this concentration of the mind, why must one reverse the smelling? When awakening occurs, it ultimately results from the exhaustion of the breath;
therefore, it belongs to the perfect penetration of the nose faculty. The section on the nose faculty of Cūḍapanthaka is concluded. △ Third, Gavāmpati.
The faculty of the tongue. This is divided into three parts. First, the prostration and formal address:
Kauṇḍinya immediately rose from his seat, prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, and addressed the Buddha, saying:
Wenling says: *Kauṇḍinya* (憍梵鉢提) means "ox-chewer" (*gomayūka*). Just as an ox, even when not eating, habitually makes a hollow sound with its mouth, this man’s mouth was like an ox’s snorting;
it was a retribution for his frivolous mockery. △ Second, the words of the confession, which are further divided into four parts.
First, the karmic retribution invited by verbal action.
I committed verbal karma in past kalpas by mocking śramaṇas. Consequently, in life after life and birth after birth, I suffered from the ailment of "ox-chewing.
Seeing elderly monks who were toothless yet eating, I laughed at them, remarking that they resembled oxen.
Thus, in every lifetime, I was reborn with an ox-tongue and constantly engaged in ox-chewing. Verbal karma is to be feared in such a manner. II. Following the Teachings on Śamatha and Vipaśyanā.

The Tathāgata has shown me the Dharma-gate of the single-flavor pure mind-ground. Having attained the cessation of the mind, I have entered samādhi and observed that the cognition of flavor is neither a substance nor a thing.
This Buddha originally intended to instruct him through the perfect penetration of the tongue-root.
Thus, he first had him cease distraction and enter stillness, and subsequently taught him to give rise to illumination from within that stillness to observe the nature of tasting.

Therefore, these first three lines represent the initial bestowal of a rosary, commanding him to recite the Buddha’s name; this is called the "Dharma-gate of the Single Flavor of the Pure Mind-ground."
This is because when recollecting the Buddha, one ceases all miscellaneous conditions so that the pure mindfulness is singular.
The next two lines refer to ceasing distraction and entering stillness, thereby first accomplishing the *nien-fo samādhi*.

The final two lines refer to subsequently instructing him to arise from stillness and manifest illumination, observing the flavor of stillness and knowing that its nature does not derive from the sense organs nor from the substance of the object.

This is because external flavors do not come to the sense organ, and the organ does not taste by itself; therefore, it is not the essence [of the flavor]. The tongue does not perceive through contact, and the object does not taste itself;
therefore, it is not the object [of perception]. One should know that the practice of *nien-fo* (Buddha-recollection) is not merely for the purpose of preventing slander;
rather, the prevention of slander is but a secondary benefit. 2. Transcending and Attaining the Fruit.

He should contemplate so as to transcend all worldly outflows (*āsrava*). Internally, he is liberated from body and mind; externally, he leaves behind the world. Although he remains within the three realms of existence, he is like a bird that has escaped its cage.
Free from defilement and with dust extinguished, his Dharma-eye is purified, and he becomes an Arhat.

Having thoroughly realized the nature of taste, one finds that it arises neither from the sense organ nor from the flavor; one suddenly awakens to the fact that its source is the *tathāgatagarbha* (storehouse nature).
Thus, the nature manifests like the rising sun, and the outflows (*āsrava*) vanish like melting frost; consequently, all outflows are instantaneously exhausted.

Internally, one is liberated from body and mind—this is the liberation of the faculties from their bonds. Externally, one leaves behind the world—this is the transcendence of the vessel-world (*bhājanaloka*). To realize this is...

The three realms of existence are fundamentally empty; only by being thus distanced from them can one be free from the entanglements of the primary and secondary bodies. Therefore, it is like a bird escaping from a cage.
This corresponds to the stage of the four fruits and the seven levels of faith, at which point one attains what is described at the end of the fourth fascicle:

"the faculties, objects, consciousnesses, and mind dissolve away as soon as they are thought of. What is now called "leaving behind defilement and dissolving the dust so that the Dharma-eye becomes pure" refers precisely to that.

The text states: "What is called 'perception' takes appearances as its object; consciousness and emotion constitute its defilement. When both are left far behind, then your Dharma-eye shall immediately become clear and bright.
The wording is entirely similar [to other passages]. I request that you examine that explanation in detail;

then you will know for yourself that this realization is not the fruit of the Small Vehicle (Hīnayāna), but is precisely the stage of entering and abiding with perfected faith. △ Fourth, Receiving the Buddha’s Seal of Certification.
The Tathāgata personally certified me; I have ascended to the path of no-more-learning (*aśaikṣa*).
As previously stated: △ Third, the conclusion and response regarding perfect penetration.
When the Buddha asked about perfect penetration, that which I have realized is as follows: returning to the flavor and revolving the faculty of cognition—this is the foremost.
"Returning to the taste and revolving back to the knower" means that by reflecting inwardly upon the nature of the one who tastes, one awakens to and enters the storehouse mind (*ālaya-citta*).
This concludes the rectification of the tongue faculty. 4. The Body Faculty (*kāya-indriya*) is further divided into three parts: first, the offering of prostrations and the formal petition.
Pilingavatsa immediately rose from his seat, prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, and addressed the Buddha, saying: "Gushan says:
This is called a 'remaining habit' (*vāsanā*). Because he was formerly a Brahmin, his remaining habits were largely characterized by pride;

thus, his cursing the river god as a maidservant was not his true heart, but rather a manifestation of his habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*). △ Second, the words of his petition, divided into [sections].

5. First, upon hearing a discourse on the Truth of Suffering, I initially resolved my mind [on enlightenment] and entered the Path under the Buddha. I frequently heard the Tathāgata speak of how all worldly matters are not to be enjoyed.

To resolve to attain enlightenment is itself to leave the household life. That which is not to be enjoyed in the world is the Truth of Suffering (*duḥkha-satya*) among the Four Noble Truths, such as the three sufferings, the four sufferings, the eight sufferings, and so forth. △ Second, the commentary on "grieving for the feet."
While begging for alms in the city, he was contemplating the Dharma-gate. Unaware of it, a thorn in the road pierced his foot, causing his entire body to ache.
The Dharma-gate is precisely the Truth of Suffering (*duḥkha-satya*). Having been instructed to contemplate suffering, he happened upon a painful occurrence;
this was truly the catalyst for his awakening. III. Investigating Bodily Sensation. This section has two parts: first, the narrative; second, the two types of sensation.

I am mindful that there is cognition. I know this profound suffering. Although one perceives through perception, one perceives the pure mind; there is no perception of suffering within the perception of suffering.

The first two lines describe the false perception that cognizes suffering, which is precisely body-consciousness (*kāya-vijñāna*). The subsequent three lines describe the true perception that is free from suffering, which is the body-faculty (*kāyendriya*);
its nature of awareness is equal to seeing and hearing. Although one perceives through perception, one perceives the pain.
This means that although, according to what precedes, there is a mind capable of perceiving and the pain that is perceived, within the body-faculty (*kāyendriya*) there is no discrimination.
The pure, awakened mind fundamentally lacks both the pain that is perceived and the perception of the pain that perceives.
△ Second, investigating and exhausting the non-duality.
I further reflected: "In this single body, how could there be two cognitions?
Two cognitions refer to the cognition that knows pain and the cognition of the pure mind. As I gave rise to this transformative thought of wisdom:
since the body is one, how could there be two cognitions? That which is one is the truth; that which is two is delusion. △ Fourth: Entering.
Kong attained the fruit.
Not long after he had focused his mindfulness, his body and mind suddenly became empty. Within twenty-one days, all outflows were exhausted, and he became an Arhat.
As for "focusing the mind," this refers to following only the true awakening that is free from pain and pure, and no longer following anything else.
He knows that the perception of pain is illusory. Before long, his body and mind suddenly become empty;
this is the ultimate state of concentrated mind, where the true and pure prevails and the illusory is severed. Body and mind open up suddenly, becoming identical to empty space.

As all outflows (āsrava) are exhausted, the nature of the treasury of true awakening manifests, and desire, existence, and ignorance can no longer be found. This is the same as for the Arhat mentioned previously.
△ Five: Receiving the Buddha’s Seal of Certification.
Having obtained the personal seal of certification, one realizes the state of No-more-learning (*aśaikṣa*).
"No-more-learning" is as explained previously. △ Three: Concluding the Answer on Perfect Penetration.
The Buddha asked about the perfect penetration of the faculties. According to what I have realized, the pure awareness that leaves the body behind is the foremost.

"Pure awareness" refers to the singular, true awakening. "Leaving the body behind" means that body and mind suddenly become empty. This combination of "leaving" and "purity" also contains the sense of "revolving.
The section on the faculty of the body (kāya-indriya) is complete. △ Fifth, the faculty of the mind (manas-indriya) arising from emptiness, divided into three parts. First:
Having paid homage and made this declaration, Subhūti rose from his seat, prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, and addressed the Buddha as follows.

II. The Words of the Declaration. This section is divided into three parts. First: Knowledge of Emptiness through Past Lives. This is further divided into two. First: Remote Penetration of Past Lives.
His life-force was not forgotten.
Since the distant kalpas of the past, his mind has attained non-obstruction; he can remember his successive births as numerous as the sands of the Ganges.

"The mind attaining non-obstruction" means that there is neither the confusion of the intermediate state (*antarābhava*) nor the obscurity upon emerging from the womb. △ Second, the reliance [on the Buddha].
He correctly realizes that both self and others are empty.

From the very beginning while in the mother’s womb, he knows emptiness and stillness. In this way, even until the ten directions have become empty, he also causes sentient beings to realize the nature of emptiness.

The first two lines concern the emptiness of the primary retribution (*sambhogakāya*). While in the womb, one is able to undergo birth according to appearances; yet, by knowing emptiness, one is able to penetrate the principle.
"Not being obscured by empty stillness" means that the five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*) are all empty, and the substance of birth is utterly unobtainable.

The next two lines concern the emptiness of the secondary retribution (*bhājanaloka*). From the mother’s body outward, extending to the mountains, rivers, and the great earth—all are equally empty and still.

This refers to the Bodhisattva of Profound Mind (*gambhīra-citta*). Both person and phenomena (*pudgala-dharma*) are empty; from the level of the objective realm upward, everything belongs to self-emptiness (*ātma-śūnyatā*).
The final two lines refer to emerging from the womb and extensively transforming sentient beings so that they together realize the principle of emptiness.

Here, "emptiness-nature" (*śūnyatā-svabhāva*) refers to the True Suchness (*tathatā*) of the twofold emptiness of person and phenomena; it is not yet the manifest treasury-nature (*gotra*), as this is only revealed by the subsequent text.

Now, abiding in the womb [of the Dharma-realm] without delusion, wherein both person and phenomena are simultaneously empty—this is something that neither those of the Two Vehicles nor Bodhisattvas at the initial stage can achieve;
how much less so for those in the profound stages of the Mahāyāna who fully possess the two benefits? What cause for doubt could there be?

Regarding the discussion of the expedient means for the initial mind, this refers to the stage of the fulfillment of the ten levels of faith (daśa-śraddhā). II. Entering through Realization by Following the Teaching. This is further divided into two parts.
Upon attaining awakening, one realizes one’s own fruit.
Having received from the Tathāgata the revelation of the true emptiness of the nature-awakening (*prakṛti-bodhi*), wherein emptiness is perfectly luminous, one becomes an Arhat.
"Revealed" means that [the Tathāgata] illuminates it for them. The true emptiness of the nature-awakening is the reflection of the empty nature within true awakening; this is the Tathāgata.
The hidden mind is pure and fundamental, pervading the entire Dharma-realm; its empty nature is perfectly luminous, such that form and emptiness are unimpeded.

This is what is called the total integration of the whole body, wherein great functions are limitless. If it were thus, what deficiency would there be for an Arhat’s realization when compared to those of the Great Beings of the Ten Stages?
The heading refers to the fruit itself; in contrast to what follows regarding the Buddha’s knowledge and vision, this is not [the case].
Also toward sentient beings. △ Second, sharing the Buddha’s knowledge and vision.
One suddenly enters the Tathāgata’s ocean of jewel-like luminous emptiness, sharing the Buddha’s knowledge and vision.
This appears to be a transcendent entry into the subsequent mind; hence it is called "sudden entry. The "ocean of jewel-like luminous emptiness" refers to what is called the One True [Dharma-realm].
The Dharma-realm is the emptiness of the ultimate truth (*paramārtha-śūnyatā*), also called ultimate emptiness (*atyanta-śūnyatā*). This is to be quiescent in the same manner as the Buddha.
The Buddha’s knowledge and vision (*jñāna-darśana*) is precisely what was previously fully manifested in the Three Baskets (*tri-piṭaka*), namely the meaning of the great light of wisdom.
This is to illuminate in the same manner as the Buddha. A separate sutra clarifies: "Subhūti was, in the past, the Tathāgata Śikhin."

Observing this, the preceding phrase seems identical to *nirvāṇa*, while the following phrase seems identical to *bodhi*. This is likely because it has already been revealed and clarified by the Tathāgata;
thus, he speaks of the profound mind (*gambhīra-citta*) himself, without further concealment. The explicit text and its clear evidence are as such.
Yet, the ancients all claimed that interpreting this as a distinction within the Hīnayāna school was without fault. Little did they realize that this explains the *Saṃdhinirmocana-sūtra*.
This is shallow. To oppose the Buddha and slander the Sage—how could one not be guilty? I pray you, take heed of this. △ Third, receiving the Buddha’s seal of approval:
sealed as one who has attained the stage of No-more-learning (*aśaikṣa*), liberated in the emptiness of nature, I am supreme.
The Lesser Vehicle realizes the emptiness of emptiness, yet this is a bondage rather than true liberation. Furthermore, its samādhi is not the emptiness of original nature (*prakṛti-śūnyatā*).
This refers to the emptiness of persons, phenomena, and both together—the principle of emptiness realized through all forms of liberation.

This is the single, true, primordially existent essence of the nature of true emptiness that is not empty. As for my being the Unsurpassed One, I have exhausted the principle of emptiness; furthermore—
There is nothing further to add. Thus concludes the candid statement. III. Conclusion and Response on Perfect Penetration.

The Buddha asked about perfect penetration; according to what I have realized: all phenomena enter into non-existence; where non-existence itself is exhausted, one turns back from dharmas to return to the Unconditioned.
This is the foremost of all marks—namely, the mark of self, the mark of person, the mark of sentient being, the mark of a life-span, as well as the mark of dharmas. It is not emptiness;
rather, it is the entry of all marks into non-existence, which is the simultaneous emptiness of both person and dharma. "The negation of what is negated is exhausted" means that...

Both the subject that negates and the object that is negated are simultaneously exhausted. The "object that is negated" refers to the various characteristics mentioned above; the "subject that negates" refers to the various negations mentioned above, namely, the characteristic of non-dharmas.
This is precisely the meaning of the simultaneous removal of both medicine and disease, wherein the emptiness that empties [the object] itself is extinguished.

The "dharma by which dharmas are revolved" refers to the dharma of the single mind—that is, the nature of cognition within the mental faculty (manas), and does not refer to the dharma-object (dharmāyatana).
Furthermore, "revolving the method back to non-existence" means that one revolves the nature of cognition back into ultimate emptiness (*atyanta-śūnyatā*).
Yongjia said: "Both existence and non-existence are discarded; it is not even empty. He also said: "All conditioned phenomena are impermanent and entirely empty;

this is the Tathāgata’s Great Perfect Enlightenment (*mahā-vajra-samādhi*). This is what is meant. Compared with the Perfect Penetration of the Ear Organ, this [passage] more clearly reveals the essence (*tattva*).
That [faculty] predominantly manifests its function. Although the point of realization for the masters of our school exists throughout all gates, it is especially prevalent in this gate.
This is truly because, whether manifest or latent, they mostly take only the single character "knowing" (*jñāna*) as their basis.

The section on the perfect penetration of the five sense organs is complete. △ Three: The Perfect Penetration of the Six Consciousnesses. (Now, at the beginning of the Sutra, the consciousness-mind was questioned and refuted, and rebuked as being born...)

This is the very root of death. Sentient beings mistakenly identify with it and enter the cycle of saṃsāra in vain; though they rely on the provisional and limited teachings for their cultivation, they ultimately achieve no real fruit. How, then, could they now enter through the perfect penetration? This has already been argued in the section on the pervasiveness of the element of consciousness (*vijñāna-mahābhūta*); I shall now state it once more.

Although consciousness is the ultimate in being a false reflection of external objects, it has no separate self-substance apart from the true seeing-part (*darśana-bhāga*). It is like a shadow in relation to water: though the shadow is utterly unreal, it has no separate self-substance apart from the water. Yet those who are deluded and attached perceive the consciousness and forget the truth, thereby creating a false state of transmigration.

This is like a foolish person who perceives a shadow but forgets the water, only to mistakenly suffer drowning. The stakes are not minor; thus, this must be rebuked. If one awakens, one realizes the truth within consciousness itself, and...

Consciousness is not outside of reality; why doubt its perfect penetration? It is like a wise person who observes a reflection and knows it is water; yet the reflection is not outside of the water, and one can still obtain the utility of the water—how could one suffer from drowning in it? Therefore, these six sages, along with Maitreya who follows them, [attained this realization].

All were able to immediately recognize and see the Truth; thus, they all realized perfect penetration (*yuan-tong*) without obstruction. As the Chan school says: "What is this thing that arises and ceases in such profusion? This refers to that very point. Question: Why does the Tathāgata not simply cause people to immediately recognize and see the Truth? Why must he reprimand them and insist on teaching them to enter through the sense-faculties (*indriya*)?

Answer: A verse states: "The nature of the Sage is all-pervading; both following and reversing are skillful means (*upāya*). For those with a beginner's mind entering right concentration, their progress—whether slow or fast—is not of the same order.

This is precisely because the objects (*viṣaya*) and consciousnesses (*vijñāna*) are both slow, whereas the faculties alone are the most swift. It is like the reprimands directed at the Two Vehicles (*śrāvaka* and *pratyekabuddha*): it is not that they will ultimately fail to become Buddhas, but rather that the kalpas required would pass through points as numerous as dust motes—a state of extreme slowness. Therefore, he rebukes beginners so that they do not give rise to such [narrow] minds. [End of section]
This is divided into six sections. First is the eye-consciousness of Śāriputra. Regarding the first five consciousnesses, there are two kinds of difficulties in discerning them.

First, because they are conflated with the first five sense organs, it is difficult to distinguish them; yet, as they follow after recollection in a coarse manner, they somewhat resemble the non-discriminative nature of the sense organs themselves.
Among the śrāvakas who cling to the literal dharma, there are none who do not become deluded by this. Thus, the *Jiugui* (Rules of Conduct) says: "It is difficult for the foolish."
This refers to the division of consciousness and the sense faculties. These two are mixed with the five [sensory consciousnesses] within the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*).
Although they are coarse and superficial, because they involve recollective discrimination (*anusmaraṇa-vikalpa*), they somewhat resemble the conceptualization of the mental consciousness.

Therefore, the Hinayana teachings do not recognize that the first five [consciousnesses] are distinct from the mental consciousness, maintaining instead that mental phenomena are unitary. Master Wuxing’s statement that "consciousness is generally prone to confusion" is likewise [correct].

This is a delusion. Therefore, scholars of the Nature School (Xingzong) ought not to neglect the Dharma-characteristics (Faxiang); this is appropriate. Now, I shall briefly clarify the characteristics of visual consciousness (*cakṣurvijñāna*);
the other four may be understood by analogy. For instance, when the eye illuminates an object, there is not a single thought-moment of movement;
it is simply like a mirror, without further analysis. This is the seeing-nature of the visual faculty (*cakṣurindriya*). Within this, the eyes function...

Passing through the various characteristics of black and white, large and small, many and few, good and evil, and so forth, such that they appear distinctly without confusion—this is the coarse discrimination of recollective mindfulness that does not yet involve verbal designations;
it is the visual consciousness (*cakṣurvijñāna*). From this, one proceeds to sequentially point out, investigate, and analyze infinite distinctions;
this is the detailed discrimination of conceptual construction (*vikalpa*) that universally clings to verbal designations. This is the [mental consciousness].

The "household" refers to the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*). It is also called the "consciousness of clear comprehension. Here, we take only the second, the visual consciousness (*cakṣurvijñāna*).
One must not confuse the nature of the sense faculty with that of the mental consciousness. This is divided into three parts: first, prostrating and making a formal declaration.
Śāriputra immediately rose from his seat, prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, and addressed the Buddha as follows.
△ Second, the words of the petition are further divided into three sections. First, the sharpness of visual consciousness.
Since the beginningless kalpas, my mind-vision has been pure; thus have I taken birth as many times as there are sands in the Ganges River.
Regarding the various transformations of both the mundane and supramundane realms, I have attained unimpeded penetration upon seeing them but once.
This also describes the long-term benefit of the eye-consciousness (*cakṣurvijñāna*) over many lifetimes. "The mind sees" refers to the eye-consciousness.
"Pure" means being without obstruction. "Worldly and world-transcending" refers to all realms of ordinary beings and sages.

"Various transformations" refers to differentiated illusory phenomena, such as the characteristics of the causal and resultant aspects of the *karmakara-dharmamukha* (the Dharma-gate of creative activity). The two phrases beginning with "one sees" mean that no effort is required.
It possesses great power. When the visual consciousness follows upon recollection and performs coarse discernment, it penetrates both the internal and external with complete clarity;
this precisely demonstrates the sharpness of the visual consciousness. △ Second, increasing awakening through encountering the teachings.
On the road, I encountered the Kāśyapa brothers following one another, proclaiming the *nidāna* and awakening to the boundless nature of the mind.
These Kāśyapas are the three brothers; they are known as Mahāmaudgalyāyana among those who attained supernormal powers. Other sutras state that I encountered Aśvajit;
this is simply a matter of adopting what the masters have said. It is correct that these accounts are not from a single person, but are mutually presented by different sources.

The principle of causes and conditions should be understood according to the perfect meaning of the Supreme Vehicle (*anuttarayāna*). As the Buddha’s verse says: "Phenomena produced by causes and conditions / I declare to be emptiness;
/ They are also called provisional names, / And are also called the meaning of the Middle Way.

These four lines follow their respective order, corresponding to the Four Teachings: the *Āgama* (Tripitaka), *Vaipulya* (Shared), *Pratyekabuddha*, and *Bodhisattva* (Perfect) teachings. Alternatively, each teaching may encompass all four lines. Regarding the son of Śāriputra...

Explanation: Because he has decisively penetrated the perfect principle, he awakens to the fact that the hidden mind pervades the entire Dharma-realm. △ Third, following the Buddha’s supreme realization:
He left home following the Buddha, saw that the enlightened clarity was perfect, attained great fearlessness, became an Arhat, and served as the Buddha’s eldest son.
Born from the Buddha’s mouth, transformed by birth from the Dharma:

seeing and awakening is the eye-consciousness; clarity and perfection are the ultimate realization. Attaining great fearlessness means possessing the four kinds of intrepidity when preaching the Dharma;
because his vision is penetrating, his teaching is without deficiency. The Arhats follow the same principle as before, as does Śāriputra.

He was foremost in wisdom, and Śāriputra was preeminent in renown; thus he was called the "eldest son. From this it is known that Śāriputra’s wisdom consisted entirely of the sharpness of visual consciousness (*cakṣurvijñāna*).
The following two phrases explain why he is the eldest son, while also distinguishing him from Rāhula, who attained realization of the Dharma-body upon hearing the Buddha’s teaching;
hence it is said that he was "born from the Buddha’s own mouth. Within the teachings, he is the eldest.
One nurtures the holy embryo; through this, the Dharma-body develops from the subtle to the manifest. Therefore, it is said that one is "born of transformation from the Dharma.

A separate sutra states that Śāriputra was, in a past life, the Tathāgata Golden Dragon; thus we know that reaching the Dharma in seven days and realizing the fruit in half a month were merely manifestations.
In total, these are not the ultimate reality. Why then must one dispute whether he heard the Dharma from a person?
[The Buddha said: "Excellent! △ Third, the conclusion and response regarding perfect penetration.

The Buddha asked about perfect penetration; according to what I have realized, the mind and vision emit light, and when this light reaches its ultimate limit, it becomes knowing-seeing. This is the foremost."

The mind-seeing gives rise to radiance; this is the thorough penetration and realization of the eye-consciousness. It is identical to the "extreme stillness where light penetrates" (靜極光通達) and the "light at its extreme where knowledge and vision [arise]" (光極知見).
It is identical to "tranquil illumination containing empty space" (寂照含虛空). Through this supreme function of clearly mirroring all phenomena, one can know its source.
The section on Śāriputra’s eye-consciousness is concluded. II. Samantabhadra’s Ear-Consciousness. This is divided into three parts. I. [The Introduction].
Having paid homage and made this declaration, Samantabhadra Bodhisattva immediately rose from his seat, prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, and addressed the Buddha, saying: "Xie Li says:

'His practice pervades the entire Dharma-realm, hence he is called Universal (Samanta); his rank is adjacent to that of the Ultimate Sage, hence he is called Worthy (Bhadra). This is not [the stage] prior to the grounds.'"
This is the Vajropama-samādhi (Diamond-like Samādhi), which stands at the summit of all subdued states; it is therefore called "Worthy" (Bhadra).

Both [this master] and Mañjuśrī are the shadow and echo of ancient Buddhas. Although there are many explanations regarding their names and ranks in the *Dàchǎo* (Great Commentary), I shall here follow only the essentials.
II. The Words of the Petition, divided into three parts: 1. Establishing Models for Aiding Transformation.
I have already served as a Dharma Prince for Tathāgatas as numerous as the sands of the Ganges.
When the Tathāgatas of the ten directions instruct their disciples who possess the faculties of Bodhisattvas to cultivate the practices of Samantabhadra, they derive their names from me.
Because he succeeds to the family enterprise of the Buddha, he is a son of the Dharma King. "Bodhisattva faculties" refers to the faculties of the Perfect and Sudden [Teaching].
"Samantabhadra practices" are the Ten Kings of Vows, wherein even a single color or a single fragrance completely pervades the entire Dharma-realm.
Throughout the ten directions of the sands of Ganges, all who cultivate the practices of Samantabhadra are named after them; this may be called the ultimate standard for emulation.
△ Second, the auditory consciousness discerns the capacities [of beings].
"World-Honored One, I employ the hearing of the mind to distinguish all the knowledge and views of sentient beings.
Wēnlíng says: "The 'hearing of the mind' refers to the auditory consciousness. To 'distinguish the knowledge and views of sentient beings' means to select the practices of Samantabhadra."
And thus they bring it to fulfillment. △ Third, universally protecting the practitioner:
If, beyond worlds as numerous as the sands of the Ganges in other directions, there is a single sentient being who brings forth within their mind the practice of Samantabhadra;
At that time, I shall mount a six-tusked elephant and manifest hundreds of thousands of emanations, all arriving at that place.
Even if their obstructions are so deep that they do not yet see me, I will stroke their heads from within the darkness, protecting and comforting them to bring them to accomplishment.

Regarding the phrase "there is one sentient being," this is said to the utmost extent to mean that not a single person is excluded; it does not mean that the discussion is limited to only one sentient being.
