that by following the same path, practitioners cultivate both the shallow and the profound together to enter [enlightenment]. Yet, one specifically selects the ear-door (*śrotra-dvāra*), while the other doors do not suffice.

Even when there are those who enter through other gates, they likewise rely on the majestic power [of Avalokiteśvara] for the sake of the immediate matter. However, in this case, it should be said: "The ear-faculty of Avalokiteśvara..."

Regarding the preceding general outline, this section demonstrates its extensive exposition; however, the underlying intent regarding the faculty of hearing is already contained within the two characters "Guanyin" (Avalokiteśvara).
This is divided into three parts. First: Prostration and Petition.
At that time, the Bodhisattva Avalokiteśvara rose from his seat, prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, and addressed the Buddha, saying:
"The name 'Avalokiteśvara' fully manifests the virtues of the two benefits [for self and others]. Yet, the manner of observation differs.

In the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*, the Tathāgata explained: 'When sentient beings afflicted by suffering and distress single-mindedly invoke this name, the Bodhisattva immediately observes their voices.'"
All attain liberation; for this reason, he is named Avalokiteśvara. According to this, that which is observed is precisely the sounds of the world.
This is because the perspective of the fruit-stage (phala-mukha) solely reveals the magnificent virtue of benefiting others. Now, in this sutra, the Bodhisattva explains it himself:
"Because I observe and listen to the perfect clarity throughout the ten directions, the name 'Avalokiteśvara' pervades the realms of the ten directions. Based on this...
That which is observed is precisely the nature of the faculty that hears sound; this is because the gateway [of hearing] predominantly manifests the profound source of self-benefit.
Thus, these two sutras mutually manifest and conceal one another, and their names are seen to be perfectly wondrous. This meaning is roughly the same as that of Gushan;

however, since we are currently discussing the gateway of cultivation, we shall provisionally follow the latter interpretation. The character "observe" (guān) follows worldly convention, and although it is written [in this way],...
The tone is level (ping shēng). In reality, it ought to be departing (qù shēng). This is because taking up sounds is "hearing" (wén), while reaching the principle is "contemplation" (guān).
Since one specifically seeks to penetrate the principle, regarding sounds one speaks not of hearing but of contemplation. Furthermore, as for the principle that is penetrated...

This is not the principle within sounds, but rather the neutral principle inherent in the faculty of hearing (*śrotra-indriya*). Nevertheless, it must rely upon sounds in order for the nature of hearing to be manifested.
Therefore, he does not speak of "contemplating the faculty of hearing," but refers only to "Avalokiteśvara" (The One Who Observes the Sounds of the World).

Furthermore, one must understand that although benefiting others and benefiting oneself are distinct, the dharma capable of benefiting them both equally manifests the preeminence of the faculty of hearing. There is no... [omission].

This has two points. △ Second, the words of the formal petition, divided into three parts. First, the original teacher’s transmission of the practice of "listening inwardly," which further has three sections.
First, the Buddhas of antiquity who share the same name.
"World-Honored One, I recall that in the past, incalculable eons ago as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, there was a Buddha who appeared in the world named Avalokiteśvara.
That Buddha, while still in the causal stage, may have entered realization by means of this very [practice]; therefore, his name and title manifest the fruit through the cause. Or...

The Buddha, discerning the timing and circumstances, [taught] that one should enter [the path] from this point; thus, his name and title correspond precisely to the teaching suited for those of such capacity.
△ Second, generating the aspiration for enlightenment following the Buddha.
I, before that Buddha, gave rise to the bodhicitta.
This bodhicitta does not transcend three minds and four vows. First is the mind of goodness, which is the vow to exhaustively sever all afflictions and the vow to study the infinite dharma-gates.
Second is the mind of compassion, which is the vow toward boundless sentient beings...
"May they be delivered. Third is the "straight mind," which is the vow to achieve the unsurpassed path of the Buddha.

According to the *Awakening of Faith*, the first, the straight mind, refers to right mindfulness of True Suchness (*tathatā*). The second, the virtuous mind, refers to the extensive cultivation of immeasurable wholesome dharmas.
The third is the mind of compassion (*karuṇā*). This refers to the immeasurable deliverance of sentient beings. Subsequently, one dedicates [the merit] toward three points:

True Suchness (*tathatā*), the Buddha-way (*buddhamārga*), and the nature of cultivation (*prakṛti-bhāvanā*). Although these have different emphases, among the four vows, the Buddha-way necessarily encompasses True Suchness;
therefore, when combined, they do not differ. This mind is the most precious; from its initial arousal, it is like a prince in the womb, whose nobility already surpasses all.

The assembly of ministers, the protective mindfulness of all Buddhas, and the empowerment of ten thousand sages—these cannot fully exhaust the description of his magnificent virtue, even with the hundred parables of the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra*.
Furthermore, it is said that if one does not give rise to this mind, all practices cultivated will be entirely seized and controlled by Māra.
Therefore, those who wish to cultivate the perfect penetration of the ear faculty must first give rise to this Great Bodhi-mind. △ Third, Receiving the Precepts.
This is the Dharma-gate.
That Buddha taught me: "Enter samādhi through hearing, reflection, and cultivation.
Once the Great Mind has been awakened, one must uphold the holy teachings. Any practitioner who does not uphold the holy teachings, or who acts according to their own whims—

[This is] the intention. Alternatively, there are those who believe in false teachers; their transgressions are immeasurable. Therefore, this section clarifies that one receives [the teachings] directly from the Buddha.

That Buddha refers specifically to the Buddha Avalokiteśvara. These three types of wisdom consist solely of the wisdom derived from hearing (*śrutamayī-prajñā*), as they differ from the conventional paths.

The cultivation through reflection and practice is likewise distinct. According to the conventional path, "hearing" refers to extensive learning—that is, the effort of hearing the sutras and understanding their meaning;
its substance consists of auditory consciousness and the discernment of resolute conviction (adhimukti) produced by the mental consciousness associated with the ear.

However, the term "hearing" used here specifically points to the nature of hearing within the auditory faculty (*śrotrendriya*); its substance is simply the principle of non-conceptual suchness-wisdom (*tathatā-jñāna*).

Thought does not then cling to emptiness or existence; it is a single flavor of "returning hearing. Externally, one is liberated from the dust of sound; internally, one merges with the principle of wisdom.

This refers, for the time being, to the practice of stillness within the efforts of dhyāna. "Cultivation" means attaining mastery in the myriad practices so that they do not conflict with this contemplation of dhyāna.
It is said that even in such acts as coughing, spitting, or turning the back, there is no moment when one is not in samādhi, let alone in all virtuous deeds.

This is based on the cultivation and advancement of a beginner; thus, [the three wisdoms] should be fully present. If one further analyzes according to the stages of entry, they should be distinguished by means of the "six identities" (*liuji*).

Wisdom derived from hearing (*śrutamayī-prajñā*) should reside in the stage of names (*mingzi*); wisdom derived from reflection (*cintāmayī-prajñā*) should extend through the stages of contemplative practice (*guanxing*) and semblance (*xiangsi*);

wisdom derived from cultivation (*bhāvanāmayī-prajñā*) should enter the stage of partial realization (*fenzheng*). If one further distinguishes them by means of the path of seeing (*darśana-mārga*) and the path of cultivation (*bhāvanā-mārga*), both wisdom derived from hearing and wisdom derived from reflection belong to the path of seeing.

Cultivated wisdom (*bhāvanāmayī-prajñā*), however, corresponds to the stage of cultivation (*bhāvanā-mārga*). Thus, there is a vast gulf between the shallow and the deep regarding these latter two types of discrimination.

If we consider the "Original Gate" of Avalokiteśvara, the three instances where the character for "hearing" (*wen*) is mentioned must all be understood as specifically referring to the faculty of hearing.

Although both sound and hearing constitute the essence of the teaching, hearing is the true essence of the teaching. As for the term "human *samādhi*," its name applies to both the initial and subsequent stages; at the beginning—

This refers merely to the designation of "attainment through concentration" (ding-cheng), yet it further relies upon the subsequent mind to realize entry into the realm of perfect penetration (*yuan-tong*), where quiescence manifests before one.
Only when both movement and stillness are simultaneously sustained without contradiction can it be termed "attainment through concentration.

However, this movement and stillness differ from the two [subsequent] objects; here, they are spoken of in terms of two temporal phases: stillness as entering meditative absorption (*dhyāna*) and movement as engaging in the myriad practices. If...
If stillness is conjoined with movement, it is ultimately not called the accomplishment of Great Samādhi. My Master’s transmission of the practice of "hearing back" is now complete.
△ Second, the sequential unraveling of the knots for cultivation and realization. This section constitutes the actual practice (*sādhana*).
As a key point of the Sūtra, it ought to be explained in detail; therefore, what is now explained shall be somewhat complete, without shying away from prolixity.
May the reader not be weary of its length. This is not like the transformation of a long river into three cascades, which lacks any essential significance.
One should know that the aforementioned resolve was the aspiration, whereas this [text] constitutes the practice based upon that aspiration; thus, that aspiration shall not be in vain.
The Master’s reception and upholding of this teaching constitutes practice based upon the doctrine; thus, the teaching does not fail him.

Nevertheless, regarding the division of the text into sections—specifically the division by means of the three emptinesses and six knots—it is because these three emptinesses were spoken by the Buddha himself within the five fascicles.
Changshui (Changluo) was also aware of following this method of division, yet he was unable to fully elaborate upon it with complete detail.
Regarding the six knots, this is understood through inference based on their meaning; it is not a forced interpretation.

This is because when the Buddha tied the cloth, he specifically intended to clearly demonstrate that both the tying and the untying possess a sequential order; yet, in explaining the sequence of untying, he merely listed the three voids.
It appears to have only three layers, yet its intent contains six knots. The previous explanation was somewhat clear; now this is precisely the main text for untangling the knots.
Does it not build upon what was previously stated? Moreover, if one carefully examines the logic and phrasing, the six sections are distinct;

this is not a forced division. It is divided into three parts. First, the initial resolution of the three knots first attains the emptiness of persons. This further has three parts. First, detaching from moving objects.
"At the beginning, within hearing, one enters the stream and loses the object.
"Beginning" refers to the initial stage of giving rise to a resolute mind and commencing the practice.

According to the constant protocol for establishing the teachings of the Tathāgata, if a practitioner has karmic obstructions or has not yet fulfilled the precepts, they must first seek a favorable response through repentance and vow to sever [afflictions].

There are four transgressions, as clarified later in the "Section on the Path. For now, we shall discuss the Great Samādhi directly with respect to a person who is free from obstacles and possesses the full precepts;

the practitioner should reflect upon this for themselves. The two characters "Wen" (hearing) and "Zhong" (middle) are the very nature of what is perceived, and they are also the principle toward which one proceeds.
Now, they serve as the gateway through which one enters and the objective realm that is illuminated. At the outset, these must be clearly distinguished. Do not...
One may fall into two kinds of errors, the former being coarse and the latter subtle; these must be clearly discerned.

The first is the error of not recognizing that this faculty of hearing is not within the physical ear. This nature of hearing is fundamentally the *ālayavijñāna* (storehouse consciousness), which is of one essence with the ocean of the mind and possesses six functions.
When it resides in the eye, it is seeing; when in the ear, it is hearing; and so on, up to its functioning as cognition in the mind. Now, we shall take the second [point].
Therefore, it is said that "hearing" is within. At the beginning of the sutra, the faculty of sight is taken as the example to illustrate the other five;

this thoroughly clarifies the turbid state, as shown in the ten successive demonstrations. Subsequently, once one is free from the two views, the deluded mind becomes the wondrously pure essence of seeing.

It concludes by stating: "The originally pure fundamental mind and original enlightenment are eternally abiding. The present "hearing within" is identical to that "seeing within," for their substance is non-dual.

Second: Furthermore, the four categories and seven elements are re-designated as the *tathāgatagarbha-citta* (the mind of the Tathāgata-garbha). It pervades the ten voids and perfectly encompasses the myriad dharmas.
This very "hearing within" is precisely that *tathāgatagarbha-citta*. Moreover, the one true *dharmadhātu* perfectly possesses the three *garbhas*. It is not all dharmas, yet it is all dharmas;
it is apart from being identical and apart from being non-identical, yet it is both identical and non-identical. This is so.
This is called the Tathāgata’s knowledge and vision of unsurpassed bodhi. Now, within this hearing [of the Dharma], it is precisely the essence of those three piṭakas.
This is because that which is most powerfully elucidated during the stage of the Path of Seeing (*darśana-mārga*) is what is applied in its entirety during the time of cultivation.
It is what is called "treading upon understanding to accomplish practice," the Great Dhāraṇī. If it were treated as a separate dharma, then previously...
Such an exposition would be entirely useless. Thus we know that this "hearing" is the state wherein the myriad phenomena are swallowed whole within the utterly empty Dharma-realm.
Second, it is not within the faculty of auditory consciousness; it is by means of this nature of hearing.
Whether there is sound or no sound, the clear mirror reflects them with perfect clarity; not the slightest detail is obscured, yet it remains free of discrimination.

This is identical to seeing one's nature, for it is like a mirror that does not engage in separate analysis. Furthermore, that which is free from the marks of thought is equal to empty space—both eternal and all-pervading.
Where there is thought, one is immediately restricted to a single location, subject to momentary arising and ceasing; [only when free from thought] is one neither partial nor biased.

"Constant. This refers precisely to the consciousness that takes sound as its object. If one falls into this [interpretation], then based on the original text, it would be identical to the "reflected images arising from the discrimination of objects" refuted by the Tathāgata at the beginning of this sutra;
consequently, the entire passage concerning the "sevenfold refutation" and so forth would be rendered utterly useless.
Thus we know that within this hearing, not a single thought arises; it is the state of perfectly illuminating the Dharma-realm, which is also the One.
This is the site of the ground of quiescent extinction, the true *āraṇya*, the place for authentic practice.
If you have not yet attained clear understanding through the sutras, you may recognize it with precision through quiet cultivation while seated. Frequently rise from your seat at the fifth watch;
when the night air is clear and bright and the myriad sounds first stir, let not a single thought arise, and awaken to this nature of hearing—it will be vast and open.
It is perfectly round and luminously radiant; mountain crags do not obstruct it, nor does darkness obscure it.

Sounds, whether great or small, distant or near, are reflected with absolute clarity and without omission. Even the slightest breeze stirring the trees or the sound of footsteps ringing upon the stairs is never missed.
Suppose that several *li* to the east, a great bell tolls; its sound is indeed distinct and clear.
Simultaneously, several *li* to the west, a multitude of drums resound; their clamor is likewise resonant and unmistakable.

Thus, even down to the lamentations on the southern lane and the laughter on the northern street, or the rattle of chariot wheels and the hoofbeats of horses—each and every one appears within this perfect hearing.
It is like reflections appearing within a great round mirror, where not even a hair’s breadth remains hidden.

When one reaches the state of profound stillness and silence, the hearing of that very stillness becomes all the more boundless. However, this merely uses the voice of Avalokiteśvara to manifest the essence of the capacity to hear as "the midst of hearing";
it does not take the perceived objects of movement or stillness as "the midst of hearing. Only upon reaching this point does one finally come to know.

The wondrous nature is inherently present; it is not something produced through cultivation. It is merely that, in ordinary life, one has neglected it by obstructing it with the distractions of a distracted mind, failing to realize its presence oneself.

Furthermore, one should know that within this hearing-nature, the so-called "fixedly real" body and mind, as well as the so-called "fixedly real" external vessel-world, leave no trace whatsoever to be found. It is a single expanse of empty luminosity.
Vast and boundless, the myriad dharmas stand in dense array, all fully possessed within the mind alone. The subtle wonder of their mutual penetration and integration is entirely contained therein.
It is neither existent nor empty; it is both emptiness and existence. This is the ultimate, wondrous state that transcends the reach of thought.
It is also the Patriarch’s Treasury of the True Dharma Eye and the Wondrous Mind of Nirvana; yet it is not confined to a single gate.
Alternatively, it may indicate the faculty of mind (manas), while stating that "cognition" (*vijñāna*) is merely a different term for it.

Take care, take care! This first phrase establishes the object of illumination with certainty; the subsequent phrase refers to the actual practice. "Entering" (*ru*) means turning back. Regarding "flow" (*liu*), there are two meanings:
first, the flow of the Dharma (*dharmasrotas*), which is the nature of hearing (*śravaṇatā*). To "enter the flow" means to rotate the hearing of sounds.

"Listening to it" means turning back to listen to one's own nature. "The two flows" refers to the pouring forth of attention. Listening in accordance with the sound and pouring outward toward external objects is called the "outward flow.

Turning back to listen and illuminating one's nature while pouring inward is called the "inward flow. Both interpretations are valid. This also requires that, in a single thought-moment, no thoughts arise;
one must turn the light back upon oneself and focus intently on listening to one's own nature, so as to bring about the aforementioned wondrous [state].

The objective realm is serene and ever-luminous, not for a single moment to be interrupted; this is precisely what is called "continuous and subtle cultivation" (*mián mì gōngfū*) in the School of the Patriarchs (*zōng xià*).

[Question: Seeing, hearing, sensing, and knowing share the same root-nature (*gēn xìng*). Yongjia said: "When cognition arises, one cognizes within cognition; this is not a cognition without an object (*wúyuán zhī*).

It is like a hand making a fist—it is not that the hand is no longer a hand. Now you say, "For a long time, hearing has heard its own nature. If we follow Yongjia’s logic, it should say: "When hearing arises, one hears within hearing; this is not a hearing without an object. It is like a hand making a fist—it is not that the hand is no longer a hand. How can these two meanings not be contradictory? [Answer: That [passage] refers to...

Once the faculties and objects have been extinguished and the wondrous nature has manifested, there can no longer be two cognitions. Now, since we are at the stage of a beginner initiating cultivation, we employ the expedient means of "forgetting the objects" (wangchen); therefore, one must temporarily rely on "hearing what is heard" (fawen) as the entrance.

When one reaches the point where "that which is heard by hearing is exhausted," this is likewise the state after the faculties and objects have been extinguished, and the two types of hearing no longer exist. Furthermore, this initial entry into the stream and forgetting of objects is identical to that initial cessation of thought and forgetting of objects; how could it be immediately the same as the state following the extinction of cognition and the abandonment of opposition?

Thus, if one wishes to harmonize the words of the Buddhas and Patriarchs, one must understand the sequence of before and after, and then there will be no contradiction. These two characters [“hearing” and “what is heard”] are precisely the union of awareness. Below...

The two characters [“dust” (chén) and “extinguish” (wáng)] refer to turning one’s back on sensory dust; this is the liberation of the deceased. “That which is encountered” refers to the dust of sound.
Therefore, the first two characters signify the revolving of hearing, while the latter two characters signify liberation from sound.

According to the second section on the "Definitive Meaning" at the end of the preceding four fascicles, it is explained in detail that the knots of the faculties arise entirely from mental objects (*dharmas*). Thus, when the objects perish, the knots naturally exhaust themselves. Now...
To understand the faculty of hearing, that which ought to be discarded must be identified as the two objects of motion and stillness.
"Motion" refers to the presence of sound; "stillness" refers to the absence of sound. Now, first, one discards the object of motion. This, moreover, is of two kinds:
first, indirect sound, which possesses semantic meaning, such as speech, songs, and the like; second, direct sound, which refers to...
Meaningless sounds are, for example, the sounds of wind, water, birds, beasts, bells, and drums.
Among these, those most powerful at drawing the mind into cyclic existence are distorted sounds (*kuṭila-śabda*). One must first sever these and never again encounter their conditions.
Furthermore, there are two kinds of such distortions: first, worldly distortion; second, logical distortion.
Furthermore, there are two kinds of worldly discourse: first, that which is powerless; second, that which is powerful.

"Powerless" refers to the critical evaluation of ancient and modern literature, events, or matters of other regions and the past that do not concern oneself; it merely indulges in distraction and lacks the power to increase afflictions (*kleśa*).
Therefore, it is called "powerless. "Powerful" refers to speaking of various objects of desire, causing [afflictions] to...
The mind gives rise to greed, speaks words of partiality, causes the mind to become enraged, slanders behind one's back, and reviles one to one's face.
All such words concerning personal gain or loss cause people to lose their composure, suddenly giving rise to joy or anger and causing them to forget right mindfulness.
These are all instances of worldly crookedness. As for the crookedness of principle, it is as when one speaks of the internal and external...

Regarding the principles of the heterodox and the orthodox, even down to the profound and subtle intent of the fundamental teachings of the Dharma-gates, one should not allow oneself to unconsciously generate interpretations based on words or engage in deliberation and calculation.
If one permits攀緣 (*pānluán*, objective clinging) toward these, it is likewise to wander following the sound.

This most severely obstructs fundamental hearing (*mūla-śruta*). Therefore, in the School of the Patriarchs and Buddhas, the verbal teachings of the Buddhas and patriarchs are treated like born enemies.
Question: Ceasing worldly affairs seems acceptable enough; why, however, do you also block off superior reflection upon the principles (*dharma*)?

Answer: One must tread upon understanding to establish practice; when practice arises, understanding is severed. If understanding is not severed, then untainted practice (*anāsrava-caryā*) will ultimately never be realized.
If this can be accomplished [by the conceptual mind], how much more so the true mind of the limit of reality (*bhūtakoṭi*)? A single movement of thought already deviates from it;

how could one allow for the lingering of intellectual interpretations or the pursuit of convoluted principles and sounds? Therefore, the subsequent verse says: "If you intend to hold the Buddha with your mind, why do you not hear that which hears itself?"

This is further because one must avoid the deviousness of worldly principles (just as a newly delivered family avoids the intrusion of visitors; if they sever ties with both distant guests and close friends, only then can they be free from peril.

If they only exclude distant guests while permitting the coming and going of close friends, the harm of intrusion will ultimately not be avoided. Worldly deviousness is like the distant guest; the deviousness of principles is like the close friend. Therefore, both must be severed).
At the beginning of the practitioner’s resolve, they first do not take any of these sounds of deviousness as objects of cognition.
If you simply turn the faculty of hearing inward so that it remains profoundly still, luminous, and unmoving, then all coarse and manifest conceptualizations will forever cease and fail to arise.
As for the sounds of flowing water, moving wind, ringing bells, and beating drums—all such direct auditory objects—they are even more difficult to eliminate.
You must apply yourself with meticulous care and single-minded diligence to the practice of "entering the stream."

[The sounds] have long since perished and vanished of their own accord. [The questioner asks: "If the merit of 'hearing inwardly' has been accomplished, does it mean that all sounds are as if in a state of drunken sleep, entirely obscure and unperceived?

[The answer is: "No. Whether sounds exist or not, the practitioner merely maintains the nature of hearing through its perfect illumination, ensuring it does not leak out or flow into the stream of sound.
[The questioner asks: "Does this mean one does not take as objects sounds that are distorted or crooked, thereby ceasing [the perception of them]?"
Discrimination is easy to examine; it does not depend on direct sounds and can cease its grasping. However, it is difficult to verify [the cessation of] these various sounds.
Even if the mind does not grasp them, how can one verify that it does not follow after the sounds when they erupt in confusion and disturb the hearing?
Answer: For one who is single-mindedly and earnestly practicing the "returning-hearing-to-its-source" (pratyāhāra), [this is verified].
The nature of hearing is eternally self-evident and distinct, like facing the clear autumn moon; it lacks even a single moment of darkness.
Furthermore, without focusing on a single sound, all sounds are universally perceived without obscuration. If one were to slightly grasp at a sound, there would be two consequences:
first, the nature of hearing would suddenly become obscured and no longer distinct; second, it would become biasedly focused on that one [sound].

Sound. All other sounds are entirely obscure. (To clarify this further through a metaphor: It is like a person suffering from vertigo who cannot cross a river by himself; he relies on someone else to pull him across.

That person instructs him to look up at the sky and not look at the water for even a single breath. If he forgets the instruction for even a single breath and looks at the water, he immediately falls over. This case is also like this. Turning the hearing back toward one's own nature is like looking at the sky; no longer seeking sound is like not looking at the water.

There will be no further affliction of transmigration, just as there is no longer the affliction of drowning. Thus we know that sound cannot be eliminated, but one must simply turn the hearing back with focused diligence—just as water cannot be eliminated, but one must simply look upward at the sky with focused diligence. Question:
"Are these various sounds ultimately never obscured? Is there also a time when they enter cessation? The answer is: "Obscuration is not the same as cessation.

Mental confusion constitutes obscuration; the dissipation of sound constitutes cessation. By turning back to hear one's own nature, it becomes increasingly clear and refined over time, such that there is never a time of obscuration.
When one externally detaches from the dust of sound, it gradually fades away over time, until finally reaching its end. This is truly because the nature [of the mind] is..."
This is because the sound that originally exists is fundamentally empty. Question: Sound is presently manifest; why is it said to be fundamentally empty? Answer:
It is like a person who, in a dream, falsely experiences the terror of thunder. That thunder is fundamentally empty, yet while one is in the dream, it seems to exist.
How could it truly exist? All sounds perceived before us are likewise thus. Question: Since all sounds are unreal, [how can they be heard?]...
"It is like a dream or an illusion. After they have dissolved away, there is ultimately nothing at all to hear.
Does this mean that those who have realized the Way are all like deaf people? The answer is: "No, it is not so. This is not true extinction.

It is merely that the faculty of hearing, which gathers sounds, has been temporarily submerged in a state of withered silence by the nearby obscuring sounds—just as one with eyes might find themselves within the realm of the aggregate of form (*rūpa-skandha*)."
It is like a dark room; before long, the faculty of hearing within the mind opens wide, pervading all of space. This is what is called the manifestation of the fundamental luminosity.

It will surely reach upward to the Peak of Existence and downward to the Avīci Hell, such that even the most recent sounds—the crawling of insects or the scurrying of ants—which were previously beyond the range of hearing, shall now all be heard.
How much more so other sounds! This is like the doubt of one who is deaf; it is base and inferior.
"How profound! Regarding this 'entering the stream and losing the object,' is this practiced only during seated meditation, or is it also practiced when engaged in worldly affairs?
Answer: "If one were to rely solely on seated meditation, what would be the use of examining and distinguishing sounds such as those that are distorted or winding?
It is precisely by maintaining the same state in both movement and stillness that one achieves Great Samādhi. Question: "It is easy to forget [the practice] while in seated meditation. Now,"
This is not to say that facing actual circumstances is easy; I now ask you about it. Suppose there is a person who, having encountered a situation, seeks out an old friend.
While on the road, he exerts effort, thinking only of returning to hear his own nature, while not grasping at any other sounds.
Precisely while the nature of hearing is serene and still, suddenly, midway through, one hears the speech of an old acquaintance from across a wall.
If this sound is not sought, the task of inquiry is abandoned; yet if it is sought, does this not constitute a state of transmigration?
Answer: It is admitted that this sound involves discursive thought (*vitarka*), yet it does not obstruct the non-occurrence of cyclic existence (*saṃsāra*).

As the verse says: "Sentient beings, deluded regarding their fundamental hearing, wander through cyclic existence because they pursue sound. If, at the time you pursue sound, you are not deluded regarding fundamental hearing, then this is merely pursuing sound;
how could it be cyclic existence? Question: Please distinguish between pursuing sound and wandering in cyclic existence versus pursuing sound without wandering in cyclic existence.
[The Master] said: "When you are investigating the nature of hearing itself, there is a sound that you seek;
yet when you focus single-mindedly on this seeking, the nature of hearing becomes entirely obscured and confused—this is 'samsara' (transmigration).

If, while seeking the sound, the nature of hearing remains distinct and clearly unobscured, such that it returns to its original state as soon as you momentarily seek, this is called 'attaining its function.'"

Stop here. How can it be said that these are the same as the cycle of transmigration (*saṃsāra*)? Take this as an example; whenever you encounter any matter, you should reflect upon it according to this principle.

Generally speaking, when a beginner practices in stillness, they gain the most benefit. Once stillness and concentration (*samādhi*) are established, one will gradually be able to engage with worldly affairs without losing clarity.
If, while practicing stillness and concentration, one has not yet achieved mastery, yet suddenly hopes to engage with worldly affairs—this is a mistake.
It is truly difficult not to be deluded. You ask how one can remain undeluded when engaging with worldly affairs;

since you say this is indeed difficult, it may be feared that for a beginner practicing "hearing back" (*pratyāśravaṇa*), it will be hard to achieve both principle and phenomena together. Answer: For those who abide in conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*), they would rather abandon principle to ensure the completion of affairs.

For those who practice cultivation, they would rather abandon affairs to ensure the completion of principle. Now, for one at the initial stage of cultivation and progress, who requires you to rely [on worldly affairs]?

In the past, you were deeply versed in worldly affairs and strove to achieve a dual fulfillment. You should know that for one who has "turned the hearing inward," even while dwelling in the world, they seek only to simplify matters and reduce speech.
In their daily life, they proceed with ease and spontaneity; when they find stillness, they remain still.

Only when absolutely unavoidable do they engage in a single matter or a single word, ceasing immediately once it is finished. Moreover, even at the very moment of engagement, [they maintain this state].

There is not the slightest bit of delusion. A single word or action that deviates from the truth is neither heeded nor regretted; one simply seeks to turn the hearing back toward its source without interruption, and the mind then becomes serene.
When asked, "What did the Patriarch mean when he said that 'this side' and 'that side' are both fully functional?

the answer was: "This is something long lost. Only by passing through total extinction and reviving again, by finding life within death, can one finally reach the pinnacle of its wondrous subtlety. It is not otherwise."

This means that from the very first thought, one is already able to act in this way. Question: Regarding this section, many of the old commentaries supplement it with the meaning of Tiantai’s Threefold Stop-and-Contemplation (San Zhiguan), treating it as the "Wondrous Pivot" for practice.
Why do you not employ that approach here? Answer: That [system] serves specifically as a separate entry point.
This is not the purport of this sutra. Furthermore, the initial stage of the three contemplations enters by means of the conceptualization of the six consciousnesses;
yet now, at the very beginning of this sutra, the six consciousnesses are discarded and no longer employed—by what means, then, will one enter the three contemplations?

The perfectly integrated and wondrous principle of this sutra is entirely the fundamental endowment of the *ālayavijñāna* (store-consciousness). This is elaborated in detail within the section on *śamatha*, though it has not yet been cultivated by the practitioner.
At that time, one first achieves a perfect understanding; yet when it comes to the stage of cultivation, practice arises while conceptual understanding ceases.

It is sufficient to hear [the teaching] once, which is extremely simple and convenient, without the need for the laborious establishment of extensive *śamatha* and *vipaśyanā*. This is what the Gate of the Patriarchs calls "entering directly with a single blade.

Furthermore, "entering the stream" accords with the principle of enlightened illumination, which is itself a concise and wondrous form of contemplation (*vipaśyanā*). "Forgetting the object" means turning away from the dust of the senses and bringing delusions to rest.

This is precisely the sublime stillness. When, after a long time, meditative concentration is perfected, then the perfectly interfused, subtle, and wondrous essence and function both flow forth from the fundamental ground—what is called "the original manifestation of the wondrously enlightened nature of True Suchness. Question: Previously, when the cloth was being tied...

The Tathāgata’s personal analogy should be understood through the Middle Way. Now, if you merely practice "reversing the hearing" (*pratyāhāra*) without clarifying the Middle Way, how could this be consistent with the analogy of binding the mind?
Answer: To examine the Buddha’s analogies of being pulled from the left and right:

they refer, respectively, to the cultivation of ordinary beings in the triple world who are attached to existence, and the realization of the Two Vehicles of the transcendental path who sink into emptiness. As the verse says: "Observe..."
The intersection of these two natures is neither emptiness nor existence. Now, at this time before one has reversed the hearing, the perfect understanding (*pariniṣpanna*) is already established;

when one actually reverses the hearing, how could one fall into those two extremes? Since one does not fall into either emptiness or existence, this is the most simple and direct Middle Way, which truly accords with the metaphor of binding the mind.
Why must one extensively establish *śamatha* and *vipaśyanā*, laboring over such superfluous growths?
The Middle Way is truly like adding legs to a snake; it is quite laughable.
The previous metaphor regarding the "three voids" within the *kambala* (head-wrap) used to assist in treating illness is precisely applicable here; one should examine this in detail. (Question:

May I hear about the stages of progress for a beginner and the states of guarding against transgressions during cultivation? (Answer: Although this practice is not exclusively focused on seated meditation, a beginner must still primarily cultivate in stillness. This is what is meant by the so-called "great forgetting of the human world" and "great death."

First: Know only how to turn the hearing back toward its own nature (*pratyātmadharmatā*). One should not even engage in any scattered wholesome deeds, let alone worldly affairs. Even the sacred words of the religious teachings should be regarded as if they were born enemies; how much more so should one regard worldly speech?

Even if someone comes to ask questions, simply settle the mind and turn the hearing inward, responding with one or two sentences as they happen, and then stop. As for all other activities—prostrating to the Buddha, burning incense, eating, dressing, receiving guests, answering calls, or moving about—one must ensure that the faculty of hearing remains perfectly clear and distinct.

Furthermore, at such times, since the faculty of hearing has been fully brought forth (*kṛtsnapratiṣṭhāpana*), and the faculty of hearing is itself the entire Dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu*), then every movement, every step, every cough, and every spittle is entirely pervasive throughout the Dharma-realm; this is the total enjoyment of the whole body. Even in stillness, one must constantly keep it from becoming obscured. At night...

Then, donning his robes and sitting upright, he should dispel drowsiness and distraction, focusing intently upon the faculty of hearing. As clarity and stillness flow together, if drowsiness reaches its peak, he should rest briefly for a moment, then immediately rise to practice walking meditation. He should continue this until the nature of hearing becomes clear and sharp, at which point he returns once more to sitting in stillness.

As it is said in the School of the Patriarchs (Zongmen): "A single thought-moment is ten thousand years; ten thousand years are a single thought-moment. Question: What is the case when there is wandering through the dream state? Answer: For a beginner, there may be wandering within a dream, but upon waking, one should immediately gather the mind back. There is no need for regret or attachment.

Even if one remains long in the dream, it is like the time of waking when one practices "hearing the sound of hearing" (*fǎnwén*); this is the good news that waking and sleeping are always one. However, at all times, seek the grace of the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas to cause the mind to open.

When practicing in this way, everything is forgotten, just as described later in the text: "like a person with eyes situated in a vast dark room"—this refers to being within the domain of the aggregate of form (*rūpa-skandha*). One must by no means resent this confusion and distress, for when the sense organs and their objects have both subsided, one will naturally become as follows:

When one’s practice reaches its ultimate limit, there will naturally come a time when the fundamental luminosity manifests; do not seek this with impatience. However, when the light of the mind reaches its peak intensity, you may see the manifestation of your original teacher appearing to touch your crown and bestow empowerment. At that time, you should act according to what is explained in the section on the subsequent path.

Silently verifying the distinction between demons and Buddhas, you must apply yourself with even greater intensity. Should various wholesome states arise—such as the first ten types of "shadow-demons" mentioned later—do not mistake them for signs of sainthood; simply continue to exert effort in the practice of "turning the hearing inward.

Furthermore, at the moment when you enter the stream and lose all objective referents, this is precisely when the mind-essence reaches perfect resonance, sharing a single nostril with the sages of the ten directions. It is at this very juncture that the culmination of your practice may stir up demons. Relying on the subsequent sacred teachings, if you awaken to this state, there will be no fault; by no means should you become deranged midway through the process.

Thus, having escaped the movement of sensory dust, your cultivation must reach the point where suddenly all clamor vanishes and only the nature of hearing remains—brilliant as the sun and moon, like the sky after a rainstorm has cleared, or like a windless sea, utterly tranquil.

Quiescence. At this time, not only do all sounds vanish, but the body, mind, and world become utterly empty; vast and open, one attains sovereign ease. This is precisely the moment of "turning back hearing to detach from sound" and entering the path.

This state is extremely vast, sovereign, quiescent, and tranquil. One must most strictly avoid being overly skillful at grasping or becoming attached. If you maintain only a single even-mindedness and persevere without ceasing, then immeasurable wondrous states will gradually unfold before you.
Should you grasp at them even once, you will lose them as soon as you gain them, and they will never be recoverable again. Take note! Take note! 2. Detaching from Motion and Stillness.
Since that which is entered has become quiescent, the two characteristics of motion and stillness clearly do not arise.

In the preceding section, one merely departed from the knot of motion; in this section, the knots of both motion and stillness are removed together. This is because when motion is eliminated, stillness manifests.

This is the principle of spontaneity (*ziran*). When effort is applied, both [subject and object] are simultaneously discarded; thus, the labor of spontaneity is achieved. Therefore, when it is said "the object," one immediately forgets the object;
when it is said "entry," one immediately enters the stream. "When both the object and the entry are stilled" means that the object has perished and one has entered the stream;
both have become quiescent. For although one initially forgets the object, how easily can the object be made to perish? Although one initially enters the stream, the stream...

"How easy it is to enter! Though it is said that one must exert effort, if not even a single thought arises, one cannot yet avoid the mind being stirred by movement and stillness, requiring constant gathering and containment;

this is not yet true quiescence. When one reaches this point where the object of perception vanishes while that which is perceived does not vanish, one enters the flow such that there is no flow into which one does not enter.
All manifold movements cease together, and as the emotions are gathered and forgotten, it is said: "That which is entered is already quiescent. From this...
Thus one knows it. That which was previously "non-existent" was merely the absence of movement;

that which is now "already tranquil" is the state wherein the fetters of movement have been eliminated and the fetters of stillness are now revealed. The next two phrases represent the simultaneous elimination of both movement and stillness.

Although these are spoken of together as a pair, in reality they single out the elimination of "already tranquil," thereby removing only the dust of stillness. Thus, it is said to be "clearly understood."

However, as for "non-arising," this refers to the state after [the mind] has already become still; through further application of effort and advancement of power, one reaches ultimate quiescence, wherein even the two types of objects are extinguished and both become unobtainable.
Question: The extinction of movement is the same as the extinction of sound.
Yet, the object of sound and the nature of hearing are as opposed as black and white, making them easy to distinguish; therefore, their extinction is easy. But when it comes to stillness...

Dust and the nature of hearing accord with one another. The nature of hearing is supremely still; when dust is still, the nature of hearing is also still. Both are without boundaries; both are without discrimination.
Like wind and space, they cannot be distinguished; like water and milk, they are difficult to separate. Truly, it is hard to analyze them, so to eliminate [the perception of dust] may not be easy.
How, then, can you demonstrate it? Answer: The only concern is that you have not yet been able to clearly perceive the nature of hearing.
It is clear. If one perceives the nature of hearing and seeing with lucid clarity, how could there be any possibility of confusion?

This is because the nature of hearing is the mind, while the stillness of sensory objects is the environment. The mind is a luminous awareness that is never obscured; the environment is dark and inert, devoid of cognition.
The environment is simply the environment, and the mind is simply the mind. As you are you and I am I, what difficulty is there in distinguishing them? It is just like in the mundane world.
Ordinary people enter deep mountains and solitary places where no one dwells;

they are all able to discern the stillness within those mountains, yet they are not aware of even a hair’s breadth of their own auditory nature. When they come to a bustling marketplace, that stillness is entirely lost.

This is because their previous state of stillness was entirely the stillness of the mountain; once they leave the mountain, how could there be any more stillness? Worldly people grasp only at the stillness of external objects.
There is nothing that does not lose [its stability] apart from the objective realm. This is because external objects are still extremely coarse.

Furthermore, there are practitioners who, having not yet seen their own minds, merely practice the concentration of mindfulness (*smṛti-saṃgraha*) until they achieve meditative absorption (*samādhi*).

As they progress deeper and deeper, relying on the power of that concentration, they perceive boundless realms and still the objective spheres. Yet, when the power of that concentration is exhausted, there is nothing that does not lose [its stability]. This...

This constitutes the internal object. It is subtler than the former. If one has not yet awakened to the mind and does not perceive the nature of hearing and seeing, then truly one does not recognize that these two are both tranquil objects;
it is not that the mind itself is tranquil. If one can awaken to the mind and clearly realize the nature of hearing and seeing, [then one knows this].
One awakens to this nature as being fundamentally and ultimately still, tranquil and boundless. It is not produced by the concentration of mindfulness, nor does it depend upon external objects.
Those who do not know how to turn the hearing inward remain entirely unaware of it. If one can single-mindedly turn the hearing inward, then this still nature is ever-present;
whether dwelling in the mountains or in the marketplace, that stillness is unchanging. Whether entering or emerging from meditative concentration, it remains the same.

Its stillness is constant and unchanging. Even if one has not yet attained enlightenment, prior to the practice of "returning the hearing," it has been fundamentally and eternally still since beginningless time;
how much more so after one has clearly perceived and practiced returning the hearing—how could there then be any talk of gain or loss?

Thus, the nature of hearing is fundamentally unrelated to the dust of stillness; for one who is single-mindedly and earnestly practicing the return of the hearing, to lose it would be exceedingly easy.

What difficulty could there be? Generally speaking, after the cessation of movement, there is no other skillful means; rather, the practice of "hearing inwardly" becomes increasingly profound and penetrating.
As the nature of hearing grows clearer and more luminous, the two sensory objects of motion and stillness are both utterly transcended.

Upon reaching this point—the ultimate limit of the cessation of objects—one stands at the stage of the practice of luminosity, corresponding to the initial stage of faith (*śraddhā*) within the first of the ten stages (*bhūmi*). In comparison to the Two Vehicles, this level is equal to theirs.
The First Fruit. Question: How is this known? Answer: The *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra* states:

"It is called 'entering the stream,' yet in reality there is nothing entered. It further states: "Because one does not enter form, sound, smell, taste, touch, or dharmas, one is named a *srotāpanna* (Stream-enterer).

This indicates that when the dust of sound is extinguished, all six objects of the senses are simultaneously extinguished; thus it is known to be so. As for the two characters "entering the stream," the distinction between the Great and Small Vehicles is profound.

The difference is this: those of the Lesser Vehicle who have entered the stream merely concentrate their minds to enter deep samādhi, asserting that the nature of dharmas is simply the realm of the three unconditioned phenomena.
This sūtra, however, treats even dharmas as objects of mental consciousness—mere reflections of discrimination.

How could it be the same as this "reversing the hearing to listen to one's own nature"? Thus we know that although their stages of realization may be equal, the depth of their penetration into principle is vastly different.
The same applies here. △ Third, the liberation of the faculty of hearing.
In this way, it gradually increases until both the hearing and that which is heard are exhausted.

While the preceding section entirely concerned the elimination of objects (*viṣaya*), this section now concerns the exhaustion of the faculties (*indriya*). The phrase "in this way" (*evam*) is a term that承接 (links back to) what precedes.

"Gradually increasing" means the intent of applying effort and advancing in practice. Regarding the second phrase, I do not follow the old commentary’s explanation of "raising the dust to manifest the faculty.

This is because the first instance of the character *wen* (to hear) refers to the inverted hearing-mechanism (*wen-ji*), while the second instance of *wen* refers to the nature of hearing (*wen-xing*) that hears what is heard.

Since the preceding section established the expedient of "extinguishing the dust" by means of a diagram, it posited two types of hearing—the subjective and the objective—to enable [the practitioner] to...
When the faculty of hearing is heard, objects vanish. Now that the characteristics of objects have been exhausted, there is nothing external for it to confront;
thus, the faculty itself no longer exists. Both the hearing-mechanism that hears and the hearing-nature that is heard are simultaneously extinguished.

Therefore, it is said: "Hearing and the heard are both exhausted. As the subsequent text states: "When objects are no longer perceived, the faculty has no partner; the flow is reversed and the One is fully realized."

"The six faculties do not function"—this is precisely what that refers to. Question: Since you have already established that the nature of the faculties is fully augmented and clarified, and have now stated that both movement and stillness are simultaneously absent, if you now further claim that the nature of the faculties is also extinguished, does this not result in total annihilation?

Answer: This merely means the exhaustion of the faculties; how can it be called the extinction of their nature? Question: Are the faculties and their nature two different things? Answer: They are not two, nor are they not two.
They are not one. Question: How should one understand this? Answer: The faculties (*indriya*) are like ice, and their nature (*svabhāva*) is like water.
Since ice and water originally have no distinct substance, they are not two. However, because ice freezes and becomes obstructed while water melts and flows through, they are not one.

What is now called the "exhaustion of the faculties" is merely like the melting of ice; how could it be like the drying up of water? Question: As for what was said previously regarding the disappearance of the two objects (*viṣaya*).

"Consider the nature of hearing: it is exceedingly tranquil, profound, and boundless. Now that the internal faculties have been exhausted, what further characteristics remain to distinguish this [nature] from them?

Answer: "By means of the skillful methods previously employed, one detaches from those two objects [of sound and form]. Consequently, one temporarily grasps the nature of hearing as 'internal' and the two objects as 'external.
Turning away from the external and facing inward, the internal faculty remains clearly and constantly present when one examines it with subtle detail. (From the *Sūtra*)
It is called "hearing within," and it is also called "entering the stream. That "within" and "entry" clearly manifest that the sense organ is internal; this is self-evident.

When the two objects of perception have been washed away and extinguished, external appearances no longer exist. Since one no longer faces the external, internal appearances gradually dissolve until they vanish entirely.
When there is suddenly neither internal nor external, this is the state in which the sense organ has reached its end. By this, one knows that what was said previously—
That which is "boundless" (ananta) is not a true non-existence. Taking two atoms (*paramāṇu*) as a limit constitutes a boundary;

now that these two atoms have been exhausted and there is no further partition, this is truly boundless. If one examines this in relation to the three emptinesses (*śūnyatā*), reaching this point constitutes the realization of the emptiness of persons (*pudgala-śūnyatā*).

Prior to this, when the sense-faculties (*indriya*) were contrasted with objects (*viṣaya*), the object was regarded as the "other-aspect" (*para-lakṣaṇa*) and the faculty as the "self-aspect" (*ātma-lakṣaṇa*).
Characteristics. By excluding others, one establishes the self; by turning away from others, one turns toward the self, and the characteristic of "self" remains distinct.

Reaching this point, both faculties and objects dissolve, and both subject and object perish. There is no longer self or other; there is only the single *dharmatā*. Without distinction between internal and external, the four characteristics—gross and subtle—are exhausted without remainder.
This stage of concentration corresponds to the seventh level of faith (*śraddhā*), equaling the seventh abode (*vihāra*) of the *Pratyekabuddha* vehicle. Regarding the Small Vehicle (*Hīnayāna*)...

At the stage of the Arhat of the fourth fruit, the afflictions of views and thought (*dṛṣṭi-kleśa* and *bhāvanā-kleśa*) are exhausted, and one realizes the true suchness (*tathatā*) of the emptiness of self (*pudgala-śūnyatā*).
This is precisely what the Tathāgata previously described as "this faculty first being understood, whereby one first attains the emptiness of persons.

Furthermore, it should be known that this is the high realization of the seventh stage of faith (*śraddhā*) within the Perfect Teaching (*yuanjiao*) of the Bodhisattva; however, in terms of severing the afflictions of views and thought and realizing the emptiness of persons, it is said to be equal to that of the Lesser Vehicle.

The four fruits of arhatship are not truly identical to those of an arhat; they are like the first rank of the world’s jinshi (advanced scholars), who temporarily share the status of a minor official.

But how could their ultimate rank truly be identical in name and position to that of the highest grade? One should know that this applies to the six supernormal powers, the eighteen transformations, and so forth.
All should be sublime. Their differences will be further clarified below. It is also like the status, rank, and titles of the jinshi (advanced scholar) qualification;
none of these can be looked up to by those of the lower clerical ranks. The initial explanation of the three fetters and the prior attainment of the emptiness of persons is now complete.
△ Second, the sequential explanation of the two fetters to achieve the liberation through the dharma. This follows the sequence previously indicated, with the exception of the [preceding] removal.

Section on Grasping. Having already clarified that the coarse forms of grasping at phenomena (*dharmagrāha*) were long ago completely severed when first entering the stream and losing the objective referent, here we address only the subtle grasping at phenomena.
This section is divided into two parts: first, the liberation from applied and sustained thought (*vitarka-vicāra*).
"The hearing is exhausted and does not abide; that which perceives and that which is perceived are both empty.

The two characters "exhausted hearing" (*jin wen*) cite the previous state where "hearing and the object of hearing are exhausted," which is the realm where these two modes of hearing have both vanished.
"Does not abide" means to apply effort and advance, passing through this realm without being dull or obstructed by it. This is because one has seen that hearing is exhausted.
If one remains [attached], their pride will increase among their peers and the city of transformation will be closed forever. The final phrase refers to the newly realized state;
for after the exhaustion of hearing, the faculties and objects are utterly detached, and the profound, singular, and boundless realm manifests before one.
What is now called "awakening" (jue) is the wisdom that illumines this realm; that which is awakened to is this profound, singular realm. Exhaustion...
If one abides in hearing, then the realm of wisdom will constantly confront it, and the duality of subject and object will persist, ultimately becoming an obstacle to further progress;
this is what Yangshan referred to as "the fullness of mind and objects.

Now, when it is said that "that which perceives and that which is perceived are empty," it means that both the wisdom that perceives and the objects that are perceived are equally empty and quiescent, such that they vanish entirely and no longer stand in opposition to one another. This...

Although both object and wisdom are mentioned together, the two—the subject that perceives and the object perceived—are both termed "awakening" (*jue*), which refers to the aspect of the mind that is awakening.

This pertains primarily to wisdom (*prajñā*). If one is stingy with this mind, regarding it as the true wisdom of *prajñā* and unable to let it go, this constitutes the "affection for dharmas" (*dharmatṛṣṇā*)—the false arising of attachment toward wisdom.
Furthermore, in relation to what follows, this serves to sever attachment to dharmas (*dharmagrāha*).
Discrimination. Question: Regarding the discrimination of attachment to dharmas (*dharmagrāha-vikalpa*), it should have been severed along with the previously mentioned coarse attachment to dharmas.
Why, then, does discrimination still exist within this [state]? Answer: This is the subtle, continuous flow of innate discrimination (*sahaja-vikalpa*); it is not coarse discrimination.

In fact, it is merely a case of "discrimination" being spoken of in the sense of being like *vitarka* and *vicāra*, where awareness is not yet forgotten. △ Second, liberation from the two types of emptiness.
The realization of emptiness reaches ultimate perfection. That which is emptied by emptiness is extinguished.

Regarding the phrase "the emptiness of the realization of emptiness," the term "realization of emptiness" (kōjaku) reiterates the "emptiness of that which is realized by the realization" (kakushosakū no kū) mentioned above;
it is used to manifest the wisdom of the double emptiness. "Ultimate perfection" (kyūen) refers to the intention of further cultivating until its full measure is attained. As for the final phrase:
"Promptly raising the emptiness" refers to this wisdom of the "repeated emptiness. "That which is emptied" refers to the preceding wisdom and its objects as analyzed above.
"The emptiness and that which is emptied both cease" means that the wisdom of repeated emptiness, along with the preceding wisdom and its objects, are all extinguished without remainder.
This is because, when the wisdom of repeated emptiness first arises and has not yet reached full perfection, there remains that which can empty and that which is emptied.

Both [the object and the subject] remain clearly present. Now, when the realization of emptiness is perfectly complete, not only does the cognitive object that is empty cease, but the wisdom of the "emptiness of emptiness" likewise perishes along with it.
It is like drilling wood with wood: once the fire emerges, both pieces of wood are consumed.
Although this is the wisdom of the "emptiness of emptiness," both the capacity to empty and the object emptied are said to be empty; thus, the objective realm is empty.

This is a matter of category. In terms of principle, it is similar [to the previous stage]. If one is parsimonious regarding this object and takes it to be the ground of the reality-limit (*bhūtakoṭi*), this constitutes the "dharma-attachment" that falsely gives rise to attachment toward the principle.
Furthermore, compared to the preceding stage, this represents the abandonment of the innate grasping at dharmas (*dharmagrāha*).

This is because, while both subject and object are empty and one has already departed from the subtle discrimination discussed in the previous section, there still remains this subtle obstruction that persists spontaneously.
It is merely a reflection of conditions. When this reflection is extinguished, one achieves liberation through the Dharma, and the true light is about to be revealed.
These two knots have already transcended and surpassed the Small Vehicle (Hīnayāna). Nevertheless, their position is fixed within the Perfect Teaching (Yuanjiao):

specifically, they correspond to the eighth stage among the ten stages of Faith; in the Distinct Teaching (Biejiao), they correspond to the eighth stage among the ten abodes, as well as the ten practices and ten transferences—these twenty-three positions.
And the dust-like delusions are exhausted. (One should know that these bodhisattvas differ greatly from those of fixed nature who turn back from the Lesser Vehicle.

This is because the bodhisattvas have already severed or suppressed their attachment to coarse phenomena, whereas those of fixed nature must first suppress and then sever all phenomena; this is why they are slow and dull. Furthermore, this is because the realization of emptiness presented by these bodhisattvas is extremely perfect.
As previously stated, the emptiness taught by the Tathāgata is perfectly luminous. Therefore, one should know that this emptiness—the object of emptiness—is extinguished;

this is precisely what was previously called "liberation through the Dharma. Having thus explained the second knot and completed the liberation through the Dharma, next we shall explain the single knot:
both being empty, they do not arise.
When birth-and-death have ceased, quiescent extinction manifests before one.

The two characters "birth-and-death" encompass both the preceding states of motion and stillness. When the faculties and consciousnesses are empty and extinguished, the six knots are entirely withdrawn;

though coarse and subtle differ, they are fundamentally all the mind of birth-and-death. First, it was explained that motion ceases and stillness arises; next, it was explained that the objects cease and the faculties [arise].

Regarding birth: although in principle there is no birth, there is cessation and persistence; birth and cessation are manifestly present. The following sections are all explained according to this pattern.

Third, one understands that when the faculties cease, awareness arises. Fourth, one understands that when awareness ceases, emptiness arises. Fifth, one understands that when emptiness ceases, cessation arises.
If, upon reaching this point, one dwells in the final phase of cessation, then one will be shrouded by that mark of cessation and will perpetually abide in total emptiness; this would be [the fault].
Because there remains a subtle obstruction at the very peak of realization, it is still called the "sixth extinction of fetters. At the top of a hundred-foot pole, one must advance even further.
This is what the Patriarch meant when he said, "There is still more to do below," and it is also termed the "final attachment."

However, one need not again exert effort to eliminate this; it is what the Confucian classics call "transformation that cannot be contrived," and what the fundamental scripture calls the "path of non-exertion" (*anābhoga-mārga*).
One simply maintains a mind free from dwelling or attachment and awaits a single *kṣaṇa*.
When the fundamental principle manifests before one, then this characteristic of cessation will be utterly transcended, as in the final verse.
It is so. However, that which is called "quiescence" is not a quiescence that exists in opposition to movement; it is the quiescence that has been fundamentally unmoving since beginningless time.
That which is called "extinction" is not an extinction that exists in opposition to arising; it is the extinction that has been fundamentally without arising since beginningless time.
This is the essence of the principle of original enlightenment, the nature of the Tathāgatagarbha, and the reality-limit of True Suchness (Tathatā). It is pure.

Pure and inherently so, it pervades the entire Dharma-realm. It is also called the Great Ocean of Quiescent Extinction (*mahā-śānti-nirvāṇa-samudra*) and the Great Treasury of Radiant Light (*mahā-prabhā-garbha*).
What is known as "quiescent illumination encompassing emptiness" merely reverses the aforementioned arising and ceasing;

yet when speaking solely of quiescent extinction, it is in fact the entire substance of the True Mind, wherein all manifold functions are fully present. When this principle manifests before one, then mountains, rivers, and the great...

The stage [of the Bodhisattva] should be conceived as transforming into supreme enlightenment. The faculties—whether separated or joined—interact such that the six sense organs function for one another;
all the superior functions described in the subsequent sections originate from this. According to the rank attained, it should correspond to the first abode (*prathamā bhūmi*).
Although one has severed a portion of ignorance and realized a portion of ultimate truth, [the remaining ignorance still persists].
By severing one, all are severed; by realizing one, all are realized. The merits of the forty-two stages are implicitly complete.

Although it is said that this is equal in rank to the first stage (*bhūmi*) of the Separate Teaching (*biejiao*), the distinction between the sequential and the perfectly integrated is as vast as the difference between heaven and earth.

(This concludes the preceding section on the "Successive Untying of Knots," which is synthesized with the final passage of the fourth fascicle: entering the stream is to maintain the true and constant, while losing the object of perception is to abandon all arising and ceasing.)

The exhaustion of hearing is itself the faculty; when objects and consciousness respond to thought, they immediately dissolve and fall away. The two types of awakening are the defilements of consciousness and emotion; the two types of emptiness are the dust of conceptual marks and appearances.

When the former is empty and the latter is extinguished, both are simultaneously distanced. When quiescent extinction manifests before one, the Dharma-eye becomes clear and bright, without the slightest discrepancy. If one understands the *Śamatha* passage from Yongjia, "entering the stream" means the cessation of thought, and "losing the object" means losing the dust.

One should also interpret the text as follows: the stream does not exist without losing the object, and the object is not lost unless one enters the stream. To lose the object is to enter the stream, and to enter the stream is to lose the object. These four lines can be equated with the non-arising of movement and stillness. Furthermore, it says: "To lose the object and enter [the stream] is to enter."

There is no one who can enter; having entered the stream, one perishes. Thus, in this "perishing," there is nothing to perish. These two phrases—the simultaneous subsiding of root and object—may be equated with "the exhaustion of that which is heard and that by which it is heard. Furthermore, it says: "In this 'perishing,' there is nothing to perish" means that objects are abandoned and do not constitute a duality. "Entering, there is no one who can enter" means that thought ceases and is not a cognition.

These two phrases—being without duality and without cognition—may be equated with "the emptiness of that which perceives and that which is perceived. Furthermore, it says: "Cognition ceases and duality is abandoned, resulting in a state of uniform profound stillness. These two phrases may be equated with "the extinction of that which is empty and that by which it is emptied."

Furthermore, it is said: "Silent and without reliance, the wondrous nature is innate. These two phrases may be equated with the passage: "When birth and death have ceased, quiescent extinction manifests before one. They seem to merge seamlessly without interval.

However, while Yongjia appears to encompass all six sense-faculties—or perhaps focuses specifically on the faculty of mind (*manas*)—this scripture specializes in encompassing the faculty of hearing (*śrotra*), which is their point of distinction. Moreover, while Yongjia is currently discussing the initial dissolution and manifestation, followed by further cultivation and refinement, this scripture has already discussed deep realization at a high stage, followed by the subsequent manifestation of functional application.

Now, when these are compared and synthesized, the phrasing and structure appear remarkably similar. This is intended to show that in the Perfect and Sudden teaching, there is no difference between the beginning and the end. Practitioners must not dismiss the higher stages as being irrelevant to themselves. Furthermore, Yong...

Jia Ge said: "The mind is the root; dharmas are the dust. These two are like stains upon a mirror. When the stains are exhausted, the light begins to appear. When both mind and dharmas are forgotten, the nature is itself the Truth. This causes one to exhaust even the subtlest attachment to dharmas, which precisely corresponds to the subsequent three subtle knots.

That which is called "the mind is the root" refers to the knot of sensation (*vedanā*). That which is called "dharmas are the dust" refers to the knot of emptiness (*śūnyatā*). That which is called "both mind and dharmas are forgotten" means that birth and death have already ceased; this correctly eliminates the final knot of cessation (*nirodha*).

And that which is called "the nature is itself the Truth" means that quiescent extinction has manifested before one. The Buddhas and Patriarchs are of one accord; from the beginning there have never been two paths. Students should take heed of this. (Successive Unraveling of the Knots)
The cultivation and realization are now complete. △ Third, a detailed exposition of the extraordinary excellence attained. The above constitutes the causal practice of perfect penetration;
this, however, is the resultant function of perfect penetration. Because the three sections herein contain extensive accumulations of chapters, it is termed a "detailed exposition.
Furthermore, as these are the words of the Bodhisattva himself, they are designated by their own title to mark their extraordinary excellence. Question: Is the causal practice for the sake of...?

The essentials of cultivation ought to be explained in detail; why then is the text so extremely brief? If one argues that the result should remain implicit so that it may manifest spontaneously once the practice is perfected, then perhaps brevity would be appropriate;
yet why is the text so extremely detailed? Answer: To clarify the result and thereby inspire and encourage joyful cultivation, it certainly should not be abbreviated.

However, in demonstrating the essential method of cultivation through the causal practices for the sake of others, one must be even more detailed. What is now described concerns these causal practices.

The reason it does not exceed a few words is that this sutra presents the Tathāgata and the Bodhisattva as equally expounding a single, perfect cause and effect, with the preceding and succeeding sections varying in detail and brevity.

From the latter half of the fourth fascicle, where the Tathāgata demonstrates the two definitive meanings, up until the first half of the fifth fascicle, which provides proof through the striking of the bell to verify permanence, there is no separate conclusion regarding the source of delusion. Until...
Tying a cloth around his head, he demonstrated the union [of the faculties]. There is a volume of scripture that explains the liberation of the faculties in detail;

its account of the cultivation of perfect penetration is most exhaustive. How could it have been limited merely to its widespread use today? As for the reason why it speaks of the "fruition-function," it simply says:
"Mountains, rivers, and the great earth shall, upon thought, transform into supreme enlightened awareness. It further states: "By means of these six faculties..."

They function in mutual dependence. The phrasing [of the sūtra] is extremely concise. Now, if the Bodhisattva’s exposition of practice were detailed, it would be redundant given what the Tathāgata has already taught regarding their application.
If it were concise, it would fail to remedy the omissions in the Tathāgata’s text. Both extremes would lack excellence.

Therefore, while the cause—the practice—may be concise, the effect—the application—should be extensive; thus both the extensive and the concise are appropriate to their respective needs. This is merely because the Tathāgata spoke in a general manner.

Regarding the "faculty of liberation" (*mukti-indriya*), [the text] cryptically points to the faculty of hearing (*śrotra-indriya*). While the Bodhisattva speaks of it explicitly and exclusively, the phrasing appears to have both hidden and manifest aspects, as well as universal and restricted applications;

yet in meaning, there is truly no difference in their intent. If a practitioner wishes to investigate the details of the causal practice of perfect penetration (*pariśuddha-āyatana*), they should consult the preceding scriptural passage alongside what the Bodhisattva has said, examining them in comparison. It is not necessary to restrict oneself solely to the Bodhisattva’s teaching.
In a few words, it is divided into two parts. First, the presentation of the two fundamental natures. This further has two sections. First, the general presentation:
suddenly transcending both the mundane and supramundane worlds, one attains the ten directions' perfect luminosity and acquires two kinds of excellence.
"Suddenly" refers to the single moment (*kṣaṇa*) of the path of liberation (*vimukti-mārga*).
