For the realization of the true essence occurs in a single moment, and the arising of function in accordance with that essence likewise occurs in a single moment.
"Transcending" means the sense of being liberated from entanglements; because one is no longer bound by the internal realms, one transcends the world, yet is not [confined] by the external realms.
Because it is free from entanglements, it transcends the mundane world. Its perfect luminosity throughout the ten directions is the meaning of "quiescent illumination encompassing emptiness";

it does not stop at the trichiliocosm. According to the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra*, this refers to the perfect luminosity of the hundred realms through the manifestation of bodies; that is, clarity and penetration fill the hundred realms.
Furthermore, the "ten directions" may also be understood as the perfect luminosity of the ten dharma-realms, such that each and every realm is fully present.
This refers to attaining the ten suchnesses. Second is "extraordinary excellence" (*viśeṣa*), which exhausts the two kinds of wondrous functions listed below.
From the very first moment of generating the bodhicitta, the Bodhisattva realizes that mind, Buddha, and sentient beings are non-different.

Thus, at the time of realizing one's own mind, one immediately shares the same essence and function as the Buddhas. However, these are all termed "extraordinary excellence" to manifest their transcendence over the provisional vehicles (*upāyayāna*).
Indeed. This is because [the practitioner] harmonizes with those above and unites with those below—states that neither of the two vehicles can achieve—and thus it is said so.
△ Second, the detailed enumeration, which is further divided into two parts. First, harmonizing upward with the power of compassion.
First, above, it accords with the fundamental, wondrously enlightened mind of all Buddhas of the ten directions; it shares the same power of compassion as the Buddha-Tathāgatas.

First, by acceding with the fundamental, wondrously enlightened mind, one is of the same essence as all Buddhas; by sharing the Buddha’s power of compassion, one is of the same function as all Buddhas.

Being identical to the fruit while remaining in the cause, and eternally pure while dwelling in defilement, it is therefore called the "fundamental, wondrously enlightened mind. This [mind] resides within every person.
Because it is inherently possessed, upon its realization, there is immediate upward convergence. According to Wuxing, the character "force" (力) is read as "compassion" (悲).

This is because the Buddha’s compassion that bestows joy must necessarily be accompanied by the compassion that uproots suffering; this is logically so. △ Second, downward convergence through compassionate yearning.
Second, it joins downward with all sentient beings of the six realms throughout the ten directions; it shares the same compassion and longing as all these beings.

Below the phrase "sentient beings of the six realms," there should also be the four characters "original wondrous enlightened mind" (běn miào jué xīn), though they have been omitted in the translated text.
Because the Buddha and sentient beings equally possess the fundamental mind (*mūlacitta*), when a bodhisattva realizes this mind, the upper and lower realms are both unified.

Through this unification, they first become identical in essence (*tattva*), and subsequently are able to become identical in their two functions: the power of compassion (*karuṇā*) and the aspiration for liberation (*anurāga*).

Regarding sentient beings, the author of the sutra omits them for two reasons: first, because the Buddha’s descent [into the world] has already clarified the nature of sentient beings; [the second reason follows].
Because they are not different, they are not reiterated. Second, the wondrous mind of the Buddhas has already been realized and possesses power;

it is necessary to manifest its union for its superior function to be perfected. The wondrous mind of sentient beings has not yet been realized and lacks power; there is no need to manifest its union.

Through union, one becomes fearless, yet the superior function cannot be made identical [to that of the Buddhas]. Although both are pervasive, the former meaning is the correct one. This is the compassionate one’s [teaching].
To "entreat" means to seek the extraction of suffering; to "look up to" means to hope for the bestowal of happiness. This intention is the same as what was explained by the one from Wuxing.
The presentation of the two versions is now complete. II. The Transmission and Elaboration of the Three Sections.

Regarding "transmission and elaboration," this is because each subsequent section contains sub-sections that inherit from those above. This is divided into three parts. First, the Thirty-two Responsive Manifestations. This also has three parts. First, the Presentation of the Transmission.
"O World-Honored One, by virtue of my making offerings to the Tathāgata Avalokiteśvara, I received from that Tathāgata the Vajra Samādhi of Hearing-Perfuming and Hearing-Cultivation,
which is like an illusion; because I share the same power of compassion as the Buddha-Tathāgatas, my body has become thirty..."
"Second, the Responsive Manifestation (*anuprāpti*):

'Entering all lands'—from 'by me' onwards, up to 'because of the power of universal compassion'—this indicates the transmission and reception [of the teaching] and reveals the name of the samādhi, thereby manifesting the vast source of the marvelous essence and function of the response.
The character 'hearing' (*śrotra*) above refers to the essence of the original enlightenment of the nature of hearing."

"Perfuming through hearing" refers precisely to what is called the internal perfuming of original enlightenment (*prakṛti-āśraya*). The character "hearing" (*wen*) in the following [phrase] refers to the faculty of hearing that has been turned back;

it denotes the wisdom of initial enlightenment (*ādikṣaya-bodhi*). As for speaking of "cultivation through hearing," this means advancing in the cultivation of perfect penetration by means of this "hearing back.

However, it was initially described as being "like an illusion," meaning that the provisional and temporary application of initial enlightenment is gradually dissolved; it is not the same as clinging to it as real.

This refers to the cultivation of purification. Regarding "ultimately culminating in the vajra": it means that fundamental awakening (mūla-bodhi) is fully manifested and is forever indestructible, yet it still possesses the power to shatter the firmest things;
it is not like the provisional vehicles, which are ultimately unreal. Furthermore, because the first two [stages] are based on the provisional and the heard, they are like an illusion;
because the final one is perfected as the single nature, it is like a vajra. Only at this point is it clearly explained that one has attained the essence and is equal to the Buddha.
The second line clarifies the shared function; only when essence and function are both present can the wondrous response of the final three lines be established.
For a Bodhisattva to respond according to the capacities of beings is "response. Those sentient beings who seek such a response must exert their own wondrous capacity for resonance;
if they lack this wondrous resonance, one certainly cannot falsely claim that the compassionate response is not all-pervasive. As for "wandering through various lands": [End of excerpt]

"There is not a single land where he does not manifest his body. Wēnlíng says: "The thirty-two manifestations refer to the manifestation of bodies within the ten dharma-realms, perfectly responding to the various capacities of sentient beings.
When expanded, there are thirty-two; when condensed, they comprise only the four noble classes and the six ordinary realms, encompassing all categories of beings.
II. A detailed enumeration of the wondrous responses. This has two parts: 1. Responding to the mind that seeks [mercy]. Seeking compassion and...

Joy: each seeks that which accords with their own mind. Furthermore, there are two [categories]. First, one should seek the Noble Vehicle (*āryayāna*), which refers to the four supramundane noble vehicles.
Regarding the seekers themselves, excluding the Buddha, there are only three; regarding the bodies they manifest, all four noble vehicles are complete.
Here, as for the seekers, there are still four, because to the *pratyekabuddha* (solitary realizer) is added the *pratyekajina* (self-enlightened one). This is divided into four. First, Bodhi...
"Śāriputra,
if there are bodhisattvas who enter samādhi and advance in their cultivation until their untainted resolute conviction (*anāsrava-adhimukti*) becomes fully manifest,
I will manifest in the body of a Buddha and preach the Dharma for them, causing them to attain liberation."
Since they are called "all bodhisattvas," they exist within each teaching and are not restricted to the distinct or perfect [teachings].
However, there are no ordinary bodhisattvas who do not aspire to attain the Buddha-body; therefore, he manifests the Buddha-body to respond to their capacities.

As for "superior understanding" (adhimukti), it refers to the wisdom of realization that arises when the causal practices have reached their culmination, according to the specific dharma-gate one has cultivated. The character "perfect" (yuan) is manifested.
This is explained by interpreting it as "full" (*pūrṇa*); it refers to the time when the realization of wisdom is about to reach completion. Xielü says:

"The phrase 'superior understanding manifests its perfection' is so named because, for each [vehicle], their respective vehicle’s principle and wisdom are about to manifest before them. Hereafter, all instances follow this pattern. Gushan says:
"If one enters the 'similar' (*pratirūpa*) samādhi and advances in the cultivation of the Middle Way’s outflow-free state, then [one attains] partial..."
The true resolute conviction manifests its perfection; even if one cultivates the adamantine untainted state, then the ultimate resolute conviction manifests its perfection.
These Great Beings all manifest the Buddha-body and preach the sudden Dharma for them, enabling them to attain both partial and ultimate liberation.
Question: Do Bodhisattvas of Equal Enlightenment (Samyaksaṃbuddha-bodhisattva) truly rely upon the manifestation of a Buddha in the First Stage (Prathamābhūmi) to hear the Dharma?

Answer: To attain understanding by hearing the Dharma, why must one necessarily seek out a person? Furthermore, relying upon a superior body further increases internal wisdom. Moreover, even a celestial Māra may manifest as a Buddha image.

Even Maudgalyāyana paid him homage; how much more so would a Bodhisattva at the first stage? That which is manifested through wondrous principle—though Equal Enlightenment (Samyaksambodhi) is honored, who would dare not look up to it?
This teaching refers only to Equal Enlightenment; there is certainly no habitual pride of conceiving oneself superior to those inferior.
If one considers Avalokiteśvara’s initial realization, it seems to be at the first stage; yet for those of the highest faculties in the Perfect and Sudden Teaching, this is indeed the case.

The task of a single lifetime is accomplished; that is to say, from the very first arousal of the mind of awakening (*bodhicitta*), one attains perfect enlightenment and gradually manifests great functions.

How could this be restricted definitively to the first stage (*prathamā-bhūmi*) alone? There is no reason to doubt that he preaches the Dharma for those at the stage of Equal Enlightenment (*samyak-saṃbodhi*).
It need not be further explained: he is fundamentally an ancient Buddha, and his liberation is likewise realized in a single kṣaṇa upon entering the path of liberation.
...Furthermore, regarding the second, the Pratyekabuddhas:
if there are those in training who possess tranquil, wondrous clarity, and in whom the supreme, wondrous state is fully manifested, I appear before them in the body of a Pratyekabuddha.
He then preaches the Dharma for them, causing them to attain liberation.

These three sections below are all referred to as "those in training" (śaikṣa), because those in each category are at the stage of cultivation (bhāvanā-mārga), where their merit reaches its peak and they are about to realize entry into the state of "no-more-learning" (aśaikṣa).
The plural particle "zhū" (諸) merely indicates a large number of individuals within a single class.
The following sections are all modeled after this. Wēnlíng says: "As for the Pratyekabuddhas (Solitary Realizers), they appear in worlds where no Buddha is present;

by observing the transformation of phenomena, they personally realize non-arising, and thus they are called 'Solitary Realizers. Delighting in solitary, sublime tranquility and seeking spontaneous wisdom, they are described as 'tranquil, wondrous, and luminous.
One should know that these are not natural-born non-Buddhists (tīrthikas); rather, it is because they have received the Buddha’s Lesser Vehicle [teachings] over many lifetimes."
Regarding the teaching of *vāsanā* (habitual perfuming): one shall pass through seven lifetimes before realizing the stage of *aśaikṣa* (no-more-learning), never exceeding eight lifetimes.
Now, in this seventh lifetime, having emerged in a world without a Buddha, the time for realization has arrived; one suddenly encounters an object and enters realization.
This appears as though one did not pass through the teachings, yet in reality, one was taught over many lifetimes. △ Third, the Pratyekabuddha.
If there are those in training who sever the twelve links of dependent origination, and through the excellence of that severance, the supreme and wondrous nature becomes fully manifest,
I appear before them in the body of a pratyekabuddha and preach the Dharma for them, causing them to attain liberation.
Wenling says: "Pratyekabuddhas are those who receive the Buddha’s teaching and awaken to the Way by contemplating conditions (*pratītyasamutpāda*).

Knowing that delusion regarding the supreme nature arises from the twelve links of dependent origination, they sever them; thus, from the cessation of ignorance (*avidyā*) up to the cessation of sorrow, lamentation, suffering, and affliction."

Thus, when conditions are severed, the supreme nature (śreṣṭha-dhātu) manifests. Because this nature is revealed through the severing of causes and conditions, it is called "the supreme nature upon the severance of conditions.
The "supreme nature" is precisely the nature of the non-arising of causes and conditions; it is likewise but a "converted city" (nirvāṇa as a provisional resting place).
The subsequent section follows this pattern. △ 4. Śrāvakas.
If there are those in training who attain the emptiness of the Four Noble Truths, enter cessation through the path of cultivation, and manifest the perfection of the supreme nature,
I appear before them in the form of a śrāvaka and preach the Dharma for them, causing them to achieve liberation.

Xueli said: "From the three fruits [of the śrotāpanna, sakṛdāgāmin, and anāgāmin] and prior, both the stage of the worthy (śaikṣa) and the stage of the noble (ārya) belong to those still in training (śaikṣa).

Through the sixteen moments of mind of the path of seeing (darśanamārga), one abandons the afflictions belonging to the four truths and realizes the principle of the emptiness of sentient beings; therefore, it is said that 'the emptiness of the four truths is attained.
Following the first fruit, one proceeds to abandon the eighty-one grades of innate afflictions of the three realms, realizing a portion of analytical cessation (pratisaṃkhyā-nirodha) for each grade."
Because it is unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*), it is said that one enters extinction by cultivating the Path. One should seek the Noble Vehicle (*āryayāna*) until completion.

△ Second, one should seek the various realms of existence (*gati*), which are the six ordinary states. This is divided into two parts. First, the various heavens, which are further divided into two. First, the celestial lords (*devendra*), which are further divided into four.
First, Brahmā Deva-king:
if there are sentient beings whose minds awaken clearly regarding desire and who do not transgress the dust of desire, desiring their bodies to be pure, I appear before them.
He manifested in the form of Brahmā King and preached the Dharma for him, causing him to attain liberation.
His mind regarding desire became clear and awakened; he realized that lust is the root cause that invites suffering.
Although desire extends to the five objects of the senses, lust is the foremost among them. This sutra discusses this point alone, for it is a profound and painful admonition.
This liberation is the accomplishment of the definitive relinquishing of desire to be born in the Brahma realm.

Although it possesses both the relinquishing and the seeking, yet to further crave and seek is equivalent to the "accomplishment of the lower" (the *adhobhūmi-siddhi*). Furthermore, that which is practiced as the *prātikṣepa* (rejection/renunciation) is also called liberation (*vimokṣa*).
Guishan says: Regarding the speaker of the Dharma, as stated in the *Suvarṇaprabhāsa-sūtra*, the Great Brahmā King spoke [thus].
This is the Discourse on Transcending Desire. △ Second, regarding the Śakra-devendra:
if there are sentient beings who desire to become a celestial lord to rule over the various heavens, I shall appear before them in the form of Śakra-devendra.
And he preached the Dharma for them, causing them to achieve accomplishment.
Gushan said: "Śakra is the second Lord of the Heaven of the Desire Realm. That heaven is horizontally divided into thirty-three heavens, over which Śakra presides.
'Preaching the Dharma' refers to the ten wholesome paths of action (*daśakuśala*). The *Suvarṇaprabhāsa-sūtra* states: 'Śakradevendra...'"
It is because of various excellent discourses. △ Third, regarding Īśvara:

if there are sentient beings who desire to travel freely through the ten directions with mastery over their bodies, I appear before them in the form of Īśvara and preach the Dharma for them, enabling them to achieve their goal.
Gushan said: "The Heaven of Sovereign Power (*Īśvara*) is the highest heaven of the Desire Realm. Its full name is *Vaśavartin*, which means 'Sovereign over Others' Transformations.
This refers to the Māra King, who achieves his own pleasure by making use of what others have produced.

Alternatively, it is said that there is a separate dwelling for the Māra King above the six heavens, which is also subsumed under the Heaven of Sovereign Power. [The text continues: "The body of desire itself..."
"Those who dwell here" indicates that these are merely the primary retributions (vipāka) according to their wishes; the following sections apply this principle.

"Wandering through the ten directions" refers to the ten directions of the six desire heavens and the four continents; alternatively, they may also reach other realms, though it is unlikely they could travel as far as the form-realm heavens.
This allows for a general interpretation across all cases. △ Mastery over the Four Great Elements.
If there are sentient beings who desire bodily mastery to fly through the void,
I appear before them in the form of Maheśvara and preach the Dharma for them, enabling them to achieve their goal.
Gushan said: "Mahādeva is the Māheśvara Heaven at the summit of the realm of form (*rūpadhātu*).

As the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* states, he has three eyes and eight arms, rides a white ox, and holds a white fly-whisk; this is him. Regarding his 'flying through the void' and being able to reach other realms, it is as the *Lotus Sūtra* says:
'He can pass over five hundred million *koṭi* of lands,' which refers to his seeking out and making offerings to the Buddhas."

If even those in the first dhyāna are capable, how much more so those at the peak of the form realm? Furthermore, when discussing the various heavens in general, one often cites a single example to encompass the rest.
While the Brahmā King appears to be restricted to the first dhyāna, he actually encompasses all four;

Śakra appears to be restricted to the two heavens of desire, yet he actually encompasses all six. The two types of Māras are mentioned separately because the two Māras do not reside within the formal heavens.

It belongs [to the category of those who do not appear]. Therefore, it is mentioned again. However, the four formless attainments (*ārūpya-samāpatti*) are omitted; this may be because they were implied but the text was abbreviated.
As for the reason why both this treatise and the *Lotus Sūtra* omit them: this treatise manifests a physical body, whereas the four formless realms do not delight in bodily forms;

therefore, [the Buddha] does not manifest there. Even if there were others [in those realms], he would benefit them through skillful means (*upāya*), yet they likewise would not enter this manifestation of a physical body.
This is an example thereof. The section on the Celestial Lords is concluded. △ Second, the Celestial Ministers, divided into three parts. First, the High Generals:

If there are sentient beings who love to govern spirits and ghosts to protect their lands, I shall manifest before them in the body of a Great Celestial General and preach the Dharma for them, causing them to achieve success.
This refers to the four heavenly kings, each of whom has eight generals with Vajrapāṇi as their chief.
Each commands his own retinue of spirits, namely those belonging to the Eight Classes of Beings (*aṣṭa-nikāya*). "Protecting the land" specifically refers to the human realm;
thus, they subdue demons and protect living beings. △ Second, the Four Heavenly Kings.
If there are sentient beings who desire to govern the world and protect its inhabitants,
I appear before them in the form of a Four Heavenly King and preach the Dharma for them, enabling them to achieve their aims.
The Four Kings ought logically to be categorized among the celestial lords; yet, in this text, they are listed after the generals, and thus belong to the class of ministers.
Furthermore, it has long been established that the Four Kings are subordinate to Śakra as his great ministers, each presiding over one of the four continents;
regarding other heavens, high or low, no such distinction between sovereign and minister is heard of. As for the world, it refers to all the lands on each side of Mount Sumeru.
...and so forth. △ Third, regarding the Prince:

If there are sentient beings who desire to be born in celestial palaces and to command ghosts and spirits, I appear before them in the form of a prince of the realm of the Four Heavenly Kings and preach the Dharma for them, causing them to achieve their goal.
Wenling says: "The princes of the four heavens are of the same class as Nātha; they are able to drive away ghosts and spirits.
According to the *Tongji*, each of the Four Heavenly Kings has ninety-one princes who serve as their messengers;

these are precisely the aforementioned generals and the eight classes of beings (*aṣṭa-kula*). This concludes the section on the various heavens. △ Second, the destinies (*gati*), divided into four parts: first, the worldly man.
This does not yet discuss those who uphold the Buddhist precepts. Furthermore, it is twofold: first, regarding the sovereign of men.
If there are sentient beings who delight in being kings of men, I manifest before them in the body of a king of men and preach the Dharma for them.
"Causing them to achieve [this].

Wēnlíng says: "From the Golden Wheel-turning King down to the 'Scattered Grain' kings, all are kings of men. The 'Scattered Grain' refers to the minor kings of various states scattered throughout the world, as numerous as grains of millet.
Question: Among the common people of the world, there are those who harbor deluded ambitions for the imperial throne.
"Is he a king? Furthermore, why would he need to borrow the body of an emperor to preach the Dharma that accords with his heart's intent? Answer:
"This person must possess virtue and cherish benevolence; unable to bear the chaos of the world, he has made a vow to become a king of the Way in every lifetime."

To govern the state according to principle, the Bodhisattva manifests for them a body that they currently admire, and speaks to them of the causes for being born into noble status as well as the virtues and achievements of emperors and kings, merely to perfume the seeds of their future lives.
This is like practicing the ten wholesome deeds as the cause for becoming a Wheel-Turning King (*cakravartin*).
How could this be teaching the arts of usurpation? One should infer further by extending this same principle.
...them. △ Second, the subjects and citizens. This is divided into four parts. First, the elder:
"If there are sentient beings who love their own clan and lineage and are highly esteemed by the world, before them I manifest the body of an elder."
He then preached the Dharma for them, causing them to achieve realization.
Wenling said: "To be a *śreṣṭhin* (elder) is to possess ten virtues: noble lineage, high rank, great wealth, majestic authority, and profound wisdom."
Advanced in years, pure in conduct, and complete in ritual propriety, he was praised by those above and revered by those below; thus he became the leader of his clan, esteemed by the world.
Observing this, we see that the title "Gṛhapati" (Elder) used in India does not refer merely to advanced age;

rather, it is a designation for a high-ranking official or a member of a great family who also possesses virtue and reputation. Furthermore, it is not a status attainable within one's present life alone.
...Thus it is. △ Second, regarding householders:
If there are sentient beings who delight in discussing names and terminology and dwell in self-purification, I manifest before them in the body of a householder.
Thereupon, they expound the Dharma for them, causing them to achieve realization.

These individuals possess virtue but lack formal rank; they may discourse on the Way and discuss its virtues to serve as teachers and models for others, or they may compose writings and establish their teachings.

To transmit the teachings to future generations is what is called "naming, speech, statutes, and regulations. This includes those like Wang Tong and Shao Yong of this region who remained in seclusion and did not serve in office.
△ Third, the administrative official.
If there are sentient beings who love to govern territories and adjudicate the affairs of states and districts,
I appear before them in the form of a high official and preach the Dharma for them, enabling them to achieve success.
Wenling says: The Three Dukes, Ministers, Governors, and Magistrates are all titled "officials" (*zhāiguān*).
The three categories above seem to be encompassed by the Confucian teachings of this land. △ Fourth, the Artisans (*shùshì*).
If there are sentient beings who delight in various arts and sciences and seek to protect and maintain themselves,
I manifest before them in the body of a Brahmin and preach the Dharma for them, causing them to achieve success.
Wenling says: "Brahman" (婆羅門) is translated here as "Pure Conduct" (淨行). It is one of the four castes.

They are fond of various arts and techniques (*śāstra*), namely the combination of divination and physiognomy, and the calculation of the waxing and waning of celestial bodies. This section merely explains these arts and techniques, yet does not clarify the methods of self-protection;
it refers to those who regulate and preserve the body and lifespan, namely the ranks of physicians. This chapter resembles the medical and divination practices of this region.
These are comprised within the category of miscellaneous arts, such as those exemplified by Guo Pu and Hua Tuo. They were held in the highest esteem in India and belong to eighteen clans.
This concludes the section on worldly men. II. Men and Women Who Follow the Teachings. This refers to those who uphold the precepts. It is divided into two parts:
first, the monastic community; second, [the lay community]. The monastic community is further divided into two: first, bhikṣus.

If there is a man who delights in learning and leaves the household life, upholding the various precepts and regulations, I shall manifest before him in the body of a bhikṣu and preach the Dharma for him,
causing him to achieve fulfillment.
The various Vinayas refer to the precepts ranging from the ten precepts up to the full ordination of two hundred and fifty rules. Second, regarding the bhikṣuṇīs:
if there is a woman who delights in learning and leaves the household life, upholding all the prohibitive precepts, I shall manifest as a bhikṣuṇī before her.
He manifests in bodily form and preaches the Dharma for them, causing them to achieve accomplishment.
Regarding the various precepts, they likewise proceed from the ten precepts to the full ordination (upasaṃpadā) and the five hundred [precepts]. △ Second, the two groups of householders.
This is further divided into two: first, the upāsakas.
If there is a man who delights in upholding the five precepts, I shall manifest before him in the form of an upāsaka and preach the Dharma for him,
enabling him to achieve fulfillment.
Gushan says: *Upāsaka* means "male attendant. One who maintains himself by means of the five precepts is fit to serve as an attendant to the ordained *bhikṣus*. △ Second, the *upāsikā*.
If there is a woman who abides by the five precepts, I will manifest before her in the form of an upāsikā and preach the Dharma for her,
enabling her to achieve accomplishment.
Gushan said: "Upāsikā" means "attendant lady. She also observes the five precepts and is qualified to attend upon bhikṣuṇīs.
This concludes the section on men and women who have received the teachings. Next is the section on women of the Threefold Truth.
If there are women who manage internal affairs and establish themselves as pillars of their households and nations, I appear before them in the form of a queen,
a state lady, a noble consort, or a great matron, and preach the Dharma for them, enabling them to achieve fulfillment.

"Internal governance" (*neizheng*) refers generally to all the duties of a woman. A Confucian text states: "She possesses cultivation within the inner chambers, yet harbors no ambitions beyond their borders.
Hence it is called internal governance. However, the inner chambers are the source of all transformations; therefore, they concern the order or chaos of both the family and the state.
"Family" encompasses those from the rank of Great Officer (*dafu*) downward; "state" encompasses those from the rank of Feudal Lord (*zhuhou*) upward. (From *Gushan*)

It is said: The "Female Ruler" (*nǚzhǔ*) refers to the Empress, the consort of the Son of Heaven, or the Marquis’s Lady (*guófūrén*). As stated in the *Lúnyǔ*: "The wife of a lord of a state is called the 'Lord’s Lady' (*jūnfūrén*).
A "Lady by Appointment" (*mìngfù*) refers to a wife who has attained honor through her husband. An example of a "Great Lady" (*dàjiā*) is Cáo Shìshū’s wife of Fúfēng during the Later Han dynasty;
she was the daughter of Bān Biǎo from the same commandery, named Zhāo, with the courtesy name Huìjī. Emperor Hé summoned her several times.
He entered the palace and was made to serve as a teacher to the Empress and the ladies of noble rank; he was titled "Dajia" (The Great Teacher). [Note: The pronunciation of "jia" is "gu"].
△ Fourth, the category of male and female *kumārabhūta* (Child-Sages), which is further divided into two sections: first, the male *kumārabhūta*.
If there are sentient beings whose male organ is not impaired, I manifest before them in the form of a young boy and preach the Dharma for them,
causing them to achieve accomplishment.
This refers to those who have the resolve to never violate the precept against sexual desire for the rest of their lives. △ Second, regarding young girls:
if there is a maiden who cherishes her own body and does not seek to be violated, I will manifest before her in the form of a young girl.
And he preaches the Dharma for them, causing them to achieve accomplishment.
"Maiden" (kanyā) is also called "virgin" (kumārikā), referring to a girl who has not yet married.
"Delighting in abiding as a maiden" means wishing always to remain a virgin and never to marry. "Not seeking" means having no desire to follow [a husband]. That is to say:
One maintains steadfast integrity; even if subjected to forceful aggression or violence, one vows not to comply.
The section on the mind of aspiration is concluded. △ Second, the mind of weary detachment (*nirveda*).

While the preceding aspiration was the hope for the accomplishment of superior matters, this weary detachment is the lack of delight in one's current station and the desire to escape from it. However, [one should] primarily seek to escape...
Regarding "entering human society": it would be appropriate to ask about other realms, but why instead seek [the path] within the heavenly realm?
The answer is that the human body and mind are suited for the cultivation of the Way and transcendence. Master Pei said: "One can thereby rectify the mind and thoughts to advance toward Bodhi;

only the human way is capable of this. This is correct. It is divided into two parts. First, the eight classes of beings. Mount Gu said: According to the *Pumen pin* (Universal Gate Chapter), this section lacks the *Kinnara*.
Luo-luo (Lūla) refers to the *garuḍa*; it has been abbreviated in the translated text. Now, these seven changes are divided into seven sections:
First, the Heavenly Multitude.
If there are various devas who wish to depart from their celestial status, I manifest a celestial body and preach the Dharma for them, causing them to achieve success.
"Emergence" (chū) is synonymous with "liberation" (tuō). To "accomplish" means to fulfill their aspiration for liberation. This shall be applied to all subsequent instances.
△ Second, the Dragon Hosts:
If there are dragons who desire to emerge from the class of dragons, I manifest in a dragon body and preach the Dharma for them, enabling them to achieve accomplishment.

From here downward lie the seven realms of existence. Although all possess supernatural powers, merit, and authority, they are collectively termed "evil destinies" (durgati) because each is characterized by its own specific suffering and affliction.
For this reason, most wish to escape them and become human beings, hoping thereby to cultivate spiritual progress. Question:

Why do you say one must seek the human realm when it is possible that one might wish to escape [the cycle of birth and death] altogether and enter the stream of the sages? Answer: This applies to those who seek the fruits of the Three Vehicles of sagehood.
This has already been included within the previous section on "Seeking with Aspiration"; it should be categorized under "Seeking the Noble Vehicle" and does not belong here.
△ Third, the Yakṣa Assembly:
If there are yakṣas who delight in delivering their own kind, I shall manifest in the form of a yakṣa before them and preach the Dharma for them.
To cause them to achieve accomplishment;
"to cross over" (du) also means "to be liberated" (tuo). Gushan said: "Yakṣa" here translates as "light and agile. △ Fourth, the Gandharvas:
If there are Gandharvas who desire liberation from their kind, I appear before them in the form of a Gandharva and preach the Dharma for them.
The Dharma causes them to achieve [this].
Guishan said: "Gandharva" is translated here as "Fragrance-Body. In the new translations, it is rendered as "Seeking-Fragrance-Walker.
This is the musical deity of Śakra. △ Fifth, the Asuras.
If there are asuras who desire liberation from their kind, I manifest before them in the body of an asura and preach the Dharma for them,
enabling them to achieve success.
Gushan said: Asura means "not upright," because their women are beautiful while their men are ugly; thus, they are named after the male.
The new translation is *fei-tian* (non-deva), because they are deceitful and lack the conduct of devas. △ Sixth, the Kiṃnaras.
If there are kiṃnaras who desire to be liberated from their kind, I manifest before them in the form of a kiṃnara and preach the Dharma for them,
causing them to achieve success.
Gushan said: The kiṃnara is a being whose form resembles a human but has horns on its head; for this reason, it is called the "Doubtful Deity.
It is the deity of the celestial emperors' string and bamboo music, and is slightly inferior to the gandharva. In the new translations, it is rendered as the "Singing Deity. △ Seventh, the mahoraga.
If there are mahoragas who desire to be liberated from their kind, I manifest before them in the form of a mahoraga and preach the Dharma for them,
causing them to attain accomplishment.
Gushan says: Regarding the mahoragas, Master Kumārajīva calls them "earth-dragons," while Master Sengzhao calls them "great pythons that travel on their bellies.
This concludes the eight classes of beings. △ Second, the non-human hosts, which are further divided into two: first, the human hosts.
If there are sentient beings who delight in being human and aspire to the human state, I manifest in a human body and preach the Dharma for them, enabling them to achieve fulfillment.

These are those among present-day humans who seek to relinquish their bodies only to regain the human form again—those who strive not to lose their human status and cultivate progress life after life. △ Second, the non-human multitudes.
If there are non-humans— whether with form or without form, with perception or without perception— who desire to transcend their own kind,
I shall manifest my body before them all and preach the Dharma for them, enabling them to achieve accomplishment.

Changshui said: "Those with form include those such as the *xiujiu* (omen) and *jingming* (spiritual clarity); those without form include those such as the *kongsan* (empty dispersal) and *xiaochen* (dissolution and sinking);

those with thought include those such as spirits, ghosts, and numinous intelligences; and those without thought include those such as spirits transformed into earth, wood, metal, or stone—all of these are not human beings.
This concludes the detailed enumeration of the wondrous responses. △ Third, the conclusion of the title and the source of its emergence.

This is called the thirty-two kinds of wondrously pure bodies that enter various lands; all are accomplished with mastery through samādhi, the power of non-action, and the subtle efficacy of cultivation through hearing and refinement of what is heard.
This is called the "Explanation of Names. All that follows explains the underlying causes. The mind is like the ocean, while the various bodies are like the patterns on the ocean's surface.
When conditions arise, they appear; yet when they come, they have no point of origin. When conditions cease, they vanish; yet when they depart, they have no place of rest.
Because they are unimpeded and unhindered, they are termed the "Response of Wondrous Purity. This is the wondrous power of non-action.

This is not like the supernormal powers (*abhijñā*) achieved through mental application (*manasikāra*) by those of the Two Vehicles. That which the Bodhisattva realizes is the ocean of great quiescent illumination, serene and unmoving;

objects appear spontaneously in response to conditions, yet from the beginning there is no deliberate action. This is what is called the "unconditioned" (*avyākṛta*) supernormal power. It is also as stated in the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra*:
the power of the roots of goodness of benevolence truly has no coming or going. Regarding "spontaneous accomplishment," it means that there is no...

"It is that which cannot be manifested. Wuxing said: "Regarding the thirty-two manifestations, although they appear and disappear differently when compared with the *Pumen pin* (Universal Gate Chapter), their general substance is the same.
Taken as a whole, they do not exceed the ten realms (*daśadhātu*).
Within these ten realms, both sutras lack the forms of bodhisattvas and hell-beings. Some say this is merely an abbreviation of the Sage’s words; others say..."
Avalokiteśvara is already a Bodhisattva; why then need he further manifest the heavy suffering of the hells as being impossible to cross?

According to the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*, the Wise One fully manifests the body of a Bodhisattva within the realms. Furthermore, based on the *Śāstra*, Bodhisattvas also transform those in the hells.
Thus we know that the ten realms must not be omitted. This concludes the thirty-two manifestations. (20)
The four fearlessnesses (*vaiśāradya*). Furthermore, these are divided into three sections. First, the declaration of receiving compassion and aspiration:

"World-Honored One, because I also, by means of this power of the unconditioned wondrous efficacy of the Vajra Samādhi—cultivated through hearing and practicing what has been heard—share in the same compassion and aspiration as all sentient beings of the six realms throughout the ten directions and the three periods of time, I cause all sentient beings to [rely] upon me..."
The body and mind attain fourteen kinds of fearless merits.

Furthermore, descending to the level of those who look up with compassion and longing, I shall set forth the names of the samādhis and establish that compassion and longing are the foundation of fearlessness.
This belongs to the section on the manifestation of the understanding of names; however, it specifically concerns the six classes of ordinary beings within the ten directions. This is truly because:
The aspirations of those above have not yet been discussed in terms of their difficulties; this is because they seek superior matters during times of peace.

This includes both the Three Sages and the six classes of ordinary beings. However, since the present discourse primarily concerns those in the midst of suffering and hardship, the Three Sages shall be treated briefly here.
This is because those who participate in the Vehicle of the Sages are necessarily of the highest virtue and thus rarely encounter evil calamities. Furthermore, those above—
Even ordinary beings within the realms do not encounter such obstacles; how much less so for the noble ones of the Three Vehicles? Question:
It is said that if the fetters of the fruit still exist, even an Arhat cannot escape them—as in the case of Ānanda’s obstacle regarding lust and Śāriputra’s obstacle regarding ghosts.

How can it be said that they have no obstacles? Answer: Those instances were mostly manifestations and not real; even if they were real, they were few. Now, following the majority of cases, we consider only...
Generally speaking, this is a brief summary of the Three Vehicles. "Causing all those below" refers to the correct attainment of fearlessness.
Regarding "my own body and mind," when a Bodhisattva practices "hearing back" (*pratyāśravaṇa*) to realize their true nature, they realize the entire Dharma-realm;

thus, they are darkly identical with all sentient beings in a single mind, interpenetrating and mutually permeating one another. According to the words of Master Wuxing, the principle of perfect penetration realized by the Bodhisattva pervades everywhere.
"Among the compassionate longing of sentient beings" means that the Bodhisattva resides within the bodies and minds of sentient beings.

"Secondly, 'participating and taking'" means one thereby knows that the ordinary and the sage are constantly in profound union; it is simply a matter of waiting for the response to the invocation, at which point the aid is immediately granted.
Regarding "fearlessness," this refers to sentient beings; specifically, those who encounter calamity are in the midst of terror, yet they receive rescue and attain liberation.

This is precisely fearlessness (*vaiśāradya*). In terms of merit, this refers to the Bodhisattva; saving sentient beings and liberating them from fear is truly the most sublime merit of a Bodhisattva.
II. Enumerating Fearlessness, divided into four parts. First: Fearlessness regarding the eight difficulties (*aṣṭākṣaṇa*), further divided into eight.
First: The difficulty of suffering and affliction.
First, because I do not observe myself by means of an observing subject, I cause those suffering sentient beings of the ten directions who observe my voice to immediately attain liberation.

Although "suffering" (*duḥkha*) and "affliction" (*upāyāsa*) are generally synonymous, it is also appropriate to distinguish them as pertaining respectively to body and mind; that is, suffering torments the body, while affliction disturbs the mind.
Among the eight difficulties (*aṣṭāv akṣaṇāḥ*), this first one serves as the general category, while the following seven are the specific ones.

Since they are already listed individually, what is the purpose of this general heading? The answer is: the individual listings are not exhaustive; all other difficulties are subsumed within this general category.
The first two lines first set forth the underlying cause. Wēnlíng says: "Not [relying on] Guānyīn" means not following the cognitive perceptions that arise from the sensory object of sound.
"Observing with observation" refers to turning back the mechanism of hearing and reflecting inwardly upon one's own nature.
Regarding the phrase "suffering sentient beings," Wúxīng directly equates the sentient beings with the observation of sound, conflating the two.

Regarding the cultivation through hearing: Bodhisattvas who cultivate through hearing do not hear sounds, yet they hear the nature of hearing; sentient beings who cultivate through hearing do not hear the nature, yet they hear sounds.

This is a contradiction. Such an interpretation is entirely incorrect. This is because the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* and the *Śūraṅgama-sūtra* each have their own detailed and abbreviated expositions;
thus, "hearing the sound by turning back" (*pratyāśravaṇa*) is the causal practice of perfect penetration (*pariṣphuṭa-prativedha*). Compassionately saving sentient beings is the fruition.

This is its application. Because the causal practice in the *Lotus Sūtra* is brief while its resultant function is detailed, it lacks a description of "turning the hearing back" (*pratyāśravaṇa*); instead, it adds:
"If sentient beings single-mindedly recite the name, the Bodhisattva immediately perceives their voices, and all attain liberation."

In the *Śūraṅgama-samādhi Sūtra*, the causal practices are detailed while the resultant applications are brief, as indicated at the outset by the passage beginning with "Not from Avalokiteśvara" and so forth;

these points are each explained in full detail. However, when it comes to the discourse on the salvation from suffering, there is a deficiency regarding the invocation of names and the Bodhisattva’s contemplation of those who invoke his name.
You argue that Master Yue must compel sentient beings to also employ the cultivation of hearing (*śruta-vāsanā*).

However, when sentient beings are in the midst of urgent distress, how many among them are habituated to the cultivation of hearing? Even if there were one or two, how could this be called "universal salvation"?

Furthermore, if sentient beings can cultivate the hearing themselves, why wait for Bodhisattvas to rescue them? This argument is not correct; you should simply rely upon the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*.
When sentient beings single-mindedly invoke the name, the Bodhisattva immediately observes their voices and causes them to be liberated.

In the text, the two characters "relying on me" (蒙我) are omitted following the phrase "sentient beings in suffering and affliction. Try reading it by adding these words; you will see for yourself that the intent of the two sutras is identical.
This uses the words of the Buddha to authenticate the words of the Bodhisattva, ensuring there is no discrepancy whatsoever. Hereafter, all cases shall follow this principle.
This is the meaning of the phrase "contemplating the sound" as it is commonly called; do not doubt this. △ Second, the difficulty of being burned by fire:
Second, when knowledge and vision revolve back [to their source], it causes all sentient beings that they even if they enter a great fire, the fire cannot burn them.

Wenling said: "The four elements of the internal and external realms are constantly interacting and responding to one another. Since seeing and cognition belong to the element of fire, when the karma of seeing interacts, one perceives fierce flames.
Now, by knowing that seeing has revolved back into its source, the karma of seeing ceases; therefore, fire cannot burn."

"Even those called 'sentient beings' cannot be burned by fire. Question: When the Bodhisattva’s knowledge and vision revolve back [to their source], how does this relate to sentient beings such that it immediately causes them to escape from fire? Answer:

When the Bodhisattva’s hearing revolves back and is liberated from sound, their seeing also revolves back and is liberated from form. Thus, fire cannot interfere with them. This is because they have realized the ultimate Dharma-realm.

Because his majestic spiritual power (*mahānubhāva*) is immeasurable, those who single-mindedly invoke his name are immediately embraced by the majestic light of his great compassion (*mahākaruṇā*) and shall not fall into the calamity of fire.
It is like entering the shade of a mountain, where the summer heat cannot penetrate; this is surely the residual power of his self-benefit.

Furthermore, it is through the power of compassionate vows that such a thing is possible; there is no room for doubt. Xielü said: "According to the Tiantai interpretation, there are three kinds of fire-disasters:
first, the fire of karmic retribution, which extends from the hells upward to the First Dhyāna Heaven; second, the fire of evil karma, which pervades the Three Realms;
and third, the fire of afflictions, which pervades the Three Vehicles. Since this is the case regarding fire-disasters, all other [calamities] are likewise relinquished."
This is so. If the three fires were to encompass all [beings] universally, then the three types of sages would also have to be included among those to be saved.

Since they were already subsumed within the two characters "all" (一切) in the preceding introductory text, one must understand that this present statement represents a thorough investigation and the ultimate exhaustion of the principle. This is something that cannot be left unknown.
△ Third, the peril of drowning in water.
Third, by observing and listening to the revolving [mantra], it causes all sentient beings who are adrift upon great waters not to be drowned by the water;
the general meaning is the same as that of fire. △ Fourth, the peril of harm from ghosts.
Fourth, by severing delusive thoughts and harboring no intent to kill, one causes all sentient beings to enter the realms of ghosts such that the ghosts cannot harm them.
Since ghosts and spirits take hidden, obscure states as the cause for their perceptions and infliction of harm as the condition for their downfall, the Bodhisattva, in response to this—

When one hears [this name], internally one extinguishes deluded thoughts and externally one eliminates the karma of killing. One thus completely transcends the mental activities of ghosts and spirits.
By the power of this complete transcendence, those who invoke the name can be spared from the harm of ghosts. △ Fifth, the calamity of war.
Fifth, by perfuming the faculty of hearing until it becomes true hearing, the six sense faculties are dissolved and restored, becoming identical with the act of listening to sound.

This can cause sentient beings who are about to be harmed—having their bodies cut into pieces by blades—to perceive those weapons as if they were merely slicing through water or blowing across light; the nature [of the mind] remains unshakable.
"Perfuming the hearing" means that when one turns the hearing back toward its source, the true hearing of original enlightenment internally perfumes the deluded hearing.

"Achieving hearing" means achieving the nature of pure, true hearing. "The six sense-faculties being dissolved and restored" means that as one faculty returns to its source, all six faculties are liberated.
"Hearing sounds in the same way" means that both sound and the nature of hearing are formless dharmas; thus, one does not fear being cut by a blade.
Now, as the six sense-faculties are dissolved and restored, the entire body merges into formlessness, becoming identical with that which hears sound; thus one can cross through the turmoil of war.

As for "like light and water," it is due to the power of samādhi. As for "possessing supernatural powers," it means one can naturally levitate oneself and likewise cause the bodies of others to levitate.
That the sword destroys the body but not the [true] self is like [the case of] Sun... [the rest of the text].

Regarding the virtue of reverence: one’s body becomes like light or water; even if a blade passes over it, there is no injury. This is like the Sixth Patriarch, yet it was solely through the power of his own self-realization.
△ Sixth: The difficulty of being seen by ghosts.
Sixth: When the brilliance of the permeation of hearing pervades the entire Dharma-realm, then all forms of darkness cannot maintain their nature in its entirety.
This enables yakṣas, rākṣasas, kumbhāṇḍas, piśācas, pūtanas, and other such spirits to be unable to see with their eyes even when they draw near to its side.
Gushan says: *Yakṣas* are as previously described. Master Zhao states there are three kinds: first, those on the earth; second, those in the void;
and third, those in heaven. *Rākṣasas* are called "the terrifying. *Kumbhāṇḍas* are ghosts who cause loathing and enchantment.
*Piśācas* are ghosts that devour vital essence. *Pūtanas* are ghosts of feverish diseases. Wenzheng says: "The brilliance of hearing-perfuming illuminates that obscurity."

It is dark; therefore, one cannot see. The first two lines state that when the practice of "hearing back" reaches its ultimate point, the fundamental luminosity is manifested, shining forth to illuminate the Dharma-realm in its entirety.
The next two lines state that the subtle, hidden habitual tendencies and thoughts of ghosts and spirits turn toward darkness and turn their backs on light.
On the contrary, they cannot endure its brilliance. This is like the owl, which sees at night but is blind by day, or the rākṣasa, who cannot see when facing the sun.

The manner in which it awes and subdues sentient beings should be understood according to what was previously explained; the following cases may be understood by analogy. △ Seven: The Suffering of Shackles and Locks.
Seventh: When the nature of sound is completely dissolved and the faculties of seeing and hearing turn back inward, one becomes free from all sensory dust and delusions;
this enables sentient beings so that they cannot be bound by shackles or fetters.

The first phrase signifies the cessation of objects. The second phrase signifies the cessation of the sense faculties. The third phrase doubly supports these two, universally encompassing liberation from bonds and freedom from constraints.
Regarding the passage "It can cause... and below, one should understand it according to the preceding explanation.

Within the section on the universal gate of responsive resonance, those who were freed from shackles and fetters by reciting the Name were not limited to just one person. △ Eighth: Perils from Robbers and Thieves.
Eighth: When the cessation of sound results in perfect hearing, it universally generates the power of compassion, enabling sentient beings to pass through perilous paths unrobbed by thieves.
"Cessation of sound" means liberation from the sensory dust of sound; "perfect hearing" means realizing the nature of the ultimate faculty, which universally integrates all things. However—
When the dust of afflictions is extinguished, there are no longer external enemies;

because the perfect nature causes all things to internally harmonize, one who universally generates the power of compassion can transform those with cruel hearts and poisonous minds into compassionate kin and retinues. As the *Lotus Sūtra* says:

"Recalling the power of Avalokiteśvara, they all immediately give rise to a compassionate heart. This refers to that. The section on being fearless from the eight difficulties is concluded. △ Two, Three.

Regarding the fearlessness toward the three poisons: it was asked, "The eight difficulties manifest as states of suffering; these may be called fearsome. But the three poisons follow the movements of one's own mind—what is there to fear?
Answer: One fears the eight difficulties because they manifest as the fruits of suffering. One fears the three poisons because they inevitably constitute the causes of suffering.
However, this must be said in reference to those who possess faith in cause and effect and thus feel dread; it does not apply to those who act with reckless abandon.
To speak thus to one who lacks faith [is futile]. The *Lotus Sūtra* states:
"If a person has much lustful desire, yet constantly recollects and pays homage to Avalokiteśvara Bodhisattva, they shall immediately be freed from desire; the same applies to anger and delusion.
This is all said in reference to those who know fear and seek liberation. Otherwise, why would they give rise to a mind of constant recollection? [The section] is now divided as follows:
Third: first, the poison of greed.

Ninth: by perfuming the faculty of hearing so that it is detached from sensory objects, one is no longer plundered by forms; this can cause all beings with excessive lust to distance themselves from greedy desire.
Turning the hearing inward to leave behind sensory dust, one becomes utterly detached from form; how then could form ever plunder the family treasure?
This enables one to conform to what was previously described. △ Second, the poison of anger.
Tenth: His pure voice is free from defilement; his faculties and their objects are perfectly interfused, such that there is neither subject nor object.
This enables all sentient beings who harbor anger and resentment to be freed from all hatred.
Sound merely designates the object perceived by the faculty of hearing; it does not yet designate the various faults of the objects of the senses.

Since sound designates both the faults of defilement (*rajas*) and obscuration (*tamas*), when sound is pure and devoid of objects—meaning that although the sound itself is not destroyed, it has already departed from the faults of defilement and obscuration—this is the identity of mind and object (*citta-viṣaya-eka-rasa*).
Alternatively, the character "sound" (*yin*) may be an error for the character "hearing" (*wen*); if so, its meaning would be consistent.

It is understood. Because the faculties (*indriya*) and objects (*viṣaya*) have merged into a single dharma, there is no faculty that can act as the subject, nor is there any object that can act as the counterpart.
That one is able to bring about liberation from anger through this absence of subject and object is because anger arises from opposition and resistance.
Now, because there is neither the adversary nor that which is opposed, anger has no basis to arise. △ Third, the poison of delusion:
Eleventh, as dust is dissolved and clarity turns inward, the dharma-realm, body, and mind are like lapis lazuli—luminous, penetrating, and unobstructed.
This enables all those of dull nature and obstructed character, including the icchantikas, to forever leave behind the darkness of delusion.

Wenling says: "Delusion arises because one is obscured by false objects and shrouded by ignorance (*avidyā*). To dissolve these objects is to be without obscuration; to revolve back toward luminosity is to be without shrouding.
Thus, the external dharma-realm and the internal body and mind become concentrated, pure, and brilliantly penetrating, thereby departing from the darkness of delusion.

To be fully possessed of afflictions of view (*dṛṣṭi-kleśa*) is to be "dark"; to be fully possessed of afflictions of thought (*bhāvanā-kleśa*) is to be "dull"; to be fully possessed of ignorance (*avidyā*) is... [to be] "obscured."
It constitutes an obstruction to one’s nature; *ātyantika* (阿顛迦), which here means "lacking a wholesome mind," is also the most profound form of delusion (*moha*).

Wuxing states: According to the Tiantai interpretation, the three poisons pervade both the internal and external realms. "Internal" refers to the afflictions of views and discursive thought (*dṛṣṭi* and *saṃjñā*); "external" refers to ignorance (*avidyā*).

For those of the Two Vehicles (*śrāvaka* and *pratyekabuddha*), delighting in *nirvāṇa* constitutes greed (*lobha*), loathing *saṃsāra* constitutes hatred (*dveṣa*), and being deluded regarding the Middle Way constitutes delusion (*moha*).

The Bodhisattva extensively seeks the Buddha-dharma and reviles the two vehicles (śrāvaka and pratyekabuddha), for they have not yet realized that the Buddha-nature is entirely comprised of the three poisons.

These profound meanings are fully understood [by the Bodhisattva], yet they are not necessarily the primary intent of this section. The correct meaning relies solely on the explanation provided by the initial heading.
The section on "Fearlessness Regarding the Three Poisons" is concluded. III. Fearlessness Regarding the Two Seekings. Question: Seeking a son...
As for women, what do they fear? The answer is: they fear that their desires will ultimately not be fulfilled.
When a Bodhisattva fulfills their requests, one immediately casts off that fear of non-attainment. This is divided into two parts: first, the request for a son.
Twelfth: Merging his form, he further hears that while remaining unmoved at the site of enlightenment (*bodhimaṇḍa*), he enters into the mundane world without destroying the worlds.
He is able to travel throughout the ten directions to make offerings to Buddhas as numerous as motes of dust, and at the side of each Buddha, he acts as a Prince of the Dharma (*dharmarāja-putra*).
For those sentient beings within the dharma-realm who have no sons and desire a male child, he causes the birth of a son endowed with merit and wisdom.

The first two lines describe the dissolution of delusion and entry into the Real; yet, this One Reality is boundless. The next two lines describe the manifestation of function from within the essence;

thus, the myriad functions are fully revealed, and the Real and the conventional are both complete. The path of the Son is perfected. From "Able to pervade" (*neng bian*) onwards, the text details the matter of his being the Son of the Buddha.
Xie Li says: "Entering into the mundane world without destroying the world" refers to the [Dharmakaya]... *fang* (square/cosmos).
Wisdom is direct, while skillful means belong to the provisional. Because the provisional can manage affairs, it gives rise to the male.

As the *Vimalakīrti-nirdeśa-sūtra* says, "Skillful means is taken as the father"—this is precisely that meaning. Wēnlíng says: "Making offerings to the Buddha suffices for merit; receiving the Dharma suffices for wisdom.
Being able to succeed the Dharma King possesses the way of a son; therefore, it can respond to such a request. [The character] "yóu" (by/through).
Because they are fully endowed with both merit and wisdom, they are able to grant sons possessed of merit and wisdom; this does not occur spontaneously without cause.
II. Seeking a Daughter.

Thirteenth: The six sense organs are perfectly penetrating and clearly illumined without duality, encompassing the worlds of the ten directions; thus one establishes the Great Perfect Mirror-like Emptiness.
The Tathāgatagarbha receives and upholds, without loss, the secret dharma-gates of the Tathāgatas as numerous as motes of dust throughout the ten directions.
It enables those beings within the Dharma-realm who are childless— those who desire a daughter— to give birth to a girl of upright appearance, endowed with merit, gentleness, and compliance,
one whom all love and revere, and possessed of auspicious marks.
The two characters "perfect" (yuán) and "penetrating" (tōng) run through both of the following phrases, while those two phrases in turn run through the two subsequent phrases.

This is because "penetrating" carries the sense of clarity, and thus implies luminous illumination; "perfect" carries the sense of encompassing, and thus implies the inclusion of the realms. Because it is luminously illuminating, the Great Perfect Mirror Wisdom (ādarśa-jñāna) is established.

Because it contains the realms (*dhātu*), it is established as the "Treasury of Emptiness" (*ākāśagarbha*); because it possesses actual wisdom (*jñāna*), it is able to receive and accord with the secret.
"Receiving and acceding" refers to the gentle virtue of the earth (*kūn-yí*); "receiving and accepting" refers to the duties within the inner chambers.
Thus, it can respond to the request for a female. These first three phrases alone differ from the Wēnlíng [commentary], while the remainder all adopts its meaning but omits its wording.
Xueli said: "To establish the Great Perfect Mirror-like Tathāgatagarbha belongs to actual wisdom (*bhūta-jñāna*).

Since actual wisdom accords with principle (*li*), and principle is capable of containing and nurturing, it gives birth to the female. This is the meaning of what the *Vimalakīrtinirdeśa* says: 'The Perfection of Wisdom is the mother of Bodhisattvas.
The second section, on the fearlessness of seeking, is concluded. △ Fourth, the fearlessness of upholding the name. Question: Regarding those who uphold the name...
What is it that is feared when one speaks of fearlessness? The answer is: those who uphold [the name] may fear that their merit is not superior and thus harbor doubt;
or they may encounter one who upholds many names and fear that they cannot equal them—both are signs of fear.
Now, those who uphold the name of the Bodhisattva are completely liberated from these two fears. Furthermore, this is divided into four sections, the first of which is the "Combined" [section].
The merits of the Bodhisattvas of this realm are fourteenfold: within this trichiliocosm, there are ten billion suns and moons;

among those currently dwelling in the world as Dharma Princes, there are sixty-two billion times the number of sands in the Ganges River, who cultivate the Dharma, establish models, and transform sentient beings according to their needs.
The expedient means and wisdom that accord with sentient beings are each different.
This term specifically refers to the three thousand great thousands of worlds, consisting of ten billion suns and moons within the Sahā world-system.
Initially, within the four continents and the six heavens of the desire realm, covered by the first dhyāna, one sun and one moon constitute a small world-system. Of these, there are one thousand...
The world-systems are covered by the second dhyāna; this is called a small chiliocosm. Within it, there are one thousand suns and moons each.

When these small chiliocosms are further accumulated to one thousand, they are covered by the third dhyāna; this is called a medium chiliocosm. Within it, there are likewise one thousand times one thousand suns and moons each.
When these medium chiliocosms are further counted to reach one thousand, they are covered by the fourth dhyāna; this is called a trichiliocosm.

The "Great Trichiliocosm" (Mahāsāhasra-lokadhātu) is so called because it consists of three sets of a thousand worlds. Within it, there are ten billion suns and moons; this is stated as a general figure to indicate its vastness.

This "world" does not refer solely to the human realm, but also includes the heavens. Regarding the phrase "those currently residing," this refers to the Bodhisattvas who, manifesting transformation bodies according to the capacities of beings, dwell together with them to benefit all.
These are the sages—numbering six hundred times the sands of the Ganges—who are known through direct perception (*pratyakṣa*). [This passage] adorns the Bodhisattvas.
There are two kinds of practice for delivering sentient beings: first, practice according to one's own true realization; second, practice according to the expedient means of others.
The current "cultivating the Dharma" line refers to the practice of true realization according to what one has cultivated oneself.

The "accordance with" line refers to the practice of expedient means that benefits others by following their inclinations. △ Second, [the section on] "already perfected, pervasive, and all-encompassing."

By means of the fundamental root of perfect penetration that I have attained, I gave rise to the wondrous gateway of the ear; thereafter, my body and mind became subtle and wondrously all-encompassing, pervading the entire Dharma-realm.
Previously, Ānanda sought an explanation, saying: "Although I have realized that the meanings of 'one' and 'six' are both lost, I have not yet reached [full understanding] because..."
Regarding the fundamental root of perfect penetration, the Bodhisattva now speaks for himself:

"By means of the fundamental root of perfect penetration that I have attained, you can see how the cultivation of the ear-door accords with the specific capacities of beings; it is what should be sought and taught according to their needs. Why wait for a selection among the various methods?

Furthermore, calling it the "fundamental root" clarifies that it is a faculty characterized by excellence in a single direction; calling it the "wondrous door" indicates that it is fully endowed with the power of liberation.

The three subtle excellences of profound and perfect [wisdom]. Manifestations and transformations are without fixed direction; this is the subtle excellence of the body’s capacity for inclusion. Wisdom and compassion are inexhaustible;
this is the subtle excellence of the mind’s capacity for inclusion. Pervading the ten realms, both the environment and its inhabitants are fully present;
this is what is called the "universal pervasion of the Dharma-realm," encompassing the dharma-gates of all sages. △ 3. The first name’s merit is equal to that of all names.
If one can cause sentient beings to uphold my name, their merit shall be exactly equal and no different from that of sixty-two billion Ganges-sands of Dharma-princes who uphold it together with them.
△ Fourth, he further explains the reason why his practice is of equal efficacy:
"World-Honored One, my single name is no different from those many names; it is because I have cultivated this that I have attained true and perfect penetration."
Gushan said: "The Lotus Sūtra also contains such comparisons. Only upon examining the present sūtra does one come to understand its intent.
This is because the beings of this region possess sharp faculties of hearing; thus, those who receive the Way are numerous, and for this reason, the transformation of Avalokiteśvara is preeminent."

Because the faculties of others are dull, those who receive the Way are few; thus, the transformations of the various sages are inferior. Therefore, one should know that although their stages of practice may be equal, they differ according to the capacity of the recipient.
Even the total number of beings as numerous as the sands of the Ganges can be matched by a single Avalokiteśvara alone;

this is why the two merits of reciting the name are exactly equal. Based on what has been said here, it is already implicitly distinguished that [Avalokiteśvara] is the perfect and penetrating one, yet this remains unapparent to those who have not yet understood.
As for this, one should further await Mañjuśrī’s detailed discernment.

Furthermore, his manifest self-assertion—that "only I have attained true perfect penetration"—makes it clear that what the other sages have attained is not the truth. Mañjuśrī’s selection merely serves to reiterate this statement.
This concludes the section on the fearless exposition. III. Conclusion of the Names and Manifestation of Benefits.
This is called the fourteenth power of bestowing fearlessness.

Regarding "bestowing the power of fearlessness upon all sentient beings," the subsequent text states: "The lands of the ten directions, as numerous as motes of dust, are all said to be those upon whom I bestow fearlessness.
"Fully equipped" (bei) means complete. Regarding "the merit is fully equipped for sentient beings," this means that it is not merely that they are liberated from that [fear].
This refers to being free from fear while simultaneously preserving one's merit.

This is because the first eleven sections merely liberate one from fear, whereas the final three sections additionally preserve one's merit; thus it is said so. The fourteen kinds of fearlessness are hereby concluded.
△ Next, the "Three Kinds of Inconceivability" is divided into two sections: first, a general summary of perfect penetration.

World-Honored One, because I have further attained this perfect penetration and realized the unsurpassed Way, I am also able to skillfully attain the four inconceivable, unconditioned, and wondrous virtues.

Although the text generally relies upon the *Perfect Enlightenment* [Samantabhadra] Sūtra, its intent actually summarizes the preceding section on "the manifestation of quiescence. This is consistent with the above.
This corresponds to the lower [classification]. It refers to the perfect penetration (*yuan-tong*) wherein the mind, the Buddha, and sentient beings are non-differentiated in three ways.

However, while the preceding sections all indicate "proceeding from samādhi" and thus still approximate the causal mind, this section indicates "proceeding from the cultivation and realization of the unsurpassed path" and therefore already pertains to the stage of fruition (*phala-bhūmi*).
It appears to be the realm of Equal Enlightenment (*samyak-saṃbodhi*), which is why Wēnlíng frequently explains it in terms of Equal Enlightenment. Hereafter...
This shall now be explained in its entirety. As for the term "inconceivable" (*acintya*), it is a praise of the sublime qualities (*guṇa-lakṣaṇa*);
the qualities listed below are so wondrous as to be beyond thought and so divine as to be beyond comparison.

As for the term "unconditioned sublime virtue" (*anabhisaṃskāra-praṇīta-guṇa*), it is examined to show that these are not produced through volitional effort (*manasikāra*) of conditioned phenomena, but are spontaneously and effortlessly accomplished.
△ Section Two: Categorization by Distinction. This is divided into four parts. First, the inconceivability of the mantra’s single-body form:
that within a single body, many heads, eyes, and arms are manifested, and from those many heads, many mantras can be spoken.
It does not depart from a single body; therefore, it is called the "Mantra of Identical Substance. This is truly inconceivable.
Furthermore, there are three [reasons], the first being that the faculties are not separated.
First, because I first attained this most wondrous mind of hearing, the essence of the mind abandoned its hearing;
seeing, hearing, sensing, and knowing could no longer be separated, becoming a single, perfectly integrated, pure, and precious awakening.
"At the very moment of first attainment" refers to the initial stage within the process of hearing. Regarding the "wondrously wondrous mind of hearing":

it is because when one turns the hearing back toward one's own nature (*svabhāva*), that act of turning the hearing back is *ādikṣaya-bodhi* (initial enlightenment), and the nature of one's own being is *mūla-bodhi* (fundamental enlightenment).
When the initial and the fundamental merge into one, both become wondrous; thus, it is called the "wondrously wondrous mind of hearing. This is the essence of the mind.

"Leaving behind hearing" means that what is heard has been completely exhausted. "Leaving behind" (yi) signifies liberation. This is because, through long practice of "turning back the hearing," one's mind becomes singularly refined and liberated, exhausting the characteristics of the sense-faculties;
hence it is called "leaving behind hearing. The two phrases regarding seeing and hearing mean that when a single faculty returns to its source, all six faculties are liberated.
"Not being partitioned" means that seeing, hearing, and so forth are no longer restricted to their respective original faculties; this is the liberation of the six.
The first is "forgetting. The final two phrases describe, to the utmost, the restoration of the inherently wondrous essence of the single True Dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu*).

To interpenetrate and function reciprocally is called "perfect fusion" (*yuanrong*); to be without obstruction or hindrance is called "purity"; for all phenomena to be fully present is called "precious awakening.
This is indeed the manifestation of quiescent extinction (*śānti*), while simultaneously clarifying the meaning of perfect function and inclusive containment. △ Second, one.
Because my substance embodies manifold functions, I am able to manifest many wondrous forms and preach boundless secret mantras.
Within a single body I manifest many forms; within those many forms I preach boundless mantras. This is truly so.
This is inconceivable. △ Third, a detailed explanation of the manifestation of forms. Wēnlíng says: "The head represents the totality of the six functions;
the arms symbolize the compassion that uplifts and receives; the eyes symbolize the wisdom that illuminates and understands.

Each is filled according to its original number, up to eighty-four thousand, which symbolizes responding universally to sensory objects based on the fundamental six functions and the fundamental wisdom and compassion."
Through diligent effort, one attains great sovereignty; these eleven stages constitute the sublime practice of perfect enlightenment.

Some say that the "eighty-four thousand" merely symbolize the Dharma. How could they possibly be applied to a single body? This is simply an attempt to fathom the Bodhisattva’s realm of perfect penetration with a conceptualizing mind.
Indeed, the body encompasses the ten voids, and lands appear upon the tip of a single hair. That emptiness...
And as for the lands, they are not merely like heads and arms. Those eighty-four thousand heads and arms are no different from a person’s eighty-four thousand pores;
there is nothing extraordinary about them. The words of the Sage encompass both phenomena and principle.
Since these are called "inconceivable virtues," one must not limit their meaning through thought or deliberation. [Eighty-four...]

Since the number one thousand corresponds to the categories of afflictions (*kleśa*), it must also correspond to their remedies; thus, [the Bodhisattva] is fully endowed with eighty-four thousand *dhāraṇī* gates.
However, this wondrous countenance should be able to manifest [them] from the very first stage (*prathamabhūmi*), though perhaps the number of instances may differ.
The Sūtra states that even Śakra can manifest a thousand hands and eyes, yet when considering his fundamental station, he...
