The three abodes of the Perfect [Stage] may be inferred by analogy. They are divided into three parts. First, the full manifestation of manifold forms, which is further divided into three.
First, the many heads:
therein, he may manifest one head, three heads, five heads, seven heads, nine heads, eleven heads, and so forth. Thus...
Up to one hundred and eight heads, a thousand heads, ten thousand heads, and eighty-four thousand *śakara* heads.
Wénlǐng says: *Śakara* means "solid and indestructible. △ Second, the many-armed [forms].
Two arms, four arms, six arms, eight arms, ten arms, twelve arms, fourteen, sixteen, eighteen, twenty,
up to twenty-four; and so on, even unto one hundred and eight arms, a thousand arms, ten thousand arms,
and eighty-four thousand mudrā-arms.
Wenling says: *Mudrā* means "seal" (yin) here; each [deity] possesses its own wondrous seal. △ Third, regarding the many eyes:
two eyes, three eyes, four eyes, nine eyes, and so on, up to one hundred and eight eyes, a thousand eyes, ten thousand eyes, and eighty-four thousand pure jewel-eyes.
It is said that the diamond eye illuminates through worldly toil; this is the function of illuminating the Buddha-dharma.
△ Second, the differentiated protection of living beings:
whether through compassion or majesty, whether through meditative concentration or wisdom, one rescues and protects sentient beings, attaining great mastery.

The aspect of loving-kindness (*maitrī*) is the aspect of joy; the aspect of majestic wrath (*vīrabhadrakopa*) is the aspect of anger; the aspect of meditative concentration (*samādhi*) is the aspect of serene composure;

the aspect of wisdom (*prajñā*) is the aspect of illuminating discernment. Each of the heads, arms, and eyes possesses fourfold distinctions. As for the protection and salvation of sentient beings: through loving-kindness one protects their roots of goodness;
through majesty one rescues them from their evil natures; through concentration one protects them from dullness and distraction; and through wisdom one rescues them from delusion.
This is "sinking" [into non-duality]. One who has attained great mastery does not exert deliberate effort or contrivance; they respond according to what is perceived, never encountering obstruction.
If the physical form can be thus, one may know by analogy that the mantra is likewise so; it too must possess these four kinds of protection. II.
The Inconceivability of the Form-Mantra of a Different Substance. Regarding "a different substance": this refers to which form should be manifested in accordance with the capacity of the recipient.
Thus, he manifests them. Since those who serve as his spiritual counterparts (*gong*) are numerous, the forms he manifests are likewise countless, and for each, he preaches a mantra.

This differs from the previous category [of the thirty-two responses] only in that multiple appearances are manifested within a single body. Question: How does this differ from the thirty-two responses? Answer:

The thirty-two responses either accord with what is sought or respond by assuming a similar form, and then preach [the Dharma]. In contrast, this [manifestation of multiple appearances] involves manifesting various physical characteristics within a single body.

Regarding the Dharma: here, we do not seek it by restricting ourselves to specific categories; rather, we observe what form it should take to preach mantras for protection and deliverance, and then manifest it accordingly.
This is its distinction. It is divided into two parts: first, liberation from the dust of the world through hearing.
Second, by means of my hearing and contemplation, I have emerged from the six sense-objects.
Just as a sound passes through a wall without being obstructed, so too, hearing is the very nature of hearing, and contemplation is the entry into the state of forgetting effort;

when the two characteristics of movement and stillness clearly do not arise, one has emerged from the six sense-objects—the following metaphor makes this clear. △ Second, causing the arising of freedom from fear, which is further divided into three parts. First, individually...
Each form has its own mantra;
therefore, I am skillfully able to manifest each individual form.

By reciting each individual mantra, each individual form is manifested, appearing before each respective capacity as a distinct embodiment. Regarding the recitation of each individual mantra: for each [capacity],...
The bodies and the respective mantras are explained; thus it is shown that distinct forms manifest individually. △ Second, the dual manifestation of protecting living beings:
through their forms and their mantras, they are able to bestow fearlessness upon all sentient beings.
Either he manifests his body to liberate them from fear, or he recites mantras to liberate them from fear. Question:
How does this differ from the fourteen fearlessnesses (*vaiśāradya*)? Answer: The fourteen fearlessnesses merely cause sentient beings to be liberated by themselves through invoking his name;
they do not discuss manifesting forms or reciting mantras. How could these two be conflated? △ Third, the conclusion on the naming.
For this reason, throughout the lands as numerous as motes of dust in the ten directions, all name me the "Bestower of Fearlessness.
That the fame of my gift of fearlessness is heard everywhere across the lands as numerous as motes of dust is because the merit of my saving those from suffering is particularly supreme.
△ Third, the breaking of stinginess and the resulting response of the inconceivable.

Third: By virtue of my cultivation of the fundamental, wondrous, perfect, and penetrating root of purity, all the worlds I visit cause sentient beings to relinquish their bodies and precious treasures to seek my compassion.
Wenling says: When the fundamental root is pure, there is no attachment to anything; therefore, he causes sentient beings to abandon all stinginess and clinging.
As for those who "seek my compassion," he accepts them out of compassion and performs the Buddha-work for them on their behalf.
○ The stingy mind of sentient beings is the most difficult to break; the mind of renunciation is the most difficult to arouse; and the seeking mind cannot be forced.
It is so. That which has been encountered now immediately moves sentient beings to break their stinginess and practice giving at my request;
this is truly brought about by inconceivable majestic spiritual power (*ṛddhi*). Who knows its vast source?

It is simply that because the faculty of hearing (*śrotra-indriya*) has been purified and rendered free from attachment through long-standing practice, it is able to produce such a corresponding resonance. Thus, those who hope for a response from the numinous—how could they seek it elsewhere?
△ Fourth, the inconceivable arising of making offerings to the Buddha. This is divided into two parts. First, by attaining the ultimate:
"I have attained the Buddha-mind and realized the ultimate."
"To attain the Buddha-mind" means to wondrously accord with the pure, perfect, and true mind of all Buddhas.
"To realize the ultimate" means that one has already entered the ocean of wondrous adornment, wherein the inexhaustible treasure-trove of the Buddha-dharma is entirely present before one. II.
Therefore, one extensively makes offerings. Having entered the ocean of wondrous adornment and opened the treasure-trove of the Buddha-dharma, one possesses the immeasurable [qualities].
From within the hands of merit and wisdom, one can produce immeasurable precious treasures; with body and mind, one can exercise immeasurable supernormal powers.

Thus, one is able to generate inexhaustible material and Dharma offerings equal to those of the Buddhas. This is divided into two parts. First: making superior offerings to the Buddhas of the ten directions.
One is able to use various kinds of precious jewels to make offerings to the Tathāgatas of the ten directions.

These various offerings to the Buddhas, as described in the "Chapter on Vows and Practices," include garments, garlands, incense, and lamps, which are as vast as the four oceans and as magnificent as Mount Sumeru.
"Pervading the entirety of empty space and the Dharma-realm," and so forth. △ Second, the section on extending laterally to the six realms of existence. This is further divided into three parts.
First, the general heading and the birth [of beings]:
"Extending laterally to the sentient beings of the six realms throughout the Dharma-realm."

Question: Since all six realms of existence include the three miserable paths (*durgati*), why is it said that one should offer [alms] to them? Answer: The Bodhisattva directly contemplates sentient beings as possessing the wisdom, virtues, and marks of a Tathāgata;
thus, he regards them all with a mind identical to that of a Buddha. Consequently, through the gift of material wealth (*āmiṣadāna*), he enables them to obtain happiness;

through the gift of fearlessness (*abhayadāna*), he enables them to be free from suffering; and through the gift of the Dharma (*dharmadāna*), he enables them to transform their ordinary state into that of a sage.
All with an impartial mind and a sincere heart, they perform these offerings. △ Second, enumerating what should be sought:
seeking a wife, one obtains a wife; seeking a son, one obtains a son; seeking samādhi, one obtains samādhi; seeking long life, one obtains long life.

Wife and children belong to the gift of material wealth (*āmiṣadāna*). This is because a kingdom, a city, a wife, and children are called external wealth, whereas longevity and life itself are called internal wealth.
Meditative concentration (*samādhi*) belongs to the gift of the Dharma (*dharmadāna*), for the teachings subsumed under meditative concentration are vast.
The stages and positions of all Arhats and Bodhisattvas are characterized by longevity;

this does not merely refer to a long life among humans, but extends to the enduring rewards of immortals and devas, all of whom are able to respond to requests and grant them. △ Third, transcending to the ultimate.
In this manner, up to the seeking of great *nirvāṇa* and the attainment of great *nirvāṇa*.
Even the two characters "up to" (*yāvat*) transcend the two aforementioned types of giving—material wealth and the Dharma; those that cannot be fully enumerated are all included therein.
Material giving refers to such things as official rank, gold, silver, and so forth. Giving of the Dharma refers to [teaching] the first fruit, the second fruit, and even the third.
The ten types of worthy ones (*śrāvaka*) and the noble ones (*ārya*), and so forth, are all included herein. Great Nirvāṇa is the ultimate and supreme fruit of the Buddha;

it also contains the sense of a comparative term (*upamā*). As it is said: "If even the supreme and ultimate fruit of the Tathāgata is bestowed upon those who have achieved [the necessary conditions], how much more so worldly wealth and minor fruits?

Provided one prepares oneself with sincere seeking, there is nothing that will not respond. Discussing this in connection with what preceded: although a person of perfect capacity (*paripūrṇa-pudgala*), though...

The initial arousal of the mind and its ultimate fulfillment are essentially no different; yet, regarding the characteristics of their virtues and their spiritual transformations throughout the preceding and succeeding stages, there is indeed a distinction of superiority and inferiority.

Within the text, these appear to be distinguishable. When quiescent extinction manifests before one, being in accord with those above and harmonious with those below, this seems to occur at the first stage (Prathamabhūmi).
Regarding the thirty-two manifestations, he personally exerts himself by appearing in person to preach the Dharma;

furthermore, those for whom he acts as a catalyst all know how to aspire to and weary of [samsara], which is a realm where superior goodness is easily transformed—this seems to be the function of the three stages of worthiness (*tri-piṭaka-śaikṣa*).

Regarding the fourteen fearlessnesses, he is able to rescue the suffering and hardships of ordinary beings through the majesty and numinous power of his name alone; thus, the power of a single name rivals that of many names. This seems to be...

These are the functions of the deities of the Ten Grounds (*daśabhūmi*). Among the four inconceivables, the first three appear to be the marks of the qualities of Equal Enlightenment (*samyaksambodhi*), while the fourth declares that the Buddha-mind is ultimate;
it resembles the realization of the pinnacle of Wondrous Enlightenment (*prajñā-jñāna*). I request that you study this text, for it is not without basis. Question:

Regarding the perfect penetration (*yuan-tong*) of the First Abode (*prathamavihāra*), why does it overlap with such deep stages as even up to Wondrous Enlightenment? Answer: For one of perfect capacity...

The first stage (*bhūmi*) fully possesses the merits of the forty-two stages without exception; it is merely that its scope of transformation is broad or narrow—what is called "possessing the substance but lacking the magnitude.
As it is with the first dwelling (*vihāra*), so it is with every successive stage.

Furthermore, although these three categories are extensive in their textual expression, they generally do not transcend the three kinds of giving, the thirty-two manifestations, and the gift of the Dharma (*dharma-dāna*). [The remaining category is] the fourteen fearlessnesses (*vaiśāradya*).
This is the gift of fearlessness. The four inconceivable [gifts] include both the two [spiritual] gifts and the gift of material wealth (*āmiṣadāna*).

It is truly so that *dāna* (generosity) encompasses all practices. My verbal explanation is now concluded. △ Third, the conclusion and response regarding perfect penetration. This is divided into three parts. First, the formal conclusion of perfect penetration.
The Buddha asked about the perfect penetration of the Way. I entered through the gateway of the ear; by means of the Samādhi of Universal Illumination, my conditioned mind attained mastery.
Through the sign of entering the stream, I attained Samādhi and accomplished Bodhi. This is the foremost method.
From "I have descended" onwards, the complete manifestation of the essence and function of perfect penetration is shown. Regarding "the samādhi of universal illumination":

when the practice of "listening inwardly" reaches completion, one understands the faculties and attains the essence; this is precisely the manifestation of quiescent extinction (*nirvāṇa*). Regarding "the mind of conditions being sovereign":

according to Wēnnǐng, this refers to the attainment of mastery over the mind that responds and transforms in accordance with conditions, which corresponds to the three categories beginning with "response. From "Because of entering" onwards, the initial stages are described in detail.
This concludes the section on cause and effect. Regarding "entering the stream through the signs [of practice] to attain samādhi":
this refers to initially turning the hearing inward to abide in the perfect, tranquil, and non-arising, non-ceasing nature; this constitutes the mind for the causal stage (*hetu-bhūmi*).

"Accomplishing Bodhi" refers to subsequently perfecting the cultivation and realization of the fruition stage (*phala-bhūmi*). The final phrase concludes its supreme excellence. To examine this in detail, all the sages are called "the foremost."
These are merely what each honored one has attained; they are not the true, supreme [attainment]. These are, rather, truths relative to specific capacities.
As for that which Mañjuśrī called "perfect penetration surpassing all others," Avalokiteśvara is the foremost. This is indeed the true, supreme [attainment].
△ Second, a supplementary clarification of the bestowal of predictions.
World-Honored One, that Buddha-Tathāgata praised me for having well attained the Dharma-gate of Perfect Penetration, and in the midst of the great assembly,
he conferred upon me the prophecy of the name Avalokiteśvara.

That Buddha-Tathāgata is none other than Avalokiteśvara Tathāgata. As for the bestowing of a prediction upon those who have attained the name "Good" (Kṣema), it is to praise the harmonious union of teacher and disciple in the Way.

Furthermore, this is a prediction regarding the cause rather than a prediction regarding the fruit; it should pertain to the time when one first realizes the stage of the First Abode (*prathamabhūmi*).

If they enter the stages above that, up to the level of Equal Enlightenment (*samyaksambodhi*), they shall receive a prediction regarding the fruit, at which time their names as Buddhas will be revealed.

Wuxing said: "According to the *Avalokiteśvara-samādhi-sūtra* and the *Mahākaruṇā-sūtra*, it is stated that this Bodhisattva attained Buddhahood long ago in the past, with the name *Saddharmaprabhāsa*.

Furthermore, the *Karunāpuṇḍarīka-sūtra* states that in the past, the Tathāgata Ratnagarbha bestowed a prediction upon Prince Animiṣa, naming him Avalokiteśvara. Thus, the *Karunāpuṇḍarīka* and the present sūtra [differ]."
These are all merely names for the concealed origin and the manifested trace. Now that he has attained perfect penetration, he is indeed the later incarnation of the Prince.
Since he manifests as being at the stage of a cause, it does not hinder his sequential demonstration of the stages of cultivation and realization. Part Three:
Further Description of His Name and Title.
Because I observe and listen to the perfect clarity throughout the ten directions, the name "Avalokiteśvara" pervades the worlds of the ten directions.

This further description of his name serves two purposes: first, it indicates that the person and the dharma share the same name and possess no second title, showing that the name and reality correspond perfectly;
second, it indicates that because his perfect penetration is all-pervasive, his reputation and fame are likewise pervasive, thereby manifesting the dharma.
This refers to the excellence of the gates. When the great assembly had each finished their discourse, △ Third, the Buddha manifests auspicious signs.

Since the various sages have each described their perfect penetration (*yuan-tong*), all the doors of the flowered mansion have been opened; therefore, the Buddha again responds with auspicious signs.

While these sages have manifested through words, the Tathāgata manifests through physical marks (*lakṣaṇa*). He desires that sentient beings, by relying on the words and contemplating the marks, [attain realization].

This is the section on "Awakening. It is divided into three parts. First, the general characteristics of perfect penetration (*yuantong*). Now, as for the principle of perfect penetration, self and other mutually penetrate one another;
this is true not only in the state of fruition, but also in the state of cause. Therefore, the Buddhas are used here to represent fruition.
The various sages manifest the cause; their radiance flows into one another, revealing the mutual penetration of the causes and effects of self and others.
Although they universally respond to all sages, in reality, this mutual penetration is equal and wondrous, yet it is the faculty of hearing that alone is made manifest.

If one can truly contemplate the perfect and wondrous nature of the faculty of hearing, who would not be fundamentally and mutually penetrating? One may thus believe that cause and effect are of one suchness. Furthermore, [it is] divided...
There are two [aspects]. First, the auspicious sign of his own penetration of the causes and effects of others.

At that time, from his five limbs while seated upon the lion throne, the World-Honored One simultaneously emitted precious light, which reached far to moisten the crowns of the heads of the Tathāgatas as numerous as motes of dust throughout the ten directions, as well as the various Bodhisattvas who are Dharma Princes.
The five limbs all emit precious light, symbolizing that the entire body has been fully revealed.
"Irrigating the Buddhas" means that one’s own fruition penetrates the fruition of others. "Irrigating the Sages" means that one’s own cause penetrates the cause of others.
However, the act of "consecrating the crown" (abhiṣeka) alone symbolizes that this principle of perfect penetration is the most extraordinary and unsurpassed Dharma. △ Second, by...
He thoroughly realized his own causes and effects;
those Tathāgatas likewise emitted precious light from their five limbs, which came from every direction, as subtle as motes of dust, to drench the crown of the Buddha’s head.
He also sprinkled [the water] upon all the great Bodhisattvas and Arhats in the assembly, so that they might transcend others and realize themselves;
their intent can be understood from this. △ Second, manifesting the specific characteristics of perfect penetration, divided into four parts.
First, the subtle and wonderful auspicious signs of sound and form.
The forest trees and ponds all emit the sound of the Dharma; their interlacing lights form a lattice like a net of precious threads.
Wēnlíng says: "Once perfect penetration (*yúntōng*) manifests before one, then every sound is the Buddha’s voice and every form is the Buddha’s color;
there is nothing that is not a point of awakening entry, and nothing that is not the principle of perfect penetration. △ Second, Awakening and Realization.
This auspicious sign was in accord with the occasion.
This great assembly attained what they had never experienced before; everyone universally obtained the Vajra-samādhi.
The first two phrases, "rejoiced," signify the realization of the meaning. This is because they had previously heard the words and now, furthermore, behold the signs.
Because they mutually clarify one another, one attains thorough awakening with supreme joy. The following two phrases refer to that which is realized.
"No further arising or ceasing" may be likened to a vajra; the nature of perfect penetration now manifests before one, which is precisely the perfectly profound, non-arising, and non-ceasing nature.
Just as a vajra cannot be destroyed, those who abide in and maintain this nature are therefore called "Vajras."
The *Sūramgama-samādhi* (Vajra Samādhi) is that which accords with and does not oppose what has been realized. △ Third, the wondrous adornment of the auspicious signs of practice and wisdom:
At that moment, there rained down from the heavens lotus flowers made of a hundred jewels—blue, yellow, red, and white—intermingled and variegated throughout the empty space of the ten directions.
It is formed of the colors of the seven treasures, with the various hues of the petals representing *caryā* (conduct). The jewels possess radiance, which represents *jñāna* (wisdom).
Thus, the first four lines are the auspicious omen of the flourishing of the myriad practices; the final two lines are the auspicious omen of the sublime adornment of all wisdoms. △
The four marks of existence merged into a single auspicious sign:
in this Sahā world-system, the great earth, mountains, and rivers all simultaneously vanished, and only the lands of the ten directions, as numerous as motes of dust,
were seen to merge into a single realm.
The first three phrases represent the mutual fusion of all phenomena (*dharmas*). The latter three phrases represent the ultimate realization of the single nature.
△ Third, showing the joy of the Dharma of perfect penetration.
The chanting of *brahmā* hymns and songs unfolds spontaneously.

This section certainly demonstrates that sentient beings will inevitably attain the Dharma-joy of perfect penetration (*yuan-tong*). However, one must generally trace back to the specific characteristics mentioned above:
first, one understands that sound and form are entirely the mind; next, one awakens to and realizes the ground of practice (*yin-di*); and finally, one truly engages in cultivation.
Wisdom is the ultimate ocean of fruition. Thus, one celebrates that sentient beings will surely obtain complete benefit.
The performance of *brahman* chants most fully expresses the inexhaustibility of the joy of the Dharma. After the Buddha had commanded the various sages to each expound one section, he finished.
II. The Buddha commands Mañjuśrī to select [the assembly]. He specifically appointed Mañjuśrī for two reasons: first, regarding the original site of the Vajra Seat...

This is the Great Wisdom, the Dharma-eye of all assemblies. Since both [the Buddha] and Avalokiteśvara attained realization through this, I have selected this sublime gate and entrusted it specifically to you.
However, there are two reasons why it was necessary to select this particular one.

First, although the Buddha previously instructed that one should enter deeply through a single gate, he did not ultimately specify which gate; furthermore, since all gates are now presented together, it is only logical that a decision be made.

Section on Determining the Single Gate: Although the preceding text slightly alluded to it, it was never explicitly taught. Now, one must provide a definitive analysis to clearly identify the faculty of the ear.
Second, as for why the other sages did not correspond to this faculty and wisdom, while Avalokiteśvara uniquely accords with the specific capacity [of beings]:

were it not for this single discernment, these points could not be fully revealed. This is nothing other than the desire to cause those who are currently receptive to the teaching to attain realization.
Furthermore, setting aside all other gates, one takes up only the gate of the ear. This is divided into two parts: first, the Tathāgata’s command for selection;
and second, first showing the equality of various explanations. This [second part] is further divided into three: first, instructing one to contemplate the various sages who teach.
Thereupon, the Tathāgata addressed Mañjuśrī, the Dharma Prince: "Observe now these twenty-five great Bodhisattvas and Arhats who are beyond further training."
The Bodhisattva is designated as one beyond training (*aśaikṣa*). Because the practice of the perfected person is identical to non-practice, it is said to manifest before one.
First the number is indicated, and subsequently the categories are classified. Second, he secondly demonstrates the perfect penetration that has been explained.
Each [of the patriarchs] spoke of their initial expedient means for attaining the Way, all claiming they had cultivated true and perfect penetration (*yuan-tong*).
What each school cultivates and realizes is uniformly termed an "expedient means" and "the real. △ Third, the correct elucidation of equality and lack of distinction.
In their practice, there is truly no distinction of superiority or inferiority, nor of priority or posteriority.

Regarding the absence of distinctions between superiority and inferiority, there are two interpretations. First, if one considers only the ultimate attainment reached, it is perfectly penetrating and non-dual.
This is like the gates through which one enters; there are indeed differences in skill or clumsiness, and speed or slowness, yet once the destination is reached, all are equal.
This is the principle that the thousand paths and nine thoroughfares lead to no other than the royal city.

Second, if one examines the intent of the Buddha’s words in detail—since he stated that the practices of those [beings] are in reality without superiority or inferiority—it seems to specifically manifest what they have cultivated.
These gates are likewise each equal. Based on this, there are further many implications: first, the distant causes of all sages are scattered throughout the ten directions;
as they accord with the suitability of each region and the faculties of those therein, how could any of these not be wondrous gates?
Second, each has many lifetimes of cultivation and habituation; by following their respective spiritual dispositions (*gotra*), how could it be difficult to enter? Third, each has many...
The afflictions are categorized according to their appropriate antidotes; like medicine administered to a specific ailment, they yield swift efficacy.

Not only does one benefit from the excellence of the medicine, but one may even attain immortality. If, furthermore, the Buddha’s majestic spiritual power is added, then as one engages with worldly toil, every single aspect becomes a sublime cultivation.
Therefore, there is truly no difference in the cultivation of the various sages. (Observe this: even the Buddha did not permit that there be superiority in cultivation.)

"Inferior! How could you allow for differences within perfect penetration? This means that all sages are undoubtedly identical in the single Perfect Vehicle (yuan-sheng). Yet, Master Yue was unable to forget his own minor traces and arbitrarily gave rise to attachments; thus, the annotations provided in the previous fascicle and in this section [are as follows]."

Disregarding the Buddha’s intent, you are intent on establishing your own doctrines. You have openly defied the Buddha’s words; this is no small transgression. Have you not considered that at the assembly of the *Śūraṅgama Sūtra*, the provisional vehicles were expressly disparaged and suppressed in order to establish the Great Vehicle of the Perfect Teaching? If one were truly of the Two Vehicles, how would they dare to participate therein?

Samantabhadra, Avalokiteśvara, and others have all described their realization of perfect penetration (*yuan-tong*). Specifically, because these sages manifested birth following the Buddha, their traces were naturally categorized as minor. However, since the *Lotus Sūtra* appeared later, their fundamental and manifested states (*ben-ji*) have already been clarified;
why then persist in rigid adherence [to one view]? II. The Intent of Selecting Those Who Appeared Later. Since it is said that [all are] equal, why is there a need for further selection?
Nevertheless, there is a profound meaning, which will be presented here. This is further divided into three parts: first, the desire to accord with the specific capacities of the audience.
I now wish to cause Ānanda to attain awakening through twenty-five modes of practice.

As for which of these corresponds to one's faculties—this refers precisely to matching the teaching to the capacity of the individual—the state of realization is certainly equal for all; yet, regarding the gateways through which one enters, how could they not correspond to the specific capacities of those in this region?
And how could they not be entirely suitable for constant cultivation and study? Nevertheless, one must cultivate them constantly in accordance with one's capacity.
One should simply take from a single gate; therefore, one must not fail to select [the appropriate one] so that Ānanda may focus exclusively on it.
△ Second, the desire to establish a model for future generations.

Furthermore, after my parinirvāṇa, the sentient beings of this world who enter the Bodhisattva Vehicle and seek the Unsurpassed Way—these post-parinirvāṇa beings are none other than those of my own lineage.
The Bodhisattva Vehicle is the true cause; the Unsurpassed Way is the ultimate fruit.
△ Third, the question: through which gate is it easiest to achieve success?
By what skillful means can [enlightenment] be easily accomplished?

It is difficult if one does not encounter the appropriate capacity (*tāyin*), but it is easy if one encounters the appropriate capacity. Therefore, this concludes the section on the gateway of encountering the appropriate capacity;

"interrogation" (*kṣepa*) here carries the sense of causing one to make a selection. **2. Mañjuśrī’s Verses in Response.** This is divided into two parts: 1. Describing the Ritual and Indicating the Verses.
Mañjuśrī, the Dharma Prince, receiving the Buddha’s compassionate command, immediately rose from his seat, prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, and,
sustained by the Buddha’s majestic spiritual power, spoke these verses in response to the Buddha:
This prostration is the standard protocol for respectfully following the instructions of one’s teacher; furthermore, it is performed in order to seek their empowerment.

The subsequent section clarifies how one invokes their majestic spiritual power. Although this concerns a Great Being who has already attained the fruit of realization, such is the manner in which the ritual protocols are manifested.

This is sufficient to serve as a warning to those who flow with the current of self-conceit (*māna*). △ Second, the detailed exposition of the verse text, divided into six parts. First, the source of the arising and the opening of the selection, further divided into three.
First, the dual demonstration of the two sources, further divided into two. First, the true source upon which [the teaching] relies.
The nature of the ocean of awakening is clear and perfect; the clarity and perfection of awakening are fundamentally wondrous. Regarding "the nature of the ocean of awakening":

the two characters "ocean of awakening" (jue-hai) manifest the essential substance and magnitude of this nature. For nature takes cognitive awareness as its substance and profundity and vastness as its magnitude;

hence it is called "the nature of the ocean of awakening. As for the two characters "ocean of awakening," they— [Note: The provided source text ends abruptly. The translation reflects the available portion.]
There are two interpretations. First, both the literal meaning and the metaphor are presented together to reveal the profundity and vastness of original enlightenment (*prakṛti-bodhi*).

This is what the Master of Wuxing meant when he said, "The nature of true awakening is like the great ocean. Second, the awakened nature itself is directly called an "ocean," rather than being taken as a metaphor for the physical sea of water.
This is because anything possessing a measure of profundity and vastness is termed an "ocean," such as in the case of the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra*.
This refers to what is called the ocean of lands, the ocean of kalpas, and so forth. If one insists on using the ocean of water as a metaphor, it still falls into the error of being imperfect;
for the ocean of awakening is boundless horizontally and bottomless vertically, unlike the ocean of water which still has a limit and a bottom.

The latter explanation is superior. The two characters "clear" (chéng) and "perfect" (yuán) directly express the meaning and characteristics of the ocean of awakening. Do not rely on [the interpretation of] Wu.
To explain that "clarity" (*cheng*) signifies "stillness" (*ji*) and "perfection" (*yuan*) signifies "illumination" (*zhao*) is not at all consistent with the meaning. Clarity is precisely stillness;

it refers to being clear, settled, and profoundly tranquil, devoid of all arising and ceasing. Perfection is precisely illumination; it refers to being perfectly integrated and penetratingly reflective, devoid of all partiality or obscuration.
The first three characters of the second line refer back to the preceding text, while the final two characters clarify that [the nature] is originally perfect.
"Penetration" (*tong*) means the fundamental source (*ben*). "Subtlety" (*miao*) refers to the wondrous function of perfect penetration.

It is perfectly complete and fundamentally without deficiency; it is universally harmonious and fundamentally without contradiction. Generally speaking, "the ocean of enlightenment" points to the essence (*ti*);

this phrase roughly indicates the greatness of the essence. "Clarity and perfection" points to the characteristics (*xiang*); this phrase roughly indicates the greatness of the characteristics. "Fundamental subtlety" points to the function (*yong*); this phrase...
It is as if they were designated as "Great. These three Greats serve as the basis for all delusions;
therefore, the topical outline (ke) refers to them as "the True Source as the Basis. △ Second, the Delusive Source as the Dependent.
The primordial luminosity gives rise to the object; once the object is established, the nature of illumination perishes. Zhenji said:

"Upon that primordial luminous nature, one falsely gives rise to the function of illumination, thereby forming the characteristics of the object. When there is a corresponding object, the nature manifests;
when there is no object, it is hidden. Therefore, the nature of illumination perishes. [This is because] upon the primordial luminous nature, one falsely gives rise to the function of illumination.

This refers to what was previously stated in the sutra: "The nature of awakening is necessarily luminous, yet through delusion it becomes the 'luminous awakening' (ming-jue), thereby manifesting as that which is characterized.

This means that awakening itself is not the object of illumination; rather, because there is illumination, an object is established. That which has characteristics appears before the mind, while that which is without characteristics remains hidden.
Just as when clouds arise they must obscure the sun. The first phrase resembles what Yongjia said: "If one looks back, it again becomes subject and object.
The final phrase resembles the idea that if subsequent cognition arises, prior cognition has already ceased. Question:
Since the object has been falsely established, why does it not give rise to your false subject? Answer: Whenever a single layer of delusion arises, it possesses two functions.
The first [function] is the ability to conceal and cover; the second is the ability to give rise to. The present verse precisely expresses concealment, whereas the preceding sutra clarifies arising.
Both meanings are fully present; the preceding and succeeding passages merely reflect and manifest one another. However, the general intent is roughly the same as that of Yongjia.
Inferring from this to the beginningless past, although it is not complete, it accords with the "mind of Chan" described by Yongjia.
The underlying intent is reached from afar; thus, it may be analogously understood. This also demonstrates that the Patriarch’s meaning accords with the *Sūtras*.
Furthermore, these two instances of "illumination" arise first and perish later; both belong to the delusory. One cannot claim that the latter illumination is true. It is as Yongjia said:
"Since the two cognitions do not coexist, one merely attains the cessation of the prior cognition. At the place of cessation..."

They serve as the objects of cognition; both subject and object are equally not the Truth. Furthermore, this arising and ceasing arises based on the aforementioned Truth and serves as the source of the myriad dharmas;

therefore, it is categorized as the "source of delusion. II. Briefly Revealing Arising and Ceasing. This refers to the coarse arising and ceasing of the myriad dharmas, not the subtle arising and ceasing of the aforementioned ignorance.
Following upon the preceding discussion of the union of Truth and Delusion, the text then speaks of the dense array of myriad phenomena.
It is complete. This is divided into two parts. First, the arising of the ten thousand dharmas:
from delusion comes space; based on space, the world is established; from the clarification of thought, the land is formed; and from cognition, sentient beings arise.
The first phrase refers to what was stated at the beginning of the sutra: "Obscuration and darkness become space. It means that space first manifests based directly upon ignorance (*avidyā*).
The second phrase refers to "within the obscurity of space, one binds darkness into form. The third phrase refers to what Wēn-líng described:
"Delusive thoughts coalesce to form the insentient realm of land. The fourth phrase refers to what he called "delusive consciousness" (*vikalpa-vijñāna*).
Consciousness constitutes sentient beings. The first two lines manifest the realm of space; the latter two lines concern the accomplishment of the environment and its inhabitants.

△ Second, the cessation and return of the ten thousand dharmas. Question: Since the arising [of phenomena] is only clearly manifested through the inquiry [into their origin], why do you suddenly speak of cessation and return?
Answer: Cessation and return is precisely the returning to the source. Now, by selecting the faculties for deep penetration, one is correctly planning to return to the source.
Therefore, I shall fully demonstrate that arising is illusory and cessation is easy, thereby initiating this discourse. This is divided into two parts.
First, I shall first manifest inferior delusion:
"Within the great awakening, emptiness arises like a single bubble emerging from the sea; the minute dust-like lands of the outflowing world all depend upon emptiness for their birth."
It is vast and without exterior; it can contain all dust-motes and buddha-lands with ample room to spare.

Fundamentally not minute or inferior, yet when compared to Great Awakening, it is immeasurably greater. It is like a single bubble in the ocean, whereby space itself becomes exceedingly minute and inferior.
Regarding "with outflows" (*sāsrava*), according to Wuxing, this refers to both [the environment] and sentient beings. This further explains "with outflows."
Even the lands of the dust-motes arise dependent upon space and do not exist outside of space; thus, one sees all the more clearly their insignificance and their falsity.
△ Second, the subsequent explanation of sudden extinction:
"When the bubble is extinguished, space itself is fundamentally non-existent; how much more so, then, are the various realms of the three worlds?"

Changshui says: Regarding "the bubble extinguishes," it is as the scripture states: "When one person awakens to the truth and returns to the source, the empty space of the ten directions all vanishes.

In this context, "three realms" refers to the three worlds of dust and lands, namely: the realm of desire (*kāmadhātu*), the realm of form (*rūpadhātu*), and the realm of formlessness (*ārūpyadhātu*).
The wondrous principle has no beginning; through delusion, the three realms are formed, like water freezing into ice. Objects...
Yet it does not transform; therefore, it is called "existence" (*bhava*). Furthermore, taking the nine *bhavas* from within [the three realms], one further opens them into twenty-five *bhavas*.

According to Wuxing, this is because they simultaneously encompass both the sentient beings (*sattva*) and the physical world (*bhājana-loka*). Like bubbles in empty space, these exist falsely though originally non-existent within the great ocean of Awakening;
thus, through cessation, they return once more to their original non-existence. As for the three *bhavas*, they likewise abide by sharing the same essence as emptiness.
The perilous matter is one. Thus, even the empty space beyond the boundaries of the world returns to fundamental non-existence;

how much more so the three realms of existence within that space—how could they not be instantly extinguished along with it? This intention expresses that because [the ultimate] is the ultimate void, rapid extinction is possible.
Had it not been void, how could it be forcibly extinguished? △ Third, the proper clarification of the necessity for selection. As stated above, the myriad dharmas can...
By means of cessation and extinction, the path leading back to the source has already been drawn forth; therefore, this section sets forth the reasons for selecting the return to the source.
It is divided into two parts. First: The Equality of All Gateways.
The nature of returning to the source is non-dual; the expedient means have many gates. The holy nature has nothing it does not penetrate;
whether following or reversing [the path], all are expedient means. The first two lines jointly indicate the one and the many:

the first line clarifies that the principle is solely one, while the second line clarifies that the gates are manifold—just as the capital region is a single place, yet there are many diverging paths to enter it. The final two lines merely set forth the many gates.

Question: Since the principle is one, why are there so many gates? Answer: This is because the nature of the Sage is universally harmonious and penetrates all phenomena, just as the main thoroughfare within a celestial ruler’s palace leads to the myriad nations.

Thus, whether entering through the twenty-five gates in forward order or in reverse order, they are all skillful means for entering the principle, just as the thousand paths and nine crossroads all lead to the imperial capital.
Gushan said: "For Avalokiteśvara, the faculty of the ear is 'concordant' (*shun*), whereas for other sages, all faculties are 'inverse' (*ni*).
This is explained in reference to the spiritual capacities of those in this region. Regarding these two terms, "concordant" and "inverse," it is as if one were to say:

that which accords with the capacities of those in this region is "concordant," while that which opposes the capacities of those in this region is "inverse. I, however, maintain that [the ear] follows the flow of sensory objects and consciousness, turning back to reach [enlightenment].

"Entering in accordance with the Way" (*shunru*) refers to the perfect penetration (*yuantong*) of the six objects, the six consciousnesses, and the elements from the fire element up to the consciousness element;
it is like following the road away from the capital to reach a distant region by way of circuitous travel.

"Entering against the grain" (*niru*) refers to turning back and entering the nature by reversing the outward flow of the six faculties and their respective elements; it is like turning back toward the capital.
It is the path that one reaches upon turning back. Observe the various faculties' perfect penetration; the term "revolving back" (*xuánfǎn*) can be seen in each instance.
△ Second, one must select the faculty appropriate to one's own root.
"The beginner enters samādhi; their speed differs according to their class.
"Initial entry" refers to the very first skillful means. "Samādhi" refers to the correct concentration (*samyak-samādhi*) of each respective gate. Regarding the difference in speed:

according to the former [explanation by] Gushan, Avalokiteśvara is swift in accordance with the flow, while the other sages are slow in moving against it. According to the latter explanation, however...

Those who follow the current move slowly; those who go against the current move swiftly. As the Sūtra says: "Between those with complete faculties and those with incomplete faculties, a day and an eon are mutually multiplied.
From this it can be seen that among all the faculties, the ear-faculty (*śrotra-indriya*) is the most swift.
Nevertheless, these two phrases must correctly appear at the beginning because they demonstrate the necessity of selection. An objection may be raised: "If both are merely expedient means, then..."

[The teaching is] equal. Why must there be further selection? [The Master] replied: "How can one avoid it? Regarding the capacities of those in this land, there are those for whom [the teaching] is appropriate and those for whom it is not.
For the appropriate, it is exceedingly swift; for the inappropriate, it is exceedingly slow. How could one not exercise selection? It is like the road to the capital:
there are a thousand variations between circuitous and direct routes; how could all of them be shortcuts? Yet one cannot fail to choose the path before setting out. [Thus he] opened the source.
The selection is complete. △ Second, the thorough examination of various categories. The intent is to cause [the practitioner] to relinquish them. This is divided into four parts.

First, the examination of the six sense-objects (*ṣaḍviṣaya*). These objects are insentient and thus most remote from the mind; furthermore, they possess both the meanings of "obscuration" and "defilement.
Being remote, they are difficult to transform; being obscuring, they are difficult to perfect; being defiled, they are difficult to penetrate. Therefore, they are all rejected and not employed.
This is divided into six parts. First, regarding the sense-object of form (*rūpa-viṣaya*):
form-perception aggregates to form the object; because the essential clarity cannot penetrate it, how could one not lack penetrating clarity? Thus, one attains perfect penetration.
The first phrase states that form relies upon deluded thoughts to form the dust of obscuration.

The second phrase states that if one attempts to penetrate this form with the essence of the mind, it will ultimately not be fully understood. This is because the substance of form is fundamentally composed of the accumulation of darkness.
How could the initial mind possibly comprehend and penetrate this? The final two lines cite and conclude that the initial mind will certainly not rely upon this to attain perfect penetration.
△ Second, the sense-object of sound is said to be partial.
Sounds and mixed speech consist merely of phonemes (*vyañjana*), names (*nāman*), and phrases (*pada*). Since one does not contain all, how can one attain perfect penetration?
"Sound" refers here to direct sound; "speech" refers to indirect sound. The following two lines specifically discuss the indirect.
This is because Ājñātakauṇḍinya entered [the path] through the Four Noble Truths, and thus he exclusively grasped the indirect [method]. "Ī" refers to "that";

as a single character, it is designated as a *nāman* (name), which expresses the intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*). As two characters, they constitute a *pada* (phrase), which expresses specific distinctions (*viśeṣa*).

"Flavor" refers to the meanings and principles contained therein. Since words and sounds have already fallen into the realm of linguistic expression, one can only grasp the flavor of those names and phrases.
Furthermore, while this principle is perfect, its verbal expression is partial; how could a beginner comprehend how a single word universally encompasses all meanings and principles?
Therefore, relying upon it, I fear it would be difficult to attain perfect penetration. △ Third, the sense-object of fragrance is not constant.
Fragrance is known through its conjunction with the nose; when separated, it fundamentally does not exist. Since that which is perceived is not constant, how can one attain perfect penetration?
A beginner practitioner must wait for smoke to meet the nose before perceiving fragrance; once separated, the characteristic of fragrance no longer exists.
Thus, this fragrance is not permanent and cannot cause perception to be constant. If perception is not constant, then the fragrance is likewise not real.
"O Constant One, how could one possibly attain perfect penetration through fragrance? △ Fourth, the objects of taste are not uniform;
the nature of taste is not inherently so. It exists only when there is tasting, and its nature is not constant or singular. How, then, can one attain perfect penetration?"
This is merely a variation in phrasing from the "tangible object" (*spraṣṭavya*) discussed below;
the meaning is identical to that of the "odor object" (*gandha*), as all three are equally known through contact. "Fundamentally so" (*bennian*) means "always so.

The second line states that one must wait for the tongue to taste a flavor before perceiving the tangible object. The final two lines are entirely the same as the preceding section. △ Five: Tangible Objects.

The realm of dust is not fixed; touch is clarified by that which is touched. There is nothing it does not clearly touch. Its nature of joining and separating is not fixed. How can one attain perfect penetration? Touch has no self-characteristic;
it depends dually upon the subject and the object. Internally, it depends on the body-faculty as the agent of touching; externally, it depends on the objects of form.
It is that which is touched. It is only through the medium [of the object] that the characteristic of touch becomes manifest. Now, regarding the statement "to clarify by means of touch":

it is necessary to wait until the object of touch (spraṣṭavya) comes into contact with the body for the characteristic of touch to become clear. The final two phrases are the same as the preceding section.
△ Six: Mental Objects (dharmas) are not pervasive.
The dharma-object (dharmāyatana) is called the internal sense-field (*adhyātma-viṣaya*). Since there must be a basis for the sense-field, there must necessarily be that which possesses it;

yet, subject and object do not pervade one another. How, then, can one attain perfect penetration? The dharma-object is not the substantial reality of the five external sense-fields, but rather their shadows; it is perceived exclusively by the mind alone.
It belongs to the realm of solitary images; hence it is called the "internal object. The phrase "there must be something" means that the mind must be focused exclusively on one place.

For the mental faculty (*manas*) has no duality; when it arises to take an object, it focuses solely on a single sphere. It abandons one only to take up another, remaining singular from beginning to end.

Since both subject and object are thus restricted, how could it possibly engage with everything universally? Because it is not universal, the beginner finds it difficult to enter perfect penetration (*yuan-tong*).
The selection of the six sense objects is complete. △ Second, selecting the five faculties and retaining the faculty of hearing. Therefore, only the five are selected. Question:
Since the faculties are capable of turning back toward their source—that is, the nature—why are they also excluded? Answer:

Although the faculties as a whole are closer to the nature than the objects and consciousnesses, among the six they are not uniform in their completeness. As the preceding text states: "The perfect faculty and the imperfect..."
The sense organs, days, and kalpas increase tenfold respectively. Here, we are specifically excluding those that are combined, superficial, or incomplete;
the intention is to select only the ear organ. This is divided into five parts, the first being: the eye organ is not complete.
Although the seeing-nature is brilliantly clear, it illuminates what is before but not what is behind; half of the four directions are missing. How, then, can one attain perfect penetration?
"Brilliantly clear" (*dòngrán*) conveys the sense of luminous, penetrating illumination. The word "although" (*suī*) is a concessive term. The second line negates its lack of perfection.
The third line specifically demonstrates the extent of that imperfection; though the phrasing is brief, it implies the four directions.
The four corners necessarily include the four cardinal directions; that one speaks only of the four intermediate points (caturvidiś) is a brevity of expression.

Furthermore, regarding the twelve hundred merits, there are eight hundred for the four cardinal directions and four hundred for the four intermediate points. Now, only the [merits of] the rear direction and the four hundred of the two corners are missing;
this is merely a deficiency of one-third. To say that "half is lacking" is a careless way of speaking.
If it were truly half, it would amount to six hundred. It is sufficient for the student to skillfully grasp this meaning.
While a deficiency is difficult to complete, the underlying intent is easy to understand. △ Second, regarding the deficiency of the nose faculty:
The inhalation and exhalation of the breath pass through [the nostrils], yet in the present state, there is no mingling of the airs.

They are fragmented and do not interpenetrate; how, then, can one attain perfect penetration? Regarding the function of the nose: the exhalation, the inhalation, and that which lies between them each consist of four hundred [instants].

Now, only the four hundred instants of the intermediate period are missing. "Mingling of the airs" refers precisely to this intermediate period. "Fragmented" means they do not connect with one another in succession.
This is because when the exhalation is finished, one cannot immediately inhale; there must be a brief interval before inhalation occurs. The same applies to inhalation.
This is precisely where fragmentation arises. For it is through exhalation that one takes up fragrance, and through inhalation that one perceives fragrance.
This fragmented state lacks any functional power; therefore, it is not complete. "Fei" (匪) means "not. "She" (涉) means "to intersect.
"Ru" (入) refers to the nose-faculty (*ghrāṇa-āyatana*). This means: if this faculty is interrupted and does not intersect [with its objects], how could one quickly attain perfect penetration?
This, along with the preceding section, serves to exclude the incomplete faculties. △ Third, the tongue-faculty is not...
"Constantly. The tongue is not an entrance without a source; it gives rise to cognition because of flavors. When flavors cease, cognition has no existence.
How, then, can one attain perfect penetration? Wuxing said: "The first phrase is inverted; it should read, 'The tongue-entrance is not without a source. Wenzheng said: "The tongue..."
To be able to perceive without depending on flavor would be groundless. Now, this is not the case; therefore, it is said that it is not groundless.
The final three phrases state that because there is no constant perception apart from flavor, it is difficult to enter perfect penetration (*yuan-tong*).
Question: It is said that the ear perceives silence when separated from sound, and this is called its permanent nature. Why does the tongue not likewise perceive [silence] when separated from flavor?

"Is it also said that the subtle [element] is permanent? Answer: "The ear is a cognition of separation. It is eternally and universally pervasive. Apart from sound, it is tranquil; yet when compared to sound, its resonance is perfect.
This is easy for people to understand. As the Sūtra says: 'In motion, it reaches both near and far; in stillness, it is without boundary. This is precisely what is meant.
Now, the cognition of the tongue-root that perceives taste does not exceed three inches. Even when in contact with its object, this cognition is inferior; yet its cognition of separation..."

The characteristic of tangibility is even more subtle and obscure; how could it possibly manifest as clearly as the constant nature of hearing? Therefore, this does not serve as a comparable objection.
△ Fourth, the body-faculty does not conjoin [with its object].
The body and its objects of touch are likewise; each is not the contemplation of Perfect Enlightenment (*pariniṣpanna-avabodha*).

Since their boundaries do not merge, how can one attain perfect penetration? The first two phrases follow the example of the preceding sense-object of touch, clarifying that they are equally incomplete gates.
These two characters, "objects of touch" (*spraṣṭavya*), refer directly to the aforementioned sense-object of touch. The meaning is that I have already rejected the former sense-object of touch.
That which is not complete—this present body-faculty—is likewise entirely identical to that object of touch (*spraṣṭavya*). This phrase establishes the definition;

the subsequent phrase demonstrates their commonality. Thus, in "Perfect Enlightenment" (*yuanjue*), the single character "perfect" (*yuan*) penetrates both characters "enlightenment" (*jue*) and "contemplation" (*guan*) simultaneously.
"Perfect Enlightenment" refers to the independent, absolute whole; "Perfect Contemplation" refers to that which is free from all dependence.

This is total wisdom (*sarvajñatā*). This body-faculty and the aforementioned object of touch are each not these two [the whole and total wisdom], for the cognition within their conjunction is manifested through the mutual dependence of faculty and object.
When the aforementioned object of touch is separated from this body-faculty, its characteristics immediately vanish;
thus, it certainly lacks an independent, substantial totality or an absolute, non-dependent total wisdom. And this...

As for the body-faculty (*kāyendriya*), when separated from the preceding object of touch (*spraṣṭavya*), its cognition also vanishes; there is no independent, absolute, and all-encompassing totality of being and wisdom.

How, then, could it possibly engage in perfect awakening and contemplation? Generally speaking, these two phrases collectively clarify that knowledge exists only after [the faculty and its object] are conjoined.
"Limit" (*yāliàng*) refers to a boundary; specifically, it refers to the boundary of the body and the boundary of touch.

"Obscure" (*ming*) means darkness; "to meet" (*hui*) means to know. One who does not "obscurely meet" means that one cannot have knowledge within the darkness at the time of separation, just as the ear has [knowledge] of sound.
This phrase states that there is no cognition during the state of separation.

The final phrase concludes that this is not the perfect penetration (*pariniṣpanna*). This is because it generally involves both presence and absence; thus, it clarifies that perfect penetration is difficult to attain.
This, along with the preceding section which eliminates those who rely on combined knowledge, addresses those of shallow faculties. △ Five: The mental faculty and its discursive thoughts.
"The faculty of cognition (*manas-indriya*) is characterized by chaotic thoughts; though it may reach a state of profound clarity, ultimately there is nothing to be seen.
Since conceptualization cannot be cast off, how can one attain perfect penetration? This passage is easy to understand.

In general, this refers to an ordinary person at the initial stage who wishes to seek perfect penetration by relying on this mental faculty (*manas*), and it serves to sever the difficulty of such attainment. "Chaotic thoughts" refers to the mental consciousness (*mano-vijñāna*). Among all the consciousnesses, only the mind...
Consciousness (*vijñāna*) is most chaotic and most stubborn; it is difficult to subdue because it is constantly intermingled with the mind (*manas*).
"Profound clarity" (*zhanliao*) refers to the state of having completely shed off mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*), a realm of profound and lucid awareness.

As for the statement that "in the end, nothing is seen," it is like entering the "neither-perception-nor-non-perception" concentration (*naivasaṃjñānāsaṃjñāyatana-samādhi*) in the Heaven of Neither-Perception-Nor-Non-Perception: though one investigates and seeks its profound clarity, it can ultimately not be found. This is the retribution.
"Ultimately they all fall"—this is correct. The final two lines conclude that these are not the perfect penetration (*yuan-tong*).

This implies that perfect penetration is originally the supreme fruit of non-discriminative concentration; since one has not yet escaped from conceptual recollection (*xiang-nian*), how could such a fruit be attained?
This section eliminates those whose faculties are not purely detached. The examination of the five faculties is complete. △ Third, the examination of the six consciousnesses. This...
At the very beginning of this sutra, it is refuted that the six sense bases and the consciousness-mind constitute the root of birth and death;

one must not rely upon them for confused practice. Yet, when the various sages personally recount their experiences, they still include these six gates, which demonstrates that the nature of the sages is all-pervasive.
When Mañjuśrī further eliminates them, he does so in accordance with this sutra to prohibit their erroneous application. If...
If beginners employ this to seek perfect penetration, they will fail to achieve unsurpassed Bodhi;
indeed, there are many who instead become Śrāvakas, Māras, or followers of external paths. Those among the Six Sages who attained correct perfect penetration are extremely few;
therefore, it must be eliminated. This is divided into six parts. First, visual consciousness is not fixed.

"Consciousness and vision are a mixture of the three harmonies; when their source is examined, they are called 'without marks. Since their own essence has no fixed priority, how can one attain perfect penetration? Xielü said:
"The Treatise states that consciousness arises from the harmony of two, meaning that consciousness arises within the conjunction of the faculty (indriya) and the object (viṣaya).

What is here called the 'harmony of three' is a combined statement of the agent and the object. Furthermore, the two characters 'consciousness' (shí) and 'vision' (jiàn) also appear to be inverted in word order; it should [be read as]..."
What is called "seeing-consciousness" (jianshi) is precisely the eye-consciousness (cakṣurvijñāna). It is the conceptualization following recollection (*anusmaraṇa-vikalpa*) belonging to the eye;

externally it confronts insentient color-form objects (*rūpa-dharmas*), while internally it relies upon the non-conceptual eye-faculty (*cakṣur-indriya*). Between these two, it falsely manifests a coarse conceptualization following recollection.

This is the eye-consciousness. Because it possesses its own substance as the dependent (*āśrita*) along with its supporting faculty and object (*indriya* and *viṣaya*), it is said to be "mixed with three."
"And so it is. Wēnlíng says: "The union of these three is fundamentally without substance; therefore, it is called 'not a characteristic' (a-lakṣaṇa).
The final two lines follow upon the preceding to conclude that there is neither fixedness nor a fixed, substantial self-nature.
Part Two: Ear-consciousness is not primary.
"Mind-hearing penetrates the ten directions; it arises from the power of great causes. Those with a beginner's mind cannot enter this—how, then, could they attain perfect penetration?
Wénlíng says: "Because Universal Good (Samantabhadra) employs 'mind-hearing,' he is able to know the external affairs of sand-grain worlds in other directions.
This arises from practicing the great cause of the Dharma-realm conduct; it is not something that a beginner's mind can enter. [This is] due to the majesty of the great cause.

It is merely a matter of exerting effort. Consciousness penetrates and hears throughout the sands of the world-realms; it is not that the ear-consciousness itself is inherently subtle and capable of following the initial mind to achieve this wondrous fruit.
Therefore, it is said that the initial mind cannot enter [this state]. △ Third, the olfactory consciousness has a dwelling place.
"Contemplation of the nose is fundamentally a provisional device, intended only to cause the mind to abide. Once abiding is achieved, the mind finds its place;
how then can one attain perfect penetration? Wēnlíng says: "Sundara was distracted, so the Buddha wished to collect and stabilize his mind by having him contemplate the tip of the nose.
This was merely a provisional device. For the true mind has no abode; to have an abode is delusion. Regarding "contemplation of the nose": at [the tip of the nose]...
One forms the visualization of white at the tip of the nose. As for "originally a provisional device," it means that this visualization was provisionally established as an antidote;

it is not something originally inherent to the olfactory consciousness (*ghrāṇavijñāna*). This is because the function of the olfactory consciousness is to discriminate between fragrances and stenches, and thus it has no relation to the "white" at the tip.
The second phrase clarifies that the original intent is solely to restrain and stabilize the distracted mind. The third phrase... [text continues].
This is because its clarity is not perfect. If it abides, it is biased and restricted to one place; by what means could it become perfect? △ Fourth, the tongue-consciousness has outflows.

"Preaching the Dharma by playing with sounds and characters, awakening those who have already attained perfection"—names and phrases are not without outflows; how, then, can one obtain perfect penetration?
Regarding the first phrase: although the preaching of the Dharma arises from the tongue-consciousness (*jihvā-vijñāna*), it cannot avoid being mixed with sounds and written characters;

thus, it is said that one "plays with sounds and characters. Yet, the ability to awaken others and achieve one's own fruition depends solely on the power of eloquence (*pratibhāna*) cultivated over vast eons in previous lives;
it is not something achievable by the tongue-consciousness of a single moment. Furthermore, this is called... [name].
Phrases are formations dissociated from thought (*viprayukta-saṃskāra*) and are subsumed under conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛta*); they are not untainted dharmas (*anāsrava*).
How could the tongue-consciousness (*jihvā-vijñāna*) participate in this to achieve perfect penetration? △ Fifth, body-consciousness is not pervasive.

Holding the precepts and violating them merely restrains the body; if there were no body, there would be nothing to restrain. Originally, this does not apply universally to all things—how, then, can one attain perfect penetration? Wuxing said: "Question:
Upāli first took up the restraint of the body and subsequently took up the restraint of the mind, and in both cases he attained mastery.

Why do you now say that it merely restrains the body? Answer: "Even when Śrāvakas restrain their minds, they likewise prevent the transgressions of the six groups and seven branches of the Vinaya; how much more so [for those who practice the Bodhisattva path]!"
Now, it is said that "body-consciousness" (*kāyavijñāna*) is contained therein. This verse specifically excludes body-consciousness;

the phrase "binding the body" refers precisely to being bound by body-consciousness, not to the body-faculty (*kāyendriya*). As for the claim that consciousness is contained therein, Master Yue’s confusion is of this sort.
Furthermore, observe the subsequent line, "originally not pervasive of all," and one will know [the distinction].
This statement regarding "binding" does not merely signify the abandonment of the mind; rather, it signifies that much more is abandoned.
This is because the realm of perfect penetration (*yuantong*) should universally integrate the myriad dharmas of the body and its boundaries.

Now, if one merely binds the consciousness of the body and restricts it to the physical body and mind, lacking the wisdom of universal integration, how can one attain perfect penetration? 6. The Consciousness of the Intellect (*manovijñāna*) Conditions Objects.

"Supernatural powers (abhijñā) originate from past causes; how could they be devoid of the discrimination of dharmas? Since mindfulness depends on conditions rather than being detached from objects, how can one attain perfect penetration?

Wuxing said: "Maudgalyāyana’s supernatural powers were obtained through past habituation. Although it is said that his mind’s radiance was manifested by turning back the turbid depths, this does not involve the manifestation of the discrimination of dharmas.
Furthermore, the supernatural powers of the Lesser Vehicle are all produced through deliberate mental effort (manasikāra) and depend upon conditions."

Things exist; apart from things, they do not exist. ○ The three characters "dharma-vikalpa" (dharma-discrimination) are simply another name for the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*), because the mental consciousness is the nature of discrimination regarding the objects of dharma (*dharmālambana*).
This point has already been clarified. Maudgalyāyana’s spiritual transformations and perfect penetration originally have nothing to do with the mental consciousness.
The subsequent sentence further states that even if it were derived from the mental consciousness, it is still merely an object-condition (*ālambana-pratyaya*).

If it were merely the dust itself, rather than a pervasive reality that transcends the dust, it would likewise be difficult to attain perfect penetration (*yuan-tong*). "Objects" refers precisely to the dust.
Examining the passages that distinguish [the faculties] from consciousness, it is clear that the six sages each attained their realization through distinct supports;

it was not truly by means of their own conscious minds that they reached perfect penetration. The selection of the six consciousnesses is complete. △ Fourth, the selection of the seventh [consciousness].

"Great. Among the seven elements, the first five are identical to the objects (*viṣaya*); the sixth is identical to consciousness (*vijñāna*); and the seventh is identical to the faculties (*indriya*).

Compared to the preceding [classification], this merely adds the characteristic of being "vast and great," yet its selection of the mental faculty (*manas*) is largely the same as before. It is divided into seven categories;
first, the element of earth (*pṛthivī-dhātu*) is not universal.
If one contemplates it through the nature of earth, its solidity and obstruction prevent penetration; being conditioned (*saṃskṛta*), how can this non-sacred nature attain perfect penetration?
Wēnlíng says: "To hold the earth and level it still involves the conditioned; it is not the true sacred nature. Only by encountering the Buddha with a level mind does one return to the sacred nature.
Because the initial mind is entirely involved with the conditioned, it is difficult to attain perfect penetration; thus it seems to be [the case].
This is easy to see. △ Second, the water-element is not real.

If one contemplates through the nature of water, such conceptual thoughts are not true reality. Since the state of suchness is beyond both perception and reflection, how could one attain perfect penetration?
Wenling says: "The contemplations of moonlight and water have not yet transcended conceptual thought; thus it is difficult to accord with suchness (*tathatā*).
This is because the principle of suchness is not a state of applied and sustained thought (*vitarka-vicāra*). "Suchness" refers to the perfect, penetrating, and true essence.
This is the dharma of non-conceptualization and immovability. Any arising of mental activity, discrimination, or discursive observation (*vitarka-vicāra*) is entirely inconsistent with it;

conversely, this clearly demonstrates that the "revolving of hearing" does not belong to discursive observation. Those who insist on imposing the three contemplations (*trividha-bhāvanā*) upon it should still investigate this point.
△ Third, the fire element is not primary.

If one contemplates through the nature of fire, this is a detachment born of aversion toward existence; it is not the truth. This is not a skillful means for the beginner. How, then, could one attain perfect penetration?
Only when both body and mind are severed, and even the nature of that severance is absent, does one achieve true detachment. Since you currently maintain aversion and severance, it is not the truth.
Furthermore, aversion toward desire is merely a provisional designation; it is not the truly real, originally existing Dharma. [The preceding] three phrases state that it is not the beginning.

The method for concentrating the mind: Since not all beings with their initial resolve possess excessive desire, how could those sentient beings who have few desires or no desires employ this method to enter perfect penetration?
△ Fourth, the great element of wind has its counterpart.
If one contemplates by way of the nature of wind, then motion and stillness are not without their opposites. If there are opposites, they are not the Unsurpassed Enlightenment;

how, then, could one attain perfect penetration? If motion and stillness have opposites, then one being in motion and one being still belong to the phenomena of cyclic recurrence, birth-and-death, and impermanence.
Therefore, it is not the essence of unsurpassed enlightenment. Question: The Dharma-gate of "listening in reverse" also enters through movement and stillness;
how does it differ from this? Answer: That [method] gradually sheds the two sensory objects of movement and stillness in order to apprehend the hearing-nature that is neither moving nor still.
This serves as a skillful means for beginners; it takes the nature of wind—characterized by movement and stillness—as the gateway for entry.
This is why there is such a great difference [between this and the previous approach]. How could one use this to challenge that? △ Fifth: Space-mahābhūta is not awareness.

If one contemplates through the lens of emptiness (*śūnyatā*), then that which is dark and dull is not originally awakening. Since non-awakening differs from Bodhi, how could one attain perfect penetration?
Wénlǐng says: "Obscurity and darkness constitute emptiness; therefore, it is called 'dark and dull. This is an interpretation that exhausts the source.

If we consider its manifested characteristics, 'dark' means profound obscurity and 'dull' means stubborn rigidity. Space is fundamentally characterized by this profound obscurity and stubborn rigidity."
Cognition has the characteristic of being aware. Bodhi, however, has the characteristic of the luminous intelligence of the awakened nature (*bodhicitta*), which is the very essence of wisdom.
It is precisely the opposite of dullness and obscurity. To seek the fruit of luminous intelligence within the state of dullness and obscurity is as difficult as trying to drill fire from ice;
it is certainly an arduous task. Those in the world who revere the great void as their original nature should awaken to this. 6. The Six Consciousnesses.
This is a great delusion.
If one observes through the nature of consciousness, one finds that the observed consciousness is impermanent; to maintain the mind [upon it] is itself a delusion.

How, then, can one attain perfect penetration? Wénlǐng says: Maitreya cultivated only the contemplation of consciousness, yet the consciousness he observed arises and ceases from moment to moment. To maintain...
If even the mind, when examined, is found to be illusory, how much more so its attainment of perfect penetration?

The first phrase states that upon generating the aspiration for enlightenment, one immediately investigates the nature of consciousness as the gateway to practice. The second phrase states that both the observing mind and the observed nature of consciousness are subject to moment-to-moment flux;
neither can remain stable. In my humble opinion, even if a beginner’s resolve is fierce...
One will inevitably fall into meditative attainments such as the Sphere of Infinite Consciousness (*vijñānānantyāyatana*). This is the third phrase, representing the ultimate limit of investigation.
Even if there is a mind that persists in existence—such as the nirvāṇa in which the two vehicles abide—it is merely a realm of the aggregate of consciousness (*vijñānaskandha*).
It is like a tranquil flow of water that appears still from a distance, yet in reality, it does not remain so; therefore, it is called "empty and false. How could this be the original mind?
Can one who relies upon these faculties enter perfect penetration all at once? △ Seventh: The Great Difference in Roots and Their Corresponding Resonances.
All conditioned phenomena are impermanent; the nature of thought is fundamentally subject to arising and ceasing. Cause and effect now resonate differently; how can one attain perfect penetration?
Regarding the first sentence: It is said that whatever involves movement or flux belongs to the aggregate of formations (*saṃskāra-skandha*) and thus falls under impermanence.
