yet at the very beginning of his resolve for enlightenment, he first felt revulsion toward the turbidity of desire. Throughout the three gradual stages, he addressed each [defilement] first, and only then did his body and mind become wondrously perfect, attaining great peace and stability.
At the initial stage of the ten faiths, because the love of desire was dried up, the nature of wisdom became perfectly luminous.

Consequently, one ascends through the stages of the Equal and Wondrous [Heavens]. Because the minds of worldly people do not wander or dissipate, clarity and brilliance arise, and they gradually reach the six heavens.

Therefore, true cultivation must first involve internal restraint and the departure from desire. Furthermore, this is divided into two sections. The first section analyzes the characteristics of loss and gain; it is further divided into three parts:

first, a general presentation of the benefits and harms of maintaining precepts versus violating them; second, [the specific categories]; and third, [the detailed analysis]. Within the first part, there is the maintenance [of the precepts].
Then one will certainly transcend birth and death.

the remaining three [precepts] are to be understood by this analogy. Wēn-líng says: "All sentient beings, because of sexual desire, establish their very nature and life, and thus remain entangled in birth and death.
If the thirst of desire dries up, then the remaining physical form will no longer continue. 2. If one commits a transgression, one will inevitably fall into the realm of Māra.
Furthermore, there are three [reasons] why you will not transcend the mundane world. First, you will certainly not escape from the dust of the senses.
You practice samādhi precisely to emerge from worldly toil; yet, if the lustful mind is not eliminated, the dust cannot be escaped.
Samādhi is precisely the perfect penetration of the ear faculty. "Dust and toil" refers to the views and afflictions within the realms.

Although a Bodhisattva does not actually depart from the triple realm, they must nonetheless attain mastery over these views and afflictions; only when they are no longer bound by birth and death can they be said to have departed from dust and toil.
Now, sensual desire is the foremost of these dusts and toils; therefore, unless it is eliminated, one will certainly not depart. △
Second, one will inevitably fall into the ranks of Māra.

Even if one possesses great wisdom and meditative concentration manifests before them, if they do not sever lust, they will certainly descend into the path of Māra; at best, they become a Māra-king of the highest grade.
The middle-grade māra-beings and the lower-grade māra-women possess great wisdom;

that is, their discernment (*prajñā*) enables them to penetrate and expound all dharmas. They have actualized meditative concentration (*dhyāna-samādhi*), meaning they are skillful in entering, abiding in, and emerging from sublime states.
Regarding those who do not sever sexual desire: during the time of meditative concentration, they do not definitively abandon or cut it off.

Regarding lustful thoughts: if one indulges in such contemplation, one will inevitably fall into the path of Māra. This is because the objective realm summons itself according to the mind, and the mind shifts in pursuit of the realm;

they necessarily draw each other along. Since what you are currently contemplating lies within the sphere of desire, and no sphere of desire surpasses that of Māra—just as water flows toward moisture—how could one not fall into its midst?
It is like wandering through the realm of the *skandha*-māras while practicing the meditation on emptiness (*śūnyatā*).
The practitioner of meditation who, instead of abandoning worldly defilements, extensively transforms precious women—this is precisely what is meant.

This occurs because the mind of samādhi and wisdom touches upon sensory objects and flows into them, thereby falling into such states. If one lacks samādhi and wisdom and possesses only the habit of lust, one will fall directly into hell;
how could there be a reward in a demonic palace? High, middle, and low [rebirths] follow the thickness or thinness of one's merit, serving as the respective gradations.
[This is] the second [point]. △ Third, they concurrently give rise to increased pride (*adhimāna*).
Those various māras also have their own followers, each of whom claims to have realized the unsurpassed path.

They claim to have realized what they have not realized and to have attained what they have not attained; this is the "increased pride" (*adhimāna*) among the seven types of pride. It is also not a fruit [of the path].
Calculating the results. △ Second, preliminary exposition on the rituals of the Māra-teachings. This is intended for people to discern and recognize them so as not to be deluded by Māra.

Divided into two parts. First, the teaching of Māra that transforms the world through lustful desire. This is further divided into three. First, a preliminary record of the final dharma age (*mappō*).
After my parinirvāṇa, during the period of the Final Dharma (mofa),
secondly, demons will flourish and propagate lust.
Such demonic followers will be numerous, blazing throughout the world, widely practicing greed and lust while posing as spiritual friends (kalyāṇamitra).
These followers of Māra are those from previous lives who practiced dhyāna while harboring lust. They come to act as teachers;

through their supernatural powers and wisdom, they secretly teach the practice of sexual intercourse as a Buddhist rite (buddhakārya), transmitting it to one another. Therefore, it is said that "it is practiced extensively.
This rampant indulgence in lust does not stop at mere thought; both teacher and disciple shall fall directly into the Avīci Hell. △ Third: The Trap.
Humans destroy the Path, causing all sentient beings to fall into the pit of craving and views, thereby losing the way to Bodhi.

"Craving" refers to the afflictions of thought (*sī-fo*), while "views" refer to the afflictions of vision (*jian-fo*). Sexual desire serves as their teaching, for the afflictions of thought are particularly heavy; yet, it is through sexual desire...

For the sake of the Way, one must also perceive the great perversion of conceptual discrimination within the delusions of view. △ Second, teaching people to sever lust is the instruction of the Buddha:
"When you teach the people of the world to cultivate *samādhi*, first sever the lust of the mind; this is called the method of the Tathāgata and the World-Honored Buddhas of the past."
This is the first definitive and pure instruction.
Although herein Ānanda was exhorted, later practitioners need not personally depend upon Ānanda;

whenever one encounters a spiritual friend, one should rely on the teachings indicated by the Sūtras to sever lustful thoughts. Those who cultivate perfect penetration are just like Ānanda, as well as Śākyamuni and—
If a former Buddha personally comes, follow him with a sincere heart. Generally speaking, when one says there is no obstacle to lustful desire, it means the Demon King has personally arrived;
one must quickly be startled and avoid him. This is explained in detail within the section on the *skandha-māra*. △ Third, determining whether Bodhicitta is achieved or not:

For sentient beings whose initial resolve aspires toward Bodhi, there are the latent causes from past lives, the permeation of the teachings, the roots of goodness, and the internal *tathāgatagarbha* (original enlightenment).
Regarding the difficulty of abandoning lust and other afflictions due to the power of habitual perfuming: this refers to the co-emergent, deeply ingrained habit-energies accumulated over vast eons.

Consequently, many rational desires wage war within the breast. At this very moment of such dual difficulty, if one suddenly encounters a demonic teacher who secretly transmits the teaching that [desires] do not obstruct Bodhi, there are few who do not joyfully follow it.
Therefore, the preceding section demonstrates how one becomes bound and falls into the clutches of Māra.

For this reason, one must exert effort to stop [such thoughts] and not follow them. Yet, fearing that there may be those whose habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*) are most heavy, they might indulge their own minds, claiming that one can practice dhyāna while still harboring lust.
They argue that although one will not quickly attain *bodhi*, one shall eventually attain it after a long time.

Therefore, for such people, [the path] is definitively severed and ultimately cannot be accomplished; only by severing [these tendencies] can one hope for success. This is divided into two parts. First, the analogy.
If one does not sever [desire], there is no accomplishment. Furthermore, there are three points.
First, to practice dhyāna while still harboring lust. Therefore, Ānanda, if one practices meditative concentration without severing lust—△ Second, the analogy of sand that cannot make rice.
It is like steaming sand and stones, hoping to produce cooked rice; even after hundreds of thousands of kalpas, it will only be called "hot sand. Why is this?
Because this is not the source of rice; it is merely sand and stone.
△ Third, engaging in sexual union does not accomplish the Way.

You seek the Buddha’s wondrous fruit with a body of lust; even if you were to attain wondrous enlightenment, it would all be rooted in lust. If the very foundation is constituted by lust, [how can you attain the Way?]
They will revolve through the three miserable realms and certainly be unable to escape. Regarding the Tathāgata’s nirvāṇa, by what path can one cultivate and realize it?
The first two lines correspond to steaming sand to make rice; the subsequent five lines correspond to being heated by hot sands for kalpas.
The "subtle awakening" of lustful meditation is merely the temporary state of the sand becoming warm. Taking thoughts of lust as the root, one gives rise to [this state].

Because of this profound realization, it is said that all [afflictions] have lust as their root. Having briefly been born in the palace of Māra, they will unrestrainedly commit great evils and pass through the three miserable realms, with no prospect of escape.
The final two phrases state that lust is not the foundation of Nirvāṇa, just as sand is not the foundation of rice;
therefore, there is no path for cultivation or realization. △ Second, the exhortation that only through deep severance can one achieve success.
One must ensure that the mechanism of lust is severed in both body and mind, such that even the nature of severance itself is absent.
Only then can one hope for the Bodhi of the Buddha. This section precisely contains the most earnest words for the present precept regarding the elimination of lustful intent.

"Mechanism" (*ji*) refers to the cause of arousal, like the trigger of a crossbow. That is to say, the mechanism of bodily lust is set in motion by the mind, while the mechanism of mental lust is released by thought.

Release. Only when not a single thought arises can one achieve the simultaneous severance of both body and mind. As for the statement that "even the nature of severance is non-existent," this is discussed from an even deeper perspective.

If the nature of severance were to persist, it would ultimately remain in opposition to desire; thus, the residual shadow of the conditions of desire would not yet have been forgotten, and it would not be a state of total exhaustion.
It is like a patient who must eliminate both the illness and the medicine to truly become a person free of disease. △ Second, the adjudication of the heterodox.
This is the correct teaching.
What I have thus explained is called the Buddha’s teaching; what is not thus explained is the teaching of Pāpīyān.
One should strive to be skillful in discernment, diligently following the Buddha’s teaching and severing the teachings of Māra. The section on the cessation of lust is concluded. II.

Regarding the precept against killing: the underlying intent of the classification and the general meaning of the text are all to be understood according to what was established previously. Only those points where there are slight differences will be explained here.
The killing prohibited herein does not refer merely to humans and domestic animals; it extends downward to include even flies, lice, snakes, scorpions, and the like.

Do not kill any of them. This does not apply only to killing with one's own hands; even consuming their flesh for one's body is not permitted. Furthermore, this prohibition extends beyond merely the physical act and speech;

even mental intention must be completely severed. This is divided into two parts: first, an analysis of the characteristics of harm and benefit; second, a detailed exposition of the advantages and disadvantages of upholding or violating [the precepts].

Within the second part, there are three sections: first, the exposition of the benefits and harms of maintaining or violating [the precepts]; second, [the section on] "If one maintains [them], one will surely transcend"; third, [the section on] "If one violates [them], one will surely fall."
Ānanda, furthermore, among the sentient beings of the six realms in all worlds, those whose minds do not kill will not continue through the succession of birth and death.

They carry their karmic debt to demand retribution; because they form the conditions for birth and death, if one does not kill, the cycle will not continue. △ Second, if one commits these offenses, one will inevitably fall into the realm of spirits.
This is further divided into three parts. First, one will certainly not escape the dust [of worldly existence].
"You cultivate samādhi, yet its origin lies in the midst of worldly toil. If you do not eliminate the murderous mind, you cannot escape from the dust of the world.
II. You will inevitably fall among ghosts and spirits:

Even if you possess great wisdom and meditative concentration manifests before you, if you do not sever the habit of killing, you will surely fall into the realm of spirits. This applies even to those of the highest grade."
They become powerful spirits (*mahābala-guhyaka*). Those of middling quality become flying *yakṣas*, various ghost generals, and the like;
those of inferior quality shall become earth-walking *rākṣasas*.
Although these ghosts and spirits are divided into superior and inferior grades, they are all equally realms of evil destiny (*durgati*). Therefore, those who enter from the human realm are called...
This refers to falling [into lower realms]. However, within consciousness there are nine grades; these three grades are likely the three grades within the superior grade.
While the middle and lower grades mostly take stinginess as the cause for falling, these three superior grades all possess powerful clarity.
Their spirits are like those of rivers, mountains, and peaks; their supernormal powers are penetrating, and they share the same fearlessness, wealth, and joy as humans and devas. This—
Thus, to practice meditation while not ceasing the taking of life constitutes a cause for falling.

There are indeed those among the world’s heterodox practitioners who accumulate merit in pursuit of attaining the divine path, yet they do not realize that falling into the evil realms or the neighboring lands of hell is easy, while ascending from them is difficult.
However, it is only those who possess a mind of killing while practicing concentration and wisdom who fall into such categories; this is not something possible for those who merely kill.

They fall [into error]. As for the powerful ghosts who immediately commit acts of slaughter while roaming among the heavens—those now venerated by humans, whom people call "Emperors" or "Heavenly Beings," are mostly of this class.
△ Third, they concurrently give rise to increased arrogance.
Those various ghosts and spirits also have their own followers, each of whom claims to have attained the Unsurpassed Way.

△ Second, a preliminary explanation of the ritual protocols of the ghost teachings, which is further divided into two parts. First, the teaching of ghosts that involves eating meat while transforming the world.
Regarding the consumption of meat mentioned here—following the previous prohibition against killing—it is because many people kill living beings for the sake of eating meat. Although...
One does not kill personally, yet by means of wealth one causes others to kill; the injury to life and the resulting karma are identical. Thus, a sutra says:

"To kill sentient beings for profit, or to use wealth as a net to obtain various meats—both are evil karmas; after death, one falls into the Raurava Hell. Therefore, eating meat is itself the act of killing.
Consequently, there are those in the world who can renounce the eating of meat but do not refrain from killing; such instances are frequently seen.
Practitioners of the Way do not show leniency toward even flies and lice, yet they recklessly kill them in countless numbers; this is profoundly irrational.

Furthermore, there are those who can refrain from killing living beings but do not renounce meat; both of these are irrational. Those with the aspiration for perfect penetration should take great pains to avoid such practices.
This is further divided into three parts; the first is the premonition regarding the Dharma-ending age.
After my parinirvāṇa, during the period of the Final Dharma (mofa), there will be two types of ghostly transformations that eat meat.
This section has two parts: first, an account of the ritual of ghostly transformation.
These ghosts and spirits will proliferate in the world, claiming that by eating meat they attain the path to Bodhi.

He proclaimed that eating meat does not hinder one from attaining Buddhahood. △ Second, the sublation of provisional teachings to prevent difficulties; this has three parts. First, clarifying the provisional transformation in the present:
"Ānanda, I have directed the bhikṣus to eat the five kinds of pure meat. These meats were all produced through my supernatural power; they did not originally exist."
Regarding the life-faculty (*jīvitendriya*):

in the Vinayas of the *Āgama* and *Vaipulya* [teachings], the Buddha permitted those who instruct Śrāvakas and Bodhisattvas to eat the three kinds of pure meat, provided they exclude twenty types such as humans, snakes, and so forth.
To now claim that this was performed through the Buddha’s supernatural power while he was still in the world would be to negate [the established doctrine].
"How could one possibly eat it again? Gu-shan said: "Regarding the five kinds of pure meat, the Vinaya clarifies three purities:
not seeing that it was killed for one's sake, not hearing that it was killed for one's sake, and not suspecting that it was killed for one's sake. What is now called the 'five' adds two more:
naturally deceased and scavenged by birds. 2. Explaining the Origin of Expedient Transformation.
"O Brahmin, your land is largely damp and humid; moreover, it is filled with sand and stones, so that grasses and vegetables do not grow.

Through the empowerment of my great compassionate supernatural power, and by virtue of my great kindness and compassion, I have provisionally designated this as 'flesh. Thus, you are able to taste its flavor."
△ Regarding the statement that after the extinction of the Three Clarities (trividyā), there is no longer the teaching:
How can it be that after the Tathāgata’s parinirvāṇa, those who eat the flesh of sentient beings are called sons of the Śākya?

This is evident. As for any instances where the Buddha permitted the eating of meat, these were all expedient transformations employed while the Buddha was in the world to gradually guide beings through compassionate教化 (huà).
Furthermore, after the extinction [of the Buddha], how could one possibly eat meat that has actually taken life?

As for the profound sutras that abolish the provisional and do not permit it, these all demonstrate the reality of the ultimate truth to protect against the errors and fallacies of the Dharma-ending age.

Those with resolve must strive to follow the reality and must not deceive themselves by invoking the provisional. △ Third, falling into suffering and increasing entanglements; this is further divided into two parts.
First, they will inevitably fall into the sea of suffering.
You should know that these meat-eaters, even if they attain an opening of the mind resembling *samādhi*, are all great *rākṣasas*.
When their retribution ends, they will inevitably sink into the bitter sea of birth and death; they are not disciples of the Buddha.

As for "the mind opening," it refers to gaining power within meditative concentration (*dhyāna-samādhi*) such that the objects of experience manifest before one. However, the obstacle of eating meat is deep;
it appears to be real but is not, for all such people are great *rākṣasas*. Because their current conduct is identical [to that of the demons], their retribution will surely follow.

Therefore, the effect is used to designate the cause. "Must sink into the sea of suffering" means that because the rākṣasas increase their transgressions and turn toward evil, they will inevitably reach a place of ultimate suffering.
△ Second, they will certainly not escape the entanglements.
Such people kill one another, devour one another, and eat one another without end. How could such people escape the three realms?
Since their karmic debts of life remain unsettled, there will be no time for liberation; by what means could they transcend the world? 2.
Teaching People to Cease Killing—This is the Buddha’s Instruction.

When you teach the people of the world to practice samādhi, they must first cease the taking of life; this is called the second definitive, pure, and clear instruction of the Tathāgata and the World-Honored Buddhas of the past.
The ritual for the transformation of the ghost-buddha is complete. △ Third, determining whether liberation can be attained. This also has two parts.
First, the analogy that one cannot escape as long as [the afflictions] are not severed. This is further divided into two. First, the primary analogy.

Therefore, Ānanda, if one does not cease killing while practicing meditative concentration, it is like a person who blocks their own ears and shouts at the top of their voice, seeking not to be heard by others;
such people as these are said to be "seeking concealment while making themselves even more exposed."

Wenling said: "To cultivate meditation in order to avoid sin, yet instead commit acts of killing; to plug one's ears to avoid others, yet instead raise one's voice—this is to desire concealment while making it even more manifest.
As for the two characters 'avoiding sin' (bìzuì), it would be better to change them to 'transcending the world' (chūshì)."
△ Second, the illustration by contrast:
Pure bhikṣus and bodhisattvas, when walking on a forked path, do not even tread upon living grass; how much less would they pull it up with their hands?
What is great compassion? It is to take the flesh and blood of sentient beings as food. Wēnlíng says:
"If one does not intentionally trample upon them, nor intentionally pull them out, such ultimate benevolence extends even to plants and trees;

how much more so regarding the eating of sentient beings' flesh? II. Exhorting toward profound severance so as to achieve liberation, in two parts: 1. Praising those who are able to sever [the habit]. Furthermore—
Second: First, he praises [the practice] directly:

"If there are bhikṣus who do not wear silks, cotton, or fine fabrics from the East, nor the boots, furs, woolens, milk, curd, or clarified butter of this land—if such bhikṣus are truly liberated in the world, they have repaid their karmic debts from past lives and do not wander within the three realms."
"Vīra" refers to coarse woolen clothing. Wēnlíng says: "It is not that there are no furs and wools in the East, nor that there is no silk or cotton in the Western lands;
these are spoken of according to what is most prevalent. Regarding the phrase "repaying past debts and no longer wandering in the three realms," the former clause should have been placed later;
this is a reversal in the translator's wording. △ Second, raising the question and explaining through a metaphor.
Why is this? Because by consuming their bodily parts, one becomes conditioned by them. It is like a person who eats the various grains from the earth;

their feet do not leave the ground. Wēnlíng says: "Feet not leaving the ground" refers to humans at the beginning of the kalpa, whose bodies possessed flying radiance. If they stepped [with their feet],...
Cloud: Because they consume the fat of the earth and eat fragrant rice, their bodies become firm and heavy, such that their feet do not leave the ground.
Regarding "parts of the body": although silk and the like are not the flesh and blood of the being itself, it is not necessarily the case that they all take life;
nevertheless, they are still a portion of that being's body, and when used, they form a condition of inseparability with that being. △
Second, one should correctly exhort others to renounce [harm] and grant them liberation,
ensuring that both body and mind do not, through either physical means or mental intent, consume or ingest any part of a sentient being’s body or its constituent members.
I say that such a person is one who has attained true liberation.
Wēnlíng says: "The body" refers to flesh, blood, marrow, and bone; "body parts" refer to furs, wool, milk, and curd.
Regarding the two paths of clothing and food, one must sever craving for them both. II. Adjudicating Between Erroneous and Correct Teachings.
What I have spoken in this manner is called the teaching of the Buddha; that which is not spoken thus is the teaching of Pāpīyān.
Having finished the refutation of killing, [we now address] the third: the refutation of stealing. This act of theft does not consist merely of pilfering another’s property;

rather, it includes all instances of practicing fraud, using deceptive speech to delude or intimidate others, and even harboring a single thought of seeking gain or offerings. All such acts constitute [stealing].

It is also divided into two parts. First, the classification of the characteristics of benefit and harm, which is further divided into three sections. First, the primary exposition of the benefits and harms of maintaining and violating [the precepts].
Second, [the section on] how maintaining [the precepts] necessarily leads to transcendence from birth and death.
Ānanda, furthermore, as for the sentient beings of the six realms within the world, if their minds do not steal, they will not follow along with the continuity of birth and death.
"The mind does not steal" means that the thought of coveting profit and desire for gain does not arise for even a single moment. △ Second, the transgression.
Then you will inevitably fall into deviant paths. Furthermore, there are three [reasons]: first, you will certainly not escape the mundane world.
You practice samādhi fundamentally to transcend worldly toil; if the thieving mind is not eliminated, you cannot escape the mundane world.
Only those who weary of the mundane dust can transcend it; how could those who crave the world ever go beyond it? II. They will inevitably fall into demonic and heterodox paths.

Even if one possesses great wisdom and meditative concentration manifests before them, if they do not sever their thievery [of desire], they will surely fall into heterodox ways and become high-grade spirits.
Those of middle quality are malevolent spirits; those of lower quality are possessed by various demons who are wicked people.

They take advantage of others through devious means, their minds are turned toward perversion, and their words and deeds are improper; thus they fall into the category of the heterodox. As for "spirits" (jīnglíng): [they are...]
There are mountain spirits and water monsters who possess various supernatural powers; they resemble immortals yet are not immortals, and resemble deities yet are not deities.
These malevolent specters appear and disappear within the world, frequently possessing people. They may either steal their vital energy or plunder their wealth.
When a person is possessed by such an evil spirit, their speech and conduct become strange and aberrant, thereby deluding and confusing others. (3)
Furthermore, they increase their arrogance;
those various heterodox groups also have their own followers, each claiming for themselves that they have attained the Unsurpassed Way.
△ Second, a preliminary exposition of the ritual protocols of demonic Buddhism, in two sections. First, the hidden enticement and delusion, which is precisely demonic teaching. Moreover—
Third: First, a prediction concerning the final dharma; second, the prevalence of demonic and deceptive transformations.
After my parinirvāṇa, during the period of the final dharma, many such demonic and heterodox beings will flourish in the world, concealing their wickedness and deceit.

They are called "good spiritual friends," yet each claims to have attained the state of a superior person (*uttarimanussa-dhamma*). They deceive the ignorant, fearing they might cause them to lose their minds;
wherever they pass, the households waste away and dissipate.
Regarding those who "conceal their wickedness and deceit," they primarily seek to acquire wealth through demonic speech and demonic conduct, or by manifesting demonic intimacy.
Claiming for themselves self-mastery, they falsely represent themselves as realized masters (*jñānin*). The foolish, unable to discern the truth, surrender their entire households to serve them.
△ Third, misleading others so they fall into hell, which is further divided into three parts. First, they initially compare their own teachings with others' to establish their superiority.
I instruct the bhikṣus to wander for alms before eating, so that they may abandon greed and accomplish the path to Bodhi. These bhikṣus do not cook food for themselves;
they entrust their remaining lives to a transient sojourn within the triple world, demonstrating a single round-trip from which there is no returning once departed.
"According to the direction" means that wherever one arrives, one seeks alms with purity; this is what is meant by "begging according to the direction.

The first four lines directly indicate the abandonment of greed, meaning not to accumulate and not to act for oneself. From the words "All bhikṣus... onwards, the reason for abandoning greed is explained.
To stay on land is called "lodging as a traveler," and to stay on water is called "mooring"; they are like passing guests. One merely relies upon...
The Buddha himself explains his original intent; there is no need for further elaboration. Second, [the text] reveals that this is a violation of the teachings and a perverted exposition.
It asks: "How can these thieves, wearing my robes as a pretext, peddle themselves like merchants of the Tathāgata, performing all manner of deeds while claiming them all to be the Buddha-Dharma?"
However, they are not ordained bhikṣus who possess the full precepts.

Regarding the path of the Hīnayāna, the first phrase states that their inner minds are fundamentally those of thieves; the second phrase states that while they outwardly borrow the monastic deportment, their intent is solely to pilfer profit.
Because they use the Tathāgata as a broker for their gain, it is said that they "peddle the Tathāgata for profit. As it says:
It is said that even the Tathāgata himself was deceived by such people. They perform all manner of karmic actions while claiming them to be the Buddha-dharma;
they employ immeasurable adornments solely for the sake of profit and as causes for falling into the realms of suffering, yet they falsely profess these to be the Buddha-dharma.
If one compares this with the true teaching of begging for alms from the past, how could it possibly be the original intent of the Buddha-dharma?
This refers specifically to those who are inverted, preaching what is not the Dharma as the Dharma. The final three phrases refute their slanderous words that delude people.

When such deceitful persons are rebuked with the authentic teaching of begging for alms, they claim for themselves that they are practicing the path of a bodhisattva, yet conversely disparage those who follow the authentic teaching as followers of the Hīnayāna path. This, moreover, is the teaching of the Dharma.
This is the inversion of what is not the Dharma. △ Third, the correct demonstration of the profound harm of such delusive doubts:
By means of these delusive doubts, immeasurable sentient beings fall into the Avīci Hell.
Hearing those who speak of the Dharma as non-Dharma, they all harbor doubts regarding the orthodox teaching, mistaking it for the path of the Hīnayāna, and follow such false slander.
Hearing those who speak of non-Dharma as Dharma, they all erroneously take karmic causes to be the true Buddha-dharma and adhere to such deluded practices;
thus, they all fall into Avīci Hell. This concludes the section on "Concealing and Deceiving through Delusive Teachings. II. The Teaching.
"Cutting off theft is the instruction of the Buddha. This is divided into two parts. First, the instruction given by himself, which is further divided into four sections.
First, teaching the relinquishment of even subtle causes regarding the body:
"If, after my parinirvāṇa, there should be a bhikṣu who resolves his mind to cultivate samādhi, he shall be able [to see] the Tathāgata..."
Before an image, one lights a lamp with the body, burns a finger-joint, or applies a single incense stick to the body.
"Samādhi" here refers to the Ear-faculty Perfect Penetration Samādhi, which is the Illusion-like Samādhi.

The meaning contained within this passage implies that there may be obstacles to superior cultivation arising from karmic debts of theft from previous lives; thus, one cultivates such subtle causes. Generally speaking, as for burning...
However, one must eliminate past hindrances and cultivate the Great Samādhi to truly establish the wondrous cause.
If it is done for the sake of wealth, profit, or fame, one will instead incur great sin. △ Second, permitting the completion of karmic debts and the emergence into the world.
I say that such a person has, at once, repaid all karmic debts from beginningless time; they bid a final farewell to the world and are forever liberated from all outflows (*āsrava*).
"Bidding a final farewell" means to take one's permanent leave. Mount Gu said: "A thief takes another’s *niśraya-vipāka* (the environment and material resources) for their own body."
Now, by sacrificing their primary retribution to provide for the supreme sages, they are able to overturn and destroy the karma of theft accumulated since beginningless time.
△ Third, looking upward to exalt them clarifies that they are near the Way.
Although they have not yet clearly illuminated the path to unsurpassed enlightenment, these people have already attained a resolute mind regarding the Dharma.

The path of awakening is precisely the path of *bodhi*; this is what is meant by perfect penetration (*yuan-tong*). Because one has only recently repented and undertaken the precepts, one has not yet reached the stage of meditative concentration and wisdom;

therefore, it is said that "the path is not yet clear. One who possesses a resolute mind is determined to believe that their past karma will surely be extinguished and the path of awakening will become clear.
Wēnlíng says: "Among all things difficult to relinquish, nothing surpasses one's own body. To be able to relinquish what is difficult to relinquish—"
Consequently, all other forms of craving and attachment can certainly be abandoned. Therefore, it is said that such a person has attained a mind of certainty regarding the Dharma.

If one merely aspires to renounce the body and forcibly alters their appearance, yet the karma of theft continues before them and they repeatedly commit new acts while the underlying craving of the root-mind remains unaltered, they will still not escape the suffering of karma; how then could they possibly attain certain, clear awakening?
How perilous it is! Fourth, as for the violation of this [precept], one must repay it.

If one does not provide even this slight cause for sacrificing the body, then even if one attains the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*), one will inevitably be reborn among humans to settle that karmic debt from former lives.
It was exactly like my own meal of horse fodder, no different at all.
To "accomplish the unconditioned" means to realize the supramundane fruit. If one does not return to birth among humans to repay past debts, [one has attained liberation].

Because there are obstacles to further progress and the deliverance of sentient beings, one must repay [one's karmic debts]. Wēnlíng says: "Because the Buddha was once a bhikṣu who had reviled others, he had to eat horse barley;
consequently, upon attaining Buddhahood, he ate it at the village of Vairaṇyā. This demonstrates that past debts must inevitably be repaid.
△ Second, the turning of the teaching according to the instructions of previous Buddhas.

"You should teach the people of the world to practice samādhi first, and only thereafter renounce stealing. This is called the third definitive, pure, and clear instruction of the Tathāgata and the World-Honored Buddhas of the past."
The preliminary refutation of the demonic Buddhist rituals is concluded. △ Third, determining whether *samādhi* is attained. This is divided into two parts.
First, using a metaphor to show that it is difficult to attain if one does not sever [the afflictions]:
"Therefore, Ānanda, if one who cultivates meditative concentration (*dhyāna-samādhi*) does not sever theft, it is like a person pouring water into a leaking cup."
If one seeks to fulfill [the debt], even if it takes aeons as numerous as dust motes, it will never be restored.
△ Second, exhorting that only through profound severance can it be attained, divided into two sections. First, relying solely on the definitive meaning to practice relinquishment and giving.
Furthermore, it is divided into three parts. First is the relinquishing of greed and stinginess regarding the body:
if monks do not store even a fraction of what remains from their robes and alms bowls, and give away the remnants of their begged food to hungry sentient beings.

"Surplus above" refers to that which remains beyond one's robes and bowl; it means maintaining restraint by being free from greed. "Surplus below" refers to that which remains after one has had sufficient food for oneself;
it means maintaining practice through the ability to give, without being stingy. △ Second, the mind relinquishes pride and anger.
In the great assembly, one joins the palms and pays homage to the multitude.

To be struck or reviled by others while regarding it as equal to praise—these two lines mean that by respecting others, one can abandon arrogance; one must contemplate the Buddha-nature as being of the same essence, seeing others as Buddhas.
The latter two lines mean that having practiced patience, one can abandon resentment; one must contemplate True Suchness (Tathatā) as being equal, knowing that slander is the same [as praise].
This is praise. △ Third, the complete relinquishment of body and mind.
One must ensure that both body and mind are abandoned together; the flesh, bones, and blood of the body are shared with all sentient beings.

The first two phrases jointly inherit the preceding [section on] practicing the perfection of giving (*dānapāramitā*) without interruption between body and mind; this is necessarily the attainment of the fourth [stage].
Regarding the foundations of mindfulness (*smṛtyupasthāna*), there is no longer any clinging to a self. The final two lines cause one to exhaust their full measure;
for once one has relinquished even one's own body, flesh, bones, and blood, how could there remain anything further of either body or mind?

It is by necessarily observing things that are suffering, empty, non-self, impermanent, and impure that one performs the work of the Buddha. Question: This is the preliminary expedient; what follows next?
One enters the *maṇḍala* to cultivate meditative concentration (*samādhi*) and wisdom (*prajñā*). Why, then, would one suddenly abandon body and life? The answer is this:

it refers to not being stingy with the parts of the body, not to the abandonment of body and life itself, for this is not the occasion for the great renunciation when emerging from the provisional [teachings].
All of these are for the purpose of accomplishing a mind free from theft. As it is said: "If even the monk’s insight requires that he abandon both body and mind, how much more so [in this case]?"
Furthermore, do not harbor a thieving mind to deviously appropriate for oneself gains and offerings. Second, do not employ expedient vehicles to deceive others;
do not take the Tathāgata’s teachings of provisional meaning and turn them into your own interpretations to mislead beginners.
Within the *neyārtha* (provisional) teachings, it is permitted to keep the one hundred and one necessary items, while only the other two are prohibited;
or perhaps it is permitted not to enter the great assembly, avoiding humiliation by refusing to accept [offerings]. Furthermore, in acts of giving, much does not reach the person's own body.
Now, we rely solely upon the *nītārtha* (definitive) teachings and do not rely upon the *neyārtha* teachings. As for the final two lines: "If, due to oneself, one is unable to offer..."

Regarding the first three precepts: should one encounter questions from beginners, yet fail to acknowledge one's own faults and instead perversely cite the provisional vehicles to demonstrate non-obstruction, the ignorant beginner will likewise believe and practice this.
This is to deceive oneself within and to delude others without; it is a crime of no small magnitude.
To acknowledge one’s fault and speak the truth—even if there were a transgression, it would be minor. △ Second, to seal [the teaching].
One attains true samādhi.
The Buddha seals this person. "Attaining true samādhi" means being sealed;
that is, being granted permission. This signifies that they will certainly realize perfect penetration. Contemplating this section on "Profound Severance" causes people to...

Feeling shame and remorse, he shed tears. It can be seen that when the patriarchs of the Final Dharma established the monastic groves (*saṃghārāma*), they did so out of compassion for the times, adapting themselves to benefit sentient beings as they could not help it.
Those who dwell within these institutions must feel constant shame at their own failure to attain realization.
Do not harbor even a hair’s breadth of thought regarding gain or profit; merely avoid transgression and offense.

Should you encounter someone who challenges this scripture, respond with sincere words of apology, acknowledging that you are unable to fulfill it in this degenerate age and must not resort to clever, unimpeded speech.

Furthermore, if there should be a person of superior capacity who masters this scripture and is able to uphold the definitive precepts, vowing to attain perfect penetration, you should feel ashamed [of your own lack].
In serving and honoring others, one must not perversely cite the faults of others to gloss over one's own transgressions.

When host and guest compete with one another, driven solely by self-interest, one ought to feel such shame that death would be preferable. The analysis of the characteristics of partiality and impartiality, as well as loss and gain, is hereby concluded.
△ Second, the adjudication of heterodox and orthodox doctrines.
That which I have spoken is called the Buddha’s teaching; that which is not spoken thus is the teaching of Pāpīyān.
The refutation of theft is complete. △ Fourth, the refutation of falsehood. There are two types of false speech: speaking what is untrue is minor falsehood;
falsely claiming to have realized the fruits [of the path] is major falsehood. That which is here to be severed is major falsehood. This must...

The conclusion is not merely the act of raising the mind; it is divided into two parts. First, a brief demonstration of the intent of the precept and exhortation, which is further divided into four sections.

First, a preliminary statement on how false speech causes great harm, which is further divided into three parts. First, following up on the previous point, it is shown that false speech constitutes becoming a māra.
Ānanda, it is thus with the sentient beings of the six realms in this world:

although they may have perfected the three practices of abstaining from killing, stealing, and sexual misconduct within their bodies and minds, if they engage in great falsehood, their *samādhi* will not attain purity; they will become demons of craving and views and lose the seed of the Tathāgata.

It is thus. Following upon the previous [discussion], this reveals that even those whose three practices are already perfected still fear this transgression; how much more so for those whose three practices are not yet perfected?
As for "great false speech," its name is merely indicated here and will be explained in its own section below.

Wēnlíng says: To covet offerings and seek one's own exaltation is called the "demon of craving" (āmiṣa-māra). To give rise to false views and claim that one is equal to the sages is called the "demon of views" (dṛṣṭi-māra).
△ Second, pointing to the reality and explaining the meaning of those words:
namely, claiming what has not been attained as attained, and declaring what has not been realized as realized; or seeking preeminence and supremacy in the world, saying to others:
"I have now attained the fruit of *srotāpanna*, the fruit of *sakṛdāgāmin*, the fruit of *anāgāmin*, and the fruit of *arhat*."

The Way of Han; the vehicle of the Pratyekabuddhas; and the various stages of Bodhisattvas, both those on the ten grounds and those prior to them—these seek such rituals and repentances and crave their offerings, claiming to have attained the Way.
"Attainment" refers to the realization of principle; "realization" refers to the attainment of the fruit. *Srotāpanna*.
The "equality" refers to the fruit; the Arhat is the path. This is because, in the principle of the Lesser Vehicle, one reaches the ultimate at the stage of the Arhat;
thus it is called the "path. Their vehicle is the same, their status is the same, and their fruit is the same. To seek the excellence of the World-Honored One, one must be reverent;
to seek his prostrations and repentance, one hopes for offerings. When a person repents before one who has attained the fruit, they invariably present offerings in abundance.

△ Third, the prediction concerning their destruction of goodness and downfall: they are *icchantikas* who extinguish the seed of the Buddha. It is as if a person were to cut down a *tāla* tree with a sword; the Buddha predicted of such people: *The Sūtra on the Great Nirvāṇa*, fascicle 24, "Chapter on the Prediction of the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Maitreya," states: "If there are sentient beings who, having heard this *Mahāparinirvāṇa-sūtra*, reject it, slander it, or speak ill of it, I predict that these people shall fall into the Avīci Hell. Furthermore, the *Sūtra on the Great Nirvāṇa*, fascicle 13, "Chapter on the Prediction of the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Maitreya," states: "If there are sentient beings who, having heard this *Mahāparinirvāṇa-sūtra*, reject it, slander it, or speak ill of it, I predict that these people shall fall into the Avīci Hell. Moreover, the *Sūtra on the Great Nirvāṇa*, fascicle 16, "Chapter on the Prediction of the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Maitreya," states: "If there are sentient beings who, having heard this *Mahāparinirvāṇa-sūtra*, reject it, slander it, or speak ill of it, I predict that these people shall fall into the Avīci Hell. And the *Sūtra on the Great Nirvāṇa*, fascicle 24, "Chapter on the Prediction of the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Maitreya," states: "If there are sentient beings who, having heard this *Mahāparinirvāṇa-sūtra*, reject it, slander it, or speak ill of it, I predict that these people shall fall into the Avīci Hell. Finally, the *Sūtra on the Great Nirvāṇa*, fascicle 25, "Chapter on the Prediction of the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Maitreya," states: "If there are sentient beings who, having heard this *Mahāparinirvāṇa-sūtra*, reject it, slander it, or speak ill of it, I predict that these people shall fall into the Avīci Hell. Thus, the Buddha predicted of these people: "They are *icchantikas* who destroy the seed of the Buddha. It is like a person cutting down a *tāla* tree with a sword. The Buddha predicted of these people.
Their roots of goodness are forever destroyed; they no longer possess knowledge or vision, sinking into the ocean of the three sufferings and failing to achieve samādhi.
Wēnlíng says: "Ekantika" is the same as *icchantika*. The *patala* tree cannot revive once it is severed by a blade;
this metaphor illustrates how great falsehoods permanently sever the roots of goodness. The "ocean of the three sufferings" refers to the three miserable realms. △ Second, expressing oneself.

The Prohibitory Edict Regarding Manifested False Buddhas: There is a prohibitory edict; all sages dare not dare to violate it. If one violates or leaks [this edict], it is sufficient to know that such a person is not a sage.

This is divided into two parts. First, a detailed demonstration that true persons must necessarily maintain secrecy. This is further divided into three sections. First, the edict concerning the esoteric transformation of the two sages.
This is further divided into three subsections. First, the designation of saving sentient beings according to their various types.
After my parinirvāṇa, I shall command the bodhisattvas and arhats to manifest their bodies within that age of the final dharma;
assuming various forms, they shall deliver those wandering in the cycle of rebirth.
The True Body (*dharmakāya*) is like space; it manifests forms in accordance with sentient beings, and is therefore called the Responsive Body (*nirmāṇakāya*).

Furthermore, within the two higher lands, these two sages possess a distinct, wondrous body of Dharma-nature (*dharmatākāya*), which appears in response to conditions within the Land of Common Dwelling.

This is merely a partial attainment of a transformation body that accords with the species of beings. It may also be produced through the Samādhi of Universally Manifesting Physical Form. △ Second, the detailed explanation.
Regarding the two aspects of following and opposing [the Dharma],
they may manifest as śramaṇas, white-robed laypeople, householders, kings, officials, boys, girls, and so forth,
even down to courtesans, widows, adulterers, thieves, butchers, and merchants.
Alternatively, he may manifest signs of downward conformity, because such traces are for the most part pure.

Likewise, he may manifest signs of downward opposition, because such traces are entirely defiled. That is to say, he manifests the three poisons to the multitude and even displays the signs of false views.
To those sentient beings who should be delivered by means of this body, he manifests it accordingly without fixed standard.
△ Third, regarding the Buddha-work, it is the same:
to engage in the same activities as others, to praise the Buddha-vehicle, and to cause their body and mind to enter *samādhi*.

This first phrase is one of the four means of integration (*saṃgrahavastu*). It applies equally to both pure and defiled matters, being identical with them in both cases. If [the activities] are the same...
While their types may be similar, their specific affairs differ; thus, they act with a mind of contrivance and defiance, not following one another in harmony.
The multitude joins them in these shared activities, intending to win their favor so as to eventually praise the Buddha Vehicle and transform them through it.
This samādhi is not fixed to the ear-faculty. △ Second, clarifying that the secret words must not be leaked.
He never spoke of himself, saying, "I am a true Bodhisattva" or "I am a true Arhat. To "leak the Buddha’s secret cause" means to speak lightly of one's own limited learning;
to "speak lightly of limited learning" means to easily disclose these words to those who are late learners. △ Third, the permission to secretly transmit at the time of death.

Except for cases where, at the end of life, there is a secret entrustment of the Dharma (*guhyadharma-parindanā*), [the Master] both manifests taking birth and manifests passing away. "Yin" (陰) means dark or hidden.

The secret entrustment of the Dharma is intended to warn that one must certainly act; yet even this disclosure is done in an indirect manner, as in the cases of Du Shun and Qingliang. Therefore, it is called a "dark entrustment."
△ Second, the reason why the words [of those who claim otherwise] must be false:
How could such a person delude sentient beings and commit a great falsehood?
If one abides, one does not leak; if one leaks, one does not abide. This is a fixed principle, just as with the three sages, Feng, Qian, and others.
It is so. If he continues to remain even after leaking these words, it is clearly evident that he is a heterodox person seeking gain and offerings; be careful not to believe him.
△ Third, turning the teaching to clarify the instructions of the former Buddhas.
"You shall instruct the people of the world to cultivate samādhi, and thereafter further eliminate all great false claims.
This is called the fourth definitive, pure, and clear instruction of the Tathāgata, the World-Honored Buddhas of the past."

The meaning is no different from what preceded. △ Fourth, determining whether the attainment of enlightenment is possible or not. This is divided into two parts. First, a detailed explanation of the metaphor that there is no attainment through non-interruption.

This is further divided into three sections. First, citing the metaphor of carving dung. This is further divided into two sections. First, clarifying that [attainment] cannot be achieved by means of the metaphor.
Therefore, Ānanda, if one does not sever this great falsehood, it is like carving human excrement into the shape of sandalwood and hoping for its fragrance;
such a thing is impossible.
△ Second, he subsequently demonstrates the contradiction with the teachings by means of his physical demeanor:

"In my teaching, I instruct the bhikṣus that at the site of the Way, they must maintain a straightforward mind; even amidst all activities within the four modes of deportment, there must be no pretense whatsoever."
"What is meant by 'claiming for oneself the attainment of the Dharma of those superior to men'? Wēnlíng says:

Jìngmíng states that "the straightforward mind is the site of enlightenment (dōucháng) because it is free from falsehood. This refers to the four modes of deportment: walking, standing, sitting, and reclining.
"Claiming for oneself" means to falsely claim. "The Dharma of those superior to men" refers to the dharmas of those who have attained the various fruits [of the path]. △
Second, the illustration by means of a false claim, which is further divided into two parts. First, clarifying the incurrence of guilt through an analogy:
it is like a destitute person who falsely claims to be an emperor, thereby bringing about his own execution and destruction.
△ Second, using subsequent analogies to manifest the depth of the offense.
How much more so for the Dharma King! How could one falsely usurp [his position]?
All fruits are the rank of the Dharma King. △ Second, citing the analogy of biting one's navel. This is further divided into two parts. First, the initial demonstration.
The cause and effect are false because the ground is not true; thus, the fruit brought forth is circuitous.
Because one takes great falsehood as the cause, it is not true; seeking progress, one instead retreats; seeking ascent, one instead falls. Therefore it is said:
The result is circuitous. △ Second, the subsequent analogy regarding the failure to achieve Bodhi:
To seek the Buddha’s Bodhi is like a person attempting to bite their own navel;
whom could such a one hope to accomplish? Wénlǐng says: In the *Zuǒzhuan*, "biting the navel" refers to being ultimately unable to reach it. [This applies] to seeking [Bodhi] through false speech.

Perfect Enlightenment. It would be like trying to bite one's own navel with one's own mouth; how could it ever be reached? △ Second, the profound assurance that those capable of severing [the afflictions] will certainly succeed:
"If bhikṣus have minds as straight as a bowstring, are entirely truthful, and enter into samādhi, they will forever be free from demonic interference."
"I certify this person. They shall achieve the unsurpassed awakening of a Bodhisattva. Wénlǐng says:
"Previously, because of being circuitous and indirect, one ultimately could not achieve success; now, because the string can be made straight, his achievement is certified.
The unsurpassed awakening of a Bodhisattva is precisely the true mind of the causal stage of perfect penetration (*yúntōng*). However, because...
The fruit of meditative concentration is also unsurpassed bodhi. II. Determining the False and the Correct:
What I have spoken here is called the teaching of the Buddha; that which is not spoken thus is the teaching of Pāpīyān.
The explanation of the four major sections is hereby completed.

First, replying to the inquiry and reaffirming the strict precepts.
Ānanda, regarding your question on the gathering of the mind: I shall now first explain the sublime gateway for training in the entry into samādhi.
Those who seek the path of a bodhisattva must first maintain these four kinds of discipline, as pure and clear as ice and frost.
At the beginning, when asked about the site of practice (*dojō*), it was explained how to gather the mind and enter *samādhi*; thus, the Buddha’s concluding response addresses that prior question.
The "wondrous gate" refers to the gate of the ear. The final phrase states that one should maintain it so that it is pure and free from even a speck of defilement.

These are minor false speech, frivolous speech, double-tongued speech, and harsh speech. This is because once one has already abandoned the coarse, the subtle will necessarily not arise.
Question: Sexual misconduct, killing, and stealing are the most coarse physical actions; why, then, are they said to be subtler than the three mental actions?
Furthermore, great falsehood is the most grave verbal action; why, then, is it said to be subtler than the four verbal actions? Answer: Regarding sexual misconduct, killing, and stealing...

The mirror in the void is detached from things and has no reliance; this is the wisdom of the Buddhas. Only that which has things mixed with it and relies upon them is able to reflect objects."
If one has not yet been able to illuminate oneself, one must necessarily attain the wisdom that is detached from objects and dwells nowhere; these functions then operate in mutual interdependence.

Only after this can object and self mutually illuminate, and mind and environment be simultaneously fused. Thus, the bodies and lands of all Buddhas and sentient beings enter into one another without the need for physical movement or the application of thought.
Every dharma is omnipresent and every phenomenon is unimpeded. Upon raising the eyes, the thousand sages appear all at once.

At the locus of touch, the myriad phenomena are clearly manifest. With a single flower or a single incense offering, one makes universal offerings to all lands as numerous as motes of dust. With a single practice or a single characteristic, one expands infinitely.
Without relying on supernatural powers and without engaging in conceptual thought, such is the fundamental nature of every dharma within the tranquil site of enlightenment.

The construction of the *dōjō* is completed. △ Second, the stages of cultivation and realization. This is divided into two parts. First, the initial seven-day period for establishing meditative concentration (*samādhi*) and wisdom (*prajñā*).

This is further divided into two sections. First, the practice of the first seven days. This is further divided into three sections. The first is the practice of prostrations, recitation, and circumambulation during the first seven days.
During the first seven days, one should with utmost sincerity prostrate to the Tathāgatas of the ten directions, the great Bodhisattvas, and those bearing the title of Arhat.

Constantly throughout the six periods of the day and night, one should recite mantras around the altar and practice the Way with a sincere heart, performing one hundred and eight recitations during each period.
Wenling says: In all aspirations, taking refuge in the Triple Gem is the primary expedient means.
Therefore, during the first seven days, one should with utmost sincerity prostrate to the names of the Tathāgatas, Bodhisattvas, and Arhats.

This is done so as to rely upon their inconceivable power to initiate practice and assist on the Path. [This is the power of others (parāśraya). Next, during the second seven days, one should single-mindedly resolve to...
Aspiration.
During the second seven-day period, one should single-mindedly and exclusively cultivate the bodhisattva aspiration, with the mind uninterrupted.
In my Vinaya, there is already a teaching on aspirations.
If one were to provide a general summary, it would not exceed the four great floods. Wēn-líng says: "According to the Vinaya teachings, one should single-mindedly make vows.
When practice and vows are firm and strong, one attains great valor. Wŭ-xīng says:
"The 'teachings on prior vows' refers to such things as the ten great vows of the *Brahmajāla Sūtra*. △ Afterward, for three weeks, one should exclusively recite mantras.
During the third seven-day period, one should single-mindedly recite the Buddha’s *pāṭala* mantra at all twelve periods of the day.

Wēnlíng says: "The time is without interruption, and the recitation of the mantra has no limit; by reciting and upholding it with single-minded devotion, one is ultimately able to move the deities through sincerity and achieve success through diligent effort.
II. On the Final Day: Concentration and Wisdom. This is divided into three parts. First, the Manifestation of the Buddha.
He strokes [the practitioner’s] head.

On the seventh day, the Tathāgatas of the ten directions simultaneously appear at the place where the mirrors reflect one another’s light; it is there that they receive the stroking of their heads by the Buddhas—this can be seen.
During the preceding three seven-day periods, they likewise possess a coarse yet settled mind, though this is supplemented by prostrations, recitation, vows, and mantras.
It is not that one does not gather the mind and turn it inward to hear [the sound]. If the water of the mind is not pure, how could the Buddha manifest?
Wēnlíng says: "Where the mirrors reflect each other's light, the wisdom of the Buddha arises; this is the mutual resonance of the Way.
△ Second, the accomplishment of the settled mind.
Immediately at the site of practice, cultivate *samādhi*.
In this method, one exclusively practices "hearing back" (*fanwen*), not allowing even a single thought to take that auditory object as its condition.

One should focus intently on the wondrous realm within hearing previously explained—that is, "entering the flow and losing the object. This should be practiced while seated for a long duration, perhaps lasting...
Practice elimination. Simply engage in the single flavor of constant "hearing-warding" without interruption. △ Third, the accomplishment of the wisdom-mind:
it can cause those who practice and study in this degenerate age to have bodies and minds as clear and pure as lapis lazuli.

The first phrase reveals that the concentrated mind serves as the proximate cause (*upādāna-hetu*), while practices such as maintaining the mantra at the site of enlightenment (*maṇḍala*) serve as the contributory conditions (*pratyaya*).
It is by the power of these causes and conditions that [the state] is brought about. The final two phrases describe the wondrous realm from which wisdom arises.

Although body, speech, and mind encompass both the true and the delusory, with respect to the character "Bright" (*ming*), it is simply the manifestation of the marks of the Great Wisdom Light of the True Body and True Mind.
Furthermore, although the word "pure" (*śuddha*) is also said to signify "true," it simultaneously reveals that the deluded body and deluded mind are ultimately unattainable;

this constitutes the reason for its being truly pure. The final phrase uses two metaphors to clarify this purity: moreover, the true body and true mind are precisely the nature of hearing (*śravaṇatā*).
When the sense-object of sound is forgotten, all six objects of the senses are discarded; thus, it is supremely clear and pure. This occurs within meditative concentration, giving rise to wisdom.
For a time, one attains correspondence with the state in which quiescence (*śamatha*) is manifest.

Having completed the cultivation of meditative concentration (*samādhi*) and wisdom (*prajñā*) during the first three weeks, [the practitioner] suddenly realizes the fruit of sainthood (*āryaphala*) over the course of two hundred days. This is divided into three parts. First: preventing failure due to impurity.
Ānanda, if among this bhikṣu’s original preceptor or the ten bhikṣus within the assembly there is even one who is impure,
such a site of practice will for the most part not be accomplished.
As for those who do not achieve success, it is simply that they are unable to realize the fruit within a fixed period. One must carefully select one's teachers and friends;
one must not indiscriminately associate with those who are not of the human path. △ Second, the formal demonstration of the completion of the period and the realization of the first fruit.
After three weeks, he sat upright in meditative seclusion for one hundred days. Those of keen faculties attained the stage of *srotāpanna* without rising from their seats.
Those of sharp faculties are those whose afflictive obstructions are both light and whose nature of wisdom is clear and enlightened. Guishan says:

"Regarding the stage of *srotāpanna*, according to the [Lotus Sūtra] stages, this corresponds to the first *śraddhā-caryā* (faith) of the Perfect Teaching. If one follows the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra*, it is the initial entry into the *bhūmi* and *vihāra* of the Distinct and Perfect Teachings.
According to the first interpretation, this corresponds to the state where movement and stillness do not arise, having severed the eighty-eight *kleśas*; this is likewise merely a stage.

"Equaling the Small Vehicle’s [attainment of] the Path of Seeing" does not mean truly attaining the small fruits. According to the latter interpretation, it refers to reaching the stage where quiescence is manifested before one;
this level is equal to the first bhūmi of the Separate Teaching (Pratyekabuddha) and the first abode of the Perfect Teaching (Mahāyāna). Both explanations are valid.

In the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra*, the names and stages of the four fruits of the Small Vehicle are borrowed to correspond sequentially to the Mahāyāna stages of abiding, advancing, and direction (*sthiti*, *caryā*, *pratipatti*), and the grounds (*bhūmi*). △ Three.
Even after the opening has occurred but before it is perfected, one still perceives the Buddha-nature.
Although their body and mind have not yet achieved the holy fruit, they know with certainty that their attainment of Buddhahood will not be in error.

According to the former interpretation of Master Yuan, this stage corresponds to the five contemplations (*pañca-vipaśyanā*); according to the latter interpretation, it corresponds to the ten stages of faith (*daśa-śraddhā*).
Next, regarding the principle of certainty realized therein, one clearly perceives the Buddha-nature.
One gains self-confidence in one's original nobility and no longer suffers from the anxiety of not having attained realization; this is what is called "having reached the stage beyond doubt.
The sequence of cultivation and realization is hereby concluded. △ Third, the conclusion and response to the request.
"You have asked how the *maṇḍala* is established; it is thus.
Wuxing said, "Regarding the ritual procedures for the *maṇḍala*, their practice in this land during the final age is exceedingly difficult. Nevertheless, as for the mantras one recites..."
The following text also permits this. Because they do not enter the *maṇḍala*, there are conditions through which they receive benefit according to their capacity.

The repeated request for the explanation of the *maṇḍala* is concluded. △ Second, the repeated request for the explanation of the divine mantra (*dhāraṇī*). This is divided into three parts. First, the assembly’s repeated request, which is further divided into two.

First, the description of the personal request, which is further divided into three. First, the description of encountering the sorcery and receiving rescue, which is further divided into three. First—

Describing his state of having heard much but not yet realized, Ānanda prostrated at the Buddha’s feet and said to the Buddha: "Since my renunciation of the household life, I have relied upon the Buddha’s affectionate favor;
because I sought extensive learning, I have not yet realized the unconditioned."

The previous error regarding reliance on affection has already been explained. In the Hīnayāna, the four fruits are considered unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*). △ Second, the account of being bound by an evil incantation:
he encountered the binding spell of that Brahmā; though his mind remained clear, his power was not free.
This is because the power of the first fruit (*srotāpanna*) is weak. △ Third, describing the reliance on mantras for transformation and rescue:
"I encountered Mañjuśrī, who enabled my liberation;
now I must supplement this with Mañjuśrī’s mantra to go and provide protection. △ Second, describing how the mantra was received but not yet heard.
"Although I have received the protection of the Tathāgata’s *uṣṇīṣa* divine mantra and have secretly obtained its power, I have not yet heard it directly.
Tianru said: "In the past, Ānanda secretly relied on the power of the mantra to resolve his difficulty regarding lust; therefore, it is said that he 'secretly obtained it without having heard it.
△ Third, the request for a further proclamation for the broad benefit [of others].
I only pray that, out of great compassion, you will proclaim it once more. Out of pity, rescue those practitioners in this assembly, as well as those in saṃsāra in the future.
By receiving the Buddha’s secret voice, may their bodies and minds be liberated.
Liberation of the body refers to the exhaustion of karma and the departure from suffering. Liberation of the mind refers to the destruction of delusions and the realization of the Truth.
△ Second, the communal invitation for a general service.
At that time, the entire assembly in the gathering all paid homage, waiting expectantly to hear the secret verses of the Tathāgata.

II. The Tathāgata’s Repeated Explanation. This section is divided into two parts. First, the actual recitation of the divine mantra. This is further divided into three parts. First, the light-omens preceding the mantra. This is further divided into four parts.
First, the Tathāgata emits light from the crown of his head.
At that time, from within the *uṣṇīṣa* on the crown of the World-Honored One’s head, there surged forth a light of a hundred jewels.
That light signifies many meanings, which shall now be briefly explained and analyzed.
This section and the following one reveal the esoteric within the exoteric, as manifested from the very body of the Tathāgata himself. The *uṣṇīṣa* is the invisible crown of the head.
The emission of light from the crown of the head symbolizes that wisdom arises based on the principle of the Dharmakāya.
That the light is endowed with a hundred jewels symbolizes that wisdom contains ten thousand functions. △ Second, the manifestation of Tathāgatas within the light.
From within the light, a thousand-petaled jewel lotus emerges, upon which a manifested Tathāgata sits amidst the precious flower.
The emergence of the lotus from the light signifies that practice issues forth based on wisdom; the manifested Buddha sitting upon the lotus signifies that practice adorns the sublime fruit.
△ Third, the manifested Buddha emits light from his crown.
Ten paths of light, composed of a hundred jewels, are emitted from the crown [of the head].
This section and the following section represent the secret within the secret, as they further manifest from the transformation buddhas (*nirmāṇakāya*).
This is precisely what is meant by "the Buddha-crown from among the Buddha-crowns" emitting "the jewel-light from among the jewel-lights," signifying this.

The Mantra King is the most honored among the honored, the most wondrous among the wondrous. The ten rays of light also symbolize the profound wisdom of the ten powers, which fully possesses myriad functions;
there is no request to which it does not respond. One beholds the compassion that embraces all. △ Within the four rays of light, the Vajra manifests.
Each and every ray of light universally manifests ten times the sands of the Ganges of Vajrapāṇis, who hold mountains aloft and grasp thunderbolts, pervading the entire realm of empty space.
This symbolizes the immeasurable secret divine power that subdues demons and heretics; there is no evil that it does not destroy. Behold this act of suppression and subjugation.
Awe-inspiring. △ Second, the great assembly listens with reverence.

The assembly looks up in admiration, harboring both awe and affection; they seek the Buddha’s compassionate protection and listen with single-minded devotion as the Tathāgata of the Unseen Summit Emitting Light proclaims the divine mantra.
"Veneration" (*wei*) means to revere his majesty; "love" (*ai*) means to cherish his compassion—this refers to the heart's embrace.

Sentient beings, through these two modes of embrace, accord with and follow the Tathāgata, such that his spiritual transformations proceed without obstruction. Within this dhāraṇī, these various subtle principles are secretly contained;
therefore, they are here set forth. △ Third: The Chapter on the Phrases of the Divine Dhāraṇī.

*tu lo oṃ phaṭ* (26) *svāhā* (27). Gu Shan said: "The divine mantras in various sutras generally do not reverse [the characters].
Among the five types of non-reversal, this belongs to 'secret non-reversal.

Within the four categories [of non-reversal], it is a case of reversing the characters but not reversing the sounds. Tiantai synthesized this, concluding that it does not go beyond the four *siddhārtha* (fourfold benefits).
Tianru said: Regarding the four *siddhāntas* cited by Gushan from Tiantai, *si* means "pervasive" and *tandan* means "bestowal.
The various sages universally bestow these four dharmas upon sentient beings. First, the *loka-siddhānta* (worldly standpoint) consists of teachings given according to different circumstances.
The first is the benefit of generating joy; the second, the *puruṣa-siddhānta*, is the benefit of generating goodness;
the third, the *pratipakṣa-siddhānta*, is the benefit of destroying evil; and the fourth, the *paramārtha-siddhānta*, is the benefit of entering into principle.
○ Secret mantras are not merely Sanskrit; they are, moreover, the secret words of all the sages and worthies. For...
The Sanskrit language is not understood here in this land; yet it is that which the people of India understand and employ in their daily lives.
As for secret mantras (*dhāraṇīs*), not only do ordinary people in India not know them, but logically, saints and sages of lower stages should not comprehend the mantras of higher stages.
Generally speaking, when saints and sages propagate the teachings, they follow the pattern of having both exoteric and esoteric doctrines, just as in the case of medicine.

There are generally two approaches to treating illness. The first is the transmission of prescriptions, which explicitly explains the origins of the disease, the nature of the medicinal substances, and the methods of processing and administration, much like the Buddha’s exoteric teachings.
The second is the transmission of the medicine itself, wherein none of these details are explicitly explained;

one simply provides the medicine for the patient to take so that the illness may be cured, without necessarily requiring knowledge of what the medicine is or how it was treated, much like the Buddha’s esoteric teachings.
Therefore, secret mantras (vidyā-mantra) are exactly like administering medicine; there is no necessity to seek their meaning. If understanding arises, the mantra is lost.
Sentient beings should simply believe in and uphold them, and they will naturally receive various benefits.

Furthermore, although secret mantras cannot be interpreted, there are also a few aspects that should be known, which briefly exhaust three meanings. The first is the power of principle (dharma). This refers to, by means of one—
The characters contain boundless subtle principles and are thus called *dhāraṇī*. This means that they encompass all phenomena and uphold immeasurable meanings;
the power of these words fully embodies the principles they express, just as in this land [of China] the terms "Yuan," "Heng," "Li," and "Zhen" [represent the totality of the hexagram Qian].
Thus, one may also avoid misfortune and bring about auspiciousness. Second is the power of majestic virtue (*prabhāva*).

This refers to all Buddhas, Bodhisattvas, and other holy sages of both provisional and ultimate [teachings], whose majestic virtue is profound and grave and who possess great power. By invoking their names, one’s wishes will be fulfilled according to one’s intent.
It is just as in this world, where if one relies upon the name and reputation of a person of influence, one can subdue evil and escape from calamity.

Third is the power of truthful speech. Because Buddhas, Bodhisattvas, and all noble sages give rise to a heart of great compassion out of pity for sentient beings, they utter words of sincerity and truth, offering incantatory vows that sentient beings may leave suffering behind, attain happiness, and transform from the mundane into the sacred.
Therefore, by reciting these, one can achieve benefit in accordance with the words. This is just as in the world, where even those who practice genuine cultivation can still offer incantatory vows.

If fortune and misfortune are accomplished merely by following one's words, how much more so for the true compassion and vows of the sages and worthies who have realized the principle and entered the stages?

How could these be measured? This is equivalent in meaning to incantations and curses. Briefly stated, it is because of these three meanings that upholding [this practice] yields unfathomable spiritual efficacy.
However, one must maintain firm faith and uphold it single-mindedly; only when the merit is fulfilled will the results be attained. If...
