Those who harbor doubts, interrupt their practice, or cease midway; or those who fail to maintain the altar and precepts according to the Dharma, yet slander the mantras as being ineffective, will incur great sin and suffering.
This is because even in the mundane world, the incantations used to restrain snakes, scorpions, sores, and malaria still yield manifest efficacy.
How much more so for that which is the dwelling place of the majestic spiritual power of the Sages and the Truthful—how could there be empty words? You must strictly guard against this.

There are those among the people of the world who say that if one recites the mantras without following the proper sequence, they will hide their vulgar and crude expressions for fear of being ridiculed by others.
This is truly ignorant and groundless slander; even those with a modicum of wisdom should not be deluded by such talk. As for the four *siddhārtha* (the four ways of benefiting beings)...

Regarding "things": it does not stop at secret mantras. Generally, when the Buddha emits light, manifests supernatural powers, or preaches the Dharma—these foremost of all skillful means—he desires that every person awaken to and enter into the Buddha’s knowledge and vision.
This is what is called acting solely for the sake of the one great causal event.
This is precisely the benefit of entering into principle. For those who have not yet been able to awaken and enter, one first provides the second benefit:

the eradication of the seeds and habitual tendencies of afflictions, which is the benefit of destroying evil. After a long time, once obstructions are exhausted, they shall eventually awaken and enter.
For those who are still unable to destroy evil, one then provides the third: causing them to give rise to wholesome minds and establish [virtuous practice].
One establishes virtuous conduct; as the power of goodness gradually strengthens, evil habits naturally recede.
If that person is still unable to give rise to goodness, one should then provide them with the fourth [type of gift], causing them to experience joy; this is the benefit of joy.

This is also a matter of planting slight and minor roots of goodness for them, serving as a distant causal condition for the [first] three superior types. Should that person still be incapable of this...
Those who, having given rise to joy, instead turn into those who harbor hatred and slander, have long been perceived by the Buddha; thus he remains silent and non-active toward them.
If we consider the teachings according to the one great period: the *Avataṃsaka* primarily enters into principle while briefly encompassing the latter three;
the Hīnayāna teachings primarily destroy evil while briefly encompassing the latter two; and the Human-and-Heavenly teachings primarily give rise to goodness while...
This briefly combines with the latter one. Among the various realms of rebirth, those who are upright rejoice solely in joy;

that is to say, by first providing protection and extracting them from suffering, one causes them to give rise to joy, and they may also gradually ascend to the [realms of] the upper three. Now, we discuss only the four *siddhis* of secret mantras (*guhyamantra*).

The sequences listed by various masters all proceed from the inferior toward the superior. First, regarding "joy in the world" (*loka-saṃtoṣaṇa*): this refers to benefiting sentient beings according to their respective regions.
For example, there are cases such as carrying [an amulet] to escape calamity or to seek wealth.

As for what Tiantai refers to—reciting the names of the spirit-kings so that the local tribes are struck with fear—this is merely one path for escaping the perils of ghosts and spirits. Second, regarding the generation of goodness in people:
this includes causing those who have not yet received the precepts to obtain them, and causing those who are not yet diligent to become diligent, and so forth. As for Tian...

Tiantai’s comparison to a military signal that corresponds [to the situation] without being subject to censure or prohibition also clarifies that it merely brings about wholesome states without obstruction.

Third, regarding the counteractive measure for destroying evil, such as causing the mind of lust to cease suddenly, Tiantai likens this to the poor man who feigned anger but whose [anger] ceased instantly upon hearing the verse;
this likewise uses a metaphor to clarify that the person reciting the mantra does not [act out of self-interest].

One knows that evil is destroyed by means of its source. Regarding the fourth, "entering the principle through the primary meaning" (*paramārtha*), this refers to such things as entering the *anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti* (patience regarding the non-arising of phenomena).

Tiantai’s metaphor of a wise minister who understands the words while others do not is merely a metaphor for the fact that the source from which the power of the mantra awakens one is unfathomable to ordinary people. In brief, this clarifies the four aspects of the secret.

It brings benefit to all. The reason for this cannot be understood through the teachings of the Exoteric Vehicle (*vyākhyāna-dharma*). If it were possible to fathom or know [its workings], why would the Esoteric be so esteemed?
Practitioners should simply have firm faith and maintain their resolve; there is no need for speculative deliberation. The formal exposition of the divine mantra is hereby concluded.
△ Second, the explanation of the benefits of the mantra. This is divided into two parts. First, its essential utility for all Buddhas is evident;

it is not only that sentient beings would be left without recourse apart from this mantra, but even the Buddhas would lack much of their functional capacity without it. This is further divided into three sections.
First, the indication of its full name.
Ānanda, these subtle and wondrous verses of the secret *gaṭha* of the *Śītātapatrā* (Cooling Parasol) from the gathered light of the Buddha’s crown—

specifically the three characters of "Crown-Light-Gathering"— were, in truth, originally spoken by the Transformation Buddha of the Crown-Light; furthermore, each possesses its own symbolic significance.
"Uṣṇīṣa" (the crown) signifies supreme excellence; "light" signifies majestic spiritual power; "gathering" signifies divine function. "Gāthā" clarifies that there are verses within the mantra.
A major section is called a "chapter" (*varga*), as in the division into five assemblies (*pañca-khaṇḍa*).

A finer division is called a "line" (*pada*). "Subtle and wondrous" clarifies that it is hidden, profound, and unfathomable. △ Second, fully manifesting its various functions, which is further divided into three parts. First, the general [explanation].
It indicates cause and effect.
It gives birth to all Buddhas of the ten directions. By means of this mantra-heart, the Tathāgatas of the ten directions attain unexcelled, right, and universal enlightenment.

The two characters "birth" (sheng) and "arising" (chu) clarify the formation of the secret cause. The two characters "attaining" (de) and "accomplishing" (cheng) represent the assistance toward the ultimate fruit and the vision of the Buddha.
From the initial resolve to the final consummation, one can never depart from these; they are truly the essential general characteristics. △ Second, the specific enumeration of the essentials.
Furthermore, it is divided into six sections. First, subduing demons and restraining external influences:
the Tathāgatas of the ten directions hold this mantra-heart to subdue all demons and restrain all non-Buddhists.
By the power of this mantra, one shall be rendered free from delusion and confusion. △ Second, the function of manifesting the body and preaching the Dharma:

The Tathāgatas of the ten directions, riding upon this Mantra-Mind, sit upon precious lotus flowers and respond to lands as numerous as motes of dust throughout the ten directions. The Tathāgatas of the ten directions...
Containing this *dhāraṇī*-heart, one turns the Great Wheel of Dharma within lands as numerous as motes of dust.
"Those who ride" refers to those who rely [upon it]. Regarding the term "*dhāraṇī*-heart," following the interpretation of Wu-xing, it refers generally to the entire *dhāraṇī* as the "heart-mantra";
that is to say, it is called a "heart-mantra. It is the most essential method within the Secret Treasury; therefore, it is termed a *dhāraṇī*.

Regarding the word "citta" (mind): if this is the case, then the character for "mind" (*citta*) is used metaphorically, as in the *Prajñāpāramitā-hṛdaya-sūtra* (Heart Sutra), where it does not refer to the six characters beginning with *siddham*.
Those [six characters] are merely the name of the mantra.

Furthermore, considering that *tadyathā* introduces the recitation of the mantra, the portion from the character *oṃ* onwards is what constitutes the actual mantra; it consists of no more than eight phrases and thirty-four characters.

The characters preceding [the mantra] are the names of the Three Jewels, along with those of various external protectors, as well as the category of "words of truth" (*satyavākya*) that assist the mantra.
If one is unable to hold the entire text, one may begin from the syllable *Oṃ*; this follows the precedent of the nine sacred syllables of the Cundī mantra.
As for "sitting upon a lotus and universally responding," this refers to manifesting the Buddha-body in the form of the marks of attaining enlightenment. "Containing" means to keep it secret within.
The meaning of "as the basis" is that one takes this esoteric principle as the foundation to expound the exoteric teachings. △ Third, the function of bestowing predictions upon oneself and others:

The Tathāgatas of the ten directions, by upholding this mantra-heart, are able to touch the crowns of their heads and bestow predictions throughout the ten directions, even before their own fruits have been fully realized.
Furthermore, throughout the ten directions, one receives the Buddha’s prediction of enlightenment (*vyākaraṇa*).
"Bestowing" (*mo shou*) refers to empowering through mantras so that one will certainly attain Buddhahood; this may be compared to the *gonglo* wasp's incantation over the *mingling* caterpillar.
That one has received such a prediction can be seen: whenever there is one who upholds this mantra, the Buddha knows that they will certainly achieve it.
Because it is the Buddha-way, he bestows this prediction. △ Fourth, the function of rescuing from suffering and distress:
The Tathāgatas of the ten directions, relying on this mantra-heart, are able to extricate and save the multitudes from suffering throughout the ten directions; that is to say, from the hells.

Hungry ghosts, animals, the blind, the deaf, and the mute; the suffering of encountering those one hates, the suffering of separation from those one loves, and the suffering of not obtaining what one seeks;

the blazing intensity of the five aggregates; and all manner of calamities, both great and small—may these be simultaneously liberated. May there be freedom from the perils of bandits, the perils of armies, the perils of kings, and the perils of prisons.
Calamities of wind, fire, and water, as well as hunger, thirst, and poverty, shall dissolve and vanish upon being brought to mind.
The eight sufferings and eight difficulties contained herein also differ from the conventional enumeration.

Ordinarily, the eight sufferings are defined by pairing birth, aging, sickness, and death with the latter four—enmity, resentment, and so forth. Here, however, the three miserable realms and the impairment of the sense faculties are substituted for those.

These constitute the eight; furthermore, they are augmented by various minor calamities (*pārṣṇy-antarāya*), which exhaust all remaining sufferings—such as the "various calamities" mentioned in the *Bhaiṣajyaguru-sūtra* being an example.
The eight difficulties (*aṣṭāv akṣaṇāḥ*) also differ from those in other sūtras; here, they are defined as:
being a rebel king, a prisoner, a jailer, wind, fire, water, and famine. Famine and thirst are synonymous with starvation; furthermore, poverty is added to these as well.
This merely exhausts the remaining difficulties. △ Fifth, the matter of serving a teacher and inheriting the Dharma:

Following this mantra-heart, the Tathāgatas of the ten directions are able to serve spiritual friends throughout the ten directions; within the four modes of deportment, they provide offerings as desired.
Within the assemblies of Tathāgatas as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, they are promoted as Great Dharma Princes.
The power of mantras can cause the four requisites to be fully provided and enable one to know the minds of others; thus, it fulfills the function of serving the teacher.

Furthermore, it can open the mind to penetrate the essential points of the Dharma; thus, it fulfills the function of succeeding to the Dharma. △ Sixth, the function of gathering and transforming those close to oneself.

The Tathāgatas of the ten directions practice this mantra-heart; it is able to gather and sustain their close karmic causes throughout the ten directions, causing those of the Hīnayāna to hear the secret treasury without giving rise to alarm or fear.
"Intimate cause" refers to the intimate conditions accumulated over successive kalpas. "Receiving and guiding" is exemplified by [the Buddha's] exhorting Ānanda; this is it.

Regarding the "Secret Vehicle of True Reality," one must necessarily abandon the three [vehicles] and establish the one. When the Lesser Vehicle hears this, they are often struck with alarm and doubt; the power of the mantra can cause them to reach a definitive understanding and be free from doubt.
△ Third, the summary of the beginning and the end.
The Tathāgatas of the ten directions recited this mantra-heart and attained unexcelled enlightenment; they sat beneath the Bodhi tree and entered Great Nirvāṇa.

The Tathāgatas of the ten directions transmitted this mantra-heart, and after their parinirvāṇa, entrusted it with the affairs of the Buddha-dharma, so that it might ultimately be upheld and maintained.
The precepts are strictly purified, attaining complete clarity.

The first section covers the period from his initial attainment of enlightenment until his entry into *nirvāṇa*; the second section spans from the True Dharma (*saddharma*) age to the Final Dharma (*paścima-dharma*) age.
In both cases, one relies upon the power of the mantra; it may be said that from beginning to end, it cannot be dispensed with. △ Third, further clarification.
It is inexhaustible.
If I were to recite this Buddha-Uṣṇīṣa-Raśmi-Sañcaya-Pāṭala Dhāraṇī from dawn until dusk,
with the sounds linked together and the syllables and phrases never overlapping, it could not be exhausted even after kalpas as numerous as the sands of the Ganges.
This inexhaustibility refers to the essential requirements of the Buddhas; it is inherently inexhaustible and does not depend on the requirements of sentient beings.
The section on the essential requirements of the Buddhas is concluded. △ Second, the benefits for sentient beings: these sentient beings, by principle, encompass the nine realms.
The text mostly follows the conventions of others. Second: first, specifically indicating its superior name.
This dhāraṇī is also called the "Crown of the Tathāgata" (*tathāgatoṣṇīṣa*).
Compared to the full name mentioned above, this is a concise designation. To call it simply "Buddhoṣṇīṣa" specifically highlights its supreme excellence, so that sentient beings may...
One must receive and uphold it with the utmost reverence, never treating it with negligence or contempt. △ Second, fully manifesting its majestic power, divided into three parts.
First, showing that practitioners must rely upon it to encourage its recitation, further divided into two. First, the actual recitation wards off demons from afar.
"You who are still in training and have not yet exhausted the cycle of saṃsāra, if you resolve with utmost sincerity to attain arhatship,
yet do not maintain this dhāraṇī while seated in the bodhimaṇḍa, it is impossible for your body and mind to remain far removed from all demonic activities."
Now, those at or below the three fruits of the Hīnayāna have not yet transcended the cycle of birth and death (*saṃsāra*); thus it is said they have not exhausted *saṃsāra*.

This refers to those who, as previously mentioned, enter the ritual arena (*maṇḍala*) with a fixed term to attain realization. If they do not maintain [the precepts], they will certainly encounter demons;

therefore, within the previous ritual arena, the instruction was to maintain them exclusively. In the current text, the passage "if one does not maintain... follows, using negative language to provide an exhortation that one must certainly [maintain them].
It must be maintained. From this, one should know that among all practitioners, who ought not to maintain compassion?

Nowadays, we see that many mountain retreats and monasteries where silent cultivation is practiced have fallen into neglect regarding the maintenance of mantra recitation. Consequently, people frequently suffer from wind-disorders or insanity;
even if they do not become insane, they often encounter terrifying or seductive visions. All of these are the result of such negligence. How could the words of the Sage ever be otherwise?
"Is it empty? [The questioner] asks why there are no bodhisattvas. [The master] answers: "There are three meanings for this. First, those who do not lack the status of a bodhisattva:
these are those whose own fruition is not yet complete, yet who have received a prediction from a Buddha, serve spiritual friends (kalyāṇamitra), and are designated as Dharma-princes.
Second, those who borrow a name to encompass the great: these are those prior to the seventh stage of faith who borrow the names of the Lesser Vehicle sages [to refer to the ten stages]."

He departed to become a great arhat. Thus we know that those who attain the stage of arhat within the Perfectly Penetrating Way (yuan-tong dao-chang) must have possessed the root-nature of a bodhisattva or have turned their minds back [from the Lesser Vehicle], rather than being of fixed [Hinayana] nature. Third, there are those whose birth is at a profound stage;

for example, like those with "decided bodhi," who have comprehended kalpas as numerous as the sands of the Ganges and awakened to the patience of non-arising (anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti)—how could they not be bodhisattvas? △ Second, the permission for non-[arhatship].
Ānanda, if there are sentient beings in any world, in whatever land they may dwell, who write down this dhāraṇī on birch bark, palm leaves, paper, silk,
or white woolen cloth according to what is produced in that country, and store it in a fragrant pouch— if these people’s minds are dull and they have not yet [attained realization]...
Recite it from memory, or wear it upon the body, or write it within one's home; you should know that throughout such a person's entire life, no poisons whatsoever shall be able to cause them harm.
"Bai-die-mao" (white cotton cloth) is an item from India, similar to paper. There are those whose value is immeasurable; such things do not exist in this land.

△ Second, a detailed exposition on protecting life and aiding the Path to provide the rationale. The reason one must certainly be exhorted to wear [this cloth] is precisely because it possesses the power to protect and assist;
hence it is called "providing the rationale. Furthermore, in the previous exhortation to wear it, the assistance to the Path and protection were briefly explained.
[This] arises; therefore, these words are spoken in detail. Furthermore, there are two parts: first, a general indication of the two meanings.
"Ānanda, I shall now further expound this mantra for you, to protect and deliver the world, to attain great fearlessness, and to bring about the accomplishment of supramundane wisdom for all beings."
The final four lines consist of two lines on protecting living beings and two lines on assisting the Path. △ Second, the specific enumeration of manifold merits, divided into two parts.

First, manifesting individual benefits in relation to sentient beings, which is further divided into three. First, rescuing and protecting from calamities and disasters, which is further divided into two.
"During one *jī* (a period of twelve years), it refers to people.
If, after my parinirvāṇa, sentient beings in the final age are able to recite this themselves or teach others to recite it.
△ Second, the actual explanation of saving from calamities, divided into two parts. First, evil conditions cannot bring about harm.
It should be known that such sentient beings who recite and uphold [this] cannot be burned by fire, cannot be drowned by water, and cannot be harmed by great or small poisons.
△ Second, evil beings cannot inflict harm.
This is divided into two parts. First, they cannot inflict harm. This is further divided into three sections. First, the inability to inflict harm... [text continues].
Spells cannot take hold.
In this way, even down to the dragons, devas, ghosts, spirits, terrestrial deities, and demonic enchantments—all malevolent spells—none can take hold.
△ Second, when poison is added, it is immediately transformed.

The mind attains right concentration (*samādhi*). All curses, malevolent insects, poisons, and drugs—whether from gold, silver, plants, trees, insects, snakes, or the poisonous vapors of myriad things—that enter the mouth of this person are transformed into the flavor of ambrosia (*amṛta*).

Wenling says: "Gold and silver, when used as medicine, may sometimes provoke toxicity. Question: When the mind attains *samāpatti* (right reception), the power of mantras sustains it to form *samādhi*.
Why, then, does the mantra for repelling evil spirits not require such *samāpatti*? Answer:
Evil spells are not solid, material objects that can be blocked by a correct mantra so that they do not affect the person. Why would one need the *samādhi* of one's own body [to counter them]?
If one is in a state of delusion, and the poison of form has already entered the body, how can that which is not the samādhi of one's own self be transformed into nectar?
Therefore, one must enter right reception (*samyaksamāpatti*). △ Third, the inability to give rise to evil.
All malevolent stars, as well as various ghosts and spirits who harbor cruel hearts and poison others, will be unable to give rise to evil toward such a person.
△ Second, they shall further provide protection.
The Pinnayakas and all the evil kṣetrapāla kings, together with their retinues, shall all receive this profound kindness and constantly provide protection.
Wénlǐng says: Because one recites the dhāraṇī for the benefit of others, all the evil kṣetrapāla kings receive this profound kindness.

Having finished the section on rescuing and protecting from calamities and disasters, [the second part] is "Assisting in the Accomplishment of the Path," which is divided into six sections. The first is "Providing Resources to Stimulate Supernatural Penetration and Clarity" (for the following).

This serves as the foundational source for all ritual sections. If one does not first develop penetrating clarity, then one will likely be obscured by the "darkness between deaths" (*yinyin*) and remain muddled;

how then could one escape the evil realms over long kalpas and attain the supreme realization of the fruits of the path? Furthermore, this is divided into three parts. The first clarifies that the holy ones protect and uphold the mantra.
Ānanda, you should know that this mantra is always accompanied by eighty-four thousand nayutas of koṭis of Ganges-sand grains of the assembly of Vajragarbha-rāja Bodhisattvas;
each one has a retinue consisting of various vajra-beings.
They attended him day and night.
In terms of their realized virtue, they were all bodhisattvas of profound stages; in terms of their manifested forms, they appeared as powerful warriors exerting their majesty.
For while calamity-averting spirits can provide physical strength, assistance on the path requires nothing other than bodhisattvas. Therefore, this is clarified at the outset.
The Bodhisattvas serve as his close attendants. △ Second, raising the point that even those with distracted minds follow [this practice]:
Suppose there were sentient beings who, with a distracted mind and not in samādhi, were to recollect this in their minds and maintain it verbally—this is the Vajra King.
"One should always follow those sons of good family" refers to practitioners who are still at the stage of gradual cultivation and have not yet attained stable, constant abiding in samādhi;
because they simply maintain the dhāraṇī constantly, they should also follow those who are neither negligent nor defiled by evil. △ Third, the analogy of the bodhicitta.
Furthermore, people are divided into three categories.
First, those who merely identify themselves as such, let alone those who possess the resolute bodhicitta.
These latter must abide constantly in samādhi while reciting mantras, aspiring to swiftly attain perfect enlightenment.
It is so. That which is the primary tenet of this sutra is the Perfect Penetration of the Ear-Faculty, serving as the wondrous *samādhi*.
△ Second, the secret empowerment that awakens and develops:
these Vajra Bodhisattvas, Kings of the Treasury, with their refined minds acting secretly and swiftly, stimulate his spiritual consciousness.
The Bodhisattva can, through the empowerment of their supernatural powers, cause the minds of practitioners to open and dispel the darkness of the aggregates (skandhas) with great speed.
This is because the essential spirit of the Bodhisattva’s mind and the essential spirit of the practitioner’s mind are perfectly fused into a single, non-dual entity.
Since the Bodhisattva’s mental power is combined with the power of the mantra, they are able to secretly urge the practitioner on, causing their mind to open. △ Three: The Perfecting [Section].
Realizing supernormal powers and clarity,
this person, at that time, is able with their mind to remember eighty-four thousand Ganges-sands of kalpas,
comprehending them thoroughly and without any doubt.
Wenling says: This is what is meant by "accomplishing the supramundane wisdom that brings sentient beings to maturity.

Although memory may merely resemble the knowledge of past lives (*pūrvanivāsānusmṛti-jñāna*), it encompasses kalpas as numerous as the sands of the Ganges and is further described as being all-pervasive, penetrating thoroughly through the three periods of time.
Furthermore, one should understand this without doubt; it appears to involve the three types of supernormal knowledge (*vidyā*).

How much more so when kalpas as numerous as the sands [of the Ganges] vastly transcend the eighty thousand [kalpas] of the Hīnayāna—know that these are still the bodhisattva’s extraordinary six supernormal powers and three types of supernormal knowledge. △ Second, distancing oneself from various realms of rebirth.
Being born among the various realms of rebirth, one may either become defiled by evil habits or fall into heavy suffering, which deeply obstructs the practice of the Path.

Therefore, those who cultivate the mind all make a vow not to be born in these various realms; thus, this section is placed within the "Aids to the Practice of the Path. It is divided into three parts. First:
marking the time until the attainment of the fruit.
From the first kalpa until the final body:

the "first kalpa" refers to the time when one first gives rise to the resolute bodhicitta; the "final body" refers to the body that attains manifest enlightenment through the perfection of causes, as can be seen.
It is evident that throughout the entire period of intermediate practice, there is no obstruction. △ Second.
They will not be reborn as gods or ghosts;
throughout their successive lives, they will not be born as yakṣas, rākṣasas, pūtanas, kaṭapūtanas,
kumbhāṇḍas, piśācas, and so forth, nor among any of the hungry ghosts— whether with form or without form, with perception or without perception— in such evil realms.
Yakṣas, rākṣasas, and others manifest the perfect penetration of Avalokiteśvara. Piśācas, kumbhāṇḍas, and kaṭapūtanas are likewise members of this retinue.
Third, one will not be born into poverty or low status.
If these good sons read it, recite it, write it, copy it, wear it, or preserve it, and offer various forms of worship,
they shall not be born in states of poverty, lowliness, or unpleasantness throughout kalpa after kalpa.
Reciting from memory is called "chanting" (jìng). Drawing and copying seals is called "writing" (xiě). Secretly wearing them is called "concealing" (zàng).

Poverty leads to the suffering of hardship; low status leads to the suffering of servitude. Both hinder one's spiritual practice (*dàoyè*). One must distance oneself from what is unpleasant, for concentration gives rise to what is pleasant. Changshui says: "This is because one upholds the *Uṣṇīṣavijayā*. **3.
Constantly being born before the Buddhas, constantly following the Buddhas to learn, and the swift attainment of cultivation and realization.** This is divided into three parts.
Regarding the collective merits of all Buddhas:
even if these sentient beings do not personally perform meritorious deeds themselves, the merits possessed by all Tathāgatas throughout the ten directions shall be bestowed entirely upon this person.
This section further explains the cause for birth in the Buddha-realm; it is only through many causes and conditions of merit that one is born there.
Now, by upholding this mantra, one can evoke the bestowal of merit from all Buddhas, and thus attain certain rebirth.
The *Sukhāvatīvyūha Sūtra* states that mindfulness of the Buddha is itself great merit, which must arise from the bestowal of wisdom. △ Second, being born in the same place as the Buddha.
By this, for kalpas as numerous as the sands of the Ganges—incalculable, unspeakably unspeakable—they are always born in the same place as all Buddhas.
"By this" means that because of the merit bestowed by the previous Buddha, they are able to be constantly born together with the Buddhas. △ Third, [the section on] being together.
The Buddha has cultivated immeasurable merits,
which— like the clusters of the akṣa fruit— have been cultivated together in one place and shall never be dispersed.
Since these merits produced in this life and in future lives constantly follow the Buddha, they share in every single one of the Buddha’s merits.
Once born [therein], one will inevitably encounter and be intimately influenced by them, remaining inseparable from them for long kalpas.
△ Fourth, the accomplishment of the various practices, which is further divided into five parts. First, the accomplishment of the complete precepts.
Therefore, it can cause those who have broken the precepts to purify their roots of discipline, and enable those who have not yet attained the precepts to obtain them.
△ Second, accomplishing diligent practice.
Those who have not yet attained diligence shall be made to attain diligence.
△ Third, the practice of wisdom:
those who lack wisdom shall be made to attain wisdom.
△ Fourth, accomplishing the practice of pure conduct:
those who are impure quickly attain purity.
△ Fifth, accomplishing the practice of the fast and precepts.
Those who do not maintain the fasts and precepts will naturally fulfill them.
If a person has karmic obstructions from previous lives such that they repeatedly desire to observe the fasts and precepts but cannot achieve success, this mantra can bring it about.

Or, if one is hindered by karma or by the physical environment, or lacks a teacher and a ritual altar and thus cannot observe the fasts and precepts, it is permitted to simply hold the mantra; this is equivalent to observing the fasts and precepts.

△ The Extinction of All Sins. This is divided into four parts. First, the extinction of sins for violating the precepts. This is further divided into two. First, the simultaneous eradication of both light and heavy offenses.
Ānanda, when this son of good family maintains this mantra, even if he has violated the prohibitive precepts prior to receiving them, by maintaining the mantra...
Thereafter, all offenses of breaking the precepts, regardless of whether they are light or heavy, are extinguished at once. Wēnlíng says:

"Those who have not yet received [the precepts]" refers to those who have not yet recited the mantra. It is evident that after one has maintained the mantra, one must no longer commit further transgressions.
△ Second, the simultaneous pardon for eating [forbidden food].
Even if one has consumed alcohol, the five pungent roots, or various kinds of impure things, all Buddhas, Bodhisattvas, Vajras,
celestial immortals, spirits, and deities will not regard this as a transgression.

Regarding this, there are three interpretations to be considered. Observing the single character "guo" (past) in the Sutra, it appears to refer to events that occurred prior to the recitation of the mantra;
once the mantra has been held, all such [transgressions] are entirely forgiven. This does not mean that the person holding the mantra may act with unrestrained license.
Furthermore, if there are those who uphold mantras who, being driven by necessity, happen to encounter such circumstances, they may all be excused; this is not a matter of indulgence or license.
Or, for those whom true compassion permits to be unable to maintain the full fast and precepts, it is likewise allowed that they uphold [the mantra].

It can immediately eliminate their transgressions, as illustrated by the analogy of water cast into boiling soup; this merely demonstrates the extraordinary excellence of the mantra. This applies according to the previous case of those who have not yet received [the precepts].

Regarding these statements, the former two explanations are more consistent with principle. If one consults the texts on the four Vinayas and the three gradual stages, then for those who seek true cultivation and rare realization, maintaining purity is paramount.
II. The Extinction of Offenses through Violating the Rules. This is divided into two parts.
First: Impurity is itself Purity.
Even if one wears impure and tattered clothing, whether walking or staying, it is entirely the same as being pure.

This is also the practice of *dhūta* (ascetic purification). Being poor and lacking in resources, one should maintain this without doubt; it is not done out of a deliberate intention for wealth or abundance.
△ Second, "Where there is no altar, that itself is the altar."

Even if one does not construct an altar, does not enter a sacred precinct, and does not practice the Way, yet recites and upholds this mantra, it is identical in merit to entering the altar and practicing the Way;
there is no difference whatsoever.
The aforementioned methods for constructing altars are extremely difficult to fulfill completely. This [practice] allows one to maintain the mantra even without an altar;
do not doubt that its merit is distinct [from other methods]. Moreover, if one can further abide constantly in the Great Samādhi, this is the true site of quiescent extinction.
It would surely surpass those who merely possess the physical appearance of an altar but lack a concentrated mind. △ Third, the eradication of the most grievous offenses.
If one has committed the five heinous crimes of immediate retribution, or the four pārājika and eight saṃghāvaśeṣa offenses of bhikṣus and bhikṣuṇīs,
upon reciting this mantra, such grave karma will be entirely eliminated— just as a fierce wind scatters a heap of sand—
leaving not even a hair’s breadth behind.
These offenses committed prior to having resolved to practice mantra-recitation can be completely extinguished by relying on the power of the mantra; one must not harbor further doubts.
It is certainly not the case that the mantra allows one to commit these evils with impunity and without restraint. Guishan said:
"The four parājikas for a bhikṣu refer to the four root heavy offenses of killing, stealing, sexual misconduct, and lying. In Sanskrit, they are called *pārājika*. This...
"Parajika" (Cloud-Abandonment) means that one who commits this offense is forever abandoned outside the boundaries of the Buddha-dharma, just as the great ocean does not accept a dead corpse.
For the Bhikṣuṇīs, four additional Parājikas are added: namely, touching, the eighth, concealing, and following. That is to say: fifth, one must not, with a defiled mind, touch the body of a man;
sixth, one must not, with a defiled mind, allow a man to grasp one’s hand or clothing or enter a secluded place [with him].
The eight matters include: standing together, speaking together, walking together in private places; leaning one's body against another's; making appointments with one another, and so forth.
Seventh, one must not conceal the grave offenses of others. Eighth, one must not provide robes and food for those who have been formally accused by the Great Saṃgha;

that is, once one has been accused by the Saṃgha, if they have not yet performed the *sahavāsa* (method of communal residence), one may not associate with them. These are collectively termed [the prohibitions].
The eight *pārājika* offenses. "That which is brought forth by the Saṃgha" refers to the meaning of exposing and accusing [the transgressor]. △ Fourth, the extinction of extremely grave offenses.
This is further divided into two sections: first, accumulated offenses not yet repented.
Ānanda, if there are sentient beings who, from immeasurable and incalculable kalpas past, have committed all manner of light and heavy karmic obstructions,
which they have not yet had the opportunity to repent for since their previous lives;
△ Second, the eradication through mantras.
If one can recite and chant this mantra, transcribe it, wear it upon the body, or place it within one's dwelling, house, garden, or villa; [the aforementioned calamities shall be extinguished].
Such accumulated karma will be dissolved like snow melting in hot water.

For those who understand how to read and recite it, it may even be kept without being written down; however, for those who do not understand how to recite it, it is especially wonderful to write it out, carry it with one, and install it [in a shrine].
△ Sixth: Swiftly Awakening to Non-arising.
Before long, they all attained the realization of the patience of non-arising (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*).

In the Perfect Teaching (*yuanjiao*), one realizes this patience at the first stage (*prathamabhūmi*); in the Separate Teaching (*biejiao*), it corresponds to the stages above the ground. To examine the previous manifestation of supernatural powers:

those were manifested through the accomplishment of the mind of meditative concentration (*samādhi*); what is now realized as non-arising is manifested through the accomplishment of the mind of wisdom (*prajñā*).

Previously, one merely understood things without delusion; it was not necessarily a true realization that all phenomena are unborn. One should know that the subsequent stage is deeper than the preceding one.
Moreover, after attaining this patience (*kṣānti*), both sin and merit are empty, and the conceptual distinctions between sage and ordinary being are exhausted.
Thus, one can regard demons and Buddhas as identical, and only then is one able to traverse all realms of suffering and evil without obstruction or discrimination. Therefore, one knows that...

This section precedes all other sections and serves as the fulfillment of the path of assistance. Furthermore, what is called "supramundane wisdom" begins with the manifestation of supernormal powers, yet it has no end in terms of their actual production.
According to the six categories of analysis: the first four constitute the *sistanda* (beneficial teaching) for human beings;
the fifth is the *pratipakṣa* (remedy) that destroys evil; and the sixth is the *paramārtha* (ultimate truth) that enters into principle.
Furthermore, the rescue from calamities mentioned previously and the response to requests mentioned later constitute the *loka-anuśaṃsa-siddhānta* (the world-pleasing teaching).

The rest may be understood by analogy. This concludes the section on assisting in the accomplishment of the path of practice. △ Third, the fulfillment of wishes and requests. The former rescue from calamities belongs to compassion (*karuṇā*) which extracts suffering;

this response to requests belongs to loving-kindness (*maitrī*) which bestows happiness. This is divided into two parts. First, the wishes and requests made prior to birth, which is further divided into four sections.
First, seeking sons and daughters.
Furthermore, Ānanda, if there is a woman who has not yet borne children and desires to conceive,
if she can recollect this mantra with a sincere heart, or if she can wear this *Siddhārthapralamba* upon her person, she will immediately give birth to blessings.
Virtuous men and women of wisdom.
△ Second, seeking long life.
Those who seek long life shall immediately obtain long life.
△ Third, seeking the fruition of rewards.
For those who wish to seek the swift fulfillment of rewards, they shall swiftly attain fulfillment.
Within this, the rewards of merit and benefit, as well as the rewards of spiritual practice, appear to be all contained together. If it concerns the rewards of spiritual practice...

[This] refers to the retribution [of maturation]. It encompasses the three types of *siddhi* mentioned above. Within the general category of "aiding the path of practice," there is already the fruit of retribution from cultivation;
this should mostly be the fruit of retribution consisting of blessings and merit. △ Fourth, seeking physical appearance.
Their physical life, appearance, and strength are likewise so.
This is long life, further endowed with intelligence and free from decay, such that their entire body remains healthy and robust.
△ Second, rebirth after the end of life.

After the end of their lives, they will be reborn in the lands of the ten directions according to their vows; they will certainly not be born in border regions or among the lowly, much less in mixed forms.
This concludes the section on how the benefits for each individual are manifested through sentient beings, based on the invocation of vows as distinct from the aids to the path.
△ Second, revealing universal benefit by way of the land. The preceding section clarified that each individual obtains benefit by reciting [the scripture] themselves;
this section clarifies that merely copying and enshrining it brings universal benefit to the entire nation, city, and so forth. This is precisely the *loka-siddhānta* (worldly standpoint).
It is divided into three parts. First, the elimination of various calamities. This is further divided into three. First, first citing the sites of calamity.
Ānanda, if there are kingdoms, prefectures, counties, or villages that suffer from famine and pestilence, or further face the calamities of war,
bandits, and strife, as well as all other lands beset by misfortune and distress.
△ Second, the installation in the city and the reception of offerings. This is further divided into two sections. First, instructing in the installation of the mantra:
transcribe this divine mantra and install it at the four gates of the city, as well as at various caityas or upon the *toraṇa* arches.
Wenling says: *Cetiya* is translated here as "a place worthy of offerings," which is a general term for a pure land (*śuddhakṣetra*).
*Dhvaja* means "banner. These two types of offerings are worn upon the person and kept at home.
May all sentient beings within that land welcome this mantra, prostrating to it with reverence and making offerings with single-minded devotion;
may the people each wear it upon their bodies or place it in their respective dwellings.
△ The three fetters are difficult to eliminate;
all calamities and misfortunes are entirely extinguished.
△ The myriad people enjoy abundance and happiness.
Ānanda, in whatever lands and regions sentient beings may dwell, wherever this dhāraṇī exists, the devas and nāgas will rejoice; wind and rain will follow their proper seasons;
the five grains will be abundant; and the myriad people will enjoy peace and happiness.

This must depend upon the entire nation knowing and revering it with faith; or else, when the sovereign, ministers, and local officials all encounter those who understand its essence and instruct the people to hold it in high esteem, only then will spiritual efficacy be attained.
It is like a practitioner of mantras: they become efficacious only after a long time;

how could they produce swift results in a brief moment? This is likewise the case: it becomes efficacious only through ultimate reverence. If, although the mantra exists everywhere, one merely binds it away on a high shelf...

Furthermore, it is an extreme delusion to fail to show respect to a stūpa, or even to place it in a position of intimacy or familiarity where dust and filth are not removed, and yet to blame the mantras for lacking efficacy.
All other cases should be considered according to this principle.
△ Third, the non-appearance of malevolent stars, divided into two parts. First, a brief indication.

Furthermore, it can subdue all malevolent stars that manifest strange portents according to their respective directions; calamities and obstacles shall not arise, and no one shall suffer untimely death.
Shackles, fetters, stocks, and manacles shall not touch their bodies; they shall sleep peacefully day and night, never having evil dreams.
△ Second, the detailed explanation. This is further divided into two sections. First, the explanation of the calamities manifested by the various stars:
"Ānanda, in this Sahā world-system, there are eighty-four thousand calamitous and malevolent stars.
Twenty-eight great malevolent stars serve as their leaders, and furthermore, eight great malevolent stars act as their sovereigns. They manifest in various forms and appear."
In the present age, they can produce various calamities and anomalies for sentient beings.
Wēnlíng says: "The eighty-four thousand correspond to the afflictions and karmic actions of sentient beings. The twenty-eight are the regulations of the four directions;
the eight are the principles of the five elements, along with Rāhu, Ketu, and Śanaiścara. When these are in accord, blessings respond; when they are contrary..."

Then calamities will manifest as their response; that is to say, "following the auspicious brings good fortune, while following the perverse brings misfortune. That which can produce disasters and anomalies merely responds to such perversity.
For instance, comets, meteors, and flying stars respond to the same category [of karmic conditions] and are not the deeds of the constellations themselves.
△ Second, the explanation of the methods and scales for suppressing and eliminating [calamities].

Wherever this mantra is present on the earth, all [calamities] are completely extinguished. An area of twelve *yojanas* becomes a consecrated boundary (*sīmā*) where no evil portents or disasters can ever enter.
Wēnlíng says: Because the power of the mantra accords with a hundredfold auspiciousness, all malevolent transformations are utterly extinguished; as for celestial disasters and portents—

One does not enter its domain. "Xiang" (祥) refers to the preceding omens of good or ill fortune. Second, the detailed exposition on protecting life and assisting the Way to emerge from oneself is concluded.
△ Third, clarifying that the practitioner will certainly attain realization to conclude with an exhortation. Section One: Exhortation to Maintain [the Precepts].
This section cites the initial practice of subduing demons to provide encouragement. This heading concludes the exhortation by clearly stating that it definitively opens the mind;
this cites the final realization to inspire joy and encouragement. It is divided into two parts. First, explaining the reason for the discourse on security:
this explains that the Buddha’s original intent in teaching was primarily to ensure the security of practitioners. This is further divided into two: first, protection and peace.
Therefore, the Tathāgata proclaims this mantra to protect beginners and all practitioners in future ages,
so that they may enter samādhi with their bodies and minds at ease, attaining great peace and stability.
△ Second, being far removed from demonic adversaries:
there shall be no further interference or harm from any demons, ghosts, or spirits, nor from the karmic debts of past offenses and long-standing calamities accumulated since beginningless time.
△ Second, the correct demonstration that those free from fault will necessarily attain realization. This also has three parts. First, citing persons of the present and future:
"You, all sentient beings who are still in training (*śaikṣa*), and all practitioners of future ages."
△ Second, clarifying the non-transgression of the four faults:
Relying upon my ritual arena (*maṇḍala*), one maintains the precepts according to the Dharma; the precept master from whom they receive them encounters pure monks who uphold this mantra-heart.
Not giving rise to doubt or regret constitutes the fourth transgression.
These four are: first, failure in the ritual procedures (*tantra*); second, deficiency in the precepts; third, defilement by the master; and fourth, doubt and regret.

If even one of these is committed, it is difficult to attain realization in the present life; such acts serve only as remote causes. Therefore, one should know that the aforementioned permissions do not authorize genuine cultivation.
...of such a kind. △ Third, resolving that one must attain mental penetration:
"If these good sons do not attain mental penetration within this body born of their parents, the Tathāgatas of the ten directions..."
This would then be false speech.
Regarding the body born of one's parents, it is said that realization does not depend upon a future life. Wuxing said:

"As for 'penetrating the mind,' based on what was previously stated, it does not go beyond three meanings. First is the realization of the fruit; this refers to sitting upright for a hundred days, which requires sharp faculties."
First, one attains the stage of *srotāpanna* (stream-enterer) without rising from one's seat. Second, the development of understanding:
this means that even if one’s body and mind have not yet achieved the holy fruit, one knows with certainty that one will attain Buddhahood without error. Third, the knowledge of past lives:
at that time, this person’s mind is able to remember eighty-four thousand *gaṅgā-nadī-vāluka* kalpas, knowing them exhaustively and without fail.

[The assembly] was filled with doubt. After the Tathāgata had finished his repeated exposition, [the third section follows: The Assembly Requests Protection. Question: The mantra possesses its own power;
why is it necessary to request protection from others? Answer: The portion following the syllable *Oṃ* constitutes the actual mantra.

The preceding sections are all requests for the majestic power of the Triple Gem, or are individual heart-mantras (*hṛdaya-mantra*), because the vows of the various sages to protect living beings are identical. Furthermore, there are the Eight Classes [of Spirits].

The names and titles of the divine kings surely have their origins in past vows, yet they also concurrently abide by the Buddha’s commands, using the merit of protecting living beings to adorn their own karmic fruits.
As for the minor deities among the common classes, they receive the wondrous power of the incantations, thereby escaping suffering and attaining happiness.
This refers to receiving and protecting [the practitioner] out of deep gratitude for their kindness.

Therefore, while the practitioner maintains the mantra through their own power (*sva-bala*), it is further supplemented by the protective power of others (*para-bala*). By means of this merit of wearing [the mantra], its majesty is immeasurable and unfathomable. Question:
Since true compassion protects the practitioner in all circumstances, why is it necessary to require them to maintain a mantra before protection is granted? Answer: The mantra...
It possesses divine efficacy. It first causes the practitioner to exert their own power, and furthermore, it employs invocation as a condition for its operation.
Moreover, the mantra is like an imperial edict; therefore, those who receive the edict—whether they be eminent and capable kings or ministers—are all protected by it.
Otherwise, those who are base and incompetent will not be protected. Furthermore, the recitation of mantras is like the study of books; it must be practiced for the sake of the world.

As for its application: there are no kings or ministers who do not provide for and promote [those who practice it]. If one does not study what is useless, then how can such provision and promotion be bestowed?
Furthermore, the practitioner is like a warrior; the mantra is like a sharp blade and armor; and the various sages are like those who assist in battle.
Therefore, those who possess armor and weapons can assist in achieving certain victory; if they do not possess them, what benefit would assistance provide?

This brief exposition of a few principles is sufficient to clarify that the protection of mantras must be combined with their ritual holding—let there be no doubt about this. It is divided into two parts.
First, external protection and support: because these involve worldly characteristics and have not yet designated the title of "Bodhisattva," they are termed "external."
However, their status as provisional or ultimate is not fixed. If they are provisional manifestations, they all secretly maintain the identity of bodhisattvas while outwardly assuming mere names.
If they are actual ordinary beings, then their outward designations are indeed real titles. Furthermore, they are divided into five groups: first, the assembly of Vajrapāṇi spirits.

When these words had been spoken, immeasurable hundreds of thousands of *vajras* within the assembly simultaneously joined their palms before the Buddha, prostrated themselves, and addressed the Buddha, saying:
"In accordance with what the Buddha has taught, we shall with sincere hearts protect those who thus cultivate bodhicitta."
These are currently manifest as Vajradhara bodies; they are not like the Bodhisattvas who appear later.

For those cultivating Bodhi, the practice of perfecting the faculty of hearing through the retention of mantras is supreme; all subsequent [practices] are derived from this. △ Second, the assembly of the most honored among the heavenly deities.
At that time, Brahmā, Śakra, Lord of the Devas, and the Four Great Kings also simultaneously prostrated before the Buddha and addressed him, saying:
"If there are indeed such virtuous persons who practice and study in this way, we shall protect them with all our hearts and with utmost sincerity."
It causes all that one has done throughout a lifetime to be fulfilled according to one's wishes;
this is like the fruit itself. "Fulfillment of wishes throughout a lifetime" refers to attaining realization and mental mastery (*citta-vaśitā*) in the present life.

This is the *tattvārtha-siddhānta* (the ultimate standpoint of entering into principle). If one were to fulfill wishes merely in terms of worldly affairs, it would then be the other three *siddhāntas*. △ Section 38.
Surrounding and honoring the Honored One,
there were furthermore immeasurable yakṣa generals, rākṣasa kings, pūtana kings,
kumbhāṇḍa kings, piśāca kings, pināyaka great ghost kings, and various ghost commanders, who likewise stood before the Buddha.
With palms joined, I pay homage. I also vow to protect and sustain these persons, causing their bodhicitta to be swiftly perfected.
I vow to constantly guard them so that the great fruit may be swiftly accomplished. △ Fourth, the assembly of presiding deities who illuminate and oversee.
Furthermore, there were immeasurable sun and moon deva-kings, the masters of wind, rain, clouds, and thunder, along with the lord of lightning and others;
as well as the officials who cycle through the years and the retinues of all the stars, who also prostrated at the Buddha’s feet within the assembly and addressed the Buddha, saying:
I, too, shall protect this practitioner, establishing them in the *maṇḍala* so that they may attain fearlessness.
"Master-Ber" (*shībó*) is a title denoting a presiding sovereign or leader. "Yearly Circulating Officials" refers to those such as the Four Rectifying *Gōngcáo*.
Those who specifically protect the *maṇḍala* are individuals who seek realization within a fixed period; I shall doubly protect them so that they may remain without fear.
Māra. It is not that the assembly of those who cultivate according to their convenience is entirely unprotected. △ Fifth, the assembly of terrestrial deities:
furthermore, there are immeasurable mountain spirits and ocean spirits, as well as all the numinous essences of the myriad things moving on land, in water, and through the air.
Together with the Wind Deity King and the gods of the Formless Realm, they simultaneously prostrated before the Tathāgata and addressed the Buddha, saying:
"We, too, shall protect these practitioners so that they may attain Bodhi, forever free from the works of Māra."

The deities of mountains and seas are the presiding lords of rivers and peaks. "Land" refers to the class of terrestrial spirits (*bhūmidevatā*). "Moving through water, land, and air" enumerates these three abodes to encompass the vast multitude.
"The refined spirits of the myriad things" includes, for example, the deities of trees, crops, and so forth.
All those above belong to the category of beings with form; those below include the formless Wind King (*Vāyu-rāja*), who resembles the Śūnyatā-rāja (Lord of Emptiness) who presides over space.

They are deities. A scripture states: "Their forms are like the wind. In the heavens of the Formless Realm (*ārūpyadhātu*), there is no matter resulting from karmic fruit; thus, they all lack physical form.
That they are nonetheless described as "bowing their heads" (*praṇāma*) is because they may, by relying on the Buddha’s majestic radiance, temporarily manifest a body.

Wénlǐng comments that it is also consistent to consider them as completing the four great elements (*mahābhūta*) of the three realms, though the fire deity is missing. This concludes the external protectors.

[The preceding section] concludes. △ Second, the protection and sustenance by the internal sages. Since both the fundamental and the manifested aspects are revealed, the sages of the internal teaching are designated. This is divided into three sections:
first, identifying the persons and describing their ritual observances.
At that time, eighty-four thousand nayutas of koṭis of Bodhisattvas, as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, who were the Vajragarbha Kings,
rose from their seats within the great assembly, prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, and addressed the Buddha, saying:
Because he has realized the principle of ultimate firmness, he is called "Vajra" (Adamantine). Because he secretly guards and maintains [the teachings], he is called "Guhya" (Secret).
Because his compassion is majestic and supreme, and because he employs both the methods of subduing and gathering, he is called "Rāja" (King).

It is his constant practice as a Bodhisattva that, when subduing Māras, he manifests the form of the wrathful Vajra holding a vajra-club; thus it is said. △ Second, revealing the long-standing protection of the source.
World-Honored One, we and those like us shall long perfect our bodhi through the merits we have cultivated;
we shall not enter nirvana, but will constantly follow this mantra to protect and deliver those who cultivate samādhi and practice correctly during the final age.
Their meritorious deeds have long been accomplished; that is, having passed through the various stages, their realization and certification are already perfected.
They do not enter nirvana, yet they do not exclusively grasp at quiescent extinction; rather, they truly abide in the three secret treasuries.

The phrase "constantly following those below" indicates that they do not abandon sentient beings, practicing the cause while manifesting the fruit, thereby repaying their original vow to protect living beings. All of this spontaneously reveals their fundamental nature. △ Third, the explicit clarification.
Regarding the protection [of practitioners], it is divided into four parts. First, protection whether in meditative concentration or in distraction:

"World-Honored One, if those who thus cultivate the mind and seek right concentration are in a place of practice (*dharma-cakra*), or elsewhere walking for meditation (*caṅkrama*), or even when their minds are distracted as they roam through villages, we and our followers shall always follow and attend to such persons."
When walking in meditation at the site of enlightenment (*bodhimaṇḍa*), it is precisely the time when one gathers the mind in right concentration;
that is, the time when one "turns hearing back toward one's own nature" and "enters the stream so that the object of perception perishes," and so forth. Even down to the following point:

after having resolved to attain awakening and begun cultivation, although the beginner’s mind may occasionally be interrupted by periods of distraction, the Bodhisattva does not fail to protect the mind on account of such distraction. For this reason...

Furthermore, when observing those who practice the recitation of mantras, they should also know for themselves that they ought to respect [the precepts] and must not engage in the defiled conduct of breaking them, out of a sense of reverent shame before the Bodhisattvas.
△ Second, the complete expulsion of demonic influences. This is divided into two parts.
First, the explicit explanation of their complete expulsion.
Even if Māra or Maheśvara were to seek an opportunity, they would ultimately find none;
as for the minor spirits and ghosts, they remain ten yojanas away from such virtuous persons.
Maheśvara is also a Māra-deva of the Form Realm (rūpadhātu). △ Second, the exclusion [of certain beings] from the arousal of the resolve (cittotpāda):
those who have aroused the resolve and delight in practicing dhyāna are excluded.
"Those" refers to various minor spirits (yakṣas); because they have aroused the resolve and are fond of dhyāna, and because they themselves protect the practitioner, they are not expelled.
Except where I permit them to approach. △ Third, those who transgress shall surely be destroyed.
"World-Honored One, if such an evil Māra or his retinue should come to harass these virtuous people, I shall shatter their heads with my precious vajra-pestle until they are like fine dust."
"‘Ruined and destroyed’ means that as soon as the precious vajra is aimed at them, they shatter without waiting to be struck.孤山 (Gushan) says:

‘The aforementioned multitude of spirits have all recovered their original mind; abiding in the Śūraṅgama-samādhi, they are able to establish great principles and manifest in the forms of bodhisattvas, devas, ghosts, spirits, and so forth, to protect and sustain the practitioner.
As for the statement that their heads are crushed by the precious vajra, it is like [the process of] nirvāṇa...'"

Pāśa killed the icchantikas, and Śāntamati pre-emptively executed those of pure conduct; all this was due to abiding in objectless compassion (*apratigha-maitrī*) and attaining the stage of the only child (*ekaputraka-bhūmi*).
Only by reaching such a state can one act in this manner. △ Fourth, always causing things to be as desired.
May this person’s undertakings always be fulfilled according to their wishes;

as for "according to their wishes," it follows the previous [explanation]. From the initial metaphor of the flowered house and the request for cultivation, up to this present passage, one should skillfully cultivate the auxiliary practices in their entirety.
Although both types of cultivation are initially expedient means, the ear-door is that which penetrates deeply. This is...

Right cultivation and the recitation of mantras at a site of practice (dojō) are both auxiliary practices. Thus, one should know that those who cultivate through skillful means possess two types of faculties:

superior and dull. Those whose faculties are somewhat sharp certainly do not require the assistance of a site of practice and the like, for they can naturally enter the perfect penetration through the faculty of hearing, as Ānanda did. Those whose faculties are somewhat dull, however, cannot enter swiftly.
In such cases, one subsequently employs the "later gate" to assist them. Question: Since this constitutes a complete cycle, why is there no one who attains realization?
Answer: Realization occurs at the conclusion of correct practice; as this [gate] is merely an auxiliary practice, there is no realization.

Within the four aspects of reality in the title of the sutra, it properly belongs to the definitive meaning of cultivation and realization. It explains samādhi so that one may rely upon the wondrous mind.

The first section, "Entering Deeply through One Door," is now complete. △ Third, the explanation of *dhyāna* (meditative concentration) to cause one to abide in perfect samādhi and to undergo cultivation and realization through the successive stages;
this answers Ānanda’s request for the "wondrous *dhyāna*. However, both this and the preceding section do not depart from the previously mentioned "Flower House" of the fundamental nature of samādhi.
The former was like entering through the gate; this is like ascending to the hall and entering the inner chamber.

The sequence is as follows: it merely combines the two causes of the prior conditions—enabling and understanding—and fuses concentration and wisdom into a single excellence. This is divided into two parts.

First, Ānanda’s expression of gratitude for the teaching and his request for the [Buddha’s] seat. This is further divided into three sections. First, the formal observance of ritual and the presentation of the petition.
Ānanda immediately rose from his seat, prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, and addressed the Buddha as follows.
△ Second, the words of gratitude for the teaching, which is further divided into two parts. First, recounting past faults and thanking for the benefit; this corresponds to the preceding section.

This could also be categorized generally as the conclusion of the preceding "Repentance for Cultivation" (xiè xiū). However, as the logic and phrasing connect to what follows, it is now treated as a section consisting of "repentance for the past" and "requesting for the future.
This section further has two parts: first, describing how one possesses much learning but has not yet practiced.
We are dull-witted and foolish, fond of mere erudition, yet we have not sought liberation from the mind of outflows.

"The mind of outflows" refers to subtle afflictions and deep-seated delusions that abide in the ground; they do not merely consist of the four abodes. Because we are foolish, it is difficult to clarify them;
because we are dull, it is difficult to sever them. Moreover, we indulge in powerful memory without single-mindedly seeking the Way; therefore, we have long remained without liberation.
△ Second, expressing gratitude for the instruction received and the benefits obtained:
Having received the Buddha’s compassionate teaching, I have attained correct cultivation (*bhāvanā*), and my body and mind are filled with joy, gaining great benefit.

"Compassionate teaching" refers to the two preceding gates of selecting the faculties (*indriya*) and preparatory practice (*prayoga*). With the distinction between the primary and auxiliary practices clearly defined, one may advance in cultivation.
There is no delusion; therefore, there is joyful and abundant benefit. △ Second, the formal request for the position [of the fruit]. This is further divided into two parts.
First, precisely indicating the stage prior to the fruit:
"World-Honored One, practicing and realizing the Buddha’s samādhi in this manner, one has not yet reached nirvāṇa."
△ Second, the sequential invitation to the various stages.
What is meant by the "Stage of Dry Wisdom" (śuṣka-vipaśyanā-bhūmi)? Regarding the forty-four mental states, at what gradual sequence does one attain the vision for cultivation?
To what place does one go that is called "entering the stages" (*bhūmi*)? What is meant by the name "Equal Enlightenment Bodhisattva"?

"Dry Wisdom" (*śuklavidarśana*) refers to the stage prior to the first [of the ten stages]. Changshui says: "The stages of faith, abiding, practice, and direction, along with the preparatory application (*prayoga*), are termed the 'forty-four minds.
The preceding [passage] cites the middle position, while the following traces the origin and seeks the end. Therefore...
Regarding "gradual progression," this refers to the first three gradual stages prior to the initial stage of Dry Wisdom (*śuṣka-vipaśyanā*).

It should be said that this marks the beginning. By means of which gradual stages does one set out to practice? And at the end, to what destination does one arrive to enter deeply into the stages beyond the ground (*bhūmi*)?

The final two phrases are easy [to understand], as they signify the ultimate limit of the causal stage (*hetu-bhūmi*). (A close study of this text reveals there is a transposed passage; the phrase "reaching what" should appear within the section on *samādhi*).

If one follows the sequence from beginning to end, there is no need for convoluted explanations. Now, to first cite the middle position and subsequently require the beginning and end is to follow error with error; it is ultimately not in accord. Please examine this carefully.
In the fifty-nine positions revealed in this inquiry, because he intends to clarify the cultivation of causes, he asks only about the causal stages.
By adding the stage of Subtle Enlightenment (*sūkṣmajñāna*), they become sixty positions. △ Third, bowing together with the assembly and looking up.

Having spoken these words, he prostrated himself with his five limbs touching the ground. The great assembly, with one mind, awaited the Buddha’s compassionate voice, gazing up at him with fixed and vacant eyes.
II. The Tathāgata’s Explanation of Dependent Origination. Dependent origination refers to the two conditions of defilement and purity, both of which arise based upon the mind.
Sentient beings rely upon fundamental awakening (*mūla-awakening*) to give rise to non-awakening (*an-awakening*);

this is defiled dependent origination (*saṃkleśa-pratītyasamutpāda*), which results in the twelve classes of beings and the boundless ocean of birth and death. The sages rely upon non-awakening to give rise to initial awakening (*ādi-awakening*);

this is pure dependent origination (*vyavadāna-pratītyasamutpāda*), which results in the sixty stages of the sages and the boundless ocean of fruition. This is divided into three categories, as praised and permitted by the Tathāgata.
At that time, the World-Honored One praised Ānanda, saying: "Excellent, excellent!

You have been able to universally act for the sake of the great assembly and all sentient beings of the future ages who cultivate *samādhi* seeking the Mahāyāna, beginning from the stage of ordinary persons."
It concludes with the Great Parinirvāṇa and reveals, from afar, the path of supreme, correct practice. Listen attentively now; I shall explain it for you.

"From afar" (xuán) means distant or prior. "Revealing from afar" means that before reaching deep realization, one first speaks from a distance about the various stages traversed, up to and including the ultimate realization of the precious abode; there is nothing that is not fully revealed. Supreme.

Regarding "correct cultivation": this indicates that all that is shown herein constitutes the cultivation and realization of the definitive meaning (*nītārtha*), and is not like that which is of non-definitive meaning (*neyārtha*).
△ Second, the Great Assembly listens with sincerity:
Ānanda and the great assembly joined their palms, hollowed their hearts, and silently received the instruction.
"Kū" (to hollow out) means to scrape and remove. "Hollowing out the mind" refers to making the mind empty and pure, such that there are no longer any doubts, substance, or points for debate;
one simply maintains a single mind of yearning and reverent listening. △ Third, the actual exposition, which has two parts.
First, a general summary, which is further divided into two sections: 1. The True Suchness as the Basis.
The Buddha said to Ānanda: "You should know that the wondrous nature is perfectly luminous and free from all names and marks. Originally, there have been no worlds and no sentient beings.
This 'wondrous nature' is True Suchness (*tathatā*) within the gate of birth-and-death, which is fundamental enlightenment (*mūla-awakening*). 'Perfectly luminous' means it is purely unsurpassed."
In perception, names and phrases have not yet manifested, and the characteristics of meaning have not yet been encountered; therefore, it is free from all names and characteristics.

Generally speaking, when one speaks of the "world" and "sentient beings," this includes both the environment (*āśraya*) and its inhabitants (*adhiṣṭhāna*). Names and characteristics are provisional phenomena (*prajñapti-dharma*), whereas the environment and inhabitants are substantial phenomena (*dravya-dharma*).

Furthermore, the first phrase refers to the perfected nature (*pariniṣpanna-svabhāva*) as that which is capable of transcending [duality]; the second phrase refers to the imagined nature (*parikalpita-svabhāva*); and the final phrase refers to the dependent nature (*paratantra-svabhāva*).

That which is dependently originated (*paratantra-svabhāva*) is what is to be abandoned. △ Second, that which is originated—arising and ceasing—exists based upon *tathatā* (suchness) while manifesting arising and ceasing.
This is divided into two parts. First, a brief demonstration of the defiled dependent origination (*saṃkleśa-pratītyasamutpāda*).
Due to delusion there is birth; due to birth there is cessation. Birth and cessation are termed "delusion.

That which is "due to delusion there is birth" refers to depending upon ignorance (*avidyā*), through which there is a successive progression until insentient matter gives rise to sentient beings and undergoes rebirth.
Cessation refers to the disintegration of insentient matter and the death of sentient beings. This is necessarily a state of mutual opposition.
Indeed. △ Second, a brief demonstration of the pure dependent origination:

the cessation of delusion is called "the True. This refers to the two designations for the twofold revolution of the basis (*āśraya-parāvṛtti*): the unsurpassed enlightenment of the Tathāgata and Great Nirvāṇa.
When one awakens to the truth and returns to the source, then the world and its sentient beings all vanish away. Through this, birth and death are replaced by true permanence;
therefore, it is said that the extinction of delusion is called "the True. This refers to the actual fruit [of enlightenment]. What follows below merely mentions the names of the fruits of emergence.
Regarding the two characters for "the True," they are designated as *bodhi*, because *bodhi* is precisely true wisdom. Regarding the extinction of delusion...

The two characters refer to *nirvāṇa*. This is because *nirvāṇa* is precisely the absence of arising and ceasing. Nevertheless, while *bodhi* transforms afflictions (*kleśa*), *nirvāṇa* transforms birth and death (*saṃsāra*);
therefore, they are called the two designations for the transformation of the basis (*āśraya-parāvṛtti*). △ Second, each is explained in detail.

This is divided into two sections. First, a detailed exposition of the conditions for defilement (*saṃkleśa-pratyaya*) shows that they universally constitute saṃsāra. This further has two parts: first, an exhortation to recognize inversion;
one must recognize the inverted results of defilement before one can subsequently overturn them to attain pure results.

This is the reason why the stages of the noble ones (*ārya-bhūmi*) are not discussed first, but rather the cycle of existence (*saṃsāra*) is described beforehand. Furthermore, there are three points: first, to establish and determine the intent of the question.

"Ānanda, if you now wish to cultivate the true samādhi and proceed directly to the Great Nirvāṇa of the Tathāgata, then for this true samādhi, you should take the 'perfect penetration through the ear-door' as your primary principle. The two characters 'directly proceed' already contain the fruit within them;
the nirvāṇas of the preceding stages are merely the ultimate fruits [of those paths]. 2. Exhorting him first to recognize perversion.
First, one should recognize these two causes of inversion regarding sentient beings and the world.

Generally speaking, when we refer to "sentient beings and the world," the world refers to the emotional world of sentient beings; it is the primary retribution and not the supporting environment. Wuxing said:
"The inversion of the world" refers specifically to the primary retribution, namely the twelve classes of living beings. This answers what Ānanda asked.

Entering the stages of realization. These stages arise from awakening and entering [the truth]. Awakening must necessarily proceed from delusion. Delusion constitutes the state of an ordinary person (pṛthagjana), while awakening constitutes the state of a sage (ārya).
Both are matters pertaining to the primary retribution (vipākaphala); they do not refer to the receptacle world (bhājanaloka). This, then, is merely a portion of the primary retribution.
These two inversions are established merely by way of cause and effect; you shall see this for yourself later. △ Third, concluding by returning to the question:
that inversions do not arise is the Tathāgata’s true samādhi.
Ānanda originally asked the Buddha about the stages within *samādhi*. Now it is said that being non-inverted is precisely right concentration (*samyak-samādhi*);
what is called "stage" (*pada*) refers to entering through awakening. △ Second, the interrogation and explanation of the two inversions. This also has two parts.
First, the interrogation and explanation of the inversion of sentient beings. This is further divided into three. First, the interrogation.
Ānanda, what is meant by the "inversions" of sentient beings?

△ Second, the formal explanation, divided into three parts. First, the formation of existence through following the stream. The character "following" (shùn) refers to the innate afflictions that arise spontaneously.
To investigate the source thoroughly, although these ultimately rely on ignorance, they simultaneously encompass both types of grasping (*dvaya-grāha*). However—
In the immediate sense, this refers to the proximate basis of the segmented [birth-and-death], which consists primarily of the afflictions of thought within a single realm.
