Regarding "the formation of existence," this refers to the arising of the karma of birth-and-death from within the fundamental state where there is no birth-and-death. This is divided into three parts.
First, a retrospective exposition of how existence arises from non-existence.
Ānanda, because the nature of the mind is luminous and the nature of the mind is perfectly full, the nature arises from luminosity, and deluded vision arises from that nature.
From ultimate non-existence, it becomes ultimate existence.

Wenling says: "The luminosity of nature" (*xing-ming-xin*) refers to the essence of True Suchness (*tathatā*). "The luminosity of nature is perfect and round" (*xing-ming-yuan*) means that it does not abide in its own nature.
Because it does not abide in its own nature, through deluded luminosity it gives rise to deluded nature; because of deluded nature, it produces deluded views.
Thus, from the formless reality, it becomes the deluded state of having form. "Luminous perfection" (*ming-yuan*) is precisely that which flows forth.
The movement of the mind means that it does not maintain its own nature; this is the principle of following conditions (*pratyaya*). Deluded clarity is ignorance (*avidyā*);

deluded nature is the consciousness of karma (*karmavijñāna*); and deluded nature-seeing is the simultaneous arising of the two attachments. All of the above belong to the category of afflictions (*kleśa*).

As for what follows—arising from non-existence to existence—this refers to the manifestation of karmic fruition that must inevitably be summoned once karma is formed. This character "existence" (*yu*) refers to...
The "existence" (*bhava*) link within the twelve links of dependent origination is the karma that spontaneously leads toward rebirth.

However, the two characters "ultimate" (*jiujing*) carry the meaning of successive grasping, fabrication, and accomplishment. Therefore, do not yet interpret this "existence" as referring to physical form (*śarīra-lakṣaṇa*).
It is only the subsequent phrase "divided segments" (*fenduan*) within the world that constitutes physical form. △ Second: Clarification.
This demonstrates that although there is "constancy," it is actually non-existent.
This "existence" is that which possesses [nothing]; it is not a cause for a cause, nor is it a characteristic of an abode for an abode. It is utterly devoid of a fundamental basis.
The upper character signifies the delusion of "being able to have," while the lower "possessing" refers to karma. The subsequent phrase generally clarifies its non-existence.
"Because" [indicates that] this karma is not the true cause, and these afflictions are not the true object-cause. "Abiding" refers to continuity.
That which is about to arise is called "existence" (*bhava*); when its characteristics are collectively uninterrupted, it is called "abiding. Thus, existence is that which is able to abide.
Delusion is that which dwells [within it]. The final phrase states in general that both characteristics are entirely without a fundamental basis upon which to rely.
Since there is neither cause nor basis, although they exist, they are eternally non-existent. △ Third, the determination that [these characteristics] are falsely established based on non-existence.
Based on this non-abiding, the worlds and all sentient beings are established.
Wu Xing said: "To base [them] on this non-abiding means that 'abiding' refers to a basis. When one traces from the root to the branches, there is ultimately nothing upon which to rely.
Non-abiding means that the delusions and karma which constitute the fundamental root are fully understood to be non-existent. These worlds exist within the multitudes...

Above "birth" (sheng), the character "and" (ji) is further added; this refers to the "dependent retribution" (yi-bao), such as the mountains, rivers, and the great earth, which are concomitantly included.
As it is said: "This root of non-abiding is not only the basis for sentient beings, but the mountains, rivers, the great earth, and sentient beings alike are all established in dependence upon it.
If "birth" were placed first and "realms" (jie) last, [the meaning would be lost].
This is precisely what is meant by the "sentimental world. The old commentaries failed to grasp the distinction between the sequence of the realms (*dhātu*) and the stages of birth (*jāti*).

Some rely on the provisional while others on the ultimate, arbitrarily dividing them into general and specific categories; they fail to notice their contradiction with the preceding interrogative phrasing, which is simply due to a lack of thorough investigation.
Furthermore, the true mind also possesses the meaning of "non-abiding," as in the case of non-abiding *nirvāṇa*, which does not linger in any single phenomenon.

That is to say: this is not the intended meaning of the present sutra. The section on "the completion of existence through following the stream" is finished. △ Second, "the false further becomes non-existent.

The single character "false" (*xié*) refers to the delusion of discrimination arising from longing for and aversion to [existence and extinction]. If one investigates its ultimate source, it remains the same as the previous category:

it relies distantly upon ignorance (*avidyā*) and concurrently involves attachment to phenomena (*dharmagrāha*). If one considers it proximately in terms of the immediate basis of the *pratisaṃdhi* (segmented) realm, it likewise consists largely of [these factors].
This refers to the delusions of view within the realm [of existence]. As for "establishing what is not so," it is because one has long wandered through birth and death;

weary and seeking restoration, yet ignorant of the essential means of escape, one engages in successive, erroneous practices. This is divided into three parts: first, that which is fundamentally non-existent cannot be restored.
Delusion of the fundamentally perfect luminosity gives rise to false construction. This false nature has no substance and has nothing upon which it depends.
False karma cannot diminish this fundamental perfection; false delusion cannot obscure this fundamental luminosity.
This fundamental perfect luminosity is precisely the essence of the unchanging nature. Sentient beings merely become deluded regarding this unchanging nature, and thus [delusion] arises.
Regarding delusive afflictions and karma born of falsehood: if one pursues the nature of this falsity to its ultimate limit, it is found to have no substantial reality and no basis whatsoever.
In brief, this means that while the True is immutable, the false is fundamentally empty. Now, since the false is fundamentally empty, there is nothing of the false to be abandoned;
and since the True is immutable, there is nothing of the True to be restored. II. All "restorations" are non-existent. Since there is nothing to be abandoned...
"Can be restored. Thus, all who seek restoration do so falsely. Furthermore, there are two sections. First, the illustration by means of analogy.
This, in turn, has two parts. First, clarifying that even the primary restoration is still not [the ultimate].
If one intends to return to the Real, once that intention arises, it is already not the true nature of True Suchness (*tathatā*).
This refers to those within the Buddhist teachings—whether of the Hīnayāna or the provisional, gradual Mahāyāna—who attempt to return to the Real by following correct principles;
yet even they do not attain the true nature of True Suchness. This is because they forcibly [seek] that which is inherently inseparable.
"Departure. This is because one forcibly returns to that which is fundamentally beyond returning.

It can be seen that only those of the Perfect and Sudden [teaching] attain it by means of "departure without departing" and "returning without returning. △ Second, further clarifying the error of false returning and its lack of benefit.
This is not a true seeking of restoration; it results entirely in non-characteristics (*asamjñā*).

This refers to all non-Buddhists (*tīrthika*) who, failing to perceive the correct principle, engage in various forms of erroneous cultivation—all of which constitute a non-true seeking of restoration.
"It results entirely in non-characteristics" means they manifestly fall into erroneous and false causes and effects, becoming increasingly entangled in their branches.

This is a departure; it violates and distances one from perfect penetration and turns one's back on the city of Nirvana, placing one in the company of the latter group of the māras of the skandhas. II.
Second, the detailed explanation:
It is neither arising nor abiding; it is neither mind nor dharmas, yet they arise from one another in succession.
These all belong to delusion; that is, they are afflictions of view (*dṛṣṭi-kleśa*). It is only in the subsequent section that they are formally categorized as karma.
This is because, upon reaching the later world-spheres, it is explained that the body itself is the fruit. The old interpretation—that the body and sensation are not [the cause]—is incorrect.

Here, "not arising" does not mean not being the cause, but rather refers to the false calculation of causes: recklessly imagining wrong practice to be the cause for producing the fruit. "Not abiding" does not mean not being the fruit, but refers to the calculation of the fruit.
This refers to the fruit of falsely conceptualizing all impermanent states as permanent. "Not mind" refers to false wisdom;
it encompasses all erroneous views and understandings, establishing its own tenet such that each individual claims to clarify their original mind.
"Not dharma" refers to false objects; it encompasses all erroneous practices and realizations, establishing various systems of dharma.
[The preceding sections were] the gates. Each [of them] individually claimed to have attained the unsurpassed Dharma. The final sentence provides a summary:

because false causes, false effects, false wisdom, and false objects mutually induce one another, they arise in a continuous succession. Thus, it is concluded that all of these are not [the true state]. End.
△ Third, the delusions of the three fetters form karma.
The power of birth manifests [karma]; this manifestation perfumes [the mind] to constitute karma.
The "power of birth" is the power of perverse delusion; "manifestation" refers to the activity of acting based on delusion, which is perfuming (*vāsanā*). This is the initial [stage].
Xun initially called this "the manifestation of awakening. Xun has long practiced meditative concentration; what is meant here is that his karma is already established and cannot be altered.

This is also the perfuming that forms karmic seeds, which will inevitably bring about the latent tendencies (*anuśaya*) for perverse fruits. △ Third, a general explanation of the induction of retribution.
"Karmas of the same category resonate with one another. This means that because there are karmas of resonance, they mutually extinguish and mutually produce one another.

This collectively follows from the two preceding sections on the two types of afflictions and karma—those arising simultaneously (*sahaja*) and those through discrimination (*vikalpita*)—to clarify the retribution of mutual extinction and mutual production that is summoned.
This is truly because sentient beings undergo birth-and-death in segments (*paricchinna-jarāmarana*) only when they are personally [bound by these conditions].

Based on the two delusions of views (*dṛṣṭi*) and thought (*saṃkalpa*), one creates karma that brings about retribution. However, these two may be mutually light or heavy, or they may be equal in proportion.
To exhaustively investigate their initial arising, it must be thought first and views later; therefore, the sūtras enumerate them in this sequence.
Regarding innate delusions and karma (*sahaja-kleśa-karma*), the text briefly describes the manifestations of delusion while detailing the delusions and karma themselves;

this is because they arise spontaneously and simply, and thus the source of delusion must be clearly identified at the outset. Regarding discriminative [delusions], the manifestations of delusion are detailed while the delusions and karma are described more briefly;

this is because false conceptualizations are manifold, and thus the source of delusion need not be recounted again. Upon reaching this section, the text then simultaneously upholds both [aspects] in their totality.
This clarifies the principle of mutual resonance. Those with identical karma will necessarily gather together because their karma is the same.

As for "mutual resonance," it means that once they have gathered for a long time, there are inevitably two types of matters—favorable and adverse—that mutually stir one another's minds. Because of this, there arises the karma of resonance.
This also establishes the meaning of the seeds of karma. For instance, when one is moved by favorable circumstances, the seed of karma for unrelenting affection is formed;
when one is moved by adverse circumstances, the seed of karma for unrelenting resentment is formed.
The final phrase briefly demonstrates retribution across successive lifetimes, thereby showing that afflictions, views, karma, and their results serve as the conditions for birth.
Furthermore, those who gather through resentment and hatred will mutually destroy one another; those who gather through affection and love will mutually give rise to one another.
This is also determined according to present karma to establish future fruits, rather than being a formal discussion of karmic retribution.
The detailed explanation within the section on "Inversions in the Lower Worlds" has now been completed. △ Third, the conclusion.
For this reason, there are sentient beings who are inverted.
"For this reason" means precisely because of these two delusions and two types of karma. Thus, it should be known that "sentient beings" is spoken of in reference to their causes.
The section examining and explaining the inversion of sentient beings is hereby concluded. II. Examining and explaining the world.
The inversion of realms is divided into three parts. First, the inquiry:
"Ānanda, what is meant by the inversion of worlds?

Second, the formal explanation, which is divided into two parts. First, explaining the enumeration of the names of worlds, which is further divided into two. First, explaining the formation [of the names].
Names are that which possess existence; they arise falsely through segmentation and are established based on these realms. They are not caused by a cause, nor do they abide in an abode;
they flow on without staying, and thus the world is formed.

This section explains the formation of the two characters "world" (*loka*). The preceding afflictions and karma constitute the "possessor," while the present retributive body constitutes the "possessed.
Through the fulfillment of cause and effect, this body of segmented birth (*paricchinna-jāti*) arises falsely from the unborn.
Based upon this segmented physical basis (*āśraya*), the realm of sentient beings (*sattva-loka*) is established; such is the designation of that realm.
It is from this that they are obtained. Furthermore, this false arising is fundamentally neither the cause nor the causal condition; it is fundamentally neither the dweller nor the dwelling place.
By its very nature, it is a dharma that undergoes moment-to-moment flux and does not abide.
It is because of this that the three periods of time are formed through continuous succession, and it is from this that the names of "time" are derived. 2. Explaining the Quantification.
The three periods of time and the four directions intermingle and harmonize, transforming sentient beings into twelve categories.
The "four directions of the body" refers to left, right, front, and back; this is based on the fundamental number of the world.

Through the reciprocal interaction of three and four, and four and three, these twelve all respond to their numerical values to produce transformations. 2. Inferring the Origin from the Six Perceptions (ṣaḍ-saṃjñā).
It forms a cycle. Question: Since it is said that this arises from "pushing forward," is this not a cause? Answer:

This refers to the time of taking birth, when one pursues sounds and chases after forms, grasping and becoming attached so as to form a cycle. This is what is called "moistening birth" (janmanirvartana), not "moistening karma" (karmavipāka).
Therefore, it belongs to the fruit and not to the cause. It is divided into three parts. First, showing the sequence of inhaling sensory objects.
Therefore, in the world, sound exists because of movement; form exists because of sound; fragrance exists because of form; touch exists because of fragrance;
taste exists because of touch; and mental phenomena are known because of taste.
Wuxing said: "The 'last' refers to the cognition of dharmas; 'cognition' is the mental faculty (*manas*), and 'dharmas' are the objects of the mind (*dharmāyatana*).

By analogy with what follows, there are likewise the principles of hearing sounds, seeing forms, and so forth. Furthermore, it speaks of the 'six disordered delusions,' which shows that seeing, hearing, sensing, and cognizing all return to delusion.
Now, although the taking of birth is induced by external objects drawing upon the mind, at the very beginning..."
First, it is moved by one's own mind that one subsequently hears sounds and so forth; therefore, it is said that "because of movement there is sound.
Furthermore, when sensory objects come to respond to the mind, sound must arrive first. This is because sound is most pervasive over great distances, and because the ear is particularly acute.
Sound occupies the first place among the six types of confusion; following sound, one inevitably proceeds to seek forms. Therefore, it is said next that "because of sound there is seeing."
Regarding form: when one approaches form, one inevitably comes to smell fragrance; smelling fragrance, one inevitably comes to perceive touch; perceiving touch, one inevitably comes to taste flavor;
tasting flavor, one inevitably comes to cognize mental objects (*dharma*). To "cognize mental objects" means that one does not relinquish conceptualization based on conditions.
This is because, from the remote one proceeds toward the proximate, gradually forming the characteristics of drawing near and grasping. All sentient beings are thus inverted.
The destinies and births all arise from this. △ Second, explaining the formation of the wheel of karma and its revolution:
because the six types of distracted false conceptualization constitute the nature of karma, the twelve divisions [of dependent origination] revolve by means of this.
"Karma" (*karma*) refers to habitual practice (*vāsanā*). "Nature" (*prakṛti*) refers to that which cannot be altered or transformed; it is what is meant by "habitual practice perfected as nature.

Do not seek the cause of karma through conceptual conjunction. Although sensory objects (*viṣaya*) are only six, each arises from a single cause and a single existence, cycling through the six positions.
Thus, they constitute twelve. Consequently, one is moved by these twelve distinct divisions to revolve in saṃsāra.

Furthermore, because the two characters "cause" (yin) and "existence" (you) refer to the sense faculties and their objects, they likewise correspond to the number twelve. △ Third, the conclusion on the revolving according to objects.
Therefore, the sounds, smells, tastes, and touches of the world, exhausting their twelve transformations, constitute a single cycle of return (*xuánfù*).
Although only four sense-objects (*cén*) are briefly cited, they nonetheless encompass all twelve; hence it is said, "exhausting the twelve transformations.
As for "cycle of return," it carries the meaning of completing a cycle and beginning anew. The formal explanation of this section is hereby concluded. △ Third, the conclusion. This is the conclusion.
The textual accounts of the world are exceedingly detailed and extensive because they primarily manifest the dependent origination of defilement and its pervasive formation of saṃsāra;
conversely, when translated into the perspective of purification, there are likewise many stages. These are divided into three parts, the first of which concludes with a general summary.
Because they ride upon this wheel of the characteristics of perversion, there exist worlds of egg-birth, womb-birth, moisture-birth, and transformation-birth;
those with form and those without form; those with perception and those without perception; and those who are neither with form nor without form, and neither with perception nor without perception.
If it were not for the state of non-perception (asaṃjñin), those who ride this wheel of inversion would immediately mount the revolving roots and sense-objects above.

This is like the successive ascent of the moisture-generating ignorance that gives rise to the realms formed by the subsequent text; there is a "below," where one then details the world-systems that are formed. At each stage...

The four modes of birth each constitute a single group. The latter eight modes of birth do not transcend the conceptualization of form; they are delusions regarding the Truth that result in falsehood.

These are fully encompassed by the two characters "form" (rūpa) and "mind" (citta). The names are listed here, while their detailed explanations will appear naturally in the subsequent scriptural text.

II. A detailed enumeration of the specific categories, divided into two parts: 1. A separate listing of the various classes of beings. Now, the cycle of rebirth (*saṃsāra*) consists of inverted, harmonious, and chaotic conceptions.

Although all categories may generally possess [all four modes of birth], they are distinguished by their respective predominance. Furthermore, there are three [classifications]. First, the four types of birth:

egg-born, womb-born, moisture-born, and transformation-born. Wuxing said: "That which arises depending on an egg is called egg-born; that which emerges from containing [the embryo] is called womb-born;
that which arises through reliance on moisture is called moisture-born; that which suddenly exists where it was previously non-existent is called transformation-born. Thus it is.

There are four modes of birth (*yoni*). With internal mental volitional action (*cetanā-karma*) as the cause and external conditions such as eggs, wombs, moisture, or warmth as the contributing factors, these are established in sequence according to the degree to which such conditions are relied upon.
Egg-birth possesses all four; therefore, it is mentioned first. Womb-birth possesses three; moisture-birth possesses two;
and transformation-birth possesses only one, namely, mental volitional action. This classification into four categories is based on the *Yogācārabhūmi*.
First is birth from an egg.
Ānanda, because the world is characterized by false, revolving, and inverted movement, the combination of vital energies produces eighty-four thousand disordered thoughts of flying and sinking.
Thus there arise egg-born *kalala* beings, who transmigrate through lands as fish and birds.
Turtles and snakes—these species abound.
Wénlǐng says: "The egg is born solely from thought; 'emptiness' (or 'falsity') is precisely thought. The essence of thought is light and buoyant, which is called 'agitated inverted thought.

The egg is formed through the intersection of qi, which is called 'accomplishment through harmonious blended qi. Thought involves much ascending and sinking, which is called 'confused thoughts of flying and diving.'"
Therefore, they evoke the various classes of beings, such as fish and birds, which either fly or sink.

As for the statement that each of the twelve classes [of beings] consists of eighty-four thousand [types], this is because each is produced through the transformation of eighty-four thousand afflictions (*kleśa*). *Kalala* is translated as "coagulated mucus";

it refers to the initial stage of entering the womb, the state when the embryo and the amnion have not yet differentiated. Regarding the *kalala* and subsequent stages while in the womb, one takes [the appropriate form] according to...
This constitutes the text; it is not that each section stands alone. △ Second, birth from the womb:

due to the inverted desires within the world of causes—the defiled cycle of saṃsāra—eighty-four thousand types of horizontal and vertical disordered thoughts are formed through their harmonious blending and nourishment.
Because of this, there is the *kalala* (embryonic stage) of womb-birth, which flows and turns through various lands among humans, animals, dragons, and immortals.
These types are everywhere abundant. Wēn-líng says:
"The womb-conception arises because of emotion; 'defilement' is precisely emotion. Emotion is born of craving, which is called the inversion of desire.
The womb is formed through the union of semen, which is called growth through combination. Emotion has its partiality and correctness, which are called horizontal and vertical disordered thoughts."

Therefore, it moves humans, domestic animals, and all classes of beings, both horizontal and vertical. *Ētuphanda* (遏蒲曇) refers to the "blister" (*phalgu*), which is the stage where the embryo and egg gradually divide.
Regarding "partial" (*pian*) and "correct" (*zheng*): according to later [teachings], when emotion and thought are equal, one is born among humans;

this is the "correct. When emotion is predominant and thought is slight, one flows into the realm of animals; this is the "partial. The worldly teachings state that humans possess the fullness of the Five Constants (*pañca-śīla*), whereas animals...
This attains a partial realization of the Five Constant Virtues. Master Huan’s intention lies mostly in the latter explanation. △ Third, moisture-born beings:
due to attachment to the world and the inverted states of the realms of rebirth, they form through the union of warmth eighty-four thousand types of agitated and disordered thoughts.
Consequently, there exist moisture-phase *piśāca* spirits that circulate through lands, containing crawling and wriggling creatures.
Their kind fills [the world]. Wēnlíng says:

"Moisture acts through union and response; attachment is precisely this union. Union arises from the stagnation of craving; as it encounters objects and clings to them, it is called 'clinging to perversity.
Moisture generates through yang-energy, which is termed 'the warmth formed by conjunction. That which is pursued has no fixed destination, which is termed..."
Because of their inverted and chaotic thoughts, they are moved by birth as wriggling and crawling creatures. "Bisī" refers to soft flesh;

it is the initial sign of moisture-born beings. Since they do not enter a womb, they lack the first two stages [of embryonic development]. ○ As for moisture-born beings, they are attracted by fragrance.
It should be revised to read: "Hearing fragrance and approaching. △ Fourth, birth by transformation (*upapāduka*).
Due to the false inversion caused by the world’s cycle of change and transmigration, the combination of contact produces eighty-four thousand disordered thoughts of new and old.
Because of this, there are transformed *kalala* (embryonic stages) that circulate through lands, undergoing metamorphosis and flying about.
These types fill [the world]. Wēn-líng says:
"Transformation responds through separation; change and alteration are precisely separation. Leaving this and entrusting oneself to that is called 'false inversion.

Touching upon categories and undergoing transformation is called 'the formation of contact through harmony. Turning from the old to the new is called 'the disordered thoughts of the new and the old.'"

Therefore, the retribution experienced is likewise so. Because one sheds the old, one proceeds toward the new; it is like a caterpillar becoming a butterfly, changing from crawling to flying, or like a sparrow becoming a clam, shedding flight for submersion.
Generally, whenever different forms are transmitted to one another, it is all a process of transformation and shedding (*parivṛtti*).
*Kalala* refers to "hard flesh"; once shed, it becomes a body that no longer possesses the characteristic of softness. From this point downward, all are termed *kalala*.

"Southern" (nam) is the general designation for all categories; it stops here. If one speaks of the fifth stage, *prasākha*, as "formation of shape," then that refers to specific appearances and is not a general designation.
Wuxing said: "That which was non-existent suddenly comes into being—this principle should properly apply here."

Tianru said: If one discusses the heavens, hells, ghosts, and so forth, they all possess transformed appearances (*nirmāṇa-lakṣaṇa*). Thus, Master Yue’s assertion that these exist suddenly where there was previously nothing also possesses its own logic;
this should be fully considered. Regarding the place of defiled birth by transformation (*upapāduka*), it is called "accomplishment through the contact of harmony" (*saṃnipāta-sparśa-siddha*).
As the Sūtra says: "In the hells and among the various devas, each and every one is born by transformation. This refers to the transformation based on the shifting support of karma.
It is appropriate to conclude that this is so, because those who are dyed by heavenly karma hear the stench when they enter hell; it is merely a matter of swift transition without difficulty.
All of these are transformations manifested through the transference of karma; they do not arise suddenly from nothing, but are wondrous transformations produced by the mind.
II. The Four Modes of Birth according to the Presence or Absence of Form and Perception. This section is divided into four parts. First: Those with Form.

Due to the obstruction of the world’s causal stagnation and the cycle of samsara, and because of inverted views, they combine and adhere to form eighty-four thousand deluded thoughts of radiant brilliance.
Consequently, there arise the kalala-stage with physical characteristics, which circulate through various lands as auspicious or calamitous spiritual essences.
Their kind fills the world.
Zizhong said: "To rely upon the sun, moon, water, and fire, and to harmonize with their light while clinging to them firmly and refusing to let go, is called 'obstructive attachment.
To be blocked by barriers so that there is no passage is called 'the inversion of obstruction. Because the essence is clear and manifest, one undergoes birth through this; hence [these names]."
Regarding physical forms, such as the stars, planets, sun, and moon: those that are auspicious are termed "restful" (*xiū*), while those that are inauspicious are termed "calamitous" (*jiù*).

This extends even to things like torches and the pearls of oysters; all belong to this category. Wēnlíng says: "All brilliant and spiritual entities are manifestations of refined radiance (*jīngyào*);
because their mental projections have already coalesced into refined radiance, they possess only form. The *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* states that the eighty deities are all... [text continues].

Because the fundamental source of obstructive perceptions remains, this subtle radiance is formed. Although this is extremely refined and spiritual, it has not yet transcended the state of being carried along by the cycle of birth and death and its inverted characteristics. △ Second, the formless realm.
Due to the causes of the world’s dissolution, the cycle of rebirth, and delusive inversions, the union with darkness forms eighty-four thousand obscured and chaotic conceptions.
Consequently, there exist formless *kalala* (embryonic stages) that circulate through various lands, dispersing into emptiness and sinking away.
Such types are everywhere prevalent.
Wēnlíng says: To loathe existence and cling to emptiness, to extinguish the body and return to non-being, is called the cycle of dissolution within saṃsāra.

To be deluded, leaking, and without hearing is called the inversion of confusion. To loathe existence and return to non-being is to rely upon the dark and obscure emptiness; therefore, it combines with darkness to form [this state].
This is termed "obscured and chaotic ideation" (*saṃjñā-āvila-vikṣepa*), which refers to the class of non-Buddhists within the Formless Realm (*ārūpyadhātu*).
Although these possess ideation, they do not constitute a substantial karmic body; therefore, they are also called *kalala*.

Furthermore, because their delusions and karma are heavy and dark, their physical form is worn away, and their substance merges with the obscurity of emptiness. Consciousness clings to this obscured state, belonging to the category of those who are empty, dispersed, dissolved, and submerged. ○ This—

There are two categories. The first category refers to the gods of the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*); this includes not only non-Buddhists but also both ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*) and noble ones (*ārya*).

The noble ones here are those with dull faculties who have attained the stage of *anāgāmin*. They possess no matter as the fruit of karma, yet they do possess the fruits of meditative concentration (*samādhi*).

Furthermore, these should be specifically categorized as belonging to space. "Scattered" refers to the scattered mind, which is the state of being empty and devoid of the marks of form. The second category refers to the deities who preside over space. As for the direction...

The pure non-Buddhists (tīrthikas) maintain that both [name and form] are absent; this should be categorized separately. "Dissolving and sinking" refers to the delusion of wrongly grasping emptiness (*ayoniśaḥ-śūnyatā-grāha*).
It means being worn away and submerged. Furthermore, in the intermediate state (*antarābhava*), there is perception but no form, yet it does not constitute the substance of karma.

On what basis, then, could it also be called *kalala*? One should rather say: although the substance of karma is absent, it does not preclude the existence of birth through the fetters of karma. Therefore...
It is also called *kalala*. This is a designation based on its essential meaning. △ Third, those with perception (*saṃjñin*):
due to the world’s cause of revolving through illusory appearances and inverted reflections, they combine their memories to form eighty-four thousand latent knots of chaotic thought.
Because of this, there are the *kalala* stages characterized by perception, which circulate through various lands as spirits, ghosts, and numinous entities.
Their kind fills the world. Wēnlíng says:
"They are empty and false, having lost their true nature. They are erroneously attached to reflected images and have no physical body to rely upon; they arise from recollection and imagination.
Within the midst of the formless, they secretly form appearances. Their spirit is not luminous, yet they become ghosts in the dark; their essence is incomplete."
Yet they disperse to become spirits; they possess no substantial form, but exist only as conceptual appearances.

○ As for "intangible appearances" (*wangxiang*), it conveys the sense that they seem non-existent yet are not non-existent. For while the forms of gods, ghosts, and essences cannot be seen, there are indeed appearances within the darkness;

thus it is said they are "hidden, obscure, and subtly formed. When sentient beings perversely long for spiritual penetration and pursue these shadows with recollective thoughts, they may at times experience a state of dazed confusion.
Upon seeing this, after a long time, one will surely be reborn and fall into their class. △ Fourth, the Non-Thinking [Beings]:
Due to the world’s cycle of dullness and the delusions of inverted views, a combination of stubbornness produces eighty-four thousand parched and chaotic thoughts.
Because of this, there exist non-thinking *kalala* (embryonic stages) that circulate through the lands, their spirits transformed into [such states].
"Grasses, trees, metals, and stones—these kinds fill the world.

Zizhong said, "Non-Buddhists reckon that insentient things possess life; they argue that metals and stones are firm and solid, or that they are like the settled ash of those practicing meditative concentration."
When thought becomes single-mindedly withered, the mind changes according to its objects; encountering things, it takes on their form.

This is exemplified by such cases as the *jing* spirit born from a flower-pillar or the yellow-headed stone formed from a human. Wénlǐng says: "Failing to understand the principle of the Truths, one stubbornly clings to ignorance.
When this dullness reaches its extreme, one becomes obstinate and devoid of knowledge, and the spirit is transformed into earth, wood, metal, or stone. △ Three.
The four modes of birth (catur-yoni) are neither existent nor non-existent. These four modes of birth are the height of delusion; they truly conform to what Wenling said:
"As deluded sentiments become increasingly false, the principles of transformation grow ever more discordant. This is divided into four parts. First: there is no form.

Due to the world of causes, which is characterized by mutual dependence, cyclic existence, and false inversion, they combine with defilement to form eighty-four thousand disordered thoughts based on causal conditions.
Consequently, there arise non-material forms that take on material characteristics as *kalala* (embryonic stages), circulating through various lands.
The various *śiṃśumāra* (water-mothers) take shrimp as their eyes; their kind fills [the waters]. Wēn-líng says:
"The species of water-mother takes water-foam as its body and shrimp as its eyes.

Originally it has no color of its own, but depends on other things to acquire color. It cannot function by itself, yet depends on other things to have utility. Thus it loses its true nature and becomes entangled in attachment."
They are floating and false; their natures differ from one another, yet they join together through defiled conditions, and thus are called "relying on causes. Zizhong said:
"Their union is a clever deception; they humble themselves to follow others, or falsely rely on causes, mutually providing support and influence to sustain their bodies and nourish their lives."
Karmic results follow one another in succession; because they do not receive a body from their own specific category, they are called "non-material" (arūpa) and so forth.

The eighty thousand families of worms within the bodies of sentient beings all belong to this class. Regarding this life, if we consider the *śiśumāra* (water-mother), it also possesses a physical form;
its substance is like bean-flour, and its shape resembles a woven rug. Since people take it as food, it does not belong to the formless realm (*ārūpya*).
This is specifically because their forms and functions depend on others and cannot maintain their own integrity or vitality; thus it is said that they do not possess form (*rūpa*).
Zizhong’s analogy of the insect in the door-latch is also quite apt. △ Second, they are not without form (*arūpin*).
Due to the nature of cyclic existence being inverted by the mutual attraction of world-phenomena, mantras combine to form eighty-four thousand deluded thoughts of summoning.
Because of this, there exist non-form and formless *kalala* (embryonic stages) that circulate through various lands.
"Cursing and incantations for suppression arise; their kinds fill the world.

Wénlǐng says: "Depraved karmas draw one another in, causing one's nature and emotions to become inverted. Thus, one mounts the incantation and entrusts one's consciousness to it, not following the natural course of life.
One falsely follows the summons, whereby worldly evil arts, cursings, spirits, and enchantments thereby [take hold]."
There are those who possess life. ○ Zizhong cites the example of a frog attaching its voice to its eggs; this is similar to [the view of] Shou, yet it is not as pertinent as the invocation of curses.
We see in the world today that there are those who cast spells upon wooden figures made of *zhāngliǔ* wood to cause them to report omens of good or ill fortune.

Therefore, the interpretation of Wénlǐng is correct. If one were to infer the cause and effect here, it must be that [the person] was constantly engaged in incantations and curses, harming things and injuring life;
as cause and effect repay one another in accordance with their nature, they receive this birth as a result.
△ Third is the perception of non-existence.
Due to the world’s conjunction with delusive saṃsāra and its inverted nature, various combinations give rise to eighty-four thousand types of reciprocal and confused perceptions.
Because of this, there arises the perception of non-existence, which forms the *kalala* and *arbuda* stages of thought; thus they flow and turn within the realms of existence.
Those such as the *pulu* (the parasitic gall wasp) and others achieve their existence through the transformation of different substances; their kind fills the world.

Wēnlíng says: "The two delusions combine, and their essential natures become utterly obscured; they achieve their existence through different substances, and their life-principles are mutually entangled."
It is like that caterpillar (*pulu*): originally a silkworm, it lacks the perception of being a bee, yet it develops the perception of being a bee.
Wuxing said: "Because its substance is different, it does not possess the characteristic of perception; yet because it is formed by those characteristics, it becomes a *kalala* through perception.

[The opponent] attempts to resolve this by claiming that cause and effect appear inverted here; this must be an attempt to deceive within the causal stage, taking what belongs to another and appropriating it as one's own.
There are. Therefore, even within the fruit [of rebirth], they are seized by other beings as their own property. △ Fourth, they are not without perception.

Due to the causes of the world’s cycles of enmity and harm, and the perversity of killing, through their conjunction with strange conditions, eighty-four thousand perceptions of eating one's parents are formed.
Because of this, there exist those who are neither without perception nor possessed of perception—namely, the *kalala* and *arbuda* stages—which circulate throughout the lands.
For example, there are creatures such as the earth-owl that take clods of earth for their offspring, and the mirror-cracking bird that takes the fruits of poisonous trees to raise its young;
once the offspring have grown, both parents meet their end by being eaten by them. Such species abound.
If one infers the origin of this birth, it was originally for the purpose of harboring resentment and seeking retribution; thus, it is said that they are not without thought.
Yet, within the delusions of saṃsāra, all such acts are designated as "killing out of resentment.

Furthermore, there is the suffering of being devoured by those who provided one with life and nourishment—the ultimate kindness and love—while there is also the act of returning in rebellion and devouring those very children who received such ultimate kindness and love.

As for eating [the flesh of one's parents]: if there were anyone who took such pleasure in venting their resentment, it would truly be unbearable to hear or see, and it would be considered an extreme anomaly.
Therefore, it is said that "eating [flesh] becomes the thought of one's parents.

If one were to investigate this through the principle of cause and effect, it must be that the person received the utmost kindness and love, yet instead repaid that grace with enmity and harm. Such instances are also very common to be seen in the world today.

Furthermore, because they were requited by their karmic debtors for this resentment, they came to be born as such. Regarding the old commentary, its tracing of the origins of this particular birth is not entirely clear;
therefore, I shall provide a separate explanation. Mount Gu said: "The earth-owl and the *pòjìng* (broken-mirror). According to the *Shiji*, "Basic Annals of Emperor Wu," it states:
"In the sacrifice to the Yellow Emperor, one *xiāo* and a *jìng* are used. Mèng Kāng [commented]: "The *xiāo* is the name of a bird."

*Shimǔ* (Eater of Mother) and *Pòjìngshòu* (Broken Mirror Beast) are names of animals. *Shifù* (Eater of Father) refers to the Yellow Emperor’s desire to exterminate their kind, whereby he mandated that they be used in all hundred sacrifices.
The *Pòjìngshòu* resembles a wild boar (*chū*) with the eyes of a tiger. The current mention of "bird" (*niǎo*) is likely an error by the translator;

perhaps the character for "bird" should have been "equal" (*děng*), which was later arbitrarily altered. The separate enumeration of animal species is hereby concluded. △ Three: The *Lè* (Leather/Strap).
The categories of names.
These are called the twelve kinds of sentient beings.
*The Correct Pulse Commentary on the Great Buddha-Top Śūraṅgama Sūtra*, Fascicle Seven.
*The Correct Pulse Commentary on the Great Buddha-Usnīṣa Śūraṅgama Sūtra*, Fascicle Eight.
Composed by the Śramaṇa Jiaoguang Zhenjian of West Lake, Capital City.
The detailed enumeration has been completed. △ Third, the formal conclusion regarding mutual falsity. This section has two parts: first, the formal presentation of mutual inclusion.
Analogously,
Ānanda, within each and every category of such sentient beings, there likewise exist twelve kinds of inversions, just as when one presses upon the eyes,
a chaotic mass of flowers appears.
Gushan says: "Each being complete" means they are mutually complete. This is because within each and every category of deluded mental seeds, all are fully present.
When one [aspect] manifests, it is called "phenomenal creation" (shizao); when the others remain latent and hidden, it is called "principle-completeness" (lizhi).

○ The metaphor of pinching a flower illustrates its falsity; the metaphor of the disordered blossoming illustrates their mutual completeness. △ Second, pushing back the false to reveal the true, thereby showing how the true becomes the false.
The inverted, wondrously perfect, true, pure, and luminous mind is fully endowed with such false and chaotic conceptions.

The preceding was a metaphor for the false; this is an investigation into the very reality. It is simply because the fundamental truth is inverted that it is fully endowed with all manner of delusions.
"Fully endowed" means that, encompassing both seeds and manifestations, they mutually possess one another, totaling one hundred and forty-four.
Birth. Although this cycle of birth and death is boundless, ultimately inverted, and unreal, the pure, luminous, true essence remains as it ever was.
If one transforms defilement into purity and advances to the stages of sainthood, how could this be difficult?

This is precisely the fundamental intent behind the teaching of the two types of dependent origination (*pratītyasamutpāda*). To explain in detail the dependent origination of defilement, it results entirely in saṃsāra.
[End of section]. △ Second, a detailed exposition of the pure *paratantra-svabhāva* (dependent origination) through which the various stages (*bhūmi*) are successively accomplished.

Because *tathatā* possesses a body that is unchanging, it is able to follow conditions without being fixed. Since it previously followed defiled conditions to universally manifest as sentient beings, how could it not now follow pure conditions to universally manifest the stages of the sages?
This is divided into four parts. First, the direct answer regarding cause and effect. [The text continues with the headings: ...various...

Regarding these stages, this cause-and-effect relationship involves both affirmation and negation. If one affirms it, each preceding stage serves as the cause for each subsequent stage, and each subsequent stage is the effect of each preceding stage.
If one negates it, only the Buddha is the fruit, while all stages prior to Equal Enlightenment (Samyaksambodhi) are causes.
Therefore, one should know that the old commentaries judge this in terms of realization (*sākṣātkriyā*) rather than cultivation (*bhāvanā*).
This is not a definitive argument. Question: If one speaks in terms of subsumption and exclusion, the causes consist of various stages while the fruit consists of only one stage.

Why, then, do you speak generally of the various stages of cause and fruit? Answer: The aspect of the perfectly interfused fruit is inherently complete from the very first moment of generating the bodhicitta.

What prevents us from speaking of these various stages? There is only the distinction between what is intrinsically possessed (*xingju*) and what is accomplished through cultivation (*xiucheng*). Thus, they are divided into ten sections.
First, regarding the three gradual stages: the previous question asked to what extent one must progress through these gradual stages to attain the "eye" of cultivation;

this refers to the "practice" and so forth, which is precisely the eye of correct cultivation. Herein it should be understood that the three gradual stages prior to the stage of Dry Wisdom (*śuṣka-vijñāna*) encompass all five ranks and ten levels of faith within the Perfect Teaching (*yuanjia*).
As for the ten levels of faith established subsequent to the stage of Dry Wisdom, they are...

This first stage (bhūmi) unfolds into ten minds, as is clearly evident in the scriptural text. This is because those dwelling in the Perfect Teaching (yuan) do not take realization prior to this stage;
therefore, they do not enumerate distinct positions. Consequently, both this sutra and the *Avataṃsaka* do not divide the stage of faith (śraddhā) into ten.
The second section, "Re-examining the Text," is divided into two parts. First, establishing the stages of the sequence of defilement and purity within the teaching. This is further divided into two.

First, the formal exposition: "Now, as you cultivate and realize the Buddha’s samādhi, based upon this original cause—the fundamental state of deluded thought—I shall establish three progressive stages."
Only then can they be eliminated.

Considering this from the very beginning of establishing the stages, one speaks of cultivation and realization as being level; how could one then distinguish the former as cultivation and the latter as realization?
Samādhi is precisely the "Gate of the Ear" samādhi mentioned in the sutra; the old commentary failed to understand the sutra.

The text runs through this point as a single unity. It is entirely unknown that this is a reiteration of the Perfect Penetration (*yuantong*) as the primary expedient for the initial stages (*zhuzhu*);
it is often judged separately, which causes the structural continuity of the sutra text to remain forever unconnected.

"Fundamentally caused by chaotic thoughts" refers to the aforementioned eighty-four thousand [afflictions] such as flying and sinking; "gradually eliminating them in three ways" refers to instructing him...
This refers to dyeing the cloth to make it pure. △ Second, the explanation by way of analogy:
It is like a clean vessel from which poisonous honey has been removed; one then washes and cleanses that vessel with various hot waters mixed with ashes and incense.
If one later stores ambrosia in a vessel that has already held poisoned honey, how can it be called a pure vessel?

It must be understood as being fundamentally pure from the beginning and incapable of being defiled by poison—such is the case with vessels made of gold or jade. This serves as an analogy for the root of non-arising and non-ceasing within the faculties.
The nature is fundamentally and originally pure, yet it possesses an immutable essence. "Poison" and "honey" are metaphors for the five pungent vegetables, sexual misconduct, killing, and so forth.
"Hot water" and "ash" are metaphors for forgetting external objects and exhausting the sense-faculties. "Nectar" is a metaphor for the holy stages that are established.
The three gradual sequences can be understood through these metaphors. △ Second, showing the stages that are established. This also has two parts. First, the inquiry and the enumeration.
Question:
What are the three stages of gradual progression? First, cultivation to eliminate their auxiliary causes; second, true cultivation to excise their fundamental nature;
third, further advancement to counteract their manifest karma.

The first two lines pose the inquiry. From "First" onwards, the six lines list the names; each consists of two lines, with the upper line clarifying cultivation and the lower line clarifying severance.
"Cultivation" refers to investigating the Truth, meaning entering samādhi and gradually attaining the perfect penetration of the ear-faculty.
"Severance" refers to cutting off delusions, meaning eliminating the five pungent roots, observing the three grave precepts, and dissolving the twelve sense bases.
Now, first, regarding the stage of cultivation (*xiūxí*): this refers to the time when, within the context of hearing, one enters the stream and loses the object.
At the outset, through study and practice, one gathers the scattered mind and repeatedly returns it toward its own nature (*zìxìng*).

However, because there are still interruptions and it has not yet become a single, unified whole, it is called the "stage of cultivation. Were it otherwise, then the five [aggregates] would have already been severed.
Regarding "pungent": it means that [the consumption of] the five pungent roots (*pañca-garaka*) is excluded. As for the mention of "cultivation" (*bhāvanā*), what is it that is cultivated?
The following two lines are omitted here. Regarding "excluding their auxiliary causes": this refers to this stage to clarify that the five pungent roots must be severed.

For the five pungent roots do not merely assist lust and anger; through their cumulative power, they can attract demons (*māra*). If so, what evil would not follow? Indeed, they are the four... [text fragment ends].
The "heavy" [disturbances] are the causes that assist [the arising of delusion]. Therefore, one should eliminate them first at the very beginning of cultivation.
Second, as for "true cultivation," this refers to the time when that which has been entered is already tranquil and movement or stillness do not arise.

This is because the effort of forgetting movement has already become a single whole upon entering the path, such that even the dust of stillness will gradually be forgotten; hence it is called "true cultivation. This is because, from the outset...
Observing the precepts is not sufficient to merit the name of "true cultivation"; it is only when one attains true samādhi that one can truly be so designated.

To "excavate their inherent nature" means that at this stage, one uses the razor to scrape away and completely sever the four kinds of fundamental grave offenses, for these constitute the inherent nature of all evils and thus must be excavated at this stage.
This is because one practices dhyāna while still being bound by the four [defiled] minds.
All such [practices] resemble the truth but are not the truth, for they inevitably lead to the paths of demons and the like. Regarding the third stage of progress:
this refers to the time when one gradually increases [one's practice] until all that is heard has been fully realized. This is identical to the "perfect penetration" (yuantong) mentioned previously;

the term "increasing cultivation" (zengxiu) is the same, leaving no room for doubt. Furthermore, while the previous gradual cultivation involved severing distinct entities and had not yet reached full clarity, this—
If cultivation and abandonment share this same single characteristic, what further doubt could there be regarding their difference?

This is truly because that which is cultivated here is fundamentally the nature of hearing, while that which is abandoned consists of the faculties and their objects; thus, one opposes the active karma by preventing the flowing faculties from rushing toward the objects.

This is called the manifestation of karma. When the objects of perception are forgotten and the faculties are exhausted, this is called "contradiction" (*viyoga*). Question: Within this context, one speaks here of "forgetting the objects and exhausting the faculties.
Why, then, was it previously stated in the first two stages that one must "forget the objects and return to hearing"? Answer: In the first two stages, one practices and studies gradually.

This present stage is where the fruition is gathered; the faculties and objects are completely extinguished. This is not the gradual training of the previous stages—how could one suddenly reach such a state through those prior practices?
It is so. △ Second, the detailed analysis and explanation. This is divided into three parts. First, the removal of auxiliary causes. This is further divided into three.
First, the inquiry: What are the auxiliary causes?
This inquiry concerns only the auxiliary causes (*sahakāri-hetu*) and does not inquire about the practice (*bhāvanā*).

Since the practice has already been explained in detail within the section on Perfect Penetration (*paripūrṇa-samyaktva*), its mention here serves merely to indicate that at this stage one should eliminate the auxiliary causes.

Therefore, up to this point, there is only an inquiry and explanation regarding the auxiliary causes, and the practice is not inquired about again. This is also like [the case] in the *Dharmadhātu-maṇḍala*, where...

This is a detailed explanation of the categories of precepts; the following sections shall follow this pattern. △ Second, the detailed exposition. This also has three parts. First, identifying the reliance on food for sustenance:
"Ānanda, the twelve classes of living beings in such worlds cannot sustain themselves by their own power; they rely on the four kinds of nutriment for their existence. These are as follows:"

There are four kinds of nutriment: edible food, contact as nutriment, volition as nutriment, and consciousness as nutriment. For this reason, the Buddha taught that all sentient beings subsist by means of nutriment.
Since he spoke of the "twelve classes of beings," this refers specifically to those within the realms of conditioned existence (*dhātu*).

Those who cannot sustain themselves [within these realms]—such as those whose nature is like the *dharmatā-kāya* (Dharma-nature body) and who have no need for nutriment—are not included here. Nevertheless, the statement that they "must subsist by means of nutriment" refers to the observation of beings within the realms.
One's physical life and the life of wisdom are bound up with one another; therefore, practitioners must understand what requires discernment and what must be restrained and abandoned. Wēnlíng says:
Regarding the four kinds of nutriment, "edible food" (kavaḍīkāra-āhāra) refers to that which humans consume, for it must necessarily be taken in distinct portions.

"Contact-nutriment" (sparśa-āhāra) refers to spirits and ghosts, who are satisfied merely by inhaling contact. "Volition-nutriment" (manahsaṃcetanā-āhāra) refers to the heavens of dhyāna; when nutriment arrives, they may simply... [text fragment ends]
One is satiated by contemplating it. One recognizes both heaven and food; since they possess neither form nor color, one relies solely on cognitive perception (*vijñāna-saṃjñā*).

Regarding "enjoying contact," this means merely touching its fragrance. In the heavens of dhyāna, there is no method for physical food and drink; thus, one should simply derive satisfaction from contemplation.
Yet, one might fear that this takes "dhyānic bliss" itself as the object of contemplation rather than the food. How would such cognitive perception differ from the contemplation of food?
This likely means that consciousness (*vijñāna*) is defined as sustaining life. To say that consciousness serves as nutriment refers to those of superior capacity.
For those of inferior capacity—such as those in the hells or among the hungry ghosts (*preta*)—even throughout kalpas, their life-force cannot be severed merely by their karmic consciousness.

This is also analogous to the categories of "consciousness-nutriment" (*vijñānāhāra*) and "mental-intention nutriment" (*manosaṃcetanāhāra*). I shall examine this further. △ Second, the teaching on abstaining from pungent poisons.
Ānanda, all sentient beings live by consuming what is sweet and die by consuming what is poisonous.
Therefore, those sentient beings who seek samādhi should sever their consumption of the five kinds of pungent vegetables of the world.

"Non-toxic" means "sweet. This does not refer exclusively to the taste of sweetness. The first three lines illustrate that the safety or peril of one's body and life depends upon whether food is sweet or toxic;
they further show that since the life of wisdom (*prajñā-jīvita*) is even more dependent on it, one must exercise extreme care in making choices. [This applies to] seeking *samādhi*.
This clearly shows that when practicing *yuan-tong* (perfect penetration), the five kinds of pungent vegetables are indeed great poisons that endanger the life of wisdom;
therefore, one should sever their use. Gu-shan said: Regarding the "five pungent plants," the *Laṅkāvatāra Sūtra* states they are leeks, garlic, chives, scallions, and *hiṅgu*.
Master Ying said: "*Hiṅgu*" is a corruption of the Sanskrit sound; it is correctly called *xing-yi*. Maitreya... [text continues].
Min Sanzang says: "The root is like a radish; when it emerges from the soil, it is pungent and foul-smelling.

When Maitreya reaches that land, he will not see its sprouts, meaning this [root] does not exist here in our own region; therefore, it is not translated. △ Third, a profound clarification of its faults, which is further divided into four parts.
First, they provoke lust and increase the fault of anger.
These are the five kinds of pungent roots. When eaten cooked, they provoke lust; when eaten raw, they increase anger.

When eaten cooked, they necessarily stimulate the fire of the physical form and thus provoke lust; when eaten raw, they necessarily agitate the qi of the liver and thus increase anger. Thus said the Buddha.
What wisdom reflects is never off by even a hair’s breadth; the nature of things is thus inevitable. One should therefore revere this truth, believe it, and take heed. 2.
The Fault of Heaven Being Far and Ghosts Being Near:
In such a world, those who consume pungent roots, even if they can proclaim the twelve divisions of the scriptures, will find that the celestial immortals of the ten directions—
Disgusted by its foul stench, they all keep their distance. As for the various hungry ghosts (preta), because of that food, they lick his lips;
yet, dwelling constantly with such ghosts, his merit and virtue daily diminish, and he is forever deprived of benefit.
Now, among worldly people, even those who observe the precepts of fasting still mostly fear and avoid those who eat pungent roots;
how much more so must this be for devas and *ṛṣis*? Because hungry ghosts (*preta*) partake of impurity, they constantly draw near to them; because devas remain distant, their merit diminishes daily.
Because ghosts are near, there is long-term lack of benefit. One constantly sees epidemics during the celestial seasons. The people of the world all say that pungent flavors can ward off pestilence;
yet, judging by the scriptures, these are actually the very source that invites pestilence. Thus, driven by the karmic power of worldly beings, they perversely increase their calamities in this way.
One must not fail to take this as a warning. △ Third, being unprotected and encountering Māras.
Furthermore, when those who consume pungent roots practice *samādhi*, the Bodhisattvas, devas, rishis, and virtuous deities of the ten directions will not come to protect them.
A powerful Māra will seize this opportunity to manifest in the form of a Buddha, come to preach the Dharma to them, and disparage the prohibitions and precepts.
To praise lust, anger, and ignorance;
for celestial beings and immortals not to be permitted to hear the sutras; for this holy goodness not to protect meditative concentration; for the superior to invite hungry ghosts;

and for this to lead to the Demon King—these views become increasingly profound. It is not that the prohibitions and precepts are the fetters of the Lesser Vehicle; rather, it is the praising of the three poisons as being without obstruction [that constitutes the error].
To treat the Great Way as something ordinary is to commit every kind of evil, such as the four grave offenses; this truly serves as a cause for all manner of evils.
One must take great care to guard against it. △ Fourth, the fault of becoming a māra and falling into hell.
At the end of their lives, they themselves become part of the retinue of Māra; when their demonic blessings are exhausted, they fall into the Avīci Hell.
The former are present evil causes, while the latter belong to future bitter fruits.
Thus, by reason of a single foul and evil taste, worldly people are led to the extreme suffering of Avīci. What is so difficult to abandon that one would not courageously sever it?
△ Third, the conclusion:
"Ānanda, those who cultivate bodhi must forever sever the five pungent roots. This is called the first progressive stage of cultivation."
Observe that this section begins by stating that one who cultivates bodhi must subsequently sever the five pungent roots;

this clearly shows that the first gradual stage must necessarily involve the concurrent practice of perfect penetration (*yuan-tong*). If one were merely to sever the five pungent roots, how could it be suddenly termed an "advancement in cultivation"?
Furthermore, how could it be designated as "cultivating bodhi"? 2. Excising Their Essential Nature. Properly...
"Nature" refers to lust, killing, stealing, lying, and so forth. The five pungent herbs mentioned above merely serve to assist and provoke these;
here, however, we are addressing the very essence of those fundamental evils themselves. This is divided into three parts. First, the introduction of the inquiry.
What is right nature (*samyaktva*)?

△ Second, the detailed explanation. This also has two parts. First, the instruction to uphold the precepts. This further has three parts. First, showing that the cause of meditative concentration arises from the precepts.
Ānanda, for sentient beings such as these to enter *samādhi*, they must first strictly maintain pure precepts;
only when the practice of "listening inwardly" takes hold can one truly enter *samādhi*. This is what is called the stage of genuine cultivation (*bhāvanā*).

It is seen that this is more profound than the previous textual discussion on the practice of seeking. However, the reason it says "must first" is because it relies upon the merit of the preceding stages.
Now, hearing and understanding alone cannot bring one’s practice to fruition.

Therefore, it is shown that only after receiving special and strict admonitions can one’s effort enter the gate and attain *samādhi*—what is known as "concentration arising from precepts. △ Second, showing that one must first sever lust and killing.
This has three parts: first, the formal instruction to sever them forever.
Permanently sever the mind of lust. Do not consume alcohol or meat; eat food purified by fire and do not eat anything that possesses life. Lust and killing are the foremost of all evils;
therefore, one must first sever them before being able to follow the various precepts.
Lust must be brought to a halt from the mind. Not drinking alcohol preemptively prevents the confusion and transgressions it causes. Not eating meat is itself the act of renunciation.
Regarding killing: in the fourfold *Saṃghāvaśeṣa* rules of the six-fascicle [Vinaya], the consumption of meat is all categorized under the taking of life.
To purify food with fire is the ultimate expression of the precept against killing. Consequently, one dares not eat any raw or fresh things that have not passed through fire.
It is shown that even those who grow plants among insentient things cannot bear to harm them; how much less could one who lives among sentient beings bear to kill them? Question:
If the cessation occurs only at this stage, does it imply that in the preceding stages one was still permitted to consume alcohol and meat? Answer:
This is for the sake of those with sharp faculties who have not previously observed the precepts of fasting; thus, they are led through such gradual abandonment. If [one had already] previously...
Those who possess the upavāsa precepts are not included in this category. Furthermore, in India, many were temporarily adherents of the Hīnayāna who had not yet severed [their afflictions];

thus, they were instructed to turn their minds toward the Mahāyāna and gradually sever them. In this land, however, those who purely uphold the Mahāyāna never fail to sever [afflictions] first when practicing;
therefore, there is no need to wait until later to sever them. △ Second, the determination through negative statement.
Ānanda, for a practitioner of the path, if they do not sever sexual desire and the taking of life, it is impossible for them to transcend the triple world;
this is because the cycle of mutual birth and mutual killing has not yet ceased. 2. Specifically Teaching the Contemplation of Sexual Desire.
One should contemplate lust as being like a venomous serpent or as encountering an enemy thief.

Lust is the profound source of birth and death; moreover, because it is habitually practiced by the mind, it is most difficult to abandon all at once. Therefore, one is specifically instructed to contemplate it.
Wénlǐng says: "Lust is like a venomous serpent or an enemy thief" because it can harm the *dharmakāya* and kill the life-force of wisdom (*prajñājīvita*).
Therefore: △ Third, the gradual progression of the precept categories in the later teaching.
First, one maintains the four parājikas and eight niḥsargika-pāyattikas of the śrāvaka, holding the body motionless; subsequently, one practices the pure discipline of the bodhisattva.

If one maintains the mind so that it does not arise [with afflictions], this alone fully encompasses the four grave offenses and the four acts of expulsion—namely, sexual misconduct, killing, stealing, and lying. For a bhikṣuṇī, this is further augmented by eight prohibitions, including touching a man and concealing another’s offense;

these also largely prevent sexual misconduct. To maintain the body by merely forbidding the seven branches [of unwholesome conduct] is still considered coarse. One who advances below this level is a bodhisattva.

The precepts of restraint (*saṃvara*) are subtle; they are to be understood according to what was previously explained regarding the ritual site (*maṇḍala*). For a Bodhisattva as well, it is sufficient to cease from the four grave offenses (*catur-gurudharma*) within the mind;
the subtlety lies in not giving rise to even a single thought, rather than [observing] the thirty thousand and eight hundred thousand precepts.

**II. The Benefits of Accomplishing the Precepts.** This is divided into two sections. **1. Liberation from Birth and Death.** This is further divided into two parts. **A. What is Liberated by Abandoning Lust and Killing.**
When the precepts are perfected, there will forever be no karma of mutual procreation or mutual killing within the world.
By severing lust, one does not procreate; by severing killing, one does not kill.
Since the causes of the karma of procreation and killing are absent, the retributions of procreation and killing likewise do not exist. II. Severing the Liberation from Theft and Robbery.
Stealing and robbery do not occur; there are no burdens of mutual indebtedness. Furthermore, in this world, one does not have to repay debts from previous lives.
"Stealing" refers to taking things secretly; "robbery" refers to taking things by force. "No burden of indebtedness" means the absence of the karmic burden of being in debt.

According to the scriptural text, it appears to speak only of stealing; however, Wuxing’s supplementation regarding "great falsehood" (*mahāmṛṣāvāda*) and his judgment that this refers to the stage of contemplative practice (*guanxing*) seem to have a rational basis.
His brief statement says: "Because one does not lie, one does not repay past debts; because one commits great falsehood, one covets offerings.

Speaking in terms of spiritual stages, this should fall within the contemplative practice of the Perfect Teaching (*yuanjia*), specifically corresponding to the ten levels of faith (*śraddhā*) of the Distinct Teaching (*biejiao*).
Thus, these seven are the virtuous ones. △ Second, the purity of karmic retribution:

These pure persons cultivate samādhi; their physical bodies as parents need not rely on the divine eye, yet they naturally perceive the worlds of the ten directions, behold the Buddhas, hear the Dharma, personally receive the holy instructions, attain great supernormal powers, and travel through the realms of the ten directions.
One's past lives are purified, and one attains freedom from hardship and peril.

A pure person treads upon the preceding stage of upholding the precepts; the subsequent stage of *samādhi* represents great meditative concentration (*mahāsamādhi*). Now, concentration is the correct practice.
The precepts are merely auxiliary practices. The manifestation of the exhaustion of the aggregate of form (*rūpaskandha*) is the sight of the ten directions with the physical eye.

This is what is meant in the later passage: "The ten directions open up clearly, with no further darkness. According to the stages, this should correspond to the first stage of faith (*śraddhā*), equivalent to the Small Vehicle’s first fruit (*srotāpanna*).

Previous judgments that place this at the level of "contemplative practice" (*guanxing*) contradict the sutra; this will be examined in detail within the section on the demons of the aggregates (*skandhamāra*). For now, I shall provide a separate judgment for each.

Do not cling to what you have heard before. The next four phrases describe the characteristics of the exhaustion of the aggregate of sensation (*vedanā-skandha*). The subsequent text states: "Going and staying are free and spontaneous, with no further lingering obstructions. It also says:
"Having attained the body born of mastery (*manomaya-kāya*), one proceeds everywhere without hindrance. Now it is said that one beholds the Buddha and hears the Dharma.

Furthermore, the statement "personally received" implies that one must have gone there in person; it does not refer to seeing or hearing from afar. That the subsequent text further states "attaining the power to travel throughout the realms" is even more consistent with the later passage.
According to the stages, this should correspond to the second or third stage of faith (*śraddhā*), equivalent to the two lower fruits of the Śrāvaka path.
The final two phrases describe the signs of the exhaustion of the *saṃjñā-skandha* (perception aggregate). The later text says: "In the mind of awakened clarity, it is like removing dust and grime."

Throughout the cycle of birth and death, one illuminates the beginning and the end with perfect clarity. What is now called "purity regarding past lives" clarifies that one has removed defilements to illuminate birth and death.
Furthermore, regarding the statement "attaining freedom from hardship and peril," since one has already penetrated and mastered knowledge of past lives, [one is thus free from such obstacles].
Except by the power of one's own vows, one shall never again mistakenly enter the evil destinies—namely, being free from the perilous difficulties and evil paths of birth and death.
According to the stages, this should correspond to the fourth and fifth levels of the Ten Faiths, which parallel the three lower fruits of the Small Vehicle.

Regarding this karmic retribution, one briefly relies on the precepts as auxiliary practice, while fully developing the wondrous samādhi of the ear-door, which encompasses all ten faiths, including the first five.

This fully manifests the purity of the six sense organs: seeing the ten directions constitutes the purity of the eye organ; hearing the Dharma and receiving it personally constitutes the purity of the ear organ;

attaining supernormal powers to travel through the realms constitutes the purity of the nose, tongue, and body organs—since all three involve the union of cognition with its objects and reaching distant places; and having no difficulties regarding past lives constitutes the purity of the mind organ. △ Third, the conclusion.
This is called the second stage of progressive cultivation.
Within this, the first half—where various precepts assist in perfecting right concentration—constitutes the stage of contemplative practice (*vipaśyanā*). The latter half concerns karmic retribution.

This corresponds to the five levels of faith and the three lower fruits [of the śrāvaka path]; within the practice of perfect penetration (*yuan-tong*), one then reaches the state where movement and stillness do not arise.
△ Third, contravening their present karma, divided into three parts. First, the inquiry.
What is the manifestation of karma?

△ Second, the detailed explanation is divided into three sections. First, the simultaneous sublation of sense organs and objects, which is further divided into two parts. The first reiterates the previous point regarding maintaining the precepts and remaining detached from sensory objects.
Ānanda, for one who thus purely maintains the prohibitive precepts, the mind is free from lustful desire and does not flow excessively outward toward the six external sense objects.
Although the term *samādhi* was repeatedly mentioned in the preceding text, it is not mentioned here because the initial stage of the mind relies entirely upon the precepts.

If one supports [the former], then the characteristics of the precepts (*śīla*) are prominent while the characteristics of meditative concentration (*samādhi*) are subtle and hidden; fearing that people might forget concentration, it is mentioned repeatedly therein.
In this context, however, the wondrous concentration of the revolving faculties (*indriya-parāvṛtti*) is fully revealed, so there is no need to laboriously restate concentration.

Rather, only the precepts are restated as the cause for the subsequent concentration, thereby demonstrating the profound principle that concentration arises from the precepts. Therefore, it begins by citing the pure upholding of the precepts.
Regarding this person, the text first cites the various precepts maintained in the former half [of the sūtra], and specifically elaborates on the prohibition against greed and lust.
This is certainly because it is the foremost of the four grave offenses and the chief destroyer of meditative concentration; thus, it serves to warn people that they must eliminate such desires.

Furthermore, from this point downward, the text formally cites the various individuals within the latter half concerning the retributive fruits—namely, those of the five levels of faith and the three fruits of the śrāvaka path—to provide confirmation.

This is because it is granted that [the practitioner] has reached the limit of their power.
