For one who has attained the five stages of faith (*pañca-śraddhā*) and the three fruits (*tri-phala*), the nine grades of afflictions of thought (*saṃskāra-kleśa*) within the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*) have already been exhausted;
how could they retain a lustful mind? Therefore, it is granted that their mind will certainly be free from greed and lust.

This is still due to the supreme merit of forgetting sensory objects (*viṣaya*). Furthermore, it is granted that the six sense objects (*ṣaḍ-viṣaya*) do not flow forth or disperse excessively. However, while it is granted that they do not [flow excessively], it does not...
As for the claim that it is entirely absent, this is because the roots have not yet been exhausted and the state of mutual dependence still persists;

it merely involves the permeation of the out-flowing (sāsrava) by the outflow-free (anāsrava), whereby [the former] gradually diminishes from its abundance. It is not entirely outflow-free, and therefore we do not grant full assent to that claim.
It is entirely untainted. This is discussed in the following section. △ Second, advancing to the attainment where objects are forgotten and the faculties are exhausted:

because the causes no longer flow outwardly, one turns back to the source and returns to oneself. Since objects are no longer conditioned, the faculties have nothing to pair with. The returning flow becomes entirely unified.
"The six faculties do not function.

This opening phrase traces back to the previous practice of forgetting external objects. For while a mind free from greed and lust is still merely the mark of ethical discipline (*śīla*), the fact that sensory objects no longer flow forth and run wild clearly manifests the accomplishment of meditative concentration (*samādhi*).
However, this is shallow rather than deep; now, he traces back once more to advance further.
Because it dissolves the nature of the faculties, it is deeper than the former; this is precisely the stage of gradual increase in perfect penetration (*yuan-tong*).
It should correspond to the six levels of faith. Next, the following lines manifest the resonance with the true nature through "turning the hearing inward.

The middle two lines correctly clarify that by forgetting objects, one necessarily reaches the exhaustion of the faculties, for the faculties entirely depend upon objects to be established. The final two lines conclude by establishing the entry into the One and the forgetting [of all].
Sixth: This refers to having attained the extinction of six [senses], yet still not forgetting one. The *nirvāṇa* of the Small Vehicle (*hīnayāna*) precisely corresponds to this stage.

According to the Perfect Penetration (*yuan-tong*), this is the moment when both hearing and that which is heard are exhausted. By the standard of the stages, it should correspond to the seventh stage of Faith (*xin*), equaling the fourth fruit of the Small Vehicle.
II. The Wondrous Nature Fully Manifested. Within this, there are three sub-sections, which should correspond to the Perfect [Teaching].
These three sections collectively clarify the cessation of the three fetters through the realization of emptiness.

As for why the language of the first two sections does not correspond [to each other], it is because what the Bodhisattva discusses in those sections is the effort (*yatna*) for untangling the knots, whereas here we are characterizing the state of realization (*adhigama-viṣaya*) attained through that very effort.
Only in the third section do the words and meaning coincide entirely; this sufficiently verifies that the first two sections are likewise not erroneous. This is divided into three parts.
First, the environment is luminous and pure;
the lands of the ten directions are brilliantly clear and pure, like a bright moon suspended within lapis lazuli.
This is precisely the realm realized through the non-abiding of all-hearing. The first two phrases correspond to the mountains, rivers, and great earth.
The thought transforms into supreme awakening precisely because one does not dwell within the realm of internal self-awareness;

thus, attachment to phenomena (dharma-grāha) is utterly dispersed, and the world is fused such that there is no longer any distinction between the sentient beings and their environment. This appearance of being vividly and transparently opened is illustrated below by the metaphor of clarity and penetration:
for instance, when the bright moon is amidst obstructing objects, it cannot pass through them, just as in the case of two [separate things].
This vehicle merely clarifies the internal realm and does not integrate it with external phenomena. Now, the Bodhisattva realizes that both the perceiver and the perceived are empty;
thus, both the inner and outer are transparently penetrating. It is like the moon reflected in lapis lazuli—how could there be anything that does not penetrate through?

This corresponds to the stage of "similar attainment" within the eighth stage of faith (*aṣṭama-śraddhā*), wherein form is sovereign. △ Second, the wondrous perfection of the primary retribution (*vipāka*).
Body and mind are blissful; wondrous, perfect, and equal, one attains great peace and stability.
This is the realm realized when the awakening to emptiness is perfectly complete. While previously there was the wisdom of emptiness, this is now the emptiness of emptiness (*śūnyatā-śūnyatā*).
Since one is neither exhausted by wisdom nor bound by emptiness, body and mind are blissful, reaching the height of liberation.

"Sprinkling" signifies the meaning of the Dharmakāya being vast and open, and the true mind being expansive and serene. "Wondrously Perfect" means it is wondrous because it is unbound, and perfect because it is unimpeded.
There are three aspects of equality: first, both the measure of the body and the measure of the mind pervade the entire Dharma-realm;
second, sentient and insentient beings share the same substance without distinction; third, the self-mind, sentient beings, and Buddhas are perfectly fused without high or low. This corresponds to...
Ninth is the mastery of the mind that resembles faith. Because body and mind are as one, the body is also the mind.
△ Third, the manifestation of the principle of all Buddhas:
the secret, perfect, pure, and wondrous [nature] of all Tathāgatas is fully manifested therein.

This is clearly identical in all respects to "the manifestation of quiescence" (*śānti-pratyupasthāna*). However, the former refers to one's own mind, while the latter refers to the principle of the Buddha;
thus, the two meanings are equal. "Esoteric" (*guhya*) refers to the realm that is secret, profound, firm, and remote, such that no one can reach it.
"Perfect" (*pariniṣpanna*) refers to the realm of perfect fusion, where things interpenetrate and mutually encompass one another in infinite layers. "Pure" (*viśuddha*) refers to clarity...
"Pure" refers to the realm where the signs of dawn are pure and refined, such that not even a speck of dust can arise.

"Sublime" refers to the spiritual wondrousness, the realm wherein all transformations and manifestations are without obstruction. These four Buddha-realms manifest within the environment and inhabitants of the Bodhisattvas.
This corresponds to the stage of the ten faiths (*daśa-śraddhā*), where the compassionate clouds resembling [the ultimate] cover the ocean of *nirvāṇa*.

Because the principle of the Perfect and Sudden (*yuan-dun*) is harmoniously fused, it causes this stage of resemblance to be entirely similar to the stages beyond the grounds (*bhūmi*). △ Third, the permission for rapid realization of the stage.
This person immediately attains the patience regarding the non-arising of dharmas (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*). From this point, they gradually cultivate practice;

according to their initial resolve and exertion, they establish themselves in the stages of the noble ones (*ārya-bhūmi*). This concluding phrase is a preliminary promise of the subsequent stages; therefore, it says, "from this, they gradually cultivate. "Immediately" (*ji*) means speedily.
"Immediately attains" (*ji huo*) is a way of saying that one shall realize it before long. The patience regarding the non-arising of dharmas refers to the first stage (*prathama-bhūmi*).
The "sacred stages realized" refers generally to those penetrating through to the stage of Equal Enlightenment (*samāyākī-bodhi*). Wēnlíng says:

Among the ten types of patience (*kṣānti*) in the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra*, the third is called the "patience regarding the non-arising of dharmas" (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*), which means not perceiving the arising of even the slightest dharma, nor perceiving the cessation of even the slightest dharma.
Free from all defilements of emotion, without action and without aspiration, to dwell securely in this path is called "patience" (*kṣānti*). Wuxing says:
"In this context, it specifically refers to the stages from the first abode (*prathama-vihāra*) upward as the 'sage-stage' (*ārya-bhūmi*).

If the subsequent text states, "By means of the three progressive advancements, one is able to accomplish the fifty-five stages of the true path to Bodhi," [this confirms the point]. △ Third, the conclusion.
This is called the third stage of progressive cultivation.
The three stages of the gradual sequence are now complete. II. The Stage of Dry Wisdom (*śuklavidarśana-bhūmi*).

This stage is clearly defined as consolidating the ten levels of faith (*daśa-śraddhā*) contained within the preceding gradual sequence into a single position. Regarding this, Gushan states that the ten levels of faith are combined to form "Dry Wisdom."

The principle is beyond doubt. However, there is also the sense of "perfectly accomplished" (here, the old commentary rejects this view simply because it sees that the name "Dry Wisdom" [śuṣka-vijñāna] is the same as in the Shared Teaching [Sādhāraṇa-yāna], and thus insists on equating them.

It fails to realize that if this name were the same as other names in the Shared Teaching, it would likewise have to be the same as those in the Distinct Teaching [Pratyekabuddha-yāna]. Now, since all other stages borrow the names of the Distinct Teaching to signify the Perfect [Yāna], this stage too should borrow the name of the Shared Teaching to signify the Perfect;

how then could both the literal and the actual meanings be identical to the Shared Teaching? One must know that the Dry Wisdom of the Shared Teaching occurs prior to the stage of faith (*śraddhā*), corresponding only to the five grades of practitioners. This Dry Wisdom of the Perfect [Yāna], however, occurs after the stage of faith, encompassing the ten stages of faith (*daśa-śraddhā*). How could it be merely a matter of textual terminology?
This is for the sake of conformity, yet in reality it is a great penetration into principle. It is divided into three parts. 1. Not Receiving Further Existence:
"Ānanda, these sons of good family have the craving for existence dried up; root and object do not meet. Their remaining physical form before them shall no longer continue to be born."
This section groups together the preceding seven stages of faith to demonstrate their complete fulfillment.

Because the mind was previously free from lustful desire, at this stage, the craving for sensual desire has withered away. While in the prior stages one merely attained the severance of both body and mind, here, even the very nature of that severance is absent;
hence it is called "withered. This is because the conditions for birth in the Desire Realm are utterly incompatible [with this state].
And so it is. Because the functions of the preceding six [senses] no longer operate, one reaches this point where the faculties and their objects do not meet.

In the prior stage, one merely attained the initial dissolution of the six sense-objects; here, however, one further reaches the state where mind and objects are mutually transcendent. Hence, it is said they "do not meet.

This is because both faculties and objects are simultaneously severed, and seeds as well as manifestations are both eliminated; thus, the conditions for birth within the three realms are utterly beyond reach. [End of section. Mò.
These two lines clearly explain the state of no further existence (*anupapatti*). The remaining physical form currently present is merely the persistence of the fruit-boundary;

there is no further continuation of birth, for the seed-boundary is forever severed. Generally, the continuation of birth takes the sense organs and their objects as its cause and craving (*tṛṣṇā*) as its condition.

When these are withered and do not meet, then both cause and condition are simultaneously extinguished; the retribution has no locus to rest upon, and thus one does not undergo further existence. Furthermore...

What cause for doubt? This reveals that the actual body of segmented existence has already been exhausted; there is no longer any bondage within the realms. [Question: Bodhisattvas do not take up *nirvāṇa*;

why then is it said they do not undergo future existence (*punarbhava*)? [Answer: This statement means they do not undergo future existence bound by karma. It is not like the Arhats, who possess neither compassion nor vows, and thus lack the wondrous body of mastery. [Question: How does this differ from what was previously stated regarding the eternal absence of mutual birth and mutual killing?

[Answer: There is a great difference. That [previous teaching] merely avoided the evil retribution of birth and killing as a form of compensation; however, the conditions for wholesome and pure birth have not yet been severed. As observed below, even regarding the pure retribution, it is still spoken of in terms of "the flesh of one's parents."

The physical body can indeed be verified [as such]. This refers to one who, among the twenty-five states of existence (*pañcaviṃśati-bhava*), no longer possesses the conditions for rebirth, nor a body driven by karma; rather, they merely dwell or go at will according to their compassionate vows, and take birth at will.

Because the old commentary forcibly equates this with the five grades of practitioners, it cannot help but conflate that state with this one. Furthermore, since this occurs after the faculties and objects have ceased to coincide, it is clearly the stage of the seventh faith (*saptama-śraddhā*).

To insist that while the names and meanings are the same, there is a difference in coarseness and subtlety—how could there be a case where names and meanings are entirely identical yet one still distinguishes between coarseness and subtlety? This is certainly not a definitive argument. △ Second, defining the name "Dry Wisdom" (*śuṣka-prajñā*).

The grasping mind is empty and luminous, consisting purely of wisdom. The nature of this wisdom is bright and perfect, adorning the realms of the ten directions. When this wisdom exists in its primordial state, it is called the Stage of Dry Wisdom (śuklavidarśanā-bhūmi).

This section groups the final three stages of faith to manifest their perfect accomplishment. Regarding "the mind of grasping," Master Yue states that it refers precisely to the mind of the two types of grasping:
that for persons (*pudgala-grāha*) and that for phenomena (*dharma-grāha*). If this is so, how could it be appropriate for these to precede the ten stages of faith?

This is because, due to the preceding state where body and mind are joyful and at ease, by the time one reaches this stage, the delusions of the two types of grasping have been exhausted, and the wisdom of dual emptiness is pure.
Because the preceding lands were already luminous and so forth, at this stage the essence of wisdom becomes perfectly bright, and its illuminating function pervades the entire realm.
Because the preceding Buddha-principle was fully manifested, at this stage one achieves the body of wisdom, awakening not through another.
The final two phrases thus establish the name "Dry Wisdom" (*śuṣka-prajñā*); the explanation of its meaning is found in the following section.
△ Third, the reason for this is presented:
the habit-energies of desire have just begun to dry up, yet they have not yet connected with the Tathāgata’s stream of Dharma-water.

Among the three—present manifestations, seeds, and habit-energies—the habit-energy is the most subtle. What is now called "the habit-energies of desire having just begun to dry up" refers to the fact that the craving of desire is at its most [subtle].

The subtle habitual tendencies (which are of the nature to be severed) initially attain a state of parched dryness; yet they have not yet received the moisture of the Tathāgata’s true suchness (*tathatā*) dharma-stream.

Therefore, it is said that there is "dry wisdom. Upon entering the first stage (*prathamabhūmi*), which is the partial realization of truth, one then connects with the flowing water of the true suchness dharma.
Furthermore, it is taught that while the names of the fetters (*saṃyojana*) originally encompass multiple meanings, their individual explanations are presented singly.

Speaking in terms of "desire" (*yù*), it appears to be somewhat deficient. Alternatively, "desire" may be taken as "desire-attachment" (*yù-ài*), while "habituation" (*xí*) refers to the habit-energy of the two attachments.

"Dry" (*qián*) means "exhausted. Upon careful examination, this stage is clearly the first stage of Dry Wisdom (*chū qián-huì-dì*) within the Vajra-mind of Equal Enlightenment (*xiāng-sì děng-jué jīn-gāng xīn*).
Furthermore, the names are identical, which makes this even more evident. Generally speaking, regarding the three stages of gradual progression, this is the... [first].

The first stage consists of the initial orientation toward contemplative practice within the stage of names. The second stage comprises the five grades [of the ten abidings] together with the preceding five levels of faith.

The third stage consists solely of the latter five levels of faith. However, these various stages, such as faith and so forth, all follow the Perfect Teaching (Yuanwei) of the Tiantai school and do not adopt the Separate Teaching (Biéjiào).
Furthermore, the scriptural text merely divides the gradual path into three fundamental stages; it never originally divided them into [sub-stages such as] faith and so forth. Now...
Because there are three points requiring clarification regarding the causes, they must be explicitly identified. First, it is to show that what follows is not "faith" (*śraddhā*).
This is because, following this stage in the sutra text, there are separately the "ten faiths," which borrow their names from conventional usage but in meaning open up to the first *vihāra*.

If one were to instead take these conventional ten faiths as implicitly contained within the three gradual stages (*tri-krama*), and fail to clearly explain them, few would not mistake the latter for the former.
The term "faith" (*śraddhā*) is used here in its conventional sense, as stated in the old commentaries. Second, this explicitly cites the "perfect penetration" (*yuan-tong*).

These three gradual stages (*jian-wei*) are merely a re-grouping of the perfect penetration—its auxiliary aspects, its primary essence, and its beginning and end—to serve as the skillful means for beginners in the subsequent stages.

However, since the perfect penetration undergoes the realization of the three emptinesses (*trividha-śūnyatā*) and actually resides within the ten levels of faith (*daśa-śraddhā*), if this were not clearly specified at this point, people...

Seeing that after the scriptural text there are the "Ten Faiths," which would otherwise cause the Perfect Penetration (yuan-tong) to be relegated to the stage of contemplative practice (guan-xing), it is for this reason that each one is specifically pointed out.
The old commentaries are confused; only Gu-shan’s assertion that the "Dry Wisdom" (gan-hui) is combined with the Ten Faiths is correct.

However, he also does not say that the Ten Faiths are already contained within the three gradual stages, and that the Dry Wisdom is merely a combination of them. [The former is distinct and the latter...]
In total, there are four stages. The first stage, Dry Wisdom (śuklavidarśana), is completed. △ Third, the ten stages of the Stage of Faith (adhimukti).

Herein, the names of the stages in this treatise do not differ by a single character from the conventional names for the stages of faith. However, the meaning of the treatise is entirely different from the conventional understanding of the meaning of faith.
This is especially so regarding the subsequent "first dwelling" (prathamavihāra), where it explicitly states that one gives rise to these ten minds, and further mentions the "ten applications."

Because one enters into the perfect realization of the single mind, it is logically beyond doubt that Mount Gushan’s explanation of this as being "opened out" from the first stage (*prathamā-bhūmi*) is correct.

Furthermore, within these six stages, each is designated with the character for "stage" (*zhù*), which provides even further grounds for reliance. Thus, the criticisms of the old commentaries are inappropriate.
In the *Jin'gang shiba zhu* (Eighteen Abidings of the Vajra), it is stated: "Why must one be at the stage of abiding (*zhu*) to receive the name 'abiding'?
It follows that all fifty-five stages should collectively be called 'abiding. Why then is this term specifically applied only to the ten stages prior to the actual abiding?

This serves as further proof that [the ten stages] are indeed distinguished as the preliminary stages of abiding. Therefore, the title of this section is now established according to the "Ten" [Abidings].
Regarding "Faith": its meaning is simply to follow the sutras and return to the initial stage (*ādikṣānti*). This is divided into ten parts. First is the Stage of Faith (*kṣānti-bhūmi*):
that is, within this mind, one flows into the center of the center; the perfect and wondrous blossoms, and from the truly wondrous perfection, the true wonderfulness issues forth once more.
Sublime faith abides eternally; all delusive thoughts are extinguished without remainder, and the Middle Way is pure and true. This is called the Abode of Faithful Mind.

As for this mind, it follows upon the previously mentioned mind of Dry Wisdom (*śuṣka-prajñā*). Regarding "flowing into the center of the middle": this refers to practicing according to the Perfect Penetration (*yuan-tong*).
Although the beginner directly contemplates the nature of hearing, remaining unattached to emptiness or existence, this is likewise the Middle Way of the absolute, numinous mind. And...

The coarse defilements fall away first; both person and phenomena are simultaneously dissolved. Yet, as one has not yet escaped the spontaneous tendency toward the emptiness of perfect luminosity, this is not yet the pure truth of the Middle Way.
Upon reaching this stage, all is empty and non-arising; the Middle Way previously cultivated becomes even more refined here.
Thus it is said, "flowing into the Middle of the Middle," meaning that by being centered within the center, one follows the flow of the Dharma-water.

"Profound penetration. The mutual functioning of the six sense organs is called "perfect" (*yuan*); the simultaneous transcendence of both the sentient and insentient realms is called "wondrous" (*miao*).
"Blossoming" is like a flower beginning to open. The following two phrases clarify that by means of this opening of the mind, one's progress increases further.

"From the truly wondrous perfection" refers to the fact that this is not the same as the "wondrous truth and semblance perfection" of the preceding stage; rather, it is the "semblance of the wondrous, true, and perfect. [The text repeats "repeatedly"].
Regarding those who have given rise to the True and Wondrous: it is briefly summarized by the single character "Complete" (yuan).

This is intended to cause those with the True and Wondrous to advance further into the Wondrous, and those with the True and Complete to advance further into the Complete. It should be that the faculties and objects mutually permeate one another, such that the body and the land become layered and gradually expand, like a flower in full bloom.
As for those with Wondrous Faith, they personally perceive that the mind, the Buddha, and sentient beings are non-differentiated; this is not the same as...
The faith derived from inference is constant, firm, and immovable; it is not like the state previously described, which was as light as a goose feather.
As for the "extinction of deluded thoughts," this refers to the simultaneous clearing away of the notions of self, the notion of phenomena, and the notion of non-phenomena;
it is also the cessation of the views of the holy and the ordinary, and the forgetting of the sentiments regarding cause and effect. The final two phrases summarize the preceding meaning.
One forms the mind of faith (*śraddhā*). This is purely the Middle Way, unlike the preceding stages which were accompanied by a tendency toward emptiness (*śūnyatā*).

Because one personally perceives this principle and possesses profound forbearance and aspiration, it is called "cultivating the mind" (*bhāvanā-citta*); this is the mark of accomplishment. To "abide" means to dwell permanently in non-retrogression.
Hereafter, all [terms] shall be explained according to this pattern. This is the faculty of faith (*śraddhendriya*) among the five faculties. Furthermore, since in this stage...
This encompasses what was previously accomplished through the stage of Dry Wisdom (*śuṣka-prajñā*).

Since Dry Wisdom combines with the ten stages of faith (*daśa-śraddhā*) contained within the preceding three gradual stages, one should know that this position represents the culmination of the ten stages of faith prior to the ultimate realization. This is why it is specifically designated as the "Abiding in Faith" (*śraddhā-vihāra*).
If it were merely the conventional ten stages of faith, how could the initial mind possibly correspond to this perfect, wondrous, eternally abiding, and all-encompassing state?
Is this not the meaning of equality? △ Second, the mind of mindfulness:
with true faith and clear understanding, all things are perfectly penetrating; the three categories of aggregates (*skandha*), bases (*āyatana*), and elements (*dhātu*) cannot act as obstructions.
Thus, even throughout countless eons of the past and future, all habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*) from discarding one body and receiving another manifest before one in the present.
These good sons are all able to recollect and maintain it without any forgetfulness; this is called the abiding of the mind in mindfulness (*smṛti*).
The first two phrases entirely build upon the preceding stage; "true" indicates that which is not merely similar, while "clarity" arises from direct perception.

"Perfect penetration" is identical to the previous "perfectly wondrous," because every sense organ and every object of the senses interpenetrates one another without exception; thus it is termed "universal perfect penetration."

The following passage establishes the fundamental state of the mindful mind. Because of the aforementioned universal penetration (*sarva-saṃpūrṇa-abhijñā*), the aggregates (*skandha*) do not obscure, the sense bases (*āyatana*) are not restricted, and the elements (*dhātu*) are not partitioned.
Consequently, one is able to recollect the distant past and future for as many as incalculable eons (*asaṃkhyeya-kalpa*).
Regarding "habitual tendencies" (*vāsanā*): these are seeds and latencies (*anuśaya*) perfumed by the power of karma. According to the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi*, there are three types, namely:

The grasping at a self through names and conventions (*nāma-vikalpa-ātma-grāha*) is a member of dependent origination (*bhavāṅga*). What is now called "neutral feeling" (*upekṣā-vedanā*) is mostly a member of dependent origination;

it is the maturation-consciousness (*vipāka-vijñāna*). However, the term "all" (*sarva*) also includes the other two [types of feeling]. Furthermore, when it exists within the state of grasping at a self, it is a seed (*bīja*);
when it exists within the state of grasping at phenomena (*dharma-grāha*), it is the subtle habitual shadow (*vāsanā-pratibimba*) left by seeds. It is like Piṇḍola... [text continues]

This refers to Śāriputra’s pride and [the Buddha’s] anger. Now, that which predominates in the past stage of the self is coarse, while that which predominates in the future stage of dharmas is subtle.
For the time being, let us set aside the two matters of feeling and habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*). If the future habitual tendencies have already been exhausted...

Yet one specifically recollects the sensation of equanimity (*upekṣā-vedanā*). If the habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*) of compassion and vows were outside these three [types of sensation], they too would endure until the end of the future.

Question: How can there be the occurrence of the sensation of equanimity for a Bodhisattva who has entered and dwells [in the stages]? Answer: Because those of the Perfect and Sudden Teaching do not grasp at the *pariṇāmi-ka* (transformation) body;

they constantly attain great mastery over the *paricchinna-ka* (segmented) body. This belongs to the two supernormal knowledges (*abhijñā*) of recollecting past lives (*pūrvanivāsānusmṛti*) and the exhaustion of outflows (*āsravakṣaya*), as well as to the five faculties (*indriya*).

Because the faculty of mindfulness (*smṛtīndriya*) is predominant in the middle [stage], the foundations of mindfulness (*smṛtyupasthāna*) are established. Generally speaking, for those in whom the two types of faith (*śraddhā*) have not yet reached full penetration, such a state is still far off;
yet here, this stage is described as "all-round penetration. How could this be the ordinary course? It is undoubtedly the stage of abiding.

Furthermore, while the preceding stage consists of deep faith in the intrinsically existing Buddha-nature (*buddhadhātu*), this stage consists of recollecting and habituating oneself to the lineage (*gotra*). These two stages...
This is to distinguish them. △ Third, the mind of diligence:

wondrous, perfect, pure, and true. From this true essence, transformation arises; beginningless habitual tendencies merge into a single, unified brilliance. It is solely through this brilliant clarity that [all is realized].
Advancing toward true purity is called the mind of diligence (*vīrya*).
The first four lines build upon the two preceding stages to accomplish the single character "diligence" (*jing*); the first two lines build upon the stage of faith (*śraddhā*).
The first phrase directly addresses the realization of the fundamental state; the second phrase clarifies that through long-term accumulation, one becomes capable of transformation.
"True essence" refers to the power of wondrous, perfect, and pure contemplation gradually becoming refined and clear over time.

"Arising transformation" means that the wisdom of contemplation is so powerful it can initiate the functional power to melt away delusions. This is because through refinement comes transformation, and as transformation progresses, the capacity increases further.
"Refined hearing. The next two lines follow upon the mind of mindfulness (*smṛti*). The first line directly follows the stage of understanding (*prajñā*) in its original state;

the second line clarifies that, together with what preceded it, the habitual shadows (*vāsanā-chāyā*) have been completely melted away without remainder, such that all become wisdom. Therefore, it is said: "penetrating into a single refined clarity.
This is because in the preceding stages there were both the fundamental and the habitual, which had not yet merged into one; reaching this point, they are entirely melted into oneness.

This clarifies the essence of the body of wisdom. The next two phrases build upon the preceding character "refined" (*jing*) by adding the character "advancing" (*jin*), thereby simultaneously establishing the dual meanings of "refinement" and "exertion.
For "refinement and clarity" (*jingming*) is the essence of *bodhi*, which is also the essence of suchness-wisdom (*tathatā-jñāna*);

"true purity" (*zhenjing*) is the essence of *nirvāṇa*, which is also the essence of suchness-reason (*tathatā-artha*). Now, it is said that one advances toward true purity by means of refinement and clarity.

"Purity" means that one is entirely in accord with the principle of suchness through the wisdom of suchness. Question: Since wisdom and principle are of one suchness, why speak of "progressing toward"? Answer:
Although their essence is non-dual, there is nonetheless the appearance of progression through the conformity of skillful means.

This is what is called "the progression of non-progressing," which is the principle that the nature does not obstruct cultivation. The final phrase concludes the name [of the chapter]. Regarding diligence among the five faculties:
This is the faculty of progress. △ Fourth, the Mind of Wisdom (*prajñā-citta*):
When the essence of the mind manifests before one, being purely characterized by wisdom, it is called the Abiding in the Mind of Wisdom.
Wénlǐng says: "Since deluded habits have been exhausted, the essence of the mind manifests before one. In the preceding stage, both wisdom and principle were combined.
This stage is specifically established in terms of the perfection of wisdom. It is only at the higher stages that one speaks of transforming the habitual tendencies of delusion into wisdom.
Because these delusions are destroyed, the true mind manifests; as the mind manifests, the essence of Bodhi is no longer intermingled with falsehood.
The final phrase concludes the title. △ Five: Concentrated Mind.
Maintaining the clarity of wisdom, it is pervasive, tranquil, and profound; this tranquility is wondrous and eternally coagulated—this is called the "abiding of the settled mind.

This stage is established specifically in terms of principle (*li*), because stillness and illumination are distinguished such that stillness belongs to concentration (*samādhi*) and [illumination] belongs to principle.
The first phrase traces back to the preceding stage; for in that prior stage, because the seeing-mind was lucid and penetrating, wisdom was purely bright, yet this wisdom...
Illumination. If there is no power of concentration to sustain it, then deluded thoughts will arise, causing the mind to be narrow and partial rather than all-pervasive;
right mindfulness will be lost, becoming intermittent and unstable. This is what is called "illumination without stillness," like a lamp in the wind.
Therefore, the second phrase clarifies pervasive stillness (*sarva-śānti*), and the third phrase clarifies eternal stillness; both are characteristics of the Great Samādhi.
The final phrase concludes the name: it is the faculty of concentration (*samādhi-indriya*) among the five faculties.
The above belongs to the five faculties, which are like the initial planting of the roots of a fruit tree into the earth. △ Sixth, the Mind of Non-retrogression.
Dīpaṃkara illuminates; the nature of illumination penetrates deeply. Advancing alone without retreating is called the "non-retrogressive mind.
From this point downward belongs to the five powers (*pañcabala*). It is like a fruit-bearing tree whose roots have been established for a long time and possess an irresistible power of function.
This section concerns the power of progress. The first two lines again double-reference both concentration (*samādhi*) and wisdom (*prajñā*); for concentration and wisdom—
If one-sided, there will be much decline and loss. The first phrase is fixed for the arousal of wisdom; when the mind is unmoving, the principle is fully revealed.
The second phrase uses wisdom to enter meditative concentration (*samādhi*); once the mirror is clear, concentration becomes even deeper. Thus, concentration and wisdom mutually support one another.
They are activated in succession without end; thus there is progress and no regression. The final phrase concludes the name. △ Seventh is the mind that protects the Dharma (*dharmarakṣā-citta*).

When the mind advances with tranquility and maintains [the practice] without loss, its vital energy connects with that of the Tathāgatas of the ten directions; this is called the mind that protects the Dharma.
This is the power of meditative concentration (*samādhi*). The first phrase follows upon the power of progress;

as for the statement that "the mind progresses," it clarifies that this is not a coarse activity visible through external signs, but rather the vigor of the self-mind where stillness and illumination flow as one.
Furthermore, the term "serene" reiterates that although the previous stage was called "non-retrogression," there was still a sense of effort involved in its diligent and uninterrupted application.

Now, because this non-awakening exerts effort, it is called "tranquil" (*ānana*). Maintaining it as before constitutes the practice of "holding," which clearly belongs to the category of meditative concentration (*samādhi*).
Since one has advanced into tranquility and achieved the power of concentration, one constantly maintains it without any leakage. This "Tathāgata-element" is the element of the *dharmakāya*;
it does not depart from the wondrously awakened true essence. This, too, arises because the state of concentration pervades all things in profound stillness.
Therefore, one is able to achieve a perfect fusion with the minds of all Buddhas. The final phrase concludes the title. Regarding "protecting the Dharma" (*dharmapāla*), there are two meanings:

if "protection" is understood in terms of preservation, it refers to internally protecting the mental dharmas; if it is understood in terms of subduing demons through meditative concentration (*samādhi*), it also refers to externally protecting the Buddha’s Wheel of Dharma.
△ Eight: The Mind of Dedication (*pariṇāmanā-citta*).

Maintaining this awakened clarity with subtle power, one can turn the Buddha’s compassionate light back toward the Buddha and abide therein. It is like two mirrors facing each other with their radiance;
within them, wondrous reflections multiply and interpenetrate one another. This is called the mind of dedication.

This is the power of wisdom (*prajñā-bala*). The first phrase refers to the essence of awakening (*bodhi-tattva*) sustained by the preceding power of concentration (*samādhi-bala*); "wondrous power" is precisely the power of wisdom.

The following two phrases indicate that although one has already been received by the compassionate light of the Buddha as soon as the "fragrance of the Tathāgata" from the previous stage was first attained, there still remained a distinction between self and other;
here, however, [self and other] have long since merged into one. This is the compassion of other Buddhas.
The light is precisely the compassionate light of the Buddha within one’s own mind; yet, it does not obstruct the distinct clarity of self and other.

Furthermore, this compassionate light is turned back toward the Buddhas of the ten directions, abiding with the cognitive realm (jñāna-viṣaya) brilliantly manifest, while in reality there is no duality of essence.

Nevertheless, because they do not obstruct each other’s distinct clarity, it is like two mirrors reflecting one another, transmitting and illuminating each other endlessly. This is simply because the two mirrors face one another.
The reflection within the illumination already contains further reflections; thus, it is layered upon layer without the necessity of multiple mirrors.

Therefore, this metaphor refers only to the two Buddhas—the self and the other—while the existence of all Buddhas lies beyond words and need not be explicitly added. The final phrase concludes the title. Regarding dedication (*pariṇāmanā*), there are also two meanings:
if one dedicates toward the Buddhas of others, it is directed toward the Buddha-way; if one dedicates toward one's own Buddha-nature, it is directed toward...

Regarding True Suchness (*tathatā*): concerning the two meanings in the preceding stage and the two meanings in this stage, in both cases the former meaning is primary, while the latter meaning is necessarily secondary as well. △ Ninth, the mind of precepts.

The light of the mind secretly returns, attaining the Buddha’s eternal stillness, supreme, wondrous, and pure, abiding peacefully in the unconditioned; having attained this without loss, it is called the "abiding of the mind in ethical discipline."

This is the power of faith (*śraddhā-bala*). The first line follows upon the preceding stage, clarifying that one's own mind merges seamlessly with the Buddha’s light, thereby attaining the immovable essence of the Buddha.

The next two lines clarify the attainment of the principle (*tattva*). The following two lines clarify immovability: "constantly concentrated" refers to the Great Samādhi of the Buddha, which belongs to the mind;
"unsurpassed, wondrous purity" refers to the Great Ocean of Quiescent Extinction (*mahā-nirvāṇa-samudra*), which belongs to the objective realm. Having attained this from the Buddha...

The principle and the mental state are eternally identical. "Abiding in the unconditioned" means remaining far removed from the functional activity of the conditioned and dwelling in the path of non-effort.
"Without loss" means not allowing even a hair’s breadth to leak into the realm of the conditioned.

This refers, in general, to the state of immovability. The final phrase concludes the title. Regarding the "precept-mind" (*śīla-citta*): it is called a "precept" because one does not commit the fault of transgression or loss.
Yet, if even a single thought of conditioned activity (*saṃskāra*) arises, it is termed a breach of the precepts; can this not be called a most profound precept?
Furthermore, because the observance of the precepts relies upon firm faith, it belongs to the power of faith (*śraddhā-bala*) among the five powers. △ Ten.
The *praṇidhāna-citta* (vow-mind).

Abiding in the mastery of ethical discipline (*śīla*), one is able to travel throughout the ten directions; wherever one goes, it is according to one's vow. This is called abiding in the vow-mind. It is the power of this mindfulness.
The first phrase follows upon the preceding mind of ethical discipline; as for the term "mastery," it is because in the prior stage [one was not yet fully autonomous].

The essence of immovability reaches this point and gradually gives rise to the function of mastery. The middle two phrases mean that one is born in the Pure Land according to one's vow without any hindrance;

this is precisely the sense of attaining great mastery. To conclude by naming it "vow-mind" and attributing it to the power of mindfulness (*smṛti-bala*) means that the vow is itself the mental recollection (*citta-manasikāra*), and that being born in the Pure Land depends entirely upon this mental visualization.
Therefore it is so. In the preceding stage, one abides in the Buddha’s *dharmakāya*; in this stage, one partakes in the Buddha’s *rūpakāya*.

Furthermore, considering the ten stages of mind as a whole, the first six cultivate one’s own mind, while the latter four harmonize with the Buddha’s virtues. The ten stages of the stage of faith (*śraddhā*) are hereby concluded.

△ Fourth, the ten stages of the stage of abiding (*sthiti*). There are two meanings to "abiding": first, the meaning of firm and constant abiding, which is contrasted with the preceding gradual progression.

The various forms of faith contained therein, though not as slight as a goose feather compared to the Separate Teaching (biejiao), nevertheless do not yet equal this stage where both practice and mindfulness are non-retrogressive.
Second is the intention of being born and dwelling in the Buddha-family; for the current text fully reveals birth into the Dharma-king’s house.
It is also abiding in the "flowered mansion" (huawu), which is not the same as [the mere state of] samādhi. Third is the gradual...
Next, one finally attains entry into the gate; therefore, the title of the major section, "Causing One to Abide in Perfect Concentration," begins from this stage.
It is divided into ten stages: first, the Stage of Resolving the Mind (Prathamacittotpādavihāra).

Ānanda, these sons of good family, by means of true skillful means, give rise to these ten minds. Their mental essence radiates brilliance, and the ten functions interpenetrate one another to perfectly accomplish the One Mind;
this is called the Stage of Resolving the Mind.
The final two lines of the "True" section summarize the preceding discussion of the ten stages. "True" refers to the mind of True Suchness (*tathatā*).

△ Third, the Dwelling of Cultivation (*caryā-vihāra*).

The mind-ground and its cognitive engagement both attain clarity; traversing the ten directions, one encounters no obstruction. This is called the Stage of Cultivation and Practice (*saṃbhāra-vihāra*).

Because its essence is thus, it is said that "both are attained with clarity. To "wander without obstruction" means that one reaches the destination through the clarity of vision.

Practice. These ten phrases all refer to that which the Buddhas originally practiced.
"Accordance with the ten directions" refers to the extensive practice of giving. The *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* states:

To the point of not begrudging even one's own flesh; to practice the gift of Dharma by teaching the equality of the three periods of time up to bodhi and nirvāṇa—this is compliance with the ten directions. As for the title "Joyful," the *Avataṃsaka* says:
"When sentient beings beg and seek, the Bodhisattva feels redoubled joy, saying: 'These multitudes are my field of merit; they are my virtuous friends.'"
It is equal [to the previous]. It is also said that it causes all sentient beings to rejoice and be satisfied; this is it.

Furthermore, other passages also contain the intent of realizing the three emptinesses (*trīṇi śūnyatāni*) and not clinging to signs (*animitta*); there is no need to cite them all exhaustively. △ Second, the practice of benefiting others (*parārthacaryā*).
Skillfully benefiting all sentient beings is called the practice of benefit;

this is the perfection of ethical discipline (*śīla-pāramitā*). In the *Avataṃsaka*, this practice is first characterized by the upholding of pure precepts, taking as its foundation non-attachment to the five desires of form, sound, and so forth, even to the point of not giving rise to a single thought of desire, let alone engaging in such acts. This is excellent.
Regarding that which is able to benefit sentient beings, the *Avataṃsaka* states: "To cause all sentient beings to abide in unsurpassed ethical discipline, up to and including bodhi and nirvāṇa.
Furthermore, it says: "Having attained liberation oneself, one causes others to attain liberation; up to and including having attained happiness oneself, one causes others to attain happiness.
There are ten such phrases in total, each of which pairs the two benefits of self and others. Therefore, they are collectively designated as "beneficial" (*rāyika*), by means of ethical discipline.
It is virtue that brings benefit. △ Third is the practice of non-anger.
To awaken oneself and awaken others, thereby attaining freedom from opposition and rejection, is called the practice of non-resentment;

this is the perfection of patience (*kṣānti-pāramitā*). The *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* initially indicates that this Bodhisattva constantly cultivates the dharma of patience; there it is termed "non-opposition" (*anupratigha*).
"Non-opposition" (wéijù) means the absence of resistance or rejection. Whenever humiliation arrives, to resist and refuse it is precisely what is called "intolerance.

Now, being without resistance is precisely what constitutes patience (*kṣānti*). As the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* states: "One is able to joyfully endure immeasurable verbal abuse and physical assault"—this is it.
What is now said regarding attaining non-opposition through self-awakening and awakening others is likewise like this.
The *Avataṃsaka* states: "When a bodhisattva contemplates that both self and suffering and pleasure are non-existent, this is awakening to oneself (*sva-bodha*).
It further says: 'I shall understand [this] and explain it extensively for others,' which is awakening to others (*para-bodha*). It concludes by summarizing:
"To awaken oneself and cause others to awaken" is identical in meaning to the present scriptural passage; both refer to "awakening.
Since [the former] refutes false and delusory views, there should be no contradiction. It concludes by naming this the "practice of non-anger. As the *Vajra* [Sūtra] states:

"If one possesses the notion of a self, the notion of a person, and so forth, then at the time of being dismembered, one would give rise to anger and resentment. From this, we know that it is characterized by the absence of anger and resentment.
This is what constitutes true patience. △ Fourth, the inexhaustible practice:

its manifestations arise in all their varieties, extending to the limits of the future, equal throughout the three periods of time, and penetrating the ten directions; this is called the inexhaustible practice.
This is the perfection of vigor (*vīrya-pāramitā*). At the outset of the *Avataṃsaka*, it is stated that this Bodhisattva cultivates various forms of vigor.
From the first type of vigor up to universal vigor, ten kinds of vigor arise.

The *Avataṃsaka* states that even those who have reached the Avīci hell will all attain Buddhahood and enter nirvana without remainder (*anupadhiśeṣa-nirvāṇa*), after which they realize their own fruition.
Only then is it truly accomplished. Now, when sentient beings reach the ultimate limit—from the Avīci Hell up to the attainment of Buddhahood—their entire species is exhausted.
This is precisely what the *Vajra* [Sūtra] means by saying that all twelve classes of living beings enter *nirupadhiśeṣa-nirvāṇa* and are thereby delivered.

"Birth" refers to the birth of all Buddhas. "Exhausting the limits of the future" means that throughout kalpas as numerous as the drops in the ocean or the dust motes in a buddha-field, one practices asceticism until the end of time without ever having a single thought of regret or resentment. "Equality of the three periods of time" is as the text says:
"One practices diligence solely for the sake of knowing the nature of equality across the three periods of time. "Pervasive penetration of the ten directions" refers to...
The text says: "It is precisely for the sake of knowing the entire dharma-realm that one practices diligence. This is correct, for the ten directions are themselves the ten dharma-realms.
Now, the emergence of various categories is the foremost mind; reaching to the end of the future is the eternal mind;
the equality of the three periods of time is the non-perverted mind; and universal penetration throughout the ten directions is the vast mind.
These four are all inexhaustible; therefore, they are collectively named "Inexhaustible Practices.

However, while the *Avataṃsaka*’s "Practice of Unyielding Flexibility" directly expresses diligence alone, this [text] presents four kinds of inexhaustibility to demonstrate the excellence of diligence.
△ Fifth, the Practice of Freedom from Delusion and Confusion.
All things are in harmony; attaining non-deviation across various dharma-gates is called the practice of being free from delusion and confusion.
This is the perfection of dhyāna (meditation). As stated at the beginning of the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra*: "The mind of this bodhisattva is without distraction, firm, and immovable," and so forth.
All things being in harmony through various dharma-gates, one maintains a single [dharma] with a concentrated mind of a single thought-moment.

It is the essence of all dharmas. The *Avataṃsaka* states that it can maintain the verbal expressions of all supramundane dharmas, and even maintain the verbal expressions for establishing the intrinsic natures of feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness.
It further states that it skillfully enters all gateways of meditative concentration (*dhyāna*).
To know that all samādhis share the same essential nature is this [meaning]. To "attain non-error" is as it is said:
"When a bodhisattva hears immeasurable dharmas, they do not forget or lose them throughout immeasurable kalpas. This is why the name "free from delusion and confusion" is established.
It is because being unable to maintain the various dharma-gates within meditative concentration constitutes "deluded concentration" regarding those dharma-gates.
It cannot avoid error; it remains a state of a distracted mind. Now, by maintaining various dharmas without error, one is free from both delusion and distraction.

Furthermore, the Sanskrit term *dhyāna* is translated here as "calm contemplation" (*jinglü*). Being free from delusion constitutes "contemplation" (*lü*), and being free from distraction constitutes "calm" (*jing*).
Therefore, it undoubtedly belongs to the perfection of meditation (*dhyānapāramitā*). 6. Skillful Manifestation of Practice.
Thus, within the identical, a multitude of differences manifests; yet within each distinct characteristic, one perceives their mutual identity.

Furthermore, they differ entirely from the usual sequence of the final five perfections. Upon careful examination, these are in fact all subsumed within a single Perfection of Wisdom. And...
This is expanded into five kinds of profound *prajñā*, just as the six root afflictions are expanded by dividing "view" (*dṛṣṭi*) into five.
Thus, it integrates the myriad practices within the first five perfections, causing them all to become supreme virtues.

This present single practice is the wisdom of the non-obstruction between principle and phenomena, and also the wisdom of the mutual integration of the two truths; it manifests diversity within sameness.
This means that principle does not obstruct phenomena; it is also the true interfusion with the conventional. To see sameness within difference means that phenomena do not obstruct principle;
it is also the conventional interfusing with the true. Thus, he is named "the Practitioner Who Manifests Well."
This clarifies that for this Bodhisattva, in each and every action, both principle and phenomena are simultaneously revealed, and the ultimate and conventional truths are harmoniously integrated.
△ Seventh, the Practice of Non-attachment:
In this manner, even unto the number of atoms filling the empty space of the ten directions—within each and every atom, he manifests the worlds of the ten directions.

Nevertheless, I shall briefly cite one gate. This Bodhisattva should likewise possess the simultaneous integration of the Ten Mysteries (*daśa-guhya*).

Regarding the manifestation of the worlds of the ten directions within the atoms of the ten directions, it is as the Sūtra says: "Within the countless atoms of the Flower Treasury World (*Kusumatalagarbha-lokadhātu*), within each and every atom, one beholds the Dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu*).

Furthermore, manifesting lands within motes of dust is called "manifesting realms" (*dhātu*). Not destroying the characteristics of the motes is called "manifesting motes.
Regarding "mutually not obstructing": when the realms enter the motes, the realms do not become small; this is the small not obstructing the large.
When the motes contain the realms, the motes do not become large; this is the large not obstructing the small. This is summarized as the practice of non-attachment.
To clarify this: how could the small and the large be so simultaneously integrated when there is attachment? The Third Patriarch said: "The ultimate large is identical to the small;
it is forever without boundaries. The ultimate small is identical to the large; one forgets and transcends all realms.
This "forgetting and transcending" is precisely non-attachment. 8. Honoring Practice.

This norm produces understanding and wisdom in sentient beings. In the *Avataṃsaka*, this practice is specifically termed "unimpeded preaching of the Dharma.
Such perfect integration and so forth also build upon the two preceding unimpeded knowledges (*pratisaṃvid*) to clarify the establishment of ultimate altruism.
This is the teaching of the Buddhas. As for the regulations of the Buddhas, they consist in revealing immeasurable Dharma-gates to sentient beings.

However, since these are based upon the perfect fusion of the two kinds of unimpededness, one takes only the Six Characteristics, the Ten Mysteries, and so forth—what is called the "Dharma-gate of a Single Syllable," which could not be fully written even with the ink of the ocean.
The concluding phrase summarizes the title, as can be understood. △
The ten practices of reality (*bhūta-caryā*).
Each and every one is pure and without outflows (*anāsrava*), being truly unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*) because its nature is inherently so; thus they are called "practices of reality.

These do not contradict the wisdom of the true mark (*lakṣaṇa*), and they also accord with the wisdom that enters reality through conditions. Regarding "each and every one": this firmly follows upon the two [preceding points].
The unimpeded practices for self-benefit and benefiting others actually encompass all nine perfections mentioned previously.
"Pure and untainted" means not being defiled by the ignorance of ordinary beings, outsiders, or those in the realms of desire and existence.

"One true unconditioned" means not laboring at the arduous cultivation and realization of the provisional or limited vehicles. The phrase "because its nature is inherently so" serves as the reason for these two points.
This clarifies that cultivation arises from the nature, such that the entirety of cultivation is itself the nature.

Therefore, purity does not belong to the outflows (*āsrava*), and its primordial state does not fall into the conditioned (*saṃskṛta*). Furthermore, it is explained as follows: "Purity and freedom from outflows" distinguishes this from the outflows of the triple world;
"the one true unconditioned" distinguishes this from the conditioned states of the two vehicles; and "the nature being primordial" distinguishes this from the provisional and gradual teachings.
Cultivation and accomplishment also apply [to these]. Regarding the designation "true" (*satya*): because they are untainted (*anāsrava*), they are not produced by false cultivation;

having reached the ultimate, they become true causes. Therefore, they are called "true practice" (*satyapratipatti*). Because they are unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*), they are not of a nature produced by effort;

they possess an ultimately real fruit. Therefore, they are called "actual practice" (*bhūtapratipatti*). Furthermore, generally speaking, regarding the five practices opened up by the *Prajñāpāramitā*, the former two are...
The essence of *prajñā* consists in the non-obstructive wisdom of the two dharma-realms, for this is the profoundly deep *prajñā*.

The following two are the functions of *prajñā*, namely the *pāramitās*, which are the function of self-benefit in the pursuit of the fruit, and the "Buddha-ordinances," which are the function of benefiting others through the preaching of the Dharma.
The final one subsumes the preceding essence and functions, as well as the preceding [categories].
The five perfections and myriad practices are all ultimately resolved and returned to one’s own nature; this is the convergence of nature back to the source.
The ten stages of practice are concluded. Sixth: The Ten Stages of Dedication (*pariṇāmanā*). According to the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra*, dedication is equivalent to making vows.
Guifeng stated that it does not exceed three spheres: sentient beings, the Buddha-way, and True Suchness (*tathatā*). The text of the *Avataṃsaka* is extremely vast and expansive; its intent is—

The various categories generally encompass all three locations; however, in the present sutra text, each is presented with varying degrees of explicitness and implicitness. For instance, when "sentient beings" is made explicit, the other two are implicit.

The same applies to the explicitness and implicitness of "Buddha-nature," "the Path," and "True Suchness. That which is explicit is directly developed and expounded, while that which is implicit is likewise contained within the intended meaning;
it is not entirely absent. Therefore, although the wording of this sutra and the *Avataṃsaka* does not correspond, [their underlying principles are identical].
Their essential meanings do not conflict. Furthermore, the *Avataṃsaka* extensively elucidates the virtues and deeds realized through the cultivation of Bodhisattvas at each stage;
thus, its prose and meaning are vast and expansive. This sutra, however, primarily investigates the reasons for attaining such names;
thus, its phrasing is concise and succinct. These are the distinctions between these two scriptures. They are divided into ten sections. First: Dedication Free from Characteristics.
Ānanda, when these good sons have perfected their supernormal powers and completed the work of Buddhahood, they will be pure, clean, and true, far removed from all lingering afflictions.

They shall deliver sentient beings while extinguishing the very notion of "delivering" them; turning their unconditioned minds toward the path of Nirvāṇa, this is called the Dedication to Protecting and Delivering All Sentient Beings While Remaining Free from the Notion of Sentient Beings.
This and the subsequent stages are all dedicated to sentient beings. These "good sons" refer to those who have already practiced the ten stages of conduct.
"Perfected supernatural powers" (abhijñā) encompass the entirety of the preceding eight stages of conduct.

That is to say, from the first stage up to the eighth—where one manifests dust and realms—their supernatural powers have reached their ultimate limit without the slightest deficiency. Having completed the task of attaining Buddhahood, they step upon the [ninth stage]...

The nine practices constitute the rules for attaining Buddhahood; they are themselves the act of becoming a Buddha. Being pure, clean, refined, and true, they lead one to tread upon the tenth practice.
Being free from outflows (*anāsrava*) is purity; being the single, true, unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*) is refinement and truth.

Far removed from all lingering afflictions, these practices collectively encompass the ten stages and bring them to final resolution. When the ten practices are fully perfected, then within the realm [of birth and death], there is no longer...

To have "obstacles of lingering affliction" (*liu-huan*) within the realms of existence; not to have "obstacles of lingering in emptiness" outside the realms means to simultaneously transcend both the mundane and supramundane worlds.

All that precedes this refers back to the preceding text, while what follows below belongs to its own proper position. The *Avataṃsaka* Sūtra first sets forth the six *pāramitās* entirely in the same manner.
This present sutra, however, follows the intent of the aforementioned ten practices (*daśa-caryā*). "When" (*dang*) means "correctly. This is because it says:

At the very moment of truly delivering sentient beings, there is the mark of extinction; this signifies that there is no sequence of before and after. "Delivering" is precisely the "delivering" of extinction.
These two phrases are identical to those in the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra*, which says: "I cause them all to enter nirvana without remainder and deliver them;
yet, in truth, there are no sentient beings who have attained deliverance. The following two phrases then provide the explanation for this.
The two characters "dedication" (*pariṇāmanā*) specifically derive from the aspect of extinguishing and transcending the marks of attainment.

Now, since one has already delivered all sentient beings without grasping at the mark of deliverance, one turns back conditioned practices and enters the unconditioned mind; this is the dedication that enters the true cause.
One turns away from the path of birth and death and heads toward the road to nirvāṇa; this is the movement toward the true fruit. These two phrases each speak of the same realization.
The intent of "one-pointedly heading toward the truth" is not that the preceding phrase accomplishes the subsequent one;
rather, if it were to form the meaning of the subsequent phrase, it should say "returning to enter the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*) in order to advance toward *nirvāṇa*.

This is because if one constantly dwells in the conditioned (*saṃskṛta*) without returning to enter the unconditioned, one will ultimately be unable to reach the path to *nirvāṇa*. Regarding these ten stages, the principle...
One should fulfill the Middle Way, for by proceeding from the stage of the Worthy (ārya) toward the stage of the Sage (ārya), one speaks of delivering sentient beings;

thus, the manifestation of the signs of extinction (nirvāṇa) illustrates the Middle Way. The old commentary’s claim that one turns back from true wisdom toward conventional compassion neither accords with the text nor captures its intended meaning.
This shall be explained in detail following the Ten Dedications (daśabhūmi-pariṇāmanā). This concludes the title: "Rescue."
Regarding "protecting sentient beings": as in the *Avataṃsaka*, this begins with rescuing them from the three miserable realms and culminates in abiding where the Buddhas abide.

This must likewise involve breaking through the five abodes and departing from the two deaths; only then can it be considered ultimate protection. The final phrase is identical to the elimination of the marks of crossing over.
The *Avataṃsaka* also states that one does not cling to the mark of sentient beings, extending even to the marks of conceptualization and views.
It is non-perverted; this is it. The purport of these two sutras is the same; this sutra merely states the essentials. △ Second, the Non-Destructive Dedication (*akṣaya-pariṇāmanā*).
To destroy that which is destructible and to remain far removed from all [notions of] detachment is called the Non-Destructive Dedication.
"Destroying" (*huài*) refers to the aforementioned elimination. "That which can be destroyed" (*kě huài*) refers to the aforementioned characteristic of crossing over.

"Various abandonments" (*zhū lí*) refers to the aforementioned abandonment of the mark of sentient beings (*sattva-nimitta*). For when one abandons the mark of sentient beings, one then abandons all four marks and five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*) of sentient beings;
hence it is called "various abandonments. "Corresponding" (*yīng*) refers to the marks of the two kinds of emptiness—self and phenomena (*ātma-dharma-śūnyatā*). Now, furthermore...
To be "distant from this" means, in essence, not ultimately grasping at the characteristics of the two emptinesses of self and phenomena (*ātma-dharma-śūnyatā*).
As it is said: although one eliminates the marks of crossing over [to liberation], one transcends the realm of craving and views;

yet, one does not grasp at the two emptinesses to the point of destroying the compassion that delivers sentient beings. The *Avataṃsaka* states: "Although one knows that all phenomena are empty and quiescent, yet..."
It is the arising of mental attention toward emptiness. As for the name "Unbreakable" (*Abhedyā*), it refers to the unbreakable activity of delivering sentient beings.
In the *Avataṃsaka*, this stage continues to extensively promote the practice of giving. When considered in conjunction with the preceding stage:
the preceding stage states that although one delivers sentient beings, one does not cling to the marks of sentient beings; this stage states that although one does not cling to marks, [one...]
It prevents hindering the salvation of sentient beings; it is the Middle Way of the dual benefit of self and others through the simultaneous operation of compassion and wisdom.
△ Third, the Dedication Equal to the Buddhas:
Original Enlightenment is profoundly still; when awakening is equal to the awakening of the Buddhas, it is called the dedication equal to all Buddhas.
The following four stages all involve dedicating toward the Buddha-way. In these stages, one first understands that one’s own wisdom is identical to the Buddha-wisdom;

this means that the wisdom of original enlightenment (*prakṛti-āśraya-jñāna*) is identical to the ultimate wisdom of the Buddha’s perfect enlightenment. That "original enlightenment is profound and still" means that when the mind and the Buddha manifest, the ocean of awakening is clear and tranquil.
This is as described in the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* as being "vast and pure. Thus, one's awakening is equal to the Buddha's awakening.
This means that one’s mental essence is perfectly interfused with that of all Tathāgatas;
it is called "harmonizing with the wondrous awakening" because the Dharma-body is complete and non-dual. To say "equal to all Buddhas" means being equal to the Dharma-bodies of all Buddhas;
that is to say, my precious, true, awakened mind is non-dual and complete with that of the Tathāgata. △ Fourth, dedication of the place reached.
The essence and truth are brilliantly manifested; the stage is like the Buddha-stage.

This is named the Dedication Reaching All Places. This position clarifies that the objective realm is identical to the Buddha-realm; that is to say, the realm of the causal ground is identical to the realm of the resultant Buddha-ground.

"Essence and truth" refers to the substance of original enlightenment; "brilliant manifestation" refers to the unfolding of its wondrous function; "the stage is like the Buddha-stage" means it is equivalent to the state of Buddhahood.

This term precisely expresses that the boundless realms contained within the mind of one’s own causal stage are entirely identical to the immeasurable lands manifested upon the ground of the Buddhas’ fruition stage.
The designation "reaching all places" (*sarvatragāmin*) signifies the exhaustion of the Buddha-realm.
In this stage, the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* describes how the Bodhisattva extensively cultivates offerings.
He reaches everywhere to the abodes of the Buddhas, and only then speaks.
His three karmas universally enter all worlds to perform the Buddha-work, even entering universally into all worlds within a single pore, and so forth. This is it.
△ Fifth, the inexhaustible dedication.
The worlds and Tathāgatas interpenetrate one another without obstruction; this is called the Dedication of the Treasury of Inexhaustible Merit.
This builds upon the previous two stages to achieve mutual fusion. "Worlds" refers to the places reached, and "Tathāgatas" refers to the Buddhas who are equalized.
In the previous two stages, self and other were still distinguished; therefore, they were described as "self-awakening" and "Buddha-awakening."
From the stage of the self to the stage of the Buddha, these are now fused into one without distinction;
thus, it is said that the world and the Tathāgata are identical, meaning that self and other are completely interpenetrated. Regarding the sense of mutual penetration:

if one says that the world penetrates the Tathāgata, then within every single pore there are immeasurable jewel-lands, adorned with subtle and wondrous beauty. If one says that the Tathāgata penetrates the world...
Regarding the realm: within each and every atom, there are immeasurable Tathāgatas turning the Great Dharma Wheel.
Those who have attained non-obstruction are described as follows: when the world enters the Tathāgata, it does not obstruct the Tathāgata from entering the world;
when the Tathāgata enters the world, he does not obstruct the world from entering the Tathāgata. [Question: Regarding the two preceding stages...

Originally, [the text] was explained by distinguishing between the realm of wisdom (*jñāna*) and the objective sphere (*viṣaya*), as if contrasting nature (*svabhāva*) and characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*).

Now that both have been received together, why has it further changed into a contrast between the mutual interpenetration of the primary and secondary [receptacles]? Answer: When the Buddha establishes the name for this stage of "equality in wisdom" (*jñānasamatā*), he states that one is already equal to all Buddhas;
thus, he immediately takes up the person who possesses realized wisdom (*pratyakṣajñāna*). Therefore, at this stage, one simply receives these two.

This is termed "conjunction" (*saṃyoga*), referring to the manner in which the Tathāgata’s body and the world interpenetrate. If one were to speak in terms of the cognitive nature (*jñāna-svabhāva*) being in opposition to its object, then one would be formless while the other would possess form;
such a description of their interpenetration would be inconvenient. This is all the more so when considering the characteristics of the primary [body] and the secondary [environment].
It is not that the nature of wisdom is not integrated; therefore, when it is said that they are mutually integrated, the nature of wisdom is contained therein.
As for the title "Inexhaustible Treasury of Merit," it is because both the Buddha-body and the Buddha-realm each possess immeasurable adornments, fully manifesting inexhaustible merit;
thus it is so called. The *Avataṃsaka* clarifies that this Bodhisattva, by means of the great vows and practices of Samantabhadra...
It serves as the foundation, for it manifests the merit of the adornments of the infinite worlds of the Flower Treasury (*Gandavyūha*).
Its phrasing is like clouds and forests; yet this sutra is further concise and exhaustive, its meaning rich and subtle! △ Sixth:
Dedication through Equality.
Within the same Buddha-ground, each stage gives rise to its own cause of purity; by relying on these causes, one manifests and takes up the path to nirvana.
This is called the dedication of roots of goodness that accord with equality.

This Buddha-ground (*buddhabhūmi*) directly follows upon the treasury of the aforementioned merits. When a Bodhisattva realizes this, they are identical to the resultant stage (*phalabhūmi*) of a Tathāgata;

thus, the fruit of Buddhahood was already fully possessed beforehand by means of these causes. This is because, in the Perfect and Sudden (*yuan-dun*) Supreme Vehicle, one first attains identity with the resultant stage of a Tathāgata through the sudden approach;
such is the nature of the Dharma. Regarding the phrase "each and every" within the ground: it is due to the merits contained within this treasury...
Virtue is inexhaustible. Just as the adornments of the six perfections, the myriad practices, and the myriad virtues are all inherently possessed, it is said that each is thus.
Regarding the "arising of the cause of purity": based upon that inherent nature, each follows conditions to give rise to the cultivation of non-cultivation.
It is like fashioning vessels from gold; every vessel is gold. How could they not be purely one and pure? Therefore...

It is said that "the clouds arise from the cause of purity. To rely upon this cause to manifest and attain the path to nirvāṇa means that while previously one proceeded from the fruit to produce the cause, here one again relies upon the cause to realize the fruit.
This is truly the principle of the mutual penetration of cause and fruit, and the simultaneous identity of nature and cultivation.
Since nirvāṇa is the ultimate and final fruit of the Buddha, this stage corresponds to what was traversed in the preceding stages and positions.
The stages of these two lands are not the same. That is the stage of the mind-ground of one’s own nature; this is the stage of the fruit of the Tathāgata.
To conclude by saying they "accord with equality" means to accord with the equality of one's own mind and the Buddha-mind.

This clearly shows that those who do not realize that their own minds and the stage of the Buddha-fruit are entirely identical are not practicing from the fruit back toward the cause; none of their practices accord with the fundamental nature.
Regarding the term "roots of goodness" (*kuśalamūla*): it indicates that these alone are the true cause for attaining Buddhahood and will necessarily produce the actual fruit.

In the *Avataṃsaka*, they are called "firm roots of goodness," and the phrasing differs slightly from this sutra; there, it mostly speaks of dedicating one's body and life through giving back to sentient beings.
△ Seventh: Dedication through Equal Contemplation.

Once the true roots have been established, all sentient beings of the ten directions are my own original nature. When this nature is perfected and fully realized, one does not lose sight of sentient beings;
this is called the dedication of merit through the contemplation that accords with all sentient beings.
In this passage, the phrasing appears to be a dedication toward sentient beings, yet in reality, it is a dedication toward the Buddha-way.

The opening phrase refers back to the aforementioned pure causes and impartial roots of goodness, which are the true roots. These roots, when fully cultivated, are identical to the nature (*dharmatā*).
Since this nature encompasses all sentient beings without exception, it is said that "all are my own original nature. Thus, once my own root is perfected, [the roots of] sentient beings...

They are perfected simultaneously. Therefore, it is said that "the nature is perfectly accomplished. This means that the accomplishment of the true faculties is itself the accomplishment of the Buddha-way.
As for "not losing sight of sentient beings": if one perceives that sentient beings are not external to the mind, then when one is accomplished, all are accomplished;

thus, there would be no sentient beings to deliver. It is unacceptable to lose the heart of great compassion. Although the Bodhisattva perceives the perfect completion of self and others, they do not...
Nevertheless, one continues to deliver sentient beings from suffering. For this reason, at this stage in the *Avataṃsaka*, one continues to extensively practice the two kinds of giving as before.
The concluding statement, "observing in accordance with equality," means that one accords with one's own mind so that it is equal to the minds of all living beings.

This makes it clear that one does not see the accomplishment of one thing as the accomplishment of all; yet, even while within such accomplishment, one still practices compassion and delivers others. All who do not do so are not [true practitioners].

This is to accord with their intrinsic nature (*dharmatā*). However, what is called "observing all sentient beings as equal" means observing that self and others share the same fundamental faculty, while remaining unimpeded in view, wisdom, and compassion.
When combined with the preceding stage, the principle that the mind, the Buddha, and sentient beings are non-differentiated becomes manifest.
△ Eighth: Dedication of True Suchness (*tathatā-pariṇāmanā*).
That is, all phenomena are free from all marks; being both identical to and detached from them, without attachment to either, is called the dedication of the mark of True Suchness (*tathatā*).
