The three stages below this are all dedications to True Suchness. "Identical to all phenomena" is as stated in the beginning of the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra*:
The "phenomena" (*dharma*) do not exceed those of the mundane and supramundane realms; that is to say, the world, sentient beings, the gates of Dharma, karmic actions, and so forth.
"To be free from all marks" is as stated in the subsequent text: "not clinging to the world, and not grasping at sentient beings."
To know that all phenomena lack intrinsic nature and are entirely quiescent, and so forth;

this refers to "detachment through separation," which will be explained extensively later, for example, in the one hundred and seventy characteristics of *tathatā*. One should examine its meaning in detail.

However, because this sutra is neither identical with nor separate from [reality], it appears to encompass everything exhaustively; this sufficiently demonstrates the wondrous skill of this sutra in condensing the vast within the concise.

For "non-attachment to identity" transcends existence (*bhava*), while "non-attachment to separation" transcends emptiness (*śūnyatā*); thus, it is the Middle Way that transcends both emptiness and existence simultaneously.
In the *Avataṃsaka*, following the section on the characteristics of True Suchness (*tathatā-lakṣaṇa*), ten kinds of equality are taught—this is precisely the Middle Way.
Furthermore, the title "The Aspect of True Suchness" (Tathatā-lakṣaṇa) is given because True Suchness takes non-attachment as its characteristic.

If one explains this by following the sequence of the preceding aspects, then the preceding stage of "Saving Sentient Beings and Attaining Buddhahood" encompasses all phenomena; it is thus "all dharmas.
To be free from the marks of sentient beings is identical to the primordial Buddha being free from all marks. The section below constitutes the fundamental position.
In this very state, one is detached; being free from the two attachments, one then accords with the characteristic of True Suchness (*tathatā*).
This sufficiently demonstrates the intention of entering into the principle ever more deeply. △ Ninth: Dedication of Liberation.
Truly attaining that which is as-it-is, there is no obstruction throughout the ten directions; this is called the Dedication of Unbound Liberation.

The first phrase follows upon the two types of non-attachment, signifying that what has already been attained is of one mark with True Suchness (*tathatā*). "The ten directions" refers to the ten dharma-realms (*dharmadhātu*).
"Unobstructed" refers to the great liberation of the unobstructed dharma-realm. This is because in the preceding stage, there was non-obstruction regarding principle (*li*).
This stage is the non-obstruction between principle and phenomena, and between phenomena and phenomena.
In the *Avataṃsaka*, one cultivates the practices of Samantabhadra with a mind of liberation that is without attachment or bondage across sixty-two aspects, filling the entire Dharma-realm.
Furthermore, one attains one hundred and fifty-six kinds of most subtle and minute wisdom; as for all other states within the Dharma-realm, where could they not be contained? Thus it is concluded.
This is called "The Nameless Unbound Liberation. It refers to entering the inconceivable liberation of the *dharmadhātu*.

This is because in the preceding stage one merely attains liberation through detachment (*visaṃyoga-vimukti*), whereas in this stage one further attains liberation through mastery (*vaśitā-vimukti*); hence the designation.
△ Tenth: The Immeasurable Dedication.
The inherent virtues (*prakṛti-guṇa*) are perfectly accomplished, and the limits of the *dharmadhātu* are extinguished; this is called the "Infinite Dedication of the *Dharmadhātu*.

The first phrase follows upon the two preceding stages. This is because Non-attachment (*asaṅga*) attains the entire substance of the inherent virtues, while Non-obstruction (*apratigha*) attains their great function (*mahā-vṛtti*).
Since both substance and function are fully possessed, it is said that the inherent virtues are perfectly accomplished. If one relies on [the commentary by] Gu...
The Mountain refers to the perfect realization of the wondrous nature of the three virtues.
Furthermore, by connecting the preceding with the following, non-attachment is itself prajñā, non-obstruction is itself liberation, and the immeasurable is itself the dharmakāya.
That the measure of the dharma-realm ceases is truly because its essence is omnipresent and its function is all-pervasive; thus, every speck of dust and every hair is equal to the dharma-realm.
There is no longer any limit; thus, that which is the cessation of measure is itself the immeasurable.

In this stage of the *Avataṃsaka*, one exclusively uses the roots of goodness from the gift of Dharma to adorn all Buddha-fields, emerging from an infinite and sovereign body that pervades the entire Dharma-realm.
Up to the roots of goodness for benefiting sentient beings throughout the entire dharma-realm, there are twenty phrases, all of which speak of the "immeasurability of the dharma-realm.

Furthermore, there are thirty-six phrases concerning "abiding in the immeasurable dharma-realm" and "dwelling securely in the immeasurable dharma-realm," all of which convey the meaning of the cessation of the measure of the dharma-realm;
the titles of these sections may be understood accordingly. Question: Regarding the eight summaries of True Suchness (tathatā), the ninth...

Question: Why are the first nine described as "unobstructed" while the tenth is described as "immeasurable," yet both are said to be dedicated toward True Suchness (*tathatā*)? Answer: Because the unobstructed nature of the ninth and the immeasurable nature of the tenth are both aspects of True Suchness;
thus, these three are identical in their locus. Although these three loci are distinguished for the sake of classification, in reality, every stage is the perfection of the Middle Way:
first, compassion does not obstruct wisdom; second, wisdom does not destroy compassion; third, they are fundamentally wondrous.

1. The integration of enlightenment; 2. The identity of cause and effect within the same stage; 3. The mutual fusion of the environment and its inhabitants; 4. The simultaneous identity of nature and cultivation; 5. The shared root of self and others; 6.
The simultaneous transcendence of both identity and separation; 7. Sovereignty over the ultimate and the conventional; 8. The perfect consummation of essence and function.
For this reason, the *Avataṃsaka* states that upon reaching this stage, the earth trembles, flowers rain down, and the various devas offer worship and sing praises. Furthermore...
These names and stages belong to the Separate Teaching (Bie-jiao) and are termed "outer ordinary beings" (wai-fan).

However, within these stages of the Perfect Reality (Yuan-shi), from the first abode (chu-zhu) onward, one is already equal to those on the [ten] grounds (di-shang). Reaching this point, one further transcends the eighteen stages of that Buddha.

This is vastly different from what the Separate Teaching can look up to. The ten stages of Dedication (Hui-xiang) are hereby concluded. 7. The Four Stages of Preparatory Practice (Jia-xing). By Xie Li.
It is said: According to scriptures such as the *Ratnaguṇasaṃcayagāthā* (or *Yíngluò jīng*), the four stages of application (*prayoga*) are not listed separately.

However, according to treatises such as the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi*, the forty minds prior to the [first] stage (*bhūmi*) are designated as the stage of provisions (*sambhāra*) for external ordinary beings (*bāhya-pṛthagjana*); thereafter, following the ten stages of dedication (*pariṇāmanā*), the stages of "Heat" (*uṣmagata*) and so forth are specifically clarified as the stage of application for internal ordinary beings (*adhyātma-pṛthagjana*).
Regarding Wuxing’s statement that "the Perfect [Vehicle] borrows the specific names [of the Separate Vehicle]," this refers to the intended meaning of those names.
They are similar in brief outline but actually different in substance. "Vijñaptimātra" (consciousness-only) refers to the stage of *prayoga* (preparatory application).

This means applying effort and practice (*prayoga-karma*) because one is approaching the Path of Seeing (*darśana-mārga*) of the First Bhūmi, the transition from the state of an ordinary person (*pṛthagjana*) to that of a noble one (*ārya*). This is a major turning point (*mahā-sandhi*) where it is necessary to apply diligent effort;

this is the point where the meaning is briefly similar. Question: This sutra establishes sixty stages of the noble ones (*ārya-pada*). In what way does it accord with the *Vijñaptimātra*? Furthermore...
Regarding the distinction between ordinary beings and sages: the answers concerning their identity or difference, and inclusion or exclusion, are both unimpeded.

If one considers the initial stage of the Perfect [Teaching], because one suddenly awakens to the fundamental Buddha-nature, they are granted the status of being identical to the sages. However, if one examines the relative depth of their practice, then from the perspective of faith and understanding (*śraddhā-adhimukti*), there is no hindrance to the distinction between ordinary beings and sages in actual cultivation.
Nevertheless, these ordinary beings of the Perfect Teaching have already far surpassed those of the Separate [Teaching] and the Voice-hearers. This is the division.
This consists of two parts. First, concluding the preceding and initiating the subsequent:
"Ānanda, these good sons have fully perfected the forty-one pure minds; next, they accomplish the four kinds of wondrous and perfect preparatory practices (*prayoga*)."
Wenling says: Regarding the "forty-one minds," there is one stage of Dry Wisdom (*śuṣka-vipaśyanā*), and ten stages each for the levels of Faith, Abiding, Practice, and Dedication.

While both the Small Vehicle and the Shared Teaching possess these four preparatory stages (*prayoga*), they are neither wondrous nor perfect; therefore, this [text] specifically designates the wondrous and perfect preparatory stages.

Because one first awakens to the perfection of the fundamental nature and subsequently gives rise to a cultivation and realization that is itself free from cultivation and realization, it is called "pure.

Yet, it is specifically termed "wondrously perfect" because, although from the initial stage up to the fulfillment of the stages of abiding one employs exclusively the Middle Way, the text has never explicitly mentioned matters concerning the benefiting of sentient beings; this is the wisdom that tends toward the Truth.

One dwells predominantly within the stage of the Ten Practices (*daśabhūmi-pratipatti*), beginning there to deliver sentient beings through explicit teachings. This is the most supreme form of world-transcending compassion.
Within the text on the Ten Transferences (*daśapariṇāmanā*), the ultimate and conventional truths are clearly seen to be mutually integrated, with compassion and wisdom operating in equal measure.

Since every stage and every vow therein perfects the Middle Way, now, building upon the Ten Transferences to discuss the stage of Application (*prayoga*), it is most wondrous and perfect. That is to say:
Regarding the principle of the Truths (*satya*): that it is neither three nor one is called "wondrous" (*miao*); that it is both one and three is called "perfect" (*yuan*). Question:
Since each stage (*bhūmi*) in the *Avataṃsaka* involves the deliverance of sentient beings, why is there no sequential progression between the ultimate and conventional truths?

Answer: Both are the words of the Buddha; each has its own specific domain. They should be elucidated through mutual illumination. Did we not say previously that the *Avataṃsaka* expounds upon meritorious deeds and manifestations? Therefore, its terminology is expansive.

Broadly speaking, they are unified; yet the *Śūraṅgama-sūtra* originally established distinct names. Thus, the terminology is both essential and differentiated, such that they support one another without mutual obstruction.

Question: Since one proceeds from the "pure middle" toward the "True" and transcends the "Conventional," and then proceeds from the "True" and "Conventional" to fulfill the "pure middle," this should constitute ultimate realization.
Why, then, is there further addition at this stage? And why are there ten stages (*daśabhūmi*)?
Furthermore, regarding "cultivation": the answer is that the ten stages of faith (*daśa-śraddhā*) are a semblance of cultivation, yet in reality they merely fulfill the mind of faith;

the three stages of worthiness (*tri-kṣānti*) are a semblance of cultivation, yet in reality they merely bring the mind of understanding (*adhimukti*) to its limit. Neither constitutes true cultivation.

Now, as faith and understanding have reached their ultimate fulfillment and one is about to enter true cultivation, it is therefore called "preparatory application" (*prayoga*). Since this is still not true cultivation, how could one rashly claim to have realized the ultimate?
Question: Prior to this stage, was there not already faith, understanding, and cultivation? Answer: These were all merely semblances of faith and semblances of understanding.

Even if there were marks of cultivation, they were merely the exertion of semblances of faith and semblances of understanding; they did not yet constitute even semblance-cultivation, so how could they be confused with true cultivation?

Furthermore, there is a distinction between those who have not yet entered the five grades and those who have already entered them, as well as between the two states of mind: the distracted and the concentrated.
This is the distinction between them. Thus, the sequence for advancing in practice has been considered by more than half.

Now, those who traverse sixty stages and are uniformly designated as occupying the rank of sage do so to honor their sudden enlightenment (*tongwu*). Those who are categorized into ten divisions and distinguished by various positions do not abandon the completion of gradual cultivation (*xiucheng*).
Only one who realizes the non-obstruction between the nature and cultivation may be consulted regarding the Way. △ Second, the specific clarification.

Regarding the four positions: although these differ from the stage of mere consciousness (*vijñaptimātra*), each position possesses its own meditative concentration that can give rise to contemplation, the contemplation itself, and the phenomena being contemplated.

Now, examining the scriptural text closely, it employs only the two characters "mind" (*citta*) and "Buddha" (*buddha*) to contrast and distinguish four propositions, thereby establishing the four positions.
This is because one gathers sentient beings by means of the mind, and gathers true suchness (*tathatā*) by means of the Buddha; this is a summary that traces back to the preceding three stages.
It does not stop at the tenth stage, but further divides it into four: first, the stage of "Heat" (*uṣmagata*).
One immediately takes the Buddha’s awakening as one's own mind. Whether it has emerged or not yet emerged, it is like drilling wood to produce fire when one desires to ignite the timber;
this is called the Stage of Warmth (*ūṣmagata*).

According to the principle of inclusion based on characteristics, it certainly encompasses the ten stages of dedication (*pariṇāmanā*); however, according to the explicit textual evidence, there is still a separate sequential progression.
This stage is like treading upon the Buddha’s awakening and coming from it. Thus the Master says:
although the preceding Buddha-awakening is said to be capable of being equalled, one has not yet attained formal realization.

Now, as one is about to approach the holy fruit, one takes that Buddha-awakening as one's own causal mind and further applies effort and practice to seek formal realization. Having first entered the stage of the cause, one does not immediately attain the fruit.

Therefore, it is like drilling for fire; only then does one obtain the characteristic of warmth. While previously one merely made vows and sought [enlightenment], here there is actual practice and progress.

Furthermore, whereas previously the perception of the Buddha was not yet forgotten and could not be merged into one's own mind, here the perception of the Buddha is finally merged so that there is only the One Mind—this is what is meant by "the Buddha is identical to the mind. The stage of cause refers to the fundamental stage; as for the fruit:

This refers to the First Stage (*prathamā bhūmi*). (According to the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi*, at this stage one enters the Samādhi of Attaining Clarity (*vidarśanālābha-samādhi*) and gives rise to the contemplation of inferior investigation (*mṛdu-paryeṣaṇā-vipaśyanā*), initially observing that name (*nāman*), object (*artha*), intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*), and distinctions (*viśeṣa*) are all empty.
△ Second, the Stage of the Summit (*mūrdhan-bhūmi*).

Furthermore, by means of one's own mind, one attains what the Buddhas have traversed—whether relying on it or not relying on it. It is like ascending a high mountain where the body enters into empty space, yet there remains a slight obstruction below;
this is called the Stage of the Summit (mūrdhan).
This stage is like treading upon the ground as if approaching the Buddha-ground (*buddhabhūmi*), for that which is traversed is the very nature of the ground itself. Wuxing says:
"Relying on the mind of the 'Heat' (*uṣmagata*) stage, one cultivates the wisdom of the Buddha-fruit. Because this wisdom contemplates the mind, it is like feet treading upon the ground;

because the characteristics of the mind are about to be exhausted, it is as if relying yet not relying. The high mountain is a metaphor for the mind of this stage, while empty space is a metaphor for that which is [contemplated].

Based on this principle: because the characteristics of the mind (*citta-lakṣaṇa*) have not yet been fully exhausted, there remains a subtle obstruction below. That the obstruction reaches such subtlety indicates that the characteristics of the mind are not many.
This is because, although the vision of Buddha (*buddha-darśana*) was extinguished in the preceding stage, the vision of mind (*citta-darśana*) still persisted;

reaching this stage, the characteristics of the mind are again extinguished, leaving only a single awakening (*ekābhisambodhi*). This is what is meant by "mind is itself Buddha" (*cittam eva buddhaḥ*). [In the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi*, this stage is called entering the Samādhi of Increasing Clarity (*vṛddhāloka-samādhi*), giving rise to the superior investigation.]
Contemplation. Repeatedly contemplating that the four dharmas—name and so forth—are all merely transformations of the mind. △ Third, the stage of patience (*kṣānti*).

When the mind and the Buddha are identical, one skillfully attains the Middle Way. Like a person enduring an insult, neither harboring resentment nor retaliating; this is called the stage of patience.
This stage merely inherits the two preceding stages in their entirety, maintaining both mind and Buddha; hence it is said that "the two are identical," which is to say, "mind itself is Buddha.

Because cause and effect interpenetrate, it is said that one "skillfully attains the Middle Way. Wénlǐng’s claim that cause and effect are both forgotten is an overextension that conflates this with the lower stage.
He [Wénlǐng] attempts to pair the state of being about to realize but not yet having realized with the categories of "neither dwelling nor emerging."

Regarding the statement that one does not differ from those who practice patience, yet neither harbors nor emits [resentment]: it is because, being able to tolerate, one does not harbor resentment like ordinary people;
thus it is said "not harboring. However, because one still maintains the capacity for endurance, one has not completely forgotten like the Perfected Person (zhìrén);
thus it is said "not emitting. As for the matter endured, it is in a state of being about to be forgotten but not yet forgotten—this is comparable to patience.

The Bodhisattva on the stage of the Path of Seeing is like one who is about to realize what has not yet been realized; it is precisely similar [to this]. (In the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi*, this stage is described as entering the "seal-impressing samādhi" (*mudrā-pratyavekṣaṇa-samādhi*) and giving rise to the "inferior correct contemplation" (*tathatā-nirūpaṇa*), thereby sealing the previous four dharmas as empty.
△ Fourth, the Stage of Supreme Mundane Dharma (*laukikāgra-dharma*).
Quantities are extinguished; delusion and awakening are the Middle Way, wherein both are beyond designation. This is called the Stage of the Supreme Worldly Dharma (*laukikāgra-dharma*).

The opening phrase marks this stage and also collectively summarizes the preceding three positions. Because both mind and Buddha are simultaneously obliterated, it is said that "quantities are extinguished.
For where there is mind and where there is Buddha, the distinctions between cause and effect constitute quantities; only here is this truly so.
When cause and effect are both forgotten, it is still said that "it is neither mind nor Buddha. The next two phrases explain the gradual dissolution [of delusion].

The two terms "delusion" (mí) and "awakening" (jué) run through the Middle Way below as a pair. However, one who is deluded regarding the Middle Way does not mean they have misunderstood the Middle Way;
rather, "delusion" refers to the state prior to awakening. Thus, being deluded regarding the Middle Way occurs within the state of non-awakening.
This refers merely to the Middle Way cultivated by sentient beings. To "awaken to the Middle Way" does not mean to intellectually comprehend the Middle Way;
rather, awakening is the stage of Great Awakening (*mahābodhi*). Therefore, awakening to the Middle Way is the Middle Way realized as the fruit within the stage of Great Awakening.
Thus, being deluded regarding the Middle Way remains the causal mind of a Bodhisattva, whereas awakening to the Middle Way...

It remains the resultant wisdom of the Buddha. Regarding these two, that which has no objective referent means that, below, one does not perceive one's own mind, and above, one does not perceive the Buddha-wisdom;
thus, both mind and Buddha are forgotten, and no numerical quantity is maintained within worldly phenomena.

This is the most supreme. This reveals that only upon ascending to the stage of a Bodhisattva does one transcend the world, and only upon attaining Buddhahood does one become the foremost of those who have transcended the world.

(In the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi*, it is said that at this stage one enters the *ānantarya-samādhi* and gives rise to the superior contemplation of reality as it is (*yathābhūta-darśana*), thereby sealing the emptiness of the two graspings and subduing and eliminating both the innate and conceptualized aspects of the two obstacles.

Now, in the first stage, the Buddha is precisely the mind; in the second stage, the mind is precisely the Buddha; in the third stage, it is "mind is Buddha"; and in the fourth stage, it is "neither mind nor Buddha."

It is not the Buddha; therefore, one does not depart from the two characters "mind" (citta) and "Buddha. Thus, the four stages are clearly manifest. (Now, there are three reasons for specifically citing the *Vijñaptimātra* [Consciousness-Only] school here: first, to cause people to investigate it clearly.

Since its name is the same as this [Chinese tradition], how can one fail to examine its meaning? Second, to show that it differs from this. For once one has mastered its meaning, one will see that while the names are identical, the meanings are distinct.

Third, to clarify that this [tradition] is profound while that is shallow. This is because its first stage corresponds to the first *vihāra* (abode) of this system; thus, its four preparatory stages (*prayoga*) prior to the ground correspond to the ten mental states (*daśa-cittotpāda*) prior to these abodes. Consequently, its four concentrations and four contemplations are roughly similar to the concentration and wisdom within the ten mental states.)

Regarding the faculties and powers (*indriya-bala*), while their essential meanings differ—being either partial or perfect—how much more so is this case of the four preparatory stages (*prayoga*)? These have already transcended the eighteen stages of that Buddha; how could they possibly be discussed as being of the same order? Furthermore, Mount Gu said:

"The meaning of deriving these from the ten stages of dedication (*pariṇāmanā*) is not without difference, yet the principle remains incomplete. For whenever one advances to realize a stage, there must necessarily be the three mental states of entry, abiding, and exit.
Now, the four preparatory stages lie between the two pillars of the stages of dedication and the grounds (*bhūmi*); they should therefore be..."

The mind that emerges from the Ten Dedications (*daśa-pariṇāmanā*) enters the first stage (*prathamā bhūmi*). If one does not open this as a separate category, there is no objection to merging it with what precedes or follows.
One may apply this same reasoning to the subsequent stages of Equal Enlightenment (*samyak-saṃbodhi*) and Vajra. This concludes the four stages of the preparatory application (*prayoga*).
Regarding the eight stages and ten positions, Wēnlíng says: "The ten stages (*daśa-bhūmi*) refer to the accumulation of the preceding dharmas until they reach their fulfillment."
All Buddha-dharmas arise in dependence upon this; therefore, it is called "ground" (*bhūmi*). Regarding this, there are two meanings.
First is the meaning of "perfected reality," for the ground takes solidity as its essence.

Second is the meaning of "arising and producing," for the ground takes production as its function. According to the end of the preceding fourth fascicle, the Tathāgata established [the grounds] merely...

Regarding the text on the two stages of cause and effect, it says: "Attaining the nature of original, luminous awareness, which is without birth or extinction, one takes this as the mind of the causal stage;
thereafter, one fully accomplishes the cultivation and realization of the fruition stage.

This means that one simply takes the fundamental mind of perfect penetration from the first stage (*bhūmi*) as the causal ground, and takes the Buddha’s ultimate, wondrous enlightenment as the fruition ground; everything in between constitutes the full accomplishment of the fruition ground.
This refers to the stages (*bhūmi*). Now, examining the original text concerning the holy stages of *dhyāna*, the second stage is named "Cultivating the Ground" (*caryā-bhūmi*).

This is because one traverses the previously mentioned wondrous mind to constitute the ground. Furthermore, the fourth section on "Dedication" (*pariṇāmana*) states: "When the essence of reality is clearly manifested, the ground is like the Buddha-ground.

Up to the four stages of "Additional Practice" (*prakarana*), each stage is designated as a "ground. These are all grounds based upon causes. Indeed, "ground" (*bhūmi*) is also glossed as "step" (*krama*).
This is because the ten stages (*daśabhūmi*) are truly the cause; yet, the mention of "stages" prior to the [Buddha] stages refers to the levels that serve as the steps toward this true cause.
Now, these ten stages should also be subsumed under the stage of fruition (*phala-bhūmi*), even though the Buddha stage alone is the true fruition.
These ten stages (*daśabhūmi*) are the levels for advancing toward the realization of the true fruit. Furthermore, in terms of cultivation and realization:
since the ten stages are called "true cultivation" (*bhūtābhyāsa*), it follows that the stages prior to them are all "semblance cultivation" (*pratibimbābhyāsa*).

Since the stage of Buddhahood is "true realization" (*bhūtasākṣātkriyā*), the ten stages are merely "semblance realization. Thus, from the initial aspiration to the ultimate consummation, although the principle is identical in its suddenness, there remains a distinction between semblance and reality.
Nevertheless, the shallowness and depth of the successive stages remain distinct in their sequence, such that the two aspects of perfect interfusion and sequential progression are mutually unimpeded.
This is divided into ten sections. △ First, the Stage of Joy (*pramuditā-bhūmi*).

Ānanda, these sons of good family have attained excellent penetration into great bodhi; their awakening penetrates that of the Tathāgatas and they exhaust the realm of the Buddhas—this is called the Stage of Joy (pramuditā-bhūmi).
Regarding "Great Bodhi" (Mahābodhi): among the five types of bodhi, it should be the Unsurpassed Bodhi (*anuttara-bodhi*).

According to the four-fascicle version of the root scripture, the Buddha himself defines this as "Unsurpassed Bodhi" by taking the three *tathāgatagarbhas*—namely, "not-all-is-all," "dual-separation," and "dual-identity"—as its total essence.
This is because within it, the one and the many are mutually identical, and the large and the small are non-obstructive.

...up to the point where it universally encompasses and integrates all things as its great function; this is it. At this stage, one has merely attained penetration (*prativedha*), yet has not yet realized the ultimate;
it remains the Bodhicitta of the enlightened mind (*cittaprakāśa-bodhi*) and is thus the stage of the Path of Vision (*darśana-mārga*). As stated previously:

"Sentient beings within the three realms of existence and the two vehicles who have transcended the world cannot fathom it with their cognitive minds (*jñeya-citta*). Now, however, it is granted that only the Bodhisattvas at this stage [can do so].

It is not merely that they are penetrating, but that they are thoroughly and skillfully penetrating. These first two phrases appear to establish the principle, while the following two phrases provide its explanation.

"Awakening penetrates the Tathāgata" refers to the fact that the fundamental awakening (*mūla-awakening*) of one's own mind and the wondrous awakening (*prajñā-awakening*) of the Buddha’s mind are perfectly interfused and non-dual.
This is what is meant by the statement: "Only through wondrous awakening and clarity does there arise a perfect illumination of the Dharma-realm"—this is "awakening penetrating."

Furthermore, as for "exhausting the realm of the Buddha," this also means that by means of the three collections (*piṭaka*), the four meanings, and the four characteristics, the entire body and great function [of the Dharma] encompass and exhaust the wondrous realm of the Buddha.
These two phrases indicate that it is precisely through the awakening that penetrates the Tathāgata that one exhausts the realm of the Buddha, thereby attaining unexcelled Bodhi.
However, the single character "penetration" (*tōng*) signifies actual realization and direct vision.

This is not a matter of inferential knowledge through words and letters. Furthermore, one should know that "Awakening pervades both phrases" refers to the stage of "the mind itself is Buddha" within the preceding four stages of application (*prayoga*).
At that stage, one is on the verge of realization but has not yet realized it; here, however, there is actual realization.

Moreover, while at that stage Awakening may pervade but not exhaust the objective realm, here it not only pervades but also exhausts it. For this reason, it is superior and thus designated as "holy" (*ārya*).
It is established. The *Avataṃsaka* states that this bodhisattva "skillfully knows" ten points, such as the obstacles of the various stages (*bhūmi*) and their remedies;

all are described as "skillfully knowing," which suggests a form of thorough penetration. The final conclusion, however, links this to "entering the Buddha-stage," at which point it appears the ultimate limit is reached.
Nevertheless, while this may involve penetrating the matters of cultivating causes on the stages, I fear it does not yet fully accord with this unsurpassed *bodhi*. Second.

The purport of the sūtra seems slightly different. The wise should examine this in detail. It is named "Joy" because, regarding what was previously hoped for, one has now attained initial penetration.
As the *Suvarṇaprabhāsa-sūtra* states: "One has first realized the supramundane mind that was previously unattained;
having now finally attained it, all that was wished for regarding the great task is fully accomplished."
One gives rise to supreme joy and bliss. △ Second is the Ground of Freedom from Defilement (*vimalā-bhūmi*).
When distinct natures enter into sameness, and even that same nature is extinguished, it is named the Ground of Freedom from Defilement.

Following upon the preceding stage, one realizes that the penetration [of wisdom] is identical to that of the Tathāgata; that is, the distinct natures of the nine realms enter into the single realm of the Buddha—this is called "distinctness."
The nature and the entry are identical. Upon initial realization, one must not forget the Buddha-realm;

yet if the Buddha-realm becomes an object of the mind, this itself constitutes a subtle defilement within that which is inherently pure. Thus, even this identity of nature must be extinguished before what is called "defilement-free purity" is attained.
Furthermore, if one traces back to the four preparatory stages (*prayoga*), it is neither mind nor Buddha.

One must apply further effort toward that state; this too is a realization of reality. Furthermore, when that which is neither mind nor Buddha has its numerical distinctions extinguished, one then enters the sameness of different natures.
Moreover, by taking this very sameness and extinguishing it as well, one advances to realize the essence free from defilement;

seeing this increase in excellence, one attains the rank of a Sage on the second stage (*bhūmi*). Both the *Avataṃsaka* and the *Suvarṇaprabhāsa* sūtras express the departure from all forms of destruction.

Regarding the defilements of the precepts, the essential meaning appears somewhat different; there is no need to force them into agreement. If one considers falling into difference as falling into sameness, this is termed breaking the precepts.
This is indeed profound, yet it also seems like a forced synthesis. △ Third, the Ground of Radiance (Prabhākari-bhūmi).
When purity reaches its ultimate limit, luminosity arises; this is called the Ground of Radiant Light (*Prabhākari-bhūmi*).

The two characters "ultimate purity" (*jing ji*) fully trace back to the [previous stage of] "freedom from defilement" (*vimalā*). In the preceding stage, one was merely free from defilement but had not yet reached the state of transcending that freedom itself;
now, one is about to distance oneself even from the "freedom" of that prior freedom. This constitutes ultimate purity, wherein true awakening becomes manifest.
Dew appears; this is the arising of clarity. It is like an ancient mirror: after being freed from impurities, it is further polished, whereby it becomes pure and clarity arises.
This is the natural principle. Regarding the identity or difference between the ordinary person and the Buddha:

once the subtle obstructions of emotional defilement are purified without remainder, the originally inherent capacity for illumination will manifest and cannot be suppressed. This is what is meant by "when purity reaches its extreme, light penetrates everywhere."
This is "attainment. The *Avataṃsaka* clarifies that this Bodhisattva’s great arousal of the six kinds of true and pure supernatural powers (*ṣaḍ-abhijñā*) corresponds to this stage.
The phrase "binding and developing light" refers to the arising of illumination. △ Fourth, the Stage of Blazing Wisdom (*Arciṣmatī-bhūmi*).
When clarity reaches its ultimate limit and awakening is fulfilled, it is called the Stage of Blazing Wisdom (*Arciṣmatī-bhūmi*).

"Ultimate clarity" means that clarity arises based on the preceding clarity; it is like a fire that has just begun to burn, where light has just started to emerge but has not yet reached full fulfillment.
This stage is like a blazing fire that has become a great, fierce mass; both consciousness and the golden light are [fully manifest].
Regarding the phrase "burning the fuel of afflictions," although this principle is profound, it must also involve the incineration and severance of subtle delusions that serve as obstructions.

As for the term "fulfillment of awakening" (*jue man*), it clarifies that [awakening] accords with the nature of reality; hence it is called the fulfillment of awakening. This refers to what is known as "quiescent illumination encompassing empty space.
In this stage, according to the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra*, one fully cultivates the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment (*bodhipākṣika-dharma*) which assist the path. These are as follows:
The factors of enlightenment (bodhipakṣadharma) are like the intent of properly burning firewood.
However, the text here expresses the birth into the family of the Dharma-king, which is similar to the four abidings (catuḥ-vihāra) of this sutra; one must not fail to examine this in detail.

In the sections concerning these various stages (bhūmi), the text for the most part establishes their sequential positions based on the depth of the realized principle (tattva), rather than—as is common in that other sutra—primarily describing the cultivation of abandonment (prahāṇa).

Future sages will not be biased; they should simply investigate the meaning and compare the respective proportions. One must not judge superiority or inferiority based solely on the extensiveness or brevity of the text.
The name "Blazing Wisdom" (Jvalanābhā) is intended merely to signify that this wisdom, like a flame, possesses the supreme function of transcendent brilliance.
△ Fifth, the Ground of Difficult Victory (Sudurjayā).
That which nothing—neither identity nor difference—can reach is called the Ground Difficult to Conquer (*Duranjayā*).
Regarding the first two lines: through the awakening of the First Ground, the distinct natures (*bhinnatva*) of the Tathāgatas are extinguished, leaving only the single realm of the Buddha;

on the Second Ground, their common nature (*sāmānyatva*) is extinguished, and even the Buddha-realm is forgotten. Thus, one returns once more to the state of primordial purity (*viśuddha-prakṛti*), where there is absolutely no obstruction.
From this point, one further passes through two stages: from purity to clarity, and from clarity to fulfillment.

Because the previous states of difference and identity have long since been transcended, they now reach a state of profound non-attainment. This is because the principle has reached ultimate perfection and integration, such that no further identity or difference can be perceived.
It is named "Difficult to Conquer" (*Sudurjaya*) because all mundane and supramundane phenomena are utterly unable to equal it.
How much less could it surpass it? The *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi* states that on this stage, the two wisdoms of the ultimate and the conventional have mutually contradictory modes of activity (*ākāra*);

yet they are brought into correspondence, which is why it is "Extremely Difficult to Conquer" (*Sudurjayā*). This refers to the similarities and differences between those two [wisdoms] regarding their ultimate and conventional aspects.

However, while the synthesis of those two is supreme, this [stage] is utterly transcendent and beyond comparison. Although the provisional and the real, the partial and the complete, differ in their essential purports, they are merely similar.
And that is all. △ Sixth, the Ground of Presence (*Abhimukhī-bhūmi*).
Unconditioned True Suchness (*tathatā*) is by nature pure and luminously manifest; hence it is named the Ground of Presence.

From the stage prior to this ground, one applies effort and practice, aspiring from the state of the Worthy (*śaikṣa*) toward the Sage (*arhat*); upon entering the ground, differences are dissolved and extinguished.

The same. When clarity gives rise to the fulfillment of awakening, one thereby transcends both sameness and difference. The conditioned functions of effort are most supreme and ultimate, such that none can surpass them.
However, when conditioned phenomena are exhausted to their limit, the nature of unconditioned *tathatā* (suchness) finally manifests;
thus, this stage is named "Manifestation" (*Pratyutpannā*). This is because for those of the Sudden-Perfect vehicle, the arousal of the mind is itself the sudden realization of *tathatā*.

The wondrous nature is the realm of the Buddha where emotions are forgotten; yet, as the five stages of dwelling have not been shattered and the defilements of the mind have not been eliminated, one’s understanding of *tathatā* (suchness) remains merely inferential.

How could it be a direct realization? Now, by progressing from semblance cultivation to true cultivation and exhausting the meritorious practices of the conditioned, one is about to reach the stage of effortless practice (*anābhoga-prayoga*). Therefore, it is only upon this ground that *tathatā* finally becomes manifest.
This is first attained through direct realization. However, the total embodiment and great function of True Suchness (tathatā) should occur in the eighth and ninth stages;
yet at the eighth stage, there is truly non-effortful functioning (anābhoga), where one merely reaches the unconditioned (asaṃskṛta) and begins to manifest True Suchness.

Furthermore, this [stage] is designated as "Manifestation" (Abhimukhī) because it reveals its nature; whereas the *Avataṃsaka* and *Suvarṇaprabhāsa* primarily clarify the manifestation of meritorious practices, which thus appears to have a different purport.
Therefore, I shall not trouble myself to cite them here. △ Seventh, the Stage of Far-Reaching Travel (Dūraṅgamā).
Reaching the limit of the reality-limit (*tathatā*) is called the Far-Going Ground (*dūramgamā-bhūmi*).
On the preceding stages, the reality-limit has only just begun to manifest; it has not yet been fully revealed, let alone traversed to its end.
Here, one exhausts its actual limit, reaching through to it without exception. Wēnlíng says: "When identity and difference do not reach [it], then the pure nature of *tathatā* [is realized]."
It is clearly revealed and manifest before one. While the manifestation of *tathatā* (suchness) is partial and limited in its realization, its ultimate limit is far-reaching;
it transcends all else and reaches the pinnacle, hence it is named "Far-Going" (*dūraṅgama*). Wuxing said: "To reach the limit of the limit of *tathatā*—this is the limit of the limitless.
Since the principle is already limitless, how could practice be anything but near? In this sutra, from the fifth stage onward, there is no longer any distinction between sameness and difference.

Then the effort of conditioned practice (*saṃskṛta-prayoga*) is already brought to ultimate completion, and the unconditioned truth (*asaṃskṛta-tattva*) of the sixth stage is already manifest before one.
Reaching this point, the limit of reality (*bhūtakoṭi*) is fully revealed. In the *Avataṃsaka*, this very stage clarifies that the culmination of effort is reached;
yet, while it speaks only of the excellence of effort and does not generally mention the manifestation of the fundamental principle, this seems to be a distinct teaching. Thus says the Wise One.
Examine this in detail. △ Eighth, the Immovable Ground (*acalā-bhūmi*).
The mind of True Suchness (*tathatā-citta*) is named the Immovable Ground.
Wēnlíng says: "Since its limit has been fully exhausted, one then completely attains its essence; as the single True Reality is concentrated and eternal, it is therefore named 'Immovable'."
Movement. ○ In the sixth stage, True Suchness (Tathatā) begins to manifest; in the seventh stage, it begins to be fully revealed.

Yet, in reality, one has not yet employed it as one’s own mind. What is now called the "One True Suchness Mind" is the state where both one's own mind and the Buddha-mind are simultaneously and perfectly dissolved, leaving only the original mind of True Suchness, which is none other than the Dharma-realm of True Suchness. This is termed "Immovable."
"Movement" refers to transformation. However, that which accords with principle is subtle and true, remaining entirely without change; thus it is said so.
When a Bodhisattva abides in this stage, the faculties, the body, and the vessel-world—down to every single speck of dust and every single hair—are all the True Suchness of one's own mind.
This is what is called "thoroughly reaching the source of all phenomena," which is unmoving and indestructible; therefore, it is named "Immovable.

Indeed, for those who have attained realization from their initial resolve, they now personally verify this truth without error. In the *Avataṃsaka*, this stage clearly elucidates the mutual manifestation of the ten bodies (*daśakāya*).
Furthermore, at this stage, the specific names of the ten stages (*daśabhūmi*) are enumerated, including the title "Youthful Truth" (*kumārabhūta*).
The verse clarifies the eight stages of abiding (*bhūmi*), which bear a certain resemblance to the eight stages of abiding in this sutra;

these should be combined with the meaning of "birth into nobility" from the preceding four stages. One must carefully discern and differentiate them through investigation; let us await the subsequent text to provide a thorough and detailed exposition.
△ Ninth, the Stage of Excellent Wisdom (Sādhumatī-bhūmi). This also has two parts: first, the explicit explanation of the fundamental stage itself.
It is called the Stage of Excellent Wisdom because it brings forth the function of True Suchness (tathatā).
While the preceding stage attained the entire substance of True Suchness, this stage brings forth its great function; it arises in accordance with that substance.

This is the functioning of the natural principle. While the *Avataṃsaka* and *Suvarṇaprabhāsa* sutras mostly point toward meritorious practice, this sutra seems to speak of the fundamental true essence acting of itself.
In the preceding stage, each particle of dust and each hair is pure and original by nature, pervading the entire dharma-realm;
in this stage, however, each and every thing mutually encompasses and enters one another—pervasive and all-encompassing—and so forth. These are the ten mysteries.
Their functions are all the functions of True Suchness (*tathatā*). The title "Good Wisdom" (*sādhumati*) should be understood as the unimpeded wisdom of the Dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu-asangajñāna*).

Question: What distinguishes this from the mutual manifestation of the realms of dust and phenomena within the sevenfold practice, or the mutual interpenetration of the environment and its inhabitants within the five stages of aspiration?
Answer: It is only upon reaching the seventh stage that these practices truly exist; it is only upon reaching the fifth stage that these vows truly exist.

As for that which has not yet been described—the direct realization of the fundamental true body and its self-appropriated functions, which are naturally and primordially endowed—it is now manifested and brought forth. Because this is a partial direct realization within the stage of true cultivation, it is vastly different [from the previous stages].
Upon careful examination of these ten noble practices, they do not correspond with those found in the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* to any great extent.
It is the same. Therefore, I rely on the sacred words to seek the ultimate principle; I do not dare to arbitrarily engage in acceptance or rejection.

If the *Avataṃsaka*, the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi*, and the *Suvarṇaprabhāsa* all state that this stage possesses the four kinds of unimpeded eloquence (*catasraḥ pratisaṃvidaḥ*) and acts as a great Dharma-preacher who most skillfully expounds the Dharma, yet the *Avataṃsaka* further elucidates that the realm of such preaching is also profoundly inconceivable, in that it can cause—
"Sentient and insentient beings everywhere proclaim the sound of the Dharma," and so forth. Zizhong said:

"In the *Avataṃsaka*, this Bodhisattva is described as possessing the four kinds of unimpeded knowledge (*pratisaṃvid*) and acting as a great Dharma-preacher, expounding immeasurable *asaṃkhyeya* phrases and meanings without end;
therefore, it is called 'manifesting the function of True Suchness' (*tathatā-vṛtti*). I say: Expounding the Dharma can certainly also be described as such.
This is the manifestation of function. However, this is but one function within the Great Function.

Therefore, while the Manifestation of Function does not omit the preaching of the Dharma, how could the preaching of the Dharma exhaust the Great Function? The other stages are not all identical; why must they necessarily be the same here?

Thus, it is only when the Ten Mysterious Gates are fully present that they constitute a function truly commensurate with reality. Yet, even so, how could they omit the preaching of the Dharma? △ Second.
To provide a comprehensive explanation of the general name:
Ānanda, from this point onward, these bodhisattvas complete their cultivation and bring their merit to perfection;
therefore, this stage is also designated as the "Stage of Cultivation."
The single character "all" (zhū) does not merely refer to those from the ninth stage (*bhūmi*) onwards; rather, it refers generally to the higher stages.
Alternatively, it may refer specifically to the four preparatory stages (*prayoga*) up to the ninth stage.

This is because the Buddha, prior to the four preparatory stages, summarized [the preceding] as "transcending forty-one minds," thereby revealing that they are the various expedient minds prior to the stage of cultivation (*bhāvanā-avasthā*). Since this [current passage] is likewise a summary, it is appropriate that it should only...

This refers specifically to the stage of cultivation following the four preparatory practices (*prayoga*). One cultivates the latter two lines by means of suddenly awakening to the wondrous nature of True Suchness (*tathatā*) at the very beginning of one's resolve.

From this point, one proceeds through the stages of cultivation and severance until the entire body and great function of True Suchness are personally realized and fully attained, without deficiency or remainder; thus it is said. Furthermore, if these two lines are distinguished separately:

This pertains to the stages from the fourth through the sixth bhūmis, where the cultivation reaches its completion because one enters the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*) according to these successive levels.
From the seventh through the ninth bhūmis, merit is perfected; this means that the intrinsic qualities of *tathatā* are fully manifested.
Furthermore, in these subsequent stages, there is only the taking of realization. The final two phrases clearly indicate that this begins from this [seventh] stage.

Previously, this was referred to collectively as "cultivation" (*bhāvanā*); however, in reality, it clarifies that during the final three stages, the intent of cultivation is slight while the intent of realization (*sākṣātkriyā*) is predominant.
This does not contradict the *lakṣaṇa*-school (Yogācāra), as these [stages] are subsumed within the tenth stage, the Stage of Cultivation (*bhāvanā-bhūmi*). △ Ten:
The Cloud of Dharma Stage (*dharmameghā-bhūmi*).
The wondrous cloud of the compassionate shade covers the ocean of nirvāṇa; this is called the Ground of the Dharma-Cloud (*dharmameghā bhūmiḥ*).

Previous interpretations have been manifold, yet each appears to be partial or deficient, and their designations and meanings do not correspond with one another (Wuxing [Zhiyi] takes the preceding phrase to belong to "compassion").

The second phrase takes the originally quiescent nature of sentient beings as the ocean of *nirvāṇa*. This refers solely to benefiting others. Wēnlíng also attributes the preceding phrase entirely to compassion, yet designates it only as one’s own fruit-virtue, while taking the subsequent phrase to be the ocean of the Tathāgata’s fruition.

He thus claims that these two correspond and harmonize; this, however, distinguishes self and other from the perspective of persons, whereas the Dharma here refers exclusively to the fruition. Furthermore, regarding the two characters "Dharmamegha" (*fǎyún*), the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi* states: "The great Dharma-wisdom cloud contains the waters of myriad virtues, filling the *dharmakāya*.

The *Suvarṇaprabhāsa-sūtra* states: "The *dharmakāya* is like space, and wisdom is like a great cloud; both are able to pervade and cover all things. The *Avataṃsaka-sūtra* states: "Receiving the office of great wisdom, one increases immeasurable wisdom and merit."

This is called "Abiding on the Ground of the Dharma-Cloud" (*dharmameghā-bhūmi*). This is all based on the analogy that the Dharma is the *dharmakāya* (Dharma-body), and the cloud is the cloud of wisdom (*jñāna-megha*). In essence, this signifies the harmonious resonance between principle and wisdom. Now, to provide a distinct interpretation:
the first eight characters constitute the meaning, while the final four characters conclude the name. Within the meaning, "compassion" (*maitrī*) is the Dharma;

"compassion" refers to the sorrow of benefiting others, while "sublime" (*miao*) refers to the wisdom of self-benefit. "Shade-cloud" (*yin-yun*) is a metaphor: "shade" (*yin*) takes the aspect of providing shelter and moisture, while "cloud" (*yun*) takes...
The body is filled [with compassion and wisdom]. Compassion is like the clouds of the *skandhas* (aggregates) and wisdom is like the clouds themselves; both possess the sense of "covering" (*āvṛti*).
Regarding the word "covering" (*āvṛta*) in the subsequent phrase, it signifies being joined, complete, and all-pervasive.

This is because the cloud-masses of compassion and wisdom are the causal virtues perfected in the ten stages (*daśabhūmi*), whereas the ocean of *nirvāṇa* is the resultant virtue that is about to be realized but not yet realized at the end of the ten stages. *Nirvāṇa*.
"Parinirvāṇa" is taken here as its essential meaning: it signifies that there is nothing true that is not "complete" (pari) and nothing false that is not "quiescent" (nirvāṇa).
The term "ocean" serves as a metaphor for the magnitude of this fruition-merit; it extends horizontally and exhausts the vertical, being boundlessly vast and bottomlessly deep.

Because the Bodhisattva’s compassion and wisdom are perfected and closely approximate this fruition, only at this stage can the name truly correspond [to the reality], and there is not the slightest [discrepancy].

This refers to a deficiency. Therefore, one should know that it was not the case that there was previously a lack of wisdom or compassion; rather, it is simply that at this stage, being in accord with *nirvāṇa* is designated as "supreme.
Nevertheless, it does not say that one is in accord with the Buddha's virtues, for fear of confusing [this stage] with Equal Enlightenment (*samyaksambodhi*).

As for designating the name "Dharmameghā-bhūmi" (Cloud of Dharma Stage), if one calls upon the meaning by means of the name, then the single character "Dharma" (*dharma*) simultaneously contains both compassion and wisdom, while the single character "Cloud" (*megha*)...
These [eight characters] are subsumed within the aggregates (*skandha*). By returning their function to their essence, these two characters invoke the meaning of the preceding eight;

thus, one may say that name and meaning correspond perfectly. (Examining this in light of both the sutras and the śāstras: the sutras are indeed the Buddha’s words, and the śāstras likewise embody the Buddha’s intent. How could one dare to arbitrarily give rise to either reverence or contempt?)

One may briefly raise points of contention; however, the essential meaning resides within the text. Since the words of the Sage are interwoven and lack fixed characteristics, one must certainly not allow personal bias toward what one has studied to undermine the objective evaluation, nor should one avoid suspicion by concealing the true meaning of the Buddha’s teachings.

Indeed, when one examines the *Suvarṇaprabhāsa*, both its phrasing and meaning are identical [to other texts]. Although the *Avataṃsaka* is vast and extensive in its applications, its words and meanings do not differ significantly from it. Yet this sutra alone is concise in its diction while its meaning is profoundly distinct, showing no signs of correspondence whatsoever.

Furthermore, in the *Avataṃsaka*, it is only at the fourth stage (*bhūmi*) that one speaks of being born into the family of the Dharma-king; whereas in this sutra, the four abidings (*catuḥ-vihāra*) explicitly state: "It is like the intermediate state (*antarābhava*), seeking parents of its own accord; through the subtle communication of the *skandhas*, one enters the lineage of the Tathāgata. This appears to be entirely identical to being born into the family of the Dharma-king in the *Avataṃsaka*.

Regarding the fourth stage (*bhūmi*), it merely speaks of the "clarity of ultimate awakening being fulfilled," yet it completely lacks the noble intent of realizing non-arising (*anutpāda*). Furthermore, in the *Avataṃsaka*, it is only at the eighth stage that the manifestation of the ten bodies (*daśakāya*) is taught; yet among its alternative names, this is also called the "Abode of the Youthful Truth" (*kumārabhūta-vihāra*).

In this sutra, however, it is already stated at the eighth abode that the spiritual characteristics of the ten bodies are simultaneously perfected, and it is named the "Abode of the Youthful Truth. Upon reaching the eighth stage, it merely speaks of the "one mind of True Suchness" (*tathatā-citta*), with no mention whatsoever of the "ten bodies" or the "Youthful Truth.

Furthermore, in the *Avataṃsaka*, the ninth stage is explicitly called the "Abode of the Dharma Prince" (*dharmarāja-putra-vihāra*); yet this sutra alone applies the title "Dharma Prince" specifically to the ninth abode. Upon reaching the ninth stage, it merely speaks of "manifesting the function of True Suchness," with no trace of the designation "Prince. Moreover, in the *Avataṃsaka*, the tenth stage is clearly described as receiving the consecration (*abhiṣeka*).

Regarding this office, the *Daśabhūmika Sūtra* clearly states that from the first stage (*prathama-bhūmi*) up to the tenth stage (*daśamī-bhūmi*), it describes the Great King of the Nation delegating authority to the Crown Prince and performing the consecration (*abhiṣeka*) and so forth; yet, upon reaching the tenth stage, it merely says, "The subtle cloud of the shade of compassion covers the ocean of nirvāṇa," and contains no mention whatsoever of the signs of consecration.

The stages of the four, eight, nine, and ten bhūmis in the *Avataṃsaka* are all identical to the stages of abiding (*vihāra*) in this sutra; as for the remaining stages, their names are mostly the same, yet their meanings do not correspond.

Even regarding the stages of abiding in these two sutras, while their names are largely identical, their meanings differ significantly. In all such cases, how could one fail to examine them without due scrutiny? It is utterly unacceptable for Wu-xing to hastily suppress the *Avataṃsaka* by claiming that its "stages" and "ten bodies" are the same [as those in this sutra].

This is because both sutras merely borrow these names as provisional teachings to entice practitioners, yet their actual meanings are as different as heaven and earth. While it is natural for one with limited vision to criticize [the *Avataṃsaka*] in this way, to highly extol the *Avataṃsaka* without carefully determining the reasons for their differences also seems to be incomplete.

This is the principle. Now, let us employ inference and test this with the wise; I do not dare to insist that this is a definitive doctrine. This scripture possesses both aspects of the unobstructed dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu*), and the intent of each part is largely identical to that of the *Avataṃsaka*, differing only in the extent of its wording—some being detailed and others concise.

Nevertheless, there is as yet no further reason to infer that it surpasses the *Avataṃsaka*. Question: Why is the "Ten Abodes" (*daśavihāra*) here currently presented as being the same as the "Ten Grounds" (*daśabhūmi*) of the *Avataṃsaka*?

Answer: The Buddha’s speech is sovereign and may follow two paths. First, the intention of inclusive integration (*saṃgraha*). For the perfect principle encompasses all within one: thus, the first abode should immediately include the first practice, the first orientation, and the first ground. In this manner, up to the tenth abode, it should include the ten practices, the ten orientations, and the ten grounds. If this is the case, then it should be so.

Each set of ten is identical; how could it be limited to the identity of the four stages of abiding? Second is the meaning of opening and closing: for the Buddha’s teachings are not fixed. Sometimes he opens what precedes and closes what follows; sometimes he closes what precedes and opens what follows.

Now, regarding the *Śūraṅgama Sūtra*, one fears that it might close together the stages of abiding, practice, and dedication (*caryā-pratipatti-praṇidhāna*) from the *Avataṃsaka* into the ten levels of faith (*daśa-śraddhā*). This is similar to how Tiantai closed together the twenty-three stages of the Separate Teaching (*biejia*) into the final three levels of faith. Let me explain their characteristics. The answer is: taking the initial planting of the five faculties (*pañcendriya*) as the meaning of "abiding" (*sthiti*); using the two powers of progress and concentration to gather all practices of both concentration and distraction;

and using the eighth power of wisdom (*prajñā*) to explicitly state the turning toward enlightenment (*pariṇāmanā*). The ninth [power] of precepts and the tenth of vows are both directed toward this intention. Because these ten levels of faith thus merge with those thirty stages, one may apply the ten [levels] of this sutra [to them].

When the *Zhù* (Abiding) stage is confronted with the ten stages (*daśabhūmi*) of the *Avataṃsaka*, [the following] questions and answers arise: Question: If this is so, what are the subsequent stages after "Abiding"? Answer: They should all be understood as the "Equal Enlightenment" (*samāpatti-bodhi*) stage, differentiated according to its various aspects.

Question: How can a single stage of Equal Enlightenment possess such manifold meanings? Answer: The ten concentrations (*daśa-samādhi*), ten supernormal powers (*daśābhijñā*), and ten patiences (*daśa-kṣānti*) of the *Avataṃsaka* correspond exactly in number to these subsequent stages; they differ only in their formal establishment. The *Śūraṅgama-samādhi-sūtra* adopts elements from others, meaning that within each of the ten stages, it takes up the three categories of concentration, supernormal power, and patience.

This is done to conform to the provisional teachings (*neyārtha*) of other schools, which establish the names of "Practice" (*caryā*), "Tendency" (*mukha*), "Addition" (*prakarṣa*), and "Stage" (*bhūmi*). This is also a means to attract and guide those followers. Please clarify their characteristics. Answer: For example, among the ten practices (*daśa-caryā*), the first four perfections (*pāramitā*) constitute patience (*kṣānti*), as each requires diligent effort and uninterrupted application.

Furthermore, the *dhyāna-pāramitā* is concentration (*samādhi*). The latter five *jñāna-pāramitās* are the supernormal powers (*abhijñā*), for supernatural powers and wisdom mutually support and stimulate one another. In the Stage of Ten Transferences (*daśa-pratipatti*), the first two are the "patience" (*kṣānti*) stage; among the ten types of patience, non-arising (*anutpāda*) is the most supreme, and this non-arising can be attained through mental realization.

The middle five are the supernormal powers: one is general and four are specific. The general meaning is as follows: "reaching all places" does not exceed the ten directions and three periods of time; it refers to the three powers of the divine eye, the divine ear, and the recollection of past lives (*pūrvanivāsa*).

The next three transferences correspond respectively to the three powers of the basis of psychic power (*ṛddhi-viṣaya*), the exhaustion of outflows (*āsrava-kṣaya*), and the knowledge of others' minds (*paracitta-jñāna*). The final three, regarding True Suchness (*tathatā*), are all concentrations of self-nature and can be attained through mental realization. As for the "stages of application" (*prakarana*), there are three distinctions: one general and four specific applications. These entirely constitute the intent of diligent, uninterrupted effort within the stage of patience.

From the first to the fourth bhūmi, these are the supernormal powers (*abhijñā*). Because they thoroughly penetrate the limits of the objective realm, the [powers of] the divine eye, the divine ear, the knowledge of miraculous powers (*ṛddhi*), the recollection of past lives (*pūrvenivāsānusmṛti*), and the knowledge of others' minds (*paracittajñāna*) all reach their peak intensity. "Freedom from defilement" (*vimalā*) corresponds to the exhaustion of outflows (*āsravakṣaya*); as clarity arises and reaches its ultimate limit, these remain the most excellent of the three types of clear knowledge (*vidyā*).

From the fifth to the ninth bhūmi, these are meditative concentrations (*samādhi*). The former [fifth bhūmi] is the inducement, while the latter four are concentrations that are preeminent by their very nature. The tenth bhūmi is the synthesis of these three: it consists of compassion (*karuṇā*), non-referential patience (*anālambana-kṣānti*), and unobstructed wisdom (*jñāna*).

This is consistent with the fixed [classification] of *nirvāṇa*. As for this opening and closing [of categories], it is simply because the stages of the "dwelling grounds" (*zhùdì*) are identical in both sutras; fearing that such opening and closing must be performed, the principle may indeed be so. Furthermore, the single stage of "Equal Enlightenment" (*samyagbodhi*) in the *Avataṃsaka* subsumes a great many [stages];

it is likely that these correspond to the various stages of "Practice" (*xíng*) and so forth in the *Śūraṅgama-samādhi-sūtra*. However, the realm of the supreme sages is known only through realization; therefore, one should ultimately not cling to fixed [classifications]. I have provisionally preserved this for the amusement of the wise. Whether to adopt or reject [these views] is a matter of personal inclination;

there is no need for severe criticism. The ten stages of the Grounds (*bhūmi*) are hereby concluded. 9. The Single Stage of Equal Enlightenment (*Samyagbodhi*). Various sutras and treatises, such as the *Ratnagotravibhāga* (Treatise on the Awakening of Faith)...
Furthermore, there are those who do not establish this stage after the ten stages (*daśabhūmi*), but rather subsume it within the ten stages themselves.

Alternatively, they designate it as the "fruit" (*phala*) and subsume it within *miao-jue* (Wondrous Enlightenment). However, since the causal stages (*hetu*) consist of many parts while the fruit consists of only a single stage, it is correct to subsume it within the ten stages.

In general, none of these approaches are as comprehensive as the present sutra, which separately establishes the stages such as the practice (*xing*), the direction (*xiang*), and the ground (*di*). Since these have already been definitively established...

Regarding the "Penetrating Patience" (tongren), it should correspond to Equal Enlightenment (samyaksambodhi). Based on what further distinction is made? The answer is: the meaning of Equal Enlightenment is extensive and subsumes the broad meanings not previously included;
since the boundaries of awakening intersect, what prevents another distinction from being made? Thus, they are divided into two sections: first, the explicit clarification of the fundamental stage.

The Tathāgata flows against the current; the Bodhisattva likewise proceeds in accordance with it until they reach the point where awakening and the limit [of ignorance] intersect. This is called Equal Awakening (*samyak-saṃbodhi*).
Since this stage clarifies that the Bodhisattva’s initial awakening (*ādi-bodha*) is equal to the Tathāgata’s wondrous awakening (*tathāgata-pratibodha*), the Tathāgata is mentioned first.
As for the term "moving against the current," it refers to the Tathāgata, who has already previously realized the ocean of the fruit of wondrous enlightenment and has nothing further to attain;
he merely does not abandon sentient beings, but instead steers the compassionate vessel against the current to emerge from it.

As for this Bodhisattva being said to arrive by "moving with the current," it means that his progress toward attainment is not yet complete, as he is still proceeding toward the ocean of the fruit in accordance with the flow.

It flows and enters. Regarding "the boundary of awakening entering into mutual intersection": the initial awakening of the Bodhisattva and the wondrous awakening of the Buddha are perfectly equal in their measure;
there is only the difference between moving with the current and against the current. It is like those who enter the sea to gather treasures:

the preceding merchant has already obtained all manner of jewels and returns against the current to the sea-gate, while the subsequent merchant is only just beginning to advance and take them up, following the current.
They flow and enter, also reaching the Sea Gate. These two ships are exactly aligned;

however, they differ in that the bow of the front merchant ship points outward, while the bow of the rear merchant ship points inward. Wuxing said: "The *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* states, 'Equal Enlightenment is illumination within stillness;
Sublime Enlightenment is stillness within illumination. This is precisely the meaning [of this alignment]. Wenzheng said: 'Bodhisattvas of the Ten Grounds blend with the mundane world...'"
In terms of delivering sentient beings, this stage is identical to that of the Tathāgata; however, it differs from the Tathāgata in the direction of its movement—whether contrary or with the flow.

Specifically, the Tathāgata moves against the flow, emerging from the realm of the myriad things; the Bodhisattva moves with the flow, entering toward Wondrous Enlightenment (Samyak-saṃbodhi). Having reached the limit of awakening, it is called "Entering the Confluence.

Because there is no interval between this and Buddhahood, it is called "Equal Enlightenment" (Samyaksambodhi); it is precisely the Path of No-Interval (ānantarya-mārga) preceding the Path of Liberation (vimukti-mārga).
△ Second, the wisdom attained:
Ānanda, from the stage of dry wisdom up to equal enlightenment, this awakening first attains the initial stage of dry wisdom within the diamond-like mind.
The first two lines generally recapitulate the beginning and end of the vision, all being termed "Dry Wisdom" (*śuṣka-jñāna*); yet, while the names are the same, their actual meanings differ.
From Dry Wisdom up to Equal Enlightenment (*samyak-saṃbodhi*), there are fifty-four stages included in the interim, plus the two encompassing stages, totaling fifty-six.
This collectively concludes the exhaustion of bonds; this "enlightenment" refers specifically to Equal Enlightenment. [From] Gold... [text ends].

"Stiff mind" (*kāṭhinya-citta*) refers to that which, prior to the path of liberation (*vimukti-mārga*), is uninterrupted, extremely forceful, most firm, and most sharp, capable of severing the subtle essence of the delusions regarding the marks of the arising of ignorance;

thus it is so called. However, to refer to this as "dry wisdom" (*śukla-vidyā*) in conjunction with the preceding term is to manifest that this is the ultimate dry wisdom, distinguishing it from the initial-stage dry wisdom mentioned previously. Wēnlíng says: "The preceding [term] is named..."
"Dry Wisdom" (*śuṣka-prajñā*): Because it has not yet connected with the Tathāgata’s flow of Dharma, this is called "Dry Wisdom.

Because it has not yet connected with the Tathāgata’s ocean of sublime adornment. Wu Xing says: "Because the ignorance that obstructs sublime awakening has first become dry, and because one has not yet connected with the ultimate flow of the Tathāgata’s Dharma.
"First becoming dry" means having initially attained it; this serves to indicate—
In all preceding stages, one was unable to attain this wisdom; it is only upon reaching this stage that one first attains the "initial drying" (*kṣānti*).
Regarding this, some masters either subsume it entirely within the stage of Equal Enlightenment (*samyak-saṃbodhi*), while others open it as a separate stage.

In my humble opinion, if one carefully examines the four characters "this awakening is first obtained," then subsuming it under Equal Enlightenment is certainly not improper. However, if one further examines the two characters "having reached" (*prāpta*), [it suggests a distinct status].
If one cuts off the final mind of these stages, then the separate opening is also applicable. Now, if we take only the fifty-five positions, they are combined;
however, if we take the twelve single and double stages along with the sixty noble positions, they are opened up.
Thus, it is appropriate that the Buddha’s words are characterized by great flexibility, such that opening and combining are not fixed, and one should not cling to a single interpretation. △ Ten.

The single stage of Sublime Enlightenment (*samyak-saṃbodhi*) involves such successive layers, totaling twelve stages—both single and combined—before the stage of Sublime Enlightenment is fully perfected and the Unsurpassed Way is realized.
The first eight characters conclude the preceding discussion on the causal stages. A single character refers exclusively to one specific stage as "single," while another character...
Taking ten stages in total constitutes a "compound" (fù) set; taking twelve—whether single or compound—constitutes a "double" (shī) set.

One should follow the interpretation of Wēn-líng, which takes: 1. Dry Wisdom (gāndha), 2. Faith (śraddhā), 3. Abiding (vihāra), 4. Practice (caryā), 5. Orientation (mūrdhan), 6. Heat (uṣmagata), 7. Summit (mūrdhan), 8.

Patience (kṣānti), 9. the Worldly (laukika), 10. the Grounds (bhūmi), 11. Equality (samatā), and 12. Gold (suvarṇa). Among these, [the first five] are Dry Wisdom, Heat, Summit, Patience, and the Worldly.

The seven stages from "Equal to Gold" (*samatā-jina*) constitute the single [final] stage; the five stages of faith, abiding, practice, direction, and ground (*śraddhā-vihāra-caryā-pratipatti-bhūmi*) constitute the compound [preceding stages].
The final eight characters correctly clarify the ultimate fruit-stage (*phala-avasthā*). All preceding stages lead toward this fruit, and only upon reaching it is success fully realized.

It is the attainment of the supreme, true, and real fruit. "Exhausting wondrous enlightenment" refers to the initial mind of the causal stage, the beginning of the perfect person's *śikṣābodhi* (initial awakening).

Although it is profound through its gradual progression, because the fundamental and the initial have not yet become one and subject and object have not yet been forgotten, it has not yet exhausted the wondrous.
This remains the case even up to the stage of *samala-āśraya-parāvṛtti* (equal awakening), where one merely reaches parity but is still unable to achieve oneness. Now, at the very last...
In a single kṣaṇa, one realizes this stage. There is only original enlightenment (mūla-awakening), with no separate initial enlightenment (ādi-awakening).
Subject and object are utterly purified; stillness and illumination are of one suchness. All phenomena and all principles are suddenly realized as a single body; therefore, it is called "wondrous.
To investigate its essence, it does not transcend the three Tathāgata-garbhas within the preceding four fascicles; its function does not transcend those four.

The meaning consists of four aspects: namely, the ten profound virtues (*śūnyatā-lakṣaṇa*), the ten profound karmic functions, and their simultaneous perfection, which is profoundly mysterious, supremely wondrous, and inconceivable.

Regarding the Unsurpassed Way: although one shares the same path of awakening as the Tathāgata from the very first moment of the Perfect and Sudden [practice], this perfect fusion does not obstruct the progression through stages; rather, at every stage, one relies upon each preceding one.

The preceding is considered inferior, while each subsequent stage is superior. Thus, one knows that among all the stages within the causal process, there is none that does not have something superior above it.
Only this final stage is the ultimate realization, beyond which nothing further can be added; therefore, it is called the "Unsurpassed Way" (*anuttara-mārga*).

What are known as "unsurpassed bodhi," "unsurpassed nirvāṇa," and so forth, are all alternative designations for this. This concludes the major section providing the direct answer regarding the various stages of cause and effect.
[End. △ Second, a general refutation that [these states] are neither real nor defiled.
These various stages are all observed through the ten profound metaphors for the illusory nature of phenomena by means of diamond-like contemplation within *śamatha*.

By means of the *vipaśyanā* of all Tathāgatas, one purifies, cultivates, and realizes [the stages], gradually penetrating deeper into the various grounds—referring here to both the aforementioned grounds of cause (*hetu-bhūmi*) and the ground of fruition (*phala-bhūmi*). Although the ground of fruition is singular, the grounds of cause are manifold;
therefore, they are described as "various. As for "Vajra," it refers to what was previously called the "Vajra-King Jewel-Awakening" (*vajrarāja-ratna-bodhi*), for it is from...

From the very first stage, one already partially realizes the position of perfect penetration (*pariniṣpanna-vyūha*). As each successive stage becomes increasingly profound, one reaches the ultimate *vajra*-mind at the stage of Equal Enlightenment (*samyak-saṃbodhi*).
Thus, one should know that "vajra" is a name for the profoundly deep *prajñā*; it is the contemplative observation of the true mark (*bhūtalakṣaṇa*).
It is like a jewel that possesses light which, in turn, illuminates the substance of the jewel itself. The former is inferior and the latter is superior; they are one.

It is simply the essence itself. "Observation" refers to illuminating it with the adamantine jewel-like awakening. Wēnlíng says: "The various stages" refer to the twelve positions, both single and combined.

As for the "ten metaphors," they are: a phantom person, a mirage, the moon in water, flowers in the sky, an echo in a valley, a city of the gandharvas, a dream, a reflection, an image, and a transformation.
*Deep metaphor* refers to that which is illuminated by this adamantine [awakening].
