Because this bird does not lay eggs, it merely takes a clod of foul soil and incubates it until chicks are formed. This is simply because it possesses [that nature].
It is merely like being possessed by a malevolent spirit; how could the evil of their residual habits and the suffering of their residual retribution not have deep causes?
Moreover, since the Buddha generally characterizes them as "repaying debts," what debt is this repaying?

One should know that since these malevolent spirits arise from the habit of greed, those whose greedy habits are heavy frequently compete for and seize one another's property, even killing each other in mutual pits of destruction. This is precisely...
This is merely to repay that debt. Furthermore, Master Huan said: "When each person speaks of 'many,' they are speaking in terms of the predominant portion of their karmic habits;
it does not necessarily apply to all cases. This statement is correct. Hereafter, all [cases] shall be understood in this way.
From this we know that those with light habits of greed are not necessarily all of the *xiāo* (owl) species. △ Second, the portents of retribution.
The ghosts of the wind-demon *pó* (hánbó) have their retribution exhausted by the winds and are reborn in the world, often manifesting as omens of calamity.

Master Huán said that these "omens of calamity" (*jiùzhēng*) are precursors to impending misfortune, such as the flying squirrel (*wúshǔ*) calling out to people or the *shāngyáng* bird dancing in the water;
these are examples of it. Now, while the drought-demon *pó* causes disaster, these transformed animals likewise serve as portents of calamity; they are surely its remnants.
This is due to habitual conditioning. △ Third, the fox category:
all various classes of ghosts who bewitch and possess animals, when their animal lives end and their retribution is exhausted, are reborn in the human world, mostly as members of the fox species.
All such diverse species are as described in the *Śamatha-vipaśyanā*.
To observe them throughout the twelve periods of the day—such as the rat of the hour of Zi and the ox of the hour of Chou—and all other animal-spirits (*tiryag-yoni* and *preta*), is precisely this.
Now, it is only natural that the *mei*-ghosts, originating from the habit of deception, have transformed into the *yao*-deluding foxes. △ Fourth, the class of poisons.

Regarding the ghosts of *chóng* (parasites) and *gǔ* (vermin): when their *gǔ* is extinguished and their retribution exhausted, they are born into the world, mostly as types of venomous creatures, such as venomous-headed snakes, scorpions, and the like.
△ Five: the class of *huí* (roundworms).
The ghosts of decay and pestilence: when their retribution for past poverty and exhaustion is exhausted, they are born into the world, mostly as classes of worms.
As for pestilence ghosts, they originally arise from the habitual karma of resentment that creates epidemics; they enter the human body to cause illness.
Now, they are imprisoned within the human body, sharing the same food and the same security or peril as the person, for such is the nature of their conditioning. 6. The Class of Food.
Spirits born of the vital breath, once their breath has dissipated and their retribution is exhausted, are reborn in the human world; they mostly become types of food.
Because of their habits of arrogance, pride, stinginess, and indebtedness, they will often become ghosts who suffer hunger or become livestock to serve as food, thereby repaying their debts.
△ Seven: The Class of Clothing.

The ghosts of those who died in silk cocoons (*mianyou*): when their existence in the dark realm has dissolved and their retribution is exhausted, they are born into the human world, mostly as members of the category of "clothing" (*fulei*).
"Mian" means attachment; "you" means darkness—the ghosts that cause nightmares in the dark.

Regarding the category of "clothing," Master Huan states it refers to two meanings: silkworms and cattle or horses. Since silkworms can produce clothing, those in the category of clothing refer to garments.
"Vehicles" (fu) are a category [of things]. Since oxen and horses can be used for vehicles, "vehicles" refers to the category of those things used for riding or drawing.
When the habitual tendencies of *wang* and *yan* manifest as ghosts, they possess humans and turn them into beasts;
these beings are then clothed and ridden by others as a repayment for the debts incurred from their oppression of people. △ Eight: The Category of Correspondence (ying lei).
When the spirits of harmonious refinement have their retribution exhausted through harmonious dissolution, they are born into the human world, mostly as "responsive" (ying) types.
Those with the habit of clear vision become ghosts who harmonize with various spirits; thus they become animals of the responsive type. Master Huan said:
Those capable of perceiving the seasonal order refer to species such as the *sèyàn* (swallow) and the *sèhóng* (wild goose). △ Ninth, the Auspicious Omens (*xiūzhēng*):
Spirits of enlightened intelligence, once their retribution has been exhausted and they pass away, are born into the human world; for the most part, they manifest as auspicious omens.

"Manifesting spirits" refers to the manifestation of efficacious responses through the power of incantations. "Extinction" means the exhaustion of the incantation's power. Generally, an incantation produces spiritual efficacy by relying on its sustaining force;
when that force is exhausted, there is no further response. Ghosts, too, report the end of their term and undergo rebirth as animals possessing auspicious signs.
Master Huan said, "They are like the auspicious phoenix and the praiseworthy qilin. I ask:

what practice did these ghosts follow, and what merit have they accumulated, that they are so fortunate as to be such auspicious, virtuous, and beautiful creatures? He replied, "These ghosts, due to the power of their karma, are driven by incantations even though they are ghosts."
Yet, if one encounters the Triple Gem, the power of their mantras and the influence of their merit will gradually dissolve one's evil habits and karmic suffering;

thus, one may participate in auspicious and virtuous matters. However, if one encounters heterodox incantations for driving away spirits, killing, or stealing, these will not necessarily result in favorable omens.
Question: The Tathāgata has generally taught that one must repay debts. As for these scattered objects [of offering], what debt do they repay?

Yes. Answer: Whether they are caught in nets and sold, caged for amusement, used for the benefit of others, or prey upon one another—in such categories as these, which are not places where debts are repaid? △ Ten: Following the Categories.
All classes of ghosts that depend on humans—when the human dies and their retribution is exhausted—are mostly reborn as domestic animals (*cunlei*).
The first two lines clarify that there are also many types of ghosts that attach themselves to shamans;

when the shaman they have attached to dies, the ghost’s retribution also ends, and they become such domestic animals, like cats and dogs that follow and obey humans. This is explained in detail below.
The section on animals concludes. △ Third, concluding that these are false and ultimately non-existent:
"Ānanda, all these beings have their bodies dried up by the fires of karma as they repay their past debts, serving as animals for others.
These, too, are all summoned and drawn forth by their own false karmic actions. If one awakens to Bodhi, then these false conditions are fundamentally non-existent."
All these [beings] below tread upon the two destinies of hell-beings and hungry ghosts. "Lateral" (páng) means moving horizontally; thus they are also called "lateral-born" (pángxing).

However, while "lateral" is broad, "domestic animal" (chù) is narrow. This is because "domestic animal" implies being nurtured; it clarifies that they lack the power to sustain themselves and must depend on others for their nourishment and care.

It is not appropriate for those who possess power to nourish themselves; therefore, it is narrow. From the phrase "these [beings]" below, this is the conclusion of the delusion and the inference of non-existence by means of the words "likewise all.
This may be understood according to what precedes. △ Fourth, the general conclusion and response.
It is as you have said. The evil karma of those such as Ratnapadmagandha, King Vairadeva, and the bhikṣu Sunakṣatra was originally produced from within themselves;
it did not descend from heaven, nor did it emerge from the earth, nor was it bestowed by others. It was summoned solely by their own delusions.
They return once more to undergo [retribution] within the mind of Bodhi; all is but floating emptiness, for it is the congealing of deluded thoughts.

Having completed their time in the three miserable realms, they are about to enter the happy destinies; thus, this section generally expresses the intent of the "knot" (granthi), which seeks to block the paths to the three miserable realms.
"As for you," and so forth, refers back to the previously asked question regarding those who fall into hell due to such evil karma.
These four characters refer to the three types of people mentioned above, encompassing all evil karma that leads to falling into the three miserable realms.
This is because Ānanda specifically detailed the hells, while the Tathāgata further included the three paths to clarify that they share the same suffering of retribution.
As for the phrase "originally revealed by oneself," it is because the self-mind of sentient beings is the *tathāgatagarbha*.
Within [this], there is nothing that is not fully present. Whenever one follows along with whatever karma, it spontaneously manifests;

whatever the retribution may be, it is like the various flavors inherent within rice, which can become sugar, vinegar, or wine. At the moment they are produced, they spontaneously manifest from within;
they are not obtained from without, nor do they come from below to be received. This precisely clarifies that [it does not come from elsewhere].
This refers to the external. This point requires the student to once again apply their attention. It is not like the worldly notion that one brings official punishment upon oneself;
for although people in the world know that calamity is self-invited, they still cling to the idea that official punishment is an external circumstance.
Here, it is shown that the three miserable realms are all transformations of one's own mind and illusory objects, exactly like a dream.
Furthermore, there are no external objects; therefore, it is said that within the mind of Bodhi, false delusions coalesce and solidify.

As for those such as Han Yu and Ou-yang Hsiu who claim that the Buddha fabricated this out of self-interest to intimidate people—how could they have even dreamed of such a principle? From this, one should awaken to the truth.

Not only the three miserable realms, but even the mountains, rivers, and great earth—the various matters of suffering and joy currently before us in this world—are all the solidification of false conceptions.
If one dwells within this awakened state, then all phenomena are fundamentally empty; why wait for them to be contrived?
It is simply necessary not to be deluded during the present moment. As the Patriarch said: "To let it pass is not permissible. How profound! To the utmost!
This is the instruction. The section on the animal realm is concluded. △ The Human Realm. Regarding the place from which this realm comes:
with the exception of the manifestations of sages, all realms of existence pass through the human realm as the common path for cultivation and progress.
All realms aspire to seek a swift rebirth as a human. Therefore, all Buddhas attain Buddhahood only among humans. (From) Master Pei’s Preface to the *Yuan* [Avatamsaka Sutra].

The exhortations of the Awakened One are indeed detailed. Furthermore, there are immeasurable distinctions between the superior and the inferior. Those who are wealthy, noble, and compassionate resemble devas;

those who are intelligent resemble immortals (*ṛṣi*); those who are fierce and violent resemble asuras; those who are poor and lowly resemble pretas; those who are ignorant resemble animals; and those who are imprisoned resemble those in hell.
Since such resemblances are so numerous, one knows that the places from which beings come must likewise be many. Now, in this regard...
This is also discussed according to sequential order; therefore, I have selectively taken up those [beings] coming from the animal realm, while the remainder are all included within the mind.

This is divided into three parts. First, following the previous section to provide a warning and introduction: Now, this chapter somewhat resembles the preceding one on the realms of existence (*gati*);

yet, upon examining the remaining text repeatedly, it should be understood as the passage providing a warning regarding the human realm (*manuṣya-gati*). This is truly because, after the hells, all the various realms...

Having once again initiated the sequence, the discussion of the animal realm is now concluded; yet, as it is begun anew with the following section on humans, there is no mention of "furthermore" (*punar-aparaṃ*) in the headings for the individual categories.

The intent is clear from this. Moreover, the suffering of the hells has been exhausted, the habits of the hungry ghost realm have come to an end, and the debts of the animal realm have likewise been settled.
Now that one arises as a human, what will serve as the cause for moistening [the seeds of] rebirth?
Indeed, this passage examines two points: the "surplus" and the "seeking of life. These are the means by which various animals nourish their existence and become human beings.
Thus, does not this section of the scripture represent the very beginning of animals arising as humans?

Furthermore, the heading "Arousing Caution" is employed to signify that the Buddha’s intention is to cause people to awaken to the fact that they must maintain a compassionate mind toward all animals.
One must not exceed one's strength. One may cease killing, yet one must not devalue life. This section is divided into two parts.
The first concerns the repayment of debts through repeated claims for compensation, which is further divided into three sub-sections. The first clarifies the repayment of original prior debts.
Furthermore, Ānanda, when these beings emerge from the realm of animals to repay their former debts, their existence as ghosts while in the animal state was originally intended to settle those debts;
thus, it serves as the starting point for their rebirth. Consequently, whenever a previous destiny gives rise to a new bond, there is always mention of "repaying a debt.
Once it is said that the debt is being repaid, they remain until the debt is fulfilled, at which point the two states no longer interfere with one another.
Second, there is the "excessive repayment" (yuefen fanzheng).
If those who receive such repayment exceed the amount owed, these sentient beings, upon returning to human form, will in turn demand the excess back from them.
"Excess repayment" (*fenyue*) refers to when the amount repaid exceeds the original debt. "Recovery of the surplus" (*zhengsheng*) refers to demanding back the amount that was over-received.

It is precisely through these causes and conditions that one returns once more to human form. Question: If the repayment is complete and one’s lifespan ends, or if one transmigrates to another birth, then there would be no excess.
However, if the repayment is complete yet the other person does not die nor transmigrate, then what of the ordinary mind?

This is because one knows that it must stop there. Answer: If feeding does not reach the standard of propriety, or if forced labor and whipping are excessive, then [the retribution] will inevitably exceed this limit;
one must take great care to keep this in mind. As for the transition at death, there will surely be a presiding lord in the unseen realm;
there is no need to worry about this. △ Third, repaying the value according to superior or inferior status, divided into two parts. First, those with power.
To repay it.
If one possesses such power as well as merit and virtue, then among human beings, one will not lose the human body and shall repay that power in return.
"Possessing power" means having the strength to maintain the human body. "Possessing merit and virtue" means that not only...

One does not lose one’s human form, yet becomes a person of wealth and status. If one possesses strength but encounters an adverse summons, one will inevitably suffer the loss and seizure [of property] by the other party.
If one possesses merit and virtue but encounters an adverse summons, it is merely a case of being improperly overcompensated for one’s debts.
△ Second, those without strength who must provide compensation with livestock.
If one lacks merit, one returns to the state of an animal to repay the remaining balance.
To lack merit means to be powerless; if one possesses power but lacks merit, one must still repay with human labor.
As previously stated in the higher section, "returning to the state of an animal" means that this person is transformed into an animal. "Repaying the remaining balance" refers to making restitution.

This is the repayment of the remaining debts owed to those animals. Having completed the cycle of repeatedly demanding and repaying these debts, △ Second, the incessant devouring and killing of lives.
This is further divided into three parts. First, it clarifies that the remaining debts are easily repaid.
Ānanda, you should know this: if one uses money or goods, or employs their labor, until the debt is fully repaid, it ceases.
This section explains that when one has repaid the remaining value, it refers to what was originally owed.
If one uses money or goods—such as the price paid for a pack animal—or employs their labor—such as providing for one's own use—it is said that...
If, regarding these two ends, one transcends what is owed, then one merely stops owing that person money or labor, but does not stop owing them their life.
One may repay it with a human being or exchange it for an animal; once the repayment is complete, one naturally ceases [the obligation]. Thus, it is said there is no difficulty.
△ Second, the actual explanation of the difficulty of repaying a debt of life.
Just as in the intermediate state, they take one another's lives or eat their flesh;
and so it continues until even the most minute dust-aeons have passed, devouring and slaughtering one another like a turning wheel, alternating between high and low status without any rest.

This is the dialectical analysis of the matter. If one not only expends money and labor excessively, but furthermore takes life and eats meat therein, then from birth to birth there will be mutual enmity and killing with no end in sight. "High and low" refers to the strong and the weak.
The strong are able to eat and to slaughter; the weak are eaten and slaughtered. As strength and weakness alternate, they prey upon and kill one another in succession.
△ Third, only the Dharma-Buddha can bring it to rest.
Apart from *śamatha* and the appearance of a Buddha in the world, it cannot be halted.
*Śamatha* is the Dharma; it is the correct concentration that turns back delusion to accord with the Truth, clarifying that the Way is attained through one's own power.
When a Buddha appears in the world, he releases them from their resentment; this clarifies that salvation is achieved through the power of others (*parāśakti*).
Only when these two conditions are met can [the cycle] be brought to an end. Apart from these two matters, it certainly cannot cease.

This is said to emphasize the need for vigilance and the impropriety of indulging in killing and eating [meat]. The preceding section on "The Warning" is concluded. △ Second, the formal enumeration of human types.
These are also divided into ten categories. First is the category of the dull-witted.

You should now know that those of the owl-like class, once their retribution is exhausted and they regain their physical form, are born among human beings and are included within the category of the dull-witted.
"Wan" refers to one who is both wicked and foolish, such that not even a hair's breadth of goodness can be transformed within them.

Thus, the Master says that because the *xiāo* (owls) devour one another by attaching clods of earth [to their young], their residual habits consist of stubbornness, stupidity, and unrighteousness. As for the term "synthesized" (*cánhé*), it means:
They are interspersed among them. Indeed, within every class of human beings, there are those who are superior and those who are inferior.
The ten types of animals are merely included therein because their habits and species resemble [those of humans], not because every member of that stubborn class was transformed by an owl.
Furthermore, even among the dull and ignorant, there are those who possess wealth and status; these certainly could not have been transformed by owls, for they were originally...

Those who emerge from the three miserable realms (triyapāya) must have had meager merit; thus we know that those among the ten classes of beings who participate in the merging [of rebirth] are all those who have recently taken on poverty and low status. II. Different Species:

As for those with ominous signs of retribution, once their karmic debt is fully repaid and they resume a physical form, they are born within the human realm and participate in the merging of different species.
Thus, the Master’s statement that calamitous omens originate from the residual habits of former licentiousness, which again manifest as strange anomalies, is precisely this.

Indeed, the small children with eyes and mouths on their heads who appear during droughts, as well as all those whose physical faculties deviate from the norm toward the bizarre and anomalous—all are such instances.
While the *pó* ghost has no form, these already possess human forms; their appearance invariably portends disaster. Furthermore—
They are the lingering remnants of calamitous omens. △ Third, the common class:
Those of the fox lineage, having received their retribution and returned to physical form, are born among human beings and included within the common class.
"Ordinary" (*yōng*) means base. Thus, what the Master refers to as "ordinary, base, and ignorant" is precisely this.
Their deluding of others must necessarily stem from their own delusion; now, these beings have fallen into the state of a seductive fox due to their habit of deception.
When they first attained human form, were they not indeed ordinary, base, and ignorant? △ Fourth, the class of the headstrong.
Those of the poisonous class, having received their retribution and returned to physical form, are born among the human race; yet they are integrated with the cruel species.
To harm things without compassion is called "cruelty" (hen). This category is easy to recognize. △ Fifth, the minute class.
As for those belonging to the category of worms, once they have fully repaid their karmic debt and regained their physical form, they are born into the human realm as members of a lowly class.
Thus, the Master’s statement that "worms are excluded from the ranks because their decaying breath clings to material things" is correct.
This refers to those who are base and contemptible, suffering from cold and hardship, and for whom nothing is favorable. 6. The Soft Class.
Those of the "Food Category" (shílún), having received sufficient recompense and regained their physical forms, are born into the human realm among the gentle class.
This is what the Master meant when he said that the Food Category arises from hunger and devouring; therefore, they are gentle and timid, lacking in courage. 7. The Labor Category (láolèi).
Those who have fulfilled their karmic obligations regain their physical form and are born among human beings, joining the class of those subject to toil;
this is what the Master refers to as "the laborers whose toil never ceases. However, since it is said that their obligations are "fully repaid," they are no longer bound by debt.

It is merely for one’s own labor. Furthermore, observing these types of clothing used for labor, it is sufficient to know that the previous meaning of taking oxen and horses for riding and transport predominates. △ Eight, the category of texts.
Those who correspond to this category will receive full recompense and restore their physical forms, being reborn among the human race as members of the literary class.

To belong to the literary class means to be proficient in the meanings of characters and the principles of yin and yang, yet to be one who falls out of harmony with others. △ Ninth, the clarification of categories.
As for those who received auspicious signs, their retribution was sufficient to restore their physical forms, and they were reborn among the human realm, joining the ranks of the enlightened.
Because they had relied on the power of the luminous mantras, they attached themselves to those of worldly wisdom, eloquence, and intelligence, imitating the minor functions of humans;
yet they possessed no great wisdom. △ Ten: The Category of Attainment.
Those various domestic animals, having received sufficient recompense and regained their forms, are born among human beings and join the ranks of the enlightened.

"The enlightened" refers to those who are well-versed in worldly affairs and understand human nature. Because domestic animals have long been dependent upon humans, they become attached to this class of beings;
thus the Master says that these are not their primary karmic retribution (*vipāka*), but rather the result of residual habits (*vāsanā*).
"By chance," it is therefore said, "they are combined. The latter three [categories] all consist of those who are merely clever in miscellaneous arts and possess worldly wisdom and eloquence;
they do not concern the matters of the virtuous and enlightened, nor of literary refinement. The formal enumeration of human types is hereby concluded. △ Summary of their pitiable state.
Ānanda, all these beings have fully repaid their karmic debts from former lives and have again taken human form.

Yet, from time immemorial, they have been subject to the delusions of karma, giving rise to one another and killing one another. Having failed to encounter the Tathāgata and hear the True Dharma, they naturally revolve within the cycle of worldly afflictions.
Such people as these are truly to be pitied.

Regarding "those who have fully repaid their past debts": this refers to those who, during their time as animals, have already completed the repayment of their debts; there are few who have not done so, for they cannot attain human status.

It should be clearly understood that among the ten classes of beings, those who take on rebirth again mostly receive only a fraction of the remaining karmic surplus; this does not refer to those who have exhausted their entire course of existence.
Therefore, such beings experience much misfortune and little fortune, much suffering and little joy; it is for this reason that they move the Buddha’s compassion. This is the reckoning of karma.
As for those who are inverted, they do not forget debts or their lives. They are born to one another for the purpose of collecting debts, and they kill one another for the purpose of reclaiming life;
these are all gatherings of unfavorable conditions. Only upon meeting the Tathāgata can they be resolved, and only by practicing the True Dharma can they attain liberation.
Were it not for these two [encounters], birth and killing would never cease; this is why they are to be pitied. Contemplate this.

This section on the "knots" (granthi) corresponds exactly with the preceding "Arousing of Awareness" (jāgarana). It is sufficient to know that this heading constitutes the main text for the human realm (*manuṣya-gati*).

The discussion of the human realm is concluded. △ Five: The Realm of the Various Sages (*ṛṣi-gati*). The first three destinies were discussed in sequential order; they do not go beyond the ten habitual tendencies as the seeds of karma.
Although the human realm is virtuous, because it follows upon the various animal realms and completes the retribution of form, it is therefore treated [separately].
Consider those inferior sentient beings who have first attained a human body; they all still carry the residual traces of the ten habitual tendencies.
Only from this realm of the immortals (*ṛṣi*) upward are they no longer concerned with these ten habits.

Now, the Way of the Immortals arises from sentient beings’ loathing and fear of impermanence, conceiving the thought that the body is eternal, and thus falsely establishing many paths—all of which are nothing other than directed toward [the pursuit of] longevity.
To seek longevity and immortality is to fail to realize that this body is merely a deluded misapprehension within the true mind.
Although those who rely upon grass and wood differ from such practitioners in their degree of excellence, when it comes to the nature of their delusion, they are one and the same without distinction.

Now, out of fear of death, you further engage in the vain pursuit of longevity; this is a mistake upon a mistake, leading to ever-increasing fragmentation and confusion, such that you remain lost in ignorance.
How deeply regrettable this is! Yet, in the ancient times of India, among the non-Buddhist sects, Maheśvara was the principal deity.

When the Buddha appeared in the world, he was hailed as the Omniscient One; yet even as he established provisional teachings according to the capacities of beings, he still ranked the "human vehicle" (manuṣyayāna) alongside others—how could there not have been a "celestial vehicle" (ṛṣiyāna)?
It is also heard that Avalokiteśvara serves as the teacher of the celestial vehicle. Considering the capacity for the Mahāyāna in this land [of China]...

The Pure [Vehicle] has not even been transmitted or practiced within the Lesser Vehicle (Hīnayāna), let alone in the Miscellaneous Vehicles (miśrayāna). Therefore, its ultimate realization has not been heard of in the teachings of the Tripiṭaka.
Here in this land, the Way of the Immortals shares the same source as Confucianism; Laozi and Zhuangzi were both the supreme exponents of the pure and quietistic within the Confucian tradition.
Those who study the arts of immortality have attached themselves to these teachings. Upon carefully examining the various techniques of Zhang, Ma, Qiu, Liu, and others, they are all...

Briefly summarizing the teachings of Laozi and the Old Master [Zhuangzi], they extensively propound the Great Ultimate (*taiji*). Their discourse on Qian, Kun, Kan, and Li originates from the *Yijing* (Book of Changes);
yet their primary aim remains nothing more than the pursuit of longevity and immortality. This is divided into three parts. First: following the previous section to introduce the subsequent one.
Ānanda, furthermore, there are those who follow other teachers and do not rely on perfect enlightenment to cultivate samādhi;

instead, they cultivate deluded thoughts and fixate their mental images to preserve the physical form, wandering in mountain forests where humans cannot reach. There are ten kinds of such seers (ṛṣi).
"Following after humans" means practicing solely within the human body and attaining realization within the human body; it does not restrict itself to the ten aforementioned classes of beings.
"Perfect Enlightenment" (Sambodhi) refers to the True Mind of Original Enlightenment (Mūla-bodhi). "Samādhi" refers to the Shurangama Samādhi, the Samādhi of Right Concentration.

It is not the case that one fails to attain such right enlightenment and right cultivation, yet instead develops a false awakening, believing there is a life-force or nature within the five aggregates (skandhas) that can be cultivated and nourished to make it grow long.

Regarding immortality: there are ten categories of cultivation methods for preserving the mind through visualization (*cunxiang*) and solidifying the physical form (*guxing*), each differing in its specific practice.

However, such visualization and solidification of the form are, in essence, nothing but deluded thoughts. As for "remote mountain forests beyond human reach," these refer to famous mountains, caves, and grottoes—the hidden abodes of transcendents (*shenxian*).
According to the scriptures, among the Seven Golden Mountains there is one mountain where transcendents dwell; this is the Way (*Dao*).
The "home" refers to Mount Kunlun, the Mountain of the Reversed Sun; it must be this mountain and not Mount Sumeru. Since ordinary people cannot reach it, it is exclusively a dwelling for immortals;
thus, it is a collective retribution of the same class. Changshui’s claim that there is no separate collective retribution is incorrect.
Second, the formal listing of the various immortals: this merely categorizes them according to the differences in their techniques for maintaining their physical forms.
I have not yet discussed the matters of maintaining precepts and accumulating merit; these will be clarified later in the section on "Refining the Mind. This section is divided into ten parts.
First is the Earth-Walking Immortal (*bhūcarī-ṛṣi*).
Ānanda, those sentient beings who steadfastly take medicinal elixirs without ceasing, until the path of food is perfected, are called Earth-Walkers.
Regarding the "Practices of the Immortals" (*xingxian*): the first five characters should be read with level tones (*pingsheng*).

From earth to heaven, these are all categorized according to the weight and distance of the steps taken, as well as their height and depth, thereby distinguishing between superiority and inferiority. This sequence likely proceeds from the inferior to the superior to demonstrate gradual progress.
This reaches the intent of transcending the world and soaring aloft. However, this category and the subsequent category are distinguished by their relative gravity and lightness.
Furthermore, both are medicinal; yet, the term "ingesting" (*e*) used here refers to the intention of processing, compounding, and forming them into pills or cakes.
By consuming these, one attains efficacy; hence it is said that "the path of food is perfected. As for the "earth-walking immortals" (*dixingxian*):
However, while their hundred limbs are healthy and strong and their lifespans are extended, they have not yet attained the ability to fly lightly; they remain those who travel upon the ground.
△ Second, the Flying Immortals (Khecaras).
One who diligently cultivates medicinal herbs without ceasing will achieve perfection in the Way of Medicine and be called a Flying Immortal (*khecarī-ṛṣi*).
Such herbs include purple mushrooms (*zǐzhī*), yellow essence (*huángjīng*), sweet flag (*chāngpú*), pine, and cypress; these are to be taken for a long duration.
The body is so light that one’s gait is like flying; even the intention to ascend heights or leap over ravines is achieved.

This is because the actual act of flying through the air is reserved for the subsequent section. The statement here regarding "medicines" as distinct from the previous "ingestion" refers to the distinction between processed and raw substances.
Furthermore, this serves to distinguish the "near" and "far" categories mentioned below. △ Third, the Wandering Immortals (Cāraṇa-ṛṣi).
Firm as metal or stone, they do not cease their efforts until the path of transformation is perfected; such are called *vihāra-ṛṣis* (wandering immortals).
Firm as metal or stone, they are like those who smelt lead to refine it into cinnabar, which is termed the "Ninefold Great Return" (*navakṛtva-mahāpunaḥ*).
As for those who wander through the path of transformation, they dissolve their ordinary bones to achieve a light and subtle body, appearing in an instant.
Ten thousand *li*. This refers to one who travels everywhere without weariness. △ Fourth, the Sky-Walking Immortal (*khaṇḍaroha*):
Firm and steady in movement and stillness, never resting; when the vital energy (*prāṇa*) and essence are perfected, one is named a Sky-Walking Immortal.

Regarding "steadfastness in movement and stillness": it refers to such practices as massage and manipulation, the circulation of qi to harmonize the body, moving and resting according to the proper seasons, and being invariably cautious in one’s daily conduct.
Regarding "the perfecting of qi and essence": this refers to what is called refining the essence to return it to qi, refining qi to return it to spirit, and refining spirit to return it to the void.
"Wandering in emptiness" means that one has finally attained the transformation of the feathered body to ascend and roam through the void.
Nevertheless, there remains a distinction of superior and inferior when compared to the following category, because "emptiness" (ākāśa) is not the celestial realm (*deva*).
△ The Celestial-Traveling Immortals (*devagāmin ṛṣi*):
They solidify their vital fluids and do not rest; as their virtue of moistening is perfected, they are named Celestial-Traveling Immortals.
This is the exhaling of the old and inhaling of the new. It is as the Master of the Ring spoke of: "Beating the Celestial Pond and swallowing the Jade Nectar.
This enables water to ascend and fire to descend, thereby forming the Inner Elixir (*neidan*). Hence it is said: "The virtue of moisture is perfected.
Furthermore, this transcends the practice of space and can reach the heavens; thus it is called "Celestial Practice" (*tianxing*). 6. The Perfected of Universal Practice (*tongxing xian*).

With firm and pure essence, one proceeds without ceasing; absorbing the refined quintessence until it is perfectly accomplished, this is called the "Transcendent of Penetrating Practice" (Tongxing Xian).
The five characters below this line should be read with the departing tone (*qùshēng*); they refer to the term for "cultivated practice.
That which is called the "Transcendent of Penetrating Practice with Firm and Pure Essence" is as the Master Huan described: "Donning rainbows and drinking mists, the refined qi penetrates secretly."

I have also seen writings of the immortals which state that one should close the eyes at dawn while facing the east to gather the solar essence (jīng) and drink it, and at night gather the lunar radiance (huá), even going so far as to ingest the essences of the five stars; these are what are called "essential colors" (jīngsè).

As for what is called "practicing the Way" (tōngxíng), it refers likewise to the circulation of the spirit and energy (shénjīng), thereby communicating with the creative transformation (zàohuà) of the cosmos. △ Seven: Practice of the Way.

The *xiān* (immortal) is one who maintains firm and unceasing incantations and prohibitions; when their ritual methods are perfected, they are called a *dàoxíng xiān* (immortal of the Way’s practice).

This refers to those who, by exclusively upholding mantras, naturally achieve the path of immortality. Within our own tradition, the recitation of the Cundī and other such mantras is likewise permitted to lead to the attainment of the immortal path.

It is so. Furthermore, by using incantations for dates and writing talismans to heal sores and diseases, to prohibit poisons and expel demons, and thereby benefiting all living beings, one possesses the aspiration for the Way that saves the world;
thus it is called "Daoxing" (Practice of the Way). △ Eighth: Zhaoxingxian (Immortal of Illuminating Practice).
To maintain firm recollection without ceasing until the visualization is perfected is called the "Illuminating Practice Immortal" (Zhàoxíng Xiān).
This is what Master Huán meant by "concentrating the mind with refined thought; after a long time, illumination and response follow.

Whether one visualizes the spirit exiting through the fontanelle (*mūrdhan*) or focuses the mind on the navel wheel (*nābhi-cakra*) to refine the elixir (*rasāyana*), these are all instances of the perfection of recollection. It appears this passage has been omitted from the current text.
Next, one should first explain the perfection of firm mindfulness and recollection using the two lines beginning with "either preserving" (*hucun*).
Only thereafter should one explain the practice of illumination using the two lines beginning with "tranquil and concentrated" (*chengning*). This alone constitutes the proper sequence.

Furthermore, I have observed in the *xian* (immortal) texts that one first binds the mind below the navel, passes through the *weilu*, ascends the *jiaji*, and reaches the *niepan* (nirvāṇa) before finally piercing the crown of the head to emit the spirit. All [of these methods]...
This refers to the act of recollecting and contemplating. △ Ninth, the *siddha* of refined conduct (*viśuddhacaryā-siddha*):
Through firm and constant union without ceasing, the response is perfectly accomplished; this is called the *siddha* of refined conduct.
Master Huan says: "Internally, the pairing of the male of the Kan trigram with the female of the Li trigram constitutes husband and wife.
What are called the 'infant' and the 'maiden' refer precisely to the union of Kan and Li, whereby one takes from Kan to fill Li, thereby forming the immortal embryo."

As for the practice of using women as sacrificial vessels and engaging in licentious conduct to seek assistance, the Inner Teachings (Buddhism) firmly rejects this as a demonic doctrine, while the Way of the Immortals likewise despises it as an inferior grade.
This is because it appeals to human desires; many who are crazed and deluded are misled by it.
Righteous men and gentlemen should simply refrain from speaking of it and distance themselves from it. I have often said that these are the degenerate currents of the Daoist tradition.
Because people have desires, they are easy to follow. Because the inner teaching fundamentally strips away people's desires, people find it difficult to uphold.
Now, wealth, beauty, and longevity are the great desires of humanity. The Way uses the two cinnabar vessels of lead and mercury—gold and jade—to cast away the desire for wealth and beauty;
furthermore, it employs the inner cinnabar of vital essence and breath to accord with the attachment to life.

Who would not joyfully follow such a mind? As for the Inner Teachings, the perfection of giving (*dāna-pāramitā*) and the pure conduct (*brahmacarya*) run counter to the heart’s craving for wealth and beauty;
furthermore, they command one to contemplate the body as a venomous snake and to discard it like mucus or spittle.

If one does not understand their profound purpose, who would not find them difficult to accept? Yet, one fails to realize that clinging to the three [realms] is the root of birth and death, while abandoning the three is liberation.

This is the essential method for liberation. Since I wish to exhaustively explore its profundity, I shall further await the subsequent text to explain it in detail. △ Tenth: The Transcendent Immortal of Ultimate Practice (*atyācaraṇa-ṛṣi*).
One who is firm and stable in their transformations and never ceases, yet has attained perfect awakening, is named the Transcendent Immortal of Ultimate Practice.
This awakening penetrates the principle of transformation and is capable of great illusory manifestations, such as those of Liu Gen and Zuo Ci.

It even reaches the point of moving mountains and overturning waters, being so wondrous as to be peerless in their time; therefore, they are called "Transcendent Immortals of Ultimate Practice" (juexing xian).

The awakening within this [category] is like the realization of Zhuangzi regarding the observation of transformation (*guan hua*) and Tanzi regarding the mastery of transformation (*da hua*); it is not the true awakening found within Perfect Enlightenment (*zheng jue*). This is correctly categorized among the [various types of practitioners].
The section on the Immortals is concluded. △ Third, the judgment that these are identical to saṃsāra:
"Ānanda, all these have refined their minds among human beings, yet they did not cultivate true awakening. Instead, they attained a distinct mode of existence, living for ten million years.
They dwell in deep mountains or on remote ocean islands, far removed from the realm of humanity. This, too, is saṃsāra, born of deluded thoughts."
They transmigrate; failing to cultivate samādhi, when their retribution is exhausted, they return once more and are scattered into the various realms of existence.
The aforementioned ten types involve distinct methods of cultivation, whereas this refinement of the mind involves a commonality in practice.

For instance, though one may maintain the precepts, accumulate merit, and perform deeds of rescue and aid, if it is said that one does not cultivate right awakening, it is because one has not attained the fundamental source.
The mind is true and eternal, yet the myriad forms take it as their own substance. Furthermore, failing to understand the cause of death, they give rise to delusions regarding birth and death;

not realizing that both are non-existent, they fear death and cling to life. They use "longevity" as a designation, but how could they realize that such talk of "length" merely describes birth as superior to brevity, and that speaking of life is ultimately intended to await its cessation?
How could they know the supreme principle of non-arising or the wondrous essence of fundamental permanence? Therefore, it is said:

They do not cultivate correct awakening (*samyak-saṃbodhi*). Regarding those who separately attain the principle of prolonging life: this refers to attaining, apart from correct awakening, the deluded principle of extending one's life.
As for "living for ten million years," it means that through the fulfillment of deluded cultivation, they correspond with that deluded principle.
Question: In the world, there is no one who does not covet life as pleasure and regard death as suffering. Now, Arhats and Bodhisattvas take many kalpas to...
It is established. Even those who, throughout their entire lives, attain rebirth in the Pure Land cannot avoid the death that appears before them.

When they suddenly hear it said that the Way of the Immortals grants a lifespan of ten million years in this world, those whose will and vision are unstable often give rise to a mind of expedient pursuit.
How can this be demonstrated? Answer: How excellent is this question! Who has not been misled by such words? It is because those words speak of the present...
As for those who attain longevity in this world, this too depends on the fulfillment of merit over many lifetimes; it is only upon reaching their final birth that they manifest the attainment.
If one traces back their previous lives, the number of times they died without attaining the goal despite their arduous cultivation is unknown.
How could everyone attain the manifestation of results immediately upon beginning their practice? If one observes only the manifestation of the fruit...

[It is] accomplished. Yet, if one does not trace back the long accumulation of its causes, it would follow that the Buddha attained enlightenment in merely six years, while those who heard the Dharma at his assemblies realized the fruits and entered the stages in the space of a single conversation—beyond counting. How could it be that only immortals can achieve realization in this world?

Question: When first beginning practice, how does one know that realization will certainly not be attained in the present life? Answer: For one who begins practice for the first time, [the previous...]

If one has already been born with the seeds of the karmic causes for the fixed destiny of short life, or if the karma of the sages across successive lifetimes has not yet reached fulfillment, then one lacks the "sage-bone" (*ṛṣi-asthi*) for birth;

thus, it cannot be attained in the present life. It is only when one possesses the defiled mind of the sage-path from past lives, and through the accumulation of effort amidst suffering throughout successive births, that the seeds of the fixed destiny of long life are finally perfected. Only then does one obtain the sage-bone upon birth, such that the aspiration manifests spontaneously.
This has been realized in the present. Thus we know that one who attains the state of an immortal at the end must not change their physical form to achieve longevity;

even in the case of "corpse-liberation" (shijie), it is merely departing by concealing the form, not a true death. Wu Xing says that his passing was a transition to rebirth rather than a final cessation.
The following clarifies that he did not dwell among ordinary people, nor was he in the heavens, but remained perfectly as he was.
This refers to the *sabhāgatā* (homogeneity) of the ear. This also correctly defines the cycle of rebirth (*saṃsāra*) from a lower perspective.
Thus we know that when the thousands of myriad years of immortals and seers are exhausted, they merely die later; it is not true immortality. It is like pine and cypress trees:

they merely wither later; it is not true non-withering. It is simply because their lifespan exceeds that of ordinary people that people do not witness their death—this is merely a false conception (*vikalpa*).

As for those who transmigrate: because within their bodies there is fundamentally no life-force, destiny, or sovereign self, they are deludedly attached to the existence of birth and death, which are both like dreams and illusions.
Thus they falsely give rise to love and hatred; what else could this be but false conceptualization? This is the case for those who do not cultivate samādhi.

This is not to practice and abide in the *Śūraṅgama-samādhi*. Regarding those who receive rebirth upon the exhaustion of their retribution: since immortals (*ṛṣi*) are inferior to devas, and even devas do not transcend saṃsāra, how much less so the immortals?

Now, if one cannot attain realization in this life through initial cultivation, and even if one were to attain it, would not still remain within saṃsāra—how does that compare to reciting the Buddha’s name to seek rebirth in the Western Land, where one attains the golden body in a single lifetime for eternal duration throughout vast kalpas?
They have escaped from saṃsāra, yet there are those who lack the conditions for faith; how tragic, how tragic! I ask those who seek to become immortals:

they falsely claim that the Buddhist teaching cultivates only nature (*xing*) and not life-force (*ming*), and that the numinous spirits of ten thousand kalpas find it difficult to enter the state of holiness.
Many are deluded by these words; I request this appended refutation to awaken those in deep confusion. In response, I say that what they speak of—both nature and life-force—is neither true.
This refers to taking the spirit and consciousness within the body as "nature" (*xing*), and the vital energy (*qi*) that forms the life-root within the body as "life" (*ming*).
Therefore, it is said that those who cultivate nature alone attain only the ghost-spirit of a *yin*-soul, lacking a long-lasting physical form;

only by cultivating both life and nature does one attain a light, subtle, and long-lived body, boasting of the marvelousness of both form and spirit. How could such people know the "nature" taught by the Buddha?
Every person inherently possesses the ocean of the nature of True Suchness (*tathatā*), which is the fundamental substance of immeasurable heavens and earths and immeasurable myriad things.
One who realizes this nature is not only able to manifest immeasurable wondrous bodies, but can also manifest immeasurable heavens, earths, and myriad things.
Furthermore, that which is manifested is not only able to cause beings to abide for hundreds of thousands of millions of years.
Although it spans kalpas as vast as the sands of the Ganges, one may cause it to abide; yet when one wishes to withdraw it, it is withdrawn so that not even a single atom remains.
When one wishes to manifest it, all phenomena are fully revealed. Attaining great mastery and great utility, this is what is called True Suchness and Buddha-nature.
For those who do not believe these words, I request that you carefully read the preceding sections on the manifestation of nature; therein, you will naturally awaken to it.
They slander [the teachings] out of ignorance. The section on the realm of the *ṛṣis* is concluded. 6. The Realm of the Gods (*deva-gati*).
The realm of the gods and the realm of the *ṛṣis* are fundamentally different. Yet worldly people do not distinguish between *ṛṣis* and gods;

those who study the path of the *ṛṣis* indiscriminately affiliate themselves with the gods, even claiming that all the gods are their ancestral *ṛṣis*. I shall now briefly clarify this. While the *ṛṣis* possess human bodies...
Those who crave longevity fear most the casting off of one body to receive another. Yet all the devas cast off their previous bodies to receive celestial bodies;
how could they be of the same class? Furthermore, the abodes of the immortals, such as Penglai and Kunlun on the seas and mountains, are not within the heavens.
Even the Four Heavenly Kings and the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven have no fixed residences there, let alone the higher realms, and let alone the Form Realm (rūpadhātu). Thus we know that the heavenly destiny—

They are the most preeminent and exalted among those within the realm [of desire], being entirely distinct from the classes of sages (*ṛṣi*) and spirits (*deva*). This section is divided into two parts.
First, the formal enumeration of the various heavens, which is further divided into three. First, the Six Desire Heavens (*ṣaḍ-kāmadhātu-deva*):

these range from the two heavens at the waist and summit of Mount Sumeru up to the four heavens that dwell in space, comprising six tiers in total. All of them possess food and drink, sexual desire, and sleep.

They sleep. Because they are fully possessed of the three desires, they are called the Desire Heavens (*kāmadeva*). Their marriage and taking of wives and concubines is also like that of the human realm.

Furthermore, there are two [classifications]: first, the division based on the gravity of their desire, which yields six categories. The first is the Heaven of the Four Great Kings (*cāturmahārājakāyika*).
Ānanda, there are those among the people of the world who do not seek permanence and have not yet been able to renounce their affection for wives and concubines;

yet, regarding sexual misconduct, their minds do not wander or run astray, and through their clarity and purity, they give rise to luminosity. After the end of their lives, they dwell in proximity to the sun and moon.
This class of beings is called the Heaven of the Four Great Kings.
The merit of the six heavens of the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*) is, in fact, entirely brought about by the ten wholesome actions (*daśakuśala*).

That we now distinguish them specifically according to desire is because we are investigating the reality behind the names. These six are collectively called the "desire heavens" (*kāmadeva*), and since sexual desire is their primary characteristic, they are ranked in their lower and higher order based on the gravity or lightness of that desire.
As for the ten wholesome actions, these are the general cause for all three realms; [they do not apply exclusively to the desire realm].
This is merely a preliminary statement. The four characters "not seeking permanence" (*bù qiú cháng zhù*) are likewise the general cause for the three realms.

Because one does not seek the fundamental eternal principle through supramundane cultivation, but instead hopes only for the fruits of worldly pleasure that are subject to exhaustion—this is true of all the gods, let alone those in the heavens above.
One should know that this phrase is restricted to this specific context, yet its meaning extends to the final [stage]. One's own form is...

Regarding lust: to have sexual relations with those who are not one's own wife is called illicit lust (*kāmamithyācāra*). This person possesses both wives and concubines, yet he does not allow his desires to flow outward toward those who are not his own.
To say "mind" implies that he not only dares not transgress with his body, but his mind likewise lacks even a single thought [of such desire].
That he becomes clear and luminous is because his lustful thoughts are regulated and his intentions are largely withdrawn.
[The text] concludes: "Pure and unsullied, the mind-ground is luminous. Yet, one must further cultivate the ten wholesome actions with diligent study before one can attain such [a state].
Hereafter, all [passages] shall follow this pattern. Regarding the statement "after the end of life," this clearly indicates that one discards the previous body only then to receive a celestial body;
it is not the same as the Way of the Immortals (*xian dao*). Question: Why is rebirth superior to long-life (*changsheng*)? Answer: Long-life is like...
Mending old clothes can never result in anything extraordinary or superior. When the various devas are reborn, it is like casting off tattered rags to exchange them for precious, elegant garments;

the difference between the superior and inferior states is as vast as that between heaven and an abyss. It is only the foolish who, clinging to the base and perverted habit of attachment to the body, consider longevity to be supreme.

How much more so when the celestial body is transformationally born (*upapāduka*) and refined in its subtlety—how could it possibly be the same as the foul impurity of womb-birth? Truly, it is not [the same] for them.
This is what was seen in the dream. This heaven resides at the waist of Mount Sumeru, level with the sun and moon; therefore, it is adjacent to them.
It is called the "Four Kings" because on the four sides of the mountain’s waist there are the Four Kings—Dhṛtarāṣṭra and the others—each residing while occupying one side.
△ Second, the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven.
Regarding their own wives, their lustful desire is slight; even when dwelling in the Pure Abodes, they cannot experience full flavor.
After the end of their lives, they transcend the radiance of the sun and moon and dwell at the summit of the human realm. This class of beings is called the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven.
This person has only one wife; however, his lustful passion for her has diminished and grown thin, rather than being frequent and intense.
As for "the pure flavor not being complete," it means that although thoughts of lust occasionally arise, they are far superior to those previously mentioned.
Regarding "surpassing the brilliance of the sun and moon," whereas the former was merely equal to them, this one is twice as high. [He dwells] upon Mount Sumeru.
The mountain peak. Because it does not dwell in the void, it remains the summit of the human realm.

Furthermore, the first two phrases are superior to what precedes them, while the latter two phrases are inferior to what follows.孤山 (Gushan) says: "Trāyastriṃśa" is translated here as "Thirty-three"; Śakra rules over it.
△ Third, the Yāma Heaven.

When encountering desire, they engage briefly; once it has passed, there is no further recollection. In the human world, their movement is slight and their stillness is great. After the end of life, [they are reborn here].
Abiding serenely in the midst of empty space, the radiance of the sun and moon cannot reach them from above;
these beings possess their own intrinsic light. This class of beings is named the Suyāma Heaven.
If this person does not encounter objects of desire, lustful thoughts will certainly not arise spontaneously. Even when encountering them, before sexual union occurs, thoughts may arise;
however, one who engages briefly only fulfills a momentary impulse without lingering attachment. Upon departure, they are immediately relieved and no longer pursue recollections.
Within the state of purity, such a person will surely possess its full flavor and gradually incline toward a concentrated mind. Therefore...
If one’s speech and actions are mostly still and rarely disturbed, one can thereby attain rebirth in the luminous abodes of the sky-dwellers (*ākāśavāsin*). Question:
Regarding these sky-dwellers, upon what do their palaces, ponds, and trees rest? Answer: They rest upon a great earth of the seven precious gems and lapis lazuli, no different from our own;
however, whenever they wish to descend, it becomes empty and unobstructed. This is just as, for example, the sages, gods, and ghosts of the human realm are all able to ascend [to those heights].
Below, it is vast and unobstructed. One should know that the myriad dharmas are illusory, brought about by the power of karma;
thus, the void and the real appear together. Those who are deluded have truly not yet realized this. This heaven is twice as high as Mount Sumeru;

therefore, the sun and moon do not reach it, yet its own palaces and bodies emit light that shines everywhere, illuminating one another. "Suyāma" is translated here as "Time-Portion. It is encircled...

The Master said: "It is by the opening and closing of the lotus flower that day and night are distinguished. Furthermore, one should know that for this person, not encountering the superior heaven of No-Thought (Avṛha) is inferior;
encountering it and having a fleeting thought is subsequent and inferior. △ Fourth, the Tuṣita Heaven.

Always tranquil, when sensory contacts arise, they are unable to cause disturbance. After the end of life, they ascend to a refined and subtle realm, never descending to the levels of humans or devas of the lower worlds;
even when the kalpa is destroyed, they remain beyond the reach of the three calamities. Such is this class of beings.
This is called the Tuṣita Heaven.
Compared to those mentioned previously, these beings are entirely devoid of lustful thoughts at all times;

however, when confronted by the pressure of sexual objects, they are unable to resist. According to what follows, this should be understood in detail: they must necessarily experience a lack of flavor during the act of union.
"Subtle and refined" refers to the wondrous realm of the Inner Court. It is refined rather than coarse, and subtle rather than easily seen; it cannot be fathomed by sentient beings with coarse minds.
Since they do not even know its location within the Outer Court, how much less so for other devas? Therefore, it is said that "it is not accessible," and so forth.
Regarding the fact that "the three calamities do not reach it," this is what is meant in the *Lotus Sūtra* when it says: "This land of mine is not destroyed, yet the multitudes see it as such."

This refers to the meaning of "burning away. A question arises: this treatise discusses the matter of transmigration through the seven realms of existence (*sapta-gati*), which seems to correspond with the external heavens.
Why, then, does it single out only the Inner Court (*abhyantarāyatana*) while omitting the external heavens, thereby rendering the other heavens inconsistent?
I have heard that even when the three Bodhisattvas cultivate the Tuṣita Inner Court, they have not yet fully ascended; there must surely be a distinct method of cultivation [for them].

Could it be that this "few desires" (*alpeccha*) alone enables one to ascend? Answer: According to the subsequent text, among the various heavens both the noble (*ārya*) and the ordinary (*pṛthagjana*) are fully present;
those such as the five types of *anāgāmin* are examples of this. How could it be that this passage intentionally omits mention of the Inner Court (*abhyantaravimāna*)?

It is merely a suspicion regarding the Sanskrit original: perhaps it first mentions the outer heavens and subsequently includes the Inner Court, but the translator abbreviated the text by omitting the redundant portion and dividing it.
The analysis lacks detail, resulting in an impression that the outer court is entirely omitted when, in fact, it is not. Now, according to my own private estimation:

the first three phrases seem to describe the causes of the outer heavens while omitting their effects; the section beginning with "at the end of life" seems to describe the effects of the inner court while omitting its causes.
Thus, cause and effect are mutually implied by way of abbreviation. I do not know if this is correct.
Otherwise, how could these devas, possessing but slight desire and inferior merit, so suddenly obtain such a superior retribution that transcends the third dhyāna?

Some say: according to the Buddha’s own examination of the texts, the superior encompasses the inferior; thus, it is also consistent for the external heavens to allow one’s mind to attain this realization.
△ Fifth, the Heaven of Transformations (Nirmāṇarati).

I have no desire; I shall comply with your actions. When you lie across me, my sensation will be like chewing wax. After my life ends, I shall be reborn in the Heaven of Delighting in Transformations.
This class of beings is called the Heaven of Delighting in Transformations.

This person lacks mindfulness when encountering objects; in this respect, they are the same as those mentioned previously. However, at the moment of union, there is no flavor, which is merely superior to the former case.
As for "lying across," it refers to being pressed by an immediate object of lust such that one lacks self-mastery.

That person is ultimately without intention, and thus experiences total lack of flavor, like chewing wax. Furthermore, as for "transcending transformation," one is able to transcend the lower heavens and is able to...
The gods of the Heaven of Delighting in Emanations (Nirmāṇarati) delight in the musical instruments they themselves have emanated; therefore, they are named "Delighting in Emanations.

Because they are constrained by their own minds in their emanations, both cause and effect are inferior compared to those of the subsequent heavens. △ Sixth, the Heaven of Controlling Others' Emanations (Paranirmita-vaśavartin).
They possess no worldly mind, yet they engage in activities identical to those of the world. Amidst such worldly interactions, they clearly transcend them.

After their lives end, they are able to universally surpass the realms of both the transformed and the untransformed. This class of beings is called the Heaven of Mastery over Others' Transformations (Paranirmita-vaśavartin).
Those who possess no worldly mind aspire to the higher realms and take no pleasure in the mundane world; they merely follow along with the world, provisionally conforming to the state of a wife.
Yet, when it comes to the moment of union, they find not only a lack of flavor, but their spirits wander to external realms, having no engagement whatsoever.
Wénlǐng says: "Transformation" refers to the fifth heaven (Nirmāṇarati), while "non-transformation" refers to the lower heavens. These are the various sensual pleasures.
As for the objects of their environment, they do not trouble themselves to transform them; rather, they enjoy them with mastery through the transformations wrought by others.

Thus, they are named Paranirmita-vaśavartin (Masters over the Transformations of Others). This is because the causal mind surpasses the preceding mind, and the resultant transformation of others surpasses the preceding self-transformation.
The analysis of the relative gravity of desire is hereby concluded. II. Determining its inclusion within the Desire Realm.
Ānanda, in these six heavens, although their forms are subject to movement, the traces of their minds still intermingle. From this point downward, it is called the Realm of Desire (*kāmadhātu*).
The term "movement" refers specifically to the agitation and restlessness of desire. Among worldly people, those who lack self-restraint find their movements [unrestrained] in this regard.
It is most chaotic and cannot be restrained. Like a torrential flood, a runaway fire, or a galloping horse, there is nothing that can serve as a metaphor for it.

Because of its delusion and madness, beings constantly fall and are submerged in the three miserable realms. Therefore, these gods of the six heavens of the desire realm gradually exercise self-restraint and turn toward stillness;
thus it is said they "emerge from movement. Specifically, the first heaven ceases external movement, while the second heaven also ceases internal movement.
[The degrees of] reduction are as follows: on the third heaven, movement occurs only upon encountering an object; on the fourth heaven, one does not resist even when the object presses upon them;

on the fifth heaven, there is no flavor during the union; on the sixth heaven, the forms join but the mind transcends. These all represent a gradual departure from the turbulent agitation within desire.
As for those whose mental traces still intersect—referring to the first four heavens—they still involve mental intercourse because they possess flavor; the latter two heavens, however, are merely...

Their traces intersect because they lack [substantial] flavor. From this point downward—that is, from this heaven below, all the way down to the Avīci Hell—is subsumed within the Desire Realm (*kāmadhātu*).
This is because the three types of desire are identical, and both sexes are fully present. Master Yue cites Tiantai’s words:
"Beyond the ten wholesome deeds, the first three heavens each additionally incorporate meritorious practice (*puṇya-kriyā*), while the latter three heavens each additionally incorporate..."
Regarding meditative concentration (*dhyāna*): it is not merely a matter of disparaging sensual desire; those who aspire to rebirth in the heavens must understand this.

The distinctions regarding the gravity or lightness of the enjoyment of desire among the six heavens of the *Kosa* (Abhidharmakośa) concern matters of the fruition (*phala*), and are not the purport of this sutra concerning the cultivation of causes.

As the verse in the *Kosa-śloka* says: "In the six [heavens] that enjoy desire, there is intercourse, embracing, holding hands, laughing, and gazing. This interpretation differs from what I have heard. I have previously heard a verse within the Teaching which states: "The Four Kings and Trāyastriṃśa share a single path; in Yāma they hold hands; in Tuṣita..."

[They] smile. In the Heaven of Delighting in Emanations (*Nirmāṇarati*), they gaze at one another for a brief moment; this is the true bliss of the six heavens. In the first stage, they should embrace and partake in the union of forms, intertwining their limbs. This may also be summarized as follows: although there is physical union, it is without seminal fluid, unlike that of the human realm.
Now, lustful desire is the very root of falling into bondage. Through the Six Heavens of Desire, one ascends gradually by means of lightness;
through the Four Dhyānas, one is loftily elevated by severing [desire]. Thus, if one does not abandon the mind of desire, even the higher realms cannot be hoped for, let alone liberation.
Is it by cultivating *samādhi* within the three realms? This is why Ānanda must rely upon this to give rise to his teaching.

(Regarding those whose karmic fetters and habits are so heavy that they cannot suddenly be severed: they must likewise cultivate shame and revulsion, make vows, or seek rebirth elsewhere to achieve ultimate liberation. Be careful not to conflate this with the superior states of realization described in the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* and other such texts; do not deceive yourself or fall into the trap of demonic teachings.
Herein there is a separate class of Mara-devas belonging to the Desire Realm, whose sensual objects and sovereign power all surpass those of the other devas.
This sutra is subsumed within the sixth [category]; therefore, it is not explained separately. The six realms of desire are concluded.

Narrated by the Śramaṇa Jiāoguāng Zhēnjiàn of the West Lake in Kāyāvati. △ Section Two:
The Four Dhyānas. Wēnlíng says: From this point upward, the eighteen heavens of the form realm are clarified; although they are free from the defilement of desire, [they still possess form].

Because they still possess material form (*rūpa*), they are collectively termed the "Form Realm" (*rūpadhātu*). Furthermore, because they have already abandoned the defilement of desire, they are collectively termed the "Brahma World.

Because they have already abandoned distraction and agitation, they are collectively designated as the "Four Dhyānas. While the heavens of the Desire Realm are produced through the retribution of the ten wholesome actions alone, these heavens are produced through both the ten wholesome actions and meditative concentration (*dhyāna-samādhi*).
Nevertheless, this consists merely of the sixfold practice of impure (*sāsrava*) dhyāna-contemplation. As for the six practices:

To loathe the desire realm as suffering, coarse, and an obstruction, and to rejoice in the form realm as pure, sublime, and free—this is the path by which ordinary persons suppress their delusions and transcend the desire realm.

Although there were occasional states of meditative concentration (*dhyāna*) in the preceding heavens, it is only in this realm that they are formally designated as "meditation" (*dhyāna*), because the previous conclusion stated:
"Though the body has emerged from movement, the traces of the mind still intermingle. This is sufficient.
He knew that beyond this point there were absolutely no women; thus, both mind and conduct were detached, with no further contact.

Furthermore, he had neither food nor sleep, and the three desires were entirely forgotten. Whenever he felt even slight hunger or fatigue, he would enter meditative concentration (*dhyāna-samādhi*). Upon emerging from concentration, he was satiated and his spirit was clear and vigorous.
Thus, he took the joy of meditation as both food and rest, gradually departing from the coarse and heavy state of body and mind. Briefly stated.
They are divided into four stages, each having its own fundamental concentration; hence they are called the "four dhyānas. When analyzed in detail, there are eighteen stages.

However, it is suspected that there may be cases where stages occupy the same location yet are categorized as distinct based on their relative superiority or inferiority; thus, it is not necessarily the case that all eighteen follow a sequence strictly by ascending and descending levels.
This will be examined further in the main text. [The section] is divided into two parts. First, the formal division of the four dhyānas. This is further divided into four. First, the first [dhyāna].
The three heavens of dhyāna. Although these three heavens enter into the ranks of those who practice dhyāna, their moral virtue (*śīla*) is particularly preeminent.

While this demonstrates that their moral virtue is especially superior, the latter two heavens briefly manifest meditative concentration (*samādhi*) and wisdom (*prajñā*). This will become clear from the text itself. Furthermore, there are two parts: first, showing the specific characteristics of the three heavens;
this also has three sections, the first of which is the Brahmakāyika Heaven.
Ānanda, there are those in the world who cultivate their minds without relying on *dhyāna* and lacking true wisdom, yet are able to restrain their bodies from practicing sexual desire.
Whether walking or sitting, they are free of such thoughts, and because no defilement of craving arises, they do not remain bound to the realm of desire.
Such persons, by virtue of this mindfulness, consider themselves companions of Brahmā. This class of beings is called the Heaven of the Retinue of Brahmā (*Brahmapārṣadya*).

The initial mention of "the world" (*loka*) indicates that this is not the supramundane. Yet, it also speaks of "cultivating the mind. Because ordinary beings practice in delusion and darkness, who among them does not claim to be practicing the true cultivation of the mind?
Even demons and spirits claim to have attained the Unsurpassed Way, let alone those in the dhyāna heavens.

Nevertheless, all the sūtras state that the dhyāna heavens consist of *dhyāna*, *samādhi*, and so forth; here, "stillness" (*śānti*) is equivalent to "concentration" (*samādhi*), which is deeper than the six [perfections].

Desire and deliberation are themselves wisdom (*prajñā*). Because they distinguish [the practitioner] from the four formless attainments (*ārūpya-samāpatti*), the Buddhas of the provisional teachings rely upon these to achieve their realization.

When it is now said that "one does not depend on *dhyāna* and lacks true wisdom," this reveals that they possess only the contaminated (*sāsrava*) meditative absorptions (*dhyāna*) and the sixfold practice for subduing desire;
it does not mean they possess the untainted (*anāsrava*) true *samādhi* of wondrous, perfect penetration. This principle should also apply here.

This connects with what follows. The section concerning the lower direction is the specific text for this particular heaven. This heaven alone manifests the virtue of ethical discipline (*śīla*), yet does not yet reveal meditative concentration (*samādhi*) or wisdom (*prajñā*).

The preceding mention of "controlling the body" distinguishes it from the six heavens of the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*); even if one forcibly suppresses the emotions, one cannot avoid bodily transgressions.

Only when this body is entirely distanced [from such faults] is the holy life (*brahmacarya*) truly accomplished. If one acts below [this level], it signifies that the mind is not unrestrained; thus, both body and mind [are governed].
Because both are pure, there is no need for divination regarding their dwelling below, yet they share companions above. The multitude are thus the common people of the Brahma-world.
△ Second, the Heaven of Brahma’s Ministers (Brahmapurohita).
Once the habitual tendencies of desire have been eliminated, the mind free from desire manifests; one takes delight in and accords with all forms of discipline.
Such a person is able to practice the virtue of Brahma at the appropriate time. This class of beings is called the Heaven of the Ministers of Brahma (Brahmapurohita).
Master Huan says: This "Heaven of Precepts" (Śīlabhava) is associated with meditative concentration (*samādhi*). The first two phrases indicate the Heaven Above;

however, there, one has merely recently become free from desire, and the characteristics of the pure mind have not yet reached full manifestation. Here, the characteristics of the pure mind of one free from desire are clearly revealed and brilliantly manifest.
The former heaven is like a sickness that has only recently been cured, not yet reaching robust health; this heaven is like being already healthy and strong, with a radiant luster.
The various Vinayas are the precepts of the Brahma-faring (brahmacarya). "Loving joy" refers to gladness; "conformity" refers to pliancy (praśrabdhi);
these are the characteristics associated with meditative concentration (samādhi). One who practices the virtue of Brahma not only purifies body and mind, but also propagates virtuous transformation;
