because there is no interval between inner mind and outer conduct, such a person assists in the transformation [of beings] once born in heaven, and is thus a celestial minister.
Thus it is. △ Third, the Great Brahmā Heavens:
Their bodies and minds are wondrously perfect, their dignified deportment is flawless, and they observe pure prohibitions and precepts, further augmented by clear awakening.
Such persons are able, at the appropriate time, to preside over the Brahma hosts as Great Brahmā Kings. This class of beings is called the Great Brahmā Heavens.
This deity manifests both precept and wisdom together. The first deity holds to the body; the second deity manifests the mind.

This deity encompasses both, and is therefore called "wondrously perfect" (*miaoyuan*). Furthermore, the first deity gathers the mind by means of holding to the body, while the second deity practices virtue through the manifestation of the mind.
These body and mind attain a wondrous state of oneness without duality, fulfilling the full measure of their capacity.
"Perfect. Regarding "not deficient in dignified deportment": walking, standing, sitting, and reclining are all wondrously perfect.
The following two phrases describe the characteristic of right precepts coexisting with wisdom; clear awakening is simply the further illumination of the wisdom of the six modes of conduct.

Just as the virtue of the former [earthly] heavens can assist the king’s transformation of the people—the way of a minister—this virtue of the heavenly beings can preside over the Brahma hosts. It is like...
"Embodiment of benevolence is sufficient to lead others; this is the Way of the Ruler. It is also because his wisdom surpasses that of the former heavens that he prevails.
The demonstration of the distinct characteristics of the three heavens is now complete. △ Second, the conclusion on suffering, the cessation of outflows, and the end.
Ānanda, these three superior classes cannot be oppressed by any suffering or affliction.
Although they have not yet attained the true Samādhi of correct cultivation, within their pure minds, the various outflows (āsravas) remain unmoved; this is called the First Dhyāna.
Wenling says: Having already departed from the eight sufferings of the desire realm, it is said that "suffering and affliction do not oppress.

Having already departed from the scattered and agitated mind of desire, it is said that "all outflows (āsrava) are unmoving. The *Abhidharmakośa-bhāṣya* states: "This is called the stage of joy and bliss born of seclusion."
This refers to attaining pure bliss by departing from the mixed and evil rebirths of the desire realm. Gushan said: There are four types of dhyāna.

First, contaminated dhyāna (*sāsrava-dhyāna*), which refers to the present four dhyānas. Second, uncontaminated dhyāna (*anāsrava-dhyāna*), referring to the nine notions, the eight liberations, and so forth.

Third, both contaminated and uncontaminated dhyāna, referring to the six subtle gates, the supernormal powers, and the clear understandings (*vidyā*). Fourth, neither contaminated nor uncontaminated dhyāna.
This is not the untainted (anāsrava) dhyāna; it is precisely the concentration of principle within the Śūraṅgama Samādhi King Sūtra.
When it is now said, "Although this is not the true, correct samādhi," this merely distinguishes the first [heaven] from the fourth.

From this point upward, they are all termed "superior flows" (viśeṣa-srotas), signifying their superiority over the various realms of the desire realm (kāmadhātu). Regarding these three heavens, there is some doubt as to whether they do not constitute a vertical progression.
Furthermore, if the celestial subjects, the celestial ministers, and the celestial king each occupy a separate layer, how can this constitute a unified realm?

Moreover, while subjects and ministers may be numerous, why would the celestial king alone reach such a number as to fill the heavens while occupying but a single layer? In that case, both parties would simply be kings.
What could they possibly command? I fear they are like the ministers of the Four Heavenly Kings, residing above and below the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven;
yet the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven has its own distinct subjects and citizens dwelling there, so they cannot be entirely subsumed under the Four Kings.
Furthermore, the Great Brahmā devas are likely not numerous either; those single deities merely occupy vast royal palaces, sharing them only with their own retinues.

As for the ministers and subjects below who perform their duties, they temporarily ascend to reside there [in the heavens], and when there is no further business, they retire to their original heavens.
If this is the case, it remains a vertical division between the upper and lower realms; however, as this is not yet definitively established, it awaits further investigation.

The three heavens of the First Dhyāna are concluded. II. The Three Heavens of the Second Dhyāna. In the previous [heavens], the power of meditative concentration still relied upon the support of precepts. This...

Thus, without relying on the support of the precepts, one spontaneously enters immovable concentration (*aniñjya-samādhi*) and gives rise to radiant light. These are ranked according to the superiority or inferiority of that light.
Wuxing said: "The *Bodhisattvabhūmi-śāstra* refers to the second dhyāna as the 'dhyāna accompanied by joy' (*prīti-sahagata-dhyāna*). When this concentration arises..."

It arises together with joy. This is divided into two parts. First, showing the distinct characteristics of the three heavens, which is further divided into three sections. First, the Heaven of Limited Light (*Parīttābha*).

Ānanda, next there is the Brahmā Heaven, where one presides over the Brahmā-puruṣas, perfects the Brahma-conduct (*brahmacarya*), and maintains a tranquil mind that is unmoving. From this profound stillness, light is produced.
A class of beings such as these is called the Heaven of Limited Light.

The two phrases [of the verse] governing this section are fundamentally similar to what is performed by Mahābrahmā; therefore, this deva is suspected of having cultivated [the path] within that heaven.

This is because he follows the previous practice and merely adds full perfection to it, thereby ascending to this heaven. Master Huan also stated that those who ascend and progress by following the practices of Mahābrahmā are precisely these [beings].
Below the phrase "clarifying the mind" (澄心) is where the superior realm of this heaven truly begins. Clarifying...
"Profound stillness gives rise to light. This means that as water becomes clear, it reflects; when stillness reaches its ultimate limit, the function of illumination is manifested. Question:
How does this differ from the "tranquil illumination" (*jizhao*) of a Bodhisattva? Answer: [In this stage,] the two attachments to persons and phenomena have not moved even by a hair’s breadth;

it is simply that by being free from desire, one attains meditative concentration (*samādhi*), and as this concentration deepens, illumination arises. This is the distinction. The following sections shall all follow this pattern. △ Second: The Immeasurables.
The Heaven of Light:
light and light mutually ignite one another, shining forth without end and reflecting throughout the worlds of the ten directions, everywhere becoming composed of lapis lazuli.
This class of beings is called the Heaven of Immeasurable Light.

Wenling says: "The power of meditative concentration becomes increasingly clear, and wondrous light flashes forth in succession. As the objects follow the light, they are everywhere transformed into lapis lazuli. Zhenji says:
"'Reflecting the worlds of the ten directions' refers to the light of concentration according to its various manifestations in the east, west, south, north, and so forth;
it does not mean pervading the entire world-system of the ten directions. According to this, although this heaven cannot reflect [the sun's light],...

Regarding the various great trichiliocosms: within their own fundamental realms, they also cover a small chiliocosm. When one thousand sets of four continents are thus filled, why would there not be worlds in the ten directions?
△ Third, the Ābhāsvara Heaven (Light-Sound Heaven).
Inhaling and sustaining the circular radiance, they accomplish the essence of the teaching; they give rise to pure transformation, and their applications are inexhaustible.
This class of beings is called the Ābhāsvara Heaven (Heaven of Radiant Sound).
This uses light to take the place of vocal sounds in order to proclaim that Brahma-conduct and transformation.
It is like how, in the mundane world, written characters take the place of vocal sounds yet also proclaim various forms of instruction; this is identical to using light to perform the Buddha-work.
The two phrases "arousing" and "transforming" clarify the propagation of the Brahma-teaching, whose wondrousness is inexhaustible.
Master Yun, based on this, concluded that from the second dhyāna upward there is no speech at all; however, this is likely not necessarily so.

For instance, although worldly paper, ink, and written characters represent speech and teaching, how could they ever completely dispense with spoken language? Having finished demonstrating the distinct characteristics of the three heavens:
△ Second, concluding the section on the suppression of the outflows of sorrow and separation.
Ānanda, these three superior streams cannot be assailed by any anxieties or apprehensions.
Although they do not yet constitute the true, correct Samādhi of the ultimate reality, because coarse outflows have been suppressed within their pure minds, this is called the Second Dhyāna.
"Anxiety (*utkaṇṭhā*) is unease. The previous statement that "suffering and affliction" are coarse and heavy refers to their pressing upon both body and mind;
this anxiety, however, is subtle and fine, involving only the mental faculty. Now, it can be known that it does not constrain joy and bliss. Wēn-líng says:

"In the second dhyāna, one is free from anxiety and attains supreme joy and bliss; therefore, it is said that 'anxiety does not constrain. It is only in the first dhyāna that [one first] attains [this]."
The outflows (āsrava) do not disturb the mind, yet they have not yet been subdued. This deva has already subdued the coarse outflows. The *Abhidharmakośa* states:

"This is called the stage of joy and bliss born of meditative concentration (*samādhi*)," meaning that the water of concentration moistens one's karma, so that anxiety and distress do not oppress him. Wuxing says:
"Huan" (懸) may be an error for the character "chou" (愁). The three heavens of the second dhyāna are concluded. △ Third: The Three Heavens of the Third Dhyāna.

Wuxing says: The *Bodhisattvabhūmi-śāstra* refers to the third dhyāna as the "Dhyāna Conjoined with Bliss" (*sukha-sahagata-dhyāna*), because the merit of this concentration arises together with bliss pervading the entire body.
Although the first two dhyānas possess the factor of bliss (*sukha-aṅga*), it is obstructed by the factor of joy (*prīti-aṅga*).

Now, because joy has ceased and there is pure bliss, it receives its name. This is divided into two parts. First, showing the distinct characteristics of the three heavens, which is further divided into three.
First, the Heaven of Limited Purity (*Parīttābha*).
Ānanda, such celestial beings have circular halos that perfect sound; they shed sound to reveal the sublime, and their development brings about refined practice, penetrating into stillness.
The cessation of pleasure. Such a class [of beings] is called the Śubhakṛtsna (Utterly Pure) devas.

Wēnlíng says: "Because the essence of the teaching from the aforementioned radiant circle reveals the subtle principle and brings forth refined practice, one becomes detached from the prior agitation of joy and gives rise to pure pleasure.
This state of serene detachment and stillness is called the pleasure of cessation (*nirodha-sukha*). One is merely able to penetrate it; yet..."

It has not yet been perfected; because it is still inferior, it is called "Slight Purity" (Parīttaśubha). ○ "Refined conduct" (viśuddhacaryā) is also a pure practice that corresponds to the revelation of the wondrous principle.
"The bliss of quiescence" (nirvāṇa-sukha) is also that which is produced when the concentrated mind finds its resting place;

it must not be confused with the inherently quiescent essence (prakṛti-śānta-tattva), for while the names are the same, their essences differ. As the text below states: "In time, it must surely perish."
Their intent can thus be seen. △ Second, the Heaven of Immeasurable Purity (*Apramāṇaśubha*).
Pure emptiness manifests before them, giving rise to boundlessness. Body and mind become light and tranquil, achieving the bliss of cessation (*nirvāṇa*). Such is this class of beings.
This is called the Heaven of Immeasurable Purity (*Apramāṇaśubha*).
The first phrase states that previously one had only attained purity; here, one further gives rise to emptiness, gradually becoming void and expansive until reaching the boundless limit.

Whereas the previous stage was pervasive quiescence and took pleasure only in the inner mind, this stage adds the body and mind, such that there is peace and happiness both internally and externally, arising from within and accumulating outwardly.
The external realm is vast and expansive; therefore, it is called "Immeasurable Purity" (Amitābha). △ Third, the Heaven of Universal Purity (Śubhakṛtsna):
World, body, and mind are all perfectly pure. The virtues of purity are fully accomplished, and the sublime reliance manifests before one. One returns to the bliss of quiescent extinction.
This class of beings is called the Śubhakṛtsna (Universal Purity) devas.

Whereas the previous [level] involved only body and mind, this adds the world-realm, which together achieve a state of pervasive emptiness and stillness; hence it is called "Perfectly Pure" (yuanjing).

This is brought about solely by the power of meditative concentration (*samādhi*), meaning that the objective realm simply transforms in accordance with that concentration; it is not brought about by the power of mental contemplation alone.
The two lines on "Pure Virtue" (*śuddha-guṇa*) refer back to what precedes them: since the world and one's own body and mind are perfectly pure, is this not the accomplishment of pure virtue?
The two lines on "Superior Reliance" (*viśiṣṭa-āśraya*) suggest that one has truly found a homeland of pure bliss (*sukhāvatī*) where one may establish one’s life and secure one’s existence.
Although the former [lines] speak of the external, they still describe a state of empty vastness within body and mind, wherein the world has not yet been integrated.
Now, all these are integrated; therefore, it is called "Universal Purity" (Śubhakṛtsna). The demonstration of the distinct characteristics of these three heavens is complete.
II. Concluding the Endowment of Peaceful Joy:
Ānanda, these three superior classes possess great conformity; their bodies and minds are peaceful and secure, and they attain immeasurable bliss. Although they are not...
Having correctly attained true samādhi, with a mind established in peace and fully endowed with joy, it is called the third dhyāna.

Regarding "possessing great conformity" (*mahānulaṃbha*): whereas the conformity to the discipline (*saṃvara*) in the first dhyāna is not "great conformity," this [third dhyāna] possesses great conformity because its pure bliss conforms [to the mind] limitlessly and pervasively;
thus, it is said to possess great conformity. "Peaceful" (*kṣema*) refers to the sovereign enjoyment [of that bliss].
Furthermore, "immeasurable bliss" (*apramāṇa-sukha*) is the ultimate limit of bliss; therefore, within the realm of desire, the third dhyāna is considered the place of ultimate bliss.

Although this stage is named "sublime bliss detached from joy" (*prīti-viveka-praśānta-sukha*), it is still said to be "fully endowed with joy" because it is distinguished by the four characters [of the mind] within a state of tranquility.
This is because joy (*prīti*) is that which is aroused by a moving mind, whereas bliss (*sukha*) is...
When the mind is integrated with tranquility (*śamatha*), even if it is active or mobile, though the mind may be described as "joyful," it remains the factor of *prīti* (rapture).

When the mind is in a state of security (*anavadya*), even if it is described as "joyful," it remains the factor of *sukha* (bliss). Master Yue held that while the names are identical, their essences differ; this is correct.

Furthermore, regarding the principle that "one should not let the phrasing distort the meaning," he failed to realize that [the term] was already used within the context of a secure mind for the purpose of distinction.
This concludes the section on the three heavens of the third dhyāna. △ Fourth, the nine heavens of the fourth dhyāna. Wēnlíng says:
From this point downward, it clarifies that there are nine heavens in total within the fourth dhyāna. However, regarding the realms of retribution for the fourth dhyāna, there are only three heavens;

the fourth, the Heaven of No-Thought (*asaṃjñisattva*), is a separate opening from the third, the Heaven of Vast Fruit (*bṛhatphala*), and constitutes the realm of retribution for non-Buddhist practitioners (*tīrthika*). Above these four [heavens]...
There are five heavens of the Non-returners (*anāgāmin*). These are distinct from ordinary beings because the noble ones (*ārya*) cultivate meditative absorption (*dhyāna*) differently.
This category is divided into two parts. First, the Four Heavens of Supreme Flow (*catur-śuddhāvāsa*): the Buddha established this classification by summarizing these four as "supreme flows.

He did not exclude the fourth [heaven] of the non-Buddhists (*tīrthika*), for both are characterized by the same state of meditative concentration associated with equanimity (*upekṣā-sahagata-dhyāna*); therefore, the Buddha judged them identically. Furthermore, one should know that these four...

Regarding the meditative absorption (*dhyāna*) of taking up and discarding: it does not transcend the three types of sensation (*vedanā*). The former heaven discards the sensation of suffering and abides in the sensation of pleasure;

this heaven, however, discards both sensations and abides solely in the sensation of equanimity (*upekṣā-vedanā*). Furthermore, there are two [points]: first, to show the distinct characteristics of the four heavens; second, to further divide them into three.
First, it indicates the first two heavens. Although the first three heavens constitute a single group, the third heaven diverges from the Heaven of Non-conception;
therefore, these are categorized in pairs. Second, the Heaven of Merit-Born (Puṇyaprasava).

Ānanda, furthermore, there are gods and humans whose bodies and minds are no longer oppressed, for the causes of suffering have been exhausted. Yet, pleasure is not permanent; after a long time, it must inevitably decay and give rise to suffering.

They simultaneously and instantaneously relinquish both the mind of suffering and the mind of pleasure. The characteristics of coarseness and heaviness are extinguished, and the nature of pure merit arises.
This class of beings is called the Heaven of Merit-Born (Puṇyaprasava).

The two phrases "not oppressed" conclude the description of the second dhyāna, clarifying that suffering has already been abandoned. This is because the afflictions of the first dhyāna have been left behind and the anxieties of the second dhyāna have been exhausted;
thus, there is no oppression. Since desire is the cause of suffering and all desires have been cut off, the causes of suffering are exhausted.

Regarding the two phrases "pleasure is not [to be felt]," they conclude the subsequent heaven, clarifying the principle that even pleasure should not be experienced. This interpretation is acceptable.

[This] is understood. Below, regarding suffering and pleasure, one treads upon the fact that this pleasure is subject to destruction; thus, the mind of dual equanimity arises. This is precisely the meritorious practice of the fundamental heaven.
That is to say, having already departed from suffering, one no longer experiences pleasure. Since pleasure is not experienced, its destruction does not arise.

"The coarse and heavy characteristics are extinguished" means that both suffering and [the prospect of] destruction have been transcended. "The nature of pure merit arises" refers to the presence of pleasure.
Receiving no further blessings, one’s own merit gradually arises. The name may be understood accordingly. △ Second, the Heaven of Love for Merit (*Puṇyaprasava*).
With a mind of equanimity that is perfectly integrated and a pure resolute understanding, amidst unobstructed merit, one attains wondrous conformity that extends to the limits of the future.
This class of beings is called the Puṇyaprasavā devas.

The preceding class was initially focused exclusively on equanimity (upekṣā) and had not yet escaped partial emptiness; since this class has reached full maturity, it gradually ceases to be obstructed by existence (bhava), and is thus said to be "perfectly integrated" (saṃvṛta).
Regarding those with pure resolute conviction (adhimukti-viśuddha): their understanding of this purity is superior to that of the former, as the former was characterized by detachment.
To desire liberation from suffering for the sake of purity is to be free from both suffering and pleasure; furthermore, it is because one is not obstructed by existence (*bhava*).

Thus, emptiness (*śūnyatā*) is the meditative concentration of equanimity (*upekṣā-samādhi*), while existence is merit (*puṇya*). "Limitation" (*saṃvara*) refers to this [distinction]. "Exquisite conformity" (*sūkṣmānukūla*) is great sovereignty (*mahāvaśitā*).
Those with great merit have no limitations in their aspirations and attain great mastery. Regarding "extending to the limits of the future," it is as the Master Yue said:
"Merit supports both paths [the human and heavenly], and does not merely pertain to the present life.
This refers to the sense that one will receive inexhaustible retribution within the two higher heavens; it does not mean true permanence. This is the name.

Regarding "Blessed and Loved" (*puji ai*): this refers to the fact that the merit of these devas is also something to be cherished and delighted in within the realm of conditioned existence (*saṃskṛta-dhātu*).
Furthermore, the merit accumulated by these devas has a distinct object of craving and seeking, namely the hope for the two higher paths.
△ Second, the judgment of the two paths.
Ānanda, from this heaven there are two diverging paths;
this heaven is the Heaven of Love and Merit (*Puṇyaprasava*). Those who enter these diverging paths from this heaven have distinct mental inclinations and karmic actions.
The meaning of this will be seen clearly in the following section. Wēnlíng says: "One path goes directly toward the Vast Fruit (*Bṛhatphala*). One...
A circuitous and deviant path leading toward the realm of non-conceptualization (*asaṃjñā*). ○ Furthermore, I have often reflected deeply upon this:

regarding the ascent [to higher realms], those who progress gradually are many, while those who attain sudden realization are few; it is like the promotion of officials in the world. Regarding the descent [into lower realms], those who fall directly are many, while those who progress gradually are few;
it is like the demotion of officials in the world. What is clarified in the present sutra seems to follow entirely from...
Practicing on the lower day to ascend to the upper day is merely a concise explanation for the purpose of sequential progression and ease of exposition;
the rest may be understood through one's own insight. △ Third, showing the latter two days: these are the two divergent paths.
This is divided into two parts. First, the Bṛhatphala Heaven:
those who dwell having cultivated and realized a state where their previous mind is characterized by immeasurable pure radiance and the perfect clarity of merit—such is this class of beings.
It is named the Heaven of Vast Results (*Bṛhatphala*).
This initial mind is the subtle, compliant mind within the Heaven of Merit-Love (*Puṇyaprasava*), which enables all that is sought to be fulfilled according to one's wishes.

Furthermore, this mind takes as its essence the perfect integration of meditative concentration and merit. Now, the Immeasurable Pure Light is precisely the meditative concentration associated with equanimity (*upekṣā-sahagata-dhyāna*).
It is profound and emits light. Within this light, it causes merit and virtue to flourish, increasing and becoming perfectly bright; one thereby attains cultivation and realization. Zizhong says:
"By perfuming meditative merit with the four immeasurable minds (*apramāṇa*), one leaves behind the defilements of the lower stages.
That which is induced by the Fruit of Vastness (*Bṛhatphala*) is called the Heaven of Vast Fruit (*Bṛhatphaladeva*). II. The Heaven of Non-conception (*Asaṃjñisattvadeva*).

If, within the preceding state of mind, one simultaneously feels aversion toward both suffering and pleasure, refining the mind of equanimity until it flows in an uninterrupted succession and fully masters the path of equanimity, then body and mind will both cease;
the mental faculties will become ashen and stilled for five hundred kalpas. Since this person has taken birth and extinction as their cause, [they shall not attain liberation].
They are unable to manifest the nature that is neither born nor extinguished. For the first half-aeon they cease, and for the latter half-aeon they are born;
such a class is called the Heaven of No-Thought (*asaṃjñisattva*).

Their prior mental state is the same as before, but whereas in the Heaven of Vast Results (*bṛhatphala*) one causes merit and virtue to flourish, in this heaven one causes the abandonment of meditative concentration (*samādhi*).
This is the primary cause for their flourishing; they falsely claim that by relying on this, one may attain *nirvāṇa*.

This is because these two types of dispositions diverge. The first two lines refer back to the preceding state of mind. The three lines beginning with "thoroughly investigating" (*jingyan*) concern the application of effort in cultivating the cause.
"Thoroughly investigating" means searching deeply and scrutinizing minutely. "Continuous" (*xiangxu*) means diligent and uninterrupted. "Completely exhausting" (*yuanqiong*) means necessarily...
This refers to seeking the ultimate. The three phrases concerning body and mind indicate that the fruit is definitively achieved.

When it says "remaining in meditative concentration," it describes a state where everything becomes entirely obscure and dark, a profound and total emptiness. Although only body and mind are mentioned, this necessarily implies the cessation of the realms as well;
this is precisely what they mistakenly grasp as the fruit of *nirvāṇa*. This lasts for five hundred great kalpas, from the first birth until the end of one’s life.
This has merely been attained after a long period. These four subsequent lines reveal the reason for its impermanence:

it is precisely because one has practiced based on the two kinds of fundamental delusions. The first line clarifies that the basis of this error is the six consciousnesses, which are the root of birth and death;

taking these as the primary cause for cultivation, one forcibly causes them to solidify like ash. The second line clarifies that this is a case of turning back toward the delusion of the consciousness-essence.
This is because one clearly understands the nature of luminous, perfect, and profound stillness—which is neither born nor extinguished—yet remains entirely ignorant of its function.

The final two lines clarify that from beginning to end, one falls into impermanence. Regarding "extinguished in the first half-aeon": having initially given rise to the practice of meditative concentration, one begins to extinguish perceptions after half an aeon.
Regarding "arising in the latter half-aeon": when the retribution is exhausted and the concentration dissolves, perceptions arise again after another half-aeon. [Question: What of the body?
The realms are both empty; how does this differ from the four emptinesses? Answer: Upon emerging from meditative absorption, they exist;

therefore, they are not the same. Nevertheless, there is only the realm of the body, for no manifold perceptions arise simultaneously. The distinct characteristics of the four heavens are thus concluded. △ Second, the conclusion on the immovable and the perfection of mastery.
Ānanda, these four superior streams cannot be moved by any worldly objects of suffering or pleasure.

Although they are not the unconditioned stage of true immovability, because the mental effort of those who still possess a sense of attainment has reached full maturity, they are called the Four Dhyānas.
Because both [the subject and object] are abandoned simultaneously, the two objects cannot move it. Wēnlíng says: "The fourth dhyāna is not moved by the three calamities;
thus it is called the 'Immovable Ground' (aniñjya-bhūmi). However, its receptacle world is not truly eternal, and its sentient beings arise and perish together with their emotions.
Although it is not the unconditioned true realm, the conditioned function has here reached full maturity. Question: Why is it not moved by the three calamities?

Question: Since it is subject to movement, why do you say that the vessel-world (bhājana-loka) is not truly eternal? Answer: Other sutras clarify that when these devas and humans are born, their palaces, gardens, and groves arise along with them;
when they die, these things perish along with them. It is simply that there is no sign of a total destruction [of the entire realm].

Furthermore, discussing the four dhyānas in general: the first dhyāna is associated with ethical discipline (*śīla*), and thus the virtue of discipline is predominant. The second dhyāna is associated with joy (*prīti*), and thus radiance is predominant.
The third dhyāna is associated with bliss (*sukha*), and thus pure bliss is predominant. The fourth dhyāna is associated with equanimity (*upekṣā*);

therein, for the first three heavens, merit (*puṇya*) is predominant, while for the last heaven, equanimity and concentration (*samādhi*) are predominant. This is their distinction. These are the four superior streams.
The section on the Deva realms is concluded. △ Second, the Five Śuddhāvāsa Heavens. Wēnlíng says:

Those who have attained the third fruit, having exhausted the nine grades of afflictions to be abandoned through cultivation in the Desire Realm, are reborn in these heavens and will not take birth again in the Desire Realm. Zīzhōng says:
The *Abhidharmakośa* states that because there are five distinct grades of mixed cultivation of dhyāna, one is born in the five Pure Abodes. Mixed cultivation...

"Those who" refers to those who practice by alternating between the tainted (*sāsrava*) and the untainted (*anāsrava*). "Meditative absorption" (*dhyāna*) refers to the state where concentration (*samādhi*) and wisdom (*prajñā*) are in equilibrium.
As for the "five grades," these are the inferior, the intermediate, the superior, the most excellent, and the ultimate.

Since the five grades of the five heavens all proceed from the inferior toward the superior, it would seem that there is no discrepancy in assigning the five heavens according to these grades. Furthermore, since they already exist...
Regarding their superiority or inferiority, is it not the case that they are ranked according to the depth of their severance of afflictions?
If this is so, then it appears that in the first four heavens, one successively severs the afflictions of the four stages of the fundamental realm (*dhātu*).

Since the fifth heaven is named Akaniṣṭha (Ultimate Form), it appears that one there severs the afflictions of the four stages of the higher formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*). This is a judgment based on inference, offered for your reference.
Since this is not definitive, even a slight discrepancy is not an error. This is divided into three parts. First, the designation of the noble fruit as a provisional dwelling:
"Ānanda, herein there are further five types of Non-returners (*anāgāmin*). Within the lower realms, their nine grades of habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*) are extinguished simultaneously;
they have forgotten both suffering and pleasure, and having no further abode below, they are established within the homogeneous class (*nikāya-sabhāga*) of equanimity."

Regarding the dwelling place, Wēnlíng says: because one no longer undergoes rebirth in the desire realm, it is called "Non-returner" (Anāgāmin). It is also named the Five Pure Abodes, meaning the abode of those with pure bodies who have transcended desire.
Since both the latent tendencies (*vāsanā*) and the afflictions of thought (*dhyāna-kleśa*), as well as their active manifestations (*samudācāra*), are extinguished, it is so called.
Both are exhausted. Up to this point, it represents the matter of the Sage’s severance of delusions, clarifying how he differs from those in the four dhyānas.

Generally, ordinary beings suppress their delusions but cannot sever them; this is the distinction between the sage and the ordinary person. "The lower realm" refers to the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*).
"Habitual tendencies" (*vāsanā*) are the seeds of the delusions of thought (*vitarka-kleśa*). These delusions of thought consist of greed, anger, ignorance, and pride. This is [the meaning].
These arise spontaneously; they are subtle afflictions, unlike the coarse afflictions found within conceptual discrimination. They are divided into eighty-one grades and abandoned accordingly.
Specifically, across the nine stages (*bhūmi*) of the three realms, each stage contains nine grades.

These present nine grades pertain to the "Stage of Mixed Dwelling in the Five Destinies" of the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*). Within these, each is further divided into three—superior, middling, and inferior. [The celestial beings...]

Regarding the superior person among humans: having passed through seven births, they sever [the defilements] by means of the "going and returning" (āgāmi-pratyāgāmi) process; yet it is said that these are extinguished simultaneously.
This refers to the realization of the third fruit (anāgāmin) through its complete exhaustion in the very last moment.

From this point downward, the text explains the reason for the five classes of deities (*pañca-deva-nikāya*) residing in this realm, clarifying that they share the same status as those in the four dhyānas. I humbly ask: why is this so?

[Question: "Why is it that [the beings] dwell exclusively in this place, which is so vastly separated from the realms above and below? [Answer: "It is because their afflictions (*kleśa*) of the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*) have been exhausted;

thus, coarse suffering has already been eliminated. Furthermore, they no longer experience the pure pleasure (*śubha-sukha*) of the third dhyāna. The meditative absorption (*samādhi*) they enter is one in which both pain and pleasure are forgotten, characterized by equanimity (*upekṣā*).
Now, when pain is forgotten, there is no place among the five destinies (*pañcagati*) for them to dwell in a mixed manner. When pleasure is forgotten..."
Thus, among the three dhyānas and their three stages, there is no place to establish a residence, as they do not share the same homogeneous category (*sabhāgatā*).
However, since it has already abandoned the equanimity associated with meditative absorption, it shares its homogeneous category exclusively with this stage of "purity of equanimity and mindfulness.

For this reason, one establishes a secure dwelling solely in this stage. Abiding here, one severs the seventy-two categories of the most subtle greed, delusion, and pride, aspiring for accomplishment.
"An Arhat. △ Second, showing the distinct characteristics of the five heavens; this is divided into five parts. First, the Avṛha Heaven:
"Ānanda, where both suffering and pleasure have ceased and the contentious mind no longer engages, such a class of beings is named the Avṛha Heaven."

According to the five grades, this heaven seems to correspond to the lowest grade. It likely corresponds to having severed the nine grades of afflictions (*kleśa*) within the stage of "joy born of seclusion.

The "striving mind" refers to the two minds of longing and aversion; for as long as suffering and pleasure have not been forgotten, one feels aversion toward suffering and longing for pleasure, which battle within the breast.
Hence it is called the "striving mind. Now that both have been forgotten, it is called "non-striving."
"Intermingling. Intense heat is called "affliction" (*tāpa*); this also describes the state of the inner mind being stifled and oppressed by heat.
Those who possess a combative mind cannot avoid this; because one does not intermingle here and first attains coolness, it is named "Without Affliction" (*Atapa*).
△ Second, the Heaven Without Heat (*Atapā*).
The trigger functions alone; there is no ground for cultivating friendships. A class of beings such as these is called the Heaven of No Heat (*Atapā*).

This heaven seems to correspond to the middle grade of the nine grades of afflictions associated with thought that are to be severed upon attaining the stage of "joy and bliss born of meditative concentration" (*dhyāna-ja-prīti-sukha-bhūmi*).
"Trigger" (*ji*) refers to the shape of a crossbow bolt, representing the releasing of thought; "grip" (*kuo*) refers to the shape of a sheath, representing the gathering back of thought.

"Releasing and gathering" (*fangshou*) also refers to beginning and ceasing. "Walking alone" signifies that one is solely focused on mindfulness (*smṛti*)—whether releasing and rising or gathering and ceasing—without any other thoughts intermingling therein.
Upon reaching this state, one no longer perceives any ground for the friction between attraction and aversion (*anunaya-pratigha*).
This implies that although such friction had not been actively cultivated prior to this, it was nonetheless still present. To be slightly troubled is called "heat" (*ūṣmagata*), and...

As for "heat also being absent": when equanimity and mindfulness are purified, and this excellence is further enhanced, the mental ground becomes cool and refreshing, entirely free from the affliction of heat.
△ Third, the Sudṛśa Heaven.
Throughout the worlds of the ten directions, wondrous vision is perfectly clear and limpid; there are no further sensory images or any defilements whatsoever.
This class of beings is called the Heaven of Good Vision (*Sudṛśa*).

This heaven likely corresponds to the superior grade [of practitioners], who should have severed the nine grades of afflictions associated with the stage of "sublime joy" (*prīti-sukha*) that is free from coarse delight.
The worlds of the ten directions constitute the magnitude of one great trichiliocosm. "Sublime Vision" refers to the divine eye (*divyacakṣus*).
Since it shares the same sphere as the fourth dhyāna, the divine eye should likewise perceive the general characteristics of the great trichiliocosm through the fourth dhyāna.

"Perfect" means filling the great trichiliocosm. "Clear and transparent" means penetrating through to the bottom. "Dust-like images" refers to the objective realm; it clarifies that there are no further obstructions or separations.
This is the realm [of the Suyāma Heaven]. "Sinking defilements" refers to the mind, clarifying that there are no further lingering thoughts.

If one were to treat these as "afflictions of thought" (*vitarka-kleśa*), yet then speak of them as being "all," how could it be that the afflictions of thought are exhausted upon reaching this heaven?

It is named "Good Vision" (*Sudṛśa*) to signify that the essential substance of the meditative concentration of this heaven is pure and clear, excelling at reflection and illumination. △ Fourth, the Heaven of Good Manifestation (*Sudarśana*).
Refined vision manifests before them, and they mold and transform things without obstruction. This class of beings is called the Śubhakṛtsna (Wholly Pure) Heaven.

This heaven appears to correspond to the superior grade; it seems appropriate that they have severed the nine grades of afflictions of thought associated with the stage of "Purity of Equanimity and Mindfulness.
While the preceding heaven’s essential nature (*tǐ*) was perfected, its functional application (*yòng*) was not yet preeminent; this heaven excels in both essence and function. Therefore—
The first phrase steps upon the wondrous essence of this heaven; the second phrase brings forth its supreme function.
"Molding without obstruction" means that, like Maheśvara, one transforms all myriad things according to the mind, attaining mastery over them—just as a potter fires tiles or a smith melts gold.
Question: Does the Sage also act in the same manner as Māra? Answer: [No.]
Since they share the same *sabhāgatā* (homogeneity), they must likewise possess this capacity alone; how could they both equally exercise greedy power as false rulers?
One who is named "Excellent Manifestation" (*Sudṛśa*) merely indicates the function of possessing the power of transformation. △ The Heaven of Ultimate Form (*Akaniṣṭha*).
Having reached the ultimate limit of the manifold and exhausted the nature of form, one enters the boundless; such a class is called the Heaven of Ultimate Form (Akaniṣṭha).
This heaven appears to be the supreme pinnacle above, and it seems that one should have severed the thirty-six categories within the four stages of the four formless attainments.
Regarding the afflictions of thought (*dhyāna-kleśa*): Question: On what basis is it measured that these [afflictions] are predominantly severed? Answer:

Since it is named "Ultimate Form" (*Akaniṣṭha*), its meaning is defined by the exhaustion of form. Yet, all four formless attainments (*ārūpya*) are ultimately free from form; thus, this is known to be so.

Furthermore, according to the preceding principle where heavy afflictions are severed individually while light afflictions are severed collectively, one may now infer that the very last, most subtle category of a single heaven may be severed collectively.
[The term] "ultimate" (*jiujing*) means thorough investigation and inquiry. *Ji* (the subtle) refers to the minute movement [of thought].
By investigating many thoughts until one reaches a single thought, it is called "ultimate. Regarding the "multitude of *ji*" (*qun ji*), this refers to the mixed cultivation of the five grades.

Initially, one uses many moments of outflow-free (*anāsrava*) wisdom to permeate many moments of outflow-possessing (*sāsrava*) states; this continues until finally, one employs a single moment of outflow-free wisdom.
To perfume a single thought of outflow (sāsrava) is called the "supreme grade. Thus, the *Abhidharmakośa* states: "It is accomplished by a single thought-moment through intermingling.

This is precisely what it means. Question: Does this not contradict what you previously stated—that the former is small and the latter is great? Answer: This [statement from the *Kośa*] refers to the wisdom that effects the severance;

therein, the former is complex and the latter is simplified. My [explanation], however, refers to the afflictions (*kleśa*) to be severed; therein, the former is heavy and the latter is light. It is as follows:
The many thoughts of outflows (āsrava) are surely grave afflictions; thus, one day’s practice alone severs nine grades, after which they gradually diminish.

Is it not the case that those at the very end are the lightest? Moreover, since even light afflictions are further divided into many grades, it is therefore possible for a single day alone to sever them.
As for "exhausting the nature of form," this refers to what Master Yue meant when he said that the mind has been perfumed from much to little.

Form (*rūpa*) likewise exhausts from the coarse to the subtle; this is what is meant. As for the phrase "the nature of nature": ordinary people and non-Buddhists take the ultimate atom (*paramāṇu*) to be the nature of form, which is to say, subtle and yet more subtle.
"Entering the boundless limit" means entering the limit of the four formless realms (*ārūpya*).
"The ultimate of form" means that form reaches its point here where it is purified and exhausted without remainder. This demonstrates the distinct characteristics of the five heavens.
[The preceding section] is concluded. △ Third, the conclusion regarding the four heavens not being seen:
"Ānanda, as for these Non-returner heavens, the various Heavenly Kings of the four stages of the fourth dhyāna merely hear of them with reverence, yet they cannot know or see them.
It is like the vast wildernesses, deep mountains, and sites of the sacred paths in this world today, all of which are inhabited by Arhats."
Because they are sustained [by the power of meditative concentration], they cannot be seen by the coarse people of the world;
this is what is meant by "consciousness-only. It is said that from the Second Dhyāna upward, there is no distinction between kings and ministers.

Regarding the mention of the "four kings," this may refer to those who are honored as preeminent leaders and are thus briefly similar to kings; the others, moreover, do not necessarily correspond to the ministers of the lower realms. Therefore, it can also be so described.

There are kings without ministers; there are those who have heard [the teachings] but lack knowledge and insight. Between the severing of delusions and their suppression, between the untainted (*anāsrava*) and the tainted (*sāsrava*), and between the noble ones (*ārya*) and ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*), the differences are as vast as the distance between the coarse and the subtle.
Therefore, one merely reveres their illustrious names, yet does not know their actual enjoyment (*paribhoga*), nor does one see their primary and secondary environments (*āśraya* and *parivāra*).
The phrase "as in the present day" below takes the human realm as its example. This refers to the sacred site of the Path (*ārya-mārga-caitya*).
Regarding the "grounds" (bhūmi), such as the Bamboo Grove at Tiantai and others, this is the case. Although they are called Arhats, they also include Bodhisattvas.

As with Mount Wutai and Mount Emei, one may only hear of them with reverence but not see them. Because of this, there arises doubt: it seems that in the Five Indias [the sages] merely dwell in the Bṛhatphala Heaven, whereas here in the human realm they are like holy ones who, while heard of with reverence, are not seen.
If the difference between the two were as vast as the distance between heaven and earth, why would this be so?
Thus it is said. Moreover, the Buddha initially spoke only of "within this" and had not yet spoken of "above this," which can still be seen.
This precisely concludes the division of the four *dhyānas*. △ Second, the summary of their inclusion within the Form Realm (*rūpadhātu*).

Ānanda, these eighteen heavens are solitary and without companionship; they have not yet exhausted the burden of form. From this point downward, they are called the Realm of Form (*rūpadhātu*). Gu Shan says:
"Solitary and without companionship" means that both are devoid of emotional desire; "have not yet exhausted the burden of form" means that there is still form present.
Because they are substantial. ○ Furthermore, the preceding phrase clarifies what is abandoned, while the subsequent phrase clarifies where one dwells.

"From here downward" refers to everything from the Heaven of Ultimate Form (*Akaniṣṭha*) down to the Brahma Assembly (*Brahmapāriṣadya*), all of which constitute the Single Realm of Form (*rūpadhātu*).
This concludes the Four Dhyānas. △ The Three and Four Empties. Wēnlíng says: From this point upward, the four heavens of the Formless Realm (*ārūpyadhātu*) are clarified.

Regarding the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*): there is no matter that is the fruit of karma, but there is matter that is the fruit of meditative concentration (*samādhi*). This applies equally to both the primary body and its environment.

Thus, one extinguishes the physical body and returns to the formless state, abandoning the various mixed dwellings of gods and humans; these are not of a single kind, yet all lack the aggregate of form (*rūpaskandha*). The four heavens of this realm all advance by relying on partial emptiness (*ākāśa*):
first, one detests form and relies on space; second, one detests space and relies on consciousness (*vijñāna*); third, [one detests] both form and space and relies on consciousness.

Third, the three cessations rely upon the nature of consciousness. Fourth, relying upon the nature of consciousness, one exhaustively investigates through cessation yet fails to attain true cessation;
these are all merely superior wholesome fruits of the conditioned, which do not transcend saṃsāra and do not constitute the Path of the Sages.
○ Within this context, ordinary worldlings (*pṛthagjana*) who exhaust form and aspire toward emptiness are its primary inhabitants;

those of fixed nature (*niyata-gotra*) who are Śrāvakas reside here as guests, while heterodox outsiders (*tīrthika*) dwell among them in a mixed fashion. This is divided into five sections. △ First, identifying the divergent paths and excluding the noble ones (*ārya*).
Furthermore, Ānanda, from within this limit of form at the Peak of Existence (bhavāgra), there are again two divergent paths.
If one develops wisdom through the mind of equanimity (upekṣā-citta), and the light of wisdom becomes perfectly penetrating, one then transcends the realm of dust and becomes an Arhat.
They enter the Bodhisattva vehicle. This class of individuals is called "Great Arhats who have turned their minds. Wēnlíng says:

"The realm of Form culminates in the heavens of the Form Realm, which borders the Formless Realm; this is called the 'limit of form. All four dhyānas are cultivated based on equanimity and mindfulness;

here, the term 'mind of equanimity' refers to the causal mind of the Peak of Existence (*bhavāgra*). Wŭxīng [says]: [Note: The provided text contains a fragmentary commentary regarding the transition from the Arhat stage to the Bodhisattva path, specifically addressing the meditative states of the Form and Formless Realms.]
It is said: In the Heaven of Ultimate Form (Akaniṣṭha), those who have attained the third fruit are divided into two paths according to whether their faculties are sharp or dull.
Those with sharp faculties give rise to untainted wisdom (anāsrava-jñāna) and, having exhausted all afflictions to be abandoned through cultivation, immediately transcend the triple world.

Those with dull faculties, furthermore, by means of a concentrated mind, rejoice in the higher realms and feel aversion toward the lower ones, thereby being reborn in the formless realm (ārūpyadhātu). "Wisdom" here refers to the wisdom of the emptiness of persons (pudgala-śūnyatā-jñāna). Regarding "contemplation":
When delusions are exhausted and the wisdom of emptiness is fulfilled, it is called the "Perfect Penetration of the Light of Wisdom.

One becomes an Arhat, immediately transcends the three realms, and enters the Bodhisattva vehicle, thereby further departing from mere emptiness. The concluding summary regarding the turning of the mind has two meanings:
first, concerning the Arhat who turns the mind, they turn back their mind that delights in the higher and loathes the lower, thereby suddenly transcending the three realms; second, concerning...
A Bodhisattva who turns back their mind is one who reverses the intention of abandoning the Great Vehicle to grasp the Small Vehicle and swiftly enters the Mahāyāna.
However, this class of person is originally of indeterminate nature (*aniyata-gotra*) and possesses sharp faculties (*tīkṣṇa-indriya*).

By contrast, those of determinate nature (*niyata-gotra*) with dull faculties (*mṛdu-indriya*) enter only the four formless attainments (*catasra ārūpya-samāpattayaḥ*). This is also discussed according to the sequential order; therefore, regarding...
This directly refers to those in the Akaniṣṭha Heaven, describing their entry into the four heavens of the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*).

In reality, ordinary beings, those in the Bṛhatphala heaven, non-Buddhists, and those in the Unconscious Heaven (*asaṃjñisattva*) are all adjacent to the formless realm; all may ascend to enter these four heavens.

Please observe what follows regarding the falling of both sages and ordinary beings, and the intent will become clear. II. The formal enumeration of the four heavens, divided into four parts: 1. The Sphere of Infinite Space (*ākāśānantyāyatana*).
"O Deva,
if one abides in a mind of equanimity, achieves the relinquishing of aversion, perceives the body as an obstruction, and dissolves that obstruction to enter into emptiness—
this class of beings is called the Sphere of Infinite Space."
The first two lines refer back to the preceding heaven; the following two lines clarify the fundamental heaven. Wên-lǐng says:

"To loathe the constraints of one's own form and resolutely cultivate the contemplation of emptiness, so as to extinguish the body and return to non-existence—this is to loathe form and rely upon emptiness. It is called the Sphere of Infinite Space (*ākāśānantyāyatana-samādhi*)."
Therefore, it is called the "retribution-born sphere of infinite space" (*ākāśānantyāyatana*). Changshui says: There are two ways of relinquishing the mind.
First, if one uses the untainted path (*anāsrava-mārga*) at the Peak of Existence (*bhavāgra*) to sever delusions and enter the sphere of space, this refers to the *sukha-vihārin* Anāgāmin.

Second, if one uses the tainted path (*sāsrava-mārga*) at the Fruit of Vastness (*bṛhatphala*) to suppress delusions and enter the sphere of space, this refers to ordinary worldlings (*pṛthagjana*) and non-Buddhists (*tīrthika*). △ Second, the Sphere of Infinite Consciousness (*vijñānānantyāyatana*).
As for the gods of the sphere of infinite space (*ākāśānantyāyatana*):
once all obstructive forms have dissolved, there is neither obstruction nor cessation; therein remains only the *ālayavijñāna* in its entirety and a subtle portion of the *manas*.
This class of beings is called the sphere of infinite consciousness (*vijñānānantyāyatana*).

The first phrase traces back to the characteristics of the fruit of the preceding heaven; the subsequent phrases describe the characteristics of the fruit of the fundamental practice and merit of this present heaven.
Wēnlíng says: "When all obstructions have been eliminated and are no more, one does not rely on form; even the 'non-existence' of non-obstruction is extinguished."
Thus, one does not rely on emptiness, but retains only the *ālayavijñāna* and the *manas*. This refers to those who, weary of emptiness, rely upon consciousness;

it is called the meditative absorption of the sphere of infinite consciousness (*vijñānānantyāyatana-samādhi*). Therefore, when reborn in the sphere of infinite consciousness, there is the eighth consciousness, the *ālaya*, and the seventh consciousness, the *manas*.
Furthermore, the objects of the manas are the three: form, emptiness, and consciousness. In this stage, one becomes weary of form and emptiness and relies upon consciousness;
thus, since the coarse objects of form and emptiness are already absent, only the subtle aspects—the whole and the half—remain. Question:

According to the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi*, the manas does not take external objects as its domain, but rather internally clings to the seeing-part (*darśana-bhāga*) of the eight consciousnesses as the self. Why then does Master Huan say that it [also]...?
"Conditioned by the emptiness of form. Answer: "Seven [factors] are conditioned by the emptiness of form; certainly, this principle does not hold.
However, since one internally clings to the *ālayavijñāna* as self, one also spontaneously clings externally to form as other.

Therefore, if the emptiness of form were present, the entire manas would be present together with it. Now that the emptiness of form has ceased, only half of the manas enters into the subtle state. Question: "Manas..."
As for that *ālayavijñāna*, Arhats have not yet realized it; how then can ordinary beings, non-Buddhists, or *anāgāmins* know it? The answer is:
this is something the Tathāgata perceives with clear and penetrating vision, and thus bestows a name upon it; it is not granted that they themselves possess such knowledge.

In their state, they simply consider themselves to have transcended form and emptiness, believing this to be the true nature (*dharmatā*). Their delusion is similar to that of the *asaṃjñisattvas*. As the *Lotus Sūtra* says: "Sentient beings abide in..."
The various stages are known only by the Tathāgata as they truly are. This is so. △ Third, the Heaven of Nothingness:
Since both space and form have perished, the consciousness-mind is entirely extinguished; the ten directions are silent and utterly devoid of any destination. Such is this class of beings.
This is called the Sphere of Nothingness (*ākiṃcanyāyatana*).

The first phrase refers back to the fruit of the preceding heaven; the second phrase refers to the cause and fruit of descending to this present heaven. "Consciousness" (*vijñāna*) here refers to the aforementioned *manas* and *ālaya-vijñāna*.

As for the statement that they are "completely extinguished," it means that by relying on profound meditative power (*samādhi-bala*), the active manifestations (*pravṛtti*) of these two consciousnesses are both suppressed and do not function.
For example, the non-conceptual state (*asaṃjñi-samāpatti*) suppresses six [consciousnesses] for five hundred eons, whereas this [attainment] suppresses them for sixty thousand eons. Question:

What is the mode of their active manifestation (*samudācāra*), and how is their cessation? Answer: When the seventh [manas-consciousness] conditions the eighth [ālaya-vijñāna], such that the subject and object are clearly distinct, this is called "active manifestation.

This is precisely when the aforementioned preceding states further advance into a profound meditative concentration (*samādhi*), whereby the subject and object of perception cease; this is temporarily termed "total cessation" (*sarva-nirodha*). That is to say:
This refers to this [state of] heaven; therefore, one should know that this "cessation" does not mean the simultaneous severance of both seeds and manifestations as it does for an Arhat.

"Tranquil and without destination" refers to the realized realm within the meditative absorption of the cessation of consciousness (*nirodha-samāpatti*), which is vast and profound, such that one can no longer proceed further.
This is the point where non-Buddhists are deluded into regarding it as the "Principle of Obscurity" (*tattva*). The final phrase designates its name as "Form" (*rūpa*).
The three realms of emptiness and consciousness are all non-existent. △ Fourth, the Heaven of Neither-Perception-Nor-Non-Perception:
the nature of consciousness is unmoving; by extinguishing and exhausting investigation within the inexhaustible, one proclaims the nature of exhaustion. It is as if existing, yet not existing.
If that which is exhausted is not exhausted, such a category is called the Sphere of Neither-Perception-Nor-Non-Perception (*naivasaṃjñānāsaṃjñāyatana*).

Master Huan saw in this statement that the nature of consciousness (*vijñānatva*) is immovable; therefore, he said that in the preceding heavens one merely loses the mind of consciousness (*vijñānacitta*), but does not lose the nature of consciousness (*vijñānatva*).

He did not examine how the nature of the mind could be divided to the extent of reaching this point. Furthermore, his interpretation of the nature of consciousness as the "profound root" (*youben*) is also [incomplete].

Examine what constitutes the profound root. If one takes the active consciousness (*vijñāna*) as the manifest activity and the nature of consciousness (*vijñānatva*) as the seed, this seems reasonable.
However, it is the seeds that slumber and dwell within the storehouse consciousness (*ālayavijñāna*) that truly constitute the profound, immovable root.

This is because ordinary beings and non-Buddhists have not yet embraced the Buddha’s dharma-gate for severing the seeds, and even *anāgāmins* have not yet exhausted their afflictions of thought; thus, they all perceive [the ālayavijñāna] as firm and solid.

It cannot be moved or shaken. Regarding the phrase "exhausting and investigating through cessation": this means forcibly relying on the power of the meditative concentration of cessation (*nirodha-samāpatti*) to exhaust it until nothing remains and to investigate it until it is thoroughly penetrated.
The following two lines judge that it ultimately cannot be exhausted; there are two meanings to this.

First, if one considers the fundamental substance of the *ālayavijñāna*, which is the *tathāgatagarbha* nature, then there is no principle by which either ordinary beings or sages could exhaust it. Second, if...
Regarding the seeds: since both ordinary beings and non-Buddhists lack the dharma of abandonment, their [defilements] can never be exhausted.

Furthermore, the Anāgāmin possesses dull faculties and is likewise not at the stage of exhaustion. Yet, in this heaven, those with initial resolve all forcefully exert themselves to manifest the desire to exhaust their nature;
however, this cannot be achieved. All that has been described above constitutes the causes for being born in this heaven, as well as the functional effort employed therein.

Furthermore, the following two lines refer precisely to the fruit of abiding in this heaven. This is because, regarding the two consciousnesses, they are like a dying lamp—half-extinguished and half-burning.
This is truly due to being constrained by the meditative absorption of cessation (*nirodha-samāpatti*); thus, while it exists, it does not exist, resembling a lamp that is half-extinguished.
Yet, because the substance of the seeds remains unmoved, it is neither exhausted nor non-exhausted, resembling a lamp that is half-burning. [End of] the final section.

Later, Master Huan inherited [the teaching] that "existence is non-existence" to establish the Sphere of Neither-Perception-Nor-Non-Perception (naivasaṃjñānāsaṃjñāyatana), and he inherited that "exhaustion is non-exhaustion" to establish the Sphere of Neither-Perception-Nor-Non-Perception.
Thus he grasped the underlying logic of these terms; for "neither-perception" is simply "not having perception," and "neither-non-perception" is simply "not being without perception.
Having thus completed the formal enumeration of the four heavens: △ Third, the emergence and fall of the holy and the ordinary.

These individuals exhaust emptiness but do not fully realize the principle of emptiness. Among those who have reached the ultimate through the noble path from the Heaven of No-Return, there is a certain class known as the "dull-witted Arhats who do not turn their minds.
Furthermore, there are those from among the non-Buddhist heavens of the Unconscious who exhaust emptiness and do not return.
Deluded, leaking, and lacking learning, they enter into the cycle of rebirth.

This section specifically clarifies that when eighty thousand kalpas are completed for those dwelling in the state of non-conception (*asaṃjñin*), those of the noble class immediately emerge from the three realms, while those of the ordinary class fall back into saṃsāra;
each has its own terminal phase. The old commentaries fail to comprehend this entirely, thereby negating the *pratisaṃvid*.
Han [Shi] still treats this as the *anāgāmin* fruit and explains only the latter half [of the verse], merely negating the *asaṃjñisattva*.

This is utterly irrelevant to the essential point; it is extremely groundless. Please examine my current interpretation in detail: the first two lines universally judge the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*), encompassing both the noble ones (*ārya*) and ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*).

These are precisely the *asaṃjñisattva* and so forth—those who previously exhausted emptiness. In the first heaven, they exhaust form (*rūpa*) to cause its dissolution; in the second heaven, they exhaust emptiness (*śūnyatā*).

He causes them to be non-existent. In the third heaven, he exhausts consciousness to cause its cessation; in the fourth heaven, he exhausts nature to cause its exhaustion. Thus, the first two exhaust the object, while the latter two exhaust the mind.
Because he seeks to render both mind and object empty, they are collectively termed "exhausting emptiness. As for those who do not fully realize the principle of emptiness:

ordinary people and externalists have not yet understood the principle of the emptiness of persons, and the lesser sages have not yet attained the principle of the emptiness of phenomena—how much less so [others]?
The principle of the Perfect and Sudden Teaching is that the mind and its objects are fundamentally empty; how could they require further extinction?
Therefore, [the text] simply states that they have not yet attained full realization. As for the subsequent distinction between the holy and the ordinary, or those who fall away and those who do not:

regarding those who dwell in the Realm of Neither-Perception-Nor-Non-Perception, if they originally came from the Five Indies to cultivate the holy path, then when these eighty thousand kalpas are completed, their afflictions of thought...
Having exhausted [all outflows], he immediately transcends the three realms and becomes an Arhat. Regarding the statement that his mind does not turn back, there are two meanings.
If one traces it to the past, it is to reproach him for not having earlier turned his heart toward joy and aversion at the Peak of Existence (bhavāgra) to quickly achieve Arhatship.
If one examines it in light of the future, it clarifies that he will certainly not turn his heart back toward the realm of emptiness.
Regarding the Bodhisattva Vehicle: this refers to those śrāvakas of fixed nature, not those of the previously mentioned indeterminate nature.

Furthermore, they are said to be "dull-witted" because they have passed through all four heavens; compared to those of sharp faculties, they have practiced for many more than two million *kalpas*. Question:

Previously, at the Peak of Existence (*bhavāgra*), it was determined that their afflictions of thought (*vitarka-kleśa*) were completely severed. I do not understand why these people [are still] in the four [heavens].
What is cultivated and abandoned in the heavens? Answer: The previous [discussion] was based on those of sharp faculties; how could those of dull faculties be the same?

When those of dull faculties are in the five heavens, they abandon the delusions of the first four heavens in the same manner as those of sharp faculties. Upon reaching the fifth heaven, they no longer possess a mind of longing for the higher or aversion to the lower;

they merely apply effort to eliminate obstacles and seek birth in the four formless realms (ārūpyadhātu). As for the delusions of the latter half [of the path], they expect to abandon them in those heavens.

Accordingly, the four *āryasatyas* and the four *dhyānas* should each sever nine grades at every stage; thus, it is only when the *asaṃjñisattva-āyatana* (the sphere of non-perception) kalpa is completed that they are exhausted.
By this standard, the highest single grade must be connected to the Peak of Existence (*bhavāgra*), encompassing all five heavens.
One should infer it to be so; let us wait for further reference. This concludes the explanation of how the noble ones emerge. Next, the falling of ordinary beings will be explained.
Regarding those who dwell in the Sphere of Neither-Perception-Nor-Non-Perception (*naivasaṃjñānāsaṃjñāyatana*):

if they originally came from the Heaven of No-Thought (*asaṃjñisattva*) or the Heaven of Vast Fruit (*bṛhatphala*), having merely cultivated impure meditative concentrations (*sāsrava-dhyāna*) until the exhaustion of their emptiness, then when eighty thousand kalpas are fulfilled, they will have no place of refuge.

One would immediately fall back into saṃsāra. Question: The later sutras state that those who falsely cling to the state of non-conception as nirvāṇa slander the Buddha at the time of death and fall into hell;
why then do they now reach the Heaven of Neither-Perception-Nor-Non-Perception? Answer: Master Yue [correctly] attributes this precisely to such delusion.

Yet you claim that [the Unconceivable] does not come; this fails to understand what is stated in the subsequent sutra. It may simply be that such a case occurs at certain times, but since the capacities and natures of beings are ten thousandfold, how could it be so for every single one?
Question: When the Buddha speaks of "various non-Buddhist heavens," how is it known that these also include the Bṛhatphala (Great Fruit) heaven?

Answer: Ordinarily, when contrasted with the Buddha, the vehicle of the heavens is considered internal teaching, whereas the Heaven of No-Thought (Asaṃjñisattva) alone is classified as a non-Buddhist path.
Now, in the presence of the Buddha, the Hīnayāna is considered the internal teaching; therefore, all the devas are collectively called "outsiders" (tīrthikas).
To say they do not "return" means that they have exclusively pursued the ultimate emptiness and no longer turn their minds to submit to the Noble Vehicle.

Having reached this point where strength is exhausted and the path is at its end, with nowhere left to rely upon, they can only fall downward. Furthermore, the phrase "deluded, leaking, and without hearing" is [the reason] for their emergence.

This is done to expose their transgressions as a warning to those who follow. It is said that they specifically fell into this state because, being deluded regarding the causes of outflows (*āsrava*), they mistook them for the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*);
lacking extensive learning (*bahuśruta*), they committed the error of exerting themselves only in minor practices.

Thus, having reached this point, they find no refuge and fall directly downward. From this, one should know that the aforementioned "dull arhats who do not turn their minds" also exposed their own faults.
This is a warning. It means that he specifically failed to turn his mind back early, which resulted in his dullness; it was only after a long time that he achieved success.
Contemplate this meaning in detail. △ Fourth, the general classification of ordinary beings and sages.
Ānanda, these various devas and their respective celestial beings are all ordinary persons receiving the retribution of their karmic fruits;

when that retribution is exhausted, they enter the cycle of rebirth. Those heavenly kings, however, are bodhisattvas who dwell in samādhi, gradually advancing along the path of practice dedicated toward the ranks of the sages.
The preceding section merely judged the matter of the ultimate exhaustion of both non-percipient beings and sages.

This [present] section, however, universally judges the devas currently dwelling within the three realms—distinguishing who is ordinary and who is sage—and thus serves as a general summary of all these heavens; it should properly follow the preceding section.

This was erroneously placed here instead of within the preceding "General Conclusion" section. "Heavenly beings and humans" refers to ministers and subjects. Regarding "the retribution of karmic fruits":
the ten wholesome actions and the eight dhyānas constitute actual meritorious deeds, and the fruits of the six desire heavens and the four dhyāna realms are what serve as their retribution.
As for "all who exhaust [their merit] enter the wheel," this refers to what Yongjia said: "When momentum is spent, the arrow returns."
[This refers to] falling. Question: Since there is no evil in the upper realms, why is it that some fall directly into the three miserable destinies?

Answer: The various seeds within the *ālayavijñāna* have not been forgotten for distant eons; they ripen in succession and cannot be bypassed. Now that the retribution of heavenly merit has ended, one falls spontaneously according to those ripened seeds.
How could one avoid the three miserable destinies? This is why the Tathāgata earnestly exhorts us to maintain mindfulness.
The Buddha [taught] by way of transverse emergence (*tiryag-gati*). The gradual increase refers to the Sage’s entrusting of cultivation and progress.

However, as for the assignment of the Bodhisattva stages to the various Heavenly Kings, the various sutras differ in their doctrinal approaches, resulting in discrepancies in names and positions; I do not dare to establish a definitive system.
Master Huan cites the third stage of the *Avataṃsaka-sūtra* as corresponding to the Heavenly Kings, yet even this is merely a broad approximation. I recall the system established by Tiantai:
Detailed [explanation]. I shall permit further examination and determination. △ Fifth, the summary of the inclusion within the formless realm:
"Ānanda, in these four heavens of the formless realm, body and mind are extinguished; the nature of stability manifests before one, and there is no form resulting from karmic fruit.
From this point until the end, it is called the Formless Realm."

In the first two heavens, both body and objects are entirely absent; hence it is said that "the body ceases. In the latter two heavens, the seventh and eighth consciousnesses are both suppressed and do not manifest;

hence it is said that "the mind is extinguished. As for the manifestation of the nature of meditative concentration (*samāpatti-svabhāva*), this refers to the time when one is actually in concentration.

There is the matter resulting from concentration (*samādhi-phala-rūpa*), which the Master [Xuanzang] cited from the *Viniścayasaṃgrahaṇī* as "matter produced by the mastery of concentration" (*samādhi-vaśitā-janita-rūpa*). This is because...
They freely enjoy the transformation of the environment and its inhabitants (the *niśraya* and *adhiṣṭhāna*). Regarding those who lack the form resulting from karma (*karmaphala-rūpa*):

at the time of emerging from meditative absorption, both body and mind are tranquil, and both the environment and its inhabitants are empty. When observed with the eyes of a sage, the three-footed consciousness-spirit appears like the intermediate state (*antarābhava*).

"From here until the end" refers to the progression from the first heaven up to the fourth heaven. As for designating these as "formless" (*ārūpya*), it is merely based on the power of meditative concentration;

for two hundred thousand *kalpas*, there is temporarily no reliance upon either the physical body or the environment. This does not mean that the aggregates have truly become empty such that karmic fruits are forever severed.
Having completed the formal listing of the various heavens: △ Second, the general conclusion of the preceding section.
All of this arises from failing to understand the wondrously enlightened and luminous mind; through the accumulation of delusions, the three realms of existence are produced.
Within these realms, deluded individuals (*pudgala*) follow their various destinies, sinking and drowning within the seven paths of rebirth according to their respective types.

This encompasses everything from the six realms of desire up to the Sphere of Neither-Perception-Nor-Non-Perception. The wondrously enlightened, luminous mind is that which, in its proximity, is fully present within the sense faculties, and, in its extension, encompasses all phenomena.

It is called "wondrous" because it is fundamentally free from the consciousness of birth and death; it is called "enlightened" because it is fundamentally free from the dullness and rigidity of form and emptiness;
it is called "luminous" because it is fundamentally free from the obstructions of ignorance and delusion. Though it is presently manifest, one does not perceive it oneself.
Therefore, it is said that they do not understand. The two lines concerning the accumulation of delusions refer to the fact that for long kalpas they have been attached to grasping and rejecting;
thus, the three realms are eternally established as truly existent, and they remain in a great, long-lasting dream. The middle two lines serve as the conclusion regarding these various heavens.

It is said that although the various devas exert their power and effort at will, because they have not specifically clarified the mind, they ultimately cannot escape drowning together in birth and death;
they are likewise termed "those of the seven destinies. [The author] deeply pities them and displays this as a warning. The final two lines clarify the reason for the classification.
*Pudgala* (補特伽羅) here means "one who repeatedly takes up existence," which refers to the intermediate state (*antarābhava*). This is because it is able to repeatedly...
They take birth and assume bodies within the various realms; thus they are so named. This refers specifically to the devas.
Among the devas, those who possess bodies and share similar karma take birth together, each forming a single group; for this reason, the text repeatedly speaks of "a class of such beings.
The section on the realm of the devas is concluded. △ Seventh, the realm of the asuras. According to the Buddha’s introductory discourse, all seven realms proceed from...
The inferior inclines toward the superior; this realm possesses both superiority and inferiority and is subsumed within the four destinies (*gati*), and thus it is situated here.
According to the judgment of the root sūtra regarding *sabhāgatā* (homogeneity), it refers merely to the abodes of the gods of the empty space and water.
Master Yue cites the Āgama, stating that within Mount Vajra in Jambudvīpa there is a palace of the asuras, with railings, rows of trees, and so forth, extending for six thousand *yojanas*.
Nevertheless, they undergo suffering three times throughout each day and night; the instruments of torment come of their own accord into their palaces.

I have also frequently seen this within the *Āgama* collections. It is likely that those who possess supernatural powers and enter the void do the same: they roam through the empty space in the morning and return here to dwell at night.
Otherwise, they would be of the same class as the inferior beings who are scattered across the earth. Furthermore—
This section shall be left blank for future verification. It is divided into two parts. First, the general enumeration of names and numbers:
Furthermore, Ānanda, within these three realms, there are four further classes of asuras.
Because they are subsumed together under this [category], the three realms are designated collectively; however, in reality, they reside only within the Desire Realm (*kāmadhātu*).
Master Huan translated the name as "Non-Gods" (*asura*), stating that they possess much anger and enjoy celestial fortune yet lack celestial conduct. He also remarked that they are not upright.
