"Investigation" means greeting [the mind]. "Transparency" means that when stillness reaches its ultimate limit, light penetrates through. "Unconfused refined radiance" means...
The light of the mind is concentrated and stabilized, not shifted by conditions of brightness or darkness. "Suddenly, below" refers to seeing objects within the midst of darkness.
The previous mention of "various objects" does not refer to items already present in the room, but rather to extraordinary objects that appear in the dark.
This is because ghosts, spirits, and malevolent apparitions constantly dwell in close proximity to human habitation, yet they do not see one another; now, [they appear].
It is because when the light of the mind becomes secretly clear and profound obscurities are revealed, various manifestations appear.
I have heard that once someone, while in a quiet room, suddenly saw one person emerge from the floor and another come from within the wall;
they conversed for a long time and then each vanished back to their original place. There were also those who saw three or five naked figures, as tall as—
"Two chi. He stealthily took rice from within the room as if no one were there; such instances could not be fully enumerated.

Furthermore, as this mind enters perfectly into the void and the harmonious fusion, the four limbs suddenly become like grass and wood; even if burned by fire or hacked by a blade, [they remain unaffected].
One is never conscious of anything; furthermore, the firelight cannot burn or scorch, and even if one cuts the flesh, it is as if carving wood.
This is called the merging of the sensory objects and the exclusive entry of the nature of the four great elements into purity. To attain such a state for a time is not a realization of sainthood.

Not giving rise to the thought of being a sage is called a "wholesome state"; if one forms a conception of being a sage, one immediately succumbs to various delusions. Regarding "perfectly entering equality":

through the intense power of the practice of "hearing inwardly," one reaches the ultimate of empty fusion; forgetting the body as if it were discarded, one thus remains unaware even of being burned or cut.
Furthermore, although the subsequent passage is repetitive, it is slightly different: in the former case, one was unaware of the burning of the skin.
It is not necessarily the case that there is no injury to the flesh. Here, it means that the skin and flesh cannot be burned and are for the most part free from injury or destruction.

The previous statement said "chopped but not pared"; this statement says "pared away like mud. This is the distinction between them. The three phrases following "dust" (*rajas*) together set forth the reason why one does not perceive the absence of injury;
this is what Master Huan meant by "the five dusts are simultaneously extinguished and the four elements are cast off."

Because their pure awareness has cast off the body, they are not subject to injury or contact. The preceding six and seventh sections concern matters pertaining most closely to the bodies and environments of this land.

It fills the entire realm of space; the towers and palaces are magnificent and splendid. Looking down, one sees the hells; looking up, one observes the celestial palaces, attaining unobstructed vision.

Regarding the tenth category: within this Great Samādhi, one is not moved by the nine preceding objects. One exerts all effort in exhaustive investigation until reaching the stage of ultimate refinement and perfection;
this is precisely the moment when one’s mind merges perfectly with the minds of the sages. At this point, the aggregate of form (rūpa-skandha) is about to be shattered;
it trembles and vibrates, and the demonic mind becomes wild and overbearing, converging at this very time. Therefore, demons cause disturbances.
It is from this point that they initiate their attack. Yet, they do not exceed two methods: either they provoke false views or they provoke wild wisdom;
both can cause the practitioner to doubt their own realization of sainthood (*ārya*). Thereafter, they seize the opportunity and enter by exploiting the interval.
Therefore, I shall now present their characteristics and clarify their underlying causes so that you may be forewarned. However—
The sequence of this text is inverted and somewhat difficult to distinguish. Let us attempt to divide it: "Seeing the virtuous one" (*jì shàn*) and below refers to the manifestation of deluded views.
The first four lines first demonstrate their characteristics. "Seeing the virtuous one" (*jì shàn zhī shí děng*) refers to what the practitioner sees for themselves in stillness.
"The transformation of physical form" (*xíng tǐ biàn qiān děng*) refers to the manifested appearance of Buddhas and Bodhisattvas.
These are images of devas, nāgas, and their male and female attendants. The following two lines clarify the reason for this.

Regarding "those with deviant minds harboring demonic influences": this means that it is simply because the practitioner’s mind was not guarded with sufficient secrecy that they received false objects;
thus, ghostly spirits deluded them, manifesting these illusory shadows rather than a true vision of the sages. The phrase "or encountering" below refers to the arousal of their mad wisdom.
The first two lines first clarify the cause. "The celestial Māra enters the mind" means that the Māra enters the practitioner’s body and takes hold of their mental spirit.
The subsequent two lines later demonstrate its characteristics. "Expounding the Dharma and attaining the subtle" refers to the practitioner speaking of themselves;
all of this is caused by the Māra’s power taking hold of them, rather than being a genuine opening of the mind.

Furthermore, this passage and the subsequent statement, "This is not a sign of saintly realization," are consistent in their logical structure. The traditional interpretation that "good spiritual friends" (kalyāṇamitra) refers exclusively to actual realized persons is untenable;
for instance, when it later says, "The flying spirits who take possession of people and preach the Dharma," it likewise points to such [false] teachings as not being signs of saintly realization.
Moreover, to claim that this also contradicts the preceding passages would be entirely unreasonable. One should...
Know this: as the practitioner applies effort, progressing from the shallow to the deep, demonic influences begin to cause disturbances, starting subtly and becoming increasingly manifest.

Therefore, during this stage and the subsequent ten objects of the *vedanā-skandha* (feeling aggregate), these influences first enter the mind in secret, causing internal agitation to arise spontaneously.

It is not until the *saṃjñā-skandha* (perception aggregate) that they manifest by attaching themselves to others to openly deceive and delude them. How could such overt deception exist at the very beginning of their emergence?
This is indeed the arrival of actual persons sent to cause delusion and confusion. The text below states: "If one relies on this prior awakening, the demons will naturally subside;
conversely, if one acts otherwise, demonic activities will break out in full force—this need not even be stated. The ten intermediate objects have now been concluded.
△ Part Three: The Section on Entrusting Protection against the Three Hindrances. First, showing the mutual interaction of causes:
"Ānanda, these ten kinds of manifest states in dhyāna are all due to the mutual interaction of the mind with the aggregate of form (rūpa-skandha);
therefore, these phenomena appear."
"Intermingling" refers to what the Master Yue called the "intermingling battle between dhyāna-observation and the deluded thoughts of the various aggregates.

This means they contend with one another for victory or defeat. For instance, when each wholesome state arises within the aggregate of form (*rūpa*), this is a momentary victory of the power of observation over deluded thought;
thus, the light of the mind is briefly revealed. However, as it merely opens for a moment before closing again, this is actually deluded thought once more.
The power of his superior contemplation remains unmoved. Therefore, the ten objects of the preceding stage all manifest at this time;
the subsequent stages are all released from this. △ Second, delusion leads to harm.

"Obstinate" refers to a lack of knowledge; "deluded" refers to inverted perceptions. "Not weighing oneself" means not assessing whether one's own capacity has been developed for long enough.
"Deluded and failing to recognize oneself" means further failing to examine how [the mind] briefly opens and then closes again—how then could there be any realization of the holy?

Thus, they stubbornly claim to have attained sainthood; how could they avoid falling [into error]? Hereafter, all cases shall be treated according to this principle. Examine the ten objects previously mentioned; they are all...
This is impelled by profound meditative concentration; it must certainly reside within the stage of contemplative practice (*vipaśyanā-caryā*), and cannot be achieved through mere names and words.
△ Third, the entrustment to protect:
"After the Tathāgata’s parinirvāṇa, you all should rely upon this and proclaim this meaning during the Dharma-ending age (*paścima-dharma*). Do not allow the heavenly Māras..."

To "attain their skillful means" and "maintain and protect them so that they may accomplish the Unsurpassed Way" means that those who rely upon the Tathāgata should practice according to the intent of his proclamations and protections.

"Proclamation" refers to the compilation and dissemination [of the teachings], as well as manifesting in person to preach the Dharma, thereby causing others to understand for themselves. "Protection" refers to the secret bestowal of spiritual power (*adhiṣṭhāna*).
This is to prevent them from falling into delusion. Hereafter, all [sections] shall follow this format. The signs of the māra of the aggregate of form (*rūpa-skandha*) are now complete.

II. The signs of the māra of the aggregate of sensation (*vedanā-skandha*). This is also divided into three sections. First, a full demonstration of its beginning and end, which is further divided into two.
First, the initial stage before the boundaries have been broken through, which is further divided into two. First, following upon the signs of the exhaustion of the aggregate of form.
Ānanda, when that son of good family, while practicing samādhi and śamatha, has exhausted the aggregate of form (rūpa-skandha),
he perceives the minds of all Buddhas appearing like reflections manifested within a clear mirror.

The cultivation of the three and two lines refers to the simultaneous practice of *śamatha* (calm abiding) and *vipaśyanā* (insight). The "gate of the ear" is the contemplation of entering the stream and the cessation of forgetting objects.

Regarding the phrase "the aggregate of form is exhausted": this means that among the ten aforementioned realms (*viṣaya*), one may have fully experienced them, not fully experienced them, or encountered more instances of similar types.
In general, it is essential to clearly recognize these so as not to be deluded by them. When one's practice reaches its culmination, [the aggregate of form is exhausted].
When the aggregate of form (*rūpa-skandha*) suddenly reaches its end, all that follows is explained by this statement.
This refers to the previous analogy of a person with clear vision in a vast dark room; reaching this point, it becomes entirely filled with light—this is the characteristic of the exhaustion of form.
This was already explained in detail below the passage "the ten directions open wide. Regarding the two lines beginning with "seeing all," Master Huan says: "The minds of all Buddhas are my own."
The wondrously enlightened, luminous mind is precisely this. Its characteristic is that it is opened wide and free from darkness.
Sentient beings run their thoughts outward, attempting to fathom the Buddha-mind, yet in the end they cannot see it. Now, one sees it within the opening of one’s own mind;
since it fundamentally does not exist outside, is this not intimate and clear? Therefore, it is likened to an image appearing in a mirror. (As stated in Fascicle Eight)

The second stage is determined by gradual progression. Having already entered the first stage of faith (*śraddhā*), one no longer relies on the previous classification of remaining in the stage of contemplative practice (*darśana-bhāvanā-mārga*).
Because of these explicit words, one personally beholds the Buddha-mind as images appear in a mirror; how could this not be the arising of true faith?
Moreover, the Buddha-mind is precisely the mind of *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.
When the various masters determine the stages of cultivation, they all take the arousal of the bodhicitta as the first stage of faith (*śraddhā*). How could this not be the first stage of faith?
Furthermore, there is an objection to be raised, which shall be examined again later under the section on the sixty noble stages. 2. Describing the realm of the *skandha* of sensation.
If there is something attained yet one is unable to employ it— just like a person suffering from sleep paralysis whose hands and feet are perfectly present and whose sight and hearing are unconfused,
yet whose mind is possessed by an external malevolent spirit so that they cannot move— this is called the domain of the aggregate of sensation (vedanā-skandha).
If there is something attained, since it is one's own mind and yet is directly perceived, how could this not mean that its substance has been truly attained?
As for "being unable to employ it," this means that one has not yet been able to give rise to sovereign function in accordance with that substance.

The following section demonstrates the place of its application; below, it is clarified through a metaphor: a person who is suffering from a nightmare while asleep clearly perceives the state of being awake.
Yet one cannot move. This is just like the state where the aggregate of form (*rūpa-skandha*) has already opened, but the aggregate of sensation (*vedanā-skandha*) covers a person.
The two phrases concerning the hands and feet are a metaphor for having something attained; the two phrases concerning the mind and touch are a metaphor for being unable to employ [it].

As for "guest-demons" (*kṣetrapati*), the character for "demon" (*yàn*) includes the radical for "ghost" (*guǐ*); it seems that this occurs because one is externally overwhelmed and oppressed by ghostly entities. Therefore...
The nightmare-demon (*yāma-ghost*) serves as a metaphor for the aggregate of sensation (*vedanā-skandha*). △ Second, the final destruction of the manifest source of delusion:
If the affliction of the nightmare ceases, the mind departs from the body and looks back at its own face; it becomes free to go or stay, no longer subject to obstruction.

This is called the exhaustion of the aggregate of sensation (*vedanā-skandha*). Such a person is then able to transcend the turbidity of views (*dṛṣṭi-kaṣāya*). Observing its origin, one finds that empty, luminous false thinking (*vikalpa*) is its root.

The first phrase refers to the exhaustion of the aggregate of sensation; the subsequent part, "its mind below," refers to the ability to give rise to sovereign function. The mind is fundamentally... [not inherently existent].

It is confined within the body. Beginningless deluded attachment takes what is not confined and confines it. At birth, one is confined to the manifest aggregate; at death, one is confined to the intermediate state (*antarābhava*).
There is no time when one is not confined by the body. How, then, could there be a state of freedom apart from the body?

In all cases, sensation (*vedanā*) serves as the root of bondage. Therefore, as soon as sensation is exhausted, one immediately leaves the body and contemplates the face, attaining freedom in going and staying.
You should know that this is not the same as passing away while seated and being unable to return;

in that case, one merely passes away while seated by relying on the power of meditative concentration within the preceding state of obscurity. This is why Jiufeng did not approve of the Head Seat Taixian.

This means that both form and sensation are opened up together, and both essence and function are designated as such; there is no obstruction regarding the past or the future. Dongshan Faqing and others were precisely such people.
The view of a self-body (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*) is the root of all views; when sensation is exhausted, one is detached from the body, and the view of a self-body is liberated.
Thus, one is able to transcend the turbidity of views (*dṛṣṭi-kaṣāya*). Only then, through direct perception, does one personally realize that the fundamental mind does not reside within the body;

it is merely the aggregate of sensation (*vedanā-skandha*) that falsely functions as reception, manifesting in vain. Based on the previous analysis, its stage corresponds to the second and third levels of the two stages of faith (*śraddhā*).
This shall be further examined below, at the beginning of the aggregate of perception (*saṃjñā-skandha*), among the sixty holy positions. [End of] volume.

The exposition of the beginning and the end is now complete. △ Second, the ten characteristics of the intermediate stage. Within these ten characteristics, they are explained by dividing them into five pairs of dyads.

This is further divided into ten sections. First, suppressing oneself and giving rise to compassion. This corresponds to the subsequent section on suppressing and exalting oneself and the Buddha respectively.
Thus, "suppressing oneself" means to suppress and reproach one's own self; "giving rise to compassion" means to feel pity and sympathy for sentient beings.
Furthermore, there are three [stages]. First, the manifestation of signs at the commencement:
Ānanda, that good man, while in this state, shall attain a great radiance.

His mind becomes luminously clear, yet because he exerts excessive internal restraint, he suddenly experiences boundless compassion toward all things therein, even regarding mosquitoes and insects as if they were... [as if they were]... his own kin.
A feeling of compassion arose in his heart, and he involuntarily shed tears.
This state is precisely when the aggregate of form (rūpa-skandha) has already opened, yet the aggregate of sensation (vedanā-skandha) has not yet been shattered.
"Attaining a great radiance" means that the ten directions have opened up clearly. "His mind becoming luminous" refers to the realization that all sentient beings are identical [to himself].
Possessing such sublime principles of luminosity, one suffers in vain through drowning.

As for those who excessively suppress their inner [afflictions], they instead reproach themselves for their own persistent delusions and for not having awakened early enough to deliver sentient beings; this is how compassion arises.

To investigate and discuss this thoroughly, it is fundamentally the compassion of shared essence (*sahaja-karuṇā*), which is inherently not at fault. However, regarding the excessive suppression of internal observations and so forth, these lead to successive errors.
If it is excessive, it will lead to the onset of demonic possession. △ Second, awakening through the teachings of name and instruction:

This refers to the application of effort that suppresses and overcomes transgressions. If one awakens to this, there is no fault; yet it is not a holy realization. Through clear understanding, one remains free from delusion.
It subsides and ceases of its own accord after a long time.
Regarding the suppression and crushing of excessive effort: this was originally intended to arouse compassion and exert oneself in order to shatter the aggregate of sensation (*vedanā-skandha*).
However, because one suppresses and reproaches oneself too excessively, losing the quality of compassionate gentleness, it results in excessive sorrow. If one can awaken to this original intent...

Because one does not conceive the thought of having attained a holy realization, there is gradual awakening and gradual cessation, and one returns once more to right mindfulness; therefore it is said that "after a long time, [delusion] will dissipate.
△ Third, showing that delusion inevitably leads to a fall.
If one takes this to be a realization of the holy, then the demon of pity will enter one's heart and inner organs;
upon seeing others, one will feel pity and weep boundlessly, losing correct meditative absorption and falling into ruin.

Those who form a "sacred understanding" claim for themselves that they have already become equal to the great compassion of all Buddhas, or that they share the same sorrowful longing as the two supreme types of Bodhisattvas.
Believing themselves to be correct, their pity and concern do not cease;

consequently, Māra enters their minds through such affinities, causing them to lose their concentration and give rise to immeasurable inverted and false thoughts. Therefore, they will inevitably fall. This applies even to those who have already entered the stages.

[If one] does not guard [the mind], one will sink into its depths. Therefore, within the *saṃjñā-skandha* (aggregate of perception), there is greedy seeking. This shall be analyzed in detail below under the section on "Skillful Means. **2.
Exalting Oneself as Equal to the Buddha.** "Exalting oneself" means loftily elevating one's own spiritual essence. "Equal to the Buddha" means suddenly becoming identical with the Ultimate Sage.
This is further divided into three parts: 1. Initiating the Topic and Manifesting Signs.

Ānanda, furthermore, within that state of meditative concentration, those good sons perceive the aggregate of form (*rūpaskandha*) dissolving and the aggregate of sensation (*vedanāskandha*) becoming clear and luminous.
As superior signs manifest before them, they are moved with excessive intensity; suddenly, amidst this state, they give rise to boundless courage.
Their minds become fierce and sharp, and their resolve becomes equal to that of the Buddhas, claiming that the three *asaṃkhyeya-kalpas* can be transcended in a single thought-moment.
"Form opens up the clarity of sensation" means that it is like removing an outer garment to clearly see the inner garment.

"Superior signs" refers to seeing the Buddha’s mind, such as the manifestation of images within a mirror. "Being moved beyond measure" means that although one has consistently heard that the mind and the Buddha are non-dual, one had not yet been able to see this directly;
now, because form has opened up [the realization], one personally attests to and directly perceives it, and thus is moved with intense emotion.
This is great valor. "One whose resolve is equal to that of all Buddhas" means that one perceives directly that the mind and the Buddha are non-dual.

One thinks that in a single thought-moment (*ekakṣaṇa*), one can swiftly transcend; why wait for three *asaṃkhyeya-kalpas*? Question: The Sudden Teaching (*dun-jiao*) does not establish stages, but rather advocates a direct entry in a single leap.

How does this differ from the present case? Answer: That [Sudden Teaching] was intended for those who over-reach by speculating about the realm of the sages, or who limit themselves to the point of exhaustion. For them, it provides a remedy suited to their specific ailment.
This is merely a medicinal expedient. It does not mean that the practice division is invariably obstructed by the principle of perfect interfusion.

I ask you to examine carefully the meaning of the "stages of faith" and "stages of person" in the School of the Gate (Zongmen); then you will see that those of the Sudden Teaching do not necessarily completely discard these stages. △ Second, awakening through the names and teachings.

This is called the fault of overreaching through forceful effort. If one awakens to this, there is no transgression; it is not a state of saintly realization. Once one attains clear understanding and is no longer deluded, this state will naturally subside after some time.

Regarding "overreaching through forceful effort," it means that while originally intending to advance and break through the *vedanā-skandha* (the aggregate of sensation), one suddenly becomes arrogant and equalizes oneself with a Buddha.
Consider this: to falsely claim that one can transcend the three great kalpas in a single thought-moment is to violate the proper sequence and act with coarse negligence;

it is to overstep one's bounds and transgress the rites. If one awakens to this and stops, one may once again dissolve [the error] back into the state of no-fault. △ Third, showing that delusion inevitably leads to a fall.
If one forms a holy understanding [of these states], then a mad demon will enter their heart and viscera. Upon seeing others, they will boast, possessing an incomparable pride;
their mind will reach such a state that they neither see the Buddha above nor see other people below. Having lost right concentration (*samādhi*), they shall surely fall into ruin.
If one falsely claims to possess the same courageous vigor as the sages and persists in such deluded self-indulgence, then Māra will likewise attach himself to such a person.
With the loss of concentration due to *māna* (conceit), one will surely fall—of this there is no doubt. △ Third, concentration is biased toward excessive recollection.
This corresponds to the section below concerning the madness of concentration, wisdom, and recollection. It is divided into three parts. First, the manifestation of signs at the outset.
Furthermore, within that samādhi, those good sons see the aggregate of form (rūpa-skandha) dissolve and the aggregate of sensation (vedanā-skandha) become clear.

Having no new realization before them and having lost their former dwelling, their power of wisdom declines and they fall into a state of desolation. Seeing nothing at all, a great parching thirst suddenly arises in their hearts;
at all times, they dwell in a state of constant recollection without distraction, taking this very condition to be the mark of diligent vigor.

There is no new realization yet before you; the aggregate of sensation (*vedanā-skandha*) has not yet been shattered. You have lost your former dwelling, for the aggregate of form (*rūpa-skandha*) has already been exhausted.
At this juncture, you should simply maintain the equilibrium of concentration and wisdom, entering the stream and losing all objective referents. In this way, you may gradually achieve success.

Yet, alas, your power of wisdom is now weakened and diminished, such that you cannot perceive that the essence of sensation is fundamentally empty, nor can you remember the objects while forgetting the senses until they are utterly exhausted.
Being bewildered and distressed, one has no direction in which to advance; therefore it is said that "entering therein, one collapses and lacks vision.

The phrase "suddenly descending" indicates the partial application of the concentrated mind, wherein withering thirst and sunken recollection are taken to be the merit of breaking through and attaining vigor.
△ Second, naming it "Awakening through Name and Teaching.
This is called "losing oneself through cultivating the mind without wisdom. If one awakens, there is no fault; however, this is not considered a realization of sainthood.
This so-called "cultivator of the mind" refers to one who employs meditative concentration (*samādhi*) exclusively to cultivate and discipline the mind. Without wisdom, one loses oneself...

"Loss" refers to the failure to possess the wisdom that perceives the objects of perception as vanished, the sense organs as exhausted, and the essence of reception as fundamentally empty; thus, one loses the skillful means for oneself.
"Awakening" means understanding through reflection. Such a person possesses little wisdom and much meditative concentration, yet returns to *samādhi* (equipoise) merely to avoid faults;
how could there be any realization of the holy? △ Third, showing that delusion inevitably leads to a fall.
If you take this to be a realization of the holy, then the demon of recollection will enter your heart and inner organs; morning and evening it will seize your mind and suspend it in one place.
You will lose right concentration and shall surely fall into ruin.

Regarding those who form a "sacred understanding": because they take this state of mental sinking and recollection to be their meditative concentration, they falsely claim that they have realized the state of a sage.

Consequently, they summon demons, which then attach themselves to them. "Cue" (cuō) means to seize; it refers to seizing the mind and holding it aloft, thereby losing its original state of concentration.

Question: The ancients said, "If you place the mind in one spot, there is no task that cannot be accomplished. How does this differ from the present case? Answer: That [ancient teaching] was for the purpose of...

Regarding those whose distracted minds are occupied with worldly conditions, they merely respond to the ailments of a single lifetime; this is not the case of one who constantly directs the mind toward cultivation as true diligence.
Alternatively, if one takes the entire Dharma-realm to be a single location, then that perfectly pervasive realm is vastly different from this [limited state].
△ Fourth, when wisdom is excessive, it leads to madness. This is further divided into three parts. First, the initial manifestation of signs.
Furthermore, within that meditative concentration, those good sons see the aggregate of form (rūpa-skandha) dissolve and the aggregate of sensation (vedanā-skandha) become clear and bright.
Their power of wisdom exceeds their concentration, yet they lose its sharp intensity; harboring various superior natures within their minds, they themselves begin to doubt that they are Vairocana.
To be satisfied with a mere trifle.
Regarding the two phrases on the power of wisdom (*prajñā-bala*): by perceiving the excellence of one's own nature, one causes the mind of wisdom to become superior.
This is essentially an excessive reverence for one's own spirit; what is called being "born too noble. Therefore, it says: "With a mind harboring a superior nature..."
This is likely a corruption of "Rushana" (Vairocana). One should know that this differs from the previous section on "Equaling the Buddha.

The former merely stated that the Buddha could be quickly realized and that it was not difficult to cultivate for many kalpas; this [view], however, claims that the self-nature is itself [the goal] and requires no cultivation or realization.
Its error is even more severe than the former. Question: The Chan school all says that one is originally a Buddha and does not depend on...
"Practicing and realizing [enlightenment]—why would this not be an error? Answer: "The Patriarchs, in guiding people, only insisted on 'accomplishing through cultivation.

Because this neglects one's own spiritual nature, they used such methods of suppression and exaltation. Nevertheless, there are also times when they cause people to undergo a great death and advance further from the tip of the staff, exhausting the present moment.
Instances of such words are beyond counting; how could it be that they ever biasedly emphasized the self alone?"
Lingquan said, "This is merely a matter of cultivation and realization. △ Second, identifying this as awakening through names and teachings:

This refers to a state where the application of the mind has lost its constant discernment and one is submerged in intellectual views. If one awakens to this, there is no fault; however, it does not constitute a holy realization.
"Those who have lost constant scrutiny" refers to those unable to constantly examine whether their own virtues differ from or are identical to the virtues of the Buddha.
"Those who are submerged in views and knowledge" are those who, through excessive faith and excessive self-reliance, believe that the Tathāgata’s knowledge and vision already exist within themselves;
because their nature obstructs their practice, they arrive at this state. If one can reflect and understand, one will scrutinize and know for certain.
The five aggregates have not yet become entirely empty; how could one’s virtuous function possibly equal that of a Buddha? It would be better to return to [the ordinary state] to avoid transgression.
△ Third, showing that delusion inevitably leads to downfall:
If one takes this to be the realization of sainthood, then the demon of "inferiority and easy contentment" will enter one's heart and viscera. When seeing others, one will say of oneself:
"I have attained the unsurpassed ultimate truth," yet you lose right concentration and are destined for a downward fall.
To take this as a realization of sainthood and then assume the role of a Śramaṇa, persisting in delusion without turning back, is to be joined by demonic influences that cause great madness.
You should know that to speak of "I" and to speak of "attainment" is to be fully possessed of the two attachments to person and phenomena; how could the ultimate truth be such?
Is it not so? △ Fifth, "Awakening to Peril and Abundant Sorrow. This corresponds to the following section on "Peril and Peace, Sorrow and Joy.
It is further divided into three parts. First, the introduction and manifestation of signs.
Furthermore, within that meditative concentration, those good sons see the aggregate of form (rūpa-skandha) dissolve and the aggregate of sensation (vedanā-skandha) become clear.

Because they have newly realized what has not yet been mastered, their [former] mind has already perished; as they survey these two boundaries, difficulties arise spontaneously, and a sense of inexhaustible anxiety suddenly wells up within their hearts.
It is like sitting upon an iron bed or drinking a lethal poison; the mind has no desire to live, constantly seeking someone to end its life so that it may quickly attain liberation.

The first half [of this verse] is identical to the specific category of meditative concentration (*samādhi*). "Surveying the two limits" means observing the two boundaries of form (*rūpa*) and sensation (*vedanā*).
Furthermore, those who give rise to perilous anxieties do so out of dread of encountering decline or loss. When excessive worry does not cease, it leads to a succession of reversals;
thus, the various deluded matters described below as occurring while seated arise. Second, there is awakening through the teachings of the Name (the secular world).
This is called losing the skillful means (upāya) during practice; if one awakens to this, there is no fault. It is not a state of saintly realization.

It is said that although one’s fundamental nature is diligent cultivation and a mind of alert vigilance, one fails to perceive that it has become excessive, and thus lacks the skillful means of consolation and understanding, leading to this state.
The Patriarch said: "The Great Way is vast and remote; why be so busy? He also said: "Silence."
Silently know for yourself that the ground is firm; with a carefree spirit, who would let their belly grow so complacent? It is further said: "Let go of the four elements; do not try to grasp them.
Through such immeasurable skillful means, one can forget all worries and return to right mindfulness.
How could one consider excessive anxiety to be the way of a sage? △ Third, showing that delusion inevitably leads to a fall.
If one forms a holy understanding [of these experiences], then a portion of the demon of constant sorrow and anxiety will enter their heart and viscera.

Grasping a sword in hand, they will cut their own flesh, rejoicing in the relinquishing of their life-span; or they will be constantly sorrowful and flee into mountain forests, unable to bear the sight of people.
One will lose right concentration (*samādhi*) and fall into ruin.

If one considers excessive anxiety to be the natural state of a sage’s mind, then when such anxiety does not cease, demonic forces will attach themselves and provoke it, leading to conditions such as brandishing weapons or the great wind-disorders of insanity.
△ Six: Awakening to Peace and Abundance of Joy. Divided into three parts. One: Introducing the Manifestation.
Furthermore, within that meditative concentration, those good sons perceive the aggregate of form (*rūpa-skandha*) dissolving and the aggregate of sensation (*vedanā-skandha*) becoming clear.

While abiding in this state of purity, after their minds have become tranquil and secure, there suddenly arises within them an infinite joy; their hearts are filled with such rapture that they cannot restrain themselves.
This cause opens up the present realm of sensation through form; it is also most delightful. To give rise to joy therein is not inherently a fault.
However, if one becomes addicted and indulges the passions so that they continue without ceasing, faults will inevitably arise.
As the Patriarch said: "Even if there is realization or proof, you must quickly spit it out. This is precisely what he meant. △ Second, awakening through the teachings of names (ling-miao).
This is called "light ease" (praśrabdhi) without wisdom, a form of self-restraint. If one awakens to it, there is no fault; yet it is not the realization of a sage.
Within the state of awakening and realization, sublime bliss is itself light ease. If there is the illuminating discernment of wisdom, then this is merely a shallow realization.
What need is there for deep attachment? The wind of joy would naturally cease. Now, lacking this wisdom, one cannot restrain it.
△ Third, showing that delusion inevitably leads to a fall:
If one takes this to be a realization of sainthood, then a portion of the demon of fondness for joy and pleasure will enter one's heart and viscera; upon seeing others, one will laugh.
Beside a roadside, he sang and danced by himself, claiming to have attained unimpeded liberation; yet having lost his meditative absorption (*samādhi*), he was destined for downfall.
If one were to say that delighting in such ways is appropriate for the mind of a sage, and thus indulges in such unrestrained abandon and excessive joy without ceasing, then this is Mara.
An afterthought: one who falls into madness will not regain consciousness. △ Seventh, arrogance toward others due to seeing one's own superiority.
This corresponds to the section below concerning the distinction between self and other through views and wisdom. It is divided into three parts. First, the introduction and manifestation of signs.
Furthermore, within that meditative concentration, noble sons perceive the dissolution of the aggregate of form (*rūpaskandha*) and the clarity of the aggregate of sensation (*vedanāskandha*).
Believing themselves to be sufficient, they suddenly give rise to groundless great pride (*māna*), and even so forth: pride, excessive pride (*atimāna*), and pride beyond pride (*mānātimāna*).

Whether it be overweening pride or inferiority complex, they may arise simultaneously; such that in their hearts they still slight the Tathāgatas of the ten directions, let alone those of lower status, such as śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas.

"To claim for oneself" means to rely solely on one's own views and false recollections without seeking the seal of a teacher. "To consider oneself sufficient" refers to the sense of self-satisfaction and arrogance;
it is the source from which pride arises. "Without cause" means both without reason and without limit.

Although great conceit (*mahāmāna*) is one of the seven types of conceit, it appears to be the general category for all forms of conceit. Regarding the seven types of conceit, the *Kaimeng* (Opening the Ignorant) states:

"Single, excessive, increased, perverse, self, and low. Its commentary explains: To consider oneself superior when one is inferior, or to consider oneself equal when one is equal, constitutes "single conceit" (*māna*).
To consider oneself equal when one is superior, or to consider oneself superior when one is equal, constitutes "excessive conceit" (*atimāna*). When one... [text continues]

To reckon oneself superior to those who are actually superior is the pride of overweening pride (*mānātimāna*). To claim one has attained what one has not attained is the pride of overestimation (*adhimāna*).

To reckon oneself as much more inferior than those who are actually inferior is the pride of arrogance (*abhimāna*). To claim one possesses virtues when one lacks them entirely is the pride of false conceit (*mithyāmāna*).

To remain complacent in one's own inferiority and insignificance before those who are vastly superior, neither showing respect nor seeking [instruction], is the pride of inferiority (*ūnamāna*). This sutra lacks only the pride of false conceit; thus, the general and specific categories are combined.

Treatise: Possessing those six types of pride, although one’s mind is lowly and all manner of conceited thoughts are driven by concerted effort, one nonetheless exalts one’s own spirit while looking down upon the sages;
speaking of its essential nature, this is *mānātimāna* (pride beyond pride).

One should know that this, moreover, exceeds the previous [type of] wisdom in its excessive delusion and is even more severe. That [previous type] merely claimed that one is originally equal to the Buddha, whereas this...
This refers to the fact that one further transcends even the Buddhas. Question: In the school of the Patriarchs, there is "reviling the Buddhas and cursing the Patriarchs.

How does this differ from the present case? Answer: The Patriarchs sought most earnestly for people to awaken to the equality of the single nature, so as to eradicate the view of a Buddha by realizing that there is no Buddha outside of mind.
How could they truly intend to increase arrogance and, conversely, lose their state of equality? △
Second is awakening through the teachings of names and concepts.
This is called "superior vision without wisdom to save oneself. If one awakens, there is no fault; yet it does not constitute the realization of a sage.

One who possesses superior vision does so because they perceive a particularly excellent nature and are impelled by a superior spirit. If, however, they possess the wisdom of introspection, [they will not fall into error].
Once one has realized the nature of equality, one no longer perceives even a single sentient being toward whom one might feel pride;

how much less so when delusions have not yet been dispelled and practice remains incomplete—how could one dare to be arrogant toward the sages? △ Third, showing that those who are deluded will inevitably fall.
If one interprets this as a realization of the holy, then a portion of the demon of great conceit will enter their heart and inner being.
They will fail to pay homage to stupas and temples and will destroy scriptures and images. Addressing donors, they will say: "These are merely gold and copper, or perhaps clay and wood;

these scriptures are but leaves from trees or folded paper flowers. The physical body is truly eternal, so do not show it reverence; instead, you truly act in a perverted way by venerating clay and wood."
Those who have deep faith, having been shattered by it, shall be buried and cast away in the earth;
they will mislead sentient beings, enter the Mounts of Unrelenting Torment, lose right concentration, and must fall into ruin.

If one persists in delusion to the end and shows no further remorse for their transgressions, they will be possessed by demons and driven to madness, bringing ruin upon themselves and others; such a state is beyond salvation.

In recent times, such individuals have proliferated throughout the world. They disparage the Buddha’s physical form as being merely made of gold, copper, wood, or clay, while regarding themselves as living Buddhas.
They revile the Buddha’s scriptures as nothing more than paper, ink, and written characters, while claiming their own words to be the true sutras. Truly...
This is the teaching of Māra; such individuals are truly followers of Māra. To verify this by means of the present sutra, they shall enter the Avīci Hell as swiftly as an arrow shot from a bow.
How deeply pitiable they are! Should they have even a slight affinity for the Dharma and hear this sutra, they must quickly repent;
this would indeed be a great blessing. △ Eight: Huian’s Self-Satisfaction, further divided into three parts. First: The Manifestation of Signs.
Furthermore, within that meditative concentration, those good sons perceive the dissolution of the aggregate of form (rūpa-skandha) and the clarity of the aggregate of sensation (vedanā-skandha).

"Vital clarity" (*jīngmíng*) refers to the Buddha’s initial demonstration of the source of consciousness as vital clarity, which was later termed the "hearing-nature" (*wénxìng*) of the ear-gate.

To "see" is simply to see; there is no longer any obstruction. As for "light ease" (*praśrabdhi*), it refers to the state where body and mind are free from all heaviness and dullness, characterized by a sense of sudden awakening and mastery.
Consequently, one considers oneself satisfied, believing one has become a sage and attained great liberation.
Compared to the preceding category, this fault seems lighter; for while one merely remains self-satisfied and does not progress further, it is not a case of further disparaging others. △
Second is awakening through the teachings of names.
This name refers to attaining various states of lightness and purity through wisdom (*prajñā*). Awakening is free from fault; it is not yet the realization of a sage.
One should know that the previous "seeing" and this "wisdom" have distinct natures and characteristics: seeing is the path of the discriminating mind, whereas wisdom is the opening [of insight].

Regarding "awakening to the realm and attaining lightness and purity through wisdom": when the time comes for the manifestation of form, one awakens to the fact that body and mind are like clouds and shadows;
having departed from heaviness and turbidity, one attains lightness and purity. This is merely a state of sudden, expansive awakening and profound satisfaction at a single moment.
How could there be any sacred realization here? Why should one be so self-satisfied? When a practitioner encounters this, they should awaken to it in this way.

If one takes this to be a realization of sainthood, then a portion of the "delusive spirit of fondness for lightness and purity" will enter their heart and viscera, leading them to claim they are fully satisfied.

They will no longer seek spiritual progress. For the most part, these will become unlearned bhikṣus who mislead sentient beings through doubt, causing them to fall into the Avīci Hell and lose right concentration;
they shall surely sink into ruin.
To be deluded without awakening is to be possessed by demons; one’s self-imposed limitations lead to a cycle of transmigration, like that of the "thoughtless" bhikṣu.

Not only does one deceive oneself, but one also deceives many others. Furthermore, by adding regret and slandering the Buddha, one ultimately falls into a great ruin. △ Nine: Attachment to Emptiness and Destruction of Precepts.

Therefore, by setting this aside, there is no fault in proceeding directly. △ Third, showing that delusion inevitably leads to ruin:

△ Third, the conclusion regarding harm and the entrustment for protection, divided into three parts. First, showing the mutual interaction of causes.
Ānanda, these ten kinds of visionary states that appear during dhyāna are all manifestations resulting from the interaction between the mind and the aggregate of sensation (vedanā-skandha).
Thus, these phenomena arise.

To speak of the time before the aggregate of sensation has been cleared away: one must guard against the arising of these errors. The meaning of "interaction" is the same as in the previous section; it is merely being pointed out here.

This also signifies the sense of mutual combat and alternating victory. △ Second, if one is deluded, it results in harm.

Sentient beings are stubborn and deluded; they do not reflect upon themselves. Encountering these causes and conditions, they remain lost and fail to recognize their own state, claiming instead that they have attained the ranks of the sages.

"Those who are deluded and do not recognize themselves" means they cannot even recall their own names;

"You all should also take these words of the Tathāgata and, after my parinirvāṇa, transmit them during the Final Dharma (mappō).

First, a complete demonstration of the beginning and end. This is further divided into two. First, the initial stage before the realm has been broken through. This is further divided into two. First, following upon the exhaustion of the *vedanā-skandha*.
Ānanda, when that son of good family has cultivated *samādhi* and the aggregate of sensation (*vedanā-skandha*) is exhausted, although his outflows (*āsrava*) are not yet extinguished,

The stage of the Sage. Having attained the *manomayakāya* (body born of mind), one proceeds everywhere without obstruction.

According to the previous classification, this should correspond to the second or third levels of the stage of faith (*śraddhā-bhūmi*); therefore, it is said that "outflows (*āsrava*) are not yet exhausted.

It is only upon reaching the seventh level of faith, when one no longer undergoes future existence, that the outflows are truly exhausted. Regarding the phrase "the mind detaches from the body": because the true mind is all-pervasive, it is fundamentally [not separate from the body].
It is confined to the body. This beginningless deluded clinging is not inherently confined, yet it is confined;
previously, one allowed its conceptual understanding to pervade everywhere, but alas, seeing and hearing merely follow the movement of the body—how could there be any portion of temporary liberation?

Even if the previous physical form were exhausted and seeing and hearing were all-pervasive, there would still be no function of independent mastery apart from the body. It is like one who is lost in a direction; even if there were someone...
I have explained this clearly; yet it is difficult to turn back abruptly. All of this is due to being shrouded by the *vedanā-skandha* (the aggregate of sensation).
Therefore, only when sensation is exhausted can one finally become detached from the body, attaining the freedom of a bird escaping its cage.

This completes the analysis of the lower four lines, which determine that one is certainly able to traverse the stages of sainthood with an ordinary body. This is because the Separate Teaching (*pratyekabuddhayāna*) is entirely based on reality.
Because one attains realization through it, one must undergo successive births over many kalpas and realize only a single portion before reaching a single stage.
How could one possibly traverse all the stages instantaneously with an ordinary body? This most keen faculty of the Perfect and Sudden [Vehicle] does not grasp at realization as being real;
thus, by means of the ordinary body, it swiftly ascends through the various stages. Therefore, the stages prior to "Abiding" (Zhù) are generally not enumerated, whereas those after "Abiding" are.
The stages (*bhūmi*) are likewise transcended; this merely clarifies that their perfect interfusion does not obstruct the sequence of practice.

It is not like the dull cultivation and actual realization of the Separate Teaching (*bhedavyavahāra*). Therefore, it is said that one traverses the sixty stages with an ordinary body. As for these sixty stages:
Within the fifty-five stages, if one adds *kandhī* (dry wisdom) from the beginning and *samyak-saṃbodhi* (wondrous enlightenment) at the end, there are fifty-seven.

If these are combined with the preceding three gradual stages, they exactly total sixty. However, since it is only during the first gradual stage that one renounces the five pungent roots (*pañca-garaka*), it seems this cannot yet correspond to the ranks of the sages;
moreover, it is only in the second gradual stage, within the purification of karmic retribution, that one clearly enters [the path].

Since this refers to the conventional stage of faith (*śraddhā-bhūmi*), one should exclude the initial "gradual" [stage] from the preceding section and include the subsequent "opening of the vajra" [stage] to constitute sixty stages. Question:

Since the Buddha has already spoken of passing through the stages only after the reception [of the precepts] is complete, does this not mean that Mount Gushan’s claim—that one enters the stage of faith only after the reception is complete—is correct?
This appears to accord with the Buddha’s words; yet why is it that one enters the first stage of faith (*śraddhā*) precisely when form (*rūpa*) is exhausted? Answer: The Buddha’s speech is sovereign.

It is specifically because the wondrous function of the exhaustion of sensation (*vedanā*) is made manifest that this serves as a sign he will inevitably pass through all the stages of sainthood (*ārya-bhūmi*).

It does not necessarily mean that the stages of sainthood begin from this point. For in the preceding stage, the ten directions were opened up and the Buddha-mind was like a mirror. When [form is exhausted],...
This marvelous essence being revealed brings forth right faith manifest before one; is this not the stage of the first faith?
And how could it not be a rank of the sages? I request that you combine the two passages concerning the gradual purification of retribution and examine them once more in detail.孤山 (Gushan) says:
"Within these ranks there are both worthies and sages; because they are all positions traversed by the Buddhas of the three periods of time, they are collectively termed 'sage-ranks'."

The mind-made body (*manomaya-kāya*) is so called because it moves as swiftly and without obstruction as the movement of thought; it is of three kinds: 1. The mind-made body that enters the bliss of *samādhi*.
This refers to the state where the mind is tranquil and unmoving, corresponding to the stage from the first to the seventh faith, which is the position of entering emptiness.
2. The mind-made body that awakens to the self-nature of phenomena. This refers to the universal entry into Buddha-fields, taking the Dharma as its own nature.

The "nature" refers to the stage of emerging into the provisional [world] through the eight levels of faith (*śraddhā*), which is characterized by similarity. Third is the "body born of the three types of mental mastery" (*trividha-manomaya-kāya*) that arises spontaneously without deliberate effort;
this refers to the realization of the Dharma realized by the Buddha, corresponding to the middle stages of cultivation during the nine and ten levels of faith.

It is like laughing at those who study the arts of immortality and take the manifestation of the "yang-spirit" (*yángshén*) as a supreme achievement, while failing to recognize that these are merely the lower stages of the three types of mind-made bodies within the Śākya tradition.

It is wondrously transcendent and beyond compare; how much more so the ten bodies of the profound stages! To nevertheless recklessly claim it is the "shadow-spirit" (yin-shen) is truly the speech of one devoid of knowledge.

II. The Ten Intermediate Phases. These are divided into ten parts. First, the pursuit of skillful means (*upāya*). This somewhat resembles spiritual transformations;
however, the underlying intent is to win people's conviction so as to carry out teaching and transformation, hence it is termed "skillful means. Furthermore, this is subdivided into seven sections.
Ānanda, that son of good family will certainly give rise to a craving for attainment.
As the aggregate of sensation (*vedanā-skandha*) becomes empty and subtle, he is no longer beset by perverse thoughts.
Within the samādhi of the luminous manifestation of perfect concentration, his mind craves perfect clarity; he sharpens his refined contemplation and greedily seeks out skillful means.

"Vast" means that seeing and hearing are all-pervasive. "Subtle" means being free from bodily activity. "Not encountering perverse thoughts" means not being deluded by the ten objects during the intermediate stage.

"Sending forth the wicked to possess others.
At that time, the celestial Māra waits for an opportunity, dispatching his essence to fly into and possess a person, who then speaks the sutras and the Dharma with their own mouth.

Although the celestial Māra was previously mentioned in summary, it has not yet been described in detail; now, at each stage, the manifestation of receiving the profound state of the "exhaustion of sensation" (vedanā-kṣaya-samādhi) is explained.

This refers to another person who has long been subject to heterodox delusions. Generally, [the teachings] cannot penetrate the heart and viscera of one whose karma is exhausted;
therefore, they use a bystander to confuse them, causing them to become further disordered. Hereafter, all cases shall follow this pattern. △ Third:
External heterodoxy intrudes and disturbs.

That person does not realize they are possessed by a māra; they claim for themselves that they have attained unsurpassed nirvāṇa and come to the place where that seeker of skillful means dwells, spreading out a seat and preaching the Dharma.
For a brief moment, their form may even manifest as a bhikṣu so that the person may see them.
Sometimes they appear as Śakra, sometimes as women, or as bhikṣuṇīs; or while one is sleeping in a dark room, their bodies emit radiance.
If the person being possessed does not perceive it, this means the person themselves is unaware.
For when Māra enters the mind, how could the person possibly be self-aware? He descends from above before reaching the practitioner’s location; thus we know that he arrives from above.
These words spoken by them are not words addressed to practitioners. This is truly because they themselves are unaware of being possessed by Māra;

they marvel at their own unprovoked ability to eloquently expound the sutras and the Dharma, suspecting that they have already attained the Buddha-way. Only then do they spontaneously come to delude the practitioner;
all this is caused by Māra’s silent attachment, which makes it so. Later, he emits these [powers], transforming his appearance and radiating light—this is precisely his skillful artifice.

This is a matter that moves the heart. It is precisely because a real person has been sent here to manifest transformations and create delusions that we know our previous encounter with the "good spiritual friend" was merely a hollow image within stillness; it is not like this. △ Fourth, the master’s delusive confusion.
These people are deluded and confused; they mistake him for a bodhisattva and, believing his teachings, have their minds shaken and agitated.
They violate the Buddha’s precepts and secretly practice lustful desires.
This is because one inevitably becomes deluded by casting oneself into what the mind loves and seeks.
Had there been nothing to love or seek, how could it lead practitioners to such confusion? One should simply settle the mind and cease all seeking.
The final two lines represent the core intent of the demon’s delusion of practitioners: that their threefold training is flawless and their progress is as swift as flying.
The palace of Māra trembled with terror. As for the schemes Māra devised to cause disturbance, they were intended solely to break precepts and lead others into lust;

thus, both concentration (*samādhi*) and wisdom (*prajñā*) would be drawn into evil, and as his own son, Māra would find peace. If one possesses strong wisdom, this situation serves instead as a primary means to verify Māra:
regardless of his unfathomable supernatural transformations, one need only observe whether he destroys precepts and seduces others into lust. Thus, [one knows him].

Knowing this to be Māra, how could one fall into such delusion? Regarding the various matters of lust and the violation of precepts in the subsequent text, all should be interpreted according to this principle.

They take pleasure in speaking of portents, auspicious signs, and strange transformations. Sometimes they claim that the Tathāgata has appeared in a certain place;

"Disasters" (*zāi*) are omens of retribution; "auspicious signs" (*xiáng*) are omens of prosperity. "Portents" (*biànyì*) refer to strange and extraordinary anomalies.
Some say that in recent times, many ignorant people among the common folk have spread such talk, causing others to abandon their homes and flee in panic;

Thus, since the Buddha stated that one proceeds from this ordinary body, it is evident that one does not yet attain the fruit of sainthood. Furthermore, when he says "ascending through the stages of the sages," it is clearly seen that...
However, these are merely passed through with speed; how could one possibly attain realization at each and every stage? It is like a bird ascending a mountain:

Beneath a thousand crags, it is known that the veil of ignorance has not yet been lifted. Since one has not yet entered perfect penetration (*yuantong*), there is no harm in the possibility of falling back.
Someone might say: "If this is so, then the Perfect and Sudden Teaching is actually inferior to the Gradual Teachings. I reply: How can such a thing be said?

It is like a flyer who relies on wings: falling is indeed easy, yet ascending is not difficult. As the scripture says: "If one awakens, there is no fault"; this means that even if one is about to fall, one returns to ascend.
How much more so for those who possess the superior faculties of the Perfect and Sudden—many are able to sever craving and seeking, such that ordinary beings and sages [are no longer distinguished].

When attachment is forgotten, one naturally incurs no fault of summoning demons or usurping the status of a sage; rather, the Buddha’s compassion provides specific entrustment and protection merely as a warning against unforeseen calamities.
It is certainly not the case that there is no possibility of falling into error, yet it is also not the case that many will sink into ruin.

△ Fourth, the naming and manifestation of the harms.
These are named the great power mountain spirits of heaven and earth, the sea spirits, the wind spirits, the river spirits, and the earth spirits;

they are the accumulated karmic spirits and enchantments of all plants and trees over many kalpas, or dragon spirits, or those who were immortals at the end of their lives who returned as spirits, or those whose period as immortals has expired.

According to the calculation of years, he ought to have died, yet his form has not decayed. Others marvel at this, for he has become possessed by a demon; having grown old, he has become a māra who harasses and disturbs this person.
Once his desires are satisfied, he will leave that body. Both the disciples and the teacher will then frequently fall into royal calamities.
△ Section Five: Awakening to the Precepts and Dispelling Delusion.
You should awaken first so as not to enter saṃsāra. If you remain deluded and ignorant, you will fall into the Avīci Hell.
△ Section Nine: Craving the Profound Emptiness. Divided into five parts. First: The Arising of Attachment and Seeking.

Furthermore, son of good family, when the aggregate of sensation (*vedanā-skandha*) has become empty and subtle, and one is not beset by perverse thoughts, the light of perfect concentration (*samādhi*) becomes manifest.
Within this state of *samādhi*, the mind desires to enter cessation (*nirodha*), investigating the nature of transformation and greedily seeking profound emptiness (*gambhīra-śūnyatā*).
Entering cessation is not nirvana; it is merely a desire to empty the body so that one may exercise mastery over its appearance and disappearance. II. The Demon Dispatches the Evil to Possess Him.
At that time, the celestial demon, waiting for an opportunity, sent forth his emotions to possess a person, who then spoke the sutras and the Dharma with their own mouth.
△ Third, regarding the matter of delusive activities through false attachments, there are also three points. First, as for the person to whom one falsely attaches:
that person ultimately does not realize they are possessed by a māra, yet claims to have personally attained unsurpassed *nirvāṇa*.
They come to the place of that son of good family who seeks emptiness, arrange seats, and preach the Dharma.
△ Second, manifesting the matter of false delusion:
Within the great assembly, his form suddenly vanished, so that the multitude could see nothing; then he emerged abruptly from the void once more.

They exercise mastery over their appearance and disappearance. At times they manifest their bodies as transparent as lapis lazuli; at other times they extend their hands and feet, emitting the fragrance of sandalwood;
or their excrement and urine are like thick rock honey. They slander the precepts and hold those who have left the household life in contempt.

Wenling says: "He wished to enter the meditative absorption of cessation (*nirodha-samāpatti*) in order to attain emptiness and stillness. His ability to appear and disappear from within emptiness was due to his fondness for the void;

thus, he relied on such deceptions to delude others. His flavors were rich and intense. Now, one whose body is pure and limbs fragrant, yet who also relishes honey, is truly capable of startling the common folk and confusing them.
Yet he instead destroyed the precepts and disparaged those who have left the household life; therefore, he is a fool."
If people dare not comply with [the teachings] and do not know how to refrain from violating the precepts and so forth, one can verify that this is the work of Māra;
thus, what is there to fear in such divine anomalies? △ Third, speaking of heterodox and delusive words.
They constantly preach in their mouths that there is neither cause nor effect, and that upon one death there is eternal extinction, with no further rebirths for either ordinary beings or sages.

Although they have attained a state of empty stillness, they secretly indulge in greed and desire; those who receive such desires also attain an "empty mind" and deny the existence of cause and effect.
To deny the existence of desire, thereby opposing the Buddha and turning one's back on the sutras, reveals one to be a Māra;
yet those who are deluded by this are truly nothing more than people whose own minds have gone mad and confused. One should awaken to this. △ Fourth, naming the manifestation to show its harm.

These are the vital essences of solar and lunar eclipses, precious metals and stones, numinous fungi and grasses, as well as qilin, phoenixes, tortoises, and cranes. Having lived for thousands of myriad years without dying, they become spirits;
when they are born into this land and grow old, they become demons. They afflict and disturb these people until their desires are satisfied and their minds give rise to weariness.
If one abandons that human body, both the disciple and the teacher will often fall into royal calamities.
Although gold, jade, and the like are insentient objects, they may be inhabited by spirits and monsters, thereby becoming sentient-like beings;

such categories as the "unconscious" (wu-xiang) are essentially the essence and charms of plants and trees that have long become part of the demonic faction. △ Fifth: Teaching Awakening and Warning Against Delusion.
You should awaken first so as not to enter saṃsāra; through delusion and ignorance, you will fall into the Avīci Hell.
△ Ten: Seeking Eternal Years. This is divided into five parts. First: Determining the Arising of Craving and Seeking.

Furthermore, son of good family, when the aggregate of sensation (*vedanā-skandha*) has become empty and subtle, and one is not beset by perverse thoughts, within the *samādhi* where perfect concentration brings forth illumination,

the mind may come to cherish long life. One then undergoes arduous toil in investigating the subtle, greedily seeking eternal years and abandoning the birth of segmented existence (*kalala-bhava*), suddenly hoping for the permanence of the subtle characteristics of the transformative birth (*pariṇāma-bhava*).
That which is sought herein is the realm of the Arhat; once practice has opened up, it is attained naturally. Now, because of this restless striving, demonic obstacles are summoned.
Gushan says: "Transformation" refers to the exhaustion of the afflictions of views and thoughts (*dṛṣṭi-kleśa* and *kleśa*), whereby one is born into the Dharma-nature land (*dharmatā-bhūmi*).
Therefore, they undergo transformation and change. Now, they suddenly wish to transform their coarse bodies into subtle substances and exchange their short lifespans for long ones;
from this point of severance, they are extended into that land. △ Second, the demons dispatch evil spirits to possess them.
At that time, the heavenly demons, waiting for an opportunity, sent forth their essence to possess people, who then spoke the sutras and the Dharma with their own mouths.
△ Third, regarding the matters of delusive seduction by the heterodox, there are three parts. First, the heterodox possession of people. ... up to [the end of the section].
That person ultimately does not realize they are possessed by a māra; they also claim to have personally attained unsurpassed nirvāṇa.
They come to the place of that son of good family who seeks birth [in the Pure Land], spread out a seat, and preach the Dharma.
△ Second, manifesting the phenomena of false delusions:
He delights in speaking of traveling to and from other regions without obstruction; though he may travel ten thousand *li*, he returns in an instant, appearing as if he were still in that very place.
Having obtained that object, suppose he were at a single location within a house, at a distance of only a few paces from east to west wall;

yet, even if this person were to walk with great haste for many years, they would not arrive there. Because of this, their mind would gain conviction and they would doubt whether the Buddha has appeared before them.
"To travel ten thousand *li* in an instant" refers to the supernormal power of the divine realm (*ṛddhividhi-jñāna*) among the five supernatural faculties (*pañcābhijñā*).

Now, he himself manifests the divine realm such that the distant becomes near, while causing others to perceive a few steps as having become distant. Therefore, those of shallow wisdom and meager learning were struck with wonder and marvelled at him being a Buddha.
△ Third, the statement regarding false delusions.
He constantly says with his own mouth: "The sentient beings of the ten directions are all my children. I give birth to all Buddhas;
I produce all worlds. I am the primordial Buddha; appearing in the world spontaneously, I did not attain this through cultivation."
Now, both sentient beings and all Buddhas are equally born from others; this is precisely the primordial Buddha of no beginning.
How could his longevity have any limit? This is also why he accords with their fundamental thought of seeking through affection. △ Fourth, naming him and showing the harm.
This is called the Lord of the Heavenly Demons who dwells in the world.

He causes his retinue—such as Cāmuṇḍa, the Four Heavenly Kings, and the Vaiśya youths who have not yet resolved their minds—to exploit its empty clarity and consume its refined vital energy; or else, they do so without relying on a teacher.
The practitioner personally witnesses this: one who claims to be Vajradhara bestowing long life manifests in the body of a beautiful woman and indulges extensively in lustful desire;
yet before a year has passed, their liver and brain wither away, and they speak soliloquies that sound like those of a malevolent spirit.
The details of this matter have not been fully ascertained by previous scholars. Many fall into royal peril; before they even reach the point of execution, they have already withered and died.
They afflict and disturb those people until they bring about their demise.
Gushan says: "The Heaven of Sovereignty (Īśvara) is located separately above the sixth heaven of the Desire Realm;
it is the dwelling place of the Māra King and is also subsumed under the Heaven of Mastery over Others' Emanations (Paranirmita-vaśavartin). Wenzheng says:

In the *Dhāraṇī Sūtra*, there is the Piśāca youth named Cchamantra, who is a Piśāca ghost subordinate to the Four Heavenly Kings. Once he has resolved his mind [on awakening], he protects people; when he has not yet..."
To give rise to such a thought is to harm others. Because they take the clarity and luminosity of that meditative power as a profit, they consume the vital essence of others.
As for those who do not rely on a teacher, it means they do not rely on a teacher possessed by a māra, yet they personally witness the manifestation of a māra.
"Speaking alone" refers to the speech of one who follows such delusions. Having personally seen the manifestation of a māra, they engage in sexual desire with him; others do not see it.
This refers to what is called "speaking alone. That person is actually speaking with Māra. If one is a malevolent spirit (*yakṣa*), it is precisely this practitioner who resembles such a spirit.
The phrases "the former person" and "that person" both refer to the practitioner who has been deluded;
as for the term "not yet detailed," it means they have not yet been able to examine whether [the voice] is that of Māra or of a sage. △ Fifth: Teaching Awakening and Warning Against Delusion.
You should awaken first so as not to enter saṃsāra; if you are deluded and ignorant, you will fall into the Avīci Hell.

This concludes the section on the ten intermediate objects. Part Three: Showing and Exhorting Regarding the Final Age, divided into two sections. First, a preliminary indication of demonic activities.
Furthermore, it is divided into three parts. First, falsely claiming the ultimate fruit:
"Ānanda, you should know that these ten kinds of māras, during the time of the final age, will go forth from home to practice the Way within my Dharma."
Some attach themselves to human bodies, while others manifest their own forms; all claim to have already attained the realization of Perfect Complete Enlightenment (*samyak-saṃbodhi*).
Those who speak of leaving the household life to practice the Way either attach themselves to bhikṣus or manifest themselves as bhikṣus and so forth.
According to the ten types mentioned previously, only the tenth manifests itself as a beautiful Vajra maiden; all the others merely attach themselves to humans. The practitioner should know this.

Whenever anyone manifests supernatural powers claiming to be a Buddha, they are undoubtedly a demon; for a Sage would never leak [the secrets]. Second, regarding those who accomplish their "transformation" through lust:
they praise sexual desire and violate the Buddha’s Vinaya. These are first the evil demonic teachers and their demonic disciples, who transmit their lust from one to another.
Such evil spirits thus bewitch the heart and the inner organs. In the near term, this may occur within nine lifetimes; more often, it extends beyond a hundred generations.

This causes those who practice true cultivation to become entirely part of the demonic retinue—demonic teachers and demonic disciples. Furthermore, the preceding ten types [of demons] were mentioned to illustrate that their harm extends into future lives, frequently destroying [the path].

This refers to the practitioner. Wēnlíng says: The *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* states that in the final age, the retinues of Māra will manifest in the forms of bhikṣus, arhats, and so forth, to corrupt the True Dharma and slander the precepts; their intent is the same as this.
△ Third, falling into the clutches of Māra and descending into hell.
After their lives end, they will inevitably become subjects of Māra; having lost right and universal knowledge, they shall fall into the Avīci Hell.
△ Second, the profound exhortation for compassionate rescue, which has two parts. First, the formal presentation of the exhortation.

"You need not first seek nirvana at this time. Even if you attain the stage of No-More-Learning (aśaikṣa), remain by your vow within that age of the Dharma’s decay, give rise to great compassion, and rescue those sentient beings who possess a correct mind and deep faith, ensuring they do not fall under the influence of demons and that they attain right knowledge and vision."
Observing the Buddha’s final testament, it is clear that Ānanda’s entry into parinirvāṇa in four parts was likewise a provisional manifestation;

yet, he must certainly have remained in the world in secret to provide salvation in accordance with the Buddha’s lingering vow. Is it not by the power of the Venerable One’s compassionate salvation that the Dharma teachings are now widely propagated?
"Rectifying the mind" means seeing the truth authentically; "profound faith" means having an insatiable longing for it.
Right knowledge and vision means that the eye of wisdom is perfectly clear and bright, penetratingly illuminating the treachery of Māra. △ Second, the exhortation to repay the Buddha’s kindness:
"I have now delivered you; you have already emerged from birth and death. To follow the Buddha’s words is called repaying the Buddha’s kindness."
To hear these instructions and not feel heartache or shed tears would be to be a person of wood or stone.
△ Fourth, the conclusion on the harm and the instruction for protection, which is further divided into three parts. First, showing the mutual interaction of causes.
Ānanda, these ten kinds of meditative states appearing during dhyāna are all the result of the interaction between the mind and the *saṃjñā-skandha* (aggregate of perception).
Therefore, these phenomena manifest.
△ Second, if one becomes deluded, they turn into harm.

Sentient beings are stubborn and deluded; they do not examine themselves. Encountering such causes and conditions, they remain lost and fail to recognize their own state, claiming instead that they have attained sainthood.
Having committed this great falsehood, they fall into the Avīci Hell.

This refers to those who claim to have attained the state of a sage; it means that they do not merely mistake deluded demons for sages, but also presume themselves to belong to the ranks of the holy ones.
△ Third, the instruction to provide protection.
"You must certainly carry the words of the Tathāgata. After my parinirvāṇa, transmit them during the Final Dharma period, causing all sentient beings everywhere to awaken to this meaning.
Do not allow celestial Māras to find any opportunity; maintain and protect [this teaching] so that they may achieve the Unsurpassed Way."

This is precisely why Ānanda compiled and circulated [the teachings], so that the sutras might be heard everywhere. This concludes the section on the characteristics of the māra of the aggregate of perception (*saṃjñā-skandha*).
