The description of the demonic manifestations of the *saṃjñā-skandha* (perception aggregate) is now complete. △ Fourth: The demonic manifestations of the *saṃskāra-skandha* (volitional formations aggregate). This aggregate was previously discussed in fascicle two. Five...
Within the *Yin-ke* (Section on the Skandhas), that [treatment] concerns the stage of delusion; therefore, it takes up the coarse, like a torrential stream.

This [treatment], however, concerns the stage of cultivation; therefore, it takes up the subtle, analogous to a mirage. Since the first three [skandhas] have already been shown to be empty, the remaining *saṃskāra-skandha* is the most profound and subtle.
It is divided into three parts. First, a complete demonstration of its beginning and end. This further has two sections. First, the initial state before the boundaries have been broken down.
Furthermore, there are two [points]. First, following upon the signs of the exhaustion of the aggregate of perception (*saṃjñā-skandha*):
"Ānanda, when that virtuous man cultivates *samādhi* and the aggregate of perception is exhausted, his ordinary dreams and thoughts are extinguished;
whether awake or asleep, he remains constant in one state. His awakened clarity is empty and still, like a cloudless sky, no longer burdened by the coarse and heavy objects of the external world."
Regarding the matter of shadows: observe the great earth, mountains, and rivers of all worlds; they are like reflections in a clear mirror—coming without attachment and passing without a trace.
They receive illumination in emptiness, utterly devoid of habitual tendencies; there is only the single, pure, and true reality.
The ten preceding stages, if fully traversed, result in either the non-arising of craving and seeking from beginning to end, or the ability to perceive the arrival of Māra beforehand.
After such a long duration, the aggregate of perception (*saṃjñā-skandha*) naturally reaches its end; therefore, this section demonstrates the signs of the exhaustion of perception.
"Sleeping" (*mai*) refers to slumber; "waking" (*wu*) refers to awakening. Within sleep there are dreams; within waking there is perception. However...

A dream is a thought within sleep; a thought is a dream within waking. Both are produced by the solitary mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*), which is the essential characteristic of the aggregate of perception (*saṃjñā-skandha*).
Therefore, when the aggregate of perception is exhausted, dreams and thoughts both cease; because there is no dreaming while asleep.
Yet upon awakening, one realizes there was no thought; thus, whether awake or asleep, it is ever-constant.

When not a single thought arises, this is the very essence of the wondrously luminous nature-awareness—how could it not be constant? It is empty yet without obstruction; still yet without clamor. It is like clouds dispersing and the sky becoming clear.
Furthermore, these coarse and heavy shadows of dust are entirely the dharma-dust (dharmāyatana) taking the aggregate of perception (saṃjñā-skandha) as its substance. When perception is exhausted...

Dust has no basis of its own; therefore, it is said that there are no longer coarse dusts and the like. The above section concerns the self-substance of the mind, while the following sections concern the subtlety of the mind’s illumination of objects.
Furthermore, the "solely projected images" (duoying) mentioned above were previously shown to be empty;

those below, being "objective realms" (xingjing), are likewise empty. The phrase "like a mirror reflecting brightness" refers to the mind illuminating mountains, rivers, and so forth. As for... [text ends]
A mirror manifests reflections; it is without obstruction. "Passing" means that after one has left the object, there is no trace—just as a mirror returns to its emptiness without lingering.
"Vastly receiving and responding to illumination" summarizes the preceding text: when the mind encounters objects, it merely receives and responds to them in a state of emptiness.
This clarifies that both the mind and its objects are empty and harmonious. The final two lines summarize [the entire passage].
"Words and thoughts are exhausted" means that they are bound by ultimate purity. "Wang" (罔) means "non-existent. That which has accumulated deeply over time is called "cchen" (陳).

"Habit" refers to habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*). Indeed, floating thoughts disturb the mind; these are truly the habitual tendencies that have accumulated over a long time and are difficult to eliminate.
Now, they are suddenly and completely extinguished; therefore, it is said they are "resolved" (*liao*). "Resolved" means they cannot be found. "Only the single, refined truth" refers to this.
This is the essence of pure, uniform, empty stillness and awakened clarity. Second, the realm of the *saṃskāra-skandha* (the aggregate of formations) is described:
the root source of birth and death is here revealed. One perceives all twelve classes of sentient beings throughout the ten directions, exhausting every category.
Although one has not yet fully penetrated the origins of each individual life-force, one perceives the common ground of birth as shimmering and turbulent like a mirage;
this serves as the ultimate pivot for the floating sense organs and their objects. This is what is called the realm of the *saṃskāra-skandha* (the aggregate of formations).
"Arising and ceasing" refers to the birth-and-death of segmented existence (*paricchinna-janma-maraṇa*).

The reason why the arising and ceasing of sentient beings within the three realms never ceases is that their fundamental root is all driven by the *saṃskāra-skandha* (the aggregate of formations). As long as the first three aggregates have not been destroyed, this fundamental root can ultimately never be seen.
Now that the first three have been entirely eliminated, the fourth manifests of its own accord and is completely exhausted. This encompasses the twelve classes of living beings.

From the heavens above to the human realm below, throughout the four formless realms (*ārūpyadhātu*), there is nothing that does not fall within the suffering of conditioned existence (*saṃskāra-duḥkhatā*); this is precisely what is meant. Thus it is said that "all its categories are fully exhausted.
Master Huan held that the causal continuity constitutes the *vijñāna-skandha* (consciousness aggregate), while the basis for arising constitutes the *saṃskāra-skandha* (formations aggregate).

He thereby distinguished between the depth and shallowness of these two aggregates. Master Yuan held that their individual designations constitute the specific characteristics (*svalakṣaṇa*), while their shared division constitutes the general characteristic (*sāmānyalakṣaṇa*). This is certain.

The distinction between the subtle and the coarse regarding these two aggregates (skandhas) should both be deeply contemplated. In the commentary on the *Zhuangzi*, the "wild horses" (*yemǎ*) have already been analyzed;

they are merely mirages (*yángyàn*), not dust motes. Furthermore, since the character "yì" (熠) is derived from the radical for fire, it sufficiently demonstrates its correspondence with a flame, representing a flickering radiance.
It refers to the appearance of vapors rising from the earth in springtime when the weather is clear, visible lying upon the ground.

It is like water that possesses light, which is like a flame. "Clarity and agitation" refer to the subtleties of speech and movement. The metaphor of the flame specifically represents that which is hidden, subtle, and difficult to perceive.
If one were to apply the metaphor of water consistently throughout both preceding and following sections, then the *saṃjñā-skandha* (perception aggregate) would still be like a great surging wave.

The aggregate of formations (*saṃskāra-skandha*) is like fine ripples; the aggregate of consciousness (*vijñāna-skandha*) is like flowing water without waves. The essence of true awakening should be like water that is profoundly still and unmoving.

Thus, the aggregate of formations is the root source of fragmented existence (*paricchinna-bhava*), while the aggregate of consciousness is the root source of transformational existence (*pariṇāma-bhava*).

When comparing these from beginning to end, the distinction between the coarse and the subtle, the false and the true, is as clear as looking at one's own palm. Therefore, know that there is only this one [reality].
"Essential and true" (*jingzhen*) is also permitted [as a description]. "Floating roots and objects" (*fugenchen*) refers to the four objects of the floating roots, meaning the physical body.
"Ultimate pivot and cavity" (*jiujing shuxue*) means that the profound root of transmigration, decay, and death lies entirely herein.
The final summary of the realm of the *saṃskāra-skandha* takes only its flickering, clear agitation as its characteristic. △ Second, the conclusion of the refutation and revelation.
The source of delusion is exposed.

If this clarity, amidst its flickering disturbances, returns to its primordial nature, and that nature enters into primordial purity, such that the original habitual tendencies are once and for all clarified—like waves subsiding and transforming back into still water—this is called the exhaustion of the aggregate of formations (*saṃskāra-skandha*).
Such a person is then able to transcend the turbidity of sentient beings. Observe the cause of this:
Deep-seated delusive thoughts constitute its foundation.
Beginning with the aggregate of form (*rūpa-skandha*), it designates the "original nature" (*prakṛti*) to clarify that this is the root-source of birth and extinction—the very substance of nature.
When the waves of water cease and subside, it is called "clarity" (*ting*). This fundamental clarity is precisely the *vijñāna-skandha* (consciousness aggregate).

"The nature enters fundamental clarity" means that the movement of subtle waves returns to the ocean of consciousness where no waves exist. Fundamental habituation is the seed of the *saṃskāra-skandha* (formations aggregate).
To once clarify fundamental habituation is to forever sever the seeds and habits of the *saṃskāra-skandha*, so that they never arise again. The following analogy will make this clear.

This fully accords with the previous metaphor of water. Wēnlíng says: "Birth and death ceaselessly continue; karma and destiny constantly shift—this is called the turbidity of sentient beings (*sattva-kaṣāya*).

Therefore, when the aggregate of formations (*saṃskāra-skandha*) is exhausted, one transcends it. The aggregate of formations shifts secretly, yet there is never any awakening to it; hence it is called 'subtle and hidden delusive thought'.

Having thus completed the detailed demonstration from beginning to end, [the text proceeds to] the second section: the ten calculations regarding the transformation of objects during the intermediate state. It says:
"Speculative views" (kalpanā) refers to the fact that these are merely various false speculations arising from what is seen within one's own meditative concentration;
they do not involve the interference of external objects or demonic activities. This is divided into ten parts. First, two kinds of causelessness, which are further divided into three.
First, the indication of falling away:

Ānanda, you should know that when these good sons who have attained right awareness within *śamatha* concentrate their clarity and stabilize their minds, the ten classes of celestial Māras cannot find an opportunity;
only then are they able to investigate with refinement the root of all living beings, and within that fundamental nature...
Regarding those who expose the source of birth: they contemplate that profound, pure, and perfectly agitated source; yet within that perfect source, they give rise to conceptual calculations.
Such people fall into the two theories of causelessness.
These ten subsequent views arise because the aggregate of perception (*saṃjñā-skandha*) has already been shattered while the aggregate of formations (*saṃskāra-skandha*) remains unshattered;
thus, this section cites the shattering of perception and the manifestation of formations as its opening. "One who attains right knowledge" means that one does not encounter perverse deliberations.
"Within *śamatha*" refers to the illumination of perfect concentration; "stabilized and unmoving" means it is steady and unwavering.

Thus, from beginning to end, one does not give rise to craving or seeking; this clarifies that there is no delusion. When Māra arrives, one perceives it first and remains unconfused, maintaining a correct mind.
Thus, one simultaneously upholds both [the teachings] without wavering or delusion, remaining upright from head to tail.
In this way, the ten classes of celestial Māras mentioned above will ultimately find no opportunity to act; only then can the diligent practitioner truly shatter them through their power.
This is the aggregate of perception (*saṃjñā-skandha*). To exhaust the root of all living beings is to first attain penetration up to the aggregate of formations (*saṃskāra-skandha*).
This above has been a sequential exposition on how the destruction of perception leads to the manifestation of formations; this concludes that section.

Below the "Root" section, the text returns to explain the manifestation of formations as the primary cause, which subsequently gives rise to ten kinds of false calculations. This is because, after the destruction of perception, the celestial Māras are rendered helpless and can no longer intervene.

It arrives. It is simply the calamity wrought by the mind’s own false interpretations; this is what is called the "demon of the mind" (*citta-māra*). "Fundamental categories" refers to the twelve classes [of beings].
"Origin of birth" refers to the aggregate of formations (*saṃskāra-skandha*). "Manifesting" means to reveal itself. "Pervasive" means it extends throughout all twelve classes.

"Profoundly clear yet agitated" refers to the subtle signs of movement. When these pervasive origins are constrained into the formation of the aggregate of formations, it is termed the "two theories of non-causality. This is...
These were merely evil views established by heterodox practitioners of the past through their mistaken interpretations of mental cultivation—views that contradict reason and oppose the correct path.

Now, the interpretation manifested in this practice coincides exactly with theirs; thus, it immediately falls into their own treatises, like a carriage following in the tracks of one that has overturned before.
Therefore, they fall together into the same pit. All subsequent arguments in these various treatises follow this same pattern.

[This is] the meaning. △ Second, a detailed explanation in two sections. This also has two parts: first, the absence of a cause from the beginning. This is established based on the fact that a cause cannot be reached in the past.
This further divides into three: first, according to one's own direct perception (*pratyakṣa*).
The first type of person perceives that there is no fundamental cause. Why is this?

Because this person has already attained the complete breaking open of the life-faculty (*janman-indriya*) and, riding upon the eight hundred merits of the eye-faculty (*cakṣur-indriya*), they see all sentient beings throughout eighty thousand kalpas. They observe the winding currents of karmic flow as beings die here and are born there;
they see only the cycle of rebirth of these sentient beings within those realms. Beyond eighty thousand kalpas, it is dark and nothing can be perceived.

The first two lines establish the definition; the following section interrogates and explains it. The "basis from which the movement of the life-force is activated" refers specifically to the *saṃskāra-skandha* (the aggregate of formations).

Its "destruction" reveals that the meaning is not yet exhausted. Since "vision" pertains to the eye, it corresponds to the number eight hundred thousand based on the merit of the eye; the figures merely correspond in this manner.
It is unnecessary to divide them according to the past and future, for such a calculation would otherwise be inconsistent. This is because [the power] is based on...
The full excellence of the faculty of the eye, conjoined with the power of meditative concentration (*samādhi*), enables one to see through all categories of past beings;
this is the supernormal knowledge of past lives (*pūrvanivāsānusmṛti-jñāna*). Question: Why is this not considered a distinct characteristic? Answer:

It is because one mostly sees the general patterns of how classes of beings transmigrate through birth and death without ceasing, rather than examining each individual case in detail. If one were able to examine each one in detail, [it would be a distinct characteristic].
Thus, the attachment to spontaneity (*svabhāva*) is not established. To refute the subsequent attachment to spontaneity, that point shall be clarified further.
As for that point: it refers to the period within eighty thousand *kalpas*. This is because the scope of their supernormal powers (*ṛddhi-bala*) is limited to this number;
therefore, beyond this number, they remain in darkness and see nothing. 2. Erroneously Forming Deviant Calculations.
They then form this interpretation: "These sentient beings of the world in the ten directions have existed spontaneously without cause for eighty thousand kalpas.
Because they do not perceive the source, they give rise to the calculation of causelessness; based on this, they are called the "causeless non-Buddhists" (*ahetuvādin*).

Master Yue states that these are none other than the *amūrta-tattva* (the principle of the unmanifest). This is because the three paths of sentient beings proceed in succession, each depending upon the other, such that one cannot reach their ultimate limit.
At the beginning, it was only the Buddha-eye that could penetrate through to the end; even Bodhisattvas still have limitations, let alone ordinary beings and those of the Small Vehicle.

Thus, when ordinary beings and those of the Small Vehicle exhaust their supernatural powers, they stop at this point. Master Yue rebuked them for not knowing that causes and consciousnesses are not [the ultimate reality].
Even if they were to know causes and consciousnesses, how could they ever fathom the limit? △ Third: Losing the Truth and Falling into the External.
By means of such conceptualization, one loses right universal knowledge (*samyak-sarvajñā*) and falls into the ranks of external paths (*tīrthika*), thereby deluding the nature of Bodhi.
Because of these false calculations, it is not right knowledge; because one does not understand that the path of karma is beginningless, it is not universal knowledge. The concluding statement says:
"Having already fallen into erroneous awakening, one will ultimately remain lost in true awakening. 2. The Endlessness of Causes. This refers to the absence of a subsequent limit in the future.
Cause and effect is divided into three parts. First, according to one's own direct perception (*pratyakṣa*).
Second, as for those who see that the end has no cause: why is this? Because such people, having already seen its root in birth, know that humans produce humans and realize that birds produce birds;
they hold that crows have always been black and cranes have always been white; and that humans and devas were originally upright, while animals... [are horizontal].
Birth is fundamentally horizontal. White is not produced by washing; black is not created by dyeing. From eighty thousand kalpas ago, there has been no further alteration or displacement.
As for the signs and marks, they are as previously cited according to the interpretation of terms; this is a detailed inference of the past used to definitively establish the future.

"Birth" refers to the various types of beings within a kalpa, while "roots" refer to that which is beyond the kalpa and without cause. Indeed, it is precisely through this absence of cause that one establishes the source of the various types of beings.
The text below [the character for "root"] explains in detail that all things are fundamentally without cause and arise spontaneously (*svabhāva*).
Therefore, this school of thought is designated as the "Spontaneists" (*Svabhāvavādins*). However, it should be understood through examination that this is merely a general characteristic;

they observe that for the most part, sentient beings remain unchanged over long periods of time, and thus they give rise to this calculation. It is like a person observing a bustling marketplace from a distance, seeing only people walking about.
One does not perceive sitting or standing. If one can examine each case individually, then even those who sit or stand for only a brief duration should be known.
This is because, among the twelve classes of beings, only the human class is easily transformed, whereas all others require a long time before they can change.
Now, because one cannot discern particulars through a general observation, one arrives at the notion of spontaneity (*svabhāva*) based on the majority of cases.
Therefore, the final two phrases conclude with the point that there is no change. Master Yue’s commentary shares this same intent;

however, his citation of the episode of Śāriputra observing the pigeon should not be considered entirely identical, for in that instance, he was able to perceive the Tathāgata through their specific characteristics (*svalakṣaṇa*). Thus, [the text] selects the aspect of permanence.
"Transformation" means causing them to observe differently, in order to encourage their progress.

Furthermore, when the four fruits of Arhatship unfold their practice and manifest their consciousness, they are able to discern each individual's life-origins and never cling to the notion of spontaneity (*svabhāva*). △ Second, erroneous views lead to deviant calculations.
Now, even with this final body, it is likewise so. Since I have never from the beginning perceived bodhi, how could there be any further matter of attaining bodhi?
One should know that today all phenomena are fundamentally without cause.
The preceding section entirely detailed the past; this section now establishes the future by analogy. "To the end of one's life" means until the end of the future.
"It is also thus" means that it is determined they shall all remain without change or deviation. The following passage explains this to completion:
"Originally not seeing Bodhi" refers to the period before eighty thousand kalpas, when one originally did not see its departure from Bodhi.

This refers to the nature of arising. As for the phrase "How could it be... and so forth, one should understand by analogy that even after eighty thousand kalpas, it will ultimately not be established.

Regarding the passage beginning with "One should know," it serves to resolve and judge the adherence to false views. Master Yue states that the character "ben" (root/origin) should properly be the character "mo" (end/cessation).
As for "the end has no cause," this means that when the eighty thousand kalpas are exhausted, it will ultimately result in annihilation, and there will be nothing further.
It is merely cause and effect. This is because that which arises from no cause would, in turn, revert to no cause and return to the primordial darkness (*ādikṛta*);
this is simply an inference based on the past, not a vision gained by observing the future.

I suspect that the *saṃskāra-skandha* has not yet been shattered, for otherwise one could not remain identical across preceding and succeeding kalpas. If this were not so, what need would there be for such repeated investigations of the past? Consider this again in detail. △
The third [point] is "losing the truth and falling outside.
Based on these calculations and speculations, one loses correct universal knowledge (*samyak-saṃbodhi*) and falls into the ranks of external paths (*tīrthika*), thereby confusing the nature of Bodhi.
This may be understood by reference to what precedes. △ Third, concluding that these are heterodox treatises.
This is called the first heterodox school establishing the doctrine of causelessness.
The two types of causelessness are concluded. △ Second, the four kinds of universal permanence, divided into three parts. First, the heading indicating the fallacy.
Ānanda, when these good sons within this samādhi concentrate their clarity and align their minds, Māra finds no opportunity.

As they exhaustively investigate the root of all living beings and contemplate that profound, pure source which is yet subject to constant agitation, if they give rise to conceptual calculations within that perfect and eternal state,
such persons fall into the four theories of universal permanence.
The general meaning is that although one has exhausted the investigation of the *saṃskāra-skandha*, it still remains shrouded and unseen;

thus, regarding its subtle, hidden, and shifting flux—which is neither universal nor eternal—one prematurely calculates it to be universal and eternal. This is called the "eternalist view" of the non-Buddhists (*tīrthika*).
Although all four types of such views arise from calculations based on the *saṃskāra-skandha*, the first three all additionally involve the exhaustive investigation of other phenomena. Furthermore...

The number of kalpas is differentiated according to the breadth or narrowness of the dharma; only the fourth [view] lacks both, and thus its kalpa-measure is not mentioned—this is the distinction between them.
Changshui said: "Because the arising and ceasing of the *saṃskāra-skandha* (formations aggregate) continues without interruption, it is called 'constant' (*nitya*);
because the four types [of views] reckoned therein pervade all dharmas, they are called 'universal' (*pariṇata*). Wénlǐng said: "Universal..."
This is precisely "perfection" (yuan). Therefore, the title here is designated as "Pervasive and Constant" (biàncháng), while the conclusion later designates it as "Perfectly Constant" (yuáncháng).
△ Second, the detailed explanation of the sections, divided into four parts. First, the attachment to permanence regarding mind and objects.
First, this person exhaustively investigates the nature of the mind and its objects, finding no cause in either of these two locations.

Through cultivation, they are able to know all the births and deaths of sentient beings throughout the ten directions within twenty thousand kalpas; seeing that these all circulate in a cycle and have never been lost, they reckon them to be permanent.
The first two lines state that this person’s perception of breaking through their practice has manifested;
riding upon this opening of the mind, they proceed to investigate the fundamental origin from which both the internal mind and external objects arise. However, their investigation does not reach far;

they see only that twenty thousand kalpas ago, things existed spontaneously without cause. This is because the phenomena being investigated are coarse and narrow, and thus the scope of their vision is limited.
This is all there is to it. As for "cultivation," this refers to the cultivation that exhausts the nature of mind and objects.

The phrase "is able to know" implies that while beyond twenty thousand kalpas there is indeed a profound darkness devoid of knowledge or vision, within those twenty thousand kalpas one personally witnesses the uninterrupted arising and ceasing of sentient beings.
Therefore, they do not reckon with annihilation beyond the kalpas, but instead reckon that the continuity within the kalpas constitutes pervasive permanence.
This differs from what preceded; the latter three cases are to be understood by analogy. II. Second, calculating the permanence of the four great elements:
Second, this person exhaustively investigates the origin of the four great elements and concludes that their four natures are eternally abiding.

Through cultivation, they are able to know that throughout forty thousand kalpas, all the births and deaths of sentient beings in the ten directions are entirely constant in essence and have never been lost or dispersed; thus, they calculate them to be permanent.
This, too, follows the mind’s opening to exhaustively investigate the source of transformation. One perceives that all phenomena arise from the conjunction of the four great elements;

thus, one applies focused intent to exhaustively examine them. Seeing that their essential nature is eternally abiding, one clearly illuminates the kalpas of birth and death for sentient beings, reaching as far as forty thousand.
Compared to the phenomena previously investigated, this is somewhat more detailed and extensive; therefore, its illumination of the kalpas—
It is several times greater than before. Nevertheless, because they calculate based on permanence, they also follow the previous people in relying solely upon the duration within a kalpa.
△ Third, the eighth consciousness calculates permanence:

these people exhaustively investigate the six sense faculties and the *manas* that grasps and maintains them, reaching the fundamental source from which mind, intellect, and consciousness originally arise.
Because their nature is eternal and constant, through cultivation they are able to know that all sentient beings throughout eighty thousand kalpas circulate without loss;
they are fundamentally ever-abiding, exhausting their course without losing their nature, and they reckon this to be permanence.
The character "gen" (根) is certainly a corruption of the character "shi" (識). There is no need for convoluted explanations regarding subject and object.
Since the *manas* consciousness that grasps and sustains [the body] corresponds to the seventh and eighth consciousnesses, it is beyond doubt that what precedes it refers to the six consciousnesses.

Furthermore, as the text subsequently uses "mind," "intellect," and "consciousness" to collect the eight, seven, and six consciousnesses in reverse order, this can still be verified. The various masters of the old commentaries merely harbored doubts regarding the *saṃskāra-skandha* at this point.

It has not yet been opened. How could one possibly exhaustively penetrate the eight consciousnesses? One must realize that the eight consciousnesses are merely the dharma-gates employed for further cultivation after this person has opened their mind.
As for "penetrating," it is certainly not yet penetrated; as for "exhausting," one may allow for exhaustion.

This is, for example, like the śrāvakas who exhaust the Dharma of the Four Truths, but only reach the limit of birth and death; how could they penetrate the realm of non-action? This applies even to the original source.
Regarding the "locus" (處), Master Yue states that this specifically refers to the aggregate of formations (行陰).
Because they are still shrouded by formations, the fundamental nature they have penetrated merely stops at the aggregate of formations, yet they falsely claim it to be true and eternal.

This is especially because the dharma-gate of the eight consciousnesses they have investigated is deeper, broader, more detailed, and more thorough than the previous four great elements; thus, the number of kalpas they know is also double that of the former.
Yet they reach as far back as eighty thousand [kalpas]. As for those who, within a kalpa, contemplate birth and calculate it to be permanent, their calculation is no different from the former one.
△ Fourth, the calculation of permanence based on the exhaustion of ideation:
Fourth, this person, having exhausted the source of ideation and the principle of its arising, no longer possesses the movement, circulation, or the ideational mind of arising and ceasing.

Now that [the mind] has been eternally extinguished, it is naturally so within the principle, becoming neither arising nor ceasing. Because they are measured by the mind, they are reckoned as permanent.
After such people have exhausted their conceptualizations and their practices have manifested, they lack the power for further investigation and thus reckon them to be permanent.
Compared to the first [level], this is still shallow and inferior; how much more so for the second and third?
Therefore, one does not establish a kalpa-length for that which can be known. Measuring what is known, it certainly does not reach twenty thousand kalpas.

By this inference, one knows that in the preceding texts, where there was originally no cause, the reason eight thousand kalpas were illuminated must likewise have been due to the power of the eye’s merit. Furthermore...
Only through the application of exhaustive investigation can one finally achieve this; it is not something that can be accomplished simply by exhausting one's thoughts. Wēnlíng says:

"The 'origin of thought' refers to the aggregate of perception (*saṃjñā-skandha*); the 'principle of life' refers to the aggregate of formations (*saṃskāra-skandha*). It is falsely claimed that the flow and cessation of transmigration both belong to the mind of perception."
Now that [birth] has been eternally extinguished, the principle of non-arising and non-extinction naturally belongs to the formations (*saṃskāra*).
One does not realize that the aggregate of formations (*saṃskāraskandha*) is the very source of arising and extinction. △ Third, the conclusion of the external treatise.
Based on this calculation of permanence, they lose the correct universal knowledge and fall into the ranks of external paths, becoming deluded regarding the nature of Bodhi.
This is called the second type of external path: the doctrine of established perfect permanence.

They conceive of what is not all-pervasive and perfect as being all-pervasive and perfect; they conceive of what is not true and eternal as being true and eternal. Thus they fall into false awakening and lose right awakening.

In this context, there is no need to follow the old commentary’s forced classification [of these views] under the five aggregates, claiming that the former is broad while the latter is narrow, for such an approach would only create confusion contrary to the original text. The four types of pervasive permanence are concluded. △ Three.

The four types of inversion. Combining these with the previous two views, there are five: second, the causeless view, which, resembling an observation of the point of cessation outside the kalpas, calculates impermanence;
fourth, the view of universal permanence, which, resembling an observation of the continuity within the kalpas, calculates permanence.

Each of these previously mentioned views was a single calculation alone; the present one, however, is a dual calculation of both permanence and impermanence. This is divided into three parts: first, the statement of the cause.

To show the fall: furthermore, among those sons of good family within *samādhi*, who have stabilized their minds in right concentration so that Māras find no opportunity, and who exhaustively investigate the root of all living beings by contemplating that profound,
pure, yet eternally agitated source— if they give rise to conceptual calculations regarding self and others, such a person falls into [error].
The four inverted views include the doctrine that one part is impermanent and one part is permanent.
Following the exhaustion of perceptions and the manifestation of formations, one exhaustively investigates oneself and others, giving rise to false and deluded discriminations.
These are further categorized as either single or dual, yet they do not transcend the relationship between self and other; it is not a case of each pair being combined simultaneously. Śūraṅgama...
Within meditative concentration (*samādhi*), one must realize that all phenomena are ultimately and firmly established as the Perfect Enlightenment (*samyak-saṃbodhi*).

Now, however, because one calculates by treating the permanent and the impermanent as equal parts, this constitutes a perverted view (*viparyāsa-dṛṣṭi*). △ Second Part: Detailed Explanation in Sections. This is divided into four sections.
The first pair concerns the distinction between self and others.
First, there is the person who contemplates the wondrously luminous mind as pervading the worlds of the ten directions, regarding it as a profoundly still and ultimate "divine self.
From this, they calculate that their self pervades the ten directions, remaining concentrated, luminous, and unmoving; thus, all sentient beings exist within the center of their own heart.
"Arising and perishing by itself, my own mind-nature is therefore called 'constant. That which arises and perishes is truly of an impermanent nature. Wuxing says:

"From 'observing the subtle' (*guān miào*) onwards, he again raises the topic of contemplative practice (*guānxíng*). From 'serenely still' (*zhànrán*) onwards, he correctly clarifies the arising of conceptualization.

This is also because one fails to understand the arising and perishing of the *saṃskāra-skandha* (the aggregate of formations), falsely claiming that the mind-nature at this stage is serenely still, and taking it to be the divine self (*ātman*). Thus he speaks.
The "divine self" (puruṣa) is what non-Buddhists call the "principle of the Lord" (īśvaratattva).
They claim that all phenomena are "mine," and that this divine self is their master. This is the final principle among the twenty-five principles (tattvas).
What is stated in the second fascicle—that there is a true self pervading the ten directions—is precisely this. One should know that one's own mind is without arising or ceasing.
One then calculates that one’s own self is permanent, while sentient beings undergo birth and death within one’s own mind; one then calculates that others are impermanent.
Thus, these constitute a dualistic calculation. △ Second, regarding other lands.
Second, such a person does not contemplate their own mind, but instead surveys throughout the lands of the ten directions as numerous as the sands of the Ganges.

Where they see places where kalpas are destroyed, they designate this as the "nature of ultimate impermanence. Where they see places where kalpas are not destroyed, they designate this as "ultimate permanence."
Since it is said that one does not contemplate the mind, this clearly indicates contemplating only other phenomena; that is, contemplating only the land.
Wuxing says: "From the third dhyāna downward, all are ultimately destroyed by the three calamities and are thus termed 'of impermanent nature.
From the fourth dhyāna upward, they cannot be destroyed by calamities and are thus termed 'ultimately permanent. △ Third, [the contemplation] in relation to one's own body and mind.
Third, this person separately contemplates their own mind as being subtle, fine, and dense, like a minute particle.

It transmigrates through the ten directions, its nature remaining unchanging, capable of causing this body to arise and perish in an instant; this indestructible nature is called the permanence of the self-nature.
All birth and death flow forth from this self; it is named the nature of impermanence.

One should observe the body and mind separately from themselves. The mind is capable of subtle transformation yet remains unchanging, thus being permanent; it causes the body to undergo birth, death, and decay, thus being impermanent.
Furthermore, there are three types of the "self" as conceived by the non-Buddhists (*tīrthika*): first, the subtle self; second, [the gross self]; third, [the intermediate self].
The vast self. Third, the great and small selves. This is the subtle self (*sūkṣmātman*). "Essential" means it is not mixed; "subtle" means it is not coarse;
"minute" means it is not attached; "dense" means it is not manifest. Like a mote of dust, it is said to be so fine and small as to be difficult to see or know.
The first two lines concern transmigration; that is, calculating that one's own mind is eternally neither arising nor ceasing.
"Able to cause" and below refers to calculating that one's own body is impermanent, subject to arising and ceasing. The final four lines reaffirm permanence and impermanence:
the first two lines reaffirm the mind, and the latter two reaffirm the body. Is this not simply a calculation formed based solely on oneself? △ Four: The Dual [View].
It is not other than itself.

Fourth, this person knows that the aggregate of perception (*saṃjñā-skandha*) has been exhausted and perceives the flow of the aggregate of formations (*saṃskāra-skandha*). Because the aggregate of formations flows constantly, they reckon it as having a permanent nature;
whereas form, sensation, perception, and so forth, having now ceased and been extinguished, are termed impermanent.

This contemplation arises from the calculation [of the nature] of the first four aggregates (*skandhas*). Because the distinction between self and other is not absolute, it is called "neither both" (*ubhayānta-vinirmukta*).

When calculating the aggregate of formations (*saṃskāra-skandha*), it is not "other," because formations are one's own mind. When calculating the [remaining] three aggregates, they are not purely one's own mind, because form (*rūpa*) includes the six external sense objects (*viṣaya*).
If one considers that the aspect of self is predominant while the aspect of other is minor, and follows the predominant over the minor, it may also be categorized as follows:
Based on the four aggregates (*skandha*), this diagram now establishes four meanings that are neither deficient nor redundant; thus, these sections are established.
The distinction between the permanent and the impermanent is easily understood from the text. △ Third, concluding the external treatise.
Because they calculate that one part is impermanent while another part is permanent, they fall into the ranks of the externalists and become deluded regarding the nature of Bodhi.
This is called the third heterodox doctrine: the theory of partial permanence.

This is because, although the designations "self" and "other"—whether taken individually or as a pair—are not fixed, the notions of permanence and impermanence they calculate are all equally dualistic reckonings.
The four types of perversions are hereby concluded. △ Fourth, the four types of having limits.

Although the text speaks of dualistically reckoning both "having limits" and "having no limits," in principle this is merely a false reckoning of the view of extremes (*antagrāhadṛṣṭi*); it is not truly [the attainment of]...
Regarding the reality of the boundless principle, it is therefore judged by means of the authentic teaching to be merely "bounded" in name.
Examining its underlying intent, it seems that "bounded" is taken to mean having a finite limit, which is not the supreme dharma; whereas "boundless" is taken to mean having no finite limit.
This is a superior teaching. For example, it is like weighing permanence and impermanence together, yet taking only permanence as superior.
This is divided into three parts: first, the heading that indicates the fallacy.

Furthermore, among those good sons within samādhi who have stabilized their minds in right concentration, so that Māras find no opportunity, they exhaustively investigate the root of all living beings.
As they contemplate that profound, pure, yet eternally agitated source, if they form conceptual calculations regarding its various states,
such persons fall into the four theories of finitude.

Wenling says: There are four divisions of position, namely: the division of the three time periods (*traiyadhvika*), the division of seeing and hearing, the division of self and other, and the division of arising and ceasing.
[The following] provides a detailed explanation of these two categories in four parts. First, concerning the three time periods:
First, these people calculate the origin of birth as a stream of activity that never ceases;
calculating the past and future, they call it "finite," and calculating the continuous mind, they call it "infinite."
Wenling says: "The source of birth flowing and functioning is the *saṃskāra-skandha* (the aggregate of formations). Because it migrates and flows, one calculates across the three periods of time.
That which has passed has already ceased, and that which is yet to come is not yet seen; therefore, they are called 'having limits. That which is currently continuous is called 'limitless.
Since one takes the present mind’s point of continuity as being without limit, one must necessarily take the points where the past and future are severed as having limits."
"Limitless. Now, regarding "the present mind being limitless," this refers to contemplating the mind as it is, vast and boundless, without shore or limit.
△ Second, [discussing] in terms of seeing and hearing.
Second, this person contemplates eighty thousand kalpas; they then see that prior to those eighty thousand kalpas, sentient beings were quiescent, beyond hearing or seeing.
That state beyond hearing or seeing is called "boundless," while the presence of sentient beings is called "bounded."
This is the opposite of the previous calculation. It is what Master Yue referred to as "mutual reversal and inverted calculation.
The previous calculation held that the past and future constitute the finite (the bounded), which is like calculating that there are places where seeing and hearing do not occur.

It held that the present constitutes the infinite (the unbounded), which is like calculating that there are places where seeing and hearing do occur. Now, however, one calculates that within a kalpa, those places where seeing and hearing occur constitute the finite, because...

This is limited to a number of eighty thousand. Calculating that there is no place for seeing or hearing beyond the kalpas constitutes "boundlessness," because it is infinite and cannot be measured or known.
Wu Xing said: "The subsequent eighty thousand kalpas should likewise be as before;
I now fear that [the text] has been abbreviated. △ Third, regarding self and other.
Third, this person calculates that because they possess universal knowledge, they have attained the nature of boundlessness. To them, all other people appear within the scope of their own knowing;
yet they themselves have never known the nature of those others' knowing. Thus, they claim that those others do not possess a mind of boundlessness, but rather possess only a limited nature.
The first three phrases [state that] one assumes for oneself a nature that is boundless.
The subsequent statement, "that person manifests within my cognition," means that such a nature exists solely within my own nature.
"I have never known that nature" means that within my own nature, I do not perceive any separate cognitive nature belonging to another. This also clarifies that such a nature cannot [be perceived].
Externally, they disregard the nature of the self; thus, with the final two phrases, they judge that [the self] possesses the nature of finitude.
△ Fourth, regarding arising and ceasing:

these people exhaustively investigate the emptiness of the aggregate of formations (*saṃskāra-skandha*). Using the mental pathways they perceive, they calculate and deliberate upon all sentient beings.
Within a single body, it is reckoned that all things are half-born and half-extinguished; this clarifies that of everything existing within the world, one half has limits and one half is limitless.

Regarding those who exhaustively investigate the emptiness of the aggregate of formations (*saṃskāra-skandha*): it is because such persons have reached the limit of the aggregate of formations but fail to realize that its domain has not yet become empty, that they consequently claim this to be the nature of true emptiness and quiescent extinction.
Thus, "half-birth and half-extinction" refers to their measuring the bodies of sentient beings based on deluded views;

from the aggregate of perception (*saṃjñā-skandha*) onwards, the former half belongs to birth, while from the aggregate of formations (*saṃskāra-skandha*) onwards, the latter half [belongs to extinction].
These belong to cessation (*nirodha*). Furthermore, they distinguish birth as finite and cessation as infinite;

yet their underlying intent is to grasp the emptiness and stillness of the aggregate of formations (*saṃskāra-skandha*) as the supreme nature of limitless boundaries. △ Third, the conclusion of the external treatise.
Based on these deliberations regarding finitude and infinity, they fall among the non-Buddhists and become deluded concerning the nature of Bodhi;
this is precisely what is called the fourth type of non-Buddhist who establishes the doctrine of finitude.
The four kinds of finite existence are concluded. △ Five: The Four Kinds of Evasive Confusion, divided into three parts. First: The Marking and Demonstration of the Fall.

Furthermore, among the sons of good family within *samādhi*, if they maintain a firm and unyielding correct mind, Māras shall find no opportunity; they will exhaust the root of all classes of living beings.
If one contemplates that profound, pure, and eternally agitated source and gives rise to conceptual calculations within the sphere of knowledge and vision,
such a person falls into the four kinds of perverse, indecisive, and chaotic speculations on immortality— universal theories of empty fabrication.

"Regarding those who harbor distorted views based on their knowledge and insight": this refers to making erroneous calculations based on what is known and seen within that state of meditative concentration.
Wénlǐng says: "Because they are perverted and mistaken, amidst their knowledge and insight, their deluded interpretations remain indecisive; they consequently distort and confuse their speech."
The depraved people of today falsely claim to have attained the Way, yet they lack internal rectitude and instead delude others; most such individuals fall into these four categories.
Zizhong said: According to the *Abhidharma-mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra*, non-Buddhists calculate that the heavens are eternally abiding and thus call them "immortal.
They further calculate that by providing unconfused answers, one will be reborn in those heavens. If one truly does not know but nonetheless answers recklessly, there is fear...

Thus, they fall into evasive equivocation. Therefore, when questioned, they reply, "It is secret," or speak in a confused manner, claiming that everything should not be explained, or providing indefinite answers.
The Buddha of the Dharma rebuked them, saying: "This is truly evasive equivocation. Hence, it is called the "Evasive Discourse on Immortality" (amarā-vikkhepa).
△ Detailed Explanation of the Two Divisions. This is further divided into four parts. First, the eighth [type] is also characterized by evasive equivocation (*vāg-vibhramśa*).
First, this person contemplates the source of transformation; seeing the locus of flux, they designate it as "change. Seeing the locus where characteristics converge...
That which is called "constant" refers to the locus where seeing is perceived. That which is called "arising" refers to the locus where seeing is not perceived.

That which is called "increase" refers to the cause of continuity, the state where its nature is uninterrupted. Within the process of correct continuity, it refers to the point where the middle is abandoned.

That which is called "diminution" refers to the various places where things arise; that which is called "existence" refers to their mutual presence; and that which is called "non-existence" refers to their mutual disappearance.
When observing through principle as a whole while perceiving with a particularized mind, there may be seekers of the Dharma who come to inquire about its meaning.
To them, one answers: "I am now both arising and ceasing, both existent and non-existent, both increasing and diminishing. At all times, such a person confuses their speech.
This causes the former person to lose the essential phrases [of the text].
Changshui says: Within the single life-phase of the aggregate of formations (*saṃskāra-skandha*), one distinguishes eight meanings through separate views, namely:
