The power [of this] goes without saying. Question: While it is certainly so regarding the internal faculties, how does it relate to the three perceptions when external receptacles are included? Answer:
As previously stated in the section on the continuity of the world, such as "solidity establishes resistance" and "the realization of solidity is formed from jewels," and so forth.

This is also a solidified false imagination. △ Second, the false imagination of the aggregate of sensation (*vedanā-skandha*). This is divided into two parts. First, the transformation of perception into sensation:
that is, this aforementioned perception of height, which can cause your physical form to truly experience a sense of acid and astringent distress.
The first two lines refer back to the preceding aggregate of perception (*saṃjñā-skandha*), specifically echoing the previous metaphor of standing at a high precipice and imagining a fall.

The subsequent two lines take only that which experiences bitterness and astringency as the aggregate of sensation (*vedanā-skandha*); this is what is meant by "perception transforming into sensation.
To speak of it as "true sensation" intends to clarify that although the perception of a high and perilous place has no reality, the form itself undergoes true bitterness and astringency.
All sensations may be understood as illusory by analogy with this. II. Expanding the argument and concluding with the name:
Because sensation arises from causes, it is able to move the substance of form. You now experience before you both the favorable and the adverse; these two manifest states drive you about.
This is called the second false discrimination, "empty clarity.

The first two lines cite the preceding false sensation of a moving substance as an example, showing that all subsequent sensations are likewise false movements. Wuxing says: "In your present experience...

and so forth, which correctly demonstrates sensation and perception. That which is favorable and beneficial is pleasant sensation (*sukha-vedanā*); that which is adverse and harmful is... [unpleasant sensation].
Regarding painful sensations (*duḥkhā-vedanā*): there are also those that are neither contrary nor favorable, namely sensations that are neither painful nor pleasant (*aduḥkhāsukhā-vedanā*).

This is merely an abbreviation in the text. Wēnlíng says: "When one contemplates empty space, the feelings of bitterness and astringency truly arise; thus, both the contrary and the favorable are illusory.

Yet, as benefit and harm manifest and race about, the aggregate of sensation (*vedanā-skandha*) has no substance—it is a voidness that is clearly perceived. Therefore, it is called 'illusory clarity' delusion. △ Three.
The aggregate of perception (*saṃjñā-skandha*) is a false conceptualization. It is divided into two: first, that which is associated with the mindfulness of the body.
Because of your mental deliberations, you cause your physical body to act; yet the body is not of the same category as thought.
For what reason does your body follow the dictates of thought to grasp various forms? The mind gives rise to formal grasping, which is associated with thought.

This section fully demonstrates the emptiness of the aggregate of perception (*saṃjñā-skandha*), which can cause the reality of the aggregate of form (*rūpa-skandha*) to correspond with that emptiness;
thus, one perceives the falsity of the aggregate of perception. Wénlǐng says: "Thoughts and deliberations are empty sentiments, while the physical body is substantial reality.
That these two, being of different natures—empty and real—can influence one another is due to their being integrated by perception. The mind gives rise to empty perceptions."
The form takes on the reality of the object, while the mind and the form have distinct functions; yet they are able to correspond because of the pervasive power of *saṃjñā* (perception).
2. Expanding the Scope and Concluding the Name:

When awake, it is the mind of perception; when asleep, it becomes all manner of dreams. Thus, your perceptions and thoughts, which stir up deluded sentiments, are called "pervasive integration" (*rútōng*).
The third deluded thought:
waking thoughts and dreaming in sleep both have the solitary mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*) as their substance; thus, they belong to the aggregate of perception (*saṃjñā-skandha*).
To speak of them as "shaking and moving deluded sentiments" is to reveal that they are all not the quiescent true mind. Wēnlíng says: "Waking and sleeping, shaking and changing."

Causing the mind to follow objects, or causing objects to follow the mind—both are deluded thoughts of mutual interpenetration. △ Fourth, the deluded thoughts of the aggregate of formations (*saṃskāra-skandha*).
This is divided into three parts. First, the lack of awakening to the shifting nature of substance.

The principle of transformation does not abide; it shifts and moves in secret with every passing moment. The nails grow and the hair sprouts; the vital energy wanes and the face wrinkles. Day and night they succeed one another, yet there is never any awakening to this process.

This also follows the previous example to clarify that the illusory aggregate of formations (*saṃskāra-skandha*) is capable of displacing the substantial reality. The first two lines cite the aggregate of formations;
"transformative principle" (*huàlǐ*) refers to the nature of transformation, which indicates that the aggregate of formations takes constant flux as its characteristic.

Therefore it is said that they do not abide. "Moving on and moving on" (*yunyun*) is synonymous with "thought after thought" (*nianian*). "Secretly shifting" (*mimi*) indicates the hidden subtlety of their movement.
Zhuangzi’s metaphor of the boat being carried away by a stream at night illustrates precisely this sense of secret shifting;

however, while he refers to it as the work of *zaohua* (the creative force of nature), here it is called the *saṃskāra-skandha* (the aggregate of formations). The following two lines specifically illustrate the substantial entity that undergoes transition. For indeed, [it is] transitioning...
From youth to adulthood, one transitions from vigor to old age. Day and night replace one another; that is, there is not a single kṣaṇa in which one can remain stationary.
Yet, one never awakens to this, for it is said that one cannot comprehend it moment by moment—precisely because the process of transition is so subtle.
△ Second, a dual interrogation of right and wrong.
"Ānanda, if this were not you, how could its substance undergo transformation? If it must be truly you, why do you have no awareness of it?
This phrase refers to the *saṃskāra-skandha* (the aggregate of formations). "If this were not you" means: if this shifting and flowing *saṃskāra-skandha* were indeed not your mind;
"how could its substance undergo transformation? is an interrogation as to how it is able to transform and change your own reality.
Is it the substance? Since you do not deny it, if it were truly your mind, why do you not perceive it?
This interrogates why you do not cognize it moment by moment;
since you do not identify with it, it is neither "not-you" nor "you"—neither can be definitively established. Thus, one knows it is empty.
It is delusory and not real. △ Third, expanding upon the point to conclude with its name:
Thus, your various formations (saṃskāra) do not cease for even a single moment; this is called the fourth subtle and hidden false imagination.
That which is "hidden and obscure" (youyin) is fundamentally defined by the difficulty of knowing its shifting flux and the uncertainty of determining right from wrong;
it also takes as its characteristic that the first three [aggregates] are concealed and cannot be seen without cultivation.

Generally speaking, although the three aggregates of sensation, perception, and formations all belong to the mind, the text emphasizes that they must be shown to be interconnected with the physical body (*rūpakāya*). As for sensation, it is able to cause the physical body...
Regarding the domain of perception: through ideation, one can direct the body; through volitional formations, one can transform the physical substance.

Furthermore, although it is said that the three aggregates pervade the material body, the essential point is to reveal that the body belongs to the category of mental ideation and is not truly existent.

△ Five: The Delusive Conceptions of the Five Aggregates of Consciousness. Divided into four parts. First: Granting and Denying the Real and the False. This is further divided into two. First: Granting the Reality with respect to its Nature.
Furthermore, that which you call "constant"—the place where your clarity and brilliance are profound and unshakable—does not depart from the body’s seeing, hearing, sensing, and knowing.
If one is truly refined and authentic, there is no room for the habitual delusion of false thoughts.

Although the *vijñāna-skandha* (consciousness aggregate) of the stage of delusion generally encompasses all eight consciousnesses, within the stages of cultivation and severance, once the first four aggregates have been exhausted, there is no longer any coarse, floating, or shifting movement;
what need is there then to mention the [first] seven? One should know that this refers exclusively to the eighth consciousness.
Therefore, these first three phrases first employ concessive language to establish constancy. "Vividly clear and unshakable" refers to the eighth consciousness.
Being pure and undifferentiated while penetratingly illuminating both horizontally and vertically is called "vivid clarity";

this is what is meant by "resembling oneness. When floating thoughts have ceased and all disturbances have stilled, it is called "serene and unshakable"; this is what is meant by [resembling stillness].
"Constant. The term "perpetually constant" (*nitya*) is precisely a word used for formal affirmation. It asks:
if one takes this very consciousness—vividly clear and unshakable—to be the true, constant, and unchanging nature?

Regarding the phrase "in the body," it implies that even if one does not practice delusion, as long as one does not transcend seeing, hearing, sensing, and knowing within the body, it serves to further clarify the faculties (*indriya*) previously indicated in the Sūtra.
This nature within is undoubtedly the eighth substance. However, while the preceding section revealed the True through the delusive, this section investigates the True to sever the delusive.
If the true essence were not susceptible to the habitual delusion, it would be as the saying goes:
"If it were truly refined gold, it should not be mixed with sand. The matters concerning habitual delusion will be demonstrated in the following section. △
Second, verifying that memory refutes delusion:
For what reason, among you, would there be someone who once saw a marvelous object in years past, yet after the passage of time, has neither remembered it nor forgotten it?
Later, when suddenly looking back upon those former wonders, the memory remains vivid and clear, without the slightest loss.
Thus, within this state of refined clarity and profound stillness, there is a continuous permeation by habitual tendencies from moment to moment; how could it possibly be calculated?
This refers merely to the fault of the habitual delusions of the eight consciousnesses, wherein one remembers and maintains what was seen many years ago without forgetting it.

Although the initial perfuming occurs through the first six consciousnesses, the act of recollecting and maintaining [the impressions] without forgetfulness is not something the first six can accomplish.
The first six are like ministers who collect revenues; the eighth is like the official in charge of the treasury; and the seventh is like the officer who handles both expenditures and receipts.
The Master [Xuanzang] knew that this treatise’s inclusion of "retention" (*dhāraṇa*) refers exclusively to the eighth consciousness.

In reality, this consciousness is capable of retaining and holding immeasurable varieties of habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*) from many kalpas, which mature in succession; how could it be limited merely to the many years of the present life?
The old commentaries failed to understand this, erroneously including the first seven consciousnesses; their loss of the essential meaning was profound. Amidst the unmoving stillness, mindfulness...

Regarding the statement that "mindfulness perfumes [the seeds]": this means that after one has seen an object, although it may seem as though the mind has forgotten it and the matter is set aside, in reality, it is perfumed and maintained by mindfulness moment after moment without a single instant's interruption.

If this were not so, how could it appear vividly before the mind when one looks back upon it later? What calculating person would say that this is merely proof that a single object has not been forgotten?
In reality, the immeasurable accumulated habits that maintain the seeds are boundless; therefore, it is said thus. △ Second, the formal presentation of the analogy:
Ānanda, you should know that this stillness is not true; it is like a rapid current of water which, from a distance, appears tranquil because the flow is so swift that it cannot be seen.
It is not that which is without outflows (*anāsrava*). If it were not the source of perception (*saṃjñā*), how could it receive the habitual tendencies of delusion?

One must take the water of a rapid current that is free from waves—the swift flow of a level stream—which appears as tranquil because it lacks the irregularity of billows and the up-and-down movement of surging rapids. The following two lines clarify its correctness.
Because the current is so swift, it cannot be seen; it is not that there is truly no current. Once, standing by this water, I observed its flow at leisure.
I cast a blade of grass upon the surface, and the blade sped away with great velocity. Only then did I realize that the current was extremely rapid and was not, in fact, absent.
Thus, when the Buddha previously tested his ability to predict the movement of objects, it was like casting that blade of grass.

The final two lines serve as a definitive judgment that one is still contemplating the source. This is because while the preceding exhaustion of the *saṃjñā-skandha* (aggregate of perception) merely exhausted coarse perceptions, in reality, this aggregate remains characterized by subtle perceptions;
therefore, one continues to undergo these deluded habitual tendencies. Generally speaking, when tracing back to the root, there is only a single deluded thought (*vikalpa*).
However, its coarse and manifest forms reach their limit in the *rūpa-skandha* (aggregate of form), while its subtle and minute forms reach their limit in the *saṃjñā-skandha*.
Regarding the aggregate of consciousness: △ Third, pointing out the time of cessation:
This delusion of yours—the mutual functioning, merging, and opening of the six sense organs—can never be extinguished.
Since this statement that the aggregate of consciousness (vijñāna-skandha) is neither certain nor truly essential, it still belongs to deluded habituation.
If so, when will this delusion finally be extinguished? It must be at the time when the six sense organs function interchangeably, after the barriers between the organs have been opened and merged.
This deluded thought is precisely what must be extinguished. However, the Sutra uses paradoxical language to reveal this truth; thus it says:
"If one does not enter the perfect through the faculties and understanding, this delusion will never have a time of extinction.

This refers to the mutual application of the faculties and the union of opening and closing, which occurs exactly at the moment when quiescent extinction manifests before one—attaining the two extraordinary excellences at the conclusion of the Ten Faiths and the beginning of the Ten Abidings.
△ Fourth, the generalization and naming of the result.

Therefore, among what you currently see, hear, perceive, and know, how many have been repeatedly practiced? Thus, there is a profound clarity within that is ethereal, formless, and void—the fifth inversion, a subtle and refined conceptualization.
The "present seeing, hearing, perceiving, and cognizing" refers to the substance of the six faculties as they manifest before Ānanda, wherein not a single thought arises;
this is like the Buddha’s previous tenfold revelation of the fundamental essence of consciousness—immovable and undying—as the "brightly pure source.
As for the phrase "the various habitual tendencies within," it refers to the fact that when one perceives an object, it is not forgotten, and each moment is permeated by karmic conditioning.
"Profoundly clear" (*zhanliao*) refers to the state within that is brilliant and lucid, remaining profoundly still and unwavering.

"Formless and void" (*wangxiang xuwu*) means that its essence is fundamentally the illusory cataracts of ignorance; it appears substantial yet is empty, and appears existent yet is non-existent. "Inversion" (*dian-dao*) refers to...

"To be deluded regarding the truth and to cling to the semblance" refers to this. "Subtle and minute" refers to the *ālayavijñāna* (the *dharmadhātu-vijñāna*). "Essential and pure ideation" refers to the essential source of the clarity of consciousness (*vijñāna*).
This merely distinguishes it from the coarse ideations of the torrential flow within the previously described aggregate of ideation (*saṃjñā-skandha*).
The detailed exposition of the five layers of false imagination is hereby concluded. △ Third, the summary of what is produced by false imagination.
"Ānanda, these five aggregates of clinging (pañca-upādāna-skandha) are formed by five kinds of delusive conceptualization.
Wēnlíng says: "The five aggregates of clinging are also called the five aggregates of grasping (pañca-upādāna-khandha).

Due to the delusion of a single thought-moment, one receives and grasps these [aggregates], thereby concealing and hiding oneself. [This concludes] the preceding general statement. From this perspective, although the five aggregates are superficial...
They differ in being deep, coarse, or subtle; yet, in sum, they are all produced by deluded conceptualization (*vikalpa*) and are not inherently present within the true mind.
This concludes the response regarding the arising of deluded conceptualization. II. Response concerning the shallow and deep levels of the aggregates (*skandha*) and elements (*dhātu*).
If you now wish to know the depth of the causal realms: mere form and emptiness are the limits of form; mere contact and separation are the limits of sensation;
mere recollection and forgetfulness are the limits of perception; mere cessation and arising are the limits of mental formations.
"The profound stillness merges with profound stillness, returning to the limit of consciousness.
Ānanda’s third question previously asked: "In this way, through these five stages, where do they reach their boundary?

The Buddha now answers this question within his second response. Regarding the phrase "due to boundaries" (*yin jie*), the old commentaries explain it according to the principle of the mutual conditioning of space and form, and so forth.

To explain this: there is indeed a sense of insentience here. Now, examining ancient exegesis regarding the eighteen *dhātus*, it is said that "realm" (*dhātu*) signifies the sense of a cause—that which gives rise to all phenomena, just as the earth produces things and serves as the cause for those things.

Thus, the five aggregates (*skandhas*) are simply the expansion and contraction of these realms; therefore, they are called "causal realms. This is merely another name for the aggregates. As for their relative depth and shallowness...
Regarding the depth and shallowness of the limits [of phenomena], each of the five aggregates possesses its own.
For instance, within the aggregate of form (*rūpa-skandha*), that which has characteristics is form, while that which is without characteristics is emptiness (*śūnyatā*).

If one departs from all forms and causes the mind to dwell in empty purity, the Patriarchal School calls this "the limit of a single form," while the Consciousness-Only school calls it "the single manifest color of emptiness. Thus, we know that one exhausts form without exhausting emptiness.
All of these have not yet transcended the boundaries of the aggregate of form (*rūpa-skandha*), and thus all forms of patience regarding emptiness (*śūnyatā-kṣānti*) are not ultimate.

Within the aggregate of sensation (*vedanā-skandha*), attachment is called "contact" (*sparśa*), while detachment is called "separation" (*viveka*). One should sever all attachments while not forgetting this state of detachment.
This is still abiding within the midst of equanimity and sensation (*vedanā*). Therefore, after teaching the departure from illusion, the Buddha further taught the departure from that very departure.
One should know that while contact (*sparśa*) may be exhausted, if departure is not yet exhausted, one has not yet emerged from the limits of the aggregate of sensation;

thus, all forms of renunciation (*pratisaṃvid*) are not ultimate. Within the aggregate of perception (*saṃjñā*), having mindfulness is recording, and lacking mindfulness is forgetting. [Excluding all...]

To be mindful without forgetting is still to dwell within the realm of quietistic mindfulness. Therefore, the Buddha said that both having mindfulness and being without mindfulness lead equally to delusion and confusion.
The Patriarch said: "Do not say that 'no-mind' is the Way; even no-mind is still separated from it by a single barrier.
Thus we know that to retain everything in memory without ever forgetting is likewise to remain within the limits of the *saṃskāra-skandha* (the aggregate of mental formations). And yet, one—

All states of non-conceptualization are ultimately not the final goal. Within the aggregate of formations (*saṃskāra-skandha*), the coarse activity of the distracted mind during the stage of delusion is the characteristic of arising, as illustrated in the second fascicle by the metaphor of a torrential stream.

The subtle activity of the concentrated mind during the stage of cultivation is the characteristic of cessation, as illustrated in this fascicle by the metaphor of a mirage. Nevertheless, these subtle activities appear to be ceasing.
It is not cessation; it remains a subtle, restless transformation. This can be verified by the fact that even a person in meditative concentration cannot avoid the growth of nails and hair.
Thus we know that while birth has been exhausted, cessation has not; one has likewise not yet transcended the limits of the aggregate of formations (*saṃskāra-skandha*).

Yet all states of cessation (nirodha-samāpatti) are ultimately not final. Within the aggregate of consciousness (vijñāna-skandha), taking "entry" (*praveśa*) as "tranquil entry" means that the flow of formations (*saṃskāra*) has been extinguished and one has submerged into the ocean of consciousness.
As the Sūtra says: "The nature of entry is fundamentally clear; once it is clarified, original habits vanish, like waves subsiding and transforming into still water.
This is what is meant. Taking "non-entry" (*apraveśa*) as "merging with the tranquil" refers to what the Sūtra calls "internally..."
"Externally serene and luminous, entering where there is nothing to enter"—this is it. The character "he" (合) carries the meaning of immovability;
it is like not perceiving the flow of a river when the current is so rapid. Nevertheless, the scope and measure of this state of "conjoining the serenity" (合湛) are no small matter.

This is because the initial mention of "serene entry" specifically indicates the very moment the *saṃskāra-skandha* (行陰) is dissolving and consciousness first enters the ocean of awareness; by this stage, one has already attained the level of the seventh faith (*saptama-śraddhā*).

While [the various methods] are equal in relation to the four fruits of arhatship, the path of perfect penetration (yuan-tong) specifically lies in the exhaustion of both hearing and that which is heard.

It concludes by merging with the profound stillness (*zhan*), which is renamed the ocean of consciousness; having long remained still, clear, and pure to the ultimate degree, the realms gradually open, being on the verge of penetrating yet not yet fully penetrated.

By station, this may correspond to the eighth, ninth, or tenth stages of faith (*xin*); as for perfect penetration, it should fall within the final three fetters (*jie*). Although one perceives the entry into profound stillness...
Furthermore, although one may suddenly attain stillness, it remains within the realm of consciousness; thus, one cannot escape being transmuted by the four most subtle phases of change.

Know that while you have exhausted the entry into profound stillness, you have not yet exhausted the merging with profound stillness; consequently, you have ultimately not transcended the boundaries of the aggregate of consciousness (*vijñāna-skandha*).
This is what is meant by "clear light shining before the eyes, yet still appearing as if lost in one's home"—all the luminous qualities of the *dharmakāya* remain unrealized.

Question: At what stage is the aggregate of consciousness (*vijñāna-skandha*) ultimately exhausted? Answer: It is upon entering the first stage (*prathama-bhūmi*) and realizing perfect penetration (*pariśuddha-vidyā*).

The Sūtra states: "It is not that your six sense-faculties (*ṣaḍ-indriya*) can function interchangeably; this deluded thought (*vikalpa*) cannot be extinguished at any time. This is a clear proof. Question:
Since this aggregate of consciousness is exclusively the eighth [consciousness], it is the *karma-vijñāna*. Yet, other sūtras and śāstras...

All [schools] maintain that ignorance and its arising-conditions are exhausted only after the mind of "subtle awakening" (*sūkṣma-bodhi*). Now, you say they are exhausted at the first stage (*prathama-bhūmi*);

upon what, then, do the subsequent stages rely for their maintenance? Answer: That is discussed in the context of the gradual teaching (*anupūrva-vyākaraṇa*), where even the first stage and "subtle awakening" are as far apart as heaven and abyss;

how could it be said so abruptly that they are exhausted? This is the principle of the perfect and sudden teaching (*yugapad-pūrṇa-naya*). The scripture clearly states: "From the mutual... [and so forth].

By means of this practice, one suddenly transcends all stages and is able to enter the adamantine stage of pure wisdom (*vajra-śuṣka-prajñā*). How could this be anything other than the final mind of Equal Enlightenment?
One should know that within the ultimate truth, the nature of the true ultimate is profoundly inconceivable; it should not be challenged as being "sudden" by means of gradualist reasoning.
Nevertheless, if we use this to generally compare the depth of the causal realms: if one merely knows form as form, [this is the shallow level].
To not know that emptiness is also form is to understand the shallow level of the realm of form (*rūpadhātu*).
To know that both emptiness and form are all form is to understand the deep level of the realm of form.

In this same way, up to the point where one only knows that the entry into stillness is consciousness (*vijñāna*), yet does not know that the merging with stillness is also consciousness—this is to understand the shallow level of the realm of consciousness. To know the entry into stillness...
"That all that is merged and profound is consciousness" refers to one who understands the depth of the realm of consciousness (*vijñānadhātu*).

This, then, unfolds the five layers of deluded thought (*vikalpa*) and may be said to exhaustively reach their ultimate limits. △ Third, the answer concerning the sudden and gradual methods for eradication.
Ānanda’s second question previously stated: "Furthermore, are these five aggregates eliminated all at once, or are they exhausted sequentially? Therefore, the Tathāgata...
Now, within the third response, this question is answered in three parts: first, the sequence of arising and ceasing.
These five aggregates fundamentally arise in succession; their arising is caused by consciousness, and their ceasing proceeds from the elimination of form.
This sequence of the arising and ceasing of the five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*) is precisely the sequence of the binding and untying of the six sense faculties (*ṣaḍ-indriya*).

Since it is now to be clarified that although there is sudden awakening (*tongwu*), gradual cultivation (*jianxiu*) is required, the arising and the cessation of the five aggregates are first presented.

Originally, there are two layers of sequence; how could they possibly be eliminated all at once? This is the fundamental text. [The aggregates] arise in successive layers, meaning they fundamentally arise through accumulation.
The aggregates are not formed instantaneously. Gu Shan said: "In terms of arising, one constructs the external from within, proceeding from the subtle to the coarse, like putting on clothes.
Thus, when deluded regarding principle, there is consciousness and even form.

In terms of cessation, one proceeds from the external to the internal, from the coarse to the subtle, like taking off clothes. Thus, when awakening to principle, form is exhausted, leading up to the exhaustion of consciousness. △ Second.
Regarding the sudden and gradual, the beginning and the end:

in principle, there is sudden enlightenment; by means of this awakening, [delusions] are eliminated all at once. However, phenomena are not suddenly removed; they are exhausted through a gradual process.
The preceding section presented both types of sequence—arising and ceasing—whereas this section presents only the sequence of cessation and elimination. And...
If one simultaneously attains initial awakening, there would be no sequence; yet, ultimate cultivation must proceed through stages.

As for the statement that "principle is realized through sudden awakening," "principle" refers to the principle of delusion, and "sudden awakening" means thoroughly comprehending that the five aggregates are nothing but a single false thought, and that this falsehood is fundamentally empty.

Once awakened to this in a single thought-moment, how could there be any sequence? Regarding the phrase "riding upon awakening, [delusions] are eliminated all at once," this refers to eliminating them...
It is the inverted perception that has persisted for billions of kalpas. It is like being startled by a stump in the dark night and mistaking it for a ghost, fleeing in panic across the wilderness;
once someone points out the truth, the notion of a ghost vanishes entirely. Regarding the phrase "matters are not suddenly eliminated":

"matters" refers to the tasks of breaking through and severing through cultivation; "not suddenly eliminated" means they cannot be removed all at once, as they must be exhausted through a gradual process.
This means that one must pass through the five aggregates in their proper sequence and gradually eliminate them. It is like the perception of a ghost:
although it may have been entirely dispelled, how could one suddenly turn back from a long journey? One must necessarily traverse the path back before returning to one's original place.
This is simply the principle of sudden awakening followed by gradual cultivation. △ Third, reproving for forgetting previous teachings.
I have already shown you the knots tied in the *kārpāsa* cloth. What is it that you do not understand, that you must inquire about it again?

As for "having already shown the knots in the cloth," this refers to the passage in the fifth fascicle where the Buddha takes the flower-cloth offered by the deity Kāpāla and ties knots in it to demonstrate their sequential order.
When it asks, "What is it that you do not understand? it means that the preceding analogy and its meaning are perfectly clear and leave nothing obscure.
This is not clear. You should realize this very point; only then will you have properly grasped the Buddha’s instruction.

Why then do you neglect that and ask about this again? If you study this with care, you will know for certain that the previous account of Avalokiteśvara resolving the six knots and entering perfect penetration is entirely identical to the present account of shattering the five aggregates and entering the first stage (Prathamābhūmi). It is simply a matter of...

Regarding the enumeration: the former [text] has six items while this [text] has five; because their opening and closing differ, they are difficult to correspond precisely. I shall briefly divide them into two sections to categorize them roughly.
From "form and emptiness" up to "penetrating stillness," these encompass the first three fetters (*saṃyojana*); only the two characters "stillness" (*zhan*) encompass the latter three fetters.
The old interpretation erroneously took the six sense organs to be the six fetters, failing to realize that a single organ inherently possesses all six.

The six knots have now been untied; since they no longer follow [the old views], the arguments regarding horizontal and vertical [arrangements] found in the ancient commentaries on this passage are all rendered useless.
Having fully answered the three questions, the section concludes. △ Second, the conclusion and exhortation to transmit and show [this teaching].
You should take this root of deluded thought and cause your mind to attain liberation;

then transmit it to all practitioners of future ages during the Dharma-ending period, so that they may recognize what is false and illusory, develop a profound weariness with their own arising [of afflictions], realize the existence of Nirvana, and no longer cling to the triple world.

"Opening and penetrating" means that regarding each and every aggregate (*skandha*), one thoroughly understands its root source to be entirely false conceptualization (*vikalpa*) and not substantially real by nature.
This teaches self-benefit. "Transmitting and showing" below encourages the benefit of others.

It causes those who recognize the voidness and falsity [of phenomena] to realize that the aggregates are fundamentally empty and non-dual with themselves. Thus, they develop a profound weariness toward their own arising.
As for the character "one" (*zì*) in this context, it carries two meanings. First is the meaning of spontaneity (*zìrán*):
once one has realized that all is delusion, a profound sense of weary detachment arises spontaneously to its ultimate degree. Second is the meaning of selfhood (*zìjǐ*):

once one has awakened to the fact that the five aggregates are fundamentally non-existent, one immediately gives rise to a deep resolve to loathe them; both of these arise from one's own delusions and must therefore be resolved by oneself.

[One] eradicates [these] by means of power. The final two phrases state that one thereby knows that the nature of the fruit—eternal, blissful, self, and pure—is inherently present, without obstruction or accumulation;
thus, one no longer clings to the causes and effects of the outflows within the birth-and-death of the triple world.
For aversion and attachment are opposites: once one has become averse, how could one still cling? From the discussion of the seven destinies up to...
Herein concludes the first major section of the main body of the text, titled "Transcending Existence and Escaping the Cycle of Māra.

△ Third, the Section on the Propagation of the Teaching (Fǎliú-tōng-fēn). Since this follows the same pattern as the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*, the text of the *Dafangguangfo Huayan Jing* contains passages for the propagation, exhortation, and praise of the scripture's merit at the end of every chapter;
these continue through the final major section of the propagation, extending for several [chapters].
Question: Since this scripture shares the same category [as the Lotus Sūtra], why is the text concerning its dissemination so meager? Answer:

This scripture follows the same track as the *Lotus Sūtra* (*Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*) in that their respective scopes of doctrinal meaning are identical. As for the extent of their dissemination, it may be briefly inferred through two points.

First, due to the distinction between doubt and faith: at the initial stage of the establishment and abolition [of teachings] in the *Lotus Sūtra*, doubt was prevalent and faith was shallow. Therefore...
The washing away of doubts is detailed, while the exposition of principle and practice is concise; for instance, regarding the true marks of knowledge and vision, only their names are indicated.
Yet, the reason for the repeated comparisons, praises, and exhortations to understand is that the intent lies in resolving lingering doubts and causing one to accept with faith.
Since this sutra has long since revealed the truth, doubts have been eliminated and faith is established; therefore, it is now proclaimed.

The detailed exposition of reasoning and practice is thorough, while the cleansing of lack of faith is concise. For instance, regarding the realization of the true nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*) and so forth, he searches and investigates with meticulous detail until they are fully exhausted;
yet, he does not extensively exhort others toward such penetration, knowing that they will easily grasp it for themselves.

Second, because it is concise yet comprehensive. Although this text of circulation is relatively concise compared to the *Lotus Sūtra*, it actually employs concise language to encompass extensive meanings;
it is not truly deficient. This is because the Buddha’s words are subtle and profound.

That this comprehensiveness enters into the text will be evident of itself. It is divided into two parts. First, the supreme manifestation of the sūtra's merit, which is further divided into two. First, the opening of the two...
How much more so for manifesting the retribution of merit! This is because by citing a small portion to serve as an illustration, one manifests the vast. Furthermore, there are two parts:
first, citing the benefit of others to manifest it further. This also has two sections: first, citing many merits to determine them through comparison. This also has two parts:
first, the Tathāgata cites his own merits and commands a comparison.

Ānanda, suppose there were a person who filled all the empty space throughout the ten directions with the seven treasures, and offered them to as many Buddhas as there are atoms of dust, serving and making offerings to them with a mind that never failed. What do you think?
By virtue of this cause and condition of giving to the Buddhas, would that person obtain much merit?
In this context, the Buddha cited examples where both the material wealth and the field of merit reached their ultimate excellence.

Since the empty space of the ten directions is fundamentally without limit or measure, how could the seven treasures filling that space have any measure? If this were so, even a single Jambudvīpa world would be insufficient to discuss;
for any description of the superiority of such wealth, however many layers of words one might pile up, it could never surpass it.
It is so. The atoms of the dharma-realm are inherently inexhaustible; how could the Buddhas, as numerous as those atoms, ever come to an end?
If this is the case, then three, four, five, or even hundreds of thousands of millions of Buddhas cannot be compared to this.
For one who extols the excellence of the field of merit, no matter how much they magnify their words, they can never surpass this. As for those who serve and make offerings, they should immediately—
The jewels filling the void are received as offerings. That "the mind does not let anything pass in vain" means that not a single one among the Buddhas, as numerous as motes of dust, is omitted.

The passage beginning with "This person... serves to have him calculate [the merit]. However, this calculation proceeds merely from the perspective of obtaining blessings and extinguishing transgressions;
it has not yet reached the ultimate point. △ Second, Ānanda calculates and determines the immeasurability.
Ānanda replied, "Space is inexhaustible and precious jewels are boundless. In the past, there was a sentient being who offered seven coins to the Buddha;

even by giving up his body for that, he still attained the rank of a Wheel-Turning King. How much more so now, when the space before us is already exhausted and the Buddha-lands are filled to overflowing?"
Even if one were to bestow precious jewels for an entire kalpa, even the most exhaustive deliberation could not equal it; how then could there be any limit to such merit?

The first two lines single out the excellence of the material gift (*dāna-vastu*). The passage beginning with "In the past... uses a double comparison to reveal the excellence of both the gift and the field (*kṣetra*).
For instance, giving seven coins to a single Buddha represents a case where both the gift and the field are inferior, yet one still attains the status of a *cakravartin*.

The excellence of the reward (*vipāka*). Furthermore, the manifestation of Buddha-lands pervading all space constitutes the excellence of the field (*kṣetra*). The bestowing of precious jewels constitutes the excellence of the material gift (*dravya*).
The phrase "throughout kalpas" and below determines that the merit obtained is inconceivable and without limit. △ Second, the excellence of the sutra’s merit by way of contrast.
One should know that the intent of this contrast lies entirely beyond the literal words. This is divided into three parts. First:
To demonstrate sincerity and inspire faith, the Buddha told Ānanda: "The words of all Buddhas and Tathāgatas are never false.

Although the merit required for the subsequent propagation of this sutra is minimal, the destruction of sins and the acquisition of blessings are exceedingly great; I fear it may be difficult [to believe]."
This is for the sake of inspiring faith; therefore, it first clarifies that the Buddha has no words that are unreal or untrue, so that one may believe them with earnest sincerity.
△ Second, the clarification of the eradication of sins and rebirth in the Pure Land, which is further divided into three parts. First, an extreme description of evil causes and their evil effects.

Furthermore, if there is a person whose body has committed the four grave offenses and the ten *pārājika* transgressions, in an instant they shall pass through the Avīci hells of this world and other worlds,
until they have exhausted all the uninterrupted hells throughout the ten directions, experiencing them all without exception.
"Furthermore, if there is a person" means that it is assumed there exists such a person. The four grave offenses (*catur-āpatti*) are killing, stealing, sexual misconduct, and lying;

these are either the ten *pārājika* offenses or the ten unwholesome paths of action (*daśākuśala-karmapatha*), though the latter lacks a definitive source. However, the *pārājika* is the first of the five categories of offenses (*pañca-vastu*), and its meaning corresponds to the accumulation of the most extreme evils.
It is explained through three senses: first, falling away and sinking; second, not being permitted to dwell together [with the Sangha]; and third, [the loss of the status of a monk].

"Falling" is also translated as "abandonment. Regarding the five punishments, such as decapitation, when one considers that the retribution for downward-directed evil is extremely grave, these four heavy categories of the ten evil deeds must inevitably accumulate to an infinite degree.

The phrase "the superior evil cause leading to the inferior evil fruit, traversed in an instant," indicates that the point of falling is imminent. *Avīci* refers to the most severe of the five *anantarya* hells.
Furthermore, "to exhaustively experience all throughout the ten directions" refers to the greatest number of hells. △ Second, a brief mention of those who temporarily propagate this sutra:
being able, with a single thought, to reveal and teach this Dharma-door to those of later learning during the final kalpa.
The person capable of mindfulness is precisely one who is on the verge of falling into hell. "A single thought" refers to the temporary arousal of the aspiration for enlightenment.
This Dharma-gate must be identified as a definitive gateway that transcends and enters deeply into the perfect penetration of Great Samādhi.
"The final age" refers to a time when the sages are distant and demons are powerful. "Students of the final age" refers to those who find it difficult to advance and easy to retreat. One must...
Knowing that the propagation of the sutra depends solely upon a single thought-moment, the sutra itself must not be voluminous—referring to what are known as "four-line verses" and the like.

Furthermore, the recipient must not be a multitude—referring to what is described as "secretly [teaching] for the sake of one person. △ Third, through this cause, they depart from suffering and attain happiness.
The karmic obstacles of this person shall be extinguished by mere thought. The causes for the suffering they would otherwise undergo in hell are transformed into a land of peace and bliss.
As for these karmic obstacles—the most severe and numerous evil retributions—they are extinguished by the single thought of propagating the sutra;
it is like a spark of fire consuming a heap of grass, leaving nothing but ashes. They are thus transformed.
Furthermore, it states that it is not merely sufficient to exhaust one's karmic offenses; rather, by transforming one's perception, one shall be reborn within that Land of Bliss.

Indeed, if even a single moment of subtle merit can cause one to leave extreme suffering and be born in Ultimate Bliss, it is truly because one should contemplate that the entire dharma-realm is solely mind.
This is precisely the verse from the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* on "Breaking the Prison," and this scripture brings it to full completion.
It reveals the Dharma-realm and fully manifests that "it is solely mind.

By upholding this for even a single thought-moment, one is thus able to cause immeasurable Avīci hells to be extinguished wherever they may be, and inconceivable lands of bliss to arise in their very place. However, one must have self-confidence to achieve this merit;
if one lacks self-confidence, one will deeply fail to realize this wondrous benefit. How tragic! △ Third, the excellence of the merit obtained surpasses the former.
The merit obtained will surpass that of the previous donor by a hundredfold, a thousandfold, ten million billionfold;
indeed, it will be such that even calculation or analogy cannot reach it.
It is said that not only will one be freed from suffering and attain happiness, but one shall also obtain immeasurable merit that is unsurpassed and peerless.

As for the phrase "surpassing those who have previously given," this refers to surpassing those who have previously offered treasures filling the void of all lands, as numerous as atoms, to Buddhas as many as the dust motes.
This degree of transcendence is not merely one or two times greater; it is indeed hundreds, thousands, ten thousands, millions, and billions of times greater.
It is even beyond the reach of calculation or analogy.

It is precisely because this sutra opens the Tathāgata’s secret treasury of jewels, enables one to obtain the naturally pervasive family treasure, and brings to fruition the Buddha-fruit in which all dust-motes and lands are mutually integrated, that it cannot be equaled by the fruits of material giving, offerings characterized by grasping at signs, or conditioned phenomena. Question: Although the entire sutra...
There is indeed such merit. How could a single thought-moment exhaustively encompass its meaning? Yet, it can suddenly extinguish manifold transgressions and instantly bestow vast blessings.

Why, then, would this not be considered an excessive reward? Answer: The realm and wisdom of perfect interfusion are inconceivable; they equal the measure of all atoms within a buddha-field, yet thoughts and eons mutually contain one another.
How could one fathom this with the limited measures of ordinary intellect regarding size or duration? One should instead deeply accept and rejoice in it.

The Buddha said: "Do not harbor self-doubt or hesitation regarding the wondrous benefits of the fundamental truth. Furthermore, you should understand the meaning implied beyond the literal words, which shall be clarified here.
For even a person who has committed the most grievous offenses can, by reciting this sutra for a single thought-moment, extinguish their sins and obtain such merit;
how much more so, then, those with minor offenses, those without offenses, or even those who already possess merit and abundant virtue?"

The extraordinary and supreme karmic retribution for propagating the sutras can be known from this: if even a single thought-moment can produce such results, how much more so for long-term propagation, continuing until the end of one's life?
If even a single phrase or a single verse can produce such results, how much more so for a single fascicle, half a volume, or even an entire sutra?
I venture to say that if even a single person can achieve such results, how much more so many people together, especially when acting on a grand scale.
Within the assembly, he extensively expounded this for others; the excellence of its karmic fruit and benefit can thus be known.
Having finished illustrating [the merit] by means of altruism, (2) he now illustrates it by means of self-benefit.
Ānanda, if there are sentient beings who can recite this sutra and uphold this mantra as I have extensively explained—

reciting the sutra means upholding the manifest text, while upholding the mantra means reciting the secret scripture— as I have extensively explained, even if one were to do so for an entire kalpa, it would not be exhausted. "As I have extensively explained" means by...
The Buddha, with his eightfold voice and four types of eloquence, extols such a person, stating that their aforementioned offenses are extinguished and they obtain the aforementioned merit;

even if one were to exhaust the duration of kalpas, one could not fully describe it. One should know that within this, there is also the implicit meaning of using external analogies to reveal the truth beyond words.
This is because by reciting sutras and maintaining mantras, one first attains the wisdom of hearing; the merit and its retribution have already been described by the Buddha as inexhaustible.

How much more so for those who advance to contemplation and cultivation—such as interpreting the meaning, practicing meditative concentration, and performing visualization—to hear back toward one's own nature, and even to reach the six perfections and myriad practices?
The merit and its retribution are all the more impossible to describe exhaustively. [Question]
It is as explained extensively above, with the addition that it would not be exhausted even throughout an entire kalpa. How could self-benefit possibly surpass the benefit of others?

Answer: This is merely a mutual abbreviation for the sake of brevity. Previously, the comparison was detailed to demonstrate its transcendence; in essence, this is because the sūtra is most excellent and sublime.
By balancing the two benefits, one attains a supremacy beyond compare; even if one were to explain this balance exhaustively, it would not be finished.
Having opened up the two benefits, the explanation of the manifestation of the supreme retribution is concluded. △ Second, combining the two benefits to deeply affirm the ultimate fruit.
"Relying on my teachings and practicing the Way according to the instructions, one will directly attain Bodhi without further demonic activities.
This section combines the two aforementioned benefits and speaks of them together. "Practicing the Way according to the teachings" means to follow the Buddha.
By means of this Dharma-gate, one benefits oneself and others; only then does one truly practice the Way according to the teaching.

This is because this sutra fundamentally possesses both forms of benefit (svārtha and parārtha). Moreover, supreme bodhi must necessarily have both benefits perfected before it can be realized as the ultimate.
As for the direct attainment of bodhi, from the initial generation of the mind until the achievement of Buddhahood, throughout the interval...
There are no further complications or devious turns; it is like water rushing into a gully or an arrow piercing the void, proceeding without any hindrance.
It is certainly not like halting within the illusory city of the Hīnayāna, nor is it like the slow progression through successive stages of realization found in the gradual teachings.
This refers to those who, without passing through the *asaṃkhyeya-kalpas*, enter directly and transcendently. The final sentence briefly indicates the reason for this:
generally, all instances of regression, discouragement, or circuitous detours in the interim are caused by the rampant interference of demonic activities (*mārakarma*).

Through the empowerment of both the exoteric and esoteric teachings of this sutra, one is forever free from demonic obstacles; thus, one directly accomplishes Bodhi without further delay or stagnation. This, then, is...
As for its circulation, the extant texts are few; yet as for the study of its words and meaning, even if one were to compile numerous volumes and layers of scrolls, one could not surpass it.
Is this not because it achieves the vast through the concise, leaving nothing behind? Thus, the saying, "I am the Dharma King, sovereign over the Dharma," is truly not false.
Having fully demonstrated the merit of the sutra, [the section] concludes. △ Second, concluding with the joy of the assembly.
When the Buddha had finished speaking this sutra, the bhikṣus, bhikṣuṇīs, upāsakas, and upāsikās;

all the devas, humans, asuras, and others in the world; as well as the bodhisattvas and followers of the two vehicles from various regions, the holy ṛṣis and youths, and the powerful spirits and ghosts who had first resolved their minds—all were greatly rejoiced. They paid homage and departed.
This section and the introductory section (nidāna) form the beginning and end [of the discourse]. Both were established by the compilers of the sūtra;

the opening phrases conclude both the main body (śarīra) and the dissemination (parivarta), as both are the Buddha’s own teaching. From the words "Bhikṣus" onwards, the assembly of those who rejoice is first enumerated.
However, this [section] and the listing of the assembly in the introductory section each encompass different aspects; thus, they are divided into two parts.

The former encompasses the praise of virtues and the time and assembly, and is therefore the "Introductory Section Listing the Assembly. This [section] encompasses the joy, prostrations, and dispersal, and is therefore the "Section on the Dissemination Listing the Assembly.

Furthermore, although the listing of the assembly in the introductory section is detailed, it is incomplete; whereas the listing of the assembly in this chapter, though concise, is complete. Please [consider this].

There is a distinction between being detailed, brief, incomplete, or complete. For instance, while the headings at the beginning of this section list the fourfold assembly, the introduction (nidāna) lists only the bhikṣus;
thus, it is incomplete by omitting the other three assemblies. Next, there is a brief mention of the eight classes of beings (*aṣṭau gaṇāḥ*);

although the phrasing is concise, it fully manifests the characteristics of these eight classes, whereas the introduction omits them entirely. Furthermore, the subsequent designations of bodhisattvas and those of the two vehicles (*dviyāna*) are all presented collectively.

This was abbreviated and not as detailed as the distinctions made in the introductory section (*nidāna*). Later, the two assemblies of the Holy Sages (*ṛṣi*) and the Divine Beings (*deva*) were added;
however, these are not only missing from the introductory section, but are also rarely seen in most other sūtras.

Nevertheless, the specific addition of "Holy Youth" (*kumāra*) among the sages clarifies that although they dwell in the realm of the sages, they practice the holy paths of the three vehicles (*triyāna*) within the internal teaching, in order to aspire [to enlightenment].
"The fruit of youthful purity" distinguishes them from the other classes of immortals.

Regarding the spirits and deities who have specifically developed a great power of resolve, this signifies their establishment of the will to protect the Dharma and their possession of great supernormal powers (*abhijñā*), whereby their strength penetrates all things without fear;

thus, it distinguishes them from those who are violent and evil, as well as those who are weak and inferior. These two groups are both capable of widely protecting and circulating [the teachings]. Eight... [text ends]

The preceding sections have not yet exhausted the subject matter; therefore, these are added here. The final two lines serve as a formal conclusion expressing gratitude for the Dharma-joy. As for "Great Joy":
having heard the orthodox teaching, one attains the fundamental, wondrous, and perfect mind; furthermore, hearing the section on circulation, one understands the ultimate benefit of its propagation.
One is freed from the near-anxiety of falling into evil realms and possesses the distant hope of realizing the Truth. This is not like that of ordinary people.
The three vehicles of the heavens obtain subtle benefits; having attained great and vast advantage, their celebration is extraordinary and they experience great joy.
"Those who depart" means they return. Each leaves the Dharma assembly of following signs and returns to the immovable site of enlightenment within their own mind.
Whether practicing cultivation or propagating the teachings, this is not like worldly people who leave the Dharma assembly and consequently fall into distraction.
*The Correct Pulse Commentary on the Great Buddha-Uṣṇīṣa Śūraṅgama Sūtra*, Fascicle Ten (End).
Postscript after the Publication of the *Śūraṅgama Correct Pulse*:
When I was residing in Shangdang and composing this commentary, several disciples such as Miaofeng and Chengyin were renowned for their pure reputations throughout the world.

His writings have circulated throughout the realm. He prays from the depths of his heart that once this draft is completed, he may obtain a single witness to verify that it does not deviate from the Sage’s intent.

Yet, he fears such a meeting may not occur. When the draft was nearly half-finished, Miaofeng suddenly arrived at Lu. [Yuan] had already marveled at this; intending to go and pay respects to the Master, he reached the gate.
Upon seeing him for the first time, his heart and soul were immediately cast down in devotion, as if they shared a karmic affinity spanning three lifetimes. He consulted [the Master].
As for his purpose in coming, he said, "It is merely to cast the pinnacle of the Wan-gu Pagoda. I replied, "I have here a version of the *Buddhapiṭaka* (Buddha-śīrṣa); you should present it to you.
He immediately produced his draft and bowed twice, requesting my verification. The Master also bowed and accepted it.

Before he had finished reading, he exclaimed in amazement, "Among the eminent monks of this age, you point out errors in previous interpretations as easily as one might replace the beams and pillars of a house. Yet here, you have completely overhauled the old and established something entirely new—truly a great feat! He then consulted the ancient manuscripts.
"This is no trivial matter. I have grasped its general outline, yet not its full details. I beg you to take it back to your lodgings so that I may study and savor it thoroughly.
I responded with respectful assent and took my leave. The following day, I went to return the master's visit and bowed my head in gratitude, saying:

"Yesterday, I opened the wondrous commentary and read it from dusk until dawn; I could not put it down. Layer upon layer of new insights appeared, revealing things I had never heard before. As for the *Śūraṅgama Sūtra* itself..."
The purport is as follows: It is like the sun first rising; were it not for the secret empowerment of the various sages, one would certainly not have reached this point.
I pray that you, Master, may focus your resolve to achieve completion quickly, lest the time for the task of carving the woodblocks should pass us by. I, [Name], shall labor on this behalf.

Having received this testimony and permission, I too prostrate in gratitude. I privately reflect: perhaps this is because the Sage’s heart has granted his approval—how extraordinary is such an encounter, and how early is the attainment of realization!
On another day, the Master again exhorted me earnestly. Moved by the warning that time was passing and would not wait for me, I applied myself diligently from morning until night.

After three years, the draft was completed. As the year drew near its end, the Master suddenly arrived once more; my joy and gratitude were immeasurable. He requested the draft as urgently as if it were a matter of life and death.
I said that it could not be entrusted to others and must not be delayed, so I set out to finalize it after the New Year. Then, in the second month of spring, I...

Thereupon, he established the practice of providing five-peak rice for the monastic community. He traveled on to Luaya Huayan Temple to observe the summer retreat; this temple was also founded by the Master himself.
During the winter, he stayed at Fen. In the following spring, he again accepted an invitation from Mount Tai to lecture on the *Commentary and Sub-commentary* to the *Amitābha Sūtra*.
In the summer, I traveled through Yunzhong and stayed at Xiyansi Temple, where I lectured on the *Śūraṅgama Sūtra*.

It happened that Master Miao, having been invited to Xuancheng, passed by Xiyansi and urged me to return to Pu. This event was truly extraordinary. I then followed him, reaching Wanggu only in the middle of winter.
Having received various forms of generous patronage from his teacher, on the first day of the second month of the following year, he commissioned artisans to begin carving the blocks for printing.
Nobles and high officials all contributed their efforts. The Master further promoted the project in neighboring prefectures and Shanggu, even selling his own mount to supplement the funds.
Thus, it was completed within one year. As for the commentary and sub-commentary, they exceed four hundred thousand words. And...
It was accomplished so swiftly that there were certainly those who marveled at it in silence. Yet, the power of the Master’s Dharma-eye and the fulfillment of his vows are especially unfathomable;
he must have possessed great karmic affinities from many lifetimes regarding this scripture, such that Kian Mong provided assistance not merely in this single lifetime.
Otherwise, how could it have arrived unexpectedly, with all conditions converging in such perfect harmony?
Is it so? I have thus recorded the beginning and end of this matter, so that one may see that the Dharma has what is realized and merit has where it returns.
On the full moon of the eighth month of the Gengzi year of the Wanli era, the śramaṇa Zhujian respectfully appends these words as an epilogue for this unworthy person (Ting).
Born in this degenerate age, my innate nature has been dull and foolish; though I have a fondness for the true Way, I regret lacking the guidance of a teacher. This...

How fortunate I am to have encountered Your Royal Highness, my elder brother, the King! You have refined your mastery of the scriptures written on palm leaves and penetrated their profound mysteries. Deeply indebted for your polishing and guidance, I have barely managed to grasp a single thread of understanding.

I have long heard that the Venerable Master Jiaoguang has been staying at Luyang and has revised the commentary on the *Śūraṅgama Sūtra*. (Ting) My spirit has frequently communed with his; I wish to pray for the opportunity to attend upon him in person.
In the year Wuxu, Master Miaofeng made this appointment.

When the Master passed through Wan’gu, he carved the new commentary on the *Śūraṅgama Sūtra*. [Wang] Ting went to visit him and received immeasurable instruction. The following spring, the Master lectured on the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra:
A Suspended Discourse* (*Huayan Xuantan*). [Wang] Ting attended as a disciple and listened to it; it was as if parting the clouds to behold the rising sun or looking up from a well to see the sky.

He suddenly felt his body and mind expand to pervade the entire Dharma-realm. At the end of the year, the new commentary was completed, and he was honored by the Master’s presentation of it. He burned [incense].
I, Xiang, have perused this work and have come to realize that the deluded mind is the source of immeasurable obstacles, while the fundamental nature is the very substance of the true mind.
To turn back the hearing is the path of effortless action (*anābhoga-mārga*). By abandoning the source of obstacles, delusions are exhausted; by beholding the true substance, the mind finds peace.
Through effortless application, one enters suddenly. The *Avataṃsaka* is indeed an inexhaustible treasury of jewels, and this scripture is the shortcut for entering the *Avataṃsaka*.
Ah! The Dharma-milk flows vast and deep; this humble body cannot repay its debt. These weeds of words are falsely superfluous, yet I venture to address my fellow seekers of the Way.
Written on the Mid-Autumn Day of the Gengzi year of the Wanli era by the disciple under the Bodhisattva precepts, Zhi-ti-xuanzi Zhu Junchan, with prostrations. Respectfully inscribed at the end.
